_childDocuments_.review: PROS:-some damage values have been improvedregular thrown items have had their damage upgraded, now dealing the same amount of damage as a punch. therefore, it only takes 3 throwables in succession to kill an enemy as opposed to 5, as it used to be. this is a welcome change for me personally, since pelting an enemy with whatever i can find has always been one of my favorite kill methods. however, it could be argued this makes throwables too overpowered, making them more of a weapon than a way to get a quick stun.-new weapon typesin addition to regular throwables that stun and deal damage to enemies, there are new types of throwables that behave like spears and shurikens. anything with a pointy bit at the end can be thrown straight at an enemy, scoring an instant kill if it makes impact with the head or chest. the "shuriken" class of throwables behave very similarly, although theyre mostly disc-shaped, therefore requiring less accuracy in your throw, but making it easier for enemies to destroy in mid-air. again, i was a big sucker for throwables in the first game, so this is a very welcome addition that would be hard to argue as a detriment to the game's balance. there's also a new gun, with its main gimmick being its insane projectile speed. as opposed to other guns in superhot, this new gun fires railroad-spike-esque projectiles that arrive almost instantly at their target, and its projectiles stick into enemies and surfaces, letting the player retrieve them by hand and throw them like spears. this may sound overpowered at first glance, but its balanced by its slow firerate and having the small clip size of 3 spikes.-melee weapons are improvedkatanas now deflect bullets back at their attackers as opposed to slicing them in half (this applies to katana-wielding enemies as well as the player), and enemies can knock throwables back at the player with baseball bats and pipes. this adds more functionality to melee weapons, especially the katana, both for the player and the enemies, but it could also be argued, again, that this makes them too overpowered. this game certainly puts the katana on a pedestal, not only adding the deflecting mechanic, but going so far as to dedicate multiple skills to improving it further. whether or not this is a good or bad thing really just depends on your opinion of the katana. i personally welcome the changes, but sometimes it feels as though the katana is the only weapon you ever really need, as its become so versatile that it debatably outranks some of the guns.-longer campaignthis one could honestly be a pro OR a con, depending on how you felt about the campaign's length in the first game. the level progression in mind control delete is vastly different from the first game, whereas the first game was very linear and this game is anything but. in the first game, the campaign was moreso a prerequisite the player had to traverse before unlocking its true replay value in its challenge modes and endless modes. here, the campaign essentially is the entire game, which, to many people, is an improvement. to others, however, i'd definitely understand preferring the short and sweet "story mode" of the first game, as its levels were more memorable and its atmosphere had more of an impact.-more enemy varietyin the first game, red guys were the only enemy you'd ever face, and they were all able to be killed the same way. this, of course, wasn't a problem, but seeing as how mind control delete has more of a sense of progression throughout its campaign, it makes sense that they'd want to add a bit of spice to their enemy roster. now certain red guys can have specific body parts you have to shoot, melee-wielding enemies can knock throwables back at you or deflect bullets, and some red guys explode upon being killed. more enemies with specific kill conditions and abilities obviously makes for more strategic experimentation, which is an improvement in my eyes. however, some of these enemies could be seen as downgrades in some regards, as the specific-body-part enemies are much less satisfying to kill than a normal red guy, and the exploding enemies can certainly become a huge nuisance over time. the invincible enemy types introduced later in the game are discussed in the cons list.CONS:-the game's tone is extremely condescendingthe first superhot had a wonderfully unique tone to it, where it was totally self-aware about making the player feel like a badass slow-mo action hero, while throwing in plenty of creepy elements that made it a borderline horror experience at times. the lack of music and its general glitchy aesthetic could easily be twisted into making the player uneasy in the downtime between its action-packed levels. mind control delete does preserve, and in some cases even bolster, the creepier parts of the franchise's atmosphere, but it interestingly also takes every chance it gets to... mock the player for enjoying the game? yeah, it's... weird. and probably my least favorite thing about the game.the first superhot was by no means a story-driven game, but it had enough "story" to make the player curious as to what's *really* going on as they mow down "red guys" from level to level. it was all relatively open to interpretation and was so cryptic it bordered on pretentious at times, but the way i interpreted it, the bottom line was that the player was being controlled to kill dudes in real life while it was all framed as a harmless simulation. is that all it had to say? i dunno. ive never really been interested in superhot's lore, and ive always been more interested in the gameplay. mind control delete somehow finds a way to mock its playerbase for being interested in both of those things.continuously, as you progress through mind control delete's "map", there are many segments that are dedicated entirely to calling the player an idiot for wanting to play the game. multiple "levels" are literally just walls of glitchy text that are meant to sound as if theyre from the player's perspective, demanding more levels, more violence, more lore, more whatever. the game's motto, in fact, is the word "MORE" in all caps, and it repeatedly forces the player to beg for "MORE" just to progress. its absolutely baffling how the devs can repeatedly mock the player for "craving violence" or whatever, yet the devs are the one who... made it. it feels incredibly hypocritical for the devs to pour so much into making a sequel with more content, then proceed to make the player feel like an idiot for enjoying it, and repeatedly urge them to stop playing. it feels as though the devs see the playerbase as a bunch of cavemen, blindly demanding more superhot simply because they get off on violence.-motion sicknessi suppose this counts as a bit of a spoiler, but its more of a warning than anything. in the game's later levels, the walls, ceilings, and floors of some stages start warping and distorting in ways that make it nearly unplayable for players susceptible to motion sickness, such as myself. it feels like a glaring oversight in terms of accessibility, as i oftentimes have to stop playing for a bit just to recover from how nauseous it makes me. needless to say, i think the game requires the option to turn level distortion off, especially since its solely for aesthetic purposes and adds no additional challenge to the game other than discombobulation.-invincible enemiesdespite my praise of the increased roster of enemies in the pros list, im not entirely sold on the game's boss-type enemies that are literally invincible. i still have yet to beat the game, but so far, ive encountered a weird glitched-up dog man that has a claw swipe attack, and a man with a glitchy slash through his face that can throw his katana at you and recall it back to him. both are good enough concepts for enemies, but the fact that they have no weaknesses whatsoever basically means theyre just glorified obstacles.i ran out of typing space oops!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most personally disappointing sequels of all time, SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE tells you over and over that you're stupid for wanting a sequel to SUPERHOT, the critical and commercial darling from a few years ago. Every lore dump tells you you're greedy and foolish for ever daring to want more SUPERHOT. As someone who thought SUPERHOT was great and SUPERHOT VR sublime, I would have simply let this pass as light metacommentary in the vein of other SUPERHOT storytelling, but as I moved past the first world and through the second, third and fourth, I realized they were right. SUPERHOT was lightning in a bottle, and MIND CONTROL DELETE is akin to cutting yourself open on the broken bottle, the lightning long since gone.Gone, too, are the impeccably designed and tuned combat encounters in favor of endless repetition of the same handful of room types. A SUPERHOT roguelite could work, but the structure of MCD is so utterly flawed it seems almost contemptuous of the player. The game is divided into layers, which are divided into levels. The levels consist of a randomized set of rooms with random enemy spawns, usually between 5 and 15 rooms per level. Every two or three floors, you get to pick between one of two hacks: nominal gameplay changes that you will lose at the end of the level, succeed or fail. Occasionally, you will come across new COREs, which allow you to have different starting abilities and new E-key powers, or new hacks, which become available in the pool. These cores and hacks come with training levels that are interesting and I genuinely think the CORE system is good. The hack system leaves a lot to be desired, but this is mostly because of how bad the structure of everything else is. If you take damage, occasionally you will be offered "heal.hack" between rooms, which heals you to full. It's a lose-lose situation; you either take the health and feel bad that you had to heal, or you take the powerup and might lose this run early, shunting you back to the tedious start of the level. This is not risk vs reward: this is choosing between fun or pragmatism. I use the term fun lightly because after World 1, you have wrung every last drop of fun out of MCD and still have a few hours left of licking the floor, hoping desperately to taste the remnants of fun you can almost remember.When I finished floor 1, I was happy. A new structure, new powers, new things to throw, a single new gun: not bad, I thought. All they have to do is keep the game interesting and I'll see it through to the end. But no. Aside from new enemy types (armored enemies that require being damaged in specific spots [good], enemies that explode into random bullets [horrible] and two unkillable enemies meant to serve as obstacles [mediocre - essentially just an annoyance stacked on top of many others]), one or two new rooms per floor, and a couple of new COREs and hacks, that's it. That's the game. From your very first room of randomly placed enemies to the very last one you do, that's all there is to it.Despite this, there are moments of brilliance amid the muddy and repetitive. The last world (SPOILERS follow) has some really interesting decisions and levels.  However, after this is the real gut punch, the kick in the teeth so that you really get the point driven home just how much the devs hate you: you are  Did I do this? Bow to their whims? No. They told me time and time again that they didn't want me playing the game, so I won't.  This is not art. This is garbage. I know the SUPERHOT team is capable of better because they made one of the best indie games and one of the best VR games. I know they are capable of new and interesting gameplay because they almost had it right. And I know that you should skip this game even if you received it for free for owning SUPERHOT. If you must play it, stop after World 1. Your time is more important than this.I'll still be here for the next game, be it a real SUPERHOT 2, a SUPERHOT VR 2, or something entirely different, but I've played few more disappointing sequels. Disaster.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a huge fan of SUPERHOT since the first game. I play the game to get away from well... other games. It might not make sense ( Neither does SUPERHOT XD ) but this game feels like it fulfils a desire no one knows they have. It has no storyline ( sort of ). Its enjoyment grows from your own search for something where there is none. You fight round after round after round after round, with no real explanation to why. It's murder in the most beautiful way possible. You go through the game dead confused, this path seems to lead you somewhere, but it feels like you've been here before... but it is so DAMN ADDICTING. I can't tell you why... even if you move on to other things, other games, in the back of your head you always long to kill that mindless body of red glass. You will always come back for more. It is not a matter of "will you?" it's a matter of "when will you?"- SUPER fun (ironically)- Controls are simple.- You can leave the game for a month come back and still know "what" and "how to" do things.- Makes you feel skilled AF for dodging, throwing, catching, shooting your way out of death.- Good way to waste some free time.- The game is unique, you won't find anything like it.- It can become a bit repetitive.- There is no real reward system (Unless senseless murder is rewarding enough for you XD )- The overall story is confusing (If there is one anyway)I love this game for how weird and unique it is. _childDocuments_.review: Summary: This game has more potential than US high school students do. It needs some polish, but the core is there.The good:*The core mechanic of Superhot is still just as amazing as it always has been*I have yet to find an unfair fight, though they are all very challenging so far.*The combination of soft-permadeath and multi-level-per-checkpoint design works well.*The increased durability you gain over time meshes well with the new roguelike format.*More types of weapons and objects to swing, shoot, and toss than I remember from the original.The bad:*Level variety is lacking as of yet- Every level feels like it is one of 3 or 4 levels.*Lack of a replay feature as of yet.*Some UI elements, such as the directional marker reticule for swords, are not in yet.My suggestions to the dev (Level Gen):*Try to convert level bits to a tileset with attachment points and very small tiles.*Make the tiles attach to only certain other tiles.*Have positions that objects can spawn from a list on, be they usable, decoration, or both.*Add elements like activatable objects that open walls temporarily, and use them to create monster closets.*Make the monster closets from the above idea activate on their own shortly after enemies spawn, spilling foes out.Other suggestions to the dev:*Add a replay feature, and possibly tie shared replays to steam workshop and allow anyone to view anyone's replay?*Re-integrate UI elements from Superhot into Mind Control Delete, such as a line or arrow swing arc for melee weapons.*Offer more optional minds and more options for between-level progression.*Add a practice mode with customizable difficulty via enemy spawns and weapon placement, perhaps?As a player I see this game going ahead swimmingly, weather you take my suggestions into account or find your own ways to deal with the flaws remaining in this game and add yet more content.

_childDocuments_.review: is the sequel to 2016's , attempting to expand on the excellent gameplay and provide, as the tagline implies,  of what made the original great.The visuals are mostly the same as before: brilliant white and untextured environments, low poly crystalline props and enemies, simple if unfortunately very basic (and sometimes screwy) character animation, and an ASCII-styled interface even more reminiscent of terminal-based RPGs. The only new thing I noticed about the visuals is expanded post-processing - you have a permanent blur filter around the screen's edges, and certain status effects apply distortion to the edges as a "minimalist" notice of kicking in. It's still recognizably SUPERHOT, which is fine, but especially the animations leave me wanting for MORE.Sound effects are much the same again. The same computer-modulated SUPER HOT voiceline, the same crystalline, crunchy potent sounds with a still-low gunfire sound effect variety, though slightly rectified by an extra weapon that has a unique set of sounds... when in your hands. The music game has been upped significantly however, thanks to The core gameplay is also around the same: time is slowed to a crawl when you stand still and goes by faster when you move, look around, or attack. Basic enemies die from either one bullet, one melee weapon strike, or a few fist strikes and thrown clutter, and you must dance through a hail of bullets in each level to progress.  changes up the progression compared to the original: you navigate through ASCII rooms on the "overworld", and when entering combat nodes you get the choice of augmenting yourself with either extra hitpoints or a new ability, including the returning Hotswap. The level selection is moderately expanded from the original, but a number of them are strung together in a random order in each combat node, broken up by opportunities to enhance your avatar with more abilities or enhancements, from stronger punches, to extra ammo in firearms, to all bullets ricocheting off surfaces and into enemies. These abilities can synergize and provide a lot of tactical and strategic variation when chosen right - not to mention fun. In addition, as you progress through the "overworld", the level sets include further variations of the basic enemy type: spiky enemies explode into shrapnel when killed, while statues are only vulnerable in a specific limb and nigh impervious otherwise.That's where the good ends, sadly. Yes, a first person shooter in constant  mode can still go wrong. Boss-type enemies are introduced in the late game: invincible mooks who chase you around the level and harass with dangerous abilities based on the alternate CORE modules you may be using, but are sooner annoying than anything since they just force you to chase down the regular enemies until the level ends. The levels, being randomly strung together instead of being based around a fairly simple narrative, now lose a lot of the context and meaning binding them together - the gameplay is now distilled in this manner to "kill, kill, kill", and unfortunately becomes fatiguing, even as you can recall thrown katanas, bouncing them between every enemy in the room, or create chain reactions of enemies being headshot firing bullets of their own towards other enemies. In half the levels, even by the late game, enemies don't spawn quickly enough to really test your decision making skills.The smug meta-narrative of the original   continues in this game too.  Meta-narratives were cool half a decade ago, now they're overdone and annoying.Even with all this added content and the promise of roguelike random level sequences, the replayability feels around the same as the original. Sure, there's MORE of anything that's cool and fun, but it all starts to blend together not long into it.It's a shame to recommend against , but, to me, it shows how the slow motion formula is finally tired. The original game was an exquisite dessert - it made you want for MORE, but was still great to play through until the end, even if the meta-narrative packaging gets annoying. Here, half the table's still uneaten with randomly combined meals.

_childDocuments_.review: I played  way back in 2013. I was in my first year of college, and SUPERHOT was just a prototype from a game jam. The concept had me immediately hooked, and the minimalist art style was striking. It was a short experience, but one that I went back to several times. My first thought was, naturally, "when are they going to make a full game out of this?"In 2016, it happened. A full SUPERHOT game. Being the cheapskate I am, I wasn't the first in line to buy it, but found the chance to a couple of years after release. It was, all-in-all, a more polished version of the prototype, with sharper graphics, the semblance of a storyline, and well thought-out level design. You would be dropped into a checkmate situation at the beginning of each level, only to unravel your way out of the constraints the game had imposed. It was pretty fun. Not a masterpiece, but definitely a well-executed and novel concept, that held my attention til the end. appeared mysteriously in my Steam library one day. I spent a few minutes trying to remember exactly when I had bought it, but a quick Google search revealed that it had been given as a free add-on for those who already owned the original game. Very nice, I thought, but this couldn't be a fully-fledged sequel being given away for free, surely?It's not. This is not SUPERHOT 2. This is pretty much an adaptation of the endless mode for the original game, stretched out into a whole new release. There are new levels, a few new weapons, and a handful of new enemy types, but beyond that, it's much of the same.The only thing is, it's much of the same, but worse. There are a set number of maps, and enemies spawn randomly throughout them. Everything in the first SUPERHOT felt planned out, whereas nothing in SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE feels totally thought out. Everything becomes a repetitive slog after a while, and my interested was waning after only a couple of hours of playing. In the absence of the puzzle style gameplay, every stage felt trivialised, and it just became a pretty standard FPS where you could stop to line up shots every now and again.Most of the elements worth praising are present in the original release. The graphics and engine are identical, and the concept is still roughly the same. There are power-ups added that slightly alter the gameplay, and I did like some of the trippy sequences they added before picking up said power-ups. The eerie storyline (if it can be called that) is pretty neat as well. Beyond that, there's little fresh content to offer.The kicker is that they're charging $25 for this.  This feels like a $10 version of SUPERHOT, and there's no way that it deserves the same price as the original. The problem is, so many people got this for free that they've likely just left a positive review without even thinking twice. If somebody were to pay full price for this as their  SUPERHOT game, they'd be cheating themselves of the more refined experience that the original has to offer. I'd recommend the original SUPERHOT. This one seems like a hurriedly made cashgrab to capitalise on the success of the original.4.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: That they gave this to current SuperHot owners for free is a big plus and reflects well on the company doing what they do for the love of innovation. The first game told an interesting story in a unique understated and frankly vague style that felt like art. Unfortunately this iteration feels more like fan service, it's okay as an expansion but is very repetitive. It somewhat feels as though that was intentional, making mention of the pointlessness of what you're doing, but the length of time you spend repeating these similar levels takes it out of the realm of irony and feels actually pointless. They would have been better served with fewer levels and removing or having the option to remove the enemy kill count to finish a level in favor of the challenging and satisfying total elimination from the first.

_childDocuments_.review: The 1st Superhot was a great puzzle action game, with a really slick super slo mo mechanic as the main device. You stop, and time slows to a crawl, and you can literally count the seconds it takes for a bullet to come whizzing by. When you move, so do the enemies at a normal pace, and so do their bullets. The 1st game however was more about memorizing enemy patterns when you got sloppy, so you could steamroll that same level like a boss. This time around however that element is thrown out as enemies are now more randomized, and the game now shifts its focus more to showcasing one of many different powerups.The core gameplay element is still intact. Time slows down when you stop, and goes back to normal when you move. But the added powerups add some new dynamics. The powerups are enabled when you beat certain sections of the game, but do not remain with you permanently. You can use them as you progress through different multi leveled sections of the game when you reach certain points. But you lhe powerups when you die, or beat that section. When you get to a segment that lets you pick a powerup, you are given a choice between 2 random powerups that you previously unlocked, so you can play a multi leveled section growing gradually more powerful with a mish mash of powerups. The powerups may include things like deflecting bullets with your katana, starting levels with a random gun, having more ammo, being able to shoot multiple enemies with 1 bullet, exploding projectiles, and more. When you get the right assortment of powerups, the levels can be a breeze, and show off some really slick sequences. The only downside I see for this game is that individual levels can be over rather quickly. Some levels can be cleared in literal seconds if you're good enough, or lucky enough to get a random set of jobbers. All in all though, it's a good game, and a worthy sequel. I would not say however that one should play this over the original. It has a different style to the way the game is approached, while still mostly being the same. It would be best to experience both and decide which one you think is better. Bonus: It's free for Superhot owners who got it before release!

_childDocuments_.review: The first Super Hot was a hand-crafted work of art with great levels and a dark story.   The major downside was that you could beat it in a few hours.  MCD exchanges those traits for arena fighting where you try to kill a certain number of enemies to move onto the next level.  Between levels you gain powerups that let you make different "builds".   Longer game play, more diversity, much less story.   Both games are great, but personally I think it's worth waiting for a sale for the first one.
_childDocuments_.name: SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE

_childDocuments_.review: So I'll be completely honest here. I loved your first two games. This one was alright, not as good as the first one though.The thing that really pissed me off to the point where I uninstalled your game, was the ending...That was highly annoying, to the point where I didn't even feel like trying to get back to the main menu.I just used Task Manager and force quit the game...If you're going to make another one, please, don't do that again.I'm reinstalling your first game.I usually don't leave reviews, but this deserved it, sorry guys.
_childDocuments_.name: SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE

_childDocuments_.review: So, mind control delete is a trip. You get a vague idea of what's going on, but as you progress, the reality of the game steadily comes apart around you. What begins as a fun game becomes a power fantasy, and then the power fantasy turns on its head. I have felt genuine fear playing this game as all my power drained away and the world began to collapse around me. If you want a fun shooter, this is for you, and if you want a psychological trip, this is also for you.
_childDocuments_.name: SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE

_childDocuments_.review: It's like the first SUPERHOT, but more challenging and with some power-ups to change up the gameplay. Would've been a 10 if it was just that. It was still really fun but the levels were very repetitive after the first few hours. Not only that, but the ending required the game to be on for 2.5 real-time hours (used to be 8 hours) just to unlock a very anticlimatic resolution. Still a solid game with fun gameplay nonetheless, 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE

_childDocuments_.review: the core game is really solid after investing some time in it. the repetitiveness is somehow interesting, since you can learn the levels and hone the needed skills, so the game is quite rewarding after some time up to one pointHOWEVER: - whoever optimized the hitboxes has made a tedious job, which makes the later levels unplayable to the point, that you have to pray to the RNG gods to put you in a favorable spot - 0 skill based gaming, you can lose more than 30 mins replaying one node just to get the proper spot on one level, even after doing a quite good job previously- balancing issues - exploding enemies spawning in front of your face is sometimes frustrating... - the unkillable enemies are another point to concentrate on - given the hitbox nonsense, most of the time it`s impossible to dodge an attack because of the narrow level design- I can`t wrap my mind around the spawn system and how even after being in a single dead end corner I still get hit in the backotherwise: - game design - 10/10- idea - 10/10 - gameplay (except the above mentioned stuff) also 10/10 - game stability - not a single crash ever and no framedrops I would greatly recommend the game after all, but with a grain of salt.

No thanks. Apparently the superhot team took that criticism real personal, because this game exists purely to insult anyone that gets fooled into purchasing it. That 2.5 wait used to be like 8 hours. What a pretentious and vindictive piece of "art".

_childDocuments_.review: The story in this game is definitely divisive. It will probably have a lot of players feeling either annoyed or frustrated. But the story isn't really the point. How does the game play? It feels AWESOME! They have taken everything that was great about the original game and made it even more fun and more insane. This is a great shooter and the time slowdown mechanic allows the player to think tactically even in the midst of a blazing firefight. And killing an enemy with a thrown katana and then killing his friend when you recall the katana to your hand will put a big grin on your face. Definitely give this game a try.

_childDocuments_.review: it's superhot, but with more weapons, levels, new mechanics, and seemingly improved ai. not all of these new mechanics are my favorite, though.level design has become smaller than in the original game, and they are occasionally reused a few times (some are reused from the original game too). the game tries to bypass this sometimes by having you play on a different part of the level than before. for instance, there was a new sewer level that looked pretty cool and was exciting to explore, but that feeling wore off quickly when i had to play it two more times. the level progression is also different, too. levels are now in sets called nodes, and it's basically a small gauntlet of levels and you have three lives to finish them. this may sound intriguing, but you're allowed to choose hacks along the way to help you and these make the game ridiculously easy. you don't even have to restart a level if you lose a life. also, levels seem to just end after you've killed a certain amount of red guys, because countless times levels have ended and there were still some red guys left for me that i would logically have to shoot. despite its flaws i'm really liking mind control delete so far, even if it's not as challenging and fun as original superhot was. but if you're here reading this review, chances are you didn't get this game for free by owning superhot before this expansion came out. this is why i cannot recommend the game; its content compared to the original is not worth it for the asking price of $25 USD (and, hell, i wouldn't even buy it right now for $15). i would say play the original superhot first, and if you really like it, then i'd say pick this one up if you can get it for under $10, whether that be in a bundle or during a sale.

So, yes, the game is a great sequel of SUPERHOT but f*ck man, that ending is actual horse sh*t.

_childDocuments_.review: SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE is a unique blend of stuntman choreography and real-time strategy game.  As each new room is revealed you have to analyze your surroundings for possible escape routes, weapon and item locations and all enemy positions.  There may be a guy coming in behind you but the very act of turning your head to see advances time for the guys already coming at you from the front.  But there is something inherently satisfying with the way the game dynamically unfolds like when you just emptied your pistol at one guy then throw the empty weapon as the next, hitting him in the head causing him to toss his shotgun in a gentle arc above your head as you look up and snatch it from the air and blast the stunned enemy in the chest.  Combat is mostly situational opportunities that keep you thinking and reacting on your feet, chaining melee and weapons combat into this organic flow of death and destruction.  It truly is the best of both John Wick and The Matrix where you can dodge bullets while killing someone with a butter knife.Full review at

Mirrors let you move through time.The government monitors people, they pay people to pretend to be your relatives and they put drugs in your foodand they film you.There's messages in every game. Like Pac-Man.Do you know what PAC stands for? "Program and Control."He's Program and Control Man,the whole thing's a metaphor, he thinks he's got free willbut really he's trapped in a maze, in a system, all he can do is consume, he's pursued by demons that are probably just in his own head,and even if he does manage to escape by slipping out one side of the maze, what happens?He comes right back in the other side.People think it's a happy game, it's not a happy game,it's a ♥♥♥♥ nightmare world and the worst thing is it's real and we live in it. _childDocuments_.review: So, after 3 years in early access we finally got the MIND CONTROL DELETE in release, and made a long way from a raw project to the finished product. But what that product is, a completely new title, a big addon or just a blank DLC? Well, the question is simple but the answer is… not really…You see, the developers decided to change the direction of the game and make it more procedurally generated rather than scripted. No, you wont be getting weird procedural rogue-like levels, in that regard we have fully finished 32 maps of different size and quality, but the enemies placement and map order is procedural. So, if original SUPERHOT felt more like a puzzle where you had to find the most convenient and spectacular way of eliminating all enemies now it feels more like a survival mode from original game, but you have a fixed number of randomized maps to pass by killing certain number of red guys on each one. And of course, that couldn’t be all the changes: now we have more weapons more types of enemies and a kind of buff system which is called “hacks” there. In short, every once in a while between these randomized levels you will get the chance to choose one of two randomly picked hacks, which are unlocked throughout the game, and differ from useful ones like more hp (yeah, now the game has hp system and you can catch several bullets before having to restart) and starting with katana to mediocre ones like blowing with shurikens every time you take damage.And by now you might be thinking that we finally got a new title in the SUPERHOT franchise, but, despite all the pros of the game, it still has some cons and still doesn’t feel like a solid sequel. First of all, because of the procedural nature of the game from time to time you get hits from seemingly out of nowhere and sometimes end up in the situations with 3+ fire-armed enemies and you not having even a single can to throw. However, these moments are not that critical and after some time you learn to avoid them, nevertheless, the game still doesn’t make it to the sequel status and end up resembling a standalone addon. The story keeps to be metanarrative-ish but still doesn’t get a real further unfolding, new mechanics decently expand gameplay but don’t really bring anything outstanding to the game. Plus, graphics and its style remained the same (I don’t say it’s bad, I actually like it, but just a fact). And the cherry on top is that the game is too prolonged, especially if you try to do 100%. If original SUPERHOT had several game modes for you to enjoy after main game’s finished, here you mostly have 1.5 game modes: endless survival and “kill-enough-enemies-to-proceed” survival and both of them happen on the same maps. So, if you are planning to complete that game at 100% I recommend doing it with sufficient breaks not to be tired of the repetitive game loop. And one small remark, about the thing that I was personally disappointed by: soundtrack. Yes, the original game didn’t have any real music and seemingly it was foolish to await it in the MIND CONTROL DELETE, but when it was announced that the game will have Zardonic as score producer, I expected to hear some relatively-fast beats to do graceful killings to (actually drum-and-bass really fits the tone of the game), but in the end all I got was one disco level track, one special mix and everything else being just deep ambient.   So, all in all, should you by MIND CONTROL DELETE? Yes, and it’s a must have if you are still hungry for more after completing the first title. Just keep in MIND that despite the games attempt to introduce new mechanics and extensions, you get used to them quite quickly and it’s better to take breaks between sessions so you won’t burn out. P.S. Oh, and all original SUPERHOT owners got MIND CONTROL DELETE for free on the release, which is a very kind move from developers, especially during these lucrative times of gaming industry.

_childDocuments_.review: MCD is an exhilarating and unique game that delivers on its promise to make time move only when you move. The concept is simple, but the execution is brilliant. Each level presents a new challenge that requires you to carefully plan out your movements and attacks. The game rewards you for creativity and improvisation, and it's incredibly satisfying to pull off a series of moves that feels like something straight out of an action movie.The graphics in Superhot: MCD are sleek and minimalist, which fits perfectly with the game's aesthetic. The levels are well-designed and the enemies are challenging without being too frustrating. The game's soundtrack is also worth mentioning, as it perfectly complements the fast-paced action on screen.My only complaint about Superhot: MCD is that it's not as enjoyable playing it without VR. The game was clearly designed with VR in mind, and while it's still fun on a regular screen, it's just not the same experience.Overall, Superhot: MCD is a fantastic game that delivers on its promise of a unique and thrilling gameplay experience. If you're a fan of action games or just want to try something new and innovative, I highly recommend giving this game a try. It's definitely worth the investment.

_childDocuments_.review: Story-wise and ending-wise (and I don't mean the ending narratively, either), I hated Mind Control Delete. However, gameplay-wise I *loved* it. Essentially, Mind Control Delete takes the formula of the original release of Superhot, adds in a slew of new maps, spawns you in different spots in them, tweaks the layout of those maps at different points in the game (i.e. you might have two entrances into a room one time, but two entrances into it another), adds new enemies, adds new weapons, adds new abilities, adds new threats ("mines" on floors/walls/ceilings), and gives a slight randomization through little rogue-lite sort of runs of series of maps.It all worked really well in my opinion, and via the trial by fire that is at least getting past the end sections (other than the 100-map node and the infinite node, anyway), I got a lot more skilled at the game. When I pulled off successful runs, it felt really satisfying and the new guns and enemies - though tough/annoying at times - definitely changed up how I had to play certain maps. If you enjoyed the gameplay of Superhot and wanted more justification to play a lot more of it without simply running the challenge modes of the original, Mind Control Delete is great stuff.Now with that out of the way, I will say that the new story elements and ending were more cryptic and unfulfilling than those in the original game, in my opinion. Worse yet, to TRULY get to the "The End" screen, you have to leave your computer sitting through 2.5 real-time hours of keeping the game loaded up. It's also how you get to start the game over if you so choose. I watched a YouTube video where the timer showed 7.5 or 8 hours or some such, so the devs may have modified/patched it since then to be less obnoxious, but having to leave the game sitting with the computer running, taking up electricity and memory to go to a "The End" screen and start the game over is asinine and disgusting.Despite my disdain for the story and "ending," the overall net of my experience (aside from the obscenities I screamed at surprise losses throughout) was a fairly big positive. If you have to pay for this, though, I wouldn't recommend paying more than like $9.99 or so for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I have to say i feel conflicted.I got the Game for free for owning the Original, as a lot of other people did.But when writing a Review I felt that I had to consider the Price it is being sold at.At the time of writing, this Price is 24,99€ in Germany. Planning new Routes on death took precedence over just improvising every time, and felt better to play. _childDocuments_.review: Superhot: Mind Control Delete is a first-person shooter centered about some of the most ludicrous stuff you can pull in a videogame. From cutting bullet with a sword to snatching a guy's gun and shoot him with it or face...people with the head of a dog that moves like the  hunting you down. A game that is a lot of fun to play and focuses on that train of thought of getting better every time and beating its multiple levels.The title gets progressively harder the more you play it, up to the point where it becomes sadistic towards the player! It can be represented with a plethora of enemies that will grow to be tremendous obstacles. The regular foes already swarm you, but then at some point, special ones will show up, these cannot be killed and have special powers just as you do. They will hunt you down as you frantically search for the standard version to beat the level before they dispose of you in a battle against time. It is just fantastic, from guys that throw katanas with mind control to dogs that will hunt you at super speeds.The other cool thing is the powers, the standard version of the game lacked this function, and here is just so much fun to use them! They are called hacks and can do things from slowing downtime even more, to rushing like a bulldozer to switching bodies with an enemy to escape a situation or be able to shoot without recharging the weapons. They come in two groups, cores ones of which you can only use one at a time and side ones that can be accumulated for the duration of the level. Mixing powers adequately can make even the harder levels seem more doable and make all the difference in the world!The bottom line is: it is a lot of fun! Users who had the normal version get the Mind Control Delete for free, and it is worth the price if you are looking for something short yet entertaining! The full game lasts for about 4-6 hours, and there is some extra stuff, such as wave mode, if you want more. Perhaps as a single title, it might pale a bit to encourage you to get it, but as a bundle, it is a sweet deal! If you want to be  in a game, then this is that game! and remember:

Like, even if some ability is stronger or more versatile, but just doesn't play as fun, you won't feel encouraged to play with those abilities. My description of "mundane" for the speed up ability does not do the seemingly basic ability justice. The sheer playing potential unlocked by one of the most simple abilities is tremendous. _childDocuments_.review: Impressive gameplay, but the improvements upon the original formula are limited to tacked-on roguelike elements. The game easily overstays it's welcome, with the only gameplay variety being in powerups you receive and the ability you choose. These don't significantly alter the play experience, and are far from justifying the absurdly long stretches of roguelike 'permadeath' content. In later stages, Superhot:MCD expects you to complete 15 stages, killing a dozen enemies in each, with an RNG-based healing system and only two hits before you die and reset all 15 stages. This fails to account for the game being more liberal in using unkillable enemies, explosives, hard-to-see traps, and enemies spawned behind you (where you may die just turning around to look at them!) and altogether creates an experience that starts as what may as well be a modded Superhot Endless mode, and becomes a frustrating slog of playing the exact same gameplay loop for hours on end with no satisfying reward in sight, only the option to engage in another level and another slog.This is, of course, amplified by the baffling decision to create a main menu with the only option being "exit game", and *tying that to the left click button.* I have wasted at least 6 hours of gameplay on retrying levels because I, with the most powerful abilities and full health, pause and alt-tab out of the game, then click back into the window, only to lose the perfect run I had spent twenty minutes on because the game provides no confirmation for exiting a level, and ties it to the most commonly used input: clicking anywhere in the game window. Not just clicking on the "exit" command, no, clicking *anywhere in the game* will make you exit out of the level and, depending on how late you are into the game, you can spend multiple hours trying to get back to where you were before.Additionally, it's worth noting how poor the ending is; it's some secret minigames and a 2.5-hour loading bar, mixed with some ominous messages. There is no resolution, no answers for the cryptic secrets of the Superhot universe, just waiting and getting booted back into the main menu. Incredibly dissapointing.The game is alright up to the 10 hour mark or so, and at that point rapidly declines into being actively frustrating and unenjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the weird and unique time-stopping action that the first two games offered, you'll probably at least get a few hours of enjoyment from the added content in MCD. That being said, if you're a fan of the mysterious lore behind SUPERHOT, or are a deepdive secret hunter, don't go into this game expecting much. There's still plenty there, but nowhere near as much as SUPERHOT or SUPERHOT VR. A lot is repetition, but I still enjoyed a majority of my playtime. Just don't try and 100% complete the game. You will probably not have fun.MIND CONTROL DELETE is probably best thought of as an extremely long expansion pack to the original SUPERHOT concept. There are many new levels and mechanics to explore, and most people could probably finish the game in 20 hours or so. If you want absolutely every achievement, lore hint, and level 100% completed, plan for 50 or so hours of gameplay and a lot of grind. Seriously, for some of the later levels, expect an hour or more of extreme repetition until you get a good run, or get lucky and gain the ability that allows you to regain hearts. All in all, MCD is pretty much SUPERHOT with twice as much content and a tenth of the story. If that sounds like what you'd want, go ahead and get the game! The price is reasonable for the amount of content included, but I would suggest waiting for a sale.One final note - if MCD doesn't quite sound like what you had in mind for more SUPERHOT content, there is a beta of an older version that you can still try out. It actually has a lot of content and provides a lot of the same concepts, and even some concepts that you won't find in the release version of MCD, and doesn't have hours upon hours of grind. Both are worth playing, but for different reasons. If MCD doesn't feel quite to your tastes, maybe take a look at the beta version.

_childDocuments_.review: So right away, I'd like to state that if you have not played the original SUPERHOT? Stop. Do not touch this game. Go buy the original game and play that first. Think of it this way; SUPERHOT 2016 will give you the proper SUPERHOT  MIND CONTROL DELETE gives you exactly what the game offers; more of the SUPERHOT gameplay, but not necessarily a new experience. With that said, MCD is a good game and does do a lot to change the gameplay of how SUPERHOT works, helping it stand out a little bit. Unlike the original game where you repeat the same level over and over until you figure out the 'puzzle' to kill all the red guys (I like to compare it's style to Hotline Miami), MCD is, as much as it won't make a lot of sense, handled more like a mini rogue-like of sorts. Instead, levels become a series of "nodes" which contain several different levels in randomly selected maps. Kill a few guys, move onto the next, repeat until you hit the bottom and complete the node. And as you go further along, you're given ways to enhance your ability to perform in the game while the game's typical "red guys" later get variants that have different characteristics, some of which can be used in your favor if you play smart. The only major problem is that the game can be very repetitive with small adjustments. I've also run into a small handful of bugs here and there, but usually it's nothing too gameplay breaking. Only maybe once or twice was it such.Good game, though not as good as the original one IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have ever played the original SUPERHOT or SUPERHOT VR, you will instantly understand what to do and fall back into the flow with ease.I do not recommend this game to new players without explaining or at least warning them about 2 things, The first being the learning curve. Starting out, you are given relatively easy challenges and once overcome will seem very obvious as with most games of a strategic nature. As you are aware, "time moves when you move" is pretty accurate but isn't truthful. without budging, time does indeed tick along. This game introduces a bunch of new mechanics that have changed the gameplay for me compared to the standard/original/first game. Every "level" is familiar and so are the weapons and their operation. There is a "story" to it but i must stress, it's not as heavily pressed onto the player as it once was in the first SUPERHOT (it's annoying writing that in caps, but that's how it's named.... so...)the first new mechanic which isn't one i am fond of but i undertsand why it was implemented was the "die and go back to the start" mechanic. not "rogue-like" but the level set. it starts out with levels labelled 1, 1a, 1b, 1c, 2, 2a etc. and each consists of a collection of levels in varying amounts. if you don't finish them consecutively and die, you gotta go back. not to 1. but to whichever grouping you're in. example: 1b has 6 levels, if you don't finish those six and die, you have to redo 1b from the start and not from, say, level 4, or the level you die on. i feel like i made that complicated. but it's there.other new mechanics are the "mind hacks" which basically, we would normally call "buff" or "advantage" or "perk". from having HP to extra ammo, or even a local explosion from the player character if they are hit and lose a Hit Point (and have health remaining). you unlock these as you progress, however, it seems optional to collect the "mind hacks", i haven't completed it yet to start again and try without picking up these hacks/perks.if you played the original, this one is certainly worth playing, especially when considering you probably got it for free just because you owned it on steam or somewhere else legitimately. if you didn't get it, but played the original, this one is basically the same game but (in the words of South Park) Bigger, Longer and Uncut. also, experienced players are guaranteed to take a few hits and get tricked/dooped by the game.i am a curious player and explore, experiment and play slowly on my first time around on most games, 4 hours in and i'm at level 4. bare in mind i've been chatting and getting distracted, so if you concentrate you'll be much further than me in the same time. i have heard this game is even longer than the original so i can only hope the zone/area/world count goes well past 4 and hits maybe 16. that would be intense. i'd be satisfied with 20 or more. but so far, 4 is a good challenge and now, it's getting radically harder for me.

_childDocuments_.review: If Superhot is an interesting gimmick that can barely be stretched into a two-hour campaign, Mind Control Delete is stretching that out even more with one of the most effective tools in the indie developer's pocket: randomized levels and bonuses. I don't like using the term "lazy" as making games takes a lot of work and it feels disrespectful, but I simply cannot stand when someone feels like any semblance of actual level design can be replaced by a slapped-together randomiser. The narrative takes a small step back, but it's still quite pretentious fourth-wall breakage that is incredibly tired by now. The game kept asking why I kept playing it, and so did I. Since I have some amount of self-control, I just uninstalled after less than an hour. If I wanted Superhot's gimmick (and only interesting bit of... anything), I'd just play Dusk with the Superhot mode cheat.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the original Superhot and the idea of a near endless Superhot with roguelike elements sounded like a great idea, and it could work if only the developers weren't really lazy with making this game. The problem is that there's just so few maps for the game to cycle through to where it gets repetitive in a boring too fast, and that's quite horrible considering how good Superhot's core gameplay look was at being satisfyingly repetitive.I mean, if you really like Superhot and get it for cheap, it's okay, but you won't really be able to play this without shaking the feeling of how much better the original was.It feels like there's no more than 8 maps that are on constant rotation, you're always at the mercy of the RNG because whenever the next map loads in you're always facing 1-2 enemies with randomized weapons without any chance for you to get a look at your bearings, they also spawn in randomly so you do run the risk of getting ganked from the back, so maybe something like a mini-map that shows enemies spawning wouldn't have been that unfair to add to the game. There's also a new type of enemy that erupts in to bullets when you kill it, and some of the hack modifiers are pretty useless. Like the deflect all bullets if you cut one bullet one is too situational, the grenade is a liability rather than a bonus and so you mostly just end up using the same basic hacks you get from the start of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had the potential to be great,But the devs must've ran out of ideas...Or, maybe they just became lazy.The start of the game lures the player in with the promise of more hacks, more cores, and more levels-- but when you do get to the later levels: the only rewards for beating them are small snippets of lore.I had hoped that at the end of the game I would unlock a Sandbox.core, or God.core, but sadly the devs decided to play a prank on their player base by making it the least rewarding ending possible.I don't mind the enemy spawning, it's like endless mode in the first game, but the level design is totally uninspired:No jumping between moving trucks on a highway, no dodging between gears inside a giant clock:-- Don't get me wrong, the levels are well-designed for fair difficulty, but they lack the novelty of the original game.When I first saw the hack mechanic I was excited to discover them all. There were some interesting ones like "lightning reflexes" and "flow recall". Sadly, those two are the height of it: there're no more to discover after them.The cores are fun to experiment with. A great idea, but like everything else in this game: it feels half-a$$ed. Only 3 unique cores? Did the devs run out of ideas?Some ideas:-H4X0r.core; press E to spawn and equip a random item. Choose from 4 hacks instead of 2. Hack: higher chance to spawn a firearm.-Worm.core; press E to brainwash enemy, enemy throws held weapon then runs to nearest foe, enemy head explodes after three seconds. Hack: brainwashed enemies become spiky OR contagion spreads to nearby enemies when head explodes.-Jump.core; press E to change between jump heights, deathstomp by default. Hack: Shockwave on landing.-Psychic.core; catch and store bullets, press E to fire them back with a finger gun. Hack: store up bullets to shoot like a shotgun OR combine 2 bullets to shoot like a sniper.-Melee.core; press E for sweep attack. Doubled enemy spawn count, faster enemy movement, no firearms. Hack: no delay between attacks.-Speed.core; everything moves faster, press E for temporary player speed boost (slow down everything else). Hack: fullstop.-Sandbox.core; select six hacks at the start. Hack: choose one additional core.-God.core; invincibility, press E to kill all. Hack: explode with bullets when hit.-Dodge.core; levels have a countdown timer, invincible enemies, press E for temporary invincibility. Hack: longer i-frames.-highway.level; convoy of trucks, enemy spawn from truck cabin (add simple animation to look like enemy climbs onto roof from window).-clock.level; like in Super Mario 64.-mirrors.level; maze with glass walls, by the end of a long level most panes will be broken.-hotel.level; penthouse suite with stairway up to roof, stairway down to three smaller rooms, and a moving window cleaning platform.-elevators.level; 4 elevators in one shaft, each moving up and down between 3 floors, each floor has enemy spawn doors, elevator doors always open, enemies path to doorway and shoot into shaft.-butcher.hack; recently defeated enemy body parts can be picked up and used as weapons.-stickman.hack; player hitbox width reduced.-antivirus.hack; player can kill special enemies.-bumpfire.hack; thrown firearms fire at nearest enemy upon impact.-highpressure.hack; increased player bullet speed.-dwarf.hack; player size halved.-randomizer.hack; shotguns can shoot like snipers, rifles like shotguns, pistols like rifles, etc.I do like this game.. I just can't help but feel that it could have been so much MORE.Imagine what it could've been if there was a level editor, custom hack creation tool, and mod support for custom cores. So much potential.To any dev who might be reading this:Did you encounter too many bugs?Did you become too fixated on the jaded meta-narrative of "less is more"?Did your focus on difficulty prevent you from experimenting more with the gameplay?Did you simply lose interest in the project?You don't have to answer me, I just had to ask.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this better than the original game? No. MCD tweaks the gameplay of the original (albeit with much easier to manipulate AI) to be more diverse and interesting, while lacking in the story and level design side. You're running through the same few maps with a few randomly generated obstacles that "glitch" out the environment. Every level is just a short endless mode (ironic though that is) that has no interesting map or enemy challenges. In SUPERHOT, there were levels that relied purely on a gimmick; running from a truck, fighting on a train, being stuck in a claustrophobic fighting pit. MCD feels much less unique, because it's designed to be MORE of the same type of game, for better or for worse.I definitely think it's worth playing if you enjoyed melee and throwing in the original, because they let you go all out with modifiers that make it better than the gun-play. Narrative is substantially weaker than the original, and it doesn't really advance the  of the original that much. Think of it more like another game-mode like SUPERHOT's endless or challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: Soft yes.It's more SUPERHOT.It won't change your mind if you didn't like the original.It doesn't feel quite like the original in that had distinct level flow and this cycles through levels randomly. I vastly prefer the original's map flow, but that does little to hinder, it just lacks the genuine changeups that could happen, like having to start the mission falling doesn't ever seem to happen.The new twists on the gameplay are welcome, offering a more arcade-like or even roguelite experience where you run through nodes, unlocking further nodes and echelons of the map you play through while individual node runs are small instances that let you keep trying from their start if you die until you succeed. These individual nodes offer 'hacks' you can pick that change the way you play, the most fundamental difference in gameplay from what came before it. The charge skill is fascinatingly gamebreaking without being too powerful, allowing you to literally phase through scenery to virtually teleport next to someone and bash their red glass head in. Other iterative changes include enemies who have selective weakpoints, forcing you to target those areas to land a killing blow.All in all, if this is the last SUPERHOT game, it certainly did a decent job of keeping things fresh enough to offer more, while still resembling what it used to be. But it won't convince anyone who didn't like the other games to convert over.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great follow-up to the original game. It's a lot of the same stuff from the first game, only MORE. More levels, more enemy types, more weapons, more everything. My one complaint about SUPERHOT was that it was too short. With how minimalist this is, you would think they could throw together more levels. Well, they did that with this game.There's a decently large number of levels, but then they mix and match your start position, enemy placement, what powerups you have, etc., so even when you repeat a level (and you will, quite a bit), it still feels pretty fresh and fun. And then they went ahead and threw in an endless wave mode for every level as well. And they gave the game away for free to everyone who bought the first! What's not to love? So if you played the first and enjoyed it and somehow didn't get MCD free (like you got SUPERHOT free on Epic or something), then I'd highly recommend buying this game. Also, if you're interested in the original or this one, I'd suggest buying this one. The first is fun, but this has everything the original one offered and more. The story is, like everything else in the game, very minimalistic, so you're not really missing anything by jumping in here, but I'm sure you can find an explanation or video of the story stuff from the first game online somewhere. Anyway, I heartily recommend this game to anyone who likes shooters, puzzles, or just really cool, stylish games.UPDATE after finishing the game (minor general sort of spoilers, nothing specific): I still recommend this, but the "story" drags it down. The more you play, the more they try to shoehorn in some "deep" message about addiction and control and video games and all, in a unique but ham-fisted way. The gameplay, the levels, the enemies, all the parts of playing the game? Great. The "story" (and I keep putting it in quotes because there's not really a story, per se), the mechanics they use to try to tell it, everything outside of actually playing the game? Dumb, tedious, pretentious BS that drags on. SUPERHOT, and especially MCD, are games you want to jump in and play a few levels then put down until you want your next fix. And for the majority of this game, you can do that. But the end stuff is just a huge departure from the gameplay and so not what I was looking for in a game like this. It's so weird having two strong yet conflicting opinions on a game, but I do. I love the gameplay, hate the "story." Still play this, but unless you care about achievements, I wouldn't even bother finishing it. Just go play the endless modes or something once you get to them.

_childDocuments_.review: Original is a masterpiece and the VR version of the original is a must have title. I recommend those with a fiery passion.That said I don't recommend this game for twenty five bucks (though props to the devs for throwing it at legacy owners for free).This is still fun, but it's like a C- at best in contrast to the A+ of the former two. It's repetitive, but in that meh way - I'm a huge roguelike/sandbox fan, really love burning time on mindless stuff to relax, and this really just gets old fast. Same series of levels over and over, no variance. Yeah you get powers, yeah you get little tweaks to gameplay, but it's still the same song and dance. There isn't really anything so new and breathtaking that it can sweep the repetition of this title under the rug, so bear in mind you will get bored of this quickly, especially if you've already played the original(s) to exhaustion. It isn't some fresh spin; it's the exact same game except you get a handful of special powers and some of the enemies can only be hit in certain areas.One other major gripe, and the key reason for the significant degrade in my opinion versus the originals is that the hit detection has taken a noticeable nosedive in consistency - the original and VR were on point, everything flowed and made absolute sense, and there was no question when a bullet connected or how a trajectory should operate. In this version, the I'm constantly wondering why I did or didn't get hit by gunfire, or why the enemies or objects did or did not. At first I chalked it up to my being mistaken, but over the course of playing this game for a couple hours I cannot deny that this is an actual problem, which is again an extreme letdown versus the polish of the first two titles. It's also confusing given this is effectively the same game, so I am curious what engine tweaks are leading to this.I'm also annoyed reading about some of the trollish nonsense the devs have included later in the game - reading some of these other reviews to see if I was alone with the hit detection/repetition gripes and seeing the asinine eight hour delete/reinstall sequence just makes me roll my eyes with irritation - get that Hideo Kojima meta ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out of here and polish your game.Overall this definitely feels like it should have just been a DLC game mode in the $10 (MAYBE $15) price range rather than its own title (unless the engine tweaks impacted the hit detection of the original game). TL;DR After my experience I would have returned it had I not received it free for owning the original.

_childDocuments_.review: I've tried very hard to like this game. I adore the first game and full admittance I got this game for free because I already owned Superhot, and I am so thankful I didn't spend money on this game. So much of the original vision is lost and totally ruined by design decisions in this game. Levels no longer are creative set pieces mimicking action film sequences. Instead levels are not a handful of different repeated endless arena levels with randomly spawning enemies and weapons. It is now nigh impossible to master a specific level or sequence due this randomness. There is now an ugly middle in which you anxiously cannot predict what will be in a set arena level, and likewise because the arenas are played, replayed, and replayed again; they are boring and become dull fast. The longer levels and set number of hits that a player can take over a sequence of levels motivates the lamest most conservative and boring gameplay possible, an outright antithetical design consequence from the original's fast and loose gameplay. SUPERHOT felt freeing and like the more you mastered the mechanics and systems of the game; the more liberally and expressive your play could be. SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE feels like I am constantly being monitored by a supervisor and can't risk or afford playing stylishly, experimentally, or expressively. This has become a game of shooting and taking cover, the very gameplay loop the first game was decidedly subverting.I really question if the creators fully understood what it was that made the first game so great.

_childDocuments_.review: SUPER–HOT SUPER– HOT SUPER–HOT SUPER–HOT SUPER-hang on, someone is watching, aren’t they? Hi, please hold the red flag. You know the chant, don’t you? Sure thing you do, it’s SUPERHOT, the indie sensation where “time moves when you do” or at least that’s what I am going to assume, things are easier this way. SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE presents itself as all solid sequels should – it is more of the gameplay that fans of the original look for but remixed in a way that make it go above and beyond what veterans of first instalment are used to. Now, imagine two indie game trends have a car accident, except nobody dies and the contents of both vehicles get thoroughly mixed together.The comparison doesn’t make any sense? Lovely, let’s delve a little further. Driving a red Ferrari F350 was the original SUPERHOT, while approaching from the opposite direction in a silver Bentley Continental was the rougelike genre, both pedal to the metal towards a fiery conclusion. The result of ensuing collision is a pleasantly solid sequel, which finds a reasonably engaging twist to a formula which otherwise might’ve seemed as a one-time gimmick.SUPERHOT has an angry relationship with its player. The original was calling out the user for their violent urges propelling the game forward, repeatedly highlighting that the only reason behind game progression is a temporary outlet for brutal tendencies. MCD at large drops the pretence of morality or being a story-driven journey, fully embracing the fact that the player is there to indulge in unapologetic carnage and that they are keen to do so. If you’ve found yourself at odds with SUPERHOT’s moralising tone, while you were just enjoying how a funny red polygon man shatters into pieces, this aspect is grossly reduced in MIND CONTROL DELETE.That is not to say that “cursed arcade” aesthetic of the original has been withdrawn from, quite the opposite. The user still traverses the peculiar world of BIOS interface adaptation, as with each completed chapter a new “node” is unlocked for the player to explore. This arrow navigated roadmap allows the player to gradually explore the system, continuously unlock new power-ups and occasionally snippets of lore. Most importantly though, every “node” is a gauntlet of several levels, which player has to handle in one go in order to progress.Clearing several challenges in a row may initially seem awfully unfair, however the player is not an unrelenting deathdealer for nothing. To facilitate continuous clearing of levels, the player has a wide variety of gradually unlocked power-ups at their disposal. Chief and first among them is having 3 lives, allowing you some margin of error rather than dying from the first hit. Notably superpowers can be divided into melee and range oriented, allowing the player to create a “build” best suited to preferred playstyle. Are you a sharpshooter, eager to use extra ammo with piercing capabilities? Perhaps you are a CQC specialist, enjoying a direct dash to an enemy while holding a katana yearning to strike? Maybe you are a jack of all trades and it would be an awful shame if the bottle you just snatched off the table turned into lethal shrapnel when thrown? MCD has it all.Introduction of the power-ups may lull you into an impression that you are an unstoppable force of nature. Fair enough, at first you are. However, SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE has a steadily increasing difficulty curve which will require you to fully employ skills learnt during the early stages, once the game properly kicks into gear. To begin with, MCD introduces a number of new opponent types: “glitches” holding a weapon unusable by the player, “concretes” having only a single limb susceptible to damage and “mushrooms” exploding with spikes once they die. Not to mention hunters wielding otherwise player-exclusive powers, further down the line.“Time moves when you do” shenanigans combined with this title’s distinct aesthetic deliver a more than solid core for MIND CONTROL DELETE to build around. However, the rougelike blocks used as a finishing touch are a much more divisive aspect. Truth be told, the first SUPERHOT was an overwhelmingly successful proof of concept. Now that the concept has been comprehensively proven, where is one supposed to go from there? MIND CONTROL DELETE isn’t a series of pre-planned engagements, introducing the player to diverse combat scenarios while sprinkling bits of story along the way. Instead, the game offers a number of arenas with defined spawn points and has the player kill several enemies before transitioning to the next level, thus eventually making it up to the player and powers selected, to keep the combat interesting. To give credit where it is due, there is a lot of levels in MCD and with varied spawns it takes a while for the repetition to sink in. That said, it inevitably does, sooner than later at that – to the point where I would recommend playing this title in hour-long sessions, otherwise it may overstay its welcome uncomfortably quickly.I cannot in clear conscience recommend the game for being exhausting, although the effect does seem to be intentional. Tedious game progression is fitting to the game’s theme of mindless grind for the sake of it. Any notion of enjoyment, accomplishment or even purpose are slowly discarded. Through and through, MCD is dedicated to those who were left hungry for more and means to feed you until your stomach bursts.As a noteworthy mention, I am compelled to highlight the game’s soundtrack by Zardonic. Powerful electronic tunes, occasionally break the indistinct ambience of this title. In doing so, granting gravity to every scene where it springs in to life.MIND CONTROL DELETE is a game that was always going to have the odds stacked against it. Novel idea was a major factor behind the success of the first SUPERHOT, now that spirit of originality is spent, any direct continuation is bound to be viewed as inferior. Nonetheless, the developers chose to squeeze as much as humanly possible out of the gameplay mechanics. Thus, a genuinely decent sequel was born, which was given for free to all owners of the original game. While I have utmost respect for this title as a part of the series, it doesn’t hold all that well on its own. Fans of the genre will likely enjoy the rougelike touch and won’t frown at inherent repetition that comes along with it. That same quality will however be a deal-breaker for those who expected MCD to deliver a journey. Should you happen to already own this title it is more than worth at least checking out. If you are to buy a SUPERHOT game, by all means do try the original and come back once you feel thirsting for more.

_childDocuments_.review: I was torn about whether or not to recommend SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE.  Mechanically, it's mostly an iterative improvement over SUPERHOT; there're more weapons, there're more abilities, there's more variety in the enemies, and there are more levels.  That's all good, and it's easy to enjoy when it's allowed to do its part.What does not work is the structure of the game's narrative and campaign.  The story is shallow (and intentionally so), and the writer(s?) have clearly mistaken hammering on that point for making some sort of real statement or constituting a story.  In fairness, I did not complete the game (more on that in a moment), so it is conceivable, if unlikely, that a story of some substance coalesces in the (presumably small) portion I missed.  As for the campaign structure, being divorced from a story leaves it very repetitive; instead of navigating stages following a narrative path (as the first did), it takes a form of procedurally-generated combats in a random selection of game's pool of stages.  The aforementioned mechanical improvements prop this up for a good while, but the player's failures quickly become frustrating when randomness in 'hack' (power-up) distribution and enemy generation can make a set of stages unduly hard (or easy, for that matter), compounded by the fact that one cannot learn things like enemy placement or spawn order (since those change every time).  I 'quit' (temporarily) in frustration several times, frustrated into waiting until the next day to repeat my attempts at clearing a 'node' (a set of stages which must be completed in a single attempt or retried from scratch--the campaign is structured entirely in these 'nodes').What killed it for me, though, and why I can't speak with certainty on the actual conclusion of the game, is a godawful sequence near what I (quite reasonably) presume was the endgame.  Continuing through a faux ending appeared to require HUNDREDS of unprompted keystrokes (with the possibility it may be quicker if one ignores the game's nominal theme; I can't say for sure).  I exited the game to eat dinner after getting through to more gameplay, and when I came back, I found myself back at the beginning of the 'ending' sequence.  Nope.  Not worth it.  I'm done.SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE can definitely be entertaining, but its structure introduces a frustrating level of randomness and the writing clobbers the player over the head with a fairly vapid theme.  As an owner of the original, I received the game for free, and I AM grateful for that.  I would not suggest paying for it.

_childDocuments_.review: You want MORE? You get MORE!This game is much more action focused than its predecessor. You get to blast your way through wave after wave of enemies, picking up special abilities in the form of "hacks" and "cores" along the way. The limited amount of maps can start to feel stale after a while, but by switching cores often you can keep things fresh. There is a certain story aspect but just like in the first game, it's very cryptic and sometimes hidden.All in all, if you liked the combat in SUPERHOT, you'll love this sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: This started out pretty fun, but quickly became repetitive. I would recommend it but the final levels just feel like an exercise in tedium. Also this is one of the worst handled endings ive seen in my life. Having to wait in a menu for 3 hours just to play the game again is such an insult after making it through the frustrating final levels. I get the story and appreciate what they are going for, but I feel it was at the cost of being fun. Go play Superhot or Superhot VR, they are better.
