_childDocuments_.review: Summary (TL:DR)Arcadian Atlas is a decent game that tries to capture the glory of FF tactics and Ogre Tactics, yet falls short on the bread and butter that is tactical combat. All the pieces are there, they just need some extra work and polish. It's a good game if you want a kind, gentle introduction to the Tactics genre of games. 6/10------Full Review------This game is clearly a love letter to games such as Final Fantasy Tactics and Ogre Tactics. From the art style and storytelling, to the tactical game play and class system. It's very clear where the creators got their inspiration from. Sadly, it's a love letter that doesn't quite reach the needed height of its love. Arcadian Atlas is a decent game, with a potential to actually be a really good one. Yet certain aspects fall short, leaving you with an aftertaste that feels lackluster.Pros:Pixel Art - The Pixel art is on point, giving a more realistic style then say FF Tactics or Ogre Tactics. Main characters feel unique and the maps are well crafted in a way fitting the area they represent.Unique classes - Classes feels unique and the class tree offers a different, welcomed change to the basic healer/dps/tank combo. Sadly it's not allowed to truly shine, due to several restrictions during game play. A good foundation that's never allowed to truly blossom.Pro-Cons:Music - The music is unique for this kind of game and setting, using a jazz inspired soundtrack instead of a more typical epic fantasy. It works well with the more relaxed game play, yet doesn't really add anything to the story or feeling of the game. It never gets the heart beating, which makes it feel lackluster at times.Level of challenge - While veterans of SRPG/TRPGs will find this game very easy, due to low number of units and fast combat encounters, new players to the series might find a good first game. It's very easy to pick up and would give a newcomer a good taste of what SRPG/TRPG games can offer. An appetizer in a way, before the main course of example FF tactics or Ogre Tactics could be consumed.Story - The story has all the ingredients to be an epic, political-heavy story line with dangerous magic and world ending enemies, yet these never really hit home. There is no weight behind choices, nor do characters get enough time to shine or build their motivations. We're expected to fill in the blanks and motivations behind nearly every character, making it feel flat and shallow. There is a good story here, but it needs more depth to truly grab on to your heart.Cons:Low unit count - As a squad/army building game where you are invited to craft your army of unique soldiers and classes, the game falls completely flat with its limited 5-6 units per encounter. Especially as the main cast of characters are 2-4 depending on where you are in the story. Combined this with the level system and recruitment system and you'll end up using the same units all the time. This also makes the battles feel small, quick and lacking of tactical depth. It's less of an army builder and more of a "DnD party battle style" kind of game.Level and Recruitment - Characters earn levels after each battle they are part of, with the main cast also gaining levels during certain story beats. New recruits are cheap and always on the same level as your main cast. This means that more often than not, you end up using either a full cast of non-story units, or your main cast, making having additional recruits feel unnecessary. One upside is that this system allows to you switch out a soldier between missions, if you are not happy with their build, but it also takes away all needed investment in them, making each soldier feel like a random mook, rather then a good, crafted hero.Combat - The combat is very flat, from the lack of elevation effects, to line of sight and just all around weird balancing issues. More often than not, you are able to nuke down a single enemy with two units, if not one with a critical. AoE can be devastating and certain map-wide abilities can completely wipe the enemy forces in one round. While this creates quick combat encounters, it doesn't lend it self to a good challenge, but rather the opposite.Gear and Gold - Gold is something you get in abundance, on levels rivaling Skyrim and Fallout. There is so much gold thrown your way that you never lack for gear or new recruits, even if you try to spend as much as possible, there seems to be more around the corner. Gear is upgraded on a speedy level, with each main-story fight opening up new gear all the time. Yet this never feels like an real upgrade, seeing as you just bought yourself the previous level ten minutes ago. Nor does the gear feel unique in any way, often just giving flat stats.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I want to recommend this game, I cannot.It just hung when an enemy Apothecary tried to revive a unit my Inquisitor had turned to undead.I had been planning on giving a thumbs-up before it hung.The positive:The story is on par with the story in similar games.The map design is on par with the classics.The negative:I was going to say the game is playable - but after the hang...Height does not matter, it is just window dressing.Walls do not block ranged attacks.Most lists do not wrap from end to end.There is incentive to leave the main characters out of combat - the fact that only the main characters auto-level,Characters can walk thru fire wall without taking damage.The music is out of place for this genre of game - moreover it is straight-up elevator music.  It _might_ work in a film noir detective game.I was only level 21 - I didn't get a chance to play with the promoted classes' abilities.  But, it was looking like there was not going to be any job switching like the classic tactics games.During the KS campaign, the designers said they were making a game like Tactics: Ogre and FFT. _childDocuments_.review: Backed the game way back on Kickstarter. I do recommend the game! I would say it makes a good introduction to the genre and there's definitely something here, but release states are important and I gotta say I'm left feeling a tad underwhelmed. It feels so close to being great but there's things mentioned by many others here that should not be missing in a game of this genre. If I had to pinpoint my biggest gripe, it would be the lack of ability to display more information about nearly everything. I wanna see more stats in the shop before buying something, I wanna see my troops' abilities before battle, I wanna see the enemy placement before I decide where to place mine, and I wanna see where my enemies can go and attack on the battlefield.I think the theme the devs were going for, "war doesn't discriminate" being my guess, shines through with the troop system. Your troops are disposable and replaceable. They are a means to an end and if one falls, you've got plenty of coin to replace them. Recruiting is random cause when you're busy fighting wars, you take what you can get.I see the passion and understand that the team is small, with a few QoL improvements I think most of the frustrations will appeased.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not very far into it but it has been great so far.  The music is awesome, the story has been good, the characters interesting and the battles have fun.  The game has strong  Final Fantasy Tactics, fire emblem, and Tactics Ogre Vibes but with its own charming little touches.  I was streaming and the chat went wild for Poncho...  The camera angle was throwing me off a bit at first but after a few battles I was used to it and it's fine now... Anyways, great game so far and if it continues on this trajectory it will surely be a great game overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this game on Kickstarter and have been following the development ever since. It's fair to say I've been fairly invested in the project for a while.Overall I'd say my expectations with the game were met. I've really enjoyed the writing thus far. I'm not always the biggest fan of medieval fantasy that leans heavily on a lot of lore and history that we're not aware of going into the story, so it's a testament to this game that the broader strokes of the backstory are introduced quickly and the characters establishing conflicts are interesting and engaging right out the gate.Combat has been relatively fun. Nothing has been overtly difficult to be frustrating but I've had enough close calls that I've stayed engage with it, and its a relatively simple turn based system that allows me to properly strategize and execute a plan. From what I've played so far, if you're a fan of real nail biting battles then this might not be for you but I also haven't played much of the late game yet, so that might change! I also prefer my games to be more on the breezy side, so its worked for me.If I had any criticisms, it's less with the main gameplay and more with pre-battle strategy and preparation. One of my favorite things to do in strategy games such as this is making multiple armies with a lot of different classes and specializations that I can build up and then if I need a particular unit type for a main mission or specific battle, I'm good to go. While I can recruit other party members and make specializations but there's no opportunity beyond limited and non-repeatable side missions to build side parties. And again, maybe this will change in the late game, but so far incentive to have a well balanced or party variety has seemed very limited.None of this has soured my experience with the game. It's been engaging, fun and breezy, with excellent art and music rounding out the package. Not perfect, but no game is and overall its a strong debut showing for Twin Otter. Hoping to see more in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute delight. It’s an indie and was made, astonishingly, by less than a dozen people. Despite this, it’s a very playable tactical RPG with some absolutely enjoyable surprises and details. The pixel art and music are wonderfully fresh. The gameplay is serviceable and tactically challenging. There’s a few rough edges here and there (some controls, camera movements, statuses) but the story is so engaging that you barely notice. I hardly touched the side quests and still enjoyed every minute of my 17 hour play-through. The story is dark – human and emotional – and is not to be missed. I know a LOT of people have tried to make a spiritual successor to FFT over the years, but this was the first one that even came close for me. I eagerly look forward to what this studio does next.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: I will most likely edit my review to be more in-depth when I play more the game/finish it but the short version is that Arcadian Atlas is clearly a passion project with a lot of soul. It might be the game that the TRPG with the most charm that I have played since the FFT franchise. From the story to the art style, animations and soundtrack the universe of Arcadia is really fascinating to see and you genuinely want to keep playing this game (which sounds dumb but is obviously a good thing).Now the game currently has a lot of very very very odd things missins or just bizarre decisions, the XP system feels like a demo placeholder, the menus are tedious to navigate both in and out of combat and so on but despite all of these flaws that would normally be fatal to me the game still manages to be enjoyable and the dev team has said they would patch the missing QoL so hopefully they improve upon that (though I have low expectations regarding menuing unfortunately).

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest issues so far-Battle mapI cannot zoom out /rotate it at all. its not fun to fight in this game when I (sometimes) have difficult time clicking on someone during a fight.and the hitting enter after every load screen makes me wanna burn it all downIf rotating is just not an option, zoom out would make it way better. Games fun just seems some QoL issues
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game, which is a shame. I've had this game on my wishlist for a very long time and FFT is one of my favorite games, so I was pretty excited for it. What the developer tried to do here is extremely ambitious, and I commend them for it, they just missed the mark.The writing and story are clunky. Nothing about them draws me in.The music is more smooth jazz than fantasy battle/political intrigue background music, and the mix is weirdly clean. It feels very computer generated, if that makes sense. The animations are all pretty bad. Movement animations don't seem to end when they are supposed to. Attack animations don't have a good hit keyframe and the timing of the hit sound and the damage counter feel off. Ranged attacks/items are slow, mismatched with the throw/shoot animations, and are lobbed waaayy too much.I'm also not a fan of the 2D dialog art, but if everything else was fixed, it wouldn't really bother me.Another annoyance is that at the start of each battle, there is no establishing shot of the objectives and the enemy locations, and there is extremely limited functionality to get an overview of the battlefield; all you can do is see two zoom levels. I find it difficult to see the whole picture and plan ahead without a better tool set here.Maybe if they hire a writer, a sound engineer, and an artist to redo the animations I'll consider this game again.I couldn't play it long enough to review the actual game mechanics and how they balance. Maybe after a few hours they would be interesting enough to keep me engaged despite the other flaws of this game, but due to the 2-hour playtime return window, I'm not willing to risk it. At least one other review already written speaks about this a bit, though, so I'm not optimistic.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: I'm 30 minutes into this game at the time of this review, so take this with a grain of salt.The graphics and music are top notch and are driving this so far.The interface so far to play the game is a bit janky and doesn't quiet behave as expected. In the tutorial, I also found myself picking a strategic starting position and ended up too far from the action so I just hit the move button a lot and the fight was over before I could even land a hit. This looks like it has potential, but the controls are a little rough so far and I just ended up clicking buttons and waiting for the NPCs to finish the first fight. I did nothing. All I've really done the first half hour is hit move and get annoyed setting my character to defend in the right direction; i wasn't attacked anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: I supported this game on Kickstarter.  I'll agree that it could have used a few more coats of paint on the UI with not being able to rotate the camera, and the related issues of not being able to click on a character if they're clumped together.  WASD and Enter is a work around for it, but it took me a while to realize that was an option.  That said, I like the FFT vibes with the character designs, the strangely chill jazz music (which you will either like or very much not depending on your own preferences), and most importantly: Poncho the Raccoon.  All media is improved by the inclusion of a raccoon. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Arcadian Atlas is what you get when someone played Final Fantasy Tactics and thought "I could do that" and understood nothing of why FFT is the GOAT in the genre. All those years on the wishlist wasted. Some of the below complaints could be fixed with some QOL patches but the core gameplay is lacking and that isn't changing. I would wait for this inevitably end up in some bundle. My SteamDeck lost internet somewhere in my playthrough so my tracked time is a bit higher than listed. Should be around 6 hours.Edit - Dev also doesn't understand how constructive criticism works. Avoid - Complaints after chapter 1 Why is FFT the gold standard? Very fun job system that is highly customizable, an orchestral masterpiece for an OST, visually pretty good looking and the cherry on top telling an above average story. The fanhacks rebalancing/tweaking have taken it above and beyond throughout the years. This game has nothing going for it except the sprite work is very good. Before anyone comments this is 100% inspired by FFT. Chapter 1 has the same setup: Tutorial battle in the present timeline you can't lose, go back to the past and see how it started, ends with a similar bridge blow up vibe then skips to the present. The "job" ability equip screen is the same, post battle rewards the same and just all around looks similar.

_childDocuments_.review: Short review: I would play this if it was a visual novel.Pros:-The music. I loved smooth-jazzy feel combined with the story/setting. It felt fresh and somehow not out of place.-The story (of what I saw) was interesting and the characters mixed well together.-Visually impressive settings and the characters looked good, although some from behind looked like they were permanently squatting or bending their knees in a weird way. The portraits are fantastic.Cons:(Note: I was not expecting this game to be FFT or anything else besides what I saw. I'm not even a big TRPG enjoyer usually so I'm really giving critiques based on the game and not any pre-existing expectations)-The game feels hollow as it is right now combat-wise. Most fights feel solvable by "have everyone be ranged".-I was excited for the specializations within classes, which I think is a fantastic idea, but they are extremely shallow.-Evasion system seems pointless, I don't think either I or the enemy ever missed hitting from the front and with increased evasion. Even if the system gets fixed, enemies will still face backwards when my whole party was behind them.-From what I could tell, obstacles didn't matter, I could both hit and be hit even I hid behind something.-Movement is slow.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with a lot of promise that didn't feel ready for full release. The first update fixed a lot of my concerns, but the UI is still pretty stubborn, its easy to send yourself to the title screen from battle, the one song that plays in most battles gets old quickly, and as others have said the height for jumps and attacks is pretty bonkers. _childDocuments_.review: I remember seeing this game being developed a long time ago, and I added it to my wish list. I was very excited to see it was officially released and I purchased it right away; particularly because I love Final Fantasy Tactics and am always trying to find games that expand on that style. I am very disappointed by the hour that I did play; this game could stand a large amount of QoL updates. If you are using a gamepad, you must click for every square you want to move, you cannot simply hold the direction down in order to speed it up; there is also some input lag when you try to do anything. If you try to inspect a unit, you can see all of the information on them, but you cannot activate a help tooltip to explain some of the information, and you also cannot look to see what specific skills that unit has(during battle). The viewpoint is fixed and the devs have made some translucency to obstacles to compensate, but it isn't enough to make it easier to see the battlefield. The level of zoom on the battlefield is not the greatest, you cannot zoom out to see most of the battlefield, you have only close and medium distance. The world map does not have a zoom at all, so you need to screen scroll around it and it feels very tunnel like when you do that, a zoom out function would have been fantastic.After each battle, all units that participated gain 1 level and 1 skill point. That's it. I did not recruit any new units to see what level they start at, but if they start at 1..that's a lot of battles to get them caught up to other units. I believe it said you need 18 skill points in a class to promote it; so that's a lot of grind for levels and skill points.In order to load to a new menu/area/screen there is a loading screen, that you need to hit start/play/menu on your controller in order to continue on...which I kept forgetting about and would sit there for a few minutes.It costs the in game currency to change an existing unit's name...which seems unnecessary.The class system leaves much to be desired; there are 4 main classes that can be promoted to 2 advanced classes for each main class. The classes also offer a tree functionality for some variety, however there is no dual class system in order to create unique builds. The trees don't lock you into them, which is nice, at the same time I would have liked to see more growth opportunities if you did focus on a specific tree or something. Once you promote a class, that's it.I overall like the aesthetics, at the same time I don't find the character portraits to be that appealing, a few of the characters portraits look like "One-eyed Jacks". I did enjoy that I could tell when sprites are doing shifty eyes. I felt like the music didn't fit the overall style of the game. There was a lot of sultry saxophone that didn't need to be there. I'm dating myself with this comment, but it felt like I was watching only the melodramatic moments from the Lethal Weapon series back to back. Overall the game has a lot of great potential and I hope it reaches it, but for now I am disappointed in my purchase and wish I had waited for it to iron things out.

_childDocuments_.review: One look at Arcadian Atlas(AA) and you can see the clear resemblance to the inspiration it wears on its sleeves. Final Fantasy Tactics(FFT). As someone who loves FFT, hearing about an indie RPG attempting to reach similar heights as that one caught my eye. And I’ve been watching their development closely. However, I should preface this, I won’t make any comparisons to the FFT, since I feel not everyone has played the title. So I’ll try and judge the game for what it is rather than what it aspires to.First, I believe developers find difficulty, to create a title where you have a clear inspiration while not retreading familiar ground. For better or worse, other titles walk the road most traveled too closely while some merely use it as a base and go off in their direction. AA I think takes the middle ground while striving to develop their own identity in a low fantasy medieval story in homage to the classics of old, especially from Yasumi Matsuno’s works.You control two protagonists Vashti and Desmond. Two lovers caught up in a civil war that threatens to shake the very foundation of the continent. I found the story to be mature, holding nothing back during the war and hitting nuances I don’t see that often regarding choices, emotions, duty, and more. Lore-wise. The added compendium is appreciative of giving background on the world, important characters, and events. Where the writing delves into a nice balance between seriousness with humor at times to lessen the gravity of affairs here. It is well placed. These strengths splinter down to the cast which I’m surprised to see how small they’re, but allow our cast both main and villains to shine. The protagonists are not overpowered at all or hateable from the get-go. There is careful precision to keep them within the realm of believability without sending me into a volcano of overriding my suspension of disbelief.A good amount of class variety here being 12 different classes and all of them have multiple skill trees to specialize in. I was able to have a raccoon archer, ronin, sorcerer, inquisitor, and shaman available. Each had their strengths and weaknesses, but for the most part, they all felt strong enough to tide me over against my enemies. The gameplay starts with some mandatory battles early on before granting you the ability to move around the world map and accept contracts. Think of these like sidequests for money and gear rewards. There is even an exclusive side quest chain here I found to be amusing so I recommend players finish these off if they require money or seek the unique side quest chain. Decent tunes to go along as you combat your way through various maps. The sax in particular I didn’t get tired of hearing. And considering how short the game is. Well to be fair, not too short. I was able to complete the game within 11 to 13 hours. Which I feel is just right for the length. Didn’t want to go through 40+ hour campaigns where the pace moves at a snail’s pace. Here the pace was quick and didn’t take long to reach the heart of the matter for plot beats. Didn’t experience any bugs or crashes either. This helps tremendously since battles can be completed within ten minutes on average. At least on normal difficulty.I did have some mixed feelings here. Not a positive or a negative, but for the sake of transparency I'll note them down. I wish the compendium would be updated periodically to show new changes to a character's background. This would grant more importance to the compendium while adding context when needed. Not much room to experiment with classes due to how experience is calculated. Bit un-traditional, which I like. But here every time you finish a battle you gain a level that coincidentally grants you skill points to allocate. I like the removal of grinding, although this doesn’t allow much room to go out of my way to go beyond the base and advanced classes and experiment since there are no repeated filler battles to test them out. Sure I could use contracts, but those are limited within each chapter. Could’ve used more objectives besides defeating all units. There are more than a handful of uncommon ones here: Travel to this tile, escort, etc. Though these are few and far between the regular. Some spice would’ve been nice to goals here to not make objectives too repetitive back to eliminating every foe. Also, I think some more flashbacks to the villain would’ve been welcome as a more show/don’t tell approach to flesh them out more and perhaps to a lesser extent our protagonists. Lastly, I believe contracts could be made more interesting beyond killing everyone. Grant us rare units instead of filler ones, give us more side quest chains, expand on the world with lore/characters, etc. I could say more, but those are minor nitpicks not worth mentioning and the developers of Twin Otter are already working hard to fix them in hot fixes and patches.Overall, Arcadian Atlas displays a serviceable amount of gameplay and classes. Delving into interesting scenes during the civil war without holding your hand throughout. All while delivering a bug-free (at least for me) and crash-free experience that doesn’t seek long hours to complete. I can’t help but appreciate the close attempt to conceive their take from looking up to FFT. And for that, I respect it and look forward to the future when this title is cleaned up of some imperfections. I admire the attempt to construct their own game while balancing enough nostalgia to design their own identity. A long seven-year development cycle with a Kickstarter budget. With only 4 members on the team to develop, only deserve praise in my eyes. Is a good indie Jrpg I recommend for those testing the waters for indies and Jrpg’s alike.7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Few hours in (7?) and having a good time. Really enjoy the music, the art, and skill systems. While it isn't jam packed full of a billion classes or go up through hundreds of levels for your characters - I've really been enjoying playing through the story and progressing the character skills between each battle. Also you get a raccoon with a shiv in your party which rules.Recommended to anyone that wants to feel like its 1997 again and you're exploring your first tactics game again. The vibes are right despite what limitations exist from a team size and budget. Worth checking out.UPDATE 8/25Ended up wrapping the campaign after 22 hours or so. Played through on stream and both my community and I loved so much about it. Everything that I enjoyed at the start of the game (music, art, and variety of skills) remained strong all the way to the end. The story itself get really intense on the third act and left me wanting to spend more time with them and the world. As much as I love a concise story, at the same time a good story always leaves me wanting more and this did that. Characters were all strongly written (for better or worse). For everything that's here it's absolutely worth your time. If you're looking for endlessly playable tactics game ala Disgaea series this isn't that though. Only two criticisms I could really lay at it's feet is I wish there was more battle music, as the most common one you end up hearing for probably half of your time with the game. Another 2-3 that rotated or changed up when you switched chapters would been a great way to keep this wonderful music special (think Trisection vs Apoplexy from FFT). The second criticism is wishing the mouse controls were more precise. Often I'd had to jump back to WASD controls to get a specific block to target, especially when dealing with various heights.Overall though, really fun experience and it's reinvigorated my desire to play more tactics RPGS. I haven't played any in about a decade now (Tactics Ogre: LUCT on PSP last) and I think I'll start by revisiting FF Tactics Advance.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: This is not Final Fantasy Tactics but you might as well enjoy it.Graphics: This is no triple A production but the pixel art is really good. Some movements might lack a more appealing animation, but I specially like the all map spells. My kudos to the Art Director.Music and sound: A lot of people have been complaining about the soundtrack, but I really liked it. The game story is pretty noir so I think it actually fits the theme pretty well. I think SFX also are quite good.Story: This probably has been the aspect I liked the most. A pretty original story inspired in some of the inspirational games to this one. I felt some parts of the story could have further development, specially towards the end of the game, but I really got engaged.Gameplay: The battle system is nice, not super complex but challenging enough. Targeting with the mouse sometimes can be straining, but can be fixed if you help yourself with the keyboard. The contract system delivers some interesting sidequests too. A lot of people complain that ranged combat is op (it usually is in this genre) but I felt that the thing that was most unbalanced was probably speed. Another thing that may need a rework is the levelling system, as the number of battles is limited, and your reserve rooster doesn't level up.All in all, I recommend this game, despite the price being a bit high for an indie project.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Straight to the point, I did a let's play of the first 45 minutes here: I think the reviews here all have valid points, but most of all I'd emphasize that this is a highly entertaining game! The story has tons of depth, and so does the combat. I got excited when I started my first group combat. There are so many options and so many ways to progress the battles. The tutorial did actually confuse me a bit, but probably just because it covered so much so quickly and parts of it seemed to need a little more scrutiny. I enjoyed the experience though and the controls are pretty good once you get them down. (Right click on your unit for action menu, first move, then attack, then wait.), If you want to explore an interesting story, but don't mind being patient with a few of the games quirks, I think it's alright. I hope that this game finds its proper place in the rank of RPGs, which is quite good in my opinion. One last thing: this is a mature game and uses mature language occasionally, but all I encountered was more like a few villains say things that are a bit sweary. Didn't bother me, but I understand if it bothers you. Anyway, that's it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, and if you like tactic games and a good story you should play it!But I also wish this was a better game.My two main issues are the user interface and the game mechanics. The user interface just feels janky, everywhere. It always takes a short moment to respond, and it is full of annoying little things. For example, you cannot go to the end of a list (shop inventory, unit abilities, etc) by pressing up at the top of the list - you always have to go through the entire list. Another example is that keeping a button pressed does not repeat the input. If you want to go to the right side of the map, you cannot just press 'right' on the gamepad and keep that pressed - you have to press it repeatedly, until you reach where you want to go.The UI is full of stuff like this. It's not terrible, but it's annoying.My second issue is that the game mechanics are just not very deep. For example, spaces on the map have different height levels, but that is almost completely cosmetic. Here and there, the height difference between two adjacent spaces is too big for a unit to jump up, but usually you can easily go around. Apart from movement, height differences have zero effect, neither for ranged attacks, nor melee, nor anything else.Positioning of unity relative to each other also almost does not matter. Units can evade attacks, and a unit that is attacked from the side or behind has a slightly lower chance to evade, but otherwise it does not matter in which direction your units point.Also, there are zero mechanical surprises. No unique units with special abilities that you could recruit, or new classes that are not available at the beginning, or similar things. Essentially, after you played the first couple of missions, you have seen everything the game has to offer, mechanics-wise.Finally, but that is a smaller issue, I felt the writing got a bit weaker in the final (third) chapter of the game. It is not always entirely clear why things are happening. It does not get confusing, but some events at the end lose some impact because they feel a bit random or out of nowhere.That was a lot of negative things about a game I liked, so again - I do recommend it. Just be aware that it might not be quite as good as you might expect.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get this out of the way first: this game is not FFT. Is it inspired by it? Clearly. But there are a lot of criticisms I've seen leveled at this game saying that it isn't enough like that game or is not enough of a spiritual successor to FFT. It's its own thing though and is not made by people with anything to do with the making of FFT. If you want FFT, go play FFT or one of its sequels. If you want to play a different game that wears some of that inspiration on its sleeve, then let's get into it.First, this game has gorgeous pixel art. The design choice is for a 2D isometric perspective, so do not expect the maps to be rotatable - that's just not how the art was designed. This can cause some slight irritation for those used to a more 3D rendered art-style and map format, but it works well enough - especially when you get a few battles under your belt. Sometimes this requires using the keyboard instead of the mouse, but I think it's worth it for the essentially hand-crafted assets. The animation on the sprites is very, very good, especially during cut-scenes. Characters move like they should and facial expression animation is able to convey a surprising amount of motivation and detail. Top notch.Fights are fun. Elevation and positioning matter, as one would expect from a S/TRPG. Status effects can either buff or debuff characters in several expected ways. Maps are a manageable size. Small squads go in, accomplish an objective (usually defeat all enemies, but with a bit of variability I've seen already in the format), rewards are collected and the story moves forward. There are no random battles and there is no real grinding. There are optional side battles that gain you rewards and levels, but nothing I would call a grind. Characters level up after each deployment (story characters level up regardless of being on a deployment or not). Nice and easy. It feels like a game that respects your time. I might like to see some tweaking done by the dev team about damage numbers that units put out, but it's a fairly minor gripe for me.Level progression works in a somewhat simplified way, but I still find it pretty satisfying. The skill trees fill up pretty quick, make a notable impact, and again, just kind of respect your time (if that makes sense?). Characters may seem like they have somewhat less to do than in other games in this format (they get one set of skills and can't dip into other classes), but it's easy enough to hot swap characters from the Recruiter to try something else.I would love it if the game auto-prompted to Save after battles. Some of the UI could be tidied up. But overall, I really like this game. I like the responsiveness of the dev team. I also like that the dev team is only 4 people: it's a real labor of love and it shows. I like the story. I love the art and creative direction. The jazzy soundtrack is growing on me (it seemed a bit incongruous to me at first). I do wish there was another battle song though.I recommend this game. It is a solid entry in a newly crowded S/TRPG space. Just know what you are getting: is it FFT? Nope, but I don't really want it to be either. I want these people to make THEIR game and I am happy they did.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Strategy RPGS, this should be right up your street. It's not perfect, and a lot of the story and class upgrades leave a fair amount to be desired. But both are still good starting points in a game that left me hopeful for the future. The gameplay is fun, and could be challenging sometime, though mostly I felt it was pretty easy fare. Still, a pretty good time. Though short if you're not going to replay. I played on Steamdeck and it worked pretty good there. The time is messed up though, I beat it in roughly 6-7 hours, not 4.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: I first played FFT when I was 8 years old, i'm 33 now.I have a deep love of the game, and alot of respect for  Yasumi Matsuno, the team responsible for the game, and especially Akihiko Yoshida's amazing Art.Is Arcadian Atlas FFT? No.What it is, is a fun experience for someone who wants a game of a similar nature.If this game would have come out right after FFT when I was a kid, I would have been Jazzed (excited).The art is good, and I think the story line has alot to offer. Especially if us, (now spoiled adults), take into consideration these games could catch the attention of a young person and set them on a love of fantasy style RPG's for the rest of their lives.I liked Arcadian Atlas, I suggest it.If you want an almost exact FFT experience, play Ogre Tactics.So thanks to the developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure why this game has such mixed reviews. Sure, it's a little cutscene-heavy, but it's a fun little battle strategy game with cool characters, nice graphics, and fun music. Perfect for when you want a game with combat but without a ton of stress. If you're a fan of D&D, I particularly recommend this, the combat is set up very similarly.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: After so many years, where most of it was simply siilence, then suddenly more news dropped on progress of this game, it feels like it was rushed, just to get it done. I'm writing a review based on the first few minutes on this game for one reason: I don't want more people to waste time on this game than necessary. It would have been better to waste no time at all from creatives, devs and players alike and consider it a failed project. The music is such an immersion breaker. A saxophone in a fantasy kinda medieval world? I love the saxophone, but only in the right context, when it comes to games. Maybe for one special character it might have worked, but in this game's setting to have it play in nearly every track is a no-go. In general, some of these tracks would fit a noir detective game far better.Character portraits feel off. Everything is retro pixel art style, but the portraits are not. It's like you're having two different art design philosophies clashing together.Another flaw: Since I couldn't stand the music, I wanted to get into action and see, how it plays. Funny enough: skipping the first scenes leads to skipping the opportunity for playing the tutorial. I've never seen that in a game and it feels like an oversight, that could be easily fixed by e.g. having the tutorial run along with the first fight.Placing my units without knowing, where my enemies are is not making sense. Specifically, if they start the encounter, I should be able to see where those characters are so I can position them either more to the left, right or center.I saw an AI character walk through an enemy unit, which after checking FFT Advanced was even considered a no-no. and you had to walk around the enemy. If I can simply march my way to specific characters without malus (e.g. losing on movement), what tactics are there to follow?After the first fight, there are more characters seemingly dead on my end in the following cutscene, although none of them died during this fight. ... How? ... Why? No explanation.Controls feel unintuitive. Why not using middle mouse click for moving around? Why do I need to open the radial menu first, if the game already switches / moves to the playable character anyways? Also, settting the directions at the end of the round isn't always working, for which I have no explanation. If my mouse cursor leans towards one direction, I expect the character to face that direction. I don't want to move my mouse around the character first and to identify, when the direction may lock in.I knew why I stopped putting a huge chunk of money into Kickstarter games. Just the bare minimum to get the game and that's it. Most of the time, even that little money was wasted. This here is an example of "most of the times".
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions with this game are pretty positive! The setting doesn't seem huge/sprawling, but is well developed (you get a good sense of what kind of world it is fairly quickly). The dialogue is well done, characterisation is well established, and the characters themselves are interesting. The pacing is also good in the first act; it doesn't drag, but it doesn't rush you from plot point to plot point. It takes time to develop the characters.The pixel art is expressive and fantastic, and the music is an interesting choice (smooth jazz, pretty unique for this kind of game). I like it! The combat is well done as well! It doesn't have the same polish as a big-team or big-budget title, but the visual design is great, attack animations are satisfying, and the gameplay has a good balance of strategy and difficulty (with difficulty sliders if you want them).All in all, I'm enjoying my time with it. It's fun and satisfying to start, and if the developer continues to polish it up, even better.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this game on Kickstarter, and I am very pleased with the final product! It really captures the feel of the original Final Fantasy Tactics. The music's great, the art's lovely, everything works like you think it should. If you've never played the original FFT, you may not be used to the slower pace of combat that this game will introduce you to, but give it a shot. I think you'll have a great time.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: So I backed this product on kickstarter a very, very long time ago and only a few minutes of play showed me how poorly polished the gameplay and visuals are. The kickstarter campaign itself was handled badly, with poor communication, extremely sparse updateds and no word on physical rewards. And maybe if the game felt polished and looked good I would be able to let that go, but this game took 5 more years than they promised and it really does not have too much to show for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Game looks great, runs great and the music is an absolute vibe. Pretty much the holy trio that every game should have. My advice would be to try the game yourself and not follow the negative reviews. i dont usually review stuff but this game is mixed for no reason. I'm 2 hours in and its still going strong and im loving the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting years for this and I am not disappointed.  First - if you are looking to play Final Fantasy Tactics, go play that. This is not FFT, despite having strong vibes and familiar looking systems.People looking for a Job System will not find it. Classes have skill trees and specialisations. It works very well. I didn't encounter any glitches, bugs or crashes in my first 5 hours of playing. So that is a very good start. I imagine we can expect to see a bit of QoL improvements - but once I understood I could select characters (Target and move) with the keyboard rather than fiddling with the mouse, it became a much better experience. This is a wonderful game. It is fun, the class system is rewarding, and the story is interesting. I look forward to seeing if this game is expanded on in the future. Well done to the team.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I've played an indie tactic RPG, and I've gotta say it left a great impression. While the game isn't without flaws, I enjoyed it from start to finish. The writing is really the strong point in Arcadian Atlas. There were surprising twists as well as plot developments I may have guessed at but played out in ways I didn't expect. The ending brought me to tears, and I always have respect when a story can tug on my heartstrings that well. Despite it being a fairly short game (Steam says 21 hours for me but my save file says 17), I really felt connected to the main protagonists and their story, as well as the goings-on in the political sphere. The soundtrack is very pleasant to listen to, but I'd have liked to see more variation in the tunes especially in Chapter 1. I do think it gets better as the game goes and as the stakes get higher. Gameplay is also great. A variety of classes and skill trees really let you build your party however you like. I was surprised to see that consumable items weren't in the game, but I appreciated the level of challenge that (and limited revives) brought to the battles. I played on the normal mode and found the difficulty very satisfying with some very intense fights. There is one gameplay bug I discovered, though; the sorcerer skill Blood Sacrifice claims to reduce the user's HP to 1, but that didn't ever happen when I used it, making it a quite OP skill.This game has pretty mixed reviews but IMO it was a pretty solid experience and I'd recommend it to anyone who would enjoy playing a short tactical RPG.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: At first it seems a basic RPG developed by a very small indie company with a lot of small issue, as you progress, you can clearly see that the game is just a watered version of what you see in the first 2 hours + some fancy bugs that make you lose a lot of time.Honestly, it needs to be both polished and get some rethink on various aspect of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Outstanding tribute/homage to Final Fantasy Tactics but with its own spin on some things.Excellent story thus far I am in chapter 2.  Battles are challenging enough with things like elemental bonuses added in the mix which were not part of FFT.  The soundtrack is incredible!  I can already see the replay value due to the depth of classes to promote to.  Has been very fun customizing my party so far with tons of possible valid combinations.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to write this as a kickstarter backer. I can see a lot of love was put into some parts of this game. But life is too short to spend many hours on things that aren't fun, engaging, or enriching in some way. This game has a host of problems:* Every single battle can be won with the simple strategy of having multiple of your units gang up on one enemy unit, kill them, and repeat. Enemy AI is very dumb, and sometimes not even aggressive. I have seen support units run around in circles healing themselves instead of attacking while I took apart all of their friends. * Other reviewers have noted how simple the class system is compared to other games of this genre. They're right, but there's more - the lack of options acts as a band-aid over how pointless many of the class options really are. Most base classes have two or three moves that you'll use a lot, and the rest of your skill points are just filler.  The advanced classes are just as bad, with the additional problem that once a unit is promoted to an advanced class you can no longer spend points on their base even if there's nothing useful in the advanced tree anymore.* Most battles only let you bring 5 units, and up to 4 of those will be plot-characters. No fights are repeatable, so those 5 units are the only ones you will ever need. * You can respec the human main characters - Desmond, Vashti, and Eda - but not the raccoon, Poncho, or any other unit. So if anyone falls behind in level or their build isn't working out, it's simpler to recruit a new character at the same level as your mains than to keep using the old characters. * Aside from accessories, all equipment is just slightly higher numbers than the equipment you had before. Money should never be an issue - by my endgame, I had over 200,000A left over. So upgrading gear just feels like a chore instead of something you have to think about strategically as part of a build or as an economic challenge. * The first two chapters are about a war in which friends, family, and lovers are fighting on opposite sides - a great premise for a grand drama. There's a decent bit of lore and character-building, but you never learn that much about the characters' histories or motivations - there's more in the in-game compendium than is ever shown in the game proper. Then Chapter 3 rolls around, the war becomes irrelevant, and it's not even clear what any of the characters are trying to achieve anymore. They're still fighting each other, but no one ever stops to articulate *why*. * I will give some praise at least - the game's music is very good. I wouldn't have expected a saxophone to work that will in a tactical battle, but it does. Also, the spritework is exceptionally expressive.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful, the music is charming.The game is not hard, the strategy very limited ( just used ligthning and water all the way till the end ) but at least it was enternaining.Some quality of life can be added.But the real problem about this game is the story. From strat to finish we have NO IDEA whatever is going on. Like nothing is explain to us, it is very hard to understand when or where or just what happens. The game want us to feel sorry or sad sometimes but it just doesn't work because we don't undersand what's going on. I'm very sorry but i cannot recommand this game because there is just better games out there even if i wanted to like it.Next time, maybe don't let the writer of your story do this alone. We are not in the head of the caracters or the writer if you don't explain us what is going on we can't possibly understand.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Spoiler Free Review from someone who completed it After beating the game I would give it a wait for sale. Story Started strong but went off the rails not fully explaining key plot devices. The character bios started strong but fell flat not updating or adding new characters. The game failed to fully explain the plot and focused more on the dynamics between certain characters without fully fleshing them out. While it did manage to tell a story, in the end it felt like a convoluted rush from the story we were expecting. Game PlayIt tries to come off as diverse and immersive but ends up coming off as bland and straight forward. Since your active characters level after every battle instead of during battles, the fighting is limited and you either end up being stronger than the encounters on par or you send in units too weak to survive. BattlesEnemy AI try to focus down one unit at a time. Because of the way healers are with only one rez per battle, no healing items, and how fast characters perma-die, You don't need to worry about losing units during battle except the main story ones. Outside of using on average 5 units, the others will fall behind so the best option is to focus on the Hero units, dismiss weaker units and rehire them at the correct levels. The difficulty is determinant on how well you manage the healing and how many rezes you bring, The battles boil down to who can blitz the others units down the fastest. Job design The jobs have 2 paths but all end up being hybrids. Most of the paths are lack luster with menial percentages and underwhelming abilities. Example Outside of Inquisitor silence which also hits hard, most of the other skills are too low to risk using versus an ability you know will get an enemy unit off the board, so you will favor basic attacks and hard hitting skills you invested in.     Final ThoughtsThe Game feels ambitious until you delve in deeper and realize so many things go off the rails. Out of the current 3 TRPGs that released Crimson Saga, Cross Tails and Arcadian Atlas, Arcadian Atlas is the weakest of the three. this game like those would have done well with a Demo or Early Access feedback phase to address the bare bones QoL, flawed design issues and weak story that will make this another forgettable "Failed Final Fantasy Tactics Successor".
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: good story enjoyable game. thew game is more like a shell of a game rather then a completed game. it has some major things missing. no consumable items no ability to multi train several classes on one character making you stuck with only one real option for each character. there is no special classes to recruit and every character generic recruit and hero are all the same strength no reason to even use the main characters. there is not a way to level up characters out side of the ones you use in battle if you skip a battle with a character it will forever be 1 level behind the rest of your team. there is no way i can find to recruit monsters. you get special currency but the option are of no value. you get so much money that money has no meaning you will never have to chose what to buy because you have so much you can just fully upgrade everything and still have several hundred thousand left. the game is worth a play threw but has no replay value
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review: Only a couple hours in but so far this game has made a pretty good impression on me. Combat feels good and is easy to understand. While you're not going to dance around a job system like FFT, the skill trees apportioned to each class feel pretty robust and encourage you to try different combinations. You can have two cavaliers in a party that feel very different from one another in just a few battles. I'm not too far along in the story, but so far I like where it's going. There's some intrigue building up along with some ethical questions proposed. Each of the players on the board doesn't seem to be morally black or white at all times, and you sort of wonder which way they may go on things. Music kicks ass. Oddly enough, it reminds me of ODST with the jazz feel, albeit with a little more spring in its step and a little less somber. Still, absolutely love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcadian Atlas

_childDocuments_.review:
Watch your back in the world of Arcadia, where a kingdom is tearing itself apart and forces more dark and ancient than the soil are about to awaken. Experience deep tactical battles across vast and treacherous landscapes as you build an army of powerful troops, customizing their classes and skills to gain every advantage against monsters, ruthless men, a daughter scorned, and a queen so cruel she'd kill her own husband to gain the throne.

Play as two lovers brought together by war and torn between the queen they've sworn fealty to and the charismatic illegitimate daughter who's risen up to take back a throne denied hercivil war threatening to engulf the destitute and desperate as battle lines are drawn and swords unsheathed.

And amidst it all, a young girl caged behind castle walls her entire life stumbles upon the Atlas, a power she cannot hope to contain. With the help of a roguish magician she'll uncover the forces that built the world, but can she control them? Or will they engulf her and the very world you're trying to save.

name: Zombie Army 4: Dead War
detailed_description: Season Pass One Is Now Free Zombie Army 4 Season Pass One is now FREE!* Sink your teeth into a whole season of content, including: 3 ADDITIONAL LEVELS Experience blood-curdling new campaign missions for 1-4 players. 4 CHARACTER PACKS New playable characters to be used in any mode. 9 WEAPON BUNDLES Weapon bundles including new weapons, charms, skins and more. 5 WEAPON SKIN PACKS Customise your weapons, with effects ranging from wrapping paper to hot lava. 4 CHARACTER OUTFIT BUNDLES Dress up your characters with new outfits and hats. *Requires Zombie Army 4: Dead War base game About the Game Hitler’s hordes are back for more in this spine-chilling shooter from the makers of Sniper Elite 4! Abominable occult enemies, epic weapons and a harrowing new campaign for 1-4 players await in 1940s Europe, as you fight to save humankind from undead Armageddon! Shocking New Campaign The resistance have defeated Zombie Hitler and cast him into Hell – but the dead rise once again with greater hunger than before! Continue the alternate history of Zombie Army Trilogy in huge new levels, and uncover a sinister plan that takes the Survivor Brigade across Italy and beyond! Fight the forces of darkness in corpse-riddled canals, survive a Zombie Zoo, and journey to dark, inexplicable places no person has been before…and lived to tell the tale! Award-Winning Gunplay Experience the genre-defining ballistics Rebellion made famous in the Sniper Elite series, and put it to good use against the shambling hordes of the damned! Upgraded Kill Cams and Dismemberment The X-Ray Kill Camera returns! Watch in gory-ous slow motion as bullets, bombs and more destroy bones and organs in X-ray. Marvel as your bullets tear off a rotten limb or two, and shiver as the dead KEEP COMING! Deep Progression and Customisation Build the slayer that suits you as you rank up! Fancy yourself a guardian angel? Take damage for your teammates! Like that turret so much? Why not take it with you? Then kill in style as you unlock new outfits, emotes and taunts! Killer Melee When the dead surround you, fight back with enhanced melee combat! Barge through crowds, stomp on heads and dispatch the living dead with fearsome takedown moves! Epic Weaponry Harness the power of fire, lightning, and divine essence to upgrade your guns at workbenches, and create homespun hell raisers! An assault rifle that shoots lightning? A pistol with a flaming Bayonet? Anything goes in humankind’s last stand! Monstrous Multitudes Take on legions of ghoulish grabbers, hulking armoured elites, terrifying shadow demons, explosive suicide generals and a host of other surprises! When you’re staring down the fleshy barrel of a ZOMBIE TANK, you’ll wish you’d stayed behind the sofa! Bigger, Badder Horde Mode Extend your SLAYcation in the expanded Horde Mode. The longer you survive, the bigger the map gets. How long can you fight back without joining the horde of the LIVING DEAD? Extend Your Slay-Cation! Want more? Additional seasons of Zombie Army 4 are out now! Unveil the secrets of the occult in the new 3-part ‘Hell Cult’ campaign and face off against the terror of the skies in the horrifying ‘Death From Above’! From extra missions to new characters, weapons and more, get ready to blow apart your undead foes in new and terrifying ways!

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: As of March 2022, the Season 1 pass is free, so you can feel free to keep that in mind.Despite giving this game a thumbs down, I actually recommend playing it. My thumbs down is simply to highlight and grab attention at what is a growing trend in scummy business practices by game developers and publishers.Zombie Army 4 is a pretty great game as far graphics, game play and technical merits is concerned. The problem is the downright, ridiculous way that Rebellion has decided to price this game. Let's put aside the one year exclusivity deal with Epic because developers need to take the best deal they can get to maximize returns on development, so as much as I dislike Epic, I can't fault Rebellion for wanting to make the most money they could. That is how all businesses operate and it is what it is. The major problem is the absolute nickel and dime pricing structure they've come up with. You can't simply buy the base game and have an equal experience to the previous Zombie Army games. Buying the base game gets you the base campaign, four characters and three guns for each weapons category. THREE!!!! This means you have three rifles to choose from, three secondary weapons (Technically, there are four secondary weapons, but the Thompson and STG are so similar feeling, I have a hard time counting them as two weapons) and three pistols for a total of nine weapons. In a game that was an offshoot of the SNIPER series, you know, a game where you SNIPE enemies with rifles and get to see awesome kills, you get a whopping THREE rifles to choose from! Unless, of course, you buy the Super Deluxe edition or you bought the base game and later on, shell out $35 dollars for one or both of the season passes ($70 for both). Or... you can buy guns individually for a few bucks a piece... And that's just the start of it, individual characters, clothing packs, weapons skins and levels can all be purchased by themselves. Seriously, go and look at the DLC options for this game and it will make your head spin. I have no problem with developers selling a season pass or DLC that's actually worth something, but breaking up all of this content to such a ridiculous degree is the most asinine thing I have ever seen! This game looks like it's trying to rival something like Fortnite with the amount of crap they want you to buy. Again, DLC is fine, season passes that make sense are fine, but this was just the messiest and most headache-inducing way to release content. It makes me angry that they would go and do this. It makes me feel like Rebellion thinks their fans are dumb and are just going to gobble up any garbage they throw out. I bought the base game at a discount price on Greenman Gaming and I didn't mind spending that, but it's unfortunate that I won't be able to experience the other levels or even the guns, for that matter, until I see a major sale. In the end, this lack of content in the base game leads to boredom much faster than it otherwise would. It gets VERY repetitive only having three rifles to choose from. In the previous games, I'd usually play for a level with one rifle and then switch it up on the next. Well, if you like doing that, after three levels, you've experienced all of the rifles there are. And that goes for the secondary weapons, too. You get three... and then you're back to repeating them again. This lack of variety turns, what should be a very fun game, into a rather dull drag. Unless, of course, you want to shell out an extra $70+ dollars or Lord knows how much for all of the additional micro-transaction garbage.Difficulty balance is also an issue in the harder modes, at least for single player, which I enjoy. I beat the game on normal, which was fine, as you'd expect. I decided to go back through again on the hardest difficulty (Brutal). Despite having my rifles upgraded all of the way in damage and most other attributes, basic zombies can, sometimes, take 3-4 headshots to die. That is pretty ridiculous. You'll often find yourself running out of ammo because zombies won't die from even several headshots and you're left running around trying to scavenge what little ammo zombies might drop (it isn't much) or looking for an ammo box which aren't always placed where you need them. This is a minor nitpick, of course, because the hardest difficulty is meant to be hard! But, I think it's a little silly that I can put 3-4 bullets straight into a normal zombie's forehead and they just keep shuffling toward me and scratching my health away. What's the point in maxing out gun attributes when it doesn't really help? It's actually a weird choice in balance. When you max out guns and you're playing on 'normal' difficulty, you can steamroll right over almost anything. But, play the game on 'Brutal' and it's like your guns are useless. At least, as far as the guns in the base edition are concerned. With all that said, this is still a very fun game. The visuals look terrific. It runs very smoothly for me. I only experienced a couple of crashes and it was at the same point in the game with DX12. I switched to Vulcan and was able to proceed just fine and later, switched back to DX12 with no further problems. The base campaign is quite lengthy. That is one area I will give it to Rebellion. There are a lot of levels and areas to fight through, so big A+ in that respect. If you're a fan of the series, you'll still enjoy the experience, especially if playing with friends. However, the lack of guns in the base game is so slimy in my opinion, especially in a game that's focused on shooting things. If you want to sell additional levels, skins or a few special weapons, I'd see no problem with that, but locking the bulk of guns that fans have had access to in all of the previous games behind additional paywalls was just an awful decision. Let me be clear, offering a ton of worthy DLC wouldn't have been offensive, but locking basic weapons behind season passes or a ton of little micro-transactions is the big issue here. The base game gets a 7/10 from me. The story was good enough for this type of game and the Zombie Army lore, the visuals are fantastic, the controls and mechanics feel so satisfying and 99% of the time, it ran like a dream. I'm running an 8700k and a 1080ti and I ran the entire game at native 4k with everything turned all of the way up, except I leave AA off. The game rarely dipped below 100fps for me. Absolutely a joy in optimization as far as I'm concerned. If they had just given access to all of the normal weapons which should have been included, my score would've definitely been higher. I give Rebellion's pricing structure and business practices a generous 2/10. If they do this in their future zombie titles, I'll be skipping them all together or looking for other ways to play them.Please see my edit - EDIT: Let me just add this to my review as well since I'm just now realizing this. Steam/Rebellion doesn't really make it super-clear what content comes with what edition as well as the season passes. If you are a person who wants all of the content. You can get it by purchasing the Super Deluxe Edition along with Season Pass 2. That will give you, essentially everything. However, if you view all of the additional content and choose the "Add all DLC to cart" at the bottom, Steam will allow you to purchase it all which works out to over $200. You will be purchasing the Super Deluxe Edition, both season passes as well as all of the individual micro-transaction garbage. Which means, you'll be buying the same content twice when you don't need to and Steam will not warn you or stop you. This is extremely troubling. This might be more Steam's fault than anything. However, this should be something Rebellion should've addressed with Steam as to not allow someone to make this mistake. If you want all of the content, purchase the Super Deluxe Edition and Season Pass 2. DO NOT add all DLC content to your cart and purchase that way.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong, this is a great arcade-y third person zombie shooter and despite owning all the DLCs, I don't recommend it because of the following:-Too many DLCs for a full priced game and the developers misread the community thinking they would fork over this much money considering most of the playerbase of the franchise consists of people getting the Zombie Army Trilogy for pennies during sales-Horde mode doesn't account for your DLC weapons unless you're playing solo so even if you play with other players that also own the DLC weapons, they will not show up, leading to repetition -The base game content is lacking, and I mean REALLY lacking. You only get 3 primary, secondary, and sidearm. That's extremely pathetic for a full priced game on top of the previous games not having this lack of content-Base game weapons' form of progression is finding collectibles called Upgrade kits and finishing stickers (which are challenges) but even if you finish all challenges and finding all kits, you won't have enough to fully upgrade all the base game weapons unless you level up to 100. This is fine but the DLC weapons have ACTUAL WEAPON PROGRESSION as in each upgrade requires you to do something rather than chase after collectibles. For a game that boasts DEEP PROGRESSION, why give that to DLC weapons and instead also give it to the base game weapons? I dont understand this direction-Game playerbase is minimal due to the issues listed above, but the biggest flaw is that you cannot play with people that have DLCs that you dont and vice versa, leading to alienation of an already small playerbase. The whole game is built as if the main game is F2P, but no it was launched at full price of $60 dollars with over 200 dollars worth of DLC. I got this game and the DLCs at a sale and it was $87 dollars. Was it worth it? Game is fun, but not $87 dollars fun. Wait for a bigger sale or wait for Rebellion to stop acting like greedy moronsEdit: They just made all Season 1 content free. Not the right move, make the main game free, not the DLC. And it's funny how this means there is a chance other season pass content will be free, screwing over anyone that paid the absurd prices for these DLCs AND incentives people into just waiting for them to become free instead of buying them. _childDocuments_.review: This game costs $50, has THREE Season Passes, and a total of $350 of DLC.Despite the fact that this is basically just a zombie mod for Sniper Elite 4 with a few assets borrowed from Strange Brigade, even the cheapest possible method of buying this game, namely purchasing the "Super Deluxe Edition" and Season Passes 2 and 3, would still set you back $150 and you STILL wouldn't have access to basic weapons like the Kar 98K, the P-38 and the TT-33 which are ALREADY in Sniper Elite 4 and are being held back for Season Pass 4 or 5.This game really is the epitome of creating "DLC" by hacking content out of the base game and then drip-feeding it out in overpriced "Season Passes" with the intent of conning people into spending more money on the game. Compared to Sniper Elite 4 or the previous Zombie Army Trilogy, you will notice this game has fewer weapons and several missing characters but every time a new $35.00 "Season Pass" comes out, you will see one of the weapons which was ALREADY in Sniper Elite 4 added to the game.The only other games which I have seen do this as badly are fighting games like Dead or Alive and Tekken. This game has an upgrade system... which I expected to be a good thing given that the lack of an upgrade system was one of the few weak-points in the original Zombie Army Trilogy which is one of my all-time favorite games. However, the upgrade system is tedious and annoying because rather than simply requiring you to collect exp or currency like in a Resident Evil game, it requires doing lots of busy-work (get 50 head shots within 10 meters, etc.) in a way EXACTLY like some of the worst CoD multiplayer games. This ruins the gameplay in that it is designed to both suck up your time AND ensure that rather than focus on actually playing and enjoying the game, you are instead WORKING. You WORK by trying to do something which would otherwise be irrational OVER AND OVER AGAIN (like letting zombies get close to you before you shoot them at point-blank range with a sniper rifle) so that you can upgrade the weapon you are using so that you can WORK again with slightly better tools...But it gets worse... even after working to complete these silly objectives, you STILL won't be able to upgrade your guns until you find "upgrade kits" which are few and far between and were OBVIOUSLY originally intended to be sold as microtransactions just like the "shared lives" which helped to ruin Wolfenstein: Youngblood.In fact, you can't even get these "upgrade kits" which have absolutely no purpose except to give you permission to complete upgrades you have already unlocked via the tedious and annoying "challenges" by replaying levels so it couldn't be more obvious that they were put in the game either to sell them OR to push the "DLC" by selling it to people who can't upgrade their weapons without buying new content because they ran out of these "upgrade kits" and can NEVER get any more without buying an expansion. Unlike many multiplayer games on Steam, this game does NOT offer remote play together. Online connectivity is also noticeably below the standard for a steam game.This game began life as an EPIC exclusive which is likely the reason for the inferior multiplayer and failure to adopt features like remote play together which if offered, would make this version of the game better than the EPIC version. (This is also probably the reason the the Left 4 Dead characters playable in the previous Zombie Army trilogy are not available in this one.)It put an invisible wall between me and the safe-room at the very end of the level so that I couldn't complete it. The only way around this was to replay the ENTIRE level all over again from the beginning. I would find a bug like this more forgivable in a game without $105 of Season Passes but if you are going to overcharge that much, you ought to at least make sure your product is reliable.Unlike the previous Zombie Army games and Sniper Elite in which you search corpses to find ammo, in this game, you need to stomp on corpses to grind them into mush because zombies and skeletons are apparently made of Jell-O. After you stomp on them, glowing ammo and medpacs will magically pop up.I like the premise, the voice acting, and a lot of stuff about the game. The sad thing is that if it had a more ethical business model, it would have been a great game and one which I could wholeheartedly recommend. This game should have been sold for $20~$40 like World War Z, Remnant From the Ashes, Senua's Sacrifice etc. as a complete game with nothing hacked out. The devs still could have made new DLC missions and sold those but these ought to have been NEW content as opposed to weapons, characters etc. hacked out of the base game.Even this game's flaws would have been quite forgivable if it were sold honestly as opposed to costing literally hundreds of dollars even with some content still being held back for future DLCs.If you haven't played Zombie Army Trilogy (which combines 1 and 2 and adds 3) then play that instead. That was a great game and it was also one of the first games I liked well enough to take the time to review it.This game on the other hand, is simply not worth the literally hundreds of dollars it currently costs, especially given that there is STILL content (such as the Kar 98K, the P-38, TT-33, the ZH-29, etc.) which is already in Sniper Elite 4 (which uses the same engine) and is obviously just being held back for "Season Pass 9" or whatever. If you feel like buying this game, wait until it TRULY goes on sale like five years from now and is actually offered at a fair price. Play some of the other games in your library and get this after you're done with those. I wish I had done so.
