_childDocuments_.review: Salt and Sanctuary is a master piece and this game is close, I will talk about the notable points of this game below.TL;DR at the end1. The art style reminded me more of lewd side scrollers than a souls like, it is also hard to tell what is in the back ground and what is in the foreground from time to time. Which can be lethal if you think a platform is in the foreground when it is not. Also I feel like some characters' art feel rather out of place compared to the rest of the game.2. The story uses elements like cosmic evil and alternate dimensions, which is fine. What is not fine is the fact that the story in my opinion lack depth, big god eating realm and hero saving the day, over generic for a souls like. There are bits and pieces of side lines that are either too short or lack continuity. Also I think the main character stated she has "memory loss" when being transported to the alternated dimension, but never stating what DOES she remember. Creating a disconnection between the player and the character. Since the player does remember everything. It is hard to immerse in a world when there is a disconnection of knowledge between the character and the player.3. The music is fine, but mediocre at best. Neither here nor there, does not make me want to mute it but it is not adding much to the experience.4. I only played one weapon: the sword, and it feels weird. The foresight parry counter registration is bad, despite the description stating "0.1" or "0.2" seconds, I can either miss time it by 1 entire seconds and still hit the parry, or hit it on the point and still not trigger the parry. I suspect it has to the with the fps the game is running on, but for a core gameplay mechanic to feel good it has to be precise and deliberate, which it doesn't. And that carries over to other mechanics like the dodge spin and execute. At times the game feels more akin to a hack and slash rather than a souls like.5. Level design is not quite metroid nor souls like, you're given most of your movement options in the prologue. So you can  reach most places as soon as you start the main game. Most areas are just linear, it is either a circle or a line from one point to another, and some areas are connected together in the way you expect them to. I never hit a moment where I went "WOW, this is a short cut to an earlier part, I would've never see it coming".6. Amount of item you can equip is rather poor, usually one or two choices of BiS for each slot. I'm the sword I started the game with is also the sword I am going to the game with. 7. The game gives you upgrades that changes the functionality of your class rather early, and the stats later. It is usually done the other way in other games. However I think it works in this game, for you to get use to the move sets early and only improve in stats later. 8. I can see from the tree that each weapon are meant to have multiple play styles, the sword for example, have a path that's focusing on dodging and a path that's focusing on parrying/block. But each branch is so short that I can take both without losing out on anything. This mean that the playstyle end up not differ from one another that much. I wish they could've given us longer brances with more choices to make so every body can play a different way even when they are using the same weapon.9. The amount of time you spend fighting bosses compare to the amount of time you spend traveling/fighting trash mobs are too low. Three things contribute towards this: lack of boss fights, vast/empty terrain and bland mob design. Make traveling feel extremely boring, you just cull through all the trash mobs. Exploring feels pointless due to the lack of good items in the game, you finding some hidden path usually rewards you with 300 gold, underwhelming. 10. Bosses themselves are fine, nothing really pops out but they are serviceable. Some bossed are too easy when you parry them and some bosses are unparriable, encouraging diversity in playstyle I guess. Only complaint is again, the bosses are unrewarding. In Salt and Sanctuary defeating bosses at worst gives you options in terms of armor and weapon, in this game, nothing.11. The game has (to avoid spoilers) three endings, bad, neutral and good/true. However the true ending is unreachable if you leave the prologue without completing certain tasks. I feel like this is a huge oversight, compare to Salt and Sanctuary where you have more than double digits of endings that are all neutral. No ending falls in the traditional definition of good or bad, which goes well with the Love Craftian tone. In Salts and Sanctuary you can always decide your ending until the LAST boss. The fact that in this game no warning/sign is given that you messed up and cannot go back is pretty lame.12. The game uses rather out dated technology of save points and save files. So if you die you need to load a save file and go from that stage. Which actually would make sense if only one choice at the end decides the ending, so you can save before the choice and go back and watch all the endings. But it does not, your ending is decided from nearly the start of the game and thus making suck mechanic out dated. Compare to a bonfire/sanctuary in other souls games, this save mechanic means if you die, not only you loose all you exp/currency you gained over the course, you also lose game state such as discovered secrets and opened short cuts.13. This game also uses a rather out dated potion system, you have to teleport back to town to buy potions every once in a while. I cannot see the advantages of this system over just having your healing mechanic replenish at the save spot. The potions cost next to nothing so they are essentially free like flasks in other games. It just forces you break up your gameplay to teleport back to town to restock. TL;DRDespite all the problems I stated above, I still do recommend this game, maybe a little expensive for its size. It is a serviceable souls like side scroller to quench the thirst until another Souls and Sanctuary comes out.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another Metroidvania ... and it's a fun one :)Pro:-free demo which allows you to play a big chunk of the first "chapter"-awesome style/graphics & music-fluid joypad controls (keyboard needs some tweaking)-quite challenging combat that allows for dodging parrying and quite a few different fighting styles.-interesting bossfights-a HUGE map to explore, with some enjoyable platforming to doNeutral:-at least one IMHO essential exploration tool can be missed quite easy, locking you out of a big part of the game (like a 3 optional bosses and an ending tied to them a little bit). Can be recovered if you missed it, but until then, there's some road-blockers that will make you scratch your head.-I don't know if it's thanks to the translation, but the first part of the story seems disjointed from the rest.-the english translation was a little rough in the beginning, but got better due to updatesCons:-there's some "points of no return" in the story, i.e. you can't go back to "before" and since some NPCs are now missing, you can't finish some sidequests, so better make a few more saves than absolutely needed.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly amazing game. I've played a lot of 2d metroidvania games (hollow knight, salt and sanctuary, Death Gambit). For me this game is straight up better than Salt and Sanctuary and Death Gambit. The story is more interesting as well, being more akin to bloodborne with some eldritch hidden mysteries. The combat is absolutely enthralling once you get a few lvls. One thing this game does well is that there is not your typical Str, dex, stamina, hp, etc talent points upon lvl up. Instead you spend your talent points on cool moves and combos you can do with weapons. This made it possible to use more than 1 play style per playthrought. Unlike Darksouls, where you make a build around a certain weapon, you can actually be for example, strong in both daggers and bow alike without feeling one is clearly better than the other. This made me feel like i could change play style and adapt to different enemies. This felt really rewarding. A lot of weapons have unique weapon arts which adds even more moves to your repertoire.Exploration feels greatly rewarding as well. You acquire new weapons, ring and spells (arcane items) that might end up good for you. As of the most recent patch, there are now items that increase your stats that you can find in hidden areas (+hp,+mana,+arcane,+stamina). Even if these bonus are somewhat small, it makes it so you are rewarded even if you are "full build". The little sound the game makes when you find a secret path is satisfying to hear.If i had to give one down side to this game, it would be the bosses. Some of them are good, but id say 40% of them are super forgettable and lacklustre.If you are a fan of 2d metroidvania or bloodborn, id 100% recommend you this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Replayed the game in full after Bounty of the Night update. For some reason, my previous save file was lost and I wasn't able to do an NG+, nevertheless I'd say the game stood the most important test for a metroidvania - replayability. Doing everything again was a blast, I was able to find new secrets I missed the first time, I tried more builds than before instead of sticking to a single (and safe) one, and was equally compelled to explore and engade in everything the game has to offer. Bounty of the Night was almost a major overhaul, fixing some map issues, reworking the english translations, adding new items, fixing some bugs (that weren't even that gamebreaking tbh) and much more. At release Vigil was a good game, now it's squarely great, although personally I'm very drawn towards it's charisma. Playing Vigil feels exactly like playing Castlevania SotN back in the day. They're very different games, mind you, but that whole essence of piecing a minimalist story, exploring a whimsical map, learning new abilities and how they interact with the environment and a non-linear progression that pratically invites you to never stick to a single route (and even of acquiring some items before you're meant to) are all there.I really can't recommend this game enough, it's fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil: The Longest Night is a fun, decently sized metroidvania with plenty of good things going for it.Combat system is fun, has a nice variety and few very interesting touches I haven't seen in other games (stamina system in particular is pretty interesting)Great exploration, a lot to explore too and it's really incredibly fun to just poke around everywhere, movement abilities are accessible rather early and cleverly implemented. Gotta say tho, binding dash to double stick tilt by default is not a good decision. Ended up changing controls a little, thanks for rebind option. Bosses are great too, designs are pretty unique and fights are fun, but default boss theme sadly doesn't slap at all. Major and secret bosses tho? Good stuff, good stuff. Speaking of OST, I found it to be a hit and miss, also audio mixing could use some help, tracks end abruptly when you go indoors and when you come back, area theme starts from beggining. Most of the tracks are straight up fire tho. It's a bit janky (encountered a few bugs) and game acts in best traditions of Dark Souls at times by not letting you know about points of no return in advance (which locks you from side quests btw if you haven't finished them yet) and typical "boss died? time to fail that one quest lmao", which I personally can tolerate, but others might not.Overall I'd give it 7.8/10? There were 2 moments that I didn't exactly like, like having insta-kill pits out of nowhere. If you like metroidvanias and somewhat challenging gameplay, I say give it a try, it's fun. Don't forget to save often tho.

_childDocuments_.review: While it has somewhat amateurish aspects like stiff animation and poor translation, it's not the mediocre Salt and Sanctuary clone it appears and has some great ideas of its own.Animation aside the actual art is as great as it looks and it has visual quality features you might not expect such as armour and weapons actually showing up on your character.Progression is guided by NPC quests with a journal that keeps track of any clues you have obtained and this adds a lot to the 'where do I actually go and why' problem games like this tend to have.Action wise the game feels reasonably smooth to play and the baseline combat system has some subtle well thought out features that certain bigger developers could do to take note of.For example, dodging is made very reliable by making it such that after dodging an attack cannot be damaged by it even after your invulnerability frames have gone, so you can't evade a swipe and then still take damage from it even though it should logically have already gone past you. Another thing like this is that some boss attacks have staggered hitboxes, wherein being in the main target area of the attack will do huge damage, but standing at the bosses shoulder for example when they swing will do greatly reduced or even no damage, only staggering you instead.According to steam this is the first game made by Glass Heart Games, and I'll be keeping an eye out for them in future. There's clear evidence in Vigil that they know what they are doing and have some good ideas, and if they work on their sound and animation and hire better translators, they could make something truly great.

_childDocuments_.review: Lifts so much influence from Salt & Sanctuary that it would seem like a must-buy for fans of that game (such as myself). It's a shame that it does a worse job in  nearly every way. Controls are frequently unresponsive. Healing in particular can't be used until the recovery frames of any action are over. This translates to a lot of missed inputs and unintentional deaths.The save system follows the traditional metroidvania of hard saves instead of the S&S/Soulslike model of auto-saving but dropping resources on death. While I don't inherently dislike this system, it does feel like a regression from modern trends in the genre. Story is pretty uninspired. Hero has unique abilities, world is grimdark with a demonic/eldritch undertone, everything is told through item descriptions, etc. etc. dark souls etc. My uninterest in the story aside (maybe it gets better later) the moment-to-moment dialogue is awful. Often feels like a poorly translated fan-fiction. There's no voice acting either so you just have to imagine how characters would deliver their lines, often to amusing results.Positives?Game looks very pretty with good light-work and hand-drawn art style (does also kinda look like S&S but hey) Combat is fun to an extent. There are only 4 weapon categories but each has different mechanics and combos. When compared to other games it does feel lacking, but for what's available it works well.TL;DR game isn't awful, but it's woefully out-shadowed by other giants in the genre. (Hollow Knight, Salt & Sanctuary, Bloodstained, Blasphemous) Made me want to replay S&S more than anything. Might play through it more to see if my opinion improves, but thus far I haven't been impressed.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil is a excellent metroidvania with very light souls elements, mostly the usage of stamina, weapon upgrading and the weird sometimes obscure questlines though frankly i would avoid comparisons otherwise. Its very much more castlevania side of the metroidvania and in general has a excellent style and atmosphere that pervades the whole thing. This is a easy recommend if you liked say, bloodstained: ritual of the night, but have not been able to find something else like it.Gameplay is fairly straightforward, you have 4 weapon types and several weapon options in those categories with unique stats and sometimes traits. Weapons may also have special attacks that you can activate via a direction and attack input shown in their info page. You have a roll and slide and later unlock a airdash as well as a ground dash with a terrible input as well as a double jump you unlock early on. Finally you have consumable potions to heal as well as items that you can throw from your stock and spells that use a recharging magic meter you can find around the world.In addition to all of that, there is a skill tree for every weapon type as well as a general. While most skills are quite useful often there are a few of dubious use, or in the case of the swords automatic counter active detriment; Luckily you can reset your tree with a fairly common but valuable item. After you beat the game and go to new game+, you also unlock straight stat upgrades you can put points into should you not care to put more into the skill tree.As for the plot i could not tell you, its both straightforward but at the same time it felt like i only got the most bare bones of the plot and the core central part. The music is usually pretty good if subdued, but there's at least 3 really good songs in there that kinda come out of nowhere but were greatly appreciated. Environments are pretty unexceptional aside from a certain place accessed via musical instrument but look great and are at least varied regardless.Overall i can heartily recommend this game, especially after out of nowhere they provided huge content updates post release adding a ton of weapons and items to the game. The main problems it had initially have been ironed out, the bugs have been fixed, and the game plays great. Give it a try if you have been looking for another take on modern castlevania or just really like metroidvanias in general.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR, 8/10, Did you play Salt and Sanctuary? Did you like it? If so, buy this immediately. If not, but you enjoy other 2D Metroidvania's, strong recommend. If this is your first foray into the genre, this is a decent introduction, but there are probably better starters.Gameplay: Smooth and responsive, but you will DEFINITELY want to rebind some of your keys if like me you're on mouse and keyboard. IMPORTANT NOTE: Your Heavy attack in this game does nothing without skills, so when you rebind it to your right mouse button and mash it for 10 minutes wondering why nothing is happening, that is why. Bosses are fun and challenging, but are very possible to beat with any weapon setup (looking at you Kelpie, I beat him with a Heavy weapon setup with 1 HP and no healing potions left). Overall I'd give this a 10/10 for gameplay on it's own.Translation: It's spotty in a few places, and there are some definite typos and spelling errors, nothing egregious and you can understand what's going on without any issue, but definitely needed one more polish pass pre-release. Overall doesn't really detract from the game unless you're a grammar fanatic.Lore/Story: Actually somewhat interesting, but like it's inspirations (Dark Souls, Salt and Sanctuary, etc.) it's fairly minimal. Unlike those games there are a large-ish number of NPCs to talk to, and a hub town filled with a variety of NPCs, some of whom will give you minor/sidequests and so on. The main focus here is on the gameplay and the art, speaking of which.Art/Style: 10/10, good lord is this game pretty, Imagine Salt and Sanctuary but actually able to drawn people (I mean this with love, SnS has some of the most unique and memorable art I've ever seen, but I wouldn't exactly call it a realistic, well proportioned, or uhhh, good). The environments and enemies are all lovingly detailed, the music is gorgeous, and frankly just watching a stream of this game would probably be worth the sale price.Playtime - Well I'm 12 hours in and I've beaten maybe 1/4 of the game, although I tend to be slow/completionist so I expect we'll see someone beat the game in that timeframe. Overall I'd expect if you play at a normal pace you'll probably get 20-30 hours out of the game, which is well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Way longer than I thought it would be. Well worth the price point, but an absolute steal at a sale.Common complaint is that quests can fail out of the blue and this is true. All I can say to help with that is, you should pay attention to the save points. The letters will guide you to where you're supposed to be in terms of quest progression. Other than that, keep a backup file or two while talking to everyone. You'll be fine.This game rewards exploration (finding secrets) and experimentation (playing with different weapons), so have fun and if you're really still afraid of the failing quests, look up when the 'big points' are. Most fail before those points, but even if you don't look them up, the story will make those points obvious.One downside for me was the writing. Characterization is okay but the text used to represent language in the game world (character articulation, item descriptions, histories, etc) feels a bit basic. If I had to make a comparison, it's like if you were reading Twilight while watching Bloodborne.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil the longest night has been a game I've had my eye on awhile. Akin to Bloodstained:  Ritual Of The night it signals a return of Castlevania-like titles that focus a lot around tough as nails intimidatingly grotesque screen filling bossies,dark fantasy folklore,and Gothic horror. In other words, this game is perfect for its' October release date!When I first got my nes as a boy my dad rented some games for me from the video store. They included Friday the 13th and more importantly,Simon's Quest. Despite its' obvious faults,Simon's Quest impressed me. I liked the very subtle rpg mechanics laid over the top of an action platformer. Aka, you could get clues from villagers and buy or upgrade items. Vigil: Longest night feels like Simon's Quest but minus many of its' flaws. Aka, the villagers you encounter actually make sense and are not made to be deliberately cryptic so you will still have to buy a strategy guide. (Looking at you Nintendo Power!)  Additionally the visuals are breathtakingly beautiful and you never really get tired of going thru the game's swamps,forests,abandoned ship yards,water falls,catacombs,sunken cities,and graveyards many times over. Yes, there is some Metroidvania trickcanery at foot here. Aka,you will gain new powers and physical feats that allow you to bypass obstacles or barriers you could not right before hand. Additionally you will collect your fair share of keys and magical abilities that fulfill similar tasks.I've already seen people compare Vigil to Dark-souls and I do understand that mindset. Aka, the skills system is very deep for this kind of game. The main heroine can learn to master a plethora of weapons and even upgrade her stamina or her arcane magical arsenal so a player can have fun experimenting with different builds. Do you want to be a mystical archer,taking out your enemies from afar? How about a mammoth sword wielding warrior that rushes straight into battle? A sneaky fast moving ranger of the woods that duel wields lightning fast venomous daggers? Trust me,whatever class you want to specialize in is there if you assign your points wisely!Some say Vigil can be too overwhelming at first. I confess that is true,the game does not hold your hand much. You may start a quest one way only to run into conflicting information or details that make you reconsider your current path or discover areas a bit "out of order" in which you are clearing out harder zones first before you stumble into an easier habitat that most likely should have been your first destination. While the villagers are helpful and easy to understand the map is a maze in and of itself whereas the places you traverse are huge and packed with secrets off the beaten path. (Then again,many gamers appreciate this mysterious semi-open-world wonder-land aesthetic as well as the challenges and rewards it presents!) For me the most obvious way Vigil strays from Ritual Of The Night is it punishes you a bit more. Aka,you can become exhausted when your stamina bar runs low. Each attack afterwards will inflict less damage upon your enemies until you reach a stunned state of fatigue. Additionally you can take damage falling from high altitudes. Miriam was a bit tougher and more resilient than Leila from the get-go. However,this is not necessarily a bad thing as over time Leila becomes a better "slayer of the dark" whilst the game adds a wrinkle of vulnerability reminding you the main protagonist as amazing as she seems is still very much human. Pretty much if Miriam is the unofficial daughter of Alucard and Maria Leila would be the unofficial daughter conceived between Trevor Belmont and Sypla Belnades. In other words, great fighting prowess mixed with supernatural powers but still tethered to the ground a tad by her limited mortality.I forgot to mention there is a story here. Pretty much Leila goes thru a ritualistic initiation to become her world's "demon slayer". There's something to do with her sister and what seems like two goddesses and a plague doctor all trying to convince Leila to be on their various sides. Yes, the game has multiple endings based upon who you align with in the end.I'm surprised Vigil" Longest Night has not gotten quite the same fan-fare as Bloodstained: Ritual Of The Night because it's obvious just as much love and painstaking detail went into crafting it. Assuming you are done with Bloodstained this is a very easy recommendation!Pros+Another game that ever so slightly continues castlevania's legacy whilst doing brand new things+Exploration,defeating bosses,and growing in strength and finesse over time remains fun throughout+Beautiful story-book-illustration-eque visuals right out of the darkest of fairy-tales.+"Perfect" soundtrack+Game is challenging but rarely becomes frustrating+Enemies are delightfully grotesque and menacing. Very much guilty pleasures to encounter, the whole lot of them!+Fluid animations+If Ritual Of The Night gave you more "Dawn Of Sorrow" Longest night gives ya more "Order Of Ecclesia!"+If you are an old timer into gaming,horror,and dark fantasy the sheer amount of nostalgia on offer here is nothing short of gleefully smiling from start to finish! Beyond castlevania you will notice easter-eggs which will remind you of Wizards and Warriors,Diablo,Hellraiser,HP Lovecraft,and even Berserk. The game is like a Doom Metal album cover come to life!Cons-A bit too "open ended" at times that can lead to aimless wandering-Certain quests become jumbled and confusing-Bosses seem perfectly scaled difficulty wise right up until you face King-Kek. You will see what I mean! -Sometimes it takes you awhile to realize you have to equip certain items to your rotating accessory ring if you want to partake in the game's various magics. (And this becomes a necessity at certain points.)-Occasionally I feel as if taking fall damage and having to worry about stamina hinders an otherwise fast paced exploration rich metroidvania experience. (However, others may appreciate the added realism and added danger. In other words,all those Dark-souls/Blood-souls/Salt and Sanctuary fans!)-Certain weapons and armors from the black smith are the price of small nations! (Luckily  healing potions by comparison are very affordable!)-Map is a riddle in and of itself until you take the time to familiarize yourself with it

_childDocuments_.review: While not reaching such lofty narrative and world-building heights as more polished games such as Hollow Knight, Vigil still manages to make up for its meandering plot (replete with typos in the EN-US version) and head-scratching map design with some very satisfying combat and varied enemy design. Once I got the hang of the sword combat (which I used exclusively throughout the game), I couldn't get enough of it. The Dark Souls influences are fairly transparent (the Equipment/Item UI is a blatant rip-off) but its boss designs are more unique and varied than Dark Souls 2's!I particularly enjoyed the swords' parry system, though some aspects of it were inconsistent - especially egregious is the insanely-tight "100ms" window for auto-riposte, which is unattainable by humans over the age of 30 (and, I suspect, bugged in some way). Frustratingly, the game does slow-roll equipment discovery (it took me almost 12 hours to find my second sword), but it makes up for it by having interesting item interactions and unique combos for each weapon. It also makes upgrade materials abundant so you have a lot of freedom to experiment with different weapons without feeling like you're limiting future options.N.B.: I played this game entirely on Linux. Works great on Proton!

_childDocuments_.review: So far i really enjoy the game, fight system, hit feedback and rolling feels reliable and fast, you got around 3 types of weapons to choose from. Sword, Axe and Bow. You can wield up multiple weapons and switch them comfortable in mid fight, thats cool. Atmosphere and Lore are immersive and cryptic. Enemy design is creative and fresh. There are also a LOT of sidequests and a ton of NPCs to talk to in the town, that makes it very different from other souls-likes. The German translation is apart from some smaller mistakes also very good.About the negatives.Cant use a controller because the DS4 support is broken, couldnt fix that. Weapon pool is super small, also due to very hard hiding spots of new items. Enemy variation is also very small; after some minutes in new areas you have seen everything. The Chests are also mostly filled with generic stuff like bombs or arrows 50% of the time, hope that will be changed.Game itself is too easy. You can cheese through a lot of mobs with special attacks or overpowered gear, especially the gold armour breaks the whole balancing. You basically just rush through the whole world being an invincible DPS cannon..The Bossfights become a joke like that.All in all its a decent game for people that are interested in 2D souls-likes that are not super hard to beat, you definetely get a solid game for your money here.

_childDocuments_.review: Trash - Don't even play it for freeIt's cheap.It's cheap in its design.It's cheap in its presentation.It's cheap in its difficulty.Levels are lazy and uninspired. Lame "metroidvania" knockoff. Barely hidden items are in obvious locations. No real sense of exploration.Mechanically simple. Usable items are banal. Different weapon types are stock standard and all play the same from beginning to end. Dodge roll. Block. Nothing more complex than "get expee > choose +1 attack or an extension to your combo or some such." Lame air combos. Simple and unsatisfying weapon crafting. Nothing you haven't seen before that hasn't already been done better in a million other games.Invincibility frames for dodging are insultingly sparse. You can dodge roll half the length of the screen and only be invincible for like two frames. Most of the time, the obscene distance you dodge will just send you rolling over a ledge.The aesthetic is every grimdark fantasy you've ever seen. What's black and white and red all over? This game.Utterly forgettable characters. Barely any dialog. Story is nonsense. Lore is nonsensical. The world premise is uninspired. It's night all the time and scary things happen. Woooh!The production "values" are roughly on par with a flash game. Animations look slick though. That's literally the only good thing I can say about Vigil.It's pathetically trying way too hard to be 2D dark souls without any of the mechanical complexity.Give it a HARD pass.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a reason Souls-Like games that have few and far between save/heal stations work: because when you die, you don't actually lose everything. Sure you may drop currency or something else to encourage you to run back to your death location, but in general any progress you made is still there. The map is still uncovered, any secrets you found remain found, and any weapons or armor you picked up or upgraded remain as well. This allows for the game play to be difficult without feeling like the last 30min were a waste of time if you die. This game however has opted for a Save system instead so that if you die, that's it. Game over, All your progress since the last time you hit a save station is just GONE. Which means you have to redo EVERYTHING that you did before. All of it. Over, and over and over again if you hit a tough patch. Yes there are extremely limited use items that allow you to save away from a rest point but they are so rare that it doesn't really solve the problem. As such despite the great atmosphere, the decently tight combat and progression systems and an actually fairly interesting story that isn't so buried behind items and lore drops that you can actually understand much of it, I just can't continue this game knowing I'll be repeating so many conversations or map progression every time I screw up a bit. If you can handle that however, it's worth a go.

_childDocuments_.review: One listen to the main menu theme song was a prognostication that this was going to be good.  I remember seeing this game back when there was a demo available, and I knew I'd buy it as soon as it came out.I won't repeat the obvious information that you've seen in the description and tags, but I want to say that this game, rather than being a "souls-like," is more of a "bloodborne-like."  It takes a lot of inspiration from Bloodborne, ranging from the blood vial system to the names of certain areas and the overall dark gothic, cosmic horror aesthetic.  Rather than copying directly off of Bloodborne, however, it sort of deviates by doing its own thing with the setting, most notably with the main character and her role.If you've ever watched the anime or read the manga called Claymore, it sort of reminded me of that.  You are a light haired warrior female with a sword who seems to have the singular purpose of taking on the abominations and horrors that humanity is plagued with but is incapable of directly facing.  If there is one thing that Vigil does very well it's the gameplay.  Dodging and general movement is very fluid, satisfying, and responsive.  I never felt annoyed that my character was not responding the way I wanted her to, possibly leading to unnecessary deaths.  As the story went on and I acquired more movement abilities, I found navigation of the environment and the combat even more smile-inducing, perhaps even to the point of being overpowered during combat, outmaneuvering nearly everything.There are four different weapon classes in the game that you can specialize in through skill trees, each with their own benefits and drawbacks, and there is an additional skill tree reserved for general skills, which encompasses everything from stamina boosts, to item drop rate, to additional mana for arcane item usage.  You won't have a problem leveling up what you'd like to by the end of the first playthrough.And speaking of arcane (yes, probably a Bloodborne reference), the arcane damage in this game is also implemented primarily through arcane item usage.  There are quite a few arcane items you can collect, each unique enough in their effects to not be confused with the other items.  I found a lot of them fun to use, but I also found myself coming back to 2 or 3 of them that were extremely overpowered and made some fights trivial provided that you had decent arcane skills.   I should mention that the items have some rather strange names if some of my review headings are any indication.It may be unclear on how to level up your arcane skills when first playing, but it turns out that  serves this purpose, which I found kind of neat.You can also infuse your weapons with gems in this game to provide auxiliary effects.  However, instead of Dark Souls where the infusions would often cause split damage with physical and the special effect scaling with a certain stat, the infusions in this game seem to only provide a net benefit by creating an additional effect on top of the base damage.  Interestingly, the items of clothing or armor that you wear can also be infused with the same gems, often creating a defensive effect instead of an offensive one.Weapons, armor, and arcane items were not very common to come by - they are something that require exploration and work to obtain.  I liked this feature of Vigil - it meant that my inventory never got absurdly crowded and more effort could be put into the weapons and items themselves by developers since this feature was not spread too thin by its breadth.The different weapon classes and specializations, infusions, and arcane items allowed for the creation of a character that was satisfyingly customizable.  And really, any build you do is viable.  This game was not particularly challenging to me personally (with the exception of some of the later bosses), and if you're a souls veteran, you definitely want to play on the hardest difficulty.I'm going to discuss three of the more artistic sides of Vigil - the art, music, and the narrative and characters.  Spoiler alert - the art and music were excellent while the narrative and characters were the weakest part of the game.I don't think the screenshots provided in the Steam store really do this game's art justice.  If you like a certain art style, then this game was made for you and it will be a pleasure to look at from beginning to end.  The best way that I can describe it is dark gothic aesthetics and monstrosities infused with a glowing, fantasy, fairy-tale-like color palette.  I've seen some people complain about the glowing and over saturation, but I personally loved it.  The world in this game suffers from perpetual darkness yet the blood and strange creatures are accented.  It's beautiful, I think.To make things even better, several of the areas were vastly different from one another with some examples being vast forests, the catacombs, an ice world, and underground mines.  They did an excellent job on the environments and the transitions between them, as well as the fast travel system.Overall, the music was a strong point, especially the main menu music and the music in the town with its melancholy, brooding tone, reminiscent of some of the more reflective tracks from the Dark Souls series.  There are not many times in the game where you are walking in complete silence - in addition to bosses having their own soundtrack, the areas have their own soundtrack as well.  Not all of them were a hit - I found the music in the forest to be a bit too over the top for me and highly repetitive, and several of the boss soundtracks were not very memorable.  It was not bad by any means, though.And then comes the narrative and characters.  Rather than talking too much about this point, I want to say that a more well developed and interesting plot, as well as more engaging and unique characters, perhaps combined with some solid voice acting, could've put this game on a whole different level.  What I'd love to see is well done souls game mechanics combined with an astounding narrative and engaging, nuanced characters - a game that is the complete package and ends up being far more than the sum of its equally strong parts - but perhaps this is too much to realistically ask.I think that if the developers of Vigil could at least hire some skilled voice actors to express the personalities of the characters in this game to get you to empathize with them, things would be more remarkable, but unfortunately, I found myself not really engaged too much with this aspect of the game.  And it's a shame, because I think improvements in this domain would've made Vigil far more enjoyable in more ways than the gameplay and art, as it would've infused it with emotion and meaning, and of course, these are the things that we remember the most as humans.So, is Vigil worth buying?  Absolutely - especially on sale.  This is the most fun I've had in a metroidvania, souls-like game in quite some time.  I knew I'd finish it within the first few hours of playing it because I kept thinking about it when I was not playing it, itching to come back and explore new areas and fight different bosses.  It's NG+ feature may enhance replayability as well, but I'm not sure to what extent things change in it.You may find yourself mashing the buttons on the controller to get through the dialogue sometimes, but the combat and environment will always make up for your lack of emotional engagement in Vigil.With the exception of a few bugs, I'm impressed that a small indie team was able to make a game of this scope and quality, and I highly recommend a playthrough for something different if you're a fan of Dark Souls, Bloodborne, or Metroidvania stuff.Enjoy slaying grotesque beasts, you blonde haired, sword wielding waifu, you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is easily one of the best of 2020, speaking regardless of genres. The story is excellent, and there's a great deal of fun and mystery in unraveling what is going on. The most refreshing aspect I found in Vigil, was that nearly every NPC is important, and talking to NPCs in between major world events is critical for progressing quest lines. Finally! A game that rewards compulsively talking to everyone, and it isn't even a conventional RPG!I have only minor quibbles with this game that are weighted far far below "this is one of the best games I've played in the last year" review: 1) jump mechanic 2) weapon options/availability 3) map fog and figuring out unexplored sections. Until the cats ring (forget the name) later on, any substantial jump = death. Jumping, and leaps of faith, are necessary for exploration and opening up the map.  Case in point, when you get to the giant tree, I'm the type of person that needs to jump from the top a dozen times to clear as much map fog as possible to make sure I didn't miss anything, because there are secrets if you jump in the right spot falling from the top of the tree. However, there are areas you really can't explore until getting the ring, which discourages exploration for a good chunk of the game, as major jumps/leaps of fath/accepting jump death is necessary and frustrating. That mechanic could be improved upon--no cat ring wasting a ring slot, cripple limb where you need an item to fix it, etc. Second, I used the same sword for the entire early game until the major transition, but had a stockpile of various daggers and other weapons. The skill tree rewards you for staying on the same track (until the cat that resets later on), so I was stuck with the same old sword, hacking and slashing away. If there's going to be x options for weapons and skill trees, there should be a proportionate amount of weapons available to use and upgrade, otherwise progression feels stunted.Third minor nuisance, the map showing topography is awesome, but being able to clear map fog in all areas isn't perfectly done or wasn't 100% possible from what I saw when I finished the game. The map is a fantastic upgrade from conventional metroidvania rooms you've been in / rooms you haven't, but it makes it inherently difficult to identify areas that need to be explored, when you can't necessarily explore that black area in the first place. I recall trying to jump off the map/cliffs by the lighthouse because the map/fog of war showed unexplored areas, but that wasn't actually an area you could get to.All in, fantastic blend of dark souls mechanics, MV exploration, and hack n slash RPG fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

I was spamming one skill most of the game, which is really broken in my opinion, Long Range, Can enter the wall, Spammable, and I am almost untouchable. I changed to a different arcane skill later on that was doing 400-500+ damage per cast and I could cast it three times, which a melee weapon will do 100 damage per hit and you will risk your body (I am sure there are strong weapons but I doubt any weapon other than lagh sword would be able to give enough damage to switch from arcane skills)+- the double jump thing was a little bit annoying because they don't want you to jump some spots that you shouldn't be able to double jump, yet the spot that needs double jump were annoying, so you may need to use some other ways for extra performance (Examples: attacking with dagger after jumping, or using bow skills, or using a special dagger that let you dodge in ait which helped like a mini air dash before getting the real air dash)- the exploaration was not rewarding to me, and I may have to say that I was using a map that shows all the treasures so I knew what I would find and where. while they have some nasy hidden spots and treasure, and playing this game without such map will give you a better feeling of adventure and exploration than I had (because i almost knew all what will i find and that it is hidden somewhere there), still I don't regret using the map, I regret bothering with the treasures specially that I am not an achievement hunter, yet I have that feeling that I shouldn't leave that treasure because I knew about it XD + good music even tho I find them not matching the area sometimes or maybe its the genre of them game, you feel like you are playing an action or super hero game while all I was doing , (spamming birds)- no voice acting in 2020It is a decent game, I just expected a better quality from it, and while it had some up here and there, I didn't get too much "thrill" playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Alrighty having just beaten the game I thought might as well actually review it and hopefully it won't be a huge wall of text (probably will be anyway lol). If you have not guessed by now this game is heavily inspired by salt and sanctuary, dark souls, and bloodborne and it shows. I'm not used to formatting when it comes to typing on steam so I'm going to do my best to separate things into categories.            In terms of the art definitely an improvement over S&S however personally I still liked S&S's artstyle. Enemy design in particular makes S&S look tame in comparison. The game simply is great to look at and I gotta give praise to the artists where it's do.          Right now gameplay wise balancing in terms of weapons is just a mess. You have 4 weapon classes being the sword, duel wielding (daggers), heavy weapons (halberds, axes, and hammers) and bows. Very quickly you will realize that right now range is king and nothing can beat the sheer usefulness of the bow in terms of exploration and killing anything with a huge health bar and the heavy weapon (specifically one of 2 halberds) which simply deletes all trash mobs the game can throw at you. Now you may be wondering "wait what did you mean by the bow being useful for exploration?" well this is because of 2 things. 1. The bow gives you access to a superior double jump. 2. You can unlock a skill with the bow that lets you reach high areas you would otherwise need an easily missed ability  to actually get to. Magic in this game is treated a lot like how it was in bloodborne where you need to find certain items in order to use magic abilities however currently unless damage is buffed for magic items its better used as utility. The skill trees honestly are best described as okay. They straddle the line of being to small and being a solid size and some of the abilities do actually have an impact in various ways.             Storywise the game is lackluster in this regard. While it may seem confusing at first once you begun to clue in you'll realize that it isn't all that great. Honestly this can be fixed by adding/improving npc dialogue in game and expanding on item descriptions but as of now it really is not all that stand out.            When it comes to OST I think the game has a very solid soundtrack. Probably one of the best parts of the game in general. This might simply be because I'm biased and really like heavy metal which shocked me as when I started the game I thought the ost would be more in line with say S&S for example but no they went with something different and honestly it worked really well.            Now for the strictly negative part. This game is currently very buggy. Lots of visual glitchs, sfx glitches, and quests breaking (had 2 glitch out and were not able to be completed) which while some are ignorable others when encountered just feel awful to experience. My literal first time playing the game I had a visual bug so bad it hurt my eyes and gave me a headache. I almost dropped the game right then and there. If I hadn't given the game a second chance I would of applied for a refund. This game could really really use a lot of QoL changes at the moment as some game mechanics atm at best are outdated and at worse are just archaic and feel like a step back compared to other games. For example the teleport screen is only names meaning you need to memorize where the names coincide with on the map to effectively use the teleport feature. Really makes you appreciate how the demonsoulsbornedietwice games actually have an image that goes with a warp point. You currently need to manually restock all of your consumables which is just tedious to do. A lot of the UI in terms of weapon stats could really benefit from being organized and cleaned up as right now it can get somewhat confusing when trying to compare stats on various gear and weapons. The english translation as of now is barely serviceable and polishing it up should be a top priority right now.            A lot of what I just said probably sounded very negative yet why am I still recommending the game? This is because despite all of it's flaws Vigil was an enjoyable experience which turned out to be surprisingly long and over all fun to play. A lot of what I just said can be patched out over time and after having briefly spoke to the devs on twitter they genuinely seemed very optimistic and gave me hope that all of this will eventually be fixed in upcoming patches. Personally I don't think this game is as good as Salt and Sanctuary yet it can still be a very good game with a lot more polishing. If I had to give this game a score it would be roughly a 7.5-8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I think overall this game was solidly "decent." It's a metroidvania that takes heavy inspiration from Salt and Sanctuary for sure, in more ways than one. Overall, I do think I liked more things than not in this game. The controls were responsive and I rarely felt that I didn't have good control of what was happening to Leila. The art style I felt was pretty unique and appealing, and the fact that (at least Leila and some bosses, not sure if all enemies) used 3D models instead of 2D sprites made it a bit nicer for me personally. Story wise, I think it's a fresh take on the souls-like formula, including messages about a strong sense of family (the relationship between Leila and Daisy) and inverting the dynamic of light, or fire, and dark on its head. Now, one thing I do want to note right away (spoiler-free) is that this game has three different endings you can get. The worst ending and "neutral" ending require no real work at all, whereas the true ending does require you obtain four key items from various sidequests in the game, specifically all items belonging to Daisy. It is important to note that it is possible to miss the true ending for multiple reasons. For me I'm a bit sour about it because, to get the true ending, you need Daisy's four items to break four seals before the final boss, but because I interacted with two of the seals before I had the key item to break them, I could not interact with them anymore. Truthfully, I did notice the interaction prompt disappeared afterwards, but I didn't think to reload my game, which is my fault yeah, but still stings a bit. So yeah, absolutely do not interact with those seals before you have all 4 items. There are also two points of no return in relation to obtaining the necessary items for getting the true ending. Both are bosses, one in the Catacombs area, and one in the Top of the Giantwood area (the latter only accessible after going past the first point of no return.) Make sure to be very thorough about exploring and doing any and all quests you get before going past these points of no return. With all the talk about story and warnings about endings aside, this is still obviously marketed as a souls-like, so how does it hold up in the gameplay regard? Well, there are some simplifications to formulas that I think really work for this game as an indie. All weapons are put in one of four categories: swords, dual daggers, heavy weapons like halberds or hammers, and ranged weapons. This never really felt restrictive to me, and I ultimately went with heavy weapons for most of my playthrough as I felt they were significantly more powerful than swords while not being prohibitively slower or more expensive stamina-wise. Leveling up in this game is much different than traditional Souls games. Unlike putting points into stats which allows you to equip better gear, you instead have five skill trees; one for each weapon type, and one general one for general improvements to Leila. For most of the early game, I found the general tree most useful as it had bonuses like increased HP, increased healing from healing potions, physical damage reductions, stamina recoup on dodge, etc. I will say the weapon trees seemed a bit lacking from my cursory glances, but the whirlwind you get for heavy weapons was kinda neat. On the topic of healing potions, these are *not* like Estus in souls where they're refilled at bonfires (owl statues in this game); instead you have to buy potions from the merchant in town (although there's not really much else to spend your money on so you shouldn't really ever have an issue because of this). To make your life easier, you can buy like 100 potions at once and send them all to your storage, which can be accessed from any Owl Statue, to cut down on trips.Bosses were pretty decent across the board. Upotancos was pretty meh for me, same for The Pale Raven. But overall, I'd say there's more hits than misses with the bosses, and even if some frustrate you for a bit it won't be too long before you get them down probably. There's not that many humanoid bosses at your stature in the game though, only one actually if you just bumrush the story and accidentally fall into the worst ending without doing any other sidequests. They're all interestingly designed though, some being outright grotesque, which was definitely refreshing to see though considering a lot of metroidvanias don't really get this dark or gritty.All in all, I would recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of metroidvanias and/or souls-likes. I didn't really mention it much, but just as much as this game succeeds in the souls department, it does succeed in the metroidvania department as well, for the most part. I didn't really feel there was much reason to backtrack to previous areas except for my futile true ending hunt, but you did get some good mobility upgrades like a double jump, an air dash, a slide, etc. The price of this game isn't too bad either, which is always nice. So yeah, I'd say if the game looks appealing to you, then pull the trigger. There's a lot of content and you can easily get twice as many hours out of this game as I did, most likely.

_childDocuments_.review: (Follow  for more reviews like this)Vigil: The Longest Night is a soulslike metroidvania set in a dark fantasy world where the sun never shines (but outdoor areas aren't really as dark as night, more like a foggy morning, so visually it didn't feel quite as dark as the story makes it out to be). You play as Leila, a member of the Vigilant Order who tries to find out what's going on - and is also looking for her missing sister.As a 2D side-view soulslike, the game can be compared to Salt and Sanctuary - if you played that and want more of that style, Vigil should be right up your alley. The game even acknowledges the similarity with a little joke in one of its sidequests, where an NPC tells you "Where I'm coming from, monsters drop salt."Unlike other soulslike games, however, Vigil does not have a "soul retrieval mechanic". Most soulslikes have your experience be a currency that you drop upon death and have to retrieve. Vigil has a much more traditional experience mechanic: once you have gathered enough XP to level up, you do so, and your health fully regenerates. When you die, you have to reload your latest save. But like in Dark Souls and its derivatives, you can only save at checkpoints. There's also a consumable item that allows you to save anywhere, but since it's a consumable you can't use it all the time. I only used it when I expected a boss encounter and haven't been to a checkpoint in a while.Gameplay is what you might expect from the genre. You have a dodge roll which allows you to pass through enemies, you have regular and heavy attacks (the heavy attacks have to be unlocked in the skill tree first), and there are several weapon types that are all used differently. I found the difficulty to be easier than Salt and Sanctuary, and any of the Dark Souls games. Your character's movement is very fluid, stamina regenerates very quickly, and at the end you can find a sword with an overpowered special attack that trivializes even bosses (but you only find it shortly before the final chapter, so it's not too gamebreaking). It's still a challenge for most of the game, and due to the responsiveness of the controls (keyboard only, no mouse), the combat is really enjoyable.But the real focus of the game is exploration. Levels are pretty huge and the world is very open. There's a ton of secrets and optional areas, including several optional bosses and a hidden island with a hairstylist who can change your hairstyle. Exploration is heavily metroidvania-inspired: some bosses will grant you new moves after you kill them, and these moves allow you to access previously inaccessible areas.Movement skills you will learn throughout the game include a double jump, a slide that lets you pass underneath narrow passages, and an air dash that can be used as often as your stamina bar allows. Especially the slide is used very often to uncover secrets, while the air dash gets a lot of use among the treetops where you have to jump from branch to branch.Overall, it's a highly enjoyable game and I can fully recommend it to fans of both metroidvanias and soulslikes (although it's a lot less difficult than most soulslikes, so if it's the hard challenge you like about the genre, this one won't be your favorite).P.S. Leila has really cute feet ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game with satisfying combat and of what I've seen so far meaningful character progression; each time you level up feels like the character is growing stronger and that's exactly what I always want from RPGs especially metroidvania games. The art style of the game is very well done and reminds me a lot of super metroid (my favorite game ever). Overall I feel it's a super nice metroidvania with well thought out RPG elements and a dark and unique art style. The music is also super nice and reminds me of donkey kong country. I highly recommend this game and commend its developers for making something I didn't know I was waiting for.and after a few more hours I feel this might be my favorite metroidvania game (it's because of the tight combat and the overall tone). There are some negative reviews where some folks think the controls are clunky but that's actually opposite of the truth: the controls require you to pay attention to each and every fight. I beat the second boss on hard and only used 2 potions. Then a minute later a lone ghoul eats my lunch because I space off for a second. Also you can equip more than 2 rings (why is this so hard to do in games? we usually have 10 fingers!) and new equipment is visible on your character. These are all the things that make a game awesome for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun metroidvania that captures the mood and aesthetics of the grimdark Souls-like world very well.The combat is tight and responsive, which is fun. Overall, once past the earliest points in the game (basically after you have pumped sufficient points into your chosen combat style) the game is not as difficult as other Souls-likes. It's also fairly easy to cheese certain enemies and bosses using ranged attacks and magic.There's not too many leaps of faith required, which is much appreciated. You can look down with limited range by holding down the down button. There is an artifact that allows you to scout ahead with limited range, a skill that auto-revives once (thus allowing you to jump into fatal drops), and a ring that negates all fall damage.Story-wise, it's told piecemeal through character quips and lore bits, so the story will probably be an unfathomable mess the first time you play through the game. Once you start piecing together enough of the lore though, it does get quite interesting. It's too bad there's so little discussion in the online community, that the plot and the lore will probably never be fully discussed and explored.One negative point in particular is the second last boss - mad pale raven, which commits the cardinal sin of making you fight on platforms, and all it's attacks are aimed at knocking you off for the cheapest insta-kills ever. And it will probably do it to you over, and over, and over, AND OVER again. Not quite enough to warrant a thumbs down, but certainly enough frustration for me to recommend just deleting the game at this point and watching the endings on Youtube.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time playing Vigil. I've played all the From Software games, Salt and Sanctuary, and plenty other similar titles. Vigil fits right in with some solid atmosphere, level/map design and inter-connectivity. It checks all the boxes as far as my expectations were concerned. However, there are lots of bugs. I will list a few so as to sanity check other players and communicate my experience.    - The Owl Feather (unlimited use homeward bone) is the first item given to the player. Its item description has two text bugs, which is a discouraging thing to show people 1 minute deep into your game. This foreshadows a lack of polish and attention to detail, but fortunately the core experience is intact and enjoyable. That is not to say these are the only text bugs; as there are plenty throughout the whole game.   - It is laughably easy to get out of bounds in Vigil.   - There is an item called "Time Deviation" or something similar that places and anchor and allows the player to return to that spot if they reactivate the ability within five seconds. It creates a Height Exploit if the player double jumps, places the anchor, lands on the ground, then reactivates the ability and double jumps simultaneously. Several times throughout my play-through I reached unintended locations using this trick which is very easy to perform.   - The Owl Feather's "Last Owl Statue rested at" pointer does not reset upon completing the game. When New Game Plus begins, the player is able to immediately use the Owl Feather and appear at whichever statue they last used before beating the game. Typically, this will be the statue right before the final boss. This means you can start NG+, instantly port to the final boss, kill it and complete NG+ in less than five minutes. This also could cause massive scripting bugs because depending on which owl statue you port to, you get gated out from completing certain quests.   - When interacting with owl statue menus, the airborne enemies will slowly drop. Needs hotfix. (sarcasm)I really enjoyed my time with Vigil, the designs and placements of both enemies and items felt great. Isolated and oppressive atmosphere was nailed, exploration was dialed in nicely, platforming felt great and wasn't overemphasized. Enjoyable experience that I definitely recommend. I think Horheristo played it as well so you know it's a banger.

_childDocuments_.review: So there's a lot wrong with this game.It's backtrack heavy. It's glitchy as all get-out. Getting the good ending involves effortlessly navigating a nonsensical web of interconnected, time-dependent choices. It runs extremely laggy on a machine that had no problem with Ori and Hollow Knight, and that lag causes genuine game issues. If your FPS is too low, the game eats inputs, making ledge-grabs, double-jumps, progression-essential stuff basically impossible. Important traversal tech is locked three upgrades deep in the bow tree, with no sign that it's used for pseudo triple-jumping. Oh, also you'll sometimes change maps and randomly fall through the floor.That said, impulse-buy this game at full price.It's good. In spite of being a whole entomological exhibit of bugs, Vigil's LONG. This gives it time to really lean into its atmosphere and its storytelling, which start off weak but become surprisingly compelling. It also gives you time to marinate in the frankly top-tier music and background art. And the monster designs and gameplay aren't bad either.Vigil straight up rips off Dark Souls' UI, but it also learns a bunch of really important lessons from DS, including pacing and ways to introduce difficult without simply making enemy stat go up.It also takes a lot from Bloodborne---in that there's religion and gore and supernatural time-shenanigans all bundled up in an atmospheric gothic wrapper---but it very clearly has its own story to tell, and honestly I like that story better than Bloodborne's rushed, unfinished-feeling one.If you're looking for Bloodborne II, this ain't that. It's closer to Salt & Sanctuary---just way buggier.But it's still good. And it's dauntingly long for a metroidvania. I'm about halfway through, at 16 hours. You'll get your money's worth.I'm hoping the game running like butts will get patched, since it would be so, so good if there was just a toggle to remove all the water effects that'll swamp your graphics card. But even unpatched, if you have a decent rig, or if you're willing to reattempt the same jump a few dozen times because it's raining and therefore the game's eating your inputs, this is a really strong title, and I'm crossing my fingers and hoping it'll do well enough to get a sequel.
