_childDocuments_.review: If there was a "meh" option, I would pick that over thumbs-down. I'm a big fan of Salt & Sanctuary and a HUGE fan of Hollow Knight / Dark Souls. If you're a fan of those games, Vigil will likely frustrate you. The play-control feels really bad compared to the games I mentioned. Attacks and movement are laggy as well as finicky. Grabbing ledges doesn't work a lot of the time, I almost never executed a slide on the first try, and the dash is super touchy. I think the dash makes the game worse. It allows access to some secrets, but isn't very useful in combat. In fact, it makes any floating-ledge boss a lot harder.On top of this, there is some really sloppy UI programming. When you hold RB to access your item wheel, pressing up or down to cycle through items will also move your character if you're near a ladder, or will transport you to another area if you're standing in a doorway. The menu overlay has similar issues. Because the Owl Feather (Homeward Bone) is considered an item, you have to switch out of it any time you use it or you will go to cast a spell and be whisked back to the checkpoint. A Yes/No prompt like in Dark Souls would make this 100% better.Another big frustration is that they use an overflow storage system like how your Blood Vials are stored in Bloodborne, but it doesn't auto-fill your health vials at checkpoints. There isn't even a quick option to say "fill 'em up," you have to manually increase the number until it says you've exceeded your weight limit (except it's not weight-dependent; it caps how many you can hold for each item-type.) I thought the game was auto-filling for 2/3rds of my playthough. At some point, I bought 50 vials but was down to 15 way too quickly. When I finally realized what was going on, I had about 250 vials in storage!!If you're played-out of the Soulsborne games, Hollow Knight, Salt, etc, and you can get Vigil for about $10, the art-style and exploration are worth that much. Some of the enemies and bosses are really unique and there are enough secret areas to keep you wanting to know what's around the corner. I played about 25hrs, got the bad ending on Hard Difficulty, looked up what I needed to do to get the good ending, and decided it was too tedious. I applaud the art and sound design, but otherwise, "meh."
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game, really digging the style and play.Don't be fooled by the tags though, this is mostly a Metroidvania with RPG progression rather than a full Souls-like.Yes, there are multiple save points and using them respawns monsters, but there is no regenerating healing items, just consumables.And if you die, there is no going back to pick up your XP, you're just dead and need to reload.None of that stops it being good though, just don't expect another Salt & Sanctuary.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Very decent 2D Metroidvania with some obvious homages to Bloodborne and Dark Souls. Appealing art direction, atmospheric score, epic boss encounters, and appropriately unforgiving Hard difficulty. I really liked the incorporation of a skill tree and weapon specializations rather than having to spend EXP on stats. On the downside, the translation is kind of a mess and reads like someone took a Bloodborne word cloud generator and recompiled the story based on that. The map can also be a pain to parse at times, and quite a few bosses and quests are missable. But with a brisk 20-hour pace, it's very much intended that you play through the game more than once to see everything. A good time.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Animations are very good;- Good variety of weapons and armors;- Gameplay is mostly tight;Cons:- Graphics is kinda washed out and not very detailed;- You level up too fast, I had the sword tree max out and some general skills at like 60% of the game;- Most bosses and enemies are very basic;- There is no back story or lore about the world in the beginning, you are thrown in the game with no knowledge of the world and that makes it very hard to care about what's going on;- UI sometimes bugs and doesn't display item info. Reloading seems to fix;Overall: 6.5/10It's an average metroidvania that took inspiration in S&S, but didn't reach it's heights. I had fun playing it, but don't have any intention in playing it again.I recommend at a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Going into Vigil I was cautious to get too excited. I love Metroidvania games and consider Bloodborne one of the best games ever. Seeing how Vigil on the surface seems to cater to both these interest it should be a slam dunk. Sadly it wasn't. I completed the game and did all the achievement, because i'm autistic as all hell but it wasn't an enjoyable experience.I'll start with the good. It looks great (if you like this artstyle), it sounds great and there is a ton to explore. If you know where to go and can find your way around.Vigil feels bloated and empty at the same time. There are  plenty of items and hidden areas to discover. On top of that there is an army of npc's with their own corresponding side quests. However, the map is an absolute convoluted mess and getting around the 2 tiered map is a nightmare. Most items don't matter, fight styles are similar and I haven't used any of the spells. So even though there is a lot to find, it's annoying to do and once you find these items, you won't use them. The world itself feels a bit bland, since all areas look similar in tone. This being emphasized by the lack of creativity in the desing of zones. It took me a bit to realize Buffonite lake and the flooded zone weren't the same area. Both dreary looking water environments.The story is also quite messy and seems to go for a Darksouls/Bloodborne way of storytelling through bits and pieces here and there. Not sure how they did it, but they messed it up. Half the time I had no idea what was going on or where I needed to go to. When I checked my notes for help I also noticed that I already locked myself out of most of the available side quests.Lastly a personal issue. I dislike how combat seems to be disconnected from the overall gameplay. It feels static where you need to stop, engage in combat before you can go platforming on. It seems Salt & Sanctuary but it doesn't make the gameplay feel smooth or satisfying.Was really hoping for better with this game and it saddens me a bit to put out a negative review.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: The game's mechanics and story were drastically scaled back part way through development, but the developers didn't both to revise anything they had already created. As a result, the first third of the game is entirely disconnected from the rest, both in terms of story and gameplay.It's sad because the first few hours of the game are actually quite good. However, the rest is a bland, unchallenging, story-less slog. For example, there are entire areas later in the game that are just corridors with the same basic enemy repeated over and over. No boss, no quests, no key items, no need to even go there.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: This is a nice, if unpolished, 2D soulvania with passable plot and clear inspiration from Salt and Sanctuary. Being a huge fan of the latter, I didn't hesitate to buy the game in question, and so far I'm OK with the experience. Nothing stellar, nothing disastrous. I liked the concept of flashy moves upgrades the most.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the better Casoulvanias (sorry, this is a thing now, I don't make the rules) out there and I highly recommend it if you like either Souls-likes, Metroidvanias, or both. First, it looks really good. It's 2.5D, but somehow it manages to actually look good (I like Bloodstained a lot, but, well... yeah, this obliterates it, visually, despite no doubt having a much smaller budget), mostly thanks to a very strong art style. It has quite a few nods to Bloodborne as well, from outfit styles to dark gothic horror to the Night playing a large part in the story.The soundtrack is of very high quality too, with some tracks definitely having that Igavania vibe.Level design is the strongest point. Maps are huge, there's lots to explore, tons of secrets to find. I found myself genuinely impressed by how new areas kept popping up when I thought I was about to reach a dead end.  There's a good variety of locales too. Combat is solid. I admit I mostly used the longsword, as I wasn't feeling the daggers and the big axes/hammers were too slow for me, but the sword was the perfect balance of damage, stagger and speed. It never got super complicated, but that's OK, because it plays smoothly, stamina and hitboxes are mostly fair, and it's largely satisfying, outside of a few occasional questionably telegraphed attacks from some bosses. I played on Hard mode and the game was appropriately challenging without being overly brutal, I would say this game is generally easier than your average Souls game or Souls-like but it wasn't brain-dead easy either (Normal or Easy modes are probably very easy though). There's a couple of Arcane tools you can use, similarly to Bloodborne, though I've found only a handful to be actually effective, but they can mix things up a bit for some encounters.A common complaint is that some side-quests will fail kind of without warning. There is a somewhat early story beat that, once you clear this boss, will wrap up the Prologue and fail side-quests automatically and the world will shift fairly dramatically, and you can't go back to those previous areas. (This happens again later at the end of Chapter 2, but it's far better telegraphed at that point at least.) The complaint is valid, as there's really no indication that killing this one boss will cause all of this, so I can understand the frustration, but I was fortunate enough to have read those warnings and was prepared for it. All that said, if you are a bit of a  completist, keep a few saves in rotation just in case to save some headaches.This game doesn't have the RPG depth or intricate boss and level design as Salt and Sanctuary, but it has probably better visuals and music and a more straightfoward story and side-quest design. Either way, it's still a meaty game and definitely worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a metroidvania/soulslike hybrid that focuses primarily on combat and platforming/exploration, but does have a story and lore for those that enjoy that aspect as well.The combat is broken up into 4 different weapon types, each with their own distinct strengths and playstyles, and each weapon has its own unique skill tree that unlocks/powers up the moves available with that weapon, so every player is sure to find one that is comfortable for them. There are also a fairly decent amount of armor sets each with their own specific strengths, allowing the player to choose sets with the stats that are most important to their style. There is also a type of magic in the form of arcane items which would serve as your "spells", but this isn't its own skill tree or anything like weapons are, they are just items you find that have cooldowns and become stronger as you find a certain item to increase your overall arcane stat, and they serve more of a supplementary role to standard combat rather than an alternative. (I'm sure players dedicated to basing their playstyle around the arcane spells could find a way to do so, it just doesn't appear to be something the game particularly WANTS to you do)There are quite a few quests that you can choose to either complete or, simply ignore if you just wanna smash enemies until the credits role. There are also multiple endings, so there would be reason to utilize new game plus for some slightly different outcomes.The only cons I really have for this game, are that it doesn't always feel the most responsive. Most of the time it is fine, but it doesn't have that second of "input memory" that souls games have, so there will times when you try to do an action immediately after another action, (say, heal after a dodge) but you hit the button to do it a frame or 2 before your character was officially back in neutral stance, leaving you sitting there for a second waiting for your action to go through and it doesn't, but this problem may be more personal due to playing many souls and souls-like games to where the input memory feels like a natural mechanic and this game not having it feels strange, so I won't knock the game for it, it just sometimes felt off to me. The only other con I have is that this game HATES the D-pad being used to interact with menus. If you map certain commands to the D-pad (dash being on D-pad down by default, for example) and you try to navigate menus with the D-pad, it will execute those commands every time you hit that button. It will also bug out elements of the menu if using the D-pad as well, like buying in bulk using D-pad right will cause it to not visually update the price, as well as often making both the confirm and cancel buttons completely disappear. This can obviously be nullified by simply using the analog stick to navigate menus, but even that felt weird as when you are in the standard menu, left and right on the analog stick will still move your character around in the background, but up and down on the stick navigates the menu, which was why I defaulted to using the D-pad in the first place. Either way, both minor gripes, but those were the biggest problems I had with the game, which I suppose means it was pretty dang good overall if that's all I have to complain about.To sum it up, I got about 30 hours out of this game on my first playthrough trying to complete every quest and obtain most armors and weapons, and there is always new game plus if the first time just wasn't enough for you, so I would say its worth it!
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a good follower of Salt and Sanctuary. From my point of view, not as good as SaS, but close enough to give it a try.Pros: - better graphic - great music. Seriously, paying respect to compositor :) Soundtrack is on a par with HOMM or Diablo.  - quests  - fresh enchant mechanics - fun to play on hard difficultyCons:- still need to be polished. For example: control on gamepad could be more responsive. Sometimes animations looks too torn.- Perk tree too simplifyed: 4 branches for wepaon types + 1 for other things... And no stats like str\int etc... As result - no interesting builds here (actually, no builds at all here, just choose your weapon and customize it).In summary, if you like 2D metroidvanias, souls-like, and already played Salt and Sanctuary, give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptionally well done metroidvania with RPG elements. Huge map to explore with nicely varied environments and tons of secrets to find. Great atmosphere; despite a large number of NPCs to talk to, the game conveys a feeling of being alone in hostile and alien world that takes me back to the original Metroid. Very cool visual style, particularly in regard to enemy design. Epic boss fights. Wide variety of weapons. Maybe the best melee combat of any metroidvania I've played, very fluid and intuitive (also most weapons have special moves which are never overly complicated). Hard, but never infuriatingly so. If I absolutely had to gripe about something, it would be that the story is a little hard to follow and some of the quests can be slightly confusing. Still, great game; paid full price and I consider it money well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: While not quite as fun as games such as Hollow Knight and Blasphemous in my opinion, it does offer a good 15-30 hours of metroidvania adventure. My only real complaint would be that magic is way over powered making bosses trivial if you use it, dash is mapped to forward x2 which can trigger at inopportune times.Other than that the story is well done and bosses are fun, with a good collection of abilities, weapons and armor (all that changes your appearance not just stats!).If youre looking for a fun game in the likes of the previously mentioned i would recommend picking this game up.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I have a self determined truth deep inside my psyche that says "I love Souls-like Games!", so i buy and play any game that claims to be one. It's strange than that i often find myself disappointed with a game that clearly has all of the hallmarks of the genre. First let me say that this game gives me that same special magic that all of the From Soft games deliver, and it does so while changing up the formula quite a bit, adding full questlines and dialogue hubs, a large skilltree, and removing the traditional die-bonfire-fetch loop that i would have thought necessary in a true souls game. this made me rethink what really makes these games special? I think it is the lovingly crafted combat and enemy animations present here that truly make it a great game. each enemy creates a moment where strategic thought kicks in and i ask myself "how should i handle this guy?", and that's the magic that games like this and Salt and Sanctuary have.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Just.. eh. Serviceable to kill time with, but not enjoyable or satisfying at its core.The combat is easy and the only way to remedy it is oneshot mechanics to offset it, resetting your progress in weird ways — having to redo dialog/interactables since your last save point and losing -some- pickups but not -all-? Frustratingly inconsistent.The quick shot maneuver for the bow didn't seem to want to proc at all, no matter the timing or practice I put into it. Traversing the map was more a matter of frustation rather than challenge, and the singular sound for it became frustrating in minutes.The story in the first few hours was dull, seemed poorly translated and wasn't a selling point for me overall.Overall, the game runs, it will keep you busy, but entertainment wasn't there for me. Worth trying on a steep discount if you can spare the money?
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels dull and "early accessy", fighting system is repetitive, most of the monsters can be killed just by bashing one button mortal kombat style. Navigation is a cryptic maze, because there are so many useless routes that bring you nowhere, leaving a puzzling feeling of not knowing what you are doing. Exploration sparks little to no joy, because items you find are useless and you will most likely beat the game with starting weapons. Overall, buy it for no more than 5$
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: There are a couple of rough edges (seemed to get a bit worse towards the end of the game) but, overall a good time. Feels very similar to Salt and Sanctuary but, with more focus on weapon skill trees and more agile platforming. Some of the later areas sort of ran together in my mind as there are a lot of tunnels and caves. One massive plus compared to it's adjacent games... It actually has a quest log so you can keep track of all the unmarked, opaque side quests! Don't ask me what the story was
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: A soulslike metroidvania done right. The combat feels good. The weapon and gear variety is nice, the level design is interesting, and the story is damn good. I particularly enjoy how you're fed a breadcrumb trail of clues as to what is going on, and as you gradually learn more. After the first "act?" of the game, a thing happens, and you return to the town and everything seems to be going okay, and all the NPC's act like things are just fine. Meanwhile, the character is like 'what? how? why?', and I, as the player, continue on with this sick feeling thinking that things are oh so subtly wrong, even though it looks like you've accomplished what you set out to accomplish. It's a really unsettling feeling, and going through the second "act" with that feeling persisting, getting just enough hints from certain item descriptions, or hints in dialogue, keeps that lovely feeling of wrongness going. Very good, narratively speaking, and very Lovecraftian. So this is definitely an underrated work of art within the genres it falls under, and I look forward to where it's going. I guess the one complaint I have is, at a certain point, combat gets very easy. It's easy to level up, and overlevel for area (which I kind of did by accident), so most of the enemies encountered present little more than a mild annoyance. But I hope that future areas will prove me wrong, and punish me for my foolish overconfidence (as a wise man said; overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer).
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Played for over 5h and did not catch me. As a huge Salt and Sanctuary fan I was hoping to have fun with this game, but it is at least mediocre. Things that bothered me about Vigil:1. Boring map design with almost linear progress routes2. Combat/dodging/moving/jumping feeling unpolished and unresponsive3. Bad and boring boss fights 4. Boring skill tree5. No automatic (estus like) healing item restock on checkpoints6. Bad and confusing game menu, shop menus not offering stat comparing functionalityIf you consider buying this game, better invest your money in either "salt and sanctuary" or "Bloodstained: Ritual of the night" for a simalar game with way higher production quality in all aspects.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: It's not very good, but also ain't terrible. Clearly the first work of developers who didn't really know what kind of game they wanted to make.For a soulslike (like the mentioned inspiration of Salt'n'Sanctuary), combat is far to boring, clunky and messy. Bosses are unrewarding and boring as well, despite the occasional OneShot-Variant.For a metroidvania, there's no exiciting exploration, meaningful backtracking or shortcuts. There are nearly no mobility or path progressing skills you can unlock, pretty much the whole map is accessible from the start.For a platformer, the controls are too unprecise ("Dash" on right D-Pad ... y tho?), as are ledge grabs and enviromental hitboxes in general.All in all, unpolished and a mix of unrewarding and mostly boring gameplay. On a heavy discount maybe worth a shot to try out for yourself, if you haven't anything better to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: It's another decent take on the "Metroidvania" genre, that was also somewhat inspired by the Dark Souls games.  It's similar to Salt and Sanctuary in many ways, but currently could use a patch to balance out some underpowered skills as well as rethink their item placement for some weapons.  The game also currently uses the analog for movement, which cannot be remapped yet.  It's fine for general gameplay, but there are some skills and weapon moves that require precise cardinal inputs, and they are very hard to get to work reliably with the analog.  Other than that, the story is simply "OK" and needs a better translation, but the general art design is great, and it also has a really good soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: A really mid metroidvania overall. Gameplay and exploration are good, but most of the systems are a bit janky/outdated and being able to lock yourself out of completing quests, getting certain endings or items is a bit annoying. Would maybe recommend if you really like metroidvanias and have nothing else to play, but wouldn't say you miss out on much by skipping this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually play these sort of games, but the art style of this one really caught my attention, After reading some reviews I decided to give it a shot and I'm glad I did. The gameplay is an absolute and the world is incredibly captivating with the music perfectly complementing that.I hope enough people will give this a try because the devs have done an amazing job with this game, they deserve all the praise they get ... and we deserve a sequel :D ... or at least an expansion
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Salt and Sanctuary so I was excited about trying this after hearing they are similar but fortunately I cannot recommend this game. Not 100% sure where it went wrong, but in general, I felt like the controls weren't intuitive or as responsive.Art is not bad, nothing about this game is really bad, but it doesn't make me want to come back to play it.Sorry for being vague.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Great Metroidvania with a compelling story and a good combat system. The evolution of the character is straight-forward but you can still create your own builds and forge/enchant a plethora of items to help you during the journey.Another good thing to mention is the OST, while it is not complex it fits the scenarios really well. Sometimes a mixture of the main character and the OST plus the scenarios reminds me a little of Valkyrie Profile from PS1 which is good.If you like Metroidvania games go for it, this is a solid choice. I give it a 8.5 of 10.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game expecting more Souls and Sanctuary, which vaulted in my fave soulslike/metroidvania ever. What I got was something very different with definite influence, but unique in story and gameplay. Didn't know if I was going to like it at first, but the controls/mechanics are solid. Music is better than SaS, but the controls are a bit less refined.  8/10 so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing this 4 hours straight on the first time I launched the game, so that's enough to give it a thumbs up.  Anyone who was a fan of Salt & Sanctuary or 2D Souls-Likes will love this.  It nails everything well without re-inventing the wheel.That said, I want to voice a major complaint/concern that almost made me stop playing around 20 minutes in.The game gives you the initial tutorials and action sequence, culminating in the first boss.  At this point it's got you hungry to start exploring and fighting.Then....Massive.  Exposition.  Dump.   And Dialogue.  This halts the cadence and forces you to go through a LARGE non-combat area which left me questioning my purchase.Fortunately, if you can get past this sequence, it gets better and stays better as far as I can tell (4 hours in, no sign of stopping, already worth the price of admission).  With a few minor exceptions it's been nonstop action after that point.  I love how truly open the world becomes, tons of options for where to go next after the Gate.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who hasn't played Salt and Sanctuary, Dark Souls, Bloodborne, or any of those other titles I've seen mentioned in reviews of this game, I liked Vigil a lot. The music by Jouni Valjakka is f***ing fantastic and really sets the mood, encompassing a lot of emotions as well as keeping the energy high when it needs to be; some areas sound Hollow Knight-esque in their sheer scale, while some feel borrowed from Castlevania titles and one cello-heavy piece even strongly reminded me of the Joker soundtrack (high praise coming from me). The graphics, while not necessarily my preferred style, definitely fit the "f***ed-up storybook" feel of the overall game and amplified many of the more horrific aspects of the creature designs, which I feel was the correct thing to emphasize given the game's dark storyline.Of course there are some nitpicks and issues I have with a few of the game's weak spots. These include ample typos, fairly-common bad grammar, an unintuitive map system, an inability to quickly look down when descending dark areas, fall damage being implemented in an exploration game (for some reason), and a very limited set of equipment options; in fact I just ended up upgrading the base sword and using that for the whole game, since everything else was either too clunky or too short-ranged. Nevertheless, I eventually adapted to these shortcomings and finished my first playthrough with a sense of satisfaction at its overall implementation, along with a desire to go back and keep exploring the far-flung areas of the game's enormous map afterwards.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful gameIt take some ideals from the souls formula but very little and is basically a love craft like story with crazy weird stuff to keep you saying "what tha ****" all the more Combat is solid and easy pick up and the skill tree allows you to be very invested in 1 weapon typeThe art choice and world building is beautiful and nightmare fuel 10/10The characters are interesting enough that i remember their names which is rare in games now days i highly recommend this game
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I could type up multiple paragraphs about why this game is amazing, why it has a super fun battle system with decent depth and fair difficulty, why the story is well written and a fascinating piece of cosmic horror fiction with memorable characters or why the level design is gorgeous and a joy to explore with tons of secrets to uncover or why the OST is a masterfully composed atmospheric masterpiece, but instead I'll just say that this game has quickly become one of my all time favorite metroidvanias and I've played far too many metroidvania games to count in my 20+ years of gaming experience.Vigil is a game that wears it's influences and inspirations proudly on its sleeve, but it wears them well and just as great as the games it is influenced and inspired by and really all I can say is if you're a fan of Castlevania, Bloodborne, Lovecraft, Dark Souls, Salt and Sanctuary or all of the above you'd be a fool to miss out on this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I am probably biased due to enjoying Salt & Sanctuary greatly, which this game got it's inspiration from... But i enjoyed this. Sure, it is not triple A in terms of graphics, writing or performance wise, but i liked it. Music was great, design of locations was atmospheric, story, though a bit twisted, is quite solid in the end. The only thing i could nag on - exploration not being rewarded enough - is currently being taken care of in patch which is currently in open beta. Also the game allows you to get quite strong pretty fast, which takes from challenge of the game a little bit, even on hard.I can recommend this to anyone looking for Souls-inspired 2D metroidvania game.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Game has a lot of diversity for playstyles and accommodates the difficulty pretty well for a first playthrough. Obviously some imbalance between different weapons and I'm not a hug fan of being able to mostly bully your way through a fight with too many heals but other than that the game is very solid.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I had a good time playing this game. It is inspired heavily by Salt and Sanctuary, which is a great thing in my opinion. It has a large, open map for you to explore at your leisure, but be warned progressing too far in the map will break questsines, with no warning. I have two story achievements I missed because I did a few things out of order. They can be achieved on a second playthrough, however.The animations are a little rough, but not too distracting. The story and lore borrow from Souls like games where they trickle details to you over the course of the game, but in my opinion, it doesn't form one cohesive plot.There are many weapon types to choose from, and each plays differently. This adds an additional layer to the fun of combat.Overall, a good game, and I'd recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic Metroidvania. If you like Salt & Sanctuary, you will likely really enjoy this as well. It's got a few mechanics that are different from others in the genre which makes it feel unique and familiar at the same time. I found the bosses a little on the easy side on the normal setting, while the exploration was more challenging. There are many secrets to find and I had a lot of fun tracking them down.While it doesn't have the same budget as Bloodstained (for example) with a more limited weapon/spell selection, I wouldn't let that keep you away. The game has a lot of heart and I've loved every minute I've been playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give this one a solid 6/10. Why only in the middle range? Well, the game does a lot of things right: Graphics are nice, sound and music as well, controls are responsive, weapon skills and variety are ok. However, the game is just... unremarkable. If compared to other similar games, even on normal, you more or less can just breeze through. In the first 2/3 of the game I did not have to learn any boss patterns, since it was completely sufficient to dash at the right moment behind him, attack, rinse and repeat. Only the latter bosses posed somewhat of a challenge, but even though, with just one adapted move (jump and attack from above) this was all there was to beat them quite easily. So, no, it is not a bad game, but also nothing too memorable either, which would warrant me to play it a second time. Good to buy on big discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:-Almost open world exploration with lots of interesting side quest.-Your decisions matter on the story-Simple and yet amazing gameplayCONS:-You will need a gamer PC to play this game, I run games like Code Vein and RE2 without issues but has problems running this game on my PC.-Underwhelming endingsMy final score 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: You play as a female protagonist who enters the world at a time of upheaval. The game gives you a lot of areas to explore, NPCs to talk to and choices to make. Where you explore, the order you explore in, the choices that you make all dictate the ending that you end up getting at the end of the game.This game uses metroidvania-like world progression and skill unlocks, some of which are even optional to discover but if you take the time you unlock more secrets or areas that you wouldn't have otherwise. It also uses Salt and Sanctuary-like combat, and has a level-up system that awards one point per level-up that you need to put into weapon or passive skills to help you progress through the game.One very important point is that progression follows the traditional metroidvania style where you have to be thoughtful about saving, and saving often. When you die the game will reload your last save and any progress you had made will be lost.I played through before the large update. There was a lot of jank in the combat, the translations were pretty mangled and you could really get yourself into trouble with quest progression or miss content if you weren't careful. I reloaded after the update and combat feels much tighter and translations looked better. Patch notes say other trouble areas were improved, so I would assume this is now easier to get into and enjoy than before.The only thing I did not like at all was the "point of no return" mechanics in the game where if you progress past a certain point it progresses the story and you lose access to any quests, items etc that you had missed. Unsure if the update addresses this somehow with a warning or something, but keep it in mind when you play. If you like to explore, do it early and if you feel you are about to progress the main story line in a significant way then just wait until you finish the other things you wanted to do.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an attempt at a completely spoiler-free review while still speaking about mechanics in specifics and storytelling in general. GREAT STORYTELLINGThis game pleasantly surprised me with its mystery story arc and the great number of NPCs that each have a separate grim background. The central village hub was an area I returned to multiple times for clues or quests, which is different to many other metroidvania games where the town is usually only a place for buying and selling things and the quests are bland and don't feel very important at all. In this game I think they do and I think the storytelling is very good overall.SOME DAY 1 BUGSI played the game during the first few days after release so there were some bugs, most notably with damage-increasing upgrades, but I could still beat all content and it didn't affect my experience very much.CONTROLS - A SMALL LEARNING CURVEThe controls initially felt a bit slow to me - not as distinct to some other platformers. I'm not sure how to explain it, but maybe that there is a slight amount of acceleration or just that it takes time to swing your big halbeard. I also had severe problems with dodging timing initially. The first time I met the first boss I got it down to 10% hp, only dodging reactively since I didn't know the moveset. The following 10+ times I performed much worse since I was dodging too fast, trying to perceive the incoming attack. However, this feeling slowly subsided and towards the end of the game I didn't think about it at all.POINT OF NO RETURNThere is one occasion, not too far into the game, where you progress to a point when some quests can no longer be completed. There is no warning and no real reason for you to expect that this will happen. This is both bad and good. It's bad if you want to complete everything in the game, but from a story point of view I think it's great, so I'm not sure I want the developers to put a warning anywhere and I still think I would prefer to not knowing this when playing the game for the first time. Instead, see it as a recommendation to everybody reading this to speak to the townspeople and resolve as many quests as possible as often as you can, if you go the completionist route. At the same time, I could get one of the rewards I missed later on in the game and could get a better version of the other reward I missed, so I don't think this is a big deal.ENEMY DROPS = $When playing it was not clear to me that basically all drops from enemies can be (and maybe should be) sold. It says in their description that they can be, but also that they could be used in some crafting situations (at least the component I was reading at the time). But for most cases unless there is a quest involved - you can sell these items as there is no such crafting in the game. You don't get much from them, but it could be good to know in the early part of the game when you typically need money. Obviously there are also weapon and armor drops that you may want to use yourself instead of selling. =)WEAPON SKILLSThere are 4 different skill trees for the various weapon types you can use and one skill tree for general updates. Throughout my playthrough this felt good to me. I initially wanted to go with swords but after trying out the first halbeard you get I was sold on the heavy weapons approach and nearly maximized this tree.I think it can be smart to focus on one weapon category. The game promotes fast weapon cycling but to be honest I never used it other than for DPS testing. I guess some enemies will be easier if you equip a bow, but I just didn't feel the need for it.WEAPONSGenerally it can take some time to find new weapons in the game, so don't be afraid to at least get your weapons up to +3 as early as you can. There are many ways to get more upgrade materials throughout the game. Only the final upgrade, +7, should be done with caution as this material is much more rare. If I have anything negative to say about the weapons it's that I found 3 different axes that were almost identical in moveset and DPS. North wind, Axe of Retribution and Northgale were the weapons I used for the majority of the game, but they felt very similar with no noticable special effects or movesets. Their DPS was also fairly close, so each upgrade didn't feel as much as an upgrade and more like wasted upgrade materials.ENCHANTINGApart from upgrading the weapons you can also enchant them. You can enchant armor too. While the armor buffs are fairly straightforward, I have a small complaint that the weapon buffs or the debuffs to enemies are not very clear in what they do. Backstab damage is self-explanatory, but what does curse even do? I had that effect on me a couple of times but noticed nothing different. Is poison better than burning damage? Is there a way to scale these damage overer time effects? I'd like some better explanation here as nobody knew anything about this during the early days when I played.MAGICI used magic occiasionally but didn't specialize much as I felt the control for this was a bit wonky and magic is available on a cooldown basis (per spell). The way you select your spells through either a wheel menu or by pushing a button for "next" didn't feel very good to me so I just put one damage spell in the wheel and then utility stuff (such as warping) for the rest.RESPECCINGThere is a way to respec your points in the game. I would say you can access it about half-way. It's a bit hidden though. Nya! =)CONCLUSIONTo summarize, this game exceeded my expectations of an indie title. The game was at least 2-3 times bigger than I thought initially and I really liked the mystery and almost detective work surrounding the story. It kept me captivated and I kept playing more or less for two and a half day straight until I had finished it and experienced all three endings. If there is ever a sequel, I'm sure to buy it too! =)

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY want to like Vigil and I would likely give it a rating of between like and dislike but that option isn't available. I am a big fan of soulslike/metroidvania like Blasphemous/Hollow Knight and Ori (and obviously souls games) so this game should be right up my alley. There is just something simple OFF about this game that doesn't kick in as much until the sunken city or forest area and despite pushing through I couldn't bring myself to play more. The most annoying thing for me was the miss able quests and items in a game and genre that should be rewarding curiosity and going off the beaten track. I struggle to comprehend how you could know some of this without using a guide otherwise you will notice yourself having failed quests in your log. Secondly the weapon skill tree is decent but some passives/actives are either poorly translated or just lack an explanation of how they actually work and are very vague so it's hard to decide if you wasted a point. The game also has an issue with giving you multiple of the same item or simply giving you a worthless ring for your efforts as there seems to be randomly generated ring stats. Lastly while the map is servicable it is far from perfect and often made things way more confusing than it had any right to be... Why can't more metroidvanias give tons of different types of markers for interesting spots to return to since there is so much backtracking???!!!The game does have it's positives such as the grim dark kind of mood and feel of the world itself which really gives a mysterious vibe. The combat itself can have its moments and there is a fair few weapons to try that are mostly different to each other. There are other positives and they are likely the elements of metroidvanias that i haven't mentioned but the flaws are really annoying. This is the kind of game I would honestly say watch a bunch of reviews or playthroughs to decide because it misses the mark but at times makes me think it could have been one of the greats. I even saw it on sale recently on switch and still considered it but reminded myself I have tried twice and quit but something about the game must have stuck with me in some way.... maybe an improved sequel?If you are still curious I would suggest a nice sale price before purchasing.

_childDocuments_.review: This one got *very* close to getting a thumbs down, if there was a "neutral" option in here it would be that.+ its a soulslike+ music + atmosphere+ combat is fun, weapons offer distinctly different playstyles; unique weapons also have "special moves", somewhat similar to weapon arts in DS3, but in here theyre triggered by combo moves that vary depending on the weapon + quite lenghty for the price + decent lategame bosses+ small thing but theres some clever enemy design that allows you to use living enemy as a platform to reach inaccessible spots, and also killing particular enemies in the right spot leaves (parts of) their corpses which you can use as a leg up +/- visuals are a mixed bag, some parts and designs look really nice (ie. town, statues of the Goddess, her design in general), but in other parts it's quite an eyesore and a  bizarre mix of painted elements and phototextures (mine area is particularly bad, especially the pixelated conifer trees); also large portion of characters have the "thanks for not aborting me" look about them; overall it looks like a mobile game - animations leave things to be desired on certain bosses - a lot of attacks are barely telegraphed, bosses go from neutral stance to full on attack in 0.1 sec with barely any indication or animation, and that includes 180 turns into full attack with zero frames inbetween (first boss is #1 example of this)- english translation is clumsy and awkward, half of the dialogues make no sense and it seems like every NPC is either high, drunk, or high and drunk; large portions of text in this game were clearly translated without context - even though its a soulslike its still using a traditional saving system, so you walk up to a bonfire and save the game manually - if you die you reload the game fully, meaning you lose all the items youve picked up between last save and dying, and so on, all progress is gone, all opened shortcuts are reverted back etc.; overall this just makes things more tedious since you literally have to fully redo entire levels and pick everything up again instead of just running through after death; you even lose the map reveal progress- for some reason Vigil insists on showering you with "traditional" quests instead of letting you organically explore the game world like other soulslikes do; large portion of those quests are very vague - horrible translation certainly doesnt help - with little indication as to where should you even look for the objectives, so you basically end up completing some of those on accident, and others will sit in your questlog for hours with zero progress; for example, youre gonna get a quest that basically states "find item x for this NPC" - where is item x? Which even general area could it be in? Who knows, it could be literally anywhere in the game world. Later it turns out its some easily missable thing in a chest in a remote place that logically had nothing to do with the quest giver. And it keeps going like this. Also, said quests can be failed by progressing to the next chapter before completing them, and the game doesnt tell you that at all beforehand- lots of pet peeves with the interface and lack of polish; ie. there's a quick item wheel you can use in this game, you activate it on by pressing up on left thumbstick - and then you scroll through by rotating the wheel.... using the d-pad. So you just have to quickly grow a second thumb I guess.  Whoever designed this clearly didn't have a controller in mind. None of these problems are there when youre using a keyboard-  - one of the basic moves you get in this game (dash) requires you to , which is extremely unreliable with the thumbstick, and you will end up accidentally triggering it at worst times; it's keyboard or d-pad on the controller in this game (unless you hate yourself and enjoy suffering); honestly it should come with a  warning considering how many issues I've ran into while trying to play it with a controllerOverall its 5/10, way below the core installments in the "2d soulslike" genre like Salt&Sanctuary. There are some good bits there, like the combat, but its getting dragged down by trying to awkwardly mix traditional rpg with soulslikes.

_childDocuments_.review: I've finished Vigil : the longest night and here are my two cents. It's a 2D metroidvania with aesthetics and UI heavily inspired by Bloodborne and likely some of the best background artwork since Ori and the Blind Forest series. Despite its inspiration, this is through and through a 2D platforming game with Soulsborne style combat where you explore and fight to unlock traversal skills to access previously locked areas. There are no corpse retrieval and you will need to reload to a previous save upon death, but consumable quicksave anywhere item exists to keep the frustration minimum. Outstanding artwork aside, the game is weighted down by rough edges and janky implementations. The character animation feels stiff and floaty. Even when playing on a PS4 controller, I have trouble consistently pulling off many of the Street Fighter style special moves. The double tap forward to dash is especially hard to do, which the developer apparently recognizes and allowed player to assign the action to a button press. The map is functional but really should allow manual adding of notes so that I remember to come back for that shiny I can see but can not reach presently, or at the very least, some kind of color coding to indicate that I've found everything there is to find in this section of the map. Moreover all the rooms are for some reason divided into three map layers that requires a button press to switch in between. Navigation would be much less of a chore if all the rooms are just shown on one map. The biggest problem I have with the game is that the platforming is uninspired. There is no moment where I would go "I can't believe I managed to jump all the way up here." or "This section used to be a slog to get through, but my new traversal skill made it a cinch." The game simply does not challenge player to anything more complicated than jump, air dash, double jump, air dash. Which is a shame as I'm of the philosophy that the heart of a Metroidvania is ultimately about the exploration and traversal, the fighting portion plays second fiddle and just need to be functional. I wanted to give this game a thumbs up on the strength of its art design, but there are just too many Metroidvania that excels in both art and gameplay. : Hollow Knight, La Mulana, Ori, Bloodstained, Ender Lilies, Astalon, to name a few that I've played. I finished the game on the second end but locked out of the third ending due to a side quest that I did not finish in the prologue. I could start a New Game to get the final ending, but I just don't feel like I could stomach the clunky gameplay anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most enjoyable metroidvania I've played so far, surely because it kinda mixes Castlevania with Bloodborne. Everything is almost top notch (few exceptions below). The soundtrack is great, the artstyle is magnificient, and the length provides you enough to do, and probably will motivate you to do a NG+ run.Some of the things that could be improved :-The controls are pretty great except for the dash, having to play with the stick will trigger some hiccups with the dash as you have to double tap the direction to dash. Meaning you'll probably fall from a cliff MANY times because of this.-The map system is, to be honest, horrible. The map is really cryptic to look into and have fun having a headache while you're trying to use fast travels too, as every checkpoint has its own name but you don't know in which area it leads... So you have to use the map for this and.. ugh.-The quest system. I love going for lore and stuff but the quest system is cryptic and annoying as hell. It will provide you minimal info about where you need to go and who you have to bring an item to. Sometimes you'll have the NPC's name, which leads you to go "Oh, let me see where this guys was!" and then you'll probably check your map... Ouroboros style, read the point just above and have fun.-The loot system: The bosses give you stuff when you beat them but it's a percentage so you'll probably miss a ton of weapons / armors because of this... Which I find weird because some people won't probably go into NG+.Except for these few things that could improve with QOL fixes, the game is incredible, some bossfights are epic as hell and the overall ambiance is marvelous.Length was about 12 hours to go for the "sad ending" because my path to the good ending was locked because I forgot one item in the prologue (which is a point of no return), but steam playtime is more of 18/19hours since I've died a lot. I'm now into NG+ and i'm trying to keep things straight to get my good ending.Played in Hard mode, Sword user(Which has a good variant from Salt'n Sanctuary that's kinda OP)

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 2: I finished the game and didn't lose my progress once when quitting the game by going back to the main menu, so I'll change the review to a positive one. Seriously, go play it, it's one of the best game I played recently. Tons of freedom, both in exploration, gameplay AND story, lots of plot twist, great music interesting lore, and stunning visuals.Edit: I did some investigating, and I figured it out, I think. Basically if you exit the game using steam big picture or alt+f4, the game simply delete your most recent save. Even if you wait for a while before quitting. So when you quit the game make sure to go back to the main menu and then exit or you'll lose some progress. Really hope this will be fixed soon though.                                                  ---------------------------------I am loving the game so far, however there is one MAJOR issue that really needs fixing: I'm losing progress every time I quit the game...I go back something like 2 or 3 saves behind... Last time it happened was when I was doing the quest called "errands" where you need to talk to a bunch of people to get medicine. I quit the game after finishing the quest, however when I opened it back up, I was still at the mill before getting the medicine. Like my most recent save was erased.I also lost every items I collected like the paintings and stuff and I'm pretty forgetful so I might miss some of them the next time I explore the area. I really hope this gets a fix soon, as the game so far is fantastic.For now I don't recommend but I'll try to change my review as soon as I stop losing progress.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this reveiw i have finished my first playthrough and am partway into starting my second as a clean up run. The long and the short of it is that i really like this game, i wasnt expecting a whole lot going in and what i got out of it was well worth it. Now to the meat of it, i will start with the negatives first: The biggest issue i has with the game was the speed of the camera, specificaly its vertical movement was slow that i would often have to wait a moment for it to catch up when acending or decending at too fast a pace.I encountered afew bugs while playing the game, two of which soft locked me and required me to reload. One was a collision issue with the geometry, the other one was during a boss fight where while i was ducking an attack and shooting arrows i swapped to another weapon and was hit by the ongoing attack, the death animation played but the screen did not change, leaving me on the floor dead unable to do anything while the boss thrashed around like i was still alive.The bow occasionally seemed to miss attacks due to odd hitboxes, usualy sliding under when i felt like it should have hit.One very slight nitpick for the start is that i think you should start with a basic version of each weapon type, as that would help a player decide what weapons they wish to focus on earlier and lastly i noticed afew spelling errors though cannot remember the specifics as of this moment.As for the positives: The Art style is fantastic and alot of love has clearly been put into it and the music to acompany it is great, im especialy a big fan with how hard the forest theme goes in which game me some castlevania vibes.Enemy design can be horrific at times which only helps highlight the art direction and wouldnt look out of place in other games with lovecraftian themes like bloodborne and darkest dungeon.The story is quite interesting, though i wont pretend that im not still alittle confused on some parts which my next playthrough should clear up.The notes system is so simple and yet for a soulslike/metroidvania which are typically very obscure by design on what you should be doing next, is incredibly helpful in pointing you in the right direction if you get lost and cant figure out what to try next. The combat is fun, im especially a big fan on the negative stamina bar that lets you keep attacking but at a penalty to attack power and punishes you if you get too greedy. i played with a sword and bow primarily and was surprised at how agile they both where when leveled up.I could go on but this is already long enough, suffice to say if your interested int this then give it a shot i ended up really liking this one alot more then i was expecting to.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:  A very solid, fun to play metroidvania / souls-like with great art, beautiful music, and an engaging story unfortunately marred by numerous bugs and design quirks.Pros:First off, the base gameplay is very fun and getting into the sword combos felt very natural right from the start of the game.  Most of the weapons seem to have interesting and varied movesets, although I only messed with the sword and dual daggers myself.  I definitely appreciated that moving forward on a skill tree only ever needs one point so you can spam through to get the moves that you want and then improve the numbers on each move later.  I also thought the tutorial boss was a great opportunity to solidify the game's mechanics and general boss strategy just a few minutes into the game.  The bosses are each unique in design and all provide a respectable challenge and spectacle to keep you interested.  During these fights and your exploration of the world, the music is a great mix of gentle ambiance with bouts of harder rock or metal that gives a very symphony of the night feel to the game.  Finally, the story hits that sweetspot of leaving out just enough information to keep you thinking about it, but without being frustratingly obtuse. Before I go into the cons I want to clearly say YOU SHOULD BUY THIS GAME.  For all its faults I feel it is definitely a worthwhile experience, especially at around $21.Cons:The save system was the biggest issue for me.  The game has souls-like "bonfires" that you rest, save, and can teleport from.  However, when you die, instead of just returning to the bonfire and losing some currency or something, you have to reload a save.  This doesn't sound like much, but it means all item pickups and xp you got are just gone with no chance to retrieve them without doing everything all over again.  Sometimes bonfires can be very far apart or you can just happen to miss one and end up losing 20 minutes or more of progress on death.  Small point, but you also have to actually hit save when you trigger the "bonfires."  Every time you sit you need to take the time to save or it doesn't count.  I also noticed there's no way to delete saves.  I tried to make multiple saves for story decisions and then found I had no way to clean them up later which was a little awkward.Another problem with exploration was the map.  I had a very hard time reading where the edges of the map were.  The difference between a fogged zone like near the ceiling of the area that you haven't and never will reach and the defined walls was very subtle and made figuring out where I had and hadn't been already very challenging. There were also areas that wouldn't be revealed on the map even after you had visited them so I found myself going back to these places several times thinking I had found a new secret only to find the chests already empty.  I usually don't end up using map notes systems, but I feel like including one here would have gone a long way.When you finally got where you were going, there wasn't always a boss there.  There were a good number of bosses in the game, but they seemed to all be crammed towards the end.  The early portion of the game has 3 bosses spaced nicely and then I probably went 10 hours before my next boss.  After a story event opens up the map, you basically have no bosses until you reach 3 in parallel far ends of the map.  But, once you reach that point, you have the 3 I already mentioned and then another 3-4 involved in the final sequence of the game almost back to back.As for bugs, I found quite a few in my travels.  These weren't gameplay bugs per se in that the game always ran smoothly and consistently.  However, I found things such one or two npc's disappearing when I returned to turn in a quest or an expensive enchantment on a weapon not causing any difference in damage.  There was also a weapon that was said to improve enchantments on it, but I did some testing and the 50% of enchantments that give status procs aren't improved at all.  That was an annoying one to figure out because the exact effects of status effects is never mentioned anywhere.  The biggest one for me though, was when I tried to get an alternate ending and instead of starting the cutscene when I killed the final boss, I was returned control of my character with a static boss in the background with no hp bar, forcing me to proceed with the normal ending.   I tried like 3 times and just couldn't get it to trigger, it was very disappointing.  There are also some typos in the npc dialogs but I didn't mind that too much personally.I will reiterate that I definitely think this game is worth a purchase.  I really enjoyed my ~20 hour  trip through the game and am probably going to play a NG+.  If you enjoy metroidvania's or souls-likes, this game is an easy buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:+ The art style is absolutely beautiful. It's distinct and unique. Very different from the other metroidvanias. No wonder the game got an award for it.+ The main idea for the game is interesting and intriguing. Most of the stuff you encounter forces you to piece the story together on your own. + While the game has a narrative, and it does tell you what to look for, it's up to you to find the places and the people on your own. No holding hands whatsoever.+ The combat is fluid, can be approached in A LOT of ways and gives you a lot to experiment with. Plenty of weapons have their own unique attack and basically everything can be enchanted and upgraded. There are 4 skill trees: ranged, axes, swords and bows. You can use them all at the same time. It's also possible to specialize in throwing weapons (which can be busted if you invest enough in them) and magic. Don't worry, you can respec your character mid-game. + The music is splendid, each and every track fits the theme perfectly.+ The bosses are great! All of them are very different from each other mechanically. It's possible to beat them using whichever style you decide to use, but once you start fighting a boss, you can tell which style you're supposed to be using. Some of them are weaker to some elements, and they also use elemental attacks, so it makes sense to gather items that provide resistance. + When you die, you are transported to the last saving spot and you lose ALL your progress. Items gathered, levels etc. Some people may not like this, but I found it stimulating, as it made me play safer and not rush in blindly.+ The game isn't hard, so I advise you to play on hard difficulty.Cons:- Some quest resolutions are still buggy,- There are still some bugs in the gameplay. For example, infinite falling down, damage not registering. It can be very frustrating when you make a lot of progress and then just randomly die and lose it all.- You can very easily lock yourself out of dlc and, as a result, lose A LOT of content. They should've made access to the dlc more straightforward.- There are no voicelines in the game, which in a way adds to the game's atmosphere. However, it also makes it harder to identify with the main character.- Some achievements are bugged, and you may need to get to NG+ and try getting them all over again on the replay.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil is a platforming game with stamina-based combat set in a dark fantasy universe with a lot of eldritch undertones and blood magic. You play as Leila, a Vigilant, which is a local order of religious monster-hunters. Majority of the game takes place around your hometown of Maye, as you seek to understand why there are so many monsters in the countryside; what is the origin of a mysterious plague; and how does your sister Daisy fit into the mysterious plot that's unravelling as the game progresses. The game borrows from the metroidvania genre, as killing bosses unlocks extra traversal abilities, such as double jump, slide and dash moves; these are all useful in uncovering the myriad of secrets scattered throughout the game's sprawling and interconnected maps; however, game's progression is largely linear (though it's possible to bypass a few areas based on some of your quest choices). There's a good chunk of RPG in here, as you can mix and match Leia's equipment, from 4 weapon types to 5 individual armour pieces (armour, greaves, helmet/cape, gloves, mask), and customize your build with skills from 5 different skill trees. Unless you REALLY grind, you're not supposed to unlock all skills in a single playthrough (though you should be able to by NG+), so build variety is supposed to matter. The game's closest comparison would be "Salt and Sanctuary" (the developers are fans, and there's even a small eEaster egg quest/collab with that game. Since I have not yet played "Salt and Sanctuary", I can't really comment on this resemblance. Taken on its own, the story is suitably fascinating, as it's all about the breadcrumbs you find in a few corners of the map, plus the item descriptions; And the maps are a blast to explore. The combat isn't my favourite part of the game, but it's serviceable, and seems you can make any of the main weapon types (swords, halberds/axes, dual daggers or bows) build work- though a few (mostly optional) enemies are basically easy mode with a bow, so a few skills in that are kind of necessary. The meat of the game is exploration and secret-hunting, though. If you look hard enough, you can find a magic item that highlights most hidden pickups (except the Arcane Items themselves), and trying to find them all without referring to a guide is one of the best parts of the game. The bosses are pretty memorable, as all of them are unique. It's not a very difficult game, but it delivers a good balance of challenge and options to tailor your build/equipment to make challenges more manageable- as a good RPG should. The music tends to fit the mood of the game nicely; I liked the art style and art direction, though that's obviously subjective; But I can't overstate this- if you like exploring 2D maps for secrets, this game is perfect. There were some bugs (mostly with NG+ progression) but the team squashed most of them and are busy working on others. Game plays great on keyboard, no clue about controllers. Buy this game. It's unique, it plays well, and exploration is a blast. If you like gothic action-adventures with RPG elements that don't require a calculus degree and optimal min-max every time, this is a perfect game for you!

_childDocuments_.review: Decent metroidvania-like game, a lot of cool weapons and spells with lots of enemy and area variety. Tons of gear that allowed for making specific builds for both the chosen weapon type and for the type of areas/bosses that were available. Would have been nice though if there were more attacks for each weapon type in the skill trees because it became very spammy after a while with the limited amount of attacks. The main quest story is interesting with fun characters but very predecible. Most side quests have boring rewards but some of them are very worth doing just to see the outcome for the characters they belong to.Gameplay I feel like has a lot of similarities to games like Blasphemous, though Vigil is way more clunky in every aspect except being way easier to complete. I wish the unlockable shortcuts made more sense, in many cases they were super strange because they were often for small specific places that didn't need shortcuts. Navigating through the world was pretty fast and easy anyways though.I'm happy with my purchase and the time spent on the game. I don't feel like doing 100% of the game, or a second playthrough, it's just not that much fun of a game for doing that. I'm pleased with the amount of side quests I completed and the ending I got.

_childDocuments_.review: A good metroidvania with a very clear Soulsborne influence and a grim story that follows the "show (in collectible notes and item descriptions), not tell" rule.Pros:- A huge world with its own history, plenty of npcs that have a lot to say about each other and react to current events.- Many sidequests, some have Consequences.- Looks good, sounds good. Cool boss designs.- A lot of platforming, albeit somewhat simplistic. A lot of stuff to find and collect in each area.- Large build variety. Four main weapon types (swords, axes, daggers, bows), many spells and consumables to use. Respec is available. Also has pretty decent Fashion Souls. You can play dress up with the protagonist, there's plenty of gear to be collected and even 3 hairstyles to choose from.- The game is stingy with money and upgrade materials at the start, but in the second half of the game you can comfortable try out different weapons and upgrade armor.- Replayability and NG+ mode. There's a lot of well hidden collectibles, a number of sidequests have different outcomes and rewards, and understanding the story definitely requires more than one playthrough.- The drawn map is fantastic, and there's a spell that can be found roughtly mid-game that can reveal all not yet collected items (except for one type of them) and which makes backtracking less of a chore than it could've been. Quest journal is present, albeit kinda messy.- Savepoint/fast travel points are placed relatively well, not too close and not too far from each other to become an annoyance.- There's a catboy.?- Combat is relatively simple and kinda relaxing even on the hardest difficulty (which can be changed at any point anyway), which can be a pro for everyone who's there for story and exploration, and a disappointment for everyone who enjoys getting killed in a single hit.- Maingame and optional bosses aren't very hard, even the final boss, but DLC bosses are a massive difficulty spike.- Imo the decision to hide almost the entire story behind optional collectibles is questionable. For example, the 'mystery' behind the prologue sequence is explained by a single piece of gear that is a non-guaranteed drop from a hidden optional boss, and is never mentioned anywhere else. Even if you go out of your way to read every single item description and find every note you will find that there's plenty of story bits that get no explanation, not even vague hints. There also appear to be some mistranslations here and there that add to the confusion. Vigil is a  story-driven game with plenty of dialogue and action (well, for a metroidvania), but at time the game acts like actually knowing its story is a crime.Cons:- ^ As a result, Vigil can be hard to play with long breaks between sessions. It's confusing enough even when you're trying to actively pay attention.- Small bugs, although afaik nothing actually game-breaking.- A couple of technical issues, too. For example, remapping a controller's buttons can be a problem, as it also affects menus in a weird way. By remapping certain buttons you can get yourself stuck in a menu, unable to exit it with the controller. Doesn't affect the keyboard afaik.- Some areas appear to be huge just for the sake of being huge, while not much is actually going in them in terms of environmental hazards, platforming, or enemy variety. It can get repetetive.- Has some combat balancing issues, certain spells and weapons are too op, others feel kinda useless. Status effects are barely explained.- A lot of shortcuts are absolutely useless thanks to the abudance of savepoints which also operate as fast travel stations. Some of them lead back to already 100% explored areas.- Certain achievement descriptions are incorrect ("collect all weapons/armor/etc" - actually require only those that were present on launch back in 2020). The achievement that requires to get to lvl 161 to obtain all skills requires serious grind even 3-4 NG cycles in with a bunch of EXP up rings.Overall, a 7/10 game. It's fun to play and you can tell that a lot of love was put into it, but the lack of polish is visible in a lot of places.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil Night is an amazing 2D action platformerPro: - a surprisingly large game (took me 18 hours for the first playthrough)- gameplay customization through equipment, primarily the 4 weapon types (axe/halberd, sword, bow, dual-daggers), among which there are some weapons with unique special moves. On top of that come unique reusable item-spells and equipment enchantments.- The checkpoint and fast travel system are great, you rarely have to waste time if you know where to go, which is also rarely a problem since there is a questbook.- Platforming and exploration are fun, aside from some control input issues (more on that later). - The combat is good. I've had more fun fighting enemies and bosses in Vigil Night than in Hollow Knight or Salt and Sanctuary. Enemies do a ton of damage, but you are agile and have fast, spamable invulnerable dodges. - Depth. It's not as complex as a regular rpg of course, but I beat the game and still have no idea what over half of the spells and unique weapons do. There is definitely room for number crunching and build optimization.- Replayability. There is a NG+ mechanic, tons of secrets, a few decisions that make some bosses easier or harder, a few occasions in which you can give quest items to different npcs for different rewards, secret super bosses, etc.Con:- The controls are awkward, especially double tapping →→ to dash or ↓ → special move inputs come out inconsistently with a gamepad joystick. Feels like you are supposed to play it with keyboard or a pad with two dpads. I don't think I would've had much fun with the platforming if it weren't for the dpad → dash macro, but that was still uncomfortable to operate (holding joystick directions with one hand while pressing the jump and dash buttons with the other).- The story and style are a bit cliched. Not "unplayably cringe" or anything, but it also didn't hook me until close to the end.- Balancing issues. For example, the halberd/axe weapon type struck me as underpowered. Maybe I missed something, but I never saw a reason to sacrifice the sword's agility for the halberd's slow charge attacks. You can probably also cheese lots of bosses with ranged attacks.- The music can get reptitive, plays non-stop in specific areas.Conclusion: it's a great game with some smaller flaws. I liked it enough that I would play a DLC expansion or sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: The good: - Neat art style.- Cool spooky atmosphere.- OK music, when it doesn't break.- Interesting mechanics for certain things.- Lots to explore, mileage may vary, it's mostly empty.- Better magic system than Skyrim.The bad:- Enemies that stunlock you. Constantly.- Awful platforming with janky air control and ambush enemies designed to kill you.- Enemies and bosses with ambiguous animations for attacks, all of them, and some are  bosses. The worst kind of bosses. Most of the time you'll be running back and forth trying to figure out which animation out of all 3 of them that look exactly the same the boss is going for, that is when the screen isn't full of projectiles, explosions, or ads. This isn't Dark Souls 2. You can make engaging AND difficult bosses in Soulvanias, it's been done before!- Trap enemies all over the place, on trees, in walls, flying THROUGH them. Dark Souls 2 up the ass, the only game in the Souls series with legitimately ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ traps and you emulate that one huh? I guess it is Salt and Sanctuary.- Ambushes are not difficulty. Stun locks aren't either, there's a bear enemy that can choose to do instant attacks more than once in a row. You literally don't have time to react to a second one and each one does half your HP even when you're way high level.- 3 weapon archetypes with fairly uninteresting skill trees barring a few perks but even if it was all good the enemies aren't fun to fight and the bad animations means the reaction-based perks are useless.- Awful loot system. What's the point of making large secret rooms that give you the same ring you already have 3 of? Stop. Delete them if you have to but this artificial padding is garbage.- Dying is not like Souls or Salt and Sanctuary, you lose progress, and you  die to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's trying to emulate Souls difficulty but still robbing you of progress when you die. Why?Overall:- This game isn't worth it unless it's on sale. Even then buyer beware, I sure as ♥♥♥♥ wish I could refund it.- If this was inspired by Salt and Sanctuary it achieved its goal of being exactly like it.- Tip to the devs, Dark Souls 2 is not the game you want to emulate.Edit: I'm not going to finish this game. I thought I was going to anyway, because I spent money on it, but I don't want to. It's not fun, there's nothing redeeming about it and it's a net loss on entertainment because even the few interesting aspects of it are horribly overridden by the awful ones.
