_childDocuments_.review: Finished in around 18 hours of solid play with minimal walkthrough help,There are 3 possible endings.The game is amazing gameplay - though make sure your using a controller.If you liked Blood Borne, Salt and Sanctuary. Deaths Gambit, Symphony of the night - then you should play this game; its worth paying full price for.It has new game+ which is important if you want all the endings - there are "point of no return" choices you can make that prevent you from doing certain things. There are essentially 5 play style options -Sword, Daggers, Bows, 2 handers and unarmed  (unarmed is very hard).Like souls games - dying without saving involves going back to the last save; the game gives you plenty of options that allow you to quick save however - You use levels to raise your power to take on challenges and unlike Souls; you spend a LOT less time dodging and whittling down enemies - HP can drop fast on enemies.The game is actually very expansive - even finishing the game I know entire zones I never even entered - the game is actually a massive game world with a eldritch horror theme. It has a bunch of quests - some which are actually very important but might not seem so. I finished the game missing multiple tools needed to open up entire maps.I do have one complaint which is that they do not make it clear you can also upgrade armor - I went through most the game without issue but never upgraded my armor till the end. Some of the bosses are really just set pieces that are easy to dodge and burn down.Music is very well done.Worth the full price I paid - no regrets and is way less frustrating then souls games but is a quality title.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best Metroidvanias I've played in a long time.  Fantastic art direction, music, and gameplay.  There are multiple endings, tons of secrets to find, side quests to complete, and builds to try out.  I just completed this recently and got the "true ending" and had fun the entire way.  I heard this game was quite rough at launch which may have been what led it to not gain as much traction as I would have expected, especially in this genre. If you're into Metroidvanias or something with a darker setting and are on the fence, do yourself a favor and play it.Update: 04/28/2024 - the developer continues to update and refine/add to this great game. I hope more people continue to recognize and pick up this game due to it's quality and the continued support from the developer.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the tags fool you, the only thing "souls-like" about the game is the narrative style.  If you enjoyed Bloodstained I would recommend this game at least as much, a surprisingly good SotN-like that I would've passed up if not for the sale price. _childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil: The Longest Night is a Metroidvania that requires tolerance for old school game design as well as some jank - Death results in a game over that sends you back to your previous save, there are barely any checkpoints, there are multiple points of no return with no warnings, there are many optional/hidden quests you can find by talking to NPCs, some of which you can fail by progressing the main story too far before completing them, no quest markers or waypoints, hidden bosses and majority of the equipment and spells are very well hidden and require exploration.To me a lot of the above was a delightful surprise, a refreshing return to those days when exploration came with a high risk, but also had that sense of discovery along with high rewards. But as always mileage may wary and if the above sounds more like a nightmare than a fun experience - then Vigil might end up being a frustrating experience for you.At the beginning of the game, you can choose from 3 difficulties: Easy, Normal and Hard. I chose to play on the hard difficulty and I think it was both good and a bad choice, while the early game drags on a little too much due to the difficulty scaling focusing on simply buffing up the hp and damage of the enemies/bosses rather than changing their attack patterns - the late game would have probably ended up being too easy due to some balancing issues in terms of the gear you can obtain.Typical to the genre, there is a decent amount of ability gating that requires you return to previously visited zones to access new areas after unlocking the needed abilities to do so. Although be it intentional or unintentional, game also allows players to bypass some of the requirements with creative usage of abilities and abusing weapon special moves.You play as Leila, a Vigilant returning to her hometown to meet her sister, only to discover that something sinister is going on and it is up to you to figure out what, while protecting your hometown from the horrors that lurk in the night. Overall the narrative and the way the events unfold are fairly interesting even if rather predictable, unfortunately the English translation holds the game back. Much due to feeling more like a direct translation, instead of a well made localization: Dialogue and notes/journals often feel very clumsy and completely lack subtlety - although it is hard to say if the latter is the fault of the original writing or the translation, several of the location/"faction"/deity etc. names are pretty bad and in addition to that there are a whole lot of typos and grammar mistakes.Despite the above shortcomings I really enjoyed my ~17 hour playthrough of the game, while the review largely focuses on the negative aspects - there are a lot of good things as well: Gameplay is solid, exploration is encouraged and feels very rewarding, majority of the bosses are fun, soundtrack does a nice job of adding to the atmosphere and visually some of locations and especially some of the bosses are great.Overall, it is a good game but with enough of issues that prevent it from being ranked up among the greater hits in the genre. Aside from the issues listed above, some of the other issues are:- Camera: Be it camera not keeping up with the player especially during vertical movement, front layer of environment graphics not fading away and blocking the visibility to offscreen hits from enemies that are often deadly.- Equipment progression and balance: Game has a fairly decent number of weapons and other gear, but it hides them a little too well before you obtain an exploration trivializing spell. When it comes to balancing, some of the weapons are simply better than the others and some such as Fallen Amaterasu are game breaking overpowered.- Instant deaths: While there aren't too many of them, they are an annoyance regardless, especially during a specific boss fight towards the end of the game.- Control/Input issues: While the general controls feel responsive, some of the special attacks (weapons) and abilities (such as dash jump) felt very inconsistent to perform on a DS4 controller, also the special dodge with the pirate daggers seemed to often ignore the direction input and perform the special dodge instead of a normal dodge.That being said, I missed a whole lot of quests and at least a couple of bosses during my playthrough. Completing the game does seem to open up some form of NG+ and there are multiple endings you can get - in my opinion it offers a decent amount of replay value at a very reasonable price point - if you're a fan of the genre, Vigil: The Longest Night is definitely worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: A solid metroidvania. It's not Hollow Knight level but it's still very enjoyable. My only complaint would be the map. It would be so much better if locked doors were color coded on the map when you discover them so you could visit them later. And also if walls were clearly defined. The map is kind of confusing because things just don't fill in like they should when it comes to locked doors and dead ends. I would revisit areas because it looked like on the map it kept going but it was actually a dead end. And it was hard to remember where locked doors were because they aren't clearly marked on the map. Otherwise I think the combat is good once you get some spells and a few weapons to switch between and the difficulty on normal felt pretty balanced for the most part.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking to play this game after I've tried the demo during Steam Indie Game Expo. Now I own it and I don't like it anymore.So, here are some things that you may take into consideration while thinking if you should grab a copy.1. I really liked the darkness and grimness of artstyle used here. New monsters are fun to discover. Bosses leave quite an impression. Death, decay and plague. Reminded me of Salt & Sanctuary and was the key factor to try it out.2. Fighting bosses & enemies in general feels good. Those dodges and charges hit well. Speaking of bosses - the few ones I've met are creative and interesting.3. And to make it three - let's say the Skill tree has some unexpected features like "Amount of health potions you can carry" & some direct parameters like damage reduction, % to find items, etc.And here is why I am not going to play more than these 4 hours:1. Salt & Sanctuary was a great game and Vigil tries hard to follow. This game is not souls-like. Yes, it has stamina and dodge, it has some similarities for combat stuff, but the core feature of "souls" and rebirth is not there. So you have a game, that expects you to die, but doesn't provide any means for you to get better. Let me explain:You stand on a checkpoint/bonfire. Ahead of you lies an area full of secrets and ambushes. You run through, chopping, picking up items, getting EXP and levelups, assigning your skillpoints, etc. And then you die, suddenly. What happens next? You re-load the game from the starting checkpoint. Do everything  again.Just why? The game would be much much better if you had souls analogue & rebirth mechanics.2. It gets really repetitive after a while. Even though bosses are unique experience in terms of fight - exploring is pretty much 2 attacks + Dodge + 3 attacks = Continue further.Same goes with world exploring - not much fun/traps/places of interest, etc. So, you jump some platforms, climb some platforms and that's pretty much it.3. Quests and story line... Well, what can I say? Run around, speak with everybody, read all the notes, find all the items. You kill second boss and blam! Some quests are completed! Yay! Kill Third Boss - BLAAAM! You automatically fail bunch of quests, as something happens and you can't revert it. As of story line - you need to talk to bunch of dull folks to hear their take on what's going on and why you should fear the old blood. Jk. Quite Meh!1. UI. It's bad. All the interfaces, all the UX elements. I still don't understand the logic on how equiping the weapons works. Why if I choose a slot and then a weapon for it another weapon gets unequipped? Special prize  for map design. It's just too clunky and horrible.2. Level design. First of all - there are a lot of loading screens between areas in this game. Each building you get in - loading screen.And boy... There will be a special level: you have to travel through chain of 20+ abandoned houses (1 house = 1 room = 1 screen location)  to progress. Yes, it's a maze of house carcasses. Guess what? 20+ loading screens! Also camera scope & level elements visibility. Many times, you won't have any idea where you should jump, or even if you can drop down or not. Moving the camera by pressing down doesn't really help, so yeah. Some kind of hate.3. Foreground elements, some design decisions and stuff like that.Pretty often you'll find yourself in a scenery where foreground elements obscure the vision of your fight area, And there are a lot of monsters who crawl, jump and shoot. And guess what? You won't see that coming. And it's not the "challenge" of fight. That's simply silly and unfair due to some design decisions. It annoys you pretty much everytime you're going to fight a regular rat or worm...4. There is only a few weapon types in this game (axes, swords, daggers and bows) and believe it or not - the gameplay doesn't really change if you pick one or another. Remember that juicy boink of "UltraSword" or "DragonTooth club"? Remember how wielding a rapier in DS changed everything? Well forgetaboudid. Not my cup.Result: This is a good looking, grim fantasy game with a bunch of really questionable design decisions that ruined the whole experience for me. Maybe you'll find it entertaining and fun, but I, personally, can't recommend this game neither as a good metroidvania, nor a soulslike game you should play. Cheers!
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Game has a wonderful aesthetic. Combat is fun and resembles a more polished Salt and Sanctuary. Weapon and item switching could be more fluent, but it does not drastically take away from the game play. There is absolutely no voice acting, so be prepared to read as you literally have to talk to everyone. Grammatical errors become glaring as you're reading so much and it can break immersion even if only slightly. The art is fantastic and the world is filled with that souls-brand dread and loneliness. Definitely recommend and this goes doubly while it is on sale. Look forward to any dlc or future products from this studio.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, in total I rather like this game, although sometimes I was not quite sure about it. But I definitely had good times with it. Graphics, Music, Controls and the whole artdesign are very good. But the game is nothing really special. The bosses are rather easy, except for some. Dialogues with NPC are sometimes a bit cheesy. The story is for quite a long time very promising and mysterious. But the end I found very disappointing since many questions remained unanswered. And the very end-game sucks! Somehow I lost fun there.A real drawback is the lack of a reference-book/help-system of some game-mechanics. Ok, in the beginning there are tutorial points in the game. But later on you'll learn some additional mechanics/moves. But if you forgot how it works you have no possibility to read it somewhere. I had to watch let's-plays to read the description when you receive a new skill. And I could not figure out how to use advanced arrows. Maybe you will be allowed to use them when you skill bowing, but in the whole skill-tree there was not a single information concerning that. That definitely reduced the fun-factor for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a worthy successor to Salt and Sanctuary!I'm not sure if it is *overall* just as good as S&S, but it comes much closer to S&S greatness than any of the others that have cropped up in the past years.In some aspects its better and in others worse. And some things are simply different and you'll like it more or less depending on your tastes:- the art style and setting are more Bloodborne than Souls.- like in Bloodborne, on a first playthrough it is easy to miss sidequests or to miss the "good" ending.Stuff I think is worse in Vigil:- replayability: there are many weapons but only three melee weapon types. And one of them is much better *and* more fun than the other two. That more useful moveset is specially important in hard mode, which you'll definitely prefer if you have any experience in these types of games.- magic balance: magic is so good (mana not only regens, but regens *fast*) than the *many* consumable throwables are pretty much not worth paying attention to.- dialog pacing: soon after starting you get to the main town. Then the action grinds to a halt until you talk to everyone there before proceeding to the rest of the game.- dashing: it is bound, not to a rebindable button, but to double "tapping" the analog stick. Luckily you don't have to dash much in this game...but yeah, get ready to dash unintentionally, and to fail to dash intentionally, many times. Stuff I think is better in Vigil:- huge map where every nook and cranny has something interesting to find.- many sidequests.- several interesting ranged options. Bow in particular has a whole tree of cool moves to unlock.- more BGMs.- more complex plot/story.In conclusion: play with swords (and in hard mode) and you'll have an awesome, definitely-worth-your-money, time.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Fun metroidvania, enjoyed it quite bit. Nice aesthetic and art, decent gameplay (though i wish weapons had some more unique movesets, they  all are basically cosmetic items with some minor stat differences).The only thing i really disliked is the save system. _childDocuments_.review: I have very Mixed feelings about this game. I like art, animation and some aspect of combat but there are a lot of things which feels weird and I didn't enjoy.Melee combat feels good but its very limited and you experience all it has to offer half through the game. Boss fights are not terrible but not very good or memorable either. But i have to point out that enemies are Unbalanced like hell, there is a lot 1 shot moves and the only way to get stronger is to find hidden items in the game which grant passive buffs and as you might guess it's a awful mechanic. There is no way to get stronger or increase your stats after certain point and most of the skill tree feels useless, this causes to leveling up gets meaningless.The map is Horrible and even when you unlock all areas, you still get lost and have to memorize the paths or just try and guess until you find what you looking for by chance! Level design and platforming don't offer much fun either.Story is very confusing and unclear, also I'm not the fan of this type of "Quests" in a metroidvania specially it lock you out of certain quests early in the game. Save system is very weird and annoying for this type of games as well and there is no point in having a manual save like this.Overall unless you are really desperate for a metroidvania and dont have anything else to play, I don't recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Not nearly through, but I can already say that this game is awesome! To me it's the perfect game of the "metroidvania" genre. It has everything. Nice graphics, an atmospheric setting with interesting story and lore, a protagonist that is rooted in the world, side missions, lots of dialogs with NPCs, a hub area, housing, good combat with a nice flow, tons of items, crafting, skill trees, a huge map and a long playtime. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A janky metroidvania that has some flaws, big and small, but still worth playing if you need a metroidvania fix. I would say that it is better off in the hands of completionist fiends, because if you just play through the story it will be over very quick with little replay-ability. Again, I don't want it understated, this game has a ton of jank. Jank city ♥♥♥♥♥. There is love put into it by the devs, though. Story: It's ok. I wasn't invested much in the story. Very dark soulsy. One of my big issues comes here because some parts of the story will advance the game into another act, leaving some items permanently unobtainable for that playthrough. I do not like this in collectible fest metroidvanias. There are some that can even get unobtainable status just because you went somewhere on the huge map in the wrong order and didn't find an npc in the right spot, specifically in the prologue. The game is broken up into the prologue, act 2, and act 3. If you are trying to 100% be aware of this and follow a guide and map. To 100% you will need to beat the game at least twice.  Graphics: Style is kind of like salt and sanctuary with more definition. Some things work while others are janky. I wouldn't ever call it beautiful, but it gets the job done. Music: Not noteworthy for the most part. Some of the jank comes in here with huge pounding music coming out of nowhere and infinitely repeating. Sometimes it will just stop randomly. I will sometimes feel like I'm about to fight a boss but I'm just walking through the middle of nowhere. Adequate most of the time. Gameplay: The fighting is okay. It's a 2d darksouls like salt and sanctuary. The dodge roll is forgiving, although hitboxes can seem wacky. Bosses for the most part were heavily uninspired. Big thing, flails around, dodge and attack. You can get super overpowered very quickly if you know what you are doing and it can make most if not all of the fighting trivial. The four weapon types work fine, with some weapons having neat special moves attached to them. Later in the game you can reset skill trees for pretty cheap so you can try them all. The skill trees in general feel like they just fully unlock movesets, without silly small damage and stamina boosts inbetween. Upgrades for armor feel few and far between, without much difference until you get a good endgame set (gold armor and weapons *cough cough*) and fully upgrade it. If you don't farm out good items sets the game might pose a challenge.Platforming: A huge issue for me is that most of my deaths came from falling. Until you get a certain ring later on in the game that negates fall damage, you will die a lot trying to explore. It isn't that jumps are hard to make, rather you just don't know if instant death awaits for jumping off screen or an item you need for completion. There is some jank here where you can sometimes cancel the fall damage by attacking in the air at the right time, but it is hit or miss. There could have been better movement skills for me, but o well. There is a double jump, a ground dash that lets you use momentum to jump farther, and an air dash late in the game. That's pretty much it. Map: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ huge.100%ing the game is a chore. It requires multiple playthroughs to get items from branching questlines, and there are a ton of items you will need to farm and collect. You will be fighting bosses and enemies over and over trying to steal their items so you get them all. You will have to grind a ton to get to the level cap. All of this, and some of the items, as stated earlier, can get an unobtainable status by moving to far in the game or by choosing the wrong option in a quest. IMO, you need a guide to accomplish 100%. You can accomplish it in two playthroughs if you are making sure to note which items and quests you need to do differently on NG+. You will be alt tabbing a ton, looking at maps, looking at wiki's, looking at videos. If this is your jam, it can be fun. This isn't a masterpiece like Ender Lilies, Hollow Knight, or Bloodstained, but it isn't the worst I've played. I think the game is skippable for most people, but if you are waiting for Silksong and have nothing else to play it will pass the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Can definitely recommend this one. It's got interesting art style and lore. The story is alright too and the game has some length and exploration to it, so that it doesn't end up feeling grindy. As far as metroidvanias go, this one's a bit average. _childDocuments_.review: Do you like Castlevania: Symphony of the Night? Do you like Bloodbourne? Great, because this is SotN with a coat of Bloodbourne paint. _childDocuments_.review: Hello and here I am again with another review. First of all I would like to thank Fextralife for making a video about this game and bringing it to my attention. Once I heard the words "similar to Salt & Sanctuary" (which is one of my favorite souls like metroidvanias) it instantly piqued my interest. Then I heard eldritch horrors and Bloodborne aesthetic and that sold it for me.So hows the game? Well the easiest way to say is a mix between Hollow Knight (Metroidvania and Souls like mechanics), Bloodborne (aesthetic, eldritch horrors) and Salt and Sanctuary (atmosphere, forboding soundtrack).On the difficulty side I only played it on normal so I cannot say beyond that, but from my perspective it seemed to be a bit on the easy side. That and I also kinda tend to over level myself in these type of games so I make my boss fights easier, but I am aware that not everyone plays like me. I finished the game at level 89 so I did grind a couple of hours to buy a specific set of armor that helped me do the second part of the game with more ease.The story is quite interesting with multiple endings and there are a plethora of side quests to do that will reward you with different types of loot you can equip. There is a lot of lore you can read from investigating books, talking to NPC's and there is also a lot of secrets that are worth uncovering more about the lore of this game.If I discount the hours I grinded in the game the playtime depending on how good you are at these type of games will be between 15-20 hours.With that said I will now do a Pro/Cons then give my final thoughts about the game.Pro:- Superb soundtrack (very atmospheric with a good ambient which adds a lot to the immersion of the world you are traversing)- Multiple endings- A good amount of weapons you can use with different effects (I think I recall 5 or 6 not including the magic powers you can use)- Moment to moment gameplay is satisfying and heavy weapons feel impactful- New Game+Cons:- No voice acting (I understand why though because this is a small indie company that decided to forgo VA and work on other aspects which I am all in favor for)- Some quests bug out if you do them in a different order and you cannot complete them- Needs some balance in some areas (easy to exploit via grinding for gold/materials/overleveling). Normal difficulty felt like easy.Conclusion: This is a game that if you are a fan of the genre (be it metroidvania or soulslike) is a must in my opinion. If you enjoyed Hollow Knight, Salt & Sanctuary, Bloodborne or any other games similar to these then this game is a no brainer.Should you buy it? YES! The asking price is good with the amount of content that the game provides.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid metroidvaina so far. It has a more involved story then I was expecting, and quite a bit of exploration without needing a bunch of gadgets or moves to get around. My biggest gripe is with the controller scheme, and the way remapping it causes other issues. You unlock a movement ability that is default mapped to the d-pad, while your normal movement is by the analog stick. Maybe it works better on an xbox style controller, but I am using an 8BitDo which is modeled on the switch pro. Long story switching between the two when trying to platform wasn't working for me, so I changed it to right bumper. Normally that is mapped to your item wheel, but I moved THAT over to left bumper, which is normally switch weapon so now THAT is mapped to down on the d-pad...Which should be all well and fine and it's what I'd recommend if you have a similar issue because tight use of the ability is pretty much required for reaching certain platforms. However this will also remap those buttons on all the menu screens, so tabbing through them (something you end up doing a lot) is now d-pad down to tab left and left bumper to tab right -_-That's the biggest thing and it is only a little annoying, otherwise it's a good time. I do feel like I'm steamrolling the bosses but I'm also only playing on medium.Ok small tips and spoiler warnings!!! while using a ranged weapon your double-jump animation changes and gives you a smidge more jump distance, and shooting at the apex of your jump also seems to give you just a few more pixels of height. So if something seems just slightly out of reach try that out! Also the guard captain's request to bring him bones is repeatable, which isn't super obvious unless you talk to him again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not bad, but it is not good either. It is somewhere between a Metroidvania and "Salt and Sanctuary".-The map is a mess. The connections between areas are too linear, it is definitely not a good design.-I have Been playing for ten hours now, and have only seen 4 bosses until now. And they are not very memorable. And even though I am playing on Hard, the last two bosses were fairly easy.-There are some pits that directly kill you, without warning.-Some enemies just take half of your health bar. Even bosses don't do that.- Areas are unnecessarily big.-The quest log is badly designed. I have to bring some things for someone, but where is that person? Well, you gotta go over all of the map to find them again. There is no indication.- I have some failed quests, without any warning. They just stand there in the log, with a big X in front of them. It is annoyingMaybe get it on a sale, when you do not have anything else to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating out of 10 Stars = Vigil is like, okay. Its not bad, its not amazing. The artstyle is a lot like Bloodstained (which is terrible imo), and the combat is just the usual bland i-frame dodge through enemy hit them behind. Also the story is incredibly hard to follow fully, and falls flat at the end. But underneath it all, I still had fun, right up until the last achievement.Bosses are decent, not really any bad ones, just a few that require AI manipulation. The combat is kinda fun, but mostly just a spam fest of a few moves even on hard difficulty.The map design is decent, large are to explore, with a lot of secrets, however most of the rewards you find for exploring are just chests of money, which becomes useless after a certain point.The achievements are good, and can all be gotten in 1 Playthrough (with a save at the end for endings). Wasn't too grindy and there are some great steam guides for the collectable achievements.----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Overall I would say its a decent metroidvania about on the level of Salt and Sanctuary or Dark Devotion. If you are looking for the next Hollowknight/Blasphemous this isnt it, but for a solid metroidvania experience I think its worth the price. Hope to see DLC!

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended for any fan of the genre. The game is rough around the edges, difficulty can be a bit wonky, and the translation could do with more work. However the map is large and quests have a bit of C&C (we need more game with fail states rather than game over!), which makes it interesting for replay. However, will likely frustrate Completionists who feel they are "forced" to replay stuff they don't like (but then why play this sort of game?).Edit: having played a lot more now, I must add how responsive the Devs are. They are only a small team and there is a language barrier but they have continued to respond to questions. And did I mention the soundtrack is awesome? You should get it too!

_childDocuments_.review: Cautiously recommend this when on sale.  Aspects of the game are very well done, (art, music and some of the level design), but the core combat mechanics have some design issues.  The game starts out decently balanced, but after you get several layers deep into the various skill trees you quickly overpower most of the enemies.  It seems like they were trying to do too much for the scope of the game:  There's too much loot, (90% of which is unnecessary), and I'm not sure that the souls-like Stamina mechanics were necessary.  They could have removed the stamina system, reduced the skill trees, (of which many skills allow you to mitigate the stamina system), and trimmed the amount of loot and had an easier time balancing the encounters.Some of the soundtracks are outstanding, and I liked the art style.  B-

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil The Longest Night makes a good case for second chances – I played the demo a while back and didn’t really jive with it, but for some reason I ended up getting it anyway and really enjoying itTLDR this is a good metroidvania with some great art and light Souls inspiration (similar to Salt and Sanctuary) but doesn’t necessarily do anything amazingly and is a little on the easy sideOverall, the best things about Vigil were definitely the artwork and world design.  It looks like something straight out of a gloomy, gothic fairytale, and the characters and backgrounds even have a bit of an oil painting feel too them.  Animations are mostly spot on, and there are some really wonderfully macabre enemy designs.  I also really liked the armour and weapons for the main character, which pay more than a bit of homage to Bloodborne. The music is also fantastic, although at times it “forgets” to kick in or comes on late.  Aside from that this is a fairly standard metroidvania with RPG progression and dodge rolling and stamina management pilfered from FromSoft.  The map is pretty huge and a joy to explore, and there’s plenty of secrets and hidden booty to rummage for.  I also liked that there are lots of rings, trinkets and weapons with differing stats and effects, so combining them and experimenting was funCombat is mostly good but a bit of a wet haddock at times.  While the weapons are cool and you can unlock some almost Devil May Cry type special moves, it feels very floaty and impact-less. A combination of floopy enemy feedback and lackluster sound effects, the combat just doesn’t feel like it has any weight, which is a shame as the special moves are really cool. I did enjoy the dual knives though.The other main gripe I have with this is that its way too easy, even on hard mode.  After I got into the swing of things and upgraded my gear a bit (not even to max) I found I could cruise through most of the game without much of a challenge.  This is especially apparent on the Bosses, which despite looking fantastic, can be felled with a well-aimed fart.  In fact, I’d say most (including the final two) fell to me on my first try and I can’t recall any that required more than 3 tries.  Its hard to get a sense of achievement with that.  Also, getting locked out of the good ending because I missed ONE item? Boooooooooooooooooooooooooooo!At the end of the day, I had a great time with Vigil.  While its not gonna knock Blasphemous off my top spot for metrodvanias on PC, it was an all around good time and I actually liked it a lot more than Salt and Sanctuary.  Hopefully, if the devs make a sequel they can sort out the combat and the difficulty.

Definitely glad I got this and will be looking forward to other games by these guys.

_childDocuments_.review: is absolutely worth buying. It is dripping with atmosphere, brimming with plot and sidequest-altering secrets, and will keep you busy for at least 30 hours (not including New Game +). The style and setting immediately evoke Ska Studio's . The game knows this and occasionally pokes fun at its influences--if you can spot them. That said,  is not a funny game. Bad things happen and if you aren't careful, you might do more harm than good, or miss opportunities to help some characters.The story is that you are a medieval ranger-type who has just returned to town after being away training, presumably for their entire childhood. The world has been plunged into moonlit darkness and that's just kinda the way things have been when the game starts. You quickly discover that your sister is missing, but don't be getting your anime Bingo cards out just yet. Things accelerate quickly. First there's a thing about "heathens" that quickly gets discarded, then human experimentation, and then Zelda-style time travel, and then a plague (ok, maybe keep those cards nearby). All this is introduced by the time the Prologue ends and the first act officially begins.The world is very compelling, the characters are likable, dialog is short and to-the-point, as it should be. The world is a very interesting place to explore. Where the game falters a little is how long you can spelunk dungeons (in my case, 20 hours) without learning anything specific about the cause of the world's problems. Worse...the game gets really easy after the prologue.  has dozens of unique weapons and animations for them; Your character can wear all the armor sets onscreen, and she has style (The art is not voyeuristic. but  fans will be pleased). But by the early middle of the game, you might not see any benefit to using more than a single move to quickly dispatch enemies. You will level up quickly. Very little grinding. The late game bosses are a nightmare though.Despite these issues, the exploration and world building is pretty good (even without detailed lore), the secrets are cool, and you will want to see how it all ends.

Ability to PAUSE the game is of critical importance to me.So the inability to pause the game is serious annoyance. Please either make accessing menu pauses the game... OR patch in a pause button. Then we're perfect.  I'm keeping this game, I like it. But I just want to highlight this small but serious annoyance that taints my enjoyment of this game.(EDIT) nvm. The map button pauses the game. _childDocuments_.review: This is a fun Metroidvania that feels like Bloodborne and Castlevania had a very broody baby. It's definitely souls-inspired (find out the plot through item descriptions, thin plot, lore-heavy, different builds, high replayablity), but that just adds to the charm; it doesn't detract form it. There's so much to explore!  A lot of the levels double back on themselves with branching paths, so keeping an eye on the map will help you explore the whole area. I'm still finding new bosses and items I missed in round 1, partway through NG+. The only real complaint I have with it is that it's visually very dark--as in, hard to see what's going on in some levels. I didn't encounter any bugs like some folks in the reviews have, and I'm halfway through a NG+. It's definitely worth picking up if you're a dark Metroidvania fan

_childDocuments_.review: I was patient up to a point...This game is a mess. Which is just bizarre to me. How do you have art this good and gameplay this fun and screw up... THE MENUS?! Huh!? DEVELOPERS! Are you listening? FIX YOUR CONTROLLER SUPPORT! Do that, and I might change this to a thumbs up. (Nerd Sass!!)I'm looking at all these reviews and I have to wonder, are they all using keyboard controls? Because first of all, eww...Here's what happens. You go to the controller menu to set your controls because the defaults are terrible, and change your healing button to d-pad up. Ok. Except now when you go to the menu d-pad up also changes panels. It does both. How did this pass playtesting?! Why aren't the menus locked to use specific controls? HOW are they contextual?!Whatever update they just did literally broke controller support. Triggers are now start and select. Start and select are nothing. What is this, amateur hour? How does a game look this good and feel like it was programmed by throwing a keyboard in a tumble dryer?All you had to do was make it work, folks. Now I have to be mean.Vigil is elevated fan art. It wants to be Dark Souls so bad, from the font to the cliche "plot". It even does that thing where the menus don't pause the action, but when you go into a sub-menu it pauses the game anyway. The difficulty settings are (Too) Easy, Medium (is too hard) and Instakill. It feels like they couldn't find anyone to play test it, or if they did they ignored all of the notes. And yet, it's not that hard because you can always- always -instantly teleport to town to buy healing items if you find a save point. I passed the first boss only after "grinding" rats for an hour. What is this game?!And I haven't even talked about the writing. It's like a high school D&D session. Characters drop modern slang like it weren't nothing, then you talk to some old lady who's suddenly a bad ren faire actress, there's just cliche "My OC!" as far as the eye can see, and I just can't care about any of these people. There's no substance to any of this. I ended up just running trough town to get to more combat, and when I saw a bear... a bear with a giant caber swinging it at me like... I mean I laughed out loud.If I could, I'd refund it. Vigil is broken, it's tone deaf, and it can't even be goofy fun because it is virtually joyless.⛝

_childDocuments_.review: While the game lacked a bit of polish at release (controls a bit cluncky, weird ennemies hitboxes and confusing map) the amazing atmosphere (visuals, sounds and music) had me playing for around 20 hours on my 1st playthrough. The weak elements of the game are no more and they also added more content, having a positive impact on the whole gaming experience.In its current build, I can definitely recommend you this game, especially if you dig metroidvania/action style of games set in a dark fantasy world.Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a very enjoyable metroidvania.Pros: - There is a HUGE world to explore. The map is gigantic in this game. It's not as detailed or varied as Salt and Sanctuary, for example, but there sure is a lot of it. - There are plenty of secrets. The game rewards you for messing around and trying things in various locations. - The combat feels smooth and responsive. - There are lots of waypoints, so there is very little need to do extensive backtracking unless you want to.Cons: - The English translation is not very good. Some parts of the dialogue are actually quite hard to understand because the translation is so awkward. - The difficulty is on the light side (think SOTN). Some items/spells/skills are OP and can easily be exploited, making many fights trivial. For example, certain spells can be spammed to kill enemies off screen and through walls/doors. Even without this, on normal mode most of the boss fights can be brute-force tanked with heavy armor, heavy weapons, and lots of healing potions.

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing that drew me to this game was the art style. It's gorgeous to look at all throughout the game. The combat is satisfying and easy to pick up. There's enough variety with the different weapon types to keep you interested as you assign skill points in the areas of your choice. I personally recommend the sword. If you can master the parry timing and followup attacks, you'll certainly feel rewarded for it.I also enjoyed the story. Nice and dark and bleak, just the way I like it. Needless to say, it compliments the art style very well.Overall, I can definitely recommend it and feel it's definitely worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine, but also not great. It would be a mixed rating if Steam gave us the option.The biggest litmus test with these Metroidvania/Souls crossovers is whether you will come back for more of the combat. Honestly, this game tries to be too much of both sides of Metroidvania hack/slash and Souls games that it comes off redundant. Whereas Hollow Knight fully invested in typical, simple Metroidvania gameplay style, and S&S posessed more of the weighty, reactionary side of combat, Vigil tries to blend the two, and it feels pretty flakey.The boss fights are also kinda bleh. 75% of them are just huge with massive insta hitboxes, that you'll likely just cheese them with the bow, considering they all run outside of your field of vision. Come the end, Vigil starts messing around with platform based Boss battles and I honestly lost the will to live. Out of the dozen or so bosses, only one was a particularly good, melee based fight.The map progression and exploration is okay, but I honestly felt like I was just ploughing through it with little thought. There seems to be a bunch of areas you can fall back to, but it's fairly awkward to even understand when and where you gain the right to examine these areas, not to mention the map isn't particularly great at showing key areas. You gain a double jump almost immediately in the game, which just about shows the lack of thought put into exploration progression. Slightly later you get a lame dash which can transport you to a few new ledges. It's all a little lowkey and unexciting.There are side quests, but ultimately the dialog and hints involved with figuring them out are so vague and easy to miss/forget that I honestly had zero clue what was going on and what to do with them. The "Notes" are really ill organized and not very helpful, given the game's translation. I managed to get to the end of the game and not have a clue what this story was about. That may be my fault, but considering I went through the entirity of Bloodborne, puzzled and perplexed, but still understanding the through line, I doubt it.Also, the game-over system... I don't see why. For a game that involves insta death by way of the environment and fall damage, this seems rather archaic and unnecessary.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil isn't a perfect game.  I would say the combat is okay, it's nothing particularly special but it gets the job done.  The performance is also spotty, especially for the recommended specs.  There are also moments of translation error--and additional moments of obvious typo.  But I'm willing to overlook these minor flaws because this is one of the best indie games I've played in a long time. The story is terribly confusing at times, but I love it--piecing this world together from the NPCs and the little story beats here and there.  World design is top tier, honestly: the map is sprawling, and it loops back into itself as a real place should.  The bosses and enemies are designed with so much unique vision and attention to detail.  Everyone knows the art style is incredible, but that really can't be said often enough.  Fans of Metroidvania or atmospheric storytelling should definitely give Vigil a play.  For such a small game I spent a lot of time with it, and that was time well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: With many of its inspirations dangling on its blood-ridden sleeves, Vigil: The longest night is perhaps one of the more interesting metroidvania's out there that sought to translate the tone and feel of Lovecraft's work and blend it with the metroidvania genre.You play as Leila, a Vigilant that is tasked to investigate the strange long night that has fallen on her hometown Maye. Your journey takes you around the countryside and has you fighting bears, wolves, mad townsfolk and strange otherworldly creatures that have infested forest, coast and mountain. As you talk to the villagers and wandering strangers you'll uncover that things aren't what they seem and that darker secrets may lay hidden underneath all the sickness and misery.Vigil's visual design really helps underline the grim story, with dark colours offset with red and blue hues that help differentiate one area from another. Because to be honest, the entire map tends to blend into itself. Sure the flooded area is distinctly different from the lake, but if you look at it as a whole? I couldn't help but need the map in order to navigate from point A to B. Which in itself isn't necessarily a bad thing. Sprawling maps with multiple pathways to choose from and stumbling on hidden paths helps breathe life into the world, but with Vigil it always felt like I got turned around; walking in circles until I glanced over the map for the actual way to go.The soundtrack had one or two interesting ambience tracks but didn't really stand out for me apart from one particular boss track that just felt... out of place.The game's metroidvania elements are a combination of key techniques, such as double jump, dash, air dash and a slide that unlocks new areas and gives the player more mobility, equipment and spells. Spells are fixed items in the world you obtain through completing quests or finding them in hidden areas. Some spells deal damage others increase or decrease stats, stun enemies, create phantom images of your character or teleport you to the last save point. I found myself using the flaming magpies a lot in the early game, but ended up forgetting I even had spells in the first place and only remembering when I needed to open a door or teleport back, and instead rely on my trusty sword to do the heavy combat.The weapons come in four types; swords, daggers, axes (heavy weapons) and bows. On the latter I can't really comment because I didn't even want to attempt a ranged build, but I have used the three melee types. Axes, or in some cases heavy weapons, are your high damage / slow attack kind of weapon. They pack a punch, but use up a bunch of stamina. Daggers are an efficient quick-kill weapon with fast attacks and long combos with the added bonus of back stab damage. Their base damage isn't terrible either. Personally, though, I always stuck to the swords. They're a mid-range weapon with average damage and attack speed. Each has their own advantages and disadvantages, and the game doesn't favour one type over another.As you level up you're given points to spend on skill trees that add new attacks and combos to a weapon and increase their base damage. There is a skill tree for each of the weapon types, plus a fifth skill tree that enhances your basic stats and abilities.Beyond your base weapons and spells you're able to pick up throwing weapons such as knives, poison needles, Molotov cocktails, grenades and shrapnel. I used them occasionally but, much like the spells, ended up forgetting these in the later half of the game as well.Where Vigil falls short, however, is some of its combat and platforming mechanics. The platforming is awful with floaty jumps, leaps of faith (assuming you haven't defogged that bit of the map yet) and controls that feel both stiff and janky. I can't remember how many times a single tap on the D-pad sent my character hurling into the night; prompting me to tap the other way only to dash off the ledge and plummet to my death. Given the 2D space there's a lack of spacial awareness and with the slow walking speed you're conditioned to dash everywhere you go, add to that parts where you have to navigate skyscraper-sized pine trees by jumping on thin ledges... Well, off you go down into the depths to enjoy a nice splatter adventure. Finding the ring the negated fall damage helped a little bit, but in the end I couldn't come to grips with the control scheme.Likewise the combat suffered from the same issues. Combos cancelled because I tapped the dash button, inputs not registering that lead to the character attacking once and standing like a lemon while the boss was in full swing for another attack. My controller has been acting up lately, so perhaps its a hardware issue and not so much a game issue but I never felt in control of the character. Instead fighting against everything she did or didn't do.Overall I enjoyed Vigil: The longest night. It's a neat addition to the metroidvania library, and for me one of the few games that handle the Lovecraftian horror themes with the love and care it deserves. Some of its aspects and its short size (My first playthrough was 6-ish hours) doesn't make it worth full price. Definitely a solid purchase on sale if you've got cash to spare.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure how to feel about Vigil. Overall, for a tldr version, I'd say that if you're a fan of games like Hollow Knight, Blasphemous, Dead Cells and the like, you'll probably enjoy this one. It won't be your new favorite, though. The combat feels fluid and engaging, with different enemies that present different timings to figure out, ranged and melee attacks and lots of poison. Like, lots and lots of poison. While in theory there are a lot of different options for your character in terms of attack approach, I found that getting a weapon upgraded at the forge and then running in to almost every situation spamming the attack/dodge buttons when prompted was so absurdly effective that it rendered the other combat options ineffectual in comparison. However, the other combat options may be incredibly viable and I just never stumbled upon the correct way to take advantage of them. The graphics are quite nice for the genre, if devoid of artistic individuality. While games like Ori and the Blind Forest, Hollow Knight and even Blasphemous have a unique artistic style that's pretty quickly identifiable to the franchise, Vigil basically looks like your average 2D platformer that can't quite decide if it's artistically inspired by Final Fantasy, Dark Souls or Castlevania. Thus, it kind of looks like a slightly peculiar mash up of all of those games in terms of artistic direction. Still, the graphics in of itself look smooth, fluid and clean. The biggest failing of this game however is the story and the way in which it presents itself. On the one hand, you're strongly encouraged by the developer to take a ton of side quests, talk to a lot of people and explore a lot of places. On the other hand you have virtually no direction or knowledge of specifically where to go and worse still, what to do once you get there. Exploration is generally tedious and devoid of meaning or genuine reward and, the characters are the most cliche, derivative and uninspired group of characters you could assemble. So while you may explore and talk to everyone in the first 1-3 hours, you'll quickly catch on to the familiarity and lack of benefit to doing this, both in terms of tangible reward and emotional connection to the game, thus you'll either mechanically continue wading around the game hoping to stumble upon a Pandora's box of loot, or you'll just quickly finish up the story/game in an emotionally detached if technically challenged fashion. This game gets direction-ally lost in it's attempt to oddly blend the story/characters of a JRPG with the punishing lack of direction of a Dark Souls or Blasphemous, and in the end it's just a bit confusing and bland.Still, I had some fun with this one in terms of gameplay. It was a fun challenge overall, and though after completing the story I'm honestly left with a sense of 'meh, alright I guess', I still would recommend it to you if you're running out of challenging metroidvanias. This'll scratch the itch, but you'll forget about it pretty quickly after putting it down.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is ... difficult to write about without giving the wrong impression. With that in mind, I'd like to start off with the conclusion: If you like intricately technical combat, metroidvanias, Lovecraftian mythos, or have been trying to scratch the Dark Souls itch this is a HARD RECOMMEND. That siad, the first thing you should know picking this title up is it feels like it's a late stage beta. More specifically the game is complete, playable, and reasonably stable but you will absolutely bump into plenty of animation bugs, dialogue issues and typos, some non-existent feedback [hard to tell when you get hit], some of the most nothing sound effects, and god help you if you try to Google info on the game because [as of time of writing] they've been so active with patches and updates that half the information available is no longer applicable or grossly incomplete. My personal favorites are an animation glitch that causes the smith to look like he's speed hammering Through the Fire and Flames on his anvil and misgendering a fairly attractive lady in the tavern [unless religious zealots living in eternal night Cthulhu world have developed some astoundingly good top surgery]. The second thing you should know is this game feels so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good to play that it makes all of the above feel quaint and charming. If the core of the game was even moderately less than great all of the bugs and weirdness I listed above would annoy the piss out of me and this would be a very different review but as it stands, the combat, the aesthetic, the exploration, the systems,  and all the little little game feel considerations are so good that when I pull an elevator lever and it sounds like someone misusing a wood box turkey call I just smile and think "that's cute". I don't want to turn this review into a novel so the last thing I want to talk at length about is arguably the best part of Vigil, the combat. You get four weapon types plus a magic system that blossom in complexity as you level with things like stingers, animation canceling, and ripostes being baked in as skills. The game even encourages experimentation with fairly liberal drops for upgrade items, the ability to reset your skill points [a bit into the second part of the game], and a decent balance between the weapons classes. Now, when I say "balance" I mean they're all fun if not viable and you can kinda break the game with all of them and, hear me out, it's pretty great. If anyone reading this has played Bloodstained you know exactly what I'm talking about. This game can really reward you for playing around and finding a dumb combo of weapon, enchantment, and equipment that can plow through many of the enemies and it feels oddly satisfying. Inversely you can forgo the cheese, master your weapon's skill set and movement options, and style on enemies with the very satisfying aggressive / counter play of the sword or dual blades, or the surprisingly robust acrobatics of archery weapons. Let's be honest though, the axe [see: heavy] class is almost 100% cheese. Thing is you have the choice and, whatever route you choose, it tends feels really good all the way through.My final thoughts on this game are that it's a very flawed title but it's so good exactly where it counts that I would happily display this game on a shelf next to my loose genre favorites: Dark Souls, Bloodstained, Hollow Knight, and Minoria.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a soulsborne-like 2d metroidvania with strong visuals and a special emphasis on boss design. It's all-in-all a game with good production value drawing inspiration from good sources, which makes it all the more baffling that it completely fails to land.The combat system contains a lot of great ideas that are let down by poor tuning. You have maybe more than what you'd expect from a game at this price: a dodge roll and backstep with iFrames, attack animations with a weighty startup and cancel-able recoveries, hyperarmor, stun bars, a parry mechanic, air combos, stamina-management, gated behind a skill-tree which provides a friendly leaning curve. But then, some options are lame traps and others are too powerful in uninteresting and boring ways. For instance, the risk to reward ratio for the sword's parry gimmick is awful in a game with such a strong backstep and dodge-roll, and this skill requires skill points to unlock. Meanwhile the axe class of weapons has enough reach to out-space most enemies, and also has an unlockable air combo with a shockwave that hits a third of the screen and costs nothing to execute.The pacing is a mess. After a short tutorial the main character enters a hub town with vendors and NPC's to talk to to receive quests and chew on dialogue. Fully exploring this area takes more time to complete than most of the combat in the early game, which is a preposterous effort for the pay off of some buggy fetch quests and very poorly translated dialogue. Around the mid-game, you enter a grimdark lovecraftian dungeon in an alternate reality with a bombastic set piece boss battle. The lead up to this weighty, occult atmosphere is a short traipse through an ossuary and 10 minutes of repetitive combat against two weak enemy types with no interesting or novel mechanics, together with some low stakes platforming. In the low tension intermission after this, you're bafflingly treated to 3 or 4 novel enemy types. All of this reeks of poor design; why so much effort spent on some mooks in the forest, and not in spicing up the introduction to the impactful boss just before them? Directly after this, you enter a palette swap of the starter town, which is now even larger and more of a time sink to explore, while the game's principal story twist lands like a shy wet fart.Narrative-wise, it's apparent the translation budget only covered the critical path dialogue, but this isn't the real reason the story and setting are bad. The basic problem is that this game was made by a cargo cult of dark souls. Let me give some examples: of course it's pretty derivative to see a description box for a pair of boots during the loading screen, but the real problem is that the flavour text accompanying the item doesn't flesh out the setting in some obscure way via some reference to lands or people or some obscure aphorism. It just... describes the item. There's no ludonarrative explanation for why your character gets to revive at a checkpoint, maybe because you actually don't, in a way; all progress is lost and you reload your save file upon death, and you need to manually save at whatever-the-bonfires-in-this-game-are-called. This game's version of undead/ashen-one/jedi/spectre is called a vigilant, and there's almost no evidence of any other ones around or much exposition as to why they exist or what they do. Furthermore it's clear that being one isn't some lonely dream-like sojourn through purgatory; 5 minutes after becoming a vigilant your character walks into their hometown and runs into lifelong acquantances, including their sister.Play it for the bosses and for playing dress-up with the stylish and well-animated main character, but there's not much else going on here.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to like about this game. The graphics are really well done. I didn't care for the style from the trailer, but in game it was actually fine, and it really grew on me by the end. The combat is very satisfying. There's a surprising amount of enemy variety, and while I eventually found an overpowered strategy that kind of broke everything, I still would switch back to my go-to daggers from time to time because it was just fun.That being said, it's not perfect, there are definitely some rough edges out there. The level design is not quite as tight and intentional as others in the genre. I felt like I needed the map in this more than other games because the level layouts are kind of repetitive. There are a lot of weapons, but most of them are just clones in one of four categories. A few of them have special attacks, but for the most part every sword has the same attacks.The talent trees are a bit boring as well. The trees are so small there's no real planning. You basically just pick one weapon type and balance that with options from the general tree. I had more than enough to max out the general tree and my chosen weapon tree by about 75% of the way through. The whole last few areas I didn't even bother spending my points.Overall I would say it's worth it if you're looking for more 2d games with souls-inspired combat. It's not the best one I've played, and I don't see myself playing through it more than once, but it was worth the price for what it was.

_childDocuments_.review: This was hard to give a thumbs down, but there are so many wonderful Metroidvania's, some that hold up even after being out for, literally, decades.This one won't. Tons of cool stuff, pretty game, little things to do, side quests, alternate endings, the game does have all the right ingredients. I just don't like the proportions. I was on my third new game + and deep into multiple hours of solely grinding to 100% the game. I feel like we have to get away from achievements that go "Find all of X, or find all of Y." - Where X and Y are both not indexed by the game, and PERMANENTLY missable.That's not good. I did like the story though, I just wish a little more time went into the game to improve the exploration and grind.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of potentials, I hope the issues could be solved in the sequel (if any).Pros:- Gorgeous art works, I really love it, details looks pretty nice even on 55 inch TV.- Some weapons have special movement which is fun (but useless as described below)- Good story and quest lineCons- Enemies are way too weak, the fact that most enemies can be killed within 2 basic strikes (even in NG+ hard difficulty)  makes combo attacks useless, so why designed those flashy attack skills?- Enemies AI is stupid, just stupid. Mobs move and attack like an idiot, most bosses don't chase you if you are out of their sight.- No souls-like mechanic that you can get your souls back, so you lost every progress from the last save point when you died, it feels like all your efforts and time are wasted. Since enemies are weak, most death comes from dropping from too high above.Throughout the game, the major problem is extremely poor enemy design which makes skill system and weapon system almost useless.

_childDocuments_.review: Bad controls ruin what I would consider an otherwise engaging game. Attack is delayed but jump is not. When you press the button to jump your character jumps instantly. When you press attack, there is about a half second delay in the actual attack happening. The easiest way to describe this is other games, like Bloodstained for example, when you press attack your character attacks the moment you press the button, but in this game, the attack delays to approx when you release the button. It's maddening. Also, when trying to use a healing potion it would not work for me about 70% of the time I pressed UP on the Dpad after assigning it to the hotbar. No reason for me to keep playing it when the core functions of the game are not working correctly. Hugely disappointed because I believe I had this on my wishlist for a year or more.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I mostly enjoyed my playthrough of Vigil. Graphics and controls are good, the soundtrack is great. I did particularly like the prologue, where Vigil feels more akin to a souls-like: The atmosphere starts out grim and lore-rich. Initial stages are cleverly designed and have few, difficult and well-placed enemies and traps. Progress is slow, but meaningful and rewarding. The plot twist at the end of the prologue got me really invested into the game. In the second and third act, gameplay degenerates to just your usual metroidvania. Enemies are plentiful and puny, while the map is too large, mostly boring and littered with trashy loot. Atmosphere and enemies, to an extent, turn less gloomy. Finally, the resolution of the plot twist breaks any emotional investment into the world and its characters you established during the prologue - instead offering "new", less likeable characters with even sketchier writing and character development.Speaking of lore, the overall storyline is somewhat convoluted and hard to piece together. This may very well be a problem of the mediocre translation - and if that's the patched translation, I do not want to know how bad the original one was.Apart from that, I had some minor bugs and gripes: A few crashes to desktop. Certain sidequests silently fail if you progress in the main story. Some sounds kept getting stuck and others were plainly wrong - walking on cavern floors sounds like banging on a metal door. Dashing controls as if it was an afterthought, but luckily dashing isn't necessary all too often.Also, what is it with blatant pop culture references in games these days? Is there anybody out there who celebrates reading GoT quotes as if these were the pinnacle of writing, peak nerdness made flesh? On a related note, I at least got a good chuckle out of the woefully inappropriate music cues in the "Depressing Forest" stage.

_childDocuments_.review: Like many, I'd say it's metroidvania x Bloodborne, in many sense. Pros:- Nice world setting and lore- Nice art- Would scratch that metroidvania itch- Not too pricey for this length and level of experienceCons:- The game has difficulty curve problem It faces the same problem as my personal experience with Bloodstain, for its first boss being so hard especially when you're not used to its control. At this point you'd quit and refund because you can't beat it or you did beat it with the feeling of accomplishment, expecting it to set the tone of the game until your next boss and onward to the end are so easy, you feel relief and also kinda let down - unless you face 2 extra bosses later added to the game, those feathery **** are another level of BS but they'll at least keep you company if every other parts of the game are too kind to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil the longest night is pretty good metroidvania sidescroller soulslike RPG with solid combat, a HUGE map to explore and a very strong art direction + accompanying soundtrack. It has some negatives in several points of no return for side quests, some balancing issues and pretty mediocre writing.As this is a soulslike let's start by talking about the combat. Combat feels smooth and responsive with great enemy variety and multiple bosses to challenge your skills. There's 3 difficulty levels to chose from, which you can change on the go, which is a big plus. Also easy is actually easy for once! This is the perfect difficulty if you wish to play the game casually. Normal serves as a good challenge and hard is if you really want to push it. However as the game is an RPG and thus has levels and gear, these aspects will determine the difficulty much more than your actual difficulty level. For example i played through the game on easy for the most part switching to normal on bosses. At the end of the game i encountered a boss which was literally impossible for me even on easy. Thus i decided to upgrade this gear i had been playing with for pretty much the whole game. The impossible boss suddenly became a walk through the park. Death's gambit afterlife also had this issue for me, i prefer metroidvania soulslikes without RPG elements but to each their own. It does offer great replayability though for a new save or NG+ which the game supports.The map is absolutely enormous and will take you quite a while to 100%, luckily the game has a very generous fast travel system free of cost! The level design isn't particularly great or varied between zones but the atmosphere changes a lot between them which does help keep you engaged. This atmosphere is thanks to the amazing visuals and brilliant soundtrack. The SFX also really help set the mood and is another top notch aspect of this game. These 3 aspects combine to make a really immersive and moody experience that isn't easily forgotten. I'd say the game is worth experiencing just because of this alone.As for the negatives it really sucks when you unknowingly lock yourself out of a side quest or item. There's even a case where you can outright miss out on a metroidvania ability (to unlock a certain type of door) as well as one of the items for the game's true ending (out of 3). This is in my opinion a cardinal sin and really shouldn't be possible. I would suggest saving often in different slots as well as checking your quest log every now and then to verify if you locked yourself out of a quest. The balancing issues i mentioned at the start are basically how gear can make you really weak/OP regardless of difficulty. This is pretty customizable though so you can experiment to find what feels right for you.Lastly the story is weird. The setting and premise itself are super cool but the execution and story telling falls short in my opinion. The dialogues are all over the place and inconsistent, probably a side effect of the translation to english (chinese developers). There's also several items and descriptions that are confusing due to the bad translation. This doesn't really hamper the experience but could've tied everything up into a nice package. In the end the game's still worth playing for the atmosphere and visuals or if you're a fan of games like these. There are better ones out there but this one is a worthwhile investment. 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only a few hours into this game, but i can already tell it is fantastic. Castlevania SOTN is one of my all time favorite games.  I'm always trying to find something with that same charm. This game is not the same as SOTN, there are similarities, but this game has it's own thing going on and i love it.The graphics are amazing.  I was able to run it at 3840x2160 and it looked incredible.  I am on a GTX 1050 and i did experience a little framerate drop, so i dropped the resolution down to 2560x1440 and it is singing at 60fps and looks amazing.  The artwork is stunning.  I do hope they address the occasional stuttering that occurs, seems to happen no matter what resolution i set it at.  That stuttering is not a deal breaker by any means, but it makes what could be a polished exp a little interrupted.  May be that i just need a new V card...The game is tough, which i love.  I spent an hour leveling up for the first boss and enjoyed every minute of it.Items items items.  One of my favorite aspects of any game, especially metroidvania style games.  This game has got it going on.  Items change the way the character looks.  They give cool effects and subtle graphic changes that are such a nice touch.  I am hoping that there are secret moves to be found with the weapons.  That was one of the things i loved about SOTN.  You could equip a weapon, and with various trial and error street fighter moves, you could discover all kinds of different abilities for each weapon.  Such a great attention to detail.Music: amazing.Story: Pretty awesome so far.  Has cult themes and subtle clues about the narrative in the dialogue.  I've discovered a few cool extra easter eggs by repeatedly speaking to characters, and by going back and having conversations again after key events. _childDocuments_.review: Vigil's greatest strength is it's atmosphere. The team lovingly crafted a world filled with cosmic horrors and intrigue with a unique art style that adds to the experience. It wears it's influences on it's sleeve and you'll be able to decide whether this is for you after watching trailers and looking through screenshots. The biggest issues I experienced while playing related to quest quality control (side quests softlocking outside of story-related progression) and several bits of dialogue that could have used additional proofreading, Despite this I really enjoyed my time with Vigil and understand that the gripes I have aren't exclusive to this game. Games are expensive and Indie studios typically have a very small budget compared to bigger studios which typically means there are less resources available for in-depth QA (Which for a game as large as this is difficult to fully do). As Glass Heart Games debut title I think they did a fantastic job and I'm looking forward to seeing what they have in store for us next.

_childDocuments_.review: A straight up banger of a game, and one I regret playing a year after it's release. Vigil provides a good mix of tried-and-true gameplay via the metroidvania style with an aesthetic and story that is both creepy and compelling. The story setting, like many "souls-like" games, is told more in the background via books in the world and items in your inventory; However the main storyline is very much easy to follow, and all the background inspiration strongly drawn from Lovecraft can be ignored with no detriment to your viewing pleasure.Combat becomes very compelling, but requires you to put your skill points into a weapon tree to unlock the funner skills for that weapon. I went the austere rout of plugging in the utility tree first, but still had fun for the first few bosses with my baby attacks. Each weapon plays differently as well, so you can find the one that feels best for you and stick to it.All in all 10/10 game, and I'm now eagerly awaiting the next release from this developer.

_childDocuments_.review: The art design is interesting, storyline was well paced, and overall this is a good metroidvania style game.two small issues that i was encountering - ground dash is difficult to consistently execute so i mapped the key combination to the d-pad (fixed that) and the second is that there are some areas that seem almost impossible to reach (the miners hall chest for example), but that could just be me and not the game.The second to last boss fight is rage inducing at times but not game breaking.The rest of the issues were fixed in the bounty of the night patch.Highly recommend, i played through twice and am on the 3rd run with the new patch
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: A solid horror metroid-vania very much in the style of "Salt and Sanctuary". Difficulty has major peaks and valleys but that is consistent with the genre. Art style is fun and in my opinion the strongest aspect of the game. Lots of good secret side quests and a couple optional bosses. There are a couple of coding issues with quests not registering or needing to hit a certain dialogue box to progress but considering the size of the game they are relatively negligible. I wish there was a little bit more diversity of play mechanic as I found myself very much in the "press x to kill all monsters" mindset. All in all we've got a strong game made by a small team. Not a masterpiece but better than most 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic Metroidvania game. Despite not having a AAA budget, this title punches above its weight, delivering a wholly satisfying experience that in some ways I enjoyed more than it's recent genre predecessor, Bloodstained. PROS:- Fantastic music- Pleasing artstyle/aesthetic- Large and engaging worldmap- Tons of weapons and armor to find, which reflects on the character model- Not groundbreaking, but totally competent and enjoyable combat and gameplay loopCONS:- Better quest journal/marker system would have been nice- Lack of voice over may disappoint someI completed Vigil: The Longest Night in about 25 hours, pleasantly surprised with its story and ending, which finished strong. This game comes highly recommended, even at full price.
