_childDocuments_.review: I real shame. I really wanted to like this game, but I couldn't.I finished the prologue, then unlocked the new, huge map and beated two new bosses (the toad and the kelpie), then i got bored.It has some truly great enemy design, but I could appreciate more in screenshots than in the game itself.The story and lore from what i have played are nicely done, but that wasn't enough to make me enjoy the game.Vigil is a perfect example of how a videogame with great art could be ruined if that game had bad design.The design of Vigil is bad because it's frustrating, but worse, it's bad because it's boring.The map is HUGE, but repetitive. Each area is filled with platform made with repeated assets and, from a screenshot, it's really hard to tell exactly where it's taken.For example, you get into a new area, you see a new background and think "that's a nice background", but then you notice the same stairs, che same floors, the same trees. Each area is just an open area filled with a bunch of repeated platforms.To make another example, it felt like Salt and Sactuary if every single area would be like the forest area, but less punishing, with some caverns all around, but without the areas being well linked like S&S.And this is the main problem, Vigil tries to be like Salt & Sanctuary without understanding what was great about that game and without trying to be something by itself.Another big problem, Vigil has a completely unbalanced skill system, with some skills being or overpowered, or useless or even bugged.I also played recently two other grear souls like games, Dark Devotion and Unworthy. Both of them are great because, other than being MUCH better beta tested and MUCH more balanced, they have a much bigger and solid identity and can enjoyed for what they are.Vigil just felt like a much worse Salt and Sactuary.I give a negative review, because I don't recommend to play it, but I can see some love in this game and, expecially, a lot of potential.I really hope that the developers could make another game, and really improve over it. Exactly like the developers behind the bad Lord of the Fallen listened at the critics, then improved by making the good The Surge, then improved even more with the masterpiece that is The Surge 2.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really well-made game.The first two hours or so are pretty slow, but the more you play Vigil, the better it gets. When you level up, you can put points into skill trees for each of the different weapon types, as well as a "General" tab for things like increased stamina and HP. Once you get some of the better weapon skills like parrying and air combos, the game really starts to shine.The story is quite good, albeit very dark and at times a little more verbose than it needs to be. You can spend 15-20 minutes in town talking to people if you want, and sometimes it gives you side quests or hints about upcoming areas. The structure reminds me of Castlevania 2 (NES) a little bit, but in a good way.The combat is tight, solid and rewarding. Leveling up makes significant improvements to your character's abilities, and I love that all the varied armor is shown on your character. There are clear references to Bloodborne and Salt & Sanctuary, but Vigil does maintain its own unique identity.If you enjoyed Salt & Sanctuary, and you like dark horror fantasy, give this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil: The Longest Night is a fairly solid metroidvania that doesn't lean into the difficulty the way a lot of similar games do, and also delivers a plot focusing on intrigue and characters that, again, similar games shy away from. If you're looking for a metroidvania with slick combat, rewarding exploration, and an interesting story, Vigil checks those boxes.

_childDocuments_.review: Whether a bad or a good one, this game was definitely an experience. So, despite the thumbs down, I’d still recommend it — see for yourself if you can handle how frustrating can it be to see a beautiful, clearly long-hatched idea crippled relentlessly by multiple horrendous design choices such as a completely obnoxious UI, a quest journal so bad it might as well not have existed, and a few other oversights so ridiculous they leave you wondering if this is perhaps early access.	The atmosphere is amazing, the art is beautiful, the main character lady is badass — what else can one wish for from a metroidvania, so you start charmed and hopeful. Of course, the story is somewhat vague and confusing at first, but all souls-likes are like that, so it’s not a problem at all. The hard difficulty is not exactly all that hard, most bosses can be tanked (I only truly struggled with Magpie), but I don’t mind that either — makes you feel cool, right?	And then you arrive at the smithy and receive a brief tutorial that mentions something about enchantments overriding other enchantments… but who cares, you don’t have any resources to enchant anything at this point, so you decide to care about it when the time is due, and move along the story only to understand several hours later what it meant — you cannot use two enchantment stones on one weapon at the same time, the new effect will override the previous one. Was there a pop-up warning you about this before you wasted your stones? No, there was a tutorial. Several hours ago. When you had no idea what an enchantment stone even was. 	Ah, by the way, once you sell something, you sell it forever. Yes,  Can you unknowingly sell a quest item (one that will lock you out of an ending, no less)? Absolutely. Is there a pop-up warning you? No. I guess I ought to count my blessings — at least some  quest items have a price of exactly one gold which makes you understand they are probably valuable for other reasons. Is there any mention about what reason it might be? You guessed it, no. 	The map… exists. And that’s pretty much all you can say about it — I guess, the devs decided you cannot get lost if you don’t know where you are and why, since the only remotely trackable quest is the main one. 	Oh. Oh, the side quests. Most of the time, you will get a vague note about “someone” potentially having an interest in an item you found. Good luck figuring out, who. Other times, you can speak to an NPC and they will request an item from you, or a task to be done — only to later relocate to another place on the map, no quest markers ever involved. Never. You also only see their name once a dialogue is already opened, so if you forgot what they looked like, you have to skip through however many dialogues  before you find the right one. 	An honorary mention goes out to the miners questline — save every miner and talk to Edward to let him know it’s done. Don’t receive your achievement, get confused, go on Google, and find out that you have to find Edward again in another location to… let him know it’s done? I guess dementia is a thing, I felt like I have it too, while trying to track these quests. I will add it again — no quest markers. 	The points of no return in the story make no effort to identify themselves as such (the devs viscerally hate pop-ups), each time leaving you with several failed quests as a result — at the first one, I was lucky to think about something like this and  to clean up my quests before proceeding, but the journal led me nowhere so I eventually gave up anyway. The further points of no return for some quests happened just upon entering a certain area, cause why bother?	The hands down most ridiculous thing — simply by dint of being so easily corrected — is the way stats are reflected in comparison. Let’s say, you get a new sword and you wish to see how it fairs compared to your old one. The stats highlighted in blue (with a + sign) would be an upgrade, and stats highlighted in yellow (with a -) would be a downgrade. Now, you see a blue stat, and you figure your new sword is better than the old one, only to start wielding it and find out that blue stat with a + sign was actually “Stamina cost” — a stat you don’t really want to increase. So, the code is written to straight up highlight everything that is getting increased in blue, without taking the meaning of the stat into the account. It might be a minor thing, but it desperately needs a better approach.	This game is impossible to approach without a guide — or is, but only for the price of skipping most of the side quests and not understanding anything of what is going on. So, as you desperately try to understand which item is needed for what, which NPC awaits you and where, where do you need to go and what to do in that location, your experience with the game scales down to simply waving your weapon and hopping around, since anything else is just way too confusing.	I still loved it, I truly did. Which is why it pained me to see such a beautiful creation being held back by so many completely imbecilic choices and oversights — otherwise, it would have been an absolutely perfect gem of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil: The Longest Night~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Vigil is a 2D, action-Metroidvania-styled platformer set in Medieval Europe, right after the effects of the Black Death starts showing its true colors; an unstoppable force of nature killing in the millions. You play as Leila, the Vigil of a damned village. Our young Heroine sets off on an adventure of epic proportions to save her family and village from this force of nature, while trying to solve the mystery behind it. Plot: Ah! Maye, a quiet little village located in a mountainous valley. Maye was so remote that it could keep its own culture and lifestyle without being interfered with by the Church.One day everything changed; the calm turned to dread, the quiet to chaos, as the Black Death ravaged this village. Infected residents wandering around the streets, creepy creatures hiding in the darkness, unburied bodies piling up at the cemetery.Seeing no other way of saving her village, Leila, our young heroine, steps forward as the village vigil/monster slayer. Leila ventures out into the unknown to figure out the mystery behind this sudden plague, put an end to it and save her people. Gameplay: The game starts off with a minimal cut scene intro, which gives a glimpse of the plot that we are about to run into, and nothing else. The story is told and discovered by textboxes while interacting with the villagers and noblemen. There are a few cut scenes here and there but the game is mostly text-heavy. And since it’s important to get into those interactions and story exploration, be prepared to do a lot of reading.Combat: Apart from the minimal intro start, there is nothing much to it. It’s a very linear start but things get complex as you start moving further. You encounter more and more creatures along your path and the only way forward is through these unholy beasts. The combat is nothing we haven’t seen before; the usual lite and heavy attacks combined with jumps, dodges, and rolls. But the combat is smooth, responsive, and very enjoyable.You get to enhance Leila’s combat effectiveness by equipping her with better weapon variants and enchanting her existing weapons with precious stones, which you can find throughout your exploration. This brings nothing new to the genre, but the way Vigil implements this feature feels fresh and positively impacts the game. There are also quite a few secondary weapons and weapons with secondary effects in the game. But throughout my play I got past most with the bare minimum lite and heavy attacks combined with some skillful dodging. Exploration: As mentioned earlier, the game starts off linearly, and then slowly but surely things escalate, and you will be running into a lot of uncreated territories. I am pleasantly surprised with the wide variety of exploration the game has to offer. Being a side-scroller, the playable areas are stacked on top of each other or hidden behind some obvious obstruction. Not only did the designers do a good job at stacking these playable areas together, but they also did a number on branching things further through hidden paths and secret rooms, spread throughout the game. The devs did a good job with this key feature in Vigil as you will find important NPCs and items lurking behind hidden rooms. Things do get a bit tedious and you will get lost often, but the reward is worth it. Thankfully the process is made a bit chilled with Owl lantern posts (Manual saving), which lets you revisit any previously interacted Owl Lantern post. Skill tree: The weapons and types of weapon that you carry will feature their own variants of the skill tree. Nothing new, but it is a neat feature that helps in the long run. Inventory and UI system: Vigil: The Longest Night features one of the most unnecessarily complicated UI systems I have encountered in a platformer yet!First of all, the game starts off with a weird PC key bind scheme that makes no sense, but thankfully it’s changeable. But what isn’t changeable is its weird UI choice, where you have to hit ESC to interact with inventory, map, skills, equipment, and notes!!! Okay I can deal with that, but why do I need to hit confirm after every action, that doesn’t have a key bind!!! Even the quick access wheel for items is one of the most complicated that I’ve encountered yet! World Design: Honestly, the game looks and feels great to explore. The world is well detailed and theme-appropriate. The structure and environment created to capture the haunting, plague-ridden medieval Europe is well done. But that glowy hue surrounding everything made me go crazy; it doesn’t really look that bad, but I hate it. Music and Sound effects: Unique, deep background music that was really good, befitting the game's theme and playing out nicely throughout my play through. The same goes for the sound effects; although there’s nothing too unique or special, it was good quality audio work. Positives: + Interesting plot + Great attention to exploration + Great attention to detail + Simple yet fun combat system + A lot of hidden paths and secret rooms+ Amazing background music + Solid sound effectsNegatives: - Same old stuff, brings nothing new to the genre - The loading screen glitched on me a few times - Unnecessarily complex UI/Inventory system Although Vigil: The Longest Night doesn’t bring anything new to the table, it more than makes up for it with its story, gameplay, and exploration. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: I will start with this: I honestly don't know why this game costs as little as it does.It is a full blown RPG metroidvania that can stand shoulder to shoulder with the greatest, like Bloodstained or Symphony of the night.It unashamedly takes its style almost completely out of Bloodborne: colors, setting, environments, monster design, parts of the story, environmental props, UI elements, rpg stats, certain mechanics - its all there, but that's not a bad thing! This isn't just a clone, it is a full, original game that could've done great without all those. I see this more as a homage, rather than just copying for a lack of ideas.Mechanics are very fun, and especially combat is fun and challenging, but not punishing. While it takes soulsbornes as inspiration, it is very clear the game sees itself as a metroidvania first. When you die, you have to reload from nearest checkpoint, and saving at checkpoint also respawns the monsters.But, you also get items to use so you can save whenever. You can get a bow very early (with plenty of arrow types), and while its not as strong as melee weapons - you can easily take down enemies that scare you or even bosses with it. Also, during one of the early major story bosses, there'll be literally a 'free loot' phase with specific items that can help you defeat the boss in a cheesier way, if you find you can't time dodge on its attacks.Graphics are great with multiple layer parallax, that at certain points can almost trick you into thinking you're walking along a 3D model.Audio is just out of this world! As you progress through the story and revisit same areas under different storyline circumstances, the music theme is there, but it changes instruments, composition, etc.If you like metroidvanias and want something just slightly different, mixed with a great combat rpg, just buy this. It is worth, imo, every cent and more!

_childDocuments_.review: On the fence about this one, which defaults to a Not Recommend. Things I liked: Art style, jumping and platforming mechanics feel nice, combat isn't trying too hard to be "git gud" with every encounter.Things I didn't like: In my experience, pacing needs improvement. At time of writing I played close to three hours and only received the starting sword and halberd. I consulted a guide to get a couple of spells. It is not good pacing to kill three bosses and be on your fourth and not find any weapons out in the world while exploring. Apparently I'm not alone in this and a staff member stated that maybe they hid the items "too well." That's not a bad thing, but the consequence was that everytime I found a treasure chest excited for a shiny new sword or what have you, it was a consumable item or some measly amount of gold. That becomes very frustrating when almost every chest is gold, throwing knife, molotov, etc. Looking at Symphony of the Night, Dark Souls, S&S etc which is ostensibly what this game is taking inspiration from, the weapons and armor would sometimes be very well hidden, sometimes they could be found very easily.Also, I spent the first 2.5 hours killing rats, bats, and various humanoid enemies, wondering if that was all I would be killing until I hit the ship area which introduced some new enemy types. It would be better if the variety was blended out a bit more.  Combat needs some polish but is serviceable for the most part. Enemies take a lot of hits to die but are not very difficult so it can be a bit of a slog. Sometimes I just dodged through and ran past enemies because it was less tedious which is not a good sign for your combat. From the few spells I used, they felt very rigid and underwhelming. Sound design needs attention, the rope "rrrreeeeah" sound when pulling levers sounds out of place for example. Dialogue needs proofreading, I encountered spelling errors and long bits of NPC text that ultimately communicate nothing  that could probably be cut.I think this game has a lot of potential and although I've been critical I wouldn't say it's "bad." If the combat was tightened up, sound design was reworked to match the wonderful art design in quality, and more weapons and armor were added and placed in easier to find locations, this would be a solid thumbs up. I'll be continuing to monitor this one and if it changes significantly I'll update the review.

Very good game, definitely worth your time if you love metroidvanias. I'm definitely going to follow these devs if they ever decide on another project.

_childDocuments_.review: I found this after searching for something similar to Death's Gambit and Salt & Sanctuary, and I was pleasantly surprised after giving it a chance.  It doesn't control quite as smoothly as those other games, the chunky roll animation turned me off at first, but the combat ultimately won me over with how stylistic the moves are as well as the hits feeling like they the have actual weight.  I was also impressed with how fun the bow weapons are to use here, the moves are stylish and impactful unlike the bows in the Salt games, which plain suck. The world is actually much larger than I expected, the enemy variety is good, and thorough exploration is rewarded with plenty of secret areas, quests and cool weapons to be found.  There are a couple different endings to unlock, and the standard ng+ with harder enemies and greater rewards.  For anyone familiar with the metroidvania/souls-like genre, I would recommend playing on hard difficulty because you will level up quickly, the xp system here is overly generous.  I see some people have criticized the story progression in the first act because of a "point of no return" that occurs and if you haven't completed your quests at that point you're s.o.l.. That is true, but I would say that if you're paying attention you will see this coming from down the block, it wasn't an issue for me. All in all I'm very happy I found this game, I would urge you to give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Really, really great game!   One of the best Metroidvania type games with challenge equal or greater to Cv Circle of the Moon and Order of Ecclesia.   Very original.   Good dark story heavily influenced by Lovecraftian horror.   Good depth of range of weapon skills and other movement techniques (aided by the awesome Time Deviation spell).   I appreciate that every piece of wearable EQ except little rings has its own graphics shown on the character.   Loading when going to another area and going in and out of town buildings is slightly annoyingly noticible but reasonably brief, at least on PC (I hear it's pretty bad on Nintendo Switch though, being about 10-15 seconds unless that version's been fixed recently).   I say definitely get this PC version over the Switch version.I'd like to warn that the steam achievement list and recent update notes contain spoilers you may not want to see until after you've played through the game.One thing unimportant to the story I wish I knew:  There's a guy Drew that begs and you give him some money.   Spend all your money or at least get down to a few gold and talk him and he will give you some money back returning the favor.   The fifth time you do this, he'll give the Stray Ring for +30% XP gains.   It's recommended to get it on your first play through and then again on your replay with your built up character for the benefit of having two!Highly recommend this game.   Get it!

_childDocuments_.review: To sum it up: 2D demon souls light.It's a platformer heavily inspired by demon souls and dark souls games, though not as difficult. (Don't let that fool you though!)Art style and animation are pretty good.Some of the level design is a bit finicky at times but very well done. (A certain tree comes to mind.)You can see for yourself in the screenshots so I’ll leave it at that.Combat is pretty smooth.It has a parry system (one traited, sword only) and you are expected to dodge.There are 4 (technically 6 *) weapon categories:- Sword = Defensive weapon focused around parry and reflection.- 2-handed = Charge attacks and big hits.- Daggers = Fast attacks that hit harder if you can keep hitting without getting hit.- Bow = Battle field dancer that shoots pointy bits. (Seriously, the dancing part is no joke. Especially in boss fights.)- *Throwing = Technically not a class, but it has it own stats and there are lots of throwing items. But requires ammunition.- *Magic = Devastating in its own right or used to supplement other play styles.Some magic is always needed as it is used to open pathways.Not all bosses are up to snuff though; some are a bit to easy compared to the rest.Gear progression is it's weakest point.There are plenty of items with different stats and ability’s but when you start upgrading you can break the entire game.I feel it would have been best if the upgrade system didn't exist or upgrade level max would be 3 instead of 7 as the stat gains make you pretty much immortal, baring a certain "bird" fight. (You'll know what I mean when you get there.)The story and quest are good enough to give a sense of the world, but they don't hold your hand to much.Forgot to do one in time? Well that's to bad now isn't it? Maybe next playthrough.O and that quest you forgot; the npc is now dead and everyone is sad about it. Enjoy the consequences.Played and finished the game in 24 hours. (restarted once 6 hours in.)Definitely one I recommend.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: In the genre of 2D "Soulslike" games, this -together with Salt N Sanctuary- is one of the best IMO.In fact if you liked S&S you can be pretty sure you will love this one too. However, where S&S had more Dark Souls inspired visuals, VIGIL seems more metrodvania/soulsborne inspired.Also you play as a female caracter in VIGIL, which is refreshing. Good mechanics, interesting weapons and spells (though a bit few) + great looking armor sets, and in general a captivating visual style. Your choices and sidequests effects the game, which bosses you will meet, how the story goes, and what ending you will get. Which to me made the replay value high.However If you are used too this type of game, play it on hard mode or enemies and bosses will be way too easy. Exploration in this game is really good, you will constantly find new paths in places you thought you had searched through, and through the game you will meet many locked paths that you will need certain arcane powers or keys to unlock that only comes later in game, so also alot of backtracking which i personally like. Over all a really good 2D "Soulslike" game.   8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil the longest night, is a game i saw a youtuber by ironpineapple featured in one of his obscure souls-like videos, and after beating it, thought id write a review and my overall thoughts of the game.Vigil, is a metroidvania in the style of fromsoftwares dark souls and bloodborne games, as well as having inspirations from other games along with it. Graphically the game is pretty grim in how it presents itself, due to the nature of the story, things are quite dark and stay night throughout the entire game, as the title may imply. While having some neat lightning and even from just visual presentation alone, the atmosphere is quite impressive, really setting the mood for each area. I found myself being rather cautious for my entire first playthrough, but also taking it slowly to just enjoy the tension and the grim feeling you'll get alot, often taking it slow for the most part. Aside from that, the character sprites are very in the style of cardboard cut outs, something you'd see in a play dating back to over 100 years ago. However, our protagonist, Leila, is a 3d model, which is a bit more obvious in motion, but on the plus side she looks great in motion as well, from jumping, to swinging various weapons, to using spells. However, due to this each armor and weapon changes how Leila will look, even things like enchants on weapons have a different cosmetic feel.As for the enemies and bosses, they are very well drawn and animated, being quite disturbing looking to some just looking out amazing, the bigger, the better looking in my opinion, having very excellent dark fantasy kind of vibes, on top of it their animations are what i'd call delicious, as I'm quite a fan of a well 2d animated sprite. The visuals get better though with the various locations, from the backgrounds looking rather cold, to seeing some caves with spiders crawling in the background, giving you a firm sense of dread or just enough detail to know what kind of location you're really in, even the town hub and its buildings really set in what kind of place you're generally dealing with.Overall, solid visuals in almost every category, some things look kinda janky at times, but overall an amazing visual presentation. The same goes for the excellent sound design. The weapon and and spell sounds are either very crunchy or just oozing with impact. Slashing at enemies and breath of the ancient guard being my personal favorites. Music is something else in this game, sometimes rather silent in some areas like the secret trail, or absolutely haunting in an area like the mines. The boss music delivers that really hopeless or dreadful type of feel you'd expect in a darker type of game, and fits perfectly.As much as I like both the visuals, music, and overall sound design. My favorite part was the gameplay and control, the controls aren't too bad, even if on my xbox one controller had some rather odd choices for button maping, so may want to mess around with that if the default buttons on your controller seem kind of so so. Despite that though the control feels rather tight and responsive, not noticing any major input delay, and jumping and moving feels just right, not floaty but not too heavy, even if some jumps sometimes were a bit harder to make than say symphony of the night or metroid zero mission.The combat in vigil is the true star though, having 4 different weapons each with their own specialities and styles. To make everything a bit more promising, the game also sports skill trees for each weapon type, granting new moves and passives. Allowing for both defensive and offensive abilities, as well as having a general skill tree for other things like increasing max hp or increasing stamina regen. Yes, this game has the whole fromsoftwares stamina system, as well as the dodge roll on top of it. However, stamina certainly feels much faster in this game to regen and generally keep up, and is a little less punishing, even after your stamina reaches zero, your blue stamina bar will change from blue to yellow. The yellow bar representing exhaustion, which decreases attack damage, but on the plus side it does allow you to get off your feet if you can manage to regain your normal stamina.The dodge roll is also really simple, press button without directions, a slight hop backwards, and directions will make you roll forward, with invincibility frames to boot. It's fairly good, and not quite as clunky as some games that use it, a little too good at times in my honest opinion.Aside from that, everything else is here, from throwing items, to your spells, which are refered to as arcane items, and of course your healing potions, which are seperated from your item selection, so you dont have to worry about switching to it. Both of these can be upgraded with various forms of armor or weapons, even the general skill tree can enhance them as well(like allowing you to use them in mid-air or even in a combo). Although some spells are kinda over-powered late game, making certain bosses more like something you stare at, rather than fight.Overall the battle system is generally not quite like a souls game and much closer to castlevania games like symphony of the night or portrait of ruin, but very fun nontheless. The upgrades also feel rather similar, most which you actually get from boss fights, so your classic double jump and slide. If you're looking to get lost in a game, vigil is quite for you. As the map gets pretty huge and honestly just exploring is quite a treat, as there is alot to uncover, as well as many secrets and items to get too. I swear some of these secret places would fit right at home in a donkey kong country game for how well they're hidden, so make use of your map and those eyes of yours, you'll be busy for quite a bit.As for the difficulty goes, it starts fairly good, enemies can put some nasty damage on  you rather quickly, even with some of the heavier armor types in the game, on the plus side you can also do alot of damage to them quite quickly if you play your cards right. Although I feel late game is a bit too easy at times, perhaps due to how many tools you have, or just how strong your equipment can be, but overall most of the difficulty is rather good, and doesn't feel effortless.There are problems however, mostly notebly in the late game areas, as getting to certain parts of the map is rather annoying, especially if you're looking to get some sort of equipment or spell and enemies or the hazards just like to fling status effects on you, and often don't feel the game does good enough for these kind of things. On top of that, many quests you'll be doing can easily be failed due to unknown areas you'll get into or a boss you fight, and the game even has areas of no return, which sometimes aren't too obvious and can make things rather confusing.How the game handles saving and respawn is also not bad, but rather odd in situations. You don't die like you would in say, dark souls where you lose some of your resources but respawn at your last checkpoint. In order to save you have to interact with these owl lanturns you find, you can also use fledgling souls to autosave where you are at, however if you dont save via these methods, everything you did will just be gone, as the save system is more akin to older metroidvanias like metroid or castlevania aria of sorrow. So in total, its kind of awkward sometimes, although it would certainly be a bit more helpful if there were more shortcuts, mostly in later areas though, early game and possibly mid game I'd say its fine.It's also been stated by others that the translation is a bit off putting, personally I havent found too much wrong with it, other than the occasional slip up, but the translation works fairly well, and is never really confusing.Overall an incredibly solid adventure, its quite a steal for its price, recommend to anyone that is a fan of metroidvanias to pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a lot of love for the game, I really hope there is a sequel (Direct or otherwise) as this has a TON of amazing content and the level of care put into things like the sound and art is astounding, but there's a lot of small things that pile up, and they're ALL gameplay. Certain things in the game are extremely annoying, like bats or the electric imps being able to phase through the walls or floors and have free shots at me, but I can deal with that, what made me quit the game was the Plague Doctor not only having a heal, poison, and multiple phases but the insane amount of effects going off on the screen to the point I LITERALLY cannot see where the boss is, or ANYTHING else for that matter. If it's intentional then that's bad design just like it's bad design to have parts of the screen hidden because I haven't past a threshold but enemies can still hit me. If you want to make a souls like game, don't have cheap hits like an enemy that rolls so fast I have 2 frames to react to from off screen. Also the controller still sucks, just copy the layout from any other game that has done this before in the last decade, it's not that hard, and fix the dodge, as it is I have a 60% chance of side-stepping into a projectile I was trying to avoid, remove the side step entirely actually, it sort of worked in the first hour but then instantly became a liability once enemies actually fought back after defeating the Ancient Guard the first time.I really wanted to finish it and see how everything comes together, I read all the notes and followed the side quests, but I refuse to endure a boss that makes me start to intensely dislike the game, because so far I'd had a lot of fun outside of those annoying instances, and it's not fair to have my view of an amazing game skewed because the gameplay design was as lobotomized as the AI of most enemies. There's a ton of small fixes that could turn this from an average game you can "deal" with to an exceptional game that stands along the likes of other 2D Soulslike/Metroidvainia games like Hollow Knight, Dead Cells or Chasm.

_childDocuments_.review: Needs polish and more variety.It looks nice. Nicer than the similar Salt & Sanctuary, for example, but that's not enough because it is a step or two behind in everything gameplay related. You only have four weapon classes (three melee, one ranged) in which to specialize - nothing more. Your char basically stays the same otherwise. Worse, the 'upgrades' in said classes - besides speed and damage - don't even seem to be helpful. The few new moves you learn can often be detrimental, (like the overhead attack on the 'Axe' leaving you open for a counter.)Spamming the light attack was always the best choice for me and that became boring after a while.I also often felt no difference between a successfull 'dodge' or getting hit. That might be on me, but in the soulsgames or in Salt & Sanctuary I knew what I was doing wrong.Itemization was also lacking. No interesting loot, the few weapons I found behaved exactly the same as the others in their respective class.Not terrible, but I can't say I had fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Every single thing in this game is okaish/fine with a few exceptions that make it really unfun. Controls are not responsive at all and you have a feeling of not being control all the time. For example, you have to tap multiple times the "drink a potion" button and even like that it may take up to 5-10 seconds for it to work. This is not acceptable in a game that tries to be a "hard" and "punishing" game. Imagine playing Darksouls with a 5% chance that every action you do won't work, yikes! Every time you die you lose everything you got since last checkpoint. This on its own is really punishing (but could be fair tbh) but if you add the absolutely poor checkpoint placement and the complete horrible input system is hell.I would not recommend this game at all since there are much much better alternatives at this price point.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're into soulsborne metrovanias then this is for you. In my opinion, the game is worth it.Here are some progression tips w/o blatant spoilers:First, the game length is on the middle-upper longer side of metrovanias. The plot only starts to make sense near the end, but you can read the clues along the way to understand the bigger picture.Second, every time something happens, talk to every NPC and check your 'Notes' for quests. You can miss most side quests if you're not careful, so use the save slots well.Third, explore the world following the order of the 'Owl Statues' alphanumerically. Use the bow's 'Air Power Shot' for early mid-air dash and its mid-air attack to lift you a little, and spam the axe's normal attack to slow your fall while moving horizontally.Lastly, hidden rooms are better seen in map- they are different in outline colors. Sometimes, the walls are either only breakable on one side so you need to find another entrance or you can break it with a 'Dynamite'.Note that most, if not all, of the bugs brought up online were fixed. It's been two years and there are patches up until July 12th this year. Plus, I vouch for it on my 40 hours of playtime (whole playthrough to all the endings) of no bugs.The Goddess is with you, Vigilant!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, an excellent game with many strong points. Here is a detailed breakdown - Graphics/Visuals: 6.7/10 - Excellent visual atmosphere, nice small details such as water reflections and background depth contribute to a strong sense of style and an interesting world. That said... I do have the most issues on this point. The game is not visually unappealing, but everything has a sort of indistinct, fuzzy 'oil painting' blurriness, which takes some time to get used to and can make it hard to clearly see things. Additionally, some of the characters/npcs fall into the 'uncanny valley' zone, with strange faces, strange proportions, and strange size scales. Some of that may be by design, but my overall impression is that the visual polish could have used more refinement. Your mileage may vary, however - the game did win an award for visual design, so perhaps my opinion in this case is an outlier.Animation: 8/10 - Leila's moveset is the best animated and looks/feels awesome while playing. The creatures/npcs are also mostly well animated, though it sometimes feels like fighting puppets, patchwork limbs stitched together over basic animation rigs.Controls: 8.5/10 - the controls are tight and responsive, if you struggle it's typically down to your own skill. A few nitpicks, however. First, it's occasionally difficult to tell where hit boxes are, though this is minor - some of the bigger creatures just have specific points of vulnerability you have to learn. Second, the controller support doesn't allow for a functional right thumbstick or clickable buttons on thumbsticks. And the menu control buttons do not rebind separately from the game skill buttons. These two factors create a gameplay problem - no good place for the dash button. The default assignment of the dash button to the D-Pad is objectively terrible to play with for ease of reach for such an essential skill. But if you reassign it to a better button, like a bumper, you have now messed up your menu navigation keybinds.Exploration: 9/10 - lots of hidden secrets to hunt for, interesting areas, and a large map that expands farther than you'd expect.Story: 7/10 - Interesting characters and story threads to follow, though they are somewhat simple and understated. Go here, talk to this person, find this thing and bring it back. But that's fine, for this kind of game you don't want story to hit you over the head, and at least it doesn't get in the way of enjoying the gameplay, for the most part. Sometimes there are consequences, which makes things more interesting.Music: 9/10 - excellent music in a style that suits the game, very well produced, and it adds a lot of value to immersion. The tracks don't get annoying even with lots of gameplay repetition, and there are some real standouts, such as the title track.Sound: 7.5/10 - the sound design that IS in game is generally solid and well done. However, there are a lot of 'missing' SFX for things that often feel like they ought to have audio, such as various magic abilities that are basically silent or are covered by only a basic activation sound, or background elements such as the blacksmith hammering on his anvil being completely silent. It just feels unfinished, like someone stopped working on sound design halfway through the project.Difficulty: NA:  I played on Normal, and the game doesn't strike me as terribly difficult, maybe even slightly easy. But that's fine, it makes for a comfortable experience. If I was to start over I might try the higher difficulty setting.I see a number of players upset over the death mechanic in this game - when you die, it is game over, back to your last save, just a straight up data load, with anything gained or changed since being lost. I would agree that the game would benefit from a slightly more 'modern' death mechanic... however, while it's less than ideal, I didn't find myself dying very often. There is a ring to completely eliminate fall damage, and a player skill that gives you one free revive from death. These help immensely.Systems: 9/10 - Fun skill trees with meaningful upgrades, lots of items with balanced, interesting tradeoffs. Even more depth could have been fun, but for the length of the game, this is just about the right amount.Gameplay: 9.5/10 - The overall experience is very enjoyable. It's empowering to the player just to jump around, slide, grab ledges, and explore. The weapon movesets are varied, distinct, and fun to do, and leave you feeling powerful.Overall Final Score: 8.4/10 - Fun, well made experience that will scratch the itch you may have for Castlevania, Metroid, or Diablo, while still standing on its own. If you liked Bloodstained, you will like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Despite not recommending the game, I would rate it a 7/10. I don't recommend the game because there are other, better Metroidvania games out there that would be more worth your while. If you've burned through every other notable Metroidvania, then this would be an alright choice, if frustrating at a lot of times.The game is rife with design decisions that scream indie-jank, such as not giving warnings when approaching points-of-no-return. Or bosses that use different moves with very similar wind ups. Or not allowing you to use consumables unless you equip them, use it, then unequip them. Bosses performing attacks that cover huge swaths of area from off screen with no distinctive sounds to warn the player.Just loads of little details that are frustrating, add no value to the game, and make it just a bit worse to play.However, past all the poor design choices is a fun game with good art direction.

_childDocuments_.review: The bad:- No savepoints available next to bosses, some you might need to fight a few dozen times before you win. Having to parkour all the way back through a whole level and loading screen every time to fight a boss is just too much. They should allow you to buy save points at the shop.- Loading screens of around 5 seconds that happen a lot when you're in town and going in and out of houses.- Interactive objects and people are often positioned right next to stairs, so I frequently enter conversations I don't want to over and over by pushing up to go up the stairs. Please devs, just shift the people slightly to the side.- People should have names above their heads, it's hard to remember who's who.- Speech text appears slowly, so you have to click twice to skip through it. I'd rather there was an option to enable to speech bubbles to appear with all text immediately, then I need only one click to advance to the next paragraph.- Saving is clunky and requires far too many clicks.- The game gives no information on level cap or max number of skill points, so it's impossible to know whether to specialise or freely try out different builds.- Skills are badly described and don't make sense half the time. You will have to search forums to understand how some of them are supposed to work and what buttons activate them.The good:- Beautiful art, animation, level design. Decent music & sound.- No voice audio.- Fun weapons and skills for variety, that aren't overly complicated.- More story and talking than Ori or Hollow Knight, so it feels less desolate. So far it also seems slightly easier than them. Without 50 different dash/flight mechanics like Ori that make climbing a cliff feel like piloting a spaceship through an asteroid field.- Gothic spooky feel to it that's very hard to find these days. A true successor to Castlevania and Wardner.- Perfect controller support, except staircase interaction is unwieldy. I've often fallen to my death off one instead of jumping.- Great tutorial level and introduction of mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Completely Exceeded My Expectations. This is an Absolute win for a Metroidvania. Does have challenging bosses comparable to souls-like, but not nearly as frustrating. It can be Comparable to Blasphemous, and Salt and Sanctuary, But the Lore, and Art style are far superior in my opinion. EDIT:  SPOILER... _childDocuments_.review: For starters i love this game, but im well aware that is in large part due to it being a perfect combination of things i really dig. Large and confusing world, check; occult themes and a nice lovecraftian feel, check; metroidvania styled progression with a fairly simple but fun combat system, check; tons of items and secrets to find, check. The point is it would've been tough for this game to let me down in the first place, I know that. But im still confident in saying this its not just me, this game is just straight up great.Ill start with what i dont like cause thats easy- english translation is pretty sketch at times as mentioned by many of the other reviews. I do feel that this affected my overall understanding of the story as well as causing other miscellaneous mixups and confusion concerning the quests in the game.- there are some bugs, who woulda guessed. A great majority of which are both rare and entirely inconsequential, but, every now and then a mission can bug out a little and give you trouble if you havnt followed the steps exactly as the game wants you too, despite the steps not always making complete sense. I should note though that none of the major quests did this so its far from being gamebreaking.- balance is just not there. It seems like for every weapon type there is are obvious "best choices". One or two weapons will be obviously better than the rest, and one skill will always be better that the rest. On top of this, the duel blades weapon type is literal garbage and borderline frustrating to play with. Additionally, many of the bosses can be absolutely curb stomped using the right combination of arcane items.- the map seemed... kinda bad. I very rarely used it for the great majority of the game and this may be why i feel this way, but using it often just confused me more. I only needed it for directions maybe three times and each time it did its job but it was admittedly harder than it probably should've been. Im fairly confident though that if you use the map throughout the game rather than just at the very end, it will serve you well.Woohoo now onto the good- with the exception of your characters 3d model, the art in this game is great. Everything looks so satisfyingly dreary and dark, the areas all stand apart from one another pretty well and all the enemies look gross and spooky... but in a good way of course. The bosses especially all look distinct and cool.- The secrets are abundant and great. Now obviously not every nook you slip into has some new weapon or significant item, sometimes its just a measly bomb. But that didnt keep me from being the most paranoid ive ever been in game thinking that i missed something because i stopped paying attention to the damn walls for a second. It was fun exploring the world and discovering hidden ledges or ladders or holes to slide through while also just trying to progress in the first place. There almost always seemed to be some hint as to whether or not there was a secret as well so i never really looked at something and thought "nah there cant be ♥♥♥♥ there" only for there to be ♥♥♥♥ there when i checked anyway.- the combat was always fun. Though my strategy for killing things stagnated around the mid game, i still always enjoyed it and new enemies were added frequently and effectively enough that it stayed pretty fresh throughout the game. the bosses were all fun to fight as well excusing some minor annoyances here and there with two or three of them and the fact that i kinda just steam rolled though the last 3 using cheesy skills and items. I consider this my reward for having acquired said items in the first place :)- the story is... something. Is there a story... yes. Do i know what it is exactly... no. Do i care, no. despite not being fully clear by the end(likely due to details being lost in translation and my own unwillingness to try any harder at piecing together names, locations, and events) it was still fun to guess at things and find clues throughout the game. It also worked as a plenty good motivator for progressing though the world and doing peoples little side tasks.- Honorable mention for the prologue to this game, which was, in terms of its story, pacing, and building of tension, better than what followed thanks to its far more linear design and short nature. It still holds as my favorite part even if the rest of the game is great too. - i dont really know ♥♥♥♥ about music, but this games soundtrack is fire af. Its hype, its spooky, it matches the feel of each area perfectly, and it works wonders for building tension in the prologue.tldr: the game is great, fun combat, great music, sick bosses, fantastic art, and fun secrets held down by just some poor translations and a couple bugged and/or unclear missions. Also use the map unless you like being lost in a big ass forest.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game now, but hungry for another run through as I missed some quests along the way. The art in this game is like Salt+Sanctuary took 5 extra years to polish theirs. Gameplay-wise, It's not like the Salt + Sanctuary/Dark souls formula where you stress so much you need to take breaks often for mental health reasons(lol), it's more in depth story-wise where I found myself wanting to find out what happens next. The ending was also quite satisfying, and generally less confusing than a souls-like.The team fixed the controller issues and now it works just fine. Very thankful for their continued support.The in-game skills and magic are kinda wild for this genre. The daggers feel like proper fun. The game has more secrets and alternate paths than the first Dark Souls. You beat this crazy area only to return to town through some nuts sewers. You get extra abilities like double jump and door unlocking abilities that open extra areas the more you explore. It's a proper adventure. Though I still haven't figured out how to unlock green areas despite beating the game.The game does feature a new game plus, and I missed a bunch my first playthrough so I'm kind of glad I can run through the main story and get a lot of those. The game does have alternating paths so hopefully this time I can change the fate of the world a little, who knows.The base game is forgiving, meanwhile new game+ is a lot less so, if you're up for a challenge. Considering the price, size of the game and the size of the team that took to develop it this game is well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: **SPOILERS** In a nutshell, I'd place Vigil into the flawed classic category. It's got gorgeous visuals that match the story's thematic elements. It's a long, winding game, and felt like a longer journey than the 20.5 hours I put in to get an ending. The plot is thin, and while Vigil tries to follow along the lines of Dark Souls storytelling, it sorta fails, because it's a mix of buried lore in items, and pedestrian dialogue from NPCs. You should at least have an idea what a Vigilant is; and cursory background info, like why it's an eternal night, etc. Gameplay is decent, with generally responsive controls,  but I was super frustrated that double-tap to dash didn't work on my controller, and I had to use the R d-pad, which made for annoying platforming. Lag was also a constant issue, with some boss fights moving through a vat of peanut butter. The map is also lacking--it's better than nothing but super annoying to have the map unmarked for the most part, and no marker system like Hollow Knight. Checkpoints are also pretty random--sometimes they're close to one another, and other times you slog. It's extremely frustrating when you die, since you don't keep the items you picked up along the way--this means you have to replay entire sections if you forget to save. Another problem is the quicksave function via item use is super annoying, because you have to equip said item. This means you have to remember to unequip it--otherwise you might accidentally use it instead of a spell, etc. It is, however, rewarding that Vigil rewards exploration. It has tons of secret areas, interesting items that really impact gameplay, and allows for different play styles. Another point (for better or worse) is that unlike Dark Souls, Vigil lets you farm unlimited baddies, so at a certain section right next to a checkpoint, you can trap a larger enemy, wail away until it's dead, and then refresh at the checkpoint for tons of XP and $. Lather rinse repeat until skill tree progression starts capping off.  (I pretty much went the Axe skilltree route, and farmed to a decent level to where I could afford a piece of golden armor. Add a ring to boost $, and an item steal spell, and you're maximizing each run.) Maximizing perks like damage reflection, and getting lifesteal items means you can facetank most bosses on Normal mode--about 1/3 of the way into the game, I beat most bosses on the first try, and could just run through levels without worrying about health potions. Enchantments are also hard to come by, and I found you can largely ignore them and focus on forging your weapons and armor instead. So all in all, Vigil's a fun trip, with some bearable nuisances that hopefully the studio will learn from. I'd put it as a B grade.

_childDocuments_.review: I almost gave up on this game in the first ten minutes because I couldn't get past the tutorial boss on Normal mode. Granted I'm pushing 40, and my reflexes aren't what they used to be. The tutorial was very sink-or-swim, without coaching on how to really time your movemnts. I had to go online and get some tips for using dodge effectively and tactical position. Once I got the rhythm down, the game got easier. Then the Prologue boss hemmed me up until I went back and found some items I had missed, including a better sword and the early Arcane spell to summon firebirds. Like a lot of Metroidvanias, there are some items that are so well hidden that you simply won't get them unless by luck or with a walkthrough.The description of the game is a good one; it's a very technically precise sort of combat. Timing needs to be spot on and you just die a lot until you start learning tactics and looking for attack indicators. I am invested heavily in an Arcane build that's working very well for me. Art direction is gorgeous, using 3D models to animate paper puppets. The music's a little repetitive but spot-on for the horror vibe. Combat is challenging but rewarding and even as you get up there in power a ways, getting careless can get you killed fairly quickly. My one complaint is going to include a spoiler: The Notes system is very lacking. This is how you track your quests, and there are no prompts on some of the quest objectives. I failed one minor quest that i didn't know was timed; okay, not a big deal, side-errand thing. The major quest that determines whether you get a good or Great ending involves collecting all your sister's personal possessions. An NPC named Hilde asks me for help in sneaking into the Doctor's house and the reward is one of these key personal items. I get no hints on how to do that, where to go, who to talk to, or when it needs to be done. So I keep grooving on the main quest until I find the three cubic stones that unlock the next quest area. I show them to the Doctor NPC and he takes off. It's only an hour later that I find that this is a 'point of no return'. I can no longer assist Hilde in her quest. Which means she won't give me one of the four key items required for a 'good' ending. At 26 hours in, it is very frustrating to realize I can't get the 'good' ending. i failed to deduce that I had to talk to Carlos to get his help with Hilde's quest. One specific NPC, out of over a dozen, way back in town, hanging out in an unobtrusive area just off-screen, for a plot-critical bit of assistance. Not even a symbol or a mark around him to let me know he was relevant to my quest. Frustrating, but, there it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Metroidvania goodness, I really like this game. Artstyle reminds me a lot of old flash games, but apparently it's moreso some paper cut thing that it's meant to emulate. It can take some getting used to, and some fights (the first boss in particular) can feel weird to react to their somewhat stiff animations.The save system can be a bit jarring; the game wants you to either use the save anywhere consumables or save as often as possible, because you can die fairly easily and if you do, any progress you did since last save is gone. It's a bit weird since the system is otherwise very Souls-inspired with the enemy respawns and healing count and whatnot, but the save system is not what you'd expect from the genre.Only other complaint I'd really have is how the weapons are generally same moveset BUT BETTER than the previous one. Since smithing materials are fairly rare, I often end up finding a vastly superior weapon soon as I upgraded the previous one, and feel a bit annoyed that I'm all out of stones to upgrade it. Some weapons come with special skills with fighting game inputs, but generally there's no difference between one sword and the other, the later game one just does outright more damage.Lore is fairly dope, your mileage may vary. Eldrich horror this and that, big Bloodborne, the main villain stuff is a bit too obvious and the game tries to play it off like it's supposed to be something of a surprise. I mean the bad guy from the prologue lived in the exact same house as the new guy who's clearly sus, is it really necessary to hint me that maybe this guy is evil by having his clothing items tucked away in evil caves that imply he might be related to the previous bad guy? Or gradually feeding me notes that imply he might be up to something nefarious? The dialogue and atmosphere is kind of all over the place too, frequently in optional quests the game is joking about itself and breaking the fourth wall, but then wants to take itself very seriously when you're back to the main questline. Bit of a whiplash at times.Anyway, big recommend. Lots of content, good experience. 100%ing was bit weird since some items didn't count until I got them a 2nd time, and I thought I was unable to get the starting sword, but turns out the smith sells it in NG+ again.
_childDocuments_.name: Vigil: The Longest Night

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid metroidvania that has heavy influence from Salt & Sanctuary.  World is pretty massive and production value is very high compared to some other MVs on Steam.  Game features multiple endings and a lot of in-game quests and content to explore.   Combat feels pretty fluid despite having zero mouse support, as a keyboard user I had no problems configuring the buttons and the character always did want I wanted it do without any jank.Leveling system features a pretty hefty series of skill trees, each node featuring multiple levels to invest in.  The general skill tree seemed to be far and away the most useful, but there is a different skill tree for each of the game's 3 weapon types.  Levels come fairly frequent so you naturally start getting them from general play without ever feeling like you need to grind.Some minor issues include the map being a little rough around the edges, literally, and lacking marking important locations on the map.  It can become difficult to remember where to turn in quests, and having some sort of map marker would have gone a long way here.  Leveling up also does no seem to innately raise your stats, so mostly weapons and armor are the main ways of growing your character's raw stats.  The shop also seems fairly bad in terms of what it sells, as I found potions to be the only thing I really used it for.  Unlike Dark Souls, the potions are all consumable and do not recharge at save points, so you are regularly going back to get them for bosses.  The good news is every save station is also a fast travel point, so jumping around the map is fairly painless once you discover more save spots.  A final word, I played on normal difficulty which seemed to be adequately challenging, which was nice.I got one of the endings in around 11 hours, probably not the best ending, and there is also a New Game+.  This means you could easily got a lot more time out of this game especially considering there are still a lot of places on the map I hadn't fully explored.  Overall a good value for your money, and I think most Salt and Sanctuary fans will enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil: The Longest Night has its moments, but ultimately it's a poor execution of the tried-and-true soulslike metroidvania genre.I got a copy of Vigil in a bundle with several other games, and I had been looking forward to trying it out. I'm not huge on soulslike-type games personally, but I love a good metroidvania, so I have played and enjoyed games like Grime, Hollow Knight, or Salt and Sanctuary.I've tried to get into this game a few times, but I just keep bouncing off of it.  For every good thing about the game, it has another dragging it down.  The core gameplay, platforming, and combat has not been enough to overcome the negatives for me. - I find the story to be overly cryptic and poorly presented.  I dislike the large town area, filled with empty quests and dozens of anonymous townsfolk who say nothing meaningful. - Worse, the quest log is full of stuff like "I need to talk to Steve".  Great, which one of these dozens of townsfolk is Steve - now I need to run all over town trying to find the guy?  -  I dislike the large amount of missable items and quests in this metroidvania game; the impossibility of collecting all items in one playthrough due to some quests having different outcomes also feels like something that doesn't belong in this genre. - I experienced a known bug with one quest, rendering it impossible to complete. - There are several points-of-no-return that are untelegraphed. - The map is large and confusing, and exploration feels kind of like a choreI am going to come back to Vigil eventually and try again, and I may finish the game at some point, but the above points for me make it hard to appreciate the good things the game does have to offer.

One is the difficulty of bosses which is not as trying and frustrating as some other soulsborne metrovania platformers like Grime, Ender Lilies, etc., but offers immense replayability due to the vast variety of weapons, armors,  accessories and magics. _childDocuments_.review: This game is killer.  If you have any interest in RPG-oriented Metroidvania or Souls-like non-linearity and dodgy combat, you're in for a good time.There, that's the praise.  The ensuing criticism is then partially intended as feedback for the developers and partially to set expectations for players who might have expected more of the game's faults.-Controls: At the beginning of the game, the controls are fine.  Your dodge is a little wimpy, the interact button being "up" is a little weird on controller (my thumb tends to drift upward on the control stick, and the input check for the game is very sensitive, so I ended up talking to people a lot when I didn't want to).  Then you start getting new abilities, and the game...staples them to the same set of buttons?  Dashing is the same sideways input twice on a .45 second (WAY too generous) input frame, which led to the extremely common scenario of me attempting to make minor adjustments while platforming to avoid sawblades or whatever other hazards and then yeeting myself off a ledge (or into a spike wall) because I accidentally pressed the same direction too soon.  Sliding--a not terribly safe maneuver--is just hitting the dodge button while you're dodging.  Why couldn't these have been their own dedicated buttons (or sliding just dodging while crouching)?  I played on a PS4 controller, and there were a full four buttons that the game never used, and it's not as if a keyboard has any shortage of buttons either.  If I had to nail down any true negative of this game, this would be it--I highly recommend that the devs add some additional flexibility to the control scheme.-Combat, Difficulty, and Enemy Design: Combat is definitely more engaging than the average Metroidvania title, but that's a low bar.  Enemies in Castlevania are dumb, programmatic, and not that dangerous--here, they're dumb (albeit in weird, unpredictable ways), erratic, and not dangerous only by virtue of the fact that they hit like wet noodles.  To which point, on Normal difficulty, the game is very, very easy.  To anyone looking for a challenge, I recommend playing on Hard, though I make this recommendation only tepidly, since the enemy design will likely ramp frustration faster than "challenge".  Enemy hitboxes (on average) come out fast and unpredictable, which makes close-quarters combat very unsafe.  Again, on Normal, this means chip damage, so whatever, but Hard will likely make any non-ranged build kind of frustrating to play.  I would have liked to see more predictable AI that punished you more for mistakes, but your mileage may vary.Boss Design: Bosses were visually sweet, but it felt like half the set just followed the formula of "giant mass of damage that runs/swipes at you a lot".  There were a few standouts (the final three bosses being the best in my opinion), and if any DLC is in the works, I would encourage the devs to flex their creative muscles a little more in this area.  Players should expect the meat of the gameplay to come in the exploration sections, though.Builds/RP Elements: Builds in this game are super shallow, which has its pros and cons, but the game also hands level-ups out like candy, which means that by the time I wrapped up my first playthrough, I had more-or-less maxed out three of the five available offensive builds as well as purchased every defensive Skill I could want (and many I didn't).  Again, depth here seems like a DLC opportunity.  It also feels like the offensive options not tied to Arcane items could use a little love--Arcane just seems vastly more powerful than anything else you can do by the end of the game (and the skill points for it are acquirable with minimal commitment, and the best spells are acquirable very early, etc.).  That may just be my own opinion, though.Again, overall, I recommend this very highly.  Kudos to Glass Heart Games--I'll be following them in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: With Vigil we got a Metroidvania Game done right. In almost every way. Fun and rewarding combat, deep lore and a wonderful story, a lot of spells, wepons, gear and builds to work with. From all the Action RPGs they throw at us in recent years, thanks to Dark Souls, this one stands out from the crowd. Very similar to another great pearl in the gerne called Salt and Sanctuary. Or even a little like Hollow Knight if you want some comparison. While SaS is the perfect DS clone in 2D, Vigil is the perfect clone of Bloodborne. You certainly know what i mean, if you have played Bloodborne and Vigil: The Longest Night. You just have to love that beautiful lovecraftian lore! Exploring can be a bit frustrating without certain items (or at least one certain ring), but with them it's just pure fun.Pros:1.) Gameworld and atmosphere2.) Story, lore and NPCs3.) Soundtrack and sound effects4.) Combat and boss battles5.) Enemy and boss design6.) Exploration and movement abilities7.) All those weapons, skills, gear, spells, rings to build around8.) No crashes or glitches encountered9.) Free DLCs and Updates! Thaks a lot for that.Neutral:1.) Saving is a bit awkward at first and different from SaS, DS, or Hollow Knight. You just have to get used to it.2.) Played with a controller, like all these games. Controls are fine and much better than Salt and Sancuary. You can't really fall trough platforms any more so platforming is easy. Some things are just a bit unhandy and i needed to rebind a bit before i was satisfied with the setup.Conclusio:Well worth the money. Got it on sale, but would pay full price every day now. So if you like the gerne, or wanna get into it, you can't do anything wrong here. Give them your money, or buy it on sale if you must. Highly recommended! And let's hope the devs will deliver more great games in the future.Ps.: Here are my reviews from the other great Metroidvania games I mentioned.1.) Salt and Sanctuary: 2.) Hollow Knight: Personal score: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun and pretty, but there's a lot of little things that add up to make me kinda mixed on it. the story  The combat is fun but the difficulty is all over the place and I personally never found many of the areas to be horribly difficult especially since you can carry like 21 full heals at all times. but to combat this the designers decided to throw a bunch of instant death pits in the back half of the game, and that wouldn't be the worst thing but every time I died to one I was surprised as they aren't very clearly marked, luckily these are few and far between but it always felt cheap when I encountered one. I'm also not happy about the weapon scaling. there's a bunch of gold weapons in the shop for like 80-90k each and I had farmed enough for them around mid-game only to be horrified that they are the strongest weapons in the game, making each and every weapon I received afterwards feel absolutely worthless. which compounds on the issue this game has with rewards, the exploration in this game is very fun but 80% of the chests you find are filled with literal garbage. they have rings labeled as "ordinary" or "rare" and they add like 4 or 5 attack or health or whatever but before you're even 10% through the game all your ring slots will be filled with actually good rings so these rings are pretty much only useful to sell but they sell for next to nothing and are annoying to sell in the UI to boot as you can't sort them from your actually useful rings. and again by mid game you will have 10s of thousands of gold, so opening a chest to find a ring that sells for 160 is the biggest slap in the face, only slightly worse than opening a chest to get 300 gold which is better since you don't have to go to the shop to pawn off the junk.  it feels like the people who balanced the weapons and decided the chest rewards wanted to do everything in their power to deincentivize exploration. if you just fight enemies to grind gold you can get some of the best equipment in the game and never have to explore at all. which is a shame as the movement and exploration in this game is so good. there's so many cool secrets and hidden rooms, but there's nothing worse than finding a well hidden cool secret room just to open the chest and get 200 gold.

_childDocuments_.review: Vigil to me seems like as if Bloodstained had a baby with Salt & Sanctuary, both visually and through gameplay. Graphics has this very distinctive style that any S&S fan will love. With a little more human-sized proportion compared to S&S. Lovely is the background/foreground paper-cut play which really adds a lot to the overall looks and depth of the visuals.Combat is a little bit more action/combo-esque once you start mastering it. Similarly to Bloodstained. with a little less emphasis on the dedicated skill buttons (there are basically none).Skill tree is not the largest but has a lot of impact so you won't feel swindled when you pick literally any trait. Plus there is the regular lvlup progression which yields you some bonus stats.Story is presented via trails of notes and bits of information here and there and of course, reading conversations (common thing among Souls-like games). There is a decent notes/quest tracker in the game to hold info regarding some of the sidequests and help you navigate and decide where to go next, in order not to wander around pointlessly.I believe there are two minor downsides to this game in my mind...Music.. Vigil has "just" decent music. it's mostly fine but nothing to write home about and not really as memorable as some of it's peers. Sometimes it's way too loud other times you get annoyed by the repetition. Sometimes I'd rather hear some quiet ambient instead.Map, which is simply terrible. It's really horrendous to navigate. You can't seem to be able to fill in all the blank spaces so you never get the right feel of exploration and areas have no visible boundaries so names won't help you much either as you are not even sure which part of the map belongs where. This has additional negative impact on teleporting which only offers names as a description of the place and most of the time you can't even locate it on the map. This leads to frustration as you will often end up stranded instead of returning to the place you wanted.Overall great game, with a lot of potential (Some minor updates could push it a long way). Vigil, will give you much more worth than you deserve for such a low price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want the short answer for "Should I play this?" Then I'll say this much: Yes, you should, but don't go in with super high standards. If you want more information than that, let me explain."Vigil: The Longest Night" is one of many games that people would refer to as a "Souls Like", in that is has quick paced and challenging combat focused around timing your attacks and dodges. Beyond that though, Vigil is actually an exploration game disguised as an action RPG. Sure, when you start out the combat can be tough and interesting, but after you've killed about 4 bosses and really tailor your build to your liking, combat becomes just another thing you do in your ultimate goal of just finding new stuff. That isn't to say that combat ever gets stale, for me at least I enjoyed ever second of it right up to the end, but combat is far from the focus here once you're halfway in. All the same, exploring the world and fighting new bosses in new areas is a ton of fun, and a lot of the secrets in the game feel rewarding and enjoyable.Now, that doesn't mean the game does this perfectly however. The game suffers from balance issues a lot, where weapon types like swords are just objectively better than things like axes and dual blades, and getting new weapons is always more of an upgrade than an option. Like in Dark Souls, you can fully upgrade a basic Bastard Sword and easily beat the game with it as long as you understand the weapon well. In Vigil, you just cannot go without eventually finding a new weapon that does more damage, which is kind of a shame if you have a sword that looks REALLY GOOD with your armour but has to be swapped.Another issue is with some of the puzzle design. There are secrets in this game that require some PINPOINT precision when jumping. I don't mind a good and challenging platforming section, but when it's just one jump that you have to attempt over and over again because you were standing in slightly the wrong spot and will always miss by a few inches, with no clear indication of how to get across besides "Try again", it gets a little tiresome.The game also isn't without its bugs. There's a whole armour set called the "Black Armour" that you get from a mini boss after an admittedly difficult jumping puzzle early on, but even if you manage to make the jump and kill the boss, the set just doesn't drop right now for some reason. Just gold. The translations are also a bit wacky at times, like how some item descriptions have a lot of typos and grammar errors, this can be forgiven though since this game came from an indie studio that doesn't speak English native.So with all that, why am I still recommending this? Because it's FUN. It has a creative story, good vision, fun gameplay, and SO MUCH TO DO. I have been sucked into this game for days now, every time I get off work I go right to it, it's great for that. And with things like Multiplayer being added eventually and a lot of the issues I've mentioned being directly addressed, there's not really anything I have to say that's super damning.The soundtrack is AMAZING, the art is AMAZING, the level design is REALLY GOOD, and clearly a ton of heart went into this project. A solid 8/10 from me. Not perfect, but worth its price point and then some.

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeously animated metroidvania that takes clear inspiration from Bloodborne but has plenty of ideas of its own. I appreciate the way it retains the more intricate aspects of soulslike combat despite the 2D format, resulting in something almost fighting game-esque at times. The enemy AI is refreshingly good across the board, too, making combat much more about fighting well instead of just rewarding cheese. Also, the lovecraftian enemies' designs are fantastic. There was one that literally shocked me to the point of dropping my controller and staring dumbfounded. All of this is wrapped up in a plot that might not be winning any awards, but still has enough intricacy and emotional weight to keep a player invested. Best of all, it's one of the rare few games whose ending is actually  Vigil is well worth your time.
