_childDocuments_.review: The first chapter or two were a little slow, but by the end you connect with the characters, and the end of the story resonates. The use of the art style has good moments and bad, but the takeaway from completing the game and the last few scenes means the takeaway from the game is it was beautiful. Would play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: I've been trying to write this intro for a bit so I don't come across as too mean but I really just hated this game. The characters range from dull to infuriating, the optional micro-fiction is excruciatingly long, and the story just feels like a wasted opportunity. So much time is spent at the beginning on useless conversations, like the game is expecting you to love these characters without actually making them lovable. When the game finally reveals what's actually interesting about the plot, it's too late; I'm beyond caring for these people. At least after that point, it's over quick.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my playthrough of the game.Graphics-wise it isn't the most impressive if that is important, but it does a wonderful job using colors to create a thematic feel that I enjoyed. Like a rusted mess being held together by rope pulled by all the characters. That's a good thing. The main joy I got out of this was the story and personalities of the characters. I went in interested in the main story with subtle interest in the side stories. I recommend being in the mood and interest in playing the game otherwise it won't fully draw you in as there is a lot of reading. I'm not a completionist when it comes to wanting to experience every part of the game. I indulged on the side stories that interested me while just focusing on the main story and that made my playthrough fun for me. There isn't a ton of interactions and gameplay but what really stood out is thinking about how much the visuals helped tell the story with minimal expressions and movement while having good dialogue. If this was a book filled with trying to describe everything in great detail I don't think it would have been interesting to me.  Give it a (expresso) shot.Other games I would recommend:Red String ClubCoffee Talk
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: A visual novel with almost Persona-style graphics? Sign me right up for that. I’ve been playing through a lot of visual novels lately with the same 2D art, so it’s about time for a change of pace.Necrobarista may have some nice visuals and music, but the plot is simply not there, killing an otherwise cool visual novel. It has some good ideas, but instead of exploring them, it instead spends more time subjecting the player to useless dialogue scenes, filler side stories, and an ending that doesn’t have any impact because the characters never got any development. It is a prime example of “all style and no substance,” and it honestly hurts me to say that because of how much I was looking forward to it.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: I had a good time with this game, and found myself genuinely liking most of the characters. It even made me cry in a couple of places. But ultimately the writing is overall a bit weak, and the plot meanders down a lot of cul-de-sacs that don't really inform the personalities of the cast, or progress the story meaningfully. This game winds up feeling deeply unfinished and fails to deliver on a lot of its premise. I'd recommend it if it was half the price it was being sold for, but at over £15 it's a disappointing product. The Walking to the Sky update is not something I can complain about too much as it's free. But while the broad strokes of the story it tells are quite touching, the dialogue is so incredibly stilted and unnatural that Tuan and Hannah feel like bad fanfiction based on their very limited portrayals in the original game.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is easily one of the most unique games I've played. Although I was expecting a story-driven experience, I did not expect it to be an outright visual novel. Nonetheless, it was still very enjoyable. Pros- The dialogue felt very real, far more so than most entries in this genre- All of the characters were excellent- Effective world building without dragging players into the weeds- Phenomenal and emotional story lineCons- I found all but the last walking around segments to be tedious at best and largely unnecessary- The dialogue among robots between chapters was annoying and I felt like it was just an obstacle preventing me from continuing the story- I didn't find much enjoyment out the word mini-game between chaptersOverall: 7/10I would recommend this game to anyone during a Steam sale. $20 is a steep price for what you are getting.Kudos to the team who made this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from being visually gorgeous with a dreamy soundtrack I can't get enough of and delightfully unique Melbournian flavour, this game has heart.Was absolutely laid flat by the loveable cast and thoughtful exploration of character, of grief, and sense of meaning, humility and grace. I loved it so much, and loved the rich sense of world and momentum and there being so much more to explore, that I hit a certain point and - I wasn't feeling too great, so I decided to leave the rest for a point when I could 'enjoy it the most'. I was so caught up in it, I didn't even realise that all I had left was the final chapter.I think to new players I'd recommend maybe *not* waiting 4 months to finish it like I did - I think retrospectively that it's a better experience all taken together. There were personal reasons why I waited though and I think I chose the right time - and the most personal time - to appreciate its final moments. It really hit me when I did, bringing tears to my ears, and making me laugh.There's a humanity to this story, an authenticity, that feels rare to experience. I'm so glad that I had the opportunity to play this when I have. Absolute work of art. Thank you to the entire dev team for the beauty you have crafted here.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is a love it or hate it kind of game. It's (primarily) a kinetic novel so there isn't a whole lot of gameplay to speak of. Let's be honest though, if you're browsing through visual novels on steam you probably aren't averse to the idea of clicking and reading for a few hours. The art style is definitely unique, in particular I absolutely adore the lighting and environment designs. The soundtrack is also excellent, if a bit repetitive at times. The game's writing is likely going to be the major sticking point for a lot of people.It focuses very heavily on interpersonal relationships between the characters, and to be blunt the characters are definitely not going to be everyone's cup of coffee. For example Maddy, the closest thing to a protagonist the game has, can be kind of a judgmental ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times. If you like the characters however, you'll probably enjoy the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Terribly slow and though I haven't finished the game I don't have any interest in continuing. The first two hours are spent explaining the rules of this universe so to speak and comes down to: there are no rules or nobody has figured out what they are. None of the characters or plotpoints are particularly interesting to see the conclusion of. If there is some hidden meaning behind it, it's lost on me. Technically it's not all that great either. All the budget went to the visuals and they're nice most of the time. There are no voice actors and some of the most important plot points are told with just plain text, no visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: A super stylish visual novel made and set in my home city of Melbourne. The Terminal is a cafe for recently departed souls and a young man walks through the door, looking a little lost.A story about grief but with plenty of light-hearted humour and likeable characters. Took me 5 hours to finish and was very worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: We don't get to choose how art is presented to us, and this game is a perfect example of that. The story, the cinematography, ambiance, everything, is compelling and beautiful. You don't get to change the story no, but that doesn't detract from its impact and beauty. Strap in, enjoy the music and the ride.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is absolutely one of the best games I have played in the past five years.Albeit short the game used its few hours to craft a finely written about accepting death and moving on towards the future, although a great game it struggles with communicating its ideas due to glitches and various errors. Another problem I noticed was how a few characters felt like they were unneeded in the game, and the story could have progressed in the same way without those characters.  these problems are nearly nothing when compared to what Route 59 was able to create.  each line is delivered with beautiful hand crafted camera angles, each as stunning as the last, this might sound like I'm exaggerating but each shot was truly outstanding and many left me sitting at the desk just staring trying to capture every detail within the vast diroramas each picture attempted to create.  this makes the game stand out in the vast ocean of visual novels.  Overall I completely recommend this game to anyone looking for a great story game without wanting to sink in the time investment like many other visual novels.  This is one of the few games I wish i could forget about just so that I could play it again for the first time.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: I really can't say for sure why I fell in love with Necrobarista. Considering the genre it was more likely I hate it. But the game got me, enticed me and in the end I fell in love. Its an amazing game, amazing characters, my favorite ones being Chay, Ashley and Ned...a game not for everyone, but definitely amazing and a good ride!
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is a short kinetic novel (a visual novel without choices) with first-person walking segments in between the chapters. The 3D look with short animated segments is original, but the text is formatted really weirdly (sometimes one word will be shunted to the next screen for no real reason) and there is so. Much. Clicking. You click between every paragraph, most of which are only one or two sentences. You click after every animation. The game took me just over three hours to finish and my wrist hurts.The story could have been interesting - there were a few parts near the end that elicited genuine emotion from me - but the Joss Whedon style quippy dialogue made all of the characters feel very same-y so it was hard to care that much about them. Also there are three characters who only appear in one chapter and seem completely unimportant to the actual plot, and Maddy's relationship to Ned still baffles me after playing the entire game.I can't recommend this game when there are better, longer, and more interesting VNs in the same price range.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Ironically, I found myself to keep passing each episodes one by one with little notice, much like a person would when captivated by a good book. The story provides a rich dialogue between characters and delivers contextual background for everyone of them. You might yourself even more interested each characters as their own, in which the game provides text that may or may not relate to the main story and shares experiences of each characters individually. There are a few of these texts based on characters you never actually see in the main story, but will provide an interesting relation to the plot.The sound track is so well executed, it involves a diverse set of styles for a diverse set of situations, each for their own placement in the storyline. How the game would come to end was unique to its own.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: The game attracts with its unusual design and gameplay. This is a kind of "semi-visual novel, semi-interactive movie." The problem is, it's neither. The plot is (for me) very boring and uninteresting. The game can be beaten in 4-6 hours, and 90% of the gameplay is pressing one button that scrolls through the dialogues (I did not find the auto forward function). And that would be acceptable if it was really interesting to read. I don't know who might like this project, considering how many good games in this genre already exist. Really good ones. I bought this game a long time ago, and for a long time I could not decide to post a review. But I think it's better to express your opinion than to remain silent and every time you see this game in your library, thinking that you still need to write a review :D
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: I read good things about this game when it first came out and I was happy that a new VN was getting popular, so, thanks to a friend that gifted it to me, I got it.While the story is interesting , the first thing you notice different from any other possible VN is that... the is no external input, as in no choices, no actions, nothing, just 11 (considering only the main story, add a couple more for the side stories) long cutscenes. Sure, they're really well crafted and surely the team behind it put a lot of work into it, but sometimes the 3D render breaks the text flow, making you skip some dialogues by mistake because they appear late in that precise scene or maybe because for some reason the sentence goes  of the scene altogether.Another problem that is unfortunately present is that the localization, the more you proceed, becomes more and more messy: missing strings, placeholder strings, typing mistakes, plenty of grammatical mistakes and even some sentences taken from completely different languages. In such a game, where reading is the most important tool, proofreading the script should have been one of the priorities and not leave it like that.To pad some "game" time, they added a lot of smaller stories, they're good but after reading few of them I grew tired and just went on ignoring them.I will finish it because I don't like leaving half-finished stories, but it's definitely not worth the current price tag, buy it only during sales if you have to (or, my strong suggestion, just choose a different VN)
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: -- Pros --  Stylish as heck  Great atmosphere  Interesting characters  Fantastic concept  Interesting twist on the visual novel concept-- Cons --  Poor mouse support (no sensitivity settings)  Does not like you having a second monitor. It's playable but the mouse will leave the screen.  No auto-read, meaning there is a lot of clickingI'd recommend this to anyone that is looking for something a little different, or a good laugh
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista - Review"A Visual Novel Where between a cup of coffee and a good conversation we will learn a lot about life and death." The game it has a fascinating history and super charismatic characters that will make the player get emotional and care for each one of them. Different from the vast majority of visual novels available Necrobarista differentiates itself by bringing a unique experience where the focus is on the way the story is written and full of details that fill the eyes of the players and encourage them to continue following this wonderful story. And to help in this reading, the game has an excellent soundtrack that blends perfectly with each text, scene and characters.Highly recommended for fans of the visual novel genre. Even if Necrobarista don't have multiple routes that lead to different endings, the experience the game offers is compared to reading your favorite comic book or book a unique story with characters you love.9.0/10
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Short, linear story (Not entirely non-interactive as side story unlocks are gathered through the main plot), but absolutely beautiful. While I'm not sure I could really call it cost efficient, it's very time efficient for a quality VN. If you are Australian, doubly so. There are the obvious marks of authenticity here, but also some more subtle aspects that I suspect the developers could not avoid.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very conflicted about this game. I went into this game very blind, only seeing the screenshots in the store page and knowing its a visual novel of sorts. And I love visual novels, trust me, I've read over about 40, So there was a certain thing I was expecting and I felt this game was lacking. Pros: 1. I wish there was more to the story/Longer, I wish the Characters did more. 2. Love maddy's design, loved how some scenes flowed. (some transitions were not that good)3. I loved Maddy and Chay but The story also made me feel for Ned.4. The OSTCon 1. Maddy looks very pretty. I love her aesthetic and the way she looks. I think maddy was the only character the devs paid close attention to because some characters just look out right derpy with their proportions or their face.2. Kishan is a very bland character and I don't know why everyone took a liking to him, no offence to him, but everyone made him seem special. Ned scouts him for the council, Maddy making him the exception to returning time to him, having him stay way past his time. 3. Side characters. I wish this was more of an array of side characters we could see maddy interact with. The one I was thinking specifically was Samantha or something? I don't even remember her name because they only gave her one scene! But I loved her interaction with Maddy, their banter was what I was living for but for some reason she didn't get anymore screen time? Why?!4. Plot. For some reason it took me about half way through the story for me to grasp the vibe of what this story was putting down, and I was expecting it to get Heavy or interesting but it just kept the steady pace the same way through. I dont know, I was expecting something more. 5. you can't save in between the story. 6. The filler 3 robot stand up banter. I could've done without. very fillery, not very interesting to listen to.I wouldnt reccomend this to anyone. Mostly because  no one in my circle of friends read visual novels. But also I would'nt reccomend this becuase there are better visual novels out there for this price. I guess this could be a beginner one but I'd wait for it to go one sale to go on this ride.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible.  i read some negative reviews saying it should have built up character development more, and while i agree with that, it wasn't that big of a deal.  it wasn't even noticeable for me through my play though, more in retrospect i wish we got to know more about the characters.  overall great game, great style, great music.  Overall amazing.  when people say video games cant be art, ill show them this.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: It's a VN, don't expect much gameplay from it but just enjoy the story. Mid way through the story and I'm loving it, if you're a fast reader you can probably blitz through it in record time.Developers are working to add some free DLC content, that's a plus. Music is fantastic.Developers, please add a soundtrack, I'd like to listen to it.Edit: They added the soundtrack, very cool.

_childDocuments_.review: Game Duration:  4~6 Hours (8th May 2021)It's a beautiful visual novel game in general. It's story is deep, emotions of each characters are telegraphed beautifully, and lore wise is very conclusive to the story. Everything connect to each other from character building, lore, storytelling, and visuals. As good as this may be, I found a bug(personally this only has happened to me once). When I wanted to read the story of an interaction item(more specifically read a previously missed page) it doesn't want to continue with the story after I gone to the present page. I needed to quit to main menu or outright quit out of the game to make it work again, meaning that I need to read it all over again. This is a minor problem, so I won't give it flak. Sometime the main story just rewinds to several dialogue back(happened to me in the 3/4th of the game, 3 more specifically). I know you can scroll your mouse wheel to rewind, but I didn't even touch mine when playing this game(since the mouse clicks are annoying at this games). I do not know if this TSLaYP(That Sounds Like a You Problem). I bought this when no sales or any form of discount, and I regretted nothing with this game. 9/10 I Confidently Recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: A very neat, somber, and sharply written unique little VN about death, moving on, and letting go. If you're someone who usually doesn't have a good enough attention span for regular VNs (someone like me), but has interest in them, do give Necrobarista a try. Its unique and well framed presentation will be just enough to keep your attention on the screen to enjoy these amazingly likable, quirky, and memorable characters.Also that OST slaps.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a great game. If you've been on the fence about it, I'd say make the jump and buy it.I really loved the visuals in this game; I've never see a visual novel set up with sort of way before and I loved it. Future VNs could take a couple notes from Necrobarista, for sure! On the occasion some of the models and such fall flat, but more often than not I was blown away by how this game looks, and found myself taking a lot of screenshots.The writing and overall story were great. At times I had issues with the pacing and sometimes the jokey stuff really out of place, but when this game broaches a more serious subject, man do they get it right. There's a lot to love about this games setting and characters - I really wish the game was a bit more time to explore all this. Still, what they did with the time given was great. I really liked the story vignettes between chapters but I wish they were not blocked by the word mechanic, I missed out on a handful because of this.Overall, great game and worth the price for sure. I look forward to seeing more games from Route 59 in the future (set in the Necrobarista world or not)!

_childDocuments_.review: Good visuals, good soundtrack, good story, this is a game worth buying.  EDIT:  Also wanted to mention after years of waiting for this game to come out, it was worth the wait.Well, it is sort of hard to call it a game, since you are mostly just along for the ride, as you read and click when you are ready to move on to the next thing.  No player choice story wise, so if you were looking for branching paths/different endings, look elsewhere.  However, if all you want is a good story, then this game has you covered there.  The game works fine with an XBox controller, but it felt better with keyboard and mouse.  Most of the game play comes after each chapter where you are allowed to move around the bar and unlock side stories that give you more insight to what the characters were up to before the events of the game, or in between episodes.  The replay value of this game is the process of unlocking all of those side stories, as every chapter lets you choose seven words which then gives you a token based on what you chose.  These tokens are then spent to unlock this side content.  Seeing how these stories require multiple tokens to unlock, you are most likely going to miss quite a bit of these side stories on your first play through, depending on what words you chose.The game takes about 5-6 hours to complete, and all achievements are able to be obtained in a single play through, without the need to do anything special or out of your way, for those of you who care about that sort of thing.

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is an interactive story about magical realism first, an interesting tale with fleshed-out characters and a unique visual look second, and only then a videogame. If you enjoy reading, and the subjects of death and of coming to terms with your own mortality, I'd definitely recommend this. It was a most pleasant surprise.More Expresso = Less Depresso

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista just falls under the echelon of elite visual novels like VA-11 HALL-A and Enigma, but is definitely worth its price of admission. The striking and unique presentation is more then just a paint job: it uses word placement and timing to real sell the emotion of a scene and help you feel like you're in the situation that's unfolding. Small sound design here enhances the use of music as it cuts in and out to emphasize points, and the writers/presenters here really understand the idea of conveyance. Strong characters in Maddy and Ashley center the fantasy story in a great place: making it relatable yet still feeling out of this world. Most everything revolves around Maddy and she's a great center piece to the story, although you do want to know more about the others in this world when all is said at done. Back and forths feel natural with down to earth writing and good use of timely jokes, and yet still is able to hit those key emotional points without breaking a sweat. The biggest downside to the game is its pacing and what seems to be cuts to the story in order to make the release. At the 2/3rd point the games pace suddenly shifts and really ends up feeling quite jarring, as a major event speeds up everything and really takes you for surprise on how fast they go through it. While this may have been purposeful in the end, it doesn't feel like it as several side stories don't seem to get conclusions and some characters just fall to the wayside. This could be the story content addressed in the upcoming free DLC, but frankly the game feels like it has a few chapters missing from it right now. In the end, it's still a worthy visual novel to add to the collection, however with its pacing issue I'd almost suggest waiting until all the DLC is out in hopes that it can fix it.  list]

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from VA-11 HALL-A and Coffee Talks I was really looking forward to this one too. Based on the premise and art style I really thought I'd enjoy it but didn't. I just couldn't get invested into the story or characters and there isn't much else going. You just keep clicking lines of text away until the end with a few walking sequences where you get to uncover memories that give you some more text to click away with none of the former having any effect on the story.My advice - watch a chapter or two on youtube before you decide on purchasing Necrobarista. _childDocuments_.review: Squanders its themes, doesn't do anything interesting or novel with the story, the memory system is bad, and it is simply not worth picking up, even on sale.Allow me to expound:-- Spoilers below this--The theme and premise the game sets up is a cafe where the dead can spend one day in the world of the living in a space with no judgement and no one asks questions. Instead of doing something interesting with the premise, the cafe is just sort of a half-way house for the recently deceased with a necromancer tending the bar. Except, early on, it's shown that spirits can stay longer than one day, and it counts against the cafe's tab with the local death council. So obviously they're way over because they don't enforce the leaving time in any meaningful way, and the councilor, who is inexplicably portrayed by real life famous Australian rebel, Ned Kelly, a real person who actually existed. So it feels weird for a real life figure, mythical as he is, to be in this game alongside the pre-teen genius inventor girl as part of the main cast.But Ned, for his role, keeps coming by to threaten the cafe and tell them they're super over their time budget because they don't kick the dead out to the afterlife. Except he doesn't do anything about it because he doesn't really want to, he's a friend to the mentor character and fatherly-ish to the necromancer who tends the bar. Additionally, they go out of the way to establish that life pulled from plants or animals can sustain the dead longer, but it's uncomfortable and mostly incompatible with people time. This seems to have eluded our necromancer who runs the place, since she runs a gambling ring in the basement of the cafe where she works which her mentor disapproves of, and she's won more than enough time to keep Ned off her back, but she keeps putting it into a tree whose roots have grown into the cafe basement. So either this is foreshadowing that the later withdrawing of the time from the tree for necromancy rituals is going to fail because of this time weirdness, or it doesn't mean anything at all because no one ever mentions it again, not even Ned, who is inexplicably present for the ritual. So why devote time to that scene in the first place if the characters who explain it as exposition don't mention it later when it's relevant? Does she already know that it doesn't work right and if so, why is she storing it in a tree if she knows it won't work for her ritual? Why not keep it in a human container until she needs it? Why does the tree have to be involved at all?So anyway, she messes up the ritual again, because it's not the first time she's tried it, and the subject she was trying to reanimate is suddenly like "Well I didn't ask to be resurrected!" And, you know, fair, maybe he didn't ask to be resurrected, but... What's just keeping him from moving on sooner, if he didn't want to stick around for the rituals? Why didn't he dissuade her sooner? He's been alive for hundreds of years by the point in the story when the ritual fails, and, sure, he was scared to move on, but at some point you think he would have stopped her after the first ritual. Be like "Hey, I'm cool with being a ghost, being corporeal sucks lol" Also, if he's been in the cafe for hundreds of years, why does he suddenly have to leave because the ritual failed? Everyone acts like it's a foregone conclusion that he has to leave, but he's been there basically forever already, so what's another 10 or 20 or 50 when there seem to be no consequences at all to the dead staying around, other than Ned Kelly coming around to be cross at them. Ultimately it's a story about letting go and accepting death, which is a weird theme for the game to go with at the end. Especially since it all seems so weirdly forced and contrived. The necromancer who is the one who needs to let go, doesn't even make the choice to stop trying, it's just sort of forced on her by the spirit. And she makes the best of it, but at the same time, it kind of defeats the theme if the necromancer isn't the one who chooses to let go. I get you can't always make the choice and have to make the most of the situation you're dealt, but it just seems a weird and contrived way to construct it in the first place.And since it's a story about letting go, the beats are very similar to any other story you may have read about people having to accept death, and moving through the stages of grief. Which is fine, but the way it's presented feels like it's wasting the setting and premise the game promises. Instead of, for example, succeeding at the ritual but having his newfound life being cut short by the human time she put in the tree, and having to accept that she made a mistake and has to let him go. Or something that takes advantage of elements that were laid prior, instead of making it more arbitrary. Life is random, sure, and sometimes the narrative can be too, but so much is wasted, or brought up for seemingly no reason. It never comes back up and is never relevant. World building is fine and good, and important for a thing like this, but the world building has to matter; it has to mean something. It has to go somewhere or contribute to the story in some way. But in this game things that are brought up are dropped and seemingly forgotten, or never become relevant where it seems they should be. The writing is charming at times, and it's not like the characters aren't good, but they seem to have no agency in their own story. Perhaps that was the intention, but it comes across as strange and contrived because the story needs to get to the next beat, the next stage of grief, the next step along the way.The memory system is how the game handles side stories. At the end of each chapter you get to pick a few from a handful of words which give you symbols. You trade in those symbols for additional content. Except the symbols you get are seemingly more or less random. So the number of side stories you can unlock in a given play through are determined by how well you can deduce which words will give you which tokens. I doubt it's possible to get all memories in a single play of the game, so it encouraged replaying the game, but the story is so meandering at times and weird in others, it's hard to sit down and replay it. I wanted to like this game, I really, really did, but I can't recommend it. Even on sale. So much doesn't add up and it's so close to being good. It's so frustratingly close to being actually worth playing that it left me legitimately angry.

_childDocuments_.review: The Terminal is special. It's a coffee shop in Melborne, Australia that just might be the last place you ever see. That's not because it's dangerous, though. It's because the Terminal is a waypoint between this world and the next, where souls can have a double shot long black before going to their final rewards.Just don't overstay your welcome. If you loiter for more than 24 hours, Terminal staff are obligated to pick up the balance on your extra time. Nothing's free, after all.Imagine a story set in a Neil Gaiman universe populated with personalities that are slightly more grounded than those of the Ace Attorney games, and you're most of the way there. Necrobarista is a witty visual novel that wears its heart on its sleeve in the best possible ways.If you had one more day...what would you do with it?

_childDocuments_.review: As of this review I have just completed the main story for Necrobarista (I'm a speedy reader), and after waiting for 2 years for this to release, I can say that it's easily one of my favourite games of all time.It's a very lovingly crafted story that raises questions and theories about what being dead and what being human really means and what it feels to have the experience of both. Every character is an absolute delight to experience, and the game's main plot tugged at my heart, nearly made me cry, then made me feel better just to nearly make me cry again. (In a good way, I promise!) The game also oozes style, one that is colourful, bright and fun but works well with its somewhat darker themes.It's well worth the money and will provide a lovely, fun, enjoyable, wholesome experience. I have yet to complete all the little side stories (I only have about 3, and it seems there were at least 10+), so I think I'm going to replay this with my partner and discover more of what these stories have to offer.Necrobarista is extremely warming. It's a genuine, loving experience crafted by a team who seem to really care about what they're writing. Please do yourself a favour and experience this game in whatever way you can. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: The art and lighting are dreamy and otherworldly.  The character design is bold and fun.  The music is evocative and reinforces the mood of the scenes (which are painstakingly staged and edited to keep you engaged on throughout this experience).The story is epic yet relatable, actualized by the potency of the writing and scene staging and timing.  The resulting mix is a well polished and unprecedented visual novel experience that emotes and tells a story in ways that VNs typically do not.  The aforementioned enables Necrobarista to take the player on an emotional rollercoaster.  I found myself laughing, or on the edge of my seat, many times; I just as easily wound up feeling contemplative and sometimes just down right relaxed during a bomb sunset over a smooth musical groove. It's rare that a game makes me cry even once; Necrobarista made me crynot once,        not twice,                  but...                       thrice!!!Necrobarista is a an endearing, bombastic visual novel that sets a new standard and pushes the boundaries of the genre forward in very meaningful ways that respects your time and senses, and I can't wait to spend more time in this world.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a visual novel with music by Kevin Penkin and a directorial style clearly inspired by Studio Shaft. If you're like me, that should just about be enough to sell you on it right there.This is a beautifully well-written visual novel with complex, believable characters. The plot tends towards the slice-of-life side of things, but there's an overarching narrative which gradually develops. It's not a very long game - my playtime represents going through the main story and both bonus stories (Walking to the Sky and Devil's Den) at a fairly sedate pace - but well worth the price, particularly since it frequently goes on sale.On the technical side of things, this is the debut game by this developer, and it definitely has some rough edges. Shadow resolutions and framerates sometimes plummet for no apparent reason, and there was some distracting z-fighting in a few scenes. At one point, in one of the exploration sections, I somehow managed to clip out of bounds in a loading zone and fall out of the map, which lead to a very unusual view of the Terminal from below. These are all ultimately fairly minor faults. What's less minor are the numerous typos in dialogue, which definitely should have been patched by now.Overall, a very enjoyable game despite its flaws. I eagerly await this developer's next project.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first experience with playing a Visual Novel and it left a good impression on me. As a VN their use of dialogue has this constant wave of chaotic energy that makes the characters genuinely interesting. The dialogue never grows old on you because there are moments in the story that ventures into a more somber tone for some of there deeper themes. This isn't something that's deep or existential like SOMA, but it's still relevant in providing an important stepping stone in understanding ourselves and other people. In this case, it is the theme of "Letting Go" and understanding what that may look like for different people. One major aspect that ties everything together in Necrobarista is the effort in breathing life into their charming cast of characters through the use of transitional animations and camera angles to draw us closer to them. They are used to convey specific feelings to complement with the dialogue and it brings so much energy because of it. Overall, this is a Game/VN worth playing and experiencing. I look forward to playing future projects from Route 59.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is an excerpt of my full review here: Is there a best way to define the ‘visual novel’ as a genre? I’m not about to do a detailed dissection of my own conception of the genre (tried in an earlier draft, ended up swearing), but suffice to say Necrobarista by Route 59 ticks my main box: most of the gameplay is clicking to reveal more text. It isn’t first-person, really, or even from a consistent perspective, and there’s no narration – text is simply spoken by characters on or off-screen (represented by a cute little icon). There aren’t any decisions to be made that affect the plot, either (though it isn’t the only purely linear visual novel), so maybe by and large Necrobarista would fall into the mechanical neutral-to-rebel end of any VN alignment chart. It is quite anime, though, so if that’s a significant factor in your conception of the genre space it’ll slot neatly in. It even has an opening theme.If you were ordering a Necrobarista, you’d ask for a visual novel – heavy on the visual, hold back a little on the interactivity, with a heavy sprinkling of rumination on life, death, and letting go. The beans would be very Australian beans, as the game is set in Melbourne. Apologies – I still can’t come up with good coffee metaphors. At any rate, Necrobarista’s focus on its visual elements offers a genuine freshness to the game – it legitimately pushes the envelope in terms of visual artistry, something that the VN genre often neglects.Necrobarista comfortably avoids overstaying its welcome, and leaves on a convincing high. It’s doubtless a low-interactivity example, but it’s a distinctive, stylish VN(ish) game – and the strength of its character designs, writing and visual composition prove that it’s a game of vision. Necrobarista proves that there’s still a lot of room for bold aesthetic envelope-pushing, and does so without sacrificing its own plotting, themes, or likeable cast. The end may even successfully jerk a few tears.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, Necrobarista is incredible. Every scene, every frame is beautiful, and perfectly conveys the mood of the moment. The music is cool too, and put to well use, the writing is often witty and sharp, and the animations and little punctual UI tweaks do the job really well. I didn't grow super fond of the characters, nor did I get involved in the story that much - I suppose me not being a native english speaker, let alone being familiar with Australia's culture, didn't help me - but let's be honest. Such a beautiful game? About such delicate and hard to grasp topics? With a duration that can actually fit in my overcrowded agenda? Of course it's a thumb up!

_childDocuments_.review: Well the FPS problem is not valid anymore, so the only reason for me to still dislike this game is that... This is wasted idea for the game. Why would you ask? Well you have so much reference for good story but nothing to make your life as barista here at the Terminal real. All you do is reading reading and more reading, not any sort of fun mini game not any sort of choice to influence the story. Hell even the story itself is just cut out to present World only at the bar itself unlocking with each chapter just more rooms of it.There is hardly any mistery in it or World creation, hardly any plot-twists. Just chilling at the bar for most part until the end. The only additional activity this game is offering is reading mementos, which you can unlock but these are even less fun to read since it's reading one page, instead of seeing people doing actual event retrospections.Even though the story is compelling and it takes around 4 hours to finish, nothing else is backing it up except music and characters. This is hardly enough since on the other side to this game is VA-11 Hall-A, Coffee Talk and also anime Death Parade. Each one of these games and anime is better than experience here. Sadly because if Necrobarista was made before them I would appreciate it more for the slice of life and death philosophy.tl;dr - It's just not enough anymore, at least not for this price. Still the game might be good for people that don't know the other stories about accepting life like this.

_childDocuments_.review: First off I'll say that I don't normally go out of my way to review games but I enjoyed this one enough that I had to encourage other people to give it a shot. This is also one of the only games I decided to 100% because I enjoyed every bit of content, while it was short it was a very worthwhile experience. The game plays like most visual novels, just by clicking you'll progress the text and read through the story. In between each chapter of the story you're given the opportunity to explore the cafe that the story takes place in with new areas opening up after each chapter. Exploring the cafe gives you access to side stories you can read (don't worry about missing some during the game you'll have access to all of them once you complete the main story) that give you an idea of what goes on in the cafe outside of the main events.Now that the gameplay explanation is out of the way I wanted to comment on how visually pleasing this game is. The shots are well done and animated unlike a lot of other visual novels. The style and the art direction is superb. The soundtrack is extremely well done, enough for me to considering buying it to support the developers because I really want to see them make more titles or even additional stories in this universe! The story was well written, the characters were lively and had a lot of personality, the topics touched on were often heavy but handled with a lot of care. Not gonna lie I cried at the end because damn I really cared about these characters! All in all if you were thinking about getting this game I would definitely go for it especially considering it's on sale at the time of this review (steam autumn sale).

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is a charming visual novel that combines a good story with cinematic visuals and a great soundtrack. It deals with a lot of heavy themes, while having a healthy amount of humour, and somehow manages to be a relaxing experience through it's entirety. The characters were pretty fleshed out, and the little exposition that was there felt natural in the dialogue. The only thing that irked me during the game was the introduction of several characters in a scene that proceeded to never appear in the story again, however the developer has confirmed these characters will be the focus of new free updates that will continue the games story. tldr; Good Visuals, Good Soundtrack, Nice Short Story of about 4 hours. I felt it was worth the price for the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: The writing in this game is really clever, and the setting is very unique. The gameplay isn't very demanding, but it's a visual novel, so whatever. The characters all feel interesting to learn about, and the game lets you explore hidden side stories in between each of the main acts. The artstyle is the strongest part of this game though, the character models are all fresh, the lighting is superb, and the animation is used in good moments. The music is also pretty catchy.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: I find it hard to describe Necrobarista.  Is it a game? a visual novel? something else?  I'm not really sure, but I really enjoyed it.What it definitely is, though, is a story, in turn thoughtful and hilarious, and a story told in a creative way.  Rather than reading from a page with pictures on it, playing it felt like standing, invisible, in a movie scene where you direct the pace and flow of the lines.  The music and the unusual, ever-shifting camera angles help settle your perspective into the Terminal, everybody's favourite coffee joint/bar/necromantic lab/gathering place for the living and the dead, and the writing makes you want to stay there.  I finished it in one or two sittings on a day off.I love reading, and I loved this game.  If you are a reader, too, then you might, also; I hope you'll give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista, simply put, is sublime. I absolutely love the look of this game, the characters and the arcs they go through are gripping and fascinating, the writing is sublime, jumping between meaningful introspection and a very modern sense of humor in a way that makes the characters feel real, and the plot is just absolutely fantastic. Set aside an afternoon, grab some tissues, and enjoy the ride.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is a visual novel with fantastic production values, and a short but compelling story about death and moving on. I'm not exaggerating when I say that there's a line of Ned's that made me weep.The game definitely leans to the 'novel' side of the visual novel space. There is almost nothing going on in the way of actual player choice in terms of affecting the story. However, the story is good enough that I really didn't care about that. It's good, it's earnest, and it's at a length that respects your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Short visual novel with great characters and some interesting concepts, soundtrack is an absolute banger.I think the characters are the major strength of this game, they have nice chemistry and are really enjoyable to watch. Some of them don't get enough attention, but the developers said that there will be DLCs some time, so I'll be looking forward to that.The art style is pretty nice, so is the way that the text is presented, it's a way more dynamic way to show text than most of the other VNs, you're going through a cutscene with the text appearing in some different ways instead of the regular still image with the text box in the bottom thing.The issues that I have with this game are technical, the FPS on some portions of the roaming sections is really low, for some reason. I played this with a controller and it was fine, the only this is that navigating trough the menus is kinda clunky, the option you're choosing isn't really that highlighted, so it took me a lot more than I expected to go trough the options and trough the memories list.But aside from that it's a really good game, I wishlisted this game a long time ago and I'm not disappointed, 100% worthwhile experience!
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: Look, if you felt curious enough to click on this game, its the game for you. Its a wonderfully small story about mortality. The characters are great, all of them made me happy. The world is kinda woolly, but if anything that adds to the game's cosiness. Its a lot of things honestly, its morbid, its cool, its funny, its heartwrenchingly sad but gives me such good feelings that I can't tell what kind of tears were streaming down my face. Play this, don't wait for a sale. Buy it now.

_childDocuments_.review: the game is definitely a short one and lacks choice, but has some masterful lore reveals/storytelling in it. It's not what I'd call a visual novel in the traditional sense (really, it plays out more like a film) but there is some interactivity/exploration and some amount of paying attention/collection in the small "game" at the end of each chapter (you get points from these games which can unlock optional lore snippets). but really if you're interested in this game, it's not for the gameplay it's for the storytelling...and necrobarista REALLY delivers. innovative magic systems come together with characters who feel real and speak in realistic ways. it's a beautiful story that will stay with me.also ost by the made in abyss guy...what else could you want?
_childDocuments_.name: Necrobarista

_childDocuments_.review: When I first saw the game, I was secretly hoping it might be something like the anime Death Parade, really good anime, do recommend that.When I saw the concept 'bartender' I at least to some degree expected some level of interactive gameplay even vaguely similar to VA-11 Hall-A (I also recommend that). Don't kid yourself, it isn't all that similar. The style is different, the level of interactivity is different.Heck, its set in basically a cafe which has some alcohol on display. I highly doubt the 'bartender' tag even belongs there if anything because it is the main characters job, which you never end up doing anyway.It isn't, and it wasn't. Instead I got thrown into basically a purely linear visual novel with a unique enough art style and an interesting enough set of characters to keep me there for a while. The main issue is the 'visual novel' bit which to most will imply some form of control over the story.Even if having a small bit of interactivity to break up the 7 hours or pure clicking through walls of texts I was doing. (Yes I played for 7 hours straight the first session I played) VA-11 Hall-A manages to give you the 'small little task' to keep your mind occupied but this one lacks anything than pure dialogue. I expect most negative reviews will end up over something similar to 'was bored and stopped playing'.(I will note someone in a review claims '6 hours gameplay if slow reading' they have 8 hours in the game, realistically that is a bit lower than the actual number I feel of maybe 8-10 hours if my guess of the story conclusion is right, I'll finish the game at a later point and maybe edit this to reflect that.)There are no meaningful narrative choices in the game, at least to the degree that there has been no visual representation that my actions in the game in the parts where I have a choice, end up with meaning unless there is some kind of 'true end' you have to play the game 3 times to unlock by either perfect choices, or to just gather enough points from the one interactive segment, to get a 'true end'. Games like until dawn make a point of representing when a choice you made affects the story, it might be unrealistic but it helps spur gamers on if they feel their choice and investments have meaning.Conflict in the story seems a bit forced, forcing the main character into an action she usually does, only to later guilt trip her and have this one instance surrounding them, be the one in a thousand that they decide it is wrong. The time where you get to do anything other than click to the next line of dialogue involves you walking around a small area which expands each chapter unlocking 'key points' for more linear reading of stories unrelated to your current predicament, they might be cute or funny stories. Might even be a better way to convey character growth and interest people through multiple shorter stories than one long one which doesn't even seem to fully focus on the main character.Meaning you have absolutely no control over character growth and development and buying the game to play it, I'd almost say is equal to just watching a mute letsplay on youtube, it would save you clicking the mouse repeatedly.While it would be a simpler option to do that, I feel the studio needs to be given a chance to develop more games.Can I even remember the games soundtrack? No, I've never been all that good with soundtracks but I'd assume playing it this week for 7 hours, I'd have at least remembered something from it.Is it 'game of the year' potential? No. But it doesn't have to be. It sets out with a goal and seems to be heading in that direction pretty well. I'd have loved even a basic relationship system or dialogue choices even if it was 'choose which insult to use next', Fake choices that could make me feel something about the main character, as oppose to just seeing the flaws they present for her.Even if she failed in her main tasks she set herself out to do, I'd probably not feel much because I've not been given a reason beyond spectator to invest myself in her situation. At most I'd feel like I wasted time investing in something so linear.If you want to know however, play it and find out, I'm not giving that away here even when I do finish the game and possibly edit this.But at the same time it sticks to its own style, stays slightly unique and still manages to get 7 hours out of me first time around. Will I complete the game? Probably at some point.The game isn't perfect, I'd have probably made a few different choices like small constant interactive bits, even if it involved walking up to a few tables and hitting a button, or pressing a few buttons on the appliances behind the counter to keep conversation moving. But all in all, the developers made something good for one of their first games on steam, and I think a bit of support won't hurt.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great, so far! It has a few obvious issues, which I trust will be fixed (namely, the game doesn't run so great, but considering the majority of the game is a VN, and the first person sections don't run *so bad* on my rig, it's pretty bearable). There are some points where the model expression look like it's clipping though but it adds A TON of expression and character having them I think! The cast is great so far and look forward to see more! The game builds the world up from the start till you hit chapter 2, that's when the story starts rolling. _childDocuments_.review: As a warning, it's definitely heavy on the "novel" aspect of "visual novel" so temper your expectations accordingly.That said, it has a very intriguing setting, and establishes a very fascinating atmosphere that feels lived in, even if some people are lacking on that front.The music is fantastic, and the writing has had me laughing several times.If I must point out a few flaws, and they are of a mostly resolvable, technical persuasion:The game will suffer from slowdowns. My computer is by no means a slouch, but even it will chug on the occasion. There was a brief issue where the mouse was separated from the center reticle, but that went away when a story point unlocked. And most importantly, as I said in the first sentence, this is very much a lean towards the novel aspect of the genre. I've been enjoying it, but so far I've yet to encounter a lot of "gameplay" really. So that can be a con largely depending on taste and the mood you're in. But hey, walking simulators are a thing, might as well have a drink while you're at it.This does remind me that I need to get back to slinging drinks in a cyberpunk bar, however. My library of bartending story adventures grows.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate writing 'nah' reviews but this one didn't grab me.Positives - the art style is really cool. The cafe itself is a very neat place that feels like a real location, and a place I'd definitely hang out...you know, for a couple hours. But the plot hinges on the idea that I'd want to hang out there for much longer and. IDK, man. Without saying too many spoilers, it felt like the story doesn't really have any stakes. I don't mind a linear story, but it's better if I believe that there's some kind of mystery or intrigue or pressure. This game never convincingly provided that. More felt like a lot of snarky people speaking filler dialog to each other.The prose, especially on the unlockable side stories, really is quite lovely in places. But also a bit long-winded, and it's unclear sometimes just what you're getting into when you're in the thick of it, until you've agreed to reading several pages of it and can't back out.This game also felt really "choppy" on my PC which can run heavy action titles no problem. Not sure if this was by design or if it was really lagging because it's kind of hard to tell with the style.I think slice-o-life (death?) may just not be my thing. But I've liked other coffee-and-bar-related visual novels just fine so maybe I just want more interactivity in my coffee simulator.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes it may just be a glorified visual novel with some nice cel-shaded graphics, to be honest I was a little disappointed at first after enjoying Coffee Talk and VALHALLA so much. I'm glad I stuck with it, if purely for the absolutely top-notch writing and the chapter and memory layout that makes it so easy to dip into this game for an hour or two like a good book.Is it a game? _childDocuments_.review: Review originally posted at -----I experienced a wholly unique feeling when playing Necrobarista. Putting it into words has proven difficult, but the closest, most succinct way goes something like this: after my first few hours I felt as though I needed to put it down—not because I wasn’t enjoying it, but rather because I was enjoying it too much. In the moment, I was able to recognize just how deep of an impression it was making within me, and actively wanted to savour the experience. That feeling persisted throughout, and amplified as its closing scenes drew closer. Now, as I reflect upon the experience holistically, any words I may have to adequately express just how much it resonated with me fall flat. It is, easily, one of the best games of the year.The game comes from Route 59 Games, an indie effort out of Melbourne, Australia. It has been in active development since 2016, and has gone through many iterations, delays, and reimaginings up until its release in late July 2020. Through the developers’ own admission, the game was delayed for so long because they’d felt as though they needed to choose between either overworking themselves to exhaustion in order to get it out fast, or valuing their mental health, delaying it, and releasing it when it felt “right.” As a developer myself, I must applaud the team’s restraint and maturity in doing so. As a gamer, though the delays were difficult (I was excited for the game ever since the announcement trailer in 2017), I feel as though they absolutely made the correct decision. The product of their journey is a refined, impactful game which showcases the team’s mastery in each of their respective crafts.It’s difficult to say which part made the strongest impact first, but one of the pieces which blew me away was the music. It consistently stood out as being a suite of high-quality compositions for every character/scenario, each with top tier production values. There were multiple times when the music made me say “yeah” aloud, to the point where I alt-tabbed away from the game to see if I could find a copy of the soundtrack. That quick search revealed all I needed to know—seeing Kevin Penkin’s name as the composer connected all of the dots. For followers of the site, Kevin composed the music to Florence (winner of our 2018 Game of the Year award for Best Music), and we have actively talked about the soundtrack to Made in Abyss multiple times on the podcast. I can’t tell you just how many times the music alone in the game made me smile, and I’d like to take a second to call it out explicitly: Kevin, we love you and your music.Another aspect which is gripping from the first moments are the visuals, art design & cinematography—I have so many screenshots saved from this game purely because of how stunning it looks. Lighting, camera angles, set design, models, characters’ expressions, text effects, colours, background art—everything about the visuals work seamlessly together. And when I say “seamlessly together” I don’t just mean amongst themselves, but with the experience as a whole. Voice acting isn’t even needed with how effectively the visuals bring the characters to life. The world these characters inhabit feels real, and every scene feels as though it was curated and hand crafted by an expert cinematographer. The marriage of the impeccable visual design, the perfectly tuned music, and story make for a cohesive experience through and through. On that note, the story…While I had saved many screenshots for the visual impact of numerous scenes, I saved even more to capture dialogue and story beats. There are very few games which compare to the standards of writing found in Necrobarista. The only one which feels immediately comparable is Disco Elysium, and it should be noted that we found that game to be especially notable for its writing. The moment-to-moment dialogue in Necrobarista is second-to-none. It can go from uproariously hilarious to soul-crushingly melancholic in just a few mouse clicks. Each character feels distinct and as though they have had months and years of history together. Their lives feel lived, and their interactions feel real. Everything they say feels like we’re seeing the genuine feelings of real human beings (and other creatures), and ultimately, the story they go through has all the more impact because we care about them as people.While the story itself covers a broad gamut of topics over its playtime, the core of it is ultimately about two things: Death and Failure. They are two very real, very raw human experiences, and it is an extremely difficult feat to convey their true weight in a game. The ways in which these themes appear throughout the story are conveyed with the sensitivity of one who clearly knows their true impact, and for a player who has had ample experience dealing with both, it hits very hard. The reason these parts of the story are so impactful is because, while the setting is somewhat fantastical (a café on the way between life and death), the human experience feels incredibly grounded. While it is a story about these dark, painful topics, it remains optimistic. It is not aiming to tell a story to leave you distraught, distressed, and fearful of these dark shadows, but rather, it offers strength and reassurance.With all of this glowing praise, are there things to criticise? Sure, absolutely, and the developers themselves have even acknowledged some of the criticisms I would offer by talking about how they’re reworking one of these systems. There are moments here and there where something like a cup will be floating above a counter, or some clothes will be clipping through an object, or a short animation might be a bit janky. I found one or two words in some of the side content which were grammatically off; but, genuinely, none of these criticisms negatively impacted my experience in any way. They didn’t pull me out of it, they didn’t make any scenes less effective, and in some ways, their presence blew me away even more. These moments of imperfection serve as a reminder that this game was indeed created by a small team, and they gave me a deeper appreciation for just how polished and premium the other 99% of the game is.“I’m Gonna Miss You, Mate”Necrobarista is a gripping experience, and one which cannot be recommended highly enough. It is a game built with passion—a passion which can be felt across every aspect of every moment. It is one of those games that I wish I could erase from my memory to have the opportunity to experience it again for the first time.There is beauty to be found in darkness, and Necrobarista shines a gentle, heartfelt light on it.-------If you are interested in a spoiler-heavy look at Necrobarista, we recommend checking out our Necrobarista Spoilercast

_childDocuments_.review: As meditations on mortality go, this one's quite wholesome. A read-at-your-own-pace sort of visual novel; nibbled into episodic chapters, side-stories, and charming bits of character lore. This is less a story and more a collection of stories that share a theme; the "main plot" is almost secondary - which I think is quite alright for the vibe here. _childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is a very linear visual novel about how hard it can be to say goodbye or move on to the next inevitable stage of one's life. It tackles this subject with warmth buried under a thick layer of millennial ennui with a touch of a distinctly Australian perspective. There's little interactivity to speak outside of a few optional side activities and some first-person interstitial segments, but the writing and soundtrack do a lot of heavy lifting here. So does the art direction, which consists of vaguely anime-esque characters models holding on keyframes, often with interesting framing choices.There's not much more to dig into without actually diving into the narrative, so that's best left to whoever's reading this review. It's strong narrative with a unique vibe, and it's very much worth experiencing.

_childDocuments_.review: For anyone not familiar with it, Necrobarista is a visual novel about a cafe called The Terminal that serves as a stopping point for the recently deceased to spend one last day (and not a second longer) to interact with the living. The Terminal is run by a couple of necromancers who are also baristas, hence...The main conflict is those two necrobaristas, Maddy and Chay, are too lenient about letting the dead linger past their allotted 24 hours, so the cafe ends up shouldering the time debt that Maddy and Chay will have to pay off themselves eventually. Who collects the time debt? The Council of Death, and they just sent an enforcer to get what they're owed.As interesting as the premise is (and the game does delve into the mechanical intricacies and lore), it's just a vehicle to have conversations and a spot of philosophizing about mortality, responsibility, and relationships. Necrobarista is a VN through and through. You're just clicking through dialogue boxes most of the time, there are no choices to make, and no actual necromancy or barista work to do.That vehicle happens to have an incredibly slick filmic flair and a soundtrack that is both ~a mood~ and ~a vibe~.The character design is obviously anime-inspired, which for the most part works except for some shots that make the 3D models look odd because of how flat some of the visual elements look. Ngl I was a bit put off by it from some of the screens I saw before playing, contrasted with the stunning chiaroscuro of the background art. Thankfully, it all comes together quite well in motion.Speaking of which, there is actually very little animation in the game. When I said it has a filmic flair, I really do mean it relies heavily on cinematic techniques to convey emotion and build atmosphere, expressed through the lens of genre anime with its slow-panning wide shots of urban fantasy vistas and interiors and dramatic dutch angle close-ups of doe-eyed characters in cool costumes. Kinda like in Wide Ocean Big Jacket, the character models transition from one still pose to another every time the camera cuts to another angle. Animation is reserved for key moments, and these only last for a couple of seconds to really emphasize their importance. It's a stylistic direction I dig. While the genre anime infusion is mostly effective in the aesthetics department, I'm not 100% onboard with it when it comes to the writing, but not so much that it completely turned me off the narrative. It's just that it still hews to certain archetypes and trope-y mannerisms that I couldn't help but feel was trying too hard, especially knowing that the devs aren't Japanese and have Western (and distinctly Australian) sensibilities that made the adherence to anime stylings... a tad fanboyish. Maybe that's harsh, but I can't shake the feeling that there's a sort of culture clash revealing itself in the dialogue that can be a little too clever for its own good and a pinch too Online™. Also there are enough typos strewn about that annoyed the editor in me lol.Dedicating a whole paragraph to that might make me sound truly bothered by that complaint, I know! It doesn't really tbh. I got invested in the main plot and the growth of the small cast. Their honest conversations and questions about the fears of dying, losing people, and continuing living without certain loved ones resonated with me. That precocious kid mechanic/gremlin Ashley charmed me with her earnest, mischievous ways. For every turn of phrase that was awkward (or maybe Australian? Melburnian? (i looked it up and hey it's not melbournian!)) or eye roll-inducing, there's an exchange or a line that had me grinning or chuckling.And hey, the very last thing got me.With the mixed feelings I have for Necrobarista, it's only fitting though that I close this out with a mix of praise and criticism for an optional system. There are text vignettes that are half-hidden in the cafe. You spot them as these floating words that are actually the vignettes' titles when you're given the chance to walk around the space in between the visual novel parts. However, you can't read the vignettes the moment you find them. You have to unlock them using these various collectible symbols that correspond to a certain story element like "Melbourne" or "Maddy" or "The Terminal". You get those from picking a limited number of words from a word cloud comprised of the highlighted words sprinkled throughout the game's scenes.The vignettes themselves are mostly good! Some of them explore the dynamics between two of the main characters, some of them highlight the one-off characters that pop up in the story, and some of them tell complete tales of characters that don't appear at all but exist in the peripheries of the world. These vignettes give a glimpse into the interiority of the cast, reflects on and adds layers to the overall themes, and does some worldbuilding to reinforce the game's fiction.It's just that unlocking them feels arbitrary because of the collectible and word cloud system. There are strict requirements for what collectibles you can use to unlock the vignettes. There's a limit to how many collectibles you can get for the walking interstitials. Knowing which words from the limited word cloud match with the collectibles you need is partly memory-based and partly guesswork. Because of this weird system, I didn't get to unlock all the vignettes when they first became available. It was only until I finished the game that I got every one, and that's because the game just dumps a ton of collectibles on you anyway with no effort on your part to unlock all the vignettes. While I appreciate being able to see everything the game has to offer without having to replay the whole thing, the gating just felt unnecessary, and I can't even come up with an in-universe reason why any of this is a thing or how this mechanic ties into the game's themes. I also bet some of the vignettes would have had more impact if I got to read them in between certain points of the main story instead of reading about half of them one after the other long past the credits having scrolled.The devs just dropped an update today saying they'll be making changes to one of the systems, and I'm 99.99% sure they're referring to that mess I just talked about. While that isn't gonna make me revisit Necrobarista, I'm definitely down for announced free DLCs about the one-off characters and that dude that was in that sick OP but absent from the game.oh god i forgot to talk about the music it's fantastic the entire soundtrack's on spotify give it a listen it's a cool collection of dark synth, electropop, melancholic keys, and chill lofi beats to contemplate your death toTook me about 5 hours to complete the game, and that includes finding all the vignettes and reading through them. You can probably mainline it in 3 hours. Your mileage may vary with the aesthetic choices and the tonal consistency of the prose (it knocked me out of the ~immersion~ at times), but there's a confidence in the visual storytelling that you're compelled to see how the next scene plays out, even just for how the camera will frame it, and the writing can be thoughtful and introspective to arrive at conclusions that ring true while also being snappy enough to not make the whole affair dreary. I didn't get teary-eyed at any point like I often do with stories that tackle such subjects, but it has put me in a pensive mood.I have a sneaking suspicion that if I didn't like the look and music so much, I wouldn't have given this game as much thought as I have after playing it, but I do like giving in to astonishment!

_childDocuments_.review: Necrobarista is the first effort for Route 59, a small studio based in Melbourne, Australia.  The story centers around a very cozy cafe which happens to be situated on the route to the afterlife.  The cafe's three employees are themselves living, but they frequently cater to the souls of the recently departed, who are allowed a day or so to come to terms with their demise before moving on.  One day, a newly dead young man enters the shop, and the staff takes a particular liking to him.  Meanwhile, a goon from an otherworldly Council of the Dead begins sniffing around, as the cafe has gained a bit of a reputation for practicing some less-than-legal necromancy, and perhaps letting souls overstay their welcome a bit more than they should.Necrobarista's tone and style feels very much like a slice-of-life anime.  The narrative is meandering, more like a gentle tide than a strong current.  We have no strong central conflict, a few minor characters that float in and out of the story, and scenes that are fun, but do not really contribute to the overall plot, such as a scene where the main characters sit around playing a board game and enjoying each other's company.  It is very much a story that is more concerned with the journey than the destination.The game plays like a kinetic visual novel.  There is no player choice, and the main story will be exactly the same each time you play it.There is an inventive little system for handling the side-content, though.  Throughout each chapter, you will encounter key phrases highlighted in gold that provide flavor text when clicked.  At the end of the chapter, you are presented with a word-cloud of all of the key phrases.  Select the phrases that appeal most to you, and they are converted into several types of tokens.  You are given the chance to freely roam about the cafe in first-person mode, and can spend these tokens to unlock optional text-based side stories before continuing with the next main chapter.  This was a simple system but it was a lot of fun and was also a nice change of pace.Unlike most visual novels, though, Necrobarista is fully 3D.  Instead of the standard sprite-on-a-2D background, the story and text are presented along with a series of cinematically-arranged 3D stills and short animations.  The presentation works incredibly well, and the visuals are a major highlight.  The soundtrack is quite good as well!  Unfortunately, Necrobarista does not have VO at this stage of the game.  While the game works fine without voice acting, I do feel like the inclusion of a strong voice cast could have elevated the game to a whole new level.  The dialogue is sharp and animated and written in a very conversational style, and I think it is crying out for some talent to bring it to life.The developers, upon release, teased three free major post-launch content updates.  The first one is out, and is an unlockable concept art gallery tied to the optional side-content.  No word yet on the other two planned updates as of this writing, but I am kind of hoping for the post-launch VO add, a la Jenny LeClue or Disco Elysium.Necrobarista is also a little short; my first playthrough clocked in at about four hours.  This was enough time to get a nice taste of the world and the characters, but was not enough time to really explore any of the game's Big Ideas in depth.  It feels kind of like a really long pilot episode, or a really short first season of a much larger series.Still, I enjoyed my time spent with this game, and I do not regret picking it up on launch to support this developer.  It kept me interested, I grew attached to the characters, and I think the big red glasses, fishnets, and bright red hi-tops make for a distinctive and memorable character design.  I would recommend giving it a go if you have the opportunity to do so.
