_childDocuments_.review: Glossary:Asuras – Half Brothers of the Hindu Gods but bascially DemonsDevas – the Hindu Gods.Once in a while, an uncut gem arrives in the gaming market. You see this game on the Steam Store, and you’re amazed. It’s dazzling splendour, it’s the fantastic art design and its engaging story. Then you realise that this uncut gem remains an uncut gem because it has more potential. It has so much potential that if expanded with DLCs and free updates, this game can become even greater. The main strength of this game is a strong story and a solid artistic design. Its puzzles are fun, but they can be complex for a beginner at first. I failed many times having to defeat multiple bosses and it was frustrating, to say the least. Many moments kept me scratching my head on how to defeat the Asuras. It’s a solid game, however, and I’ll try to evenly look at the positives and negatives of this game. It is a perfect game for introducing children to Indian mythology, and the strength of the narrative often lies in the mythological tales as you encounter ancient ruins and explore mythical realms. Each of them gives a balanced, simple view of Hindu Mythology. Which to be honest with you, is ripe for the triple AAA Market. It’s a shame.The team at Raji were often short of cash, meaning one of their developers had to mortgage their houses, investors in the Indian gaming market were woeful, not wanting to invest in such an expensive game, and many investors they went too only wanted the gaming mobile market which is alive and well in India with Fornite and PUBG.Now, seeing the success of Raji, I sincerely hope it convinces Indian game developers to stop being shy and to create more video games based on Indian mythology because there is so much that can be done here. I mean Chinese video-game companies are making games on Chinese mythology and Sony I believe is making a video game based on Sun-Wukong (A mythical creature from Journey to the West) so why can’t Indian game developers do that instead of just going for mobile gaming? The reason is being that most children spend their entire lives in India studying. The second reason is peer and parent pressure. The third is that games are just looked at as a waste of time and effort. Hence, you have this reason in societal issues that cause problems for Indian game developers. I’m wanting Raji to become even more popular, to break this stereotype in Indian society (I know because I’ve belonged to it.) I sincerely wish that Indian game developers would make a triple AAA game on Hindu Mythology. Because there is so much potential here.One of the main weaknesses in this game is, however, the multiple bosses you get to fight. Let’s name a few. The Demon Chieftan. Rangda. The main boss in the end. I managed to find a glitch with the Demon Chieftan and managed to destroy him. He was stuck in that position. Here is my screenshot. Then when it came to Rangda, who is inspired by Balinese Mythology as you’ll see in the design of the demons (Asuras in Hindi) the only thing I had to do was to destroy her fingers and boom. Some interesting dialogues were coming Rangda, but it didn’t work for me. Some of them felt cliched.  Like say: Did Vishnu aka meddler train you?I understood what it was trying to do. Hindu Mythology from a simple lens is good vs bad. But if you interpret it once again, it becomes very grey. Because the Asuras (Demons) and the Devas (Gods) are siblings to an extent with the Asuras being half-brothers to the Devas. Let’s put this in a nutshell: The Asuras worship the Devas, then get weapons from them, and then go and attack them. It’s quite amusing when you think about it, but there’s a lot to Hindu Mythology that if you even read it, you still wouldn’t scratch the surface. But I understood what they were going for, I would have wanted more dialogue from Rangda but it had to be very sharp. Lord Vishnu (The Balancer of the Universe) and Maa Durga (The name for Durga, a fierce Goddess is of War, Strength and Protection and combat evil that destroys purity) – provide a good direction and backstory aiming to introduce the player. They got the best dialogue lines in my opinion and I would have wanted to seen more Gods explaining their narrative.Even the final boss I was able to defeat using the Vishnu Chakra (a final endgame weapon that bascially destroys the annoying Asuras I had to fight with.) In the Land of the Mystics, I failed 10 times. Yes. You read that right. 10 times. To defeat those lurching Asuras that spit purple and green fireballs I assume, and then to defeat the ninja style Asuras which were more highly advanced than I could defeat them. I feel disappointed here. The balance of the bosses vs defeating the normal asuras was frustrating to me. I had failed plenty of times defeating wave after wave of normal asura. Then how I ponder, was I able to defeat the bosses so easily? That’s from my perspective. The puzzles in this game were unique, and the way the camera angle works. I’m mixed. The lack of Hindi Audio was also a pain because the dialogue would have worked much better in Hindi than English in my opinion.On the one hand, if this is a linear game as it is, it worked fine. But on the other, you can upgrade your weapons. The upgrading system didn’t work and many times, I was assigned these new weapons, there wasn’t much to work with here. However, they were fun when fighting against the asura. There needed to be more clarity on the keyboard commands because many times I was pressing Q, W, E often not knowing what I was doing. More on special attacks. Granted, that the tutorials were good, but there needs to be a training arena mode. Before you enter that specific combat area, you can and should be able to practice to get better. An option could be like: Do you want to train before entering combat? A simple yes or no answer.On the other hand, there should be a first-person camera mode and a third camera mode as well. A screenshot filtering mode as well. I’m still mixed on the camera angles. Also, I appreciate the level design that went into the arenas you fight in. But it was all wide open circles and some squares. I’d have wanted more variety in the type of demons I had to defeat, and more hexagonal shapes. Now, moving onto combat. Combat is not that hard to figure out, it’s your use of the keyboard and the mouse. I’m again mixed. Because on the one hand, you are fighting against endless hordes of asuras. Then, one of them comes and just wipes you out. All that progress you made has gone and you start over. That is something I just didn’t like at all. On the other hand, it’s the same variety. There isn’t much combination but then again, Nodding Heads was strapped for cash, and therefore I think there were much bigger plans to make combat even more challenging. However, because of the money issue, they must have resorted to just a normal combat system that everyone can play as opposed to a good combat system that can give you more challenges. Instead, combat should have been designed in a variety of other ways: Like give us a circling ball and Raji has to keep her balance while we fight for more asuras. Make Raji fight in a game of chess. Make Rajii fight in the galaxy through a variety of other levels. What I’m saying is, the puzzles should have been wide, extensive, and the combat should have reflected that. When I was in Lord Vishnu’s city, Hiranya, there should have been more verticle style puzzles to solve, more spiraling staircases.It may seem like I’m being too critical, but it’s because Raji has immense potential to become even better. Let’s focus on the strengths: The music of this game is good. I would have wanted more cinematic soundtracks if I’m rather honest. The mythological stories are an excellent foundation for anyone to get interested if they want to learn about Hinduism. The developers wanted to show that India’s more.

_childDocuments_.review: You can clearly feel that almost all of the platforming elements is inspired from Prince Of Persia and the final level gave Journey vibe. But the devs are open about taking the inspiration from those games. On a very objective level graphics are good and charming, combat is passable, enemy does have a good variety but the AI doesn't force you to be creative in dealing with them so you just hack and slash your way the same way for all the enemies. Boss fights still to some extent are creative and force you to change your tactics and timing but they are not quite challenging(may be they are not meant to be, as its not targeted towards just souls fandom). And I have played some games that uses same gameplay style of fixed camera with birds eye view such as castlevania(3d) games and their level design is far more detailed and complex as opposed to simple and linear levels of Raji and obviously the length of the game is short(5+ hours)But on the other hand we need to take several factors into account, unlike Castlevania's Konami, Nodding Heads is not a billion dollar company either. They had a very limited budget and financial struggle of devs is well documented already. This combined with the fact that homegrown Indian games and industry is practically non-existent and so Nodding Head didnt really have a focal point or anything to iterate over in regards of how to do an Indian game. And on that regard I am quite pleased with how they dealt with it. As an Indian, I haven't quite played a game that depicted and explored the hindu lore and mythologies at this level(I guess Far Cry 4's Shangri-La sequence comes closest). The cut-scenes and narrations were done pretty decently and each location did have a different theme and variety to it. It might not be a ground breaking indie game but its not bad by any means. You can breeze through this relaxing game in a few hours. But what I am really hopeful about is that if enough people support it and they start building and iterating over this game with sequels and dlcs, soon we can have some pretty unique and exciting product to play that can match the top indie games of this genre, because they have built a pretty solid base game with their first release. After all CDPR, the most loved gaming company today didnt blow everyone away just with their first game, it did take them years of experience and several releases to become the best gaming company in the world.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10 Let me start off by saying I had low expectations from the game to begin with, since it's a young studio with its first proper ambitious venture, but it still managed to under deliver.Pros:1) Unique in the sense that it's based off Indian mythological lore. I like the way the devs decided to tell us the mythological stories.2) The music was enjoyable3) Bugs were surprisingly less than I had expected4) I liked the art in the game, i.e; the concept art and the environment, more so than the characters themselves. The desert at the end looked beautiful and the lighting was really well done5) Loved the puppet themed cinematics6) The weapons looked alright7) Particle effects for combat were pretty goodCons (oh boy where do I begin):1) Level design? What's that? Let's just make a few straight forward or otherwise vague paths.2) The story was extremely lacklustre from start to end, with an abrupt ending. No flow what so ever and you don't feel attached to Raji at all throughout the story.3) The monster character designs were very generic and efforts put into detailing them (except the bosses) were in vain. They still looked better than Raji did though. Raji's design has nothing interesting or striking about it.4) Texturing needed more attention, you can actually see areas with the textures blurring out.5) Combat was just plain annoying. I don't understand why a character wielding a bow would actually want to jump TOWARDS the enemy while attacking them. Lots of unnecessary frames in Raji's attack animations as compared to the enemy, which causes a delay, giving the enemy plenty of time to hit you meanwhile.6) The voice acting for Raji gets annoying at times when she keeps shouting "Golu"7) The music that plays upon death is more frustrating than dying itself.8) Combat gets repetitive as monsters spawn for the sake of it, just so you have to kill them. Their presence doesn't have a link to progressing in the game.9) The choice of combat modifiers make no real difference. The game could have stuck to just lightning and omitted the other two elements and it wouldn't have affected gameplay. By the time you get the ice abilities, you're almost through with the game. The modifiers don't even work while fighting bosses.10) Mobility is an issue because you get hit during mid-dodge animations at times, and it gets very easy to miss pillars when you try to use them while fighting enemies.I do not regret purchasing the game, and I'm happy I got to support the devs, but to be honest, I would not recommend it to my friends. I wish you guys all the best for your future endeavours, but next time I'm gonna wait for reviews/gameplay videos before actually buying the game.That being said, I really hope you guys take into account all the shortcomings in this game and are able to make the next one a lot better!

_childDocuments_.review: Raji: An Ancient Epic is a fast paced, top down, action bash em up game. Visually its beautiful, has a great audio; music, voice narration, voice actors, weapon & skill feedback. Story was simple and enough to give users the motivation to push through the campaign. Interesting skills, tons of lore on the gods. Unfortunately, it has some issues with controls during battles and the inconsistency of terrain of battle will leave you baffled at times; when and where you are able to jump. You do lose control of your char for a few seconds, not so obvious solutions for puzzles, some balance issues on certain enemies and one disappointing ending. It was free fall once you meet the final boss. anti-climatic and confusing story that revolves around golu and raji at the end. Felt rushed or incomplete or that they really didn't know how to conclude the journey. Nonetheless, this product is fun, creative and holds so much promises to grow. It probably needed a little more tweaks on certain areas of the game to make it feel more polished.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend this game if ONLY you're here to appreciate the Indian aesthetic, support diverse devs, are interested in Indian myth and folklore AND don't mind going through a frustrating, but thankfully short, game. My positive review is LITERALLY just for those points I mentioned. If you care about any of the following things, I DO NOT recommend Raji: An Ancient Epic:1. Wonky controls. The game is so janky that it makes both combat and exploration a chore.2. Boring combat. Enemies have a lot of HP and come at you with wave after wave of minions, you don't have a lot of HP and no really reliable way to heal up, your weapons and abilities are all over the place and the character progression tree just has a lot of choices that feel like they have very little impact. The game jams in a lot of half baked mechanics that don't really mesh well together or are competent and fun individually.3. The voice actor for Raji has such an annoying and whiny delivery. Durga and Vishnu are so much better in comparison so I don't really understand just what they were thinking when selecting Raji's VA.4. No replay value. After your first playthrough, there's nothing to do and you're just sent back to the first mission. At least a level select option would have been nice but the game has a single autosave and no option at all for manual saves or quicksaves.5. Bland story. I get that it's supposed to be like a fairy tale and simple but I just have so many questions.  I didn't get a satisfying answer to any of these questions and the game just ends on a cliffhanger. I guess they're making a sequel but that leaves this game in a pretty unsatisfying spot.6. A lesser complaint, and purely subjective, but the shadow puppetry cutscenes seemed excessive. Yes, they're pretty and culturally appropriate but they were so overused that I didn't even recognize the villain when the final boss fight happened lol. And the only time that I was actually impressed with any of the cutscenes was in the literal last cutscene when the in-game animation takes over.Even with all these complaints though, at the end of the day, I'm still happy to support devs from different parts of the world with unique visions. I hope that they can learn from this game, see where it fell short and elevate their next title to a level that can really catch people's attention.

_childDocuments_.review: The game had promise but it does not have enough to keep it going throughout its length.Let me start with the positives, the music is fantastic, the setting and mythology it is based around is very good and something new which I am glad to see, there were also very few bugs that I could tell. This unfortunately is where the positives end for me.The combat is so-so, the animations for Raji are too long and this sometimes means it is hard to get an attack in before the enemy can hit you. The story is generic and bland (typical rescue story). The skill tree is very lazy, it makes me wonder why the developers bothered to implement it at all to be honest. The camera looks like it is operated by a child that has just found the zoom function, there is no rhyme or reason to the panning of the camera, it seems to just do what it wants. The platforming is passable, not much to say about it really, if you have ever played a platformer, you know what this game has. The level design is pretty but poor, there is this illusion of having multiple paths but instead there is just one, there is always multiple dead ends and then the way you have to go, you keep wanting there to be something along the other paths but there is always just a dead end. If you are going to make a linear game, fine, don't give the illusion of it being multipathed though. There is nothing to discover outside of the only path which is a missed opportunity, I am sure there are many more stories to tell inside of the Hindu religion and this would have been a great opportunity to tells these, but alas it was not to be. There are only about two puzzle types, they are just presented in a different way to make it seem like there is a bigger variety, this was also a missed opportunity, this type of game is screaming for puzzles and puzzle variety, this just was not on offer here. Yes this game is an indie game and is only charging an indie price but the product still needs to be fun to play and this just wasn't. I can't help but feel that if the devs had spent more money on the development and less on the DRM, this game could have been so much more than it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, but lacking the depth and polish of something really good.First of all, it's short: Only about 5-7 hours of content split between a tutorial level, 3 main levels, and a short final level with the last boss. This would be fine, per se, but the game elements never really have the time to  develop: platforming never really develops beyond hitting the spacebar to jump or climb, combat never really develops beyond mashing the dodge and attack buttons, puzzles never really develop beyond "line up the pieces", etc...The game can be played on KBM or controller, but it doesn't feel optimized for either. If you use KBM, some of the platforming segments become a little wonky, but if you use a controller, you can't effectively use your bow during combat (as you can only aim in the direction you're facing).There is a primitive upgrade system in the form of a skill-tree, but the lightning bonus is the only one which gives a tangible advantage (as far as I can tell), and by the time you have access to all of your weapon and upgrade combinations, the game is basically over.The ancient Hindu aesthetic gives a big boost to the game's personality, but the storyline is mostly told through expository dialogue and a series of barebones cutscenes which depict shadow puppet representations of the characters. I guess the devs never heard the expression "Show, don't tell"...Once you've completed the main story, there's no additional difficulty settings or game modes to unlock. Basically no replayability, so far as I can tell.Purchase if you really like the Hindu mythology angle and want to kill 6 hours with an okay action adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently in 4.8 hours of playing this well acclaimed game. At first, the controls are a bit of a learning curve since the mouse pointer greatly affects in battle and in traversing different areas that require climbing and jumping from one point to the other, but once you get the hang of it, the game becomes a breeze afterwards. Not only are the visuals stunning but the lore of Hindi Mythology is very rich and much like a storybook tale all in one. Just like in any adventure game you get to claim vast weaponry and elemental upgrades from the gods (lightning, fire and ice). By this time, I have already completed an elemental upgrade, and the customizing aspect of it is a very nice touch, so could focus on one element with full stacks! My only downfall for this game would be the isometric camera view of the game and the characters proportions are quite small considering such beautiful visuals the game has. At times, during battles the camera would zoom out for a large battlefield with only four enemies making targeting with the mouse quite uncertain and chaotic whether you are actually defeating a character or not. Over-all this is the game is very good and once you get a decent elemental upgrade, the game becomes enjoyable both in battle and the Hindi Mythology. Getting this game at 50% off was a good deal. Worth playing and learning culture at the same time!PROS:+ Good visuals/ graphics + Voice acting and in game music+ Customizing of elemental upgrades+ Enriching lore of Hindi Mythology CONS:- Isometric view proportions- Mouse pointer for battles is a learning process to getting used to.

_childDocuments_.review: Raji: An Ancient Epic~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Raji: An Ancient Epic is an action-adventure game set in ancient India and offering an amazing representation of the old world. This is a beautifully crafted world full of colors, ancient monuments built by both men and Gods, an excellent selection of music, intense combat, well-scripted, good voice acting, narrations, and much more. But what puts the game in the spotlight is its incredible story of a sister who will go to any length to rescue her brother. She was chosen by the gods to stand against the demonic invasion of the human realm. Her destiny? To rescue her younger brother and face the demon lord Mahabalasura.The game also features lore and mythology from ancient India, wars between the demons and the gods, the God’s origins and powers, the history of Hinduism and ancient architecture, etc. Plot: A young village girl named Raji and her tiny world that revolves around her younger brother, Golu. Her world was small and they were happy with each other’s company, until the day the demons took Golu away from Raji. She tried desperately to reach him in time but failed. Now Raji and Golu find themselves separated in the middle of the Great War; a war between Gods and Demons. However, the Gods themselves did not intervene. The gods have plans for young Raji. As she sets out to find her younger brother and confront the powerful demon lord, Mahabalasura, Raji finds herself in the hands of the great Goddess, Durga. With the blessings of Durga and other Gods, Raji sets out on an epic journey of great difficulty. Many hurdles will come in her way, and many demons will cross her path but the goddess Durga is confident that she has the strength and desire to reach her brother in time and confront lord Mahabalasura.Gameplay: Having an intimate knowledge about Hinduism and ancient India, I was very comfortable getting into the game. The game features a lot of lore from ancient India, which is amazingly depicted through narration and beautiful artwork in the form of murals, shadow puppet shows, structures, etc. which gave the game a great flavor. These featured lores affected the story and gameplay greatly. As I know a few things about the ancient Indian culture and Hinduism, I raced to find inaccuracies and errors, but to my surprise a lot of them matched up, and I got to know a few new things as well, and missed a lot while marveling over the beauty of this game. Our main protagonist Raji is an acrobat, which plays an important role throughout the game. As she utilizes her skills of acrobatic performance throughout the game and combat. The in-game movement plays out very well with its top-down and side-scrolling camera angles. The movements are basic with WASD to move. But jumping, vaulting, sliding, etc. is where the game shows its impressive animations covering Raji’s skills as an acrobat.The only downside to Raji’s impressive movement animations and skills would be her speed and clunky movement at places; for such an agile and limber person, Raji should have been much faster. And as for the clunky movements, they led to me to fail quite a few easy jumps, just because I was a bit to the left or right. But other than that, it was smooth sailing to the end.Combat; this game brings some intense yet easy to handle combat (a little bit too easy). Blessed by the gods and weilding the weapons given by the gods, combined with her impressive acrobatic skills, Raji is one tough nut to crack! As you progress through the first phase of the game, you will get all the required tutorials for the combat machines and get to try them out on the demons at the same time. Raji features quite a few impressive and bold combos for you to perform. To perform each combo you will need to run and jump off polls, carts, and walls. Also, as you pull off these combo moves, you will see some stunning attack effects and lighting. Each are very well designed and animated, and if you think about an actual acrobat, the moves would actually be possible to pull off by someone skilled enough, which was refreshing to see. As you progress, Raji faces stronger opponents with impressive skill sets, but Raji being Raji, an absolute star blessed by the gods, the combat sessions are mostly easy. However, as mentioned earlier, Raji’s clunky movement machines fail to implement its amazing combos.  Getting into the right angles at the right moment is important to pull off a combo move, which is not that difficult, but while you are doing so the smaller demons will stack upon you, resulting in a fail. Puzzles; Raji features a few well-placed puzzles, which were very easy to complete and each served a purpose in-game. The puzzles were mostly aligning pieces to view a bigger picture or to open gates and passages. Or shifting gears to start a function. World design: Raji features a stunning portrayal of ancient Rajasthan. The world is constructed around ancient man-made and god-made structures, which were well-designed and era-appropriate. With the absence of UI and no vision hindering structures, there is nothing to stop you from enjoying Raji’s amazing art style and lore. The game also seems to pay a great attention to lighting and reflection, which in turn made the game look absolutely gorgeous. Voice acting/ Narrations: Raji is being watched by the gods, and as she passes through places of great importance, the dialogues between the gods and narration of the events will kick in. I must say the dialogues and the narrations are well-scripted and acted. Strong Indian accents were present throughout the game, which did not bother me (but I did wonder what the game would sound like with the whole game narrated and acted in Hindi.  Music: Well-selected and implemented music throughout the game, which added great flavor. Positives: + Rich Story + Enjoyable gameplay+ Full of ancient Indian lore and mythology+ Good selection of music and sound effects + Simple yet fun puzzles+ Great attention to lighting + Strong female protagonist + Beautiful world design Negatives: - Clunky movement issues at places - Easy combat - Predictable- Linear storyGoing through temples and fortresses, dividing heaven and Earth, Raji’s will to reunite with her brother is as strong as any demon’s might. An excellent combination of story, art, and mythology. 9/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

We finally have a game which we can call it our own in every sense of imagination. Raji: An Ancient Epic is an action-adventure video game developed by Nodding Heads Games based out of Pune is India's first homegrown full game. With a small team, almost becoming bankrupt to selling own house the story of the developers is no less engrossing than the game. _childDocuments_.review: This is a competent 2.5d combat\platform game centered on Indian folklore and religion. It's quite interesting since is something that you rarely find outside historical games or niche jrpgs. There is no prior knowledge required, everything is explained in game clearly. Combat is very punishing at hard, there is no farming or rpg mechanics, you fight with four different weapons and special powers, that’s it. Beware the game heats a lot the cpu (for me it’s 70° which is extremely high considering is an U5 game with an average graphic) so probably it could have been done better.
_childDocuments_.name: Raji: An Ancient Epic

_childDocuments_.review: When I first heard of this game, I was very excited to see what it would be like to immerse myself into a story built on our ancient lore ! And it lived up to my expectations! The movements are heavily inspired from Prince of Persia (and it does seem slightly weird that the protagonist is accomplished at parkour!) - but that's absolutely fine! The variety of attacks is decently good, with different combinations of the elements. The music is wonderful, and the storyline is pretty good too! Truth be told, I was a little surprised when the game ended so soon, and on what a note! But for a first Indian game that has just , I believe Nodding Head Games have just announced themselves in the nascent Indian Gaming Industry (May it grow by Leaps and Bounds!) with rather a Big Bang! The creators have neatly woven in the ancient myths and legends into the plot of the game and this adds a certain human (read mortal) relatability to the divine. This game is worth playing for the way it has brought the Hindu Mythology to life! Very well done, Nodding Head Games! :-D However, I wonder at the possibility of a sequel - was that a cliffhanger the game ended on? Looking forward to more, Nodding Head Games! :-D

_childDocuments_.review: If you think it is a cute story adventure that will be easy, think again... I mean, it is cute and beautiful, but the combat can be hard and brutal even on Normal difficulty.  A few bosses require using the correct strategy, notably the right weapon among the total of four you discover along the way.  If a fight seems too hard, look for the correct strategy, such as constantly jumping up poles to avoid attacks. There are also some mild "puzzles", but they are quite easy and are used to tell the story. In terms of story, it is mostly original for folks like me who know almost nothing on Hindu lore.   It is not a RPG and there are no choices to make.  It is simple and the pleasure is learning the Hindu god stories. The graphics are quite nice and even offer (optional) RTX for shadows, reflections, etc. It took me about 7 hours to 100%. ( I surprisingly beat the last boss on my second attempt on Normal, simply because I guessed the trick early on.  The game uses autosaves, so losing a fight only means you reappear to try again immediately.)

_childDocuments_.review: It’s always refreshing to see something new represented in games. In an industry where trends are chased and so many games share similar themes and feel so much alike, it’s always nice to see something different. In the case of Raji: An Ancient Epic, it’s great to see a game where Indian culture is proudly represented. Much like Aurion: Legacy of the Kori-Odan represented an underserved culture of Africa, Rjai does that for India.You play the role of a young girl Raji, on a quest to save her younger brother Golu, as you face off against Gods and other beings from Hindu mythology. From the very beginning of the game, you can tell that it looks just fantastic. Throughout the game there are gorgeous set pieces and vistas that I found quite impressive for an indie game. From lush vegetation, to a vibrant color palette, Raji is a real looker.On the gameplay front, I found myself being reminded of Prince of Persia: Sands of Time. You have single button combos along with aerial combat as well as some light platforming and puzzles. Obviously, this is more of a modern take, with different weapons and upgrades, but I was reminiscing about Sands of Time in the best possible way playing this. Despite the combos not being super intricate, I did not tire of the combat as the game gives you enough weapons and augments to keep combat fresh throughout.If I had any complaints it would be that the static camera can make some platforming a bit cumbersome. There were a couple of spots where I wish I could have taken control of the camera. Additionally, the checkpoint system can be suspect at times. There were a couple of moments where I died and got put back a couple of minutes. I didn’t have to fight any enemies again, just simply walk back to where I was. I found this a bit irritating and simply a waste of time.Overall, I greatly enjoyed my time with Raji: An Ancient Epic. The visuals and overall polish (voice acting, soundtrack) were top notch and the combat and Hindu mythology were good enough to make me want to finish it. While the $25 price tag for 4.5 hours of gameplay may be steep for some, I’d have no problem recommending this on a sale if someone was hesitant about the value. As a freshman effort from Nodding Head Games, I found Raji to be an enthralling experience and I can’t wait to see what the studio does next.

The platforming and combat could've been a bit more challenging/fresh. But these are minor nitpickings. Definitely a very decent game I'd recommend

_childDocuments_.review: Not a fan of this game.It looks nice and has detailed environments. But the combat doesn't feel good at all. Enemies are damage sponges and they don't react to your hits at all. Worse, they're overly aggressive, attack quickly which leaves little room for you to actually do anything because most of the time there's 3, 4 or 5 enemies all coming at you at once and all you can do is roll around over and over to get a moment of breathing room.The game wants the gameplay of Devil May Cry but here it just ends up mashing buttons, hoping for the best. _childDocuments_.review: Raji is a decent attempt at isometric roguelike but suffers a lot due to poor implementation of combat which other games in the same genre do well - case on point: Hades which really is one of the best games I've played in this genre. - The story is set in Indian mythology, primarily in Rajasthan. The graphics are good, cinematics are hand-drawn puppetry style and very cute.  - Audio subtitles are available in English and Hindi both and the Hindi version is done well. - This game fits well in the "relaxing" tag popularly associated with it on Steam. It is not that long or too hard - the campaign takes 4-5 hours to finish. - Levels are quite distinctly different from one another in terms of setting, area and the landscapes were beautiful (many pretty screenshot worthy areas). - Not very graphic intensive, can run on mid-tier PCs with little bugs, crashes or FPS issues.-  You get only 4 weapons which are progressively unlocked and limited combos, the combat suffers heavily as it becomes limited fairly quickly. The game also indirectly forces you to use a specific weapon in each level (which is unlocked around the beginning) discouraging players to use older weapons and restricting the freedom to experiment with different fighting styles. - As you progress through areas you start getting enemies which can only be defeated with a specific weapon and so my question is, - And that is not the end of it. The enemies are constantly rushing and staggering Raji and if she gets stuck in a stun-lock you basically spam the dodge key a couple hundred times and hope it saves you. - Fairly frequently the game also forces you to spam combos heavily relying on environmental aspects - spam the spacebar key on a pillar or a wall and do heavy attacks which becomes boring and saturated very soon. But at least in non-boss waves you can regain your health, it's not the same for boss fights as you have no way of regaining lost health. - The bosses were mediocre. The only boss I liked as a challenge was the first one called the Chieftain and even that was bugged with incorrect hitboxes. The second boss Rangda tries you grab you 10 times with each finger, you cut off it's 10 fingers (one at a time of course and in a really dragged out fight) and it just rage-dies. You also need to use the shield to block it's screams or it eats away at your health and this was not sufficiently made clear. The final boss Mahabalasur  was too tanky and unpredictable almost making the fight a chore than fun. You are only supposed to use the final weapon for the final boss as the ones before become useless. And the final weapon has no scope of heavy attacks just the same light attack with janky aim. - The camera angles are rubbish. Ultimately I found more joy in learning about the different Hindu gods and goddesses via narration and murals than actually doing the fighting or following the story and that is primarily why I would not recommend this game to anyone.

This was a let down because the combat looked very promising, i liked the  overall mechanics (3 weapons/3 elemental damage) and fluidity but the developers didn't really capitalize on it with such basic fights.Boss fights are pretty underwhelming. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR below.Fair warning: I am writing this from the perspective of a gamer who is heavily biased in seeing the gaming industry emerge with rich Indian cultural content by Indian talent.I have played many a number of games on various platforms, from Western (primarily American) and Far Eastern games (primarily Japanese). And at the end of playing such games, one thought would always enter my mind: ‘What if one day there was a game set in India or made by Indians of similar caliber?’ To be fair, there have been attempts to capture it by Western developers, such Prince Of Persia: Sands of Time (the upcoming remaster of which is ironically being made by Ubisoft Pune, an upcoming first for them) or Uncharted: Lost Legacy. Now this game is NOT in the vein of, say, God Of War or Assassin’s Creed or even ICO, Shadow of the Colossus, The Last Guardian offerings. What this game is more similar to, are games like the classic Prince of Persia side, Trine or Limbo. It is a 2.5D game. And it’s game size reflects the same: a measly 5.12 GB. Not going to lie, I did want my Indian God of War game, but I do know I am asking for too much.  Also, all mainstream AAA games are built on top of existing games before them. If there was no Tetris, there would never have been a God Of War. And this game is the Tetris of what I hope is an upward climb of quality Indian narrative games.The story starts on a simple note: Raji, a Rajasthani circus performer and the titular character of the game has to undertake a journey to rescue her only brother who has been abducted by demons. Her story is omnisciently narrated by Durga, the Goddess of War (there you go guys, something of ‘War’), and Lord Vishnu, the God of Sustenance who for reasons, have a degree of investment in her success on her journey. Along the way, Raji is endowed with more and more powers and weapons by the aforementioned omniscient narrators of the story.The journey takes the player through wonderfully designed environments reflecting expected Indian architecture and the game designers’ own variations and exotic takes on a few monuments. Quite a few environments made me pause to take in the view, which is something I usually do in third person free-roaming games and not side-scroller games, which is a testament to the quality of the design.You get access to three weapons, starting with the trident or Trishul and moving on to other weapons. You can easily play the game with a specific weapon that fits your playing style, or you can mix and match. You can also acquire special blessings that imbibe your weapons with lightning, flame, and freezing effects. Through inquisitive exploration, you can also stumble across special Orbs that can be used to add variations to the effects earned from the aforementioned blessings upon your selected weapons. The combat is fairly well designed, but some of the UI is a bit confusing when you play it for the first time. Rotating between blessings, weapons and special effects can be a bit confusing until you get used to its system.  My preference was using a bow and arrow (and a late-game weapon I won’t spoil) in tandem, which seems to suit my playstyle for this game. The game doesn’t really force you to use which weapon against specific enemies, but you might be more inclined to be a ranged fighter, as health can only be earned from defeating enemies. Any overconfidence in melee tends to be rewarded with starting over from the last saved checkpoint.There are certain weaknesses within the gameplay design. The attack animations and attack feedback are fairly satisfying, but there are times when the kill animations feel a bit less engaging. Obviously, it may come from the need for keeping things safe to play for most ages (even as the story deals with dark things happening to children), but I do wonder what the developers could come up with fewer restrictions. As far as traversal is concerned, it does a good job of evoking Prince of Persia style 2D parkour. Aside from minor clipping issues, I did once encounter a weird issue in one bug, where I skipped a traversal section and jumped directly into a combat section by accidentally falling to my death during the traversal section. But really, these are minor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.The cutscenes, which convey most of the narrative, are things of beauty. They employ 2 dimensional Rajasthani kathputli, a special type of storytelling that uses marionettes. That leaves such an impression that the developers really want the story told in a special way. And the music composition by Linus Tzelos and his team is quite charmingly haunting, with the right mixture of sitars, tablas, violins, and castanets that prepare the setting quite nicely for either combat or sight-seeing.There are also a couple of puzzles, but they are fairly simple. Not a lot of time was spent in designing them to be challenging, but it is nothing that might count as a negative point, as they make up for their simplicity with beautiful imagery. The sights are way better than the puzzle gameplay.One drawback I would say with the narrative quality of the game is the voice acting. Now, I am completely aware that the game has to sell to a wide audience, but the English voice acting is serviceable. Also, sometimes some voiced lines do feel redundant when the visuals themselves are able to convey the story. However, I would be totally open to a complete Indian vocal localization of the story, as I feel it would add to the narrative quality. The only localization currently in this game is Hindi subtitles which are not enough. I can only imagine how much richer this game would be with authentic Indian dialogues and voices, similar to many Japanese games. Another narrative drawback emerges from the characters in the game, Raji being the most obvious herself, but it is not unique for female protagonists to be mere ciphers in their first iteration of the games. She comes off as desperate and emotional but not relatable. Her stronger character traits come when in the cutscenes with her brother Golu. But Lara Croft, Samus, Commander Shepard, Chun-Li, too started blandly but acquired much richer character in later games. I look forward to the evolution of this character should Nodding Head Games choose to advance the story forward.And of course, one can’t complete the narrative coverage without observation of the usage of Hindu mythology in this game. One must understand, this is a very sticky wicket in the current political climate and that there are sections of Indians who do take umbrage with even the littlest of deviations from the majority accepted view of our Hindu deities. Thankfully, there is an aesthetical integration of various Hindu elements into the gameplay that should not hopefully offend even the most conservative practitioners of the faith. The game also, more importantly, segues you into these stories in a very organic way through beautiful murals you will be curious to stop and observe along your journey. Now, for the gamers who do not have the investment as I do, I believe they will still find the experience worth the price of entry (an equivalent of trying out a new KFC/McDonald's menu item). If I have to compare with other side-scroller games that I have played, it’s not going to dethrone them gameplay-wise but I do feel it is a solid entry in that space. You get gorgeous and unique Indian visuals and feel-good-if-imperfect 2d combat. So get it if you appreciate a unique aesthetic and have the cash to do so.TL;DR:The game is simply beautiful in its presentation of the story-telling cut-scenes and level design, with a satisfying but imperfect combat system. While the narrative slightly stumbles behind its design, it is serviceable and promises a start of a unique set of games representing an all often neglected Indian culture at a performative level that can be compared to other culture-oriented mainstream games.

_childDocuments_.review: Raji AE pleasantly reminded of my long time fav games like God of War (hack n slash and camera pull backs), Prince of Persia (Parkour fight moves, wall running and the mechanical waterworks level) and even other indie gems like Rime and Journey, the influence of these games was apparent in Raji. However, devs Nodding Heads Games clearly put in their hearts into this experience showcasing the Hindu mythology through immaculate art and rich environments. Having said that, the game does have it's share of flaws despite receiving an enhanced edition namely being lack of tight controls for movement (avoid using KB and Mouse, use a controller instead), progression impeding glitches like no movement on input and a glitched achievement i experienced 'Favor of the Gods' (which unlocked after loading my save tho). The cons mentioned are nothing compared to the sheer beauty and unique gameplay, I especially loved the engaging narration on the gods. PS : I hope Indian devs grow big enough to someday make a game on Kartikeya - the Indian/Hindu GoW.
_childDocuments_.name: Raji: An Ancient Epic

_childDocuments_.review: You can tell that the devs wanted to put out a good game. I think it could have been an amazing game if they had polished it. The art and the level design is beautiful and well built. The fight and bosses are actually good and not easy with good action sets BUT the moves are kinda janky. There is a tree for weapon enhancement which was nice, but since the game is so short, you don't really have time to have a strong build. I really like how our character fights (with the pillars and the walls) but I would have liked to have the opportunity to use those during boss fights. The cutscenes had a nice art style (puppet show) but they were too long and I didn't care for them. Puzzles were kinda fun too. And finally the voice acting is hit or miss (either there is or it's AI, I dunno). So I do recommend this game but it could have been so much more.
_childDocuments_.name: Raji: An Ancient Epic

_childDocuments_.review: I have to recommend this game to show some love to these guys who DARED to make a linear action game, a feat that seems almost unimaginable in this modern gaming age. The art direction is obviously great but I didn't like all the glowing stuff, i get that attacks and health are supposed to be clearly visible but this is a bit too much and it kinda clashes with the rest of the environment. The combat system is quite cool even if it lacks a bit of feedback on hitting, weapons and power ups are different enough but what I liked the most was the fact that Raji expertise as an acrobat is translated really well in gameplay. You can chain 3 different jumps/dodges super mario style and attacking during a dodge will result in 3 different powerful strikes. The main letdown is that not only the game is short but it is also quite padded with really useless platforming and a couple drawn out boss fights.
_childDocuments_.name: Raji: An Ancient Epic

_childDocuments_.review: Raji is pretty unique, can't say I've seen any other game explore Hindu mythology and for that alone it gets some brownie points. That said, if Steam had a sideways thumb option, I'd probably pick that but lean towards up. It's worth a look for at least one playthrough but I feel the game would have excelled more as a visual novel because the graphics is by far the best most enthralling feature. It's a very nice art style for cutscenes. The actual game isn't bad either - the scenery is definitely beautiful.The story is decent as well - although I'm not quite sure about the ending. I felt like I was missing something and it just ended all the sudden. Oh well. I also like the optional murals to examine to learn more about avatars of the various Gods. The game really drips with the Hindu flavor and it's quite welcome!However, gameplay wise I feel the game is rather clunky and could use polishing. Platforming was frustrating at times. Many actions are tied to the jump button so sometimes I would roll when I meant to jump, jump when I meant to wall run, etc. The fixed camera made platforming difficult at times with being able to tell if I am jumping at the right angle. Was really annoying to jump off screen because I was angled slightly off. There is at least a visual cue to see if you're lined up but was still annoying. But the game has forgiving checkpoints so if I missed a jump in the end it was no real big deal.Combat is the other big chunk of the game. It's okay. It's not going to be dark souls/sekiro level of combat, but it's not really a cake walk either. If you just run in spamming attack, you will probably die. There's also dodging at your disposal and wall jump attacks and so on. There are four weapons (one is only gotten at the very end) but it seems to me the bow is hands down the best weapon.  Just spam the aimed arrow rain and pretty much anything dies quickly, even the final boss. In contrast, if you don't use the bow, battles can drag out annoyingly long at times. I think the melee weapons could use more balance to be more worth using.Some aspects of the game just seem to drag or take too long despite the game being short already. I don't mind a short game but these moments really tested my patience. For example, there is a boss where you basically hide and run. OK, sure, that's a staple of these kind of games. But it just kept going and going for far too long. There was also a boss that seemed to take way too many hits to kill - basically you take off one finger at a time. I found a way to speed that fight up a bit - can just use an ult on the hand and it will damage all the fingers and allow you to take them out faster.Anyways - despite these minor annoyances I do think the game is worth a look and I'm curious to see more games set in Hindu mythology. Definitely at least give it a look for the beautiful art.

_childDocuments_.review: Hmmm, you know, I'm leaving my positive recommendation, but with a major caveat that the game ends on a profound anti-climax. I am... very mixed on my feelings now. It feels like the last five pages of the story were just ripped out, and the game ends there. The experience leading up to it was still quite enjoyable, with beautifully realized world. But knowing what I know now... it makes the experience feel that just less satisfying. A bit of a shame. Maybe more will come, however.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a pretty good game with excellent visuals and art direction.The visuals and art direction were amazing with nice atmosphere and landscapes.The story was fine with my only nitpick being the cutscenes (i'd prefer the cutscenes being animated in 3D rather than 2D puppet type cutscenes). But it's just a nitpick. The story did contain some hindu stories which were nice touch to add in the game and I just hope they continue this as the Indian culture is so rich and has so many great stories.My only gripe with the gameplay is it being a bit stiff and not as fluid as it should be to become compelling for a second run. The gameplay lacked that impact of hit and combat flow of a game like HADES. Still, it's a pretty good game for a first try and I hope the devs will continue making these games. Good luck!

_childDocuments_.review: One word: WOW!I reviewed this game several months ago before the latest update and was negative about the combat, abandoned my playthrough at chapter three, and didn't look back. Thankfully the developers invited me to replay it after the latest update and I'm SO GLAD that they did, because this game is now a masterpiece.The graphics are beautiful, the story moving, and the setting stunning (how badly do I want to go back to India now?!) And, best of all, the combat is FUN!! It is a rare company these days that will, after release, take the time to improve difficult areas of their game, and the developers have done just that, cleaning up the troublesome combat to make this a truly enjoyable game. I'm so glad that they have done so: this is clearly a passion project and they have made it shine.9.5/10 -- Highly recommended.If you're curious, here is my old review. Needless to say, the combat hitches I complain about are now gone:This game is so beautiful and such a clear work of love, and I really REALLY wanted to love it too. Unfortunately, those gorgeous elements are badly undercut by a very frustrating set of controls. I tried really hard to push through the title after rage-quitting once during the tutorial and kept finding sections that I just adored, but just when I started to forget my frustration some part of the gameplay would get in the way. I don't want to actively NOT recommend the game because it is absolutely stunning, and perhaps those with more patience than I will be able to get past the gameplay hitches, but I wanted to post a warning in the very least.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for November 2022, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before December 6th, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.An exploration of Indian mythology. Raji is a story about a circus performer whose brother is kidnapped and she has to save him while battling monsters.  The Indian Mythology is pretty fresh and is explored well here.  The world though is exceptional with the game’s backgrounds just being beautiful.  You often see parts of the level you’ve traveled through or will traverse later and the animations are incredible, showing off the character’s acrobatic background. I played this on Game Pass, and I’ll say the first twenty to thirty minutes is a little rough.  After you get a good handle on the combat, the game starts letting you use upgrade points and then gives you a second weapon, and suddenly everything clicks, but that opening is looks amazing but is on the weaker side.Pick this up if you’re like a solid platformer with good combat, or are interested in Indian Mythology.  The story here works extremely well and the character and world design are exceptional.  I enjoyed this game quite a bit the first time I played it, and I am thrilled to have added it to my collection and will be giving it another playthrough. _childDocuments_.review: RAJI - AN ANCIENT EPIC PROS :Beautiful graphicsLevel design is amazingEnemy variety is ok-ish for a 4 hours gameCamera pans out to take in a lot of the landscape, occasionally showing jaw-dropping artworkBackground music is greatThe way the gods interact among themselves to discuss Raji's fate is pretty interestingPopular tales from Indian mythology are recounted in an interesting mannerLots of different divine weapons, which change how they are used on upgrading. Fire, ice and lightning - each feel distinctly different - with ice, after fully upgrading - freezing enemies to their spot, and fire raining down bombs from the sky.The way cutscenes are depicted in the form of a puppet show is really unique.Plenty of fun puzzles and mechanics - corrupted trees, hidden treasure, gears...etc.Extremely cheap on Steam - 540/- for this is just a steal deal!Cons :No lock-on available which makes hitting enemies, and particularly the first boss, a bother.All the bosses are a cakewalk, except the first boss. which still presents a bit of a challenge to some.Story ends too abruptly with an open ending, though this might mean a sequel in the works.Weapons become too OP as the game progresses, which makes the later levels too easy, involving just simple button mashing. and the final weapon makes the last boss fight child's play.Backtracking is prevented in a lot of areas by randomly generated barriers, so a wrong turn will make you miss a whole hidden secret.A couple more levels could have been included, replacing a huge level in the middle, and two similar looking levels at the beginning and the end.I personally would have liked the game to have some INDIAN asuras/demons in an Indian mythology setting.Overall, the pros more than make up for the cons. 8/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: OMG! Where do I start? I got a few key points that I would like to focus on instead of ranting on and on. Here are the things that I liked:1. The use of shadow puppets for cinematics was a brilliant touch on how story telling goes in ancient India.2. The music was heavily cultured specially, with the use of Matka (Literally a pot that is used to make music played like a drum) and the tablas.3. The scenery was breathtaking with the camera showing what it had to offerHere's a list on why I don't recommend it, (contains spoiler):1. Starting off with the over powered final weapon that can one shot enemy  making the boss fight so easy to the point where I could keep dodging and attacking.2. All the cinematic had narration which was pretty much exposition. As the player, I did not feel connected to Raji during the cinematic.3. The ending fight was abruptly cut off with a cinematic and I thought there would be more as the gateway had opened but the game ended.4. I was hoping for a plot twist where Golu would be corrupted and I would have to fight him because of the pond scene where it showed his head turning into a demon head.5. Before the final weapon, the second weapon, the bow, was over powered. Using the heavy attack, one could fend off a swarm of enemies and it could even one shot the shrine that summons more demons.6.  A lot of stories from Indian Mythology that had nothing to do with the game. It was nice to learn about it but it was just an info dump as if the devs are trying to shove in how much they can about Indian Mythology. Skipping ahead these story doesn't make much difference in the overall story. Its not like it provides tips or secret paths for the game.7.  The camera angle changed as per the player location and as someone who played it on PC with a keyboard, its hard to navigate some obstacles because he angle to jump at is sometimes between E(East) and SE(South-East) which doesn't exist within a keyboard.8. There is no menu so people who are hunting for achievements have to play over and over as there is no level select.9. The ending felt hollow.Overall thoughts is that the game is rich in music and cultural heritage and the visuals, but looking at it from a point of being a game, it lacks in gameplay and story. They should have worked more on those than the music or the art.

_childDocuments_.review: Too many fingers.That's the problem with boss fights and practically nobody being able to design interesting ones. Repetitiveness. Grind. Carpal and mental fatigue.Ragda, if that's her real name, has too many fingers to cut. At the end of the first hand I was already bored to death, but it didn't end there as I was seriously hoping it would. When rigor mortis took over my body, by the 7th finger, I slipped and died as expected. Cos' that's the only challenge provided by these mindless fights, innit ? Sapping your will to keep at eroding a mountain with a cheese-grater.As you imagine, devs who can't design a smart boss fight can't design smart checkpoints either. So it's back to finger #1. Or that is what devs would expect, because in the sane world it results in so long, uninstall, thumb down... I have no time for being counter-entertained during my entertainment time.Obviously, it wasn't the first straw on the camel's back. The general gameplay is mediocre at best, and had me progress in many short-only sessions. The combat is neither smooth nor tactical, and quite repetitive already. I found that, when a fight appears difficult, button-mashing will magically solve the issue as long as you alternate the buttons. Lilipads... repetitive mechanics again, that become frankly annoying when random-length timers are added (in the form of fish) to ruin your efforts and insta-kill you with full reset of the entire process.A pity, because this is one of the very best-looking games I've ever played. incredibly  gorgeous.Then again, the camera would not let you enjoy the landscapes, when it should. No control there, not even a zoom. It's also used to hide secrets, which is not the right way to go about it, and is plainly unfair when you choose to go left before right but then can never go back to see what was on the right.Beauty can only take you so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Raji: An Ancient Epic is a fun action adventure game that reminds me a lot of an isometric version of Prince of Persia in terms of gameplay style, but with less danger in the platforming.Combat is fun and feels mostly pretty responsive, and the variety of weapons and enemies keeps the game fresh during it's run time.The environments are very pretty, and the game does a good job presenting them through the game's perspective.There's also a big emphasis on lore and story, which does a decent job of relaying Indian Mythology and telling an enjoyable story. I liked the use of the gods as narrators, and Raji was a good main character.HOWEVER, the ending makes the game feel incomplete at present time, like there should be an extra level or two. No closure is given and it leaves a lot to be desired.If you like Indian folklore or want to know more about it, it's an enjoyable time at about a 6-7/10, but with a proper conclusion it could have been a great game and scored higher.

_childDocuments_.review: Brief: Visually stunning game with simple gameplay that taps into unexplored (in video games) Hindu mythology. It's a small yet good game, but could've been better. I'd give it a 3/5, recommending a play through for the visual setting and if you're interested in mythology. Getting into the details here (no spoilers), the gameplay was very simple. Some running and around and jumping with simple combat. The combat had some good combos, but the combat had no difficulty setting, rendering combos useless. Random smashing of buttons gets the job done. There are a few boss fights which were fun, though the final boss disappoints. You get three major weapons for the majority of the game, and you can switch between any of these weapons at any point. However, the combat design was too simple and you could always fight with a single weapon. They could have improved the combat to make us use the combos effectively, and choose the right weapons for the right demon, probably add in a difficulty setting as well. There are very few puzzles in the game, which were very easy to solve. This aspect I felt had more potential for improvement.The setting was beautiful. There are different places they take you through which look really amazing, and the story takes you through this setting. There's isn't much room for exploration, most of the exploration is part of the story itself, though I would've liked if there was room open for exploration, finding collectibles or such, that could make you enjoy the view while playing. I liked the soundtracks too, was a really good fusion of classical Indian elements with modern music.Now coming to the main part, I enjoyed the way they told the story through the puppets, though some part of the storytelling could've been done by gameplay too. However, the story was disappointing. It felt like it was building towards something big, but it just fell flat at the end. For the most part, the story felt like it was introducing you to Hindu mythology more than exploring the main character and her relationship with her brother. And while they could've done much better with the story, I'd like to add that the exposition of Hindu mythology was well done.

_childDocuments_.review: Pro:+ Beautiful+ Learn Indian MythologyCons:- Dull gameplayGameplay consists of minor platforming elements, extremely minor "puzzle" sections, and combat. Lots of combat. Platforming is adequate. The "puzzles" of this game are easy but I can forgive that since they are not the focus. But I do wonder whether the puzzles actually contributed to the game outside of a palette cleanser. For the combat in this game, all you need to do is mash the attack button and dodge roll. True, you could spice up combat with a variety of different attacks for each of the game's weapons, but few can seem to manage just the raw attack output of button mashing. This is compounded by the fact that your ability upgrades are chance based, so more hits = more abilities going off. Furthermore Raji controls a bit stiffly for my taste.Furthermore, the game has sections that control differently from the main game, causing confusion, as well as a general lack of explanation. You can learn a lot by experimenting, but you could also find yourself ignoring portions of the combat system out of confusion as well.Overall the gameplay just feels like it was made to be "good enough". It works, it's functional (barely at times), it does a good enough job.- StoryAs someone who despises spoilers I will only say that it story is rather... abrupt.Furthermore, the Indian mythology seems to just be... there? Like at times you will come across some beautiful pictures and can choose to trigger markers where the narrators will dictate mythology to you, but the mythology has... absolutely no bearing on what you are doing. None whatsoever. It's just an info dump.- ShortI can't see a so called "average" gamer spending  more than 10 hours on this, and I feel that is  stretching it.Overall this game is beautiful, but also short, dull and with no real payoff. Nothing you haven't seen done before in other, maybe even cheaper games (price atm is 50% off 25$). If you want to learn Indian mythology, there are probably many cheaper venues to peruse.Would not recommend, except to satisfy a burning curiosity. Even then only on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty solid effort from an Indian Game Dev startup in creating a story-based singleplayer game that explores Hindu culture, which feels like a nice, fresh change in a market saturated with typical multiplayer games or singeplayer games with other cultures. Don't get me wrong, I love games based on other cultures too (e.g. Celtic culture in Hellblade or the mixed cultures in The Witcher games), but it feels good to know that someone is tapping into the rich depths of Indian culture too.If you can enjoy the fact that this is a short (~6hrs), simple combat-platformer game with mechanics somewhat similar to a Prince of Persia game, that is based on Hinduism, with narrations from Lord Vishnu and Durga Devi, you'll like this game a lot.- Pretty well designed and polished, with an attractive art-style, with several beautiful locations/set pieces.- Finally a game that tries to explore the vast, rich and diverse Hindu culture.- A pretty good story, with narrative conversations between Durga Devi and Vishnu Dev that are enjoyable.- I personally like the stick propped puppet animation style used for cutscenes.- The soundtrack is pretty enjoyable too; consists of a lot of classical Indian instruments.- Combat mechanics are interesting - simple to learn, but take practice to master. If you've played a Prince of Persia game you'll find a lot of mechanics in the game pretty similar, and might feel right at home.- The graphics are good enough for this game to look pretty, but not too extensive, so it can run on most medium level PCs/laptops too.- Priced pretty cheap in India (₹600) compared to US ($25) or other markets.- The combat mechanisms and fighting the gadasura demons can get repetitive after a while.- The voice acting for Raji could've been better; I feel like they could've chosen a better name for her brother than 'Golu', especially since her shouting GOLUUU becomes annoying after a while.TL;DR a pretty good first effort from an Indian Game-Dev startup to create a polished, high quality game, with a story based on Indian Hindu cultures, which, combined with it's amazing art-syle, soundtrack and narration, makes for a really enjoyable gaming experience, despite some minor flaws and issues here and there. Go for it without expecting it to match western AAA titles' quality, and you'll have fun. Worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually do recommend this game but if you're reading negative reviews you probably want a more rounded review.PROS:- gorgeous- the only game I've ever played that portrays Indian mythos so respectfully- as an Indian playing this game, seeing myself represented for once really meant a lot to me- decent enough gameplayCONS:- confusing upgrade menu- locks weapons behind story progression, but the game is so short you don't get enough time with the final ones- gamebreaking bug where if you save and quit before the last boss, you can't move. Luckily there's a fix where you start a new game with a different slot, get to the first cp, then load your original save- the ending is vague and unsatisfying. it plays like a bad ending so you think maybe the true ending is in ng+? nope, only one ending. seriously soured the whole experience.Again I still recommend it, but its really flawed and wasn't worth it even on sale. Feels unfinished and not worth more than $5 sadly, despite how much I wanted it to be good.

_childDocuments_.review: is a good action-adventure game set in ancient India mythology. The unique storytelling via paper character animations and colorful stone murals with narration are memorable and listening the stories of Hindu deities is pleasant. _childDocuments_.review: In the last few years I have been reading mainly history, and as a result I started looking for "cultural" games, games that in some way represent a culture, its history or mythology. That's how I came across Raji.The game is inspired by Indian history and Hindu mythology, both visually and in terms of its world, and this is its greatest strength. The story itself is very simple: The main character is Raji, a circus acrobat whose brother is kidnapped by demons, and with the help of the gods, she goes to rescue him. She is not much of a character, her monologues quickly become repetitive. What really carries the game is the presentation of Hinduism-inspired lore and the narration by Vishnu and Durga. Part of the reason I loved their commentary is that the game has Hindi dubbing. I don't speak Hindi, but listening to a language that is appropriate for the context really enhances the experience for me.The visuals are also spectacular, with Indian architecture and paintings brought to life to make our journey memorable. I particularly liked the murals illustrating the lore. The design of the enemies also deserves praise. The excellent music helps establish the atmosphere, of course, mainly with traditional instruments.As for the gameplay, it's a simple action platformer. Neither the jumping nor the easy quasi-puzzle parts along the way caused any difficulties, but the combat was something else entirely. The battles are very fast-paced, the enemies attack relentlessly, and you have to dodge all the time with very few opportunities to strike back. The final boss was particularly ridiculous in this respect. I started the game on Easy, but I still got destroyed plenty of times. So, the combat didn't work for me as much, but overall, the game was absolutely worth it. I really enjoyed this journey. Certain aspects of it could be criticized, but as a complete experience, it was fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely unique. And that's it's main selling point.Pros: It's the only game set in mythological India as far as I know. You get to hear Vishnu and Durga narrate and you learn the tale of many Hindu gods and demi-gods and avatars and whatnot. I am a huge Hinduism nerd. I have the Mahabharata on my phone, read the Gita three times and have some Upanishads on my desk right now. That's why I absolutely loved the game.It's very atmospheric. It looks ... decent. It's well designed, though pretty low budget. The music is amazing. The voice actors are great. Cons: It's a mediocre game. It has a few ... strange design decisions. Weapons progress linearly. You just can't use the trident after you get the next weapons. Same with the boosts.The bow is outright trash. You have to use it for damage purposes, but it's moveset is just garbage. There's also a part of it's "tutorial" (when you have to use left-mouse-click while mid-air on the dummies) that just doesn't work. It took me half an hour to hit the three effing dummies.Overall, worth it. It's a small dev, so they deserve our support.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: Good; recommendedPros:- Super nice music- Beautiful environments and aesthetics, especially of the gods who are sweet- The gods narrate about you in the background just like they talk about the mortals in the Iliad- Likable characters (Raji, Durga, Vishnu)- 3-4 weapons and an OK skill system that adds a little flavor- Neat lore that teaches you about Hindu mythology- Meet / learn from the super cool Hindu gods and mystics- Fight badass Indian demons- Its style gets it close to being in that "games as art" category which distinguishes itCons:- Bit short (~4 hrs?). Basically it feels like "chapter one" of a four part series. I assume with how it ended there will be later releases that will develop the whole story. (Knowing about how financing a game works, honestly I think this type of release is the wisest plan a team can take. It lets them fully finance for later if part one is successful.)- Combat gets a bit repetitive and boring for me.- Would be nice to have more RPG elements - talk to the guards or the king in the fort, talk to the gods - would be more immersive.- Maybe have a bit more character development / improvement so you get invested more. Increase a few stats? Specialization in one area (ranged, sword, etc?) Maybe different clothes or armors? Maybe be able to play Golu?- Standard platformer / puzzler overall. Reminded me a lot of Psychonauts and Zelda. Distinguishes itself due to the story and aesthetics.I recommend buying it if all of the above sounds OK to you. And if you like this kind of stuff your purchase will support this team, who I assume will go on to complete the series. Nice job guys.

_childDocuments_.review: Raji: An Ancient Epic follows in the spirit of Never Alone to bring a people's story to life in an exciting, interactive way. While the combat is somewhat repetitive, it never quite gets boring thanks to how fluid the movements are, and the voice acting, music, and art all are a pleasure to experience. So much mythology was presented through a coherent plot, and yet much more was teased-- hinted at, referenced, just out of reach-- that it stoked a desire to look further into it on my own. On those grounds alone, I would recommend this game to any who hold an interest in expanding their worldview.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say that this is a beautiful game with an engaging story and atmosphere, but the fight mechanics often feel rather floaty at times (which is a lot of the game). I quite enjoy/like the game, so I would still recommend it to anyone who wants to play a short and enjoyable game about mythological retelling of ancient epics from India such as Mahabharata and Ramayana.Honestly makes me want to go to the bookstore and buy the thick copies of those stories to read further into these stories.Some of the art directions are truly so beautiful, especially in Hiranya Nagari (Vishnu's Temple level) which is definitely my favorite place in the entire game; the watery scenery with giant lotuses floating in the air and fishes swimming under you throughout the level, truly a breathtaking view. The enemy designs are also well done, each unique in design and attacks. I do feel that "The Ruins" and "Land of the Mystics" sort of feel like the same level, even though the latter is a late game are, the design feels like it pales in comparison to what Hiranya Nagari has offered in the previous level. To give it credit, I think overall the assets are absolutely pretty, but I think they could've went further with designing the "Land of the Mystics" level.Overall, I think it's a pretty good game. Definitely would recommend to people just to have a breath of fresh air in a rarely adapted mythology in the video game genre. 7.5/10 🌟Also: I'm bugged at completing Vishnu's Shrine and it seems to not count and of my listening actions. Otherwise I would've already 100% this game
