_childDocuments_.review: Probably among the games with the most beautiful and detailed environment design in sci-fi that I've played. The retro futuristic tech is on point and the scenery on Regis III is both beautiful and oppressive in its vastness devoid of life.The lack of HUD elements like minimaps, waypoints or current goals is refreshing and definitely helps with immersion. On one hand it lets you fully focus and appreciate the beautifully crafted environment, on the other hand you are left to be your own guide in this alien world really putting you in the shoes of the main character looking for a way out of this dead planet.I'm not really a fan of walking sims but I found The Invincible quite enjoyable. Starward Industries for sure hit the nail in the head as far as game length goes and the last autosave being very close to the end allows to experience most endings in single playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Flawed gem. Starwards did a great job in adapting Lem's philosophical scifi to a digital experience. It's a remarkable example in how walking sims should be made. Strong character writing and dialogue. Stunning visuals and sound. No forced gameplay to extend game time. Almost every place you go has some meaning to either the story or lore. Handcrafted with great care.It has many flaws like annoying navigation, occasionally stumbling pacing or a few bugs making me reload a save. Also Id love to see more of the original books lore. But ultimately the Yasna and Novik duo are always there to save the day. Plus you get to launch the nukes.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: There's not much to game play for this one. It's more of a walking movie with some small interactions and searching for clues/gear. If you don't mind that type of game, this is a great one. The graphics/environment are absolutely beautiful. It's a pleasure to walk around and explore because of it. The story is pretty engaging as well, though I found the several endings available fairly inconsequential. The voice acting was really well done by almost all of the cast. If you're in the  mood for a 5-7 hour story on a gorgeous far away planet, definitely give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Stanislav Lem is a great name and the reason I bought The Invincible.Unfortunately this is not even a game. This software is the pinacle of boredom. All you can do is walking nerve wrecking sluggish along a scripted path and when a white circle appears: You have to click on it. Then the dim-wit protagonist babbles something trivial or does someting trivial. What ever you chose in the dialogue menu: It doesn't matter!If you can't walk at all: Look around, there must be a white circle. Found it? Click on it! Now you can continue your sluggish way along the scripted path and discover more white circles.Really, that's not a joke: You don't even have to think what is important and what you should do like in an adventure game.These devs put everthing they want you to do inside a big, fat  white circle. The only thing you can do in this "game" is to click on it. This is not even a "walking simulator" oir adventure where you have to solve puzzles. From the Steam Discussion Board in case people don't believe that such a piece of scrap software really got sold as a game:- -  All in all it's the epitome of boredom.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Good walking simulator. There's normally enough dialogue to keep things entertaining. They give you a sprint button but your character runs out of breath after 3 seconds so it's pretty much worthless. Story is engaging but the end "boss" is a bit of a letdown. Voice acting is great. Everything else is good.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Short (7hrs) but sweet, and a stunning invocation of Science Fiction era from the 70's.  If you are a fan of  Stanisław Lem like me then you will love this little trip down memory lane.  Everything was recreated with obvious loving attention to evoking the feeling from Stanislaw's book, from the isolated loneliness, to eary undiscovered danger, and utterly alien landscapes.  A gem.  To those unfamiliar with SF from that era, this is a first person story where the journey is the adventure.  No shooting at aliens, no dodging return fire, and in truth not many dialog options which will change the story outcome all that much.  Think of this as a gentle trip accompanying someone on their lazy drug induced dream of exploration in the outer worlds. Something to be quietly enjoyed on a rainy Sunday afternoon. Delightful.Any negatives? Well frame-rate stuttered a bit at max setting, and there was one glitch where I fell through the landscape, but really I totally enjoyed myself here.  It's two thumbs up from me!
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: I had the pleasure of reading the novel first, and it deeply influenced my first playthrough. It made me excited to see how the game would take it if the average player already knew the outcome, and I wasn't disappointed. Regis III is beautiful, and its easy to forget the game is kind of a walking simulator. I grew up loving atompunk and retrofuturistic aesthetics so this game was an easy sell for me anyway. Just like the book, the game does a good job of making you question our place in the universe, through dialogue and through the things you see and find. The music is haunting and beautiful. I can't speak enough praises for this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: The Invincible is very cool visually, the art direction is great they executed the 60s space vibes well, and it is very atmospheric; I found myself looking around very frequently. A compelling narrative, great music and sounds all set this up for an amazing 6 hours of entertainment.  My main issue is that it is maybe the most walkiest of walking simulators.  It was so railroaded sometimes the only part of the game that had mechanical gameplay was finding the next part of the "tracks" to take.  But if you go into it with the expectations of experiencing an interactive movie, it is quite an amazing production, def one of my fav walking simulators, and it has generated a lot of interest in me to read the book.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not so much a game as it is a story based on the events of the novel that you the player are immersed in, and have to experience from the point of view of that character. You do have to drive the story forward with your actions, but there are not very many decisions that you can make as the character that have any impact on the story, except towards the middle of the game and to a large the very end of the game.The game is highly intriguing though. It is a complex mystery that you have to solve alone stranded on an alien world with dangerous otherworldly things happening around you and to you. It’s like an Agatha Christie murder mystery but instead of a murder mystery you are trying to figure out the mystery of what is happening on this planet. It requires a lot of attention focus, though if one is to truly comprehend what is happening around you.There are complex and deep moral as well as philosophical discussions that you partake in during your time on the planet as you experience the events that unfold. There are several moral choices you have to make, and experience the consequences of. That made this “game” quite engaging for me.The game does not have any wokism or modern politics in it, contrary to what I originally suspected. All of the characters in the game are complex and deep, even if they do not appear to be at first glance. They all have limitations and motives that seem real and add a layer of complexity to the game.I recommend this game looking for a deep sci-fi exploration space opera mystery experience. Although the game does demand deep thought, there is not much action involved or game play skill required.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: As pointed out, it's a walking sim.  I generally don't like them but the graphics, the potential for a good story and the price (got it for $20) made me give it a try and it is so far enjoyable and absolutely NAILS the feeling of being on a barren planet.  I've found myself just looking at the landscape and the skyline in awe of how great it looks.  Not going to be everyone's taste but I've definitely spend more money on way worse.As for a VR version ... yes PLEASE and I would gladly pay for it (DLC or discounted as an owner as I would have purchased a VR version if there had been one).  I am of the mindset that walking sims are perfect for VR, and I think this would be spectacular.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: As long as you go into this, viewing it as an interactive story rather than a game, you'll find this worth picking up, at least on sale. At times the controls can be aggravating - mainly because this is a slow-paced, short story unfolding so the controls are wrested away from you to keep you on the storyline. Much of the gameplay is on-rails, much like an amusement park ride. The biggest drawback of the story (at least on my initial play-through) is a rather long exposition dump at the very end which was slightly disappointing. Clocking in at a hair under 6 hours and contemplative story telling make for a different experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: As a big classic science fiction fan this definitely had my jaw gaping at some of the details they put into this game. This game was clearly made by people who love the genre. Hearing the words 'positronic brain' had me grinning.Anyways, for everyone interested, this is an interactive story and doesn't have much traditional gameplay. That said its expertly crafted, and you can feel it in everything you do. I felt viscerally jealous of the artistry in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Yes with caution.  This not a game!  It is a very well done, linear, walking sim with narrative.   Graphics are great....remind me of being in the middle of Canyonlands NP.    As prequel, it succeeds.  This is not a sandbox, you are limited to a defined path.  Some of the repetitive dialog is tiresome.I enjoyed the story, again not a game but a well done story.    9/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Even when noting the considerations of its limited exploration and janky movement, I still adore most everything about —the retrofuturism of atomic age meets eastern bloc aesthetic, throwback analog synth score, phenomenal voice acting, and the narrative combination of Andrei Tarkovsky's molasses-slow pacing with classic early  sci-fi intrigue, all make for a game I should, under normal circumstances, enjoy to the fullest.Unfortunately, the persistent, migraine-inducing mass stutter that occurs once you reach the Alliance base (and never once ceases from this point onward regardless of settings and far exceeding recommended specs), sucked out every ounce of joy.Optimize this, and I'll gladly give another go. Until then... consider me deeply disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: This game is short (I beat it in about 6 hours) but if you're a fan of classic science fiction the aesthetics and philosophical underpinnings of the story are fantastic. It's a bit of a walking simulator which is usually a bad word but the frustrations of occasionally feeling my time was being wasted very often were more than made up for by a set-piece that would immediately follow. There are branching paths in the story at major decision points but I didn't feel like it would be worth sitting through the parts that don't change in order to experience the parts that do.I'm very grateful for this studio allowing me this experience. I hope to see more from them in the coming years.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Spectacular. I felt like I was legitimately stranded on this planet. A meaningful 6 hours of game-play or, more aptly, an immersive narrative. Some of the visuals were absolutely stunning. A few glitches here and there, but overall the stylized world created provided an unforgettable experience. Kudos!
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: The Gem!!!"The Invincible" is a great adaptation of the book of the same name. And I think it's a really good description for this game, because it's more like interactive movie or a book. Let me start with the word for audiovisuals and design, so these are truly exceptional, this kind of retrofuturism very much reflects the atmosphere of the world. About the story, so the "real meat" of the game. I think it's well told, however the pace is a bit uneven! Story starts slowly, revealing bits of the world. Some of them come without additional exploring, other need it. And it's a really suits the theme, after all everything is about exploring The Unknown. A nice feature is the interactions with the world, yes, they are scripted, but they add a lot of depth and immersion to the game. And the way they are animated is really cool! But as I said, the uneven pace, so the last two hours are too rushed! As someone who has read the book, I feel the final part, especially theory reveal and last scene, deserves much, much more time! What I think was done brilliantly was the relationship between the Yasna and The Astrogator.Overall, I highly recommend this game. It's not for everyone, but those who enjoy story-driven games with rich conversations and exploration will have a great time!My final score: 8/10Pros:+ Atmosphere+ Some scenes are really brillant+ Audiovisuals+ Design+ Story+ Voice actingCons:- Limited player mobility- Rushed final part- Minor bugs- No lights on helmet/rover (a big con, especially in dark areas)P.S.For those who enjoyed the story, I highly encourage reading the book as well. While it may not offer many surprises, it's truly a great story. I also suggest exploring other works by Stanisław Lem; for example, "Solaris" would be an excellent starting point!
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. I love this game. The story is so unique and exciting, the graphics are top-notch and the voice acting is great! I'm literally on my second round because I want to see what happens when I make different choices than I did last time. I love the song she hums through the game, I love the exploring/discovery aspect to it...I just love it. What a brilliant game all together.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: The game is short, but I think it's a worthwhile experience. It is a beatifully crafted world that really does feel like an interactive Lem novel. The story is very linear, and only takes around 7-8 hours to complete with not much gameplay involved besides traversal, but between the beautiful graphics and the freshness of the retro-futuristic esthetic it was a great time that will remain memorable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Guys, this is not an ordinary game. In fact, it’s not a game at all; it’s an interactive adaptation of Stanislaw Lem’s book The Invincible (great guy, by the way). Basically, there is no gameplay, but sometimes it’s good to take a break from killing and destroying and just go for a walk. For me, it was a unique experience that not everyone would enjoy. I would highly recommend this game to those who like science fiction. I’d rate it 8/10. ❤️
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like about The Invincible: it's beautiful to look at, the science fiction of necroevolution is fascinating, and the voice acting is stellar. It's a compelling story and even though it's largely a walking simulator it's consistently engaging.It misses the mark in two fundamental areas that make it impossible to recommend, though: movement is excruciatingly unpleasant both walking and driving the rover, and the team clearly ran out of budget before they were able to complete the game so no matter which of the several endings you get it just... stops without any kind of actual ending. Abrupt enough that I thought it was some kind of bug, but... nope. Just stops. So, a walking simulator where walking (or driving) is painfully bad paired with a game that ran out of money 2/3rds of the way through the project so they cut the entire 3rd act = can't recommend.It's a real shame because the ingredients of an amazing experience are all here.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Engaging story of exploration on an alien planet, with superb voice acting, beautifully detailed skies and rocky landscapes and easy gameplay (keeping things simple since it's a narrative game after all). The story develops well and flows steadily, it's really well written. I didn't feel stuck at any point, just little lost sometimes and I'm sure that's how it would feel in their situation..Loved it so much!This game captivated me more than I expected, and I can not stop thinking about it , even after finishing. Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing and unique walking simulator.The Invincible reminds me a lot about Firewatch, but in Spaaace!!!It's a bit of a mix between Firewatch and a more mellow science fiction movie, like Moon. We have had sci fi walking sims before, but not so well put together like this.As a walking sim enthusiast I recommend this without any hesitation, it's great!
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: It's very much a beautifully visual novel, adaptation of classic Sci-Fi. You control a character, roam around, there's a lot of dialogs, you get to make some choices that have consequences, etc. but otherwise it is somewhat linear and slow paced.If you expect and enjoy a visual novel, you will love it. If you expect more of a game, you might be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: This game delivers what it promises in the trailers: a slow, quite calm progression, with a very limited interactions bordering on making it an interactive graphic novel; a harsh beauty of it's barren, yet awe-inspiring environments; a splendid voice acting, I daresay on par with some other great VA jobs that year 2023 has blessed us with (vide cast of BG3, of Phantom Liberty, etc.).What however makes it unique (and definitely sets much higher than what the somewhat sceptical "professional" reviewers might make you think), is the tremendous way it captures the spirit of Lem's writing. His novel are infamous for being very difficult to translate into other media, with some attempts failing quite definitely (Soderbergh's "Solaris"), some other finding their own, definitely intriguing, but different from the original, ways (Folman's "Congress"). "The Invincible" however manages to capture that original spirit, while also being able to take its slightly different angle on the Lem's story.It does it visually, with some terrific representation of the atompunk style, that moves you all the way to 60-ties and the ways, how the people back then imagined the future. It does it narratively, "taking it slow" and focusing on exploration, on discussions, instead of action. Finally, it does it thematically - dipping into the topics of how narrow our understanding of life might be; and how futile our attempts at comprehending the marvels and perils of space might be.If I would have to point out any weakness - probably I would name a lack of a definite closure. Having some form of epilogue, that would gently underline the tone of the ending you have reached. Even if the game questions the objective existence of "good" and "bad", these human concepts are perceived by us the same way as by the humans in the game, ergo some form of "happy", "sombre" or "scary" coda would do it a good service.I acknowledge, that this game is definitely not for everyone. If you enjoy hard Sci-Fi - and especially if you're familiar with Lem's works, do not hesitate. If you simply like "walking simulators" - definitely put this on your radar, but I'd understand if you'd want to wait until it goes for sale. Me, personally, I am happy to pay a full price for it and reward a very solid premiere game from Starward Industries. The quality of OG CDPR lives on :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game which successfully tells the daunting yet highly existential story about space travel, humanity, and its place in space, coupled with a very appropriate eerie atmosphere. It is a very visually pleasing game, my PC's SSD might be crying because of all the damn screenshots from the built-in Camera mode.There were some gameplay quirks here and there, admittedly, such as frame rate dropping, but they are certainly not deal breakers and for me did not ruin the experience at all.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: The Invincible by Starward Industries is a masterful sci-fi adventure that captivates with its stunning retro-futuristic visuals and thought-provoking narrative. Set on the desolate planet Regis III, the game’s environment is a meticulously crafted blend of alien landscapes and nostalgic, mid-20th-century science fiction aesthetics. The visual design, characterized by intricate details and atmospheric lighting, immerses players in a world that feels both ominous and intriguing. The story, inspired by Stanisław Lem’s novel, unfolds at a deliberate pace, inviting players to piece together a narrative rich in existential themes and ethical dilemmas. Yasna’s journey, driven by sharp writing and compelling voice acting, is a slow burn that rewards patient players with profound moments of introspection and tension.While the gameplay leans more towards exploration and narrative than action, it is this minimalist approach that allows the story and environment to take center stage. The first-person perspective and intuitive controls enhance immersion, making the world of The Invincible feel immediate and personal. The sound design, from haunting ambient noises to a subtle, evocative score, further deepens the game’s atmosphere. In essence, The Invincible is not just a game but an experience—one that resonates deeply through its powerful storytelling and evocative visuals, leaving a lasting impression on those who appreciate a thoughtful, narrative-driven journey.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: The game is slow paced and it's not compensated with interactive world to explore or rich surroundings to enjoy looking at. Controls are not great, not intuitive and that led the devs to leave too many annoying but necessary hints around the interface. Could not even finish the game since it crashes, but this may be fixed soon, I guess.I like the idea of such a game based on some sci-fi novel, and this one, while it could be so much more, is not a complete failure. It tells a story, kinda able to create a certain atmosphere, but that's pretty much it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Its like watching a science fiction movie that you can interact with. Does have some technical issues, like DLSS has ghosting artifacts that are most notable in dark lit scenes; UE stutters; pop in textures. Plays decent on Steam deck. No option to adjust settings on the deck, and it runs at 30 FPS. Also, no noticeable stutters, but there seem to be problem with texture streaming at times, where the texture does not fully load on some objects. Overall, good experience, interesting story, performance is decent. If on 15-20% sale, would recommend buying
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous game, it's a walking simulator of course but that's my jam. Whatever complaints I have are very few, the screenshots from this experience will be timelessly great backgrounds. Voice acting was great too, loved the characters. 10/10. If you like Sci-Fi or really just casual story focused games, I can't suggest this one enough.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty and with an interesting story, but with just absurdly bad controls, tooltips, pacing, and player direction, especially considering - as a walking simulator - they had just one simple job.  Somehow they even managed to make dialogue selection tedious.Most of your time will be spent wandering around at an extremely slow walk, wondering what specific thing they expect you to click on before it stops blocking you from walking toward the next area, and trying to find the exact right distance you need to be in order to actually click on the thing for it to work.Meanwhile the character you play is extremely annoying, unable to do anything without first being told to do it, and constantly whining about how hard everything is and how she's ready to just give up and die after minor inconveniencesIt's honestly kinda impressive how they managed to make a walking simulator so annoying to experience
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10 This game is a walking sim but a good one! The game is about 5 to 6 hours in length to beat depending on choices you make and how much you want to hunt for extra lore bits. If you like retro scifi settings and narrative choice driven games then you will love The Invincible. Also it has multiple endings
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: 5.5/10, for a short game its reallllly slow and dull especially the dialogue which is pretty important in a walking sim. The controls are clunky you can sprint for about 2 meters, but only if you're holding directly up on the control stick, no side ways sprinting allowed. I got stuck multiple times and had to restart from checkpoints. The story is ok - I guess the book it's based on would give a better experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the story, exploration, and voice performances in this game.  The decision making, and uncovering of the central mystery are executed well, and the game performed and looked great.  I did encounter a number of bugs during my time with the game, which were frustrating, characters getting stuck in animations, story beats not triggering, inconsistent checkpointing, all of these detracted from my experience with the game, and while I did end up shutting it down in disgust and setting it aside for a few days as a result of a bug or some lost progress, I always did come back and I'm glad I saw it through to the end.If you are a fan of this type of walking sim, I think you'll like this game. The Sci-Fi ideas are interesting and the voice performance really is exceptional.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: So in total it took me 6 hours to "beat" this game.  I put that intentionally in quotation marks because it's less of a game and more of a visual novel that you progress with pointing and clicking similar to all other games of the genre such as "Heavy Rain" or "Detroit: Becoming Human."  The difference is that there is no puzzles or specific objectives to complete as much as you merely make choices to advance the plot along in a visual novel style.That being said, I would recommend this game as it has kinda reignited a fascination with the science fiction genre for me and now I am curious to read the book this game is based on and I have a feeling it might do the same for you.  The scenery is absolutely beautiful, especially if you set it to epic quality like I did.   You'll definitely get some good shots in the photo mode for sure.  I would say that this game is fair at $30 on steam, but definitely not much more than that.  I'd say wait for it to go on sale for $20 then it'd be more understandable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very good adaptation of the novel even though it's not an exact adaptation. The game is about a new story that happens just before the novel's story. Both the theme and the descriptions of the planet is aligned with Stanislaw Lem's writings. So, the book and the game promote each other. Well done. Well done. Yet, if you are not into science fiction genre, maybe you won't enjoy conversations as much as scifi fans would do. The Invincible also keeps the main story journal in the form of comic pages. I totally loved this choice.
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

_childDocuments_.review:
The Invincible is a first-person Sci-Fi thriller set in a retro-future timeline. Waking up as a space scientist on a hostile planet, you embark on a mysterious mission to find the missing crew of your spaceship. Survival is a matter of your correct choices, taken whilst uncovering the secrets of the planet, bigger than anyone thought.

You are a scientist onboard an interstellar scientific expedition, suddenly thrown into a life-or-death rescue mission. Landing on a planet Regis III you have to find the missing crew members using some advanced space equipment, whilst relying on your brains and instincts to survive on the planet which quickly occurs to be unwelcoming. Soon you'll discover that Regis III holds terrifying secrets which are uncovered while you're piecing together the fate of your crew. And as you delve deeper into the mystery, you realise that perhaps you are not alone, and that some places like this planet are better left untouched. But it's too late to turn back.

Features:

* Retro-future atompunk setting reminiscent of the space race
* Analogue yet very advanced technology allowing for drones and autonomous robots to support or spoil your mission
* Immersive gameplay with a non-linear story shaped by your relationships, choices and persuasive skills
* Beautiful, state of the art graphics powered by Unreal Engine
* Intriguing story inspired by Stanislaw Lem's seminal sci-fi cult classic of the same name
_childDocuments_.name: The Invincible

name: Neversong
detailed_description: Upon waking from a coma, Peet's girlfriend is nowhere to be found. Thomas Brush, creator of Pinstripe, invites you to investigate the screams coming from the heart of Blackfork Asylum, the increasingly violent behavior of the grown-ups, and the strange truth about Peet's past in this hauntingly dreamlike fable. Discover what's lurking beyond the doorbell in this strange tale that started almost a decade ago. From Red Wind Field to the haunting halls of Blackfork Asylum, explore six moody, illustrative levels. Fight your way through hordes of bosses, monsters, and blood thirsty grown-ups with your trusty baseball bat. Immerse yourself in a breathtaking piano-centric soundtrack. Join your quirky child-hood pals and trusty pet bird on an adventure to discover the truth about your recent coma.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked Neversong. I think it's worth the price. But I was a little disappointed with some things.The Good:-Amazing art-Interesting characters and story-Great music and sound effects-Collectables that do things :O!-Skateboards + Umbrellas The Bad:-Combat felt very unintuitive. I can't tell if it's how far out the camera was zoomed, or how small the attack range was, or how fast the character moves, but it can be hard to be precise with your attacks without running into enemies.-All of the bosses except the final boss felt too easy (but that might be just me). And there was a lot of waiting for bosses to reveal their weak point. Also, some of the bosses would look exactly the same when they were dangerous to touch as when they were not.-But they throw health at you constantly so the game wasn't much of a challenge. There weren't very many enemy types. Most enemies would respawn so they seemed to not be worth fighting.-I didn't even realize I could kill one of the enemies because they didn't seem to show any signs of damage.-I didn't like how long the game freezes between hits. And I didn't like that sometimes particles block what you're looking at.-Platforming had a similar issue like the Combat. It was hard to be precise because the character is fast and has no deadzone or scaled speed, and the camera was so far away. But it was only really annoying in a few areas and it only wasted a little time. -You can't let go of the rope swings to drop down to a lower notch. It would be a huge quality of life improvement if I could just hit B to drop down.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say that the 1st reason i bought this game is because Thomoas Brush(the dev) inspired me into starting my own game dev career.The game is very atmospheric and fun to play! The story is pretty interesting with a "funny" dark twist to it.Sound is amazing, from the wind to the voice acting...everything is superb!Well Done!
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: There are a LOT of very good aspects to the game. The visuals are wonderful, the sound is moving and the characters are quirky, funny and voiced very well. The package seems very polished and fun to play. There is a spooky atmosphere throughout the game that isn’t particularly scary but it is slightly disturbing and the story has many hidden meanings and is presented very well.On the other hand  I defeated all the bosses on my first attempt without knowing their patterns or what was going to happen. In fact, I only died once in the game. You are given far too many lives and your lives are replenished after defeating enemies, which are also incredibly easy to defeat. The puzzles were never really taxing. Some of them needed a bit of thought and exploration but I was never really stuck on any of them and although they felt interesting, due to the atmosphere of the game, on reflection they weren’t particularly original.   Peet wakes up from a coma to find his best friend and companion, Wren, has been kidnapped. All the parents have disappeared and Peet is alone apart from a host of children left wondering where their mothers and fathers have gone.Peet sets out on a journey to find her and is aided by a bird and (sometimes) helpful advice from the children.The story is by far the most interesting aspect of the game and has quite a lot of hidden meanings and imagery. You really have to pay attention to all the cut scenes and poems as they will reveal subtle hints as to what is happening. The story is delivered in quite an interesting and unique way with poems that rhyme and cut scenes of certain incidents in your past. Neversong includes aspects of puzzling, platforming, fighting and character interaction. To gain access to the bosses, you are going to need to solve some puzzles. They are not particularly difficult. Often it is a case of reaching certain heights or having a particular skill or piece of equipment. For example, you will need a skateboard to jump ramps, magnetic gloves to swing on spider eggs and an umbrella to drift on wind currents. The platform sections mostly involve swinging on spider eggs once you have obtained the skill. There is a technique where you can swing fast and propel yourself over great distances. Mostly you will be jumping from vine to vine to reach far away platforms. You will fall quite a lot as the swinging is quite unpredictable and it is difficult to judge. Later you can cut the vines to drop bombs which can destroy obstacles in your way or reveal secret items.You also have an umbrella where you can drift on air currents to traverse chasms where vines are not available. There are enemies which you will encounter and a total of four bosses. The enemies are easy to defeat. There are around four or five different enemy types. None of them are particularly difficult and once defeated they will give you a note or a heart. Collecting one hundred notes awards you an extra life on top of your existing lives. A heart replaces any lost lives. I think I ended up with eight lives and only died once in the whole game. The amount of hearts you are awarded for defeating enemies is unbalanced and too generous. I don’t think any hearts should be awarded, just notes, and at a hundred notes all your health should be restored. Enemies also respawn if you go out of the level and back in again so it is easy to replenish your health when needed. The boss fights are also far too easy. I defeated every boss first time. That doesn’t particularly bother me as I am a fan of story games. I wouldn’t buy this game if combat is your primary goal though. The waves were predictable and easy to avoid. I could see that there were puzzle elements in the fights but they were also easy to work out and administer. There is quite a lot of backtracking to do as you will need to revisit scenes to open locked doors or return to play the songs on your piano. There are a host of collectibles called coma cards to collect. Certain cards will give you the ability to change your appearance. Some of them are very difficult to find and as far as I am aware nobody has collected all of them. There are loads of interesting characters to interact with. They are all fully voiced and sound professional but comical. They are all children and behave immaturely and uncooperatively resulting in a few laughs. You are sometimes given a choice of answer but choices do not matter and will always result in the same outcome. Visuals are wonderful and imaginative and are a strong plus point to the game. The game oozes atmosphere and each character have a distinct and highly original personality. The bosses and the characters are drawn to make them look weird and bizarre and there are some disturbing psyches. Sound is impressive and is an important aspect of the game due to the fact that Wren liked to play the piano. Music is an important part of her life and that comes across in the game. There is a melodic soundtrack throughout with good effects. The voice acting is done well and full of childish emotion and hyperbole. Curator Info: This game was received for free through curator connect.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10I've been following Thomas Brush/Atmos Games for quite a while; this is my fourth game of his that I've played (including Zero Deaths).This game felt simultaneously rushed and delayed at the same time. Some things had a whole bunch of polish, like the voice acting and the songs, but some of them felt extremely lackluster.Some of the puzzles were decent (the only one that I couldn't complete on dead-brain auto-pilot, but most were entertaining enough), but the overall level design was a little meh, with lots of backtracking (and not the fun kind, like the Ori games), and the whole game felt like a bunch of dead ends, honestly. The load times were quite long, and on my beast of a computer, that's actually an issue. Most AAA titles load faster than these levels. The special items you get felt unsatisfying, like one-trick ponies (the skateboard is mostly useless except for a couple spots). The bat-jumping feels almost exactly the same as regular jumping (I didn't notice a difference). There are errors in the dialogue like certain characters telling you things even when you say "no thanks, I'd rather not hear that again" (or equivalent) in response.The biggest problem though isn't in the gameplay mechanics and level design, it's in the story. It just makes no damn sense. It's like he had 3 different ideas for a story and tried to put them all together, but there's no depth to any of it. The juvenile "booty bum" "punky" "skunky" etc. stuff was there to be juvenile, the creepy "adults are gone and/or knife-wielding maniacs and/or monsters" part was just there to be creepy, and the crux of the story (Peet and Wren) felt like a skin-deep story just glazed over the top in order to make the whole game not feel pointless.Pinstripe got a 9/10 from me, I loved that game, and played it multiple times, and spent hours looking up the lore online to make sure I could squeeze every last tidbit out of it.Neversong, however, gets a 5/10 ... it's just not worth a replay, and even though there's obviously "New Game +" stuff that you get after the end credits, I unlocked both obvious additions, and they're rather lame. Like, almost insultingly lame.Neversong feels like a passion project from 10 years ago that hasn't aged well, and it's clear that after Pinstripe was a success, this old turd was brought out and polished. Don't get me wrong, the original Coma was charming, but Neversong feels like an overproduced song or movie that doesn't have a soul at the middle as Pinstripe did. This game recycles some of Coma, but doesn't have the charm of the original, and feels like a crappy sequel, but it's still not as bad as Wreck it Ralph 2: Ralph Breaks the Internet, so at least that's something.*Just some random questions I have (if you're worried about spoilers, skip this list):*1. Why is there a "2020" joke taking place in 1952? And was that a Donald Trump reference? Honestly, wtf.2. How does Simeon teleport to places faster than you? He's always random places, and it doesn't make sense.3. What's the point of collecting any of the cards other than trying to 100% the game? They're functionally useless.4. Why is there such a disconnect between creepy/macabre and juvenile and the heartstring-pulling stuff?5. What is the significance of Bird? Why does she say she lied to you? That feels like a dropped plot point.6. Why do some of the grown-ups disappear, some turn into knife-wielding maniacs, and some into monsters?7. What's the significance of Peet's full relationship with Dr. Smile? That is completely unexplained and confusing.8. I know it's supposed to be a coma we're in, but that honestly can't explain most of the choices made in development.9. Was most of this game's creation done before Pinstripe? That game definitely feels like more complete of an experience.10. Is there any worth in going back and playing through the game a second time with the other key? I'm guessing not.When I was about 20 minutes into the game, I already had a frown on my face. When I was 2 hours into the game, I was slightly intrigued and so decided to finish it. It had to be a decent amount longer than Pinstripe, and I was willing to sink the time in, because Pinstripe was excellent and moving, if a little quaint compared to say, Limbo or the Ori games. When I was almost done, I was like "the story hasn't even CLOSE to begun to make sense yet, they better start dropping knowledge bombs on us quick" and at the very end there was a small revelation that only raised more questions. When I saw "The End" on the screen, I was like "... what? that feels like half a game's worth of story, but with gameplay that doesn't make me want to play again at ALL, even if there IS the promise of "more content" (which turns out to just be a tongue-in-cheek "making of" video, as well as a "supporters names put in the game" graveyard, similar to Pinstripe) ... super not worth it.The 5.5/10 this game gets is a testament to the wonderful voice acting, catchy music, and I guess for the potential of this game to be improved in the future. If I was grading solely based on gameplay, replayability, and the story, this game would get a 3/10 at best. Which is a severe disappointment after Pinstripe.If you want to turn your brain off and run through some mediocre platforming for a few hours, buy this game.If you care about a coherent story, like interesting characters, and want to support Thomas Brush, buy Pinstripe instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Coma in 2014. To this day it remained my favorite flash game. I don't really know why, there's a load of insanely good flash games out there, but Coma just stuck with me. Something about it just kept on generating an overwhelming sense of both longing and serenity whenever I'd come back to play it. Just a calming game made to feel feelings. With a terrifying worm thing that makes a freaky mouth sound. So no matter how many times video games have taught me to keep my expectations low, damn right I was hyped about Neversong. And taking a lil bit of nostalgia into account as well, here goes a bunch of rosy retrospection. I'm writing this mainly for myself, to sort out some thoughts and to try and answer a single question since plenty of others have already reviewed it as an independent game - do I think Neversong stayed true to the same impeccable spirit of its ancestor? Well. Yes and no.The vibe sure has changed. There was not a single moment when I felt all alone in quiet, dreary fields. No eerie shades as characters to vaguely guide me around, keeping things mysterious. Compared to Coma, Neversong feels quite crowded. There are more npcs with so much stuff to say (featuring some fellow kids moments ngl), new game mechanics, now with enemies and collectibles and whatnot. And that's valid, it's no longer a mere flash game and it never claimed to be a full remake, gotta fill it up somehow, gotta cater to the gamers. The problem is, none of it is particularly memorable. And for me at least, it suppressed that sense of longing and drove away the serenity. Gotta smash all the props as I go to see if there's a funky card inside. Gotta nyooom on my brand new spankin skateboard. It's still a fun game to play for sure, but compared to the original, rather less atmospheric at its core. And it certainly doesn't help that it's so incredibly similar to Pinstripe in that matter. Same exact jist with a different ambiguous story. Speaking of the story, it certainly expanded upon Coma. But maybe not for the best. For Coma it worked the way it was because it mostly remained untold yet still felt liberating in the end. Here it offered more detail but ended up being pretty mediocre. I feel like I didn't gain an interesting closure, only lost the ability to imagine it myself. So, with no strings attached, would I hold this game in high esteem for years to come? Not really. It would get me 3h of moderate entertainment. Keep in mind that still doesn't make it a bad game. Moderate entertainment is still entertainment. That's what we're here for.On the other hand. The soundtrack. HOH boy. Always been a sucker for those. Wanna see me burst into tears the second the Red Wind theme starts playing in Neversong? Wanna see me do it again during the credits? Took literally a second. There's really nothing more refreshing than a ruthless slap of nostalgia right to the face. Glad to hear the original music completely unchanged. It's only what it deserves. The rest of the soundtrack worked really well too, in fact so well I ended up buying it. Furthermore, having played Coma, there were moments in Neversong I absolutely adored to bits. Seeing what used to be important parts of the flash game now cleverly incorporated as details in this one. Loved going through certain areas only to stop for a sec and go 'oh wait I've seen this before'. So rather than trying to see a remake, it all fits into place much better if one looks at it and regards it as a nice homage. And holy hell it's such a pretty game to look at? That foliage??? The backgrounds??? CRISP.TL;DR I'm far from being swept off my feet but I'm not disappointed either. And it's only natural. I guess what I expected was to be teleported back to 2014 and live my best life but no amount of immersion in a game can grant me that. Things have changed, I no longer hang out on Newgrounds every day, I'm no longer in high school and life feels complicated now. More than anything else, Coma is a relic of those good ole days for me. And Neversong made me realize that. Even if that were the only thing it had to offer, it would still be a good game.Oh and before I conclude, one thing that bothered me more than anything. If you play d-e-b-a-b on the piano it doesn't do anything? At all??? HUGE easter egg opportunity missed. Smh my head.Lårge thanks to my friend ewyy for the gift.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally called Once Upon a Coma, Neversong follows a young boy named Peet. Told in rhyme, we’re told that Peet’s world was devoid of life and color until he meet a girlnamed Wren. While she may have been the prettiest in town, they went on adventures and she even taught Peet how to play a piano and how to read sheet music. However, on one of their adventures they made a wrong move. Upon entering an abandoned asylum, Wren was kidnapped by a big shadowy man with a creepy smile (who is amply named Doctor Smile). The shock of this all, in combination of feeling too weak, was too much for Peet and resulted in him falling into a coma. We come in right as Peet wakes up right on top of the piano both him and Wren played together. Venturing out of the house, you realize that all the adults in your village (Red Wind Village) have gone missing. Though, you can still talk to the other kids that live in the village. Each one of them are pretty weird, but entertaining to talk to, like Jon who’s obsessed with jumping a billion times, a kid who loves parkour, or Simeon who is terrible to Peet but inflates. Not only that, but these kids do give valuable information concerning what’s going on and occasionally have puzzles that involve them. Anyway, not long after waking up, you’ll gain access to a bad and after venturing outside Red Wind Village you’ll be joined by Bird.Thus, you set out to find and rescue Wren. Of course, Dr. Smile is going to be right there, seemingly one step ahead just to tease you and creep you out in Neversong’s storybook poem cutscenes. Every location you’ll be visiting is just down the road from Red Wind Village, with the only thing that’s stopping you from going there early is not having the required item. Each area are designed well in my opinion, as it gently nudges you to where you need to go with the main block being if you need an item or solve a puzzle before you can continue. The puzzle here are fairly easy. Most of the time it just requires you to use one of your items and show that you know how to use them or just paying attention to what a character said. I suspect the only difficulty people will run into are the two puzzles where you’re pressed on time for rolling bombs into the right place and one of the end game puzzles which is really just trial and error. Platforming wise, it’s mostly easy as well, though there was one platforming section where I just couldn’t jump on the fourth platform for the life of me.While you’re exploring each location, you can also find coma cards. These cards give you a short description of who’s on it and, depending on the card, will let you equip it for an accessory. Like you can give Bird a rainbow trail or have Peet wear a headband.There are also enemies hanging around ready to take your health away. The only way to defend yourself is to either run away (though, that won’t be an option in cases where you’re blocked in until every enemy is killed) or use your trusty bat. If Peet touches anything that can hurt him, including things like spikes, he’ll lose a point of health. Each time you defeat an enemy, which can take one hit to seven depending on the enemy type, it’ll drop some sparkles. Every 100 sparkles, which are also scattered around each location as well, will give you another heart so you can last longer. In addition, enemies will drop hearts, assuming you don’t have full health, so you can gain your health back. Though if you do die, it isn’t all that punishing. While it seems like it sends you back to your last save, it really doesn’t. You keep your sparkle count and you spawn in with full health, with the only thing that resets are puzzles, enemies, and boss fights.Talking about bosses, their difficulty are going to depend from player to player as it could be easy for some while also being just right for others. Unlike normal enemies, bosses have weak points that needs to be vulnerable so you can damage them and they each have attack patterns. Once you hit them enough, they’ll belt out a song note, give you a heart, and move onto their next phase which will change their appearance and change up their attacks (whether that be adding in an attack or seeming more desperate in their attempts of staying alive). Once you defeat them, you’ll gain their song, which you can play to get an item you need to progress. You’ll get grip gloves so you can swing on magnetic eggs, a skateboard, and an umbrella.How easy these fights will be depends on if you know their attack pattern, react well to their new attacks, or just have enough health so you can take a hit while you learn. The third boss for me was the main example. I had difficulty with dodging one of her attacks (as well as immediately getting hit with her new phase attack), but on my second try I managed to defeat her so quickly she wasn’t able to do that attack since I knew when to attack. Personally, it was just right for me and while people have complained that you get way too much health, I was surely thankful. I have to say that the soundtrack and voice acting was great. The music really sets the atmosphere, especially during boss fights where they ramp it up. The voice acting in it’s own right enhances the characters they belong to. While there was one kid where their voice seemed to be lower than the others, these characters wouldn’t have been so entertaining or appealing without the voice acting giving them more personality. And that’s not even mentioning Dr. Smiles’ voice acting which was downright creepy. I dreaded hearing his voice again whenever I spotted him up ahead because it creeped me out so much I wanted to slowly back away and get out of there.Even though Neversong is going to be an easy game for some people, it’s still a nice adventure platformer that nails it’s creepy atmosphere every step of the way. Although while I didn’t mind how easy the game was (or will be for others), I did have some annoyances with swinging on the magnetic eggs in certain areas (I may have spent too long trying to swing over a big gap and falling down a notch without just falling off the rope altogether is a pain), the rhyming cutscenes were okay, and the ending was a bit confusing. Nonetheless, I had fun playing Neversong and there are genuine moments where it’s going to surprise you. I’d say pick this up if you want to experience a story about loss wrapped in a creepy atmosphere and you don’t mind that it’s probably going to be easy for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I have had this game on my radar for quite some time now and was thrilled to get a chance to play it.  (formerly ) was brought to us by  and , with Thomas Brush at the helm of the project. What caught my eye was its fascinating art style and the mature-themed story it promised to tell, all neatly tucked in a 2D adventure platformer. centres around the loss of someone near and dear to us. It's something we'll all have to deal with at some point in our lives, those time freezing words: "We have bad news...".  Preparing oneself for the inevitable does seem like a sound way of lessening the impact of heartbreak and pain, but what happens when we dont have that time to prepare? When your entire world goes from light to darkness in a blink of an eye?I won't go into further detail, as Ill enter spoiler territory most likely. But I do want to mention the characters you meet. They all have  to say. At first, it may seem like pointless dialogue, but they give you small clues that are important for understanding the overarching story and events of the game. So pay attention.The very first thing people notice about  is its unique art style. The 2D hand-drawn is the meta in the indie scene. But for a good reason. It brought us some majestic games over the years, produced by incredibly talented people. Due to there only being like three enemy types, they quickly lose that "wow" factor. The bosses fared better,  mixing human elements with a dose of monstrous abnormality, making them unique and memorable. Also, Handsome Squidward makes an appearance...The ambient music plays an important part in setting the overall tone of the game. And  does such a great job here, creating this bleak and  world feel. The voice acting is decent, with the narrator stealing the show with a spectacular performance. The others you meet are unique, having some distinct mannerisms to set them apart and stick to your memory. And of course, each boss has a great score accompanying it, giving these fights a pump, with how  it is.But how is the gameplay? Well, while narratively strong,  did feel like a mixed bag in the gameplay department. The combat was rather simplistic and restrictive. It's a basic button mashing approach, with one weapon and no variety in attacks or any upgrades that could possibly affect how you use it. The enemies also offer no real challenge, with easily telegraphed attacks. They follow the standard mantra of enemy design -  And that's it! With only three enemy types, the encounters get repetitive fast. And this is the biggest reason I loath the combat. Making me kill the same enemies over and over in every location wasn't fun nor enjoyable. It was tedious and monotonous. Cut out at least half of the encounters, and the game would have been better off. Honestly, it felt like a cheap way to prolonge the game. It's not important how long your game is, but how enjoyable the time playing it was. And no, you can't just skip them. You are locked into an area and have to kill every enemy to progress. The only enemies I liked, the first few times, were the flying butt looking bugs with, you guessed it - . But even they become stale after a while.Now the bosses are a different story. They each required different approaches and had mechanics that relied on other abilities, not just pointless button mashing. Utilizing them during boss battles felt organic, and this was the only time I enjoyed the game's combat. It showed creativity, and I wished we got more of that and less of dull button mashing.But this isn't a boss rush game (sadly), and there are also puzzles and a bit of platforming involved. It almost has that Metroidvania feel to it, with you needing new abilities to move forward. The puzzles are simple but adequate and effective in breaking up the monotonous combat with mobs. These segments were decent enough and never felt out of place or tedious, thanks, in large part, to the tight controls. Do be warned - there is also a substantial amount of backtracking, be it for story reasons, to figure out certain puzzles, or just finding all the collectables.So, if you are in the market for a casual adventure game that places all of its bets on its captivating story, then  may scratch your itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Heart & Soul on the piano at the start and got an achievement called "Cheater."That aside, this game is well-made and the environment is well-built. Still, I just felt upset throughout my playthrough. At no point did I feel good (nor did I feel scared or sad in an enjoyable way) and the game just doesn't achieve the same beautiful strangeness that other games with similar ambiance do (see games like Fran Bow) and doesn't commit to any aspect of the game, instead opting to do poorly in combat and puzzles both.The boss fights are incredibly easy - basically everyone has the achievements for beating the bosses quickly, and because you get constant healing, it's never challenging. The puzzles themselves often feel like busywork, where the solution is clear from the start and the game feels like a walking simulator.I did care about the characters, but not in any remarkable way. It felt similar to Edgar Allan Poe - but again, it fails to commit to the act.Graphics are neat, but never good.There were no noticable bugs.The game is short, but it feels pretty long. It drags on, especially towards the end.All in all, the game is fine, but not worth full price. There are better games to buy. I wouldn't recommend it to a friend, but I wouldn't go out of my way to tell people not to play it (although one could argue that's what I'm doing right now).6.4/10

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I wanted to, I can't really recommend this game. It definitely has some good parts; the art style and sound design are both really well done and I can appreciate some of the zanier bits of humour, but the rest of it just falls a bit flat. Combat is extremely one note, most enemies are so weak that you can afford to just run up to them and smack them, getting reliably healed up once they die without any real effort or strategy, even into the late game. The 'power ups' are extremely one dimensional as well, even when they really didn't need to be. The skateboard that you unlock feels like it should be a really cool way of getting around the map faster, but the limitations on it and the fact that you can't actually move yourself forwards with it (seriously, just a button to tap to push your foot against the ground would have made it a thousand times better) makes it feel useless outside of the few designated puzzle areas, much like the umbrella. The 'song' elements that I thought would be more integrated given the title and advertising were more like keys than anything actually impacting gameplay and there is just so much slow and tedious backtracking even in a minimum percentage playthrough. Almost fully completing the game once (I missed one collectable somewhere) only took me ~ 3 hours, of which at least one was just having to wander back and forth across completely empty and danger free environments.The final boss fight especially is extremely bad and left me with a very sour taste in my mouth, essentially boiling down to standing in the middle of the room until you had to dodge one attack (if you feel like it; by that point I had enough health I probably could have tanked) while waiting for the boss to do the same thing over and over again. I felt comfortable putting my controller down to check my phone, which is rarely a good sign for a game ending boss, and while the other bosses weren't as bad they also weren't great, mechanically (though I will say that their designs and the way they degrade over the course of the fight is quite appealing).Most controversially, I really struggled to even get into the story on this one. The ambience is there, sure, but the  and the weird non-reactions from all of the NPCs really made it hard for me to get into the sort of tragic mindset that the game seemed to want to put me in, no matter how hard I tried. The end result was that the final 'twist' just kinda made me shrug.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: It was a long wait, and it definitely didn't disappoint. Challenge level is in that sweet, salty butter zone--harder than insultingly easy, but nothing was sadistic or punishing and very little if anything was counter-intuitive. And the story? It strikes yet another butter zone between creepy, and fun, and just plain weird. Not to mention I teared up at the end, and that takes some doing these days. The Pacha meme is outdated these days, but I think it would be a wholly appropriate description for Neversong--the gameplay hits your brain, and the plot hits your heart just right, and this game sings. And in many cases literally--some of what was done with Neversong's soundtrack could give Toby Fox a run for his money. I'd pay for the album, are you reading this Thomas Brush?If I had to point out an imperfection though, I'd have to go with the final boss fight. It seemed like something of a step down from the final boss of Pinstripe, geared more toward sowing confusion than trying to be challenging. And there was one pattern/attack/whatever that I really wasn't sure what the idea of was supposed to be. That's all I'm going to say on the matter, must avoid spoilers you know! But I'd hope that most who've finished it know what bit I'm talking about. So yeah. Absolutely a solid 9/10 from me, and I hope you keep making games Mr. Brush!

_childDocuments_.review: , the follow-up game from Atmos Games, creators of , is based on an original flash game that went by the name of .  deals with themes of loss, loneliness, and madness, as it places the player in the role of a young boy who wakes up from a coma in a strange world after his girlfriend has been kidnapped. Armed with a meagre load of childhood tools, he must battle strange monsters while trying to find and save his friend. is a fusion of the platforming and adventure genre but as a game never really ends up succeeding at either. Platforming and combat are weak, so those looking for a tight and refined experience are best left looking elsewhere, and the puzzle solving rudimentary, which I suppose makes the game more approachable for a wider variety of players. The game's narrative never really dives deeper into the meat and bones of the story which also only ends up making it a frustratingly surface-level experience.Where  earns points is with the game's atmosphere but even this aspect of the game feels somewhat underdeveloped, given the nature of the story.  is a short experience, easy enough for most players to complete in 3 or so hours, but I would be hard pressed to recommend it over other far more promising indie titles in the genre. I am giving the game a recommendation but take this more as sideways "meh" than a full on recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Neversong is like if you took the gameplay of the opening thirty minutes or so of gameplay and level design of Hollow Knight, setting and characters of Into The Woods, and didn't understand how to do any of these aspects well. The combined product of these pieces is also worse than its parts.I do not like to compare this game to others, because I can't say for certain that the developers took inspiration from them. The comparison I made is just to frame for anyone potentially looking to buy this game what they might be getting in to.First, I''ll address my problems with the gameplay. Some people may consider this a metroidvania. I do not, because even though you do get upgrades (only three, not counting the basic weapon) these are pretty exclusively used to progress in a linear fashion. There are little, if any, puzzles to go back to in previous areas. You are expected to use your upgrades after you get them, and any backtracking that you do is shallow and unrewarding, with the only rewards you get being cosmetic if anything.That is not to mention that traversing the world, combat, and any of the upgrades that you get are anything but tedious and annoying. As an example: Traversal of the environment is infuriatingly slow. Even when you get something that should allow you to move faster or easier, the world isn't actually designed to let you use them in any meaningful way. These upgrades don't actually work outside of maybe ten puzzle-specific areas of the game combined. Finding this out was infuriating, as the game even blocks you from using it, or makes it actually slower than walking to do so. Combined with the baffling length of the loading times, I honestly dreaded having to backtrack anywhere.The puzzles in the game are terrible. Their complexity maxes out at "one of the puzzles from an annoying Legend of Zelda dungeon." Just imagine one of them with bad controls and you probably are imagining something better than what is actually in this game.Moving on to the story and characters, the only positive thing I can say is that "yeah, I guess I didn't see the ending coming." That being said, it's not because of some clever twist or unconventional-yet-satisfying direction it decides to go in. No, it's really just out of nowhere, and doesn't even really try to tie together most of the games motley collection of motifs in any meaningful way. The characters are named and voiced. I won't remember any of them, but they made the effort to get them voice acted at least.Particularly, the main characters are poorly made and written. Their initial relationship is established like if Pixar's "Up" never had the opening ten minutes. We are told they are kids in love and they both enjoy the piano. The game never builds on that, and doesn't really say much about the two, let alone show that they had any affection or bond whatsoever. The MacGuffin girl you are chasing is the only one with any real character implied by anything other than the game saying "This person is like this." or a character saying "I feel this way. I don't like you or this other person. Just wanted to tell you that." The game makes a big deal about them playing the piano even, giving you an Ocarina of Time-like ability to play music on one. This is never used or integrated into the game, characters, or world beyond a single room in the game exactly five times.The game is trying to be deep, but just has a bunch of shallow elements stitched together with no real idea for how to fit them together. Yes, I finished it. I didn't miss some bigger idea or the point of the story. There just wasn't anything meaningful to miss. No, I don't really know why other than I could tell it would be really short and I didn't have much else to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Not what i was expecting definitely.Im not a big fan of Thomas Brush works, but this one looked really interesting. In the end, it felt like a smaller and less polished game than his previous work, Pinstripe, which i enjoyed way more.The story is a cliche already exploited in tons of indie games, the graphics felt like a step back compared to Pinstripe, the combat feels wonky, and with an excessive and annoying amount of screen-shaking, the hitboxes are really imprecise, and on top of that, the game is extremely short for the price and full of bugs.No replayability at all, except for those who seek some achievements like speedrun, hitless, etc... which btw, despite been an absurdly easy game in every aspect (not only combat, but puzzles too) i dont recommend to try because of the gamebreaking bugs and the inconsistency of the hitboxes.To say something positive, the music is beautiful, the graphics are, as i said, inferior to Pinstripe, but still good looking, and can fill that gap for those anxious to play some atmospheric puzzle-platformer kinda like Playdead games, which are very rare nowadays. You can also feel the amount of effort and charm put by the creator on this title, despite the final result not be as good as expected.Wait for a sale if you really wanna try it.

_childDocuments_.review: I discovered this game through YouTube.  One the creators, Thomas Brush, is very active there with his channel on game development, and he's done a lot of videos on the development cycle and has been a really great resource for other indie games developers.So how is Neversong? It's very nice, quite a lovely little game. First off, the good.  It's short, just about 4 hours in length. The art is beautiful and always amazing to look at. It's some stellar artwork and really drives the tone and feel of the game.  The tone & style is reminiscent of The Nightmare Before Christmas meets Grimm's Brothers.  It's the kind of fairy tale that hasn't been sanitized by Disney. It starts off pretty cheerful and whimsical, but slowly becomes much darker as the story progresses.  The music, art, and mood all work together perfectly to tell the story. Another standout is the children, they are wonderfully voice acted and written. Next up, the gameplay itself holds up fairly well. Combat is very simple, but feels good, and the game has a focus on simple environmental puzzles.  There's a nice progression of upgrades that keep the game flowing along with cool collectables to find.  Character movement is just a bit fidgety and you'll find Peet sometimes moving around a bit to much when moving or jumping. The game is fairly easy, as almost every enemy you defeat gives you back health, but that's fine, the game is meant for you to experience it's story, not test you to your limits, so the difficulty is just about right.On the not so good side, there is one game play mechanic I absolutely hated that involved swinging on rope/vines, and unfortunately there was a lot of it. I also experienced one game ending crash that caused me to lose about 30 minutes of progress. Last, the story.  This is a story driven game and the story is memorable, well told and well written, and I enjoyed it very much. There's a late game surprise I didn't guess. However, because this is a story driven game, I have to add that I feel like there's a little more they could have done in the final act. After the surprise, I was expecting them to push things a bit further and explore the themes of the game a little further. If you are expecting a "To The Moon" experience in terms of characters and story here, it doesn't quite reach it.Those minor points aside, Neversong is a fun and memorable game, and a brilliant piece of art. The developers have a lot to be proud, they've crafted a game that's worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following Atmos Games aka Thomas Brush on YouTube for awhile, and have been looking forward to Neversong for awhile.The game's atmosphere is stunning; the sound design and art are superb. This game is more of an experience rather than a challenge, and the mechanics, puzzling and platforming are rather simple. That being said the writing is top notch and the story invokes complex emotions not usually found in video games. I can definitely forgive how easy it is based on how compelling the story is.Definitely worth a play through to burn through an afternoon. Playing through the game once allows you to unlock previously hidden areas if you want to finish a collectibles run and experience the story a second time to pick up on the subtleties in the writing.Story - 9/10Visuals - 9/10Mechanics - 6/10Sound - 10/10Replay Value - 4/10Final Rating - 7.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Neversong is a beautifully designed piece of art with an incredible soundtrack and a meaningful story that includes humor, tragedy, friendship, and adventure. If you like short story games and aren't big into actual game play this is for you. If you aren't huge into story games without complex game play mechanics and bigger boss fights and character progression, you can plan to not be amused.Pros:- The art is incredible. It is an amazing game to look at visually.- The music fits so well and is original. I thoroughly enjoyed simply "listening" while playing.- The sound effects and feedback in the game are wonderful. When you hit an enemy you know it and it feels nice.- The story in this game is engaging for the most part and you're always made curious about each characters background and wondering what the next encounter will be like.- The game is only about 3-4 hours to complete in full. Which for this type of game, is great. Since there is no character or level progression or even replay-ability, short is what you would want and expect from this.Cons:- Though the combat was very smooth, I was always confused as to why I was getting hit by enemies that I felt I wasn't quite close enough to be damaged by.- The boss fights are fairly easy. The mechanics are very interesting and the fights are decently engaging, but there's just not enough "risk" associated with the fights. They are very casual fights.- There is no way to take the game out of essentially its "full screen windowed mode", so I would find myself dragging the mouse over to my second monitor during a fight and the game would minimize itself.- I was not a fan of the camera movement up and down when W/S were pressed. It just felt strange. It's hard to explain.
