_childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong, I have nothing but respect for the game creator, I played Coma (The game this is a reboot of) on Newgrounds when I was younger and loved it.  But for the price tag you're going to get a  more out of many other games. Games like OneShot, Undertale, Hollow Knight, Little Inferno. (It has a similarly chaotic energy) and more. In fact I even recommend you check out Coma on newgrounds. It's free and still pretty good if you want similar weird energy.Despite this game being gorgeous with stunning effects to elevate the experience and stellar music with FULL voice acting it just really wasn't fun to play.The game has full voice acting and even a narrator throughout the game during cutscenes. But this doesn't elevate the gravity of the situation and the game spends a lot of time trying to get you invested into a character that you're supposed to want to protect without ever really having any chances to know her. So while I wanted to save her, I felt like the game was trying to force that reaction rather then letting my experiences in the game let me want to help.None of the side characters you meet are pleasant to be around, they're all differing degrees of unkind. Often rude, self centered and self absorbed.  The game constantly puts the protagonist down, claiming that something you did. (Falling into a Coma) was the reason for your friend being kidnapped.On top of that, while the old game was weird and uncomfortable at times this takes it to a whole new level.Lets not even get started on . A plus sized boy who gets inflated and needs your help by poking him with a needle. He puts you down throughout your experience with him. Only for quite a few awful things to occur with him and his final appearance being one focusing on his weight, how unhappy he was and the like. While having also gotten plastic surgery to give himself disturbing tumor like muscles on his chest and biceps. Clearly meant to poke fun at him, first for being plus sized and then for what would essentially be a disorder effecting his appearance. On every level, that was uncomfortable and unpleasant. The worst thing was for basically anyone who is plus sized, that just felt like a really weird and unexpected element to the game that nobody asked for. It was also like the worst thing to decide to keep out of everything from the first game.He was one of the worst characters to deal with but by no means the only unpleasant character. it seemed as if each character was meant to be a stand in of some kind for either physical disabilities or mental ones. (Like OCD). I just don't think Neversong's attempt at covering these topics had any nuance or depth and I felt as if Neversong spent more time trying to get us to laugh at these character or dislike them for their unpleasant personalities. Okay, we've gotten past characters for the most part, but lets not forget actual dialogue. The narrator only speaks in rhythm and at one points use the term "Tool" (Like calling someone a tool) To try and imply gravity to what was meant to be a disturbing scene.  There were quite a few cringe pieces of dialogue that were just that bad. For instance one of the weird little creatures you fight is called "Piss Boi" Combat is bizarre, you have a weapon which should give you enough reach to hit an enemy. Knock them back some and allow you to stay mostly on the attack. But for some reason it causes you to move forward a little even if you're standing still. So what tends to happen is you end up being to close to the enemy and get hit by their hitboxes before landing your attack. So often you will always get hit while trying to attack them. While you can put more focus into fighting to be more careful this sort of combat should become second nature to the player. In a game like Hollow Knight for instance you and the enemy both get a slight bit of knock back this stops the potential of you getting hit in a way that feels wrong.Neversong FEELS like you should be able to run around and attack things while jumping and shifting about but actually doing that isn't really viable. Which is why I think every enemy gives you a heart back.This sort of small weird control issues plagues through Neversong. While it doesn't ruin the game per'se it also stops you from ever being fully engaged. It's clearly meant to have that satisfying tactile feeling when you jump, use an ability and attack things. But it's just off. If it had a bit more polish I think the experience would of been a lot better.Going from combat, it's platforming feels similarly odd, Most of the game depends on you using "Eggs Vines" As a way to go from one spot to another. A lot like a grappling hook, including having to use the momentum of your swinging as a way to get further. The problem is, that this isn't precise enough to feel good either. Often you can over swing and fly right past what you were aiming for or in some cases ruin your projection enough to end up in a spot that forces you to redo way more then you want to. A lot of the game, both in it's small attempts at puzzles and in time sensitive spots requires more trial and error. You end up knowing exactly what to do, and even how to do it. But will have issues nailing it the way it's meant to be.A good example of this is the awful bomb mechanic. Eventually you get a way to cut bombs down from those hanging vines, it then has a timer that shifts to red and changes sound the closer it is to blowing up. However the phrase where it shifts to red is weirdly long. Which means when the game wants you to toss a bomb at something in a split second it's hard doing that at the exact time the bomb will go off.Neversong fails to be scary, because it is to predictable. Neversong fails to do platforming and combat right because it didn't polish these elements enough for them to feel good. Neversong fails to make engaging characters who you care about because it doesn't make the likeable or engaging as people. And it fails to capture the same intense concern for Peet as the first game because it tries to get you invested in a relationship that you never see develop and never have any reason to care about.It's dialogue isn't engaging enough and the characters don't matter enough to warrant full voice acting either. What it does succeed in is art direction, music, effects animation and atmosphere. That isn't to say Neversong is bad, it has a lot of good things. But I can't recommend it as a banger like I can many other indie games because it's difficulty in succeeding at those elements makes it hard to be engaged, and to have fun with it.With that said, if it's on sale? Might be worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: It is honestly disappointing. For Thomas Brush fans who have played both Pinstripe and Coma, this game is like the theme and gameplay mechanics of Pinstripe stuffed into the storyline of Coma, only it has take away both the picturesque exploration atmosphere of Coma, and the platforming/puzzle experience of Pinstripe. Boss fights in Neversong are simply unmemorable.On the subject of substance abuse, which is the signature of Pinstripe, the heartwarming/children-oriented background of the original Coma game has effectively undermined what was beautifully addressed in Pinstripe. What has really happened to the 2 main protagonists is also pretty confusing.I understand Thomas Brush's frustration in our expectation to relive an ancient game that he has long grown past, but I feel like his talents would be better spent if he's left to his creative freedom without the constraints of his old games. I will look forward to his next game in line.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game with a deep message, a game that manages to create a rarely seen atmosphere by putting the spotlight on difficult topics such as grief and the nightmares that plague children. Artistically it is a beautiful but short escape into horror. A beautifully crafted little world that draws you in with fantastic visuals. It's dark but full of witty dialogue, strange creatures and great piano music.A boy named Peet is looking for his kidnapped girlfriend Wren. During the game you get various things that help you in certain situations. Each area has a fun boss fight that requires you to use skills learned through the game to destroy them. After each fight you get notes that you play on the piano and unlock a new area and a new thing. The attack animation is similar maybe even the same as in Hollow Knight (I didn't play, I watched my friends:D)The very beginning of the game is sick and you have a small puzzle, after that it's quite cheerful and as the story progresses it gets darker. The puzzles are relatively simple, but they are carefully laid out so that the game doesn't tell you exactly where to go, you have to figure it out for yourself and notice. It's easy because almost every enemy you defeat gives you back a ❤️ and that's fine, the game is meant for you to experience its story and not to test your limits.An interesting part in the game is how children and adults are depicted. Children are shown as innocent beings, pure souls who only want to play, while adults (parents) are shown as monsters who destroy their children, all this represents a harsh truth. Of course the game has another hidden message that you have to discover. This game also has its flaws:-Very short game, only 3-4 hours.- Although it is visually charming and despite the unique atmosphere, the game world seems somewhat empty.I played it on the controller because it's much easier and doesn't have a lot of controls, you have to jump, run, skate and hit.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing this game in the late 2000's. I was around 10-12.A bit after flash died, I suddenly remembered this game and went hunting to see whatever happened to it, if the creator made anything else. I discovered Neversong and got immediately excited. I thought it was a fantastic remake that told a wonderful story, Of course I have a preference for the "creepy" atmosphere the original carried. I love to see the difference, the growth from just a little 15 minute flash game to this full ~4 hour game. 13-15 years later still a classic for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Short review:It's a good, atmospheric, 2D story-driven adventure. About 5 hours duration to complete the game without getting all of the collectables. Visually appealing, with an intensely engaging plot. Overall score 7.9/10.Detailed review:A lot of time and effort has clearly gone into the art style and the visuals of this game. For a one-man effort, the character and environment art is really good. There are layers of fog, particle effects and an absolutely gorgeous lighting effect that leaks from the background to the foreground through gaps in trees and leaves, just stunning. Would love to see Thomas make a YT video on how that effect was achieved. Having said this, I find the vector art style to be a little too rigid and square. There are a lot of unnatural looking corners on the characters, platforms and environments that broke my immersion at times. Overall visuals get a 7.5/10 from me.Animations were mostly very well done. Almost everything felt like it had the right mass and 'squishiness'. 9/10.The controls felt a little imprecise, but overall good. I played with a controller as recommended but found that making precise movements, especially very short distance jumps (little hops more like), weren't possible. However the ascending and descending timings on the jumps were a real treat, the player-character felt intuitively weighty. If the left/right movement precision were just tuned a little more, this could have made for some fantastic platforming controls. Perhaps because of this, platforming areas were quite sparse. Most of the game takes place on 'the ground'. This seems like a missed opportunity to me. Swinging on vines felt fun but similarly imprecise at times, and the spacing between vines could have been improved. Combat felt like the bat swing could have had just a bit more reach to it, accidentally getting to close to the baddies and losing lives felt frustrating. Coupled with imprecise horizontal controls this could get annoying at times. The skateboard was so damn fun and the slopes so pleasant that I had a moment where I really thought you could get another (hyper-casual) game out of just this mechanic. Though getting on and off of the skateboard didn't feel intuitive. Overall controls 7/10.This brings me to level design. Unfortunately I felt like this was another missed opportunity. So much of the game takes place on the ground, and there aren't really enough nooks and crannies to justify going 'off-script' and exploring for a little while instead of just following the next objective. Some more verticality and platforming would have been lovely alongside some minor tuning to the horizontal controls. Having said this, plenty of elements in the level design are quite clever, and there is enough here to enjoy the short journeys between nuggets of plot development 6.5/10.The plot is where this game really shines though. The game is intensely focused on plot and paces this out so nicely. You really feel like you're following the breadcrumbs through a Hansel and Gretel fairy tale. At all times there's a feeling bearing down on you that something isn't right, but you can't quite put your finger on what it is. The way the characters and plot normalise what would otherwise be repulsive or alarming, and the way the story is told, feels vaguely similar to reading a Roald Dahl book. Just like Dahl, most of these peculiarities are left unexplained and that adds to the tension; you are never quite sure if everything in this world is alien, or if you're the alien in this world. I do wish some of the red-herring plot devices would have been explained though. Plot: 9.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Neversong is aesthetically pleasing and the writing & narration makes it so much more enjoyable. Length of the game is short and linear but it does have some simple puzzles throughout the map for progression or for collectibles which makes every second of it worth playing.It is combat-oriented with mechanics slightly similar to Hollow Knight but its a lot more simpler compared to that so there is no need to worry about difficulty, anyone can play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely did not expect THAT. On a first sight, your average, runny jumpy platformer. Got to admit, first 20 minutes I wasn't sure if I will even finish this game, but once you grab onto the story, once you realize how simple yet perfect the background music is, that's where it gets good.It's an ambitious recreation of an old online flash game Coma, made by Thomas Brush (Atmos Games), that absolutely exploded on Kickstarter. Once the potential for something more was noticed in that little 15 minute game, that's where Neversong started to form. First thing you notice after beginning the game is a great somber narration that leads the player through the story, fully voice acted, which only adds to the atmosphere. It starts off slow and innocent, but quickly turns dark and twisted, more and more the deeper you get through the story. Gameplay wise it reminded me of Fancy Pants Adventures with a storytelling of Fran Bow.Once you get through the intro, you wake up in a beautiful, peaceful world, fully hand-drawn. You get to know the basic mechanics of the game, movement and controls are highly intuitive, so no worries there. Personally I played with a controller - as I mentioned, it's great to just lean back and enjoy the experience this game will treat you with. You will find yourself talking to some random kids scattered across the world, area by area, each stunning you with a different ambience. With time, you'll be more equipped to traverse the world, centered around your starting house, yet thanks to the smart level planning, there's not too much of backtracking either.Even thought the idea of a typical hack-and-slash platformer might not make your head spin with excitement, the creator of the game went the extra length to push it above the limits and make it as creative it could get. In no time you'll find yourself fighting against some twisted creatures, like... Grandma, Piss Boi or Simon's Mother. Yep. Both sound and art design are just excellent, changing accordingly to the mood of the story and area you're currently in. And at this point, if neither visuals, audio nor even the idea of the world didn't catch your attention yet, it's absolutely worth it to just push through the game only to see how exceptional storytelling skills you are dealing with.There's also a ton of puzzle elements throughout the game to keep you invested and make sure this experience won't end after 30 mins. But don't get discouraged by it, neither fights nor puzzles are not tough, it might require a minute to figure some stuff out, but it's all within the reach of everyone, even if it's your first ride with such type of games. For those wanting more, there are collectibles and achievements as well, so that provides some honest replay value for those who want to pump out 100% out of it. But since lots of you are after a nice, one-time adventure, Neversong is a great choice to spend one evening with. And believe me when I say this, if you will take up on this game, you really want to finish it, it's definitely worth it.:To put it all together, Neversong is a dark, beautiful story, accompanied by immersive music and illustrative levels. Definitely, an experience to remember and recommend all around, without hesitation putting it on a shelf next to To The Moon and Fran Bow. I'm glad I could play it, review it and love it - trust me, you will too.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: Neversong is a dark fantasy adventure game about a young boy Peet on an adventure to find his kidnapped girlfriend Wren. However, strange things have happened in RedWind. The missing adults, mysterious creatures, and creepy screams are all over the town. Players must battle through various eerie incidents to uncover the truth behind this dream-like world. I really adore this game and its variety of well-thought designs. Like I said, besides gameplay, Neversong delivers more than just the enjoyment of video game. A simple yet strong story decorated with clean artstyle and ups and downs really helps convey the theme of this game. If you like me who loves myself some good story-rich game with clues to puzzle out the main event in game, Neversong is easily a recommend for me.This is easily a spoiler-alert.  Everything in Neversong is cleverly put to aid the player to picture out the story and possibly the ending. I said it at the start the review and I will say it again: this game is a good example why I love video games, a great storytelling medium.I was introduced to Thomas Brush artstyle through the other game of his, Pinstripe, and I really like the way this kind of art works. Simple, yet charming. The art in Neversong is an improvement compared to Pinstripe. The color, however, is a different and proper approach. In contrast to Pinstripe's cold, sombre blue, Neversong utilizes the warm color orange to signify the joy and innocence of childhood memories. The music in both games also does a job working in concert with their corresponding theme. While Pinstripe's OST has a smooth touch, like a winter breeze coursing through a snowy Northern village, Neversong's OST has a quick light tempo of various instructments, making the stages feels more lively, like children heartily running around the town.Now in terms of gameplay parts, Neversong is a hack-and-slash platforms with a slight metroidvania element in it. For a story-rich game, I am quite surprised to see this game as not-blatantly easy as the others. The combat is simple:hit your enemies and outpace their attacks. The platforming is simple: jump here and there. The puzzle is simple: some memory tests and items utilization. And yet somehow Neversong makes all these simple ideas work, fun and straightforward. To further incentivize the gameplay, hidden cards are placed around the levels. You are immediately rewarded for some cosmetic options for Peet once you discovered the cards.After you experienced everything and know the truth, everything feels different. Same cheerful tune, but somehow withholds a certain depressing feelings– may this moment never change.I by no means mean that their designs are bad. Every boss has its own gimmick, more like solving a puzzle. What I think can be improved is the general concept of "songs". Songs and music notes play an  important role in Peet's childhood, and since this all happen in his coma. I think the boss fights can be more rhythmic to the songs they are guarding. Their attacks can somehow match the music notes in the song, sort of like higher pitch hits narrower but harder and lower ones hit slower but wider. I am not really the one to  talk about this kind of things since I have little knowledge about music, but I do think this feature would genuinely fit well and creatively, lore-wise and gameplay-wise.Mainly about the explosion effect and spike attacks during the final boss. Both of them have deceptive range. The color of  explosion raidius needs to be deeper rather than translusent. The spike attack, on the other hand, is a different case. It's funny to see that spikes on platforms are meant to discourage you from standing on it, even so you can just keeping running into wall to "avoid" being registered as taking hits.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: Caught somewhere between Hollow Knight, Night In The Woods and a sprinkle of "Metroidvania", Neversong is a tight, emotional package. The game can be finished in a single sit down -- which is a big plus (personally) in a year full of enormous games. There are a ton of nice touches that help make every scene memorable; The music is great, the story is strange (and sometimes even spooky), and the controls have just the right amount of "good floaty" to make the jumping and traversing satisfying.I also had an incredibly strange bug when I first installed the game, which you can see here: I'm glad a quick reinstall resolved the issue so I could enjoy this little gem, but this is one of the strangest things I've had happen to a game on steam.If Neversong has popped up in your discovery queue, I highly recommend you check it out. As soon as I finished it, I picked up the dev's previous game called Pinstripe which I can't wait to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely beautiful story-driven puzzle platformer. The artwork is mesmerizing, the music is enchanting, and for a one-man indie production, the level of polish is jaw-dropping. You could have easily told me this was a Double-Fine production, and I would not have known the difference.Unlike a lot of other great games in this vein, it is challenging but not punishing, so you can focus on the story but still have a blast. Combat is very forgiving, platforming is tricky but fun, and the characters/personalities/voice-acting remind me of the golden age of Tim Burton's work. There is so much detail in the background and foreground, and a lot of interactive elements that you can knock over or smash with your bat just for fun (gives you that feeling of slashing grass looking for rupees in the Zelda games). A cool surprise were the unlockable abilities, which I did not expect from this game based on the trailers. I absolutely recommend this to anyone who has ever enjoyed a story-driven platform adventure puzzle game. 10/10!
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I backed Neversong on Kickstarter when it was originally called Once Upon A Coma.  If you want a challenge this is not the game for you.  If you want a simple but fun game, look no further. Worth Every Penny.Pros:- Beautiful Art and Atmosphere- Great Storytelling- Great Music- Great Voice Acting- Controls were smooth, even on keyboard.- Easy Game, Quick to Finish.- Creative and Good HumorCons:- Backtracking - I felt this artificially extended the games length for the first play through. Ultimately if you know what to do, you could beat the game in under an hour as there is an achievement for that.- Coma HD DLC does not work properly and am unable to find support to troubleshoot.  EXE in Coma folder doesn't work and shockwave player crashes constantly.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: Only put as not recommend because i wouldnt recommend this to another friend - and at first having another friend game with me in a "play through" - he too did not enjoy it at all and wanted to give up on the whole game. I personally got this game through kickstarter and was more than happy to see this come to life and play it all the way through to the end. many mechanics are a bit rough and movements in the swing and skateboard are not that intuitive from experiences playing in other games. As a story game first - the combat takes a back seat and is very forgiving, it can be both a good or bad thing depending on what you are looking for. In my case, i was fine with the easier fights due to the fact its still a story driven game and if it were harder or more punishing while the controls are not as refined/sharp as other games then it might be a bad time. I personally got lost in the goals of the missions at time, and miss features like "maps" "journal/notes" that will help keep a player on track to move the story forward - though some moments of being lost is my fault, but it did make things harder than it should be when I would like to get back on track again. In the end - its still a fine game if anyone reads this and understand its minimum combat and more story - voice acting is good and charming, music is quite good for being a title of the game as well.but I'll still wouldnt really recommend this game to a friend and thus is my final verdict.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a amazing looking 2D art style.The audio/music is good, I even listen to the soundrack when im studying :)Animations are fun and playfull.The story is great and doesn't explain everything and that's something I like. You have to figure some stuff out on your own.The only 2 things that I didn't really like are the combat and the swinging/ball mechanics.The bosses are fun, but they are really simple. Not necessarily a bad thing, I like it this way. But the combat for the smaller enemies can be a bit annoying. Sometimes you have to get really close to the enemy and by the time you're close enough the enemy already hits you. (maybe im just not that good, but it was annoying at times).The other annoying part was the swinging/ball mechanic. It's not that big of a deal, but you cant drop down with the press of a buton, so you have to jump perfectly or you have to jump of again and swiggle around till you get the right ball. It wasn't a big deal but it can get annoying after a few tries. A simple drop options would have been better imo. I had alot of fun with the game and im still comming back to it sometimes to experience the game again and maybe hunt some achievements :)
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I've been thinking a lot about whether or not this game could get a recommendation from me. I know it was made mostly by one guy, and that is very impressive, with the visuals and how well it played. In the end it simply wasn't very good, as far as i'm concerned, story wise. There is no challenge here, the characters aren't very interesting, and the twist ending is... better than nothing, but it fell flat for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I tend to play games a little slower than I see others play them, so I got a solid five hours out of this one. You can tell a lot of love went into it by Thomas Brush and others who contributed. It has a dark aesthetic, and has dark humor and at times immature humor. It works. It's an enjoyable 2D melee-combat light-platformer with beautiful artwork and sound design. I'm also happy that it had some areas that were especially difficult, but not so difficult I had to rage quit. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I love indie titles like Hollow Knight and Celeste which combine great gameplay with a fascinating world/story, and Neversong is no exception. Great atmosphere, lovable and hateable characters, simple but fun puzzles which break up the journey. You can tell it was mostly the vision of one guy which means it just feels cohesive and like a lot of love was put into it. It's short (which may annoy you) but for me as an adult with kids, short games are my jam now. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I refunded the game because in my opinion, at this stage of development, is not worth the tag price.My reasons:1) A lot of backtracking, i personally don't appreciate it.2) The combat system. Too many particles and lights that disturb me without any usefulness. The combat hitboxes of the enemies, are clearly bigger than what you see on screen, and that cause the hero to be hurted while i am not having any contact with the enemy, but "i am near" him.The story, instead, is very interesting. The atmosphere and the mood of the game clearly are the main focus of the Dev (and he is pretty good at it, well done, this is very nice in my opinion).At this stage of development, and in it's current state, i am afraid that i can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: So I absolutely loved Pinstripe. The art, the music, the story, it was wonderful. Of course I was excited to play Neversong! Unfortunately, it just didn't hit the mark for me.The story is lackluster and simple, the puzzles are more annoying than fun, the ending isn't satisfying, and the boss combats are soooooooooo boring. I'm not happy I spent the money on this. It's more of a $5-$8 experience than $15. Buy it when it's on sale, but not at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: NeverSong is a delightful 2D platformer that I completed 100%, and it was an absolute blast! The gameplay was smooth and engaging, with precise controls and well-designed levels. The captivating story, exploring themes of loss and friendship, kept me hooked from start to finish. The hand-drawn visuals were stunning, and the haunting soundtrack added to the immersive experience. With high replay value and a satisfying ending, NeverSong is a must-play for platformer enthusiasts.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: A cute, creepy, atmospheric metroidvania that just felt way too short. I had hoped we would get to play through multiple episodes. The art and game play mechanics felt very satisfying, though the game itself still seemed sort of empty overall in a retro, early 00's way. I was really left wanting more. More time, more story development, more cohesion, more interaction. I do feel that Neversong successfully captured a sort of mid-autumn childhood nostalgia. It's definitely worth a play-through. I'm very excited to check out this developer's other works as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: Last year I played Pinstripe, and I gave that game a 7.75/10. I was definitely looking forward an improved next game by the same team. And that game was supposed to be Neversong.But it wasn't.The art style and music were very much similar, and that is not a complaint, since I really liked it, especially the voice acting. The gameplay was just as limited, making more emphasis on combat this time rather than puzzles. I liked its simplicity but I believe the game had a lot of potential for both traditional and platforming puzzles.For controls and usability, they were fine, although game options are very limited. No screen resolution, aspect ratio, language, key remapping or any of that. I had no problems with the game in its current state but they could have been nice additions.Both level and game design were fine, nothing much to highlight there. The game never felt repetitive and the upgrades were fun to use. Would have liked more of everything. This is a short game, beatable in 2 to 3 hours, so more levels would have been appreciated.The story was okay, not great, not terrible. Pinstripe takes the lead in this aspect with a darker tone overall and a more well-told narrative.And yeah, it was fun. Again, I was expecting much more as a second title from the developers and I got, in my opinion, less. That was my biggest disappointment. But the game is not bad by any means, just "okay".Score: 7.5/10. If you really want this game, check out Pinstripe instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game to support Thomas Brush, a game developer that I follow. This game, was not what I expected at all. It's music, art and atmosphere, as well as it inferred story, touched me deeply, and I would recommend this to anyone that likes to play a game, volume turned up, and just enjoy the experience. It is something that I think reminds me of games such as Hollow Knight, though of course of a much smaller scale, it is definitely the same feeling.I would not recommend this game, however to those who play games for the challenge. The puzzles and usage of Items are very fun and interesting, and I think the pacing is exciting and suspenseful, but the combat is not the most difficult, despite the fact that swinging that bat is the most satisfying experience in the world. If you are in it for the combat, I would say play Hollow Knight for your fix, and then come and buy this game anyways just for the heck of it (:
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: The atmosphere and art style of Neversong creates a warm, cozy feeling when playing. However, gameplay aside, the story of this game felt rushed. Through out most of the beginning I was hooked! This story had so much mystery, I couldn't stop playing. Though, as I got closer and closer to the end, I found the plot more and more confusing. The story began to make less and less sense. When I finally got to the end I found it rather disappointing. I can see what Thomas was going for but he could have told it better.Knowing that Thomas Brush created the beautiful yet tragic story that is Pinstripe, this game felt like it lacked potential. In all honesty, this was a step back for Thomas. You tried your best, but I still wouldn't recommend buying this game. Spend your money on something else like his other game - 'Pinstripe' which is actually worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: is a short, but sweet, action platformer with horror elements and themes. Paired with a fantastic soundtrack and a haunting, yet beautiful, color palette, this is truly a game worth experiencing. It isn't especially difficult, but it keeps your attention. The combat/platforming is diverse enough between each area that it stays fun and refreshing. It particularly appealed to the part of me that loves childhood adventures in a dark, twisted world a la  and . Definitely recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: if you are buying this I don't recommend buying it for gameplay, in my opinion it's kind of shallow and even tedious at times. The music is good and I wish someone would post the ost on youtube, or maybe I will. The visuals are very good and atmospheric, great colors and a lot of depth. The story is probably the best thing about this game imo, it's morbid and just good, it is a bit messy at times though.Overall you should buy this game for the artisitc value more than the gameplay.6/10 it's good
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: My wife, roommate, and I really enjoyed ourselves playing this. I'm a starting indie game dev myself and have followed Atmos Games on Youtube for a while. I originally just bought the game to support my fellow developer, but we carved out a day off to play the game and we thoroughly enjoyed ourselves, it is a small game, but masterfully crafted with stunning visuals, top notch voice acting, and an unnerving atmosphere. I cannot stress enough how you should play this game. That being said there are a few issues we had with the game. We soft locked on the title screen and ran around in the beginning are trying to figure out an imaginary puzzle until my wife looked up a play through and realized it never faded to black as it should have. The controls could have been finer tuned with sometimes my character continuing running long after I tried to stop and with the heavy air control, floaty jump, and non responsive jump and movement, it made some of the tighter platforming frustrating. Lastly the ending was very confusing for us. None of these minor annoyances even comes close to a deal breaker and I would say you would be robbing yourself of a truly special experience if you let any of these gripes get in the way of giving this game a shot. Honestly every character could be our favorite character, but Preston was precious and we will probably talk about him for a long time. long story short, play this game; you'll have a good day and won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: A short, unique narrative game wrapped in a puzzle-action-platformer package.I would say the gameplay is secondary here. This is a game I personally very much enjoyed for the story, characters and atmosphere the game delivers. You have a great mix of comedy & creepiness that blends together and creates a great vibe.It's sort of like a children's book... but a horror game. For me they nailed this feel and it came across really strongly.The art and music compliment this really well too.    Gameplay-wise, the game is a mix of puzzles, platforming and action. The game is not that long so none of these get boring or outstay their welcome. It's fun exploring each area, solving what you have to do and doing a bit of fighting & platforming. All of the puzzles feel fair even when a couple get tricky, the fights aren't overly difficult but each boss might kill you a couple of times.It's fun and stays interesting and helps the game delivery what it needs to.There are secrets scattered around too but I didn't delve into these too much.I would recommend this to any fans of shorter, unique indie games, especially those after good story and atmosphere. Though if a metroidvania fan wanted a shorter, chill experience I'd also happily suggest this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot say exactly, in words how I feel about this game. That's not to say I think bad about it, quite the opposite. I played the Coma demo a few years ago and was so hyped up that when it finally came out, I snatched it right up.The artwork is superb, the voice acting is spot on, and the puzzles in the game are not too hard, yet not too easy.For being 15$ (right now :/) the game is very reasonably priced. I have just beat the game, and I'm at exactly 5 hours game time.It's a twisted little game, very enjoyable for someone like me, however if you're not into puzzles or a twisted story, this may not be the game for you.It's def in my top ten games, if you give a damn about that, and I'm extremely satisfied with my purchase and experience with Neversong.To Thomas Brush, I'm just sorry I couldn't donate to Kickstarter.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful game. The art, soundtrack, and story are not just amazing in their own right but work together. This is not just a platformer where you battle monsters and bosses. This is a person battling inner demons. If you are looking for a game that challenges your abilities as a player then look elsewhere because that is not the point of Neversong. However, if you've ever read a good story and wished you could take an active part in bringing the story to its conclusion, then that is what this game is all about.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: Good casual adventure game that blends platforming, puzzles, and story admirably. My favorite part of Neversong is the story. The kids in this town are so outlandish and switch between friendly to devilish in an instant. The main enemy is Dr. Smile, who is sufficiently creepy. Going through the game and interacting with all these weird characters is so much fun. You're never sure who, or what, is going to pop up next and that's why it's my favorite part.Anyway, the mechanics of Neversong are constantly changing which is exciting. It's a linear game with limited backtracking and each of the new areas introduces a new mechanic. Which I don't mind, I like a game that doesn't waste my time and keeps it interesting the whole time. The puzzle elements are nice but limited. The game blocks your progress until you find the thing that allows you to pass. It's usually some bit of text that you need to find. It does give some clues about the story which makes it mean more but it's simplistic.While all the mechanics are fun Neversong is pretty easy. I didn't break a sweat getting through it.Overall, Neversong is a fantastic casual action game that I thoroughly enjoyed. I always enjoy the concise games that don't waste my time. The constant introduction of new mechanics and bazaar characters keeps the game exciting. Everything is delightfully strange.If you prefer a video,
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: The game has beautiful and original graphics, music and story, and if you are only interested on that this is your game (only easy difficulty). In fact, the plot reminds me of Thomas Brush's previous game, Pinstripe, but with that unexpected change of events in the final stretch (I liked that ^u^ ).BUT...Although it's short, the first half part is slow and almost boring. The bosses and the puzzles mean no challenge, and it wasn't until I got all the items that I truly started to enjoy the gameplay, when puzzles were complex enough to not disappoint me.I think there should be more places and situations to test ingenuity and make the most of the items; and the bosses could have one or two more attacks, or even be faster, something to have the player in constant alert (Also, I expected a blade instead of a bat to fight). I mean, I only died 1 time for being reckless!And finally, something that pisses me off so bad (in most of the games) is the translation into Spanish.I wanted to play the game in English to fully enjoy narrative, but the texts showed up automatically in Spanish (I guesss it's because that's my default language), and it's horrible. Sometimes it's like they forgot to translate some lines (especially in the poetic cinematics), used directly a translator or just didn't know how to do it. At least It was decent enough to follow the story and the characteristic font accepted accented vowels (which I'm thankful for).CONCLUSION: Beautiful art and story, but not challenging and bad translation into Spanish.
_childDocuments_.name: Neversong

_childDocuments_.review: QUICK BACKSTORY:I found Thomas Brush's YouTube Channel when I started trying to learn Unity & try my hand at game development.  Long story short that led me to Pinstripe & ultimately Neversong.  It's rare that you put a face with a game, but in this case, I was thinking of all of Thomas' YouTube videos as I played.  I purchased the game simply because I wanted to support his work.  I am not sure how much this influenced my review, but I wanted to be transparent about what brought me to the game.REVIEW:Neversong is an artistic story filled with lovable characters, dynamic visuals & scenes, & quality audio.  The game didn't require dialogue audio tracks, but I am glad the time was invested because the voice actors did a fantastic job.  Now what about the gameplay?  Truthfully, I enjoyed the story & puzzles more than the combat.  The only time I felt I was enjoying the combat was against the multiple bosses.  Simply because the bosses fit so well into the story.  The abilities make a lot of sense & work fairly well.  I would also point out that I have played several platformers that had several bugs that took away from the experience & I am happy to report I experience zero bugs while playing Neversong.VERDICT:If you like platformers that are driven by puzzles & story, you will definitely enjoy Neversong!  For the price tag, this is well worth it for the enjoyment you will get out of it.  Fantastic work to everyone involved making it & especially to Thomas.  Well done!DEV FEEDBACK (spoiler free):I wanted to provide some feedback about a few things I noticed.  I found myself wanting to ride the skateboard more to travel & it seems you cannot propel yourself with your other foot.  You can only kickflip & gravity does the rest.  This is by all means not a problem, I just felt like it was only useful during puzzles & couldn't be used any other time, unless there was a hill & it wasn't grass.  Lastly, the final boss (again spoiler free).  I'm in my 30s & throughout the game I was pretty freaked out by him during the cut scenes.  So finally facing him felt partially scary & I was ready to pull a "Negan" on him with that bat.  Truthfully, it felt too easy.  I realize there aren't difficulty options & you have to balance that for everyone that plays (not to mention people playing on iOS devices).  So I take all that into consideration.  I think I only took damage two or three times.  Maybe randomizing the attacks or combining some of them (the knives are awesome btw) would make it more challenging, ultimately making it feel more satisfying when the fight is complete.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Skip this one and play Thomas Brush's earlier game Pinstripe instead.So this is a hard game to review for several reasons. One, because this is a story-heavy game, and while there is actual gameplay here, with platforming, puzzles, boss fights, and even collectibles, the game is really there for the story and characters. And while there is enough gameplay challenge to sink your teeth into, whether you like the game will come down to whether you like the story, dialog, and art style. FWIW, it does a good job of the cute/creepy Tim Burtonesque vibe.Two, this game is VERY similar to Thomas Brush's previous game, Pinstripe. It reminds me of Zero Punctuation's review of Bioshock Infinite, where he speculates that the maker of System Shock, System Shock 2, Bioshock, and Bioshock Infinite is being told by a stern school teacher to "Do it again, but PROPERLY this time."  Either that, or the creator can't afford a therapist so instead he uses these games to explore a specific trauma in his real life and he had some leftover issues from the first go-around. The plot in both is basically you chasing a creepy man who has kidnapped your loved one.  A lot of the similar themes are repeated, the allegories are super heavy in both, the art style is very similar, and the villains in both are essentially identical. Of the two, I preferred Pinstripe, but you might feel differently.And finally, I am not recommending this game basically because I didn't like the ending. I don't want to spoil it, but let me just say that the story is one of those where you don't have a strong resolution. It's up to you to piece what actually happens at the end. So if you're annoyed by that, just skip this game. As I said before, the gameplay is secondary to the story, so your enjoyment will come down to whether or not you like the story.The game (and story) isn't bad, there are some good characters there, and interesting stuff happens. Gameplay isn't as smooth as something like Celeste, but the challenges you face also aren't nearly as taxing. You might have to redo a jump because the ledges don't end where you think they do, but the challenges aren't so pixel perfect and complex that you have to redo a ton of stuff if you miss. Boss fights are a simple challenge, I think the final one was the only one I died more than once on. The characters are quirky, and if you like the Tim Burton vibe, you'll like the weird people and creatures in this world. But for me, the ending just left a bad taste in my mouth which undid all my previous goodwill about the game. I could maybe play it again and look for more clues (the game encourages you to do this with achievements and some chests you can only open on the second playthrough) and it's short enough that it's feasible to do so, but I just didn't care that much. I liked Pinstripe better, and did replay that one to try and see the bigger picture, but it was also a much clearer picture if you know what I mean.So if you like the vibe of this game and think story is as important (or more important) than gameplay, maybe check this game out, but you'd probably be happier playing Pinstripe instead. The only people who I would recommend this game to are die-hard Thomas Brush fans, but those people don't need Steam reviews to tell them to buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game! It's a longer reboot of the old Flash game "Coma", a little 15-20 minute game that I absolutely loved when I was younger. While there are similarities to Coma, there's enough new content that it didn't feel like I was just replaying the game. The art style is amazing and the music, as always, was great (I got stupidly excited when I heard the Red Wind theme from the original game, that one's been my favorite for years.) The voice acting is awesome and the controls weren't anything crazy. The game does run a little shorter than some, maybe 3-4 hours of playtime.My favorite thing about this game was that the puzzles/boss battles weren't super difficult. I found myself quickly figuring out what I need to do and how to do it and when I did get stuck, it was usually some simple misstep. I think this definitely helped me to enjoy the game more as there was little frustration. I'll definitely be keeping an eye out for any more games from this team!

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10 It was alright. Super polished, and absolutely gorgeous. It followed the original flash game just enough, but does flesh out the whole game a lot more. You can beat it in about three hours. I take issue with the story and combat. It feels like the game has a lack of direction.With both this game and Pinstripe, Thomas treats exposition and moving from point A to point B as the "story", but there is no real plot. Every character is static, and the structure doesn't come close to resembling a hero's journey. The end reveal is underwhelming because I am not invested emotionally in the characters. (In this instance, Pinstripe does a better job of this)The combat is satisfying, but there is no depth to it. Enemy patterns are easy, boss fights are not a challenge, but have you sitting and waiting for simple patterns to repeat with little to no danger. Difficulty could have been ramped up by introducing some of the later enemies sooner, and using them in combination more to force the player into managing the attack patterns to get in a couple hits. I found myself just running up to anything and smacking it until it died since nothing posed a real threat.The music and art is too good to give this a negative review though. I wish there was more to explore in the world. I don't think this was a bad game, I just wish there was more to it. Thanks for continuing to make games Thomas!

_childDocuments_.review: Neversong (formerly known as Once Upon a Coma) is Thomas Brush’s newest baby and another successful Kickstarter campaign, after the tremendous impact of his previous game .Thomas is a one man army providing the vision, the story and the whole concept to his games. This started, for me at least, back in 2010 with Coma. Coma was a narrative masterpiece that pushed the boundaries of its Macromedia Flash limitations and it was one of the gems in that wonderful dungeon of creativity that was Newgrounds. Neversong is like a remake/continuation of that idea and offers an emotional story that is told to us with wonderful and intriguing characters that are very well written, luring us into this fascinating world. I believe that a loyal companion to Thomas games are his production values. He pays attention to every single detail; from the wonderful soundtrack to the subtle animation work. The platform aspect of the game works wonders with simple and intuitive controls. The same can be said of the puzzles, which are there more as a conduct to the story than to give you a headache. Neversong is a must have one game that should be in your collection.  To be honest, I will be surprised if Neversong doesn’t pop up topping every single list of the best games of 2020. **=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+=+**If you enjoy my short and sweet reviews, please follow our curator page  We are the Indies of Curators!#StaySafeStayInside&PlayGames

_childDocuments_.review: DEBABI played Coma 10 years ago. And i don't know why, this game has been stuck with me ever since. _childDocuments_.review: Fans of Pinstripe will feel at home playing Neversong. The game is beautiful as expected from Thomas Brush, with great music, script and most of all awesome voice overs. Especially the voice overs help a lot to flesh out the characters and draw you in. The story is quite interesting, again following the example of Pinstripe in terms of structure and narration. The general feeling of the game is quite creepy at moments, giving nice horror vibes.Regarding gameplay the game doesn't reach excellency. The platforming and "battle" mechanisms are just sufficient. The biggest drawback for me was the use of a melee weapon. Unfortunately, there is not enough depth in the battle system, there is a small variety of enemies and small challenge, depriving a part of the fun. In comparison using a rifle in Pinstripe was more fun and more forgiving for the devs. There is no comparison with Hollow Knight (since it is referred in a trailer quote). Bosses also are not something to remember, they are well designed in terms of backstory and aesthetics, but again there is not something memorable in terms of gameplay.I mostly recommend the game to fans of Pinstripe or people interested in a nice story with great aesthetics and atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is broken as ♥♥♥♥ and the devs don't care.The loading is the biggest problem and it's atrocious. The game actually loads WHILE YOU ARE PLAYING when you first open it. It might as well not let you move when it does this because it takes like 30 seconds to register and input. Once it finally ACTUALLY LOADS (when the boy icon is gone) it plays much better."Much better" is relative. The game isn't hard to beat, but this performance inconsistency makes the "beat the game without getting hit" achievement the literal worst thing I've ever seen in a videogame. What the ♥♥♥♥. There are lots of points where the game saves but doesn't tell you (no fly or other loading icon) and if the game glitches there, you're just screwed and have to start the whole thing over. I was lucky enough to not encounter a game-breaking bug in my first playthrough, but not so lucky the second time. I beat the final boss and the game got really slow for his death animation and collecting his song. Then the final area just didn't load and it was a black screen. I waited for 10 minutes and nothing happened. I had beaten it before so I knew this shouldn't happen. I was actually able to pause and I checked my inventory and I hadn't actually got the song, so I assumed the game didn't save. Well when I opened the game again to fight the final boss he wasn't there. The game saved when I beat him (without telling me) but didn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ think to save in the final area. The boss music played, but it was impossible to progress. And since the achievement I was trying to get is for beating a new game +, that means if I want the achievement that I EARNED, I have to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ play this game FOUR ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ TIMES total, instead of two. That wouldn't be so bad since it's pretty short but all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loading and bugs is too much to deal with. If you can't make an autosave system work, then maybe DON'T ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ PUT IT IN THE GAME. The manual saving works perfectly fine. I'd much rather have to re-do 10 minutes of gameplay because the game crashed than have to play the entire whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing again just because the game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up at the literal last minute. I guess I should talk about the other parts of the game. Music is really good, easily the best part. Voice acting is fine, kind of jarring when you encounter the few lines of dialog that aren't voice acted, seemingly inexplicably since they're from characters that are fully voice acted otherwise. Just another thing that points to the game being unfinished. The game looks pretty in places but I much prefer the style of the original flash game this is based on, Coma. Like if you're gonna make an expanded FLASH game so graphics-intensive the literal least thing you could do is put options in to turn them down, assuming that's even the reason that the game loads and runs so poorly and slowly. The story is ok, there's a twist which I guess is fine but it doesn't really make anything you did in the game any clearer. I'm probably going to replay the game twice again anyway, just because it's not hard. But don't be like me. Of all the premium flash games and games based on flash games I've played on here, this is by far my least favorite, and even if it ran perfectly Super Chibi Knight, Mr. Bree+, The Binding of Isaac, The Cube Escape games, The Henry Stickmin Collection, Dino Run DX, Crystal Story II and Epic Battle Fantasy 4 & 5 are all better and deserve your money much more than this game does.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those weird little games that even though it has some glaring issues I still love.  I bought this off a whim last steam sale because, well, I liked the aesthetic.  And to be fair I still think it's a very good looking game.  It's a solid story with some awkward writing here and there, nice characters, and an interesting world.The problem is the game has quite a few drawback as well.  For starters the platforming can be really awkward as the physics kind of just do their own thing.  Momentum stops dead when you stop swinging or get off a ramp it can be really jarring and frustrating.  The game suggests you use a controller but it doesn't use the D-pad (the cross).  This wouldn't be so bad if the way you swung your bat didn't depend on it.  More then a few times I'd want to smack up only for my character to swing wide or vise versa all cause my joystick was angled a tiny bit to far up or forward.  And for some reason, and this may just be a me problem, the controller it shows is a PS4 controller (the one I used) but all the buttons are shown as their Xbox counter-part.  How does your game know I'm using a PS4 controller but doesn't know the button layout?That's a lot of complaints so why do I still recommend this game?  Well, for starters it's nice and short.  It doesn't overstay its welcome so the world itself doesn't get boring, you'll always be discovering something new.  The characters are fun and the dialogue, though a bit awkward in places, is still fun and really feels like how a kid might talk.  And the gameplay is satisfying enough to keep you playing through.But most importantly, the biggest reason to pick this game up, is the passion behind it.  Despite it's flaws this was made by a tiny team of developers (mostly by one guy) and you can really tell he put his all into it.  It's a creation made by the passion of game making rather them an incentive to sell copies.  Obviously a lot of love was put into it's creation and that alone is worth something.6/10 - above average, though short and a bit clunky at times there is still an unmistakable charm that carries the game through.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the original Flash game like I did, you will love this. So far, this game has taken me down memory lane back to when I was in 3rd grade. When I had the opportunity at lunch to go to the library and use the computers, when Flash games were popular back then. I would always find myself coming back to this little game called Coma, a game that I could never understand the full story probably because I was too young. I recently played the original flash game on another website, that's when I found out that the developer had created Neversong, which was a direct remake of that original game. I'm in university now, but I knew I had to get this game. I haven't finished it yet, but so many lovely characters have made a return, as well as familiar locations and music. I'm really enjoying the game and I would sooooooo recommend it even if you didn't play the original.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is sadly very mediocre at best. I don't even put this review as a positive or a negative, it just felt rather lackluster and left me unsatisfied with its end. And as someone who adores Pinstripe, I was really hoping I'd get the same feel from this game, but that isn't the case. While the music and art is amazing as ever, the gameplay was wonky and some of the puzzles were frustrating to get through. Once you know what you're doing (which can be fairly quick), the boss fights are extremely easy to fight and don't give off much of an actual challenge if that's something you're looking for. The story felt very disjointed, and I wasn't sure what I was following until the end parts of the game. After I finished the game I had to look up online of how I was supposed to connect the story and get from other peoples' analyses on it. Neversong is certainly a game I don't hate, because there were moments I found it to be enjoyable. However, it is a game I would not replay ever again, including since there's no real motivation on collecting all the cards or achievements unless you want to 100% it. Like other reviews, I'd rate the game at a 5/10, and only recommend it if its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Neversong was an incredible game that was absolutely able to sympathize with my current situation while I played. Although the combat was a little precarious at times, and the 'Coma God' achievement was ridiculously trivial; I enjoyed this game thoroughly and would seriously recommend it to anybody. Aside from the dark and depressing themes of the game, it is also filled with plenty of humor from top to bottom that had me giggling throughout my play sessions.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to love about this little puzzle adventure game. Thomas Brush's music is a soothing masterpiece, the art style is delightfully quirky and Burtonesque, the voice acting is incredible, and it has a surprisingly heartfelt story... but adventuring around the beautiful map and swinging at the grass with Peet's baseball bat is probably my favorite part of the whole experience. Some of the puzzles are mind-bogglingly frustrating, though... there's a point in Neverwood Cemetery where you have to launch a bomb from an elevator at exactly the right moment to break some obstacles. Every time I play the game I spend nearly an hour trying to do that stupid maneuver, getting it wrong hundreds of times. I have actual nightmares about that.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing Coma on a school computer around 8 years old. I was just starting to develop my fascination with surreal horror and such! I remember that game having an impact on the media I enjoy. I remember humming the notes that Peet plays on the piano. I had no idea Coma went viral. I did not know a full game would come out. I was over the moon when steam just so happened to recommend a different game, I can not remember the name, but it was made before Neversong. I found Neversong and did not really understand which of them was a remake/based on Coma. I say Neversong had the Coma DLC and I was over the moon, I could not believe the game I treasured so dearly would become its own thing.I am rambling a lot, but I'll get on with it. I love this game, with my entire heart. It was a lot of charm. Coma did not have any combat or boss battles, but I did not realize the addition of it would bring it to life so much. The combat felt nice, the hits felt solid. However, the only major issue I had with the game is that some of the flying enemies just would not come down and that felt so unfair. That is really the only issue though. The sound track, the atmosphere, and the story was all lovely. I loved the twist at the end and I also love how vague the ending is.Neversong is a wonderful game, if you have the time and like surreal horror please play it! Its amazing!!

_childDocuments_.review: A reimagining of the 2010 flash game  that makes a few small missteps, but otherwise improves on its predecessor across the board. Puzzle-platforming is fun despite occasionally wonky physics, combat is simple and forgiving (perhaps to a fault), the visuals and music set an atmosphere that's equal parts beautiful and uncomfortable, and the emotional story it tells left a surprising impact on me. Worth the 3 hours it takes to play through the story, but 100% completion is more trouble than it's worth.  is an action-adventure game about a boy named Peet, who slipped into a coma after the kidnapping of his girlfriend and must navigate a dreamlike world in order to get her back. Formerly known as , this is a reimagining of the Newgrounds flash game , made by the same developer all the way back in 2010. I became a big fan of  when I first discovered it in the mid-2010s, and although it's taken me longer than anticipated to get around to the sequel, I'm glad I finally got the opportunity to play it.By and large, the gameplay is your typical 2D adventure game fare: some exploration in a map with hidden collectibles, some light platforming challenges, and a handful of different puzzles in the middle of it all. --nothing serious enough to stop my playthrough or anything, but enough to cause some mild frustration. For example, one time I managed to perform a step in a puzzle out of order, leading me to find an item I knew I needed but couldn't pick up because the game didn't want me to have it yet. Most of the hiccups were in the platforming, as . The specifics are hard to explain, but it was mainly a problem with two mechanics: ropes you swing from that can have unclear speed and trajectory, and large ramps that will only give you the right momentum to reach nearby platforms if you start and end your travel at very specific points on the ramp. Again, nothing too serious, but don't expect everything to work perfectly all the time.The biggest departure from , at least as far as gameplay is concerned, is the introduction of simple combat mechanics. You have a basic swing attack that can be aimed forward, up, or down, and there are no extra mechanics like blocking or dodging.  Every enemy will spawn a recovery heart on death if you're missing health--as does every boss each time you clear one of their five phases--and defeating enemies can drop currency that automatically increases your max health every time you collect 100 of them. Alongside common enemies are four bosses, and each requires you to first solve a multi-step puzzle in order to unlock their fight. : your first attempt will likely result in some heavy damage, and you might even fail; but every boss has some kind of cheap tactic that lets you beat them with little to no injury, so every fight becomes trivial once you discover it., with the world in a state of perpetual twilight that's filled with a lovely color palette of contrasting oranges and blues. It feels almost inviting despite its twisted undertones, maintaining a solid balance of whimsical and unsettling in its design that will often tip towards the latter when the plot demands it. , and it maintains a more lighthearted tone through nearly all of its songs, almost as if it's acting in direct opposition of the visuals and their darker slant in order to restore that balanced tone. While we're on the subject of tone, I do want to mention something: I wouldn't go so far as to call  a "horror game", but it will use gross/creepy imagery that can be unsettling for some players, and there are several moments set up for no other reason than to put you on edge. That said, this game is almost entirely devoid of jumpscares--there was one moment at the end that got me to jump, but I think it was telegraphed and I just wasn't paying attention--so you can let your guard down a bit if you're like me and don't enjoy those.Like everything else thus far,  fleshes out the vague concepts behind  story to create something much more cohesive and engaging. , and it's one that admittedly hit me a bit harder than I expected it to. The core of the story is laid out pretty clearly, but there is some hidden symbolism scattered throughout the game for those that want a little more to chew on--shoutouts to  of the story that helped clear up a few details I missed. The only gripe I had with it comes at the very beginning, as ; or, at the very least, it helped me guess the game's ending long before I think I was supposed to figure it out.One last thing to note, strictly for completionists: . The process will demand multiple playthroughs, as there are separate achievements to beat the game twice, under an hour, without dying, and without getting hit. Even just going for all collectibles will most likely require at least two playthroughs, as the last location will prevent you from backtracking without prior warning, and trying to reload your file post-credits will just send you to the beginning of a New Game Plus run. The main game is fun, but the achievements I've referenced have less than 5% total player completion for a reason--you have been warned., and although I've harped on a bit about the issues I ran into while playing, they were minor at the end of the day, and nowhere near enough to stop me from recommending this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd been looking forward to Neversong for quite a long time, back when it was still Once Upon a Coma. The game I played, however, doesn't live up to the hype.The combat is quite simple and healing is ridiculously easy - something that I actually appreciate, being something of a bullet magnet in games. Still, all the fights, from regular mooks to bosses, felt very flat and difficulty is never ramped up as you progress, except for beefier-looking enemies getting one more HP. That's it. No special moves or anything until the final boss, and even then the difficulty is negligible.The controls hurt. Trying to attempt a higher jump with a special mechanic seems to never work properly, instead being overridden by other commands. The skateboard mechanic feels like it was still in the first stages of implementation when the game released, as you can only go one speed and changing directions isn't even explained. Heck, honestly I feel like there's something wonky about the very physics of the game.The writing is... dear God. I haven't played Pinstripe so I don't know if this is something Mr. Brush is known for, but the dialogue is so childish and uninspiring - and sometimes, frankly, just weird. How many times do I have to listen to some brat call me a "puke" or read about the infamous "Booty Bum" gang? I grew out of this in grade 4. I don't understand why a serious, seasoned developer would write dialogue like this.The ending felt rushed and gave me more questions than answers. Think sudden tonal shift. That's another thing, the storyline just suddenly shifts from one looming threat to another. First it's the creepy doc who's kidnapped your girlfriend, next every adult has suddenly gone wild and is swinging around a machete, shirtless. With no explanation. What is this game.Also, Bird is an insult.I still finished this game and logged 6 hours into doing so. Despite having to suspend my disbelief and bite my tongue, I still enjoyed it somewhat, but I'm easily entertained. I honestly feel kind of bad for disliking it so much, knowing how much this game meant to the developer, being a remake of one of his early games. I'm very nostalgic about my old projects, too. However, sometimes those past works are best left as is, and our talents and energy should instead be focused on future endeavors and the improvements that come with them.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty good game with decent bosses. A good player would finish this within 2 hours without even trying. I did pretty much everything there was to do in about 3.5 hours, and I'm not good at anything platformer related. Platforming is not exact at all. I'm glad there's not too many times where exact platforming is necessary because he can't jump at any point, he only jumps the next moment his foot is on the ground.
