_childDocuments_.review: The game has more promise than the developers have allowed. It is sold as a "story-based exploration game" but the latter part is lacking and the former is not as smart as the writers nor the players in the comments seem to think.In terms of art and sound design the game is wonderful though not original. The voxel graphics are nice, the audio mixing is clear and the sound effects for rain and picking up objects crisp. There is a calm to driving around the city and the different sections are all pleasant to see however, since we are 40 years past blade runner it would be nice to see some innovation in regards to the cyberpunk aesthetic. It is well done, but do not expect anything you have not seen before. No major graphical or technical issues however there are noticeable slow downs where fog appears. The soundtrack is excellent soothing electronic jazz and while a common trope to be expected in this genre the composition stands out when it needs to, but also recedes as background noise when needed. The voice acting is admirable but it was a small team with actors putting on different voices. The game may have benefited from more abstract voice design since the graphics are abstract. Human voice/face for voxel-man is a little jarring.Though the city is described as "open" you cannot just park anywhere and explore. It is pre-built zones rather than an interconnected city and there is relatively little to do or interact with once you set your car down other than find collectables which one can sell or sometimes give to NPCs (which mostly gives money anyway). Driving the car is moving from point A to B marked by HUD elements. Unfortunately most modern games, even those now describing themselves as "exploration" games, disallow players from actually navigating the level or game-space with signposts, landmarks, NPC-given directions or maps. Clearly, this game would be much improved and have some much needed challenge introduced if players were tasked with finding delivery locations themselves rather than following a green diamond markers, which encourages staring at the mini-map rather than looking at the gorgeous world they made. The dialogue attempts to make quests tense by hinting at there being consequences for missing deliveries, but there is no mechanic for this. No time limit for deliveries. Which is quite contradictory to it being a delivery quest game and makes all the story tension rather false. If they felt it integral, quest makers could have been an UI option or an in-game unlockable. The lack of navigation mechanics cripple the level design to some extent and so the open world becomes more repetitive and the game relying on NPC dialogue or story beats to give the illusion of variety. The parking locations are often disconnected with players waiting for elevators instead of walkable paths, with some local areas annoyingly being divided into separate parking spaces.The game would have benefited by borrowing design elements from immersive games like deus ex. Even though that is an FPS, the ability to actually jump or move objects around in the environment would have added to the exploration side of the game. You are supposed to be doing something illicit to "make ends meet", yet cannot rob cars or hack ATMs. Though you can fuel your car and stop at designated locations, it seems like a halfway-house between immersive design and the more boring walking sims that plague the games market. More fail states from falling off ledges to failing deliveries would have made the game feel more free and less of a casual time-waster. For a game that blathers on about the meaning of freedom in the story it does not seem willing to give much of it to the player.In terms of the story and themes, I find it difficult to tell whether this is a game for adults or children. It is a game where they reference terrorism and prostitution, yet every-time a story decision is to be made the game dialogue plays "Hmm, should I do A or B? If I do A the company will be happy, but the person will be sad." "But Rania! If you do B you might get in trouble!" "I need time to think about this one!" There are no real consequences if you go against your delivery company, sure the story references something happening, but nothing happens, not even visually in the game world, the simulation just continues. Every theme is something we have seen before. The private sector managers run everything in a quasi-police state and you are someone just trying to get by by dropping into shady activity. Everywhere is either a slum, a nightclub, or an utopian complex. "Life is complex and how does everything work?" - which the game contradicts (when you speak to the engineer he mentions how they don't know how ancient technologies work yet somehow you make a delivery of a device which has a mechanical ticking/timer mechanism? How did someone build a mechanical device if nobody understands anything anymore?). Themes of nihilism, love and robots. These themes are not so clever and have been explored in a more intelligent and interesting way by sci-fi authors for decades.The developers and/or writers are attempting to criticise or satirise society at an extreme, imaginary end of capitalism where commodity production and money relations rule everything, even domestic life and state politics, while selling their own game as a commodity while working under a firm structure themselves. So it is a shallow criticism; nothing unique to this game but worth mentioning the hypocrisy. Why mention it for a small indie title? Because the writers are so far down the liberal sinkhole that they seem to regard prostitution as "honest work", criminal delivery work as "just trying to get by" or selling family memorabilia as "I need to eat". Women being forced to sell themselves into sexual servitude is a reality that can be explored, but the developers have tricked themselves into thinking that anything that is paid is "work" and "sex work" is just another source of income, coming off as supportive of prostitution. Now consider what I said about whether this game is for children or not. It is pretty shameful of them to present prostitution as another form of work, and this game is laced with themes that legitimise the activities of the lumpenproles. Though they mention a class-system operating ("the merchants are as far from the clouds as they are the gutter") we do not explore much of it. There are no workers to interact with, mostly just middle-class merchants and other lumpenproles. If they had bothered to flesh this out, they may have found some answers to their themes around purpose and what constitutes labour i.e. "work".Some of the dialogue is skippable but some parts are not. If it is dialogue associated with the main story-line then it is usually not and you find yourself waiting around for it to be completed. Also perhaps it is just me but resurrecting your dead dog as a car AI and then chatting with it is all sorts of morbid and strange. I get the game is going for a bizarre world with bizarre character interactions, but I think this was meant as wholesome. Dogs in real life do not talk as far as I am aware, and why would anyone who missed their pet want it back as a talking car siri? It makes the whole relationship unbelievable and unrelatable. In the blade runner adventure game, he has a real dog and that is why it is nice going back to the apartment. So they could not even get that part right.While the review is scathing I would not categorise this as "bad game" but one that is disappointing. Once you move past the initial presentation there is a lack of depth to both the story and the mechanics that means the game is tricking people into thinking there is more there than there actually is. The "story-based exploration game" does not really exist and it is more just another rehashing of cyberpunk tropes.

_childDocuments_.review: InSync CLOUDPUNK ReviewPLEASE NOTE: Game reviewed at Story completion. MINOR SPOILERS! In Synchronex's own, confusing words...The future is a bleak voxel-based dystopia... At least this future anyway. We will have pixelated faces, harbour very specific feelings about this seemingly endless city and soar into it's clouds - or, more likely, drop way below, into it's depths, disregarded, like rubbish.This city encapsulates actual modern humanity and beyond; how cruel everything (and everyone) really is and how no one cares as long as they can make it to the top both figuratively and literally.The "strong" as it were, live amazingly lavish lives at the top of absolutely massive spires, completely oblivious to the lives of most if not all else. The "weak"? They barely survive under the clouds and below, down into a city apparently tearing itself apart. The weak is anyone not willing to sacrifice every piece of humanity they have left to be at the top, in some instances, physically as well. The weak...is everyone else just trying to survive.... Are they really the weak ones?Amongst this physical hierarchy of strong & weak, rich and poor is the, at best, shady delivery service known as Cloudpunk. Illegally moving packages around the city and across the figurative and literal voids that exist in day to day life; to and from it's many citizens that are only just hanging on...or having the time of their life.Which is where you come in, the newest delivery driver for Cloudpunk. Your shift starts tonight and you had better be ready to do your duty..or else.- - -Cloudpunk is one of those games you weren't expecting. It starts out simple enough, move packages from point A to B. Fly your HOVA through the cloud traffic and to the destination. Fun stuff. This, and a slight bit of walking encapsulates the entire game. So right from the get-go you are experiencing everything it has to offer, in terms of gameplay. The car you fly is a bit janky and the controls are a bit weird but this is all fine and quite enjoyable really. What's not expected is the story and the subjects it touches on. It does it's best to bring you into the mood, top voice acting, fantastic scenery everywhere and is quite a well-written noir journey.However, the main character, doesn't seem the slight bit interested in anyone's life. (this quickly becomes relatable). Which is all well and good, that is until the word android or something is thrown in and she all of a sudden cares and has big opinions, which always came across as a slightly too "goody two-shoes" point of view of our real-life problems with humanity and how they are bad. Like we didn't already know. Like the game was often trying to directly tell us this is bad don't do it. This is acceptable but it is not subtle and is peppered throughout the entire game.The real problem comes when you are waiting for the latest, annoyingly bright - or dark - character to finish up telling you their life story and inevitably how this has anything to do with loving - or hating androids and the city as a whole... not to mention actually where their package is going...just so you can fly your ass to the next destination and experience more of the "game" so to speak. This puts a real hold on the gameplay itself. Just as soon as you pick up your latest, you want them gone. Now, this is not a negative comment on the voice acting itself, quite the opposite actually. The voice acting is brilliant, conveys exactly the type of character you are dealing with (annoying as they are, they are meant to be) which means they are doing a good job. The problem comes from the fact you must experience the story, in many cases, while sitting still. Waiting for the next prompt in a city that just wants to be explored. Not playing the game but rather listening to it. The story, in many cases, holds the gameplay hostage, with no benefit. Sure you can fly around the city while they talk (sometimes) but in many cases this will bring you further away from where you need to be and, ultimately, be counterproductive to advancing through the game.Now, I understand this sort of thing must put a hold on finishing up an objective so each character's dialogue can be fully realised, however, waiting a good few minutes for them to ramble on about somewhat irrelevant details at times sort of killed the immersion in moments it should have aided it and this was the main problem. It felt like the "game" was trying too hard to be a visual novel (vaguely referencing real-life issues, even racism or wage gaps) that you sort of just fly around to get to the next page and continue. It was jarring to the story as it couldn't be progressed (even if urgent) until the latest intense character shut up. At times this was also jarring to the gameplay.Though it may not seem like it at times, this is all (mostly) justified. The setting & feel of the game keeps you playing and keeps you just interested enough. Playing in first person really helped the immersion. A particular highlight (and minor spoiler) was when my obviously old and ugly HOVA needed to be replaced. I got to experience exactly how a new one is chosen in this future, was instructed to fly to a used car dealership complete with the classic "used car salesman" character, (which absolutely nailed it I might add). I not only got to look around the place & the cars but actually choose a new car, making it my own in doing so. This and a handful of other instances (such as discovering your own apartment) demonstrated how there is a bit of a game here and immersion took over from there.All this being said, as a whole package, the game is fun and interesting, though more of an experience than a game. It's an enjoyable, if somewhat depressing, little look into the dark future of humanity with an artful & creative take on futuristic cities, living in them, how they will work - and what will happen to them and indeed humanity once push comes to shove.Story: 7/10 - A decent story but it holds the gameplay hostage at times.Gameplay: 7/10 - Fun flying around and exploring but that's all you can do. (Added Immersion of 1st Person Cockpit camera has bumped this to a 7)Audio: 9/10 - Fantastic voice acting, cool beats but not often enough.Graphics: 8/10 - Awesome looking scenery, not a fan of the pixel/voxel characters.Overall: 7/10Similar to: Space Taxi 2, Audiosurf (Visuals), Cyberpunk 2077 (Setting)Personal comment: "What can I say, it was one helluva night".
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool game. It's narrative focused. Very enjoyable aesthetics. Sometimes it's worth to hide the HUD to enjoy the visuals. Pros: Rania is just great.A few notes that almost discouraged me to keep playing but changed later on: - You will be able to improve the vehicle.- A lot of the dialogues seem pointless or feel like they are just lore but they will often open quests and give rewards soon enough. - Don't quit save mid mission with a timer... there is a good chance you will be screwed with less time to complete by spawning outside of your car. I like how there are no indicators of stats as in movement speed/hunger. You can just "feel" when to use a buff or not. Its very narrative driven and has no combat. And it grows on you. Even some of the jokes... e.g.: I liked the exchange between Rubrick and Rania:  "Rubrick: It takes a lifetime to learn this city. Rania:"Well, the sooner I start the longer it will take then." To the devs: Why we can't keep delivering packages after the end of the story? (You CAN keep playing but I am not sure if there are packages at HQ)  Just add a generic "Control" line followed by a nav point and random money rewards... (I will edit if I learn it is possible)

_childDocuments_.review: Cloudpunk is not only gorgeous, it also oozes neon bright charm and hyper future cyberpunk grit. This is a narrative experience but it also helps that the gameplay is a quiet, relaxing, and fun courier/taxi missions. Not only that, but the developers are planning to add more gameplay and missions to the game soon. _childDocuments_.review: To be honest, I was at a pretty low point during the beginning of the pandemic. I found this game during the Spring Sale and decided to try it out. I've played through the game twice and to my astonishment, I had just as much fun as I did the first time. I get that there's loads of voxel slander nowadays but I think Cloudpunk did it very tastefully. The new updates have given it a whole new life with first person and some glitch correcting. Now that we have the current abomination that is Cyberpunk 2077, it really is comforting that there's a developer that focuses on the fine tuning and releasing of games as cleanly as they can make it. This game has so much potential even now after some of these updates. Personally, I would like to see more explorable interiors, maybe different car options, along with more side quests. I owe a lot to the game devs for creating such an awesome game that really helped me get out of my mental rut and thoughts.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Confusing, visually assaulting, overwhelming.  I felt like a leaf being blown around by winds I couldn't see, but knew there was a whole living world around me. Slowly I became more comfortable - the passing of vehicles and people not so much chaos anymore, but I could start to see a rhythm, a kind of mad logic to the place.  Soon enough, I felt completely at home and revelled in the enormity of the place.  Immerse yourself. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing!The city of Nivalis is wonderful, it feels alive, is fun to drive around, explore, meet interesting and often strange people. Truly great worldbuilding and atmosphere.I loved most of the characters since they are well developed and voiced, which to be honest I don't know why but it was a surprise, I thought the game was gonna be more text-heavy. Some characters are hilarious, like Huxley, I think he deserves a mention. In a city where money and social status is the only thing that matters, honest people should be treasured, and true friendhips are often rare to find.Bear in mind this is an exploration and story oriented game, there's really not much gameplay depth here. You'll be driving around the city, doing errands, walking, talking to people, but its made in such a way that is very fun to play.Good for a change of pace, I'll be looking forward for more of this!
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Joy to play.  Thoughtful story. I'm a fan of the original Blade Runner, so the atmosphere and substance of the game was very much appreciated.  Mechanics and progression were great, if you're like me and want a game that's slower paced and more exploration/collection based.  And, yes, like other comments state, your decisions do matter.  Thought provoking themes and some very touching moments that were a lot more emotional than I expected!  But, I'm a softy, so...there you go.  Very cool game.  Great job developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: So I don't normally write reviews but felt this one earned it. If you are looking for an open world game you won't find it here. However, if you are looking for an excellent Cyberpunk experience then Cloudpunk is the game for you. Every time I have played, I literally get lost in the ambiance of the game. From the graphics, to the top notch music, I am fully immersed. Well done Devs, keep it coming!
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game has a fantastic premise. My absolute favorite thing is the atmosphere. I think the Cyberpunk-feel is captured really well. If you enjoyed Bladerunner, I think you're in for a treat with Cloudpunk.There are, however, a couple minor nitpicks. When turning the camera, the falling rain moves with you. It is like it is stuck to the screen which kinda ruins immersion, but it's possible this was done to free up some graphical real estate. The dialogue is super drawn out and often results in me skipping through. The faces of the people you talk to don't match their character. For example, if you approach a man with brown hair, the picture in their dialogue box will show a blonde guy with an eye patch. Not a big deal, but again, immersion.Sounds effects can be a little wonky sometimes. When increasing altitude in your HOVA, the sound of the engine ramping up will play for a few seconds and then restart (and loop) until you are done ascending.Regardless, the story is easy to get behind and I am hooked. Easily worth $20. If you're on the fence about getting it, get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: I love cyberpunk; however, I am not really a fan of pixel art. Even so, I definitely recommend this game if you are a fan of cyberpunk. The pixelation can be a bit odd at first, especially when some other things are no where near noticeable as far as pixelation, such as water puddles, clouds, and some of the displays. If you love pixel art as well as cyberpunk then I highly recommend this title. If you're more like me then just think of it as someone implanting wonky visual translation software or funky ocular implants. Either way, this is a title worth at least a bit of your time in my humble opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I was pleasantly surprised by this game. It's relatively short, depending on your pace and if you choose to complete side missions and specific achievements, and while it's not a perfect game, it was a great ride. Yes, it's essentially fetch quests since you're a delivery driver in a dystopian world, but what keeps Cloudpunk from being too repetitive or dull is the interactions you have with NPCs, as well as choices when faced with let's just say more suspicious packages. The soundtrack and overall sound design was solid, with synthwave tracks and a rainy background to vibe to. The navigation points were easy to follow, despite Nivalis feeling quite expansive and disorientating at times (only when going to specific locations to finish side missions and talk to folks, as well as collect random parts shown on the map). Certain areas were also quite layered, with lifts and tiers to keep the map from feeling flat and like you had no room to search and walk around. There were quite a few sections of the city to explore, with the option to stay on the freeway or take shortcuts through side streets and try not to swipe your HOVA on buildings or other cars (which I did a lot). I thought it was pretty realistic that you had to actually search for parking. It made the game feel a bit more interactive, rather than have you get close to your objective and drop it off from a distance. In most instances, you also had small conversations when dropping or picking up packages, and even though the dialogue could be cringey or cheesy at times, it somehow worked for this game and made it fun with the different interactions. It also made certain characters endearing, even if the dialogue became a bit campy.The addition of Control and Camus kept the game interesting and preventing it from feeling "empty", or without any additional insight into Nivalis. I think there was a great balance between following the objectives, and also picking up extra parts to trade or collect, like the punch cards for Evelin to help her, which you could choose to look for or not. There were also a few timed missions but otherwise you could decide to cruise around between pickups and dropoffs or simply continue the story.The biggest criticism I have is that I found the voice acting to at times be lackluster, ranging between stiff and robotic voices, which seemingly worked for the android characters, to overacting by side characters or merchants and vendors. But I didn't go into this game expecting flawless execution and to be blown away by every character. Initially, the acting took me out of the game momentarily, as some characters seemed like they were not engaging enough and rather reading off of a script with no inflection, but as I played, I got more used to Rania, and realized since the game is more chill and not as action-based, the voice fit her character, who is just trying to get used to the city, feeling like she doesn't belong, and is doing her best. As long as the voice acting doesn't distract you too much, stay for the story and atmosphere. All in all, there were some interesting decisions to make that furthered the conversation of what is moral in a dystopian society and what will serve the greater good, and the atmosphere of Nivalis (and the seven major areas in it) with social commentary on how humans and androids are treated based on status and class. The narrative could have been more focused in places, but I really enjoyed my playthrough and the time in between missions to cruise and explore the city, while meeting humans and androids alike who share their diverse experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Wow! This is a narrative driven game so you would be listening to characters talk and moving the story forward 80% of the time. The game for me lasted about 7-ish hours. The Story fits the world the game creates. It is a linear story, but I would think of it as each "mission" is it's own episode within the theme. And the main story left me with a little disappointment in that I wanted it to be more complex than it was. However overall it was enjoyable. I absolutely loved the PI story line and would hope they would do a DLC story with just that character an his other stories/cases. That I would buy and enjoy. Cloudpunk Noir lol.Gameplay is the same throughout the game. The Pattern is Story/Mission start > Travel & Land > Run to NPC/Location > Leave.) No combat in this game at all. Strictly story and player decision based game.This game really shines in its World building. Great Level Design, Great Audio Design, The Voxel style fits and adds to the world. Character designs each character is different and some of them are amazing. to the developers I will say AMAZING JOB!This game was very enjoyable and left me wishing that is was longer. I would consider this to be a masterpiece, but the story's lack of complexity holds it back just because of its lack of impact emotionally. I would have liked to have more emotional connection to a couple of the main characters like CORA.This game is worth 20$ buy even though I got it for less on sale. If you like video game novels, then this game is good.

_childDocuments_.review: Down thumb, but deserves a sideways thumb. Recommended for anyone who really likes the Cyberpunk theme or who does not value game play. I could see this game being fantastic if it had a much larger budget behind it to meet its ambition. GameplayThe least interesting aspect of the game. Most of your time will be spent walking or driving. Walking is horrible because you must slowly navigate annoyingly maze-like areas, in which you will have to backtrack often. Driving is a little better, but surprisingly un-fun for a game where your vehicle is a hover car. The limited vertical motion you can make while driving is one of the most disappointing aspects - restricting you to about a 200ft tall area. Horizontal movement is also pretty un-interesting since there is not much to impede the path of your car in the lightly-trafficked sky roads and wide-open spaces between buildings. The WorldYou drive around a handful of medium-sized areas connected by loading screens that look almost identical to one another. Each area is disappointingly horizontal with every point of interest constrained within a few hundred vertical feet. Exploration is kinda pointless since everything in the game you could want has an icon on your mini-map. The atmosphere of the game is otherwise good, if monotonous. The voxel aesthetic looks pretty good for buildings, but not as well for people. SoundThis part of the game also gets a middling review. The music is background filler and never stands out. Sound effects are similarly un-noteworthy. Voice acting is sometimes good and sometimes bad.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: TL/DR: Really cool and laid back game, but leaves a bit to be desired. A perfect Steam Sale game for all cyberpunk lovers.The idea of driving a flying car (named HOVA in the game) up and around a cyberpunk city sounds like a dream, and for the most part they achieved just that! The city looks gorgeous, and it's full of that "gloomy wonderland" cyberpunk feeling. Unfortunately the game doesn't do a good job in a few aspects. - Exploring the city on foot can feel pointless. The only incentives are a few items that quickly lose relevance and a few npcs you can interact with. Problem is, a lot of times those items and npcs are not easy to reach. You can't park your vehicle anywhere, and often the thing you want to reach is on the opposite side of the parking lot, meaning you have to go all the way there and then make your way back to your car. Usually just looking at the city could be enough incentive, but that brings us to the next issue:- Even with enough npcs walking around, the city can still feel empty. This is probably because you can't interact with any npc aside from store clerks and quest-related ones. They don't make a sound and you can't even bump into them, it's like they're ghosts wandering aimlessly. There's no background chatter too, aside from a few city announcers and voice adverts.- The on foot free camera is very iffy. It's clear the game was designed to be played on its fixed camera, because the 3rd and 1st person controls are all over the place, so much so that I stopped using them entirely. To be fair, playing with the fixed camera proved a much better experience. The city is designed with the assumption you'll be seeing it from those fixed angles, so you'll miss a lot of details by playing as 3rd and 1st person.- The story is... okay. It kept me engaged enough, but I think it could've been explored much better. Some of the side quests proved very interesting and showed different perspectives from people around the city. Also I can appreciate the devs for not turning everything into a political debate.Overall I had a good time, it's a very laid back chill game with a few intriguing moments here and there.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cyberpunk, scifi driving game where your main task is to pilot a flying car around an eternally dark and rainy city. Unfortunately the driving is monotonous with dissatisfying controls, though it is better than the long on-foot sequences. Luckily the driving is really a way to connect the different plot points and it doesn't get in the way of the rest of the game too much. The premise, the story, and the ambiance are quite good. It's an enjoyable little narrative game and any fan of the cyberpunk genre should pick it up. Anyone looking for action, racing, or a GTA style game will be sorely disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: I don't finish nearly enough games, this one kept my attention. From the unique visual style to the fun of driving a HOVA around I really enjoyed it. Without giving away any spoilers, I feel like the writing could have been a liiiiiitle better, but I loved all the voice acting. Some characters stood out more than others but overall. They all did pretty good. It was a neat story with some interesting decisions in an interesting world. Also pretty low key, low stress kinda game. Sit back, relax, and work through it. Was just nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Very good story, fun gameplay, delightfully emotional. Voice acting is good and fun. Graphics are very pretty and do a successful job at establishing the gritty atmosphere. Storytelling is organic, the whole "package delivery" deal doesn't feel like railroading the player to make up for play time. Side stories/quests are integrated to the main plot naturally. I really don't understand how anyone can accuse this game of being "too political" when the setting is literally a cyberpunk dystopia - and a well-handled one at that. To anyone looking for a good little story or some dark cyberpunk vibes (or both) I recommend giving Cloudpunk a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, I really do. The graphics, aesthetics, and ambiance truly capture the spirit of classic 80's cyberpunk. However, the shine wears off rather quickly, and you're left with a rather basic paint-by-numbers story. All the elements common to cyberpunk media exist: massive wealth inequality, questions regarding the distinction between human and non-human, etc, but none of it is ever really explored to any satisfying depth. Not every game needs to break new boundaries, but  the themes are presented at their most basic and simplistic. I can't help but feel this is a result of cyberpunk being boiled down to a simple aesthetic and nothing more.Watch a walkthrough if you really must; the game is just tedium and caricature .
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game however I couldn't. Visually it is very nice, at least the environment. Character models are borderline stickman.  But in my opinion character models and environment doesn't match. I'm not saying they should be a fully polished 3D models but little more detailed models would be better. This is an art choice of course, you might love it. All subjective. There are two major issues for me. First one is gameplay. It is dull, Take a package from A and deliver it to B. As a dedicated ETS2 player I thought I wouldn't find that boring but it is boring. Over and over you carry packages for too little development in the story. Also the puzzles you get are only about figuring out where to deliver the package. You see the dot on the minimap and try to figure out how to get there because you can park your car only on dedicated parking spots and then you'll need to run to the place. There are elevators etc so sometimes you end up spending 10-15min just running around like a headless chicken. "Finding your way" isn't puzzle for me, it's just frustrating. Second issue is the voice acting. This is one of the worst voice acting I heard recently. It's not voice acting, it's just someone reading a script from a sheet of A4 paper. Kills the immersion so badly I couldn't get attached to the game. Shortly after I turned the voice off and start reading the text instead. If you want to give it a try, go ahead. I'm not refunding the game because it's not horrible. But it's not good enough for me to invest my free time in its current state, maybe at some point there will be some mods etc to change stuff a little.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great walking sim that has the Cyberpunk theme to it while waiting for Cyberpunk 2077. Its a different game when the devs added first person view and cockpit view when driving that delivers a rather different experience than when the game first released with no first person view or cockpit view. It is a very story driven game where everyone you meet shares story of their lives in the city of Nivalis. I got one ending and it feels like there might be another out come or 2 depending on your choices throughout the game. Sit back and take a hit of that good good to enhance the walking experience!
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe I should have played this game more to give it a chance, but then again I can't get a refund if I play more than 2 hours; I didn't really feel motivated to be patient with this game anyways. This game was quite disappointing, but let's start with the good parts first. The atmosphere was nice and was well aided by the good soundtrack. I really enjoyed the "cyperpunk" feel from the color palette and the soundtrack that aided it.Let's move on to the downsides. The voice acting was definitely low-quality. It did not help that much of the dialogue written for these characters was awkward and seemed like it was written by a person who had never had a real conversation before (in some ways it was the bad voice acting that made me feel this way more than the script itself). Awkward script combined with awkward voice acting led to a very cringe-worthy performance. As I drove around the city, I had to endure the dialogue to get to my next package or just to wait for them to stop talking. Not only that, there were times when the voice acting did not even match the transcripts. It seems that whoever voiced it was reading off of an older or altered version of whatever made it into the game. The main character was quite honestly so annoying. This could be down to personal preference, but she would not shut up for the life of me. It did not help that at many times, she was talking with her AI system "Cammus" whose "awkward AI but loveable personality" was also unbearable. In many instances it was as if the script was trying to make us, the player, laugh at its cluelessness or ignorance from being an AI system with no common sense, but the performance and the jokes themselves were nothing close to funny at all. To me it was as if whoever wrote Cammus as comic relief (at least for the first part of the game that I played) was trying so hard to be funny that it just wasn't.This next part is more of my own preference and what I expected from the game before I bought it. I thought that this game would allow me to have the freedom to choose dialogue that would dictate my story and my ending. While there is some choice in the delivery of packages (e.g. the location) and other in actions, most of the time I got the impression that this whole story was already set in stone and was just slowly revealing itself to me. Now some people might be okay with this, but I am more used to and enjoy games more dictated by actions AND dialogue choices. In many instances I wished that I could have been able to answer the NPCs differently, in some cases act more rebellious and in others more subservient. But alas, the MC's non-stop talking decided my own fate the whole time. Another main point is the concept of time. In my first deliveries, I was told to be quick and without asking any questions (of course the MC asked questions though) deliver the package. Maybe this is just because it was the first missions so it was easier but I didn't really feel that time urgency. There was no timer or clock from what I could see anywhere in the main interface when I'm driving in my HOVA or walking around. Even with a "dangerous" package in my car, I felt no real sense of urgency. In one delivery I got lost for some time because I wasn't ascending high enough; I thought that maybe my delivery would have a penalty because it was a lot later than my usual deliveries but the dialogue with the receiver of the package carried on as usual (nothing indicated that I was in trouble for taking a long time). Not even Control reprimanded me for taking so long. For a game that emphasizes efficiency so much in their first dialogue, I felt that I could take all the time in the world to reach my destination. Here are some other issues I had but aren't as major as the ones above: There is some aspect of exploration outside of the deliveries but from what I could see it was very limited; I would be walking around to pick up a random item placed right in the middle of the ground or some other awkward position. Granted some of these items turned out to be useful after initiating dialogue with specific NPCs, it's just that the placement or location of them was very unnatural within the setting.One last minor problem I had with it was that the NPCs clip within each other and the player. When walking around, I noticed them walking right through each other without a change in stride. This is  inconsistent with when the player finishes a dialogue with an NPC. After talking, sometimes they will try to walk past you but seem to be running into you so they cannot get past; however in other cases I could just walk right through them. This isn't a huge issue but more of something to take note of. Overall I was very disappointed with this game. In some ways it just wasn't the type of game for me but in other ways it was just low quality. I really enjoyed the idea of this game but in practice it was just cringey. Some people might argue that I should've waited longer to play the game--bear with the bad voice acting and get deeper into the good storyline; if this game really was worth my time and money I wouldn't have to wait more than two hours to finally enjoy it. tldr; disappointing and cringey.

_childDocuments_.review: Cloudpunk is an RPG set in the cyberpunk city of Nivalis. You play as Rania, a delivery driver for the semi-legal delivery company, Cloudpunk. You drive through the clouds and towering heights of Nivalis, delivering packages, hearing stories, and unravelling the tangled threads that lie at the heart of Nivalis. Mechanically, the game relies on two elements - a driving element and a walking element. As a delivery driver, Rania, of course, has a flying car that she uses to make deliveries. The player uses the car to navigate the city (preferably without ramming all the other cars along the way, though I was bad at that part), flitting from one floating platform to another. The city itself is divided into discrete districts, with floating platforms within those districts that require the car to move between them. The player can also leave the car to explore these platforms on foot, collecting items and talking to people along the way.There’s a lot to love within Cloudpunk. The world built through its writing is a compelling and vibrant one, and its writing does a consistently excellent job of drawing the player into not only the story of Nivalis, but the smaller stories of its inhabitants as well. Nivalis is a city that feels as alive as Night City or any other setting in the genre, and that is an accomplishment in and of itself. The deliveries Rania goes on further that worldbuilding and create a world that feels worth exploring. I sought out characters to talk to, not because they furthered any particular game objective, but because I was curious about the stories they would tell.However, Cloudpunk is also deeply flawed. For all the power of its writing to drive the player forward, the actual world that writing inhabits often feels empty. I drove my hover car to my deliveries, pausing on platforms to collect items or talk to characters, and found that the environment never really changed. The districts are not particularly distinct, and walking through an area feels less like an exploration, and more like a sad, soggy slog from one mini-map marker to the next. The sense of mystery and adventure is muted by a minimap filled with colourful markers, telling you which areas will be interesting and which will not. Similarly, the landscape, though beautiful from a distance, is made of voxels, giving it a distinct look that I found off-putting and immersion-breaking. The voice acting is sometimes oddly delivered, and conversations sometimes slow actual gameplay down to a crawl, creating a reluctance to actually engage with a character, lest they suddenly hijack your game and force you to do something you didn’t intend. The game presents moral choices, but these are generally shallow and don’t feel like truly meaningful choices. I find it difficult to come to a final conclusion about Cloudpunk. There’s a lot here to enjoy, but it feels lost behind the reality of a slog of a game. I don’t want to play a game that is sitting in traffic, struggling to find parking, and getting trapped in long conversations. That’s already life, and it’s less interesting than it sounds. I want to cruise and explore a cyberpunk landscape, but equally, Cloudpunk doesn’t effectively allow that, having built a world that is somehow empty, despite its myriad of minimap icons. Cloudpunk is a game of contradictions. I wanted to enjoy it for its writing and story, but couldn’t get past the slog that is its gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: I’d recommend it, but I can see how this would not be liked by everyone. The story by itself was engaging, but the gameplay was a little bit lacking. Sure, I found myself enjoying driving around uselessly and exploring Nivalis playing servant to its citizens. But I wish the UI was as immersive as the story that came with it. Having a driving and delivery service game without seeing a HUD for how broken the car was?  Or not even having a keybind to show more information about the car? A bit strange. A better skip option for the long winded dialogue would’ve been great too.
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: Its unusual for me to be so ambivalent about a game, but Cloudpunk has traits that I love and some I hate.Pro's:Visuals. The game is BEAUTIFUL to look at. This was the main reason I bought it. The charming voxel graphics. The atmospheric rain. The dark night contrasted by the bright neon that is glowing and flashing everywhere. So pretty. I HIGHLY recommend you mostly play with the cinematic view activated (thats the long range 3rd person camera) and just occasionally switch to the close range first or third person view to look at some things up close. The cinematic camera will give you the best visual experience. Characters. There are a bunch of interesting people/animals/androids that you will meet on your journey. Some of them are pretty likable. This games voice acting has been criticized, but I believe the flat voice acting is absolutely appropriate for many of those characters, so I was happy with that aspect of the presentation.Story. Considering there isnt much to do in the game other than follow the main story, its pretty important that its decent and thats what I found it to be. I did roll my eyes a few times at some SJW type moments, but still enjoyed it overall.Cons:Challenge. This game has virtually no challenge. There are a couple of moments where you race the clock, but other than that, you just drive from point to point and talk to new people. If you ding your vehicle up too much, you have to get it repaired or it will drive very slowly - but you cant make it explode or anything. There is no way to get a "game over" screen here.Combat. There is none. Similar to my comments above, the only thing in this game that will keep your brain occupied is driving (which is fun) and listening to characters talk. For this reason, I think its best to play the game in short (1-2 hour) bursts, for most people. Overall I'd give this game a 6/10. It looks so nice and I really enjoyed absorbing the visuals and the citys atmosphere, but the complete lack of challenge did bore me a little. I'd still recommend it to people who can enjoy a very slow paced game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece, every aspects of Cyberpunk is inside: mad AIs, augmented humans, digital conscience, transhumanism, machine rights, etc... The narrative is rich, you grow more and more attached to the different characters as you progress through to story. Sometimes the game will ask you to make tough moral choices, unfortunately it doesn't really impact the outside world. Ideas for improvement: - Make decisions impactful (should I save humans or androids etc etc) - Enable CorpSec cars to make pursuits if you hit them like in GTA - Mini games !

_childDocuments_.review: If you love cyberpunk environmental games and movies, you must play this game. _childDocuments_.review: What a unique little gem. It's super peaceful to fly throughout the city and get to know different characters whilst listening to the OST. _childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting experience, which I can only describe as reading an interactive book. But you're doing a bit more than just listening to the story... The gameplay is nothing special, it's a fancy cyberpunk-style fetch quest, but it's made by design, considering that the very work of the protagonist is basically a futuristic mailman. But everything that happens between the tasks? THIS is the main part of the game. The game manages to include you, a small person, an insignificant cog in a dying machine, which is the city, where everything is happening, into the wildest stories! Having no connections to the majority of people around you, the only thing that you do is helping others around. Usually, because it's the very thing that progresses you further.But it's worth it, as the stories that you find out and others tell is truly the main selling point. The voice acting and open-ended nature of your orders and dialogues you keep is making the experience intriguing and gripping. Pluses:+ Awesome voice acting, immerses you really efficiently! + A good stylized "blocky" graphics with magnificent neon lighting.+ Unique stories of unique NPC-s, making you crave for more.+ The atmosphere is immersive! Minuses:- The gameplay may become repetitive.- The driving of your vehicle is feeling a bit off (just like in Cyberpunk, lol), and it makes for an irritating experience from time to time, especially when you have time events.- While the individual NPCs' story is the selling point of the game, it has a tendency to infuriatingly to cut abruptly without any tangible resolution.- The world, so vivid and full of life, always feels a bit undeveloped, because you expect more out of so many individual situations and unique locations.In conclusion:The game deserves a praise and your time to play it! Or, at the very least, try it... The stories are gonna be the very thing that would make you crave for more content and development. The voice acting will only add to the experience. And finally, the graphics and music will make the game worthwhile!
_childDocuments_.name: Cloudpunk

_childDocuments_.review: If you want to drive around a future cyberpunk city and hear random stories this game is your dream ticket. If you want high action and adventure then avoid. I'm personally finding Cloudpunk to be a pleasant relaxing experience to play through and the short stories that you listen to on your travels are mainly worth the slow pace of the overall game. I do think that once I have completed Cloudpunk once though, I won't be back.

The story is fantastic, the city of Nivalis so detailed and alive, you can get lost exploring all the beauty of busy metropolis driving in your HOVA or just walking around. Grab it now and jump into your HOVA and start your journey with Rania and begin your Cloudpunk delivery service today!

_childDocuments_.review: With amazingly beautiful visuals and set pieces despite the voxel based models; an incredible story spanning a single hectic night; and with no need for gunplay, dialogue options or cutscenes to pump up the action, Cloudpunk brings so much more to the table than it looks like on the surface. Before passing my first hour of gameplay, I found myself fully immersed and ready for plenty more.While the game is not incredibly long, that doesn't matter, for it finds its end just at the right point where you feel like it has given you all you need from it.Compelling characters, great environmental- and dialogue-based storytelling, as well as a killer soundtrack keeps the story rolling (or should I say "hovering") with great efficiency!If you're looking for dystopian gunplay, blood, mutilation and no-stop action, this is in no way your game. However, if you're looking for great storytelling, this is likely something from you!(Still spoiler-free)I was sceptical when I bought this game. I wasn't sure what kind of experience I was about to walk into, only that the gameplay I had seen that same day looked very pretty. The game itself also seemed quite unique. I figured I might as well try it, and thus I bought it. This turned out to be one of the best decisions I've made on a whim in a very long time.Cloudpunk puts you in the boots of Rania, an outsider new to the gigantic city of Nivalis, on her first night on the job as a delivery driver. And that's all you're getting at the start of the game. No dramatic flashbacks or narrations. No cutscenes or explanations. Everything else you've got to figure out on your own. However, the game doesn't make this hard in any way whatsoever. Everywhere you float or walk, the environment tells the story of the city. A story I won't spoil here. You get  story and that of others through dialogue, the main missions, side missions, random little interactions, as well as your precious automata of a sidekick, Camus.Very quickly you'll realise the city of Navalis is filled with as many monsters and horrors, as it has casual citizens just trying to get through the day. The game is dark and gritty at times, but also heartwarming and wholesome at other times. You will make both friends and enemies very quickly and the choices you make when you're at a crossroads will at times come back to bite you (or help you) later. I often found myself pulling my hair out over even the most basic of choices. In the end I found myself wanting to know if I'd feel different afterwards had I made the other choice presented to me. I found myself feeling right just as often as I felt myself feeling I might've made the wrong choice. Morals and the individuality of the player comes into this a lot.In the 14 hours it took me to complete the story and every side mission I could find, I only ran into some minor bugs, most of which has already been fixed at the point of me writing this review. Flying your HOVA (your car) around takes a bit of getting used to, but I quickly got the hang of it. Even after many hours though, I still found myself getting iffy about the slow rate at which it ascends and descends, even after I bought the upgrade available to improve it. That's a very minor thing though and overall it took nothing away from the experience, nor my willingness to continue playing. I also recommend playing this game with a controller if you have one. Makes flying the HOVA around a little easier.Cloudpunk proves that you don't always need guns, gore or total destruction to tell an amazing story. Sometimes, all it takes is a sassy protagonist and a city which never sleeps.With that said though, if you're looking for gunplay and non-stop action, this game is in no way for you. Best thing about that? This game doesn't try to be that kind of game in any way. It's about the story and the player will get that story. By the end, as well as on the way through, it's absolutely worth it.Overall, this was a very satisfying and wonderful experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty torn on this one. The game is shallow and a bit dull, but it has its charms. The gameplay is the main weakness - repetitive and unengaging. Drive here, drop object off here. Press E to finish quest. The vibes are strong but often times not strong enough to carry the game. The overall atmosphere is nice - especially in regards to the music - but the city, while pretty, feels hollow. Minimal things to interact with, mass NPCs walking in straight lines, many of the areas look and feel same-y. But a few strong character interactions make the world feel a bit more lived in. Difficult to recommend this one to anyone not already interested in the textbook cyberpunk look/feel. But if you're a sucker for it like I am, then the vibes, characters, and a few plot beats make it worth a playthrough. Get it on a deep sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this one just recently, so reviewing a version with many updates since launch.Graphics: Ugly character models that look like they've been squished in a trash compactor.  Hover cars and cityscape are better but get to feel pretty samey after awhile.  Would be hard pressed to find your way around without the minimap.Sound/Music: Good albeit generic music, Good ambiance. Occasionally humorous PA announcements.  Main characters have decent VA work.Story/Characters: full of pretty cringey dialogue.  Preachy morality lessons from ignorant writers who get their morals from TV and the news.Gameplay: there  isn't much.  drive from point A to point B.  Find a spot to park, run slowly to a waypoint to press the use button, listen/read poorly written dialogue, run back to your hova.  Rinse. Wash. Repeat.  There's lots of random stuff you can pick up off the ground, and some random NPCs you can have awkward dialogues with that usually result in more distaste for the main character.  Sidequests also exist in the form of additional fetch quests. Overall:  If you want a game with a cyberpunk aesthetic, there's a ton of better indie games on steam.  I got this on sale for < $10 and still feel like I paid way too much.

_childDocuments_.review: You play as a female delivery driver from CloudPunk. So the RPG parts are not big since it's mostly a delivery driving simulator, but for the cyberpunk world. There's is only a few choices of choosing to deliver a package or discard, BUT that's only in specific deliveries you get in certain parts of the game. You can buy some upgrades for your car (HOVA) and I recommend to save some cash for fuels, repairs, and things you might need. There's are side quests, but you only get them by visiting the icon of a person's head. Though I recommend to explore and get many collectibles as you can. There's a quest where you need to collect punch cards for your neighbor (and it's alot; I recommend you to stock them up before you start it).  So is it fun? I would say yes, if you not worrying about playing as a self-insert and expecting RPG elements like fighting, choosing words, etc.  I recommend to drive fast since....mostly you just drive and not worry about the mile limit. I finished within 5 hours, bought all the upgrades, and have 6k left over. Once you are done with the game, you can keep playing to get all the side quests and/or collectibles done.I got it on discount, but if you like these games I recommend to go ahead...but if you feel skeptical and interested, get it on discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write many reviews, but I'm absolutely loving my time with this game and I think more people need to know about it ! I'm playing on a PC and the graphics are breathtaking. The city itself is a work of art, each building is unique and when you see hundreds of these incredible neon-lit structures stretching off to the horizon, it's truly something to behold. Exploring by foot is fun, but I absolutely LOVE the flight mechanics. It's the most exhilarating feeling to climb into your hover-car and then soar into the clouds just as the Vangelis-esque music kicks in, leaving the hubbub of the crowded streets far below. It's probably the closest I'll ever come to experiencing the world of Blade Runner.I totally get the criticisms that the gameplay isn't very deep, and that some of the writing is a bit clumsy. All fair points, but for me these negatives are far outweighed by the incredible ambience and the intriguing story. If you're looking for a relatively simply game to relax with at the end of a long day, I can't think of anything better.An amazing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic cyberpunk atmosphere and story that innovates on the genre to present some truly unique and fascinating worldbuilding.  I have to agree with other reviews when I say I want more of this story and these characters!!!!  Camus especially, the dog automata stuck in your HOVA's frame, is wholesome and hilarious and I love him so much.  Huxley too. And Pashta. At this point I'm just listing character names I can't give you context for because of spoilers, so I'll just leave it at saying the story is captivating and I couldn't get enough. There is not a ton of player choice, but the main character Rania's charisma and charm more than makes up for that. But on the rare occasion Cloudpunk does decide to give you a decision to make, it is never black and white. Especially the 'final boss' decision - which is what it functions as mechanically in this story driven game - with what it asks Rania (the player) to consider about their entire experience of Nivalis thus far, and the people that she has met along the way.I guess my one compliant would be the buggy and difficult to use camera. There are three different camera modes: tracking shot that is custom to each location, 3rd person, and 1st person. The game allows you to zoom in and out in 3rd person which is nice, but I noticed a lot of bugs with the camera's state machine that required a restart to fix. Getting stuck at the slanted drifting camera angle, the camera whipping around wildly, random gradual FOV changes when switching perspectives, etc. It definitely isn't indie-early-access buggy, but the lack of UI polish makes it feel clunky at times. Which is sad because the rest of the game is so perfectly executed and I love it to pieces.  8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Cloudpunk is a kind of visual novel interspersed with driving and walking through huge, multi-tiered city blocks. The city of Nivalis feels very much straight out of Blade Runner and the atmosphere and music really sells this comparison.The core plot is that you play as a country girl, Rania, who makes her way into the big city to make a living, due to problems of debt. The game focuses on the first night of Rania's job at Cloudpunk, a courier service, albeit one of questionable legality. During this night you'll be driving your vehicle around the city, delivering packages, acting as a taxi for a number of odd characters and making ethical decisions. You're accompanied through the journey by Rania's AI dog, Canus, who occupies the car, along with the Cloudpunk dispatcher. The story is delivered through voiced dialogue while you're driving from map marker to map marker, and while you're walking through the city on foot to find pick up or drop off points or people you need to talk to. I'd call the voice acting serviceable, not amazing by any means, but there are some decent moments. The writing is alright in general, and does deliver some actually some burst out laughter moments from time to time. The story, however, is not well written. It has a tendency to throw new characters, ethical dilemmas and meaningful events at you, then immediately forget about them, leaving no impact on the lasting plot. It's more like a series of vignettes than a full story, so to speak. There is an overarching plot, mind you, but it doesn't get anywhere near as much attention from the game as it deserves. The main story builds up, disappears for a while then comes back at the end, resulting in a baffling ethical decision that isn't properly led up to, and is delivered through an exposition dump at the end. It doesn't feel deserved by the main character at all, and isn't met with any particular gravity. It just happens, really. Very disappointing.It wouldn't be good scifi without some attempt at answering big philosophical questions, or attempting to reflect society, and this game does an OK to bad job. Throughout the game it hints at the ethics of following orders without considering the results of your actions, but really does not follow through with it at all. For example, one of the early missions has you delivering what your character believes to be a bomb. You can deliver it to it's intended destination, or dispose of it safely. Delivering the bomb causes it to blow something up, but it's never spoke of again. The main character kinda feels bad, that's about it. This theme of ethical questions with no follow up happens throughout the entire game, and it's disappointing.The game also makes commentary on class, race and identity, as well as what I interpret as trans rights. The class aspect is mostly childish, where all the rich people are presented as comedically silly and unethical. Some characters in the game speak radical-left rhetoric, but it doesn't really go any further than "rich man bad, i am mad" kind of stuff. There's no thoughtful criticism to be had, but I'm sure anyone who considers themselves a socialist, communist or anarchist will appreciate that someone is speaking to them.Scifi with robots or some form of synthetic lifeforms tend to like using these characters to make commentary on the meaning of being human, or use them to portray real-world social issues. Perhaps unsurprisingly, Cloudpunk uses it's android characters to make a statement on race and trans rights. Androids are portrayed to be human-like, but with some robot-like trappings such as an unnatural voice, that almost always make them stand out from humans whilst in conversation. The game dialogue mentions android civil rights, and tries to draw a comparison to African-American civil rights in the United States. It doesn't really go anywhere it, it just makes references here in there. There are also some comparison between androids and trans people. For example, an android is referred to as "human-passing", and one that feels that they are a human and needs you to acquire them some skin. Much like the civil-rights aspect, it doesn't lean into it much, though this is the first time I've seen a video game reference trans issues like this. I'm not terribly educated on the topic, but it bares mentioning.So is this an "SJW game"? It kinda is, but I see it as a reflection of the creators' politics and their goal to create a game with meaning. It feels mostly genuine to me. There are some cringe-inducing "SJW" moments in Cloudpunk, where it's politics feel preachy. But the worst of it is far between, as long as you can get over the main characters cringy hatred of rich people. There is at least a story reason for this, so I'll give it the benefit of the doubt and put it down as a constructed character flaw with some bad writing. If you're allergic to leftist attitudes, don't buy this game. People who care less will be able to tolerate this game.Moving on to presentation. Graphically, it's made using voxel-style graphics, though less voxely than that other voxel game, Minecraft. What makes this different from Minecraft is it's generous use of lighting and post-processing effects, giving it a very stunning and very Blade Runner aesthetic. The voxels tend to just melt away in the city, and you tend to not notice them most of the time. The character models just don't look great, however. The "resolution" of the voxels is much lower on the characters and give them a blocky look without the charm of Minecraft's voxel characters. I find this to be the only flaw in this games' graphics. It's by no means a deal breaker, and you spend most of the game in your car looking at the city and the road anyway. One noticeable graphical issues is around how the rain is depicted. It's simply an animated overlay on your HUD and does not change perspective. So if you look up towards the sky, the rain is now going sideways. It's a silly mistake, and I hope they patch it.The gameplay isn't particularly interesting. You drive around in your hover car, called a HOVA, getting from point A to point B using a marker system. The challenge is mostly in not crashing into other cars or the walls, and getting to a destination quick enough. If you crash your vehicle enough, you'll need to get it fixed, costing a sizeable amount of the income you receive from finishing missions. There's a limited amount of upgrades and customisations to unlock and buy, in order to increase your cars speed and handling. You'll max out your car in a couple of hours of gameplay. Fuel is also consumed while your flying around. I'm not too sure what happens when you run out, it never happened for me.Other than driving, you'll also be walking around parts of the city, in order to pick up packages, talk to people as a part of missions or deliver packages to their location. You drive to your destinations, park your car and navigate the multi-level streets on foot. They are quite maze-like, but it's more frustrating than exciting. Still, it's a great feeling walking around from an aesthetic point of view. There are some merchants around that sell food and drink, and there are collectables to grab. You'll spend maybe 20% of the game on foot, and it feels like enough to me.Other than that, there really isn't much else to say. I finished the game in around 7 hours, and I feel satisfied with that length. There's some bits of content that I missed, but I don't feel like finishing it. It's a shame, since I think I should really like this game, but I just don't. The one thing it does right is the atmosphere, but I can't recommend it just for that, even if you're really into cyberpunk aesthetics like I am. The rest of it is average to messy. At least the price is right. Buy this if you really like cyberpunk aesthetics and want a quality representation of it. Don't buy this if you want a game.

_childDocuments_.review: I will talk of the best part first, the sound! The sounds of this game would make me feel like I was actually there, if it weren’t for the graphics. The soundtrack is amazing, and is currently my favorite game soundtrack.Next up is the graphics, which could be significantly better. They are keen to Minecraft in regards to the people and other similar moving entities while moving throughout the environment. When you talk with someone, a small avatar image is shown, but the image rarely looks like the ‘Minecraft’ entity and the game has static interference over the avatar. There are situations where you are being called that this makes sense, but when speaking face-to-face with someone, the static is there too.The story line is captivating, and although it tries to keep you moving, the timeline doesn’t progress on its own; there is no world clock triggering events or causing you to miss deliveries. This allows you to ignore your current mission to go and explore, which you often are rewarded for. Overall, I intend to play this game several times through as it does offer game changing choices, the first of which is less than 5 minutes into the game.Overall, if you can get past the graphics, and you like story driven games, you will enjoy playing Cloudpunk.

_childDocuments_.review: Your name is Rania. This is your first night working for Cloudpunk, the semi-legal delivery company based in the sprawling city of Nivalis. You go everywhere, from the Marrow below to the spires that pierce the grey clouds high above before scraping the edge of the troposphere. name: The Sinking City
detailed_description: The Sinking City is an adventure and investigation game set in an open world inspired by the universe of H.P. Lovecraft, the master of Horror. The half-submerged city of Oakmont is gripped by supernatural forces. You're a private investigator, and you have to uncover the truth of what has possessed the city… and the minds of its inhabitants. An oppressive atmosphere and story inspired by the universe of H.P. Lovecraft. A vast open world that can be explored on foot, by boat, in a diving suit… High replay value thanks to an open investigation system: each case can be solved in a number of ways, with different possible endings depending on your actions. An arsenal of weapons from the 1920s with which to take on nightmarish creatures. Manage your mental health to untangle the truth behind the madness.

_childDocuments_.review: I have waited for this game for so long and... To be honest I have mixed feelings about it. The game was in some controversial situation, if you followed it you know what I am talking about. I am not sure if this is the version the dev team wanted to deliever or not. I want to start with positive things: the atmosphere is incredible! You see this gloomy, wet, dangerous and hostile city of Oakmont and you get into it. Quests were pretty well-written and interesting to complete. I did almost all of them and decided to abandon last two just because I wanted to see the ending as the final act is pretty intense. I liked the feeling of being powerless in this world as you always have no ammo and just have to either run or crawl. Monsters are pretty spooky and they can scare you. The world building is great and you are really invested in reading all the info you find. There are many references to different H.P. Lovecraft's stories and I liked it. The main character is pretty good as well. In my opinion one of the best things about it is investigations. You do real detective work and you figure out a lot during it. Loved this part.Now onto the bad things and there are a few: I wish the city lived its life. Let me explain. In the beggining of the game you see the disclaimer that says: there was segregation and discrimination and we want to show it. And they did it just for a second. I mean when I saw when two guys were kicking a citizen on a street I was like " wow, the city if alife" and then I saw the same 5 or 7 assets of citizens just patroling the circles on the street sometimes cleaning the ground for some reason or frying a rat thing. It was cool first couple of minutes and then you just don't see them as living things. I understand it's very difficult to make but during the final act when, if I am being honest, I and any other normal human being would panic, those guys are just chilling on a street. It ruins the vibe in the game to be honest. Also the game has a lot of bugs. Many NPCs are super broken and sit somewhere in the air and doing god knows what. Fighting and stealth were meh. And those damned crates and ledges! You need to be in the exact spot not an inch to the left or right to open or climb them and there could be a life or death situation. If you can put up with those problems, then you should get the game. Maybe it's a good idea to wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of both Lovecraft's work and video games, I was beyond excited when I heard about The Sinking City. And after playing through the game, I can confidently say that it is a gripping and immersive experience that truly captures the essence of Lovecraft lore.From the moment I stepped into the fictional city of Oakmont, I was immediately drawn into its eerie and foreboding atmosphere. The dark and decaying environment, coupled with the unsettling sound design, created a sense of dread and unease that stayed with me throughout my entire playthrough.One of the things that impressed me the most about The Sinking City was its attention to detail when it came to Lovecraft's stories. The developers have clearly done their research, as evidenced by the numerous references to Lovecraft's work scattered throughout the game. From the iconic Necronomicon to the various cosmic entities, every aspect of Lovecraft's lore is brought to life in this game.But what truly sets The Sinking City apart is its unique take on Lovecraft's mythos. Rather than simply retelling the stories we all know and love, the game presents a new and original narrative that is both engaging and thought-provoking. By weaving in elements of mystery and psychological horror, the game manages to keep players on the edge of their seats, never knowing what twisted truth they will uncover next.Of course, no review of The Sinking City would be complete without mentioning the impeccable visual design. The city of Oakmont is beautifully crafted, with every building and street oozing with Lovecraftian vibes. The character models are also incredibly detailed and realistic, adding to the immersive experience.I do have to mention that the game does have its flaws, particularly in its combat and technical aspects. However, these minor issues pale in comparison to the overall experience that The Sinking City offers.In conclusion, The Sinking City is a must-play for any fan of Lovecraft. It is a true love letter to his work, expertly crafting a new and captivating story within his vast and terrifying universe. If you are ready for a challenge, both mentally and emotionally, then I highly recommend diving into the depths of The Sinking City.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is a rushed game and feels like a console port on PC. The game is so lifeless and there's no polish to be seen anywhere.The city is too big for it's own good and almost all the buildings have extremely similar layouts on the insides. There's some unique environments, but it's far too little. There's a ton of duplicate building exteriors, entrances and other props that just makes it painfully obvious.The characters on the streets just pop-in right in-front of you and there's only like 3-5 different animations / actions for them to use. There's also far too little designs for them, so it's likely that you will see two similar AI next to each other. The performance of the game is just terrible too. I had the game on my NVMe and the loading times were bad as it didn't make a difference compared to my HDD. The game had stutters while loading in new data and it's also capped at 60 FPS, which just makes it feel more like a console port.The story itself is decent, but I wouldn't really recommend playing on any other difficulty than easy. There's no reason to and it would just be a waste of time if you want to play it just for the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Before we get into things, I am aware of the bad blood between the developers (Frogwares) and the publisher of The Sinking City (Nacon / Big Ben). However, I will not be factoring this into my review as I am going to review solely on its own merits and the experience I had playing it:The Sinking City is what I would call a diamond in the rough. The game itself is incredibly atmospheric, really hammering home the bleak nature of Oakmont and the state of the city, as well as the living conditions of its inhabitants. The sounds of the game, coupled with the musical melodies only help to strengthen this atmosphere.I would also like to commend the choice to embrace the "not so politically correct" aspects of H.P. Lovecraft. Many people criticise his thoughts and opinions of various groups and cultures, whilst profiting off of his Cthulhu mythos. The Sinking City features a healthy amount of moral choices, in which you can actually choose the more violent or distasteful outcomes. This will probably upset those who only enjoy idealism, and prefer stories in which everyone gets a happy ending. Personally, I prefer the added weight to the player's decisions and it helps to make these decisions feel more impactful.The Sinking City also features a strong focus on the mental instability of dealing with unspeakable horrors, leaning heavily into the sanity effects and making combat a test of both physical and psychological resolve. I played through the game with both the combat and puzzle difficulties set to medium, and I thoroughly enjoyed my time in Oakmont. The game did not hold my hand in the investigation aspects, forcing me to figure my next move, search for relevant records across the city and risk trips into areas infested with Wylebeasts to gather some resources to help prolong my own existence.Yes, the game is not perfect as there are a number of bugs, such as NPCs disappearing on the streets, or popping into reality before your very eyes. I personally feel that this actually added to the experience, rather than subtracting from it as it almost played on the "hideous visions" and uncertainty of what is real and false in the city of Oakmont.Overall, I would highly recommend The Sinking City to anyone who enjoys the Cthulhu mythos, gritty "Noire" style stories or survival horror as a genre. I purchased the game on sale for £6.99, and I had an absolute whale of a time. It definitely scratched that Lovecraftian itch for me, and left me very satisfied with what I had experienced.
