_childDocuments_.review: Very nice game.I got it from 6€ despite many complains about it feeling janky (specially the combat). I can say that combat is not the best, and performance isn't either; in two or three situations I've got the screen absolutely frozen after shooting (i think due to some problem related to the shotgun). Otherwise yes, janky combat but otherwise fine.The game feels much more menazing at the start because you have barely any resources. It's not like it's dangerous, but rather because you don't want to chase enemies with your silly spade.Now, for the last bad point... exploration doesn't feel very rewarded. You can place your own markers on the map, but plenty of times I found empty locations that I'd have to come later for a specific quest. In the end, that makes you feel like you have a whole map, but it's just not worth exploring.I learned soon that doing secondary quest is better if you don't chase them, but rather do them when you happen to be around them. Otherwise you can find yourself using all your ammo for a random objective and then find yourself unable to keep going with your actual quests.That said... I really enjoyed the game. The story is good. Ambient is very nice. The characters are OK, not great but interesting enough, and the game really forces you to think twice most of the time; neither reaching to conclussions or taking choices is easy and I think that's a great think to do in a game.I got 25 hours of gameplay for 6€ and I really enjoyed it despite its flaws. _childDocuments_.review: This isn't a bad game, just a tedious one at times. You have cases to solve using a rather complicated and not well explained system of evidence collection, picture taking and travel with markers and a map you have to keep pulling up to reference. This part of the game should be much more straight forward, as the main emphasis is on figuring out what to do next and how to get there. Getting anywhere is slow and the map can't be pinned to the playing screen so you have to keep referencing it and most of the canals have Y junctions where the path isn't clear. That and the overly dark streets and canals make for a depressing and tedious exploration. There are some icons you can use as markers across the bottom of the screen, but they are so small you can't see them, even on my 50 inch screen. No idea what most of them are for, even after hours of play. The worst part of the game for me are the slow loads after dying, which auto returns you to last checkpoint. Yes, you can load your last save, but only after a long wait for a load to the last check point. Do you really want TWO long loads? The long load times become especially tedious while trying to reach a destination in the infested zone where you actually fight seriously bad monsters that require some strategy. You usually die several times. When approaching these areas you might want to have a few aids, like explosives, on hand. While the infested areas do contain a lot to help you in that search, staying alive long enough to get to get to the materials is not fun or easy, especially with the long loads. Normally I would forage for some supplies elsewhere, but almost none of the doors you pass open, making traveling between locations both boring and unproductive. The world is reasonably large but not very interactive. More open exploration would have made the game much more interesting. A lot could be done with this game to enhance play. Given the small interest group is commands that is probably unlikely. I could have been a great series but this first outing would have to be much more engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is boring, feels empty, and makes a horrible first impression. Chambers coming to mind. You don't feel any stakes and are just "present" and, after watching a cinematic with as many frames as your average PowerPoint Presentation you wish you weren't. But that is nothing compared to the frustrating visual and sound design this game is a victim of. Maybe this game gets better after the first hour of play time, but I would rather bathe in sulfuric acid than suffer through one more minute of this. tldr; not fun

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is an investigative third-person shooter hybrid where you play a private investigator in an HP Lovecraft inspired Sandbox City. The game feels like a tuned down clone of Red Dead Redemption with a Noir skin. The quality of the presentation is noticeable, but the game is so tuned down to bare essentials, that it could never be rated as well as other famous Sandbox games.You begin your work on the docks of Oakmont, an half-submerged city, besieged by strange forces after a flood sank more than half of the roads into waterways. From the beginning, the investigate aspects of the game are introduced by short exchanges and questioning on the docks. Sinking City does not challenge the player very far with how to construct an investigation. All the tools, clues and journal notes are highlighted and updated automatically. All you need to do is look around rooms for hand icons or dots, or some premonition effects. Charles, the main character, can see illusory walls and has visions helping his work.  The only time-consuming activity investigating, is reading map coordinates as street corners, having to plot them manually on the map.Once you're acquainted enough with Reed's investigative tooling, you'll be challenged by the Wylebeasts of Oakmont. This is when you realize Sinking City isn't a very good shooter. All the beasts move so fast, they can dodge bullets. When I played, this meant, I would revert to use melee to defend myself, except against the bigger critters. You don't get a shotgun or a rifle right away in the game, but it doesn't matter because both are quite limited by the amount of bullets you find or that you can craft. Bullets are used as money in Oakmont, but you'll spend those about 3 times over the course of the entire game.The biggest issue in this game, is it's easy... To game it. The Save/Load system in Sinking City is completely brain dead. Whenever you save, if you reload, the game will have you start back at a fast travel spot, resetting all in-game containers. All the resource rarity in the game is no longer effective. All you need to do is go into a house, clear the spawning critters, loot everything, then save, then reload. Rinse, repeat. All the scenes, where you're supposed to be stressed by magical spawns of critters: Run into them, save, then reload, then run it back.Another big issue with this game, is it's not really a RPG. Yes you have a skill tree with experience and skill points you can invest in that tree, but the majority of all purchase-able skills have very little to no impact on the game. The best skills you can grab are for sparing resources crafting, so you can stop the save/reload scumming for resources. You can also increase the amount of Molotovs and Grenades you can carry so you can fast-track the poorly designed combat system. (spamming melee is still more effective imho)After roughly 50 hours of gaming in Oakmont, I completed everything I had to complete. Unlocked all the suits in the wardrobe, another decoration, and got my fill. For a game at its regular price, it's rather disappointing. I love the presentation, I love the story line, but everything else is just not worth recommending. I bought Mad Max for around 30$, regular price, and it's worth this game 3 times over.Would I check Sinking CIty 2 if it's ever published? Maybe, with a good sale, hoping Frogwares invested time in crafting game mechanics with a little more value.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Atmosphere = COOL and GROSS, Story = PRETTY GOOD, General Gameplay = NOT BAD COULD BE BETTER, Combat = MEH AT BEST, OUTRIGHT AWFUL AT WORST, Gathering and Exploration = WHERE IS EVERYTHING THIS IS A JOKE. Overall = NOT AMAZING, NOT BAD EITHER.I tentatively recommend this if you enjoy slimy seaside aesthetics of New England Lovecraftian horror. Come for the view, stay for the mystery - overall not a bad plot for a story like this though it may show its hand early by having some of the first people you talk to be the ape-like Throgmorton and the fish-like Innsmouthers, and a lot of the street names being things like Yellow King and such. I also recommend it for how varied you can approach cases with moral choices in deductions - some of which you may come to regret with information learned later in the story. The aesthetics of Oakmont and its culture somehow also present themselves as completely normal in their own world - the fact the librarian has a stitched up mouth is completely normal as a punishment in this city and you are just kind of told "it is what it is", and that works perfectly in its favor - it's a weird almost-familiar place while also being completely foreign.Middle of the road is the gameplay loop of how your investigations go as they can seem repetitive after a while unlike Frogware's Sherlock Holmes games that vary things from time to time. You will also have to navigate yourself - there are no quest icons to guide you through a mystery, if you are looking for a location you will need to find the street you are looking for on the map. You may also be taken out of the immersion with some of Frogware's self-referential humor (a large poster for Sherlock Holmes and the Case of the Creepy Watson for example), and since this game was I believe crowdfunded of COURSE they have to make the headstones and urns in the cemetery in-game dedications to their funders with funny little epitaphs and everything. You may also begin to notice that save for some deterioration placement and objects that the overall structure of most of Oakmont's interiors are identical. This gets weird once you find more than one fisherman's shack that has a ramp built from an improvised lifeboat in the middle of the room.I do not recommend this for the gathering, crafting, combat, and underwater segments. Gathering comes in the form of finding containers with a hobo symbol on it and hoping for the best but more often than not getting very little. Crafting is one of the only other ways you can get ammo - since Oakmont works off of a bartering system you cannot buy ammo and supplies (there's no bartering system either despite this, sometimes you can give someone a bullet as payment for something), and in conjunction with the gathering and how tedious it can get it's lackluster.Combat is mid at best and a miserable slog at worst. Remember how you can craft your own ammo? Even with the right skills and dedication to somehow crafting maximum ammunition, you may be unable to carry all that much and after a combat situation with the local wildlife (human and otherwise) you will find you are entirely lacking one type of ammo especially given how some enemies are incredibly dodgy - especially since it seems that the firearms are all hitscan rather than projectile (but I could be wrong). Entering melee without the skills to give you a harder hit is a terrible idea as a lot of this stuff can three shot you on easy. When you are killed in combat (on the surface) you will be transported to the nearest phone box (fast travel). This is not a checkpoint. Your ammo is still gone and you need to make more. The game has a little message sometimes that insinuates you DON'T have to get into combat, that fleeing is just fine - it even lets you throw bricks which distract foes (VERY WELL might I add, I was impressed how much attention that give which makes me hate what I'll say about the underwater section in a bit all the more infuriating), but you will be forced to engage in mandatory combat in places and it's a chore at best and outright unpleasant at worst, especially if you have been unlucky while gathering and crafting. I had to repeat several times to finish off a scripted fight because I kept failing to find materials for medkits and bullets, and my opponents had shotguns that could take half your health in one shot.The underwater sections are clunky, clunky, and clunky. Yes, I appreciate that trundling around in a deep diver suit from the 1920s underwater makes our character move like he's really heavy. I hate how they mix this with gas vents that damage you overtime if they are active which are often in places you cannot avoid them, forcing you to take damage. There are two types of potential underwater enemies as well: a tentacle that if you can significant ground from will just despawn it seems, and a sort of squid monstrosity. You are given a harpoon gun that takes until the heat death of the universe to reload sometimes to deal with some of this. The actual harpoon is merely a stun that barely works. The flare is a light that is said to distract the latter kind of enemy. Not once have I seen this actually work. Once the squid sees you it guns for you and cannot be shaken. Combine this with how vertical travel underwater (like on the surface, press spacebar near an elevated surface to climb) is INCREDIBLY finicky and difficult to navigate just right - you be smashing space at a ledge trying to find just the right place to clamber up. Fortunately these sections are not TOO long and are pretty straightforward, but I wouldn't miss much without them personally.Something that I have had difficulty placing in any sort of negative or positive way is the warning you are given upon starting the game that Frogware has opted to keep the 1920s looking like the 1920s by including the prejudices from those times present rather than pretend they don't exist. Then about five minutes into playing the game you see a black police officer who gives the white main character a really stern warning if you interact with him - I was streaming this and most of us agreed that the warning seemed to be for nothing. Then I got later into the game, walked into a building, and was shot at by Klansmen. The game is rife with xenophobia but from a more local perspective where everyone outside of Oakmont ("newcomers") are given the side eye and threatened but you never see this go to incredible extremes it seems. Theres ONE anti-German poster from World War 1 that depicts a monstrous ape in a helm (an actual piece of recruitment propaganda) but there's not much else besides the KKK. Not sure if it's depicted as bad as it could get Despite my ranting above, I cannot say I hate this game! Frogware kinda shot for the stars with this one and while they didn't quite make it, it's really cool to see them making it to the upper atmosphere at least. Just stick to the main storyline which takes about 12-13 hours to complete since most of the side quests seem to more or less be excuses to explore some samey locales. To my knowledge there are three endings that are entirely based on choices you are given at the end, each with a suitably eerie epilogue cutscene.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic.The bad reviews is because of a drama between publisher and developer; I don't know who is right and who is wrong, but I ain't going to review-bomb a great title because of it.The game is probably the best Mythos game ever made. Level design is top notch. Gameplay is adventure-like in its core, with simple combat and sneaking as a side dish. It reminds me a lot on previous Mythos game, the Call of Chulu, with its investigation system.No icon or a guide is given in the game to you for free: you have to read documents and mark things on the map by yourself. As you discover things, you get pointed towards clues, which are special type of information that can be correlated one with another, to form deductions. Deductions is how you complete your investigations, and they form an explanation for your case. Some deductions have alternatives, and depending on what you select - you'll be offered different case explanations.t sounds complicated on paper, but simplest explanation is this - take any Batman Arkham game, and its "detective mode". Everything you wanted _there_, this game has. To think of it, it sort of reminds me on LA Noire.The combat is simple: you have weapons, ammo and a melee attack. You can crouch to sneak to avoid detection. Crafting resources are scarce, and you use them to craft yourself whatever you need at the moment - medikit, more ammo, etc. You get them via quest rewards or through exploration.Final note - while exploration pays off because you get resources, just walking (or driving a boat) around this open world city is so immersive that you'll want to do it just by itself. There's a lot of weird people around, doing their thing. I saw two drunk bums fighting in the street, or a guy walking around with a backpack full of gore and guts.Storywise, I have no idea how will it go because I have barely just started - but game is totally worth its full price.Huge thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: A deeply immersive game set in the Lovecraftian world, Sinking City has been a joy to play and a strong recommendation. There's something satisfying in walking through a city during the early 1900s with your collar high on your neck and madmen walking past you muttering and talking to themselves. An eerie feeling in the air and talk of strange creatures circling around a flooded city buried in secrets.. Interesting characters with their stories and motives. Details you can find scattered around houses that complete the picture and urge you pay attention to everything. This is my first venture to the Lovecraft world in gaming and it has exceeded my expectations. It is not a perfect game however and I should note some its weaknesses. Assets and locations have been extensively reused and one can't help but noticing it even if they don't try to complete it's far-too-many side quests. Some of the side quests have had interesting stories but many others were repetitive quests of killing mobs and interacting with one or two things. This wouldn't be a problem if coupled with some variety in gameplay and design but unfortunately it is not the case. Choices matter, in a sense, in this game which welcomes a second playthrough. I, however, don't think I'll be doing so because of its dragged out side-quests and a general "fatigue" I realised I felt playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a horror game:  there  be blood, and lots of it.  This is also an AA-game with a blend of action, adventure, and RPG elements:  so there  be the expected jank -- but not so much it overwhelms the fun of the well-penned supernatural mystery, the richness of the setting, or even the enjoyment of the marginally glitchy combat.  I took in the sodden sights, inhaled the fishy aroma with savor; I farmed 's small handful of monsters with real, long-term pleasure (though the run-down apartments I fought the things in were copypasted more often than I would have liked, reproduced down to the same rotting mound of fish).  The game's deficiencies, such as they are, are counterbalanced by raw passion -- by the heady, squirming eel  of the world the devs set out to build, and by a cast of truly excellent voice actors (Reed and Throgmorton are my two favorite performances -- greasy, weatherworn gumshoe and half-monkey upper crustman have never been represented so accurately in auditory form).Story and hero:  Charles Reed is a tired-eyed detective and a traumatized ex-Navy diver, a scruffy, hardbitten man haunted by visions of sunken cities and mind-blasting Lovecraftian abominations -- visions that lead him, ultimately, to a Massachusetts town you won't find on any Rand McNally map:  Oakmont, the Eastern Seaboard's number-one locus for supernatural events, crazy cultists, aggressive corpse monsters, and fish-faced, Dagon-worshipping freaks.  Reed has come here to ferret out the wherefore of his maddening daymares, only to discover that many others are thusly afflicted, and that their own inner compasses have led them to the same creepy town.The thing you'll notice before even getting off the steamer is the concentrated quality of the tentacled, slimy, 1920s-period-eldritch atmosphere -- it's  stuff!  The city of Oakmont has recently been hit with a catastrophic flood of mystic origin, and its rotting, salt-eaten streets put one perfectly in the mind of an Americanized stab at Harlem or Venice in some gloomy, seaside sector of Purgatory.  It rains more often than not, and the damp nights feel demon-haunted indeed; the never-quite-sunrise, filtering through the perpetual overcast, is hardly less oppressive.The second thing you'll notice, however, is the aforementioned .  The refuse-strewn waters constantly clip through your motorboat; all too often, the game stutters like a shy nerd asking a girl to the school dance precisely when a wylebeast charges you; whenever you whip out your camera on the street to get a zoomed-in look at something, every hagridden inhabitant of Oakmont who takes offence at having his picture snapped gesticulates angrily  -- looking like they're breaking into the Thriller dance together.  The jank is pretty funny at times . . . and that's  it is (save for the antics of the occasional FPS gremlin when you're fighting, and a death never sets you back too far).  There are no game-breakers, nor serious frustration-makers, just funky slips and sudden smiles.We fell into this fishy, accursed, and good naturedly janky world, my brother and I, flushing pods of Stygian Harvesters of a Friday evening, rifling through the stacks at the Oakmont Public Library for clues all Saturday morning, digging up new and interesting sidequests around town that, whether they were thickly scaled snake's hands or had some tangential bearing on the main thread, were  very well-written.  The three endings were far too short to put a satisfying cap on this adventure for us, and despite our forty-odd hours with the game, we feel like the final decision came with boorish abruptness.  My Reed -- our Reed -- was a red-eyed Droopy Dog of a golden-hearted killing machine, and he deserved a grander send-off than any of those available to him.  I truly miss the man, and Oakmont too -- NoClip ghost water and back-up dancers included.

_childDocuments_.review: For all it's faults there's nothing like this game: true Lovecraftian unease in the form of an open world detective game.I was surprised when I discovered you not only have to look up leads at the police station and newspaper office but the location of people, places and things (except for a few general landmarks) all have to be placed BY HAND. You read the notes, talk to the people, find the streets and follow the clues. It really does feel like you're following your own investigation.The combat IS clunky and sometimes the ambitious outweighed the technology with a few extraneous NPCs clipping or popping into existence, but at it's best this game oozes as rare atmosphere of dread. Strange creatures skitter through the dingy piles of sodden debris. Everywhere are derelict boats and shuttered houses, some halfway submerged. While tooling around in my boat I could swear I saw tentacles slither out of sight into the depths.The voice acting is great: everyone hitting the right notes and sounding strangely grounded given that many interviewees look almost alien. But this mix of oddness and neutrality I find incredibly compelling: people who look like fish just going about their business, discussions of missing persons like this is something that happens all the time, literal monsters treated like pests that come with the territory. The lore is DEEP with factions vying for control and bloodlines having it out for other bloodlines. Some beats will be very familiar to Lovecraft fans especially but they've never been done with this kind of immersion. Go exploring! A lot of rooms simply exist to build the feeling of Oakmount as a place, like the abandoned printing presses, a statue declaring 'death from the depths' and secluded rooms used for esoteric rituals. Not every place has items, but if you're like me you aren't just looking for bullets: you want visions, scraps of paper, details about this world. Fair point the shooting is jank and at best standard. It almost didn't need to be here except maybe to keep you on your toes. But the core gameplay is solid, exploration is fun, and if you look there's no telling what you'll find.

Weird things here and there regarding progression that made me think "Uhh...sure, why not.". It played on the "madness" well, everything was unknown to you, eerie atmosphere with a great, eerie ambient soundtrack to go with it. That being said, gameplay isn't anything special. Combat isn't great, it's very clunky but you get used to it after a while (or just run away unless the game forces you to fight which isn't too often). Ammo is scarce, you'll have to craft ammo and other items. You talk to people, you get evidence, you piece together the evidence to form conclusions in "The Mind Palace". I thought it was a cool idea, however, some of the evidence "connections" seemed completely unrelated to one another and the conclusions drawn from them seem out of the blue. I had to turn my brain off for that one.  Also, you may know where a location is, however if you didn't discover or learn of the location in a way that the game intended you to then it won't let you progress unless you do it the way the game intended. It wasn't terrible, but it definitely led to a lot of backtracking. At a certain point this game turns into "Fast travel here, gather evidence, fast travel here, talk to this person to get more evidence, make mind palace conclusions, fast travel here, gather evidence, form conclusion, mission complete". Once you unlock fast travel points you learn that walking is for peasants. All in all, I liked the game but it's not for everyone. I'm a simple man, I see Lovecraftian/Eldritch horror game, I buy.

_childDocuments_.review: When a game proposals a story based on Lovecraft's tales, it’s important to reminisce that it’s an adaptation and interpretation of the writers and developers. So there won’t be an idealized Lovecraftian game, but rather a narrative bet from various points of view in the imaginative process of the game. This is the problem when people confuse the narrative ideal, the idealization of what should be and creative inventiveness. Let the game tell for itself.On the other hand, if you discern  games well, you’ll immediately understand that its gameplay elements are based on the detective style of . The similarity rests in a logic, but its difference for this game consists in an unfeasibility of elucidation in situations that exceed human understanding. The game develops in a noteworthy way the paranormal, the madness or the cosmos approached from a materialist point of view. Demented visions are whispers of incomprehensible entities. The human is nothing more than an insignificant and futile piece of matter whose destiny is to serve as a pawn to the other gods.The story takes place on a city not found on a map with the name of the Oakmont. Charles Reed, a private detective and survivor of the Great War, persuaded by visions and cases of people from Boston ending up there, decides to investigate what’s happening. He realizes that the city had an inundation whose cause is enigmatic. Furthermore, he discovers that many people have similar visions: a city sinks and a creature lives in the ocean. It’s for this reason that almost everyone is attracted to Oakmont.Albert Throgmorton in his last desire advises about the endless cycle, where Cthylla the daughter of Cthulhu can be awakened or kept asleep by the seed, the chosen one. Charles unearths that he’s the seed, whose purpose will guide him to choose the fate of humanity and the dreamer's daughter.I’ve been spellbound by the way the story developed. The plot is performed through cases as chapters. The game efforts to immerse us by searching for clues to the facts. With them we gradually discover the development of the plot and the destiny of the protagonist. The storyline successfully provides an enigmatic and incomprehensible air as we encounter scenarios and events related to unknown divinities. There’s an impression of supernaturalism and madness attached to the Lovecraftian gods. The narrative becomes dense and pessimistic with each step we take in the progress of the story. Which the game achieves by providing us a horror tale where the character has an insignificant destiny.The game has main and secondary cases (side quests). Some of them have an unnerving and spooky stories that they integrate into the context of the city. This is how it tries to be immersive through its plot. As if that weren’t enough, the script conveys a gloomy impetus without becoming lyrically dark. It’s simple, modest, but with personality expressed in each character in the game. The dialogue is polyphonic with a selection of several responses. It’s logical, but inside it has quite a bit of a cryptic enigma where the conjecture is the vision, the madness and the creatures of a nightmarish world.The characters have outstanding voices and the clues in the lines of dialogue be conspicuous a lot. The animation is decent (such as gestures, facial expressions, or footage); and what’s worth noticing is the contextualized and detailed setting. The game is open world. It’s set in the 20's. To get inside, it becomes atmospheric and decomposed, mouldy and off. The dwindling lighting makes things pale and because of the colour palette —without the constraint of marine colours. Although it does combine architecture with marine facets such as corals and dead fish. Also the city has changes in time and weather. This provides the illusion of transition and movement.The context of the city also reveals oppositions between rich and poor, which manages to represent the circumstances of how its citizens live —a hermetic city that rejects outsiders. Thus the game is usually detailed. But don’t confuse it with coherence and hyperrealist, because it isn’t a simulator. Certain cases have details and niceties, they’re part of the setting, character, and environment or it’s a narrative image. A case where a foetus came out, its detail consists of seeing footprints on the walls and floor, giving that intrigue to know where it went. Or people walking at night offers a feeling of being in a city that never sleeps since it’s part of story. Under no circumstances do they want to sleep or they’ll end up perishing in an unspeakable way.The city has vivacity, life and verve, this is reflected in the behaviour of its inhabitants in a disturbing, hallucinating, common or particular way. Although they’re spawned in a procedural and spontaneous way, they still manage to give a feeling of partaking with them in their city. Although not everything is a city —it looks like a Lovecraftian Venice between canals and streets —there’re also underwater explorations and caverns where it propounds us another ambiance and sensation. It’s petrifying and eerie at sea, while on the surface it’s cryptic and enigmatic. Various stories and sects are interwoven. The game has achieved to present an immersive world with an attention-grabbing story.The game is integrates of main and secondary quest, all of them as cases. Because the game is open world, we must look for clues in other places to specify and connect the evidences to expose the fact. For many this was difficult due to the need for deductive ability and intuition. For example, evidence may be hidden in plain sight or to search for information you ought to proceed to a specific location (patient location = hospital, suspects = police department). If you’re not used to it, with time and patience everything will be more affordable due to the learning path at all times.The game is oriented towards the survival horror type, where you must manage resources to craft ammo, meds or supplies. The character has a sanity bar that’s affected by situations such as combat, seeing bodies or hallucinating. If your bar is reduce, you’ll have visions, a great thing is to offer disturbing images while you go crazy, and they’ll produce a damage. The goal is to solve the cases, explore and survive.In many places you’ll obtain supply boxes. There’re also dangerous places infested with creatures. Each action performed, by the way, will earn you experience points. You can exchange them for some skill. Personally, there were skills that never worked for me, so I had extra points to spare. Telephone booths allow quick travel. Everything is reasonable as detective gameplay that’s paced as the player desires.The game draws inspiration from Lovecraft’s stories, adapts it with contextual weaves of the epoch and the madness that comes from visions of ancient gods. It’s a human story but amalgamated with the unknown. It also takes reference from other games related to cosmic horror, whose city is in a struggle for power at the hands of worshipers of Hastur, Dagon or Cthulhu.It’s a game with an interesting story. You can also unlock outfits as rewards for solving cases, which is motivating. The bad thing is that I didn't like the DLC, I don't consider it necessary to have the full experience of the game. It’s an unnecessary extension. This is another alternative narrative set in a Lovecraft-style world that’s worth a look. As if peering into the precincts of the abyss, whose pulsating stars are nothing more than cold reflections of enormous mirrors hanging in the immensity of infinity.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is a very different take on a Lovecraftian game, with its more open structure and a focus on gathering clues and unraveling mysteries. In this sense, it's more true to the Cthulhu Mythos experience and the Call of Cthulhu RPG than officially licensed games of the same name. The writing is very strong, the voice acting is good, and visually the game captures the essence of what it's going for very well. The designs of characters like Innsmouthers with Deep One blood are some of the best I've ever seen, and the game pulls from parts of the Lovecraft canon that I've never seen represented in a game before. It also doesn't shy away from the racism of the time period, which is a bold choice that I appreciated.That being said, it isn't without its flaws. Despite having a rig that meets the recommended specs, the game suffered from framerate drops and stutters that I couldn't remedy no matter what I tried. The crafting system isn't very robust, many of the building layouts are identical, and the lack of item storage means that quest rewards will frequently be wasted because you'll already be carrying the maximum amount of the item in question. Combat is fine, but nothing special; in my experience the shotgun has a serious problem where firing it causes a massive frame-drop that lead to me dying more than once (though I can't find anyone else reporting this issue, so it may not affect you.) And despite the excellent story, the endings are very underwhelming; much like Deus Ex: Human Revolution, they boil down to you picking from one of three choices at the end regardless of what you've done up to that point, and the endings themselves are short and not very satisfying.All that being said, the journey to get there is an entertaining one. If you're a big fan of the Mythos like I am, The Sinking City is more than worth putting up with its flaws for. If you're not as invested in the Mythos but still enjoy a game with a strong focus on investigating mysteries, I'd also recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I came here from playing other Frogwares games (Sherlock series) and thought I'd give this a try too. I enjoyed the world building and the Lovecraftian nature of the game. I definitely got jump scared a few times with monsters appearing suddenly, but for the most part any scariness was more along the lines of creepy and thinking "what the hell is going on here?" Some folks might want something even scarier, but I was happy with the unsettling creepiness/uneasiness. I would also say many of the choices in game don't really feel like a choice between good and bad and instead one between bad and worse. Even though it was sometimes hard for me to choose, I appreciated the moral dilemma and difficulty. I'm looking forward to seeing what the Sinking City 2 is like when it comes out.I will say that I think there was a bit too much running around. I had a similar complaint when I played Sherlock Holmes: Chapter One. Personally, I think the game would've benefited from a smaller map. Especially since much of Oakmont feels rather empty and you don't get much reward for exploring either through interesting loot or side stories. I ended up doing everything there was to do in the game and I can say I enjoyed most of it, however I wouldn't recommend doing any "side case" that involves searching for more than three or so items. These were just fetch quests without much reward besides some experience and a new outfit. You also learn some lore though these cases, but it's all through reading and although it was interesting, I don't think I would deem it worthwhile. Obviously if you really like the combat then maybe it would be worth it since most involve clearing out an area and finding something. I bought the game on sale so I can't say whether I would be satisfied with it if I paid full price. Thinking about the overall experience, I do think $40 is a fair price.

_childDocuments_.review: ### The Sinking City - A Dive into Lovecraftian Mystery**Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)**#### Pros:**Atmospheric World-Building:** The Sinking City excels in creating a richly detailed, eerie atmosphere. The city of Oakmont is filled with dark, moody streets, crumbling buildings, and an omnipresent sense of dread that captures the essence of Lovecraft's work.**Intriguing Storyline:** The narrative is compelling, with a well-crafted mystery that keeps you engaged from start to finish. The investigation mechanics are solid, and the story does a great job of blending personal and cosmic horror.**Freedom of Exploration:** The game offers a large open world to explore at your own pace. The city is filled with side quests and hidden details that reward thorough exploration.**Engaging Investigation Mechanics:** Using the Mind Palace system to piece together clues feels satisfying and encourages you to think critically about the evidence you gather.**Creepy Creatures and Visuals:** The monster design and overall visual style effectively convey the horror theme, making encounters with the unknown genuinely unsettling.#### Cons:**Clunky Combat:** Combat can feel awkward and clunky at times. The aiming mechanics are not as smooth as they could be, and enemy AI can be frustrating.**Repetitive Quests:** Some side quests and activities can become repetitive, involving a lot of backtracking and similar objectives.**Technical Issues:** The game suffers from occasional bugs and performance issues, including frame rate drops and texture pop-ins.**Limited Fast Travel:** The lack of a robust fast travel system can make traversal tedious, especially when required to move back and forth across the map frequently.**Voice Acting and Dialogue:** While the main storyline is well-written, some of the voice acting and dialogue can feel stilted and out of place.#### Summary:"The Sinking City" is a must-play for fans of Lovecraftian horror and detective games. It nails the atmosphere and provides a captivating mystery that keeps you hooked. Despite some technical and gameplay hiccups, the experience of uncovering the dark secrets of Oakmont is well worth the time. Dive in if you dare, but be prepared for a few rough waters along the way.Would I recommend it? Absolutely, especially if you're into story-driven games with a heavy emphasis on exploration and atmosphere. Just be ready to forgive some of its mechanical flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a very good game. In this short review, I will first state the bad, then the neutral, third the good things about it, and finally my general assessment of the game. The bad:My computer isn't really good enough to run the game properly, but luckily I could still play the game through. Several times the game almost froze during combat, but I still managed. Loading times may be a bit long, but that wasn't a big problem for me. The scarcity of ammunition in the game annoyed me a bit, but ammo was not that important anyway. The player character is a bit too clumsy and inept at climbing, running, and such - even incapable of jumping; but that doesn't matter much in the end. The guns were very unrealistic though, and even had made up names. I would have preferred real names and more realism in their use. The neutral:The game uses an autosave and load mechanic that I usually don't like, but this time it was done well enough: evidence discovered before the character's death remains discovered upon autoload, which is nice. I generally prefer first person view for immersion, but I guess the third person view in this game was needed to show the effects of insanity on the player character.The good:The game excels in the story, with the Lovecraftian elements especially.  The atmospheric music is very good and well suited for the game. The insanity effects are quite nice as well. The voice acting is very good too. The way investigation is done is a really good idea, and I enjoyed using the archives etc. to find the clues. The psychic ability was well done as well.Overall assessment:Generally speaking, while the game might not have great basic mechanics, the good aspects of the game by far outweigh the bad. Especially fans of Lovecraftian cosmic horror will love this game!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give this a thumbs-sideways if i could. A lot of good things happening here in this game. HOWEVER, I played 30 hours and I only did a few side quests before just tunneling through the main quest to finish things. After about 10 hours...it got pretty tedious and even boring. Crafting bullets is broken and lacking, monsters are the same few kinds and the hit boxes seem to change like the wind. There is lots of fetch questing and nothing in between the areas you have to travel between. The plot is fast and loose and leaves you very confused and exposition is almost all in reading notes. Graphically, it looks nice, but is not anything extraordinary. It is reminiscent of fallout as far as that goes. I recommend it for the experience as there are great points to the game and its a nice addition to the Lovecraft horror genre overall. But...just know what you're getting yourself into here and don't expect to be blown away. The endings were quick and anticlimactic and none of my choices mattered in the end.

There's no Sierra/Lucasarts stupid item interaction ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ here. The combat makes sense thematically, but isn't fun and is not worth engaging with at a higher difficult level. The endings are all miserabilist bummers, which in an odd way are somehow more and less in keeping with Lovecraftian themes than the rest of the game. _childDocuments_.review: 5 hours into this game I was frustrated, bored and ready to quit and leave a negative review. Then I looked up some guides, reduced the difficulty to easy so I didn't spend hours searching for ammo to fight the bullet sponge basic enemies (ammo is rare and bullets for every gun need to be crafted) and figured out how to navigate the detective system. After that the game just felt so much better. Locations were easier to find, enemies didnt just soak all your resources and the main and side quests felt engaging and much more fluid.Following this line of gameplay makes the game feel like GTA Lovecraft. Its flawed, buggy but also beautiful and grim with some dark subject matter but engaging and fantastic detective moments. Learning about locales, suspects, organisations and the threat behind the flood is all very immersive.The Sinking City is a weird one to recommend as its extremely niche. Behind the jank and the flawed interface and gameplay there is a rough diamond waiting to be discovered. If you are an eldrich horror fan that enjoys deep one mythos and can handle a large map with constant travel, exploration, fish people and KKK vs Monsters vs Insane cults and recycled environments its a must play. Do yourself a favor though, turn down the difficulty. I was reluctant to do so but the game is not that hard, just frustrating for the non hardcore audience.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is a fun game that would be much better enjoyed if you're familiar with the Cthulhu mythos and short stories. It suffers from forgettable combat, lack of impactful choices, some technical problems and a map that is too large for its own sake, but it has an outstanding atmosphere and some good choices in visual design as well as somewhat interesting mechanics, which makes it a somewhat memorable experience that should take somewhere between 15-25 hours to complete (without DLC, which I didn’t play, nor do I intend to). You play as Charles Reed, a detective who, driven by hallucinations reaches the city of Oakmont. Oakmont is an amalgam of Atlantic northern towns in the US, and it draws inspiration from multiple locales found in short stories by H.P. Lovecraft, namely Innsmouth. Within this city, Charles will need to make use of his detective skill, namely via locating specific places in the game map, and deducting information from sources as police reports, newspapers, medical records and records in the city hall. After getting information, Reed then proceeds to the “Mind Map” in which he connects all the available pieces of information and deducts outcomes and so on. This is by far, the most interesting element of the game and I found it quite fun, however, is for the most part just a bunch of menus and the process of deducting information is not as involved as I would have liked. It’s a great mechanic, that I hope is refined and improved in future games by the developers.Combat is not terrible, but it is forgettable and just not very fun, namely because Charles Reed is very sluggish to control and aiming, while serviceable, is just not good enough to make it an enjoyable experience. Resource management also comes into play, since on some occasions is just better not to fight. In my opinion, to increase the enjoyment, reduce the difficulty level of combat. There are two different choices for difficulty: One for combat and another one for the number of hints given to solve the cases. This last one, the default level seemed good enough, since more difficult levels only differ in notifying whether all the clues have been gathered in a location or not.The game provides you with multiple choices on almost every main quest and side quest, but none of them feel particularly impactful. For example, early in the game, in one of the side quests two factions are looking for a mirror. If you take the time to listen to both factions’ goals, you realize that they both want the same thing. I think this would be a great opportunity to try to broker a collaboration between the two, but no. Despite Charles knowing both, the game forces you to choose one or the other. In general, choices don’t really matter all that much, save for the final one, but I’ll briefly discuss that (no spoilers) at the end.My main criticism for the game is the map. Is just too large for its own good and it is subdivided into seven sections, but most of them are just not that visually distinct enough to tell them apart. I mostly remember three sections: The wealthy area, the port and the poor area. Furthermore, most of the map can’t be explored on foot because of flooding, which forces you to traverse the town on a boat. This way of traversal doesn’t really add too much to the experience, and I think that the map should have been at least 25% smaller; this is evident since the northern most area was clearly cut during development (You can only explore about half of it, the rest is blocked). But having said that, the game has an amazing atmosphere, and it does gel very well with some of the ideas and fears explored in some stories of H.P. Lovecraft, namely “The Shadow over Innsmouth”, and it serviceably explores some ideas about racism, tradition, filial obligation ion an acceptable manner. However, it does not explore any Lovecraftian thematic in any meaningful or interesting way. It is a fun game, but I would argue that other games explore in a more interesting way ideas and themes commonly attributed to Lovecraft, such as Eternal Darkness, Bloodborne, Alan Wake and Control. This is particularly evident in the choices made towards the end of the game, which fall squarely in line with what you expect from a Lovecraft and nothing more. It is a fun game if you’re familiar with the stories and are interested in the detective mechanics, but otherwise it may not be as enjoyable for the rest of the audience.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, 7/10. Pros: Great atmosphere, interesting story, interesting investigation mechanics that are novel but not too challenging, chock full of Cthulhu Mythos lore/easter eggs/etc. If you dig atmosphere, this game is for you.Cons: Gameplay, while functional, can be repetitive, especially combat. No real boss fights or enemy variety, which is weird for a game where your potential bestiary is the wildly diverse Cthulhu Mythos. Combat is never particularly difficult or varied. A *lot* of recycled interiors and NPC models. The open world, while sufficiently dreary, is pretty empty with almost nothing to interact with outside of the quests themselves and random loot chests. NPCs on the street cannot be interacted with in any way aside from combat, but there are no loot drops or XP for killing them. There are no random encounters out on the streets, which I think would have spiced things up a lot. The various interpretations for clues usually leads to a simple binary choice about quest outcome.I would like to see a remake and/or sequel of the game that addresses the above issues, particularly the enemy variety, interactivity of the world, and NPCs being literally anything aside from just background filler. Still, I had a great deal of fun and think that overall the games positives outweigh its negatives. I'll likely play this again in a year or so.

_childDocuments_.review: Much like the works of H.P. Lovecraft, this game is a puzzle or a paradox.Lovecraft was a well-know racist and a bigot. This much is undeniable. Even for the people of his time, his views were exceptionally vile and repulsive, born out of an extreme ignorance about people living in the world outside his home town. But while the man himself was ghoulish, it's equally undeniable that his work, spawned by that very same ignorance and bigoted fear, hit upon something deep and meaningful in the human psyche. The fear of insignificance in the face of the cosmic unknown, which he codified with his work, has struck such a profound chord that he has become one of the foundational authors of modern literature. is as close as we've gotten to an H.P. Lovecraft version of : a sprawling, open world saturated with references to literature and mythos, capturing the tone of the original work inside an original story.  accomplishes this for Lovecraftian literature. In this regard it is a resounding success.Unfortunately it's also a game that shows its budget limitations right out the gate. It's janky, buggy, very repetitive and it does not escape the trap many open world games fall into, that of being filled with "content" rather than *story*. The multiple fetch-quests that send you searching for various nondescript trinkets are evidence of this; I would have taken one single voice-acted and original quest instead of 5 serialized item fetch quests.Combat is another problem: it's kind of a chore, and not entertaining. I *get* what they were trying to do: giving you minimal resources and making you face against overpowering odds in a judicious manner captures the spirit of the  TTRPG, where fighting is usually a death sentence. Rather than an expansion of combat, what this game needed was a focusing of it. Fewer guns, but more effective and more impactful ones, with better animations and feedback.This game's strong points are its vision, its design and its atmosphere. It knows  what tone to capture and how to manufacture a feeling of hopelessness and gloom mixed with cosmic awe. The enemy monsters, the wylebeasts, and actually an unsung triumph of creature design. The weather system is perfectly designed to make Oakmont feel as miserable as it needs to. The worldbuilding strikes an excellent balance between pulpy 1920s hard-boiledness and the unspeakable Lovecraftian weirdness undergirding every aspect of life in the city. The writers should be commended for all the excellent work they did.On that last note - as far as I'm aware, the publisher Nacon acted very badly towards the developers of this game, Frogwares, and the Steam version of this game is lacking patches and features of the finished product (available on Gamesplanet). There is a guide on Steam for how to enable those features in the Steam version of the game for those interested.7.5/10 - flawed, but the passion and dedication that went into  are evident. Frogwares has much to be proud of.

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER: Third Person Shooters and RPGs generally aren't my favored game genres.TLDR; If you like RPGs and/or Lovecraftian games then try this game out.What I liked:    - The "madness" mechanic: hallucinations, suicidal thoughts, etc.    - Eerie environments - Fantastic use of random creepy sounds and unfounded dramatic music crescendos.  It kept me on my toes and even continued to "get me" with jump scares in the last hour of the game.    - Interesting world    - Best "gentle guidance" compared to all the other Detective/Story driven games I've ever played: "hobo" signs, land marks, amber/green "good"/"great" detective indicators, case book, map marking, etc.    - Imperfect Moral Decisions - Much like Dead of Winter's Crossroad's card, there was hardly ever a good decision to make.  I like that in a game.What I didn't like:    - Even though the "gentle guidance" was the best I've encountered, it was still easy to get lost.  Mildly unclear where to "research" facts/clues.  Also, sometimes an unobtrusive piece of evidence in a non-crime-scene(?) location was the single key to unlock the next chapter of the story missions.  The last two story missions were lousy for this.    - There are bugs.  They're not game crashing bugs.  They're still annoying though.  Glitched animations: monsters stuck in walls, monsters walking through walls, NPCs hovering, weird clothing animations, etc.  PRO TIP: Don't strand yourself by running a dinghy on dry land/a dock.    - The passerby animations are lazy.  NPCs walk into dead ends and disappear.  NPCs randomly change direction for no apparent reason.  NPCs spawn in locations they probably shouldn't have.I enjoyed the game but it got a bit mundane towards the end.  I liked this better than the Call of Cthulhu game.  I don't think this game has good replay value though.  Full disclosure... I received this game as a Christmas gift (who does that?!) but I'm not receiving any compensation for anything.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking CityDetective Reed arrives at an island city flooded by unusual weather and cursed with strange creatures called Wyldbeasts.After embarking from your ship you are greeted and given your first set of missions in the warf, your first encounter with wonky investigated skills and combat become very apparent, Jarring even... the setting and warn city looks amazing even though some graphics and poppin on ultra seem obvious..The music and voice acting is also pretty ok, I like some of the character models they went with and how some of the missions develop... though there some major glaring issues to accompany the bad combat / bullet sponges enemies and speculative research..The way you have to travel through the city is... f*cking boring.. I wish there was more to interact with, I feel the size and scope was to ambitious for this Dev team, fast travel sucks because you have to travel to a spot.. then fast travel to another location, very tedious, the side missions besides being forgettable are very hard, I will walk into a house I need to explore and swarmed by huge enemies that all my ammo can't seem to kill, then you are left with this garbage melee attack that is slow and can't be interrupted when swarmed.Lots of glitches, items in my inventory getting lost or can't craft, clues in your journal is incredibly vague and you have to find all the locations regardless how important it is, nothing populates your map with out finding certain streets to fill it in on your own time...Overall I found it very encumbersome to do anything, investigations are oddly done, zero and I mean zero f*cking hand holding, good luck idiot is how I feel this game treats me, the weapons suck and do very little damage for the highly limited ammo you get, lastly.. its not scary or even that suspenseful, I don't care about the world since it's half baked and I can't seem to get deeper into the lore.A honest, unfortunate 6/10I really couldn't recommend this game at 45$, maybe 5-10$ on sale.Give the regular asking price I say this is a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a charming experience with an absolutely amazing ambience of the Lovecraftian dark and dreary Mythos. It features a lot of interesting mechanics that put you right in the shoes of a private investigator that actually has to work to puzzle all of the evidence together to get a result, which is surprisingly enjoyable - a lot of games get that element to be frustrating not fun - but not , here it is a pleasure. The whole thing is glitchy to seven hells. If you fully embrace the concept, that the main character is just an unreliable narrator, and all that happens is just a wild fever dream, as his mind succumbs to madness, it does not break the immersion as much. It still feels lazy on the end of the devs. Nothing game breaking tho!Everything feels like a one giant fetch quest. Especially the side missions are just pointless in the grand scheme of things. Which is just a shame really. Just a bit more effort would go a long way.Choices don't matter. They just don't. Do what you like, it will not impact your story or the city in any meaningful way.Whole of the scenery is just beautiful. Attention to detail is fantastic. Bit a shame that every single interior is the same. Every warehouse is the same warehouse. Every living apartment is the same apartment. Lazy.The underwater segments are just plain boring and repeatable. Most of the time I wish I could just skip them. Which is just sad because you can see how much work was put into level design. Why Frogwares, just why?Overall the story is engaging. The characters make me care about some of them, sadly there is little to no follow up, no impact on the world whatsoever.You kind of expect from a Lovecraftian tale to be scary. It is not. Not a single part of it. And the breaking whats left of immersion with the stupid jokes? C'mon "the creepy Watson"? And all the gravestones? Could you please take your game seriously? it feels like the Exec was an unpaid intern. Good grief. The story is decent. Mechanics are great. It could be just so much more. So much more.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has stunning graphics, and pretty manageable gameplay. I struggle with 'you should really just run not fight' and get myself eaten in infested zones a fair bit, but other than that, I enjoy it. The investigation part is very fun, and the setting really interesting. I love Lovecraftian themed games, and it's nice to have the sort of grungy, dilapidated feeling that the Fallout games give me in one of them. The monsters are suitably nightmare material, and the characters are very well modeled. My biggest complaint is that every sitting npc seems to have a 80% chance of spawning floating over their seat, which is funny but a bit immersion ruining. The visuals are the opposite of accessible. If you have trouble with motion sickness, warping visuals, etc, just don't play it. The sanity mechanic warps your vision as it degrades, and this can't, to my knowledge, be turned off. This means that it can get rough even for myself, who has very little motion sickness issue in games, to play for a long time without disorientation and nausea. They pretty much make you feel as gross as the character does, which is not ideal.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. You could tell there were some budget limitations--reused locations and cut scenes,  and the city, while vast, often felt very empty, with very few places you could actually visit. NPCs were also super basic--they had no interactions, and they mostly walked around like zombies. It would have been nice to have a few more side quests. The story, however, was a lot of fun--a nice Lovecraftian/detective noir combo. I would have liked more insight into the characters. We learn very little about our hero, and the character of Van Der Berg (or whatever his name was) was a particularly glaring lapse. Any time you meet a well dressed, stereotypically German character with spectacles, you are going to suspect them of being evil, and it was never entirely clear to me what the guy wanted or why. There were lots of other characters you meet once and then never get to interact with again. I can only imagine what this dev could do if they had more money to flesh out the world and put more, well, stuff in it. I didn't think any of the cases were particularly challenging, and 90% of the effort was the time it took from point A to point B. A particularly annoying part was that, if you died, you'd go back to the nearest save location (the phone booths), which were often very far from where you'd been (cue retracing of steps, over and over, especially if you're bad at combat, like I am).  The enemies and locations could get very same-samey after a while. Most of the houses and buildings had the same layout, with only a few of the furnishings changed, and everything started to look identical after a while. All these quibbles aside, I enjoyed the story, and thought there was some good worldbuilding here. The environment and atmosphere, while heavy on the "gross"/body horror, was right in line with the grotesque/horrific and otherdimensional Lovecraft vibes. How a city full of ape and fish (ahem, "fisk") people living travel distance from Boston has gone unnoticed by the world, and why everyone didn't just leave and go somewhere else after the flood, remain my primary unanswered questions.  Oh, and for a small city, there sure are a lot of cults, gangs, and nefarious organizations.  Anyway, I do recommend this one, although be prepared for a little tediousness, especially when traveling by wonky rowboat.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say anything for the people that lost their DLC. That really sucks, but I did have something similar happen with Control (bought the ultimate edition on steam, and cannot buy the DLC which it said was include (it wasnt) because of the code or something?) Anyways, I guess something similar happened to people with this game. I now buy games without DLC included because for some reason its okay for Steam to screw users over like that? Anyways, the core game itself if you are a Lovecraft fan/fanatic you will deeply enjoy. Many things come directly from his mythos, and there are definitely things that are either expanded upon/interpreted within the universe he set up. There is a huge push for psychological/cosmic horror in this game as you would expect with it being based on Lovecraft's works. The good:The voice acting, core story, and gameplay are generally great. It has an interesting premise, solid voice acting cast. the story has plenty of characters and different choices you can make throughout the game. (Deciding to turn people in or not, deciding their fate in a sense). The mix of FPS with horror/survival is fairly balanced and the shooting feels good enough for what they are doing. The bad:There are definitely certain things that could be improved within the game graphically. I had some strange artifacting in one room during a mission, and I have only played a few hours so far, so I cannot say if it happens too often. It was only in one small portion of the room but basically a black line appeared (made of what appeared to be a bunch of triangles) that moved around the screen slightly as you moved. The ugly:Some of the cutscenes seem to have something off... not sure how to describe it, but one seen it was almost as if it was rubberbanding like you would in a multiplayer FPS when your connection is poor? I do not believe it is my PC as the current specs are all less than three years old, and still considered lower end high tier. (2700x, 2080Ti)I have also seen cutscenes that run flawlessly. Sometimes there's jitteriness, but it seems to quickly resolve itself and only be between a cutscene ending and the gameplay beginning. Also, the game does not do a whole lot of explaining outside of text screens. You basically have to read everything that you want your character to do and teach yourself each thing. Most games have some sort of tutorial that will go over the basic mechanics of the game. This game kind of just throws you in, and then doesn't say anything about any of the controls, or anything. ... for me this is not a big deal at all as I'm an avid fan for challenging games, but do think it is a drawback to many casual players. Overall the game runs  smooth, but could definitely use some improvements in some areas. I haven't had any unreasonable loading times, or huge frame drops. The core gameplay feels tight, has interesting mechanics, and the story is excellent. Lovecraft fans will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: The depressing atmosphere in this game is absolutely on point, instilling an overlying sense of dread, and if that's what you came here for, great. For those looking at the "Third-Person Shooter", bluntly, this isn't really it. Of course you wouldn't expect superb combat mechanics in a game about solving and unravelling mysteries, but the game's main combat can feel slow or uninspired consisting of primarily a point and click style with little to no mechanics. Of course there are different types of weapons but it's more of putting a bandage on a bullet hole when it comes to the game's enemies with ai and placement that rather challenge the player to sneak around or think critically about their actions, enemies are simple bullet sponges to brute force through.=Spoilers maybe??=The story in The Sinking City is incredibly well made in it's world building, however this is the reason why the ending of the game happens to be so disappointing , consisting of a simple choice between 3 options, where none of your decisions throughout the game actually matter. Leaving the game ending on a horribly anti-climatic note.

Voice acting is stellar, atmosphere is downright brilliant, the investigative bits are easy (or can be hard depending on your difficulty) and without being a diehard of a fan of the Lovecraft mythology this is very good. _childDocuments_.review: A very fun detective thriller experience set within Lovecraft mythos.  You play as private investigator Charles Reed in the cursed city of Oakmont, Massachusetts circa 1920.  Plagued by horrid visions, you set out to cure yourself of these nightmares, only to discover you are living in something much worse.  The game is gorgeous and the game play I would best describe as a survival horror LA Noire written by H.P. Lovecraft.  You interrogate witnesses, solve crimes, and defend yourself from abominations with a very limited supply of resources so use them sparingly.  An excellent choice for anyone who is a fan of true Lovecraftian horror, with references to his work such as Cthulu and Dagon.  Your choices matter as far as narration is concerned, but ultimately you will end up with three choices to end your journey with. What kind of man will Charles Reed become?  Will he solve the mystery of what is tearing Oakmont apart and save the innocent along the way?  Or will he fall victim to the evils that torment him?  Its up to you to decide.  A great story.  Worth playing.  As you always should with any Steam title, whether its a AAA or indie title,  try to get it on a discount because why pay full price when you don't have too?

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game immensely. I have always liked the ideas of Lovecraft and the monsters he thought up. If you go through the story on your own, then you are much smarter than me sir!

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, the Cthulu Mythos as well as the 20's setting really makes it feel you are a character in Lovecraft's story. I have not played many detective games, or even games where you occasionally have to be a detective, but this is by far the best one I have played. The cases are interesting, the fact that the outcome changes depending on how thorough you are as well as the fact that you have alternative conclusions really help this game stand out. Furthermore I always liked solving the cases, it really helped me practice lateral thinking and I felt very smart when my intuitions were correct. Even when I was wrong I didn't mind as it provided an opportunity to learn.I also like the crafting system, very basic but enjoyable enough and does not distract from gameplay. The combat is also simple but effective.There are some problems however.1. (Spoiler for this one): Bullets are meant to serve as currency in the game, however you only spend bullets once or twice in the entire game. I don't like this as you can earn bullets for jobs but there is nothing to use them on except combat.2. The game is sometimes too rigid, ironic for a lateral thinking game, for example I found out the address of a house for the quest. However I had to specifically go to find the address in records before I could actually proceed, despite literally finding the house beforehand.3. The open world is very underdeveloped. Many houses have exactly the same interiors, This made it feel very copy/paste for a lot of cases and discouraged exploration. It occasionally got to the point where I could literally predict where the clues or supplies were because I knew where they were in countless other copies of the houses.4. The NPC'S are daft, the NPC's are doing their own thing whilst you play, that is nice but occasionally it can be bad. A lot of NPC's will fight, harm or even murder each other, the other NPC's just walk along as though nothing happened. I even tried to intervene a few times and the police tried to attack me! It wasn't part of the case but I was still stopping a random murder! Also its dumb that if you clear a house full of monsters, if you pop outside for a moment the police will assume you are hostile and attack you. Once I even cleared a house only for a policeman to blast me with a shotgun just as I arrived outside! Ridiculous!4. I liked how the player character can have different outfits, but I hated how every cut scene showed you in the same outfit as you started with. What is the point of even having an outfit if you cannot see a scene with you wearing it? Furthermore this made me wonder why they even had the option of different outfits in the first place. If there is a sequel I would want the outfits to mean something. Perhaps you can only progress on certain quests with certain outfits?Despite my criticisms however, this game was so much fun. The detective work, the film noir feel, the Lovecraftian story and the overall feel of the world. I loved this game and would be more then happy to play it again and I am hoping for a more polished sequel.A really good game, I thoroughly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of this game is amazing: A private detective on an actual mission to solve cosmic horror madness. The gameplay itself is entertaining. After taking my time in the game itself, I did a speed-run through all the endings to see if I had chose the wrong one. The problem is none of them are very satisfying. It is still worth playing though.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very pleasantly surprised.The game starts out confusing and daunting, this is a detective game more than it is a horror or exploration game, and it doesn't hold your hand.It's probably the closest to morrowind's exploration as we're gonna get in modern games; it tells you where you need to be, but you get no markers. Read and figure it out. Place your own markers.The game is both blessed and cursed to not be a AAA game. It can take liberties where it wants. They can focus on one thing and do it exceptionally well.But for that same reason, it has its shortcomings as well.I was very pleasantly surprised by the graphics, ranging from solid to even impressive.On top of that, it has a rather large open world to explore, I definitely had fun taking in the sights.But despite that, unfortunately, you'll notice this isn't a big budget AAA title. Interiors will quickly start to feel familiar and recognizable as there are very few variations.Combat feels like an afterthought. It's simplistic, it's bad.It does somewhat remind me of Silent Hill, really. Careful ammo management and often relying on melee, but both are clunky and slow. And neither has a real kick to it.And as for the story.. it's complicated.It starts all mysterious and interesting, it wastes no time setting up.It captivated me and kept me going for a good 25 hours out of my total 30.But then, around the last 2 chapters, the story starts to stumble all over itself. New characters and groups get introduced and very quickly put aside again, all of which felt unnatural and out of place in this story.The game also gets a little too comfortable with supernatural stuff towards the end. There are sidequests that have nothing to do with the main story that include actual magic and everyone just shrugs it off. No second looks, not even a "huh?"The last 2 chapters of the story feel short, rushed and confusing. I'd even say forgettable. The best part of this game is the first half, and what an amazing experience I had with it.Now naturally it's impossible to write about this game without mentioning the legal battle so.. Whoopty-doo.There's no DLC included, though I don't think you're missing out on anything. There are two !unobtainable! DLC costumes listed in your wardrobe unfortunately. Patch the DLC in manually if you like, it's possible. If you REALLY want the full, frogwares-approved experience, get it on Origin.But for what it's worth, this version is solid, with no game-breaking bugs as far as I can tell, no crashing, no ads.Just a simple base-game version and imo totally worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I  waited a long time to play this game and what a disappointment! The price is exorbitant for what it offers: 1$ at most. The level design is completely off the mark, often illogical, counterintuitive and repetitive. The character movement is frustratingly slow, making the experience really painful.The potential was there but was annihilated by a mediocre implementation. Promising ideas that are poorly exploited, poorly staged and poorly executed. The open world is vast but empty, with no significant interactions with the environment or NPCs. We find ourselves wandering aimlessly, tossed from one point to another without any real interest, from trigger box to trigger box.Admittedly, there is a certain visual coherence in the game's universe. The dark and oppressive atmosphere is in keeping with Lovecraft's writings. But that's not enough to save the game from its repetitiveness. The environments all look the same, the enemies lack variety and the quests are repetitive (again) and uninteresting.We get the impression that the developers were content to create a superficial world with no depth. There is no surprise, no discovery, no real sense of accomplishment. We quickly get tired of this game which has nothing to offer but frustration (especially after playing Call of Cthulhu).To make matters worse, the game is riddled with flaws. The combat is boring, the voice acting is mediocre and it is impossible to change the language of the voices and texts independently.Only Lovecraft's universe allowed me to stick it out. Without this attraction, I would have given up long before.I tried to salvage the experience by changing the character's speed, but it was a lost cause. This game simply doesn't respect your time. While it pays homage to Lovecraft's universe, everything else feels half-baked and leaves you feeling unsatisfied.If you are looking for a Lovecraftian horror game, look elsewhere. This game is neither beautiful, nor immersive, nor fun. It is just a frustrating disappointment.NDLR : I couldn't solve a search because my proofs showed 'looted tomb' and 'looted tombs', and I had to choose the right one, the one with the tiny icon. Really ?

_childDocuments_.review: 3 hours into the game and I decide to stop.I have this game long before the huge discount happens, but it is what reminds me to play.The Sinking City has a good story set up - A flood made almost everyone in the city sick, and they started to see illusions. You play as a detective to sort things out, by collecting proofs and making conclusions.The first hour felt great. The gloomy atmosphere, yourself is kinda involved as you gain superpower to see the past scene, which tells what happened and the answer leads to a new question. You combine 2 pieces of evidence into a proof, eventually the proof leads to a conclusion and the crime is solved. For the few detective games I played I know these are no new tricks, but at the end of the first chapter it allows me to tell the truth or hide it, and I like it. Though What ruins this game is the open world set up. Too many missions require going from point A to point B, usually a long distance for minor items, even within the fast travel at telephone booths I still feel painful. I understand this is a budget game, but for all the 3 blocks I discovered so far they look alike. The interiors also look alike. Few NPCs wander on the street, the only one to interact with is who gives you a mission. Dialogs are too plain. If I run the map for 3 mins just to get 3 lines, why not make this NPC a neighbor.This game may need a better lead on where to go next. There are notes tell what to do, but once I go to a mansion in chapter 2 as the note asks, only to find I go too early. But this could be my problem only.There are monsters, rigid, and the shooting is horrible. You have very limited ammo and the gun is only given within the game proceeds. Every object you may interact with has a claw mark on it, and in my 3 hours of gameplay, they are either 1) Doors and 2) boxes for crafting material. There is really not much to craft.If I have a lot of time to kill or no good things to do, I probably will continue. The fish and monkey people are interesting, the story still makes me curious. But the time I spent does not equal the little content I got. A shame this game could have been better.
