_childDocuments_.review: Combat is simple. No bosses or special monsters except that one floor mouth thing.Investigating also not very complex once you figure out the weird and unintuitive mechanics. The world is tiny but feels large because hero moves slowly on land or water, and the fast travel is limited to hubs. The game loads quickly on nvme and theres almost no loading screens except when you first begin and when you use the hub fast travel. Exploring gets tiresome very fast. Almost all neighborhoods look exactly the same, there isn't much variety or quantity in loot. NPCs are mostly mute and just wander randomly, often unrealistically. Nobody interacts.Nothing special to accidentally stumble across. Main story is pretty good, visuals are lovely in UE4 but also repetitive. Underwater sections are boring but look nice. You can grind for XP in the infected zones, boring. Leveling up is boring, you can pick perk points but you may not ever need them. A good player can probably get by with the bare minimum of levels.Choices don't really matter and you have little effect on the world until the end game, where you can save and watch all 3 endings none of which were impressive for such a story driven game. Overall, only recommended if you buy it dirt cheap and expect to play it exactly one time. I give it a 5/10 for the Lovecraft horror setting and the visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly this game isn't terrible, just really annoying. Combat can be boiled down to "optional" fights, where bullet sponge enemies are spawned in almost every main quest location. This wouldn't be the worst thing if the game allowed a cool arsenal of weapons or gave you a ton of ammo, but it doesn't. You just have to keep looting the very same buildings where the sponges spawn. I could forgive all this if the other mechanics or story of the game were good, but they aren't. There is a perk tree, but it only effects combat and looting. There are choices, but they don't effect the actual ending of the game (although I will say that the choices themselves are difficult to made and have a lot of nuance). There is a cool detective system, but every investigation plays out the same way. This game has really good atmosphere, and the overall mysteries were intriguing enough to get me to the end of the game. However, I had to put the game down multiple times due to how annoying and tedious some parts of this game were.

_childDocuments_.review: This game starts off on a pretty high note, and is good for the first 1/4 or so, and then basically falls off & proves to be a disappointment..  Best to watch a video of it rather than playing.+ Music is well suited to the game, but needs more variety.+ Voice acting isn't bad overall.+ Excellent review of Lovecraftian Lore, brought to life very well.+ The "Grand Theft Auto" open world map is decent, if repetitive.- Individual setpieces (i.e. buildings) are extremely repetitive.  Maybe 10 or 15 different building designs.- At most, there are 20 character models.- The levelup system is okay, if unrewarding.- Your "super detective powers" are really cool at the beginning, but like I said, you basically use the same 3-4 powers on every single area.  I wish that the character development system simulated you developing & unlocking new perception and understanding as they game advanced.- The insanity mechanic was neat, but wasted.  The game should be pushing you to experience more & more insanity to resolve puzzles, since a sane human mind isn't supposed to be able to perceive this stuff.  You shouldn't be able to take a pill & be right back to normal again.- Choice doesn't matter at all.  The game was rigged from the start.  Pick a color for your ending.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was weirdly zen-like to experience, because of the atmosphere & the detective routine you fall into, in the excellently rendered Oakmont city, as you're technically doing a lot of running from clues-to-clues, interviewing people, going to city halls, libraries or patient archives to browse for more information, to then chase those leads down, marking manually on your map your clues & their potential locations-- It just becomes this roleplaying experience of being a detective, with some flawed but sort of respectable combat on the side.By no means perfect, it's a budget AA title, credits are surprisingly short even for AA teams, closer to an indie sized team I imagine, & you do see some limitations, so I'll start with those first, if these are deal breakers then best be aware what you enter into.Still, despite these limitations, I enjoyed this game a ton, finished it & ALL sidequests (I checked), but I 100% DON'T recommend anyone to actually do all sidequests, particularly:Why? The ones listed, are all very basic fetch/collectathon "quests", there's no dialogue, no talking with NPCs or investigating scenes of crimes, just notes, pages to read, XP & a lot of combat while exploring the more recycled locations in the game.By the end of the game I had all skills maxed out & 9 Skill points left that I couldn't use on anything, so you'll find all the skill points you need by focusing on the other side quests & main quests without experiencing the worst of filler content.BTW, I did like the side quests in both of the DLCs, the ones that weren't the filler ones listed above, But you don't *need* the DLCs, I think mainly consider them either on sale in the full game bundle, or if you liked the game a ton and want to support a small borderline indie studio for a cool niche game.I haven't played Frogwares other titles, all the investigation-focused Sherlock games, they could be cool, but to me, this felt pretty close to Mass Effect 1 or maybe Witcher 1 in ways, as it's pretty much a slight variation on an RPG where you go around solving mysteries, talking with NPCs, sometimes have difficult choices to make as some cases aren't black&white, while having some combat which I think I appreciated more as being there even if flawed & frustrating, but I feel like the variety combat brought was something inbetween all the other stuff to keep the pacing at a decent flow, so that detective work never got too boring on its own, I do hope Frogwares maybe makes a Sinking City 2 that just copies more homework from say Resident Evil 2 & 4, the movement, feel of combat in RE2 with the attache case from RE4 (you do start with a backpack after all), & have a tighter focus on what the combat should comprise of (stealth? traps? if those are going to be a part of the combat then seriously reconsider spawning enemies around players, make more bespoke enemy patrols, less FPS arena design, or cut them & lean into RE2-style encounters and gameplay mechanics with a better resource management system that's as rewarding as shooting, not a frustration).The city ambiance is great, I don't care if some weirdos think this is "last gen", it still looked great, with the fog & rain, long shadows cast on these slightly dreamlogic american streets straight from a 1920's film noir, or the fact that the city is sinking, most streets are flooded, you'll go around on a boat, & the atmosphere while driving around, bumping into furniture, coffins, other weird debris, looking at the stranded whale carcasses blocking streetways, the fishermen huddling around makeshift fires, with the fitting low-key moody soundtrack playing in the background, it just looks great and is a big part of propping up what could be boring running back-&-forth between a police station to look at criminal archives to the next clue to talk to a witness again in another part of town-- But having all of that detective work, in the backdrop of a fantastical 1920's Lovecraftian haunted creepy weird city with towering monoliths, oppressive weather, ruins that hint at the cataclysm that came before & what more is to come, with the occasional fighting Silent Hill looking weird monsters-- Even if many parts in isolation are a bit weak & done better before in other games, the whole package is still a bit more unique, combat might be weaker than Alan Wake 1, RPG stuff is similar but different & scaled back from Mass Effect 1, detective work is probably simple compared to other games like say Shadows of Doubt-- Still, overall, I appreciated this a ton, liked the experience, recommend it if anything here rings true to my hypothetical reader, and I hope Frogwares takes another stab at this, polish the jank, tighten up combat & inventory management (just copy other successful homework, still other stuff here to make it unique) and I think you'd have a killer sequel to a comfy interesting niche game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has many quirks. Some of them are extremely irritating so in short:I love this game and look forward to replaying it. If you play it, I suggest go with the easiest setting because the combat is frustrating with limited resources, and keep in mind the ball doesn't really get rolling until you get the shot gun. Not all missions require combat; you can complete several and earn XP just by using crouch to go unnoticed.Resources are everywhere just keep an eye out for any box, crate, trunk, trashcan.The long version:I played this game, got frustrated and took a break. After the break I discover an update rendered all of my saves unusable and was VERY upset. I had gotten to Fathers and Sons.I restarted the game, and went in with a better idea of what to expect, and new knowledge that you have fast points you can use to travel instead of walking/boating everywhere. This greatly reduced the repetitive nature of the game.That was a literal game changer. I also played on the easiest setting because despite the combat being painfully obtuse, the story an investigations were intriguing. Fast travel points and this setting were literal game changers for me. Some other tips I have include going around to explore and find resources; it isn't necessary to enter homes. There are caches everywhere in streets. These little tricks helped. The only thing I still wish was different is the visual quality of the cut scenes. The rest of the game looks fantastic and those, which have a lot of important scenes, are less so.The Sinking City has a lot going on, and its attention to detail drew me in. This game is like reading Shadow Over Innsmouth. If you like Lovecraft's stories, they put a lot of the lore and built Oakmont straight out of his works, and combined them into a city that's really rich with history and culture. Take the time and explore all of the characters and locations, it's really engrossing. The cases are slow, and frustrating, especially the first three main ones. There's a lot of build up about what's going on, a lot of questions that you don't get immediate answers from. This game is a "slow-burn" so be prepared for that. It's also creative in how skills are assigned, and how your character arrives at his conclusions through the investigations. You have choices and your actions matter. They might be limited, but with all of the other stuff going on I don't think this is a bad thing. Once you reach Deal with the Devil, the game really takes off because weird stuff is already going on, and it's like a big mystery about to come unraveled.I don't think the plot was anti-climatic. It makes perfect sense for what this genre is. I do wish there were longer epilogue scenes, though. Again, for this genre, that isn't unexpected. My only disappointment would be that the ending scenes were not longer, and as with all of the games other cut scenes, I wish they were clearer. If you like Lovecraft's works, then you will appreciate how many stories were put into this game while making it its own. It's really genius. The detective work is fun, intuitive, and really interesting. The combat before acquiring the shotgun is frustrating, but manageable with some strategy. The world is immersive, and the story is fascinating. Even finishing it, it has replayability to try different options or do some of the other quests, and I actually enjoyed the character enough to want to play again! For me, this was an imperfect, but great game!

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be summed up in one word...Meh.Get it on sale if you like Lovecraftian horror, and keep your expectations low. Still, I did give it a thumbs up...If I had to offer one word to the designers as advice, that word would be, "verisimilitude." Don't cover your start area with monsters. Ease the player into the horror of the world. The starting harbor should be be a harbor. Maybe a few strange hints foreshadowing the horrors to come, but it's a little much to see piles of dead fish, half eaten sharks and octopus, and mutant rats... cats... crats... whatever they are... running around as soon as you step off the boat.On the up side, it's a decent (if flawed) open world experience. The story is a bit of a cliche, but it does seem to have a player influenced path and (while I normally disapprove of deconstructing classic genres to appeal to "modern audiences") I do rather like the way it has strayed from Lovecraft's simple-minded (and completely racist) "purity of blood" moral tropes and replaced it with more modern commentary about power and corruption. It made for a much more complex world, and made it much harder to decide which path was the "right" one. I also loved the way the game treats the KKK as a bunch of self-aggrandizing clown shoes. Lovecraft is rolling in his grave and I'm OK with that. I adore the man's horror, but he was a POS human being and he deserved to die penniless and unrecognized in his day. This is one of many instances where a mediocre world's inability to recognize genius has actually proven a just force in the moral curve of the universe.The save/inventory/rest/healing/combat systems are hopelessly outdated. Whole maps are copied and pasted to the point that all the building interiors are basically the same. The insanity meter is stupidly executed. The game only managed to reach a fraction of its potential... But, while it's not worth its current $40 price point, it is worth playing.Just... Wait for it to go on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this is in 2022, I regret my earlier hesitation, primarily based on the initial critical reception of this game. It is what I thought and wanted it to be, despite all the bugs (heavy FPS drops in certain places/situations, enemies clipping through walls, lack of sound like voices from NPCs etc) and the somewhat lacking worldbuilding, showing all the hallmarks of a low budget open world game (much of the world is not interactive, most NPCs seem to just wander aimlessly and many faces and buildings become repetitive after a while). I feel like I understand what they wanted to make, and even though it should have cooked a bit longer in the oven, it's still a very atmospheric (both visually and audibly), dystopian loveletter to Lovecraft. You also get to feel like a real detective. Conclusion: all in all it's one of the best lovecraftian games out there, even if it's surely a diamond in the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is what you may expect from a Lovecraftian setup: grim city close to the sea, weird inhabitants and unspeakable horrors. Still, it really falls behind in every aspect. I choose to try to finish all the achievements in one go, mostly because the game was too boring for me. The story, even though it has every note as a classic Lovecraft one, felt to generic. In fact, i found the entire game really similar to Call of Cthulhu (the old one, not the remake). Graphically is really bad; not much details. The locations are all the same (in fact i think there are two or three "house models" that they reuse beyond what it should have) with the exception of a chair here or a plant there. The gameplay itself is pretty boring. The character is slow, even running (so discovering the fast travel points are a MUST). The "detective" part of the game is decent, but after playing a couple games with similar mechanics (in fact, the one of Sherlock Holmes of a couple years ago has almost the same Mind Palace; but i guess TSC did it first), i have to say that "being a detective" in a game, although it may work on paper, on practice gets boring and repetitve quite fast. In TSC, is not the exception.The cases are mostly unconnected in between, but just to give you enough information of what's going on and what to do next. The city itself is bland and uneventful. From all the case, i think the best and most interesting one was the side case of Granny Weaver (needed for an achievement); but the rest felt all too similar or unremarkable. In fact, i didn't complete all side cases; only the ones needed for the achievements.The decision making is very flat; and mostly, you don't have a "good path" and "bad path". More like a "bad path" and a "worst path", so the game's main focus (i think) is to make you choose the lesser evil throghout the game. But even that, to unlock some achievements, you have to go even with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ option, so i personally didn't like that too much (in fact, a couple of times i got the achievement, and the reloaded a save just to pick a less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ option). Luckily, non of those decisions change the final outcome (which is excellent to unlock the 3 endings on one go). The 3 endings are grim, and the cinematics on each one are short (not more than a minute each) and boring; without too much explanations nor fireworks.All in all, i don't think it was a well executed game. If i had pirated the game, i would probably had stopped playing after the first or second mission.  Also, as i said, it felt too similar to a 15-year old Call of Cthulhu; and the graphics and gameplay didn't help to make it better. Maybe for hardcore Lovecraft fans, this is a banger of a game, for i think that for the rest, is pretty mediocre.Not more than a 4.5/5 over 10

_childDocuments_.review: I almost didn't buy it after reading the flood of negative reviews, what I found is a lovingly crafted atmosphere along with rich storytelling and immersive gameplay.This game has extremely dark themes; self harm, family abuse, racial injustice etc. On the other hand there is also some clever dark humour. The genre is a mix of Detective, RPG and Survival Horror. I guess some of the negativity comes from people who only wanted one of those things.A common complaint seems to be "The Combat" and I have no idea what their problem is, I found it to be a very simple and intuitive experience with satisfying gunplay. At first it can be intense but is very easy to figure out and it is not punishing at all, if you do somehow die it just reloads the last checkpoint which is never far away. The concept of limited resources is executed perfectly imo, I always seem to have just enough bullets to survive a situation and it feels rewarding to be prepared, scouring for more when needed. Venturing into barricaded streets marked as "infested area" is one way to find more but is completely optional so it's funny to see that complained about too. You can also earn from side missions (they're actually good too) and search any empty houses you come across.The only really bad thing in this game is "Optimization", it lags sharply at some moments but at least stabilizes itself pretty quickly. I can see how frustrating it is hand-in-hand with having a combat system at all, since it is prone to happen when a new area and several enemies spawn all at once, but I see it as it's own separate issue, besides it never actually caused me to die. The Detective work in this game is generally pretty easy but not always. It lets go of your hand sometimes and you just have to read through the clues you collected so far and piece together where to investigate next e.g. you may need to look up a birth record or business address at the newspaper or city hall archives, I felt a real sense of accomplishment in figuring these things out. Naturally this type of game requires some patience and attention span, to fully appreciate the depths of the story and cases. For me the most tedious part is to go over some crime scenes with a fine-toothed comb to collect every clue, but at least the game tells you once everything has been found in an area.Traversal can also be daunting at first but gets easier when you find all the phone booths to "fast travel" between, it's such a detailed environment anyway that it can be nice to just soak in on a boat ride or jog while thinking about your next step. In 30 hours I beat my first play-through of the main story alongside about 7 side missions (it's a good idea to multi-task them) However this is one of those games that doesn't return you to the open world after the final mission, so make sure to do a manual save a bit before the finale.I will also give it a replay anyway since there are many multiple choice moments with interesting plot results.In conclusion I highly recommend giving The Sinking City a chance if it calls to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Version:Not a bad game. Not a great game.Heavy on the investigation, light on the combat. Great on the theme.Long Version:Sinking City is a solid narrative work. The story direction and dubious choices the protagonist has to make creates a compelling scenario. The lack luster end of it is that the choices have little impact on the story at large. Going particularly one direction and then immediately changing one's mind at the very end has little repercussion. Choosing one side or another, likewise has little impact. I think that momentary notice of helplessness and hopelessness ultimately helps adds to the atmosphere of the game. The notion of human suffering meaning nothing to the entities involved comes through time and again. What point does morality serve if there is little change one way or another in the long run? There are some fun concepts to be had in this game's universe. The game is best summarized by an investigation interrupted by complications. Every investigation hits one or more complications. Even the simplest of tasks becomes far more intricate. I feel like it takes the concept a little too far. In short spurts, it is okay. I found myself having a guide open on another window to help speed things along and help out so I could move forward a bit more. If the person playing is really into investigations, that's great!Though there is another problem. The game does not really allow you to take shortcuts. If you come to the correct conclusion earlier than the game anticipates, it still will not allow you to progress. The player needs to have the correct flags flipped in order to get through complete objectives. This in turn can become very tedious as the player can search repeatedly only to eventually find a clue hanging on something from the ceiling, only accessible from the floor above. Combat is okay, if a bit stale.There is arguably two boss fights in the game. Both are technically optional, which the player can make a choice to avoid one, or complete the actual objective and run from the other. Other than that the enemies are very recognizable. The conflict could be ramped up for a more intense experience, but I did not find myself really enjoying it enough to want a harder challenge. Balancing some measure of dodging (not dodge rolling, but more shuffling out of the way), stun locking with melee attacks, and liberal gunfire, I was able to deal with conflict with only two deaths (and admittedly, I stopped dying once I got half-way through the game).The level up tree is nothing to really write home about. Nothing really stood out to me to go "Oh man this is a game changer". After about midway through the game, I did not really need to concern myself with leveling. After that my levels just made me more efficient.All of these things are moderate to bad sounding for the most part, but the best of this game is its atmosphere. Some doors are in the concrete. Some containers are bugged. There are repeated and rather stale voice lines. But the lighting, the story, the feel of the Sinking City, is great. For all the other problems going on in the game, I still found myself getting all sorts of inspiration for different games and things I wanted to write.Picking Sinking City is more about picking a Lovecraftian investigation game. This game delivers. It tries to do well with combat. It does not deliver on Dragon Age: Origins of intricacies of plot and dialogue. It puts the player in a maddening situation, asks the player to solve the case, and gives them a gun with just enough bullets, because the character is not Rambo. Sinking City nails it intent, with colors from outer space.

_childDocuments_.review: Sinking City is a game set inside the H.P Lovecraft universe, to be precise from the "Shadow over Innsmouth". Our tale begins and ends in the city of Oakmont, Massachusetts which depicts flooded and mysterious island blooming with lovecraftian vibes. Hostile open world doesn't welcome you nicely with gang activities and lurking monsters in the shadows. The atmosphere in this game is absolute banger but after a while it gets a little pushed aside by the clunkiness of the combat. Sinking city is heavily influenced (gameplay-wise) by Sherlock games which makes sense because both games come from the same developer and don't get me wrong having many possibilities and choices is always great but I wish the devs spent more time on combat or just made less space for it in the game overall. Pushing combat aside the game and its mystery is pretty good and even great if you are a Lovecraft's fan. Overall the game has its downs but also ups, pretty mediocre to be fair.

_childDocuments_.review: While this game did captivate me with its premise being more or less a spin-off/follow-up of H.P Lovecrafts novel "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" it fell a bit short like many other games that have tried to tackle the Lovecraftian mythos. With this said, it did a decent job of making you try to solve more or less supernatural cases in the city of Oakmont. You are forced to use multiple resources such as dialogues, archived information and obviously clues that can be found at or near a crime scene in order to solve many of the cases. The gameplay idea itself feels interesting, which gives me even more reason to want to like the game, but this also falls short as it devovles into a repetitive loop relatively quickly. One of the better sides of the game would be the characters with their personalities and agendas but many times you find that the characters are only part of the game for as long any given quest line requires them. After that, they will either be gone or standing in a given position with one line of dialogue. On the flip side, one of the less impressive parts of the game would be its combat. While fights against outlandish creatures in the original works of Lovecraft seldom play a part of the novels, the enemies of this game felt like they could "realistically" be defeated through the use of weaponry. The combat itself though felt relatively uninspired with close to no variation in enemy behaviours and very simple gunfighting mechanics.All in all, I don't feel like I wasted my time playing the game and it did captivate me enough for me to finish the game, but along the journey it didn't offer me much more than a mediocre detective game with a touch of cosmic horror. When it comes to the endings, without spoiling how they play out, they were sadly very lackluster. Not only was the quality of the cut-scenes less than mediocre, but while being open, which is not a bad thing per se, they left you without showing you the repercussion of your choices.All in all I would give this game a solid 6/10 IF you are an avid fan of H.P Lovecraft or cosmic horror in general. A game with a lot of good an interesting concepts but a lack of polish and depth.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be one of the few reviews where i had a poor experience with a game. The Sinking City was something i had anticipated to be a great lovecraftian game filled with horrors, mystery, and thrills, but it was ... disappointing. Implementing many mechanics that seem needless while attempting to be a third person shooter/mystery solving/back and forth quest solving game, but i'm going to go into detail on what exactly i found to be the issues with the game and tell you if it's ACTUALLY worth playing.World and the mechanics in it: As you start off you immediately get the idea that you are a detective or P.I.  immediately going into your first case, and getting a handle on how you initially play. Camera for evidence, guns where you have to craft your ammo (which is initially is mentioned to be a currency type but ultimately are just bullets so no bartering can be made), loot-able chests, area types, and basic movement/combat abilities. However as the game progresses, you find a majority of the mechanics and knowledge to be almost useless, such as the camera, which is only used for 2 missions before becoming useless and needless. Area types divided into investigation zones, or infested zones; which hold a lot of loot. However the infested zones become a mute point of exploration because you can basically get any resource you need through normal game-play exploration. The mind's eye feature gives needless puzzles to create the illusion of progression after investigating an area, and managing resources are barely needed after leveling 2 portions of your combat branch skill tree (which again, feels needless) this could have been over looked if not for the limit of every bullet type being at the bare minimum, and enemies ranging from annoying, to just a mess, since the only handy weapon is the shotgun in long term, and you can use grenades and fire bombs for crowds, which are constant. As per standard in many games you have two bars, the first being your health (which is easily depleted after a few drops or hits) and sanity. Now sanity is probably the most ill managed feature in this game, strictly because it rarely ever goes down to a point where you feel like you are going to be in danger, it drops when solving magic puzzles or fighting enemies but it barely takes enough time to really cause you any inconvenience, and even then, you are able to heal it with your inventory, which is near constantly full as mentioned before. Primary exploration is on foot, and by boat ... look at glitches and annoying issues for more info on those.Story and character portrayals:The story attempts to pull you in, a case of madness spreading throughout a city mired in monstrosities, cults, and gangs .... that is all over looked when you realize you need to look at your map constantly to find out the exact roads each person lives, and travel there, and back, or look up information on them despite the game's focus trying to be exploration based solving, but i am getting off topic. Several characters in the game stand out, but are very short lived because of the little interaction, their status is shown, their motives revealed easily, but it becomes mute when their portion of the story is done, and there is nothing more for them. I'd have liked to have felt something more impactful when interacting with each one of them but it felt ... like just passing by without a care, which i suppose is the result of the monotonous style of game play and progression.Glitches and annoying issues:When traveling via boat it is almost impossible to properly steer and control without the camera glitching out of control, being consistently stuck on a small objects, or your controls seeming to inverse if you try to back away from a corner, or being literally thrown in your boat and landing on the nearest pier which backtracks you. The collision issues apply to the walking traveling as well, small rock or ledges of a sidewalk can prevent you from moving forward, climbing mechanics are oddly selective, for any and every surface, and will barely work, causing you to struggle on getting to another section. And section will always need to re-load textures for their environments, it never stays loaded in even if you leave very briefly to complete a task, which adds to the already frustrating loading time.Should you buy this game?:The long version is ... maybe. If you are a fan of the tedious dredging (this being a personal opinion) game-play that requires the less than ideal back and forth style of exploration with no reward it can be your thing, and i am phrasing it like that because the game tries to put in a reward feature in some amalgamation of story, puzzle, and combat style game-play that does not mesh well. I'd recommend getting it during a sale as this feels like the type of game that would be find in a bargain section in most pawnshops. The attempt to make this game as wide set multi-layered of diverse game-play was an interesting concept but the execution was not ideal, and it barely insight any moments of genuine amazement. Wait for a sale as that is likely the most it's actual worth will equate to.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty quick game, all told. By about six-ish hours in, ammo stops being scarce, assuming you hit your shots and get the skills that make crafting cheaper. By the mid point of the game, you spend more time griping about the resources you're leaving behind because you're full, than you spend griping about the resources you don't have. I enjoyed the game, but there are two big downsides: One is that enemies can spawn on top of you or behind you. They don't spawn at random, necessarily, but in set locations that you trigger the spawn-trap for after passing or stepping on. So If you see a wide and empty area, assume that once you're closer to the middle of that area than you are the edge of it, 2-4 enemies will spawn. The second downside is the sheer amount of running around you'll have to do, especially in the early game as you unlock fast travel stations. An exploit I made rigorous use of to save time was to play and explore a location as normal, and once I knew where I had to go next, save and then reload that save. Your progress is maintained, but you'll be teleported to the nearest (discovered) fast travel station. From there you just fast travel closer to your target. One fun thing I noticed was that if you led a monster out of a house and into a place where police patrolled, they would kill the monster for you. I personally didn't make any use of this mechanic but for the one time when I stumbled across it on accident, but if early game it might be helpful. The game is also pretty easy to pick up and put down despite the emphasis on investigative work. The casenotes are thorough, so if you're halfway through a mystery, take a break for a few months, then come back, you'll be able to stumble back on track and continue from there like you never left.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played and completed the game after the whole scandal and when it was under Frogwares completely.The most concise way i could describe this game is a good 10 hour game wrapped in 50 hours completion time.Yes its exactly that type of repetitive stretched out story you never want in a game, it kills the pacing and makes something that would be short and sweet a real slog to complete.Being a completionist i wanted to see everything this game had to offer and it isnt that much, the theme was very interesting but in the end the boring and repetitive combat, crafting system and mission design really drag this game down.This is one of the closest games that i would not recommend you play at all, but after reviewing all my time with it, if you play only the main missions you do some side missions that are in your way you will have a somewhat good time. A very mid game and an open world you didnt really need and wont explore because there isnt anything there really besides some collectibles and repetitive quests.My advice for the sequel is drop the open world and make a more focused and polished experience, not a broken or incomplete game but a very lackluster experience for the price its asking even on discount, barely passes the thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game, but also had a good idea of what I was getting into based on having played Call of Cthulhu (the TTRPG) and games set in this universe before.  This game probably isn't for everyone. Deep Ones are underwater-living creatures which serve the Great Old Ones and sometimes humans breed with them, leading to odd mutations.  Great Old Ones are ancient deific creatures that slumber in the depths, waiting to cover the world in water and reshape life in their own image to serve them. Wylebeasts are creatures spawned near where Great Old Ones slumber.  The presence of Wylebeasts and Deep Ones herald the coming arrival of a woken Great Old One and the end times. The presence of any start driving people insane with visions and special powers.You play as Charles Reed, a former Navy diver who had an encounter with something horrible during the service that took the lives of the rest of your submarine clue.  You've become a P.I. because since then, you've had a second sight of sorts for clues and evidence, but with it has come horrible visions and nightmares. The town of Oakmont calls to you, a city appearing on no maps that is gripped with flooding and decay. This is, at its core, a Call of Cthulhu game which takes place in that universe in the Prohibition era (as most such games do).  In CoC, players should know going in that there will  be a happy ending and that you will see some disturbing things.  However, though there is a warning on load that the old prejudices of this time period are present and represented, skin color is mostly ignored, instead focusing on people known as Innsmouthers who have amphibian features.  Outside of that, the KKK is present in the game, though it's brief and they usually die in particularly horrible ways. Gameplay controls similar to Dead Space, and in a similarly open world, allowing you to tackle side cases and gain resources for crafting. Graphically, it's beautiful, particularly for the time released.   Creepy areas are creepy, eldritch monstrosities are grotesque and creatively designed, and the way clothing looks in the constant rain is rather well represented.  The AI on the enemies is also not too shabby; they know that a gun pointed at them is a danger and will attempt to move out of the way if they are nimble enough and knowing their weaknesses is rather important, especially toward the beginning. The story is quite good and leaves a lot of choices to be made. SANITY as a health bar-style mechanic is also well done, leading to hallucinations as it depletes and spawning enemies to attack if it gets too low.  The choices are also very "human" choices.  While they don't affect the endings (except for the final choice), they do affect the world around you as you play, and the implied outcome of the ending you choose. They felt visceral and often didnt' have a "good choice" but without making it feel like there is a missing "good choice" because of the situation. This game is buggy in 2022 on a powerful system with a 3080Ti.  Load screens sometimes take a long time, and when firing the shotgun (arguably one of the most useful weapons in the game), loading the sound for the blast would often freeze the action.  There was also some load-time lag when the enemy count is large in a location (most appear in ruins or houses that are part of your investigations). This game also seemed to struggle with its own identity. It is, at its core, a mystery, but it has survival-horror elements like crafting of ammunition and curatives, You gain experience points, which unlock carrying more ammunition, extending your stat bars, reducing enemy damage, and dealing more damage, so there it's like an RPG.  It's an effective translation of several aspects of CoC to video games, though they usually involve less combat, and that makes the combat here feel like filler, especially as there are only one or two "boss fight" style battles at all. I also want to complain about the research system.  It's rather brilliant on one hand; you find clues that lead to researching the records at the library, police station, newspaper, or city hall to refine those clues into new clues that help complete the story and unlock locations.  However, it's not always clear which stacks you need to search of the three, and it's used rarely enough that just handling it all at City Hall would have made sense and been less time-consuming.   Also, when unlocking a location, all you get is a description like "At the corner of A Street and B Road" and you have to place your own waypoint on the map with this information, which feels like a pointless extra step.Ammo is currency, but there are no stores.1. Set combat difficulty on "Easy".  This makes the game playable if you're getting the same asset-load lag I got, which is rare compared to the rest of the game (but you'll need the shotgun, which causes it)2. DO NOT expect there to be a "happily ever after".  In CoC games, it's usually a safe assumption that one or even all of the party members will be dead before the end.  This vibe is still here with The Sinking City. 3. Frame the Donald Trump analogue for murder so he gets executed.  You'll get a chance.  10/10 just for this.

_childDocuments_.review: I never knew a Lovecraftian horror inspired RPG was missing from my life until I played this game. It's eery, atmospheric and engaging. It isn't the most polished game in the world and the gameplay loop can become a little bit repetitive, but what it does it does exceptionally well.The city is gorgeous and a joy to travel around. The layout is interesting and the visuals are very pretty.The combat is not terribly challenging and the enemy AI isn't great but it doesn't really detract from the experience.The story is the big winner here. It's bang on theme and appropriately conveys that sense of desperation and hopelessness that pervades Lovecraft's works. If you've ever read Lovecraft or are even just curious about him this game is a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun detective romp in the Mythos with a bit more action than we usually see with these types of games.While you'll be spending much of your time running around the decrepit city, putting together clues, talking to people and trying to not go insane while staring at weird things you'll also get into more than a few scraps with monsters lurking in various areas.The presentation of the Sinking city is pretty good, the entire city gives off a unnerving feeling that rarely leaves you. Combined with the music, the grotesque appearance of the monsters (and some of the locals) and just how fragile your detective is and you'll be on edge more often than not.Animations while good most of the time have no in between frames which makes watching some of the NPCs with any degree of closeness annoying. For monsters its a different story and some of their animations just make them more unnerving.Speaking unnerving you'll have to manage keeping our intrepid detective from going insane by looking at said creatures too long amongst other things. The sanity mechanic is a nice touch but i really feel like its still not done as well as it could have been. You get hallucinations of varying types, hear whispers, the screen tilts etc...you even see black phantoms once you get the bar low enough. While these are all very harrowing for our detective they aren't so much to YOU.I feel they could have made things throw the player off more. Cause the phantoms to actually harm you, have the voices and sounds you hear be similar to the creatures you fight, mess with your controls or even your interface, i feel the game Eternal Darkness back on the gamecube put the bar of "making the player question their sanity" very high though the attempt here is not without merit and does a good job unnerving you still.Combat feels ok surprisingly. You slowly gain a variety of firearms during the main story and theres a simple crafting system for keeping yourself stocked. While early on you'll be doing your best to avoid confrontations once you get a few weapons in your possession and learn how some of the creatures fight you'll find even the larger ones trivial unless they come in force.I know there was some past drama between the studios or rights holders of the sinking city, im not sure how deep this went or what exactly was the main issue but i'm glad the final product is something as solid as this and i can say this is one of the better forays into the Mythos i've seen in a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: A joyless game. Given how much of it is stitched together with copy-pasted environments and monotonous fetch quests I get an impression of the strong contempt the developers must've fostered for this title. It's reminiscent of the way a student might tweak the margins on their document to turn a 3-page essay into a 5-pager.Since 4 hours of playtime I've been hate-playing to try to see if the writing gets any better but I'm approaching my limit. As it stands at my current 10.5 hours I'm led to believe that the only research the developers did on this genre was to google image search 'H.P. Lovecraft'. There's no dread, fear of the unknown, or exploration of the limits of man's comprehension. Just a robotically stoic protagonist killing some fishmen and tentacles.EDIT: After finishing the game I can verify my earlier assessment. The game has its moments but overall it's very very rough. The devs put a lot of work into certain details but neglected huge swathes of the experience and the end product is a game that doesn't really work as an open world or an adventure strung along with a story that doesn't really work as a detective mystery or a tale of eldritch horror. If you came into this with the right expectations it might be enjoyable to sift through, but I wouldn't pay more than $10 for the opportunity.

_childDocuments_.review: I still didn't finish the game, and probably will do it because I have too much spare time... But since it's on sale, it's a good time to make you think if you want to invest your time here.The good points are atmosphere and setting, which are truly great. The city looks and feel really weird, as you would expect from a Lovecraftian setting, but mind that it's mostly empty, in the sense that there is little interaction with NPCs and few cool things to discover. It was build with procedural generation and assets are repeated to exhaustion, but that wouldn't be a problem if there were interesting stuff to do in them. Unfortunately, gameplay is really, really shallow, with many lazy design choices.The "investigation" side is simply a matter of finding white dots and clicking on things in correct order. Eveything is quite linear and little is left for you to figure out. There was a point when I used a couple of brain cells to put 2+2 together and figured out my next objective... just to get there and find it still completely empty, since the game wanted me to go click on things in two different places to actually "figure out". Oh, sure, you have to make , but 16 hours in it and I still didn't see any relevance on the ones I made.The "combat" part is not that great, but also not that bad. You can't avoid it sometimes, but it's not something you would go after because it's fun gameplay. Spawns are random, but not in a good, everything-can-happen way. You may step inside a building and find a bunch of incredible strong enemies spawned, then just run outside, walk away a little bit, come back and find just a couple of weak ones.The game wants you to think that resource management is relevant, but it isn't. You have limited carrying capacity, but you find resources everywhere, and they always respawn (when you reload or simply go away and then back, I don't know). So if you get low on something, you can just loot again and again the same boxes. The only moment where you may run out of some resource is during the short time you stay inside the buildings, because, as noted above, if you go out and in again, enemies respawn (no, it's not a timer or the like, it's literally just stepping a few meters out).All of this makes the side quests irrelevant, because they don't bring any different challenge, and only reward you with resources that you don't need. Sure, you gain XP to spend on barely significant skills. Be sure to get the inventory upgrade ones, because if you are already full and get some resources as mission rewards, they just... vanish forever. Yes, it's that lazy...So, well, if you want to experience the few good points by yourself, go on and get in on sale. Take a look at the pcgamingwiki page to tweak the graphic effects to your like. Don't worry about resources, side quests and just follow the main story, which is standard derivative stuff (apparently there is just one story that Lovecraftian games can tell). Between this, Call of Cthulhu, Dark Corners and friends, it's hard to believe that the only  Lovecraftian game may still be the first Alone in the Dark....EDIT: finished it! And it surely overstayed its welcome with a lot of "click-fastravel-click-fastravel"... I never dashed so fondly for a "bad ending" before... >D

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the best Lovecraftian game I've played. The story, the environment, the characters and the endings are superb. You are drawn into Oakmont and its mysteries the minute you start playing.The game truly makes you feel as a detective, as the investigation is not limited to look around a room or two. You also have to talk to suspects, make deductions, find things in your map and check records at different places. Of course it also has some negative things. First is the lack of a tutorial. When you start the game, you are bombarded with a ton of gameplay mechanics and explanations in the form of text / help. It kinda works, but it feels like something that you would see in a game 15 years ago. It's a bit overwhelming at first, until you master all the mechanics.Also, at some point the game starts to feel a bit too long. Probably because the nature of most missions is a bit repetitive, after a while you start to feel like an errand boy running from one place to another.But even so, I loved the game. Every Lovecraft fan should play this.

_childDocuments_.review: OMG, a publisher taking advantage of a small time developer with an incompetent legal team?  My stars!  How could that possibly happen in this day and age?  Where's the eye roll emoji on this thing?  So here's what really happened:  Frogwares got greedy and signed with a poorly managed, struggling publisher, who anyone could see couldn't possibly deliver on what they were promising.  So many lessons to be learned here!  1.  If a business deal sounds too good to be true, it most definitely is.  2.  Do your homework-- know who you are working with.  A five second glance at Nacon's investor report would have sent up several red flags.  3.  When you're in the business of creating IP, don't sign the first piece of paper someone shoves in your face because you like the number on the top of the page.  4.  If your lawyers are rubbish, get new ones!  Surprise!  Frogwares went through nearly the exact same thing with Focus Interactive back in 2019 over one of their other games.  5.  Publishers, like all businesses, are in business to make money.  They don't actually care about getting "maximum exposure for your title."  They only care about getting maximum money for a dev's blood and sweat.  In business, if someone is giving you something, it is only because they are planning to get something more valuable from you in return.I get it:  publishers are the worst.  They're like the CEO of a company.  They sit around, do absolutely nothing, and get paid 100 times what the people that actually do the work get.  (To be fair, at least publishers actually sell something, rather than just shuffle paper around)  It's an ugly thing, but hey, that's capitalism...spoiler alert: it's terrible for everyone except the 0.1% at the top.  Rant over.It's an awesome game (even though half the level designs, and visuals were lifted right out of Cyanide's CoC game...what was I saying about IP theft?) and there doesn't appear to be anything missing, outside of the usual DLC cash grab, though I don't know why anyone is complaining about that.  And no I don't miss "achievements" either because I'm not an 8 year-old who needs a participation trophy.  The .exe version is 4.20.1, dated 6-2020 in the manifest, so it doesn't appear to be an "old version" as some are claiming.  Get it, it's great, and if Frogwares is really in the right, they'll get paid eventually anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: This game's had a lot of drama, from its beginnings as Call of Cthulhu, prior to Cyanide taking over that project, to more recent issues between the developer and publisher. Compared to Call of Cthulhu, this is the superior title. Flawed, sure, but no more than a lot of other massive, open world titles offered today. Combat is definitely the weakest aspect here, but you can almost completely avoid it. The storyline is incredibly engaging, though lacking depth during a lot of the side cases. The environments are gorgeous, but somewhat repetitive, and there's not nearly enough places to enter, explore, and enjoy. _childDocuments_.review: I have waited a very long time to play this game. For so long I wasn't sure which version was the "real" one: the version that would both support the devs and be supported by the devs. Once it became available, I was really hesitant, as I feared it would be an experience tangled in production hell for too long to be enjoyable.I love being proven wrong.I'm not far into the game, only having played a few hours, but I already find myself excited to come back to it, and thinking about how to approach cases in different ways to find new leads. So many Lovecraft-inspired games take themselves so seriously as to be unplayable, either technically or emotionally. I'm finding The Sinking City to strike the right balance of humor vs. horror beats. The writing is great, all the way around. Collecting lore never feels like wasting time.The character movement is stiff and combat is awkward, and both buggy. I can't deny that. However, I don't find that it overtly affects my experience. I can understand why it might not be for everyone. When the movement bugs show themselves, it helps to remember that this is primarily a game of deduction.This is a game that rewards patience and exploration. Everything from the UI and menus, to understanding how to navigate Oakmont, requires your own brain, first and foremost. There is a helpful tips section from the menu that is extremely helpful when just getting started.If I were to name my biggest wish for this game at this point: I would love t to have shortcuts directly to every tab in the menu. For instance,  an 'I' for inventory, a `J` for journal or casebook, and so on. I'm not suggesting those are the right key-bindings, just giving examples of how it would be helpful to have keybindings into the menu tabs.At any rate, congrats to the devs on finally reclaiming their IP, and I'm so happy to finally explore Oakmont! I'm having a blast, and it's so clear that the writers appreciate both the beauty and the flaws of the Lovecraft mythos. <3

_childDocuments_.review: I love Lovecraft, I have had high hopes about this game and though atmosphere is great and I am pretty patient player, this game is simply broken - fight system is horrible. I am not capable to shoot or hit monsters fast enough to kill them efficiently.  Save system is a mess. I saved game several times in hope that I won't have to travel by boat across the whole map, but after monsters killed me and I loaded my save, I was in fast travel place (far far away from the place I saved my game). Atmosphere is so great, but fight system, save system both make the game so anoying that I can't recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: 7.6/10Overall a generally decent game. While The Sinking City doesn't do everything perfectly, or even well, it's a fun experience and I enjoyed the story and setting a lot. The combat is very clunky and not great and the graphics aren't much to write home about but the experience of the game is still worth it.If you're okay with some mediocre combat and enjoy a solid detective experience in an Lovecraftian setting you'll probably enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was an option that was less binary than a 'yes, recommend' or 'no, don't recommend.' According to the news, Nacon released this game behind Frogwares' back before the devs were finished. Unfortunately, it shows. I would say that someone who loves Lovecraft and sees this game on sale should nab it up and give it a shot. Personally, I got it for $8, and I'm very happy with the purchase. But I'd also say that if you're meh on eldritch horror, give it a pass. On the positive end: 1. I can tell that there were people who really love Lovecraft behind this. I felt like their take on a sanity effect was the most creative and affecting that I've seen in a game so far. Some of the imagery, especially in the hallucination scenes or underwater, is really breathtaking in how it makes you feel so unsettled just using silhouettes, off-kilter perspectives, and uncomfortable scale. 2. I have fun in this game. It took me a bit to get to it, but I'm still having fun and I'll probably keep playing. 3. I like the investigation mechanics. You have a mind palace for deductions, you gather evidence, you use psychic powers, you hit up different research sources for information... You're playing as a detective, and the game lets you FEEL like a detective. On the negative end: 1. It's clear that the game needed another milestone to cook. The game economy and difficulty curves are clearly not what the devs intended--you have a tip screen saying that ammo is scarce and it's better to run from most monsters, but I haven't been able to pick up any craft material in a good hour of gameplay because my inventory is full of bullets and all the materials to make bullets. The difficulty of dealing with monsters varies widely based on the weapons you have and your skill level--and it's very straightforward to make your character OP within four levels if you take the right skills. 2. As a corollary to that: it's clear that the combat design didn't have a chance to cook either. Unless a designer put a physical blocker in to stop the monsters, they'll all spawn and come at you at once except in extremely limited circumstances if you enter a house. It breaks my heart as a developer myself because I see the places where it's clear the designers INTENDED to have more staggered, interesting combat encounters, but the combat AI and trigger system just wasn't there when the game released. 3. The tutorializing and conveyance in the early game leaves a lot to be desired. I wasted a good two hours wandering aimlessly until I figured out that only SOME icons are automatically populated on my map, and others need to be populated manually. This is a game that a player really shouldn't be shy about looking at a guide for, because it fumbles on explaining a lot of its many mechanics. 4. The city feels empty. It's clear that there were meant to be more explorable spaces, but the devs just didn't have a chance to fill them out before it was released behind their backs. Traveling can become tedious because of how empty it all feels, and I think the game would have benefited from the city being shrunk by 50% if the devs weren't going to be allowed to polish the space. I've played nine and a half hours, and I still haven't entered half the neighborhoods. You see this kind of lacking polish in a lot of things, whether that's by the effect indicating if you're right or wrong on certain deductions or if that's by the player randomly getting new weapons at the end of certain quests without any indication that that's what's happening until they happen to look at their inventory. 5. This is more of a personal taste matter, but I've played this character so many times before. He's a frowning middle-aged white guy With A Past and a deep husky voice, and there's nothing to make him stand out or do something new. Honestly, I've played this long and I still don't remember his name, he's that forgettable. Especially for a Lovecraft story--a genre that's so defined by who is 'othered' and why--I would have liked a character with more intimate personal connections to the struggles faced by being 'othered' or dismissed.

_childDocuments_.review: The Short:It's a story driven mystery game with very little physical action. Nothing is very impressive about it, but it's well done. If you can enjoy a decent mystery time-killer with a Lovecraft story theme, you can grab a tea and enjoy this game. And I would get it on discount.In Long:Just 4 hrs into this and I feel like I want to say something, but I don't know what. I can definitely say this game is "unremarkable", meaning not very special, but just still a decent time killer. I can definitely grade the game with a A- (A minus) on all counts: graphics, acting, gameplay, interface, etc. Nothing seems great, there's no passion, no soul. But everything works, it just makes the grade.One thing that absolutely sucks is the introduction to game-play. I don't know if I missed a tutorial or what happened, but I had to figure out everything on my own, and even refer to a wiki once.That being said, I'm interested in how the mystery is unfolding, and the way they immerse your character into the story actually works pretty well. I am the kinda player who can blindly "follow-the-arrow" and forget why I'm even playing. This game doesn't allow that. You have to stay on your toes, pay attention, read your notes, put the pieces together. And for all of these reasons - the game is holding me on. Ergo... Thus far, I give the game a thumbs up for just this alone - The immersive story and mystery engagement. And everything else just good enough to pass. They could have done it in 8 bit graphics, and invested more into passionate voice acting, or even just replace acting with text...I would love to see this exact game model revisited with more passion, more art, more soul.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be a cautious thumbs up for me. If you are into HP Lovecraft lore and elder gods and things then the atmosphere and story will truly speak to you.  Just as in most any game involving HP Lovecraft, the fighting is difficult. Not just because you have limited ammo and simplistic controls for fighting but also because fighting a monster will cause you to lose sanity. Which will in turn cause your character to become very dizzy (which will make your screen go crazy and hazy!) Unfortunately for a game that is about solving mysteries and finding clues, it ends up throwing a ton of monsters at you for (I guess) difficulty's sake.  I suppose that you should be able to handle it, but it gets slightly ridiculous when there's 10 things surrounding you and you basically have to blast you way through the area. I truly was not expecting this game to become a 3rd person action shooter. Finding clues becomes a bit of a chore. It's quite easy to miss a clue and you can go up and down and everywhere believing that you've searched every nook and cranny. Only to realize about 30 minutes later that you have indeed missed the footprint at the front door and have thus wasted your time.   The map is pretty huge!  It almost feels like an open world game until you realize that there really isn't much to do except to go from point A to point B for your various quests. Unfortunately there isn't a fast travel system (at least in the early hours of the game for this review) So you must hoof it everywhere. Get ready for old school cartography!  Yes, you must always look up exactly where to go on the map. Thankfully there's an marking system for you with a note of where the region/streets location are. It's honestly not difficult so why not just mark it on the map for us already?Overall a solid Lovecraft game that even beats out the branded games of the like (I'm looking at you Arkham Horror) However, this game fails to recognize whether it is a 3rd person action shooter or an old school sleuthing game (with elements of fighting).

_childDocuments_.review: For a game called the Sinking City, the game just seems very shallow.....and for the price of $40, it really is pushing its fanbase hard to accept this price point for an almost half-baked game.Let me explain...CONTEXTAfter playing Call of Cthulu 2018, I got interested in the Sinking City because I heard that Frogware was the original developers before splitting away and making the Sinking City. And boy, do these two games be the exact opposite of each other. Call of Cthulu leaned heavily on its story telling and investigation mechanics whilst to me the Sinking City leaned more into the open-world action-survival genre. It is sad that the developers had such a hard time with their IP, as I believe thats why the game turned out the way it is. There are some things I liked and some things I disliked, but if I were to described the game, it would be this...A SHALLOW GAME THAT HAS EXTREMELY HIGH POTENTIAL!In my honest opinion, the game was not finished the slightest. It felt like the game was at an Alpha stage of the game development. There were alot of things in place, but it lacked refinement. Not to mention the large technical problems that are still in place. The combat was bland and the monsters are the same handful of monsters every encounter. Here are some things I feel like it did right though.WHAT THEY DID RIGHT!The atmosphere of the game is very well done.The city map and is very, very well-detailed and interesting. I love the art style of the characters and the map itself. The overall setting of the game stays true to Lovecraftian.The investigation was pretty decent, I liked that you can use the archives to find more clues about a case.I LOVE that it dosen't try to hold your hands and only gives you addresses and vague points of interest to find your clues.WHAT FELL SHORT AND COULD'VE BEEN MORE...The story overall is too cliche and it felt like the writers was trying too hard to fit too many short stories from H.P's short-stories into their game. It isn't bad, but it definitely wasn't very memoriable in comparison to Dark Corners of the Earth and Call of Cthulu 2018.The dialogue and character interaction could use more variety. Whenever you talk to a character, you will almost always get no more than 2 or 3 dialogue options. When in comparison to Call of Cthulu's dialogue system, where you can have as much as 7 dialogue options, with some options only unlocked if you find hidden items during your investigation or you talked to other characters dialogue tree or find some interesting clues during your investigation, the Sinking City has literally a yes/no/more option, with the vast majority being a simple, Yes, go on. Yes I'll do it. Yes I did it. No variety in dialogue or even a dialogue tree in general. Not even a choice to say no to a quest, you just have to accept it. No ability to ask more questions about a crime scene or about the town in general.The main character is....like the game. So, very shallow. He shows very, very little emotions whenever he talks to individuals and it dosen't help that the character model uses the same body gesture and pose everytime. And lets not get started on his facial expressions. I don't think I've ever seen him make any other expression except the same old "tired, drank too much coffee can't sleep" look... His voice acting isn't bad, but it is so monotone that it makes him feel like a robot. A main character that lacks character....WHAT I HATED IN THE GAMEThe combat mechanic is soo unfished and clunky and it is unfortunately EVERYWHERE in the game. The moment I enter a building to investigate a crime scene for a quest, a monster attacks! The moment I try to pass an infested district, a mass of monsters attack! The moment I try to do investigation mode, ANOTHER MONSTER ATTACK! The game just tries to choke you with these monster attacks without giving variety. Its the same monsters over and over again. There is like only 4 or 5 monsters with slight variations and a handful of unique human or boss battles. The issue rises when its the SAME monster over and over again for 80% of the quest you accept. The sidequest are a drag. It is a very simple, pick up, go here and investigate, go to the otherside of the map, investigate. The story elements of these side quest aren't even very interesting. I find I've spent almost 50% of my time just walking....walking walking walking from one end of the city to the other.Lastly, the open-world aspect that they tried to sell just feels so empty. There is no real point in exploring except to just loot stuff and go to the next checkpoint. It's sad because I truly, truly felt that it was suppose to be something way more if they weren't ♥♥♥♥♥♥ over twice by publishers.So, in conclusion, is it worth the $40 price? If I knew what I got, I probably wouldn't have bought it for that price. Even then, if I were to get it on discount, the draw for me playing the game is just not there. I just keep having that nagging feeling of an unfinished game whenever I try to finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10I can't really recommend this game. It is not as bad as many say it is but it is still frustratingly lackluster. There is so much potential, and yet it seems as the development of this game turned out so bad that the end-product suffered beyond repair.The Sinking City is a 3rd person detective game with some combat, a basic crafting-system and a focus on sleuthing. The usp comes from the game being inspired by mothos written by H.P Lovecraft, with eldritch horrors beeing commonplace in this game. A little too common, if you ask me. You play as private investigator Charles Reed, who is suffering from strange visions and horrible nightmares. He seeks an answer to why he is having these visions and travels to the island-city of Oakmont, who is "recovering" from a terrible flood. The city is filthy, destroyed and flooded, with you having to travel by boat a lot. This sucks, as it does not involve any other gameplay-element other than just going by boat, which is kind of slow and repetetive. The city is quite large, and you spend most of the game running back and forth between different important spots, talking to NPCs, looking up information regarding your current "case" in an archive or breaking into houses to scavenge and investigate. That is really it, there is barely anything more to this game. The story is very slow and very few characters grow on you (as most die, either by your hand or by someone elses), the combat involves <10 enemies that are all defeated by just shooting them until they die and there are so many reused assets that you have seen everything that the game brings within the first two hours. Frogware has tried to make sleuthing interesting by not giving you waypoints to mark quests but instead forcing you to read and figure out adresses and where to go next. This is fun in theory, but as every place you travel to is identical there is never a sense of discovery or mystery. When you are sick of looking for road-names on your map, look up a guide.But how about the H.P. Lovecraft??? Is that part any good? Meh, it is alright. It is, again, repetetive as repetetive goes. You see the same monsters, figure out the big mystery within the first few hours and then jksut truck along and let the rest unfold. It is no wonder to me that <10% of all players have finished the game, you get so bored so quick.+ The game looks alright, but has reused assets everywhere+ Voice acting is good+ Tone is actually decent, I like the nods to works done by H.P. Lovecraft every here and there.- City is too big and repetetive, gameplay gets old fast- Crafting system is unimaginative, and ammo being "scarce" is rarely an issue- The story presents itself so slowly and the characters never get enough room to grow.- Your actions have little to no consequence.- Endings are absolutely dreadful for the 21 hours it took to get there.My advice, read a book or play a TTRPG inspired by the mythos instead. This game won't satisfy,

_childDocuments_.review: It's a horrible game that's hyped up everywhere for no reason - graphics are really bad and nearly everyone experiences stutter - devs haven't done anything to fix it - - The telling of the story of hp lovecraft, is literally just bad. It's like a very cheap ripoff of his entire genre. I don't know how to describe it, but in hp, generally, the setting often sneaks up on you, it's made clear that something is afoot, but it's not until the very end that everything comes to the light - but in this game, just every single step is a new reference to cthulu or something - every moment is some kinda "hah, see, that's lovecraft" and that's literally it. There's really no depth to it. Sometimes you see things and then that's it. There's no explanation or ingame response, almost like it's being framed as a sort of aesthetic or easter-egg - not really pertaining to the story overall - -something I really dislike is the amount of cthulu stuff that's literally shoved in your face without any explanation or awareness - There's no mystery about it, or sublety - It feels like everything to do with lovecraft was slapped on adhoc-One of those games where extraordinarily easy achievements exist, for example, you've completed the first mission, and somehow less than 80% of the players have gotten it - I decided to continue with a cheat engine table - Other things I disliked were the plot points are just really vague, finnicky, and questionably connected, like, the way you find things out sometimes is a complete leap by the protag, based on nothing -- along with this is one of the major gameplay mechanics where you find evidence and investigate how it came to be - and so you'll see like a scratch on the ground, you'll see an artifact - and then investigation time comes and suddenly you see literally everything that happens down to every word in a conversation, you see things that you couldn't have possibly surmised under any context, in a cutscene sort of way, and it really doesn't feel good, authentic, or reasonable, like you're being pulled along watching a movie you don't understand. -Another quip is the fact of how clue finding works, you see a white emblem that shows that something is important, you click it, protag says a line, you click it again, protag says the same line repeatedly. Skyrim unironically had better investigation moments than this. The investigation parts are really really forced on you, it's not subtle once, very much babying you to understand what it's telling you happened. And then when you're finished, it's not like "hmm based on what i've found I should do this next" it's like, "you've found all the evidence." that's it. How do I know I found all the evidence? It says you did. :l - Insanity is in this game, it's an effect that you experience because you see horrible things, but often it's so superimposed that it's really absurd - You'll see something in the distance and instead of the insanity slowly draining, it's just suddenly halfway down, you're not sure what you've seen - but now your entire perspective is filled with hallucinated monsters - those monsters are 10 x spookier than anything you might have seen, it's really just in the way, another inauthentic cthulu being crammed into your face like a cream pie. -again because I used cheat engine, I started trying the combat areas, and yeah, again, it's kind of irrelevant to the storyline - It seems like it should be very relevant - But instead it's just present for no reason - and it's very inauthentic experience, you just get attacked, the monsters one shot you, and dodge the crosshair, seems more stereotypical than necessary - like they just said **** it and forced it in. It's another feature that just comes off inauthentic and forced. So idk in summary, the game just feels very absurd and forced. Everything that happens is fed to you by the plot that's forced. All the things that happen outside of the main storyline feel like they shouldn't have happened or been inside of the game. it's extremely not immersive in the sense that it tries way too hard to insert cthulu into everything - Had a funner time writing this dog**** review than playing the game

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't really have that much going for it other than atmosphere and even than was tainted by the fact that they kept all the problematic parts of Lovecraft. The combat is janky with almost no enemy variation, my resources were almost always full even though the dialogue kept insisting everything was scarce, investigation mechanics were pretty ok. The metacognition and scene ordering mechanisms were interesting but the majority of investigation was just clicking on everything. The trailer says the game doesn't show you were to go which is technically true, there aren't automatic way points, but it just means that you have to place way points yourself and the game tells you what street or intersection its on.  The main reason why I'm refunding this, which I've never refunded a game before, is that they kept all of the racism from Lovecraft. There's a blurb when the game loads about how the kept depictions of racism to be "historically accurate" which is fine: depictions of bad parts of society is important in media. The problem with Lovecraft (and this game) is that the depictions of people and groups are problematic. One of the first npcs you meet is Robert Throgmorten who is half ape half man. He's base on "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and his Family" which is about the horrors of a white man having a child with an African woman (who is depicted as a literal gorilla). Africans being gorillas is not historically accurate.
