_childDocuments_.review: Foreword is that I liked the game, but don't suggest buying it on Steam, hence the thumbs down. Why? Because as I hear there's been some legal issues were Frogware accuses Nacon/BigBen Interactive of having stolen their game, uploaded it themselves and ran off with the profits. Now, I'm just a layman with no idea how that legal process went, so grain of salt, but I am inclined to believe it given the issues the game has had with missing content and the odd end credits where you get one from Frogware and a separate one from BBI. Sus.If you don't care about outside factors like this and only want the game, or just find it too much of a hassle, no judgement from me; I just want you to make an informed decision. If you do wanna support Frogware, I hear Origin and Gamesplanet (sites I don't use myself, mind you) sell the Frogware version of the game.==EDIT==Due to Frogware becoming the sole publisher of TSC, I've changed my rating to a thumbs up.Gameplay: 6/10Anyways I had some fun with The Sinking City, I especially enjoy the investigation gameplay and how you need to look up the streets and pin your own map pointers, giving it a feeling of doing your research. Combat wasn't very good, but thankfully the game gives you two separate difficulty rating to modify, one for combat and one for the investigations, so I could reduce the burden and make it not interfere too much with bulletspongy enemies I've already encountered multiple times in the first half of the game alone. There isn't a great deal of variation of enemies you face.The way you follow clues from one to the other is usually by trying to investigate various places from crime scenes to residences to monster-infested abandoned sites to try and locate clues of various kinds. You also possess a sixth sense vision of sorts which slowly drains your sanity to use, but may grant you supernatural insights into the scenes from giving you a vision into the past to peering past illusionary walls or sometimes to lead you to the clue you need through trippy visions you follow. It depends on the particular mission you're on and is something you follow rather than invoke. Some missions have branching paths, primarily the main missions, and said main missions also have a mechanic where you piece together the clues to form a wider narrative. You also sometimes have to do a bit of research at various archives for things like citizen records or information about books, which you do by piecing together three categories that match what you're searching for. That one took a little getting used to since you got to select the exact part of the mission you wanna research and can't just select the categories wildly to see what sticks, and there wasn't too much of a game or information you'd get out of those archives, but it did provide enough to make your next clue and continue whatever narrative you are on. I guess I wish it had more to it though, either more gameplay to puzzle stuff together, or more reading material that you can uncover extra information from if you do your homework, even if it's just for flavor. Or maybe unlock hidden endings? More work, yeah yeah, but it'd make the game's rating go up a point and leave a more lasting impression and impactful salespitch, that's for sure.Atmosphere: 6/10The city is huge and has a certain attention to detail, which is cool. I loved looking through the streets on the map and gradually familiarize myself with the place, making me feel more and more like a resident. Albeit a new one. What my primary thoughts are though is "the devs did as much as they could with limited resources." I find it dark and gloomy which I enjoyed, but I also saw reused assets everywhere, often on the very same street, where the same kind of signs were used multiple times over announcing some old business or so, and while the furniture may change a bit, the layout of every residence picks from a small selection that isn't gonna change much. And also people could pop in or out on the street which is immersion breaking. These things take away from the atmosphere in my opinion, though I still was invested in the story, my role as a private eye (and Charles Reed as a person) and enjoyed the general uneasy feeling in-universe. All in all while the game could use more polish and resources, I never felt like I wasn't part of the world the game presents me.Technical: 8/10I had no strong issues with running the game. Music worked fine, ambient noises were there and played as they should, and I never ran into invisible walls or bugs that I can remember. My main issue? I had to mod the game files, with some effort, to be able to walk. Give me a damn walk button, especially in a game like this when I need to take my time to explore smaller areas for details! Once I got that solved, I had no further issues with the game. But I do understand some content is or were missing from the steam version, so I'd subtract a point from that. Maybe I could argue it's mildly annoying how you can't save at the exact spot you want, but rather get thrown to the nearest checkpoint (with all the items and clues you've gathered intact, mind you), but I won't go as far as subtract a point for it.Overall Rating: 6/10I had fun, I was intrigued and I enjoyed going through the story. Endings weren't much to write home about and left me wanting. Combat was lame, investigations were fun. But most of all, now that I've played through it, I don't feel much need to revisit it again. I know what goes down, I know all of the mysteries unless I missed a side-quest somewhere and I know the story ends. Would I recommend it? If you like investigation gameplay and/or the Cthulhu Mythos sure. If you are more action-oriented, not really for you. What I can say is the only regret I have for my purchase is that I didn't know ahead of time about the Frogware/Nacon legal dispute and am worried, if a bit ignorant and unsure, about my money not going to the right place.

_childDocuments_.review: I...don't recommend this. I very much enjoy Lovecraft, and this is certainly one of the most faithful and detailed representations of his best material, but that superficial enjoyment quickly loses ground to what is just a bad game. The Sinking City was probably designed to be a more linear (or at least more condensed) investigation experience with a dash of combat, and in this form I think it would've worked well enough. Unfortunately, some chart-hound from the publisher must've jumped in at a late stage and insisted it be converted to an open world game with crafting mechanics, you know, because Fallout was popular. So what you get is an empty, oversized, half-baked, repetitive, and still only somewhat open game that the already clunky UI scarcely helps you navigate, and which will punish you for exploring spaces too soon (as you're almost bound to do). The combat isn't good anyway, what with hollow sound design, bullet-spongy creatures, few clear tactics, and storage limits on crafting materials, although I imagine it would have been polished up if that time hadn't been wasted on the game world. As it is I just don't think this game is worth your money or time.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is an open-world mystery game with a strong Lovecraftian theme in a classic noir setting. Its price of $45 is reasonable, but I'd prefer to wait for a sale.*This is a spoiler-free review*The graphics are average for games of this genre. They're nothing earth-shattering; even at release, the visuals would have seemed a couple of years behind. I noticed during my playthrough that the game uses relatively few models for NPCs. After 5-10 hours, you'll see the same models are recycled with various clothing options and facial hair to make the city feel populated. NPCs randomly wandering the city helps with immersion, but they do wander randomly. NPCs will pop in and walk into walls, parked cars, etc. If you don't pay much attention, it sets a nice backdrop, but if you look too closely, you notice some oddities.Overall, visually, there's a consistent tone and theme, which is maintained throughout the game and helps keep the player immersed. There are some cracks in the facade, but if you don't look too closely, you can suspend your disbelief.All the dialogue is voiced, and the voice acting is good. The ambient audio is immersive and doesn't get in the way.The decent music mainly consists of unobtrusive background audio which helps set a menacing, horror-ish tone without drawing attention to itself.If you're familiar with the Lovecraftian genre, you can probably guess the plot after 1-2 hours. There aren't many substantial plot twists; it's all pretty conventional. That's not a bad thing; it's common because it works, but the plot isn't going to win any awards for innovation.There's a bit of a branching story here, but the choices you make only impact the journey along the way to the multiple endings. It's structured so that each possible ending is available to you no matter what decisions you make along the way. Your choices as you play alter the world around you, and you'll notice the impacts. Newspapers and current events stem from your decisions, but ultimately, none of that affects how the ending happens.You can undertake several side quests to get achievements and cosmetic items, but none of them will impact the main story, so you're free to complete or ignore them as you please.The main story took me about 20 hours to finish, and the side quests all add on top of that if you're looking for more content.Most of the plot makes sense; it all interconnects and is easy to follow logically. If I'm honest, the story isn't really the highlight here. The main draw of this game is the gameplay itself. The plot serves to facilitate the mechanics, which it does well.The protagonist is a Private Eye. The main game loop is roughly as follows:This is the highlight of the game, and I really like the way this system works.Most of the game will consist of the above loop of investigating a location, then taking the info you learned/deduced, talking to an NPC, pointing you to another place you'll explore, etc. Your decisions will depend on your deductions from the evidence you've found. You can also visit various Archives and do research, which is a cool mechanic that makes you feel like an investigator piecing all the clues together in a way that isn't dull or boring.The movement and combat mechanics are a bit clunky. They get the job done, but it's definitely a weak point of this game. The difficulty in combat mainly comes from the fact that ammunition for your weapons is pretty sparse, although there are a few ways you can effectively get unlimited ammo (certain crates will reset and refill if you walk a certain distance away, so you can just go back and forth looting them over and over) which makes it much easier to just blow through every monster and bad guy.This game is open-world, and I enjoyed how open it feels. Every time you're told to go to a location, it's in the form of directions to a particular street intersection, which you then have to use in-game street signs to navigate to. You'll quickly become familiar with the city and the main streets and locations because you have to navigate most places manually. It's a small thing that really enhances immersion. (You can also go to the map and place down a waypoint, which will show up on your HUD if you don't want to bother with street signs and maps and all that.)At almost any point in the game, you can stop whatever you're doing on the main storyline and just do whatever. Visit the hospital, talk to the librarian, help out crazy Frank the grave keeper with a side quest, run through a dangerous infested area to scavenge supplies and get XP, or explore one of the many unlocked houses or locations around the map—all that and more.There is fast travel, but the first time you go anywhere, you have to do it the long way. The fast travel waypoints are limited to two or three per city district, so you'll still have to do some walking, but most of the time, they're located relatively close to wherever your current case is leading you. In conclusion, The Sinking City is a fun, open-world detective game that captures the feeling of being a private eye, investigating crime scenes, and piecing things together to solve the mystery. The combat is clunky, and the visuals are a bit dated, but those aren't the game's main focus, and they don't detract from it too much. I'd recommend buying it on sale if you like the idea of being a detective, investigating crime scenes and piecing together evidence to solve mysteries.

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this after completing my first play through with the intention of coming back and 100% the game for achievements, as for achievement hunters this is an easy 100%. SPOILER FREE. Also note if you are a frogwares fan and want to support the Devs this game shouldn't be purchased on steam. There is also a DLC for this game that isnt available on steam at all. OVERALL RATING: 7.6/10LENGTH: 15-20 hours100% ACHIEVEMENT EASE: 2/10 (Every achievement is story based, but about half are missable due to choices. You can save throughout your game and get them, but I did not do that.)WORTH THE PRICE?: Buy on sale. $30 USD or less is a good price point. PROS:Being a detective in this game feels real, and doesn't feel unnatural, and definitely doesn't feel like the game is giving away the answers. I felt like i actually had to put clues together and figure out what was going on. This part of the game is a 10/10 in my opinion. I have seen a lot of comments about the gameplay being clunky, i didn't notice that. With that being said i played mouse and keyboard. Clunkiness might be felt on controller. The city is pretty interesting, but I wasn't overly enthusiastic about exploring it. The story is very interesting, and while it is choice based it doesn't seem like choices matter for the long term.  I really enjoyed how even though you have an unnatural ability being a detective, you don't feel more or less human. The movement speed isn't faster, you are not stronger. Overall you just feel like a normal person with the uncanny ability to solve puzzles. CONS:This game doesn't explain anything to you. Fast travel, healing, weapons, or crafting. None of it. You kind of just have top figure that out for yourself. This isn't a game to appreciate the ending, it is meant to appreciate the ride. NO New game+, and once you finish the game, you are just done, and cant do anymore side quests unless you create a save. No real variance in enemies, and they all are pretty easy to kill. SUMMARY: Good, fun, enjoyable detective game. If you enjoy Lovecraft games, or police games this is definitely a good choice for you. This is the detective game L.A. Noire should've been. Overall i highly recommend the game. I had about a 20 hour first playthrough. This includes all side quests, DLC, learning the mechanics it doesnt teach you, and very little exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello there, detectives.While The Sinking City suffers from severe case of 'copy-pastism' it is not a that bad of an experience overall. I think main mistake developers at Frogwares did was picking a scope too large for their resources to accomplish and that decision leaks through every nook and cranny of this title.  Technical issues is underlying experience of this game. From severe frame dips depending on the area ( I was getting anywhere from 50 to 144 fps on RTX 3070 ) and micro freezes every time i shot a gun to more bizarre and honestly  borderline funny issues like NPCs dropping from a thin air in a giant clump and then dispersing in different directions. Game was seemingly saying ' wait , wait! I'm not ready yet ! ' on every turn and throwing spawning/despawing NPCs in these giant 'balls' left and right. Funny , but a definite issue with the AI/Engine.Story is your typical by the numbers lovecraft , which i'm perfectly okay with because that is what i came here for. Being an open world game there are numerous side quests besides the main story line and they are ... fine i guess. General quest structure in game is a bit trash honesty, it devolves into this neverending chain of having to help someone so he can help you to help your previous help asker, couple of hours into the main quest you are 10 people deep into 'helping' them all , you get the idea. Even though Oakmont city itself looks and feels very nice , just to stroll around , but whole open world aspect is very basic. There are some buildings you can enter to , for quests or just loot , but there are probably 3 or 4 different inside layouts in a whole game so you are basically just entering the same few rooms for the entirety of the  game. There supposedly should be survival horror aspect of managing your limited ammo and resources , but since all the lootable containers just respawn there is zero chance of you running out of stuff or having to conserve anything.This game could and should have been way smaller experience . It had no need nor resources to be 20+ hours open world experience because there's hardly any content for 5 hours game here.ButI got it for under 10Eur and i think that is there price is right. If you are just after some lovecraftian atmosphere and want to roll in some familiar settings this is a decent buy for that price and that is why i'm ultimately recommending The Sinking City for under 10 euros. Just keep all the rough edges in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game, I played quite a bit of it, almost completed it... and then I heard of the legal mumbo-jumbo. I was gifted the game by a friend, and hadn't bought it on its initial release because of it being an Epic exclusive, and I do not support Epic's practices.With the shenanigans going on with legality(which from I can tell, both the studio and the publishers were stupid as hell), and the fact that this version of the game had old saves deleted, the game simply isn't good enough to play it again.The combat is okay but way too reminiscent of the 2002 The Thing game, the choices don't impact the game's story itself much, the crafting/skill systems are awkward, there's too many one-hit-kill enemies, there's too many straight up impassable areas for ?????? reasons, the voiceacting is extremely awkward in many sections, the game itself is buggy and models jump around often, enemies clip into the floor, etc. Nothing was a surprise, and most of the time it was simply annoying to get through sections.The 'boss fights' entail dying repeatedly to one-hit attacks until you figure out what you're *supposed* to be doing. The mysteries are non-mysteries, you wander around a room and try to find random objects, and then when you do so you're given the entire story in front of you instead of having to solve it yourself. The lovecraftian horror is also fairly nonexistent, it's just extremely vanilla body horror.All in all, while I enjoyed it, it was exhausting to play.I don't recommend the game due to the entire lack of replay value, interesting content, and the legal tomfoolery going on. It isn't short enough to tolerate the jankiness of it(like the most recent Call of Cthulhu game) and while it has a lot of content, almost all of it is the same, just different flavors. Go here, do x. X didn't have what you needed, go to y. Etc.The soundtrack is great though.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a long history of Publisher and Developer feud unfortunately and didn't deserve any of it cause it's a great game and savagely underrated. First the EGS Exclusivity for a year then the ownership issues which led to lots of criticism by the community as well.Now coming to the recent release on Steam which was released back on Feb. 2021 it was a pirated version and faced major criticism again as it should be, finally in June they released a big 14 GB update which brought back working achievements, deleted all the pirated DLCs from the game including the Save files (which some players like me had who played the pirated version for a bit) and made the game legit, then it had only the Standard Edition.Now very recently in 16th Sept they added yet another 200 MB update and also included the Necronomicon Edition for purchase which includes The Investigator Pack and Worshippers of the Necronomicon story DLC, lastly making the game complete and a legit purchase for the first time! Some people who bought the pirated version back in Feb/June(60% sale) are complaining like idiots that they bought the Complete Edition which they didn't at the first place, now that Nacon fixed the game and started adding DLCs they are demanding free DLCs which shouldn't happen at all.Finally coming to the game itself: Frogwares did a commendable job in creating an underrated Masterpiece! I mean what a game it is, literally all of the time it gave me chills of horror and suspense at the same time when roaming around the game's open world solving mysteries and Side cases which are plentiful, this game also has nice boss battles with monsters in some Story/Side cases and in the open world full of infested areas where they spawn indefinitely which can be used to farm XPs, Skill points, Crafting materials and ammo.The story of the game is inspired from H. P. Lovecraft's work and focuses on a Detective named Charles Reed who comes to Oakmont  to solve the mystery of his strange psychic powers/visions which granted him supernatural powers of deducing mysteries and cases like no man could.My Rating: It's a fully open world non linear Detective action adventure and crime/mystery game interesting boss battles and combat, best part of the game is solving cases through Mind Palace and deducing hints and connecting them to another theory (bit like Sherlock Holmes). The hero also got lots of outfits to choose from and enough weapons in his arsenal to take down enemies. 9.5/10 Knowledge points from me.*No game should suffer like The Sinking City, it deserves all of the recognition it gets after all it's a great game for the suited players. I'm thankful that i finally got the game on Steam and i bought the Necronomicon Edition as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Sherlock Holmes + Call of Cthulhu Dark Corners of the EarthThe Sinking City is one of the most impressive games I've ever played. It has impressed me unexpectedly in so many ways. The game's atmosphere is dark, lonely and very depressing. The Wylebeasts fighting scenes are exhausting, horrifying, yet surprisingly rewarding and satisfying. The game world is quite huge. Many parts of the streets are flooded waterways, on which the player has to travel by boat to navigate through. The soundtrack is lonely, depressing. As I walk through the city of Oakmont, looking at people in rags walking by, with the depressing soundtrack playing in the background, I actually felt like this is real, and I'm the lonely traveler Charles Reed.The "madness" effect is really cool. Straight out of the classic psychological horror games. It's filled with whispers, blurred vision and Mr. Reed's panic attacks, to build up psychological horror. This effect takes place whenever Mr Reed's sanity is low. His Sanity drops low quite often, whether it's fighting monsters or solving cases.Player has to gradually gain experience to fight monsters, finding loot to make bullets and explosives, as well as taking advantage of the fast travel points to travel across the city of Oakmont. The missions are not many, yet they take very long to complete. Each case has different ways to complete, and can achieve different endings. There're lots of twists and turns. For example, if you trust Anna's husband instead of Anna, then you'll never find out that Anna, despite her kind and innocent look of a lady, is in fact a vicious and evil witch from the EOD, who will not hesitate at all to lure you into an ambush and kill you. If you don't help Johannes Van Der Berg's shooter to get his family back from the kidnappers, then you'll never find out the truth about your witness Milton Pierce, or Lewis Flynn from the prologue. Turns out Milton Pierce was indeed paid to lie about identifying Mr. Reed as the shooter. And Lewis Flynn, who murdered Albert Throrgmorton, was indeed a trained killer from the EOD, instead of just an innocent Innsmouther facing injustice...... There're many other examples. Different decisions lead to different endings. The main story is revolved around the protagonist Charles Reed, who's a chosen one. He set on a quest to Oakmont to find a cure for his strange visions. With his investigation went further, he gradually found himself to be able to decide on the entire city of Oakmont's fate. In the end, he can choose to break the cycle (Safely leave Oakmont and return to Boston), end the cycle( being swallowed by the dreamer's daughter monster), or restart the cycle (restart everything, sacrificed himself). The side quests are also captivating. Some of them were treasure hunts, go to a place, kill all monsters, get the treasure/ fulfill the objective. Some of them has engaging stories: Cannibal restaurant chief, magical books collection, investigating the origin of the Wylebeasts, help a woman reunite with her Clay-man lover...... Mr Reed uses his Sherlock Holmes investigation skills to complete cases.The game lore is glorious. Many of these "peoples and places" are insinuating certain real-life groups in the US. ( Except the 3K group, which is exactly the same as the real 3K group.) There're three grand families: The Thorgmortons, The Carpenters, The Blackwoods. Thorgmortons are the most prominent family, and Mr Thorgmorton has been mourning the loss of his son, Albert. The Carpenters is a gangster family. But the young Carpenter is working with the Cult of monster worshippers to murder the Old Carpenter and take power. The Blackwood family has all gone underwater and became fish-men. The only Blackwood left, was hell-bent on becoming the chosen, and possesses the magical power to call monsters to appear.  And then there's the Innsmouthers, who insinuate the real-life immigrants. They have the lowest social status in Oakmont. It insinuates some of the tensions between different social groups in US: The Innsmouthers (immigrants) are taking the locals jobs, because they're better at fishing. Which has angered a lot of the local fishermen. The Thorogmortons  (local prominent residents)  despise the Innsmouthers the most.Now, it is a game made in 2019, after all. So inevitably, it's  a little "woke", and has certain "progressive values". Such as, in Milton Pierce's apartment, there's notes that shows Milton Pierce's policy when he ran for congress, is the same as that of the 45th President, such as immigration policy, build the wall, and "Oakmont first" (America first). The purpose is to mock at 45th and conservative policies. There's also examples of insinuating Innsmouthers (immigrant and minority) mistreated by the prominent local residents, local police and 3K group. But it's a game set in 1920s, so those depictions are probably accurate and understandable.However, despite these little "woke" elements in it, most importantly and preciously: The game has backbone, and it didn't bow down to progressive feminism. Which is especially rare, in a year like 2019. It's chauvinistic and principled. Harriet is merely the "First female university professor". Charles Reed also looks quite handsome in his fedora. I love it.Johannes Van Der Berg is immortal, it would seem. He's a supernatural being. The scene that I enjoy the most, is when Johannes Van Der Berg came back from the dead, and appeared in Mr Reed's hotel room. They had a long, profound conversation. Quite like the one Sherlock Holmes was having with Watson, after he came back from the dead, from that cliff where he and Professor Moriarty fell down together. It's really cool. As someone who read Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes growing up, I'm a huge Sherlock Holmes fan. And I love this game. If you're a Sherlock Holmes fan, or Lovecraftian fan, I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: The best Lovecraftian game I've played, forgivably riddled with minor bugs and gotchas.NOTE: This is not a blessing of Nacon in its litigious war with Frogwares; this is just a review of the game.Pros:* Absolutely nails the hopeless, dreary ambiance (graphics, music, NPCs, etc).* Lots of crazed characters to interact with.* Excellent reason for a PC's "super-vision" power.* Great take on the "monsters cause insanity" genre.* Combat is not my forte (I put it on 'easy' this time), but I enjoyed it.* Fairly realistic take on pre-Internet PI research methodologies.  No multi-quest stoolies, but lots of research resources.* Fun quests, and lots of side-quests.Cons:* New weapons are only located by following the main quest - which makes exploring really tough and wasteful on crafting resources, in the early part of the game.* Random NPCs are... bizarre. - Extreme cultists & people toting severed limbs/heads, bumping elbows with fishermen/cops w/ no comment. - Their routines are silly. (eg: Queueing up to take turns kicking a sleeping homeless person) - They just don't matter - they routinely disappear in front of you or when your back is turned. - Don't bother defending any who's attacked by another random NPC, you'll just go "insane" as a reward.* Quest rewards are usually ammo - but since I usually make more ammo after I use it, and there's low caps on how much you can carry, I usually end up not getting anything.* Acquiring crafting resources is broken - easiest way is to locate a building near a fast-travel point that has a few chests, then loot it.  Save/load/repeat.  If any monsters spawn, save/load/repeat - there's usually at least one chest you can loot before you have to run.* Climbing can be twitchy, especially when diving - makes it a bit tense/frustrating, sometimes.* Some side-quests can be hard to locate the starting point of.TL;DR: Expect n-i-g-g-l-e-s, but nothing game-breaking.  If you're looking for a good Lovecraftian game, 9/10; if you just love exploring or creepy sh!t, 8/10; else, 7/10.NOTE: Had to hyphenate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, because Steam thinks it's a bad word.  ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game for Lovecraft fans and for those who loved Dark Corners of the Earth, Call of Cthulhu and alikes. The game looks good, sounds good and plays well. The investigation mechanics are refreshing and involve plenty of reading and puzzling of clues. Combat seems solid and pretty straight forward - nothing new here, but who expects frequent shooting is wrong here anyway. The visualisation of madness is well done and the game delivers the expected lovecraftian atmosphere - decay, desperation and madness everywhere.I bought the game before I got wind of the dispute between developer and publisher. After seeing the negative reviews here, I started reading up on the topic - however I wont pick sides as I dont know the whole picture and its also not my problem. From what I read, both sides broke the contract unlawful and the court will clarify the rest. The game definitely contains (at least some of) the DLCs, so no idea why some people complain about them being missing. Personally I dont care about achievements, I have a real life and if something is worth being achieved, then its definitely there and not in my computer.Furthermore, the game runs absolutely stable on my machine and does not seem in the need of patching for playability. Sure here and there a few minor fixes wouldnt hurt (glitching/randomly spawning NPCs and maybe audible conversations between them), but thats really crying on high level and the game is fun enough for someone who does not pick cherries all the time.Overall I clearly recommend the game for Lovecraft fans, especially now while its on discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Whenever I find a game based off Lovecraftian tales that I might enjoy, the best part for me is seeing how different developers choose to depict the unspeakable and unfathomable horrors of this mythos.And to be fair, it's all very much here: the city of Oakmount is big and heavy with despair, looking half sunk and half forgotten. The soundtrack is tense, slowly drilling a sense of helplessness into your mind. Visually, the game is great, with fine textures and lightning that really sell the mood. It's once we get to the gameplay that it really starts to sink. There are some great detective mechanics going on here and I love them! You're actually required to read the notes and clues you find in order to know where to go and what to do next. You even have a mechanic that lets you search around city archives, the newspaper and hospital/police records for more evidence. My biggest issue with these is that they are overused and rapidly become very common.But it wouldn't be as problematic if there wasn't this much backtracking. That and the mediocre combat really sunk the game for me - the game loop is extremely repetitive with you talking to someone, going to a "crime scene", finding clues, going through your notes and repeat until it's closed. There are only a few enemy variations and shooting is just not fun.This was conflicting for me - I didn't want to give it a bad review, and I really wanted to go deeper into the story, but every attempt at doing so was met with another favor, for another guy who had information that I needed to progress through the main investigation and it just did this way too much for me.TL;DR: A fantastic foundation that hits the genre right in on the nose, but suffers from a lack of focus in the core loop and a vast, dread filled city that's mostly and sadly empty.

_childDocuments_.review: HM. well, if you're considering this game, make sure to read the reviews first so that you know what you're getting into. i did that and i think it helped a lot, i went in with low expectations and i got what i imagined. the reviews will tell you that this game feels a little bit unfinished, that it has a flat plotline and a LOT of repetetive quests that test your patience. almost all quests have the same mechanic - find a place on the map, go there, investigate, maybe kill some monsters, go look for the next place on the map. sometimes you'll have to check the city library or some other archive to find out where to go. in the meantime, you can do some exploration on your own, but don't expect to find anything engaging - maybe future quest locations at best, empty until you get the right assignment. this is what most reviews mention and its 100% correcthowever, what most of those reviews don't mention is just how fascinating the setting is. and i think the game is worth playing just for checking out the titular sinking city. the devs really put a lot of effort into desiging it and the citizens wandering it. when i finally unlocked access to the main part (the first part of the game is in the port outside the main gates), i simply ran around for at least an hour, exploring the city, watching the people inhabiting it. it's a really amazing concept, to see a city ravaged by a supernatural flood and its citizens trying to cope  with the world ending around them. some have succumbed to the madness and you'll see them weeping or even banging their heads on the walls, some carry on like nothing has happened. the city districts feel unique, you get the wealthy and oppulent area that was barely touched by the flood and then the outskirts, covered in squelching mud, full of completely submerged alleys. i REALLY enjoyed exploring the city -- but my own curiosity wasn't rewarded by the game. running around the city doesn't actually give you anything. there are barely any side quests to discover, no unique interactions or npcs. even though the city and street npcs have so much character, the fascination wears off quickly once you learn that theres no point in exploring the city. it's better to wait for the main quest to tell you to go somewhere. a huge waste of potential. i understand the release of this game was troubled by some sort of scandal, i don't really know much about that but it does feel unfinished and unpolished. but i picked it up because i enjoy lovecraft mythos and because i like open world games focused on a city. and despite the overly simple plot and repetetive gameplay, i don't regret the 20 hours i put into this game. it's not amazing, but it gave me what i wanted. just go into it knowing that it has its issues and you will find something to enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a phenomenal spiritual successor to Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth (2005). Jack's story ended, but Innsmouth and, all that it was, remained. The graphics are at times awe inspiring, and the story... wonderful. It really begins to pick up as the ending draws nearer, and it assisted in the feeling that time was beginning to run out. That said, I feel that there are several loose strings that left untied character wise. It could be a narrative device to further display the active lives going on above you at the end of the game when you have to make your choice, but to me, at least, several characters were just dropped and never addressed again. This is especially true with Throgmartin. He was with you most of the game, but there was no farewell, even though he was an insufferable creature more often than not. I wish that there was more of an incentive to explore the map, especially because of how intricate the visual story telling is. The Letters from Oakmont aren't even a good incentive to explore and look around because most of those locations held high-level enemies from the start of the game, effectively punishing exploration. Same for the All that Glitters quest, the rewards are not worth the risk and should be avoided. And, the combat, oh the combat, it is so lack-luster. they are a threat, yes, and the Field Research quest is cool, but the game would lose nothing if it was removed entirely.Still, good game, would recommend, especially for those who are interested in Innsmouth and the Lovecraftian themes. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. I'm not familiar with Frogwares' previous works, but to my knowledge this is their first shot at an open world game, and they did pretty well. There isn't a whole lot to really *do* in the open world between quest locations, but the art direction and atmosphere of the half-sunken city of Oakmont is phenomenally well done. Just wandering around, gawking at all the landmarks, faded posters, disheveled citizens, and Mythos references was immensely entertaining on its own. Oakmont really feels like a place that could be slotted perfectly into the world of the Cthulhu Mythos like a puzzle-piece.

And you spend way to much time going to one of way to many archieves and looking for stuff, where you can only find stuff if you are on the quest. And the over world is just boring. Nothing ever happens. No fun, no random events, no side quest or rewards for exploring. There is no reason at all not to go to where the quest tell and nothing more. And plotting in the map makers to go anywhere gets very tedious. Some of caves are cool looking and the eldritch art in there looks awesome.The diving segments are very boring. Slowly shuffle along the single path and try to avoid the tentacles. You have camera, you can't take great pictures and display or sell or gather for collectibles. It's just used for a few quest where it doesn't really matter. _childDocuments_.review: As you explore areas (particularly Grimhaven Bay), civilians will often randomly attack you on the open street in broad daylight, for as little as venturing too close.If you're unfortunate enough to be attacked by two of them in the same fight, and you decide to kill them out of self defense, you will automatically drop dead like a ragdoll (because of your sanity meter).After this happened to me for the third time, I finally realized my time is better spent elsewhere.Additional issues I would highlight:- Most of the budget seems to have went into the trailer cinematics. They absolutely do not paint an accurate picture of the final product. They aren't even included as cutscenes.- You pick up what seems to be an entire magazine of machine gun rounds, only to receive one single bullet. Every... damn... time.- Game encourages you to place your own map markers all over the map. However, after ~20 markers, you are not allowed to place any more.- As you explore, you are able to prematurely waltz into areas that you're only supposed to discover later. This allows you to explore sometimes fantastic and detailed environments with absolutely nothing to pick up or examine, ultimately resulting in nothing but wasted time.- Whoever came up with the concept of illusionary objects should never go near a game design board ever again.- There are only four kinds of monster-type enemies, all of which you will no doubt meet in the first few hours of the game.- Monster-type enemies feel like one-trick ponies: they always spawn right around you once you walk past a certain trigger. This artificial difficulty is the only way for them to become a threat, since it prevents you from picking them off from a distance. Also, their ability to spawn in from thin air makes zero sense.- All of Lovecraft's works appear in the game... as a series of collectibles and easter eggs. It makes no sense for them to be present in this context. The Necronomicon is lying in the middle of a street (you pick it up, shoot a boss, get some XP and call it a day). Brain containers are scattered all over the city, but no one as much as raises an eyebrow (not even the protanonist, as he finds them).- Besides all that, the game feels like you're stuck in a Lovecraft universe side story that takes place far away from the real action. Instead of Arkham or Boston, you're stuck in never-before-heard Oakmont. Cthulhu can't be bothered to show up for this gig... so it's his daughter this time around. I watched all the endings on Youtube after I ragequit the game, and all three possible endings feel rushed and atrocious, with no sense of payoff.- There are several other issues that I won't go into, as other reviewers already pointed them out dozens of times - copy-pasted repeats of internal environments and the like - but my pain threshold is high enough to look past those.I consider myself a fan of both Lovecraft and Frogwares, and I'm generally onboard with all the positives mentioned by other reviewers so far. However, I also believe that here, the negatives unfortunately far outweight the positives. I hope The Sinking City 2 will distance itself from the first game and change all of that. Unfortunately, those overblown cinematic trailers are already casting a very familiar foreshadow...

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a little over 21 hours to complete the game (I tried to 100% at first, but gave up on that after side-quests were too repetitive & difficult). This is a good dark, gritty mystery game that is heavily influenced by Lovecraft mythology. You're in an Eastern American fictional city of Oakmont that's been flooded and thus the city is literally sinking into the ocean depths. The city has internal strife with Newcomers, Innsmouthers (fish people) and Ape-like nativists (and human klansmen) composing the city where normal seems to no longer exist.You're a detective with visions who is looking for answers for his visions. You're in the middle of cosmic events beyond your control. I won't say anything more as I don't want to spoil the story, but there's a lot going on in the narrative and I enjoyed the main campaign for this game. Unfortunately, everything else was either mediocre or subpar. The biggest issue was performance issues. On my RTX 3080, I was getting dropped frame rates from a steady 60 fps at the highest graphical settings (on my 2560 x 1440 monitor) most of the time, to variable frame rates of down to 15 fps usually during combat. The variable frame rate did effect gameplay as it made combat more tedious than it had to be. Combat already isn't good in this game, even despite the optimization issues. You're seemingly always out of ammunition if you choose to try to shoot at enemies rather than run away most of the time.Combat is slow, clunky, and repetitive. It seems like your bullets miss if you're too fast on the trigger. There are definitely hit detection issues with multiple enemies on screen. If that wasn't bad enough, there are several underwater sequences which are repetitive and just difficult to navigate due to unresponsive controls and bad camera angles. The sidequests are boring. There's almost no story to them. They consist of repetitive actions which are seldom rewarded as bullets are scarce and doing these sidequests usually leads to having less bullets at the end of them than you did at the start. Trying not to shoot is viable sometimes, but a lot of the times it just makes the quest a lot harder, especially if you're out of materials to make health packs.In the end, there is quite a bit of content in this game, especially if you're trying to 100% it. However, the game is much better if you forget all the filler, and just focus on the main campaign. In fact, the game would have been much better with some of the content cut out as the game starts to feel stale by the end since the main gameplay loop is the weakness of the game. The game is held up by the good narrative though. There's a lot of mystery here that is interesting to uncover. Especially if you enjoy the Lovecraft mythos, I recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to but I really couldn't enjoy this game. It has its moments, definitely, but it wasn't enough for me to keep playing.Pros:1.  The city is dirty, damp, desolate and miserable. We're in the aftermath of a flood and I can't tell you how bizarre it was to talk to a perfectly poised character amidst what is essentially a giant dumpster they're presumably live and/or work in. Lovecraftian fishing town through and through.2.  I wouldn't say it's great, but it is really really good and I enjoyed getting to know the characters.3.  Some of the "passive" animations and scripted reactions impressed me. E.g. when detective Reed's sanity starts to decline he's prone to hallucinations both auditory and visual. What I did not expect the first time it happened was him to put a gun to his head. I don't think he actually pulls the trigger if you hesitate long enough, but the whole scene stuck with me.Cons:1.  The city is dirty, damp, desolate and miserable. Just as miserable as I was, trudging through its wet grey streets, dreaming to see one building with no holes in the walls and without a layer of mud covering every surface. It looks really impressive and atmospheric the first time you see it, but after playing for 5 hours it just sucks all the energy out of you.2.  I'm usually pretty good at navigation. I remember game maps pretty easily and get used to navigating prominent areas without consulting said maps pretty fast. That being said, I could not tell you how much of a chore it was getting from one point in Oakmont to another. Forget fast travel, all streets in one area looked exactly the same to me and I could not make two steps without consulting my map.3.  First, I was really excited about placing the markers for investigations myself. Finding the right street and the right corner, and then leaving markers for your notes or important items. I loved it! But then you actually get to the place you've marked, and you have  where you're supposed to go. I was doing everything short of scaling the walls to try and find where exactly on the street I was supposed to stand to access the right door.4.  There are people in Oakmont, okay? They walk the streets, they say their scripted lines and they shoot the monsters (or each other), if threatened. In fact, I was caught in crossfire more often than not, because police officers don't just shoot actual mutant beasts. They also target-practice on innocent puny detectives from mainland who just happen to pass by the actual mutant beasts. One of the more realistic aspects of a cosmic horror game, I imagine.The actual issue was the fact that you talk to a very small handful of people. Most of the time you're just walking/sailing the streets in complete silence with nothing to break the routine. From point A to point B, to point C, then back to A with a short stop at D. Rinse and repeat.5.  Get rid of it. Toss it in the bin, light it on fire. It's clunky, it's tedious and it's boring. Leave the med kits and the sanity drugs that you can buy for bullets. I get it that detective Reed carrying a gun makes sense plot-wise, but I can't tell you how little I enjoyed the actual enemy encounters.Neutral Points:1.  This one is a bit weird because the narrative definitely wasn't bad but it wasn't exciting enough either. Also I didn't finish the game, so I can't judge too much. So far I liked the mystery, the investigations, the who did what and why. However, I enjoyed much less how little my decisions affected what was happening in the town. Aside from some notes found here and there, there wasn't much impact.Overall, try it, if you enjoy cosmic horror and the very specific type of atmosphere that is Lovecraftian fishing town. Definitely not my cup of tea.But I gave this game a fair shot, and it didn't meet my expectations. Maybe it just isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: To put it short this is a detective simulator with some action and RPG elements.Our hero - Charles Reed - arrives in the remote forsaken city in order to find the answers for the visions he suffers.The main gameplay consists of scanning the crime scenes for evidence and hidden clues. In addition to conventional means our character also possesses a supernatural ability to sense certain traces of the past events and recreating them in his mind.Sometimes we need to consult the city archives in order to find the extra information for the particular case. Doing this we need to decide which archive to use (police, municipal and so on) and which search criteria to use.Between the detective work we also have to occasionally shoot some bandits and monsters, who block our way in the particular investigation.One of the unusual things in the game is a journal and map presentation. Unlike most of the modern games this one does not mark the quest location on the map manually. Instead it provides an approximate address for it and we have to mark and find it manually.It appears interesting at the beginning as it provides the feeling we actually perform some “detective” work, and we have to decide whether a particular quest requires visiting the particular location. But up to the end it simply becomes annoying. Any clue, which is related to the location, is marked by a special icon in the journal - so you can’t miss it. While searching a particular crossroad on the map to place a marker only consumes time.Either a journal should also require more manual work, or map markers should appear automatically.While solving particular cases often there are different conclusions which can be made based on collected evidence. And we can decide which one we will pick, altering the further events and our relationship with different people and factions.Despite the game being inspired by Howard Lovecraft’s novels, it has no decent horror atmosphere. We meet monsters and mutated humans, but the game presents these as something ordinary. It appears like “a fish-faced? - they all come from the same village, all the people there look like this, so what?”. There is no feeling that something big is hidden from you or the locals are hiding some terrible secret. Instead the game appears like some fantasy, we just have fish-faced people instead of orcs and elves.There is a “mental health”, which can be depleted by witnessing shocking events or particular enemy abilities. But it does not change the atmosphere.The “open world” and various choices eliminates the feeling of the struggle with overwhelming forces. There is no clash with some mighty enemy, no feeling of opposition to the mystical secret society and so on. The final quest to deal with some ancient god looks like it has been pinpointed here.Besides the main story we can pick up many side quests and explore the city. Unfortunately the world locations mostly have been designed using the “copy-paste” method. There are several types of building interiors, which are re-used over and over again. Even the loot is placed at the exact same places. At the end of the game there is a feeling the authors are mocking you, eliminating any desire to sweep all the side quests.Exploring mechanics is also disappointing. Our character is unable to jump over a half-meter long pit, unable to squeeze through the opened window and so on.There is no money in the game. After the flood the people in the city use only barter.There are no shops or exchange mechanics. We are unable to exchange one type of bullets to another or exchange bullets for a first aid kit.Also prices and rewards look ridiculous: a single drink in the bar costs 1 bullet, but after solving a complex crime case we receive 2-4 bullets as a reward. Considering that bullets can be crafted from junk found in the streets, any decent work seems to be pointless.The inventory has strict limits on the amount of ammo and craft materials, which can be held. At the same time we carry 2 pistols, 2 rifles, a machine gun and a dry suit without any trouble like these weight nothing. Graphics is decent enough. It has high quality and reflects the flooded city atmosphere nicely.The characters have been rendered with care and in high detail.Sound is unremarkable. There is nothing to catch the ear, but nothing bad either.Total rating - 6/10.As a “detective simulator” the game is interesting. But many things are disappointing and could be implemented in a better way.Also the game does not meet the common expectation as it does not feel like “Howard Lovecraft” style.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated for 2024: I know this release is highly controversial, but this version is the actual full game, published by the devs themselves (minus DLCs, which are sold separately on Steam) and has all working Achievements.  If you're like me and have been waiting for a proper release on Steam, this is it.  The game itself is great if you like the Sherlock Holmes games from Frogwares, only with a Lovecraftian focus and some exploration and combat.  The combat itself is serviceable, but not great.  It does have that "survival horror" quality of "making every bullet count", and scavenging or crafting for more resources, but its janky and unsatisfying.  Luckily it's pretty infrequent unless your doing the side quests or are late in the main story, and not really the reason you play a game like this anyway.It's a detective game where clues must be found, deductions made, cases solved, local archives researched, etc.  There are no way-points or quest markers except what you add to the map yourself.  You find notes and clues, which you can then take to the local police station, newspaper office, or hospital, and use the clues you found to research people/events/births/deaths/arrests/past investigations/etc to get more clues which you can then assemble in the "Mind Palace" and use your deductions to place your way-points and markers.  Most missions end with a choice of who you will side with based in your deductions, and whether you were right or wrong are all in the details you either found or missed, and the game continues regardless of your choice.  I really enjoyed this part, and really made me feel like a detective.Atmosphere is suitably eerie, and scary.  Environments are well detailed.  Game was clearly made by fans of the source material(s).  As much as I like the visuals, they do have a muddy color scheme and aren't as sharp as I'd like, but that also adds to the wet and muddy feel to the environment.  Great graphics and sound, decent controls, lackluster combat.  Overall very good game if you're into Lovecraft (even though this is at least the 3rd Lovecraft inspired game to feature a Private Investigator as the protagonist), and it is different enough from 2018's Call of Cthulhu that I would recommend it to any Lovecraft fan looking for a great immersive dip into the mythos.

_childDocuments_.review: After sinking 35 hours into the game I finally finished it today. I am a big fan of everything Lovecraft and after playing the Call Of Cthulhu game and liking it, I craved more lovecraftian gaming experiences. This game was that - a great lovecraftian vibe and basic enough story with semi-complicated detective and combat elements. However, that is all it is. The detective work becomes stale after so many side missions that I gave up on trying to do them all fairly early on as each one had the same rinse and repeat process. Only the story missions each felt genuinely unique, but even they became stale toward the endgame. The combat is clunky, and there are only four enemy types that you ever fight, so it gets boring fast. Another problem- the ending is the most underwhelming experience of any game I've played. There's no boss fight, so there ended up being no reason for me to mass-craft ammo and bombs before the final mission and no reason to progress my combat skill tree. Each of the three final decisions end in a 30 second cutscene that doesn't really leave you satisfied no matter what you pick, because your previous decisions through the game don't effect the ending choices at all (cough, telltale, cough). All in all, this game does a great job at the vibe and lore of the source material, but unfortunately due to the devs' pressure from the publishers, it is an unfinished, unpolished game. I'd say it is only worth buying if you're really into lovecraftian horror or detective games, and only play the main missions as not to waste your time. And don't pay full price for it, wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The best Lovecraftian experience I ever had.The story is engaging, with characters fitting what you can expect from the setting. As the storyline progresses, you feel more and more like an ant in a world controlled by the ancient ones and their minions.The story is well-made and reveals itself to you in various plot-driven investigations. Lovecraftian themes are strong in this one.The sound design is eerie, and the music tracks fit the narrative like 1920s silk. Beautifully gruesome environments that smell like fish and fit a gothic aesthetic. They also fuel the feel of a city being on its downfall.I loved how the detective works on higher difficulty settings: you really feel like a detective gathering clues, interrogating people, and drawing conclusions about your case in your mind palace.The creature design is on point, and their distribution fits the idea of a "sinking" city.The madness mechanic is narrative and fits well within a storyline that brings the feel you are looking for. I hope to see more DLC to scratch this itch.Congratulations to the devs on regaining control of this title.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game, but by watching reviews one would think otherwise. They judge the game by metrics that do not apply in this type of game. I saw many complaints about combat and how little ammunition we can carry. First off, it’s supposed to be a horror game, you are not supposed to be a one man army, you are supposed to be afraid of enemies and run away here and there. People that do complaints like these miss completely what the genre of the game is all about. Although it’s much more of a open world game and soon enough you become so strong enemies are not a threat anymore, and in my opinion it’s a negative. The difficulty of the game shouldn’t become trivial as you progress.Others yet complain about how limited the “RPG” elements are in this game, and nowadays any level up mechanic is enough to make a game be considered a RPG. The game is not an RPG, and I’m glad that still it has this mechanic, otherwise killing monsters would feel like a waste of time. So, in my opinion, having a Character progression of any type makes killing the enemies more rewarding. Even thought I think we become too strong after leveling up everything.Anyway, I avoided the game for a long while, feeling sometimes attracted to it, but also I was never really interested in horror games, mainly because of ammunition scarcity. When I heard this game wouldn’t impose that, it became much more interesting and made me play the game. Story and dialog heavy games are usually not my thing, but sometimes it works for me. If I was to criticize something is that the loot is always the same in the same places, and it resets anytime we load the game or go far away. I think many don’t play this game because they think it’s a horror game, if they knew it is more of an open world game, more people would play.But the game do have some issues. When I shoot using the shotgun, the game almost always freezes for half a second. Sometimes when enemies come into view, the game also slows down a lot sometimes. It’s not like the game have this super graphic to justify being so heavy on the hardware. Also most of the NPCs are quite ugly, all the women look the same, for example, in contrast with our character and some important NPCs that are full of details. Many NPCs have a cartoonish face and look like an art style. But it’s not, otherwise the main characters would also look cartoonish.Most of the voice acting is quite good, but when they tried to make some of the female disturbed voices, like the mad mom, the witch and the mayan vampire, they sounded very contrived. Still, overall, the game is very good. But the main character is very likable, and normally American main characters they either don’t have any personality or they act like jerks all the time. Here they could really make a main character with a moral grayness enough that we can imput our own values in what he says many times, although not always.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite this game having some simple game flaws, like NPCs just popping in and out of existence, and some of the world feeling a bit empty since its sort of that GTA open world style, it has a really really solid foundation as a game. The combat is a little less than good, but the game does a great job of making the HP lovecraft lore come to life. The voice acting is great, the story itself is the best I have seen in a Lovecraftian type of game in a while, it ♥♥♥♥♥ all over the Call of Cthulhu game that came out before it. The mind palace mechanics and thought mechanics are reminiscent of Disco Elysium, and the sanity system is really really great, it pulls off the same sort of vibes that Amnesia the Dark Descent did. Overall, this game is instantly a classic for me, despite it's flaws, definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: (strictly for Lovecraft fans)I've played 6 Lovecraftian games and "Sinking" is the first where I believe in the city.It's big, even travelling via boats takes minutes from one district to another; it's populated, walking crowds, cultists, tentacled cats and bigger INDESCRIBABLE creatures in darker alleys;It has records and archives, which keep lore and you'll visit them a lot.You scrupulously study walls and floor for a missed evidence (hello pixel hunting).You use logic to connect a crime sequence - literally marking 1, 2, 3 clouded events.Then you visit one of several records/archives and search for the last information through key phrases (filters) i.e. time period, places, names, events.The feeling when you got another clue is truly rewarding!There's crafting, you loot trash bins and tables for the crafting materials to create bombs and bullets.There's skills tree, you shoot with less recoil, carry more items and have a chance not to use crafting bits.The same diving and ascending cut-scene for all underwater episodes. Ok...I wish there were more underwater episodes. The first time you dive it's like... Oh-ho! O_ORandomly transparent heads.Lots and lots of freezes when inside houses during gun fights.Play only if you like detectives and/or Lovecraftian myths.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having an unexpected amount and quality of fun. I was pleasantly surprised, to say the least.The Sinking City combines three -very-important aspects of Lovecraft that most "experts" tend to ignore: the horror that lies in the unknown -rather than the realization of the object of horror itself-, the quick adjust-or-go-crazy transition in the character's behaviors, and the weird sense of humor that HPL showed from time to time, like powder of Ibn Ghazi in an insecticide sprayer, brains in jars, human faced rat spies, just to name a few. Gameplay is mostly action-oriented, with a healthy dose of investigative work added in. Your investigator has some unnatural abilities to help solve the cases, and these are both fun to use and to watch. There are a lot of "gamey" elements, like different weapons, med-kits for the body and the mind, clothing to unlock, and a whole city to explore. You will find very little ammo aside from the rewards for missions, yet, if you really look, your inventory will usually be overflowed with crafting elements. This gives some sort of balance to the game, even when many times you will be running away from monsters rather than doing combat. Story is solid, mood is TERRIFIC, the city looks like Innsmouth would once the deep hybrids had settled in and asserted dominance. The extra touches of Lovecraft lore, like people acting strange on the street, sporadic episodes of violence -both self-inflicted as well as upon others-, the townspeople in different states of transition to deepness, the abnormal normality of it all... these things make evident the fact that this game's developers don't only read Lovecraft; they deeply know and love his works, and avoid the one-more-game-of-The-Call-Of-Cthulhu-Story path to bring something that is both a great homage to cosmic horror, as well as innovative and, most important, FUN. To sum this up: this game feels like Lovecraft, and plays like a game. It sparks your interest and curiosity, with gameplay that is fun and engaging, although it can turn repetitive if you play a lot of it in one sitting. This crew did something amazing that must not be missed if you love and enjoy Lovecraft and games, beyond the already way too corrupted "lovecraftian" term (geez, I've come to hate that word...). Sadly, I am not well informed about the problem this study had with Steam. Whatever it was, I hope it's been solved, and the responsible part - aaaat-steamCHOO! - stop that kind of money-grabbing schemes... I mean, we almost lost the chance to play this wonder. Then again, corruption is everywhere and taints everything... as Howard told us long, long before. Buy this game. And have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: H.P. Lovecraft inspired world, acceptable voice acting, lack luster combat but decent atmosphere. For the same price you ought to get Vampyr, which has a better story, narrative and combat (though different).Story: As P.I. Charles Reed, you are tasked to figure out why both you and Oakmont's inhabitants are plagued with visions. Being inspired by H.P. Lovecraft, there is heavy influence of Cthulu and Stygians. While it is interesting, is doesn't bring enough to the story to make it deep. Gameplay: While combat is acceptable enough, it doesn't take long to have experienced the lot of it within around an hour of the game. The weapons are few and the enemy variations are fewer.The crafting system is a nice addition but feels a bit odd and unnecessary. There are a variation of tagged containers which contain crafting materials.There are infested areas which are where the most amount of crafting materials can be found, and one should know that upon exiting and reentering it, enemies will respawn and so will the majority of the loot caches.There are cases to solve, which require you to gather information through dialogue, exploration, or sometimes simply searching through archives. After enough progress and upon finding enough clues, you can draw your own conclusions and often choose between option A or B, which are often antipodes. This is where one would assume that such a big decision would have a big impact on the world, but it is very lackluster.Each kill and every case solved grants you XP. When leveling you get a ''knowledge'' point that you can spend in one of 3 talent trees, making the game slightly easier (you can level everything to the maximum rather easily).You'll spend to majority of your time running through empty streets after a fast travel, then killing some repetitive mobs, then, hopefully, find the story bits interesting. Graphics: While the game looks fine, at first, and offers a good ambience, the fact that everything looks very similar and that you can go everywhere very early on in the game renders the whole exploration aspect moot. It's too bad since if the game would have been a tad better divided, exploration could have been fun. Instead, I just started fast travelling everywhere and rushing to get where I needed to be. Audio: The ambience is good, the music track non existent. Voice acting is okay, but could've been better. My 2 major gripes are with the cinematics and when the the character recollects events. During -many- cinematics, the audio has a delay. During the recollections, the audio cuts 1 second before the end of every dialogue. It gets annoying.I could recommend this game. Heck, I should, cuz I don't regret playing this game. But it is waaay too highly rated for what it is. If you're dead set on buying it, do so on sales.

_childDocuments_.review: !!!PLEASE NOTE!!!: After three years, Frogwares have re-acquired the rights to the game and have released a new build of the game on Steam. While I don't think it will change any fundamentals, it's very possible that some of the technical aspects of the game have been cleaned up, so please keep this in mind! My original review follows below:Unfortunately, The Sinking City is a game in which almost every aspect of the experience is either unfinished, doesn't work or just isn't well thought out. I'm convinced the developers were quite passionate about this project, but its clear it was probably too ambitious for Frogwares to pull off. I'm quite fond of a lot of their games in general, so it does pain me a little to  leave a negative review. There were times were I did get some enjoyment out of the game, but there are so much elements which are constantly working against that.Let's go over some of the aspects that don't really work in this game. It's supposed to be an open-world game, but there really isn't anything to do within that open world. You just get a few assignments throughout the game (as part of the story as well as a few side-missions) which you completely by visiting certain locations. There isn't anything to do outside those locations. There are no interactive element in the entire city, aside from the random passersby NPCs on the streets. They show very little reaction to your actual presence, aside from complaining a little when bumped into or running away when you briefly flash your gun out in the open. They don't even have a lot of voice clips. Strewn throughout the city are some "infested areas" which contains randomly spawning monsters. These areas have almost no point as you can just avoid them by taking another route. Most of the time you do not need to be in an infested location. I don't think these areas have any point at all and could have been removed from the game. Overall, it's one of the most lifeless open-world cities I've ever played, and this aspect feels extremely undercooked.Then there's the gunplay. This is the first Frogwares game I've played that has any gun action in it (that I can recall), and it's not pretty. All your guns feel extremely limp, your shots have very little impact, and you'll be missing 50% of the shots you take. Combine that with how extremely feeble your character is, and you'll soon dread the tedium of the shooting action. You have a few guns and some extra gadgets, but none of them are satisfying or fun to use. I found it rather hard to avoid many of these encounters, as most enemies appear in places that you need to thoroughly and methodically investigate. Overall: not pleasant.The game also has a few underwater diving sections. These amount to pretty much nothing. You can just run forward mostly and you'll do just fine. There is the occasional Horror Fish, but you can just shoot them a bit and run past them. There's even a flare gun that's supposed to be able to distract enemies, but I think it doesn't work.Then there's the story elements. There are some interesting tidbits here and there, and the smaller contained stories can be pretty decent actually, but the overarching plot is problematic. At first, it does seem like The Sinking City is trying something a bit different. Basically, many of the Lovecraftian elements are already out in the open. For example, Innsmouth Syndrome is an actual thing that people know about, and many hybrids live inside the city. Several sea-deities are actively worshipped in plain daylight, and flesh-eating monsters occupy the city, and this infestation is public knowledge. It's an somewhat interesting idea. For example, the game uses the most likely racist ideas behind "The Shadow over Innsmouth" as reason to involve the local KKK chapter in the story, which is interesting.However, the game makes you more or less numb to the horror elements by assaulting you with an overload of Lovecraftian themes. There's just too much of it. Every single cosmic horror cliche in the book is thrown at you from the second you arrive in Oakmont. You'll start to feel numb to it all before you know it. But worst of all is that the game captures some of the imagery, but not the feeling of Lovecraftian horror. Often times it feels like the game is more keen on showing you tons of tentacles than it is in making you feel what this genre is supposed to feel. Case in point: in a genre where the central focus in on humanity's insignificance in the face of vast, unspeakable cosmic powers, your character actually takes center stage in their affairs. That just doesn't work for me. Every once and a while I came across something that was just so over the top that it almost made me laugh out loud. it just doesn't work at times, and it's a shame.Then there's also an extremely undercooked experience and skill system. It feels very throwaway and doesn't really influence that much. I just dropped some random points in some skills and I did just fine.But worst of all are the game's technical issues. Performance isn't good at all. I struggled to maintain a solid 60 fps with a more than decent rig. The game has some of the worst stuttering I've ever seen in any game. It's almost unplayable, and I think many people won't even bother with the game because of this very issue. Whenever I shot an enemy with my shotgun, the game would stutter/freeze for about 0,5 seconds. It's truly awful, and it makes the terrible gunplay even worse.Then there's the pop-in. When you're walking down the streets, random objects and NPCs will just appear right in front of your eyes. Often times you'll be able to see them spawn in the air and witness them drop a good 20 centimeter to the ground from where they are spawned. Sometimes NPCs spawn in bad places, such as on top of cars, where they'll be starting at you, remaining forever immobile.While some of the hybrids look quite good (the Innsmouthers are well-done I feel), the other character models look fairly awful. They look like cartoon characters that are in the first stages of Innsmouth syndrome themselves, with their weird lips, strange faces and bulging eyes. To be clear: this effect was not intended by the developers. Animations are equally stiff, especially in conversations.I should stress that I encountered *NO GAME BREAKING BUGS*. I was able to finish the game from start to finish without major issues. I had no crashes, and never got stuck or broke sequence. The game is perfectly completable in this stage, and I did everything there was to do in this game.  Despite my harsh assessment, I did still have some fun with this game. I admit that I'm basically any game that puts you in the shoes of a detective-style character, and indeed this is the best part of the game. I enjoy sniffing around in houses and putting clues together, and while its not as good as Frogwares' Sherlock Holmes games, it can still be enjoyable.I think there should also be a special shout-out to some of the art in the game. Frogwares' artists clearly had a blast creating this game, and some of the scenery looks fantastic. Some of the underwater caves are really breathtaking. Oakmont itself can get quite repetitive, but I nonetheless think it's of high quality when assessed in isolation.Overall, I'd only recommend this game IF you are a fan of lovecraftion imagery AND you are a fan of detective stories AND you are capable of stomaching the technical qualities of this title. I'd advise caution to everyone else.However, I do hope Frogwares makes a renewed attempt at revisiting this title. I'd love to see some of the many issues addressed in a sequel or spiritual successor, because at the end of the day this is a fairly unique game. Again, I definitely did get some enjoyment out of this title, it was just drowned out by much of the bad stuff.

You do feel like you're stuck choosing between only bad options and there is no "good" ending. The cosmic horror element is very strong, and much more than just tentacles.
