_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City takes place in the desolate city of Oakmont, an immersive Lovecraftian environment filled to the brim with nightmarish monstrosities and maniacs. Unfortunately, your visit is not under the most pleasant of circumstances. An unexpected flood has swallowed the city and brought with it a few uninvited guests. As a private investigator from Boston, you've travelled far across the ocean to uncover the source of your dreams. But be wary, for once you step foot inside Oakmont, there's no escape. Don't expect any kindness or hospitality from the locals' newcomers like you are nothing more than dirt to them. If you wish to fit in, you better not question their culture, even if outlandish at times. Something horrifying yet marvellous is rumoured to lurk underneath the murky waves of saltwater. If you're foolish enough to go for a deep dive to uncover the secrets of this hellhole, then you must've already been driven mad.GAMEPLAY:You'll spend the majority of your time doing detective work, uncovering secrets while trying to please your employers. A small portion of the game will also have you fight wylebeasts among other things. Usually, a case goes something like this: Discover new locations until you have enough clues to track down who/whatever you're looking for and have 1-3 encounters with wylebeasts along the way. The game's 90% detective work / RP'ing and 10% combat with wylebeasts or inhabitants of the city. Overall the gameplay for me is 8/10 as long as you're in it for the story.THE STORY:This is the main selling point of the game! The story is filled with lots of choices that impact how the story is told, you got multiple endings and it always keeps you on your toes. The main story is pretty long, I'd say about 15-20 hours depending on whether or not you get lost or use a guide. The game's side stories add another 10-15 hours of content and some of the side missions are almost more interesting than the main ones. I don't wanna go into details when it comes to the story but it's definitely worth checking out. The story itself gets a 9/10 from me. It's really well written in my opinion.ENVIRONMENT: The city and its inhabitants all look absolutely stunning... well for the most part. If you got a keen eye you'll, unfortunately, notice a handful of clipping issues with the environment. The most common ones I've spotted are staircases within houses and doorsteps outside on the street. There's also an issue with random citizens outside. You see they sort of just warp into existence out of nowhere and the paths they walk are far from natural. This is definitely not enough to break the immersion doing missions but it certainly does drag the final product down a bit. You'll also start to notice that the infrastructure of buildings are VERY similar as in they copy-pasted the inside of certain buildings a lot. I'd say there's a good 20 different buildings and of course, they're decorated differently to make them stand out but you can still tell they're getting reused. Don't get fooled, I absolutely adore the world of The Sinking City! But unfortunately, it does have some cracks that could've been polished. The environment part of the game gets a 7/10 from me.DIVING:I have to dedicate a section to this aspect of the game cause it needs more attention. Occasionally throughout the story, you'll have to dive into the water wearing a diver's suit. These sections are absolutely dreadful and deprive you of all fun. You can barely move while underwater, there are rarely if ever any secrets to find, you'll walk in a straight line till you reach your destination and sometimes have to deal with a couple of underwater creatures while using the poor underwater combat mechanics. These sections are rare doing the early game, but late mid-game, they'll start to become a frequent activity that you have to take part in. This part of the game gets a 2/10. The only positive is that the underwater environments sometimes can look absolutely horrifying and that you'll never have fight any boss doing one of these deep dives while wearing the diver's suit.BOSS FIGHTS:Another weak aspect of the game is arguably its boss fights. The Sinking City has a total of 4 bosses, with 2 of them being optional and the other 2 skippable. Since combat isn't one of the main selling points of the game it's pretty obvious that giant epic boss fights were never a priority. I tried to conserve ammo doing most of my wylebeast encounters and ended up with a crazy amount of spare ammo. This led to me being able to one-shot 2 of the bosses. And when I say one-shot I mean I killed them in 5 seconds after the cutscene that spawned them ended. There is 1 insanely cool optional boss that you most likely will randomly encounter that adds a few points to this aspect of the game. Boss fights gets a 4/10. 2 of them you can one shot, the 3rd is a puzzle and the 4th is a scary bullet sponge that jumpscares you (I didn't list them in the order you encounter them)FINAL VERDICT:The Sinking City is a 7.5/10 game with a handful of flaws but it's a beautiful game at heart that's trying to tell an interesting story. The majority of the negative reviews I've seen are from people who complain about the legal issues with the game or the fact that it was an Epic exclusive for a while. If you're a fan of everything Lovecraftian then you have to checkout The Sinking City.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking city is a mid game. It's not necessarily the best game, but I found it mostly enjoyable for the most part.Highlights for me are as followed:- Great Atmosphere, very spooky, very foggy (maybe too foggy)- The Case mechanics and the mind palace are very neat things, It was really cool putting the cases together and having to cross reference archives. - I like the Innsmouthers, they're really cool and I love how many of them are somewhat fleshed out with stories.- Got to fight racists which is a big WLowlights:- I don't know why but whenever I used my shotgun the game lagged and bugged out. I don't know if that's just my game or a consistent issue.- The Music wasn't great. I honestly turned it off in the first 5 minutes because I felt that it distracted me from the game as a whole.- Your Choices don't *really* matter. Perhaps that's meant to be the point of the game and I'm being obtuse, but nothing you do really changes the outcome of the game. All you get is a passing statement from a character here or there that "Hey I saw you do that". In the end the only choice that really matters in the game is the one at the very end. That said, there are specific choices that you can make which help you in the long-term, by which I mean help you avoid fights.- The World building is one of my favorite aspects of the game, but I feel it's sort of lacking. There is a fine line between "leaving it up to interpretation" and "Not adding any depth or elaboration at all." The Game makes references to various things within the Lovecraft mythos (no duh), but then doesn't really explain it. Like, who is Kay? Is Kay god? Usha mentions Kay, so is Kay some eldritch being? We don't know and it's never elaborated on. It might be that Kay is Cthylla, some have said that Kay might be K'baa the Serpent or Kthanid, MAYBE they mean the big G, I don't know it's never explained. It's not critical to the story but it would be nice to know! Dagon you don't really need explanation for because if you know Lovecraft, you know Shadow Over Innsmouth. In fact, Shadow Over Innsmouth and several other Lovecraft stories are mentioned in the game multiple times. Literally everything in the game is a Lovecraft reference, and I don't just mean "Yeah it's a Lovecraftian game, it's going to have Lovecraft references and the likes", I mean the ENTIRETY of the setting is just reference after references. The Whately name is plastered everywhere, the Street names have Alhazared, etc. also the Monoliths in the city are everywhere but no one seems to go "huh that's weird, is that connected to the flood perhaps?" Like gee I wonder if the eldritch monoliths are related to the fact everyone is going crazy and dying? I can't tell if this is a case of "Real Lovecraft fans will get these references" gone wild or if it's like a "Fanfic turned into a game".- The world feels kind of empty, NPCs and side quests are limited, but they're enjoyable. - The cutscenes are glitchy and choppy, they're low res, but it's not the worst thing in the world.Final Thoughts:This is a good game, it's fun to play through, but it could also be so much MORE! It's annoying to me how this game could be so much better, because right now this highlights some great core concepts and mechanics that I'd love to see in a game that is much more fleshed out.5/10, Fun for a time

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game but only when it’s discounted to ½ price or more.It’s not a bad game but it’s clearly unpolished and clunky.The main story is pretty decent and interesting, albeit standard Lovecraftian fare. The visuals are good, and the voice acting is nice.  The concept of investigation through the game is nice and I wish it was fleshed out more. There is an “RPG” mechanic where you get skills as you get XP as reward for quests, and it’s pretty ok However, all side quests are basically fetch-quests. Rewards for quests (aside for XP) are just crafting materials, but since there are some places in the world that you can easily loot over and over again easily (just outrun the monsters) you really do not need it.Overall, the world of the game is not that interesting to explore because all exploration is the same “find thing on map – go to place – fight a couple of monsters – loot the place”. You can feel it was a rushed game.The combat is serviceable but boring. Overall, I would have much more preferred if this game mainly focused on investigation, finding clues and making deductions. The mechanics for it are there, but I wish they were better fleshed out. Now, lots of the problems in the game derive apparently by issues between the developers and publishers and essentially we got a game that is half finished… and for this reason buy it half price, because full price (about 35 USD) is not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: My expectations were low, so I was pleasantly surprised.  I find the gameplay and UI overall agreeable.  I mostly appreciated the role-playing decisions and the game does a great job making you feel like a gifted detective (finding clues and making deductions), even though it is rather easy in reality (do not expect actual puzzles).  Some reviews make it sound like a deep challenge, where you mark clues on your map...  Sigh.  Not really.  What is different is that the game does not always show you where to go ... which felt immersive, but not really hard either.  For example (not a spoiler), after finding clues, the game might utterly tell you the person may be hiding at the bar, but the game will not mark the bar on the map.  Many clues will tell you were to go, and it is rather easy to find an intersection of streets on the map and add a marker if you wish (it's optional).  The important thing to know is that it is not hard; it just holds your hand less than in other games. After the first investigation / intro, the game feels open-world, with a huge city map and sometimes you will need to use your logic to know where to go (well, just reading the clues properly usually tells you what to do).  This open-world feeling adds to the immersion.  You can do many secondary investigations in any order (the main story is linear, but with some role-playing decisions, and three endings).  Honestly, while being cautious, I was not really afraid.  It did not feel like a really scary horror game to *me* anyhow, which is a good thing for my taste.  It is a mystery adventure, a bit fantastic (it does not seek to look real, I mean with many inhabitants looking like new races of Humans), and with a really not-subtle at all Cthulhu theme.   A lot more combat that I imagined from this genre of game.  You are not super-human, so avoid being hit.  There is a limit to how much ammo you can carry, which is only a challenge at first.  You can craft freely as you explore/loot the map and I recommend choosing the crafting perks first (there is a skill tree). The only criticism I would make is that the mystical or Cthulhu theme is too overt, explicit, in your face, to the point of being amusing rather than scary. All in all, I found the game systems fun.  * The Detective difficulty is recommended, as it is almost exactly like easy: the only difference is it will not tell you exactly which action to take (but the clues are logical and it is easy to guess).  It still shows you that a clue requires an action or if you should take a picture, etc.  If you want more challenge, there is one higher difficulty. * The game tells you when you have found the key evidence in an area.  You must gather at least the key evidence.  It also tells you when you found all interactables (so-called "All evidence").  Sadly, there is no achievement for finding ALL evidence, though one achievement is called "All Evidence Collected", but it actually is for collecting all other achievements (aka Platinum or 100%). * Decisions are role-play, for the story of how you want to play the detective.  Your decisions impact the life/death of some people you meet, but they do not impact the endings.  The 3 possible endings are your free choice no matter your past decisions. * There are no achievements for skills, clearing areas, etc. If you focus mostly on the main story, probably 25 hours.  Trying to do everything is about 30 hours or more.

_childDocuments_.review: Very disappointing game, honestlyIt had so many chances to not be terrible and disappointing, but here we areThe story is honestly pretty good, for what it's worth, but nothing you do leading up to the end makes ANY difference on the actual end of things. There's a lot of good elements, but there's a lot that can just be confusing non-sense if you don't know enough of the mythos to start with (looking at you, helpful dude from the start of the game). The animations are not great, the voice acting is alright (with notable exceptions on both sides of the spectrum but not where you'd want them), the city feels excessively static, the NPCs are metaphorically made of the thinnest cardboard, the resources are said to be scarce and feel like they are but only in the wrong ways: they're not hard to find, they're just hard to find when and where you'd like them, and you can only carry a small amount of each things, but it's super easy to refill literally  everything you want in 15 minutes in one spot next to a fast travel node. I enjoyed playing the game for a lot of it, but i can't recommend it to anyone. The ending is too infuriating and disappointing (all of them), to the point where it sours the time i spent leading up to the end, which is honestly quite the shame.  It should be a good game. I could be a good game. It's not a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: A very atmospheric and compelling storyline with interesting characters and a very Lovecraftian plot.+ the different enemy types force you to make difficult decisions during combat+ the crafting/ foraging mechanics interplay really push you to explore the environment fully + it feels like you're really figuring out each case as you progress, sifting through evidence as you go to try and figure out whats going on.+ the sidequests allow for more content inspired by the lore.+ the underwater sections are very claustrophobic and tense, it really triggers a sense of panic and helplessness when you have limited speed and options- many characters feel like they need more development, especially the Grand Families and their interactions.- the locations feel very copy/paste; it may have helped compress the size of the game but more variance would have been with the extra discspace. - for all the development that went into the game, there really could have been more quests that flesh out the world more.

The stories within game that I discover - both the main and the side quests - makes me want to read his writings.This is a well-developed game for what it is. The world you're in feels both small and huge, probably because of the way you're forced to travel (slower than most games, but there are fast-travel points around the city that you can use after you discover them).I really like this game and I took a risk on it, hoping it would keep my interest for at least a few hours. _childDocuments_.review: As far as gameplay goes, it's a decent game if you don't mind quite a bit of combat in your investigation game or vice versa. The main gameplay loop involves figuring out a location from the clues you've gathered, going to investigate, being attacked by eldritch horrors (and/or people), figuring out how things played out, speaking with someone, searching some archives, and repeat. Thankfully fast travel is available for areas you've already been to.The controls aren't really complicated so it doesn't take much time to become used to them. 4/6 enemy types will begin side stepping once they notice you pointing a gun at them so that makes combat a little more interesting. The thing is that the game tells you to avoid combat in order to save on bullets (which are somewhat limited), but it doesn't specify that this should only be applied to certain areas since investigation scenes need to be cleared of enemies.There are also underwater mini-levels which while they look cool and don't really feel bad, seem like a gimmick rather than a fleshed out part of gameplay. They are all really short and feature a total of 4 challenges: , , , and . I was expecting something more from the underwater experience of this title.The story involves a private investigator (the protagonist) going to Oakmort city in hopes of figuring out the source of his visions and ridding himself of them. In the process, he gets caught up in something greater.The game features a well sized cast of characters which you interact with (semi)regularly, and often gives you a choice on how to progress the plot. My issue is that (minor spoiler) . Also the endings (minor spoiler) .I've managed to complete the main story and about 2 or 3 side quests in 18 hours or so, so it's not that long of a game.As for visuals and sound design, the game does a really good job at bringing the city and its events to life. The creature design looks interesting in my opinion, and the semi-stylized graphics work in favor of this title. The voice acting is also one of the better ones I've come across.The music falls mostly on the ambient side, but this isn't really a clear positive nor a negative since it depends on the one playing the game. Personally, I think the music is very fitting.I haven't encountered anything game breaking so far. The worst case of a bug I've come across involves an enemy teleporting inside a wall and being stuck there, which just made things easier for my investigation. Also I've noticed that NPCs will often just pop into existence right in front of the player which breaks the immersion quite a bit. Other than that, there is nothing else to write home about in my experience.Overall the game seems to have been made with at least some passion but perhaps either the budget or short deadlines resulted in it missing some polish. This review might seem mixed, but ultimately I enjoyed playing the game.I don't think it's worth the 40€ price tag but I got it on sale for -90% (4€) which is definitely worth. Maybe 20€-25€ would be a more fitting price for this title.

Launches SteamVR, despite not being a VR game or even a 1st person game.2. Cannot be streamed on Discord, regardless of what video settings used. _childDocuments_.review: It is a so-so game, but there's not such an option on Steam.You are a detective haunted by visions who came to the town isolated from outside world by massive flood. In an attempt to get rid of your nightmares you shall solve a number of cases, each giving you a new clue how to progress. There are also side cases but I was able to level up my character to very satisfactory degree solving only few of them. Throughout your investigation you shall recognize various motives from H. P. Lovecraft short stories if you are familiar with them. Developers also wanted to give you a strong feel of scarcity. Monetary trade is gone in the city and people barter useful items and parts. They are advising you to think twice before firing a bullet and to consider whether running is a better option. Nothing can be farther from the truth, namely game has a glaring bug that literally cancels mentioned game mechanic - every time you load your game and every time you use quick travel world resets itself and all containers are refilled again and again. That means if you have enough patience you can refill your ammo and first aid just by raiding free containers that are situated in a hotel main character uses as his base of operations. Another weird glitch I noticed is that game does not save your difficulty preferences, you should visit settings every time you play the game and set preferred difficulty if you don't play on default. Optimization: Graphics are excellent but this game mightily heats both processor and graphic card. If you minimize your game and open browser temperature shall fall over time. The game never crashed in my case (Win 10 user here).Fun: I enjoyed cases very much at the beginning but past my 20th hour in game repetitive work bored me and I just wanted it to end. Difficulty: I have ironmaned the game on Detective / Normal level in slightly above 31 hours. If you are not reckless I believe many of you can do it too.

_childDocuments_.review: The theme definitely does the heavy lifting in this game due to mediocre mechanics and puzzles but it was still a very enjoyable experience that doesn't overstay its welcome... as long as you are able skip past the repetitive and boring sidequests. _childDocuments_.review: An unpolished gem, but a gem nonetheless. If you like H. P. Lovecraft and/or detective games, this is for you. Yes, the games sometimes seems unfinished, and yes, the gameplay takes a while to get used to, but once you know what to do (you must place locations yourselves) and how to get on, it is a great game. Easily the best Lovecraftian game I have played. I'd also recommend this for anyone into the 1920s and/or New England. The flaws of this game do not ruin it at all. Issues with the game: NPCs sometimes pop up out of nowhere or disappear, or behave oddly; sometimes you  can't easily find a way to climb something, especially annoying if you're in the water. But it's all easy to overlook if you're interested in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: + Interesting investigation mechanics + Scratches that Lovecraftian horror itch- Super janky- Very much overstays it's welcome- Backtracking: The GameWorth looking into for Lovecraft fans who have a lot of free time. Otherwise play Call of Cthulhu instead.A lot of the Lovecraftian vibe is there, the sanity mechanic is played well, you know you're in a Lovecraftian horror story from the outset. There are also many interesting things done with the investigation mechanics (you have to locate places on the map and place your own markers, browse archives etc.) and while these are relatively janky, I did like the addition. The writing isn't award winning, but it overall seems to fit all the characters and is mostly fine. Voice acting is good as well.Now other than all that, the visuals are very much stylised and fitting, but clearly dated. The whole feel of the movement and combat is very janky and it mostly just gets in the way. There are some things done to make it more interesting like weak spots on enemies, but honestly it's 90% reloading a save and hoping you manage to get lucky because while the enemies do have patterns and do telegraph, the whole system is so clunky that when fighting two or more enemies, you just have to hope they get stuck and attack one at a time not phase shift behind you and chomp down. The combat itself isn't that challenging, it's just that at times you are thrown against many strong enemies with little to no choice of avoiding damage while getting stuck on level geometry. And for the worst of the bunch - backtracking. Like okay, I don't really mind backtracking in itself. But that has two important caveats - either it has to be quick or it has to have substance. In Sinking City you backtrack A LOT. I mean I think there were cases where you had to go back and forth between one single place like four times at least. Yes the game has fast travel points between the main locations, but often times they are still like a minute away from where you need to go. In worse cases you need to run, boat and run again to reach the destination from theses points. And there is 0 substance in between. The first time around you might see and mark open doors and random locations or blocked roads you come across, might happen across a mugging in the background or looters fighting over scraps, but after that there is 0 content (except maybe some monsters in the no-go zones). I would have much preferred the city be 5x smaller but maybe have more roads blocked off and areas barricaded etc. so you'd actually have to map out the changes on your map. When starting out I marked two huge blockades on the map and thought how cool that idea was and then figured out that those two were pretty much all I needed to mark. If this game was 80% less running and fighting and 50% more of the investigative stuff, I would have gone for the 100%. But as is, I was just super glad that it was over when it was. A very taxing game in terms of how much jank and nothing you need to experience to get to the good parts. If you're willing to suffer through that, you'll probably like this unpolished gem, but for people with jobs that just want to experience a game and move on to the next one, better skip this. Only recommended because there really is good content in all this, but be warned.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever tried to play 'Call of Cthulhu' by Cyanide Studio, then I can confidently say this game covers everything that one does not. CoC focuses on the statistical aspect of the original tabletop game, letting player choice direct the story without any need for skill or planning, and often times the stats of the character will funnel it in a specific way. I personally disliked that Call of Cthulhu game (for a number of other reasons as well).This game is not that. The Sinking City has been described as the GTA of Lovecraft horror, and I have to agree. The open world aspect of the game is impressive, and I love how much it feels like a whole city. The effort you put in to locate quest objectives and manually mark the map does add to the investigative aspect, though it can get a little old. Unfortunately the streets do reuse assets from time to time, and the civilians don't communicate at all beyond a default line when you bump into them. Just a limitation of the development cycle I assume.Players with lower levels of patience may want to simply focus on the main story and not do the side quests (though the lore is quite interesting for those side adventures) because half the game is running around trying to complete a goal, and it's probably much more fun to just go through the main plot if you just want to get to the core of the gameplay.Combat is interesting. It's what I expected, to be fair, as fighting Eldritch horrors is quite hard when you're just a measly human. I was delighted to see things beyond just Cthulhu and undersea themes, like the King in Yellow's cult showing up, along with mentions of Shub Niggurath, and the Innsmouthers being a big plot point.However, there are only 4 fightable monsters in the game (5 if you count humans) which each function slightly differently. I would have loved to see more enemies overall, like flying ones, or non-aquatic ones? It does feel odd fighting a reasonably hard enemy in the main plot, then fight the exact same thing in a sidequest that is themed after a cult that wouldn't really summon that creature. There's a lot of variants with different abilities, but at a base they're the same 4 monsters (small, medium, large, huge).I'm just nitpicking, I suppose. I also wish there were some things from Lovecraft, like Shoggoths or Nightgaunts, but with the scale of the game, the complex story, and all that they fit in, it's understandable they couldn't fit in too many more. (I do wish we could have seen Deep Ones, but afaik at the moment they don't actually make an appearance?) As you progress, the limitation of bullets and resources is less pressing thanks to the upgrades and stockpiles you become familiar with, though it's always a bit of a grind for them.Overall, I think this is an amazing premise and step up from the 'Call of Cthulhu' game that Cyanide Studio developed, and definitely has a lot of things I missed in that game. If a triple A developer took this system and upscaled it, making it a bit smoother and a more fleshed out world (akin to assassin's creed, since that's similarly open world/free roam) then I think that would be amazing. It has the drawbacks of being a little repetitive, but completionists and fans of Lovecraft's original work will love the little nods to different stories and achievements that you can get by doing different things.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended only on *heavy* sale & willing to put up with jank.This isn't much of horror, mostly combat horror (think Resident Evil 5). If you're a fan of Lovecraft themed games this is pretty interesting as it is deeply entrenched in it. There is a good amount of detective work, quests locations are rarely just given to you, you have to research people and places at police station/newspapers etc, to find them. There is a good amount of mystery and tension here and there with the main quest line.The combat is the weakest part, just mindless run and gunning hampered heavily by the limited ammo capacity (which you have to craft). There also seems to be little rhyme or reason to enemies, you just wander in a random building and BAM some giant horror just chilling there that no one seems to notice or care about.This is one of those "janky but has charm" games that, if it appeals to you, you are willing to overlook the flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want an indepth detective style game with a little bit of action and a lot of Lovecraftian horror this is an amazing game for you! my 19 hours was a single playthrough, the city is very big and there's a lot of quests to take. If you've played other Frogwares games before you'll be familiar with their unique crime scene investigation systems that are really fun and flow well. Your conclusions in these investigations and sway what happens in the city and shapes the world around you. Not everyone will come to the same deductions which I found very cool. I loved all the Lovecraftian stuff in this game, and for once it's not just the cult of cthulhu. The city dwells many cults that you'll recognise and lots of intrigue behind the scenes. The difficulty can be changed depending on what sort of game you prefer. I had my settings as more difficult for the investigation but normal combat so I could be challenged where I wanted to. Everything is voice acted, so you're only left to read the notes and books all of which are quite concise and have info that actually matters even if it has flavour. Only thing I would love this game to have is a minimap. Having to flick open the map everytime I'm trying to find my way through alleyways was a little annoying. Hoping for this feature in Sinking City 2 when it comes out. The graphics are also very good especially considering this was originally a 2019 release from an indie studio. Overall fantastic game and experience. Very keen for the next one that's in development!

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a good game. The meat and potatoes are in the investigations and their places in the overall world, but some things like the enemies, the things NPCs say to not make me shoot their head off (which is policed by a kinda cheap but understandable insanity gauge), and even the house interiors. Most houses are copies of other houses, and locations like the Asylum or the university are quite underwhelming from the inside; these monolithic, legendary locations end up looking pretty cool from the outside but just the same as most other public/commercial buildings on the map. Major letdown (Sad face!!!!!!!!!)Some things are fun about it. Getting to choose how to solve your investigations are fun. I like the underwater stuff  too, and the NOVELTY of the insanity thing (it wears off fast). but the overall commitment to Lovecraft's world and references like "The King in Yellow Street" (I dare not say his true name) are nice to see. That said, I am looking forward to the sequel and hoping they make their NPCs, monsters, insanity effects, interiors and even the "omens" more gooderer. (Like some kind of dynamic besides having shadow people point in a direction like you're following signs). Plus, I hear you can ♥♥♥♥ the monsters and become just like the Innsmouthers if you fail sanity checks!! _childDocuments_.review: Just wanted to put a recommendation out there for anyone unsure about this games worth...Presentation is top quality - Visual and audio design is great!Story - Amazing!! Very captivating!Characters - Very well animated faces, interesting characters to meet and talk toGameplay - Solid and varied. Interrogate people, investigate crime scenes and collect evidence. All done very wellFor the money it is definitely worth it for those gamers looking for something interesting and slow paced. The action is there but it is not the focus. See this as L.A. Noire set in a Lovecraft world/dream/nightmare!!Highly recommend this so far - I can't stop playing it!!Will do a complete review when I've completed my first playthrough - I'm playing blind with no help whatsoever so it might take a while!!Concerns:* The action is questionable!! The shooting lacks impact and "feel". The enemies movement is very erratic sometimes so to have such small hitboxes on them along with very limited resources it makes the combat something I've always tried to avoid. It sucks...it's frustrating and it kinda poops on the whole experience to be honest. The dev's really should have employed someone with a bit more experience in 3rd person action games. Your character is military trained yet you can't hide behind cover, peep around corners or even switch arms/change the over shoulder view!!! It's do-able but nowhere near the fun it should be...* Underwater Sections - Very small, enclosed spaces populated with annoying "enemies" that you can only stun and not kill. Not the funnest parts of the game!!* Jank City!! Quite a bit of weirdness with NPC's appearing out of nowhere...bad pathing...getting stuck in the environment. I just found a train with a box on it...I went to jump in the side of the carriage and couldn't get in. I was floating between the entrance and the floor. COMPLETELY unable to get this loot box due to JANK!!I also just found a curb I couldn't walk over!! I had to walk to the side and around to past...it's kinda amazing how this has been left in the game. Sometimes when investigating buildings the enemies will spawn OUTSIDE of the building?!?! You end up running around inside looking for monsters that aren't there...it just sounds like they're there!!* A blank/empty City! The presentation is great...the streets, the lighting, the weather...walking around at night with your torch is amazing BUT there is just nothing to look for in the world other than staring at static buildings (most of which you can't enter), static vehicles and quite a few NPC's that don't talk and you can't interact with them. The whole world feels empty in terms of gameplay. There is just nothing to look at outside of the main plot and side missions. If you find somewhere it's probably a side quest you haven't found yet...* A Copy/Paste City? Hate to see it and I hate to say it but man...the dev's cut some corners and it's not great! This game COULD have been really, really cool and special if more time (and maybe money) had gone into making Oakmont a real treat to explore. Dynamic events would really help. NPC's to talk and interact with. Just more stuff going on would have been amazing. The love and attraction I had at the start of playing soon faded after a few hours as I realised that I should simply follow the missions as exploring independently from it only showed me how little there was to discover...A HUGE DISAPPOINTMENT!!* Waste of Potential - This game could have been a real game changer. Give it better combat and shooting mechanics along with more dynamic events with a world populated with more people to talk to and things to interact with (a shop to buy gun powder would be nice, a bar to go and chat to the locals...) and you'd be looking at something a lot of people would enjoy playing. I hope a sequel learns from these mistakes...I'd love to see this game living up to it's fullest potential!!* Performance - Whilst performance is pretty stable providing 60fps you will find that when enemies spawn in large quantities your frame rate can get hit very hard! I've seen drops down to 20fps sometimes!! IT RUINS the combat!! Post Process in Graphics settings is set to low by Nvidia's drivers. The frame drops are not so epic on Low but barely any different to setting Post Process to High or Ultra?!? Think it just comes down to bad optimisation. The game is very static so I see no need for high VRAM...* The Ending - Kind of hollow...to have spent so much time leading up to your final decision and then...credits roll...left me feeling like I didn't get complete closure of the story. P.S. I do recommend the hardest setting for the detective work (i still have action set to Normal as it's not the focus for me at the moment). Hard mode means no hand holding...no tips...you work everything out and piece it together...and it works. It's not overly confusing and seems very logical...worth it if you enjoy a challenge!!!7.5/10 - The detective/story half is outstanding to be honest. The world and the characters are some of the most enjoyable I've encountered in gaming in a LONG TIME!! The gameplay mechanics for solving crimes and obtaining info are superb and could even do with having more depth if there is a sequel in the future. It's the combat/action half of the game that let it down overall. If the story half could be mixed with an action part as solid as The Evil Within/Resident Evil then detective games like this would REALLY take off and might even become it's own genre that gets a lot of attention. Too many survival horror games lack depth...the dev's are definitely onto something with this formula...please carry on...I can't wait to see what you do next...

_childDocuments_.review: Update: 10 hours later and several main and side quests later, I still see nothing that implies this is not an official, full game. There's really not a lot more to be said. Maybe just a slight criticism about reusing the same buildings and room layouts, but I honestly like it. I do feel confident in saying you'll probably appreciate it more if you don't pay full price. $40 feels a bit steep for something that would have been cutting edge a decade ago. But it definitely takes its investigative angle pretty seriously with you having to use clues in order to cross reference information in order to progress plots. Admittedly, there is a point in the main plot where your character decides to lecture his employer on bigotry. While I have no issue with addressing concerns such as that, it honestly felt shoe-horned in and, frankly, flat. It goes out of its way to ignore the pain of a parent losing a child, rationalizing that such is the inevitable result of the parent's intolerance to a group of people, that said intolerance leaves those people with no choice but to radicalize and kill their 'oppressors'. In the proper context, this could be an extremely poignant narrative, but, again, in this instance, it just feels like a puzzle piece you jam in and make fit when you look at the story as a whole.To be clear, my issue isn't with addressing social concerns and such, but rather whether or not doing so interferes with the story/journey as a whole. It's not as bad as many games/movies/shows, but it does smack of the heavy-handedness we've seen in other media. I feel that, if the writers really thought they wanted to address this issue, they could have done so far better with far less obvious and dubious dialogue. The way they did this feels more like an after thought, as though someone said 'hey, we should put a monologue here chastising a grieving father for his prejudices using debatable talking points.'We can do better, people.Original: Like a lot of ppl, I was wary of grabbing this because of the reviews saying it was 'pirated'. However, a bit of research led me to wonder just how accurate that claim was. It seems the dev and pub are in a feud and that initially led to the game being pulled from 3rd party platforms. In a court decision, it was stated that the devs were in violation and that they were to honor the contract as it is. More here: As it says in the article, one reason the game seemed to not be complete on steam was due to the devs not releasing the master version to the pub. Whatever the case was, it now seems the full DLC and Achievements are back.So far, I haven't messed with the main storyline more than necessary to get access to the rest of the city. I like my sidequests. I have finished the necronomicon DLC without issue. I have recieved achievements and have been awarded DLC rewards.That is to say, it seems the game works just fine. I had one crash, which may or may not be related to the game or simply my settings. But I lost nothing in it and, aside from the clunky combat and some monsters clipping, I haven't seen anything that makes it unplayable.If you're a fan of Lovecraft type media, if you like puzzle solving, if you like games with lore, if you like a bit of creepiness, I'd say get it. I don't know that I'd recommend at full price just because it isn't all that smoothed out in the 'action' front and plays more like an late 00's, early 10's mid tier 3p action game, but I won't say it isn't engaging or enjoyable despite the combat issues.A couple new player tips:1. Find the phone booths in each area you come into before exploring(after you reach the Inn). Don't explore without having those locations available if you don't want to risk having to re-travel half the map.2. Pay attention to your sanity and just run if you encounter something. Cthulu games are not in the habit of being combat focused and are in the habit of discouraging combat.3. Do the Necronomicon stuff first, tons of xp and points to be had and it's not all that hard. You might need one or two hints on a couple of the books to get them.3a. 3b. 4. If you followed 3's advice, and you looted in the book areas, and in general, you'll probably have a good amount of components and will be able to keep your kits and ammo(at least 2 full mags/cylinders) maxed, unless you're relying on your guns(melee is usually enough if you get the hang of it) or not running enough.5. Unless you need to hang around an area threatening your sanity, if it starts to get low,  just run around away from any 'disturbing' stuff. It'll regen on it's own. I'll update this if I encounter any issues that seem worthwhile to point out.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally bought this from Greenman gaming when Frogwares wasn't getting paid from the publisher, luckily they now have the right back on the steam store.Frogwares gave me a Steam key from my Greenman gaming purchase which is really nice.The game itself is a blast! It really put you into a position where you feel like you're snooping around for clues. You have to mark everything on the map yourself, there is no "go-to-waypoint" on the compass. You've gotta read where things are and it does a very nice job of snipping out the important details on where things are to keep you on track so you're not reading the entire thing.All of the clues are bite sized chunks that are very well sorted in your log book so it's easy to connect the dots. While you can just spam on guessing the deductions and make progress if you're really not sure, the clues give really good descriptions and I like to be sure before I attempt to make a guess, most of the time I'm spot on.The lack of resources and ammo puts you into a position where you don't feel like a killing machine. You're fighting other worldly creatures, even when I'm loaded with ammo and meds I never felt like I was on top of the foodchain. I personally prefer this as it keeps you on your toes.It's well made, lots of polish for a small team that made this. Looking forward to what they come up with in the 2nd game.

_childDocuments_.review: I spent two hours after the tutorial/introduction scouring every inch of the city for literally anything to interact with. I found all the records/archives locations, a single side quest, and no NPCs you could interact with beyond your initial meet and greet lines. The map was big but practically empty, the visual glitches would literally blot out the sky on occasion, i fell through two stair cases and couldn't get out (there's not jump, just a contextual climb), i kept having mobs of about 15 NPCs just appear in a big cluster behind me when I exited buildings, and the combat was almost forced on you, yet totally unpolished in every sense.  It's really a shame that there is likely a very interesting and twisting story line hidden under the unintuitive game mechanics, visual glitches and game game breaking bugs. Even greater shame is that the voice acting was incredible, and it made me really want to interact with everyone I came across. But you can't. Only the 10 or so specific NPCs spread across the vast wasteland disguised as a city.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some jank. Combat is kinda rough and takes some getting used to. The UI can be a bit clunky. There are some bugs here and there.But if you can get past that it is a really good game and I enjoyed it a great deal.It has a decent story. The voice acting is pretty good. But more importantly the setting is incredibly evocative. The environment and design of the city oozes atmosphere that is perfect for a Lovecraft inspired game and story.It also had some ideas that I thought were interesting. I enjoyed the archive system for example, and there are a couple of secrets in there too. I feel they could have done more with the underwater segments but you don't really spend a lot of time down there anyway.But if you're looking for a Lovecraft inspired game and can get past the initial jank, this is well worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is the platonic ideal of a AA game: an incredibly ambitious project that punches way above its class and does so quite successfully, but that also feels limited at every turn by its technical and financial constraints, a game smack dab in between the Sherlock Holmes graphical adventures Frogwares had developed up to this point, and a third person shooter with RPG elements, whose enjoyment of will squarely depend on your capacity to keep the forest in focus instead of the janky ass trees that form it.The game follows the path of Charles Reed, a private investigator who arrives at the city of Oakmont following strange dreams and visions that seem to drive people towards it. Over the course of this investigation, our detective will delve deep into the multiple happenings into this city, battle eldritch horrors beyond comprehension, and resist the madness emanating from its citizens. Why is everyone acting so crazy? What lurks below the city? And why the hell does this town have so many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ men's clothing stores?!tSC is divided into several cases and side quests consisting of a rather straightforward loop: Find clues, find the location these clues point towards, arrive at location, put a cap on some Deep One ass, put everything together, and advance to the next case; all the while navigating the open world-ish city of Oakmont, exploring its fog-ridden streets against a rather limited selection of enemies during combat sections featuring music that is between ethereal and industrial. Yes, this is pretty much Silent Hill 2 At Home with an investigation-oriented gimmick, and trust me when I say this without an inkling of negativity.The art style is, frankly, quite impressive. While most of it comes from the technical prowess of UE4 like lighting, physics and volumetric fog, the characters and scenery also feature really great looking assets, and this is one of those games that you will just gawk at while going through it. Boats and fish corpses litter the semi flooded streets, people wander the street muttering to themselves and acting crazy, and hey, I'd also be a little nutty if my entire town had only 4 faces to share between all its inhabitants.Staying true to its source material, Oakmont is a seemingly organic location, but once you start paying attention, its veneer will slowly crack, showing its true, janky self. First of all, the city has not been affected by a flood, but a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Kaiju attack. Cthulhu himself has risen up from the depths and dragged his scaly ballsack all across this city: it's littered by boats straight up yeeted into buildings, cars appear to have suffered horrific accidents in places where they could have never even managed to get up to speed even if they tried, and calling the state of its buildings "squalid" would be making them a kindness. It looks positively post-apocalyptic, and while it's super cool to navigate a location that gives out the feeling of dilapidated, unsettling and hostile that one imagines when reading a Lovecraft book, it's... Like, at first it will feel creepy and unsettling, but quickly you will realize that no, it's just that the level designer went a little too overboard with the ambiance to the point of caricature. The bartender at the Under the Keel inn will stay there buffing the one spot in his counter, while the floor under him is chock full of seaweed. You'll see people sweeping the floor, in a rainstorm, next to a pile of rotting, half eaten fish. The people in Oakmont might be a touch off the rocker, but I'm sure they at least grasped the essentials of sanitation, or at least they'd keep enough of their sense of smell. It's these incongruous details that will keep breaking the otherwise great immersion, and you will soon be able to see the reason: tSC is a painting made with only half a palette of colors. It's a massive city created on limited assets, and as a result, you're going to see a lot of copy-and-paste design that not only looks off place, but also quite repetitive after a short time.There's only a handful of interior location plans, shamelessly reused over, and over, and over throughout the investigations. Even major locations like the Throgmorton manor will be reused multiple times, and in most of those locations you will expect to fight the same 3-4 monsters in several waves and configurations. Combat in tSC will start feeling clunky and dangerous, but soon you will realize you can just peace out of most combat encounters. At the start you will only have a melee attack and a pistol to your name, but as you complete investigations and level up, you will obtain new weapons and improve Charles' abilities, gradually becoming a force to be reckoned with. Fights can easily be cheesed by kiting enemies or stunlocking them,  and your main hampering is the very limited ammo count per weapon; but at the same time you can just craft ammo and supplies mid fight. The combat is nothing to write home about and it's quite limited and repetitive, but it's never not satisfying to blast a bunch of Chtonians to kingdom come. Keeping an eye out for lootables is also very important to stay topped on materials, but I rarely felt like I was so short that I had to deliberately go out of my way to scavenge more.Having said this, you might wonder what the point is in making a massive city if most of it is going to be copy-paste buildings and repetitive combat encounters, right? Credit where credit is due, the streets themselves do feel quite organic and lived-in, but most importantly, unlike games with a purely decorative open world like Cyberpunk or LA Noire, the core of the game's cases will consist on opening your map and manually locating where you must go next. I'd hesitate to call it a "minigame", but it is a little problem solving exercise that you will have to do for practically every objective, multiple times per case. Thankfully you will unlock quick travel points as you explore the city, and navigating it never felt tedious or stretched out for me. Much like the combat, both consulting the corresponding archives to figure out where to go next and actually getting there felt quite satisfying to pull out, despite how straightforward this loop is. The game also features a few gimmicks like visions where you have to put a series of embarrassingly obvious events in order, or dispelling illusory walls with your "inner eye", which are probably the more annoying and dragged out moments in the game, but overall, it wasn't too terrible.Look, there's something that has to be appreciated about a game that knows its limits and tries to make the best of it. During my playthrough I never encountered any game breaking bugs, or collision issues, only a couple of times enemies spawned either below the floor or above the ceiling, and none of it was game breaking, or resulted in unwinnable situations. It's a game that maybe does 4-5 things, but it makes damn sure it does them well, even throwing little gimmicky flourishes like underwater sections, or letting you travel the debris-chocked flooded streets with a surprisingly solid feeling motorboat. It really feels like Frogwares only delivered the quantity they were confident to deliver with quality, which is something rare to encounter in the current gaming landscape. A bold leap from their previous work, and a landing they could hardly have stuck better, given the circumstances.The Sinking City is a very solid game that tries to do the best with what it can, and that has the right amount of focus on the right places to deliver a mostly alright experience, As long as you are within this wavelength, that will provide 30-ish quite entertaining hours of content, and while I would not buy this game at full price, I would absolutely recommend experiencing if you can snag it at a 30-50% discount.7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is a doozy. As always, every judgement you read here is subjective.The short version: I've had a lot of fun with The Sinking City (TSC for short). The long version - that's the rest of this review.TSC has a story that is at times confusing, strange, but for me, always captivating. I'm not big on Lovecraft's work, but for those who are, the game could potentially hold much more value. There's secret societies, malevolent monsters, unsettling myths, nightmares, visions and all sorts of strange occurrences. Best of all, you get your hands dirty with all of them. They're not just lingering distantly in the background, so thematically, the game is absolutely on point.Visually, much the same - the graphics are not stunning but the art direction and style is just weird, unsettling and creepy enough to keep this constant atmosphere of unease hanging over the more tense parts of the story. Of course, it's not constantly like this otherwise the game would become suffocating to play. You see touches of elegance, beauty and society in the midst of an otherwise barnacled, run-down city with basically everything fallen apart or in the process of doing so. However, lots of interiors are re-used, leading me to wonder whether they could have made do with a much smaller, but more uniquely designed and densely packed game world. It would have saved all the running around, which is not fun unless you enjoy taking in the sights (which I did, so I didn't mind).Mechanics-wise, it's pretty good. There are no quest markers, which is lovely - every location is roughly specified by a road address and you have to locate and find what you need. Few games bother doing this, and I'm glad they tried to make it more investigative. Speaking of which, the investigative elements are great. You have to actually search through crime scenes, note clues, and through some "premonition" ability discover what happened. Then you can come to different outcomes in each case based on your interpretation of the clues - there's no right or wrong answer, no fail state, which is brilliant. It is a genuinely good investigative gameplay loop, where I knew exactly what was coming but I still enjoyed doing it, since it's so deliciously involved. Full props for this.The combat is not great until the end - at least, that's how it was for me. There's not too much mechanically wrong with it, just that it's tedious and not really "fun". TSC comes as a clear recommendation to anyone who enjoyed Vampyr, but the combat in that game - while tough - was utterly fair, challenging and fun. I tried to avoid combat in Vampyr when I could because of fear that the opponent would be too strong. Here, I've avoided combat whenever possible (in the early game) because it's just not fun. Later on, once you get a bit more competent and powerful, it's actually enjoyable.RPG mechanics are next to meaningless in terms of variety of possible builds, though I imagine the game was not designed to offer different build options - you can pretty much unlock every skill tree completely with a regular playthrough and minimal side-questing. With that said, some skills do make a marked difference in gameplay and that's always good to see (e.g. the skill that sometimes lets you save materials when crafting. Came in handy more than once).Speaking of which, the crafting is serviceable, and loot respawns whenever you move across locations so every time I find some stash I mark it on the map and revisit the area when needed. All cool.What I really enjoyed is how the sanity mechanic is used. The player character, Charles Reed, suffers from disturbing visions (e.g. eldritch monsters attacking him, his own body hanging, etcetc) and every time you are in a region with otherworldly influences, your sanity starts dropping and these visions appear on screen as overlays while the screen as a whole swims around, distorted. It's beautifully done, though you can turn off these effects as far as I know, if they cause any epileptic reactions, for example.The ending is lacklustre. But did you really come to this game for the ending? Nah, it's really the journey that counts. Reed is a monotone but fascinating character and I really came to enjoy his perspective on things - allowing us to actually connect with his detective abilities really makes him that much more relatable. His journey is enjoyable, macabre and overall, defeinitely worth your time in my opinion.The side characters are all equally interesting - the voice acting is fantastic, and there's rarely a dull moment when you're interacting with a character. My only wish would have been to see some real consequences of our in-game decisions (which usually come at the end of each case). The aforementioned Vampyr did this fantastically by re-evaluating every district's "Health" based on our quest decisions, our choices of who to embrace and so on. Not just that, this Health actively affected the gameplay experience, as lower Health districts spawned more and more challenging enemies. With that said, it took me about 20 hours to complete the game without doing any of the side quests, which I expect complete sometime in the future during another playthrough. I enjoyed my experience more and more over time, and if any of the points mentioned above really tickle your fancy, consider this a recommendation from me. Have a good one!

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I'm not really into detective games; Sherlock Holmes and the likes... Yet something about The Sinking City intrigued me. They're also working on the sequel, but lemme tell you about this one. IT IS GOOD.Let's put aside the detective thingy in the game. I never really dig into such a thing, made me have to read every word in lores, notes and others a bit more carefully and I don't really like it. It probably is the basic of any detective games to begin with. But what made me intrigued, you asked? It is so many other things! Pros:1. GraphicsAt first, the gloomy city looks... so cringe & ass. The rain, the NPCs horrible looks. But then when the rain stopped. The city started to look jaw dropping. Sinking City has its own style in terms of graphics, which you will immediately noticed some time later in the game and it will all make sense later on which made it just so perfect with the lore and all. The weather change is really nice. The foggy night, the a bit sunny rain at day.2. Almost open world mechanicThe map is HUGE and it feels huge. There are games out there with big maps but there are just so many places you can explore. Sinking City got a massive map size and what made it feels huge is that it has that open world game mechanics where you need to find the cases to be solved. The game is not holding your hand (except maybe when putting up clues, which I suck at). You need to explore to find cases (missions if u wanna call it). You're free to explore and roam around, which is so nice cuz not a lot of detective games have this kind of mechanic. What made it even more interesting is that there are certain areas with monsters to kill. So, whenever I feel bored, I just go to this areas and started gunning down.3. It feels alive, aside from certain thingsYou're a detective, not some one man army who can mow down any monster u encounter. The only super power u have, is the ability to see things in different perspective to find clues of a case that other people might not be able to see. Every time I took an aim, my arm feels heavy, u can feel the character is adjusting to the recoil after each shot. Every shot if not time properly gonna miss the crosshair. Similar to resident evil mechanic, thus every shot count. In a game where resources are kinda scarce, this mechanic made me love it even more.4. Alive NPCsMaybe not as alive as in so many other games out there. But every now and then when I bumped onto NPCs, they gonna curse me. When I aim a gun to their face they gonna surrender. Some would even return fire and shoot me when I was dealing with monsters, cuz they feel threatened. I mean honestly, it's more than I ever asked for.Cons:1. Bro is stuckSometimes a 1" obstacle made the MC stuck and can't even jumped over. Made me wonder why. This happen quite often and well, kinda frustrating at times.2. Mouth playIf you're a fan of talkative realism, this game definitely doesn't have that. Mouths definitely not working precisely as the words go, but I don't really care much about it. The detective also not a big of a talker. He barely say anything, except in dialogues. A strong silent type, which I like, but maybe some people don't. Maybe.Yes, there are other detective games out there and maybe even better than this one, heck Idk. Like I said, not a fan of detective games. BUT! The Sinking City is definitely worth checking out, especially on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember reading some negative reviews for Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments.  Some of the people wanted less "hand-holding" and the freedom to move anywhere.  Sadly, Frogwares listened to them, instead of sticking to the tried and tested (and successful) format used in the aforementioned game.  And the mess that is The Sinking City is the result.Open worlds and adventure games just do not fit together.Open worlds are perfect for crime games such as the GTA series, the Mafia series and the Watch Dogs series.  This is because you are primarily driving cars to get to locations, and usually have only one location available at a time (except when outside missions).  The format also worked well for L.A. Noire, since it was a similar sort of game that just happened to be based on investigating and solving crimes rather than committing them.  But this format does not fit an adventure game, where the primary objectives are investigating places for clues, solving puzzles and the like.The point-and-click format (or some variation, such as the ability to move freely within a small area) is what works best for adventure games, and this is the format The Sinking City should have adopted.  Frogwares did it in a modern style for Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments.  It was done for Blacksad too, where it also worked.  Why couldn't The Sinking City be similar?  Why stray from a format that works so well?Call of Cthulhu also made some diversions away from the traditional adventure game format.  But those worked for that game.  It didn't go overboard by creating a vast open-world full of various locations, with no clue where to go.  The combat sequences were very scarce and you weren't always left out of ammo, like happens in The Sinking City.  The stealth sequences could be annoying, but weren't too frustrating once the layout of the area was known.  Likewise, the run and hide sequences weren't great either, but were used sparingly and not too difficult to master.And this vast open world in The Sinking City can only be navigated either by running down streets or rowing boats.  There are cars but you can't drive them.  And while running down the streets, you can suddenly end up in "hostile areas", places where creatures will randomly appear and attack.  This does not belong in an adventure game.  For action shooter games, it's fine - we expect it, but not here.The archive systems were very complex, and very different from the ones Holmes had in the Sherlock Holmes series.  And there are multiple locations where different types of archives can be accessed.  Can I use the archive system at the beginning of the second case?  Do I have enough "evidence"?  There is no clue at all.  Why not make the places inaccessible until we need to go to them?  It would have simplified things.  Frogwares should have kept the simple system from the Sherlock Holmes games.The plot of the game is admittedly good.  It has an interesting initial mystery behind it, much like adventure games of this type often do.  It is atmospheric.  And the deduction system is great in any mystery/detective game.  This is where the good points largely end.It took me a while to work out the controls.  On the PC version, unlike the console version, there is no hint telling you how to use the Mind's Eye system.  That wasn't good.  And I spent about half an hour at least, stuck on what to do after finding most of the clues in the first location because of it.  When I got it working, the game became interesting again and I solved the first case easily.The rest of the game is all downhill from there, though.  And it's a shame because it could have been a good H.P. Lovecraft-inspired game, like Call of Cthulhu was.  Instead, Frogwares made a complete mess of it.You've already guessed by now that I do not recommend this game.  If you want a good H.P. Lovecraft-inspired game, play Call of Cthulhu.  It's not a masterpiece.  But it's a game with elements that mostly work together in an effective way to provide good pacing, some unsettling moments and a great atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: Sure, if you can look past its Eurojank trappings (of which there are many) then you can find some enjoyment here. Both the soundtrack and the overall aesthetic make for an unnerving atmosphere that nails the sense of cosmic dread. Performance, at 4K/60fps on ultra settings, was fine and while the visuals are generally okay you can definitely see the lower budget throughout. The investigation mechanics are decent but never surprise the player and you quickly find yourself going through the motions with every case.Which is where my main criticism comes in and why I wouldn't recommend this game, especially at full price.  is very very repetitive and by the final few quests I found myself just skipping through most of the dialogue and wanting to be done with it. It's also rather predictable and if you've read or played any other Lovecraft inspired works then you know exactly what to expect. When you're not sleuthing around you'll be running (read: fast traveling) through 1920s inspired city of Oakmont filled with dead eyed inhabitants that more often than not seem to glitch out with every step they take, which is a shame as the world is otherwise well realized. But seeing citizens fall through the geometry, bump into objects or repeat the same exact lines of dialogue over and over again really pulls you out of the game. Who knows though, all of that might be the result of the curse of the sea they keep mentioning?  Anyway technical issues not withstanding you'll eventually be interrupted, on many occasions, by nightmarish looking creatures that you have to fend off. _childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is a game that I found delightful. As the name suggests, it is set in a sunken city that is full of references to famous writers such as Lovecraft, Poe, and Heinlein, among others. The city is half-flooded with water, which creates a unique gameplay experience where players can travel on foot or by boat. The boats spawn near every harbor, making it easy to navigate the city. enter image description hereOne thing that stood out to me in this game was the absence of automarkers on the map. Instead, players are given descriptions of places, and they need to use their own intuition and exploration skills to find the points of interest. This added an extra layer of challenge to the game and made it more immersive.enter image description hereAs a private eye, players spend most of their time investigating. These investigations are usually split into two parts: finding all the clues in an area and then recreating the sequence of events. While the puzzles aren't too challenging, it was still a fun mini-game to search different archives for clues. I appreciated the attention to detail in the investigation gameplay.The game has some interesting side quests, one of which involves hunting down a witch that sewed a librarian's mouth shut. This side quest includes a boss fight and a video sequence, which I found impressive. The-Sinking-City-Screenshot-2023-04-19-22-55-45-21I also appreciated the self-awareness in the game's dialogue, where a police officer explains why he dislikes the protagonist:The-Sinking-City-Screenshot-2023-04-19-22-55-45-21The choices players make in the game are more subtle than in other games and are influenced by The Witcher. For example, one quest involves choosing between a necromancer that resurrects the dead to torture them and a Mayan vampire that eats people at night.The-Sinking-City-Screenshot-2023-04-19-22-55-45-21While both choices are bad, I appreciated the nuance and thought that went into the decision-making process. However, it was disappointing that the choices players make do not ultimately affect the ending.The game gives players weapons during key sequences, but the process is not shown. Additionally, while the investigations in the game are enjoyable, they can get repetitive as they all follow a similar pattern.enter image description hereOverall, I found The Sinking City to be an enjoyable game with plenty of references and interesting side quests. The lack of automarkers on the map added an extra layer of challenge, and the investigation gameplay was engaging. While the choices players make aren't consequential, they still add an interesting layer to the game's story.

_childDocuments_.review: There's no way to sugar-coat this: The Sinking City is a glitchy mess. NPCs pop in and out of existence with merry abandon and invariably spawn floating a foot or two above the ground before realising their mistake. Strange rectangles of differently textured water surround floating objects depending on the weather. Quite a few of the ostensibly normal inhabitants look scarier than the monsters, while the monsters themselves have only a passing acquaintance with the laws of physics.It's also an extremely repetitive mess. The city feels realistically expansive, but that means the limited graphical butter has been spread over an awful lot of bread. Outdoors, it's not so bad: there's enough detail and props to mostly disguise the small variety of storefronts and other buildings. Inside, though, it's quickly apparent that there are only a handful of building layouts (Think Day-Z, only less so) re-used over and over, to the point where I sometimes thought I'd accidentally gone to the wrong place.Finally, combat is just a mess. Its saving grace is your trusty shovel, which has a generously inclusive swing and can be employed with success against all but the largest enemies. Make frequent use of it and you will find your stockpile of ammunition is never in danger of running out, at least on the easier difficulty setting.Yet I am recommending it - why?What The Sinking City does well is atmosphere, story, setting, and a compelling sense of being involved in an investigation. Once you grasp the core loop (inspect everything, use your sixth sense when prompted, clean out each location, place new way-points on the map, visit various archives to search for clues) it becomes quite addictive, with the right amount of head scratching and the right amount of trudging around at either end of the fast-travel nodes to even out the pace. The various factions and recurring individuals are all intriguing and there's a constant thread of worry that you might be about to choose the wrong side and/or bring an end to humanity. I'm normally a complete white knight when playing an RPG involving moral choices, but here I've felt unexpectedly open to taking a darker path from time to time.Ultimately, the game's strengths win out over its weaknesses - at least for me. Without the ever-present glitches and with a larger palette of graphical resources, it would have been an all-time top-ten contender. As it stands, it's an engrossing and worthwhile experience that's worth forgiving its flaws.A quick tip to avoid frustration: ignore side-quests until you get the shotgun; they tend to be more combat-heavy than the main plot.Also, when you die or load your most recent save, don't be alarmed to find yourself somewhere you've never been. I was convinced for a while that the game was screwing up my save, but all that's actually happening is that it just spawns you at the closest fast-travel point to where you saved.
