_childDocuments_.review: This is an ambitious game, especially for one with Lovecraftian storytelling.  For those only familiar with Lovecraft's work through online Cthulhu-memes, H.P Lovecraft was a horror writer whose works only gained true recognition long after his passing.  His unique form of horror and storytelling would later go on to inspire numerous other authors with each of them adding over time to what collectively is known as, "The Cthulhu Mythos".  Cthulhu itself being a creation of Lovecraft's that appeared in his now famous story, "The Call of Cthulhu."Lovecraft's writings were unique because he often did not describe the various horrors encountered by his protagonists, who were nearly all men of science and logic (intellects, professors, researchers and such.  People known for the grasp of the material world and how it works) that would encounter things they, in all their gifted minds, could not process.  The various horrors of the Mythos are so Alien, so "Other" that the human mind cannot handle the sight of them, no matter how formidable that mind is.  This is where the "Sanity" mechanic that many Lovecraftian games use comes from.  Sinking city is a game set just after the end of World War I and follows a former Navy Diver who after a brief stint in a medical facility treating him for Halucinations brought on by the Bends after managing to be the sole survivor of his unit, becomes a Private Detective.  Then he begins to have haunting dreams and visions that plague him until he finds himself in Oakmont, a city that has recently suffered a catastrophic flood.  In the aftermath, looters and squatters wander the streets while a madness spreads among the survivors.Immediately you're confronted with numerous references to the Cthulhu Mythos.  Names of figures or even streets pay homage to the entire Mythos collection.  The infamous "Innsmouthers" from "The Shadow over Innsmouth", another of Lovecraft's most famous work are present here.  Its very clear that the developers are big fans and they've taken care to craft a world and story fitting of that very mythos.Gameplay is a mixture of investigation and gunplay.  You gather clues that either open up dialogue choices or require you to access the archives of the local newspaper, police department, city hall and etc to try and piece together three subjects or terms to find the relevant information you need on where to go next.  Your character has a unique psychic ability to see into the past as well.  Every major clue you find gets added to a "Mind Palace", a place where you try and turn two clues into a "Deduction".  Each case will eventually form a "Corkboard" in your head of various deductions that you connect to make certain decisions about the case.  Every case has at least one or two deductions that are multiple choice and will affect the outcome of the Investigation.  This is a fun mechanic and I hope to see it expanded upon in the sequel.The ability to add notes and clues directly to the map (and sort these collections of markings by case) is also both useful and a good idea.  It helps sell the Investigation gameplay and the need to look things up at various public Archives is a very "Private Investigator" move.  I also hope to see more of this in the sequel as well.Gunplay and Combat can be pretty unforgiving.  Thankfully if you just prefer using your brain there's different difficulty settings for combat and puzzles each.  Weapons are period appropriate, but ammo and supplies are scarce.  This is where crafting comes into play, however outside of the initial crafting recipes you must first discover the item in the wild before you can begin crafting it for yourself.  Considering how spongy certain enemies are and how difficult it is to hit their weakspots, you will constantly find yourself running low or empty on ammo and resorting to your hand axe.  There aren't very many enemy types in the game, which is disappointing considering you have the entire Cthulhu Mythos to draw inspiration from but what is present is suitably horrifying.  From mundane foes such as Prohibition Bootleggers and Cultists to the "Wyldebeasts", horrors that have popped up in the wake of the Flood.  Unfortunately there's really only four enemy types, with maybe one or two variations of a few of them, not including the two underwater enemies.Which brings me to the "Diving" mechanic.  At several points in the game, the protagonist will get to dust off his Navy diving skills and go for a walk in an old fashioned diving suit.  Enemies are rare and thankfully easily avoided or deterred as long as you're careful but these segments are thankfully short because you move very slowly underwater and there are some weird detection issues with the terrain when you're trying to find a spot on that ledge to climb but it won't take.  The diving segments are mostly atmospheric and outside of a few moments, feel like they were just tacked on despite obviously having been an intended mechanic at some point.  There's just not a lot to do underwater. While the city is vast with plenty to see, only select buildings can be entered in any fashion.  Many of which enemies will spawn inside as you explore them.  Unless you enter one of the walled off, "Infested Areas" you won't find monsters roaming the streets or anything.  Said roaming will consume most of your time with the game.  Fast travel can be done between phone booths as you unlock them but you can't just open your map and then teleport somewhere.  You gotta use the phone booths, and considering your character isn't particularly fast even at a "Run", it can feel a little exasperating and ruin the atmosphere the game otherwise works pretty hard to cultivate.The recycled use of interiors (outside of key locations buildings seem to all have the same overall floor plan and maybe two or three variations of interior.  This makes it laughably easy to discover hidden walls, doors and objects once you become familiar with the layouts.  Revealing these hidden objects usually requires you to see through an illusion put up by some mystic means, which means your sanity takes a hit.Sanity effects are hard to get right in games.  Eternal Darkness remains the undisputed king of implementing sanity effects and I feel not a lot of games take after their excellent example.  Dark Corners of the Earth did this a little but not quite as good.  Sanity effects in The Sinking City mostly consist of disturbing imagery and a visual filter becoming more prevalent until dark, oozing shadow versions of various nightmares start appearing.  That's about it.  There's the occasional cut scene that's part of the story and those are pretty good but during regular gameplay, the sanity mechanic feels not very well thought out and pretty tame.  Which is a little strange because there are plenty of disturbing and gruesome stories and scenes to be found among the city and it's survivors.  Clearly the creativity is there but it just doesn't land as a good Sanity mechanic.Overall The Sinking City's ambitions are mostly successful outside of a few outliers and really only the lack of a faster way to travel the city is the only true negative in my mind.  If you like Lovecraft stories this is definitely a must play.  It's a Private Eye Simulator with a strong horror element.  Strong voice acting combined with good storytelling makes the Investigation parts of the game fun and interesting while the Combat is fine.  It works but Combat shouldn't by the highlight of a true Lovecraft game anyway so as long as it's serviceable I'm happy.  Final Score: 8/10, 7/10 if you don't like Lovecraft.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is a third person action adventure game, feat. Charles Reed, a WW1 navy diver turned sleuth (private investigator). The game takes place in the fictional city of Oakmont, Massachusetts, a 1920s dreary and downtrodden backdrop to the stories of The Sinking City.I say stories, as opposed to story, because while there are a smorgasbord of intriguing lovecraftian inspired stories throughout the Sinking City, clearly drawing inspiration from every corner of popculture Cthulu/Lovecraft and derivative works, that's also the cornerstone of the problem surrounding the story, it's one big melting pot of references and easter eggs, leaving the overall arching story very incoherent. Rather it feels like an anthology of loosely connected stories. Main antagonists and side characters come and go, and major ones aren't even a part of the later parts.The game presents a series of morale dilemmas throughout the game, letting you choose what happens to various characters you meet along the way, but ultimately like other games before this, they have no impact on the story you experience, and certainly no impact on the ending at all. Johannes van der Berg, an enigmatic fella you meet in Oakmont, hinted at consequences at one point, but the next story following are the same, regardless of your choices. This makes the "dilemma" inconsequential.Which leads to a rather anticlimactic ending, or rather endings, as there are three, fortunately you can experience them by simply reloading the final area of the game.So what else is there besides the loosely fragmented story, well the game features exploration, if you go by the Steam product page. "A vast open world that can be explored on foot, by boat, in a diving suit…" it says, this is disingenuous because there's no exploration in Oakmont, while you could spend your time running around aimlessly, you won't find things that aren't a part of the quests/missions, and only when they are active, at least outside a few tedious side quests that are triggered when you pick up specific objects.The boat exploration? It amounts to getting from point A to point B, while traversing Oakmont, as it's as the name of the game implies, flooded in various parts. As for the diving segments, they are entirely linear platforming segments, whose only redeeming aspect is that they induce thalassophobia the first couple of times you experience them, but they overstay their welcome, with their tedious hotstreams and infinite health "fish" monsters.There's very few unique locations in the game, locations are often repeated throughout the game, with at most a handful of different houses, once you've experienced a few of them you'll know the layout and the illusory walls in all of them,m as well as the component containers, as they never change.You're a detective, so there's some detective work, via the Mind Palace, where you put together the clues you gather and try to deduce the outcomes of the missions you are working on, but it seems like these don't have that much of an effect outside of outlining what your various options are. Mr Reed also possesses a supernatural power to deduce crime scenes and events as if experienced them himself, but like the Mind Palace these never take a step further mechanically, leaving them a bit of a missed opportunity in the end.Both the main as well as many of the side quests leads to lots of needless running around and fast traveling, as a lot of them are busywork fetch quests, go here, pick up this, shoot some monsters which inevitably gets in your way, craft some more ammo, go to the next location. Rinse repeat.So the game has a lot of combat, horrendous combat which boils down to little more than a slug fest, as you hurl bullets after the monsters in a given area you are in. There's various weapons but some of them are simply too unwieldy or too ammo inefficient, like the Submachine Gun, to be of much use, as it's not like you can snipe the enemies from a distance with the Battlerifle as the vast majority of all encounters are up close and personal, favouring faster and quicker reloading weapons like the Pistol or the Revolver, or the Hand Grenades. As Krazy Ivan said in the old PS1 game, grenades are better with fish, and that goes well in Oakmont. On top of that the character controls are janky, you can only sprint directly ahead, and while that may be more realistic, having more freedom of movement is just less frustrating to control.On top of that you're boggled down by a tedious resources cap and crafting elements, as you repeatedly must restock on ammunition after every encounter in the game, as you simply cannot carry that many bullets at any given moment, neither can you carry that many crafting materials. which leads often to the situation where you cannot pick up ammo, or materials, because either is full, and then you must backtrack after crafting some. A frustrating experience. The loading tips even says ammo is scarce, but it really isn't, it's just tedious to manage.This leads to the skills and unnecessary RPG mechanics, there simply aren't interesting choices. Okey you gain xx% more experience, okey you can now carry 3 more bullets, great? There's also not enough skills available to spend EXP on, with all the repetitive sidequests granting so much exp. Not every game needs experience points, progression systems can be handled in various different ways.At the end of the day, the gameplay is incredibly repetitive, from the repeated combat to the repeated locale and mission design.The game is certainly more about the journey than the destination then, but is the journey worth it in the end? Hmnm, no, it wasn't. The sum of its parts doesn't make the journey interesting or worthwhile enough.Final note: Warning, if you adjust the ini config files to support 60+ FPS, the game has a gamebreaking bug during 'Fathers and Sons', the character cannot take a step up on the raised plateau in the Crematorium barring further progress. Why this is still being done to games I'll never understand, The Sinking City isn't that old a game for it to be an excuse anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay gets repetitive so freaking quickly, you won't even finish first half of the game when you start noticing how monotonous your game actions are: accept the mission, check archives, go A, kill some monsters, search clues, do "retrocognition", connect clues in a "mind palace", go B and repeat everything above 20 times. Monsters are shown from the very beginning, world feels empty and not motivating for any further exploration - you only need , it's the only meaningful purpose of wandering around. There are three difficulties in game, but combat mechanics are so clunky, that you automatically choose easy difficulty, because you don't want any more problems game is already giving you. Characters aren't recognisable and not very convincing. Deep-dive sections are boring, slow-paced and needless.All these shenanigans with the predestination of the main character didn't persuade me in responsible choosing of the game ending - I didn't actually care about the world itself. Cutscenes are awful - any time I was seeing it, I have been always wondering - why I was shown this scene? It didn't affect the immersion into the story, it was badly implemented into what's currently happening in the game, and didn't answer any of the story questions. The only cutscenes that matter are at the finals. The checkpoint system is locationally attached to the place of the nearest fast-travel spot, so any time you exit the game, kindly remember the heck you was doing last time, and where you stopped at. Save system stores only couple last autosaves, so if you screwed up with some achievements/choices from the previous chapters and didn't save, replay whole game from the very beginning.Some faces are well-done, but general textures of it are copypasted with the only difference - having moustache or a beard. The same goes about level design - apartments and the streets that you visit are always looking identical.The only thing that keeps you from quitting is the main story (and achievements), but the narration isn't good and transition from the middle game into an ending feels rather abruptly. If only I knew that the specialty of repeating gameplay exists from the very start till the very end, I would simply skip doing all side-quests and stick straight to the main story without any distractions whatsoever.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this title up on sale because I am a fan of the mythos (it is based upon) and the setting.  Overall I have to say I'm pleasantly surprised and please with the game and am enjoying it greatly.It has the aesthetic down completely, and the lore and story seem spot on.There are a few negatives that should be mentioned.  The inventory system is rather annoying.  "Can't carry any more" is a common message, but exactly what you are carrying too much of isn't obvious.    While this is annoying, a counterpoint is that you don't have to manage inventory squares and play the usual tetris with your storage space.  When you need something to craft on the fly, your character sensibly just picks it from the inventory.  This aspect is good inventory management.  You see the amount of crafting materials you have, but you don't have to micromanage the actual crafting process.  Just "I want that" with one click and the materials are combined and you've got the item.  Fair trade, I say, for your limited hauling capacity.Many people have found combat too hard/challenging/imprecise.  This is true in that your character seems rather anemic at combat and the firearms (at least the early stage ones) don't seem to have much punch graphically.  That's alright; filthy casual players like myself just put it on "Easy" and that seems to solve the combat issues so I can enjoy the story.NPC animations aren't always the smoothest, with characters appearing out of nowhere and sometimes aimlessly meandering.  I don't tend to notice this much and setting the graphics all the way up and draw distance all the way out pretty much mitigates this.Investigations are interesting; collect clues for the main quests and then analyze them in your "mind" interface.  Instead of just selecting dialogue options for decisions, you actually combine clues and draw different conclusions, leading to different dialogue options.  This adds a little more interest than merely selecting "he did it" or "he didn't do it" in a conversation and I enjoy this mechanic.It may feel a little unpolished, but overall I greatly enjoy this game and plan on playing it for some time to come.  I like this experience better than Call of Cthulhu (which is also a great title itself).Big bonus points: it runs great on SteamDeck.Also, I understand the publisher, Frogware, is now the master of their own destiny.  Congrats!  I hope to see more from this IP in the future.Edit: I can't seem to put this game down.  Just like an eldritch tome in the Mythos, it sucks me in deeper and deeper...!  Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly recommend and enjoy this game. Though it is victim to Eastern European jank in some gameplay mechanics, in my completion of the game I've never found anything to be completely game breaking or to actually hinder combat - it's merely smaller things like invisible walls or the awkward environmental details. The voice acting is of a shockingly good quality, and though the facial models can seem a bit... familiar (via multiple NPCs in the game using the same base face with only different scarring, hairstyles, and facial hair) the animations themselves do properly match the emotions and lip-syncing of dialogue. There's no issues like ME: Andromeda or any of the AAA titles you've seen endlessly meme'd online.The soundtrack composed by Sergey Sedilar is an *INCREDIBLE* composition that the game would be inferior without. It is every bit as atmospheric and horrifying as it needs to be, and never falls victim to recursive loops nor the bad habit of the music being either too boring or too epic for the moment at hand. His work is heavily grounded in the setting it takes place,  mixing subtle jazz chords of the early 20th century's detective noirs into an endless ethereal abyss is incredible to listen to in real time, and it's a shame that this isn't brought up more often when talking about this game. It reinforces your role as a detective in... well, a sinking city. One that's slowly being dragged down into one inevitable end or another.The setting itself is stellar. The architecture, technology, weaponry, and even the slang and lexicons of Oakmont's residents reflect the time period and location in breathtaking detail - something often ignored by bigger studios. Of equal note is that Frogwares, being a Ukrainian development studio, doesn't have stake in either covering up or outright ignoring the disturbing history of the Prohibition Era. Seeing the horrors of things like the Klan committing its disgusting crimes against those perceived as inferior, and being critical by exposing the racial and class divide excessively found during the Great Depression in the United States, definitely adds to the deepening hole of emptiness felt in Oakmont. After all, even with the horrors of Lovecraft and the existential threat of the occult, humanity still finds excuses to massacre and torture each other in the name of ignorant concepts like racial purity and "God's will." This, I feel, is often lost on Western developers - either in the name of whitewashing a dark past so that they can pretend it wasn't that bad, or in the name of inclusivity and equality by ignoring the dark history in their entirely.Now, a lot of the reviews talk about drama in the real world between the developer and the publisher, and legal battles. Frankly, that has no basis on my review. Considering that the developer's nation of Ukraine is currently facing invasion and constant attacks by the Russian military, and that the developer's studio is in the capitol of Kyiv currently being drone strike'd and cruise missile'd every few days, I doubt that its their top priority either. I'm only here to play and review a game, not court documents, and this game? It's now one of my favorites.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game for one run. Took me 25 hours to finish and get 100% achievements and I played it in 2 days which speaks for itself. You don't play a bad game for 12 hours a day.Story, dialogs and characters are ok but feels sketchy. You want to know more about motives and such but game sometimes doesn’t work very good explaining things especially if you are not familiar with Lovecraft’s works. A lot of parties are involved in a story and at some point you can lose track of who is who and why they do what they do. Game very much loves to play in shades of gray moral wise. In short most of them are crazy cultists and/or not a very good people wanting to use you for their cause so you feel like you are on your own but I believe this was exactly the devs intention.Atmosphere is nice with neverending rain in a ruined city, dead fish, strange people and creatures everywhere. But as other reviews mentioned there are only a few repetitive types of house interiors.Choices almost doesn't affect the story except some cut scenes but there are a lot of achievements that are bound to your decisions so take it in consideration and use a guide if you want to get all of it in one run. Believe me you won't want to replay the whole game to get missed achievements. Also most of the achievements are bound to, well, let's call it bad choices. BTW there are almost no good choices in the game and most of the time you choose between two evils which feels unsatisfying but adds to the atmosphere.Combat system and controls has its flaws and reminds me of "Remnant: From the Ashes" (aiming, movement, view angle) except you don't have any dodge. You die pretty fast so you need to kite enemies avoiding attacks as much as you can. I'm really not a fan of survival elements in games i.e. crafting and lack of ammo. Also in this game you can't hold much ammo and resources. You can't farm resources and craft tons of ammo for future and forced to craft everything literally mid-combat. It gets even worse when you get tommy-gun with a magazine of 30 ammo and maximum amount you can hold is 40. Why not 2 magazines at least? What they expect me to do? Craft 20 more mid-combat to have full magazine after reloading? It's annoying so I cheated ammo and just enjoyed the story.Detective part is very repetitive but it was something new to me and I didn’t get bored till the end except for hours and hours of backtracking. I’d wish game has better ways of fast travel. Otherwise it’s fun searching through the archives defining what clue to choose and what search filters to use and then manually marking the spots on the map.In short it’s not an masterpiece and has some flaws but definitely worth playing if you can stand hours of backtracking.

_childDocuments_.review: The game's premise draws you in at first, and the investigation mechanics should be familiar to anyone who's played the Frogwares Sherlock Holmes games. And yeah, it has the usual Frogwares jank too - which is actually kind of charming.What isn't charming, and what makes this such a worse experience than other Frogwares games, is the combat. It's clunky, frustrating, and relies on bullet-sponge enemies in a way that feels too bland to evoke the tension of survival horror but too slow and chunky to evoke anything approaching a quicker, more visceral model of combat. Basically, it's the worst of both worlds and that combined with the emptiness of the open world makes this an otherwise decent game simply not worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a love letter to Lovecraft's work; is it amazing? No. Is it a decent game with flaws? Yes. If you don't mind overlooking the flaws (and a little bit of repetitive grind in some cases) then pick it up.The game interweaves many of the Cthulu Mythos stories into a mostly coherent main plot; graphically it looks good, but they reuse interior assets far too often so it gets repetitive. Lots of NPCs litter the streets, but you can't interact with most of them and the AI and NPC spawning (and vanishing) takes away from the immersion.Combat isn't horrible but I wouldn't call it great, the crafting system is good for what is available, but the inventory system is frustrating; they should have given each item a weight value instead of a maximum of each allowed (your character carries a massive backpack around for most of the game, but is limited in carrying items that could fit in your pocket???)The main character tends to blandly interact with the world for the most part; although in perspective, since he routinely hallucinates, is delusional to the point he can't tell reality from the visions/dreams and does regularly take anti-psychotic meds, so....if you take that into account, he's fine.The investigation portion of the game has a lot of potential but it does miss the mark in coming to the conclusions, especially since you can figure out what has occurred in some of the cases without using the character's supernatural vision, but the game won't progress until you do. Some of the conclusions seem contrived, like they were trying to put forward a "moral quandry", but it never came across as such.The ending fits the Cthulu Mythos (there is no "happy" ending) and if solving mysteries in a condemned city sounds fun, then embrace the sanity loss.

_childDocuments_.review: The more I played, the more it devolved into pandering, progressive woke nonsense. Every checkbox is ticked here and shoved in your face:- oppressed illegal immigrants that did nothing wrong? check- rich individuals who wont share their wealth with the poor? check- charitable individuals redistributing the rich one's wealth to the poor? multiple check- secret ♥♥♥♥ relationship heavy handedly shoved as an afterthought you discover from a photo and never mentioned again? check- women's rights movement? checkThe game also clearly bashes  you over the head with what the creators think is the correct moral decision(the PROGRESSIVE one) in each instance. You're given stupid choices like: expose a clearly evil person part of a dark cult by poisoning the food they distribute to the poor in order to gain members or simply leaving her alone. I mean, seriously, what the actual F?Oh and the gameplay is pretty clunky and just annoying. You run out of ammo so damn fast then have to scrounge for more. It's not like you can AVOID monsters, most of the time you do have to fight them and they take so many hits to go down. What's the point of giving the player supposedly better and better weapons if those don't 1-shot weaker enemies? 4-5 shotgun blasts to take down a giant, same for rifle I only gave this a chance because it really did start out very promising and had SOME elements from H.P. Lovecraft done well. I should have suspected the level of wokeness when the game went exclusive to Epic for so long.Don't play this, play Eternal Darkness, a perfect adaptation of H.P. Lovecraft themes. Oh how I wish they would just make a remaster of that instead.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a truly weird game and I understand why the achievement completion score shows such a dramatic drop off in players so early into the game. This game explains nothing to you besides giving you a poorly designed text dump to show how everything works. This is prevalent throughout the entire game, it almost never explains anything to the player and assumes you will simply figure it out. There's no waypoints, you have to actually look things up on a map and mark them yourself. I think this is an easy game for people to fall off, but if you meet it on it's terms, it has a lot of really interesting things to show. Once you get the hang of the systems and the slow pace though, you'll find a truly dark and complex series of events that your character is embroiled in. Investigations often lead to bad choices where you need to choose your own personal lesser of two evils, and the game pulls no punches on how bad these outcomes will be. There are no easy choices, no hand holding, and certainly no escaping your fate. Gameplay does suffer from a serious frame lag in combat though.

_childDocuments_.review: The sinking city is kind of a mixed bag, it has alot of good things to its name, but also some on the bad side.The visuals\atmosphere\music\themes are all spot on. i signed up for a lovecraftian experience and i certainly got one. the story itself isn't exactly the pinnacle of writing or anything amazing, and that's absolutely fine, because it simply doesn't need to be. its a detective kind of game so i'm glad more effort went into creating the cases, i was actually surprised with the amount of content the game had, if you go out of your way to do the side cases as well you could end up with around 15+ hours of content (or more depending on your pace?). i also like that alot of the cases will have different endings depending on your actions and choices while solving them, it kind of gives your actions a sense of accountability and reason.Now all that said, the sinking city is not exactly perfect either. The core gameplay mechanics are very repetitive, while solving the cases, even tho they have different stories and conclusions, they still all feel the same. because you're just doing the same things over and over. collect X amount of evidence, guess the order of the events, get a tip and go to some archive and follow a trail. it gets stale after a couple of  times and rids the whole detective work of any life and originality. even tho some of the cases were really interesting but just doing the same exact things really ruined alot of the fun from it for me. another really bothersome thing was just how janky the controls are. running and sprinting was very limited and slow. fast travel can only be done from certain points which turns alot of the game into a running simulator(it's aids). you can't jump. climbing is jank. combat sucked and felt forced and annoying. the constant need to loot is annoying and gets in the way of the game. the visual diarrhea you get everytime the mc sees something spooky got really annoying and was unnecessary.Overal tho. would i recommend this game? it kind of depends. if you enjoy lovecraftian theme'ed media and detective stuff. then give it a go. if you stick to the main story line and ignore the side stuff you'll probably be just fine. the main story is actually pretty engaging and fun to go through. on the other hand if you're not exactly into the themes and genre then you'll probably not enjoy what the sinking city has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an okay AA game that you buy on sale and play it once. I completed the main story and most of the of the side cases, and I clocked 36 hours of playtime.The Good*The amount of voiced dialog is surprising for this caliber of game, and the voice acting is pretty good.*The graphics are fine and you can run this at 4k@60fps on a mid-range video card.*You get to make choices.*Multiple endings.The Not So Great*There is a lack of variance when it comes to NPC and building models. Multiple times I spoke to an NPC who looks nearly identical to a previous NPC and it almost confused me. Many building interiors are literal copy+paste of each other. Walking down any random street feels nearly the same as any other random street. There are only a few types of enemies.*Half the play time is spent running from point A to point B.*Too many bland side cases.*This one is subjective: The choices you make along the way don't determine the ending. You get to choose which ending you want regardless of your play style.*There is a skill tree but it provides very little benefit.*There is gun combat but it never evolves; you shoot the same enemies with the same guns for the entire game.*There is an sanity bar, but it's mostly ineffective.Conclusion:This game is too long with too little variance. The devs should have spent less time creating cases and more time creating different models. There should have been new, tougher enemies as the story progressed, and the player should have found better guns to fight them. If the game was half the length but double the variance and had more fleshed out mechanics, it would have been a much better experience. Having said that, I am curious to see what they do with Sinking City 2. PS: The deciding factor that convinced me to give this a thumbs up - I perused other $40 games on steam and it seems like The Sinking City is actually on par with the level of quality you can expect at this price point. If you think the game looks interesting, you can buy it on sale for $12.

_childDocuments_.review: It's one of those games that make a good impression when you watch the trailers, but disappoint in real life. I haven't encountered anything in particular that I can pinpoint as bad, but nothing stood out and caught my interest either.The start feels like repetition of other games, without knowing exactly why. It's darkness and visions. People going mad. Such a mystery. Why, oh why? But you already know why. Because of some giant Octopus McSquidface.The gameplay itself is mostly about fooling around in a small city. You can't interact with anything, unless it has a certain symbol painted on it. The only things that do are doors and garbage bins. The doors themselves are always intentional locations for quests (or cases), so there's nothing outside the main or side quests to be found.Every time you walk through a door, there's a 99.999% chance you'll encounter annoying monsters. Most of the time, you'll encounter the biggest fat ass that exists in the game, and you'll do that right from the beginning of the game when you only have a pea shooter. It's frustrating.You feel pretty smart and try to run out from the house to get more space, with one of those things chasing you. If you run too far, the monster will disappear and you have to restart the fight. If you stay too close and shoot the bastard, what do you think will happen!? Police officers start shooting you, since you are trying to defend yourself illegally. Obviously! They don't even mind the monster.You try gathering resources to take on the bastards. After hours of gameplay, having collected tons of bullets and stuff, you still haven't found a single rag to make a molotov, or a grenade. Something's off with the balance there.That's what the game is like all the way through. So what does it have that's good? Mostly atmosphere. I love the atmosphere. But there isn't much more to say about that.Finally, when reaching the end of the game, you get to make a choice between two options. I did something, thinking it would give me the opportunity to make that choice... But no. The action itself was the choice, and I didn't even know what choice I made! And I still don't. There was no end game cut scene. Only credits. Pretty much an anticlimax.So this game does NOT come recommended. It's all right pasttime if you have nothing better to do, so get in on sale if you have to.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't like many things about the game. I'd give it recommended if you were to do the main quest line only and nothing else. I've realised that the game isn't worth that much of my time. The thought came to me as i was doing second to last side case in the game. Some things that i looked past until a certain quest:- got stuck many times while fighting in the open in infested areas, not even that - it still happened a few times while i was on few of the many tedious walks,- TEDIOUS WALKING - mentioned second time to make the point clear, it was not fun. If the scenery was more diverse. I kid you not after a few hours every building looked the same,- Ctrl+C/Ctrl+V buildings, outside AND inside. I firmly believe i wouldn't care for that if I played the campaign only but that wasn't the case. I've done all sidequests except one and came to the conclusion that devs literally made 7 or 8 types of buildings and said it's good enough,- swimming in the boat - got stuck on some reef and lost good 10 minutes trying to shimmy my way out and continue with the story,- constant screen shaking as if i had severe motion sickness or been few hundred shots deep of some vodka or moonshineThings above are the ones i looked past while playing. SPOILER belowThis one, albeit small, made me lose my marbles - While doing main quests, Self-defense to be exact, i encountered a mistake in writing or so i thought. I came to the theatre to encounter dead Johannes van der Berg, proceeded to gather evidence of the crime. Reed's comment on the lying bullet casings next to the body said: "0.38 revolver shell casings - SAME AS MINE". It in fact wasn't same as his. Weapons we get in the game are: the pistol - using the 0.38 bullets and the revolver using 0.44-0.40 bullets along with other weapons not relevant here. I thought, oh, it's some irrelevant mistake by the devs, but then i learned the whole quest is all about framing Reed for the crime he didn't do and that was one of the evidence used against him. In a game, where you impersonate a detective, you investigate crimes that take place in the city. The game makes you pay attention to details and you encounter something like this. That just felt like half-assing the job you were ment to do. From that point on i just played to finish the game. Didn't really care what was happening in the story. Also, from what i gather, the game was made in times when there were many psycho-woke people getting mad at any inconvenience or deviation from their "norm". That's why devs put some racism and xenophobia warnings when turning the game on and thats why during one of the first quests where Reed talks to Throgmorton he tells him that not every Innsmouther is the same. I think it was in the first quest where you can find a note that says Innsmouthers are hated in Oakmont, noone wants to deal with them etc. Except every Innsmouther is the same. The story and lore shows how innsmouthers are either associated with EOD or with Blackwoods and Marshes. Both are cults, both were commiting atrocious crimes like kidnapping and raping women of Oakmont to make more Innsmouthers, the shooting in the fish market was blackwoods and marshes doing. They took it by force from the citizens of Oakmont. At first, seeing the note, i thought to myself, damn they need all the help they can get until i realised they ARE the bad guys, they sit right beside the other scum of that city. Now, there is some really hard stuff in this game besides the murders. The rapings, hangings, people killing themselves in the streets, people killing others in the streets, suicides by hangings, acts of cannibalism and the one thing Frogware decides to warn about is racism? I think i won't understand it even if i tried. Not recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings to mind a few words, like superficial, unfinished, scarred. Why is that? What we have here is a solid fundation of a game, but not much more. The tone and setting are spot on and very nice, but it is hard to feel immersion, in a world where people seem to walk, without any real goal, just to populate the streets. It is hard, when there is a few animations of the people walking the streets, doing things, but 0 interaction or when they just pop in due to unreal engine (it sucks). The diving segments as the segments on your little boat are very much nothing. You go from A to B, there isnt much here. While diving, there are a few obstacles, but they never pose any challenge or threat. The wound and sanity system is a joke if you compare it to something as old as the one from Dark Corners of the Earth. All of that makes this game feel very superficial. Then you have things like combat, the Lovecraftian Aspects, the Story and Side quests, the economy. The economy is running on "bullets" but that seemed like a very easy solution to saying: Yeah, we had to crunch to make this work, since there is no economy in this game. You have very little influence when you get anything, and what you get. In addition, this game runs on "The Last of Us" logic regarding to gathering items. You arent trustet to have a real inventory, you can carry x amount of y and not more, doesnt matter if you can still can carry so many of z. A real pitty. The combat shifts from mostly feeling like you throw marbles at beasts and zooming in and  out of "dangerous zones" for loot (which is conviently stored at the entrances) to carrying an arsenal, limited only by the artificial carrying capacity of the protagonists. The way to upgrade is the main quest, by some weird way of the cosmic, everybody seems to think it is cool to just give guns to you. But buying any isnt possible on your own. The Lovecraft aspect is coming to me, just having finished this game before writting this review down, as very low. It is there, and on some parts it is very on the nose (Insmouthers) and then it often feels like it is missing. The creatures you fight are never really much in detail, and it is hard to tell there origin, and what is their connection to the world of H.P. Lovecraft. They are, after all, your average, run of the mill beasts, small and fast, tanky brawler, shooting, and roaring tank. They have a few variations, which is nice, but that is it. There could have been more of the classic Lovecraft creatures, bosses, and even locations. Apart from a generic cave, that only has one big set piece, and the end, you never really visit any big locations. Which is a shame. The stalking down the hall ways in DCotE still remains with me. The story itself was very much obvious in oh so many ways. It hurts on the fact, that often characters are not returning, or just die off screen. The sidequests are mostly a joke, of fetch some quest item off some place infested with creatures. No combination, no puzzling, no interaction with objects. Which is a shame. It would have helped the game if you could have some little lock picking, mystic puzzles, or other objects to manipuilate and interact, more so then turning them around and pressing a button. This is where this games seems unfinished. But there is still a lot of potential, and I still had alot of fun. The fact that much of the game was made from recycling a few assets hints at what Frogware did, despite the Publisher shennaigans. It is sadly just a pitty, the game seems to be to scarred, to give a more in depth system, for wounds, sanity, exploration and locations. If you want to explore a sinking city, and would liek to do some "light" detective work, then you are right here. Just down expect a AAA title.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I have ever critiqued a game primarily for it's bad geometry, but then, it has been a long time since I've played a game with geometry this bad. And it is *bad*. Your character will climb things you don't intend to that don't seem to be climbable. He will not climb things that are. This combination makes it extremely easy to get stuck in the geometry if you do any sort of exploring, or to fall to your death because you stepped off a rock, or fall in the water and be unable to get out despite being in a beach, or being unable to advance along a wooden pier until you "climb" the inch high board, or whatever. Since dying or loading reset you to a seemingly random location, sometimes to some place you've never been, this can be frustrating. If you can avoid feeling the need to explore, it's definitely a better game.Unfortunately, the rest of the game is still lackluster - the basic gameplay loops (movement, both boat and pedestrian, investigation, combat, dialogue) are all shallow and uninteresting. These aren't helped by weird keybinds and bad controls.The story is alright, but nothing to write home about.Really wanted to love this game, but man does it make it hard.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is enjoyable and the graphics, voice over, and general atmosphere are superb. Loved the clue system.The game is repetitive. It is not an open world, but a large gauntlet. The controls feel a bit sticky; the character stops at unexpected times; the collisions may need adjusting. General game play gives the illusion of "challenging" but is just annoying.There is little variation in the enemies, other than some are weak and some are ridiculously overpowered, forcing you to expend rare resources. It is often far more wise to run than fight.Enemies reappear in cleared buildings and loot can re-spawn. Story triggers can change that behavior. Enemies spawn in response to triggers, often surrounding you. This screams "console game" more than "open world."Saves are all at checkpoints. Again, not a feature of an open world.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally I thought about buying this game when it launched but was convinced otherwise by some bad reviews following the release.I should have stuck with that, but instead decided to buy it at discount for me and my friends Lovecraft evening on Saturdays.The game starts promising enough with you entering the city of Oakmont and some decent storytelling surrounding the murder of a member of the city elite. We had lots of fun in this first section and while we were constricted to the small section within the city harbor the game seemed flawed but ultimately decent.Unfortunately, after this section, our opinion of the game continued to drop until we finally reached the end.The city itself is the first reason for its ultimate demise. I was under the impression that it would be a mysterious place, sparsely populated after the calamity that had befallen it, with some survivors either trapped or too stubborn to leave. However, the game seems to spawn people in front of you wherever you go, the barricaded "dangerous areas" being the one exception where the streets are truly abandoned. While there are quite a lot of different kinds of Oakmont residents, with different clothes depending on the district, you will see so many people/twins strolling around at once that you wonder if anyone actually died in the cataclysm.The buildings themselves are another disappointment. In the beginning, we were following a side quest leading us around big parts of the first district to gather notes about some weird occurrences that happened there.Here we happened to notice that most of the buildings are just copy-pastes of each other, with just some furniture moved around. Later we learned that this was not only the case for side content but the main content as well. Not even the impressive villa of the most powerful family of the city gets a different treatment, its clone is just on the opposite side of the street. And why do we need three nearly identical bars, when one interesting one would have sufficed?The next problem is the game’s story: I don’t think it’s very compelling. In their effort to have as much Lovecraft in the game as possible, a trap that a lot of Lovecraft games seem to fall into, the story ultimately feels very generic and barely worth your time. They go as far as having a gang called “the yellow kings”, whose leader messes with you for no other reason than to be mysterious. The related quest is a gigantic waste of everyone’s time, its main purpose is apparently the statement: “Isn’t Hastur mysterious and weird?”. “Giant waste of time” is a reappearing theme within the game’s story, with many decisions being made by the time the game finally ends being entirely or at least in part pointless except maybe for roleplay reasons. Do you kill this guy or his son? Does it change anything significant going forward? Not really, but hey one seems to be kind of a ♥♥♥♥ so you might as well. Do you side with the obvious Dagon cultists or with the dude causing a bunch of collateral damage? Well even if you side with the cultist, which by the way due to a bug was the only option for us, the alliance lasts for an entire staircase before ending in gunfire.Here less would have been more: Have fewer choices but have them make a bigger impact.Good gameplay can balance out a mediocre story, but here the game fails again. The gunplay is absolutely dreadful and unresponsive. With every mouse click for a shot, the game takes 1 ½ seconds to decide if you actually fire your gun. This, combined with the need to craft most of your ammunition, makes you waste a lot of your bullets just shooting walls or the floor.Frequent combat is indeed a problem in itself, while the creatures, even the non-aggressive vermin in the street, were interesting, even scary, at the beginning of the game, the game pushes combat on you during every quest making them very unthreatening and boring after a while. The typical case goes like this:First, you are given some sort of hint of how to proceed, the solution being to travel to one of the many “archives” in the city, for example, the newspaper archive or the city hall, going to the desk with the symbol and matching the story with categories like time, people and places. While this may sound fine at first remember that you will have to do this at least once per quest just with different desks and categories. Even the most interesting “archive” in the game, the library, is just another place for the matching desk and the changing categories don’t make up for the frequent visits.After that, you will receive a clue that the place you are looking for is in Lovecraft street, between Yellow King road and Arthur Jermyn lane. You look at your map, mark the spot and begin your travel.The travel takes you through streets being entirely populated by twins, canals that are entirely safe as long as you stay on your boat, which will always spawn on the nearest shore, and maybe some “danger zones” where monsters exist. You don’t need to engage with the monsters as there is more than enough time to loot some of the area’s chests and then just climb over the nearest barricade. In fact in my experience actually fighting the beasts is just a waste of bullets as the whole area doesn’t give you enough resources to make up for the tedium of combat and the bullets wasted.When you make it to your goal look for the one door marked with signs and enter. Once you take a few steps you can hear the maddening sound of non-optional combat. After you fought through however many enemies spawned from the ground, keep in mind that this is neither fun nor rewarding, you will then interact with clues in the room. We once got stuck because we missed a bottle in a corner of the room that added no additional information, so you have to be very thorough. Then you will enter “spooky vision” where your piece together which of the shown scenes happened first. This normally results in the next clue, rinse and repeat until you get to the decision of who you want to kill this time.If you are particularly unlucky part of your quest will involve “underwater fun time”, where you dive with your diving suit. Even disregarding that the same cutscenes play every time (who thought that this would be a good idea?) “underwater fun time” is where the game shows how bad things can be. The ground is littered with small geysers, your movement is even more unresponsive than during combat, making it hard to avoid the damage. Climbing up rocks is a nightmare, especially if there are geysers nearby, as it’s hard to judge what part of the climb is just for show and which one is the one you actually need to climb.Underwater combat at least gives you infinite ammunition and it works a lot smoother. This may be because the game doesn’t need to calculate damage because shooting a monster only stuns it for a short time before it will follow you again. So it would be a good idea to look behind you while you sprint away if your way here hadn’t taught you about the geysers.I would have loved for those underwater walks to just being mysterious sections of the game without enemies, where you take in the sunken parts of the titular Sinking City and wonder what the strange shape in the distance is and whose tentacles are waving over there. Sadly it wasn’t meant to be and so underwater is like land but worse.It’s no wonder then, that even finishing the game is worth a golden achievement, but that seems to go for a lot of later quests. I was hoping for it to all be worth it in the end, having an ending that would either leave us with some dread about the cosmic horror lurking between the stars or at least be so bad that it would be entertaining. As the 5-second ending cutscene played we realized that this was neither, just disappointment.TLDR: I didn’t like it very much. Neither the story nor the gameplay nor the city itself wowed me and our excitement about this game dropped at every turn.

_childDocuments_.review: As with most things Lovecraft, if you're already a fan of the genre and mythos, you'll probably like this game. Otherwise, hard to say.Pros: The map is fantastic. This is by far the most immersive Lovecraftian world I can think of in all of videogame-dom. Combat actually has some gravity to it. Resources are scarce, and just about every monster encounter deprived me of most of my ammo. Combined with the fact that respawn points could potentially be really far away from where you died, you really have to learn to be a crack shot and make every bullet count.The story doesn't always hold your hand. It is a detective game, first and foremost, and oftentimes you have to actually do some deducing to figure out where to go next. However...Cons:...this eventually gets very old. Every investigation pretty much requires the exact same steps to solve. There's zero nuance, in that department. In fact, repetition in general is the biggest con. All of the assets, from scene props to the interior locations themselves are reused over and over again.I didn't find the story to be all that interesting. I appreciate that it wasn't just a straightforward adaptation of an existing Lovecraft story, but it just moved so slowly, with so much busy work (I'll help you if you do a favor for me first) that it's hard to get sucked into it.All in all, I do recommend it, as it did keep me engaged for almost 20 hours before I lost interest. But it did lose me, eventually. Again, it's hard to say if it would have kept me interested for even that long had I not been a Lovecraft fan. But I do think that any Lovecraft fan would at least appreciate it for a while. A solid-ish entry in that genre.

I was surprised that you could do so many stuff in one quest line.I just wish it was more polished and put more time to the story with additional add-ons like  Either way, its a very fun game to play and spend some time. Highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably one of the best Lovecraftian games out there. It's like a mix of The Evil Within and one of those open world hero games (i.e. Arkham Knight, Marvel's Spiderman, etc.) There's tons of exploration, tons of horrific lore, and tons of enemies that are inexplicably unnatural entities from beyond. Also, if you set the difficulty right, you'll find that there's little in the way of handholding, allowing you to immerse yourself into the world of this sinking city.The atmosphere is perfect in this game too! Not to spoil too much, but you'll find that there are citizens of this city that are, shall we say, appropriately designed for the demonic supernatural theme of this game. The music is perfect, the scenery is perfect, the combat isn't particularly extraordinary, but this game really isn't focused on the combat. Also, fair warning: a lot of the content in this game is reading. It's totally worth it if you have the patience, but I understand if some don't.tl;dr - A fantastic and utterly essential horror experience for any Lovecraftian fans like myself. It has a lot of reading and lore to discover, very few (and mild) bugs in my experience, and combat that isn't exactly it's greatest strongsuit, but totally functional and appropriate for the setting of this game. It's not for everyone, but it is for fans of the mythos.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a "wait for sale". The skill trees are forgettable, the combat's main positive is "ammo is scarce"... sorta. So I could just save, load, turn around, and fast travel. Save the walk back.The game functions, and the plot's... well, it's cthulu. It's not told badly, but it does feel a bit padded. You have a number of story choices that... do not matter, but are presented like they do. It's fine, not great.

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is not a bad game, but it is also not very good one.The game is set in Lovercraftian universe but it is not a horror game unfortunetly.It is adventure/investigation open world game. But despite technically being open world, nothing actually happens if you are not on right quest. You can stumble upon empty locations, that look interesting but has nothing going on, just to discover that there is quest leading there later on and suddenly they are populated with monsters and loot ....The main story and story of the city is interesting but shallow, also the game is way too long for what it actually offers.I wasn't fan of the combat or the crafting/looting mechanic. It seems pointless to have limited ammunition and having to craft it bullet by bullet if the loot respawns endlessly as soon as you exit and reenter the house. Also apparently medkits are made by combining alcohol and coil springs .... who would have thought.Buying this game for 8€ in sale, like it is right now, is not bad deal, but is it worth actually spending time on?I cant recommend this game, there are so many better games out there I feel like your time is better spent elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: I am willing to give this game a positive review due to the heavy influence of H.P. Lovecraft in the story.  The game doesn't hold your hand and starting off can be difficult.  It is mainly open world after you complete the first investigation and you can easily run into areas where you are easily overwhelmed and you end up dying a lot.  The investigations and clues remind me a bit of the old NES game ♥♥♥♥ Tracy.  You are sometimes given clues that are straight forward such as "located at the intersection of such and such" and at other times you have to visit the police station or other places to search their archives.  I started using a walkthrough and it helped enormously because I was close to giving up.  Give it a try.*Edit*As I have been playing this I have found some things that help out tremendously.  One thing is that lootables respawn when you end a game and come back in.  There are several places in the game that give you a lot of loot to craft bullets with.  One such place is Billy Drunnon's hideout that you will visit later in the game.  There are a ton of bullets here especially for the machine gun.  On the way there is the cannery where you can get a ton of gun powder and shell casings.  Mark these and other places on your map and visit them if you ever find yourself running low on bullets or crafting supplies.

_childDocuments_.review: its an incomplete game. it tries to be a detective game, with some twists that could have been interesting, but its all half assed, half baked.the detective part can be interesting some times, with some compelling characters and interesting backstory. but the gameplay always gets in the way. whenever you have to engage in combat is a huge pain, one of the worst shooting experience I ever had.and the big map is completely useless, with "NPCs" that wander around but you cant interact and all you do is walk long distances unless there's a phone booth teleport around, that you need to find first before you can use.all in all, its a sad miss, 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: We need more games like this in my opinion. Took me roughly 36 hours realistically to beat the game in normal difficulty settings with only missing one side quest.

_childDocuments_.review: Played on Linux using Proton Exp, I do like this Game so far and have played around 19 Hours of mostly Side Missions, Graphics are Great, Sound is Great, Game Play is Okay, I say okay as I've only done mostly side missions which are go here, get that, go right over to the other side of the map and get that, and repeat, the main Game Mission seems a lot better as you get to solve cases, etc.But the Game Does have a few bugs at the moment, Like walk up some stairs fell though stairs and could not get out so had to reload last auto save which was a fair way back in the game, This happened a few times when playing, also the Boat seems to get stuck on something, you can still just about move and at some point it will unstuck itself, again this happened a fair few times, I did not have Frame Rate Issues I've seen other people bring up, So maybe plays a bit better on Linux using Proton?, My specs are old Intel I7 6700, 16GB Ram, Nvidia RTX 4060 and still using Hard Drives.As a patch is incoming which will break the Save Games from old version i will stop playing and await incoming Patch and start all over again.

_childDocuments_.review: At last Frogwares got back rights for their own game from disgusting nacon.I have been looking at this game on release and can say that now it is in a very good state at last.From newer Lovecraftian games this one is the best, really. Although it is not a AAA title, but it is anyway a great game.Pros:+ Lovecraft and Shadow over Innsmouth.+ Great depressing and dark atmosphere.+ Main questline is good.+ Secondary quests can be gross and unpleasant, superb addition to overall feeling.+ Progression and shooting are OK, I guess they fixed it in new patches.+ Visuals are very good.+ Ukrainian localization.+ There are no quest markers, you have to pin the on map manually, searching for mentioned streets and street intersections.+ Detective gameplay is nice.+ In a lot of quests there are no good or bad choices, all of them have both in each selected choice. And you need to choose what outcome is worse in your own opinion.+ Survival aspect, when you need to collect resources to craft bullets, medkits and all other stuff. Every bullet counts. Ah, also bullets are used as money here :)Cons (they are very small IMO):- There are several endings, they all depend on final choice and all are pretty short, just one cinematic in each basically.- Some secondary quests that have easter eggs from other Lovecraft's works are the same: find and collect N of things.- A lot of buildings inside are the same with minor differencies.- Some faces are reused with minor changes.I can absolutely recommend this game for everyone who likes Lovecraft's work. It is really good and authentic.Thank you, Frogwares, it was an awesome adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovecraftian horror and detective work in a city that you do not belong in...Your choices change who lives and dies, and the makeup of the world around you.It's up to you to put the pieces together. Literally. I loved this game. You have to use your character's abilities that cost you your sanity in order to put together cases that no one else is able or wants to. You are in charge of using context clues to make your OWN deductions and bring the clues together in your mind palace. And there are very sparse marked locations on the map, YOU have to make your own points of interest and travel to them among the many varied streets with their own stories and npcs.I only really had gripes about the underwater/diving sections that have some of the most annoying vents that you WILL take damage from and die. It is the most aggravating part of this game, seconded maybe with the learning I had to do to learn how to use the Archives correctly. I usually had the right idea to use an archive, but I was at the wrong one.Other than that, the combat was so unique and was a little dicey, but was super fluid in when you could swap from detective to gunslinger. You had no constraints on when you could pull out weapons and traps, which was great when I walked into ambushes of Wylebeasts and gangsters alike. There were also PLENTY of solid and unsettling narrative stories, both the main and side quests felt so satisfying to solve, and at no point did I feel I wasn't leveling up enough. If you love Lovecraft, you enjoy putting pieces together in mysteries, you like to be unsettled and scared, and all of it in a wet yet beautiful city of Oakmont, you will enjoy this game. My sanity was tested, and I was found sane, among the beasts of the world that sought to make this not so. Wyles, humanity itself, or those that lurk beyond the edge of consciousness...
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game on sale, and I think that's exactly how you should play it too. Is it a fantastic game? Nope! But I liked the atmosphere. I liked the moments of disturbing implication that come from just walking into a house and making your own deductions of what happened. The detective gameplay had no challenge to it, but it still felt engaging anyway. I'd feel cheated if I'd spent $40 on it, but since I bought it on sale, it was well worth the money!I have also yet to play a detective game set in the Cthulu mythos that is really fantastic. This game handles gameplay, atmosphere, and detective work much better than Call of Cthulu at any rate. If you're craving something totally passable with some brilliant moments set in that universe then check this out! Just don't pay $40 for it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes in order to appreciate a simple and bland mashed potatoes you have to go hungry for a few days.And with the current state of the modern-day lovecraftian games sometimes you have to play the Sinking City in order to reevaluate your previous thoughts on other games. For example i honestly thought that the 2018's "Call of Cthulhu" was a  mediocre game with an obvious plot, linear storyline and primitive investigations. But compared to this sinking king of mediocrity, i feel now that the "Call of Cthulhu" was not so bad at all.I can't even say that the Sinking City is truly "bad" - the game does have it's "moments" sometimes, but overally it's just so very mediocre. Good moments are offset by the totally devoid of life city (even Cyberpunk 2077 street crowd feels adequate compared to the mob in here), constant running back and forth, bland enemies, broken inner logic of the game (bloodhungry monsters are separated from the strolling crowds by literally a single half-rotten wood plank), copypasted buildings and many other small things, with suspension of disbelief being first among them.My personal stance on the game - avoid it if you are an ordinary gamer seeking for the good game (hence downvote). If you are a lovecraftian fan, who simply craves for an another dose of the sea-soaked eldritch horror - you can probably get this one on a sale to quell your thirst, but do expect this beer to be watered down. The game starts strong and the first 1,5 hours are actually very promising, but after that it will mostly slump into a gray and repetitive gameplay. If you are in a search of good lovecraftian games, let me recommend those instead:Call of Cthulhu: Dark corners of the Earth (old but gold)ConariumNo one lives under the lighthose (ugly... but brilliant)Call of Cthulhu 2018Games to avoid (unless you absolutely need a new eldritch dose)The ShoreMoons of MadnessThe Sinking CityThat is not dead which can eternal lie,And with strange aeons even death may die.Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthulhu R'lyeh wgah'nagl fhtagn, fellow cultists!
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't have bought it at the full price though. Not worth forty bucks. But about the actual game:- I love the main story... Pretty interesting how it's set up. I really love how it's set up as a bunch of really short cases instead of one big long case. That would get boring real fast.- The side cases are fun, they let you level up a lot without buffing you up with super powered items. My personal favorite case is probably "Silence is Golden" because -I didn't like the combat at first, but as I learned the enemy's patterns and  learned what to expect, it got a lot more enjoyable. The first time I encountered something other than a Stygian, it was nerve wracking, which I guess is what they were going for.- Mechanics are AWESOME. I absolutely love the Retrocognition mechanic. Getting the order of events right is so incredibly satisfying. All the tools at your disposal to solve cases (Retrocognition, Mind Palace, Archives) are fun to use and figure out. When you here the audio cue telling you that you've figured something out, it's just  amazing.-World building is alright. There isn't a lot of variation between set pieces. But I guess some of the areas get a pass. Oldgrove, for example, is basically an HOA for rich people, so the houses are all pretty similar. In Reed Heights, most of the buildings you explore are apartment complexes, so the layout of them is pretty similar. All the other areas don't seem to be very similar though.But yeah, uh...4/5 stars. 1 star has been deducted the npcs could use some work.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: This has been a fun journey, one that I'd definitely recommend, now that you can often grab it for 8-15 quids.The setting (pulp Cthulhu mythos), the eerie atmosphere, the dark comedy (like a particular cake that shows up in a particular mansion after a vigil), the dialogues, the characters all add up to a very enjoyable CoC experience.The definite strongpoint of the game are the cases and the decisions you can make. No black and white, no right and wrong, this is a very crooked city with very crooked people all around.The concept is absolutely smashing it!Then there is the delivery of all these. Now that's a bit janky, and that's why I recommend it on a sale but not full price.The game has a single color pattern. Models and animations are lacking. NPCs and sometimes even adversaries are spawning into walls where then they are stuck for an eternity. The combat is a bummer, it's flat and tedious. Traversing the terrain gets real boring real fast.Now as I said, I very much recommend this journey, because the story and investigations, the atmosphere makes up for all the jankiness; but it1s only fair to say that presentation and gameplay is not its strongsuits.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: Ignoring the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boat physics glitches (boat getting sided making the camera lopsided or just overall getting stuck somewhere), it was enjoyable and made me very depressed that Oakmont exists in my head.Would recommend to Call of Cthulhu players or people who like Lovecraftian themes in-general. (Suffer with me.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: The Sinking City is a very well written game, in my opinion. I honestly can't remember the last time I was so completely absorbed by a game, to the point I was ruminating over it all day while at work. As soon as I was home and my cats were fed, The Sinking City was loading and I'm ready to delve back into it. The atmosphere and art style is very convincing, it draws you in deeper to the game. The ambient sounds and the music scores are extremely complimentary, I highly recommend using headphones while playing this. Especially if you are a pluviophile; it never stops raining.The jump scares are on point, monsters are horrifying, especially the developers take on the human centipede, and the process of going through and solving the mysteries is very satisfying. However, use caution if you have issues with hearing voices in your head. No joke, they did an excellent job of portraying schizophrenia. Yes, there are some bugs, like this chick over here strutting down the road with her skirt up over her head, or this person over here trying to get around this wall and failing, or this random dude just walking in on a crime scene while I'm deep in the blue-zone of figuring things out (he's lucky all he got was the business end of a shotgun in his face and some soil in his pants...could have ended far worse for him). But I found these rather lightened the mood for me at times rather than simply breaking immersion. So I wasn't too bothered by them.All in all, I really enjoyed this game, which I was rather surprised by since I don't really care for horror. Even more surprising, I'm actually considering reinstalling it and playing through again, even though I cleared most of the side quests.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game for people who enjoy mystery games or Lovecraftian work. It's essentially if you played as a mentally ill Sherlock Holmes with a gun. The choices feel like they matter, and seeing all three endings for yourself is super easy, and doesn't require you to start a completely new playthrough. Some of the side quests are a bit tedious and are pointless, but they're fun to go through anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: Unbelievable rip-off of the works of H.P. Lovecraft. Literally everything has been plagiarised. The main quest is a pastiche of The Call of Cthulhu, the NPCs are all facsimiles of Lovecraft characters and the side-quests are all re-hashes of Lovecraft’s many novellas and short stories published in the pulp magazines of the early 20th century. Even the names of streets, buildings and districts are taken from Lovecraft’s work, or that of other writers that collaborated with him or extended upon his mythos.It's fortunate that Howard Phillips Lovecraft’s works lie in a state of Cosmic Copyright Indifference, otherwise Frogwares would have a Mountain of Madness for their legal team.Would highly recommend for any fans of Lovecraft’s work 😊
_childDocuments_.name: The Sinking City

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully crafted open lovecraftian world that have all the right ingredients for a masterpiece but for the lack of a better luck fallen in to some hardships development and otherwise DO NOT let this keep you away from this adventure especially if you are a fun of lovecraftian mythos the way the game is designed is beautiful and add allot to the atmosphere of what an actual cthulhu mythos  game must have!!example with NO spoilers !you take on a case you need to interview the witnesses  look at the clues manually mark locations on the map based on your clues travel to your local police station,library, and other places to go through the archives !and the best part for every single case there is not only one solution it comes down to go you to boil down the whole case to what you believe is about and what happened all by exposing your self to terrifying and unknown truths  gun down abominations or run for your life and in the end solve your case And this is but the idea behind a single mission/investigation in  an open world game

_childDocuments_.review: If you really like the Lovecraft universe, don't try to play this.Quite a rail game in which your qualities of point A, the choice of point B, as well as other actions do not affect anything. Ultimately, you will get stuck halfway because the developer requires you to unquestioningly follow the game's script. A conditionally locked door will never open until you, through careful selection of information, find out that it has been open all this time. The real peak of absurdity! Among the four NPCs, the fifth will not appear until you come and activate a special script, permanent binding to the script scripts...You cannot find and research something yourself until you receive information about it.
