_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: First off: don't look up anything about this game; I played this game knowing 0 things about it, and it blew my mind all the more (I got it on a gamble and am so glad I did). If the start of the game throws you off a bit, stick with it and things will start to build.Secondly: This game doesn't spoon feed you anything. Lots of people seem to be put off by not knowing what to do. There's no hand-holding, you just gotta go out and start messing around with the universe. This game is about exploring, information gathering, deducing, and following clues to uncover mysteries. It takes a lot of initiative, paying attention and putting together what you've learned. If you don't pay attention, you'll get lost, stuck, and bored, which seems to be where some of the negative reviews are coming from. Expect to feel lost at first, but revel in it. You'll feel like a sleuth at the centre of a complex plot which will lift you from confusion to revelation, and it will feel fantastic and enlightening. The game is incredibly clever and deep, and you'll feel clever and deep for making it through. I kind of wish I could wipe my memory of it so I could experience it all over again.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Wilds is a very special game.It is, mechanically, a game of archaeology and puzzle solving.  Reconstructing what happened in the past, exploring, and solving physics puzzles are the core mechanics here, and are mostly done very well.  I found there to be some difficulty spikes in the puzzles that didn't match the surrounding area, but otherwise the difficulty curve is smooth and forgiving.But beyond its mechanics, Outer Wilds is a game with a profound and haunting story that kept me pulled in for days. I usually enjoy writing long reviews, I feel it is best to have this game revealed in playing, so I won't critique the story here.I would wholeheartedly recommend this game.Minor technical note:  as a Linux user, this game works perfectly under Proton version 4.  As of this day, it has some issues for me with the Steam Linux Runtime and Proton version 5.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Not actually great. This is barely average. Maybe 2/5. Not sure what everyone is raving about. I finished the game because I wanted to complete it not because it was fun playing it, tbh.The mechanics is interesting, but the story is honestly somewhere between boring and confusing. The story line about the sun exploding naturally into a supernova, which is a main part of the game, is actually nonsensical -- it goes from looking like a yellow dwarf star at the start of the cycle to a red giant and a supernova in the span of 22 minute. Yellow dwarf stars don't actually explode like that. This doesn't make sense and interferes with a different part of the story, where the sun station was supposed to trigger an artificial supernova... The canonical ending isn't obvious, so you have to google what to do next at almost every step. It's also not very good and doesn't make any sense. Other clues are also well hidden and you have to go around for a long time until you stumble upon them or just google what is where. The Anglerfish at the beginning are interesting, but after a while they become annoying. You need to go beyond their lair to do some other stuff, but they're always there... It's irritating. There should have been other mechanics that would have simply removed them altogether in late game.Graphically the game is also average/below-average. Some canyons looked very cheap and unfinished. Don't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: This game is crazy good!You are in a tiny (once you play it makes sense) solar system that has a myriad of different mysteries scattered through out.You are a four eyed, humanoid creature that is set to explore the space, but you'll soon discover that there are more secrets than it seems, and those are waiting for you (every 20 minutes or so)
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to truly put into words how good this game is.  I think it really is just the kind of game that everyone will enjoy, similarly to the Portal series. My only request is that you go in completely blind. More so than any other game I have played in my 7+ years, spoilers will ruin this game like you would not believe. Thank you, and please, play Outer Wilds.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: With little exaggeration, and admittedly coming off of literally just finishing it, Outer Wilds is easily top 5 games I've ever played, and considering the emotional state it left me in as the credits rolled, might even become my favourite in time. It's deceptively difficult to write about this game since it is an experience best simply played - but yet, I will try. I had heard vague musings about it and its quality but it was not until I sat down, gave Outer Wilds its time of day and really invested into its world and systems that I truly began to fall in love with this game.On paper, it doesn't sound so exciting - you play as an alien astronaut (yay) who is exploring other planets purely in the name of researching an ancient alien race called the Nomai (not necessarily so yay). Though it seems like a premise that doesn't provoke much excitement, the sense of freedom and exploration that kicks in as soon as you are given your ship is almost overwhelming. Unlike many space exploration games, Outer Wilds truly gives you all of its tools as soon as you step into the cockpit of your disastrously unsafe-appearing spaceship. But that's the thing that's beautiful about Outer Wilds - knowledge is what allows you to unravel the mysteries of the solar system you inhabit. How did the Nomai so suddenly disappear? How come there is a black hole in the middle of Brittle Hollow? What in HELL is the deal with Dark Bramble? These are all questions that you will come to find the answers to simply by exploring, and following the breadcrumbs of your previous discoveries.Oh, and did I mention that there's a time loop mechanic? This is arguably the hook of Outer Wilds, alongside its brilliant narrative structure and storytelling - not only the fact that you have to unravel these mysteries, but that any given time you wake up you only have 22 minutes until the sun supernovas. But, of course, you come back every time you die with greater knowledge to help you on your further travels. Another brilliant aspect of the time mechanic is that it allows planets to change in such a way that for some objectives, you have to be laser-focused on what it is you will do with this loop, incentivising you to find out as much information as you possibly can before you see that final brilliant flash of light that spells your doom. This is the genius of Outer Wilds - with the time limit you have in the loop and goals in mind, you are determined to get things done on each loop, discover new things and become equipped with greater knowledge. Somehow, it gives reading ancient Nomai texts a sense of danger and exhilaration as you wonder - do I have enough time to be doing this, or will I meet my unsightly demise?  This, paired with a genuinely interesting mystery that leads you on a quest all around the solar system, fantastic writing for both the ancient and modern characters (the former of which feel just as alive as the characters you do literally speak to) and a BEAUTIFUL soundtrack composed by Andrew Prahlow makes Outer Wilds a truly mesmerizing and hauntingly beautiful experience. As long as you are willing to sink in the time waiting, reading, exploring and (most importantly) understanding, Outer Wilds will likely be one of the most engrossing gaming experiences you ever have. It is existing proof of the power of video games as a medium to be deeply and beautifully effective in its exploration systems and narratives, inextricably intertwining the two in a masterful way to engross the player in a way very few games have ever done so for me. Play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is it. Outer Wilds made me feel the sense of wonder, doubt, curiosity and unpredictability that i only felt as a young boy starting to play games in the 90's, unaware of many things. I specially remember a little game called , which made me feel absolutely clueless as a child of what was going to happen, where should i go, what should i do, what did all of that mean etc. I've never finished it, but i can easily remember how it made me feel back then. I really didn't think it was possible to evoke, even if for only a couple of days, such intrinsic feelings again at 30, having seen as much of life and living through it's miseries as i have.There are no objectives, no acomplishments required, no skill trees, which is quite unusual in games today. Guess what? The developers captured what first made humans want to create what we call games in the first place: the desire to escape reality to a different place in which imagination could be brought out: the unknown, the curiosity towards something new, the freedom of choice and the sense of being inside a story, instead of controling a specific character. There's no script to be followed, and that makes YOU feel as the protagonist here. As you explore, the game slowly opens up adding to the atmosphere and to your understanding of the universe (or universes) and, as it does that, you see that despite being a game that seems innocent, many scientific concepts are brought to your attention and are actually alive around you or will become alive depending on what you do.Life itself is a journey which comprehends knowledge, unfortunate mistakes and regrets, the need for true friendship and connection,  and, if all goes well, the chance to share your own journey with someone else on a deeper level. Well, this game encourages you to value your journey and the people around you, and this point is important. . There's no focus on violence, hatred, vengeance, competition and any other manifestations that correlate to bad emotions, except for the certainty of decay, death itself at some point - as it is with real life. I didn't expect this, and i'm happy i was unable to predict the direction of this game for a considerable part. I encourage those who have already completed the game to watch on YT it's making of interview video. Search for it... Those guys did a fantastic job.You can feel both cozy with a beautiful music composition (another aspect of this game that deserves much recognition!) while around a campfire in the woods and also in distress to think you should probably give it a couple of days before playing again once you know what you have to or should do: . Outer Wilds enables you to dwell on two separate states: the happiness of ignorance and the haunting knowledge of what's beyond your world. Once you get to the second state, it's impossible to keep yourself in ignorance, even if you would prefer it to avoid dealing with reality... Isn't life exactly like this?I wonder,: maybe the guys who made the game never experienced what i described, due to their prior knowledge of everything, isn't it sad? Like a mentioned above: This puts many AAA titles to shame.10/10.

When you want to explore and just discover things by yourself without the hand-holding and without the pressure, this game gives you that with a story that you learned based by your experience, a different experience that no one else walked or played or seen. I can only describe this game as Ocarina of Time without the hand-holding and just being pushed out of the Forest and forced to learn the world by yourself without knowing anything.Personally, I haven't played the DLC yet, but a recent talk of this game and just recently listening to the OST made me want to put more words to this review. _childDocuments_.review: So as a huge fan of Annapurna films, the moment I found out they made video games I rushed to buy this one in The-store-that-shall-not-be-named-on-Steam, where I’ve put in about 40 hours.What I was expecting was this sort of space- meets , but man was I mistaken.  Outer Wilds ended up being more like a mash up of , , and .  In my humble opinion and despite it’s quiet launch, Outer Wilds is probably one of the best indie games of the last decade.  Here’s why:✔️ GAME LOOP (LITERALLY) Within the first ~20 minutes of the game, you realize you’re stuck in Groundhog’s Day.  You have a set amount of time before everything resets, and all you do to uncover the mysteries of your solar system have to be done inside that loop.  Nothing persists except your memories, which you log in your ship.  This loops is like  on steroids, and creates an excellent setting to explore and solve puzzles in since everything is accessible in the loop timespan..  Like , it is possible to win the game in the first 25 minutes, but only if you have learned the right secrets, and there are  of secrets.✔️ PUZZLE MECHANICSOne of the aspects of this game that gave me  vibes (despite the lack of confectionary) was that every planet has its own puzzle with unique game mechanics for you to discover and solve.  They’re not on the level of  outside the box challenging, but they’re up there.  I don’t want to give any spoilers so I’m going to avoid even mentioning the individual mechanics, but I felt a feeling of surprise and reward on discovering solutions that immediately made me think of .✔️ C H I L L VIBES:This didn’t hit me until later when I beat the game, but this is the most pacified experience I’d played in a while and had fun doing so.  You are not some space marine sent out to conquer alien invaders, nor are you a miner sent to exploit resources on other planets.  You simply exist as a space explorer stuck in a time loop, and are trying to piece together the scattered mysteries to solve it.  The other explorers you encounter are all vibin where they are, without any need for rescuing or escort missions.  ✖️ POLISHThe simple-poly graphics fit the universe in the game quite well, and the music, while not memorable, is used appropriately in certain situations.  The part I would have liked more is to have voice-overs for the conversations or even the recordings you uncover, but it's all text-only.  It’s not game breaking but would have been appreciated.✖️ REPLAYABILITYI found myself disappointed upon beating the game that it wasn’t longer.  The exploration and puzzle solving is rewarding, but I was left wanting more.  Even with the multiple endings, they’re essentially the same outcome.  I feel like there was missed opportunity here for replayability.❌ CONTROLSSo Outer Wilds isn’t all sunshine and roses.  Getting the hang of zero G and low-gravity jetpacking is a challenge, but the ship takes it to the next level.  You will slam into planet surfaces and you will burn up in the sun.  This is inevitable, but not impossible to master.  There is one point of the game, though, where you need to keep thrust under one bar, and it’s super difficult to do even with a gamepad.  Can be a little frustrating.Ultimately, if you’re a fan of puzzle and exploration games, like , ,  and others, then this game is for you.  If you’re looking for a crafting, survival, or FPS experience, you won’t find it here.  Your mission is to explore and understand your solar system, and try to prevent a tragedy, all while repeatedly resetting.  I can't think of any games out there to compare it to since the sum of it's parts is so unique.For me, I was personally glad that games like this are still being made.  I highly recommend it at this price, especially if you’re looking for a chill, space-themed puzzle solving adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Wilds has earned a spot in my top ten games of all time, it is a must-play. You never get the sense that you were "meant" to find anything, it was just there, just existing and it was only by luck, determination and a spark of genius that you managed to uncover it. _childDocuments_.review: I thought I should finally give Outer Wilds a proper reviewBefore you read any further, just be aware that you can play this game once. Anything you learn about this game before playing it will rob you of the experience of learning about it in the game. If Outer Wilds looks at all interesting to you, just buy it and don't look at anything else relating to the game until you beat it. It'll be worth it, trust me.Anyway, I bought Outer Wilds early 2021. Almost 4 years later and this game is still living rent free in my head. Since I played Outer Wilds it has held the #1 game of all time title for me, and I don't think that title will ever be put onto a new game. I bought it just looking for stuff to play because I vaguely recognised it from a random YouTube video, and I went in completely blind.That was the best decision I ever made. This game is a true one of a kind experience, in the almost 4 years since i've played this game I've only found one game () that even comes close to how Outer Wilds felt to play. As a general description, without spoilers, in Outer Wilds, you explore a solar system filled with mysteries and puzzles to figure out what happened. You will be doing a lot of reading ancient texts, solving complex multi-layered puzzles, and generally trying to piece together how things work. Outer Wilds is a completely open ended game, you can do anything and explore anything however you like, once you launch there is nobody telling you what you need to do. Outer Wilds is completely driven by your own curiosity to explore and seek answers.Outer Wilds also has a DLC, Echoes of the Eye. Echoes is an excellent addition to the base game, somehow seamlessly fitting itself into the solar system, almost as if it was always there. Echoes, in my opinion, is best played after already beating the base game, as it has no crossover with the puzzles and exploration of the base game, but as is the theme with Outer Wilds, nothing is stopping you from playing the DLC whenever you'd like.Echoes adds a significant amount of extra Outer Wilds goodness onto the base game, around an extra 15 hours, with it's own story, puzzles, and location. The story from Echoes is almost as good as the base game's, and it's setting is perfect. The puzzles and mysteries of Echoes are quite a bit more difficult than the base game, so be prepared for some hard thinking, but they are still very good. Booting up the game with Echoes will give you a warning that the DLC is quite scary, and that there's an option to turn off the scares. Echoes is quite scary, so be warned, but I really did enjoy the spooky nature of Echoes.There's so much more I wish I could say about this game but I cannot without spoiling things. Outer wilds is a true perfect 10/10 game. If I could erase my memory and start fresh again I don't know how many times I would end up playing this game again. Once again, If this sounds anything like a game you would be some-what interested in, give it a go (+ Echoes if you want to). Outer Wilds is a once in a lifetime experience.

_childDocuments_.review: If I were to describe Outer Wilds in a sentence, I would say that it's about dealing with big things. After a short initial jaunt through your home town, you launch yourself into space, where you are made to contend with objects, forces, plots, and concepts that absolutely dwarf you and your tiny planet. You'll brave storms that toss your ship around like a leaf in the wind, chart lightless depths full of unknown danger, and fight the gravity wells of stars and black holes in a desperate attempt to avoid death. If you're so inclined, you can leave your star system behind and fly off into deep space. Alone in the void, forever.If you have a fear of darkness, of emptiness, of loneliness, of the incomprehensibly large, or of the strange and unknown, you're in for a ride. Outer Wilds will make you face those fears, and ask you to deal with them if you want to get anything done. It will ask you to rely on yourself and your own knowledge when nothing around you makes sense. It will show you the sheer insignificance of your race, 'any' race, on a cosmic scale, and that inevitably, you and everything you know will one day be gone. Outer Wilds comes in a friendly package, but it has some very bleak elements to it, and a not-insignificant undertone of cosmic horror. In fact, if I were to describe it in a second sentence, I would call it the most horror-esque non-horror game I've ever played.So why play? Why leave the comfort of home and hearth to deal with all that? Well, because there's things to see. People to meet, places to explore, stories to read, and mysteries to solve. Outer Wilds is a game about experiencing the world you've been given. Death may be inevitable, but that doesn't make life meaningless. The universe may not care, but that doesn't mean you shouldn't. The contrast of it is melancholy, beautiful, and, in my opinion, very much worth experiencing.It's difficult to recommend this game as much as it deserves to be, even if I weren't concerned with spoiling it. On a practical note, if you plan on playing, definitely avoid said spoilers as much as possible. This is the sort of game you can only experience once.

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously I'm writing about my experience with this game.I mostly love this game.  It's beautifully made with this amazingly intricate story that unfolds as you explore and work out what happened in the past, what is happening in the present of the game and what lies in store.My issue, and something that I think is important to be aware of going in that will make this unsuitable for some other players, is that playing Outer Wilds sent me into a depressive state of mind.If you're susceptible to depression I would recommend you look after yourself if you play this, and maybe give the game a miss.I found it to be laced with ongoing, pervasive, melancholy.  The premise, which shouldn't be a spoiler, is that you're in this little solar system where the sun is set to explode, though your character has been somehow made to start over every time they die.  So the basic fabric of this game is one where you die over and over again and start over.  On top of this, much of the exploration and uncovering what is going on is about getting to know and understand an ancient extinct advanced civilization - you can read their written musings and dialogues, and get to know them as (long dead) individuals.  It's fascinating, but again, steeped in an essential melancholy.  Not to mention that exploring their cities involves dealing with the physical decay and destruction of what is left of these long dead people.  And to top it all off, of course, is the looming question of "is there anything that can be done?"It's beautifully done; it took a while for me to get back to feeling on a more even keel.  Look after yourselves playing this.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best game I've ever played.  No game has ever made me felt this way, and the ending is something I can't describe.The closest example games might be The Witness, The Stanley Parable, and obviously, a lot like any repeating game like Majora's Mask.   The aspects of those games, the big reveal you get in the Witness, exploring every path in TS  are similar to this game.  But there are no tools or level ups you acquire in this game.  It started as a college thesis with the simple premise that knowledge is the tool you acquire.  It's a fantastic open world mystery game where there aren't so much puzzles, it's more like figuring out riddles.  Every piece of information you acquire leads to more understanding (and opening up new paths) or more things to try or places to explore.  Do NOT attempt to look up anything, it's all there, be patient.  If I got stuck, I'd put it on the back burner, and even sleep on it, and it didn't take long before the solution came to me.  If you skip any of that, you are only robbing yourself of this games limited but amazing experience.From my first two example games, you might think this is a walking simulator, but the space suit with jetpack and ship combined with small planets, solar system, and fun orbital dynamics makes that normally boring aspect of games like this lots of fun.  The music is absolutely perfect, and the bright-eyed attitude and "summer camp" vibe make this extremely fun and uplifting.  With an ending so incredibly profound and inspirational, you'll never see anything half as good in a AAA title.

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Wilds is like opening a book to a random page and starting to read.You get the gist of it but ultimately understand nothing. No context. No direction. No familiarity with the characters or the world. The information you gained by itself is essentially useless, so you move on.You jump to another random page. You're given another piece to the puzzle, but you'd be insane if you expect it to fit together with what you learned before. No connections can be drawn, no epiphanies can be made. You have so little to work with, so, again, what you learn is useless.At this point you have one of two choices.You either concede to the absurd nonlinearity of the experience and forfeit any opportunity to discover what lies just beyond the horizon...Or you keep turning those pages.If you keep reading, you'll find yourself with piece after piece, all of which seem to have nothing to do with any of the others. You turn those pieces around in your head, spinning them and jamming them together and hoping that you found a clue, an answer, anything that makes sense.You will fail. Gloriously, in some cases. Horribly, perhaps hauntingly, in others. But the more you read, the more pieces you have. And slowly, very slowly, a picture will inevitably form. You have what it takes to see it in its entirety, but you have to earn it. Step by step. One page at a time.

_childDocuments_.review: Deeply frustrating and very disappointing. Above all, the game is sold broken for mouse and keyboard, as there is a key section (which must be completed twice) that is possible but extra difficult using keyboard controls, as the thrust limit function was not implemented for the keyboard. This turns parts of the game into a punishing trial and error grind that is not rewarding in any way. Don’t attempt it using this input method.That feature aside, this is a game made far too long by its core design, and stretches a 10 hour exploration into a 20+ hour marathon. The game loop is this: the player has a journal, and entries are found all around the game world. The player tries to avoid death and use mechanisms to find more entries to complete the journal. During the course of this they will discover a series of secrets which allows them to end the game. The game actively works against the player throughout. The environments are bland and visually disorienting which makes them tedious to navigate, further hampered by obtuse controls that have only been partially implemented. Though sold as a mind-expanding game of discovery (and buried beneath its features, it is), this is above all a timed roguelike with jumping puzzles. Any sense of flow or direction is subverted, as each location devolves into a frantic search for clues that will update the ship’s log before the player dies or is reset. Like Heaven’s Vault, this is a game that depends on the player’s curiosity about the world to provide motivation, yet at the same time punishes that curiosity with tortuous processes to return to places to pick up where the investigation left off.Things that would have helped this game include free saving (at the very least being able to save inside the ship, and at the very, very least an autosave before running the gauntlet at the end), and a log that could be read at any time, as there is no way to know if something has been missed while away from the ship. Yes space is hazardous and the player will die, and a time loop is a way to include player death as part of the gameplay rather than separate from it, but there were better ways to solve this.Nothing could be better than a compelling game about space archaeology, which makes the way this turned out doubly disappointing. Those looking for conversations with friendly aliens would be better served by Mutazione, those looking to gather lost remnants should instead look to Heaven’s Vault (though that game also is far from unproblematic), for puzzles in strange environments try Obduction. Next time, developers, please think of the player.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a game that starts off promising enough, but gradually deteriorates into tedium, repetition, and frustration due to a handful of terrible game design choices made by the developers.  Ultimately, your two options to complete this game are to wander around the game's universe for somewhere between 20 and 500 hours until you stumble onto the game's more obscure solutions, or to do what I did, and cut your losses after 25 or so of those hours and seek out a guide.  Normally, that is not my MO, but when a game repeatedly forces you to play the same ten or fifteen minutes over and over and over again in order to do something slightly different in minute number 16, then it quickly saps the endurance of even the hardest of the hard core gamer.  The Outer Wilds is a game that trusts the player to infer the universe's rules and solve its mysteries way too much, and on top of that, it adds in a "world reset" mechanic which means that you frequently only get to test out your hypotheses after waiting around and completing the same mundane tasks for the fiftieth or the hundredth time.  Whatever sense of awe and wonder it inspires at the beginning is long gone by the time that you reach the game's nonsensical and disappointing ending. I wouldn't say that I hated this game or that it was without merit.  The first ten hours or so, when curiosity and exploration are being rewarded logically, it is very enticing and it almost feels like you are playing Myst all over again.  The solar system is beautiful, albeit pretty small.  This game had potential to be a great one.It's frustrating to see games with such massive design shortcomings be so universally praised by the writers and journalists that we entrust to curate this hobby for us.  Overall, Outer Wilds was another disappointment for me, after I read so many good things about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Wilds is a game best played completely blind. Even more so than other games that have been christened that way, as literally every tidbit of information you have about this game takes away from the experience going in. Literally. This game's whole gist is that any potential thing you encounter will be related to what you know about its world and story. Any thing you have before going in runs the risk of ruining that for you. So, I'll be brief.Every 22 minutes, the sun explodes. You explore an adoringly crafted Super Mario Galaxy esc star-system for its many, many secrets in a constantly changing environment before getting incinerated by a superheated wall of deadly plasma and then take that knowledge into your next attempt. Can you solve the mystery of the doomed Ash Twin Project?Outer Wilds touched me like very few games ever have. This game easily makes it into my "Best games I've ever played" list for its wonderful soundtrack and more than a little bit engaging story. Anyone who's played the game knows about the thing that happens just before the very end that will suddenly make you aware of your own mortality and the consequences of your actions. I feel comfortable saying that because spoiling just that tiny bit will not make it hit you like a brick any less. I played a super early development version a long time ago and am proud of where this game went. I adore it, and hate it just that tiny bit for the existential crisis it gave me.Buy this hecking game dumbass.

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Wilds is a space exploration game with a great twist. A game that will keep you wanting to play for hours and hours and hours until the end. Everything in the game keeps it at an S-Tier and it is one of my favourite games of all time.Game's Story - 10/10The game's story is amazing, and interesting. The game was able to get me invested in the story, and is incredibly well thought out. There are only a few parts that weren't thought through, but for the most part especially for a video game the story is very intact and is great.Visuals - 10/10Despite not going for a completely realistic look, the game is beautiful and scary. Space is amazing and so are all of the planets.Audio - 10/10SFX - 5/5I have no complaints, there are no weird sound effects or lack of sound effects they are just work.Music - 5/5By end of the journey, the amazing music will have sentimental value.Gameplay - 10/10On both gamepad and PC the controls hold up, there are tons of great mechanics that ensure the game is still simple to play. It may take some getting used to flying the ship and flying in 0G but you will get the hang on it.The achievements are also good, while they I did have to look up solutions they are all good achievements that you can get just by messing about (excluding the Archaeologist achievement which takes time and you will definitely need to look up a guide for).Value For Money - 10/10At £20 while it may look a little pricey the overall quality you get for the game is totally worth it, and you can always wait for a frequent sale to get it for around £7 cheaper.Overall - 10/10This game is a masterpiece from its story to its gameplay. I enjoyed this game to the ends of the solar system and I am excited to see what Mobius have in store for us next.The only catch with this game is that you can only experience it once, make it count.

_childDocuments_.review: No matter how I look at it, it's miserable to actually play. The vaguely-Newtonian controls make everything feel like wrestling while covered in oil, in a ring full of oil, against an opponent made of oil. This is patched by giving you an autopilot and a match-velocity button, which make things boring when they work and just add a layer of frustration when they don't. Five years after Kerbal Space Program, a projected-trajectory wouldn't seem like too much to ask. The Little Prince style planets present very short horizons and very densely-compacted interior levels with a lot of blind turns. This is patched by giving you a 'scout', which is fiddly to use, provides at best an unclear idea of what to do, and seems to have encouraged the addition of a bunch of "can't go through here! haha, enjoy your photos and spending ten minutes fighting the controls to get back here later" puzzles, though the word is being used generously. The platforming is awkward, fiddly, and provides various mechanics that cannot, for reasons of nonlinearity, be in any way tutorialised. Are you supposed to be jumping between the glowing transport beams, for example? How many times trying that am I supposed to fall into the abyss, reset and enjoy the painful bus-in-a-tornado ride back? Am I supposed to learn not to make the attempt, or am I supposed to learn to Git Gud (though consider that "skill issue" is hard to pinpoint when you have no consistent frame of reference - jumps you can make on one planet's gravity are impossible on another's, and will drastically overshoot on a third), or is it only possible if I'd gotten there sooner? Or would it be possible if I'd gotten there later? Or are the places you're going even accessible here, rather than at the other end of the solar system through warp points? And again, let me remind you, making the wrong choice is going to cost a lot of time. It's a shame, because the writing is poignant, the theming cohesive. The soundtrack is beautiful, the artstyle maybe a little questionable - it's more a comedy style, in my mind, and the story is surely a tragedy - but well-executed. If I had one complaint other than the gameplay, it would be the characters - you can talk to exactly two characters about what's going on, and they have extremely limited responses. The vast majority of characters exist only in the first ten minutes of the game, and are forgotten immediately. It may be meant to heighten the feeling of loneliness, but mostly it comes across like a missed opportunity.Overall, a disappointing game, but not without merit.

_childDocuments_.review: What appeared to be a confusing and slow snoozefest at first turned out to be one of the most epic story-driven games I have ever played.You have about half a hour to explore your solar system... before your sun implodes and vaporizes everything! But it's ok because you were (un)lucky enough to be caught in a temporal loop, being able to repeat these minutes again and again every time you die. You are the only one aware of said loop and is able to remember everything between your deaths, will you use your infinite lives to gather clues and hopefully save your entire galaxy from dying? Or will you spend your days lazing around and eat marshmallows? Both are fine when you are immortal!Very interesting zero gravity controls and immersive exploration instead of boring menus and walls of text will keep you engaged and eager to find new places, this together with stunningly beautiful and creative planets turns this game into a strongly remarkable one-time experience. As someone who hates puzzles, I was also pleasantly surprised to see that all your clues and information are all simplified and summarized in your spaceship computer after being found, no need to be worried about remembering a random text you found in a cave hours ago. It's not perfect as the flight controls can be hard to get used to, some later areas can be very cryptid to access, and the graphics can also take a big toll of your hardware. But these are very minor annoyances that shouldn't affect your experience too much.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending outer wilds is difficult. as you've most likely noticed a lot of these reviews -and pretty much anyone who liked playing the game- will say "don't spoil it for yourself, just play it!" now, there's nothing inherently wrong with this statement, it's just not much of a review. So i'm going to write a review of this game, but i'll also warn you that there's going to be a few things spoiled here that happen rather early on in the game. so if you don't mind that, keep reading.i'll go ahead and start with the "cons" of this game. Because as much as I absolutely adore it, there are some things that become pretty grating to me. or they might be to youFirst of all. you will die, a lot. Because you always start right back where you started, dying at the end of your time limit and getting engulfed by the supernova, or just slamming into the wall really hard, is part of the experience. this isn't always a good part of the experience, though. respawning at that campfire over and over again can get a little tiring when you made a simple mistake that killed you, and now you have to wait for later in the loop. this brings me to my second con.There's a good amount of waiting around in this game. now, this doesn't seem so bad when you can just rest at the campfire for a little while. but why this isn't unlocked the moment you start the game is beyond me. there aren't that many campfires to visit, so if you don't want to go near them, you don't discover that there's a "rest" option that allows you to speed things up significantly.There's this guy on a specific planet. He can give you the ability to end a loop early. but for some reason, to trigger this, you need to talk to him in 2 separate loops. This ability is already immensely helpful if you simply want to continue, but can't find an easily accessible way to end your life. So why did they decide to put this on a planet so far away? this planet was one of the last ones i explored, and i didn't end up talking to this guy twice, so i completed the game without the ability. it's confusing why they didn't make this faster and easier to get.Lastly a more technical complaint, this game doesn't.... run very well? a lot of times, and i mean a LOT of times the framerate dropped super hard. i have a pretty strong laptop, so this was kind of surprising and disappointingalright. Are you still with me? Then let me tell you about one of my favourite games of all time, and what makes it amazing.To start with, the visuals are nothing to sneeze at. It's nothing groundbreaking, but the aesthetic works really well. and there's some gorgeous designs and characters. the atmosphere is oozing from every nook and cranny, the world feels LIVED IN. and aside from the fact that some places get pretty dark at times. this game is an aesthetic wonderAdding to the already great visuals is one of the best soundtracks for a game i've ever heard. If you're a fan of the music you hear in this game, buy the soundtrack too. It's worth it. Andrew Prahlow has absolutely knocked it out of the park and I would toss pennies at him violently for making the music that pushed me from slightly depressed to outright bawling in some moments of the game. Speaking of moments..The story in this game is rather unconventional. since the game is built in a nonlinear way you can experience it in a different way than others have. and that's one of the truly great parts about this game, this is *your* expedition in this universe. Some moment's made me cry because I was sad, other's made me cry because of how beautiful it was. i can't guarantee you'll cry as well, but knowing that this game gets people to CRY over it must mean something. You solve a lot of mysteries in this game, and in hindsight none of these mysteries are extremely hard to figure out, but the game really makes you feel smart for figuring it out. There's no upgrades or physical rewards you get for exploration. your reward is the rich lore and knowledge you gain over the course of your journeyThe gameplay serves its purpose well, it's not the defining aspect of this game as much as the others are, but the important part is that the game *works* really well. and that's impressive considering all the things happening in it. I'm not praising this game for it's impeccable controls, but I will give it a pat on the back for not playing like an absolute nightmare.To finish it off, the game has some exceptional themes and atmosphere. You will die in this game, but only at one point does it feel like dying really matters.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game, but overall I'd recommend it. I have fond memories from my time playing it and it's just really cozy. The soundtrack is good (very midwest emo-esque) and the maps are designed really well. The way the maps change over time is such a spectacle, and it's evident that a lot of care was put into the game. However, I don't really like how the 'puzzles' are designed. They feel very arbitrary and unintuitive, especially near the endgame, and the order that one experiences certain gameplay milestones can have a massive effect on how these puzzles are interpreted. This is because of the massive amount of freedom inherent to the game's design. The community places a lot of emphasis on going in blind and not looking up anything about the game, but getting stuck for hours on a puzzle that's so unintuitive just feels bad. Despite this, I think the game succeeds as piece of art, because I view it as an abstracted microcosm of real life. In real life things aren't always perfectly designed, and the context in which you experience something for the first time CAN have an effect on your understanding of the world as a whole. For example, in ancient times, mental illness was often attributed to supernatural causes, and it was only later that we discovered the neurobiological origins of psychological dysfunction. Our neurological makeup wasn't necessarily designed to be understood in the first place, yet we have entire fields of study dedicated to making sense our own brains. It's all about curiosity and the pursuit of human knowledge, which I think is very much in line with the themes of the game. Outer Wilds is a riddle game, not a puzzle game.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: A great game that's not for me. You will not enjoy this game if:- you have limited time to play daily- you like exploration games that don't require speed running- you actually want to read the dialogue options or visit places without panicking.You can read all the positive stuff about the game from other reviews, which I also loved but things I especially hated:- You are both punished and rewarded for exploring. if you check out something far away, that run is dead but you get some info, which is nice.- I don't know how many times I landed on the hollow rock just to explore more but I'm guessing the game just expects us to grab the core info and never come back here, which is sad because a lot of stuff exists here.- I found myself not reading anything or looking through in detail to whatever those black pools were towards the end due to panic and just reading it from the computer which sucks and breaks the immersion. - One of the twin planets has a cave system that can be explored but you have around 10-15 mins every time because the planet is filled with sand. You will still not be sure if you have seen everything because everything gets covered up pretty quick.- Once you explored the above, lookup and see that the sand planet you just explored has a complete new set of places to see and very limited time to see them due to `reasons`. This was the end for me because I have to wait for that planet to be accessible and time is super important in the game. it would most likely take above 5+ runs to get through that area, not to mention figure out the connections to other places.- Planets have warping stations on them that work with reading and a bit trial and error. You also need to use them.- It is advised to revisit explorers to get new info but I just couldn't bare going to each again and losing valuable time.- Also after landing on the ash twins, on every run run start I suddenly got black screen. This is apparently a known bug but at this point I couldn't bother to fix it to play this game.I think this is a beautiful game for people to spend time and patience with. It can be a good family activity as well with the puzzles and all if it's ok to land on a planet 10+ times to explore it fully. I don't feel bad about spending money on this along with the dlc but wish the time between cycles and all the timed stuff was longer or could be made longer.TL;DR; If you work with Agile methodologies, this game can be called a 3 day Sprint overloaded with 6 weeks worth of tasks that are stuff you need to learn for the first time. You can choose to drag out the sprint tasks to other sprints but to what end.

_childDocuments_.review: Spectacular game! It's been about a month since I finished it, and I'm still thinking about it. The story, the art style, the music, the feelings it made me feel; it's all sticking with me. How can a simple space exploration game leave such an impact? That's something no review can tell you. There was no huge game-changing moment, no final boss fight to spend hours attempting, and no story to tell you what to do. The game never changed; everything was always there, waiting for you to find it, for it is you who changes and discovers the reason why you want to play the game. And it is only you that can discover that. And when you do, I guarantee it will be worth it.Then there is the DLC; oh man, so many feels. In many ways the DLC is a very different game. It shined a whole new light onto the game in a way that I will never forget.I will say, it's one of those games that you have to go into blind, and as a result, if you are anything like me, you might not like it at first. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR This game is a lovely, well balanced, playable novella that is truly masterful in its execution, and balance of it's subject matter. This is a true example of how a video game can be an interactive art form; an experience that cannot be replicated by books, movies, or television.I rarely play puzzle heavy games like this, and I went into it thinking, "Oh, this is a quirky, Rated E-10+ adventure game with puzzles! What a great relaxing experience before I go back to college!"I wasn't wrong. However, what I failed to anticipate was how fun it would be, and how profoundly heavy the contents of this game could be. Below its cute, goofy exterior, this game contains hope, heartbreak, beauty and terror. I truly felt like I was experiencing the unknown, unraveling a mystery while on an epic journey that resulted in philosophical contemplation that I never thought I could have from a game like this. It's playable art, and I can only hope that other people can have as much fun as I did.

_childDocuments_.review: **Addendum: There is now DLC available. I would highly recommend NOT installing the DLC before completing the original. The DLC is amazing, but almost completely self-contained. In my opinion, it is better to experience the original game alone first. It will save you from some potential distractions, and it really improves the experience of the DLC when you've seen all the base game has to offer. Might be the pinnacle of "Don't look up anything, just play it" games. Outer Wilds is an experience not quite like anything else I've played. It's probably best described as a mystery and exploration game, in the purest possible form. You get dropped in with just enough direction to get you started, and from there, you pretty much just follow your own curiosity. There's no crafting, no combat, just discovery. The payoff is incredible. There were some minor annoyances I found over the course of playing (time-based discoveries and puzzles, some easily missed clues) that I imagine some players could be put off by. But after it all comes together, all those complaints have practically faded from my memory. I still think about this game all the time, even months after playing it through. Worst thing I can say about it is that it doesn't last longer, as once you've found everything, there is very little else to do. Oh, and the music is incredible. Subtle yet powerful, it will stick with you as much as the rest of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: What day is it? It's Space Groundhog Day!This a good sandbox explorer that shares some elements with Heaven's Vault, but I can't in good conscience recommend it unless you're at least a bit into exploring, mostly because the game's developers made some decisions which waste a lot of your time. It's pretty great for the first third of the game, the rest is good but you'll spend a lot of time just waiting around for no particular good reason - you'll run out of stuff to do that doesn't involve waiting. So you need to go to a place, wait 5-10 minutes for a passage to open up or a small window of time where you can do a single thing that's critical to progress. If you're too slow you either need to wait until the next window or restart. Keep in mind that if you're late to a place you'll likely need to schlep over to the place again to find anything you missed. If you don't want to do that, go ahead and skim the lovingly crafted texts, the clock's ticking.Campfires help a little bit with having to wait, but they require you to wait instead of a simple "wait X minutes" command. Sometimes, it's not really feasible waiting at a campfire long enough, as orbits change so much that you'll miss a window to reach a place. The latter would have been simple to rectify with the option to wait/rest while you're inside your ship.Additionally, the endgame run is an exercise in unnecessary frustration.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Best gaming experience I've ever had. I don't play many games and boy howdy was I grateful to play this game through to its end. _childDocuments_.review: Truly once in a lifetime experience, masterpiece for both technical and virtual standpoints. There is no word that can describe how revolutionary this game is. _childDocuments_.review: Massively overrated. _childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Wilds is simultaneously brimming with and devoid of life in a way that is both beautiful and haunting. I am firmly in the camp of people who will say "wow, it really was  good." But I think it's important to go in with realistic expectations, because it definitely will not click with everyone.If you have even a cursory interest in space or astrophysics, you owe it to yourself to try this. If you ever had a childlike wonder at the depths of space or have daydreamed about what it would be like to explore the planets and solar systems, with new discoveries behind every corner, this game will very specifically scratch that itch. It may make feelings you thought were long dead come bursting back to life again. It might even hurt you.The first couple hours can seem pretty rudimentary or even underwhelming. The hook is not immediate. In a way, there's not really a hook at all. There is no sudden revelation or plot twist that is going to overturn centuries of human storytelling. The magic happens in the way that the game interacts with the player. The narrative breadcrumbs, and the way that they are presented, either ignite your curiosity, or they don't. This is very much a "the journey is it's own reward" type of experience.I've tried to avoid using the word "game" throughout this review. I think it's really important to try to NOT engage with this like a typical video game. It really is more akin to a piece of interactive art. If it isn't jiving with you, I think it's fair to trust those feelings. It isn't a fault of yourself or the artwork; you just weren't the intended audience. But for those of you who are, it may leave you with feelings you'll carry for the rest of your life.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent story, great setting, innovative idea, frustrating gameplay. I can see how people can like it. I didn't like it.I lost patience after a good couple of hours, because I found myself doing speedruns in order uncover more of the plot and solve puzzles. The restart mechanic, while integral to the plot, removed any enjoyment i had for the game. I wanted to gobble up as much clues and story as I could between restarts, and this ultimately put me off so much that I decided not to bother, spoiled myself, watched all the endings on youtube. By doing so, I have perhaps unlocked the best, secret ending, having realized the futility of it all before sinking more hours of my life into this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game, relaxing songs, and curiosity is the key to enjoy this game. The game mechanics is way too unique to me, and made me, somehow, to like it a lot. Watch some non-spoiler videos if you need more information about it. Avoid spoilers at all cost, this is my advice. And get a game controller.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: My main bit of advice is that, while there are puzzles to solve, you'll likely have a better experience if you approach this as a mystery/story-telling/exploration game rather than as a mere puzzle game.Stop and smell the roses, appreciate the little details (both from a world-building and game design perspective), try dumb things to see what happens. It's okay if you die a lot. It's okay if you get stuck on something for a while (and you should expect SOME frustration along the way). If you feel like you're missing pieces of a puzzle, feel free to leave it alone for a while and go explore somewhere else until you find that bit of info you need. The payoff is absolutely worth it in the end.::)
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: played this game in the dark, headphones on, 3 nights in a row from 10pm-2am. My love for gaming has been reinvigorated. _childDocuments_.review: At first I wasn't sure whether or not I would enjoy this game...I got absolutely hooked. _childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Wow what to say. This game leaves you breathless, scared, anxious, curious, and craving more. In my opinion this is one of the more unique games i have ever played. This is is not a racing or action game, beyond that i think its everything else. Instead of being so vague and broad i will line my thoughts up.So this is a "open world", or in this games setting open solar system chock full of mysteries you piece together to obtain knowledge once lost. Your question will only lead to answers followed with bigger questions. Even with what you find there is a considerable amount of puzzles to impede your journey throughout the solar system. This game utilizes a "life time loop" system. That means coming to terms with gut decisions or becoming the cat that curiosity killed. This game is not NPC heavy, and instead offers more story rich development through that what you uncover. This is a great value for $25 and the DLC is just as impressive. If you have a space itch to scratch, this might get the job done. 5/5 That's my piece.

_childDocuments_.review: By the majority of the reviews here, I was really expecting another type fo experience. Don't get me wrong, the game's still really awesome - hence this positive review - and deserves all the praise, but some expectations need to be adjusted here. Mainly, this is NOT a chill experience overall. There's a strong time-based aspect to some of its parts that rushes you to do substantial parts of the gameplay - and I'm not even talking about the main time loop you find yourself into. For starters, . You find yourself repeating some chores over and over again just to learn to get it right within the little timeframe the game provides, which can be a frustrating process. Also, if you're easily scared, you might get really stressed out in some parts, because There're mods out there that fix those issues and make the gameplay experience a little bit smoother though. _childDocuments_.review: I decided to play this after seeing a Games Done Quick speedrun of this and nearly crying just from seeing a tiny tidbit of the ending cutscene. If just watching a small portion of the cutscene elicited an emotional reaction out of me, you can guess how the rest of the game went for me.To be honest, I was a little intimidated at first. After initially getting in the rocket and blasting off (the rest of which I won't spoil for obvious reasons), I was kinda worried that it would take a long time to explore everything and eventually get to the ending.What I found over the course of 16 hours though is that the game, true to its word with how the developers designed it, has you naturally curious, and that natural curiosity is what leads you to your goal. Finding a small thing in a random planet soon leads to a rabbit hole of searching for things that act as leads to other things. Explaining further than that is spoiler territory, but you get the idea. The game also has a sense of urgency going on, and with some sections towards the end being very tough and precarious, it really has you on the edge of your seat and tensed up.As well, the soundtrack is beautiful and really aids in getting the player settled in the atmosphere. I come from a region in the US where country music is a favored type of music and is ingrained in my identity, so the folk-country music in this really hit home for me.10/10 from me, and easily one of top 5 games ever made.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to play this game 2 or 3 times, bailing every time, because I was frustrated with the controls (especially on mouse & keyboard) & I kept dying. I even wrote a negative review. Now look at me, years later, giving it a thumbs up.  The thing is, I kept hearing people talk about how great this game is, as good as Subnautica with exploration. So, I figured, all right already, I'll give it one more try. I'm really glad I hung in there.  Once you realize you're SUPPOSED to die, A LOT, things get a easier. Also, even with mouse and keyboard, I was able to complete the game (not without heaps of trial and error and error and error, though). I lack hand-eye coordination so I probably took wayyyyyyyy longer doing things than most people, but I eventually got the hang of it. This game can definitely be tedious. You have to try and fail, again and again and again and again and again, until, eventually, you find the right approach. The dopamine hit when you finally make it, though--priceless. I will say I had to do the "end" puzzle a bunch of times (maybe 20?), which made me nearly lose my mind. The bleeping anglerfish!!!!!! And there were a handful of times I had to look up hints because I had no clue what to do next. But I did find myself totally immersed in this game for nearly two days straight, unable to stop playing (let's just say I had cereal for dinner, more than once). I love it when I get fully absorbed in a game, and I especially loved the carefully crafted story. The universe made logical sense, and even the mechanics of the puzzle seemed "realistic" (as in, something an alien race would reasonably construct). The story was a reward for your hard-earned space exploration--with each new area you discovered, you unraveled more of the mystery. In the end, I didn't just like this game--I loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10 (no spoilers)In the beginning it felt as though I had nothing to do.  I was mulling around for hours.  The connections I made, the horrors I faced, and the fun flight kept me going into an almost obsessive streak near the end.  I've never felt as much shock as when I connected reading logs in this game - in every other game, I usually hate reading logs, but logs are the language this game speaks in.  I will say some puzzles are very confusing and the game will at certain times not lead on enough on what to do; that's what hints from friends are for.  Everyone online seems to cry at the ending.  I didn't connect with the ending enough to do so.  From my point of view, everything seemed simple and understandable, and the characters and world didn't make as much of an impression on me.  That being said, I think this is a good piece of media that's more of an experience rather than a game which should be viewed as such to enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Wilds (and it's DLC) land in the category of games that you wish you could completely forget so you could play it all over again with the same sense of wonder as your first playthrough. It's almost impossible to sell the incredible uniqueness of this game without spoiling the moments of discovery that make that experience so cool. All I can say is give it a whirl, be curious, and give this game a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: (TLDR Short review): Overall (9/10) absolutely fantastic and only kept from a 10 because it has an end.Gameplay (8/10) Extremely engaging but might leave some stumped at certain pointsControls (7/10) Might be a bit hard to get used to for some unused to basic flight mechanicsSoundtrack (9/10) Gorgeous and fits the game perfectlyStory (10/10) Very engaging and has an excellent payoff--(Bonus Round for DLC)--(10/10) If you enjoy the base game even a little then get the DLC, more of the same goodness(Long wall of text review):An absolutely fantastic game that I already had loads of hours in before it released on steam. It's sort of become infamous for the community around it guarding any and all information about gameplay to avoid "spoilers". And while at first you might think that there's no way that a game could have practically everything including locations on the starting world be spoilers, let alone ones that should be kept secret so carefully. Oh how wrong you are. Outer wilds is truly a special experience that can only fully be understood by playing through as blindly as possible. The sheer amount of "Ah-hah!" moments that leave you proud of being clever enough to reach is ridiculous. There are no unlockables, there are no checkpoints (at least in the traditional sense), there are no bonuses for extra completion besides an equal sense of wonder at all you've discovered and disappointment that you can't do it all over again. The progression of Outer Wilds is based entirely on the knowledge you acquire yourself by exploring a solar system that uses every planet to its absolute fullest to keep you engaged and excited to explore more. Every planet you explore has fragments of the overarching mystery that the game presents for you to solve with nearly every one of them giving you clues about another on one of the other planets, meaning that even when you think you've reached a dead end you have plenty to still explore with plenty often leading you back to the same dead end and showing you were simply missing a key piece of knowledge. If you know what you're doing you can easily beat the entire game in under 15 minutes, but the adventure you will go on to get to that level will keep you invested for hours upon hours while you hope that the experience never has to end. Add in on top of all this a newly released dlc that matches and in some cases even arguably exceeds the base game both in terms of content and quality, and you have a game that can easily be considered one of the greats and one that is so unique and charming and packed with wonder that you're doing yourself a disservice not jumping in now while you still can without the mysteries getting spoiled for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: There is a line between open exploration and giving you no direction whatsoever. This game falls into the latter category. You are given next to no directions on what to do or where to go. I spent two hours wandering around a planet, could not translate any information, or learn anything of real value. Oh, and I had to reset every ten minutes because the sun exploded..
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've ever played. Do not look up anything on how to play it or you will ruin the experience. The game is a puzzle, and any outside knowledge will ruin the game for you, and once you know the answers you can't unknow them.10/10, can't wait for the sequel.UPDATE: Expansion pack is also a 10/10. This is a game you must play before you die. Maybe the best game ever made.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: A profoundly unique gaming experience, unlike anything you've played before, with one of the best soundtracks ever composed. If you want a captivating, non-linear, story-rich, puzzle game with incredible world building and physics-based engine, consider this masterpiece. I'd advise you to keep in mind that the best way to have a once-in-a-lifetime adventure with this gem is by going in blind without any prior knowledge of it's essence and mechanics.The first hour or two might be a bit confusing, but trust me, if you stick with it, you'll soon end up praising it and wishing you could forget everything about it and experience it again.Truly a remarkable piece of media. :')P.S.: Watch out for that ravishing music! Right away, the title screen opens with an enchanting melody that conveys a sense of the game's frolic exploration and somber solitude and foreshadows the musical ensemble that's going to melt your heart and play with your emotions like Riebeck plucking the strings of the banjo one last time.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: 2/5. This is about as much fun as a hole in the head. Navigating the ship is a pita, and autopilot helps by repeatedly flying you into the sun. Or, if you're smart, you fly to another planet first, and then crash because you accidentally hit the cancel button instead of the map button. Every time you die, you have to start over from your initial launchpad, meaning any progress in the more tricky parts you have to do allll over again. Your flight suit is also a pita to try and navigate in. I spent a majority of my time crashing into things, and very little of my time having fun. I did like the alien race you play, and the mystery surrounding the ancient ones that you're helping to find out more about. But the mechanics of the game, and the save system, made me quit and give it a low review.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Never before was I able to say my favorite game came from hearing a single song... until now. I was introduced to this game simply from the 'Travelers Theme' which I had accidentally stumbled across while roaming through YouTube and I instantly fell in love. From that point I had made a mental note that I needed to play this game, even if all I knew about it was gathered from the one song in the soundtrack.From the first steps on Timber Hearth I knew I would love this game, as the visuals themselves immediately caught my eye. I was unable to run the game at it's fullest potential, but I still adored every nook and cranny, and all of the hard work and detailing put into each of the individual planets and accompanying satellites. Never once did I feel like the game was holding my hand. I was encouraged to find the new pieces of the mysteries presented in front of me on my own time in my own process, leading to my own sense of accomplishment when I did finally find a large piece of this galactic puzzle.The storytelling was phenomenally orchestrated in a way in which you could follow the whole story without having everything lined out in order. Learning of the race of the Nomai and their affairs gave me more and more reason to scour every corner of the universe looking for more about them, never failing to leave me awestruck at their work even if all I was observing was the aftermath.I adored being able to piece together how to advance myself further through little tidbits gathered from other places, such as the method of discovering the proper method of entering the outer core of Giant's Deep, even if it took a couple of tries ending in my accidentally suffocating in space. As well as the fluidity of the potential realities of the presented paradoxical situation in which you find yourself. Waking up to gasps of air after having suffocated in space helped solidify my immersion and kept me tied in for the entirety of my current 16 hours of gameplay, hours which I plan to add more to as I do not wish to stop just because I've discovered what could be called the 'True Ending.'To say I would give this game a 10 out of 10 would be undercutting it. I absolutely loved this game, the gameplay, the characters, the storytelling, the soundtrack, all of it, and I highly recommend it to anyone and everyone with ears.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most unique gaming experience ive ever played!And ive played a lot.Really there is not much to say here except that this is an absolute masterpiece and i can share the sentiments of many others. Don't let yourself get spoilered.The game, story, world and puzzles are all phenomenal.Masterpiece!
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I begin with Outer Wilds? The visuals are simple yet beautifully artistic, the sound design is very satisfying, and though the controls for your ship take a bit of getting used to, they are quite intuitive. Aside from a few frame-rate snags here and there, the game is well optimized. Oh, and being able to swap your controller buttons is an amazing feature.In my opinion, the best part of the game is simply getting lost and exploring the unknown, especially with Andrew Prahlow's beautiful soundtrack.Unfortunately, I can’t say anything else about the game, and I haven’t scratched the surface yet. If you’re thinking of playing this game,  Besides, if I went into any more depth, I’d go into spoiler territory, and I really don’t want to do that for this game specifically.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Wilds is an open world space exploration game set in a fictional universe where you take on the role as an Outer Wilds pilot sent off into the star system to explore.Put simply, the Outer Wilds is a transformative experience. This is hands down one of the best games ever to exist. It’s so difficult to put into words how fantastic of a package this game truly is. First off, Buy this game. It goes on sale often enough to warrant a purchase from hearsay, but with how much of a masterful experience this is, paying full price is just as reasonable.So let me try and explain, WITHOUT SPOILERS, just how magnificent this game is. Starting with gameplay and environments, the Outer Wilds manages to create such a beautiful array of planets in a star system that's at first glance surprisingly small. Each planet is filled to the brim with so much dense atmosphere and mechanics that make each individual location so unique that it is difficult not to want to go out and explore each one. On top of that each planet has tid-bits of the story scattered throughout that you are encouraged to find and piece together. It's such a uniquely interesting and rewarding experience to feel like you’re actually the one finding and connecting all the dots to the narrative. In what other games will achieve with lore or cutscenes the Outer Wilds hinges on the sole idea that you will want to explore and find for yourself all these pieces. And none of it feels forced or out of place because in the end YOU are the driving force behind it all. YOU are the pilot, YOU pick your path. It's such a fun time exploring every single nook and cranny that I will reminisce constantly about the first times I stumbled across certain landmarks or managed my way through dangerous terrain, because in the end, I’m the one who did it all.The Outer Wilds, while an impressive feat on its own when it comes to gameplay and environment design, but it would not have been so impactful if it wasn’t for the sound design and music. Straight up, this is some of the BEST MUSIC put into a video game. It’s almost as if during development, Andrew Prahlow was given every detail on each environment and location to create a unique and different track to set the atmosphere. There are so many locations in this game that would have felt like empty husks if not for the music that swells and explodes at the perfect moments to make your discoveries that much more of a hallmark during your journey. I will never forget so many of my discoveries because of how well the soundtrack and sound design expertly wove into the experience. Even in the emptiness of space, a brief stint of the opening theme song will play to kind of nudge you along while you’re traveling between destinations, its so well curated to the entire experience that I felt awestruck at monumental points in the game because of the masterful timing of the soundtrack.Sound design too, just helps that much more with immersing the player into a one of a kind experience, that I felt such a vibrant spectrum of emotions that I simply could not recall experiencing in a video game before. Real quick I want to touch on art direction and lighting (since I consider myself something of an artist myself) and again the lighting effects and visuals in general are so impressive that I can't leave any stone unturned. Lighting here is beautiful, genuinely so impressive and again lends itself so well to the immersion of the player. So many environments hinge on the perfect amount of atmosphere and each and every single one nails that balance of mystery, fear, and intrigue. I cannot recall the last time I actively noticed lighting and visual effects in a game. There are moments in the game that are so much more heightened than they otherwise would be if it weren't for the cooperation between lighting and effects. It feels like such a natural partnership in making everything in this game accurate and beautiful and interesting to look at. The beauty of this universe is so awe inspiring and gradually more impressive after each passing moment that I can't help but commend the work done here. Same with the visual style. It strikes such an ingenious balance. I can’t really describe the look of the game without saying cartoony, since it's so much more than that. I’d liken it to a Pixar film where there’s real world influences but artistically distinct choices in making the world feel lived in, and real, without delving into the hideousness of the uncanny valley. It’s such a wonder to take in all together, and pay attention to all the details surrounding inhabited nevorments, and even some of the more desolate landscapes, there’s an appeal to their restraint, having just enough to seem comparable to something you’ve seen elsewhere. This game is visually stunning, ‘nuff said.The Outer Wilds is the best video game experience I've had in a long time. I’ve had suggestable experiences, stuff that’s fun and I'd recommend to others, but not until now have I felt like video games have transcended the genre past what was previously known. I honestly believe this game in its entirety is the most beautiful, awe inspiring, visually gorgeous and emotionally compelling that it may just bring a tear to your eye. I felt such an array of complex emotion at the end of this game, that I couldn't help but nearly fall apart at the thought of ending the best interactive experience to ever come to the medium. Play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: The coolest mystery/puzzle game I've played so far. Extremely interesting and intricate, feels really good to explore and learn bits of the puzzle and fit them all together and realize something BIG that changes how you move forward. One of the absolute best possible implementations of an exploration- and mystery-focused game.It's hard to say much about it without risking spoilers, and you definitely want to know as little as possible before starting - because all progression in the game is knowledge. Learning things. And once you know something, you can't un-know it. My only regret about this game is that I can't really ever play it again because I already know all the things!

_childDocuments_.review: No other game compares to how amazing this game is. _childDocuments_.review: Don't understand the reviews touting this as the greatest video gaming experience of their lives, I honestly found the story to be pretty mediocre with quite a few plot holes. The puzzle solving was fun for maybe the first 10 hours, but the second 10 hours was just an absolute slog of double checking random areas and trying to find missed clues. Also, I went in 100% spoiler free and can confidently say that you do not need to play this game blind or avoid spoilers like the plague like some other reviews say. Nothing that would've been spoiled was all that groundbreaking and I found the way people talk about spoilers for this game to be very pretentious and off-putting.I'd give it a 6.5/10.
