_childDocuments_.review: What can I say. It's the greatest game you're not allowed to talk about. It gave me great hours of the enjoyment of exploration and puzzling. It distracted me from all what happened this year. Honestly. I wish I could forget everything I know about this game so I can play it all over again.I would like to make a quote:"The Outer Wilds.There are so many games out there that feature space travel, and yet none of them really get it. The horror of an endless dark vacuum so intent on killing you, that just ninety seconds in its inanimate presence is more than enough to freeze, suffocate and explode you inside out. Space is literally the worst place in the universe, people always think of space as, above us, but it's not really. You don't have to look up to see space. You have to look away from safety to see space. Then, when you're out there in the nothing, there are joules, unprocessabley large balls of fire and light held together by their own ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ anger. Rocks that can range between husks of nothing, or everything some life ever knows, and an endless amount of phenomena that would take our scientific knowledge and ♥♥♥♥ it from ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to breakfast.But video games just don't get it- they just don't get space, video games set in space are either just men with big swinging ♥♥♥♥♥ firing at bug-eyed monsters. Or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ truck-driving simulators. If exploration does happen to be the main focus, you'll find out that the main difference between the endless majesty that is life in this universe is the color of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grass.Yeah, you're in space but it- it feels inaccessible, like a fingerprint wouldn't take on it. Like it's behind glass. The Outer Wilds, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hell The Outer Wilds gets space. It doesn't care about scale. Or scientific accuracy, it gets the "feel" right. Yeah, you're ships made from wood and the majority of the planets are the size of a badly stocked IKEA, but watching all the stars in the sky go out one by one, like far off fireworks. And knowing that each one could be destroying an entire history and having you do that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ every twenty-two minutes; Nothing, nothing has made me feel like that before. No game, no book, no movie. It’s beyond extraordinary. Its planet's, ♥♥♥♥, it's planets each one is a bizarre impossible place. Riddled with life and death and decay and nonsense. Each one dense in history and vandalized by time. Each one, nightmarish and so, so beautiful. And in twenty-two minutes, they're gone. Because the outer wilds isn't even really about space, it's about the question. The most important and terrifying and unanswerable question anyone ever asked. Why? Why bother? Why bother with any of this? People die, stars burn out, the universe will go quiet, and dark, and cold, and in the longest run nothing, absolutely nothing matters. Everything dies, the universe included. So why sit around the fire playing music into a void that doesn't care? Why huddle around the light, why play?Because- well look at it. It's mad. All of it. Life is a big stupid blob of meaningless nothing yet from that, we find meaning.People, things, animals, art, sofas, cereal, Rubik's cubes, silly little games about space, whatever. None of it matters in the grand scheme but ♥♥♥♥ the grand scheme. There's no logical reason for life and nobody's gonna mourn it when it's gone. But that's what makes it fantastic.Life is a little song that we hum to ourselves, and I wouldn't want it any other way. The Outer Wilds, is an optimistic game about Nihilism. It's a game with no invisible walls, you can complete it in ten minutes if you know what to do, which you won't for hours. And the only limit is knowledge. It's a game literally like no other. The universe is big, and long, and impossible and daft. And you, you happen to be experiencing it at the exact same point that you can play The Outer Wilds as well. Embrace that coincidence. C'mon, what are you waiting for? The sun could explode tomorrow. "-Daniel Hardcastle 2019

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't get into this game. The controls are very obnoxious. Piloting your ship is a pain and if you use the autopilot it will crash into things. Not much of an autopilot if you ask me.Nothing I did seemed to result in anything happening. I believe the point is to explore and discover the narrative but it just felt too open ended to me. There is essentially no guidance and it relies on you being curious and trying everything, but with so little feedback from the game other than translating some alien text it felt like I was making no progress. I went to several planets and there was nothing to do. I believe there are puzzles built into the environment but I wasn't finding them, everything seemed empty and pointless.The game is also set on a timer and loops over and over. It's an interesting concept but I just couldn't seem to get into it. Which is a shame because the narrative seems to be based around an ancient civilization that you're finding clues about which is a very neat idea to me, but it did very little to suck me in. _childDocuments_.review: A disappointing adventure.A lot of people love this game, so perhaps I had too high expectations, or maybe this is one of the things that will be forever out of my appreciation reach (just like the band Neutral Milk Hotel). The first moments of the game are really great. Leaving the planet for the first time and feeling the awe of having a whole solar system to explore, and how simple it is to enter a completely different celestial body, was incredible. But as soon as you set a planet to explore you realize that a pattern exists, a pattern that will require time management, notwithstanding the management of oxygen and fuel that you also need to be aware of. This macro time management is frustrating by itself, but it is not the only one: the planets that contain more information are falling apart, so not only macro time management exists but also micro time management depending on where you are. I don't think time management is fun. Besides being difficult enough to explore things at the appropriate pace in a 22-minute cycle, sometimes trial and error are an inevitable part of the experience. It's true that no puzzle required to beat the game needs to be solved by trial and error, as the information is out there somewhere, but if you are looking for side content, such as the Lakebed Cave, where there is no indication about how to navigate through that maze, you will have to taste some of the bad design that the game sometimes offers, because trial and error is not fun or clever in any way. Even the ending was kind of underwhelming as well, considering that the stakes were aimed at the sacred experience reported by others. The abstract imagery and ambiguous meaning may successfully work in space contexts such as 2001 (or Interstellar to a lesser extent), but at the same time it is almost a cliché for the space genre (if space is a genre) that as the ending was approaching I wished this would not happen here too. It happened. And although I can have my own interpretations about the whole finale I don't think any of these interpretations compensate for how frustrating the gameplay aspects mentioned above were.I liked some things. The music is great, and so is the narrative. Getting the Archaeologist achievement was rewarding, not only because it gave a sense of purpose that the game for the most part fails to provide, but it was genuinely interesting to put every piece of the story together. The characters also had enough personality considering how limited their interactions with the player were. However, I can't truly recommend this game, and I think the secrecy the community built around it doesn't help.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most unique games I've ever played. It's difficult to recommend because the more you say about it the more you'd be taking away from someone else's experience. What I can say is that it's a free-form exploration game all about the pursuit of knowledge for the sake of uncovering the mysteries of the world. The joy of learning, if you will, although less puzzle based than other games that carry this theme. And it's an awesome world too, full of jaw dropping environments that are both impressive and fascinating on a technical level. I can't, and don't want to explain why, but you'll understand when you get there.When I say free-form exploration, I mean that it could technically be finished in less than 20 minutes if you just knew exactly where to go and what to do. There is no combat, there are no upgrade systems, no new abilities or equipment to obtain. Your only form of progression is knowledge, and the challenges come from figuring out the rules and workings of the different areas, and you can visit them in any order you like. So instead of 20 minutes, the average playthrough will last about 20 hours, and in that time I can just about guarantee that you'll continuously have the rug pulled out from underneath you as you keep on exploring the world, from the first half hour of the game to the very end of it. If what I've described sounds interesting to you, and you're somehow reading this without having watched any trailers or read anything about the game, I suggest you keep doing that, take a leap of faith and just jump into this completely blind as I did, with absolutely no idea what to expect. Of course, if you have watched some of the promotional material, the game isn't suddenly going to suck, you'll still have a great time, but some areas might just surprise you a little less than they did me. I seriously did not know anything about this game other than that it's apparently very special and very good, and I'm very glad I went into that way. I thought the whole game would take place in some forest and be heavily about camping and survival or something like that, just based on the promotional artwork for the game. Well, turns out it wasn't that at all, it was something much more exciting. For me at least.The only real downside to this, which isn't really a negative quality of the game, is that it has no replay value. At least not immediately. You can't unlearn the things you've learned, and as such there is nothing keeping you from just making a beeline straight to the end once you've figured out what it takes. You might try looking for some additional bits of information or go for some achievements but that's it really. I do very much look forward to the day a decade or two from now when I'll have forgotten most of the details about this game, then I'll finally be able to revisit it and enjoy it all over again. I have no doubt in my mind that it will stand the test of time for that long and longer still.

_childDocuments_.review: Holy **** this is one of the best open-world games I've played in a long time. I read some Steam reviews saying that I should play this game "blindly" and I'm so glad I did. It was a great experience and I felt so many emotions as I explored the planets and over time realized the implications of my discoveries. There might not be any voice acting but the characters are still very likable. And the art direction and music gave such a lasting impression that I'd love a sequel or spiritual successor to Outer Wilds.In terms of gameplay, you're given all the tools you need to explore space; there are no unlockables. Instead, you learn about the solar system's planets and use that info to help you navigate previously unreachable areas. The space ship and suit movement feels very fluid. It's a lot of fun landing on moving planets. And while some planets are pretty peaceful, others can be dangerous if you're not flying carefully around the gravity strength and environmental hazards. Overall, the simple focus on exploration and story makes this game incredibly replayable.Now onto my thoughts about the story (SPOILER WARNING):I highly recommend Outer Wilds to people looking for a unique exploration experience. The developers have done a fantastic job and I look forward to the DLC expansion that was recently announced. Be warned that this game takes a lot of patience, so those who get bored easily by slow progress might have trouble enjoying it.

_childDocuments_.review: Early review, but I have to dissent from the vastly positive reviews here. There will be spoilers.What is this game? Most of the reviews were of the form "just play it", because I guess it is impossible to describe. It's not impossible to describe.You're an alien, on an alien planet, in an alien solar system. You're given a spaceship. You are head out on exploration of the solar system. You encounter some mysteries, involving another alien race, and set off to understand them. Every 20 minutes or so, the sun goes super nova and kills you (if you haven't died by some other cause yet). You're stuck in a time loop. On each death, you're back to where you started, and you hop in your spacecraft, and try to learn a little more. Rinse and repeat. You don't loose your progress. Your previous findings are still recorded. Everything you do is on a 20 minute timer.This game is beautiful. Exploring the several planets I've seen so far looks amazing. The scale of the solar system is vastly smaller than reality. The planets are more like small asteroids, and the distance between them can be flown in a few minutes or less. Flying the spaceship feels great. Makes you wonder how a AAA game like Starfield can get away with completely punting on this aspect of gameplay. The game is beautiful, but you can't enjoy that if you're on a 20 minute death timer. Want to explore that planet? Better make it fast. It feels like there's a way they could have maintained the essence of the mystery here without it.I've read ahead a little about the story. It's definitely deep and complex, but I don't know it stands out as special when you compare it the body of sci-fi literature we have. If you're impressed by the story here I could recommend 20 books that would blow your mind.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my most favoritest games in the whole wide universe, truly.That said, it is not for everyone. Touting that it is 'the game of all time' and 'everyone must play/enjoy it' would be an exaggeration; although like for many, the strong feelings that produced those reactions were present for me, too. But love takes work, and boy, this game makes you work. I find the work is duly rewarded by little details in every location, yet the amount of fiddling with physics and time based puzzle shenanigans will wear on your patience, and anyone who says they were not the least bit frustrated at some point is a liar! The point is, when you reach The End, you reflect on all of your labor and what you have seen among the rubble to come to realize that it was a good old fashioned adventure complete with conflict. However, gameplay wise I actually did thoroughly enjoy it on a controller; I've played this a bunch between here and Epic for 57 hours total. By now everything feels very second nature but not everyone will get used to the drifting and sliding, or even get sick by it.If you dislike reading, zero-G navigation, and sappy stuff like love and life you may not find this one worth your time. That's perfectly OK, whatever your reasoning. If you are put off by the mechanics alone and want a story, I would happily recommend a let's play along the lines of TitaniumLegman or NerdCubed.I find this story comforting from my position on a planet that often feels on the brink of death day-to-day, and like a warm plate of food I memorize the feeling even after it's gone. That is why I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I took the advice of people who were praising this game like crazy and went into it blind. It's something I ended up really regretting, and after about 80 minutes, I had enough and gave up on it. I love mystery games and puzzles, but nothing in this game during 80 minutes hooked me. Never before have I found a mystery game which I didn't like either, so this was a first.To start with, the controls (when piloting the space ship) are some of the worst I've ever seen in a game. It's clunky and just really badly designed, meaning it's so frustrating to fly around (and that was with a controller, the recommended way to play the game).The game is based around random exploration - which feels awful due to the awful space ship controls - and solving puzzles to find out the "story". And all the story parts are just presented as text. No cut-scenes, no voiced lines, just text.Even just still pictures together with the text would've made it way more appealing and voice acting would definitely have been a plus. Honestly, I would probably have liked it better as a visual novel, because then it would've made much more sense to only have the story revealed as text, and you wouldn't have to suffer with the awful space ship flying.To put it all simply - this game is not fun to play. And I'd recommend playing some other mystery game.

_childDocuments_.review: My only regret from playing this game is how I wasn’t able to play it all at once.Outer Wilds is an interesting experience. The core gameplay is simple: fly around in your ship exploring planets and unraveling mysteries. There is technically one ending, and a bunch of other interesting yet not central endings. In other words, you have a true ending and other endings you can obtain from doing something that has you go, “What if?” I don’t want to explain further, but just keep in mind that there is one genuine ending and once you get it, you’ll know it was THAT ending.What about the story? The story is phenomenal. You aren’t tasked with a grand quest or anything. You play the first time around only to die from flying your ship at like 50000 miles an hour into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ moon, . The only thing you’re meant to do is explore; specifically, learn about the Nomai, an intelligent race that have been dead for millions of years. Only when you find out pretty much everything you can would you then learn what can be done. Enough explaining of the game, what do I think about it all?Flying around your ship is an absolute blast. The exploration is just amazing. You’re given complete control over where you want to go, and what you want to do. It’s like playing Skyrim after getting out of Helgen; you can go wherever you want and do whatever you want. Only difference is that Skyrim had a main story quest that you probably prioritized in your first playthrough. Outer Wilds, as I’ve said, doesn’t task you with anything except to explore. As a result, you’re given even more freedom because you aren’t directed to go anywhere specific. You just choose a planet and think, “That planet looks sick as hell, I’m gonna fly there.” The freedom of this game is just outstanding. Naturally, you are not able to go outside the map, but such a thing is understandable. What’s the point in going 5000 miles away from the solar system if there’s nothing to explore outside that? There is no point.The story was both gripping, grim, exciting, and many more emotions I am incapable of expressing due to my poor vocabulary. There was no narrative; the game’s story is all about reading notes left behind by the Nomai. There’s also other NPCs you can talk to, and some mechanisms you can interact with to learn more and more. Due to there being no narrative, it is hard to think about how you can actually end the game. I went through this game learning more and more about what happened with the Nomai and what they were doing. If you were to learn about everything in a certain order, I can say that once you learn everything, you just have a eureka moment. All of a sudden, I realized what I could do, and I was incredibly pumped on doing so. All these hours I spent exploring and learning all boiled down to an absolutely thrilling climax that led me into unlocking the true ending and going through one of the most beautiful endings I’ve had the pleasure of experiencing. There’s so much to this game, but talking about anything more would only spoil. Anyone who has played the game would say this: “Don’t look up anything. Learn everything on your own.” I share the same thought, but I would also recommend not being scared of looking something up if you’re truly stuck. While you can go through this entire game without the need of looking something up, there will surely be something you missed or had forgotten that would completely stop your progress, and you have no idea what that thing is. Don’t be ashamed of looking something up; I’ve stated that my only regret was not being able to play this game at once. I was quite busy and unable to binge this game immediately. As a result, I forgot quite a few details that would’ve definitely helped me in other areas of the game. Don’t be ashamed of looking something up. You’re meant to enjoy the game, not put yourself through turmoil due to being stumped over something. Another tip I’d say is: if you’re stuck in something, go do something else. Can’t reach an area or figure out something? Simply go do something else, such as explore a different planet. The game will have info on one planet that would help you explore another planet. If you can’t figure it out, go explore something else.With that all said, I’d rate this game a solid 10/10. The game offers an unique experience that you simply cannot find again that easily. If you persevere and not give up in the middle of it all, you’ll have an absolutely wonderful time that’ll make you pop onto Discord to tell all your friends to buy Outer Wilds. I did that, but everyone I spoke to ignored me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! I completed the story in about 25-30 hours. Its a great open world discovery game that lets you go wherever you want and explore. Not only is the story good but the graphics, physics and gameplay itself is great. Its fun to just fly around in your ship looking for new things. If you need tons of hand holding its not the best because it wants you to use your brain to figure out what to do next and what to discover. Its important to read all the notes and messages for clues. I went into this experience blind and I think that made it even better. There is a DLC that I am excited for. _childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool setting and intriguing world to explore. I like the way the lore unravels in a non-linear way depending what you find. I would maybe give it a mixed review if that was possible, as I have some problems with it: the controls can feel awkward and the main gimmick feels at odds with wanting to take time exploring; it's super-annoying finally managing to get somewhere only to end up rushing or getting kicked out. _childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game to others? In short - yes. It was interesting and the mechanics were challenging to get at first but fun once you figured it out.However...well...I guess I had too high of expectations for this game from reading other comments on Steam and on Reddit. There are many who would lead you to believe this is the greatest game of all time. I finished it and was just disappointed by the conclusion of it all NOT by the story but rather by the players who led me to believe it was a more than what it was.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: This is a rare adventure game in which the journey is more important than the destination. A beautifully designed game with a very well written story in which you have to explore and solve the mystery of a trapped solar system. It's one of those games that manage to hold your attention from start to finish and keep you interested all the way through. The controls will take some time getting used to, but they are manageable with practice. Outer Wilds was definitely above my expectations. It's a game that will make you relax and fill your evenings with positive emotions. If you're a fan of sci-fi mixed with a little bit of mystery, this game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Everything it needs to be and nothing it doesn't.One of those rare puzzle/mystery games that doesn't lie to you. No tricks or secret levers to pull to magically unlock the door at the end or make all the pieces fall into place. The only thing keeping you from solving the puzzle is you and your lack of knowledge.That knowledge is put into a somewhat simple, but powerfully effective story that is spread out over a solar system that is fun to move around in, very interesting, and amazing to look at. Your rewards for exploration aren't little check marks on a list, rather moments of 'a-ha' that you get yourself.On top of everything else, the music, though not always there as it should be, slips in at the right time to not set the mood, but just confirm the mood that you are having in that given location. The main theme is also catchy and its tone can shift over the course of your play through.The only flaw I can think of is that this game is unforgettable, which is unfortunate because I would love to play it again for the first time.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolutely amazing! If you love story driven games, do not look any further than this comment as you will only spoil the adventure ahead. I'm sure many people will buy this because they saw someone else play it, but if you are the lucky few that have seen nothing about this game, just buy it and start playing. I am a vinyl record collector and happened to snag the soundtrack to this game, prior to even playing it, after seeing the overwhelmingly positive comments about the music and the game. I must admit, they were all correct!It has been a very long time since I've fallen in love with a story this detailed and unique. _childDocuments_.review: I will try to keep it short with this review, since the game has been praised almost unanimously, by nearly everyone who played it. So then it should not be a controversial statement, if I call it a masterpiece of game story telling.Starting off in Timber Hearth, talking to everybody and getting to know the basic rules of playing the game. Tutorials in this starting area are great, and successfully mask themselves as reasonable things one could expect from a location in which they are located. Best of all - they can all be skipped entirely, if one only chooses to go straight to where you are supposed to, and not indulge any people with conversations. While by no means is it a revolutionary feature, nor has it been done for the first time ever, it sets the tone for the game masterfully, letting all the players know that one of the main attributes they hold in this world - is their freedom to do, or not do, anything they want.The gameplay is not particularly revolutionary either, except for the wonderful sense of liberty, that few games have the guts to grant their players. The interactive part of the game is mainly focused on exploration. Few puzzles exist, that don't prove too difficult even to people who don't normally have half a brain to solve such things (I'm speaking from experience here). However, overall, most of what you do is jump, use your jetpack to boost yourself, and walk around exploring... Oh, and also reading... There is a LOT of reading. As a person whose attention span is barely enough to go through more than two pages of a book in one sitting, the game's texts never bothered me in the slightest. Because of their placement, contents, and form (of being divided into smaller, shorter messages that aren't difficult to comprehend) the game always made me giddy when I found any reading material, leaving me excited to find out more about its story. The way the story can be understood starting from its mid-point, or from the end, really intensifies the feeling of freedom. Having no order, of uncovering the plot, be imposed on you was so refreshing I can hardly put it into words. It was very unexpected, for me, and I found it was much more of a benefit to the experience, than I initially thought it to be.Outer Wilds is the perfect example for the argument that games can tell stories just as great as books, if not greater, attributing this potential superiority to its interactive nature. I think everybody who likes good science fiction novels, and enjoys innovative games should at least give this one a try. It was an experience I will think about for many years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: Going into this blind was a gift I never knew I had. This game has a sense of wonder and discovery like no other. A true adventure game that requires brain power and a heart. Simply one of my favourites of all time.A little plot about aliens not unlike us and their lust for exploration allows you to uncover such a deep history about the species that came before them. The story is about individuals coming together as one to facilitate something bigger than all of them and it is told so beautifully over the course of puzzles and experimentation done by the player.This feels like a gem that only comes along a few times in a lifetime. I will sing the praises of this game until my death and hope to see more like it in the future. One of those games I wish I could play for the first time again.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

Congratulations dev team for such achievement.For all the people that still didn't play this game, don't waste your time and buy this one now! We need more games like this.

There isn't much replayability, but I think everyone should try experiencing this at least once. After more years pass, I will definitely come back to this game and play it again. _childDocuments_.review: Literally unplayable without a gamepad. That's not hyperbole.I don't remember seeing anything on the store page that said you have to have a gamepad/controller to play this game, but the first splash screen upon launch tells you to use one, and it's literally impossible to leave the starting area of the game without it. The forums are filled with users complaining about broken jump and other functions when using keyboard and mouse, despite them being correctly mapped in the settings. The workarounds some users suggested don't seem to work either.I genuinely can't fathom how a developer can release a PC-Based game that isn't playable on a PC with default settings. Worse, their "official" documentation for this issue references a setting that apparently no longer exists in the current version. I ended up having to request a refund after about half an hour of futzing with the settings.Until they release a major fix for this, you'll have to sit this one out if you're a KB&M player.

_childDocuments_.review: this game is absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fantasticbutouter wilds is not really a normal video gamey video game. it breaks a lot of video game conventions, and if you go in to it not knowing that, you might have a bad time. this is *completely* spoiler free btw.when you start outer wilds, it might feel a bit like a metroidvania. you go somewhere and see a locked door, so you leave expecting to come back later with a key. but outer wilds has no keys. you do not unlock new abilities, you do not get new tools. EVER. you ALWAYS have all the tools required to get anywhere, from the second you boot up the game. what you will find, rather than a key, is knowledge. knowledge of how the world works, and in time the experience which allowes you to master it. when you encounter a locked door, all you are missing is the knowledge of how to open it.outer wilds is a Knowledge Based Game. the gameplay IS finding ♥♥♥♥ out, thats how you progress and how you eventually beat it. this means that unlike most games, where most text you find is meaningless flavor text, *all text in outer wilds is important*. every single piece of writing in the world of outer wilds either gives you a hint for some puzzle, a piece of the games story, or contributes to one of the main themes, save maybe 3 specific occasions. if you dont like reading, theres a decent chance this will not work for you.outer wilds is a knowledge based games. this means that spoiling it is literally removing content. that is why you are told to stop asking questions and just to paly it already. if you know nothing of the game, i am begging you to stop reading reviews and to buy it now. if you cant afford it, feel free to acquire it in less moral ways and pay for it later if you want.

_childDocuments_.review: This was the first game i played after my dad died. It helped keep me distracted, but as it went on, it felt like this was an experience i was meant to have. You go on an adventure to learn the mysteries of the universe. You realize how small you really are in relation to it, and how everything will eventually meet its end. Yet you appreciate every moment. From solving a puzzle to meeting another explorer from home to making discoveries of other intelligent life. It shows how beautiful of an experience life really is, and its okay that it has an end. I absolutely cannot recommend this game enough, regardless if the meaning i took from it was intentional from the developers or not.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to say so much about this gem.  Instead, I will say that this is one of those games you buy off a whim.  Either you saw a friend review it, or you heard someone talk about it once.  Once you've played it, however, you will be hard pressed to find a game that fills the hole it will leave in your heart.
_childDocuments_.name: Outer Wilds

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game with a very very fatal known flaw. Save files can be easily corrupted if the game crashes. I had nearly 14 hours into this game and was nearing completion when the game crashed. I thought that was somewhat annoying, but no worries - I would just restart the loop I was on and quickly get back to the task I was in the middle of. I was wrong. I logged back in to be welcomed to the game as a new player. Searching online lead me to hundreds of people who had experienced the same issue. There is even a tweet from the developer from 2019 that they are aware of the issue and are working on a patch. I guess they never got the issue figured out because it still exists. I tried the troubleshooting steps to recover my game file, but nothing worked. This is a good game, but not something I am interested in playing another 14 hours to get to where I was prior to the game failing. I ended up uninstalling and watching the ending on Youtube. Unfortunately I was not able to get my money refunded since I had played more than 2 hours. I suggest you consider this warning before spending money on this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really don't know what to say about this game, I could be wrong but I don't think I've ever had an experience so full of emotions and freedom in any other game. _childDocuments_.review: One of the greatest implementation of space travel and exploration i have ever seen. I have been putting off playing this game for a few years now, mainly because i didn't know anything about it. Every time you google what this game is, everyone tells you to just go into it without looking anything up to avoid spoilers. This kind of kept me from playing, but also caught my interest. when i had some time on my hands and ran out of games to play, i just said ♥♥♥♥ it and bought the game. Well, i completely see what everyone was on about in terms of spoilers. That's why i too, wont go into detail about what this game is about, sorry. All i will say is, that this game is one of a kind and implements every mechanic it includes incredibly well. The game is about exploration, and that is exactly what you do. you explore and learn. Progression is very non-linear, but still kind of "straight forward". I did struggle to progress a few times, but never to a degree where it got frustrating. My biggest tip is, if you ever get stuck and really don't know how to keep going, look for tips on the r/outerwilds Subreddit. the people there are amazingly helpful, and other than online guides, will do their very best not to spoil you. I had to look up a few things there, and every time they managed to nudge me in the right direction without actually giving me a straight answer. (Just try to use the search bar, don't make a post for every minute question)All in all, if you can afford this game and have time, play it. if you even remotely enjoy puzzle/story games, I’m sure you will have a blast with this. It really is as good as everyone says.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the only time I'll ever bother to write a review, and I'm going to keep it short since you folks have heard it all by now.This is my absolute top favorite game of all time, and I can never play it again. Now that I know the mystery and solution, this game is over for me forever.But there's been not a single thing in the years since my early childhood that's ever rekindled these deep feelings of wanderlust and the terror of the unknown. The first time I tried to land on that planet quickly realized that I was plummeting through it's outer atmosphere, and then emerged into that wild mess, I was TERRIFIED in a very real and old way. I want to be an astronaut again.This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sick. Buy this game instead of spending $25 at like Olive Garden or Bevmo or some ♥♥♥♥. You'll thank me.Bless.

_childDocuments_.review: People need to understand you don't really need a straightforward plot or the best ever graphics or the most convenient and personalized controls to have the closest to a perfect game. It's underappreciated by those who'd rather have a window with objectives listed at the side of your screen. It literally gives you full freedom. If you ever think of doing something within the game's capabilities then just do it, nothing's gonna stop you. And if you get stuck on one thing just go do something else. There is no main objective per se. The plot is basically nonexistent to those who don't seek for it. This is an exploration game, after all and exploring is well rewarded. If a place looks interesting it probably is and if it isn't it probably isn't simple as that. You just have to open your eyes, mind and want to explore. If your imagination is vivid and your attention span is longer than just scrolling through colorful short form content then this game is definitely for you.alsopaying 20 bucks for a game thats little over 20 minute long is an absolute scamloved the experiencewould recommend.

name: Firmament
detailed_description: ABOUT FIRMAMENT Firmament is a new puzzle-adventure game by the legendary game studio behind the best-selling games Myst and Riven. Featuring deep storytelling and world-building, discover the story of this seemingly abandoned world as you explore and unlock the mysteries of 3 unique Realms… and beyond! EXPLORE THE WORLD Featuring a unique steampunk aesthetic, Firmament invites you to explore the legendary deep world-building Cyan Worlds is known for. Firmament is a fantastic visual feast, with thrilling new sights to see around every corner. At the same time, the world of Firmament feels completely plausible; as though it were constructed with a bigger purpose in mind… A purpose you will be compelled to discover as you play. SOLVE THE PUZZLES You carry with you a device called an “Adjunct” as you explore. This Adjunct is your interface as you interact with the various devices throughout the Realms of Firmament. Employing the Adjunct to solve the puzzles you encounter will bring you ever closer to unlocking the secrets this place holds. DISCOVER THE STORY You are not entirely alone in Firmament. In addition to The Adjunct, you are joined by a mysterious apparition, who has a story of her own to share with you. As you explore you will be introduced to 3 Realms - each with secrets and mysteries to reveal. What purpose do the Realms serve? Can the spirit who accompanies you be trusted? REVEAL THE MYSTERY Are the realms of Firmament abandoned? What are these giant, mysterious machines scattered throughout the world? What is their purpose? What part do you play in this grand mystery? Explore, Discover, Solve, and Reveal the mystery for yourself by playing Firmament! TECHNICAL DETAILS Built For Both VR and 2D Displays Firmament supports both 2D and VR play. The VR experience of Firmament includes both Free Roam and Teleport modes. Additionally, Firmament includes many “comfort level” features for both new and experienced VR users, including the option to enable smooth or snap turning, quick travel up stairs and ladders, vertical height quantization, and more!

In addition to The Adjunct, you are joined by a mysterious apparition, who has a story of her own to share with you. As you explore you will be introduced to 3 Realms - each with secrets and mysteries to reveal. What purpose do the Realms serve? Can the spirit who accompanies you be trusted? REVEAL THE MYSTERY Are the realms of Firmament abandoned? What are these giant, mysterious machines scattered throughout the world? What is their purpose? What part do you play in this grand mystery? Explore, Discover, Solve, and Reveal the mystery for yourself by playing Firmament! TECHNICAL DETAILS Built For Both VR and 2D Displays Firmament supports both 2D and VR play. The VR experience of Firmament includes both Free Roam and Teleport modes. Additionally, Firmament includes many “comfort level” features for both new and experienced VR users, including the option to enable smooth or snap turning, quick travel up stairs and ladders, vertical height quantization, and more!
short_description: Firmament is a new puzzle-adventure game by the legendary game studio behind the best-selling games Myst and Riven. Featuring deep storytelling and world-building, discover the story of this seemingly abandoned world as you explore and unlock the mysteries of 3 unique Realms… and beyond!

_childDocuments_.review: Having just played the rerelease of Myst and hopping over to Firmament afterwards, I have to say, I'm quite disappointed. The puzzles themselves are not too bad, if a little finnicky sometimes because of the targeting of the Adjunct (your tool to solve most puzzles), and they were generally fun, but what felt like it was underdeveloped was the world and the story. We have this narrator of sorts (with just okay-at-best voice acting, which was already a rough choice for the game), leading us through this world to complete tasks as we are apparently supposed to as is our character's job. And then the narrator tells us a little tiny bit about the past in various locations, and then there's a quick twist at the end once you've done everything, that I don't want to say "came out of nowhere" but it just feels inconsequential at best? And then finding out that a lot of the "background details" were AI assisted, all the letters and journals and such you can find in the background, which just speaks to me about the level which they didn't care about the world they were creating. When I backed this game on Kickstarter, this was not the type of Cyan game I backed. I didn't want a puzzle game thrown together with little regard for the world it takes place in, I wanted a game where the gameplay and the world are inextricable from each other. This game, unfortunately, just fell flat for me.EDIT: having read up on Cyan's responses to the AI assistance stuff, i want to add an addendum here. Apparently, they only used it for ideation and trying new things out, and created and wrote everything themselves. Then I guess they just actively wrote a pretty underwhelming world and game. I was willing to give them the benefit of the doubt that the weak parts came from their overreliance on AI but if their official claim is that all actual texts and such in the game are written by humans well then they're just not very good, which sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a visually stunning VR puzzle adventures, Firmament VR is exactly that. Some aspects look so mind-blowing & lifelike that I can't help but to leave my jaw agape for extended periods of time. I’ve enjoyed about 6 hours of gameplay thus far and still have a ways to go.I've not played any other Cyan Studio games yet but Firmament had my eye even before it launched (I'm excited for Riven VR to launch). The game doesn’t hold your hand as far as what to do in certain areas but everything needed to complete a task is in the environment. So it’s very challenging and can feel slower paced at times or make you want to swear trying to figure out what to do. There are areas of low performance but that’s because the game is one of the best visual experiences in VR. It can be quite demanding on even my 4090/7950X PC alongside my Pimax Crystal (but I'm able to render using the max render resolution of 5100 x 4312 per eye, which is stunning). Even using a Quest 3 it can be a lot to handle. Playing on medium graphics settings and running 72Hz the game looks and plays gorgeously with very few hiccups in certain areas.The game also has some slight gameplay issues that don't ruin the game. Climbing isn't very fluid but that can be negated within the settings menu. Also, often times rotating your main device doesn't work properly so you will need to simply retry simple rotations. I know the game didn't have the best launch but it has been improved and is a solid VR experience that is quite unique.I've been live streaming Firmament VR the past few Thursdays and I can't wait to jump back in to complete the rest of these unique & challenging puzzles. With around 250+ VR titles in my library, there are dozens of puzzle experiences among them, which I enjoy. VR does puzzlers fantastically & Firmament is testament to that. It’s not the greatest VR game but is a great puzzle adventure that will leave you in awe from the environments.TLDR: If you value life-like visuals in PCVR along with a challenging puzzle adventure, Firmament will scratch that itch and scratch it hard.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this a thumbs up recommendation not because it is a breathtaking new release from Cyan whom I have come of age with, as have many fans, since the glory days of my youth in the Myst series.  I'm am showing my support for a small company that has done ground breaking things and even took risks and accepted failures with concepts of game play that were ultimately too advanced for their time (Uru).What we see in Firmament isn't a polished Cyan creation in peak form as some of us came to know in their earlier titles.  We are, I believe, seeing a remarkably artistic and innovative company in transition.  The creative and passionate founders are reaching their retirement years and I believe we are beginning to see a passing of the torch to a new generation that will take Cyan's world building to new platforms with different voices and views taking the development reigns.In such a time as this as many games start off and are released as early access Alphas and proofs of concept, sometimes indefinitely, Cyan always resisted doing so with a history of providing a solid product, stable game play, and an enjoyable experience.  That expectation was fudged slightly with Obduction and its limited budget development thru crowd funding resulting in game play hiccups and bugs. In the end, after some patches, Obduction was a success and had a certain freshness to it in the world design, puzzle solving, and story telling after many years of living with the D'ni.Firmament feels like a Cyan that hasn't found its footing yet after probably scraping by to survive a multi year global calamity and probably the weight of considering the future for the company and its leadership.  There is unquestionably beautiful Cyan visual artistry in Firmament, but it feels like a game that was shaved down to the basic elements and released as quickly as possible to have something to show for 4-5 years in development after the splash it made on its first announcement and subsequent content teasers.Firmament is simply unfinished art.  I'm sure if it had more time and money it would have been another jewel in their crown of unique worlds and stories.  It is only a foundation of what it could have been had circumstances been different and in favor of expanding what is offered to a more completed artistic, world finished, and story built state.  We could have altered the seasons forming and cutting the ice blocks moved about, taken seeds from the vault and seen things growing in field after field of botanical diversity after turning on irrigation, interacted with (and perhaps used in world) personal objects of the keepers and main characters, seen the wind blow thru the trees as an omniball wooshes by, sensed the acidic waves crashing around the shores of the battery, heard the stories of the workers lives and of the crew that captained a vessel of ironic paradoxes of technology, how naivety and deception controlled some and the greed for power emboldened others, gazed in to a twinkling, moving, expanse of stars and worlds unseen while being awestruck with the enormity of a space ship, felt the rumble and power of harnessed energy from the Spires and Arches of the 3 realms brought together in a quantum drive engine to take all to a new world to inhabit...  Firmament is a prisoner of its own snow globe.But... the complete and possible totality of the game did not come to pass, unfortunately, and our imaginations are left with the task of filling in the massive holes where a fully fleshed out game could have transported us to the sublime, unexpected, and beyond.It seems clear Cyan's future gaze is looking towards VR.  I hope the stepping stone of Firmament, as small as it currently is, transports them to firm bedrock on which to build even greater things with younger generations developing their art, expanding on new technology, and providing us all new worlds and stories to take us all into the great beyond.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Over a year has gone by, and Cyan still has yet to fix the major technical issues plaguing this game. My save was softlocked twice. Do not play this.Standing completely independent of Cyan's previous work, I think that Firmament is a completely serviceable experience- but coming from Obduction, the Myst remakes, and even the original Myst series releases, it's a major disappointment on almost every front.The things I can confidently say stand on their own are the visuals and audio (although with a considerable performance caveat for low-end setups.) Eric and the others have once again completely blown me away from the kinds of visuals they can pull off using only composition and scale, and their uniquely stylized realism on top of that wraps every scene together beautifully even compared to Obduction. The audio is similarly masterfully vibrant, and although the lack of music for most of the game is a bit sad, Cyan's distinct sound pulls through at just the right times.Another positive worth mentioning is the quality of individual puzzles- unlike Myst, Riven, and Obduction, _every_ single puzzle this time around is entirely localized and spatial. The Adjunct isn't truly that unique from a purely mechanical perspective, but the freedom it gave the design by giving the player the ability to move and look around while manipulating puzzle pieces let them take on entirely new forms (in theory!). This made what are normally the least interesting segments of Myst-likes for me a lot more enjoyable, and combined with the gorgeous visuals resulted in some breathtakingly striking structures.Unfortunately, this is about as far as I can stretch my praise. Lots of titles struggle to hit the level of quality Firmament does on these fronts, and I can't deny that I came out satisfied having seen it through to the end, which is why I still feel comfortable making my review Positive. But in every other aspect, it comes nowhere close to Cyan's standards for a puzzle game.Starting with the biggest and most glaring issue- the game is absolutely drowning in bugs, on every level of severity. Visual issues with the interface like text being way too big or too small, or in the world with floating or misplaced setpieces, are everywhere; but these pale in comparison to the sheer amount of jank and game-breaking softlocks pervading nearly every puzzle involving a moving platform. For a game of this length and mechanical scope, the amount of these I encountered across my playthrough was nearly inexcusable- I used the "teleport to safe spot" option more times in Firmament than I have in pretty much every other game I've played combined. In one case a platform necessary for solving the puzzle was completely invisible, with no amount of reloads making it appear. I had to find it by complete chance. In another I nearly softlocked my save and lost 2 hours of progress by managing to put a rotating platform in state limbo, and only managed to continue my game by having it luckily still form the shape it needed to. Some things feel outright unfinished, the best example I can give being the Camelus vehicle section. I played Obduction far after it stopped receiving updates, so I can't say whether or not this problem is new, but I can say that I had zero issues on this level on a game I played for three times as long; and right now you have to have some real patience to put up with Firmament in its current state. I can only hope that Cyan continues to push updates to continue fixing it because right now it is undeniably the largest thing holding the game back.In a similar vein to the bugs, there are some big missed spots in terms of polish, particularly involving the Adjunct- the worst and most confusing to me being the constant unintended disconnections. On a technical level, disconnects seems to work exactly as intended- when any piece of geometry intersects the wavy blue path between you and the device, it immediately leaves its socket and flies back to you. For puzzles, this aspect only comes into play maybe once or twice involving concatenated socketing; otherwise, it's a constant annoyance. The path makes no attempt to curve or adapt to your movements, and with the way that some puzzles are laid out this means that the entire point of the Adjunct existing is nullified by it disengaging from the socket whenever you turn around or take two steps in the wrong direction. For some interfaces it was a constant struggle to look at what I was doing and keep control at the same time- if the extremely basic advantage of having to use the Adjunct is taken away like this, then it just becomes a burden. Other polish-related issues are more minor, like getting caught on edges of platforms, some instances of weird collision, including one that could cause a massive endgame spoiler, and poor visual communication, which are easier to forgive but are still very much present.The last issue comes down much more to my own personal preference and expectations- as a full experience, it simply doesn't compare to Obduction. My favorite aspect of Obduction was how it put a new spin on the classic Cyan formula- the puzzles of each Age were deeply interconnected both physically and conceptually (compared to Myst having each puzzles mostly be contained to one Age), and they all flowed together into a wonderfully paced sequence from beginning to end. Combined with the gripping narrative, to me Obduction felt at or above Riven's level by the time I finished it (the only weak spot maybe being the conclusion.) Going into Firmament, I had hoped for similar improvements to the formula and storytelling that Obduction gave, but ended up being sorely disappointed.Starting with puzzles, like I said earlier, each *individual* puzzle is fun- but it doesn't feel like they come together to form anything, even compared to Myst's similar implementation. There is almost no interconnectedness; all three realms are just sequences of puzzle boxes, nothing is ever recontextualized or expanded upon. Similarly disappointing were the Adjunct upgrades, which outside of one singular puzzle, only ever acted as colored keys for colored doors (one of which explicitly just let you interact with special colored sockets.) I felt completely belted along from place to place, not even having to fully understand the goal I was working towards- I just knew I needed to go to the tower, raise the spire, lower the water, hit the button. Certainly a far cry from even Myst, it never felt like you needed to question a single thing you were doing.Narratively the game is a complete bore, barring the very end. Obduction comes out swinging, filling you with questions about even the smallest details. Throughout the majority of Firmament, the only truly interesting piece of delivery was hearing the first couple announcements over the loudspeaker- any other semi-interesting aspect of the world was directly explained by the floating fart cloud on the bottom left of your screen with dry delivery. I think the end is a huge improvement to Obduction though, and was maybe the only part of the story I was eager to take in (although I was spoiled on a pretty large bit by the aforementioned camera clip.) Otherwise, I never felt compelled to examine anything in detail past the first hour- even the center of storytelling, the Swan, feels artificial. I understand a lot of the game's content was created with the assistance of generative AI; we don't know with certainty how much was leaned on, but I can say with certainty the end result was a huge let down for me.All in all, I can still genuinely recommend Firmament to those who enjoy the type of puzzles it presents and can put up with some nasty bugs (and maybe people who really, really like pretty graphics.) From anyone else, it'd be decent, but it's a far cry from Cyan's best work.

_childDocuments_.review: Played entirely in VR.  Yes there are some bugs and the LODs are SUPER aggressive so a lot of models don't always look great in VR.  But I played on Epic settings with DLSS enabled and overall the game looked amazing.  It didn't always run smooth, but it was playable.  I have a 3080ti and 32gb of ram.  It also sometimes felt like I was ankle deep in the ground.  As if the collision wasn't correct in VR.  I had one time where I got stuck and had to reset myself.The viewpoints and vistas of the three different worlds are beautiful and awe inspiring in VR.  Exploring the worlds was great in VR, but I will warn that you better have your VR legs 100% ready on this one.  There are some rotational puzzles where the platform you are on rotates and... ugh it literally felt like my soul was leaving my body on those.  I had to close my eyes to get through them when rotating.  There's a number of "rides" you go on and they are amazing.  They remind me a lot of the "rides" in Riven.  In fact, this entire game has a Riven feel to it, from the music to the visuals to just the overall vibe of the environments.  I do wish you could interact with more of the environment though.  Everything is pretty much static.  You can't touch or pick up anything except for a few books and papers.  It's really disappointing and I think it would have helped making you feel like you were in that world.  Unfortunately you only interact with the world using this special tool called an Adjunct.  It's fine, but I really would have loved some more variety to the interactions.  I want levers to pull, buttons to push, and knobs to turn, but there is none of that here.  It doesn't take advantage of VR really at all (not like games like Red Matter 1 and 2 do for comparison).  It's more just a bonus "Look you can play in VR too!" type of thing.  Unfortunate.Some of the puzzles really... well they sucked.  There's one in an underwater section which I just found annoying.  It wasn't even much of a puzzle, just busy work, and it wasn't fun.  I dreaded anytime you had to put that diving suit on.  Maybe it's better on a flat screen, but in VR it was not great.  I also didn't enjoy the electricity puzzle.  Rotating platforms and then you have to do it a second time... really guys??  I wouldn't say any of the puzzles were particularly difficult for me.  Some were interesting, but I think the limited interaction was a let down on a lot of them.  Send Adjunct out, turn it, find next port, send Adjunct out, etc.I also want to mention that I really liked the ending.  I thought it was really cool and it explains everything.  And it was an unexpected surprise for me.  So, in conclusion, the game is good in VR!  It's not perfect, but I really enjoyed exploring all the worlds and I plan to replay it on the flat screen.  The puzzles are not the best, but I think the environments make up for that.  If you like Myst, Riven, and Obduction I'd definitely give this one a go!  If I compare it to Obduction, I'd say the puzzles in that are much more elaborate and harder with more interaction and times where you really had to think. So Firmament is a step back there.  Everything is pretty straight forward in Firmament.   A good game though and I'm glad Cyan is still making games like this!  I've been playing them since 1993!  Took me about 8.5hrs to finish.
