_childDocuments_.review: just finished the game. and while it could be longer /have more lore itemsits fairly good game i'm actually surprised i never ran into any bugs.though if you look though the reviews i would make sure the minimum playtime is set to something like 3 hours as most of the negative ones seem to under 2 hours or so.also while iv seen comments on how few books/lore note are around they always seem to massively lower the actual number as while there aren't anywhere near as many as their could be there's much more then just 3/4 iv seen commented on.i will admit the ending is a bit of a cliff hanger disappointment "don't want to put any spoiler information here".i hope they decide too add something to the end even as a dlc in the future.for the focus on VR in design/development i do think it held it back a bit as were still a few years at least from VR being more common "for sales" or improved haptic systems. i ultimately didn't attempt to play it in VR as i have headsets but no haptic controller like the steam VR ones.for the controls it did get a bit clunky at some points like with the robot walker but otherwise the main issue would be that it takes a while to get into using that control scheme at times.one future idea for them would be modding tools as this would probably work well in the vein of portal 1/2 maps.for puzzle difficulty it never got that hard the longest hold up was at the acid vat when i kept overlooking the socket higher up to lower it. and a couple that ended up not being solved purely the intended way because for example an irrigation one wanted me to chain sockets but the walker was misaligned slightly causing it hit a wall and fail and i ended up getting a angle and doing it from the walker top.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge team Cyan fanboy.  Check out my other reviews if you don’t believe me.  Firmament is not bad but it just not something I would expect from the makers of Myst and Riven.  It’s almost like my heroes have lived long enough to become the villains.  Firmament feels like a VR tech demo, a really pretty one.  But it’s really hollow, lifeless and lacks the vibrancy of a lore filled world I have come to praise Cyan for in the past.  Complete and utter disappointment from me and it truly pains me to badmouth one of my favourite developers ever.

_childDocuments_.review: Was prepared to overlook the glitchy puzzles, minimally-functional story and developer-test-track narration because the lighting is nice – when it works – and the audio direction is solid, before I found out half the game's wordcount is machine-learning sludge (and yeah, it reads like it). _childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is pretty. The puzzles are OK and the story is fine, for someone who has played Cyan games since Myst was released, this is not anything even close to Riven, for example (which I think was the best of all their games).It is quite short (I played through all of it in 9 hours) and that is with plenty of padding of the game length by requiring lots of back-tracking. This is explained by the in-game-story, but still, it artificially pads the game length by quite a bit.But the most aggrevating part is that the game has been so poorly play-tested. I managed to soft-lock myself several times, get stuck on geometry and put machines in state where I could not get them out again. There is an in-game feature to reset stuff (from the Settings menu) but that of course completely breaks the immersion.The game seems rushed and quite frankly, the graphics is not as good as games like Outer Worlds or Satisfactory. Something I would have expected from Cyan.If you wait a bit, maybe they will fix some of the issues, but most likely not now that they have gotten their kick-starter money and have probably started the next project.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament is a disappointing first-person puzzle game from the team that gave us Obduction. While it tries to bring some narrative content via a companion ghost, it fails monumentally with cryptic delivery and terrible exposition. Players interact with puzzles using a remote-control tether, called the Adjunct, and although it works okay, it can be clumsy and annoying. The eight-hour adventure consists of long walks between sparse interactive points across three bland realms. While there are a few okay puzzles here and there, most are not satisfying to solve. A few even broke, resulting in lots of time wasted. As much as Firmament looks like a spiritual successor to Myst, it doesn’t come close.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE:Bugs fixed. Did a second playthrough and no game breaking bugs were encountered. Good jobs guys.As a fan of Myst I want to love this game. Thus far, however, the game is just too buggy. In just two hours I've encountered two major soft-locking bugs that prevented me from advancing, and a myriad of minor yet annoying bugs.For the first major bug; I was able to Second major bug at which I am currently soft-locked;  The entire structure says it is blocked from every angle and is unmovable. Sure, I could teleport to a safe location, but how do I now solve whatever puzzle this is? How do I get BACK on the platform? I don't, unless I load a long-ago save and solve a bunch of previous puzzles to get back here. That's far too tedious, and I didn't buy this game to have tedium thrown at me. That's what my real job is for.The problem here is that I wasn't even trying to make these bugs happen. I was simply playing around with the mechanics of the game/puzzle to understand how they worked. Honestly, that's pretty unacceptable for me in a puzzle game.For a few of the minor bugs, I first played this game on my Deck, and only when I switched to my PC did I realize that a TON of dialogue had been missed because they simply never got triggered when I entered an area on the Deck. Only the first couple in the starter area ever played. Another minor (but very annoying) bug are some graphical glitches, like shadows constantly flickering. These, for me, entirely defeat the purpose of fancy high end graphics. It's only as strong as it's weakest link. To be clear though, this wouldn't entirely prevent me from buying and enjoying the game.If these major bugs become fixed soon, I would easily change my recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: After seeing the reviews about VR implementation, I started my first playthrough in 2D, and i'm glad I did I think. I'll defintely replay it in VR, but I'm stunned at how beautiful this game is so far. Not very far in at the time of writing, but so far the wait has been worth it.EDIT AFTER COMPLETION:I don't really know. I'm not going to get into story details as to not spoil, but I kind of agree with other folks - I don't feel like this is a very well written story or world at all. The world itself is quite stunning in my opinion (I LOVED practically every visual in Juleston), but overall the puzzles, world building, and lack of interaction was kind of jarring for a Cyan game. I 100% recognize the talent and effort that went into this game - and btw, if the devs are reading this, I love each and everyone of you - but across the board I just kind of felt let down in the storytelling department.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks amazing, great design, architecture, geography. Personally, I liked the plot and ending.Interesting puzzles: some pretty straight forward, others harder.I only wish there was more to do - there is a huge amount of real estate (but not much too see or do other than enjoy the expansive view) and many, many items of set dressing (but you can't interact with any of them).
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This was classic Cyan fare. The graphics were beautiful and the VR experience was fantastic. I only played pieces in VR, but you can tell this game was built from the ground up with VR solidly in mind. It definitely felt more like the first Myst game as far as puzzle play and story, which is good, but not quite as rich as Riven or even Obduction.The game mechanics are a little boring if you are not playing in VR, as there is not much to interact with, but the adjunct was a good way to feel immersed in the VR aspect that you were really there interacting with the sockets.The puzzles were challenging enough, but definitely felt easier for a larger audience than the difficult puzzles Cyan has created before, though the way you had to interact with the surroundings made it feel closer to Riven than Myst in that respect, which is a good thing. They felt natural and real to the world, if not a tad monotonous. The puzzles were almost immediately "figured out" and you know what to do, but you have to do quite a bit of maneuvering to get there. It felt like work at some points, instead of mentally stimulating. They felt dropped into the environment just to get in your way, with not alot of REASON all these different blocks stopped you from moving forward.My only real gripe is the thin story layer applied to the game. Hearing a ghostly voice give me random snippets in my ear didn't give much in the way of story building, and by the end, the info dump didn't really make you feel like you were in a completely thought-out world. I would have liked more to read, see, and understand about the world, more of the history of why you ended up in the predicament you ended up in by the end, and more about the people that are spoken of in passing. Though it is VERY challenging to read alot in VR, I would have still liked some way to get more immersed in the story.I didn't have many game bugs to deal with, and the few I had were not world ending or ones that sent me too far back in my gameplay. The updates happened quickly to fix bugs by Cyan and they did a great job. All in all, I would say this is well worth the wait, the money, and the play-through. Even if this is not Cyan's best game, even their worst games are a mile ahead of the rest in the puzzles/adventure world. No one can touch their authenticity and aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: 3/5Firmament evokes elements of the Myst series, but is a totally different animal.  It was somewhat enjoyable to play, but much less so than the Myst games.Gameplay: You are in an open world environment that you can only manipulate via a tool called the Adjunct, which basically allows you to link with various sockets that open doors, turn levers, etc. It's built for VR, but you can play without a headset.  There were definitely some creative puzzles, but the focus on using this tool severely limited the types of puzzles you could solve. It got very repetitive opening doors and raising elevators after a while.  Environment: The worlds were well-done graphically, but they were shallow and sterile. Myst games excelled at creating magical worlds with incredible ambiance, but this game failed miserably. You had no backstory (in fact very little reading at all).  There were no animals, people, plants with cool features, etc. The worlds did not feel "lived in."  And similar to Obduction, the worlds were too Earth-like. The Myst games really took you to different worlds, and the more bizarre, the better. Firmament reminded me of being in Colorado with mountains and pine trees.Story/Narrator: I still can't tell you what the story was about because it was so boring and the narrator's voice was grating. The choice of having a narrator with what seemed to be a fake foreign accent speaking to me every 5 minutes absolutely killed the experience. Nothing she (or some of the other voices you hear once in a while) added anything useful or interesting to the game. In fact, opening the game with her speaking was a warning sign it was going to be bad. Bugs: I got stuck several times, especially when operating the vehicle. There is an option to unstick yourself, which puts you back somewhat close to your current progress, but it would have been better if they just fixed the bugs themselves.Despite all of this, I would still give it a positive rating because it was entertaining and I am always delighted to see games from Cyan Worlds. But I think I speak for many fans when I say that they should really revive the Myst series. The Myst games captured lightning in a bottle. Cyan's recent games are clearly inspired by Myst, but their attempts to deviate from Myst only leave fans wanting Myst more. A new Myst game using modern game technology would be absolutely amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for fans of Cyan games but that's about it.  As others have said, the game is a bit sparse.  The majority of the story/lore is packed into the final act, leaving a kind of empty/lonely feeling, even with the mentor talking to you once in awhile.  The game is also quite buggy.  Do not go near a ledge or you will often be stuck there unable to move.  A crane I was operating in Curievale got stuck in place and almost hard locked my game.  Thankfully I had the presence of mind to save a few minutes earlier.  On a couple of puzzles I looked up the solution just to avoid the headache of being stuck and having to unstuck myself in the options and run all the way back to where I was to finish the puzzle.  But even if none of these bugs existed, the game feels too short.  I looked at the world around me and saw so much more potential than what actually ended up being in the game.  I was sort of expecting a final puzzle or something more to do in the final act.  The visuals are incredible.  It's a Cyan game after all, this is what they do best.  St, Andrews in particular is beautiful.Sound/music is great.  The song during the end credits is really good.  The story itself is pretty nice overall.  The end reveal is good.  But up until that point there's very little story or lore to entertain you.  The puzzles can sometimes be a bit tedious.  This is because you know the solution but just have to go through the motions of moving things into place.  There is not much in the way of deciphering clues as in past Cyan games.  Again, just recommending for Cyan fans.  I enjoyed Firmament despite some flaws but it could have been better, maybe with a bigger budget.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I enjoyed it but...This would have to be the easiest game from Cyan I've played and I think it's due to the one dimensional nature of the gameplay. You get given an item called the adjunct, a gauntlet which acts as a key that allows you to interact with objects in the world. Aside from 1 or 2 exceptions it's the only way of interacting so you don't have to pay any attention to details within the world and instead just look for the slot to put the adjunct. This means you can quite easily fluke a lot of this game just by walking around and randomly interacting with things. They do manage to pull off some interesting things with that one mechanic though. However I felt the upgrades you get for it as your progress were underutilised.Unlike other Cyan games before it, there's no note taking necessary. There's no clues or symbols to take note of. There's barely anything to read or listen to or memorise. I felt a bit disappointed about that because that's what Cyan games are known for and that was my expectations going into it.The worlds they created did capture that awe inspiring but mysterious cyan look and feel so I was happy about that. I enjoyed exploring the worlds. I found the puzzles to be decent enough albeit not as challenging as I was expecting.Unfortunately this game has performance issues and a few bugs. Very choppy framerate but with FSR and lowering a few settings I managed to make it acceptable for the most part. There were a couple of occasions I got stuck in the terrain and had to reload my save. There was also one occasion where it let me go somewhere without a way to get back out, requiring a reload.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get it out of the way; Day one bugs are obvious but everyone's system is different. While the idea that devs should figure out most bugs before release is a legit thing, a lot of people somehow think THEIR BUG is always the *one* that should have been included. I'm seeing people report bugs I've yet to see while playing it in VR myself while my own are a lot more immersing breaking (my character will constantly rotate to the right throughout the game, especially kicks up after using the adjunct; and issues with releasing adjunct but only a bit, and seen some narrator text over itself.) Besides some graphical background issues (its VR, I don't expect perfection) that's it for me so far after 2.5 hours and solving a puzzle and a half maybe, mostly exploring and opening up areas.Would I recommend? Sure. But I could also recommend waiting for some intial patches if you're really THAT concerned about "immersing" breaking (very PCMR phrasing, that while I GET IT, it's another thing to complain about like not getting those last few FPSs when you're already 120+). It's also VR reviews that are mostly negative, and let's be honest, the VR isn't the forefront of the goal (but surely high as it was their intent). So I'm not gonna knock for something that CYAN will fix. I mean come on, it's freaking the people of MYST and Obduction, give it a bit before trashing it with complaints. It's been a day as of this writing, let them get some reports and logs and a patch or two out for those odd custom systems and then try it yourself.BEYOND that all, it looks AMAZING and I already see the old school puzzles I've long missed and awaited for since the kickstarter began. I am excited to continue and give it time to get some updates while I jump between games to allow it do so. Maybe it could use a lil more overall umpf in details but A, I've only played through a single puzzle so far and B, I'm on VR which is ehhh occasionally and some locations have looked beautiful but limited due to VR monitor).TL;DRProbable CYAN simp but I know whatever kinks there are they'll work out, it's worth it either way, even if you wanna wait for a  perfect patched version. It will be worth it.For specs: I run their recommended specs but with a higher CPU, with Rift S, except on W10.

Not everybody is right handed, or able to use WASD, developers.There is a talking companion that pops up throughout the game. She manifests as a cloud of smoke. _childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a middle option between recommend and do not recommend. I've been eagerly anticipating Firmament, hoping that Cyan would continue to produce the great work they did with Obduction. Maybe my expectations were set too high. The world they've built in Firmament is spectacular as always. It's mysterious and you're not quite sure why you're there, so you start following your guide and fiddling with the environment. That's where things got disappointing for me. The puzzles leave much to be desired as they are incredibly simple and do not require much thought at all to complete. If anything, they require hunting for the right angle to attach to a node so that you can manipulate the environment. Obduction was a return to form for Cyan that had mechanical puzzles reminiscent of their older games, Myst I-IV. Firmament is more like Myst V, but with shallower puzzles that require substantially less trial and error. I don't recommend this at full price, but it's worth playing on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: No wonder Firmament feels so lifeless: it literally is.[SPOILERS ALERT!]Sorry but Firmament looks more and more like a mismanaged trainwreck that had to resort to AI to make up the time lost doing God knows what.The released game is half-baked at best, buggy beyond redemption, with a barely stitched together plot and basically no lore (and the little it has is AI-generated, it turns out). The story simply doesn't make sense, it's not coherent even within its own wild premises (a physically impossible steam-powered generation spaceship), the Mentor is so much not a character that they didn't even bother giving her a name, but has an incredibly high capacity to decompose (from healthy middle-aged woman to perfectly clean skeleton in just 7 years!). It's not even explained why she died at all, she definitely wasn't an elderly. I guess she just got bored.There's so little plot exposure during the game that they actually had to leave conveniently scattered backstory prints just before the end. You have literally no idea of what you're doing and why throughout the whole game, the Mentor... just doesn't mentor, as in she completely fails to provide a motive. And not to mention that it's so lazily implemented that 90% of her lines will be provided by a green sentient cloud at the bottom left of your screen. You'll only see her animated character at the beginning and end of the game.Sorry Cyan, I loved all of your games, even the ones with awkward mechanics like Uru or Myst V, but I cannot bring myself to appreciate this one. It feels rushed, lazy and plain incompetent. Please don't screw up the Riven remake.

_childDocuments_.review: Another amazing accomplishment by Rand and his team at Cyan Worlds.  They continue to set the example for any games that attempt to get into this type of play style.  From the original Myst game which was practically one of the only reasons to get a cd rom for your computer in the early 90's to Riven, Uru and Obduction.  I have been playing these games since I was a child and know people to became influential in the Uru live beta testing along with the Cyan team.  Firmament embraces all of the aspects that Cyan games have become iconic for,  from the stellar and amazing world design, art creation, amazing landscaping and unique puzzles to solve.  Fans of any of the Myst games or Obduction will enjoy this addition to their library.I personally do not have a VR system to utilize while playing this game, but the overall quality of playable experience from initial launch is on the next level from other major games that have failed to provide a mostly trouble free initial on launch game play experience.  I won't mention them, but any gamer around initial launch of Firmament will know.

_childDocuments_.review: Diehard Cyan fan here! I played through all of their games (and even chose a carreer in 3D because of them) and I must admit that i am quite disappointed in this new release.Barren and gigantic environments feel empty and lifeless. Walking through them sadly feel like a chore. I also broke 3 saved games using some of the interactable machines; making me loose about 2h total of gameplay. So yeah... this game is very short (~5h) and very buggy too.At this point you might be asking yourself "Then why the positive review?"Here's why:-The scale of this game is gigantic compared to the size of their team that has shrunk considerably.-They also dared to try something new with an interesting multi-tool game mechanic that works very well. It opens the possibility to tons of fun to solve and just hard enough puzzles.-The story is also quite original, and progression flows fantastically well.So In the end, my disappointment boils down to: I only wish there was more to find.More lore, more secrets, more details, more variety and more environment based storytelling.I can only hope that Cyan will bounce on this misstep and solve this new puzzle of their own.Why not keep expanding the Myst universe?It's been AGES ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Review from a Myst superfan:What makes the Myst series great has always been the lore. In the original Myst series, you got a narrative payoff for every puzzle you solved. As you unlocked each area, you learned more about the culture of the people who had lived in the worlds, how the world had been created, what had happened to everyone. The D’ni lore was rich and complex, as was the narrative of Atrus’ family. In the first few games, it was a pleasure to learn about Sirrus and Achenar. They had distinct living spaces and environments—Achenar savage and brutish, Sirrus intellectual and calculating. You were constantly trying to puzzle out what had happened to break the family apart, and as you explored, you’d have those “ah-ha” moments. The D’ni were also super cool—who doesn’t love learning about ancient alien civilizations? I explain this because it helps to understand why Myst fans are disappointed with this one. There is very little lore to this game. The revelations are more visual than narrative—the more areas you unlock, the more you get treated to visual feasts—cool steampunk environments. There’s some great sound and visual design, and if you’re only after those steampunk vibes, this game will hit the spot.But Myst fans like me are wondering, “where is the lore?” Although there’s voiceover narration, most of what the voice tells you is stuff you can figure out yourself, by looking at the environment. There are a handful of clickable objects, but few journals, and those journals mostly repeat the same ideas the voiceover character already told you. Most of the real story revelations come in a rush in the last few minutes of the game. You arrive at your final destination, and you must sit through a five-minute monologue before the game ends. You have no choices—you just sit there, and passively watch the game end. The problem is that you had little narrative payoff throughout the game itself. You solve a puzzle, get to a new area, solve another puzzle—no unfolding of the story. You certainly unlock environments, but there are few papers or journals to find, and from the simplistic room design, everyone in Firmament seems to spend their time looking at marble busts and reading Human Anatomy textbooks. The other keepers have little in the way of backstories or personalities.I did like the revelation at the end. . Also, like all of the games by this dev, I love-love-love the way the puzzles make logical sense. There’s a reason why things operate the way they do. My favorite puzzle was the battery puzzle; I felt quite proud of myself for figuring out how the machine worked (it took me way longer than it should have, but I’m bad at math—don’t judge). For a Myst game, the story was simple and straightforward, although once the game ends,  you are left with many, many unanswered questions, and much of the plot doesn’t make sense from a logical perspective. All this being said, this is certainly a beautiful game, and I had no issues playing it on my PC. I wished the game was a little longer, and there were more puzzles and lore, but I understand that they had a limited budget as a small developer. I would gladly keep backing more Myst games, forever and ever, although it would be grand to have another game set in the same universe as the linking books/D’ni. I never get tired of being Atrus’ “friend,” and that’s the reason why I think I’d much rather go back and replay some of the earlier games, before I’d replay this or Obduction. But I’m a narrative gamer, and visual impressiveness is less of a priority for me than a good story.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of both the Myst series and Obduction, I was excited going into this one. I think the game met my excitement, but only just. There's a lot to like about the game: the puzzles and clues are presented well, with the solutions intuitive and context clues guiding you along the way without any sort of tutorial windows or NPCs laying everything out for you. The plot is interesting enough to keep you wanting to move through the game and figure out exactly what's going on. The locations are varied and quite beautiful to look at, at least if you don't look too closely at the trees in one of them.If you've been following Myst and played Obduction, you may be curious about performance and load times. I will say there is some stuttering, though it's not as bad as say, Elden Ring in that regard, and it clears up once you've looked around an area for the first time. Loading times are still there, but far more tolerable than Obduction.Which leads me to my criticism: this game is SO similar to Myst and Obduction in structure it's disappointing. There's something to be said for Cyan playing to their strengths, but this game just feels unambitious. A hub world with different, uninhabited realms, each with a similar primary objective... I've seen this too many times before. And with my completion time being at less than 8 hours, that makes this shorter than Obduction. I should also mention a couple of the puzzles are buggy. There's a "teleport to safe location" button that I had to use I think 4 times due to 2 particular puzzles either putting me in an inescapable spot or bugging out and preventing me from progressing.Overall, I'd say it's a 7/10. Fun puzzles, interesting world and story, but too formulaic and too short for the $35 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Being a long-time Cyan fan, it was inevitable that I would back the  Kickstarter as soon as I learned about it. A couple of years of waiting later, and now I got to play it.The game follows the Cyan tradition of being a first person adventure in a richly detailed 3D environment that sees the player traversing a hub realm (or "Age", if you will), that in turn sends you to a couple of distinct other realms filled with puzzles, gorgeous vistas, and no other humans. Also included are many lifts and other ways of transportation, that are often a bit convoluted but extremely enjoyable. Without them you'd really ask yourself if you even are playing a Cyan game.The title was clearly made with VR in mind, which is reflected by how the player interacts with the world. Instead of having a lot of items that  or do something, the world is filled with bright yellow sockets that can be manipulated with a gauntlet, tying the interfacing to the rules of the world instead of making essential items just lit up in gold with a weird sparkling sound, like a certain other game (yes, this review has a  reference and it's not about the Art Deco similarity). As a result there is never any doubt when the player is expected to do something at a certain place. This could be seen as either a remedy to "pixel hunting" or simply railroading the player. I lean to the former, though I understand people criticising the game for the latter.With my playthrough clocking at 10.5 hours, the game is either a bit short or a bit easy for a Cyan game (this may be the first time I finished one without consulting a guide once). I do not think this is a bad thing though, it told its story without feeling that it is dragging.My main criticism is the game stability. I've had a large amount of crashes and a softlock at the crane puzzle - often enough to be notable and frustrating. I get that with some of the physics/collision puzzles it is hard to iron it out completely, but a quick save option would be a nice feature in the meantime. Seriously, you need to save often or you will cry.Wrapping up I think this is a near essential experience for those that love Cyan's backcatalog. For people that go in more blindly, it's still a solid puzzle adventure with good but not overly hard puzzles, great visuals, and solid sound design.

_childDocuments_.review: You'll spend quite a few hours at first wondering why you're doing this, what's going on, where's the storyline, etc. Trust me, all gets revealed in the end, including why the game was a bit light on explanations/story early on. Not as difficult as some of Cyan's other games, and some have said it's more like if Cyan attempted a Metroidvania-style puzzle adventure game, which is one way you could describe Firmament. It still has absolutely gorgeous worlds to silently wander through, though, even if some of the puzzles felt more abtract and not as well-integrated into the world as with some of their past games.Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid adventure / puzzle game true to Cyan's design principles.The Myst / Riven DNA is unmistakable. The game looks great in terms of both graphical fidelity and art style. If you remember the original Myst, the rocky island landscapes will feel vaguely familiar (Julestone realm in particular). Mechanical and architectural designs are finely crafted, as expected from Cyan. Attention to details and great use of lighting make some scenes look like pre-renders. Wish I could see it in VR mode.The puzzles are seamlessly integrated into the game world, a hallmark of Riven and later games from the Myst universe. They can take a while to solve and require careful observation and deduction. This is a game for patient players, although I must admit that at one point my patience was tested. If fiddling with strange mechanisms for half-hour stretches does not sound fun, this may not be a game for you. On the other hand, there were genuine "eureca" moments when a solution suddenly struck me after a period of head scratching. Overall, the puzzles had the "right" difficulty -- challenging, but not to the point of forcing me to consult the walkthrough.Some critique can be aimed at storytelling. You only get short, scarce pieces of lore throughout most of the game. Perhaps this is an intentional choice in order to hit the player with a grand revelation at the end. Firmament's greatest problem is the inevitable comparison to Riven which set the bar very high. When compared to its spiritual predecessors, Firmament may seem not as varied, deep, or ambitious. But I still don't get the negativity in the reviews. In the era of braindead games filled with loot boxes and microtransactions, Cyan stayed faithful to their heritage and creative vision. They have yet again created something beautiful and imaginative, and I applaud them for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am sorry Cyan, but this game misses the mark, its not what I love from Cyan.  I backed this project on Kick Starter.The good?  The music is awesome, as usual for a Cyan game.  But it hurts me to say there is nothing else I love about this game.  Aside from the glitches, which I ran into two (one is currently game stopping, the other I was able to glitch out of) this is what I just don't like about Firmament:- First and foremost, the new mechanic of the gun think that controls everything.  It completely removes the mystery from the game, just look for the socket and that is something important.  No socket, not important.  Controlling anything in this game is SLOW, Clunky and tedious.  The first puzzle you come across, an ice crane, lowers so slow I thought it was glitched but I just had to hold Q to solve the puzzle.- And on the new mechanic its also a bad UI out of VR.  In my opinion this is the result of trying a bit too hard to make a VR game.  If you come across something like a crane that can move left and right as well as lower and raise, its two different interface modes.  So interact with the node, use Q and E to move left and right, then hit Tab to use Q and E to move up and down.  Then if you want to move the crane again, hit Tab again to move left and right.  What happened to a control panel with four arrows?  One click, result.  Not click and hold, Q, then right click.- The story, well, I really don't care.  The Russian chick that welcomes you and just randomly talks to you the entire time I find annoying.  I want to immerse into the world and she just starts talking.  Or I am in a boring tunnel but she starts talking so I stand still so I don't accidentally cut her dialogue off.  Also, what is my end game, figure out why everyone is gone?  None of the puzzles feel like they are working towards that story.  I am just moving machines to move to the next part of the world.- The world, it started out great but after 5 minutes in each world you can clearly see the copy / paste going on.  Each Spire is an exact copy paste between the worlds, why doesn't the frozen one have ice in it or the "Jungle" one can have vines growing on it?  Instead, its not like anything has fallen apart its just like...no one is home, but it doesn't look like anyone should be home.  Everything looks well kept, just powered down.- The size of the world is WAY too big.  I spend so much time running through open areas with absolutely nothing to do or look at.  I looked up a few solutions to some of the ice world because I didn't want to waste time of running back and forth and using the clunky mechanic to teleport around the world.  I tried looking once but just didn't see it as fun to go back.  Cyan, think of how much you were capable of in the small worlds like Myst, Riven...Exile.  Those worlds were 1/20th of the size or smaller and had so much to do.  It was not so spread out.I love Cyan but I honestly hope they ditch the VR initiative.  VR can allow you to immerse more but the sacrifices you make to game play to play in VR is too much especially for a puzzle game.  Maybe make unlockable areas that players can visit in VR and explore without puzzles as they progress in the main game, this would be a great way to reward puzzle solving and allow you to make a smaller, more involved world.But I just cant recommend this game the worlds quickly go stale, puzzles are not hard just very tedious.  Lots of move something and run around to see if it lined up.EDIT 6/21/23: I hate to come back to this, but the music is far worse than I thought.  In game, the first few worlds the music fit.  But after that, it became very similar.  I downloaded the soundtrack and played it to only discover I really didn't know what tracks belonged where or when one ended and another began.  Also, the newest update nuked my saves, they just wont load anymore.  I am not repeating all of the monotonous stuff so I do not intend on finishing this game.  Sorry Cyan, I really hope your next title has better story, immersion and is not VR centric.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m a fan of puzzle games so I really wanted to like Firmament, but ended up feeling decidedly “meh” after finishing it.STORY: Pretty much all of Firmament’s story is told in the first few minutes and last few minutes of the game, leaving the middle 98% of the game as a narrative vacuum. The intriguing teasers at the beginning go nowhere until the very end. 99% of the way through the game, I still had no idea of what was going on, why my actions mattered, or what the stakes were. This lack of narrative progress made it difficult to stay invested, especially throughout the second half of the game. The reason for the narrative void is to set up a twist at the game’s conclusion. However, this twist came too late and opened up too many plot holes to feel satisfying. Firmament could have really benefited from a slow but steady drip of meaningful story details throughout the game to provide a sense of narrative progress.PUZZLES: Overall, Firmament’s puzzles felt a bit disappointing. Only one puzzle really captured the magic of puzzling solving. The majority of the puzzles were “object shuffling” puzzles (think Tetris on a large scale) that rely on spatial reasoning: move Object A out the way, so that you can then move Object B out of the way, so that you can then slide Object C over and access a switch. Then slide Object C back so that you can reshuffle Object B so that you can reshuffle Object A, etc. Although the particular “objects” vary, the majority of Firmament’s puzzles have this sort of feel. It’s a perfectly fine type of puzzle when used once or twice, but grows stale when encountered too many times. A number of puzzles required running back and forth to fiddle with a particular control in order to get something in just the right spot. The puzzle was mentally solved, but the actual execution then took six trips back and forth to get that device is juuust the right position. This felt tedious. As a general rule, satisfying puzzles should take a long time to mentally solve and then little time to execute, not the other way around.The lack of puzzle variety, combined with the lack of narrative progress, made my interest wane during the second half of the game. I was hoping to gather clues, jot down notes, and perhaps decipher some cryptic symbols, but alas, there was nothing of the sort. All of the puzzles are self-contained (meaning you won’t need information from elsewhere to solve them), and only one actually required me to scribble things down. On a positive note, all of the puzzles are contextualized, meaning that they have an in-game reason for existing (in contrast to puzzles that exist solely to be puzzles). However, some of the puzzles would have been easily bypassed if my character could jump, scramble over debris, or step across a short gap, so these puzzles still felt contrived. I wonder if it would have been a better move to include less contextualized puzzles simply to increase variety of puzzle type.VISUALS: Visually, Firmament is beautiful. It has a great steampunk aesthetic that I thoroughly enjoyed. I wish the world had more environmental storytelling, however. Things like journals, notes, artifacts, and other personal touches would have made the world feel more lived-in and given a sense of what life was like before the player showed up. These personal touches are absent beyond the opening minutes, leaving a world that feels oddly sterile and impersonal despite having once been populated. GAMEPLAY: The game was glitchy when I played it. It crashed at least five or six times. Another time I fell through the ground into the endless expanse of game engine. I’m sure these glitches will soon be patched.CONCLUSION: Firmament isn’t a terrible game, but it isn’t a particularly great one either. It feels like a missed opportunity, especially in regard to storytelling. I wish Steam had a “so-so” rating. I would only recommend Firmament to die-hard puzzle game fans who need that puzzle itch scratched. Otherwise, let it pass until there’s a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: So recently I saw the game receiving positive reviews and I decided to give it a shot before the new Riven drops. I have been a tremendous fan of Cyan's MYST series and fondly remember playing MYST, Riven, Exile, and Revelation as a family growing up. I introduced my wife to MYST and we are going to play Riven together once the remaster drops.So with so much love for this company's most beloved franchise, why would I not recommend this game? In short, because it does not survive comparison. I strongly urge you to play MYST, Riven when it drops, and Exile and Revelation are each exceptional. But Firmament, which was Cyan's first foray into a new IP fell spectacularly flat for me.What Firmament is missing is what made the MYST series of puzzle games truly special; the puzzles didn't just challenge you; they introduced you to a world space worth discovering. You would first read of a place in Atrus' library, and after developing an appreciation for the world, would explore it on your own, discovering for yourself Atrus' various projects and witnessing with similar dismay how his sons Sirus and Achenar warped it to their respective purposes.Firmament does none of this. It drops you in the role of an amnesiac, where you are solving 3 by 4 logic puzzles or wrestling through process puzzles which are more a challenge of your ability to see what you're working with rather than an actual test of wit or ability to reason through problems. Adding to that how much space was left unused, it made me believe the game fell short of a grander vision. This is only further hammered home when at the end of the game, it is hoped you will remember the keepers and their stories... stories which you never actually got told as you played the game.I am largely convinced (having seen the backers in the credits) that this was a crowd-funded project that promised more than it managed to deliver for some unfortunate set of reasons or another. In the realm of compelling exposition, this game simply does not. Some may fault it for not having the ability to jump or being rough around the edges with movement. I don't because I am intimately aware that these things are not a focal point for Cyan Games. Their focus has consistently been aesthetic appeal and expository puzzle game-play, the quiet impactful moments you experience as you discover the lovingly crafted world they thought through. A company like Blizzard rotating into First Person Shooter game-play is beyond just unusual, so I was ready to forgive Firmament in this sense. But to take such a massive step back rather than push their unique form of computer game forward really hurt to see. Here is hoping this was an unfortunate stumble and not the beginning of a tragic trend.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this with moderately high expectations given how good Obduction and the Myst remake were. Overall it was pretty good, and I think lived up to them. The art style and locations were captivating in similar ways to Obduction, and the puzzles felt pretty unique as well. One or two stumpers - one I broke out a pencil and paper for, but the other unfortunately had me scouring streamer VODs to see how they overcame it.There's a bit of jank with a couple of them as well, which hopefully gets sorted out in a patch, so I recommend using the manual saves just in case the autosave happens after you encounter one of these.I liked the story more than Obduction's, and the discoverable books and papers at the beginning and end were nice. I may have missed a couple (I'm 3 achievements short of a full clear), but I would've liked a few more scattered along the way.Overall I recommend it if you enjoy Myst-style games that are more about puzzles and atmosphere and less about dialog / NPC interactions.

_childDocuments_.review: Bafflingly ..."Not good".After the "disappointment" of Obduction, I thought Cyan would take the hints and correct course, and make something that the fans, and newcomers want. Unfortunately, this is not it. Maybe THIS time they'll take the constructive criticism, and fix their thought process, and go back to form.As I write this review, it pains me to my core since I am a DIE-HARD-MYST/CYAN fan. I have been, since 93 (no, I didn't play Manhole, but Cyan wasn't really Cyan at that point, if you want to get real)I have played EVERY Myst game, multiple times, for the past 30 years. Through different iterations, consoles, editions, remakes (remasters), etc. I have multiple posters, shirts, mugs. I have MYST and RIVEN on my phone and tablet. I even have my Saveedro action figure, hoping to get it signed by Brad Douriff at one point. I AM a hardcore MYST fan.And when it was announced that they were working on a new, original game, back around 2013, I was stoked. Hoping that it would be a new game that has taken all the good lessons from the great games, and not brought the bad parts of the "bad games" . Unfortunately, it took very little from the great games, lots from the bad games, and added some new problems that should have been left on the cutting room floor. Cyan, as of the last 10 years has had this obsession with making a "VR" friendly, and First Person Shooter-perspective/controls-friendly game. Something that kind of "started" with Exile, where you could "look around with the camera, "freely" - for the sake of "immersion". The problem is, these games being "puzzle" at their core (or at least they should be), it's counter-intuitive to lean so heavily on that "mobility" and "freedom" aspects. This makes Obduction, and by extension Firmament, feel like a half baked First Person Shooter, with bad controls, that just happens to have some puzzles in it. So now, to capitalize on these problems, we have Firmament, the latest installment. Which, honestly, it feels like Kramer, from Seinfeld, with his latest "get rich quick" scheme, where you thought he would have learned his lesson from the last couple of times it didn't work out - but no, he leans into a new one, never learning from the past.Firmament has a couple of "main" issues, in my opinion: 1. VERY easy, simple puzzles.2. EMPTY, LIFELESS World.3. Controls and environment are VERY Imperfect and buggy lots of times.And my biggest issue with this is that all 3 of these are BECAUSE and MAINLY DUE to the reliance on making the experience VR Friendly. Sure, I understand that that was the whole point, but it SHOULDN'T be. Unless they were making a strictly VR game, that shouldn't be the case in a new Cyan entry. The game should be the game first, and then a VR Experience. Instead, you can feel in the first 2 minutes of playing that YOU are in the wrong for not playing it on VR. YOU feel unwelcome, out of place, and inadequate for playing it on a standard display with regular Mouse and Keyboard - how dare you!?I would take this all back if this was called "Firmament - VR". But it isn't, and it isn't meant to be a VR game that was given the "standard display" treatment. It's a regular, next entry, Cyan game. In modern media, it's become a cancer that companies and corporations have no new original ideas, and just regurgitate old ideas, but remade, or remastered, and don't even bother to consider new IPs. When it comes to CYAN, I feel exactly the opposite way - at this point, they need to STOP MAKING NEW GAMES, and remaster, remake the old ones. (yes, I'm obviously talking about RIVEN, namely).Do I regret being a day-1 backer on Kickstarter for Firmament, and paying the High Level Tier, for it? No.But if I found a friend who has never played the MYST games, or who only played the first four (maybe V), I would very much tell them to skip this one.Does it look great? Surprisingly no. In 2023, in the era of Red Dead 2, Farcry 5,  The witcher 3, Ghost of Tsushima, Horizon, God of War.......No, it does NOT look great. Sometimes, dare I say, some specific instances looked WORSE than some images of even RIVEN or EXILE - 26, and 23 year old games. I'm NOT EXAGGERATING. (no Ray Tracing is inexcusable)Does it sound good? Not really. There's nothing that stands out.Does it play well, control wise? Absolutely not. I have not tried it on VR, I expect it's slightly better. But no.Does it have graphical or gameplay  glitches? Yes, lots.Does it have challenging puzzles? No. N-O.Does it have a compelling story? Not really, no. Especially if you're of a certain political demographic.In conclusion, if you're a hard core MYST/CYAN fan - you WILL play this game, whether you want to or not. We are, as fans, very limited with our entries. We don't get a release every year, like some other game Developers. So, we take what we can get. But where will it rank on the list? Let me put it this way. I have slightly more interest in revisiting URU than Firmament. For the hardcore fans, that should tell you something. For the non-harcore fans, just take a look at the review scores for it. I'm disappointed that this isn't the great new CYAN game we were hoping for - especially with the empty feeling that Obduction left us with. I'm not ready to give up on this company yet. But I'm not so sure I will pre order, or crowd-fund another project. For now, I will only do one thing: Wait, patiently, for the RIVEN remake.

_childDocuments_.review: In my eyes, Riven was the perfect adventure game for its time.  It delivered AHA and WOW moments that stay with me to this day.  Firmament is the only game in the genre to match it since.  It has modern design concepts such as "while you explore" narration rather than "make you wait while I talk" narration.  The puzzles are embedded in parts of the environment that have reasons to be there rather than "here's a puzzle just because".  Play it -- and be patient, because another modern design concept is to aggressively point you where you're supposed to go, which is not what we have here.  This game rewards careful observation, and thinking about what you're observing, by not letting you progress until you've had the needed realization on you're own.Note: it'll probably get patched, but for now the first big thing you can move can get stuck while you experiment with it.  Just know that if this happens it's not you, it's the game.  Use the teleport to safe place function in settings to reset the thing as well, or reload from autosave.

_childDocuments_.review: I have thoroughly enjoyed my immersion in the world of Firmament. I have been adventure game player from 'The Hobbit' on a Sinclair Spectrum. _childDocuments_.review: First of all, I'm not here to argue with anyone.  I love the graphics.  The scenery is very immersive.  I like games that let you wander around and discover little tidbits and clues.  Some of them may be important.  Some are just interesting.  This is also what I love about Cyan Worlds games.  Yes, there is an end in mind, but the journey to that end is as much, or more fun than reaching the end.  That's not true for everyone, I know.  It is true for me.  This is why Cyan is my favorite game producer.  The only thing I have found that almost touches it is The Room series.  I'm not done with the game.  I'm taking my time and enjoying the journey.My edit for the end of game: SPOILERS!I finished the game.  Still missing 3 achievements, but honestly, since I knew where we'd end up, I just wanted to get to the end.  I did enjoy the game.  Many players won't remember an old movie from 1972 that starred actor Bruce Dern called 'Silent Running'.  That movie was playing in my head while I played this game so I paid attention when I saw all the blood stains in the Swan and listened to the Mentor.   I enjoyed the puzzles a lot.  Even the frustrating ones.  I still recommend the game although I think you need to take a look at 'Silent Running'.  It is going to feel SO dated.  It's over 50 years old!

_childDocuments_.review: Being a big fan of Cyan's game catalogue I went in with the expectation that this would be a similar experience. Yes, again we have beautiful steampunk realms with puzzles to solve, but this time I feel like it missed the depth I came to know from earlier games.I was looking forward to another journey where clues from the environment itself would slowly unravel what was happening, and the compulsion to take notes as you go because you know a clue in the form of a document, symbol or encountered situation would not always be immediately useful, but probably important somewhere else.Instead, all areas were very self-contained without having to explore or stumble upon a clue elsewhere. I never had to abandon an incomprehensible puzzle to go explore somewhere else, to then have this nice eureka moment for learning the rules to solve a situation I encountered earlier. It was also not needed to traverse the realms in a certain order/way to reach a goal (apart from a few upgrades blocking the second half of the game), while Obduction actually did a very good job at this with the way you traveled between worlds. This time it was just a series of discrete puzzles while the story only got vaguely told by a voiced narrator and only really got explained at the very end.Some puzzles involved some clever placement of objects to be able to progress which was nice, but I especially missed the information-based brain teasers with codes or other knowledge that would require some offline thinking. Instead, most problems involved making sure not to overlook a socket and just activating everything until you could continue. I understand that the game being VR-centric limits the offline problem solving gameplay / note-taking that you would traditionally inclined to do in these kind of adventure/puzzle games, but in this case I think it simplified the gameplay aspect a bit too much.Visually it looks great. I did get stuck a few times where I could not move or some mechanism got permanently blocked, but loading the latest autosave always cleared that up. It’s still a decent exploration/puzzle game, but you’ll probably be a bit disappointed if you’re used to Cyan’s earlier titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, it feels like Cyan and plays like Cyan, introducing a new way to manipulate the world with a kind of power glove which connects to sockets in the world. This is probably best used with a VR controller in VR, but after some time you get used to controlling it with the keyboard. There are bugs, most of them expected when you allow free roaming physics puzzles, but there is a way to set the player to a safe spot if you get really stuck. The world is amazing, huge, well crafted as a we are used from Cyan, and the puzzles are nicely integrated in this world. If you love puzzles and don't care about occasional glitches, get it right away, or you can wait until Cyan patches the issues, which they will.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Firmament is a beautiful game, the worlds contain an interesting mix of steampunk machinery and art deco-style architecture embedded into visually stunning landscapes. The puzzles are generally fun to solve (minus one or two slightly tedious ones) and are mostly on the easier side, i never got stuck for more than a few minutes, as a fan of Cyan games i would have enjoyed a few harder ones but i understand that not everyone feels that way. The socket-based puzzle mechanic is a bit of a mixed bag for me, one one hand it provides an interesting set of new ways to interact with puzzles, on the other hand though it takes away from the exploration to a certain degree (if an area doesnt contain a socket theres not much reason to explore it further, which lead me to rushing through some areas quite often). Story-wise Firmament feels a bit weaker than previous Cyan titles such as Obduction, with only a bit of narration and a lot less environmental storytelling, a bit more depth and detail in this area would have been nice. I do have to say that the twist at the ending was excellent though. Overall the game felt relatively short compared to its predecessors, with a completion time of under 10h which is significantly less than Obduction, with that being said i still enjoyed the experience quite a lot and can definitely recommend checking it out, i just wish there was a little more if it.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember a few years after Myst IV was released a fan asked Rand Miller if he liked the game. Rand said something along the lines of "I've been doing the very first puzzle where you have to set the frequency right, and the game just kept telling me - Turn it a bit to the left... now a bit to the right... no that's far, a bit to the left - and I said to myself - Who can enjoy this? Who could think this can be enjoyable? - and I never bothered to play it ever again." Now, two decades later Cyan releases the game that is exactly that, essentially. A set of several dozens of valves and dials that you have to turn a bit to the left and then to the right, paying little attention to narrative, environments, progress, etc. Just hardcore valve swivelling. There was a little commotion on Steam forums after the game release with people complaining about the use of neural networks during the production of Firmament, after which Cyan released the statement describing exaclty what was made using AI. I can now understand what made people worried. The whole game feels like it was generated by an AI. It is totally lifeless, simulated, schematic. A perfectly sterile and abiotic puzzle-solving experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Sideways thumb.  Long time Myst fan, playing in VR.  Some stuttering but reasonably playable.The main problem is that there isn't really any story to speak of. _childDocuments_.review: I really tried to enjoy this game (Full disclosure, I backed it on Kickstarter), but in the end, Firmament is a disappointingly shallow game and a technical disaster, as well as a harsh reminder for Cyan that their approach to designing games no longer seems to be working with modern tech.Instead of intriguing and challenging puzzle design that Cyan are known for (and which Obduction delivered), the vast majority of puzzles involving gratuitous backtracking which, with pre-rendered backgrounds gone, translates to a lot of time being wasted with nothing to even ponder about due to the puzzles' simplicity.The physics of various machines also lead to either frustrating exercises in trial-and-error patience or to blatant game-breaking states (at the point of writing this review, I got a certain crane stuck in terrain, with no way to move it out of its state).The only plus I can give to Firmament is the world building which has historically always been one of Cyan's strength and continues to be one. This one upside however does not justify buying this game imo.

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament - When Karl Marx results in tragedy and death. Accurate on that count, in fiction and real life. I have a few observations.Puzzle Mechanics - I know we're supposed to suspend disbelief to a certain extent, but I kept running up against the "clever to be clever" design philosophy here. What is CTBC? Its when you construct a puzzle with some needless steps that make zero sense, only to prolong playtime. To be fair, Myst had a rather insane puzzle with that underground pod-on-rails that wasn't so great, but this game takes that idea and expands on it. Did you hate the "maze" puzzle in Obduction? Oh boy, you're gonna LOVE these.Assets/Design - There are landscapes that look really good, but its Unreal Engine and that is one of its strengths, so I'm not surprised. What did surprise me was the asset re-use that kept happening. A more cynical observer would say they designed all these "Spires" and "Arches" in such a way that it was conducive to not designing unique things for each realm. Maybe I'm spoiled, Myst and Riven had unique areas riffing on a common theme, but for some reason that was out of scope for this game. (No, making one frozen ice and the other a verdant green landscape doesn't count.)Another design oddity, for instance, on the scaffold/paths used in the Sulfur/Acid pit level, I noticed that there was a 'good enough' thing going on where no intermediate joining pieces were made, just slapped together because who cares, right? Well, as a backer I CARE. And again, I recall Riven making things have a coherent design sense, so maybe I'm expecting too much - but it grates at me. If you're going to take the time to world-build, why not flesh out the details that is what made these games so good? Also, the effect of the acid discharging from the storage tank into the pond beyond had such a wide radius, that it undermined the visual 'anchor' of the storage retaining wall. It just made it look like a floating non-interacting piece, which killed the immersion.Don't get me started on the "Seed Vaults" - you can open every single door and it really doesn't make much of a difference, other than a way to slow you down on the tram bits. And the growing platform things inside, some have full circle paths and some not - and I get this to set up the puzzle, but why not add details that make it seem embedded to the world? Some could have had paths sheared off, decayed, rusted, broken - whatever. Just some effort beyond "Hey this one just happens to have a quarter circle of path around it, nudge, nudge, wink" to it. It just smacks of lets-get-this-done-and-push-it-out, so I don't know who to blame, the art director, the producer or the people at the top, but I noticed.I know, at this point the people who love everything Cyan will counter with "where's YOUR game, huuuuuuh!?" - and I'll respond that if you ask for money, you are setting certain expectations. Your entire game catalog sets these expectations. If you meet that bar or exceed it, great. If you flail around and produce something that doesn't, someone will notice. I did. If it was free, I wouldn't care. But it wasn't.Voiceovers - This isn't directed at the voice actress, a gig is a gig, after all. I just couldn't take this seriously after a while. I started to dread it, because I explored every corner, (and accidentally got every mentor convo achievement), she just kept going on and on. After a while I started mocking it when it started, because a french accent sounding like you're tripping hard on shrooms isn't the best choice stylistically.Lets talk about that announcer guy. Again, a gig is a gig so I'm glad someone got paid. But to hear the dialog barked out with stunners such as -  "We eat", followed by other similar quotes over and over in these levels didn't make me think "gosh, great story and world building - please, repeat this again so I can break into a wide smile". No, it made me think that if these people were so stupid they needed some male robotron reciting their creed over and over, they were no better than fleshy robots, which made me care for them even less.Sure, making games isn't easy. Which is precisely why if you are going to bother to do it, you should pay attention to details. I saw some models with badly repeating UVs, for instance on narrow parts. That shouldn't happen if you're trying to produce quality and not just shove it out the door.I'd add that in this kind of game, which is explorer/puzzle based, its even more important, because people are not going to be running by at breakneck speed to the exit. They're going to look, and look pretty closely at what you made. Especially if you charge for it.Some final gripes - I supose "spoilers" but whatever.The story says the "Embrace" is a method to shift all the realm pods/domes/whatever to a configuration that allows the vessel to do whatever burn maneuver to shed speed before their final destination.I just had to laugh. Your OWN STORY says that the gravity was produced by spin, and now you're just going to fold up all that and have every single water filled reservoir, acid pit and caustic battery enclosure just fly around these carefully constructed environments willy-nilly in huge globules, with the acid probably burning the living eff out of the plants and everything else.In the end, when I got to the skeleton sitting in the chair, I just wanted to be able to shift that bag of bones on the floor so I could at least enjoy the view before the end. No luck there.I also wonder how the other backers felt when the credits came up, rotatiing at a brisk clip, about 2 seconds a page, where it made it nearly impossible to even point and say "oh there I am", to yourself or a friend if they were watching. I guess it was too much to ask for a mechanism where there was a user-interruptible credit crawl, or a Myst-like device in a small room where you could peruse it at your liesure.But like other things, I guess it was just a step to far. Eff it, lets shove this sucker out.I wish I could say I will support you in the future, but honestly, my willingness to do so is at the bottom of the ice cube mines.

_childDocuments_.review: Like other Cyan titles,  is a beautiful game with fun puzzles and a deeply unsatisfying ending.*  was released with more than its fair share of glitches (I lost my progress once due to a failed save, and I had one puzzle fail to resolve until I restarted), but Cyan seems to be taking patching seriously, so I won’t ding them there. Ultimately, I had fun and found the length to be well matched to the scope of the socket-only interface, which is not particularly deep but does a great job keeping exploration from becoming a grinding search for hidden switches and buttons.  also improves upon some past Cyan games’ tendency to make the player walk for minutes just to test out an idea. _childDocuments_.review: BRAVO!!!!!!!!MYST was the first PC game I ever played, back in 5th grade, and it made me nag my parents to get a PC. Since then I've played every MYST game and MYST-like Cyan game. I didn't back Firmament on Kickstarter, I basically let it fly under the radar for me. As soon as I got the email it was out, I dropped everything else I was doing and started playing.What a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ masterpiece. This is better than Obduction and End of Ages. Is it as good as Riven? Maybe...? A modern, slightly more accessible Riven? I mean, god, I just finished the game and my face is wet with tears. It was beautiful. I usually get stumped in games like this, but I felt so immersed and aware of my surroundings that I was able to figure out every puzzle organically just by using my common sense. That felt really good.The story and world building in this is fantastic and incredibly immersive. It's feels a bit like an immersive sim, something like Prey, Bioshock, System Shock 2, in that it really forces you to be aware of your environment and what tools you have available to you. The game trains you really well to recognize opportunities to use your tools and it just felt really organic and natural to me throughout.It's a shame the game seems to be having issues for so many people. I ran into two issues:- At one point, I used a Conveyance Pod and ended up with a black screen, and loading the auto-save just loaded the black screen. Luckily, I had a second recent save and that one allowed me to keep going. After that, I just made a manual save before I used any Conveyance Pods, but I never had the issue again.- The infamous crane did glitch out on me. When I used the "unstuck" option in the menu, it not only unstuck the crane but mostly solved the puzzle I was trying to solve for me. That's okay, because I was seconds away from solving it myself, so it's not a big deal.Overall... a masterpiece. Honestly, Cyan, you've lived up to the legacy of your name. Kudos, bravo, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is quite short. It feels notably shorter than Obduction. You will definitely spend wayyy less time than one whatever early Myst games.That said, and even if it clearly isn't the "comeback game of Cyan on the Godlike level of Myst" I wish it would be,it shows without doubt that Cyan Worlds still got the spark of creativity.To be very honest, the whole lore doesn't really keep together long, but I relaly don't mind it because : - the game never pretended it would ;- it is an inventive narrative concept ;- it is audacious and fun, and the internal logic is holding great.It's good fiction. Fiction is not always plausible down to the last screw. I relaly like the ending, especially the way it is constructed and how you slowly, step after step, understand what is going on.I will, once again, wait for their next game eagerly. For years, probably.About the puzzle side of the game : Puzzes are really not that hard, I would have like a bit more difficulty but it works and is enjoyable.Hard Myst or Riven fans are probably going to think the game is "very easy" but I feel like for a wider audience it is enjoyable as well.It can feel a bit linear but I believe this is simply because it's well built, and you easily understand where you need to go next.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played through the entirety of the game and while there are bugs, there also things in the game to help get around bugs really quickly if you get soft locked.Before I say anything else, I played through Myst, Riven, Exile, Obduction and finished most of Revelation. I love the Cyan Wolrds games. Riven is by far the best game and my favorite, with Obduction as a close 2nd, and the others evenly tied for third.That being said, I loved this game. The puzzles were really fun and I thought they were as interesting as most Myst puzzles. I don't understand why other people thought the puzzles weren't complex when the reality is that they definitely were. I think people are turned off by the idea of Sockets - instead of using machines like you normally would in Myst games, there's a socket system that lets you know what you should interact with. Makes it less about finding the thing you're suppose to play with more about figuring the solution to the puzzle in front of you.The twist (which I won't spoil) in this game was really good too. I really enjoyed the story progression and how everything played out. I wasn't expecting it either which was a nice surprise.That being said, there's bugs I ran into but teleporting to last safe location always fixed it. You can wait for Cyan to patch or you can just play, and have to reset every once in awhile. Thankfully, teleporting resets specific things that are needed for multiple puzzle solutions and doesn't reset your progress in game. I only ran into two different pieces I opreated that became stuck or bugged - and their reset patterns were quick.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't hate Frimament, but I don't love it. Like Obduction, Firmament is spiritually a Myst game. Unlike Obduction or the better Myst titles, the puzzles in Firmament are generally uninspired and *very* simple, which results in a short game. The architecture and overall aesthetic is fine and make for some nice screen captures but, with a single exception near the beginning, nothing truly astonished me or gave me pause during play. The novel way in which the player interacts with the puzzles was a risk. I don't think it paid off but it could have with some deeper puzzles. As implemented it's shading into gimmick territory. I ran into a game breaking puzzle state bug and from what I've seen around Steam I'm not alone. I have confidence these will be fixed and there have already been two patches as of 05/24. I also ran into a handful of physics engine/graphical glitches that, while not gameplay-impacting, are hard for me to overlook considering how few moving parts the overall package has.I rarely write reviews on Steam and I realize this one may come across as though I'm just dumping on Cyan. This isn't my intention. I'm a big fan of the genre and previous titles from Cyan and Rand Miller in particular. Taken in a vacuum, Firmament is *fine*. My criticism stems from the knowledge that Cyan has done better and the belief that they could do better. Firmament is just kind of a misfire for me. If you like adventure games, buy Firmament when it goes on sale by which point any critical bugs will likely be patched out. Otherwise, I can't immediately recommend it at launch.

_childDocuments_.review: *review contains spoilers that are blacked out* Ugh man. This is tough. I love Cyan. Riven is one my most favorite games of all time. Those early Myst games were so intriguing, creative, and very challenging. Hidden pathways/buttons, weird mechanical contraptions, interesting creatures, mind-bending ideas/concepts, over-compassing epic puzzles, and constantly getting stuck and feeling like there is no way forward. Then when you have lost all hope and you want to give up... you figure it out. And that feeling is incredible -- that is the Myst franchise experience. Even Myst III (Presto Studios) and Myst IV (Ubisoft) kept up those same aspects quite well, considering they were not even developed by Cyan.Obduction, their 2nd most recent game, yet again; held true to the fabric of the Myst franchise and gave us a large amount of interesting, weird, creative, and difficult puzzles.  Here we are now: Firmament. I've been waiting for this game for years. The trailers for the game are beautiful and they gave me goosebumps. Sadly they revealed pretty much all of the locations/realms. It kind of killed the "wow" factor a bit. This is an issue Hollywood has sometimes -- trailers that show too much.Firmament fails tremendously. I feel horrible for saying that and thinking that. I don't want it to be true -- I don't want that to be my opinion because of how much I love Cyan, but it is how I feel. Here's a summary of the game without spoilers: Adjunt (move) this, adjunt that, and adjunt that thing over there. Adjunt this platform, adjunt that platform, and adjunt that other platform over there. Game Over.Now a summary with spoilers: Why does this game fail, tho? The game lacks puzzle creativity and interactive variety. The positives of the game are yes; the environments are beautiful. And also a lot of architecture in Firmament resembles Riven. And even though most of the puzzles are the same style, some did have me stumped for a while, not sure what to do next. And true to Cyan games, as well; they were rewarding once you figured it out after being stumped. However the negatives outweigh the positives heavily.It makes me sad; because, like I said, I love Cyan. This is a miss. I still look forward to their next game.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimers: I backed this on Kickstarter; I haven't finished the game. I wanted so badly to love this game. Unlike some players, I haven't had any bugs that interrupted my gameplay (though some textures got glitchy at times). I think I'm about halfway through the game. But I don't really want to finish it. Myst was not just one of my very first computer games but also one of my earliest experiences with mystery and wonder. When I played Riven it felt like discovering that that feeling of mystery could be even deeper and somehow maintained even with an understanding of its structure. Basically I've played a bunch of Cyan games and enjoyed them. Obduction (which I also backed) wasn't mind-blowing, but I enjoyed it and even played it through a few times for friends. I backed Firmament on Kickstarter because my past experiences were so positive. I don't mind waiting for games, and I pretty much ignored all the backer updates because I like to go into stuff fresh. Firmament feels stale. Like it's a remaster of a game that came out a decade or more ago--the visuals are crisp and beautiful, but they're laid over puzzles and structures that feel kind of empty and bland. Aside from your sci-fi socket wrench, there are a small handful of books you can read, and that's it. No touching any of the carefully designed objects in carefully laid-out rooms (which also constantly repeat the same assets). No variation in movement, which is often frustrating and janky (hope you like getting stuck on tiny, invisible corners). Again, haven't finished the game, but all the puzzles so far have been tedious variations on moving objects back and forth to get to the end of a linear path. There's no interesting meaning to what you're doing, there's no implied story, no real culture behind the actions (as there was in Riven, for instance). You just do the puzzle because it's the thing you have to do next to progress the game. What little story there is so far is not so much implied through environments and exploration as hammered at you by a narrator with an awkwardly shifting accent who talks with the kind of Big, Vague Trope Names that sound portentous but are ultimately a cover for weak writing. I kinda want to finish the game, but from talking & reading about it, I feel like if I do, I'm just going to be more disappointed. More sliding-things-around puzzles with a fancy, touchy socket hand. More potentially interesting environments that might as well functionally be blank walls, because there's no meaningful connection between the puzzle structures and the place you're supposed to be inhabiting. What the hell happened?! I hope we can get some fascinating in-depth documentary at some point, because this isn't the kind of thing I expect from Cyan. I will fall all over myself to talk about the interesting things that Myst and Riven do. I will probably also fall all over myself to convince my friends not to bother with this game. And that kinda breaks my heart.
