_childDocuments_.review: Not a backer so I'm not here to shill out my huge recommendation, but Firmament is fun. It's exactly what you would expect from a puzzle exploration game.4 years in the making though? Yikes. I was able to finish it in under 6 hours but i recognize that I'm the kind of person who is very good with games like this and if you're familiar with game mechanics that force you to use all of your tools, you'll breeze through Firmament.The hardest part about the puzzles is not figuring out how to do them, it's what the pieces mean and how they connect, but it gives you some sense of confidence when you complete each one, despite being pretty easy to figure out because the game gives you almost zero direction, which is a good thing in my opinion.The visuals are stunning. It's definitely an entertaining play, but if you're like me, this game is going to be a walking simulator with some lightweight puzzle solving.I wouldn't say it's worth the full price, but it's definitely worth getting on sale and i had fun while playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I've felt compelled to review a game on here. I grew up playing the Myst games and am a big fan of this mostly extinct genre. I thought Obduction was a strong come back for the legendary studio after some questionable releases and quiet years. I'm sorry to say Firmament is a miss, though it has it's moments and a healthy amount of Cyan DNA.The first harbinger of things to come is the logo, in brass texture, looking like a big steaming pile of caca. Someone in development must have thought about this and said nothing. I wish they would have. The second is the incessant disembodied voice delivering the same assortment of empty, simplistic slogans in an irritating tone for what turns out the be the entire game. Sadism is the only explanation I have for this, because it does nothing to advance the story or sense of emersion.Many of my complaints stem from a lazy Mac port. It needs to be stressed that Riven, a Cyan game from 1997, looks substantially better than this game does on a modern Mac machine. I recently played the new Psychonauts game and it both looked great and performed seamlessly, so I know it is possible to deliver for Mac in 2023. For reference, I'm on a one year old M1 Macbook Pro. I very quickly had to reduce the quality settings to keep this game from breaking, and still experienced painfully slow frame rates in the underwater portion. (They also rendered the bendy water effect over the inside of the dry suit, smdh...) I continued to experience glitchy lighting effects, clipping and dull scenery throughout the game. I wouldn't have minded a retro click-through mode just to experience the environments as they were meant to be seen.The artwork itself is fine, even gorgeous at times, but over-all felt like a phoned in Myst style universe (as well as story line.) There isn't really any advancement style-wise, only nostalgia with reduced inspiration. Don't get me wrong, the iconic digital revolution meets art nouveau aesthetic is a big part of why I continue to play these games, and it's something I missed in Obduction, but I've come to expect more winding pathways and unpredictable environments than this game could deliver. Early on there is a wall of what is supposed to be different people who signed their name, all in exactly the same script. How difficult would it have been to ask the staff to each write a character's name, or at the very least attempt to imitate more than one style of writing? This felt laughably unfortunate. Add to this many repeat and/or ai generated assets and you get a feeling the studio stopped caring after a point.The plot remains muddy up to the anticlimactic end. The nature of your spirit guide's existence and how she is speaking to you is not explained. Her presence, and the feeling she is always watching, detracts from the serene sense of isolation that made these titles famous among introverts. You get the sense in the beginning that the story will be slowly revealed slowly as you turn up clues, but no, just vague gesturing to people you don't know and some sort of troubling event that led to your being here. Her speaking to you instead of leaving notes serves no narrative purpose and is pretty confusing.The puzzles felt tedious and I solved most by fidgeting before I could or wanted to fully understand the underlying mechanism. I don't mind Cyan experimenting with the "socket" dynamic but found it deeply disappointing that the player can't interact with any physical objects besides the sockets, save for a very scarce amount of cheap AI-generated copy. Some of the many charms of the Myst games are the enthralling doo-dads that serve as sly hints for forthcoming puzzles, as well as the story-rich texts that make the worlds feel real. There are no hints in this game besides some ugly technical schematics on a few walls that you probably won't need.My biggest gripe with Firmament is this: There should never be a puzzle that relies on an obstacle that could be easily bypassed by the average healthy and upright individual with a simple side-step, hop or climb-over. This is a concept Cyan has always understood to my memory. This game seems to delight in creating these scenarios. It completely breaks the emersion and is utterly bizarre.The game is fairly short and ends abruptly. After finishing the three known realms you are taken to what looks like the set-up for a final act and at least one more head-scratcher. But no, you pass through this section with jarring ease and Finally, I'll opine on Cyan's controversial use of AI...their response to the criticism felt defensive and failed to address issues of plagiarism and corner-cutting. There are plenty of talented artists who could have drawn those lame wartime propaganda inspired banners, and plenty of living, breathing English men who could have irritated me for fourteen hours. I understand machine learning has a place in game development, but it sounds like it was used in all the wrong ways. We want games with feeling and we want to know they aren't relying on cheap amalgamations of the fruits of other people's artistic labor. Reading a "book" in a Cyan game is the last place I want to detect notes of Chat GPT. I very much hope they'll refrain from using AI, especially for artwork, dialogue or text, in future titles.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to play Cyan games in VR. Unfortunately, they are unplayable because of bugs and usability/design issues. This isn't the first time, either -- Myst suffered from the same issues. In the first 5-10 minutes of Firmament you'll struggle to figure out how to open the menu (you must hold B on the left controller, but don't you dare squeeze the controller at all). The menu itself hides the laser pointer, so it's very difficult to navigate and select what you want. There's a graphical bug where distant fog and nearby light renders with the wrong depth, which is very disorienting. I finally limped my way to the solution to the first puzzle, but  I was trapped!That was the last straw. I'll tolerate visual glitches and I can suffer my way through bad UI, but when the game itself starts to break, I've got to call it. I really hope these things get better, though. Cyan, if you read this, please play test your games more in VR.

_childDocuments_.review: Waited literal years for this to come out, but unfortunately I cannot recommend in it's current state...game looks great and is running ok, but ended up glitching out of the world and borked my autosave and lost some progress....SAVE OFTEN!!!....also saw some major pop in where an entire section of the world did not load until I went all the way through a door...so far the puzzles seem as well thought out as expected from Cyan and the environments look beautiful...cant really speak on the story just yet as I havent got far enough to really uncover, but I am confident it will be really well done...havent tried VR yet, but based on reviews so far, i'll hold off until its more stable...after a few patches, ill update my review if these issues are fixedUPDATE: Beat the game...first, the devs really fixed a lot of issues, I didnt see anymore pop in, unloaded areas or falling through the floor glitches the rest of the playthrough, so kudos there...that said, I did still get one more hard crash that killed the game, and the main menu was bugged after the end credits.....but that is ok, and is forgivable as these kinds of bugs happen...however, I still cannot truly recommend the game....the rotary crane in Curievale is broken in a way that can soft lock the game, and it happened to me many many times (thankfully I had a save) before I got to the final solution...I understand there is a teleport to safe space, but the fact that the thing can get completely stuck is bad design in the first place...also the game is quite short and the puzzles are relatively easy as almost everything revolves around looking for a place to use the Adjunct, which eliminates so much of what the older games brought, which often required more exploration, reading (of which there is almost none in this game) and an actual understanding of the world to solve the puzzles....additionally the story ends up lacking as there is very little outside the cryptic narrations to tie everything together until the very end, where I still have questions (unsure if there are multiple endings or thats it)....lastly, it does not translate to VR well, even though I thought it was meant to be a VR title first and foremost, as basically no objects in the game have physics or can even be inspected and there are no buttons/levers/switches etc, to give it a tactile feeling, again, everything is pretty much done with the Adjunct...overall, its not even that it is a bad game, i'm just disappointedtldr: environments are beautiful, puzzles are easy although well-designed (except for the Curievale crane) due to using only one main mechanic, game is fairly short overall (my Steam time is not indicative of total game time, i started over after a few hours due to bugs/glitches and left game running for a bit at one point), story leaves a bit to be desired and bugs are prevalent, albeit much improved since launch, so if you do play, SAVE OFTEN....not a terrible game, im just disappointed more than anything

_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I am sad to say that this game is just okay. The expectations for Cyan games are high no doubt, but the writing in this one was just not strong. There was to little to read and almost nothing connecting the playable story to the overarching one. Only in the last 20 minutes or so did we learn anything of importance. I usually expect a lot of environmental storytelling, but was disappointed when the worlds mostly contained keeper-propaganda with nothing much added to it. Some positive things: The gameplay itself is absolutely fine and I like how the implemented the tool thingy. The atmosphere is nice, even if the worlds are a bit empty. We can see nice vistas and a lot of detail in the different styles of the worlds wich was always nice. So the classic Cyan feeling of abandoned mysterious places did work afterall. The elephant in the room of course is the fact that they used AI-assisted writing for parts of the game and it shows. The few texts you can find in the worlds are basically irrellevant to understand the relatively obvious story and its "twist". In Obduction Cyan showcased what they can do, it was amazing! But Firmament dissapointed me. Beside the fact, that AI writing is usually terrible there are countless reasons why no one should use it to replace actual artists. You all know the reasons. I'm sure they know that this game was not their best ant thats fine. I just hope they take a few lessons away from the outcome and do better next time. I will buy their next one as soon as it comes out.Sad but hopeful.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate giving a Cyan game a thumbs down, but I'm going to have to give this one a thumbs down (especially as a kickstart contributor). It really missed the mark on storytelling and world-building, and eschews "show, don't tell" almost completely with a bunch of tedious puzzles, reused assets, and barely any plot revealed through disembodied dialogue. The core game mechanic becomes "meh" after a few hours.There's also the glitchy graphics and physics (I got stuck at one point and had to reload a save).Much preferred Obduction... or The Witness, Quern, or especially Outer Wilds.

_childDocuments_.review: The one sentence version: It's fine. _childDocuments_.review: NOT GREAT BUT NOT BAD, JUST MEHVery disappointed TBH. It was, riven and myst that i found my love for these puzzle games and i have played my fair share of them since. I didn't get excited about this one as i wanted to, mainly as i was disappointed with there last game obduction.I could not connect to this world/s, as i did with myst and especially riven, it felt very soulless.The musical score, the world ambience, is what really gets me sucked into a world. _childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game, but with a warning that the storytelling is a bit different than other Cyan games. (I was a backer of this game)Having just finished the game, I was truly awe-inspired by the "final act" ... "HERE'S the story!" I thought... after wondering what the heck was going on for weeks... which seems to have been by design.  Unfortunately, the effect is that the appreciation for the game, the story, comes so late in the game that there's no where left to really explore.The game does feel short.  The story does feel less whole than Obduction, for example.  It lacks the investigative element of all Cyan's other games, where you encounter journals, or clues to events, objectives, or characters' lives.  Some puzzles I was totally frustrated by, and others that I was totally engrossed by (that cold, underwater one I loved).  There are some really innovative puzzles/mechanics here, but perhaps because of that newness, they can sometimes feel a little chaotic and frustrating. The environments are beautiful, but somehow feel "washed out" - I'm not sure exactly why.  The architecture and design of the worlds and location are really wonderful. The music was great, but it seemed non-existent for long stretches of the game.Without the copious notes and journals and other artifacts to examine, as in Cyan's other games, it feels difficult to engage emotionally with the world.  Still, it's a world and story worth exploring, and Cyan put a hell of a lot of time, design, expertise, etc, into it.  And it's still better than 99% of the games you can find on Steam, so I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the first Cyan game I've completed in full without looking at a walkthrough even once, whether that's a good or bad thing is the reader's decision to make.  While it still has moments that evoke the charm of previous Cyan titles, it's also on the shorter side at 8-10 hours to complete.Amidst quibbles like occasionally clumsy controls, getting stuck in terrain mesh more than once, an unresponsive puzzle element that required a restart, and my computer churning out heat like an industrial furnace in certain areas, there's still a perfectly serviceable environmental puzzle game paired with a decently-executed story.Caveats aside, Cyan managed to get a VR-First game delivered during a pandemic, which is quite the feat unto itself.  While there was clearly a larger vision constrained by that reality of pandemic, Firmament is still a decent effort and worth picking up at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid narrative puzzle experience from the creative minds at CYAN. It's somehow more streamlined and more obtuse than other offerings. Mostly due to supporting VR and classic controllers at the same time. This mean that most of the interactions are done with a hand stand-in. The targeting for this could use a bit of QA, and the constant use of shoulder buttons and the D-pad made many interactions ESPECIALLY vehicles a bit of a chore. The level design also artificially pads somewhat with areas that require a lot of superfluous back and forth. That said: everything else was an absolute delight. Cyan is on top game with the writing and with the world design. Some puzzles were a bit tricky, but I managed the full 8 hours without any hints. The playtime is also just right to balance engagement and interest. Very happy I played it, and you probably will be too.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I am surprised by all the negative reviews. I enjoyed the game play, completing the game is a couple of days. I had one problem getting stuck on a rock in the first hour. I loaded patch 1 and the problem was resolved. After that game play was straight forward. As always with Cyan games, the views are spectacular. I am playing on a high-end system with a late gen 20 core processor, an NVidia 4080 gpu, and lots of ram. I experienced no lags or other issues. Not into VR, so I am playing on an OLED monitor. There are a few frustrating sections in the game play. Most notably the underwater, melting the ice section. Since I did this one first, I didn't have the same level of frustration by the end of the game that some players have reported. I would recommend completing the ice world first or second. Some users have complained that the story is unclear, vague, or otherwise hard to understand. One of the points of the game, much like Cyan's previous works, is that you don't know what is going on in the world. Part of the challenge is to figure it out. [Possible Spoiler]I have watched 6-7 persons finish the game and have noticed. During the last world, while unlocking a door and passing through, there are some historian documents on the left of the path. Almost to a person, as the players are so frustrated, they walk right past the historian documents thus depriving themselves an important part of the back story that explains the entire keeper world in some detail. Once you pass this area and move on through the next door, there is no way to return, short of reloading from a save, to get back to the area where the documents are located. While i consider it a shortcoming by Cyan that the world needs to be explained in a few pages of written documents at the end of the game, rather than some continuing aspect of the game providing the full story, at least the explanation is forthcoming. That is if you don't walk by it!I did support the game through kickstarter. Supposed to receive some physical materials, but so far nothing has arrived. Still everything I purchased was immediately available as digital content immediately online. Some might say I paid too much, but frankly, I would support Cyan again if they should decide to do another game. There are not enough smaller game developers and publishers in the world - they need our support.  In case you are wondering, I have no affiliation with Cyan - just a fan of their work. Hate it or Love it either way - play the game to completion yourself and form your own opinions.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to give this a mixed review. before I start I have top specs CPU and 4070 graphics card. Full working fan flow, liquid cooler and my CPU never gets over 41% (Just to clarify its not my hardware/software)This game is so buggy. The main title options screen, have no arrow when you point. You can hear it clicking, so you have to guess and hope you have hit the right option. If you don't you have to try again. You notice that instantly before game has even started.The game itself. Ifs a very similar MYST game, explore the worlds / realms. Alone solving puzzles. I have completed about 50-60 % so far. I cant lie I love games like this and have been loving this. That's until the bugs start to hit. From experimenting over the past week. It seems the long you play, the worse they get. After an hour or so gameplay, you can sense it getting slower and more jittery. especially traveling up and down in lifts. And there are a lot of them. It then gets to a point that you cant even run without it stuttering / jittering, the screen shaking. Its like the character is running in quick sand. Slow motion and painful in times. Some times you see the screen blink a couple of times like you cant move forward. Then suddenly you are 3 steps ahead. Bearing in mind you are travelling in some wide open spaces. If you chose the walk option it would take you forever and still buggy.I did think maybe it could be Virtual desktop throttling it after a while , or doing something. However I have played all my games through VD and never had this problem ever. That includes myst, expect you to die trilogy. 7th Guest. Fisherman's tale etc. I would say some scenes in some of these games are more demanding than walking across a field in this game. Yet never had anything wrong with them. Without a doubt this is the game itself. Which is so frustrating as I like it so much of what I played bug free.I am not going to go back into this until they get a fix. I would like to say I'll play it for an hour then stop and do that every so often. But there is no fun in that having to time and switch off. Plus the last time I tried to do that. _childDocuments_.review: I was sorely disappointed in this game. Speaking as a fan of Cyan's work from the original incarnation of Myst, I've become accustomed to their interesting world design, their mind-teasing puzzles, and their interesting characters. Sadly, the only bit of quality that has survived is their world design, and only just; it's pretty, but not altogether interesting. Each "realm" is an Earth-like sandbox that's incredibly limited in scope and focuses on a gimmick or two.The puzzles are very few and far between; the bulk of interactions can hardly be called "puzzles". Rather, you look for a slot to jam your tool into, give it a twist, and away you go. The interaction points are glaringly obvious and there are scant few instances when the answer isn't "find your way to plug that slot over there". When you find something more involved, it's all blind grasping at things without much feedback to tell you if you're on the right track or not, and in many case, you simply cannot see what you're moving around because you're stuck in a hole, tethered to a half-enclosed tower, or some other location that leaves you half-blind as you stumble through it.Of the three tool "enhancements", one is completely useless; it's impossible to tell which plugs need more 'torque', because they all appear the same. The enhanced length mod is just a gatekeeper to ward you away from the second half's puzzles. The "chaining" enhancement is the only one that actually makes things moderately interesting, but the number of times you need it for a non-obvious solution can be counted on one hand, with fingers to spare.The most egregious sin of all is the cast. I use the term lightly because there really is no cast. Like any good Myst-alike, you don't really run into people. And yet, like a fart that just continues to linger, you have a voice going on and on in your ear that thinks they're the most important thing in the room. The dialogue is hollow and banal, the acting itself is miserable, and the models are...passable, I suppose. Not good, of course; don't get me wrong. Nothing about this game can be considered "good" except for many of the visuals. The story was so awful that I was actively committed to pushing it out of my experience as much as possible; I turned the dialogue volume to 0 and let the subtitles fill me in on the important details. If I had to listen to that smug acting through the whole game, it would have resulted in a quick refund. Having finished it, that would have been the much smarter path.Cyan, you used to excel at blending art with wonder and wit. If this is what you feel proud of releasing after all this time, then I beg you: move on. Don't make me hate the company that gave me so much fun with the D'ni story.

_childDocuments_.review: “A captivating narrative with a twist you don’t see coming”After embarking on two playthroughs, I can confidently affirm that Firmament embodies all the classic hallmarks of its genre. While it may not stand as Cyan World's lengthiest title, it adheres faithfully to the tried-and-true formula that the studio is renowned for, echoing the legacy of games like Myst URU and Riven.Crafted on the Unreal Engine, Firmament stands out as one of the most visually stunning additions to Cyan's gaming repertoire. It seamlessly incorporates cutting-edge features such as DLSS and FSR support, elevating the overall gaming experience. Notably, the game has undergone significant optimization since its original release, contributing to a smoother and more enjoyable gameplay experience.If I were to voice a singular critique, it would be that the puzzles, albeit well-designed, tend to skew towards the easier side. It seems evident that this decision was made to broaden the appeal to a wider spectrum of players, striking a commendable balance. Nevertheless, as a seasoned veteran who has engaged with every title from Cyan since the age of 13, I found myself yearning for more complexity and depth in the puzzle dynamics.As for the narrative, without delving into specifics to avoid spoilers, I can assert that it stands among Cyan's most compelling writing, though it doesn’t quite rival the esteemed Myst franchise given firmament is but a single entry so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: It wasn’t an easy decision, but I decided that I cannot wholeheartedly recommend this game. I backed this game on Kickstarter as a long-time fan of Cyan games like Myst, Riven, and Obduction. These games defined for me how an immersive puzzle game should look like. Firmament just doesn’t live up to this standard.Is it a terrible game? No. After the latest round of bug fixes, it’s reasonably playable. But the puzzles are very streamlined, very localized, and most importantly, most of them just don’t make any sense. And besides those puzzles, almost nothing in this world is interactable.If you like puzzle games and this one goes on sale, there’s no harm checking it out. If you’re a fan of the old Cyan games, you will most likely be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: If you are into puzzle games, this one will appeal to you. Typical for the creator of the puzzle-game genre, starting with "Myst", CYAN has made this game another visual treat with its unique design elements, and engrossing narrative. It also has their usual 'mystery' aspect to it. As beautiful as the game is, however, be warned that some of the puzzles may take some time to solve, while others are relatively straight forward and completed quickly. Nice to see the studio still active after all these years, and look forward to more releases from them.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: OK! Got this thing cleared, let's review it!Hi, Rand Miller! I was one of those weirdo teenagers that grew up playing Uru Online and obsessing over the Myst quintology during class. I feel strongly that there is something very human and primal in the artistic visions you guys put out. I don't know how else to explain it. I really hope you take the words here and from others to heart -- we're fans for a reason and only want you to succeed.I did very much enjoy my time with Firmament, HOWEVER, Firmament as a technical game application did not enjoy me. Let's get the techie stuff out of the way first.- Multiple states where the UE engine would outright crash with a dialog box. The worst was at the very end! I had to swap to my Steam Deck just to finish the game! It was easy to tell when this would happen, because on the pause menu, the Save option would be greyed out. This was super annoying.- The ice cranes in Curievale are laughably easy to break. This needs another close look at, as they broke the most of any puzzles in my playthrough. Ice cubes can be dropped at odd clipping angles, and the crane can get stuck on odd geometry/clipping constantly. I had to use the 'Reset Position' feature at least 5 times to solve rotational crane puzzle. Not good! Additionally, I was able to cheese this puzzle by moving the bridge adjacent to the backwards-facing gate and opening it, instead of pulling up the ice cube blocking the path.- The 'invalid/error' noise from your Adjunct is way too loud compared to the other sounds in the game and needs tuned down.- Hitboxes for the ladders on the Curievale rotational ice crane are too big. Kept accidentally climbing it when trying to use the Adjunct right after descending the ladder.- Various odd clipping/pathing/hitboxes around the levels. Some breaks in the terrain mesh where you can see through.- Still very easy to softlock yourself on the Juleston rotational platforms by simply running to the edge when they're not connected.- LODs for some models suck. They constantly flicker between model versions regardless of my distance.Let's talk about the game!- The visuals here are top-notch. Cyan is very clearly approaching the threshold where real-time graphics in the UE engine will be able to match their 90's pre-renders, which is NUTS to me. I think this is most apparent in St. Andrew; absolutely gorgeous.- Same with the music! The tones fill the rooms and spaces beautifully.- I actually really liked the narrator once it got working! Stellar performance.- FMVs: I know some folks missed FMVs but honestly I couldn't care either way. I enjoy FMV's over models as a technical novelty but that's about it. Full 3D acted models are just fine.- Story/Lore: I'm of two minds here. Because of the ending, I actually feel this is one of Cyan's stronger narratives in their library. However, you're really waiting quite awhile for that payout. Honestly? I would take another pass at each of the worlds, and add some scattered lore and diary books, visual easter eggs, and other visual designs that people actually lived in these spaces. What were their hopes? Dreams? Fears? These are alluded to by the narrator; what were they? The Swan is the biggest offender -- show us who these named Keepers were. They're more than names painted on a wall. Where are the madman scrawlings in the corners of the bunkers; signs the Keepers may crack under pressure? You've gotta throw the lore nerds some red meat!- Additionally, there is quite a lot of asset reuse that becomes apparent. Maybe take another pass to differentiate the arch interiors and St. Andrew vaults a bit more.- I actually feel like the game length is juuuust about right. Maybe another puzzle or two on the ending act would've rounded things out, but not a big deal.- Puzzles were good! Once it became very obvious in the first world that the game was VR-oriented, I was able to work myself around the puzzles without too much issue. I liked that they weren't barbarically hard, but also not too easy either.- Camelus was great! Every Cyan game should have Camelus or an equivalent.At the end of the day, Firmament doesn't quite hit the scope of Obduction, but that's fine -- it carves its own space, and has its own story worth telling. But strictly speaking, as software, this does need quite a bit more work for the technical issues. I also hope someday Cyan will go back and flesh out the environments a little more.Cyan, we know you're going to knock Riven out of the park. You're obviously hitting your stride when realizing these complex environments in Unreal. They look amazing. BUT, take these feedback to heart, as you're still hitting growing pains in terms of the technical side. Firmament should not have been released in this state.If you are a Cyan fan: Get this game, but perhaps wait a few weeks for most of the technical issues to be smoothed over.

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament is a pretty good adventure-puzzle game. The environments are strange and beautiful and the puzzles are engaging. I wouldn't call any of them too hard, but at least one requires a bit of real-world knowledge that most people may not have, one was a little disorienting, and one was a little buggy (I expect they'll have it fixed soon though).The story covered some heavy themes and was necessarily a bit obtuse; I didn't always know whether or not information being withheld from me was on purpose or a bug, and I felt a little anxious at times not knowing what the results of my actions in the game were or whether or not it was something I wanted. Believe it or not, this is actually a good thing, and I think it enhanced my overall player experience in the end, which was a bit of a surprise.Overall, I have mixed feelings about Firmament. On the one hand, it doesn't entirely feel like Cyan at their best (but I may be biased by several other games in the genre coming out in recent years as emerging development tools have made making Myst-likes easier, and as a lifelong fan of Cyan's games, comparing Firmament to what they've made in the past). But on the other, it also feels like this may be a part of them getting their feet wet with new software and technology (as some of the puzzle interfaces feel very much designed for VR, and I played on PC), and I'm excited to support their next venture. Nevertheless I caught glimmers of Cyan's trademark wonder in different pockets of the game. I think how much you will enjoy this game depends a lot on you. If you enjoy 1st Person puzzle-adventure games like me, I'd say it was definitely worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit skeptical and did not expect much due to the mixed rating, but I was actually pleasantly surprised.It's not a bad game, although it is nothing special either. It is pretty short as there are only 3 (well, technically 4) worlds to solve and not much puzzles to go through, but I did enjoy exploring various environments and some puzzles were kind of fun.Graphically the game looks fine but it did not leave any deep impression on me. The music is the same, it does not impress nor offends. Just mid.As the story goes, it felt more like a afterthought than anything else. Some French gal who claims to be dead just keeps talking to herself for the entirety of the whole game and never shuts up. If I understood it correctly, you are supposed to learn from mistakes you don't remember making? It made no sense to me. Honestly, I feel like muting the dialog audio and disabling subtitles only improves the game.The controls are pretty meh and you cannot redefine anything. It seems to be heavily designed either for controllers or VR and they probably considered keyboard to not be worth any effort so take that in mind. At the very least there is a FoV slider.Long story short, it's not great and it's not terrible. It's playable, it's enjoyable, but I would not pay the full price for this. Wait for some sale if you're interested.

These elements, stitched together seamlessly, serve to stimulate the cerebral faculties in a manner few other experiences can match.This exemplary standard set by Cyan is what I had anticipated from 'Firmament', and it pains me to express that the game scarcely managed to deliver to these expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those cases where I wish there was a middle thumb option for a rating, but while I do recommend the game, that recommendation comes with some big caveats. For anyone who likes first-person environmental puzzle games, it’s pretty solid. For anyone who is a fan of the Myst games like myself, this is easily Cyan’s weakest effort in that genre.Good stuff first. The visual presentation is excellent throughout. The graphics aren’t photorealistic but the quality is there and it makes a great first impression. Controls are simple, with both a keyboard and mouse setup as well as a controller. As for the puzzles, none of them are particularly hard and ultimately amount to figuring out which things need to be activated for you to progress. Turn on the power, open doors, etc.All of this is likely nothing you haven’t seen before, but I was okay with that kind of familiarity. There’s also a rather generous autosave as well as the ability to save anywhere, which I would highly recommend (more on that later). And while I was stumped a few times, this isn’t a long game, which for this genre is a blessing.But as I played, the issues piled up. As I said above, I’m a huge fan of the Myst games, and this is a far cry from those efforts. While the visuals are strong, the music is unremarkable. There’s nothing here that mimics the somber tones of Myst’s Ages or Riven’s consistently haunting melodies. The setting itself is also rather bland. Concrete buildings and metal railings are everywhere and there’s little to differentiate different locations. And while there are references to other people, the game is entirely empty and doesn’t feel at all lived in. It feels sterile.And speaking of references to people, one of the two biggest issues with the game is the Mentor, a character you briefly see right at the beginning who serves as a sort of narrator throughout, and boy does she have a lot to say. She talks frequently, including every time you enter a new area, and she tells you about people and names and organizations using in-universe jargon and you have no clue what she’s talking about. It simultaneously destroys any hope of immersion, usually a strength of this genre, and only serves to confuse you.There’s a story here, but it’s very poorly told, and the above Mentor speaks like you’re supposed to know everything already, which brings me to this game’s second big problem: there’s no “why.” You simply are a person in a place walking around, turning power on, solving puzzles. You don’t have a mission, you don’t know why this place is important, or why you’re bothering to progress. In contrast, take Riven, arguably Cyan’s best game. In Riven’s first 5 minutes, you learn Atrus’s father is evil, he’s kidnapped Atrus’s wife, you’re going to an Age that’s unstable, it’s not safe, and you aren’t alone. Excellent, compelling purpose for the player. There’s none of that here and I was constantly asking what the point of all this was.I should also note that the game does have quite a few bugs still, despite the updates. I fell through the floor a few times and one puzzle bugged completely, which confused me greatly until I reloaded an old save (like I said above, save often). In spite of all the bad, if this genre is your jam, I would still give it a cautious recommendation on sale, but for the players out there expecting another Myst or Riven-esque effort from Cyan, this will be a significant disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Another CyanWorlds game! Can't believe it's been seven years since Obduction was released.I'm a bit conflicted about this game. With Firmament, Cyan presents us an absolutely beautifully crafted world with (positively) interesting creative choices unlike anything I've seen before (but simultaneously with very clear influences), incredible environments, lighting and sound. More often than I can count I've just stood there admiring the landscape. And unfortunately, pretty visuals and cool aesthetics are pretty much the best part of what the game has to offer. In the 'gameplay' aspect, it's a bit lacking, especially if compared to Obduction. I would like to compare this to earlier Cyan games, but that's a completely different development team with an entirely different budget, so that might not be a fair comparison. For one, the puzzles are....different. It's probably the first Cyan game where I've never really felt like picking up a notebook, scribbling down little maps, symbols and drawings of puzzles. As for puzzles: Firmament gives you a handheld tool (the Adjunct) to manipulate so-called 'sockets' within range. The Adjunct lets you enable/disable machines, open/close doors, and generally serves as the single method of interaction. Sockets are sometimes blocked by movable objects, out of range, or require upgrades to the Adjunct to activate. In the former cases, the puzzles essentially revolve around getting these sockets in an accessible position so you can manipulate whatever is attached to them. In the latter case, the puzzles cannot be completed without the upgrades, so you first should go elsewhere to get these upgrades. Where this elsewhere is isn't mentioned, though.The manner in which these puzzles are used are fairly varying, but they all share one common factor: They're . In fact, they're more tedious than , and sometimes hard to envision as there's no good way to see the whole puzzle at once. It's a little like a jigsaw puzzle where you only can see two pieces at once. There's also a fair deal of backtracking involved during these puzzles, though at the end you can usually open a path straight to the start and activate a teleporter destination so it's easy to move around the world. The environments the puzzles are in are very well-crafted and look amazing, but the puzzles themselves could use a little more variation. It's usually either "move objects to uncover a socket" or "move machines to get to new location". I wish the Adjunct/Sockets mechanic was just one of a few different mechanics instead of the single way you interact with the world. It feels much more like a Portal-style game than the point and click puzzler games they've made previously. This isn't bad, and I do think it's a good thing to explore other avenues, but the end result doesn't work well for the entire duration of a game. The overall realm 'completion' mechanics are also a bit too straightforward; in every realm it's the same general idea: restore power/resources to the area in one way or another, go to Big Building, get an Adjunct upgrade and activate a tower. In terms of sockets, it's basically "activate socket, get cool visual'' over and over again. Besides that, the world feels a little empty. There are puzzles, but the density of puzzles is much lower than ie. Obduction, and the amount of lore notes to read is shockingly low. So far I've found about ten at most, of which half aren't even lore related but mostly relevant to the puzzle near which they're located. To make up for this, a large part of the game is narrated by a "ghost" that pops up at certain locations. I have to admit that when I first played the game, there was a bug where the narrator showed up exactly once and then never again, so until that was patched I just didn't get any more info on the story of the game. I can't say too much about this narrator due to this, but this should now be patched.From the bits of lore I did get from the narrator, lore notes and game world, I can say the story definitely is original and interesting, but I'm missing a lot of context. I should mention that despite missing most of the lore I can complete the puzzles just fine, so if you're not interested in reading lots you can still play Firmament without issue. Without lore context it might feel a little weird though: why am I doing all these puzzles?Due to the semi-linear playstyle of the game, the narrator often makes vague comments related to the location you're in and drip feeds you lore, instead of telling a linear story. A downside of a narrator mechanic like this is that you can't really go back to re-read a note to look for clues or more information on the story. The audio played, and it won't repeat.Having the ability to either recall audio or to read a transcript somewhere in a travel log would have been great. It's noticeable that QA focused on playing the game through the intended paths as much as possible and didn't really have time for making sure any unintended interactions were covered up. It signals "rushed", as it's likely meant sure as many players as possible can make it through the game without many issues. This is especially noticeable in one of the puzzles where you pilot a gigantic walking vehicle; the colliders cover the intended paths well, but walk into a cliffside just outside those paths and you'll find yourself clip through with no effort. There are also paths that visually signal "don't take this path, it's blocked", but if you actually try to walk over it, you can do so just fine. (I have sent a bug report, so chances are that this will be patched out soon, though!)In other puzzles involving vehicles (of which there are a few) it's currently quite easy to get them stuck, or to get around puzzles in unintended ways. This is also likely to get patched soon. One feature of the game that I do really appreciate is the "teleport to a safe spot" function; in case you get stuck due to bugs, this button teleports you back to a safe spot, and resets vehicles you were piloting as well in case they break or get stuck. It's a very helpful feature in a game that currently needs a little more patching. All things considered, I think Firmament IS worth its while if you can look past its flaws. It isn't perfect and currently has quite a few softlocks and bugs, so I hope those get patched soon.I would suggest waiting for a while until it's a couple patches further down the road. It is  a beautiful "walking simulator"-style game that might even be interesting for people who've liked Portal's puzzle style (minus the portal gun, of course). However, it's definitely not one of Cyan's most expansive games and definitely feels very short. Though if you're not an experienced puzzler this game might take you much more than 15 hours to complete. I'm wondering to which target audience Cyan is catering with this game, as it really seems to be a much "easier" game intended to be suitable for larger audiences, but which seems skip over their audience they have already established with their previous titles. I wish I could like this game more, but it's just not what I'd hoped it would be. I did enjoy playing it, but I think the visual quality far outweighs the quality of gameplay.With its current bugs fixed it still won't be a perfect game, but at least it'll be a lot less frustrating to play.Edit: very vague ending spoilers below.(I would like to write more but I've hit the character limit apparently, sorry!Continuing in the comments.)

_childDocuments_.review: I've grown up playing Cyan's games, and this is the first game I played all the way through without using hints and solutions for its puzzles (okay, actually one small hint in one particular area I really could not understand how to go about making progress on).This is credit to its great game design. After completing the game, I don't think that I missed much besides direction on what to do. I was continually asking myself 'why' I was doing what I was doing. The voice lines would have helped with that. Also, one particular puzzle, I didn't appreciate, had me looking for lights in cracks. I would have liked more non-puzzle interact-able objects to make it feel less like a set and more like a lived in environment, More time was needed to refine all parts of this game.  I do mean all parts, including the story. Maybe they will refine it more after release. All that in mind, If you make manual saves frequently, the core of a Cyan Worlds game is still there. Touch everything and figure things out. There was a lot wrong with this game but I had fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I kickstarted this game hoping it would live up to Cyan's other games, and in short it does not.The main stumbling point for me was how the story was presented, and how often I felt like there was no plot.  There was huge info dump in the last part of the game, and not enough story beats for most of the game to connect to it.  I honestly felt less connected to this than any Myst game I have played due to the lack of environmental story telling, books, and narration during most of the game.Now the game is beautiful and is fun to play.  I love the sound track, and the voice acting is good.  Also some of the puzzles are just fun to work.  But as others have said, this is very short game you can run through in one sitting.  Also most of the puzzles were easy enough that I was able to figure them out without much thought.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated review. I'm afraid I can't recommend this game, having switched from marginally positive to a marginally negative one.Bugs aside (which, to be fair, were quite minor in my experience & didn't bother me that much) it was just bit of a mixed-bag for me. _childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This is a leaning yes. It's not like I'd sit here and preach from the rooftops about this one.Firmament is, at its heart, I think a solid idea. The story is fairly basic, but it works, and puzzles are puzzle gamey. The sound and music design is very well done, and the voice acting is... about on par for Cyan games in general, so... not the best, but it works. Graphically the game's great.So why am I on the fence? Well, remember when I said puzzle gamey? About half of this game feels like a lived in area, where you're Myst puzzling your way past obstacles. They're not "there" per say, but you're getting around issues. And the other half is obtuse hunt and peck frustrating head scratching irritating obstruction, clearly for the sake of obstruction. It's not like Myst or Riven where you're trying to get somewhere and you're trying to weed through Atrus' mind to logic map the mechanical nonsense the guy's written to make this stuff work, you're finding frozen over connection points, and turning valves for hours on end, backtracking , and even walking from point A to B for the arbitrary reason the game wants you to do that for some inane feeling of connectivity and ability to hear more or less constant indoctrination as opposed to chasing a narrative. It's immersive, but it's immersive in the irritating sense. I got a real solid reminder of the ads you'd hear from TV's in electronics or a best buy, on loop every 15 minutes. I might hear some of the audio blurbs in my sleep.Narratively, the game doesn't throw a surprise at you, and Weirdly, this game dumps 100% of the lore all at once, pretty much in the last 30 minutes. And what it does land is... pretty underwhelming. After great annoyance in two of the worlds. If you managed to plow through the second half of two of the worlds without any issue whatsoever, hats off to you. I kept having severe issues with noticing what I was intended to notice. Not sure why, but, 9 hour game sessions will do that I suppose. I flew through the first half pretty quickly in comparison.  Either way after those worlds I was hoping for a lot more in depth information about characters, and really, I think you get a solid scratching of the surface. The narrative is just so... short story, in a game with so much potential for novels of lore. Heck, after big reveals the amount of backstory could fill a novel. But we get a small blurb, and one you could miss if you were hurried. The characters' effects are minimal, we only have one real voice to listen to, and they're a bit biased. There's so much limiting factors on what the narrative is, and the story is linear and not branchable. Unlike Obduction where you could get multiple endings dependent on your observance.I don't think this game's bad. Honestly, I enjoyed it. But there's still quite some jank in the controls and interactivity, and I got stuck several times. Save often folks. All in all I think it's worth a few play sessions. Maybe keep a guide handy for especially stubborn natural 1's you roll for perception in real life. But not for more than 20 dollars. It's about 9 hours. Yeah, Myst can be beaten in a minute. Provided you've read for hours and watched or played it before and it was made 30 years ago. This one feels just way less glued together than Myst, Obduction, and others. Riven's much more cohesive, and far more rewarding too.It probably sounds like I hated it. I didn't. There's just a lot to critique. If you like puzzle games, you'll like it. If you really like Cyan games... You actually might be let down. This one just needed something. I can't shake the feeling it feels incomplete. Despite that though, I enjoyed it for what I think it wanted to be, rather than what it was. Because what it was was really average. What it could have been was honestly a lot more, and I don't know why we have what we have instead of what could have been produced. It doesn't hit the heights of Obduction. Not even close. But honestly, it's still good enough to warrant a playthrough, just don't get on a hype train to do it, it's much better if you don't.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: unremarkable story, tedious but easy puzzles, walking simulator disguised as puzzle game, maybe buy when it's at least 75% off.I'm not a long time fan of Cyan. I've played Obduction when it came out and tought it was such a masterpiece. Definitely one of the 10 best games I've ever played. I got curious so I tried the remastered version of Myst. I've played for about 5 hours without being able to achieve any kind of minimally satisfying progress, so I quit.I was still interested in Cyan's new game so I bought it when it came on sale (I paid 33.74 CAD including taxes). I was a bit skeptical about the bad reviews but still decided to give it a try. It was an OK experience, nothing more. I wish there was a neutral choice for Steam reviews, but if I have to chose between Yes and No, then it's definitely No.My two major gripes:1) The story is almost inexistent. You get bribes from a narrator throughout the game, then at the end you get some rambling explanation, but it's cheap and weak and doesn't really refect any lore you could see or read during your playthrough.2) It's my 2nd Cyan game, but it's becoming increasingly clear to me that the devs like to make puzzles uselessly convoluted and long to solve just because you never get a full, global perspective and because you constantly need to go back and forth between areas without any direct or quick path, often including unskippable animations (probably hidden loading screens). Most of the time, if you could just fly away and look at the puzzle from far away, the solution would become instantly clear, or at least much easier. To me, that's just lazy puzzle design (go with Talos Principle 2 if you actually want to stop and think about logic solutions).In any case, I can't think of anything really positive about this game, but I can't say it was all bad. I'll just never play it again and forget all about it soon. If you're really looking for something puzzly to play and there's a good discount, it can still help you pass the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Not having that continual story that Myst did is a big feeling that I felt missing from both this game and Obduction. That being said, I enjoyed Firmament AND Obduction, great logic puzzle games, and I do mean great, with unparalleled world building and atmosphere. May not be what you were looking for in Cyan Worlds but it's great none the less. Worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a disappointment from my favourite studio. Overall I thought the puzzles were fun and the environment design was good but the game is riddled with bugs that will lock you out of the game unless you load another save or reset yourself to a safe position in the menu.The worst part is the complete lack of writing. The realms feel so shallow with only a few pieces of writing per realm (maybe like 10 things to read the entire game total). Then to rub salt in the wound they used AI to assist with this game, including journals and newspapers. For such a successful kickstarter and a game that already has next to no text, it's a complete shame that they used AI to write half-baked journal entries. Literally had lines repeated between journals in different realms. It's such a downgrade from the fleshed-out and lived-in worlds that Cyan used to make.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: It's worth a play for fans of the genre or people new to it. If you're in-between these two and looking for the best of the best, skip this one.Cyan didn't outdo themselves with this, but I think it's just how the projects' direction went, not really a testament to the studios quality.Now to Firmament. The game is beautiful. The realms are really well crafted and before buying this, I looked at other reviews and must say, I disagree. The wonder of the realms is there, and the increased size of some of the areas doesn't really dilute it. The detail of each area is adjusted perfectly to which distance you look at things and how long you spend there. Everything emanates a feeling of craftsmanship, elegance and believable wear and, what isn't always done right, also feels lived in. The machines look like they could work but at closer inspection are full of improbable or extremely unnecessary complexity, this gives it its magic though ...The puzzles, on the other hand, are not really noteworthy. While they are amusing at times and did make me think, I never had to take out my notebook, which is disappointing. If they get to this stage, they run into the danger of just feeling like blockers to exploration and this becoming a walking simulator ... but they aren't there yet. Mostly upheld by how satisfying it is to setting things in motion.Concerning how you interact with the world. This is notable, different from what we've seen before from Cyan. I like how it works here and would argue that it is better. It does force you to have to look at the display sometimes instead of the world but allows for more involved puzzles without the need of having to move the character. When it feels clunky, it isn't due to the interaction, it's the puzzle's fault.One of the puzzles required understanding of how the machine worked and had me tinkering around for a bit too long. The reason I didn't get it wasn't due to the interaction or even due to having to move back and forth, it was an impossibility in the structure of the machine, in how the artists rendered it on screen. That made me think it worked differently than it actually did. This was the only point in the game where I really got a bit annoyed at it, but at the same time it also was the most rewarding, after I realized what was happening. It also clearly showed in the display, but I didn't notice. Confirmation bias. Otherwise, it was fine.Now to the actual meat. The story presentation. That was phoned in. Common Cyan. The story was fine and doing an exposition presentation can work, but it felt like I was playing the game with commentary on. The budget for that part was much too small. There are only two animated or motion captured scenes! The lines were clunky sometimes. I didn't like the accent, I usually play with subtitles off deliberately, and there just wasn't a face to look at. There's a reason content creators show their face when presenting, it's part of the interaction.Cyan, if you choose to do it this way, I appreciate not having to read as much, but please go all in and record voice and motion capture at the same time. Even if it's just the head floating in the corner, it would have been enough. The way it is done here, I would have preferred reading or even finding audio logs. Or ... just dump most of the lines in one text after completion of a realm. Just have nothing in-between.The main issue of this game is that the whole premise just isn't as interesting as Myst or Obduction.Obduction was a huge comeback. That world is magical because ... well, it is magic. It tells a story and shows something that bend my mind and while there were hints and I could see what might be behind the veil, it was a treat when it came together.Nothing in Firmament comes close. They masquerade something plausible by pretending it being magic and when all the hints draw you closer to the truth the world becomes less exciting. I think the peak being about two thirds through the game when you get to see the ancient, beautiful, implausible but wondrous machines come to life. Just to be outdone later.Maybe that's how the narrator felt. Possibly, that's the point.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: For the price its a good short little experience but it leaves you wanting more than you get, and has practically no replay value. An important thing to understand right off the bat is that this is more of an adventure game than a puzzle game. You are presented with problems you need to solve. In Myst nothing exists by accident. Obduction depends on the player understanding how the various environment overlap on each-other, but still has myst-like puzzles which require reading and paying attention to the environment. Here in Firmament the hardest thing you have to do is possible to get through via trial and error. In the fullness of time I think the game will stand as much like a monument; Its nice to look at but is ultimately just a construction. There isn't much to read or learn about in the game that isn't literally told to you. Much of the value one gets is from exploring the amazing environments, but again they are mostly static. On the subject the game has very poor VR support, which at the moment means it is rife with bugs and issues, but in a broader sense nothing about the way the game plays or has been designed does much with the concept of VR. I was excited to try and play it in VR but with the bugs present in the opening minutes I ultimately decided to play it on desktop and I feel its a better experience there anyways as you get better rendering of the environments. The are no physics based interactions or tactile interactions with objects that you might expect of a VR title. In hindsight I feel its a bit sad that you could make a pretty compelling myst-like game with the Half-Life Alyx mod tools but here this game can't manage it very well at all.For the price its a good short little experience but it leaves you wanting more than you get, and has practically no replay value.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Gorgeous visuals and great puzzles, but the story does it no favors.[This review includes marked spoilers.]This game pretty much immediately captured me from the title screen. The upholstry background with the style of the logo on top evoked an aesthetic (I think it's art deco?) that reminds me of bioshock infinite, and is honestly not used enough. The actual environments (called Realms) don't disappoint. They carry the same vibe that's very familiar from Cyan's previous games, combined with aforementioned gorgeous art deco aesthetic, impressive graphics, and rich environmental ambience. Walking around these locations is a joy, and the puzzles are worked into the environment very well. I had a few complaints while playing (one puzzle was incredibly overwhelming, and for a couple I required the help of the strategy guide), but even reading the hints I didn't feel like any of the puzzles were unfair. Most of the time I'd just missed something. The game is on the shorter side, so a relatively small number of large puzzle sequences make up most of the game, but they rarely feel tedious and I'd often find myself losing upwards of an hour on them without realizing. However.What bothered me from the start and frankly hindered my appreciation of the Realms in the beginning is the constant story exposition. From the moment the game begins, a character is talking in your ear rambling exposition and this continues throughout the entire game. It was legitimately so bad that I just completely turned down dialogue volume and being left with just the environmental sounds was a much more enjoyable experience. Through the subtitles, I could tell that voice lines became much less frequent after the first hour or so, but they sill popped up quite often. Because I muted the main source of story, I'm sure I missed a lot of story details (subtitles were on just in case, so I caught little slivers here and there), so I can't talk about the nitty gritty, but I still have major gripes with the ending. That being said, if you're going into Firmament expecting something akin to Cyan's previous works, I don't think you'll be disappointed. In general, Cyan's experience in making these types of environmental puzzle games shines through, and the gorgeous graphics only elevate that experience. The way the story is conveyed is a little annoying, but if it really bothers you, you can always just mute it and turn off subtitles like I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game, not Cyan's best work, but still quite enjoyable. I've been playing since the days of Myst and I appreciate games like this which is why I was a backer. Spoilers ahead if you haven't played itOverall, great story. I wish there was more of the story elements and clues in the various realms. One of the things I liked about Myst, Riven, Obduction, etc was finding little areas that had more of the story to tell. For the first 95% of the game, the swan held the vast majority of the story elements. I liked the talking cloud, but I wish there were more reading and other elements hidden throughout the game to discover. I also missed the story choice at the end. I think this is important as it gives the player motivation to get into the story to figure out how to get to the good ending. Next, the puzzles were too simple. I found that most of the time I was doing somewhat mindless tasks instead of actually engaging in any real thought. What I liked about Myst and Riven, is that the player had to know what the hell they were doing to advance. Not just opening every valve they find or turning on every heater. I like it when I get stumped. I worked on a couple of the puzzles in those old games, and even in Obduction for what felt like days. Refusing to look up on the internet what to do. Finally figuring them out generally brings me joy. If the puzzles were more challenging, doing things like raising the towers would fell much more rewarding. I think Cyan needs to look at their audience, and if I had to guess, the backers want tough puzzles. At the very least, it would be amazing if they came out with a master quest or something similar for this with more complicated puzzles. There also needs to be some consequences for failure at times. With the acid vats, if something was wrong, it could force a reset for the player to have to deal with. I missed the red herring puzzle like from Obduction. I wish there were puzzles to just get to story elements, but that was lacking. Which leads me to my next point...Finally, I would say there was a lack of polish on this game that others seemed to have. Besides some of the obvious bugs, I feel like the puzzles were paid attention to and anything much outside of that really wasn't. One of the great things about half life Alyx, as a relatively recent example, is it inspired the player to look in every nook an cranny of the game. This felt like it needed another 6 months of development at least.Overall, all of the elements were there. I love the grand nature of the various machinery, the huge set pieces, a couple of the puzzles, and the overall story. I think creating a master quest that adds in some of what I mentioned would really make it even better.

_childDocuments_.review: Some of this is a review, some of it a life story - but in total, a love letter...so be prepared.Most of us have been waiting for this game for approximately 50 months, with said waiting period landing during possibly the wildest and craziest part of our timeline. Much kudos to Cyan for keeping fans in the loop as much as possible and delivering on their promise through that time frame where everything from COVID to inflation threatened almost every artistic project in development.Rewind 5 (!!!) years: I did not play Obduction at launch but rather about 18 months later, and I absolutely fell back in love with Cyan and computer gaming in general after like a 14-ish year hiatus (I'm almost 37). They know how to create some real beautiful, bizarre, head-scratching landscapes and the puzzles, mysteries and lore are unmatched by basically any other media. It is up to the player to get what they want (or need, depending on the puzzle) out of the game and resolve it on their own accord. No battles, no dying, no jump scares - just good old fashioned storytelling through exploring, all the while toying the balance between relaxing, rewarding and frustrating.Firmament is no different in visual grandeur and its potential scope. Immediately upon entering the first age (sorry, couldn't help myself) it's trademark Cyan. However, Rand Miller had announced about mid-way through the development cycle that the scale and difficulty of the puzzles would be toned down - in the final product, the friction is there in the environment and there are plenty of barriers and environmental puzzles (some quirkier than others) but eschewing much of its "pen and paper" and story-driven solutions compared to all their other IP. However - the sound, music and atmosphere are all on-par with Cyan and I'm so grateful to be able to experience yet another release from them, and its ending (while feeling a little rushed compared to the story-telling of Obduction and the Myst series) is absolutely fantastic.But...with some lingering hesitancy, I can't in good faith give this a perfect 10. I know they set out to do this exclusively in VR at first. At the time (2018) VR was still in relative infancy - only a couple years after the real market breakthrough. in 2019, they formally revealed this project and released a tech demo which I really, REALLY liked. You still had to interact with some buttons, levers and the floating adjunct was a new concept that was still being refined. However, it seems like at some point this was compacted to avoid the possible over-complexity and cumbersomeness of what this might present to the player...so now everything (literally) is all (slightly re-designed) adjunct based manipulation. While this is a cool concept - I really wish this wasn't the only way to interact with the environment. It gets repetitive quick (when you see two adjunct ports next to an elevator lift - one that's a "call only" and the other is the on-board operation of the elevator lift) it takes me out of the moment when that call-only port or several other things could've been a button you push adjunct-less like in the other games. The ability for this game studio can get you excited about a button or a lever is both amazing and amusing...and I wish there was a little more of that "non-adjunct" environment to spice it up and keep it nostalgic and better fused with the environment. I always felt just a *little* disconnected from its beautiful, sprawling world(s).Back to VR...you may be familiar with a little-known title called Half-Life: Alyx. Bar none, this is the best video game ever created insofar that I label it the Breaking Bad of this industry. It raised the bar a little too high for me as far as VR's true potential, and it's not just Firmament that falls short (in fact, pretty much every other VR platformer pales in comparison except for the Red Matter or Lone Echo series which rely heavily on "non-flat screen" mechanics for player mobility). This was a valiant effort by Cyan for VR but after the St. Andrews section, I defaulted to playing the rest of it flat-screen like Obduction. Not only does it look better, it is less glitchy and I'm just so used to playing Cyan's games in non-VR that the flat-screen experience was doing it for me FAR more than the VR was. Maybe I'll revisit it, but for now - I really would recommend the monitor version.Despite any of these relatively minor shortcomings...I had an absolutely wonderful last 4 days playing this beautiful gift from my favorite gaming studio of all time. I will fund anything and everything Cyan puts out, game or not. They've been an enormous part of 80% of my life. I credit my affinity to academia and my eventual pursuit of science and technology in my adult life in HUGE part to the skills I acquired through their games. They've gotten me through some of my most formidable and difficult child- and adult-hood years respectively. The only way I can repay that debt is to support all they have to give.Thank you AGAIN, Cyan.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Like many people looking to buy , I've been playing Cyan games since around 1993. And like all of their other games, I think there's a lot to love about . You get classic Cyan world construction, breathtaking vistas, awesome (and melancholy!) music, a sparse but interesting story, and very engaging puzzles. Reviews suggest VR performance is not great and there are a handful of somewhat serious bugs so you might wait for a patch or two (surely by mid-June, these will be resolved), but otherwise there's no reason to sleep on this game. If that's all you're looking for, then my review has done its job. The remainder of the review is more a reflection on how the game sits within Cyan's catalogue and what future lies for Cyan. I think one of the difficult things many fans are going to have to grapple with is that the choice to design around VR/the "Adjunct" mechanic informs the entire game design downstream. The Adjunct is a wrist-mounted gauntlet that can remotely manipulate switches and objects. Every single puzzle in the game involves manipulation of objects in space, and the UI/UX for the Adjunct is definitely VR first. Unlike most previous Cyan games, the puzzles are generally not built around synthesizing knowledge from elsewhere in the world. They can all be solved in situ. You have what you have in front of you, and there's no inventory. You look for a socket (a point the Adjunct can manipulate), assess the types of interaction the Adjunct can make with the socket, and work to solve your way through. The puzzles can be challenging, but the overall space of possible solution concepts is smaller than most Cyan games. There is no language to decode, no counting system to learn.  might be the first ever Cyan game that neither requires nor notably benefits from taking notes while you play. I chalk that up to both VR (where note-taking is unpleasant) and the puzzle design. Additionally, because many puzzles involve physically lining things up, there are moments that feel finnicky in terms of being slightly misaligned, or off by a pixel maybe. On the other hand, building a game around free movement, as in their previous game, , allows for larger, more open areas which inspire a real sense of spiritual awe. The single-minded focus around a mechanic reminds me a bit of , though the Adjunct is significantly better and more fun to use than the tablet system was there.At the risk of turning this review into real navel-gazing, finishing up the game also filled me with a sense of quiet worry about the future of game-making for Cyan. The team is quite small, perhaps a dozen credited people worked on it. A slide in the credits suggests the use of AI assistance to generate a number of background assets and objects. Even so, the game has relatively few assets and there are obvious signs of scope constraint. When you have so few people, there's a real tradeoff between competing on asset polish, visual fidelity, and completing development in a reasonable time. One way of putting this is that the team made a Herculean effort to significantly out-punch their budget and they should be commended for it. Another way of putting this is that more than ever, there are signs that the team has to compromise. Of course there were cuts for time and budget made to all of Cyan's games (and everyone else's too). But in , you see the seams of those cuts just a little more. Here the most evident limitation is frequent asset reuse and almost no non-puzzle interactive objects. The worlds still feel lived in, as all Cyan worlds always have, but more than ever there's a hope that your imagination and your charity fills in some of the holes left by gaps in the budget. I've been playing Cyan games for 30 years, and  and  both count among my favourites. I grew up taking notes and solving puzzles with my father. He's been gone for 8 years now and more than any other games, the release of both  and  served as sad but palpable milestones of remembrance: my life goes on without him, but I think of him when I play. And now I wonder how many more Cyan games I will get to savour until that is my fate too -- hopefully at least a few of them with my own children, so that they can serve as a bond that will last when I am gone and they too need to live on.

_childDocuments_.review: Cyan Worlds is second to none when it comes to creating an atmospheric puzzle games that make sense in their setting. For fans of the Myst series and Obduction, this is a must play, but there are some major differences. Where Myst relied on journals to deliver large chunks of story at a time, now you have a steady drip from a narrator. The other big difference is that you use your Adjunct, a gauntlet with an electrified tentacle, to interact with nodes scattered throughout the world. It's an interesting mechanic that doesn't get old. It was imperative for them to make that feel right, and I feel like they succeeded. You can expect Cyan puzzles to be difficult but doable, and Firmament delivers as well. You'll often see what you want to accomplish, but figuring out how to get there is the hard part. My only tip is to pay attention to the contents of the adjunct HUD - sometimes that's the key!! I loved this game and if you like beautiful environments populated with Cyan style puzzles, you'll probably love it too.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and the effort put into creating this game is obvious.  The sad "mixed" response due mainly to the VR play is unfortunate and I hope that once whatever problems with VR play are resolved, those reviewers will amend their reviews.  I haven't encountered the bugs other reviewers complain of in (I assume) standard play, but hopefully those glitches will be resolved with a patch as well, and they'll adjust their reviews to rating the actual game once they can play it smoothly.Games like this are rare and I for one applaud the developers' efforts and how beautiful and detailed and challenging (but doable) this game is.  Myst was a revolutionary game in its time (and it still very much holds its own  three decades later).  The whole Myst series was/is incredible.  Obduction was/is impressive, too.  This game incorporates the beauty and attention to detail embodied by its predecessors, new elements that have come onto the scene since, and some new original dynamics, as well.   I expect that I will spend many hours with this game.  Thank you, Cyan!EDIT:  So, I've played about 10 plus hours now, and I'm not taking away my thumbs up... but I have to start ALL over - the crane got stuck and couldn't fix itself (I wasn't stuck so transporting to a safe place didn't help).  I loaded a saved game but then fell through the ground (which was visually interesting but it still meant, "too bad for you").  Restarting, reloading didn't help.  So, sigh.  I wish I had saved more often and not just saved over the last save (and then started to rely on auto-save).
