_childDocuments_.review: Cyan’s new intellectual property Firmament is one of those games that you either hate or love. As open-minded, longtime gamer and Myst - Riven & Obduction fan, I loved it. (Even though it has little in common with the previous Cyan games, with regards to puzzle design.) Review based on 2D, non-VR mode. (I am a Kickstarter Backer.)As soon as you were dropped into the abandoned, majestic world, it builds up an amazing, dense atmosphere in terms of visual design, landscapes, architecture, surroundings (with great attention to detail), music, and sound design. The world is divided into realms: The Swan (hub & final destination), St. Andrew, Juleston and Curievale. Each of them features a unique Steampunk setting.  I love to get lost in there, others may find them boring, empty, and not much to discover. They introduced a new game mechanic called “Adjunct”. It serves as both a key and a tool. This is the only way to progress/solve puzzles. They are all mechanical/physical, environmental based.  To embark your journey, it is necessary to advance your tool (“Adjunct”) abilities.Do not expect hardcore, brain demanding puzzles or challenging riddles. No pen and paper needed. If you are a true challenge seeker, this might not be your coup of tea. They are not that easy, but felt like work at times, trying to guess where to go next and how to get there. Some puzzles are very heavy on free form moving, running back and forth and shuffling things around to get machinery in the right place. This could be considered tedious. But still, it felt great if you solved them and moved on.To be honest, I had some frustrating moments, because I am a casual gamer. You are joined by a mysterious female apparition which revels the fascinating story of Firmament. Storytelling is mostly through dialogue less through discovery. Don’t want to spoil a single bit of it, but I really liked the twist at the end.Skilled players can possibly beat it in 8 hours, I did it in 14, with lots of help.  Be aware, you only have 2 manual save slots and a single autosave.There are no more game breaking bugs! (I fell into the abyss two times. Couldn’t move inside the harvester, etc.)As far as I'm concerned, it's a clear recommendation and thumbs up, because of the game world and story! Give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so the environments are gorgeous, once again, as Cyan are known for crafting beautiful worlds.However... this definitely falls short of Obduction in terms of story, puzzles, bugs, and gameplay.Story is pretty standard. I guessed the 'twist' almost immediately.I get that they wanted to make this more VR friendly, and the puzzles show it the most. Except that there are fun VR puzzle games like Shadowpoint that do it better. Most of my frustration was immediately knowing what I had to do, but either waiting for slow events to play out or tweaking cranes/mechs to be in the exact perfect spot.I inadvertently bypassed environment load triggers multiple times leading to doors opening to massive amounts of empty space. BOTH cranes segments were frustrating, slow, and I encountered clipping bugs. While I never fell through the world, I did almost clip out of bounds several times. The tool locks on erratically if you have multiple interaction points in close proximity too. I did not play in VR so I cannot speak to that end.The harvester segment is a prime example of the, quite frankly, bafflingly bad design choice present in several segments. Driving a mech, fun right? How about you can only see in front of you, but at least twice you have to reverse with precision over a small point with no way to check except by running to the back. Underwater ice segment is also just awful, bad visibility, reduced sight, and unclear objectives. There are also multiple areas that where you traverse a circular platform leading to an elevator but UH OH you went left instead of right and you can only enter the elevator from one side but it only goes down.But then you get to some sections and they don't even have a puzzle where you would expect one, just flip a switch. Ok... fun.Even the aesthetics of the final cutscene, that is arguably one of the most beautiful set pieces in the game, is marred by a GIANT doodad in the middle of the giant window you're supposed to be looking out of. Excuse me but I just need to scooch to the right and now I'm viewing this segment from a skewed angle instead of drinking it all in front and center.It's very pretty, don't get me wrong, but the rest doesn't really measure up to the legacy of Cyan. Especially after Obduction, which I spent about twice as long on to finish (to be fair, I would have finished this much faster if it weren't for all the bugs and slow, finicky puzzles) this just feels like a misstep.EDIT:While I appreciate that you are fixing bugs and other technical issues I encountered, these will not change the core design choices that were made that actively work against the experience. My primary memories of this title will be, in order, the frustration of the 2 worst puzzles I mentioned, the other mentioned poor design choices that actively made my otherwise boilerplate experience worse, and the beautiful environments.

_childDocuments_.review: Being a fan of Cyan's previous games, I was hoping this would be up to the same level of quality. Sadly, I just couldn't get into this one.As gorgeous as this game looks, that's really all I was able to enjoy about it. The puzzles I experienced felt like a big step down from Cyan's previous games. Where those were excellently crafted logic puzzles that had you exploring the environment for hints to get a solution, Firmament's puzzles are more like slide puzzles. You'll know the solution right away, but getting there is rather tedious.Any I was able to find during my brief time with this game also felt lacking. There are many books in the Swan, but most of them are the same copypasted poem. The ghost lady who follows you around is also very vague about what's happening and mostly just points out stuff you can get by looking at the environment. Other reviews mention a bug where she doesn't talk at all and I almost wish I had that bug because I found her to just be annoying (especially with how she's placed in your vision in VR mode).Speaking of VR mode, that also feels very lacking. The only objects you can interact with are the books, and even then those interactions are limited. Your hands have no collision and you can't even jankily pick up objects like you could in the Myst remake. The fact that you can only activate things using the adjunct only makes your interactions feel even more limited since there are no levers or buttons to grab or push. Even Obduction's VR mode felt more immersive and the interactions in that game were basically just a mouse click.After reading other people's review and seeing that the rest of the game is like this, I don't feel any motivation to play any further and have requested a refund. I'm sorry, Cyan. I love your previous games and I really wanted to enjoy this one as well, but it just isn't doing it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up playing Myst and became enraptured by Cyan's games ever since I was a kid, so naturally I had to pick this one up. It is missing some things I came to love about Myst, Riven, and even Obduction, which are frequent lore books and notes, and interactable objects to find. However, the game brings around a talking companion that is always there with vague enough hints about things that are happening, which is an interesting new approach. Even though I wish there would be more lore and mysteries to discover I feel very happy about this game and the journey it took me upon. It brings back childhood nostalgia from sitting at my desk hunched over trying to figure out Myst's obtuse puzzles and I am pretty confident in saying that fans of the series would enjoy this game as well. I am eagerly awaiting any future titles from Cyan, for they always manage to bring out an enthralling and intriguing masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first heard about this game a few years ago, I was very excited at a Cyan Worlds game that was designed for a "VR first" gaming experience. The idea of doing environmental puzzles with the immersion of VR sounded amazing, but unfortunately, the game does not seem to deliver on its promises. I suppose this may have been inevitable because the game is to be played for VR and traditional flat screens. Myst, Riven, and Obduction are some of my favorite video games, but so far Firmament has been a disappointment.Without spoilers, the puzzles (so far) are not in any way enhanced by being in VR.  In fact, I think many puzzles are made more annoying due to their verticality. Very very very few items are physically interactable, which is one of the main drawing points of VR. Furthermore, the game is very buggy in VR, which you can find descriptions in other reviews. Some bugs have been patched, but the game feels very unpolished for VR.  This feels very disingenuous from the Cyan Worlds; this game does not feel designed for VR in any way.Disregarding the VR experience, the 2D flatscreen experience is quite enjoyable. The visuals are beautiful and the story-telling style seems similar to previous releases by Cyan, which is expected. The puzzles so far are fine, though I am concerned that the game may be a little short on content.Overall, I would recommend the 2D experience for most players.  However, given the promises of a VR title and the general expectations set by Cyan Worlds, I cannot recommend this game until significant improvements are made to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Having finished the game, I'm really not sure why there are so many negative reviews (granted, I played after four patches were delivered, so maybe some of the early bugs that people complained about were already addressed by the time I got to it). I found Firmament to be an engaging and immersive experience. It took about 11 hours to complete. There were a few navigation experiences that were a little obtuse (the crane got "stuck" in the wall for me at one point and I had to use the "Teleport to a safe location" in Settings to resolve), and some puzzles weren't as challenging to decipher as in previous Cyan games. Overall though, I thought the environments were beautiful and the conclusion was satisfying. I'd recommend playing this one--if you're on the fence, maybe just wait until it's on sale?

_childDocuments_.review: I am actually flaberghasted I'm giving Cyan. CYAN! A negative rating. And yet... here we are. Where to start...It's bad, it's actually really bad. At least it's relatively unobtrusive for most of the game... But then the ending comes. And oh god its so terrible. Not only is the ending nonesensical. It's also somehow extremely predictable. I mean I saw the "twist" coming from the very start of the game, and I still came out asking a billion unanserable questions about the insane plan that got you to it. Because the narrative hits you over the head with the foreshadowing from minute one, but apparently never bothered to question why it would work that way.And in case it just being plan terrible wasn't enough. The ending is a downright monologue, that takes so long, specially for such a short game! Even worse due to the game's buggy nature trying to use the teleporter while the monologue is going on can lock it down and make you treck all over the map to another capsule. I know because I did.And then there's that. The bugs. The ice crane takes the cake for glitchiest bugfest as other comments pointed out. But even leaving that one aside. There's multiple gates that can be accessed early just by saving and reloading the area after trying to activate them. I found it out accidentaly by opening the bunker on Juleston this way. Tried to open, didn't, saved and went to get pizza, reopened the game, magic! Suddently its raised! The game also fails to communicate why some gates need the extra strength upgrade which for a while convinced me the bug was the gates not opening without reloading, not them opening by reloading. Guessed the animation was busted. But no it was the other way around. Did a chunk of the game early before the Camelus forced me to figure that one out. Oh and also I managed to clip into the floor a few times by accident, happened around the bunkers more often than not.It's nonexistent. Ok, ok. This is Cyan. They've never been too comunicative to the player. I'll admit that. But this time it was specially egregious. Maybe precisely because of the bugs, which make you question if its not working because of you or because the engine's dying in front of you again. So many things just dont work for seemingly no reason at first. And worst part is that this lack of communication is the only real hardship of the game because the puzzles are insanely easy and repetitive! So all that keeps you from beating the game fast enough to ask for a refund is how much time you spend wondering wtf you're supposed to do or go to next. Bonus points have to go to that one sphere on St Andrews. The one that takes you to the camelus, and which just so happens to be the only one in the game with 3 stations instead of 2. Which wouldn't be so bad if there was any hint of this or if going to the 3rd station wasn't vital to open up most paths early on. So until you realize the rails keep going, you're gonna be left stranded wondering wtf is happening and why can't you progress anywhere. The other 2 upgrades are gated behind actual puzzles and yet this one was the hardest purely because the game simply doesn't give you any hint how to get to it. Oh and before I forget, the way to enter the sulfur station is also just painful, because I guessed it first thing, but because its a very small path on what looks like a plain I tried to go in, got blocked by the invisible wall, and guessed it was all invisible wall, then proceded to waste a lot of time driving carts around until I finally tried again and found the path.So as for the puzzles... Most of them are just "find the socket", I mean 99% of them. My eternal hatred goes to that one underwater section in Curievale, you know the one, the guiding the steam one. I won't spoil it but it is actually painful. Actually all underwater sections are because the claustrophobic suit's AI is literally migraine inducing if you, like me, get motion sickness from low FOV. But that one was extra painful because it's the longest and least enjoyable. I mean at least the sulfur one made me go "aha! that's what I was supposed to do, glad I could figure it out", Curievales just made me go "finally, that's where I was supposed to shoot, can we move on now?". Aside from these there's technically a couple puzzles like the electricity one, which was my favourite part of the game despite not being much because, well, at least it made me think for a bit. But that's about it, really. Even the Camelus puzzle is just "find the socket", except it takes much longer than usual due to the poor controls.I don't get this. I really don't. I mean, at this point I don't expect a jump button, great as that would be, but you spend most of the game flipping switches with Q and E, or switching between switches with tab. Plus since you get unplugged when you look away when you're dragging things like the carts in the sulfur mine or just looking for switches to connect between you have to keep this awkward backwards look to stay plugged in. Was there really no better way to handle the mechanics? I mean at least let us aim like in Obduction or something. Or just don't unplug us against our will. That's all I'm asking for at this point.This was an extremely short game, with a frustrating ending, very few decent puzzles (none I'd say were good), very poor communication with the player, terrible story, and so few mechanics even this very studio's previos title beats it... And it doesn't even have the decency to be stable. If you want 3d point and click-ish games then go play obduction, it's genuinely one of the best if not the best on the genre. Then go play through myst, tho do beware the later titles are also a bit buggy at times, and keep going until you've played every other game by this studio... And then, and only then, maybe if you want to torture yourself you can play this and try to figure what went wrong.Hope the next one isn't a thorough disappointment. Because this one was.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr go play Obduction instead.First of all, I love Cyan. Their games have meant so much to me over the course of my life. I've played every Myst game, including Uru in its current state. Cyan has crafted some of the best puzzle games in the world over the course of 30 years.But this game... just isn't it. This is the only game I've ever refunded on Steam, and it physically pains me to have my only return on this platform be a Cyan game. The first room had texture issues, regardless of texture quality settings. But I could have gotten past that. However, the very first puzzle with the crane completely broke. The crane clipped through the ground and I couldn't get it back out, effectively soft-locking me. I fiddled around with it for the entire 2 hours I spent in the game trying to get it to work, and it just didn't. So I resorted to watching a longplay of it on YouTube, and to be honest as awesome as the final reveal is, the lackluster and tedious puzzles that this game has to offer just doesn't quite make the ending worth it. And what little worldbuilding/lore you get along the way just isn't enough to keep interest until that wonderful reveal at the end.I would say that I'm holding out hope that their next title will be better, but from how the development of this game went (and especially the backlash about the use of AI), I don't actually know if Cyan can recover from this enough to warrant crowdfunding again. Fingers crossed, I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: [EDIT: I've come to understand the extent of the AI content in this game. I thought it was probably just a few touch-ups and some of the writing, but now I realise that it's a lot of the 2D art, all of the writing, and there are no actors credited - the voiceover seems to be entirely generated. Cyan have insisted that there was an actor, but since they're not credited, we must assume that either they were barely involved, they didn't want to be associated with it, or that it's not wholly true and it [i]is[/i] generated. Now, I can't say that the voice wasn't realistic enough to convince me. Maybe the accent masked it a little. But the point is, that was somebody's job you just wrote off. Ok, maybe you couldn't afford actual actors, but that's how you started out with Myst and you made the best of it, and it worked. Bad form, Rand. Very bad form. And this from the studio that created a series of games and books about responsibility over the worlds you create/discover/foster. As someone on Cohost put it "Gehn move, honestly".Using exploitative, appropriative,  practices like this is against the messages of everything Cyan has made previously. I will die on this hill, and right next to my gravestone will be one that reads, .So, this is enough to make it actually a deal breaker. I can't countenance AI generated art, especially from Cyan. I still recommend that you play the game if you like the genre, with adjusted expectations, but I can't give a thumb-up to a game made with so much unethical lacklustre. Sorry.Previous review follows.]---I don't normally write long reviews, but I have complicated feelings about this game. It's a thumbs-up, but with strong caveats."First-person adventure-puzzle-game where you explore the beautiful, lonely ruins of a worlds-spanning fallen civilisation, and by solving environmental puzzles piece together a mysteriously tragic backstory" is my all time favourite ultra-specific genre niche, and Cyan have always been masters of it. (Surpassed only by Outer Wilds, if we count that.)And I think Firmament (which ran absolutely fine for me, except a couple of times I got stuck on the scenery) has got to be in the upper echelons of that niche. Top 30% easily. It's very good compared to an Aporia or a Haven Moon or a Memorrha. It even holds up excellently next to a Quern or a Heaven's Vault or a Rime or Vane or dare I even include Scorn.But the thing is, you're not weighing it against those, are you? You're weighing it against your favourite Myst or Obduction, and in that case it left me with the feeling that it could've been a lot more.Firmament just lacks meat. To the puzzles a bit, but mainly the story. The Realms are gorgeous, and like most Cyan games, the idea is that if you scratch just below the surface of these beautiful places you'll find evidence of the poignant tragedy of the people who were here before you. Firmament doesn't convince me that there were people there before me at all. A key feature of a Cyan game, to me, is the way that the biggest puzzle of all is the story. I want to stitch it together myself. I want the big summative boss puzzle to be a test of whether I picked up on the themes and metaphors, but what we get is more like an exposition dump. Right at the end, the character says to you "I taught you all about these people," and I thought, "I wish you had!" A few journals in some characterful living-quarters would've gone a long way. But all we get are some very bland workplace to-do lists, and some empty spaces that feel like they probably contain backer-only art objects.Perhaps they ran out of time and money for writing. Seems likely, as it turns out that Cyan used AI "assisted" content for some text, voice and 2D art. It really shows in the few bits of writing that there are. It's just flat. It's kind of a shock to me that Cyan would use generative AI in their work. That's the disappointing part for me, that Rand Miller couldn't've gotten out his paper-press and beetle-ink and written a page or two, instead of using exploitative, plagiarising AI to write, literally, a page or two. At least, it's only a page or two.This might have ruined my respect for Cyan, but I’d count this as an example, a very rare example, of a time AI generated content was included in a piece of media and didn’t completely ruin the media object itself. Maybe that’s only because it’s so sparse. It would normally be a deal-breaker for me. That all sucks, but I’m glad I played it anyway.Because this game, the setting and style, the big reveal (that you totally know is coming, but that's fine), the sci-fi metaphors and themes as they finally shake out, are totally my jam. It's close to amazing. With the care and attention to writing and narrative design that you usually hope for in a Cyan game, it would be amazing.But. I'm giving it a thumbs-up despite that. In the "first-person adventure-puzzle-game where you explore the beautiful, lonely ruins of a worlds-spanning fallen civilisation, and by solving environmental puzzles piece together a mysteriously tragic backstory" niche, it's still in the top 30%, to be fair. Just, whatever your favourite Myst is, or Obduction, take that expectation and dial it back a bit, and you can still have a nice enough time with this.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Cyan games since Myst came out on Playstation,they are the reason I got hooked on puzzle games all those years ago and continue to play puzzle games to this day. I've loved every game they've put out and will continue to be a fan of Cyan no matter what. I backed this game in Kickstarter and have no regrets.In typical Cyan fashion the views are incredible and the atmosphere is deep and enjoyable. As has already been mentioned in previous reviews this is not on par with prior Cyan offerings. I was expecting to get out my paper and pen and start the long deep dive into a world that requires tons of notes and puzzle solving skills. Instead i breezed through the different realms scratching my head wondering when the difficulty was going to start.I think the 800 lb gorilla in the room hasn't been addressed yet and that's the fact that this game was made during the Covid pandemic which was like trying to work on a project with one hand tied behind your back while blindfolded. I think given these near impossible working conditions they did the best they could. I have no doubt that future games from Cyan will be back to the standards which they set so high with Riven and Obduction. Get the game on sale, it's a fun experience and worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game. 🙂 Typical Cyan Worlds game, if you liked the Myst remake and Obduction, you'll surely like this one too. A few bugs, some of them have been fixed via the first update, but, there are some remaining ones, which surely will be fixed in the future, like, getting stuck in some places, hovering grappler mechanisms, or the inability to save after certain actions (which can be xifed by proceeding in the game.Performance is pretty much the same as in Obduction, I would say. Cyan Worlds is a small company, and, they simply don't have the ressources to optimize the games as bigger companies have.The game is a bit more straight forward and less difficult than Obduction, which I appreciated. _childDocuments_.review: I was hoping the negative reviews for this game were just being harsh, but unfortunately, the haters were right.  by speaking gibberish to you right out of the gate, and that never improves; the game will yap over every potential moment of awe or intrigue, never giving you a moment to first take in your surroundings and be a little mystified. The story falls on its face right from the start and never recovers.; instead, opting to waste your time by hiding sockets and building in long stretches of walking/climbing/lift-riding back and forth. There's a lot of knowing what to do, but it takes much longer than it should to actually do it. All interactions that aren't just plugging into a socket and turning it on are summed up with "slowly move the platform or object to the correct position." Most of the puzzles can be brute-forced because there's no real complication to them; they're just a list of steps that usually only have 1 way you can interact, so if one socket isn't working, go to the other socket and,  The few puzzles that do something cool when you complete them are few and far between. A lot of the time, you get nothing or just annoyingly loud sounds instead of getting to see something happen in the world because of your actions.

_childDocuments_.review: As a backer I probably have too high expectations. Obduction and Myst (new Version) have a lot more detail in world building. Firmament seems to be a little bit unfinished: Repeating textures and assets. The scale of the gameworld seems to be larger, but somewhat repeating. There are moments where you find yourself in a more detailed part of the environment, but then you find repeating assets. Some of the textures look really basic, like they are ment to run on a mobile platform. I had no bugs or performance issues in VR and in 2D. But wished the games graphics would be more polished. I also don’t like the puzzles in VR, because a lot of times you are moving platforms/elevators which cause motion sickness (for some people).It should be a thumbs down from me, but I hope that they can polish the game with a few patches and use its income too deliver on the new Riven, like they did on Myst. Some quick fixes that really annoyed me:- German localization is not perfect - Closed the game accidentally (no popup "are you sure?"), also a translation problem: "Schliessen" means close (menu or game), better wording would be "Spiel beenden" (end the game).- The "error" sound of the adjunct is too loud and really annoying, should be something subtle.- Also the alarm sound of the speakers, followed by the voice saying "we are ..." is sometimes very loud.- Music was sometimes very repeating (e.g. at the puzzle with the vaults/crane)- Please add a more detailed version of the vegetation, especially the trees
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful environments. That's the best thing about it. But they're far more sterile, less human, less interesting than Obduction. You can't make up for that with audio (even if the actress is quite good). The story, if I read an outline of it, would be a fine thing to build a game around, but it's put into the game in a half-baked state, the narrative script missing a lot of needed connective tissue. The character animation is similar: good direction, good performance, but not enough staff to match the realism suggested by everything else in the game. An attempt was made to hide the deficiencies with particles, which was actually a great idea, but they just don't get the job done this time around. Environmental storytelling is neat and relatively thoughtful when it happens, but it happens pretty rarely, and the game would need a lot more of it to help sell a lot of what's said in the audio narrative. For instance, visual evidence of the activities of any character other than the narrator. Lack of resources and time explain most of the problems.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high expectations for this game, given the pedigree and history of the studio who produced it (I backed it on KS), but have been left wanting something more from the game than it had to offer.The game is visually stunning, barring the odd glitch (floating ice blocks anyone?). The worlds are thematically rich whilst also being distinct (yet with reoccurring themes).However.The game play felt flat. The puzzles were... one dimensional; being all tied to the same overall mechanic meant that every puzzle really felt too similar.  Run here, toggle a switch. Run there, toggle a switch.  It is an exercise in just hitting switches (and not even necessarily in a specific order either).The story, whilst ambitious, is also delivered in a disjointed way that makes it frustratingly hard to follow. Delivering all of the story by voice acting, whilst nice, also means that going back to remind yourself about a story element isn't possible.  This is further frustrated by the sheer lack of any written story. I'm sure the developers are tired of hearing about the 2 books fault, but honestly... 2 books that just get pasted around everywhere. Really Cyan?Overall, the game just feels... flat and unfinished. Which is disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very excited to know that Cyan finally made a new game, after so long ago masterpieces as Myst and Raven, this one was really a great one. _childDocuments_.review: Beautiful worlds.  Relaxing atmosphere.I'm a huge fan of Cyan because of Obduction.  Firmament delivers the same experience when it comes to exploration and wild new environments.  But this doesn't have challenging puzzles and it's about half as long if you take your time and enjoy the views.  I did not try this with VR and after playing I'm glad I made that choice.  I'm not a fan of running around in VR and there's a lot of that in Firmament.  The mechanics are as simple as flipping switches over and over again.  Can't flip a switch?  There must be another switch you have to flip first.  Find, flip, repeat.If you're looking for the same experience as Obduction, this ain't it.  It's closer to a walking simulator with a few easy puzzles in a very imaginative world with plenty to look at.  It's still easily recommended for anyone looking for a chill, easy 6-8 hour playtime in a beautifully handcrafted world.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished playing, and it took me about 14 hours to complete this game. I am a long time fan of Cyan's games, and I always eagerly anticipate their new work. I found Firmament to be a worthy compliment to their library of beautiful and thoughtful games. Firmament is visually beautiful, which is something that I have come to expect from Cyan. I think of them, to some extent, as the Studio Ghibli of game developers. The art and story are always central to their creations. As usual, there is a nice blend of natural environments and science fiction elements in both the worlds they have created and the story they have imbued them with. The ambient music was also excellent and a perfect compliment to both the visuals and the story as it unfolded. The story in this one is delivered primarily through dialog and maintains a nice sense of mystery right up to the final twist at the end - one I definitely did not see coming. I enjoyed the way the story was delivered as it was a refreshing change from the usual "journals" that are used in these games. There was always just enough of a hint of what was going on to keep me interested and enough mystery to make me want to press on and learn more. Like most Cyan games, this is a peaceful experience, though the story contains some darker dramatic overtones. This was true of the Myst games as well. There is nothing violent or frightening, and the game can be played at your own pace, allowing you to explore and experiment with the various puzzles. I generally find Cyan's games to be thoughtful and meditative and this is true of Firmament as well. The puzzles are, in true Cyan fashion, integrated beautifully into the environments and the story. They are not hidden or overly obtuse, but they fit in well enough that they don't break the immersion by screaming "puzzle here!" either.  I found the puzzles in this one less difficult than those in Obduction (which is also excellent,) and generally enjoyed the balance between having no clue what to do and the AH-HA moments that come when the connections are finally made the puzzles are solved. I did experience a couple of small bugs, but nothing game breaking. At the time I am writing this, two patches have been deployed and apparently have fixed the only issues that I had. This is another testament to the quality of Cyan's art.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly so disappointed with this, I love the Myst series, I love Obduction, I cannot say I love this.After having a crane lose its cable and getting stuck in the floor for the 4th time I have to turn what would just barely be a recommend into a do NOT recommend. I thought Cyan would learn from the unoptimised release of Obduction that poor releases hurt reception but I suppose the 1.4 million they received on Kickstarter for this made them forget.Typical Cyan fashion would dictate this game to be mostly focused on the environment and puzzles involving both clues from and interacting with objects in said environment. Unfortunately, this game lacks anything requiring you remember details or even possibly take notes, favouring a gameplay loop of *interact with machine, path to next machine is clear* This ends up working however since, on release, the disembodied voice that acts as both guidance and main avenue of lore is bugged and often will not speak, going totally unnoticed until you watch a youtube video where it speaks almost non-stop. They could have done with replacing a lot of the world building and voicelines with books or notes like their previous titles are known for.The actual environments are pretty, textures are not the highest detail but plenty of work has gone into making the areas look pretty and I do appreciate that. The music was good and it felt suitable for the moments it played on. The story is decent and though I won't spoil the ending If you do buy this then either wait for a sale or until the major bugs are resolved and until then you could always play Obduction or any other of their great games.

_childDocuments_.review: Ive only played a few hours but I was really hoping this would be the pinnacle of Cyan's VR experience. Ive been playing Cyan games since I was a kid. I was absolutely engrossed in Obduction. Unfortunately this game falls flat. I have yet to dive into the deeper puzzles, which I will, and maybe I will change my review at that point but right now it comes down to this: In VR, I'm expecting to be immersed and be able to interact with nearly everything, much like Alyx. Even Obduction I could interact with a ton of elements and it wasn't tailored for VR. In Firmament, I cannot touch anything that isn't a book or adjunct socket. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic!It's not perfect, as it falls into many of the common pitfalls of puzzle based adventure games, and the VR first approach to gameplay can be a bit cumbersome at times, but all in all, I am extremely pleased. Nothing Cyan has done since Riven has ever lived up to the hope and dreams I have for it, but those are lofty heights, and I might go so far as to say this is my favorite title since then. I'd certainly call it the most cohesive and succinct. Could they have increased the complexity and fleshed out the length a bit? Probably. Would that have made it a better game? Probably not. There were some bugs, frustrating puzzles, and while playing I definitely had a list of things I might have done differently, but after playing through to the end, they all seem minor and unimportant, because at the end of the day I had a lovely time.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game. I am a longtime Cyan fan and have played through all Myst titles, as well as Obduction. I do think this is one of their weaker games - the puzzles were easier than I expected, and the game was a bit buggy. I felt that I wasn't given enough clues about the world and backstory before the very end. But I still enjoyed solving the puzzles, exploring the worlds, and soaking up the ambience. I played this game a few months after release, and many of the bugs mentioned in reviews were fixed. I did not play in VR. Summary: A weak Cyan game is still a good game

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give it a 'not recommended' but I'm just too disappointed right now.I backed the Kickstarter 5 years ago as I've loved every other Cyan game. Especially since it was boasted to be "VR first" and I own a Valve Index. Now, 5 years later, I have no idea what must have happened at Cyan because this game is, amongst other VR titles, very very basic. Lots of other VR games let you pickup stuff, peak in corners and such to add to the immersion. In Firmament you can't pickup anything, not touch anything, nothing. You have a device which let you control obvious 'controls' making it almost a point and click experience. So zero points on interactivity. Climbing ladders is horrible and I even got stuck at some points while the design clearly showed I should be able to descend.The game design itself is very nice and well thought through, has to be said. The rendering however.... The lightmapping is very bland and badly done. When setting the graphics to high or epic the game glitches all over. Shadowmaps for instance flicker in and out of existence and glitches are different for each eye so very annoying. So if you like 8 hours of puzzling, do play it because the puzzles are ok but don't go for the VR because it's not a VR game, certainly not VR-first.I'm mostly sad that in 5 years they clearly did not check out any other VR games because a lot of mechanics like climbing stairs and picking up objects had been ironed out by other game studio's years ago.I stopped playing it in VR altogether[ADDED LATER]Forgot to mention some annoyances:- when I start the game in headset (Valve Index) I have to ALWAYS manually set audio output to the headset- space walk level is severely bugged. Doors that should be open were closed and vice versa- Menu in VR is unusable. Z-order of the rendering is wrong so you can't see where you point- the menu point-beam even flickered out of existence when trying to click some options
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I backed the Kickstarter and I only just now realized that this game is priced at $45.00 CAD... At that price I wouldn't recommend the game, but if you can find it on sale, I say give it a go, especially if you're a Cyan fan. If you haven't played a Cyan game before, then just go back and play Myst, Riven and Exile before you even think of playing Firmament. PROS:-This game has nice environments, which is a huge reason I love Cyan, so I would say they were successful on the setting and art. I would often enjoy taking in the nice views and structures, although there are a lot of repeated assets which can get a little bit tiresome. But overall I give the art 8/10-Nice middle ground for the puzzles. It wasn't so challenging that I ever had to look up a solution online but there were some moments that had me thinking things through and coming up with solutions in a satisfying way, so I think they hit a good medium here. In the past I never finished a Cyan game without consulting a walkthrough for at least one puzzle, and I do prefer the old style overall, but if this is the way the studio is going, I'm not complaining. 7/10-I like the adjunct tool that the game equips you with, it's pretty intuitive, although slightly buggy at times. For the most part it is satisfying and it allows the game to highlight puzzle elements so you're not pixel-hunting, so I appreciate that.CONS:-I just don't care about the story here at all. Not even a little bit. The ending was predictable and the voiceover just felt meaningless cause I didn't have a solid connection to the world or the characters. The realms were cool but again, they didn't really feel grounded in anything real, in the way past Cyan worlds have. Thinking back to Myst and Riven, and even Exile, the games all begin with pleas for help and interesting mysteries and books to read, and fun character dynamics. It felt like all of that was missing here. 2/10-In the past Cyan games they played around with multiple endings, I wish they would have done that here too. I always liked going back and experimenting to see what could have happened if I did something different. This story had nothing like that, and I missed it.-Some of the puzzles didn't feel fully playtested. One puzzle in particular I just brute forced it because it felt like it didn't have consistent logic. I looked it up online afterwards and found out that you're just supposed to assume something about the puzzle that they don't signpost anywhere, I found that pretty frustrating, but at least it was relatively easy to brute force. -I only encountered a softlock a couple times but in general this game is way buggier than it should be - the camera jitters, you can get stuck on invisible geometry, if you try to interact with something while the adjunct is engaged you can freeze the game, etc. At least in the menu they have an option to teleport out of softlocks but in an ideal world they wouldn't need that option. CONCLUSION: Again, wait for a sale. It's a pretty good puzzle game but falls short on some of the aspects that made past Cyan games special. I don't think they could ever make anything as good as Riven again but I still think they have the potential to get close to it in future games, at least I hope so. Firmament was lacking but still enjoyable (although I was a little bit appalled to see in the credits that they implemented AI-generated text to fill out the reading material in the game, blech).

_childDocuments_.review: Terrible VR implementation! It looks like its trying to do 3D effects or something and messes with your eyes like fog looks strange. Also the fog patch that appears when the chick is talking is horrible, thought I was getting cataracts! Your hands go through EVERYTHING and there is no interaction with any objects. Climbing ladders is painful, just turn on the magic teleport ladder option...its safer for your sanity.Tried it on monitor also... Nothing modern about the game at all. water is horrible textures are bland and every puzzle seems to be to turn that gun thing with a bolt of lightning. I got stopped on a walkway by an invisible wall but there was enough for me to shimmy along, denied. terrible!I did like the female voice person thing, but thats all I can say positively about Firmament. _childDocuments_.review: I love Cyan, they're one of my favorite developers. I've supported them since the 90s. However, Firmament is not a good game. I have a very strong system built for VR and the graphics and framerate is honestly not my problem. You can optimize that, hardware will get better, over time it becomes less of an issue, so I'm wholly ignoring performance when I made my decision to refund this game. I just do not like the control mechanic, or the puzzles. The 'mega man blaster' thing does not feel good to use in VR, it feels kind of bland and lazy, if I'm honest. VR shines with interactions like pulling levers, pushing buttons and opening doors. The universal puzzle tool feels like a cop out for a game that was long touted as 'built for the ground up for VR'. It connects to what basically is a USB port and then you turn it left or right to control it via a menu. I hate that, that's not good VR UX.The puzzles themselves are also very easy and not like they require any sort of thought and I really hate how far I got in 90 minutes. This is a game I'm willing to revisit later with some updates, at a cheaper price. But for now, I would not recommend this one.I like the art and atmosphere a lot, it actually does look and sound really nice, I just feel like they fumbled the execution.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game shortly after the remake of Riven because I was hungry for more Cyan, and this gave me exactly that. I enjoyed every bit of the exploration, narrative, and world building without ever getting too stuck or frustrated on a puzzle. It's dope.

_childDocuments_.review: After anticipating this game since its initial announcement, I am hugely disappointed.  Completed the entire game and the hardest puzzle turned out not to be a puzzle at all -- I missed finding a path that was a bit hidden.  Very linear, look for the socket, activate it, look for the next socket.  I played through the normal PC experience (not VR) and didn't have any issues graphically.  The only bug I encountered was that the crane pushed the ice block below the level and skipped some of the intended challenge in moving it around.  I was really hoping for 10x the number of puzzles than are actually in the game.  There are 3 "upgrades" and as far as I can tell you only actually needed 2 of them and them and there was never a point where I had to stop a puzzle and go back to it with an upgrade to complete it, so they feel like they're completely unnecessary. _childDocuments_.review: A great game for anyone looking for a relaxing exploratory adventure. The music, atmosphere, and environments are all a treat to immerse yourself into. This game very much has the DNA of the original Myst games that you'd expect from Cyan; all except for one thing.I've seen many complaints about the type of puzzles in the game, and that's fair enough. The puzzles aren't the arbitrary kinds of roadblocks that an in universe character has set up in order to hide something, or to test the player, that those familiar with Myst would expect. Instead they feel much more a natural part of the environment and infrastructure that exists in the game. This can be good or bad depending on how you feel about it. I rather enjoyed them.The game is on the shorter end, but then so were Myst games. However it doesn't feel incomplete, and it leaves you wanting more without overstaying its welcome. As final notes, I can't speak for the VR, as I don't have a VR set in order to play it that way. I also helped with the kickstarter campaign, so take the potential bias for what you will. In the end, I'd highly recommend this game. As said before, if you are looking for a relaxing, atmospheric experience with puzzles and a mystery that unravels around you, then this is for you.

Hopefully for me there is a gamepad support which allow me to play.2) Level design requires long back and forth walk3) I locked myself 2 times. I discovered it by pure luck.4) Puzzle are complex to solve beccause you cannot see the entire effect of the command you are activating. Best examples are the crane and the camulus. I had to go up and down the ladder to check the position of the crane. From the cockpit, I tought it was good position but in fact not.5) I didn't see the point of the "upgrade" of the Adjunct. It does not bring any fun.6) There is one side of the crane you can use to go further just because of a step of 30cm... Best (or worse) example) is the Camelus (a four legs vehicule).9) french translation is poor. Even google would do it better. And there is a mix between english and french.

_childDocuments_.review: **I was VERY close to giving this a negative review, and I'm a die-hard Cyan fan. I'm giving Firmament the softest of recommendations because at the end of the day, it was enjoyable, and I fully support Cyan as a developer. Anyone who has played a Cyan game knows that they don't make cash-grabs. They're one of the few fully privately owned game big-name developers out there, still self-publishing, and I have a ton of respect for that. This review is long, because I'm passionate about this game, and Cyan. Bear with me. TLDR review at the end.Having said that, this is a game you want to love, but in its' current state, it's really tough to do so. First, here's what the game nails:- The environments are gorgeous, and there's a lot of that inspired Cyan environment/level design in here. The levels feel fresh and make you remember why Myst was such a big deal. They STILL know how to make a world that just sucks you in, and I love that. The art direction is fantastic, and on my PC, I didn't have any framerate issues. - The sound design is excellent. You'll want to play with headphones.- I consider myself a longtime Myst/Riven fan, and I actually really liked the puzzles. It's nowhere near as difficult as Myst, Riven , or Obduction, but it was pretty clear from trailers that it wasn't going to be. Many people are disappointed by this and that's fair given Cyan's pedigree, but I actually think this is a nice, new middle ground for Cyan. I wasn't looking for another Myst. We have plenty of those. Firmament is a much more breezy affair  - this one will not require detailed notes or giving up and consulting a walkthrough like Cyan's other games, but by no means is it "walking simulator" territory. I really liked using a single tool for solving puzzles. This cleanly removes the frustration of pixel-hunting that can make puzzles go from difficult, to just unfair. There was still plenty of logic required to operate machinery, figure out how to unlock new areas, and string together a few sections to solve a greater puzzle. To some it may feel like"diet" Myst, but I thought not having to backtrack millions of times or miss tiny details made this feel like a modernized adventure game. I never was so frustrated that I wanted to quit, and yet I definitely had to use my brain continually through the game. I can't think of a better balance than that. It all feels just short of some of Cyan's best puzzles... but why? See below.Unfortunately, this game is marred by some BIG downsides, and I think most should wait to buy for these reasons:- It's UNBELIEVABLY buggy. For a studio that isn't being bulled by a publisher to release, and who raised almost $1.5 million for this game, this is totally unacceptable. This studio is not known for shipping games in unfinished states, so I really don't understand what happened here. It's not a long game or technically complex game, which makes this even more unacceptable. This is Cyan's second game on the Unreal engine and Obduction was pretty stable on release, so the magnitude and amount of issues is shocking. I'm talking total game-breaking bugs - platforms that get stuck and can't ever be moved again, falling off of edges/railings into nowhere with no way to reset, and the game frequently crashing when loading a level. This is compounded by the fact that you only have 2 manual save slots and a single autosave... why!?? I'm not exaggerating when I say that strategically saving out of fear of another game-breaking bug was more of a challenge than the actual game puzzles. By complete luck I was able to load to prior saves and avoid having to start a new, but I constantly felt I was just one step away from completely breaking the game. Some puzzles are very heavy on free-form moving, and the worst bugs seem centered around these parts. That sucks, because they are otherwise the freshest parts of Firmament's gameplay. it all feels like Cyan is somehow getting the hang of making a game that *isn't* point and click... as if it's still 1998.- The story gets there eventually, but rather than have the plot spread out across the game to intrigue and entice you, it's hours of nothingness, with everything shoved in your face in the ending act. I really liked the plot and the ending, but in addition to the bugs, this gives a feeling of this game being oddly rushed despite - again - 5 years and $1.5 mil. How did it come to this?? Also there are all of TWO books to read in the game, and even stranger, the same 2 books are scattered multiple times across areas of the game. This doesn't make sense from a gameplay perspective, and it doesn't make sense from a story perspective. Again, this is Cyan - their games are usually packed with lore, and finding the same 2 books over and over feels lazy, and rushed. It's like there was going to be more but they ran out of time and hit copy/paste on every written item. It would have been better to just have no books than the same two ones, constantly reminding you they didn't come up with any other written words for you. Combined with the bugs, it's clear little to no playtesting was accomplished. There is surprisingly not much to motivate a player to solve all these puzzles besides blind faith that Cyan came up with an actual ending. They did, thankfully, but you wouldn't know it from the first 7 hours.- On that note, recycled assets galore. The environments are great, but they are filled with the same props, over and over. Why? This is the Unreal engine, and it's 2023. It's so easy to add, find, and make assets. The game even has a footnote that mentions some assets were AI generated. Your opinion of AI-generated stuff may vary, but this is insultingly lazy to me. How the heck was this determined an acceptable approach from the studio that pioneered handcrafted virtual worlds? For the 3rd time in this review, I'm hit with the feeling that there was a different game in mind that was scrapped and a replacement rushed in the final months. It all just feels so bare, so lazy, and so incomplete for the budget/legacy of this studio.- The last big one, and maybe the source of all of the downsides - VR. I totally get why Cyan loves VR. I own a headset, and I absolutely get the allure of VR promising a fully immersive world. But it's clear that the current state of the technology means you either need to make a game designed 100% with only VR in mind (and accept those big limitations to make a splash) or just ditch it and make a good traditional game. I'm personally convinced that this game was going to be a much more involved VR ordeal, and that VR design attempts ate up most of the budget and resources that should have been dedicated to foundational stuff. I think VR should have just been left well enough alone, and I think had the VR ambitions not been there, we would have had a much better game for it. I didn't try this game in VR, and I have no real desire to, given how buggy the flatscreen affair already is.A very, very TL;DR:- 9.5/10 for graphics/environment/immersion- 8.5/10 for puzzles- 2/10 for stability/performance- 8/10 story/plot- Negative 5 bags of popcorn for a story that doesn't start till the last act- Negative 10 bags of popcorn for AI generated assets and re-use of props/assets- 3/10 for needless VR- Winner of the Defunded Libraries of America Award for having only 2 readable books... from a developer whose bestselling game is about books!!!

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, atmospheric game with striking worlds, graphics and sound design. Graphics ran smoothly, with very occasional pauses for loading textures. I played on a gaming laptop and Steam Deck. I can imagine the game is breathtaking in VR. Fairly short. Took me about 12 hours. I can imagine other players completing it in 8.Puzzles are similar to those in Myst or Obduction, but more accessible. The Adjunct, a portal or gravity gun like device, works well as your main way of interacting with the world. Good voice acting from the mentor/narrator helped tell the story. I would have appreciated a little more supporting narrative in journals and notebooks around the world. The game was made by a very small team of developers, and on a second playthrough you can feel where they would have extended the world if they'd had more money and time.Some of the puzzles use a physics engine. This creates a more realistic feeling world, but can occasionally cause bugs. There is a button in the menu to reset things if they get stuck. I had to use it once on my first playthrough (and not at all on my second).Before the first patch there were bugs where not all the narrators lines would trigger. This seems to be fixed.Overall, a beautiful new Cyan game. A little short, perhaps due to the small team and using techniques like motion capture and physics engines not normally seen in Cyan games. Now they have the experience I'd love to see the developers reuse these techniques in another game.

_childDocuments_.review: Still playing through it and will update my review once I'm done.  If you liked the Myst remake and want a new challenge with similar abstract puzzles, this is pretty cool!Update 5-31-2023:Thanks again to Cyan Worlds for a review copy of the game.  I have a full playthrough of the game starting here: The game is excellent for a variety of reasons.  If you like Cyan's other titles, you already know what's up and you won't be disappointed.[NOTE: I care a lot about spoiling anything--this is a general review but as a brush stroke I will talk about some of the design--so if you don't wish to hear about that, despite how limited it is below, just get the game and stop reading now!]Some highlights and thoughts:Each puzzle is unique, you're not solving 'the same puzzle' the entirety of the game.  Each puzzle will have new and different challenges.  If you do get stuck, the game is open enough that you can find other puzzles to work on until you get a new bit of inspiration on where you may be stuck.The game makes very clever use of the entire environment whereas a lot of other 3D puzzlers could simply be in 2 dimensional space. (e.g. here's a book, the book has the code to the door and it doesn't matter it's in 3D as it could have simply been clickable images)There are some bugs, but they really make no real impact on actually playing the game.  They do not interfere with the gameplay, only if you actually try to break the game and it's outside the bounds of actually solving puzzles/doing what you're supposed to be doing.  Just have more than 1 save (you get 2 + an autosave).  There is a plan to patch them out already announced but just not released yet.  The game receives high marks from me for how well and clever so many of the puzzles are.  The logic of these puzzles has been worked through and tested well.  All of the puzzles are fair and contain a clear solution that feels wonderful when you solve it.It may not be the most difficult or abstract Cyan title, but these puzzles are primarily more 'in front of you'/technical than they are abstract.  A really clever design element of the game is the adjunct, which you use to interact with objects.  I feel for a general audience, where I don't know how skilled my riddlers playing the game are, it's built quite intelligently in this manner.  It is built in a way I can give this to a kid or give this someone with little patience and the game is fair and approachable to essentially anyone.  At the same time, someone like me who wants a really challenging puzzling experience, I was still absorbed into the world and still found it satisfying to solve each puzzle.I highly recommend this game.  Regardless of your puzzling acumen, I don't think you'll be disappointed.  It's such a fun experience to see what Cyan Worlds concocted.  The worlds are so immersive and they each will draw you in in ways other games simply just can't.

_childDocuments_.review: Re-review on May 21st:I couldn't wait much after all and completed the game shortly after the first patch was released. It still runs poorly on my Mac, and some bugs are bad-enough that I had to ditch some progress by loading an older save. Apparently there's a "teleport to safe location" feature which might have helped in some cases, but I didn't know about it at the time. The fact that this even exists is pretty suspicious though. At least, the game didn't crash once past the first hour.Apart from the technical annoyances, I liked the game overall. The world looks pretty good and reminded my of the Myst saga quite a bit. The story is neat, even though I didn't feel really drawn to it until the ending, which was worth the journey.The puzzles felt simple, perhaps too simple for some. I approached every one with a Myst-mindset where I imagined over-the-top solutions to each blocker, only to find out that it was much more obvious than I expected. Most of the puzzles still were somewhat satisfying, but not up to Myst’s standards for sure.So yeah, Firmament definitely  a good game. It needs a bit of polishing and, if you’re expecting a new Myst, maybe lower your expectations a bit, but you should have fun regardless.Thanks CYAN for yet another cool adventure. Hope to catch you again in a few year for the next one!Original review:The game looks awesome, but it doesn't run great on a MacBook Pro M1 Max and crashed twice in the first hour or so. I can't really recommend it until some of the early issues are ironed out. Can't wait to dive back in once the game is in a better shape.

_childDocuments_.review: The core of the game is largely what you would expect from Cyan, but with its own twists, so props there.Unfortunately, the game is very short again ( around 5 hours if you can go straight through and depending on how used to Cyan games you are ), the visuals are a weird hit and miss ( some stuff will be very highly detailed and beautiful, others will be completely flat, no modeling, etc. ), but the real killer that kicked this down from "Recommended at the price" to "Not recommended" was the absolute bugginess of it.And I don't mean Cyberpunk "Lol, this is bugged...anyways, continuing on", but unfortunately you are constantly running into potential game breakers. Crane bucket separating from the crane, able to climb off a crane but not back on, pushed through geometry and auto save at the same time ( and you only get 1 autosave + 2 manual saves, that's it. ), losing the ability to interact, crane getting permanently stuck ( A LOT. ), the list goes on.It took me around 4-5 hours to beat it, I had about 3 hours AFK time, yet my played time is 11.1 hours. The difference is constant reloading saves because things broke, including losing about 2 hours at 1 point before I realized how bad the save system was.If they can get enough of the bugs worked out, this would go back to a recommend for the price point. It's short, but it's classic Cyan. But it's not ok for 1/3 of your played time to be "The game broke again."

_childDocuments_.review: I have played all the Myst games (with Riven as favorite) and Obduction. Was a Firmament backer.I have now played Firmamant twice.The game has great environments and steampunk feel (artists did an excellent job), good performance (GTX 2080/9900K), and good music kept mostly in the background.I admit I totally missed the story. Got to the end of the game with a “huh?.” So, I played it again. And I am still not a fan of the story, seems contrived. It did not help that there were so many frequent “Bong, Bong, Bong” announcements that I even started to ignore the ghost lady, and thus probably did not get the story. And then ending felt like a long monologue.As for the game itself, some enjoyable challenges, in nicely constructed environments. Perhaps a bit too much going back and forth with a lot of elevator up and downs and teleports between realms. The last steam puzzle felt like a tedious pixel hunt for adjunct sockets in a dark bubbly tank. The conservatory puzzle was OK but also became a bit tedious after a bit. I did not think driving the Camelas around was fun because of the adjunct. Maybe if the game had not been buggy the first time I played (in my second run only the lower crane in Curievale misbehaved), I might have had a different opinion. But overall, this game had fewer “aha” moments than other Cyan games, and some tedious moments. With a story that, for me, missed. So, I cannot recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Translated by Google...After four years of waiting, I have now played through the PC version and soon also through the VR version with Oculus.The wretched crane was also for me a troublesome part that took me many hours, but apparently I have finally understood how it works because in the VR version I just moved it where I wanted without problems.Since I waited so long, I didn't want to play through too quickly either.The flower elevator was hard too but I liked the first ones at the beginning of the game as well as the Harvester and St.Andrew Trailer puzzle.But of course, I needed hints about certain problems, good help where I got tips on what to do but you had to figure it out yourself.Played the Myst series and Obduction and appreciate that Cyan's Legacy is also visible here.I can recommend Firmament!

_childDocuments_.review: I love Cyan games and I've been playing them ever since the original Myst came out. This doesn't feel like a Cyan game. I know their stories can be rather simple but they at least have notes and journals scattered around, rooms that look slightly lived in. Things that, you know, build the world. There's none of that here. There is nothing until the last 10 minutes of the game that advances the story or the mystery of what's going on. The puzzles are easier than other Cyan games as they all boil down to "flip the switch." Which was nice in some circumstances but due to the camera and the environment became a headache in other areas. The only times I ever got stuck were because I wasn't looking in some random direction to find a switch behind a bunch of objects in the game.The environments are good looking, especially in the first area. It's clear development got front-loaded and they worked on the design of that area, even though the literal first puzzle glitched out on me. Which the bugs, hoo boy the bugs. In regular mode I clipped through geometry, got stuck in objects, some puzzles wouldn't complete until I reloaded the game.I tried the game in VR (Valve Index) and it was a completely broken experience. Subtitles were appearing to my left, I was stuck in geometry and couldn't get out. Controls didn't work, menus didn't work. Despite repeated attempts I couldn't make it more than 10 seconds in VR before getting literally stuck. It's clear the game is half baked and rushed. It doesn't feel like a Cyan game at all. There's no charm, there's no intrigue. It's just switch puzzles all the way down.

I found myself lost a few times because I did not find a hidden path or the next action. But all in all a great experience. I was a bit disappointed when it ended, I could have stayed in this world a bit longer...
