_childDocuments_.review: Short version: It barely functions as its supposed to, it's tedious as hell and frankly it's barely a puzzle game. Go treat yourself to The Talos Principle 2 instead.Long version: You know Myst, that eternal evergreen classic puzzle game that Cyan did way back when? You know how that game is really really good? You know what made that game really really good? Clarity. Poke around enough and you'll discover that the game literally hands you the answers to every single puzzle on a silver platter, the trick being that you need to write them down and find the correct place to apply those answers. Exploration was the main meal of the day with Myst, which lead to a joyous sense of wonder as you wandered about the surreal pre-rendered worlds. Firmament completely misses that by a country mile and then some. Firmament is a game about ignoring everything around you apart from the next magical hole that will let you make some amount of progress, and then having you solve utterly inane puzzles that you'll barely figure out before dying of boredom over how gutwrenchingly slow and tedious it all is.Generally, when it comes to puzzle games, I play up to the point where my brain turns into a fine paste, and then either leave it for a bit or maybe if I'm well and truly stuck and out of ideas, I'll check for a hint or a nice little push in the right direction. With Firmament, I felt that I outright *needed* the guide in order to actually make any real progress with the game. See, this game is nonlinear in the bad way, where it will happily let you wander around the areas and futs about with the stuff in those areas, but there's secretly a specific order that you need to be going through in order to actually progress. There's nothing that indicates this, and there's nothing that implies this either, you just have to basically make it enough way through one area to realize "oh wait, i'm scuppered here", or look at a video walkthrough for a specific puzzle and notice that literally everyone else has two more magic upgrades for the magic fist that goes into the magic holes that you magically dont bloody have. "But Myst is non-linear and you were praising it just a moment ago!" Ah yes, it is, but the trick with Myst is that there's literally no set path you have to complete the game in. The order you go in in Myst doesn't matter a single bit, it's just pick a place and solve it. Not so with Firmament.Initially, I was quite on board, honestly, wandering around going "ooh" at the pretty visuals and finding the adjunct mechanic neat. And then you press forward, and realize that, oh, the entire game is just that opening segment but with varying levels of complicated and/or tedious design. Tedium is definitely the best word to describe this game. There's nothing fun about playing Firmament. Feel free to explore the worlds it drops you in, but you better remember the exact path you have to take to get to specific part sof said world otherwise you have to go on a longwinded walking adventure that takes up even more of your time. And that's before we even touch upon the actual puzzles. The puzzles in Firmament are equivalent to you holding a really heavy box and a guy breathing over your shoulder going "put it over there. no, not over there, over *there*! no, no, not there, over here instead." constantly until you finally find the correct place that makes it happy.And even if you're able to look past THAT then you still have to deal with the incredibly nothing story as told through a floating orb of dust with the voice of an cliché coy French lady that needlessly reminds you about how she's dead and you can't talk to her, for whatever reason. And then there's little things such as the game forcing you to go to the hub area just to change to a different world even though the entire system is set up so you can pick your location you want to go to, which just begs the question of why are you literally enforcing two loading screens on me just to go somewhere else?And above all else, the game just straight up fails to function well at all. It's glitchy as ♥♥♥♥ to the point that even the devs couldn't be arsed to fix some of it and just slapped a "teleport to safe spot" option in the menus (which, by the way, puts you back at the start of the area so have fun trekking back to where you were!) The adjunct only sometimes will go where you're pointing your camera at, sometimes it just decides to fly off and go somewhere else instead. Some interactable objects just wont work until you move slightly or repeatedly press a button. And it's not a bug but frankly I'm shoving it under failing to function because it wastes your time the longer you play: You can't stop movement of an object mid way through to change its direction and you cant queue or hold a direction to move in. You have to connect the adjunct, hit the button to move it, wait for it to slowly go to its next set position, and then hit the button again. And you do that for as many times as you need to get things in the right spot. Why. Just why.Cyan, you are better than this. How did you let this ship out in this state? Why is everything designed in such a tedious fashion? Did you look at that one puzzle in Obduction that was so egregiously bad in its design to the point that a guy on YouTube who does nothing but look at and research game design stuff  and think "yes that's exactly what this game should be"? I'm just...shocked and amazed that this exists and plays like this. But most of all, I'm upset. Even on sale this game is not worth the hassle it brings upon you.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Game length: About 5 hours for me This game is beautiful. The environments and atmosphere of all areas are fantastic. You could remove the story and puzzles, turning this into a walking simulator and it'd be still work some amount of money. I would turn many of the areas in this game into VR worlds to hang out in by the visuals alone. If the atmospherics interest you and you get value from that kind of thing, this game is probably for you. Puzzles are built into the world well. This game doesn't fall into the common trope of building a world, then adding the top flavor-of-the-month puzzles as door locks that some puzzle games do. All the puzzles in this game felt like they were part of the world, and the game was way better for it. Puzzles were generally unique, you only run into a single kind of puzzle once.(puzzle difficulty)  A story does exist in this game! That being said don't expect too much, the story helps give some flavor but it's not the meat of this game. (How the story is provided)  - I originally got this as a VR game; at launch at least, do not play this in VR mode. The fog in the world renders at incorrect distances for each eye and it really screws with your head. FPS is also very inconsistent, and on low the screen resolution takes a lot away from this game, and the visuals really make the game. That being said, I switched to desktop and had a much better experience! - There is a button in the settings menu to reset yourself, and it will take you back to a viable location and reset objects that may be in the soft locked state back to a valid state. If you find you believe something may be invalid, use the button. I did find that sometimes not all objects reset, but doing a save and load then fixed the last few pieces of the world that didn't reset properly.(spoiler describes a particular bug, it brings up a particular object but nothing related to how the object is used or puzzles around it) - Be sure to wait for her to stop talking, then resume your journey. She will talk over herself if you advance too quickly. (Spoiler describes the importance of the narration with regards to the story)
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: What a game! What. A. Game.Been a fan of Cyan games for many, many years since playing Myst way back in the early 90's. They have always produced beautiful, story-rich games, and this is no exception, this game is absolutely stunning!The visuals are absolutely astounding, as one would expect from any Cyan game. Beautifully rendered into a fully realised world that feels real and believable along with a deep and intriguing story with one heck of a twist right at the end... and talking about the end... an astounding track by VNV Nation over the end credits just adds a whole new level of feeling and depth to the overall narrative. Honestly I can't praise this game enough. There were one or two minor glitches when playing in VR, but nothing game-breaking or anything that spoiled the enjoyment of the experience. If this is the quality of any future games by Cyan, I am  so excited for whatever comes next. I absolutely LOVE this game!!
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Ok Cyan made this game and they also previously made the excellent Myst series.But seriously it doesn't warrant the fact that most bad reviews for Firmament are from people complaining about how much this game is not Myst.For me Firmament is a good Adventure/Puzzle game with a VR compatible gameplay and good graphics.As an old Myst fan it still took me 11 hours to beat it While still missing two achievements.Some bugs are presents but Cyan is working on patchs, the third one being released two days before my review.Just save regularly and you should be ok.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Big disapointment overall, mainly due to the puzzle being way to simple and super repetitive. The gauntlet system is one of the main reason for it. There is almost no time where you have to guess how things work or their use. Finishing a cyan game without taking any note and full sprinting from one piece to an other is a shame ... The visual quality is ok/goodThere are a lot of bugs/crash present in the game.I'd rather like a point and click with Myst like quality of gameplay (Difficulty, Investigation, Hypothesis, Trial/Error, Notes, Reading, Slow pace, with a lot of meaningless details, etc) than a 3D VR beautifull game that has completly abandonned the reason why we came to play games of this genre.Go back to the roots !
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: So glad game didnt dissapoint me! Only minor bugs and visual glitches (rocks glittering here and there, playing on 6700 AMD). Otherwise no stutters, good optimization and visual feast so far and yes, most importantly intro story is so much better then Obduction to me, real Myst vibes... Worth every Euro cent ... Kudos Cyan!
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This game is effectively a walking sim with sparse story up until the last 10 minutes, where what little story there is, is just dumped on you.There is very little content, taking approximately 8 hours to beat, which includes plenty of time to stop and look at the scenery. Unfortunately that is all there is to do, as the game includes only a handful of interactive objects and puzzles (there are only 3 real puzzles in the entire game).That being said Cyan does make some very pretty worlds and this game is no exception to that.Therefore, this game can only really be recommended if you really like Cyan's style and want to experience a little more of that.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Finished it in 5.5 hours. There aren't any challenging puzzles, you just go around and point your tool at stuff. There's no ambiguity as to what you might need, no "maybe this does that in the other world" type situation. It's very mediocre puzzle game, where no puzzle makes you really think. There's literally a "puzzle" where you encounter locked door, walk away for several minutes, press a button, walk back and the door is opened + several sections that pad out the game by requiring you to walk without doing anything, and if in Obduction that was kinda the point (still not great design), here it stands out and just disappoints.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Cyan and Myst, I recommend this game, but it disappointed me.Good: Graphics, Lore, Music, Sound, Atmosphere.Bad: Gameplay (and Gameplay bugs).The game looks great. Some locations like the hub area are absolutely breathtaking. Although I would have liked more diversity in locations, and to have things looks less "earth-like". Amazing sound and music. Some locations I just stayed there and soaked the music in. This ends up in a great atmosphere.I think we deserve better character movements. It feels amateurish (pressing two directions at the same time makes your character move faster, and the character collision capsule falls off ledges everywhere...). I was softlocked and had to reload a save multiple times because of that.The puzzles are not bad, they are thematically making sense within the world, like other Cyan games before it. Puzzles are solved using a mechanical device that controls sockets at a distance. I think the developers only scratched the surface of the device's potential. There is an "upgrade" system that gives additional abilities to the device, but they are very basic and uninspired (except for one). Most of the game's length is waiting for machines to do their things or moving from point A to B.I would love to see Cyan invest more into their puzzles and gameplay, and try to truly evolve their game design to the new age. While playing the game, I felt there had been a lack of development time and polish (or manpower).Let's see what the Riven remake, my favorite puzzle game, will look like.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Cyan is my favorite game developer so I jumped on this game day one.  I absolutely loved Obduction so my hopes were quite high, but I'm sad to report that, while good, this game feels more like an expansion or a indie game than a full studio game.  This game has jank galore and I highly recommend keeping at least one backup save as I soft-locked myself at least twice while playing.  I also had to make use of the "teleport to safety" feature at least once -- a feature that, while helpful, is very amateurish.  The story is fairly sparse and is mostly delivered via about 2 pages worth of disembodied voiceover.  I was also sad to see Cyan moving from their hallmark FMV sequences to motion capture, however I respect their right to grow as a studio.All told, if you're a fan of Cyan, I'd jump on this right away, though you may be a bit disappointed.  I'd happily have paid 2x the price for a game that was longer and more fleshed out.7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Got immersed in this right away. Like i did with all the "Myst" games since I was a Kid. I know there's no official tie to Myst.. but in playing this game i can tell it's Cyan, which is what draws me to these types of games in the first place. I've got everything Cyan ever made, they leave their mark on everything they touch with the style of puzzles and atmospheric visuals and sound. Looking forward to playing more. This is a huge thumbs up for me. Unfortunately the game has crashed several times while in VR (Quest2) and i'v had to restart the pc. But i could also be the method i'm using to run it. It would be nice to have some guidelines on what settings are recommended for someone with a quest2 and a really good gaming rid (3060Ti)
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played a Cyan game before, you'll feel at home.  It has the Art Nouveau / steam punk feel of the other games.  There are familiar transitions and activities I like and enjoy. There are new ways to interact with your environment while many of the controls are familiar and welcome. However, it is much eerier than the Myst series or Obduction.  There is much going on that will unsettle one about both the long history of the background and the recent history which brings your character into the game.  It's been enjoyable and fun to explore and understand the worlds in Firmament.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: great, until you hit Act 3.  Then, disappointment.The first 2 Acts of the game develop a sense of mystery around a repeating event found in each world and the secrets behind it... what is it for, what is it's purpose... and then just throws it away to do something else... I had all these ideas and theories about what was going on in the game.   and they died a quick sad death.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: It's heart breaking to do this because I loved Myst 2020 and I want to see Cyan succeed in this brand new IP. However right now the path to that is murky at best. This game is glitchy, rarely game breakingly glitchy but enough to have a "Teleport to last safe location" button which is normally further back than you'd expect. I hesitate to talk about puzzle difficulty but something here feels a lot more obtuse than Myst in a way that is more frustrating than gratifying. I'm going to keep powering through it and hope for a patch or two. Maybe a few more brain cells wouldn't hurt either.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: What an experience! Firmament drops you into a world full of beautiful scenery and mystery. The story unfolds slowly, tantalizing you as you wait for it to all make sense. Puzzles are a little different for those of us used to the previous games from Cyan, but the Adjunct mechanic is a lot of fun.I think the highest praise I can give is that halfway through the game, I thought to myself, “I am a Keeper!” And I was—I had become something new, reveling in my time maintaining the realms, and eager to uncover each new mystery. Highly recommended. Don’t go in expecting this to be the next Myst game, but keep your mind open to Cyan applying their expert world crafting to a little bit different gameplay concept and you’ll enjoy the ride.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give it a recommend but it's more of a "meh" because, honestly, I'd rather just play Myst or Riven again. The game is beautiful but I don't have VR so this game isn't designed with interesting and challenging puzzle mechanics for folks like me. I'm looking forward to the Riven remake but hopefully that isn't entirely made for VR, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles are satisfying and in-keeping with the Cyan style of being plausible parts of their environment.The environments are gorgeous and incredibly detailed, it feels like a set of real lived in places.The plot is fantastic, a lovely slow burn Story with plenty of subtle clues and a fascinating conclusionI played non-VR and didn't encounter any serious bugs or performance issues.My only complaint is that the game was a little short, but I'm very satisfied otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: After 6 hours i finished the game, puzzles in this one are quite a bit easier then obduction. Then again i did enjoy the game and liked most mechanics. Obviously there are some bugs here and there but at no point did i get really stuck. Thanks to Cyan for another cool game, visuals in this are really stunning.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you for another wonderful journey, Cyan! The game has a few hiccups here and there, but nothing game breaking (by patch 2). The game's visual and music score is simply amazing and I felt completely drawn in. The puzzle difficulty is a far cry from the puzzles from MYST, but that's not necessarily a bad thing! For once I didn't have to resort to an endless stream of guides and walkthroughs when im lost! Thank you again Cyan. I can't wait for what you do next! (Moooooore Myst maybe?)
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, but compared to Myst or Obduction, it misses the mark.  The steampunkish nature to the puzzles is fun, but in all they're pretty easy to solve except for a few where you're just having trouble seeing the targets you need to spot.The total number of puzzles is lacking as well. Really not a very long or difficult game.  I finished the whole thing in under 10 hours and went back for another half hour to finish off the last 2 achievements i was missing for 100%The story and world felt pretty lacking. I can see what they were going for, but it really feels like they put most of the budget into the visuals and didn't bother fleshing out the script.Visually beautiful but not much to it. Happy I played it though, so I'm giving it a thumbs up. I wouldn't spend more than $20 on it though... or $10 if you're not a huge Myst or Cyan fan.

_childDocuments_.review: NON SPOILER PORTION-------------------------------------------------------I really enjoyed this game! It was the perfect dose of Cyan for me, and I'm really sad to see all the negative reviews.  I did not play in VR as I do not enjoy playing games in VR which have First Person movement, so I can't speak to those issues. My time in game is a lie because I played this alongside my Husband on his account, we beat it in 15 hours. But I wanted to leave a ranty review about it after finishing. I did run into one massive framerate drop during a major cutscene, as well as some minor bugs, but nothing which detracted from the game for me. Most of the bugs I ran into were getting stuck from accidentally stepping out of bounds, I was going out of my way to walk in weird places looking for secrets when these happened, it never did on the clearly defined paths. There is one puzzle which is particularly.... buggy. As someone who both plays a lot of games and has some experience with programming I 100% understand why it bugs the way it does. Due to saving just before starting into it, I had no issues completing it and found the experience enjoyable still. I would highly recommend saving before you start into any big puzzles so this doesn't cause you any heartache. I play a lot of puzzle games and have my entire life. I did not find this game particularly easy. Is it as difficult as The Challenge in The Witness? Well, no. But I also don't expect that going into this game. There were several puzzles I spent hours working through still, and my husband who is very new to puzzle games definitely did not breeze through them. The game is definitely easier than Riven, but I actually find it about on the same level as Myst if not more difficult. Myst was only as challenging as it was because of the time period, new people coming into the experience often breeze through the puzzles after a little bit of messing around, and I think thats a positive thing because Myst's puzzles are figuring out how a foreign world works. Its not supposed to be difficult if you are part of that world. Driving a car is easy, but if you drop someone into a car who has never seen or used one before, figuring out how to drive will be a "puzzle" involving lots of trial and error, and thats exactly what this experience is, and what I would argue my favorite Myst games are. If you are reading this and want a spoiler free experience, please stop here! I will be getting into spoiler territory now.SPOILER SECTION-------------------------------------------------------Although there will be some spoilers here, I am going to still be slightly vague to hopefully not completely detract from your experience! The story. I really liked the story, but my husband had some issues with it which I also saw repeated in some reviews. I don't believe I missed any of the narrator dialogue, but if you do that would definitely detract from the experience as much of the story is filled in that way rather than through written word. You do get some written interactions at the beginning and end, but thats it. There are a lot of things not explicitly answered which I believe could cause you to dislike the game more depending on your personality. One thing I saw mentioned in a review which my Husband also complained about was the ending monologue, which I actually really enjoyed. The complaints I've heard is that it falls on deaf ears because you are not the person she is complaining about, and therefore you don't care. I personally still cared about what she was saying, in an empathetic way rather than a guilty way which I believe some people thought they were supposed to feel. I also 100% would have done the exact same thing in her shoes. You may not have the opportunity to yell at someone who has deeply hurt you for whatever reason, but I am the type of person who finds it therapeutic to try to on paper, or videos, or email drafts the relevant people will never actually see. Because of this, I was able to relate to her choices and appreciate it. One thing that I haven't seen mentioned yet, but which did stand out to me, is that the ideas behind this game have been used in a prior Cyan game, which made large portions of it easy for me to guess. In my time playing the very similar portion of a game in the past, the people I talked to about it and interacted with regarding it absolutely LOVED the concept and said it was one of their favorite experiences in a Myst game, but it probably doesn't have the same "kick" the second time around. It definitely didn't for me, but I still felt that this game did enough differently for me to appreciate it. It made me think of some ideas and situations not presented in the similar game, and although I wasn't surprised there was still more for me to soak up from it. I am making some assumptions here, but I do think that may be part of the reason for the negative reaction from hardcore Myst fans. To wrap up, I would highly recommend playing this game! But don't expect Riven, this is a new experience in a new world with new technology!
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Very disappointing effort from the people who brought us Myst, even without considering the quantity of assets generated using *Machine Learning* to... cut corners in development? I guess? The story is bland and uninteresting with a "oh, is that IT?" twist at the end, the script borderline nonsensical thanks to a.i. meddling, navigating around from place to place can be kind of slow, and the puzzles are pretty much all variations on three dimensional sliding blocks or 'random fiddling with simple mechanics until something changes'. Oh and they don't *appear* to credit the voice actor(s) who then go on to have their work artificially manipulated, which isn't a good look.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it. If it was twice as long and took more time to elaborate on the puzzles they invented, it might have been great. The bugs will get ironed out, but the game is finished. It's a solid 8 hours of game, so it's a fair price for a pretty game with a cute, if under-explored, core mechanic.However, one has to wonder if having such huge vistas was worth it? Take something like The Witness which is conservative in art, but beautiful and crammed full of puzzles and metaphysics, and it seems clear they hit some big challenges during development of Firmament.You can see the ambitions, but you can also feel where the cuts where made and how the game was padded for time: 3 upgrades that don't really have enough puzzles to support their inclusion, very limited lore, and it feels like some distances were set to increase player the time in the game. (It's not a bad time walking around, it's a lovely environment, but.)All in all, if you want a neat puzzle game, it's good, even at full price. You'll be disappointed that there wasn't more, but only because you enjoyed what is there.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: So, I was excited for this game. I even backed it during it's Kickstarter! But... I just have one question. Where did the money actually go? This is such a letdown, I'm sorry to say! it really feels like a bashed together game with concepts from Portal and Bioshock on a single devs budget. The overall environments are beautiful but feel utterly lifeless, the voice over feels cheap, and to be honest, hard to understand at times. The mechanics are just awful! Restrained to essentially the same type with no variety and finding yourself frustrated rather then satisfied by the time you get to the solution. Also, the plot is beyond generic! I just... I really think it's a step down for them; to tell the truth. I wish I could recommend, but honestly, I wouldn't pick this up.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament is a rare gem of a game! The artistry of Cyan shines through with every pixel, drawing inspiration from their past games without being bound by them. They have created a beautiful steampunk art-deco world that is simply breathtaking! There are a few minor technical hiccups, but they can be overlooked and will likely be ironed out with patches anyway. Fair warning: some of the puzzles require patience to avoid frustration in certain spots. Overall, it's a charming game that is well worth the price of admission. If you enjoy a solid narrative puzzle experience, you don't want to miss it!
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I am a seasoned Myst aficionado for 30 (!) years. This game will please even new players. As a Backer I was unable to play till 3 months after release due to a move to another age (state). Luckily when I downloaded there had already been 3 patches included.  I have always imagined the scope of the games to be a bit larger than they turned out to be, but this was balanced by my slow pace of play.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament has amazing visuals, atmosphere, world design and puzzles. The quality of the images is on par with that of Riven but it is much more immersive due to its real time graphics. My only disappointment was that although the mystery of this world was intriguing while |I was playing the game, the story is revealed abruptly at the end and it does not feel plausible. The story in games like Riven and Obduction was  much more fascinating, was well integrated with the puzzles and was slowly being revealed each time you solved a puzzle. Overall though I definitely recommend the game, especially for Cyan game fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: A much appreciated Cyan title after loving Myst and Obduction. The feel is unmistakable: you're dropped into a now dead world of steampunk technology with only book clippings or video recordings to help you piece together what happened. Where is everyone? What used to go on here? How can I power up that sweet orb on sky tracks? Scenic places to visit and appreciate, though it's no Obduction in that respect. Great little story, with a great twist ending.Best part? HIDING IN A VAT OF ACID hahaha no joke you for real submerge in a vat of sulphuric acid! (Here's a ladle if you need proof...)
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: It was good. That's about all I can say about it. It wasn't great. It was a typical Cyan game, lots of amazing scenery, good story, but it felt short, and the ending felt a bit rushed. It had the usual one or two very difficult puzzles, but most were manageable. Overall it felt like a similar game I played many years ago. Same sort of puzzles, same feel to the ending. I won't spoil the game by giving that title though . If you like Cyan puzzle games, it's a good entry in their collection.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Played in VR (rift). Awesome world that looks and feels huge with some pretty awesome moments. Puzzles were good to alright and follow the main mechanic but still varied enough to not get old or repetitive. Only problems with VR were that sometimes after menuing a blank banner would hang until I loaded a save and on one save I fell through the map when loaded. Luckily the autosave was less than a minute before mine so lucky I guess. Not as great as Obduction but still good
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: 3/5If you play the game as if you know all the solutions beforehand, this game works like a charm. Otherwise you can mess it up like I did, ruin your save file (I got stuck) and be forced to restart the whole game.The story is told by a ghost in your ear (I love her accent by the way), and at ONE(!) occasion she quietly tells you what's expected of you in the beginning, but without any emphasis or weight. It's so easy miss, so the gameplay easily becomes a matter of just trying to move forward because you don't know what else to do. And you don't know why you are doing any of it.This game follows Cyan's same recipe as all their older games - different deserted worlds (always deserted for some reason) that apparently cannot exist physically next to each other, but have to be in different "realities". I guess it's fine, but it's been done so many times now.The puzzles all revolve around beautifully weird and pretty stupid contraptions. Like a crane mounted on a circle, controlled from two "cockpits" that individually revolve around this circle... Yeah. Did I say weird and stupid? How about a greenhouse where only a selected few plants can get water, despite an automatic watering system, unless you manually move the plants around? It's like having a fixed garden hose, and moving the garden around under the hose to water it. It's fantastic. 😆The puzzles range from annoyingly bad all the way to great. The bad ones depend on you standing in the exact right spot to be able to shoot your "adjunct" where you are supposed to.The game has its bugs. The one I mentioned above - leaving the crane but not able to jump back up on it - is completely game breaking. Others require a restart of the game, like a stuck junction that's supposed to move when you interact with it. Yet others can be solved by interacting with stuff in random order. The bugs are mostly about those sockets that you connect to that refuse to do what they are supposed to. It's almost the only game mechanic after all, and one of very few things that can go wrong.As long as you can live with said bugs, and a few annoying puzzles, I think it's a nice game, relaxing and fun, with a rather simple yet nice story.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I hear and understand some of the criticism of Firmament, and comparisons to other Cyan games.  Full stop.  This is a stand alone game that needs no comparisons and no rating as to where it lies in the range of games from Cyan.  For me it is enough that it comes from Cyan, and in my estimation is a worthy game for  that alone.  Cyan games have a "feel" and personality unlike any other developers products.  Even for those of you out there that played in the cavern and on the old Ubisoft forums, if there are any, and I am sure there are, I think you will love this effort from Cyan.  Anyone who remembers what it was like in the cavern when all you had to work with was dial up will love how smoothly this game runs.  Yes, there are some bugs, but they are only of momentary annoyance.  I particularly love the fact that all of the "puzzles" are so well integrated into the game that you don't even realize half the time that you are solving a puzzle.  My only complaint is that I wanted it to be longer.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Having spent an hour with the VR version, I cannot recommend this game right now. Performance has been awful, menus are broken, and the graphical glitches are headache inducing. I sincerely hope these issues are fixed soon because there seems to be a lot of potential here, but if you're wanting to experience this in VR you're best off waiting for some patches.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was enjoyable. The puzzles are not quite as challenging as the usual fare from Cyan, but the use of the Adjunct to interact with the world was kind of a fun idea. It limits the type of puzzles, but it's kind of cool. The worlds were lovely, the music was nice. The only thing I would wish for is a bit more story, and a bit more characters. That's not to say the story was bad, it was wonderful, I just wish there was a lot more of it. Next time, I'd like to meet some of these characters that are described by the single person you interact with, I'd like to be able to go deeper into the story if I want to. She describes one of them briefly towards the end, but it would have been great to find their journals, or some recordings, something to enrich the storytelling. There's a lot of unrealized potential to this story, I'd love to have more.Be that as it may, I still loved the game. The one character you do interact with is interesting and mysterious, very fun. The puzzles are pretty good and interesting, the visuals are great, the final reveal is satisfying, if a little short. I am an original backer.I think if the main fault of this game is that I want more of it, it's not a terrible thing, but Cyan, if you're reading this, give us more of that good stuff next time around. Story and characters. It wouldn't be too difficult, just include more storytelling artefacts in the worlds. Sometimes the best part of the game is the stuff that takes root in our imaginations, not just what's on the screen.

_childDocuments_.review: Sad to say I don't recommend the game. Which is a shame, 'cos I was quite looking forward to it. And it largely comes down to the story, though I was disappointed by the puzzles as well. Beautiful visuals, but the story is lacking to say the least. A disappointment particularly when compared to Obduction and the older Myst games. Spoilers below.tl;dr, the story offers almost nothing, and is mostly told by exposition, either by a single NPC or by three pieces of paper in the third-to-last-room rather than environmental storytelling that had been so strong in other games. It might have been generated in part by AI which would explain why the story is so incredibly weak.The Puzzles!Long story short, it's not an awful game, but its setting is empty and its story is empty. Cool visuals, but lacking in substance. If you played the Myst games and Obduction and are coming to Firmament expecting a good story, expect to be severely disappointed. Do I regret playing it? No. Do I regret paying $45 NZD for it even with the initial 10% sale? Sorry Cyan, but yes, I do. Myst V had a more compelling story, and that's kinda saying something.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite genre of game. The things I enjoyed most about Firmament were the massive environmental puzzles. The two areas where you had don the suit (no spoilers) - especially the last one - were insanely immersive. The worlds were beautiful, the sound design sparse and effective, and the transitions between worlds fast and smooth.I see a lot of talk about game breaking bugs, but I only got stuck twice - once in a wall with the walker and I forget the other. The special teleport to safety saved me both times. Not saying there aren't others, but that was my experience.Hard as Myst, Riven or Obduction? No. Shorter? Yes. I think I'll replay that next. Thanks Cyan!

_childDocuments_.review: While I can't recommend this game, I wanna say I do appreciate what Cyan was trying to do. I played the game with keyboard and mouse, but I bet it's really cool in VR. I write a negative review in hopes the developers take my feedback seriously and learn from their mistakes. I'm glad Cyan is trying new things, but they've done it at the detriment of what has always made their games so special. This does not play nor feel like the Cyan games we've come to know and love. If you've never played a Cyan game before, this shouldn't be your first. If you're a fan, it's a massive step back from Obduction (and all their games really), so set your expectations on the floor, and you might still enjoy the experience. Buy it on sale, or don't if you want to support Cyan.Overall, the game completely lacks the depth and mystery we've come to expect from Cyan games. Although the environments are gorgeous, you get little to no information about the world or the people that once inhabited it. The most intriguing aspect of Cyan games is wondering where you are, who the people were, what happened to them, and how you fit in with this massive story that's already in motion. Since you aren't given any information to piece the narrative together on your own, it gives you little reason to continue playing the game and there is no satisfying incentive for solving the puzzles. Usually in Cyan games, as you solve puzzles, you gain access to more information. Although the game mostly keeps inline with Cyan's design philosophy of "no arbitrary puzzles," since you're left completely in the dark about what's going on, it very much feels like puzzles for the sake of puzzles.I think what happened was the developers optimized the game for VR. As a result, they had to sacrifice a lot of elements that otherwise make Cyan games so mesmerizing and engaging. Reading in VR sucks due to the limitations in headset resolutions, so I think that's why there aren't a lot of journals to read and why the little info you get is from a single narrator in voice over. Since you can't take notes in VR, the puzzles were dumbed down so they relied more on linear logic and brute force, rather than creative thinking. I took no notes for this game...I usually take tons, that's half the fun. This wouldn't be a problem except so many of the puzzles are done spatially using vertical and horizontal space. While novel, the field of view limitations of a computer screen made it incredibly difficult to see everything! This might be fine in VR where you have a HUGE FOV, but on a 2D screen, it was often hard to see what you needed to do next.This makes the game feel extremely claustrophobic at times, which is crazy because the landscapes are insanely expansive...TOO EXPANSIVE. Half the game play is spent traversing large and empty landscapes. Again, this wouldn't be the end of the world, but because of the way the puzzles are designed, there is a TON of backtracking. It's crazy that this was one of the biggest complaints about Obduction and they seem to have doubled down on it! Again, I wouldn't care so much, but the distance between some puzzle elements takes SO long to go back and forth, I looked up guides to confirm I was on the right track simply because I didn't want to waste time doing the wrong thing!The design language is questionable. It can be easy to overlook the interactive ports for your device, the Adjunct.  Often times they blend into the scenery because the ports glow amber...but they also use amber lighting in most of the game. So if you're not scrutinizing everything, it's easy to overlook the ports as lighting. Since the game lacks detail, you're not trained to inspect the environment with a keen eye that would otherwise find the more obscure interactive elements.It's cool that the game introduces game mechanics as the game progresses, but it doesn't do a good job of teaching you all of the possibilities and doesn't use them frequently enough for you to keep them in mind when trying to figure out a puzzle.Lastly, the game concludes with an info dump about the world and its lore. This means when you're at the climax and you are excited to get to the resolution, you're forced to stop, consume the little writing there is, and just sit and listen to the narrator. All of the momentum is lost.

_childDocuments_.review: The world-building and scene design in Firmament are in line with their consistent standards and taste. Most of the core puzzles are cleverly crafted, leaving a lasting impression on me. The game does have some issues, such as long scene loading times and occasional glitches when moving between vehicles, which hopefully the developers will address in future updates. Compared to their previous title, Obduction, the overall gameplay length of Firmament is shorter. However, despite its flaws, I believe that Cyan has created another gem, and I hope they continue to produce even better works.

_childDocuments_.review: Too many "Towers Of Hanoi" puzzles, gave up at the Conservatory, four sets of platforms go up and down, and everything spins when you get far enough down to rotate the entire assembly,  I've gotta either build a state diagram or fiddle with it for hours.  Yeah, spectacular steampunk graphics, but no actual fun.Did I mention only TWO saved game states?  Yeah, Myst was fun (except the part where I had to get out my frequency counter to do the musical puzzle) and I was looking forward to more of that, but this is just crazy complexity with zero hints, and even walkthrus are either multi-hour videos watching someone else fiddle with it, or "solve the puzzle and get out the other end". _childDocuments_.review: Back in the late 90's, I had a 486SE Gateway, and it could play Myst in a reasonable fashion.  I've had every Cyan title since, from the Good to the Gooder to the Not So Much.I backed the Kickstarter campaign for Firmament and was looking forward to it.  Other than a couple of minor technical issues, It has not disappointed me.  In fact, I find it to be refreshing.I can go to other games and put on power armor, pull out my MasterBlaster and teach them all the mobs a lesson.This game, this takes me back to when none of that even existed.  To a time when a puzzle was a challenge, where there had to be a solution and you just had to figure out how to solve it.The environment that's been developed with the artwork, music and ambient sounds is first rate.  Game play is linear, but still allows many side options for how to progress.  The Adjunct is a great invention - very cool and something that I hope Cyan are able to use again.In closing, I would like to say this.  If you're looking for a shootemup, this ain't it.  If you would like a gaming experience that literally takes you to another place - a place with a story, a setting and a purpose - you might want to check this one out.

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous environment in which to walk back and forth, over and over, wishing there were puzzles to solve and MYSTeries to explore.I Kickstarted this, and I say skip it. Are you looking for a gripping storyline? No line to be found. I'd say a story point, but I wouldn't want to say there was a point at all.For the majority of the game the dialogue will be provided by a green fart in the corner of your eye, waffling about nothing in particular.But who cares about that!? We're here for PUZZLES, BAY-BEE!There's like, 2.Seriously, I can't bring myself to call anything other than the vertical tracks and vaults, and the battery lake a puzzle. _childDocuments_.review: First impressions are pretty good. VR is a bit scuffed, but 2d mode works really well. So far the ambience is supurb, I love the aesthetic and feel when it comes to the environment. I backed this long before it came out and so far I'm hardly disappointed.Edit: After thoroughly playing through this I'd say this game is a solid 7.5-8/10. The world is splendid, the scenery is gorgeous (if your pc doesn't cipple), the story was pretty fun with a neat twist. _childDocuments_.review: Loved the atmosphere, solid world design and graphics, interesting environments, and a very cool sense of scale. Puzzles were good for the most part, but frankly the Adjunct tool was pretty much always kind of annoying because it limited the types of interaction that were possible, which greatly reduced the variety in the puzzles. I'm not sure if it was supposed to be a concession to make the game work for both VR and flatscreen, if so, too much was lost, and there were many other options on that front.While I am a big VR fan, I mostly played this on a screen so I could enjoy it with my partner. I have played it in VR and while it looks very cool, performance is not great. I can't help but feel more could have been done in this regard, but it's certainly playable in both modes.Overall, I would still recommend Firmament, and it's pretty sad that it's currently at "Mixed" given that it's a solid game. As a huge Myst fan I can be honest and say that the best days for Cyan are in the past, but that's a high bar, and both I and my partner were counting down the days to this release. We were not disappointed, and we'll no doubt be counting down the days to the next one too.

_childDocuments_.review: Long time fan of Cyan, Riven being a big favorite from my childhood. I backed Firmament many years ago as I believe Cyan overall is a great developer. Unfortunately I would consider this one a miss overall and do not recommend it.The main reason being I can't even motivate myself to finish it. The art is beautiful but feels kind of hollow. The world feels sparse and has much less to discover than Cyan games generally do. The story is delivered largely through disembodied voice-over that feels like its trying to be mysterious and foreboding but mostly just comes across as kind of random rambling.All of that aside, however, the biggest negative for me personally is that nearly all of the gameplay is reduced to a single mechanic where you just look for sockets in the world, connect to them, then slide things around. Platforms, train carts, trolleys, levers, doorways. It's all reduced to a simple connect and button push. I normally love interacting with all the objects and devices in Cyan Worlds'... worlds, it's part of what makes exploring them so fun and interesting, but in Firmament this is all flattened into a single mechanic. It is rarely interesting and often feels very trite. It makes the world less believable and makes all of the different modes and mechanisms feel samey. This surprised me as their games are usually even simpler in a way, just clicking, but adding this interface has a way of highlighting the simplicity and making it feel like you're not causing action in the world, you're just pushing buttons on your wrist device.I will still excitedly keep an eye on Cyan for their next endeavor as I strongly believe companies with such strong track records should be allowed to try new things and fail. For Firmament though I overall found myself unable to get sucked into the world and story as I normally would and after a few hours of running back and forth socketing and hitting Q and E to slowly make progress lost the motivation to continue onward.

_childDocuments_.review: There is potential here.  But like so many games, this is riddled with bugs and problems.  I've only played this in VR so far, so not sure how much of this effects the flat version.  Right away, you'll notice the aiming beam from your hand gets hidden behind the menu layer, so you can't see what you're trying to select in the settings.  Then as soon as you load into the game, you notice that shadows and reflections are rendered differently in each eye, making for a glitchy looking flickery mess in VR.  I ignored that because the environments and graphics are very nice looking.   Then you start using the manipulator tool that you get right in the beginning of the game, and realize it's full of bugs and glitches.  I took a transport pod to another area, and when i went to leave, I wasn't able to open any of the pods, so I thought maybe there was more I needed to do before I could leave, but it turns out the pods just wouldn't let me open them if I was using the manipulator in my left hand.. as soon as I used the tool with my right hand, the open/clone functionality worked.   I think this one needs a little more time in the oven before it's really ready for the world.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended (With Reservations)As one of the Kickstarter backers for this game, I went in with big expectations. The story of this game's release is one of perpetual setbacks and delays, and when the release was drawing near at the end of last year and an update was pushed to the backers that the game had to be delayed again because it wasn't ready for release, I had a sense that... well, at least the game will be done when it releases. We've waited 3 years, what is another six months?The answer is, surprisingly, not much. Not that the additional wait was odious, but that ultimately what was released was still quite unfinished.Other reviews have already mentioned the game-breaking glitches, the lack of polish, and just the general beta-version vibe that Firmament has. Those issues are not terribly important to me, in spite of having to restart my game a third of the way in due to a game-breaking glitch involving bad hit detection on a moving platform yeeting me into the void combined with an overzealous autosave function. As frustrating as those issues are, they will eventually be patched out. It is both the blessing and the curse of modern development cycles that no game is quite done until after the initial release, sometimes years later.No, when I say unfinished what I mean is that this is still only half a story. Beware spoilers ahead.Alright, so, that's a lot of complaining. But still recommended? Yeah. Because I think ultimately the game still delivers on what most people will be expecting when they hear that a new Cyan game has released. Its beautiful, its strange, it's 7-10 hours of confused backtracking and puzzle-solving. It just could have been so much more than that, and that kinda hurts.

_childDocuments_.review: A true Cyan game. Everything they have made over the years are just amazing games to play.Puzzles were complex, but the goal was clear. Some puzzle mechanics got bugged (ice lift being one of them), which required me to load a save game to an earlier time... A quick google search prompted me to load a previous save as other people have experienced the exact same thing.But the worlds are beautifully made in true Cyan fashion. _childDocuments_.review: Firmament has a couple of novel interactive mechanisms, and one realm that is interesting to unravel in places, but the majority of puzzles feel abstract and arbitrary rather than emerging from historical functions that make sense.The adjunct tool doesn't help in that regard, since its linear update path highlights the arbitrary gating of certain puzzle.Overall the game feels thin, with storytelling nearly exclusively delivered in scripted audio-logs before a final text-lore dump at the end; and with environments particularly sparse in terms of meaningful details.This sparseness is narratively consistent , but if a design choice, it feels like a big miss, as it prioritize the neatness of the story space over making that space interesting to explore for players. The art is really well executed, but the direction itself feels very rehashed for the studio and the genre.Sadly, Firmament is a huge step down from the idiosyncratic richness and thoughtfulness of Obduction - curiously, it had a similar Kickstarter budget, and a one more year of dev time than its predecessor... it's very strange.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit (June 8th):Original review posted May 20th, had to come back after learning that large portions of this game were generated using AI -- I will no longer be supporting Cyan as a company due to this extremely disappointing practice. A shame.  Original review below:Credits have just rolled on Firmament and unfortunately I did not enjoy this game.  Game development is extremely challenging, and I've been a big fan of this studio's previous games, so I want to be as measured as possible in writing this negative review.  While playing I thought it definitely had potential, both in terms of possible puzzles that could come from the game's unique gauntlet mechanic, and the narrative, but in the end I found both to be pretty disappointing.  If you're at a beginner level for puzzle games and are a fan of VR experiences in general and do not mind cliched plots with all telling and no showing, there's a chance you'll like Firmament.  Detailed review, spoilers from hereon.This game's puzzles are extremely easy if you regularly play puzzle games.  That isn't inherently bad, some games (such as Portal) have easy puzzles but the solutions are fun to execute.  Most of the puzzles in Firmament are neither challenging or fun.  The best puzzles of the bunch come from Curievale, one of the three realms in the game and the only one I consider to be good.  These puzzles require you to think outside the box in terms of your own positioning as well as manipulating the machinery around you to move through the environment, as well as some genuinely fun moments (busting through the icicles with the crane being one).  This realm also has by far the most puzzles in it, with double the number that appear in Juleston and St. Andrew, and it also has the best diving suit section in the game.  Unfortunately, the entire game is not Curievale.  St. Andrew begins a section that has all the creativity of a sliding tile puzzle and requires very little thought to solve.  As an intro puzzle it would be suitable, but it is one of the realm's three puzzles, and the puzzle that follows it barely raises the difficulty bar by adding a rotation element to the figurative vertical sliding tile puzzle you are once again doing.  2/3 puzzles down, and the last one?  Isn't a puzzle.  You simply have to move around a clunky vehicle, and turn 4 switches.  I was genuinely shocked at this point, but St. Andrew was not as bad as the third realm, Juleston.  Juleston's introductory puzzle has you moving energy pylons to equate to a specific voltage to get the power running.  Okay, sure, a quick intro puzzle that'll unlock some complex machinery or electricity based challenges afterwards, right?  Unfortunately no!  The next puzzle (again, one of 3 puzzles this realm has to offer), has you concoct some acid and requires virtually no thought to complete whatsoever, just the tedious carrying out of pretty obvious steps.  Even if you add both vessels of sulfur into the machine at once, you still have to process two separate vats of acid to complete the "puzzle", which brings you to the third puzzle-- which is literally doing the realm's first puzzle. A second time.  Hilariously, it's actually possible to get back to 115 volts in a single pylon move upon returning to the first puzzle, mercifully letting the realm end quickly if you make the right move.  Now, onto the game's narrative.The big reveal about Firmament's 'true setting' is nearly identical to one shared by another adventure game released a few years prior, and so unfortunately it failed to be an exciting revelation to me.  And if you've consumed a bit of media dealing with amnesia, you, like me, may have guessed the game's twist the moment the Keeper tells you she will lie to you, then immediately begins mentioning Turner.  The 'you were Turner all along' twist cliche was predictable, but not my biggest gripe with the narrative.  Adventure games have the unique opportunity to cram those environments full of objects to look at, things to read, mementos to collect, visual storytelling to analyze-- and Firmament's environments, though pretty, have very little in the way of indirect storytelling.  The two additional bunkers you find in St. Andrew and Juleston only have checklists in them, and the small number of accessible rooms in the Swan have very little personal detail injected into them that might have helped players develop an idea or an attachment to the previous keepers.The vast majority of the narrative is lore dumped at the very end, and the fragments you get from the Keeper about herself and the other keepers completely fail to flesh anyone out as actual characters.  In the final scene, she gives the player a long, emotional monologue that completely fails to land because the game has done almost exclusively telling and not showing the player the impact Turner had on the other keepers.  The Keeper gloats as she reveals that she used you to carry out her plan, and hopes that you'll feel "enraged" and "remorseful", but the game has done nothing to actually put us in Turner's shoes, and so her monologue leaves you feeling even more disconnected from the player character than you likely were before that scene.  She states "you were our god" and "our monster", and had the narrative and the game done anything at all to demonstrate this, rather than simply tell us this, that scene could have had a powerful impact.  But the game didn't do that, and so the ending was just as disappointing as the rest of the game. I said up top that game development is extremely challenging, and it is.  This studio has produced incredible experiences in the past, and I hope they will again in the future, but this was not good.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan since the beginning of Myst.  Loved the last one, Obduction.  So far, I am progressing pretty quickly, but the clever nature of the game so far is wonderful!  We've never had an ice world before, I don't think?  I have not experienced any glitches that others have.  I could care less about VR, it makes me sick anyway.  I will see how it goes, but I don't get all the comparisons to Myst/Riven (30 years ago).  It's new, and we've had plenty of great story since then. Uru and Obduction were my favorites.  Hopefully it is indeed as provoking as all of those, only time will tell!  So far so good!  Beautiful too, it actually tells me that my 8 year old graphics card sucks and needs updating to really see it in its prime lol, it put me on low, but I think it still looks great.  If you love running through games at full speed and have no patience, this game is not for you.  I suspect that a few people played level 1 and called it dumb right away. _childDocuments_.review: Regarding the puzzles, most were quite simple and environment based where exploring was the biggest part of it. Some elements where not difficult but just extremely tedious. Overall i'd rate the puzzles a 6/10.The environment was actually really nice, and fit in with the mechanics really well. 8/10What bothered me the most was the amount of bugs and glitches in the game. During the puzzles I got soft-locked 3 times. I had a weird texture glitch where all of the textures were partly covered in random pixels. And I fell out of the map and glitched out a couple of times. This game really required a lot more polishing and should never be allowed to release in its current state. 3/10
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a lot of fun!As is to be expected with anything from Cyan in recent years, it is a bit graphics intensive. But even my mid-grade graphics card did alright, and the environments are very beautiful as always. A few minor graphical glitches, but nothing too bad. The story is great, it raised so many fun an interesting questions! I liked that there was a bit of down time between puzzles for me to soak in the views and think about what might be going on behind the scenes of the story, since it is a bit of a mystery. I actually found the puzzles to be mostly pretty simple, I wish they had been a bit more difficult. They are definitely easier than Myst and Riven, about on par with Obduction. I had two points in the ice crane area where the crane got physically stuck or I got stuck and couldn't get out, but the "Teleport to Safe Area" feature is able to get you out without having to reload a save. And it sounds like they have fixed those situations in patches since then anyway! Overall a lot of fun to play, I would definitely recommend it to fans of Cyan's previous work, and anyone who likes a good story or puzzle game!
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended if you're a fan of Cyan's other games. The environments are gorgeous and top-notch, but the puzzles and story aren't quite up to the same level of excellence as some of their other games. There are some good puzzles and intriguing story elements, don't get me wrong, but the whole package feels a bit shallower than something like riven or obduction. _childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Completed in VR and NOT satisfied. This release is a heavy blow to the reputation of Cyan.The good: The game is beautiful, it really is. Nice steampunk vibes are all over it.The bad: Everything else.This is an appalling bug-ware, it really is. It had produced a crash for about every 20 minutes of playtime. Once so violently that I had to reinstall graphics drivers. This software is barely matured for beta testing, selling it as a finished product for 30+ euros is a scam.Mechanics are annoying. Even though the title was advertised as a VR-oriented project you can not interact with the world. You only use special 'keyholes'. It is 'point and click' very clumsily implemented.The world is very inconsequential. A spoiler-free example: In your very first 100 meters you pass by 6 shovels while following a freshly cleaned path on snow-covered mountainside. Wow! A 6-strong team is working here? Where they are, who they are? Nah, those shovels are there just to look good. Details have not any significance here. Even physics has no significance here.The story is barely worth mentioning. A net woven from plot-holes. The lore... What lore?I will not start lamenting on the puzzles, many players did it before. Some puzzles are OK, but most of them are quite dumb and painfully tedious indeed.By completing the game I feel entitled to declare that the Keepers are obtuse zealots and they should be looked down on for their goofy designs. This is my considered opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lukewarm recommendation coming with major caveats.The graphics are really good, especially considering it's made by a small team. The worlds are a lot of fun to explore and the strong Cyan mysterious mood is very real realized.The puzzles are a mixed bag. There are a few great puzzles, many ok puzzles, a few ones I didn't like. Overall the puzzles were mostly enjoyable. Strangely, compared to previous Cyan games, the puzzles require little to no note taking, very few clues are involved, they are more mechanics-based puzzles. I somewhat miss the older style of puzzles, but on its own terms it's alright.The story is very thin, you get a little bit at the beginning and the rest at the end. In-between, there is minimal story progression.On the bad side though, this game struggles badly with physics issues. I go stuck on geometry multiple times (there is a teleport to safe location feature in the menus, I had to use it way too often...). I also had issues with a crane getting stuck, or with cart tracks suddenly no longer wanting to move. The physics issues get really problematic to be honest. I really hope they can fix them as they really spoiled the enjoyment I had playing this game
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: It was pretty good, I don't know if I'm just getting better adapted at these sorts of puzzles or this was much easier to figure out than previous Cyan games.  I do think one thing could have been done better, there are comments in a final dialog about getting to know the other Keepers that seemed without substance.  There were no other persons narrating, there was very little literature that gave background to the other Keepers, yet you are told she wanted you to get to know them and follow their journey.  Did I miss something?  Other than that these are always good games and great exercise for the brain and heart.

_childDocuments_.review: I love challenging puzzle games, but this one is less challenging and more tedious to the point of testing your patience at every turn. There is so much pointless running around, and as you often have no idea how to even begin to solve a problem, you will be running back and forth between seemingly unrelated locations in the hope that you've overlooked something.Cyan has even invented a way to make fast travel...tedious and slow. Congratulations.Some in-game notes you could discover, or any sort of hint on the equipment, would go a long way to making this great looking game actually fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it. The puzzles were unobtrusive, and allowed for a good flow from beginning to end. It didn't overstay its welcome, and was the better for it. I do feel the story, which was strong conceptually, was let down by the lack of narrative delivered throughout the play-through via the game itself. There is a striking lack of written context for a Cyan game as one example. This resulted in some interesting conceptual story beats all hitting at the tail end of the game, rather than being built to. So, not perfect, but I enjoyed it. 7/10P.S. Cyan, if you read this, please add the option to turn off the repeating loudspeaker chants. On multiple occasions I chose to turn off the game when stuck on a puzzle due only to how grating hearing that on repeat became.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This is a rather painful one to write. The game isn't "bad" per se, but when compared against Cyan's legacy, it is probably one of id not worst game they have put out. While I'm not some old school Cyan fan, I do have deep respect and admiration for the company for what they have achieved int he past, ad how they have managed to stay afloat, even if it is in a severally reduced capacity from their glory days. Still, I don;t think that is an excuse for the how the game turned out. There is still a very distinct kind of game that people expect from a "Cyan" game which has some rather high standards to meet which is not easy to do which this game fails on, yet even when compared to Obduction, their most recent game, it falls short of that too.I really hope this is just a one off and not a new standard for Cyan, as if they continue down this path they will likely just utterly destroy their legacy which will be the most disappointing part of all.Even though so many years have passed, I, like many others still believe Cyan has the talent and energy to do what they have always done best, as the environments in this game are the same quality you come to know from them. Which is why it is a shame that everything else is some major steps behind. Maybe with time and resources some changes and additions can be made to the game, otherwise I hope this is taken as a real wake up call for whatever comes next.

_childDocuments_.review: A disappointing follow up to Myst - on rails, with most puzzles being "find the button that says finish puzzle", complicated by fumbly mechanical puzzles that tended to break the game. I was hoping for a lot here, but the number and difficulty of puzzles, and luke warm story, just didn't create a successor to Myst.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it by the end, but it took a while to get going.I think compared to Cyan's previous games the puzzles are generally more straightforward than usual, and I never hit a point where I felt like the solution required so much note taking/comparison that using a guide to simplify even parsing what the "problem" was was necessary. I found myself slightly disappointed by how there wasn't as many "eureka!" moments for me while playing as I had in Myst or Obduction, but at the same time I still enjoyed solving them. There's something to be said for puzzles being more about base-level logic and spacial awareness/navigation as well - it definitely helped keep the pacing pleasingly brisk.The environments are also huge and lovingly detailed/designed, as you'd expect of Cyan. The game looks wonderful and the puzzles at several points are on a scale that'd qualify as a "setpiece" moment in Obduction for me - there's fewer overall to solve, the game is a lot shorter in general really, but I definitely found myself impressed by the scope of some of them. The main area of the game I had issues with for most of its duration was the narrative. I found it consistently a letdown how little there is in the way of "lore" through most of the game - compared to Obduction, the "cast" you grow to learn about is tiny (I'd say more comparable to Myst) and the actual backstory is delivered mostly via monologues triggered at set points from the mysterious woman speaking to you rather than finding notes, journals, and other articles plus cues in the environments. I went in wanting to get lost in the world of the game and finding out about it as I explored, but it never really scratched that itch for me.And then the ending happened and suddenly everything clicked into place and the emotional impact of it was tremendous compared to the level of investment I felt in it before. While I still think the game should and could have fleshed out the array of characters alluded to but never "seen" throughout it, I can't say I left it still unsatisfied with the story.I can see why this game has proved to be somewhat divisive with Cyan's fanbase but for me personally I had a very good time with it and left it feeling more than satisfied. I never encountered any bugs that broke the game, got me stuck on geometry, or otherwise posed a noticeable technical issue but the game does run oddly poorly at points. It was never for a protracted period but there'd be times where the framerate would dive for me by 30% or slightly more - and I'm not referring to traversal stutter, I mean certain scenes just seemed more demanding on my hardware than they should relative to others which ran better. I'd say performance is a bit rough still but not so bad as it apparently was before the patches. Have not played it in VR and cannot comment on that.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved Myst, Riven, Exile, Obduction and now Firmament.  There were a few puzzles that had me a little frustrated and one that you have to go back and do again when you think you are done that just had me think "why ?"  However, I loved that Cyan feel and for anyone looking to scratch the Myst itch this is worth a go.  I have to say overall I enjoyed the puzzle difficulty sometimes it felt like you could just brute force your way through and I kind of liked that but I still have PTSD from Myst Revelations and unlike that torture of an impossible puzzle game, this one is very fair. _childDocuments_.review: With Firmament, Cyan seems to have violated their core ethos of weaving story, environment, and puzzles into a seamless, immersive, meaningful, and satisfying experience. Obduction was masterful in this respect. Firmament by contrast is a vapid, dreary slog trough meaningless friction serving only to prolong the concealment of a plot reveal (veiled but potential spoilers here) that we've seen many times before in games like The Forgotten City and more recently on Netflix's (also dreary) 1899. Aside from the cryptic voiceover and a few scraps of paper, there is neither character nor story development along the way, with the only reward for solving one puzzle being the next puzzle. Firmament tells its entire tale in the last 15 minutes of the game, by which point I'm regretting the previous 15+ hours' toil (many of those hours were spent trying to navigate a plethora of bugs, terrain glitches, and graphical issues). This game is either unfinished or the premise doesn't work.Update: After the fifth patch, I tried three times to give this game another go and quit less than halfway though every time. (One graphics issue still isn't fixed.) Firmament has absolutely no replay value. Knowing how it ends, very little of the "hints" and "teases" in the early narration pay off or even make sense in hindsight. Phrases like "awaken the embrace" are grammatical and logical nonsense. Cyan goofed around making a THIRD version of Myst that no one asked for, and that is likely the reason Firmament is such a root canal. I've rarely harbored such passionate hate for a game. The next Cyan title should be "Retirement."
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Long ago, Cyan taught me the first rule of a good puzzle: The fun of solving a puzzle is figuring out how it works, not entering the solution. If I have to press ten buttons to learn which one is the right one, pressing the right one is satisfying. If I have to press one button to learn which ten are the right ones, then pressing those ten is tedious. Sadly they seem to have forgotten their own lesson with this game. There are at least three puzzles in this INCREDIBLY SHORT game that I really don't ever want to solve again because, while figuring out their rules was simple, entering their correct solution was not. One of them, the game will make you do twice. They're not all bad, some are fun and satisfying, but you probably won't be needing any scratch paper, let alone a journal. And the puzzles are rather poorly integrated into the world - unlike in Riven where the puzzles were so naturally integrated into the environment, here there's a big billboard with the word "PUZZLE!" and a old-timey hand pointing the way. Just look for the adjunct nodes. I mean what purpose do these things actually serve in this world besides being an annoying gate to another basic section? How did these people do their day-to-day jobs?Speaking of the adjunct, I'm sure it's a great way for VR players to interact with puzzles in a virtual world with no other form of haptic feedback available, but admittedly it does make the game a one-trick pony. The upgrades do add some interesting new tricks, but it's pretty much the only way you're going to be performing any. Point, connect, twist. This game is light on story during the actual gameplay, but what few actual tidbits you do get out of the otherwise vague and purple-ish monologue do pay off in the end. I was honestly not expecting the ending. And good news - the ending is only ten hours of tepid puzzle-solving away! I really wish there had been more world-building related to the actual story. Everything is just so uncharacteristically vague for a Cyan game! I'm used to seeing little details sprinkled around that implied events that took place here; there's very little of that in this game and none of it is made any clearer by later revelations in the story.And the numerous opportunities to soft-lock yourself. Save often! Also there's an option in the Settings menu that you can use to get unstuck without losing your progress - the soft-locks were honestly much less annoying after that. But yes, they happen a lot.Bottom line though, I am glad that I played it, I did enjoy seeing a new Cyan game, and the graphics are stunningly beautiful and the music is really good, which is finally something that's on par for Cyan. Best-looking game my poor old PC has ever run (it's well below minimum specs, but it ran surprisingly well with only the occasional lag spike when loading new areas and long loading transition times). If you ever see it on sale for like ten bucks, go for it. But full price? Nah.

_childDocuments_.review: Kickstarter backer that took their sweet time to finish this.Game's not without its bumps and issues, a few minor sticking points here and there, some of which I saw get patched out as I played through due to my procrastination. >>;If you're going to play, make sure you update your graphics drivers before playing, i was stubborn about it and fussed for far too long before caving and just committing to a graphics update, fixed many visual issues I was having once I did that.
