_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Cyan games since Myst first came out when I was a child. I think the only ones I haven't played are Myst 5, and the Myst Online multiplayer game. Obduction had an interesting gameplay mechanic going for it, which I appreciated - but I'm not quite sure what to make of Firmament. It seems fairly 'simple' in the sense everything is a nail, and you have a hammer (except replace nail with socket, and hammer with Adjunct). The sockets all look the same, so the game kind of feels "samey" in the sense that you spend all your time holding your Adjunct in "ready" position, just searching for the tell-tale glint of red crosshairs (there's a socket, but it's too far away) to green crosshairs (you may now launch your Adjunct into the socket to do whatever specialty actions that particular same-looking socket allows you to do).The puzzles were fine, very environmental based. Nothing like Riven and placing a bunch of colored beads on a grid; these are very contextual puzzles that you might not even realize are puzzles until you're in the middle of them.The graphics are great looking, for the most part. Cyan's developers seem to be getting the hang of working with Unreal Engine, since they used it in Obduction too. It is still somewhat discouraging to see that when you're in a naturey-area like St Andrews, there are weeds and plants growing out of the cracks in the stone around you, but there's no wind; the plants don't move. In the Juleston realm, you watch liquid pour out of pipe, and there's no splash against the wall next to the pipe. So really, while things look good, it does still seem like having things 'interact' with each other; wind on plants, liquid on other surfaces nearby, needs some work.The music is generally pretty sparse, and only kicks in when you're entering one of the "important areas" in each realm for the first time. Other than that, the game is mostly silent except for P.A. loudspeaker repeated announcements. What little music there was did seem to have the telltale Cyan vibe that I remember from Myst and Riven. It was pleasant.I do wonder if the voice actor(s?) who Cyan insists in their A.I. assisted content statement chose to be uncredited for privacy reasons (are they French? Russian? What is that accent the mentor has; it's driving me nuts) are part of a voice actors' union. It does seem a little eyebrow raising that there are at least 3 different voices I can think of (the loudspeaker male-presenting voice, the mentor's female voice, and then a voice right at the end of the game which is also male-presenting) and the statement Cyan gives, the "actor" mentioned appears to be singular. Was A.I. used to turn a single non-union actor's performance into 3 separate ones as a means of cutting cost: not hiring union professionals, and only hiring a single actor instead of three?...I don't want to believe the beloved company of my childhood would behave in a scabby way like that, but with lack of further clarity beyond their statement (that I have been able to find at least) what else are we, the customers and audience, supposed to think?In any case, I still do recommend the game, but on sale. It did take me about 10 hours to finish, and I think I only looked up one thing when I couldn't figure out what to do next (I had missed noticing a tunnel at some point that I needed to go down to progress). It was a bit bland, but still pretty, and I did enjoy the ending closure.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with gorgeous settings and wonderful attention to detail. _childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - it's fine. Visually beautiful, with puzzle gameplay alternating between enjoyable to tedious (sometimes within the same puzzle). You'll play it if you're an adventure puzzle gamer and probably enjoy it (bugs notwithstanding), but it doesn't quite sit neatly within the conventions of that genre which I think is what has led to a lot of the negative reviews. Required the fewest hints for me of any Cyan game to get through, but still enough head-scratching moments to keep me entertained.Longer thoughts:The Cyan game this reminds me most of is, strangely, URU; fairly linear level design, with a lot of "world" surrounding more sparse puzzle elements that are generally about physically progressing to another area of the world. One of the consequences of this is it can make each world feel quite game-y, and people who were expecting a Riven-like immersion are perhaps rightly disappointed. Likewise, people who are expecting more typical logic/code puzzles as in Myst-likes won't find them here. But you can't say that Cyan hasn't been designing levels like this for a long time, because actually this represents a culmination of a decades-long trend in their level design away from anything resembling "puzzles" in a traditional sense. The non-Cyan game this reminded me of is Firewatch. Which, admittedly, I haven't finished, but Firmament seems to contain a lot of similar elements: essentially an environmental task simulator with exploration/adventure elements, coupled with a voice-over companion to keep you company (although in Firewatch you can talk back to her; that wouldn't really be Cyan's style). I actually enjoyed the story and the reveal at the end; I guessed part of the twist but not everything about it so it was still a good payoff for completing the game. Help yourself and avoid spoilers before playing.My personal take on negative reviews below: I work as a musician, and often see the same problem in my field when legacy artists with a huge past reputation try something new. Yes Myst and Riven were great, but if you're going to be an artist, you have to keep reinventing yourself. Even if it doesn't measure up to a nostalgia-tinted view of the past, you still have to let artists be artists. They put a lot into this game; give it a try.That being said; Cyan, if you're reading this, remember for next time that not everything completely realistic is necessarily fun. Real life is tedious. Video game puzzles needn't be.

_childDocuments_.review: It is not often that I write reviews, but I feel compelled to do so in this case.I have played the game in non-VR mode, so I cannot comment on the VR aspect at this time. However, I am likely to revisit it for VR in the future.I really enjoyed it. Although it does have some quirks and optimization issues, the core gameplay is solid. Despite using a not state-of-the-art graphics card and a 4K display, but the implementation of FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) works its wonders for the game.If you are a fan of this genre of games, I suggest giving it a try. The worst-case scenario is that you may have to play it at a lower resolution or revisit it later. The artwork is incredible, and I particularly appreciate the "Art déco Science Fiction" style it embraces.I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the puzzle-solving, the gorgeous and meticulously put-together worlds that are all centrally linked. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game but was a little underwhelmed.Usually in Cyan games the starter areas are a little more linear, just to get you up to speed on puzzles and how to navigate the world. All of the worlds here are beautiful, but they all felt like starter areas -- short and mostly pretty linear (although you go to each twice), and the puzzles are constrained by the VR interface (which I think was a smart idea but didn't pay off).Throughout the game I expected a moment where some sort of "curtain" would get pulled back and additional complexity would be revealed. That sort of happens, but it's at the end of the game and there are no more puzzles afterwards. Without getting into spoiler territory, if the game continued at that point, and you went back to the worlds and realized there were more things to do with additional implications, that would have made the narrative arc feel like it pays off somehow. As it is, you did some things and heard a story. It's an okay story, and it fits well with the structure of games like this, but it just scratches the surface of what it feels like the game could have been.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: This was an OK game. It was a bad Cyan game.I liked a few of the puzzles. Most of them were tedious. None of them made me pay any sort of attention to the worlds in order to solve them. There was no subtlety in clues. You can ignore the environment and your surroundings completely and solve all the puzzles. You don't have to ever read a single thing. I also like the voice acting, although I find the studio's insistence on the anonymity of the voice actor very strange; people use stage names all the time. But, OK...The worlds are pretty, but it doesn't matter, because the worlds don't matter, because all that matters is your multi-tool and the things you plug it into. There's, like, nothing to read :( There are a very few scattered pages, but no tomes of lore. I guess that's probably because the story doesn't make any sense at all, and applying any sort of deeper lore to it would immediately showcase everything wrong with the idea to begin with. It just doesn't work. None of it makes sense. One of my multi-tool upgrades didn't actually seem to do anything. Apparently it did stuff, but I never had any idea that it was happening, nor did I have any clue that I couldn't do that thing before. The upgrades are never used in tandem, which I really thought the game was leading up to, and is generally how multi-upgrade puzzle games, like, work!I expected the "...and Beyond!" portion of the game to incorporate puzzles with all the upgrades working together.  But, no, that just doesn't happen. There is not a single puzzle in the "...and Beyond!" portion of the game, just a long walk to another socket to plug into, and another long walk back. And then a long monologue to try and forget that none of what you're learning makes any damn sense.One very good puzzle is literally repeated later, just with different values. It's in the same exact location, and has the same exact complexity. Your previous solution is simply invalidated, so you just have to solve it again, in the same exact way. Come on!I don't know, y'all. It seems like something just went very wrong here. I guess sometimes we all hand in half-assed assignments, but as a credited backer, I sure am sad that THIS is Cyan the game I chose to kickstart.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR : A beautiful game in VR, okay story, and a very meh delivery, but worth a play.I'm giving this a very tentative thumbs up, with my love of Cyan certainly coloring my opinions. I played MYST when it launched in 1993, as well as all the various MYST incarnations since then and every other Cyan title and their various releases. I'm also a backer of the FanGamer financing campaign for "Firmament" back in 2020.Firstly, tech background... I'm playing in VR on a relatively high-end rig with a 3080TI running a wireless Vive Cosmos Elite and Index Knuckles controllers. The game is running under Nvidia DLSS with Epic graphics settings and it runs smoothly with no performance issues worth mentioning. Finally, I played the game to completion prior to the 1st patch release.In short, the game is beautiful in VR and is very obviously a Cyan game in style and presentation. Some heavy BioShock design influences, but... 🐔 or 🥚... 🤷‍♂️. The lower resolution textures, tree designs, and general chunkiness of levels scream MYST and are part of the Cyan aesthetic for me, not a design failure. I did take a peek at the game running outside of VR and it appears the textures could be the same, so Cyan may have erred on the side of using the chunkier VR resolution textures in both presentations to save on development resources. In any case, it means playing in VR feels like stepping right into the desktop game... fully immersive. I doubt I'll ever bother playing outside of VR. My one gripe with game play so far is the lack of interaction with objects in general... very little you can actually pick up and inspect.I haven't encountered many of the VR bugs detailed in other reviews, but I agree with reviewers seeing flickering with clouds, fog, shadows, subtitle windows, and game menus. The game menu interaction is the biggest issue for me... my controller pointers are overlaid by the menus... I can still make selections, but it's difficult to see where I'm pointing. As for story and delivery... meh. I would have appreciated a lot more "show" and far less "tell." The story is much too dependent on the narrator for exposition. You're reading a book 2 minutes into the game, but only 2 or 3 more books in the game total and you're done?  I'm also a bit disappointed in the quality of the narrator audio and acting... but, again, cheesy voice acting and over the top dialog are kind of Cyan's thing. 🫢Finally, the "twist" and final act... not bad in substance and I didn't see it coming, but the story feels rushed post twist. A few bits of text deliver what should have been shown via game play discovery throughout. Definitely felt like there was a rush to complete the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I held off of playing Firmament because of the mixed reviews, but in the end I enjoyed it much more than Obduction. The feel, the story, and the environments were simply much more to my liking. I particularly found the story very compelling in its build-up and revelations towards the ending, which all felt very original.The puzzles are on the easy side, but very enjoyable in their execution. Cyan still knows how to make machinery with satisfying sound effects!It's as they say, Cyan doesn't make puzzle games, they make exploration games, and Firmament is an excellent example of that. Sometimes their games will have tricky puzzles, sometimes not, I tend to enjoy them regardless.My biggest criticism is that it's a bit on the short side, about an hour or two less than I spent on most of the Myst games.

_childDocuments_.review: The latest instalment from Cyan is definitely a treat to play, with a few caveats. The pros: the story, mechanics, and visual effects were amazing. _childDocuments_.review: A non-VR reviewCalling it a disappointment is putting it mildly. I know there was Covid during the development of these. But I don't see five years worth of work here. The bugs are numerous, graphical issues. Puzzles can literally break on you, forcing you to 'teleport to safety' and restart them. But because of how slowly some of the puzzles move, this can set you back ten to fifteen minutes because a crane literally gets impossibly jammed between two walls.The lack of FMVs is disappointing, the narrator is currently broken and inconsistently talks. Which is kind of a problem because she is the only real source of 'story' to be had. The grand total of 'lore' you can find is two, a book with two poems, and a book with minimal explanation about your puzzle tool. She is literally the only NPC.While the environments are nice, closer to what I expect out of Cyan. It's missing so much of what made cyan great.The puzzles are not puzzles, every single one of them is just orientation based. Rotate platforms to get a certain number, but it's random because there is no logic to the numbering system for the platforms. Complete a sliding block puzzle where you remove X block, on an X Y axis, orientation, figure out just the right spot to stand in a convulted enclosed space to hit  a switch, and each switch has to be in order, you can't get it wrong, you just have to find the right one and the right spot, orientation.There are no actual logic puzzles to be had here, even Obduction had far superior puzzles to this. No need to write down a note from one area to help you solve a puzzle in another area, no little things to investigate that make you understand a number system (The counting device in Riven school).  This is a lifeless, poor excuse of a game, that doesn't justify a $40 price tag. I expect more from Cyan, more from a kickstarter that raised $1.5 million, which to compare to obduction, raised more than Obduction. Obduction had multiple FMV actors, actual puzzle elements, lore aplenty to find and dive deep into the world. Where the heck did all the money for this go? Because I don't see it.Cyan, Rand Miller, you were so influential to my childhood, I know you are capable of doing better. Please, it's so upsetting to see this game come out of your studio.Take your money somewhere else, this is a barely more than a  VR walking simulator.Edit to respond to DeveloperI didn't see FMVs advertised anywhere, in fact I kept pretty low key on how much info I allowed myself to get. Saw the annoucenment, new Cyan game, decided I would get it.But why was I expecting to see FMVs? You are literally Cyan Worlds, the pioneering studio of taking FMVs in this type of game to the next level in the industry. Even your last game Obduction, had FMVs. FMVS and Cyan studios mostly go hand in hand. Myst, Riven, Exile, Revelations, Obduction < All FMVs, Uru and End of Ages no FMVs (Y'all we're even criticized for leaving out the FMVs in the Myst remake) So, uh, yea. FMVs are an expected product given your legacy. I will admit the mention of a '90s style physical box' listed on the Kickstarter did give me slim hope that this would be a return to form, and 90s style Cyan Worlds is FMVs all in. Did I make an assumption, sure. But again, it's literally your legacy and a rather large chunk of why the Myst Franchise is so beloved.As far giving it a try again, why? I beat it. There is literally nothing more to gain because it's a poorly realized universe that looks pretty but doesn't really have anything else going for it.

_childDocuments_.review: To start off, the visual design and atmosphere of nearly every environment in the game is amazing. I found myself stopping and admiring the view more times than I can count. This is the one aspect that I can say the game really excels in.The story is barebones and many things aren't really explained, as you might expect. The mystery was enough to keep me motivated to get through the game, but the actual dialogue from your "companion" often felt annoyingly vague just for the sake of being mysterious. The way the story ultimately wraps up is kind of so-so in my opinion. Satisfying enough, but it's not likely to stick with me either.Unfortunately, when it comes to actually playing the game, the majority of the puzzles felt annoying, tedious, or both. The last one (which I'll just refer to as "the steam puzzle" to keep things vague) made me seriously consider just quitting the game then and there. I've enjoyed many of Cyan's previous games, and for some reason, most of the puzzles this time felt more annoying than actually fun.On the technical front, there are definitely still some bugs that need to be ironed out, but based on the size of the patch that just dropped earlier today, it seems likely that all of the most common issues will be addressed. The worst I encountered were a few instances of various movable objects getting "stuck", and while it was certainly frustrating, the "teleport to a safe location" option in the menu was always able to solve those issues, so it was usually pretty easy to get past. No crashes or anything more severe than that, thankfully.Overall, the experience was much more frustrating than enjoyable, even as a fan of Cyan's previous games with some idea of what to expect.

_childDocuments_.review: So as a (relatively newer) fan of the MYST series as well as Obduction, I went into this with fairly high hopes. While most of the puzzles in this game pale in comparison to Cyan's other works, being almost solely based on you Adjunct tool, the game is still fun and with the right amount of difficulty and frustration one comes to expect from them. The ending took me completely by surprise, and that's as much as I'll say. The game felt like it would be short at first, and while it isn't too long, it was a 12 hours well spent. Also, if you have RAZER stuff in your setup, especially a keyboard, pay attention to it. The effects are sooo cool, starting even with the logos uopn launch, with my keyboard proudly displaying Cyan's logo. To whomever did the Chroma effects for this game, bravo. I want to have those patterns saved for my setup.As for VR mode, I did't play much at all in vr, just a few mins. As I'm sure you'll see other reviews mention, it rather feels like an afterthought, and I would honestly recommend just going in flat with a good pair of headphones and a dark room, so the Razer Chroma effects can really show.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start? Well... Since the the release of Riven in the 90's I am an avid fan of these games because they take you on a journey of fascinating stories in worlds which mesmerizes. The way they engulf you in one fantastic world after another combined with mindblowing and beautiful puzzles which fit perfectly into these magical enviroments is breathtaking. Often almost combined with physical pain of virtual grieve the moment you realize you have to leave a specific world after solving the puzzle because you are so desperate to learn more about these worlds...And then there is Firmament. – Let's say: Firmament is the weakest game Cyan ever made. – beside the real bad technical issues like being irreversibly stuck in a machinery which happended to me several times –• No magical worlds.• No variety in "puzzles". • No real puzzles at all but "plug yourself in to go from A to B, and figure out how"• No real obvious goal.• Very sparse environmental story telling which usually is the key signature of Cyan games.• It is uncharactaristically short. • My 16 hour playtime is only because of long distance walks from A to B and not because of puzzle time.  • The moment a real story finally might unfold the game ubruptly ends. Two issues I personally think which helped to block any variety in creating cool world environments and puzzles:• The Unreal Engine which seems not to be the best gaming tool for these kind of puzzle games.  • More severe: The tool you've been given to solve puzzles / obstacles – to me that was the initial killer of and an adamant restricting device to any creativity for the puzzles. This time was my first time being a backer for this game. But I am not disappointed in doing so due to all the beautiful games Cyan did before. And it is a small studio. They still absolutely deserve it. Awaiting a Cyan game I was prepared with color pens and a sketchnook. But all the highly creative color, sound, time, lever, picture puzzles in magical landscapes with their weird characters I missed dearly. – Nothing of this is present in Firmament. Would I recommend the game? I don't know. Neither yes, nore no. But that is not an option here on Steam.So, I have to choose... let's say yes.

_childDocuments_.review: Love Cyan, really do. Grew up with Myst and Riven - these days I play all the games through again every other year and I even hop on Myst Online every now and then. Uru was kind of like another home for me when I was a kid. Shorah! Also, I have to say, I really enjoyed Obduction, and I pitched in on the Kickstarter to re-release the Myst games, and I even have Ghen's inkwell. The rich stories and original mechanics still feel fresh today.That being said, I implore you - do NOT buy this game just to support Cyan. Buy it if you think 5 hrs (if even?) of broken gameplay in a Cyan world is worth $35. I highly doubt it is. Firmament is simply not worth your time and money. This game is terrible. I have no clue what happened. Where did Cyan go? The mechanics are mind-numbingly tedious and unoriginal. [Run here to activate a crane. Run somewhere else to move the crane. Run up a ladder to raise/lower the crane. Sorry, can't get there yet! Backtrack back to find out what you did wrong! Oops, you somehow rotated the double crane too far and it's now stuck in a wall and won't respond! Hit Esc and go to your settings to unstuck and restart! Oops, you somehow rotated it the other way and then it got stuck in open air and won't respond! Hit Esc and go to your settings to unstuck and restart! Want any of these janky cranes to let go of an ice cube? Sorry, the crane can't let go of what it's carrying!] It's fascinating to see Cyan Worlds, who brightened the eyes of this little baby engineer in the 1990s, struggle to handle something as simple as a crane picking up an ice cube. Yet here we are.The game is lonely and lifeless and there are 3 puzzles total. Each puzzle is extremely simple. The story reveal at the end is truly lackluster and forces you to run in literal circles and go up and down ladders to listen to the narrative. I'm really not sure what else to say, because there is truly so little here to even talk about. Where are the invented languages? The different numbering systems? The ciphers and lore? Man, such a letdown. Wasted potential. In the first 10 minutes, entering The Swan, you really do get those goosebumps as if you're embarking on a glistening Cyan Worlds adventure, it's beautiful.. but then reality hits you in the face. There really are only 3 simple puzzles, each with zero ingenuity. Janky broken crane physics requiring unstucking.. Gosh, what in the world happened?

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament gets to the essence of what makes Cyan games special: puzzles that exist as part of a world, rather than just being placed for you to solve. The game has you perform the regular maintenance duties of the "Keepers", operating machinery and clearing away debris. Often the only real puzzle-y part is understanding how the controls of a device work - but these aren't made deliberately obscure to increase difficulty, rather they feel unfamiliar because they are intended for someone who actually lives in the world of Firmament. I found this mode of environmental storytelling very satisfying.That said, I can understand why people are disappointed. You likely won't have to break out pencil and paper, and there's no hidden language or number system to decipher. Most of the challenge comes from spatial reasoning and noticing connections between things in 3D space. This *can* mean spending time manipulating parts of a puzzle after you've already worked out what to do in your head, so I think you need to be on board with the atmosphere of the game.I think I'm past midway through the game, making progress towards the major objective in each area. I waited until the initial patches and haven't experienced the sorts of bugs called out in other reviews, though I believe them because of how much puzzles rely on movement and physics. Though I have not tried Firmament in VR, it's worth noting the game feels very much designed for VR: lots of standing on a moving platform you control, or walking through (gorgeous) areas between set pieces you can interact with, while listening to a disembodied narrator. I wouldn't call this a bad thing - really, it's more or less how Myst was laid out - but it definitely contributes to the emptiness of the world, beyond just the intended presentation of the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Played in VR on Reverb G2.This is a beautiful atmospheric game. The puzzles are challenging and if you enjoyed Myst or Obduction this is for you. Firmament has high graphics requirements so I can only play it with all the graphics settings at low.The game auto saves as you progress and you have only one manual save. If you use your manual save you lose the auto save. I played for about 5 hours and the auto save would not load, my manual save was at the start of the game so all progress was lost! When I re-started I copied the saved games, just in case of a repeat, but it was a one off.

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament is a wonderful world full of contraptions and intrigue, and I've enjoyed every second of it. Some folks have their complaints however, and I would like to do my part as a Cyan fanboy to provide a counter argument. The primary issue that people are discussing is that the game is a bit short for the budget invested into it. Well, while I don't have a fly in the wall to any development issues, I do know that your main tool has a vastly different design from the demo, with reports that it was overhauled because no one figured out how to control it autonomously (you were supposed to point the drone at an object and recall it with a wave). While needing a mulligan is a good excuse for the game's length, I don't think that it needs an excuse, as A: the price is reasonable for a high end indie, B: us kickstarter backers had years to recuperate from our investments anyways, and C: you can play the same game more than once, my guy. The other "complaint" is that the puzzles are too difficult for some, to which I point at the Devs' 90's puzzler pedigree and inform you that most people could get through those by writing notes like a conspiracy nut. My brothers in christ, they're going easy on you, if this still isn't your cup of tea, you could just do that, or if not, just watch a guide or something... Oh, and stay away from the upcoming Riven remake If you feel not up to this challenge, but if you power through until it clicks, I will be glad to eat my words. Game on!

_childDocuments_.review: Without a doubt, Firmament is first and foremost a loving ode to great cinema. One minute you are running along the top of a gigantic crane just like The Rock in that movie about a new skyscraper, and every so often you will feel sure you're being followed by Michael Myers!I could go on but I'd be revealing too much of the plot. Suffice to say, this game is chock full of awesome movie references. One of the best is a super cool Star Wars ability! How many can you find?Oh, and by the way, if this has whetted your appetite for steampunk puzzle games, I highly recommend you check out Quern - Undying Thoughts.Meanwhile, I'm off to watch Halloween again. The 1978 original, of course.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like writing negative reviews for games that I want to like but I feel like enough missed the mark with this experience it is worth writing about. For reference, I have been playing Cyan games since the original Myst on PC, have played Riven-Uru, Obduction, Quern, The Witness and I am a big fan of puzzle games. If you are a Cyan fan, wait until this is on sale for $20 or less. Its an interesting experience, albeit a hollow one, and is not worth release price. If you are a just puzzle game fan, I don't recommend Firmament. The "puzzles" are rarely fun or challenging and tend to be tedious and and uninspired. There are very few in universe "read-ables" to help flesh this world out. This is very little to flesh the world out at all. The environments are all different but share similar to-dos, so it gets old fairly quickly. There is little to push the player to the end. Narratives should drive the game even if it is superficial. Bugs and glitches are everywhere. I am writing this at release so hopefully this will be patched for future players. I got out of bounds more time than I could remember. I soft-locked the game multiple times and it autosaved after I broke the game, so I had to replay entire sections. Not super fun. There are issues when the game has a dedicated "teleport me to a not broken area" button in settings. I really wish Cyan would go back to stories like Riven, where you can visit a world that feels fleshed out and "real." Even Obduction, for all it's issues, gave the illusion of a "real" or tangible world. The closest I've gotten to that sense of immersion has been Quern and The Witness. Both exist in a "reality." The only reality present in Firmament comes across like a mashup of Bioshock asthetics crammed into a VR point and click.
_childDocuments_.name: Firmament

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I had a really good time with Firmament! There are a few bugs on release but I trust Cyan to hammer those out. Nothing game-breaking for me, but definitely could have done with some more polish at release time.Looking past that, this is a great, atmospheric puzzler. Trademark Cyan in these new realms... stunning vistas, otherworldly locations, giant machines to unlock. The graphics are gorgeous, and it really shines in VR if you have that option. I found DLSS Quality mode to be the ticket to great visuals and nice frame rates.This game is different from the normal Cyan fare in that you don't need to read and understand a broader culture in order to solve things. The problems are usually right in front of you, ready to be "logic-ed" through. This can lead to some frustration, in that you know what you need to do, but you have to fiddle and dink with things until they are the way you need them. This is unlike the usual "aha!" you would have in a Myst or Riven. They are still satisfying to solve though. I never lost my desire to explore and unlock the mystery around me.The soundtrack fits the vibe well and has some really nice pieces that come in at pivotal moments. All the atmospheric and mechanical sounds are there as well. It really is a nice feast for the eyes and ears. I personally found the length perfect and the ending satisfying, another couple of common complaints. I definitely was not expecting to learn what I learned about Firmament there at the end, that was a cool twist in my mind.Anyways, aside from the bugs at release, I think people just need to go into it not expecting Riven 2.0. Cyan tried something a little different here, and while I would have loved another game like Riven, I am not going to judge Firmament against that selfish desire. I will judge it for what it is, a beautiful and well constructed puzzle game with some fun and satisfying mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike your mentor in Firmament, I will not lie to you; This game is Cyan pushing their limits and taking their fans to their trademark mystery realms/ages/worlds in full VR immersion. After beating the game I look back and enjoy the journey as much as the intriguing and satisfying narrative conclusion. I played on flatscreen - apparently there are reports that the VR has some bugs to iron out. I have no doubt Cyan will address those issues swiftly as they did with their previous title Obduction. We are the Firmament.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played all Myst games as well as Obduction, I want to summarize how Firmament holds up, as a puzzle game and also a Cyan Worlds game. TLDR; Decent puzzle game. A little short and easier compared to mentioned games. Expect a few bugs. Classic, maybe dated visuals. But overall I had a pleasant experience with no complaints.- Environment -If you've played any of the mentioned games from Cyan, this will immediately look familiar to you. Beautiful, vast scenery, across multiple worlds. A feeling of loneliness and exploration in a world that was clearly inhabited, but for some reason is abandoned.I will say, that the game does not have ground breaking graphics that will blow your mind. If anything, it does actually feel like the other Cyan games. I personally didn't dislike the dated visuals as it had a feeling of familiarity and nostalgia for me.- Puzzles -The puzzles themselves are pleasantly challenging. Definitely NOT as difficult as any of the Myst games or Obduction. I never had to take any screenshots, and I only had to use my notepad once or twice to test out a solution before I apply it in-game. The Adjunct is a very welcome addition to the puzzle solving experience, with clear explanations of what you're interacting with, and friendly controls and even a display for some puzzles that you don't have good vision in. You're no longer left to figure out what the puzzles are for, or what their components are. That is not to say it detracts from the experience. There's still a bunch of clever solutions you need to do to progress, as with all Cyan games.- A Few Important Notes -Length - Compared to the other mentioned games, Firmament was to me, shorter, and also easier with less obscure puzzles that required me to backtrack.Jank - Having played through all the Myst games just recently, it wasn't really unexpected to see a few bugs. There are a few that could hinder your progress in various puzzles, as well as other more minor game design bugs. I highly recommend SAVING before you attempt any solving just in case you run into a bug that gets you stuck (I encountered a few instances of such in later puzzles, but nothing too annoying or game breaking)Performance - I have a pretty old pc, i7 7700k with an RTX 2080 Super, and I set the graphics settings to max, with no super sampling. Even though I did get 45-50 FPS in some very particular spots in the maps, overall I had a very smooth experience, mostly locked at 60FPS.FINAL NOTE: YOU'RE SUPPOSED TO HEAR A NARRATOR AS YOU EXPLORE THE GAME. IF YOU'RE NOT HEARING THEM, THEIR DIALOG IS PROBABLY STUCK IN A PREVIOUS MAP. I realized this only at the end of the game lol but it didn't really hinder my progress as I still understood what I was doing and why and still finished the game with the important dialogs occurring and understood the story.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish Steam gave you more options than just "yes" or "no". There are good and bad things to say about this game, but forced to one choice I have to say no, I do not recommend it. What I write below might give readers that impression that I hated it from beginning to end. That's not true, there were a lot of great moments in my playthrough. I'm focusing on the things that stood out to me most though, which unfortunately were not at all positive.The puzzles are few (I think a lot fewer than Obduction), and padded out in three main ways: 1) Forcing the player to wait or backtrack to find information.2) Blocking off direct navigation between important locations and forcing the player to take detours everywhere.2) Reusing assets and forcing the player to solve the same puzzle multiple times. The game tasks the player with operating and piloting various pieces of machinery to gain access to new areas. The process of solving most puzzles was very frustrating. I often found myself knowing what needed to be done, but not succeeding because I'd positioned some piece of equipment just a hair in the wrong direction. In many cases, this would require sevearl indepth steps to correct. To a shocking degree, I was made to try to pilot these machines blindly, my target on the other side of a wall or behind my head, having to rely on simplified UI elements and cryptic error messages in order to fumble my way through. The message "Blocked" was a mainstay, I can't express how many times I was shown that message. Machines would lock up and I would find that I couldn't move at all in any direction, until all of the sudden I could again. In most cases, I never discovered exactly what was blocking my path; I just blindly wiggled the machines around until they finally landed where I wanted them to. In the same vein, four times I found myself stuck and had to use the pause menu feature to reset my character to a safe location. This is not a feature that should be necessary in a finished game. Navigation was broken. The story is given to the player through pre-recorded messages from a character who is dead at the beginning of the game. Her comments are vague and incredibly withholding. These musings were presumably added to set up the pieces needed for the big end reveal, and to maintain a sense of mystery throughout the game, but my curiosity was dashed when I realized that I was being given only questions and no answers. The player is given absolutely no explanation as to the overarching task they're trying to accomplish beyond "go here and hit this button, then do it two more times in two other places, because I said so." It's only during the final sequence that concrete information starts to come in. I will say that the ending does cleanly tie together everything the player has been shown. It made sense and had a surprising darkness and subtlety to it. The key notes it hit were not original though; I think it's safe to say that anyone who has been exposed to science fiction has seen this reveal many times (including in a recently-cancelled Netflix series). For me, the nice ending didn't make up for the slog I had to go through to reach it.I found this game to be a big step backwards from Obduction, which I felt had already struggled with trying to bring the Myst DNA into the modern world. I badly want to see Cyan pull off that task, but I'm concerned after playing Firmament that that I won't get to see that happen.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gorgeous and incredibly satisfying game in the typical Cyan (Myst/Riven) genre. Puzzles take the form of mechanical devices in the world so everything feels very tactile and routed in physical objects which feel like they mostly behave the way you would expect them to.The story of the game is interesting with a nice conclusion and I really enjoyed the voice acting of the person who guides you through the game.After finishing this and thinking about it compared to other Cyan games this one feel like it was a little smaller in scope in terms of how much you get to explore, but I don't in any way feel short changed by it. Really, my only complaints are some of the bugs and glitches. Some of them are really minor like objects not displaying, or bugging out but there are some out of bounds bugs which can mean you get stuck in the geometry and whilst there is an auto save I found that it was a little too aggressive in how often it saved so, after getting stuck I tried to reload and it had already saved me in the bugged out location. I ended up having to go back to a save from a day before which meant having to redo several puzzles.I also tried this in VR, with controller and with mouse and keyboard. Experiencing the world in VR was wonderful but performance issues meant I couldn't get through much of the game in VR because it was uncomfortable to play. I played for a bit with a controller because it felt like the Adjunct had been designed with that in mind, but I ended up switching back to mouse and keyboard which I found worked the best for me.Overall really enjoyable. I think I still enjoyed Obduction a little bit more though. Either way, Cyan are still masters of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR don't expect a typical Cyan experience and you may enjoy.I wasn't sure whether to post this review.  On one hand, I would like Cyan to do well so that they can continue to produce outstanding games.  On the other hand, this isn't an outstanding game and I am severely disappointed by it.Firstly, due to its very simplistic puzzles, it is a very short game.  I was expecting an experience like their previous games, where you take information from one area and hold onto it before finding its use somewhere else.  This game however is a series of linear puzzles - you go to one area, solve the puzzle there, then move onto another area and so on.  Knowledge about the world isn't needed.  A lot of the puzzles are very similar also: go pixel hunting, adjust your view to find the angle you need, then click.  The puzzles not like this are enjoyable but they are still too simple.  A possible reason for this is that the game is designed for VR rather than PC: most puzzles involve reaching out and moving your arm left or right; most people don't play with VR so I think that designing the game this way is a big mistake.Secondly, in the updates for this game, Cyan said that it was lore heavy but it really isn't.  There is no piecing together of lore as you go, instead you get a massive exposition dump at the end.  This is a massive disappointment.Thirdly, a minor annoyance just for me is the appearance of the vehicle you travel along rails in.  Riven and Exile had an amazing vehicle where the journey was like a rollercoaster in places and just beautiful in others.  It is entirely spoiled here by having a big metal bar in the forward direction so you can't easily enjoy the view.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. Couldn't stand in place when I saw a new game from Cyan was coming out.The environments are appealing, and I wanted to immerse myself in this world that, at first glance, looked full of interesting lore and mind boggling  puzzles. Also, I'm a VR player and I've waiting for a long time for a amazing game to play with my headset and thought a Cyan game would be more than perfect for that!Trust me, I really wanted to love Firmament... but unfortunately, I was disappointed with almost every aspect. -  Lore, narration, storytelling. I recon they tried another way of storytelling; but honestly it didn't work for me at all.The lore seemed flat and poor, and didn't success in engaging interest and commitment. -  The puzzles. While doing them, I was lacking a sense of goal; I was solving puzzles, but very often I didn't know to what end. Maybe it lacked contextualization?- The bugs.Even though I know this won't be forever, it bothers me a lot that a game comes out with so many bugs. It's no fun at all to stress-save every minute, and to ask yourself at all times if you missed something about a puzzle or if the game has another bug (I lost hours of playtime because of those).-  The VR part :(Too many graphical bugs and lags to enjoy it, I finally had to play on my PC.-  Nice views, environments, and places. It was very pleasing to go through them :)-  I don't know if that's what was intended, but it's bold to try and reinvent oneself when you have such an established style of game. I salute nonetheless the efforts and the meaning behind it, I guess the goal was to have a more dynamic way of playing than the other games where you have to read A LOT. Which I don't really mind but I understand where it came from.Overall, I was motivated to finish the game because I hoped there were more to it until the end... and I'm really sorry, but I wouldn't recommend this game.To make a little comparison, Obduction, for example, was richer and made you very curious about every bits of lore (and had sick puzzles!); this one doesn't because you know there isn't more to discover :(.

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament opens up with an interesting premise and just a dash of Cyan's signature intrigue. Unfortunately the game does little to offer the player any meaningful lore or world building to ground them in the beautiful worlds they have created, making most of the journey feel like a theme park ride through beautiful set pieces, completely deflating what could have been an amazing ending to the journey.The game is still in a bit of a rough state technically right now, with numerous bugs and performance issues across 2D and VR versions. I think it's going to take a few more patches to get the game to a place that feels smooth to play, especially in VR. That being said, they've already released a major patch to start addressing these issue, so I have no doubt the game will get there eventually.Puzzles in Firmament ended up being a bit of a mixed bag. While some required a bit of environmental observation to figure out the solution, they never felt unfair. Other puzzles (one section comes to mind) ended up feeling like an exercise in frustration, as the solution was to interact with something that was behind something else that was slightly clipped into something else (I'm being intentionally vague here to avoid spoilers). Then there were the puzzles where the solution made sense, but the game forces you to run back and forth, and back and forth. These were the worst offenders of the bunch, and there are unfortunately a few of them.Firmament was so close to being something really special, but unfortunately falls short of that mark. Was the game enjoyable? Yes, and is still something I recommend to any fan of Cyan's previous works, so long as you understand that this title falls short of previous efforts.I'd love to give this a neutral review, but in its current state it's hard for me to give it a thumbs up, and am surprised it was even released in the state that it's in right now.. I'd wait a bit until they're able to iron out the remaining issues, and will update my review if/when they do.

_childDocuments_.review: I super enjoyed this game! It had everything I wanted: beautiful locations, sensible puzzles that exist in context, lots of mystery. In a lot of ways this is an essential Cyan story. It also felt a lot more MYST-like than Obduction, not that it's a bad thing Obduction did it's own thing. But if you were craving that sort of steampunk monolith vibe that Riven had, Firmament has it in spades. It's also the first time I've felt like the real time stuff looked *as good* as the pre-rendered locations in Riven. That sorta worn in detailed aesthetic is very strong. I played regular style with WASD on my monitor, but I'm tempted to run back through in VR just to see some of the locations up to scale.Highly recommended if you're a Cyan fan, or a fan of adventure games in general.

_childDocuments_.review: A mixed positive review for me.  I played in VR and 2D.    The game is beautiful, the sound is well done and it kept me engaged.  The puzzles were interesting overall and its nice to experience the Cyan style worlds and gameplay again.  The game suffers from too little exposition til right at the end but when it comes, it is rewarding.The game is glitchy and you want to save before messing with any machines as they tend to get stuck in my experience.  I had to use the Unstick me feature a few times to fix my positionor reset the machines.  Theres only two save slots which is ridiculous.  Many times when I was messing with a puzzle and I got a weird result I started to wonder, "is this glitched or is this working as intended?", which is a terrible spot to be for a puzzle game as you're not sure how to proceed.The VR mode sadly felt underdeveloped, it didnt take advantage of many of VR's strengths, and the puzzle design that involved a lot of backtracking/complex traversal is more cumbersome in VR. The graphics got a little glitchier in VR mode as well but Im sure they'll iron that out.  After a bit I switched back to 2D mode and was much happier.

_childDocuments_.review: Firmament has issues with soft locking, related to player or object positions in the game. I had TWO instances in my play through:The first time I pulled an autosave to back up a few minutes, the second I used the game's built-in "teleport" feature to reset back. In the end these issues weren't deal breaking, but they needed to be noted.With that out of the way... The environments and engineering are beautiful and intricate, and the realms are wonderful to explore. The story is intriguing and has a fantastic ending that pulls the pieces together very well, though overall the character development and narrative are on the thinner side.The puzzles are mostly fun but not as prevalent as hoped. They are also bigger and more "stand alone" without necessarily affecting one other, or other areas of the world. The feelings I remember in Myst and Riven of "oh, I solved this, so it affected that way back there" were not as present here. The game does allow access to more than one area at a time, which is a plus in the event you're stumped you can take a breather and go explore elsewhere.A couple puzzles in particular are frustrating not due to the mental acuity required, but because you feel you're fighting against the game's design to get them done; puzzles that work well in theory but should've gone through the ringer a few more times before implementation. Unfortunately they're both in the same realm.The game is on the shorter side, on average most folks will hit 7-8 hours. It's a fine length for the experience and price point, but you can't help leaving Firmament feeling like it could have been more - more realms, more characters, more puzzles, more interconnection. But budgets will be budgets and Cyan is an indie studio, they did a fine job with what they had to work with.If you loved Myst and you love Cyan, or you enjoy exploring lovingly-crafted environments and generally well-thought puzzles, you'll love this. Simply bear in mind you'll be sitting down to an excellent appetizer, rather than the belly-filling satisfaction of a main course.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a fan of the Cyan line of puzzle games since forever and I am so happy to have been a backer and helped to get this game produced.  So many of these new 3D games give me intense motion sickness and Firmament is a slow enough game that does have a lot of bouncing in it, which made it playable.I am giving a positive review since I very much enjoyed the game, and would like to see more from Cyan, though I was able to complete it start-to-finish in a single week during the evenings.  I would rate this as a beginner-level puzzle adventure.  That every puzzle in the game needed to be solved with the help of the adjuct made the puzzles very obvious.  Unlike what we have become accustomed to with the Cyan brand, there were no non-traditional puzzles that needed to be solved by sound, for example.My primary complaint with this game is the lack of a good backstory.  Myst was a story about two brothers rebelling against their father, where the depth of the brother's depravity is revealed gradually over the course of the game.  In Firmament, we are immediately greeted by, essentially, a ghost, which at the outset makes the story somewhat unbelievable at the outset.  There are no subtle clues that hint at the true nature of the ghost.  Others have mentioned that it was strange to have the ghost be aware of the characters actions--but also not aware--at the same time.  More realistic might be to have the ghost reappear at critical stages when something related to attaining the goal was accomplished.  Instead, the ghost floats in and out as you wander in and out of rooms.It is not clear until the very end exactly why the Keepers are keeping, or even what exactly they are keeping. There is very little in the way of references to the unique culture that the Keepers would have developed over the years.  Exactly what happened to all of the other keepers is a pressing question that is not answered satisfactorally until the end, and even then, not very well.  I never developed an emotional connection to any of the characters.  There are musical instruments about that can't be played, books that can't be read, et cetera, that would in some way make us feel for the absent keepers.  It is also very clear that the ghost knows exactly what the protagonist is there to do, yet the ghost was unable to accomplish the same things that the protagonist does while she was still alive.  If the ghost was a keeper, and the protagonist entered the world to be a keeper, what exactly is the secret that the protagonist knows that the ghost/keepers didn't that kept the keepers from learning the truth?  Finally, we never emotionally react to the depravity of the protagonist, as revealed at the end.I liked that Myst was set up so that it could easily have sequels that expanded upon the main Myst story.  Because it came so suddently, the ending of Firmament has a finality to it.  With machinery so advanced, why need people at all?

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I just finished Firmament and I was really blown away. Every time you think you're quite far in the game, the worlds just keep on expanding. The game is so much bigger than I thought and it holds many surprises. The gameplay is challenging, but in a very satisfying way. Compared to Obduction there is less time involved in travelling and you can keep your focus on what's in front of you, which makes it much more enjoyable.If you know previous Cyan games, then you know Obduction was meant to be a spiritual successor to Myst. Firmament, on the other hand, reminded me much more of Riven and a little bit of URU. That has everything to do with the scale of this game.I highly recommend this game!!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very wonderful game when it's not lagging.The environments are breathtaking, the puzzles are a delight to solve, and the story is captivating. The adjunct, although obviously meant for VR, actually improved PC gameplay by eliminating the dreaded "pixel hunt", leaving the player free to explore the world without worrying about what they can and cannot interact with. Which brings me to what made the puzzles so brilliant. There were no convoluted brain teasers in your way for the sake of being in your way-only tools you used to overcome natural obstacles. Although you always knew when you were in a puzzle, they never FELT like puzzles. The best part about the story was you couldn't tell where it would end up. Would this be some Randian parable on the evils of "we"? Would your stated mission destroy the world? Is your guide out to destroy you? There were so many twists and turns you never quite knew.Overall Firmament was a very wonderful experience-if you know what graphics settings to use.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: This game uses extensive AI-generated assets. It's mentioned briefly in the credits, and I assumed it was just for a few images near the end of the game. However, it actually goes deeper than that. For one, most (all?) of the in-world journals/notes/stories are AI, as well as banners and other textures. But the biggest issue is that the actual voice acting in the game is entirely AI. This definitely explains why the game felt so oddly lifeless and devoid of any real substance. I cannot recommend this game knowing how blatant its use of AI generated assets is. I knew something was off originally but this just confirms how soulless and bland this game really is. I wonder how much of the plot itself was even authored with intent... A truly shameful showing from a developer I formerly respected.Original review:The world of Firmament can feel a bit bare-bones, and the puzzles lack the same intricacy of Cyan's previous works, but overall this is still an enjoyable adventure with an intriguing atmosphere. It is short (I finished it in 8 hours), but honestly I didn't mind that. It definitely doesn't overstay its welcome.If you're a Myst fan it's well worth a play through, just don't go into it expecting the same depth as something like Riven.
