_childDocuments_.review: Sable is 2021's best game to be thoroughly tainted, but by no means ruined by bugs. I'm not going to talk about that here because many already have, but if you don't feel like reading this very long review just know that if you like exploration-heavy peaceful games or walking simulators in general, you will like Sable. It's not a walking simulator, but it is completely devoid of conflict or any massively active gameplay systems, which is fairly unique. The world of Sable came from a humble place: What if Rey never left Jakku in the Force Awakens? That's not a joke mind you that's straight from the developer's mouth. But Star Wars tribute this is not, while there are still some heavy remnants of that inspiration and is also what first sprang to mind when I originally saw the game a couple of years ago, Sable has safely formed its own identity throughout development both from the developer's own imagination and the influence of other inspirations. The artist Moebius is the most obvious as his enthralling style of Sci-fi art wraps the entirety of Sable in this distinct science fantasy charm.It's easy to imagine that a game that solely features desert areas for its environments would get dull, but the artists never shied away from using strange alien colors or extravagant landmarks of both the natural and human-made variety to keep things spicy. Sable would be a visual masterpiece without the bold lines and colors ripped from Moebius' art, but those added elements elevate it from great to one-of-a-kind. There's a fascinating mixture of things to see from the cities built up by the planet's current residents, ancient spaceships that have laid there defunct for centuries, and rolling orange sand dunes which make up the bulk of the map. But Sable's true brilliance is that it's never scared to mix all this together, combining artificial, structural beauty with the alien landscape to make the world feel properly lived in. You're exploring a planet whose residents have already lived through a lot, and never does the game try to trick you into thinking that you're the first person to discover something. Everything has the mark of those who've come before or those there right now, but that doesn't weaken the experience because it's still the first time you, and the main character, are seeing it.Sable, the main character, is a young member of the nomadic Ibex clan whose entering her gliding---a coming of age rite that every person in the world goes through. It's a journey of self-discovery that's told in a unique way, Sable is not a silent protagonist, in fact, she regularly makes her opinions on various matters very obvious. But instead of standard dialogue this is all done through narration more reminiscent of a novel than a video game. Sable, as someone with some knowledge of the world but not all of it, gets to learn a lot herself while never over-explaining something to the player. Worldbuilding in Sable is fairly lightweight, mainly meant to be interpreted from the sights you see while exploring, but there's still a solid sense of culture to everything, and the world's history does bring forth some interesting ideas once you get around to unraveling it.This brings us to how you unravel it, the gameplay, which may be Sable's weakest link. Inspiration from Breath of the Wild is a given the moment you start playing. You have a stamina bar that appears next to your character whenever you run and climb, and yes you can climb anything. A gliding mechanic which encourages getting to the game's highest points just for the sake of gently floating down. And you start in a fairly contained area meant to teach you the basics before you're let loose on the larger world where you can go anywhere.There's no big overarching story, in fact, you can complete the final quest in the game after just four hours of game time if you want. Sable does not force you to experience any part of it, but it makes it clear you'll be rewarded for staying in its world as long as possible. Various settlements dot the map with plenty of NPCs to talk to and receive quests from which is the main bulk of Sables content. Every quest directly points towards one of the game's major landmarks for either an item or event. Once you do a lot of these you'll begin to notice that no developed part of the map is left alone from these quests. Every notable area has a quest tied to it, making it clear the developers, likely for budgetary reasons, were unable to develop other areas that could just be stumbled upon naturally. While Sable may not force you to do anything, it also doesn't want any piece of content to not be used to its fullest.There's plenty to see in Sable, but hardly anything to find. Unless you purposely avoid quests, which you can, but you'll be missing out on a lot of awards and it's clearly not how the developers want you to play.How you traverse these areas is also iffy. While running and jumping felt fine for the most part, a large portion of gameplay here will be spent riding Simoon, your desert surfing hoverbike. Even this is not left untouched by Sable's world-building and style mind you, this bike is, at the very least, treated as a living creature in this world and you're expected to build a level of attachment with it. That didn't particularly work for me, I found myself more frustrated by it which we'll go over soon but the intent is important.The hoverbike mechanic is Sable is a messy one. The bike constantly flips out on the game's terrain---literally. At first, you may think handling it is just tricky, but the more you play the more you realize there's obviously some technical jank going on here. Add in the horrible performance drops experienced when driving the bike and it doesn't make for the greatest time. When everything works it's wonderful, but that's less often the case than when it isn't.Which is a big blow, as is the map's empty feeling anywhere that's not a quest area. Sable's biggest strengths are its writing, style, and the things you can see in it. I spent so much build-up talking about them because I think they're worth the shortcomings of the gameplay.I truly think Sable is on the next wave of relaxing, exploration games and it balances laidback gameplay excellently. It would've been easy to add gear management or item crafting for the sake of ringing out a few more hours but Sable's design is very intent, it knows what its wants to be and how it wants you to engage with it. Which I found very refreshing, and I hope will trickle down into future relaxation-focused games in the future. But for now, Sable is a good enough case study to hold me over.

_childDocuments_.review: (It says played for 5 hours on here but I had this game on gamepass first when it was free for 3 months, so i've already completed it, im working to 100% it now) It does what it says on the tin: its a beautiful world to explore. You won't find that its a complete botw-like with combat or lengthy puzzles, and it certainly does nothing to really fix that feeling of emptiness its predecessor struggled with. But the reality is that's just not a huge deal for me when the game looks and plays this good. Its just fun to wander, to get really completely lost somewhere.By not cluttering the world I also think a lot more effort went into the few more elaborate quests. You have some shenanigans, ask some big questions and find some really big answers. Your reward for doing things isn't really money or cool new outfits (though you do get those too), its getting to learn more about the world. And every detail has that depth and character to it. Even your cool bike has a story, so you never really feel alone. You're not taking this journey *on* her, you're taking this journey *with* her. Basically, the devs put a lot of thought into the presentation of everything. Rather than trying to make a game you could play for 100 hours, they made a game you can replay 100 times.

_childDocuments_.review: Sable is the porch beer of Breath-of-the-Wild-likes. I spent a whole weekend casually playing this game to completion. I didn't 100% it, I think getting all the masks kind of defeats the purpose. I really tried to allow myself to be immersed and it was a great choice. I still have a fun time going as deep as I wanted without having to exert *too* much effort. Really just going places that looked interesting and following interesting quest lines, I presume, as was intended. This lead me to completing 88% of the achievements in the game organically. When Sable's gliding ended, I felt like my story exploring this world could have continued and wow there are some mysteries I would love to sink my teeth further in to, but unfortunately Sable did come to a satisfying if appropriately anti-climactic end. I took a moment to let it sink it in while the credits rolled, and then read what shockingly little I could find about other people's experiences with the game.The game fought my machine every step of the way. Really the only difficulty at all was from the multitude of bugs, in one case several beetles glitching out and making a quest (and questline) impossible to complete. There were so many times my hove bike would clip through the ground and cause it to weightlessly bob around for 10 seconds while it slowly reorients itself to the direction of its momentum.  Sometimes NPC dialog can be a little robotic, clipped or repetitive. It definitely needed a little more polishing than it received, and it's really unfortunate that so much of what makes me hesitant to recommend it is mine and others' experiences with the frame rate. Around hour 17, I finally decided to play with the settings a little and found that the performance could really only be improved by running the game at its absolutely lowest possible settings at 1920x1080, which included drastically reducing the draw distance. I immediately regretted this choice because I couldn't see Chums off in the distance as well anymore, which by then was the only real quest I had left that wasn't bugged out or completely uninteresting to me. So I drove around, finished up what I was doing and ended the game.All that said, I still recommend it. Like I saidI ended up with 88% of the game's achievements without really trying over a lazy weekend. I probably would have liked it more if I was on the couch though.

_childDocuments_.review: The gaming sphere is riddled with coming-of-age tales, but few have been as effective as Sable.Sable sets out on a journey, and the pace you set is completely your own. There is no danger, there are no threats. This may seem odd, but this lends to what Sable does best: Exploration.The Sable team has a strong sense of what makes a good open world. The game is littered with secrets and questions. It recognizes that the open empty world doesn't need to have a collectible every 10 feet, or a million mindless side quests. It never wastes your time.The 160 or so collectable eggs are condensed around landmarks the player will naturally want to explore, making the completionists job much easier, while simultaneously encouraging exploration among more casual players.The open areas of the map may be a bit barren, but they serve perfectly as a playground for Biking, or just gorgeous scenery as you travel and explore. Quests are far from checklists in Sable. I remember every single quest I've done in the game, each felt sufficiently unique. There are no "Side-Quests" as it were. Every duty that you can undertake is a vital part of Sable's story. You make friends through these quests, learn lessons, and discover more about the lands and histories the world is hiding. This game has more heart and life in its characters than the last 3 Assassin's Creed games I've played combined.Do the thing. Play Sable.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to give this a thumbs up because it really has some lovely parts and has a great heart, but I'm doing so with some caveats. Firstly, it has some really annoying bugs, nothing totally game breaking that I came across but small things like the pointer disappearing on menus, sometimes all buttons being locked to making me run forward for some reason and the fishing mini game becoming virtually impossible due to not being able to cast the line. Secondly, for a cosy exploration game like this, the exploration sometimes felt clunky and unsatisfying. The art direction is excellent and sometimes just walking out from a building on a high plateau into the sun and seeing a vista before you was genuinely breathtaking, and the moment when you first set off on your journey with the main theme playing is really special. But that theme only seems to play once, and a lot of your journey is spent plodding, upending on your hover bike, or struggling with camera angles and unclear rules and grab points in platforming sections. If this was a slightly smoother experience it would be one of my all time favourite games, as it is, its a solid fine.

_childDocuments_.review: This may be the most impressed and disappointing I've been with a game, ever. I'm currently not finished with the game so I won't be judging it as a whole, just the whole of what I've played so far. The art style is absolutely STUNNING! The art department went absolutely crazy on this one, I love the almost cyberpunkish aesthetic whilst also taking place in a very open desert along with other locations. The sound design, let me clarify, the design of the sound, is quite amazing. But it's also incredibly gltichy with sounds rapidly stopping and starting and breaking the music apart and/or other sound effects. The game is also horrendously buggy and glitchy in other areas too. The camera goes through the ground sometimes if you're running uphill, your character turns invisible while driving the vehicle, the frame rate goes from being very smooth to very choppy in denser environmental locations, ground texture's dissipated earlier when my character turned invisible for maybe like the 5th time in my 6 hours of playing. _childDocuments_.review: If you like extremely chill wandering games then get it. Your glitches might not be that bad! If you don't want to gamble maybe wait for patches. If you prefer life-threatening danger or skill trees, this is not your game.Not done with Sable but gotta get the words out anyways. Header's the important part. Some folks see show-stopping glitches, but I haven't (system details below). Glitches yes, show-stoppers no.Chill. Pretty. Non-lethal so far. Game style is No Man's Sky meets A Short Walk: lots of wandering, figuring out the world, its story, and the people in it. You're figuring out who you want to be, so the side-quests  the game.Setting is sci-fantasy wasteland. Reminded me of Numenera RPG. Most — but not all! — capability progression comes from upgrading equipment. Hoverbike controls are clunky as heck until you get you some better parts and learn how to drift, then it's fun as heck. Quick travel to known landmarks is nice when you don't feel like driving. Many gorgeous vistas. Lots of climbing. Not good for acrophobics.Sometimes I miss faces.Not near as bad for me as for some. I've been able to get at everything I would expect to within world rules, and (unmeasured) framerate stays consistent and playable.- camera clipping is noticeable and distracting but I've just decided it's part of the aesthetic- Moebius-style flat shading and crisp lines don't always translate to the screen; some antialiasing would be nice- there are some visual artifacts tied to location that I haven't figured out yet if they're glitches or a mystery to be solved; if they go away in a patch update I'll have my answer- the inventory menu confuses me; still figuring out what buttons to push where- it would be nice if the keyboard + mouse control felt smoother, but this is clearly a game for controllers so I won't fuss too much- OS: Win 10 19044.126- CPU: i7-9700K- RAM: 40GB- GPU: AMD Radeon RX 5600 XT VRAM 6128MB (v21.6.1; avoiding latest because of issues in other games)- Controller: Logitech Gamepad F310Sable did  like my VOYEE Wired 360 controller. Frequent "disconnected" complaints and unresponsiveness. Thought it was a game glitch until I figured out the connector was going bad. Explains some issues I've had elsewhere. Absolutely fine with the F310 though. So  Sable is more sensitive to controller issues?

_childDocuments_.review: ’s debut at E3 2018 captured my attention with its graphics, which resembled the work of the late Mœbius, an influential French artist. It looked like it could have been something that the artist would have drawn as a graphic novel at some point in his career. Yet,  is more than just its visuals. Beneath the enchanting exterior lies a mesmerizing open-world adventure/exploration game that’s unlike any other game that I’ve played to date. is a player-driven game, in which you play as the titular character. She embarks on a rite of passage journey across the desert world of Midden in search of her life’s purpose. As you traverse the desert on your hoverbike, you’ll occasionally come across people whom you can help, as well as points of interest that are worth exploring. You can decide to help whomever you want, explore wherever you wish, and end your journey whenever you feel like it.This game is really a game of side quests, which provide some loose structure to your exploration of the vast desert. Major locations, which may be discovered from a distance by pillars of smoke, their architecture against the natural landscape, or their sheer verticality, aren’t marked on your map until you’ve visited it. Aside from a couple of puzzles, there is no time constraints on what you do. You can abandon or resume a task at any point without penalty, should any of them prove uninteresting or too challenging. Thus, Sable is as freeform as you can probably get with an adventure game. Upon completing some tasks, you’ll be awarded badges; and with enough badges, you can earn masks. Each mask represents a role or life purpose you can choose to ultimately assume. Your experience in accomplishing each type of task may influence your decision at the end of your rite of passage journey. So, it’s worthwhile to take advantage of the freedom that the game gives you: take your time with your quests, explore the wonders and mysteries of the desert, and reflect on what’s meaningful, interesting and important.I was wary at first of the mileage  can get with just side quests, let alone not having any combat or death sequences at all. However, I was surprised by how mesmerizing it is to just explore the game world at my leisure, especially when there are plenty of breathtaking sights to take in, marvellous locations to discover and visit, and secrets of Midden to unearth. With your character having the ability to climb almost any surface, and to glide down gently from great heights, it’s rather refreshing to just focus on adventuring without ever worrying about fighting or dying.The confidence with which the developers presented this game, with a simple of premise of finding one’s life purpose through side quests, without the need for combat or violence, is admirable. Yet, at the time of this review,  still has a few glaring bugs (e.g., clipping, sudden high jumping or floating, framerate and audio stuttering). None of the ones I encountered were game-breaking in any way, but they did make the game experience less refined. is a game that I will whole-heartedly recommend to anyone who enjoys adventure games, wants something relaxing and different, and/or a fan of Mœbius’ work. It’s truly a hidden gem amongst headline-grabbing AAA titles. Sadly, it doesn’t get more positive attention than it deserves, as the developers continue to iron out some bugs. Don’t let the few rough edges deter you from checking this game out though, for  is definitely one of the more refreshingly different, visually captivating games that you can play.

_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: I remember hearing about this game a few years back, and didn't really look into it at the time, which is a shame because I absolutely love this game now. I always fantasised about exploring a vast desert when I was little, and this game satisfies that nostalgic memory in me. I saw it again back in 2021 before it released and became interested, and this game did not disappoint. This game is beautiful, from the art to the music and the story and characters. The only thing I didn't like was thinking about how I can't experience this for the first time again.What's the game about though? To put it very briefly,  I really don't want to spoil anything about it for people who may be planning to play it, as it would definitely be a better experience going in without knowing anything about it.There are quite a few bugs here and there, but nothing major and won't stop you from playing the game normally, just expect some around. Overall, I think Sable has become my favourite game... ever? Right now at least, but personally for me it'd be hard to top this game. It's disappointing to not see as many people talking about the game as I expected, and I hope that its popularity increases soon.For me it had an overwhelming feeling that was like leaving your childhood home, feeling unready. But at the same time you know that you are ready, and things will change.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful open world coming of age story with an excellent soundtrack. Sable reminds me a lot of the Legend of Zelda series, particularly BotW in the game's openness and soft-apocalyptic aesthetic, and Majora's Mask because of, well, all the masks (One of my favorite parts of the game was collecting the unique masks). The soundtrack is excellent and I was delighted to find it on Spotify, although some of the in-game tracks are nowhere to be seen in the tracklist, meaning that if you want to hear themes such as the Sodic Waste or the daytime version of the Badlands, you are forced to scour the internet for a recording if you aren't willing to somehow record it yourself, which makes it a bit disappointing when wanting to listen to the otherwise magnificent soundtrack. The game, despite its excellent aesthetic and overall atmosphere, is severely hindered from what feels like rushed development: dialogue from out of the way NPCs feels underdeveloped or simply missing, giving you an empty text box where it feels like a farewell from a character should have been. I even encountered what seemed to be swapped dialogue between two Cartographer characters. When the player asks for significant land marks from the Hakoa and Badlands cartographers (if I remember correctly) they will provide landmarks from the other region, not their own. These issues as well as frustrating menu bugs, visual glitches. and clunky collision on some surfaces can leave you a bit frustrated. I found it wasn't very hard to overlook these bugs in favor of enjoying what the developers got right: the beautiful, intriguing desert riddled with spaceship wrecks and ancient ruins. I hope that this game receives the love it deserves in getting polished up in the near future, as this game -despite its roughness- is a gem and a great time to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: I had initially wrote a negative review of the game since I encountered a bug not allowing me to progress, but since that was patched, I have to say that this game is really neat! Is it one of the best open world games out there? Not at all, but it's definitely worth a buy. Although it is a really impressive game, especially for such a small team. It has a really simple yet effective story, and dialogue in the game has lots of meaning. The game is also really nice looking, and is interesting to explore! However, there is a ton of content in the game, and not all of it is necessarily high quality. Many quests will have you walk to a place and interact with an item, with not much substance, and surprisingly climbing and puzzle solving are not as frequent as I would have expected, especially in a game like this. A lot of it is riding around on your hoverbike or walking, leading to a rather boring gameplay loop occasionally. I still recommend it, (After all, it's only around 8-10 hours in length) but play The Pathless, Vane, or Shadow of the Colossus before, since those are all a bit more fun to play than Sable.  7/10

_childDocuments_.review: i'm still only 4 hours into the campaign so i cant really review the game but the visuals are great, soundtrack is amazing and the game just gives you an urge to go out and explore by yourself that feels so good.   apart from some weird bugs that'll probably get fixed soon sable is currently one of my favourite games ever
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: The game is mildly fun, but what really ruins it is the art style, not to mention it is very buggy. The art style is very unique, and I appreciate trying to do something different, but between the low frame rate animations, and the cell shading that blends everything together, I found myself being more frustrated by the art than anything. There was no moment in the game that took my breath away, so I can't even say it worked on that level. However, the music was fantastic! It worked so well with the story and locations that I would occasionally stop just to listen to it.Probably the best part of the game was discovering the background story of how the people came to Midden. But even this was a letdown because it never reached a conclusion, and it wasn't even the main story.But the worst part has to be all the bugs. In a game where you spend most of your time on your glider bike, I can't tell you how many times I had to dismount because the bike suddenly froze, or the world disappeared. To their credit, these glitches never caused a fatal error, but still it was frustrating.So while I did mildly enjoy the game, I would not suggest it to others unless you can get it at a steep discount, and don't mind the other issues mentioned above.

_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start off by saying the story (so far) has not held my interest, and the way the dialogue is presented hasn't helped.  Instead of just dialogue the game describes your character's and the NPC's reactions, and inner thoughts which if it was a visual novel I'd be fine but this isn't so I can do without that extra writing (I usually just ignore it until I see the actually dialogue pop up).  Also the animation is very stiff and is really noticeable when your character is moving (specifically running where it looks like you're getting a frame or two of animation), and the lack of fluidity is almost to the point of causing eye strain.    Oh and the animation when you find a Chum Egg is really stiff to the point of being comical (looks like cheap 70s animation).  Other than those two gripes the rest of the game is pretty decent.  The main reason I wanted to play it was exploration and the world here is (from what I've seen so far) pretty big although not as populated with things as I would like.   The glider bike is slow and cumbersome at first but their upgrade parts that improve performance over time.   This coupled with the climbing makes for some fun wandering and explore time wasting which so far has always lead to a discovery or two.    Oh and there aren't (so far) any hostiles so exploring isn't fraught with danger.Graphics are decent.  There are times where the color palette narrows down to a few colors (mainly at night) and can look really weird but there are times during the day when the lighting works and it looks nice.  Edit:  I totally forgot about the fishing that was added to the game not too long ago, and I must say it's some of the best fishing mechanics I've played with in an adventure game in awhile.  The mechanic is simple, but easy to pick up on.   You cast your line, press a button when an exclamation appears over your head and then you simply try to keep a colored box over a fish icon that moves erratically across a line.  The box changes color from dark red to blue and once you keep it in blue you catch the fish.   Simple, but a lot of fun.Overall it's worth it if you want a big world to explore without a lot of hassle.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Despite its many technical issues and somewhat one-note gameplay, I couldn't help but become immersed within the world of Sable. Immaculate vibes, calming gameplay loop, and treasures hidden around every corner kept me invested all the way through my 20hr playthrough. The story may not be the most intriguing and the characters not very fleshed out, but the world of Midden is just so captivating. Each biome was a delight to explore and even if the climbing mechanics never really evolved, I still had a blast trying to climb the highest viewpoints to take in the views because, yes, this game looks very pretty. If you're looking for a new world to explore and don't mind a more laid back, peaceful gaming experience with few challenges, I would highly recommend Sable.

Not only is the world awe-inspiring, well constructed and thought out, but the traversal is super fun. A bit janky, but yet, super versatile, with the bike, the gliding and the climbing. The dialogue is also worth mentioning, as it's at the same time sweet and suited to the world you inhabit. But, yeah, performance can be very bad at times. Highly recommended. Please patch ;-)

_childDocuments_.review: The bulk of the game is a focus on exploration similar to Breath of the Wild, but with a more meditative and minimalist approach to the gameplay. There is no combat, no fall damage, no health, no fail states. Only an uncharted world with something new to discover over every dune. The narrative is a warmly presented journey of personal growth and leaving home that blends nicely with the open structure of the game. There are terrible performance issues (of the traversal stutter, frame pacing variety) but the content of the game is strong enough to make Sable worth checking out in spite of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: My goodness, Sable. I am in love with this game, I don't feel quite equipped to review entirely considering I haven't finished but I really want to support this game as the devs deserve it. Sable at first or twice glance, though having a unique style, seems like another well cared for open-world experience, and that it is! But there is so much to Sable that makes this world feel entirely real and occupied, and most importantly the knowledge that this journey is not a pilgrimage to conquer, but trying to find out whatever the hell you want while exploring this vivid and truthful world. I think what makes Sable so... beautiful to me is the writing. The dialogue is so beloved, in a way: and even behind masks the great writing makes you feel the subtle quirks and ques that a person's face and inflections house. I think I am geeking out over this because I love writing, but the point still stands! The emotion of the people you know and the people you meet, the non-pretentious but poetic diction (like I have a good judge on what is non-pretentious), how every character is distinctly themselves but not in a way where they are just an idiosyncrasy with occasional thought: a lot of the reviews rightly praise the landscape and relaxing nature to Sable, but I think the stellar writing is so well blended, we take it for granted. Even the interlude dialogue where this character and you have nothing much more story wise to say, the line is usually "I had a lovely conversation with Llhor.". This is a small detail but it shows well how cherished and true these characters are. It is so gratifying and special to see a game be a work of art and use its means to convey its heart: this is a newish thing, seeing games as art, and this strikes that *elusive* middle precisely. The slowness, the hours that accumulate, the permanence, this is only a thing a video game could do, and Sable's beauty lies within that. You learn this familiarity and endearment just by being in game that no other artform can really do. Say for instance a book is talking about a big quest, and details the interesting things that happen on your way there. In Sable you see each and every step for yourself, and have a hand in it. So, so good. I do like, too, that you have a hand in how she is, but ultimately this is Sable's journey that you are witnessing and slightly guiding. Sable isn't an emissary for us to imagine how we are in this world, Sable is earnestly and ruthlessly herself, and this is the same for the world at hand. Some offshoot quests don't resolve cleanly, I think the famous one being Power to the People one. I won't get into its details but I imagine in real life that such a sticky situation is not able to be cleanly resolved. Corruption and preconceptions aren't merely roadblocks that if we tinker around enough they dissolve. They are built out of many sad and hidden decisions, ones unseen to us. Feeling realistic also sacrifices satisfaction and completion, and I think it works well in this case.Onto the gameplay and such, how that all blends in: the hoverbike feels freeing and fun crossing the topography upon, seeing scenic sights, sometimes important, sometimes not. You do tons of sidequests, in fact I think your quest persay is to do tons of sidequests, but they all feel distinct and novel, specifically with the dialogue and writing being the stitching. I really like finding chums, for some reason. Maybe I am a simp for the Queen, I suppose I will be fine with that. It is mostly a  relaxing feeling of gameplay with the occasional intensity being some really poignant and harrowing storylines. And puzzles! They are reminiscent of portal though still definitely have their own feel. Most of them are quite fun and fascinating, but there is a dud or two (I am absolutely calling out Centre of Brunswick, leave no uncertainty there), I think I am bad at reviewing gameplay but Sable is fun, in a particular way, it is a subtle excitement of returning and proceeding, and I haven't felt anything like it.A brief few things to mention before I address its flaws: such a nice soundtrack that feels intimate and always fitting, though there aren't any bops but I think that is intentional. One big issue I have is that the colors of the world are really vibrant adding such a vivid and immersive feeling, and fittingly night time reduces that to an umbra, but sometimes I feel like I should put off an experience until it is daytime so that I can actually see it. It would be nice if there was a way to sleep or heck, even a lantern of some sorts would do. It is very much a bad sense of flow when I reach an exciting new place but have to wait in the pause menu or just drive around for a little while until I can actually see it. I don't mind the darkness at all, in fact I quite like it, but I don't think a lantern would do any harm. I am not really sure where to put this point in so I'll just put it here: there is a seamless inclusion of enby characters that is so refreshing to see, to the point where you don't necessarily notice it. It is not only nice to see, but feels entirely organic. Also a dress would be nice. Don't get me wrong pants are really nice but I want to a skirt to flutter upon Simoon. Oh! And different colors or ways to mark waypoints: after a short while I have not a ton of ideas as to what all these blue flags mean, and it is nearly impossible to navigate without checking the map going "Okay yeah, it is that one.".The problems of Sable are mainly bug related, I don't believe there are any gamebreaking bugs left but I don't know entirely, I only encountered one devastating bug once where I clipped into the roots of the Hercules Beetle Nest while looking for Simoon (a glitchy aspect in its own right) making it so that I could not get out or move. The situation did enlighten me that there is fast travel but I could imagine that not being an option yet and this leading to data loss, or the one where you cannot go to manually save and I had a brief but intense panic; the solution being you can pick up an item or warp to trigger an autosave. I think leaving a bad review on this game for the bugs is a quite short-sighted reason, but these complaints are valid and generally make it feel less polished. I notice tons of little insects, a hive of slightly-to-very bothersome bugs. The most pesky one being menu difficulties, or clippings that aren't gamebreaking but do set you back a bit, the weird system of calling Simoon where sometimes she just... disappears? Evaporates? As in where she appears on the minimap is physically impossible, and the distance at which you can call her varying wildly. I'll have times where I am in a balloon and I accidentally press Y and I see her fumble around on the minimap, but other times I could be directly looking at her and she doesn't acknowledge me. I like to think that this is her being a sentient thing and not listening if I have crashed her into something too many times but I don't think this is the way it is intended. And an absolute plethora of little ones: music lingering from one area to the next, weird physics with launchers needed for puzzles (Shadow of Neave, mainly), me dropping a thing for a puzzle and it departing from existence apparently, Sarin's dialogue titles saying names at the incorrect time, the mask reverting back to the leftmost mask when you save and come back, also the Shadow of Neave's name displaying constantly though I am inside of it, quests being unactivated without any input on your end, and a few more I have experienced that I am forgetting. This game is obviously cared for and loved by its creators (it is a breakout game from 2 devs, that's wonderfully remarkable!), so I don't think it is negligence, it just needed a bit more time for bug-squashing and play testing. Ultimately, you are able to have a splendid experience without much trouble despite this, so please do not let the bugs deter you from playing this.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful adventure this game turned out to be! I loved it, beginning to end. PROS: It really succeeds at making you feel like you're in another world entirely (more so than some AAA games I've played lately, lol), and it has just enough content within it to not be overwhelming but still feel full of life. Mechanically, I think it borrows a lot from Breath of the Wild, at least the climbing & gliding feels very familiar, and it executes those mechanics quite well! I like that there's no combat, just because that's too often the meat of most games. Instead we focus solely on exploration, interaction, collecting, and puzzle solving. The story is super wholesome and meaningful & visually, the illustrated look is an absolute delight to play in. The character, vehicle, & environment design are all spot on as well. I could gush about this game for a while, lol.CONS: It's certainly buggy in spots. I had one major puzzle (potentially) glitch out on me where I really didn't think it should have been solved yet, and the game popped out the reward early. That only happened the one time though. Consistently, the game ran kinda chunky anytime I was on my hover-bike, which was a bummer. There were also MANY audio glitches throughout my run (usually a sputtering of sound effects or music). I have very few problems playing graphically intense open-world games that (I believe) should run heavier then Sable, so I think it might be an optimization issue. None of these issues were game-stopping for me though, just minor inconveniences.I got the game on sale for 9.99, but after finishing the game, I'd of paid full price. I liked it enough to buy a second copy for my wife, so that's saying something! I will definitely be keeping my eye out for more games from Shedworks, this was a delightful diamond in the rough.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Great (small) Open-World game with the twist, that is no health bar, no enemies, no danger, no skill tree, etc.Then this means there is more exploration and collectibles focused, which i really appreciate.Although there are many bugs in the game which i had a few tantrums, cause of getting stuck, no mouse or keyboard working, buggy settings and a lot more. So keep atleast this in mind of playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Sable is rife with minor bugs and glitches and that is where its negative points end. A rich, cultured world with a palpable history; a distinctly unique and unbeatably gorgeous art style; the ability to explore the open world as much or as little as you want; and a story that makes you feel every single moment it hands to you are just some of the high points. One of those bittersweet games that just leaves you Feeling when it's all over.10/10 Chums :)
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Magnificent game of exploration.Gorgeous, obviously.What you don't get from the trailers is that the sound is as brilliant as the visuals.The world building is exceptionally good, among the best I've seen in a game.The narrative, story structure and resolution are so simple and sensible that they've got to be the most clever ever.The map is a worthy open world full of amazing places and surprising secrets.The non-violent nature of the game means that you'll find your challenge essentially in platforming and puzzling. Maybe in fighting your acrophobia.It also means that the game is perfect for all ages.Not much to say on the negative side.It's glitchy, yes, but not in a frustrating way. Nothing that doesn't get fixed by returning to the main menu before continuing the adventure, for example when your hoverbike stops responding to your calls.The one reason Sable doesn't end up in my list of favourites is its single-slot saving, which might be good enough for corporate consoles and rail shooters, but is not worthy of a PC, an open world or an exploration title.Most spectacular and memorable.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Sable is a beautiful, peaceful game with simple gameplay and a lovely story of the titular character's journey, albeit a journey with a lot of bugs.  So, firstly, the game's biggest and most prominent issue:  The Bugs.  There will rarely be an extended play session where you will not encounter some form of bug in the game.  Things not spawning or spawning beneath the terrain, unzoomable map, NPCs becoming un-interactable, and UI menus become completely unusable have all been regularly occuring in my journey to 100%.  Thankfully, most are easy to fix by either fast-traveling to any location or exiting to the main menu and reloading your save.  If you're willing to bear through it, the story is amazing, but it can be completely immersion breaking.Gameplay wise, there's really not much to talk about.  You can run around, climb things akin to Zelda, and drive around a bike.  You can change your character's clothing (which has no gameplay effect) and the parts of your bike, but bike customization is minimal, and quickly overshadowed by a few parts being just objectively better.Sable story and art are beautiful.  The art direction is straight out of a music video, akin to Mr Fear by SAIMES, and I highly recommend adjust the color setting in the menu to "High Visabilty" simply because my default the colors dim out almost completely at night.  Sable matches it young, vibrant art style with a story about the titular character's journey into adulthood, with well done dialogue, humor, and worldbuilding.  If you are feeling lost or directionless in your life, Sable may be a game worth looking into, if only to insert yourself into Sable. The story also lasts only as long as you wish it to, with you being able to reach the ending as soon as you get your first mask.  Continuing on and collecting more masks is entirely your choice.And that's Sable, a gorgeous piece of art that could really use a de-bugging.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: What attracted me to this game was Its art style and it seems to be the only point of this game after all. The main story is light and feels empty, while there are a lot of side quests which however feel unfinished, unsatisfying and chore-like. I watched Skill Up’s review on this game and he stated “It’s not about doing extraordinary things but doing ordinary things”. I kind of agree with it but at the same time I’m suspicious whether it is what the devs intended. There were several moments where I made it all the way to a place but there was just a light interaction with some NPCs. “There is a mysterious building on top of the hill and smoke is blowing out of that place. There must be someone interesting”, ''I collected all of what the quest required. It must reveal some ancient mystery” “I solved all the puzzles. It must reveal secrets of this big place”. The reward you’ll get is some interaction with NPCs or items and that’s it. You may face a lot of “That’s it?” moments in this game, especially if you are overstimulated by AAA open-world story rich rpgs like me. The music is so comforting, relaxing and wholesome that it is one of the highlights of this game, but there are moments when the music “bugged out?”: when you enter a town, each part of the background music doesn’t match, like bass, drum and main melody counter melody are off beat (pardon my poor English). And sometimes you hear a mysterious sound which must indicate you achieved or reached something but I couldn’t figure out what it was about to the end. And there are a bunch of minor downsides such as occasional absence of button prompt, the vehicle being incapable of going backward on drive mode (so you have to switch to hover mode to go backward) and most of all, unstable fps. It really ruins the exploratory experience which should be the main point of open world games. Finally, I like the art style, music and writing, which often made me giggle, but that’s all. I enjoyed mindless exploration in the stylized open world and the photo mode was lovely. I feel bad to write a negative review but all in all, I can’t confidently recommend this game to the public.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game that is unfortunately hampered by many performance issues. If you like a game without combat that encourages exploration, sightseeing, and rich dialogue that interacts with an interesting lore, this is the game for you. It feels like a mix of Breath of the Wild, Journey, and Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind. In fact, you'll immediately recognize the sprinting, climbing, and critter finding mechanics of BOTW, the world design elements of Nausicaa, and the artistic grace of Journey. Not to mention that this game's score was recorded by none other than Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast! This game is a visual and musical treat. I only wish it didn't have so many graphical and sound issues like stuttering and clipping. I also wish that the game had more sections where you could hear lyrical music. Also, I think it's kind of weird that there are some bike parts that are objectively better than most others. I really wish the bike parts came with true side grades.Overall I give it a 4/5. Would be a 5 if it had more time to bake in the oven to get those performance problems and minor gameplay annoyances tweaked.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Sable was a fantastic and emotionally touching adventure, through and through. It's an open world game taking place in this ruined desert world, and you're sent off into it with one goal: discover who you are and who you want to be. You meet interesting new characters along the way, discovering this vast world, accompanied by your bike and a stellar soundtrack. If you're a big fan of curiosity driven games like Outer Wilds or Breath of the Wild, you'll get a kick out of Sable. That being said, some of the puzzles were frustrating at times, though rather infrequently. Specifically, there are a few puzzles which can only be solved at a certain time in the day/night cycle, meaning that if you want to solve that puzzle before heading off to do anything else, you just have to sit there and wait for the clock to hit whatever time of day you need to progress.I think my favorite thing about this game, though, is the climax of the journey. It suddenly dawned on me at the end how much of a connection I had made with my trusty bike, and it really struck a chord to leave the adventure behind and make a decision as to what I wanted for my Sable.Overall, I'd give Sable a solid 9/10, definitely worth the time and money to experience it yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is visually stunning, and as far as video-game art styles go, just seeing and exploring the world is a joy to watch.The game-play and story line itself is fairly simple, you explore the world completing tasks for different guilds, and in doing so you earn badges which can be exchanged for masks. There's no combat, no death, it's just exploration and adventure. The game is very slow paced and is as short or as long as you want to make it... and 100% completion is entirely achievable.The downside to Sable however is that it's a little buggy in places, and It suffers with a lot of screen tearing... and I mean  It's tolerable, and after a while you forget it's even happening... but it is an issue. If you love art and visual experiences I would give this a go, It's not the most exciting game, but, (screen tearing aside) it's a beauty to watch.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and chill game that's more than the sum of its parts.The aesthetic strongly reminds me of Hergé's Tintin comics and it rules. Perfectly matched soundtrack to go with it too.The gameplay is all exploration with no combat, just taking things in at your own pace and helping people out here and there. Your only goal is to explore and find the path you want to choose in this easygoing world. Climbing is the biggest challenge and it's a pretty fun one, there's a lot of variety in the places you can go.It is buggy and that's the one letdown. Mostly minor things but calling the hoverbike rarely worked for me and that's a primary game mechanic. It should always work. Still, I have to recommend it despite the flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Sable is a truly gorgeous game, and exploring it is deeply satisfying. It's rare and wonderful when a game's mechanics and narrative match so well, but Sable manages. I've yet to find a quest or puzzle in it that felt like it dragged. I love how it has me looking at its world and thinking not "I wish they made that place explorable" but "how do I actually get up there?" Narratively, I find it hopeful and affirming, especially the characters Sable encounters on her Gliding--Eliisabet in particular.

_childDocuments_.review: This would be my favourite game.Pros.1. genuinely the most relaxing game i have ever played.2. makes exploration feel great3. the art style is A W E S O M E would definitely recommend if your a Moebius fan :))4. the characters and dialog kinda feels like reading a comic book, most of your interactions feel like that nice person you met at the shop who made your day :)Cons.Fps.Im running a Ryzen 9 - 5900HX16 gigs of ram and a 3070(pehaps windows 11 or directx 12 may pose a problem idk)Point is, even on lowest graphics major cities are basically unplayable which really sucks if the story cant progress without you doing 10 different missions in them... even then, open wasteland will also give you regular lag spikes, especially when out of the starter zone, that's the only place that feels properly polished...So I really do want to love this game, and recommend it to everyone i know, but until these major immersion breaking issues are taken out of the game i simply cant... i want to love zipping through the desert but not with regular drops to 20 fps and floor clipping...I very much look forward replaying it and writing a positive review when its properly polished if that ever happens, but its 2 years down the line so we'll see :)

_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: This had been on my watchlist for quite some time due to the Moebius inspired art style, and I was fortunate to grab it on sale. A welcome reprieve from so many competitive and stress-inducing games - Sable presents its own challenges and rewards exploration in a wildly atmospheric and enjoyable setting. Random bugs (player model disappearing, clipping through surfaces, NPCs walking into walls or structures, finicky tactile landscape) briefly jolt the player out of immersion but it's quite easy to sink back in. Initially I felt that the empty landscape was detracting from the game, but as I sank more hours in I felt myself getting even more immersed. Maybe it's meant to parallel the lonesome journey of gliding. Regardless, I'd highly recommend this game to anyone. The characters were multidimensional, the aesthetic was top notch, and the underlying story was heartwarming. Definitely play Sable.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly frustrating and buggy experience.For a game that encourages exploration it sometimes forgets to give out of the way places collision so you can walk through walls at times. A certain sidequest in a massive temple couldn't be completed because a button simply refused to work. The bike is fun to ride with the exception of when it decides to go spinning out of control because you ran over a small bump. I also experienced numerous interface and sound bugs.There is certainly a good game in there, but its layered under so much frustration that I simply cannot recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Sable shines in what is unsaid but stated nonetheless. Ephemeral dust clouds spray over distant dunes, whispering come hither. Explore. Glide, child. Empty, but not unwatched temples speak to the long line of ancestors who came before you. You tread among interstellar graves, a voyeur into stories past of people you will never know.Which is not to say Sable is lonely. Your hoverbike has a spirit, a name. She is Simoon. You are inseparable, and her company is welcome in this vast, tranquil desert. Your Gliding is as much about discovering who she is as it is discovering who you are. Aside from her company, the game does not lack in other sentients to meet. People dot the desert, each handful adding their own story, their own impression.Consider purchasing if you love excellent art direction and beautiful soundtracks. If your curiosity drives you, not competition. There will be no test of your twitching reflexes, only of dutiful hands and feet placed one over the other, seeking the next unturned stone. Sable is your nature walk in the desert, without the constant risk of death.Also, seeing the reviews mentioning stuttering: I have a GTX 1660 and have had zero issues? So I guess if you're a functional adult without unlimited PC budget or time to camp out for components, this game might be for you.It's definitely for me."May all the gods turn their faces from you."

_childDocuments_.review: Basic premise/StorySable is primarily an open-world, coming-of-age, non-linear story. She must travel beyond her tribe into the vast unfamiliar dunes and discover what it means to be a 'glider'. Along the way, she will learn what it means to be truly independent and meet a colorful cast of characters who impress upon her valuable lessons. Whether it's good/bad/weird/funny/thoughtful.I first heard of Sable several years ago back in E3 2018. And was immediately drawn to the unique art style depicting a young hooded girl with a mask on an alien planet traversing the dunes with nothing but the clothes on her back and a cool hover-bike. Four years later, I’ve now had the pleasure of playing the game from beginning to end, completing all side quests and achievements to get the most out of what I can from the game. And was it worth it? Well…Unique GameplayI’d say the first 20 minutes were boring. Sable(Yes, that is our protagonist’s official name). Doesn’t have access to her hoverbike at the very start of the game. You have to go through a tutorial to get used to the controls, from there you must undertake a very small trial to receive the gliding stone which will allow Sable to glide indefinitely, but still descend. An immensely useful item throughout the whole game. From there and this is close to when the 1st-hour mark ends. Where you’re tasked with building your hoverbike. What awaits is just you, your hoverbike, and the vast dunes awaiting you. Sable is quite an interesting indie from past games I’ve played within the genre. It doesn’t have a compelling story, to hook individuals off the bat, nor does it have an addicting gameplay formula to keep you coming back for more in the sense of you can’t wait to come back to play again. The soundtrack isn’t a breathtaking experience everyone needs to hear. And the world isn’t filled to the brim with absolutely mind-blowing locations at every corner to check and collectibles to find. Instead, Sable caters to the niches of any of the hooks above. Where patience, effort, and grit, are maintained solely by the player’s will to continue and discover more. In which the value and depth of an area can be fully appreciated, once you dig a bit deeper than the surface level. And it is here I feel Sable shines magnificently. If you ever played games like Shadow of The Colossus(Sotc)/Death Stranding(DS), and even Breath of the Wild(botw). Sable takes the best parts of these and made me come back for more. In Sotc I wanted to explore/learn more about the world, but couldn’t. Here I could. I can converse with the inhabitants in small settlements and larger settlements to learn more about their culture, jobs, likes/dislikes, current events, and more. In DS I had a fulfilling satisfaction going from job to job delivery. And here it’s no different with sidequests making me travel to distant regions to complete another sidequest. And receiving that oh-so-familiar feeling once again. Not so much as a fetch quest, but more akin to doing more activities. And being satisfied with a job well done. Whether it's being challenged to climb the tallest peaks, collecting different assortments of beetles, asking for information to lead me to a person gone missing, and more. I was captivated by Sable’s world and each time I would go forth to my next destination I would become distracted by another unfamiliar structure on the horizon. An ancient ruin here, large rings deep in the sands as I raced through them on my hoverbike to unearth a hidden mechanic. Entering megastructures and solving puzzle rooms, and sometimes buying clothing/bike parts to customize my looks/bike. It's reminiscent of my time in Botw. Since I would do nothing but explore the vast world it had to offer and the game let me. Sable operates much in the same way. The world is fully explorable and you can go to any area and undertake any side quest at your leisure. I didn’t have something in the back of my mind to worry about. Nor did I need to do anything or accomplish a task within a small time frame. It also helps that Sable is quite an interesting individual herself.Whenever she would converse with any individual during her travels she would  have something to say about them via an internal monologue. It’s a small detail, but one I greatly appreciated to get a feel of who Sable is and what she thinks from time to time. She has this aura of naivety about her tempered by young adolescent wisdom that can from time to time spring some insightful comments. Sometimes she can respond wittily to people who give her sass and other times she can give answers which make the other recipient ponder the answer for some time. It is an incredible experience to witness from the start of her journey until the very end. And her growth upon meeting new people and sharing experiences is one I found particular joy in. The dialog is wonderful here in Sable. There isn’t pages upon pages of exposition and the writing isn’t too overly complicated to bombard the reader. Rather, the game is minimalist in the approach to give only as much to the player to be understood without the need to go deeper. Yet, leaves seeds throughout to nudge curious minds to dig deeper by way of exploring. And this I feel is one of the main strengths of Sable. The story being told through gameplay. Anytime, Sable would converse with an inhabitant, every time she would complete a sidequest from an NPC. And every time she would travel through the sands on her hoverbike and uncover whatever is lurking behind a puzzle room. There are some major/minor breadcrumbs being conveyed and I love it. Final thoughts/RuminationsWitnessing Sable’s journey from start to finish is an enjoyable affair. Much akin to a slow burn, you’ll only get as much out of it depending on how much time you put into the game. Luckily the game is more on the short side. My 15-hour playthrough could’ve been cut by more than half if I had decided to finish it early on. I think after the fifth hour I could’ve seen the end credits haha. And yet, despite that, I continued. Luckily the game didn’t have any bugs/crashes. Although, the game could’ve been optimized a bit better I feel. I had constant frame drops in areas I’m pretty sure my pc could’ve run flawlessly. Despite tinkering with the settings. Yet, for the most part, my fps was constantly above 30 reaching 60 in some areas. Didn’t impact me in a major way, but I feel it's worth noting. Nonetheless, the game’s incredible art-style and ambient soundtrack helped give so much life to the game. Ultimately, my time with Sable was worth it. Certainly in the beginning it sure didn't feel like it. But over time, the beauty and silent alien world captivated me. The inhabitants shared their personal experiences, the otherworldly ruins gave me awe. And riding my hoverbike through the dunes never failed to bring me a sense of satisfaction of tearing through the sands to jump high into the sky. Similarly, I felt the same contentment climbing any plateau or structure. The mysterious lore surrounding the planet, kept me intrigued to find out more. And lastly Sable's spunky, sassy, blunt attitude never fails to amuse me any time she converses with anyone. Sable is not a game for everyone, but for those looking for a game to give you a sense of wonder and freedom in a coming-of-age story? Look no further and take a wild ride on the hoverbike of Sable and go forth and find out!Total Times Beaten: 1Score: 9/10 Hours Played: 14.7 hours

_childDocuments_.review: Sable takes place on the desert planet of Tatooine where, as Spidergirl (without the ability to shoot webbing from her hands), you undergo a spirit journey to find your own Cosplay mask, as wearing Cosplay is a mark of being an adult everywhere on Tatooine. Equipped with the ability to surround yourself with your own fart-bubble, which shields you from gravity, and a hovercraft speeder-bike like seen on the planet of Endor, your journey is... to journey and collect things all while facing seemingly zero opposition or danger from anything or anyone in the world around you. Any attempt to escape or challenge this vast, meaningless existence is futile as literally nothing on Tatooine can kill you, whether its your own speeder-bike sending you into cliff-faces or face-planting into the ground, or trying to end it all by jumping from a spectacular height (since your fart-bubble explodes forth at the very last second before meeting sweet release). There are buckets you can pick up and throw, but impossibly, the local livestock do not seem to mind.

_childDocuments_.review: On its surface, Sable is a game about collecting masks by completing sets of specified missions. From climbing towering mountains, to uncovering ancient ships, to catching cute little beetles, the game offers many avenues of progression. At its core though, Sable is a well-composed tale of exploration with a principal theme of self-discovery. When first venturing out, the world is sparse and deserted—Sable, as a character, is anxious about what is to come. Although as you explore the frontier, the world becomes more and more populated by opportunity. There is a great sense of growth as you uncover what the dunes have to offer. There is a great deal of choice in this game as to where you want to go, how you want to gear up, and who you ultimately want to become. Nevertheless, despite the beauty of its vast mesas and badlands, Sable still suffers from various mechanical annoyances. These annoyances include but are not limited to: audio cutting out while sprinting, the glider constantly getting stuck, awkward camera movements, and the menu not detecting your mouse. All things that could easily be worked around with, although still annoying enough to detract from the game’s immersion.As of writing this review the game has only been out a week or so. Overall, it’s still a well-crafted game definitely worth its price—although I’d recommend waiting a bit for these issues to be patched prior to purchase. In conclusion, Sable is a brilliant coming-of-age story set amongst the dunes of a vast painted desert, limited only by its mechanical annoyances.
_childDocuments_.name: Sable

_childDocuments_.review: Sable is, at its heart, a game about freedom. You start as a child ready to go on her coming-of-age journey and are given little freedom in your tasks.  But then as soon as you complete the tutorials....you're handed the entire world at once. You can just ride around on your hoverbike to every corner of the map without anything trying to impede you beyond your own creativity in climbing. The gameplay in Sable is fun. It's key focus is exploration. There are no enemies, there is no game over or failure mechanics. Sable lets you enjoy it as you want. And at the end, a choice that takes your freedom awaits.There is some jank, but not enough to make the game any less fun. Mostly with the map not loading if you've been playing for too long or for more fun sometimes jumping on edges launches you around. I suggest this game very much.

I'm blown away by the design, visual styling, and sound.  The visual style reminds me very much of the cartoon art of French artist Jean Giraud, AKA Moebius. Played 4 hours at the time of review, I'm sure it will be many more.  I don't think I could recommend it more highly.

_childDocuments_.review: Sable is a beautiful game, not just visually, but musically, aesthetically, and in the ideas it is trying to convey and the way it is conveying them. Yes, it looks stunning and commits itself to a bold and inspired aesthetic in every aspect of it's visual presentation -but it also has a wonderfully melodic ambient original soundtrack by Japanese Breakfast. It also has writing that's full of personality and heart. This game doesn't really miss, for me. The end result is what I can only describe as an immaculate vibe. This is a game about exploring, and climbing. Exploring and climbing a barren world, with ancient, derelict technology tucked away in it's corners- the few powered up remnants of tech lit against the monochrome night with striking neon pastels. It's also a game about a young person exploring what they want to do with their life, going out into a strange world, and trying to build themselves up. Again, there is a consistency of tone and goal between all aspects of the presentation and story here that really works for me.On a more mechanical level, this game lives in that AA release space where it's not jank, but there's just the occasional whiff of jank. The camera can clip through some ♥♥♥♥. Sometimes climbing looks funny in that Skyrim way, but these are essentially non-issues. That full camera control allows you to drink in a world that is among the most stunning ever rendered, and the climbing is organic in a way that lets you forge your own paths to make it to the top, with it's breath of the wild style stamina system. Is there a jump or a ledge that looks maybe just barely reachable? You can try, and it often is. You'll climb dilapidated towers, creepy ancient temples where rituals take place, spinal columns of giant-sized creatures, crashed spaceships, and your standard red rock formations.I've only played this game for 2 sessions- and let me be clear- I don't know how long this is, I don't expect it to be some behemoth of content. There's no combat and very little conflict. You are going to run around and climb things and be like "wow, that's so beautiful," and you're going to hear some nice, well crafted dialogue that speaks to people's motivations and feelings as they deal with the world. It's all incredibly earnest and incredibly nice. For me, that's perfect. That's exactly what I wanted.Despite my short playtime as of this writing, I was so moved playing this game last night that I feel compelled to slap the heartiest recommendation I can muster here on this page. If any of this sounds cool, if the videos look like your style, please pick this up.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give this game an 8/10. I loved the story, the characters, and the world. I loved exploring this strange world and collecting masks. Each character had a unique story and it was fun seeing them interact with each other and with me. I am deducting some points tho because the game is a little janky. There were times where the camera would move in a weird way, Sable would move in a weird way (not grabbing onto walls right away, doing a weird half walk half climb, etc.), or the flowwy parts of my clothes would clip through Sable. None of these were game breaking but were a bit annoying. All in all, if you can look past the jank I think this is a wonderful game and well worth at least one play through.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend it because it's not bad. But I don't think it's very good either. Before I go into what I didn't like, I will say that it does look very unique and cool, and I respect it for that. Okay so, my main problem with the game is that it quickly starts to feel a bit pointless and samey, like, sure you can explore all these places and do all those quests, but to what end? And I didn't find it interesting enough mechanically for the process alone to make playing the game enjoyable. I dropped it halfway through because it got pretty bland. For a game about finding a purpose and place in the world, I think it is ironic that everything you can do feels a bit meaningless and tedious. It didn't manage to make me want to wear any of the masks. It's still serviceable and obviously has a lot of work and dedication behind it, but I was disappointed. I hope your experience with it will be different.

_childDocuments_.review: Sable is a beautiful game with an immersive world, incredible and unique artstyle and soundtrack by one of my bands at the moment, Japanese Breakfast, and that's why it disappoints me immensely to say this game is borderline unplayable. Currently the game has an issue where it stutters and significantly drops in frame rate seemingly on a whim. At first I thought it was because I was playing on Steam Deck, however after moving it to my decently powerful desktop rig, the stutter continued and frankly felt even worse. Upon investigation, even people with a 3090ti can't escape the stutter. Sable shouldn't be Steam Deck verified in the very least. Quite frankly, it is such a disservice to all the creative individuals involved for this game to perform as poorly as it does. I want to love this game so bad but I've had to put it down for now in hopes that it will eventually be fixed.
