_childDocuments_.review: First two big-tiddy women I met were named "Hazel Nutt" and "Melanie Jugg", I immediately knew this game was a 10/10.Kynseed is an interesting farming sim / life sim.Even though it looks similar on the surface to Stardew, Sun Haven, and all of the other pixel-farm-life games that aren't worth naming, it definitely has its own vibe.They heavily marketed it as being inspired by "Fable", and was even developed by "Fable alumni Charlie Edwards and Neal Whitehead", and it definitely shows.The art style, for one.It's retro pixel-art, just like almost every game in this genre, but it has its own flair.It ranges from charming to downright ugly- but to be honest, I appreciate it more than another "everything is cute and perfect" CoZy game.Everything stays true to a visual theme, and everything is surprisingly detailed. The character design definitely took some getting used to, and there are no "more detailed" sprites in conversations like there are in other genres, so what you see in the trailers is what you get.Whoever their artist / artists are for this game, they did an outstanding job.The music is the first thing that REALLY stands out to me as something reminiscent of "Fable".It has that haunting fairy-tale quality to it, and it's almost never outright "cheery" which is refreshing.Every tune I've encountered so far has a mystery to it, and it makes me excited to explore.The fishing minigame is more realistic and fun than they usually are in these games (thank god), there's no meta "tap A to keep this bar on the fish!" or "try to land your cursor on the icon to hook the fish!"You cast your line, you jig your bait, and when a fish bites you set the hook and reel it in.No meta immersion-breaking minigame, just plain ol' fishing. It's so refreshing.Most farm-sim fishing minigame difficulty ranges from "Braindead Clicking" to "middle-finger directly from the dev", with no room in-between.This is probably my favorite system I've encountered so far, as far as the mechanics go.I gotta say, the UI needs some work.I can definitely see what they were going for- the UI *looks* great, but the usability-factor isn't good.I constantly find myself accidentally removing things from my hotbar, dropping things, throwing things, it's takes a lot of getting used to.I like that you get a mount right from the start- I can't imagine how tedious it would be traveling around on foot considering how big the map seems to be.Plus, being able to drift a pig around corners is way more fun than you might think.It seems like there's a minigame associated with most crafting / activities in the game, which makes the systems a lot more engaging than just "drop resources in a table / wait for it to finish making itself".For example, selling something at a market-stall has customers trying to haggle with you for a lower price, with you trying to haggle them to a higher price- and it's represented by a timing minigame, trying to land in a "green zone" on a circle.Smithing seems to have several of these minigames associated with it, all of them (plus the quality of your ingredients) can positively or negatively effect the end-result of your smithing.It's a really deep version of Fable's money-making minigames.Great game, the only things I really have to complain about are:>The UI being a bit wonky regarding menus / items.>The game throwing a lot of stuff at you right at the start, without really giving you time to "learn" your current task before it moves on to the next one.>The art style has grown on me, but some of these character-designs are positively grotesque- in a "Raggedy Anne doll brought to life" kinda way.Big strengths:>Humor is actually humorous.>Atmosphere nails the "Fable" vibe beautifully.>Music is great and chill, without falling into "generic cozy game" territory.>Minigames make all of the classic farm-sim activities feel so much more engaging and fun.>Depth of systems is intimidating, but once you start to get them down it honestly feels better than a lot of other games.>The art style (aside from a few NPCs) is amazing.9/10 for me. Thanks PixelCount! I really hope to see more from you in the future- whether it's in this game, or in another game in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I figured I might as well write a review considering I gave the game a fair shot. This is by no means a terrible game, it is pretty pleasant but it definitely needs some improvements before I can thumbs up it! Pros1) The concept of the game is very unique. I loved the idea of being able to have kids with better stats than yourself, and then pass on the torch to them and have them know all your skills etc. 2) The minigames, the exploration, interactions are all fun and engaging. 3) There are unique regions each with their own culture, vibe, and it adds to the game. 4) Making friends by guessing gifts, hearing rumors of birthdays, likes and dislikes, are all a fun mechanic imo.Cons 1) While the game is unique, it definitely is unfinished. I think everyone expected Stardew Valley's design on bonding with villagers, this game definitely doesn't do that. Bonding gives you free items, but beyond that, adds very little to the story element. Hell, your own sibling barely says anything to you after the prologue. 2) The prologue is extremely slow, and restarting the game can be a pain. I've heard inklings of devs wanting to change this.3) The game definitely feels like a grind after a certain point. Your objective is to increase your reputation, and the story gets slower the more you continue. (I will give the devs the benefit of the doubt and say they're working on it. All in all, it's a fun game, but it loses its appeal after a few hours. It'd be super cool if the devs added side quests that were engaging to each area you discover. (So far, I have only experienced one but it was tied to the main story line.). If the devs improve on this, the game is definitely going to be amazing, but until then, it isn't the best. It's not bad, but doesn't deserve a recommendation until improvements are made.

_childDocuments_.review: **3rd Update**Game Owned for: 3.8 yearsStatus: Send HelpEvery time a major update launches for this game, I give it a whirl. A brand new save, a brand new attempt to enjoy Kynseed. Surely, I think, every time, they will have developed this into something enjoyable and playable. Each time I'm wildly disappointed.Without boring you with the details of everything wrong with this game, I will say this: the major problem with Kynseed is that the developers have no direction, no quality control, and no discipline. For example, the update which gave us a blacksmith shop was one of the very first. Now, on their most recent update, I read a statement by the devs that they're "revamping" the smithing minigame. Can't wait to get that update to the update. The developers do this with -everything-, from the UI to the core game mechanics, repeatedly and with no real improvement each iteration. You expect that when a major update comes out for a $15 EA title, the content is all but polished, requiring only testing for bugs and balancing. Kynseed, on the other hand, uses these updates to hype the game with every intention of going back and reworking it to something playable later. Goddess offerings, skill development quests, chat prompts, general stores, and many other things like this have gone through so many iterations, but not in the normal way you'd expect. A major update will come out that "adds" these things, but because they are always so poorly implemented, they require modifications which often leave them looking and working nothing like they originally did. This isn't normal evolution through beta, this is wasting time. Why are there even animals in your game? It's so -bad- taking care of them, the system has already undergone several overhauls and there will be countless more I'm sure. I'll save anyone reading this- the animals are buggy, statless, pointless creatures that wander all but roughshod around your farm and have been for 4+ years of development.Chances are, all the content and updates you get now will work and look completely different in the finished version of this game, whenever THAT comes out. They say some cutesy stuff on the front page about how "game devs are notoriously bad at guessing time" but that's their way of saying "we'll milk this cow til it's dead." My unironic, no-exaggeration projection for Kynseed finishing development is 2028. I can't possibly predict its quality because I doubt it will be much like the game we have today. If you're willing to wait that long, go ahead and give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: It really hasn't changed all that much from its Early Access period. Someone very stupid once told me it was a game where "you could be and do anything", but lo and behold, this very stupid, very simple man was wrong.I do have 160+ hours in the game. I try to put in a good 50+ hours before I make up my mind about something, and I did this multiple times in EA as well as after 1.0 release.The general shop is OK because you can sell whatever you want. I did have some fun selling baked goods and pretending to be a baker. Until I got over how utterly tedious it is to restock your shop with new baked goods and just started selling ingredients instead.All the shops are like this. Tedious. Boring. Samey. Zero customization, zero drama, zero difficulty.Once you're done the prologue, you're aged up to 18 or so. For plot purposes, the game has taken away your family and now you're all alone. If you don't want to be alone, which is one of the presumed purposes of this game, you must find a partner. Well, I was a year older than two of the "eligible" bachelors (they were 17, I think), so they weren't valid partners. There was actually no one within my age range unless I wanted to wait a year (and why would I do that if the point of the game is to have family and mine was taken away?), so I settled on John Bows, a man who was a decade my senior. It kinda squicked me out a little bit, but whatever, it's a game.So I started dating John Bows. I took him on dates, to his preferred location, and upon arriving, he screamed, "MORE!!" and then I had a new quest to go somewhere else. That is 100% of all dates. "MORE!!" until it's over. There's nothing interesting. You're not revealed anything special about their character. You don't even get to know them. Just "MORE!!!" and then it ends. When he screams "MORE!!!" I picture a fat medieval lord like Robert Baratheon gobbling down a fatty turkey leg, covered in turkey grease. It's just gross.When I eventually got to the point where we could marry, I had to do a ridiculous multi-part fetch quest. Get this, get that, get this other thing but only on a specific date. Propose on a specific date. If you accidentally miss it because you were restocking your boring shop, oh, well, too bad, you have to wait another week. The game doesn't pop up and tell you it's a specific date, you have to keep track on that in your head, by reading your calendar and simultaneously opening up a book on the "agreed upon ways of marriage" and following the instructions step by step.Once you're married, your partner gives up what little personality they had and moves in with you. They don't interact with you, don't interact with your children. They have zero personality, not that they really had any to begin with.Probably the most interesting and personable characters in the game is Uncle Bill, with the exception of old man Jakob (). Uncle Bill is one of the only characters in the game that's nice to you off the bat. Uncle Bill's story was more interesting when he adopted you and forced you to call him Father in the very early version of the game. Your sibling is a forking jerk. From the moment they wake you up to start the game, to when they . At the end of the prologue, he (it was a he for me, for you it may be a she) .  Your sibling should stick around and help you. They should be your family.You cannot place furniture, rearrange it, or decorate anything on your farm. There's zero customization. All the set is already designed and there's just a few spots where you can interact (your kitchen, your family chore board, your bed). You are given the ability to feed your pets various items they like - which you judge namely by watching their reaction bubbles, where meaningless hieroglyphs appear above them and you're meant to discern their meaning through your intuition. You can feed them gassy apples and then pop them, giving at most a couple ingredients, but then you have no pet. You can buy new ones from the sales auction, and at this point from your crappy shops you probably have a lot of disposable income so it's a viable form of ingredient farming. But your animals do not breed, and have very little in the way of interaction. There are also no horses - which I love horses in games, but every game does them dirty, and I guess PixelCount wasn't sure they could do horses well either as they've made them "extinct" in Kynseed's lore. To sum up, animals are for the following: wasting ingredients to feed them, popping into very few ingredients, or riding. There's no animal husbandry mechanic to be had here.As for farming crops, crops can be placed in a few static areas. If you are unmarried, you have to water them yourself or they won't grow (unless it's raining). There's zero new mechanics with crops, and like many farming life sims, crops are boring, although they get extra points for being boring as you can't even choose where they go.There are herbs that you need for certain recipes. You can actually only access these items after the prologue - even though you'd probably like to make several of the recipes you already have access to, you are actually really limited. Many of these herbs do not grow on your farm, though there are a few that do, as they have static growing areas. They are even less dynamic than the other crops.Ultimately this game isn't about family. I guess it isn't about romance. Or farming. Or owning/running shops. Or exploration. Or going through the weird forests with weird combat mechanics (it's almost as if they didn't want to add combat but shoehorned it in somehow to appease those players that need combat in every game they play).While the game does have interesting, "tactile" minigames, an interesting art style, and an interesting lore, it also suffers from extreme lifelessness. There's little to do and it can be easily be completed well on in the beginning of your life. The generational mechanic is worthless because there's never a reason to play that long. The humour tries too hard and likely would appeal more to a juvenile audience. So what's this game about? Nothing, really. There's no purpose to anything. It should be about your LEGACY but it falls very, very short. It's lifeless, shallow, and once the art style has lost its novelty and lustre, there's nothing to keep you around.I really wanted to like this game, I really wanted to play the game that the Devs wanted to make. But they didn't make that game.

_childDocuments_.review: A (magical) slice-of-life sandbox RPG with more than enough potential despite the current early access. With lovely retro graphics and enchanting music that reminds me of a very "Secret of Evermore" vibe, Kynseed so far has a lot of the elements that fans of this kind of genre look for: farming, mining, foraging, exploring, fishing, task completion, bug-catching, and getting in good with the neighbors. The vastness of the map and quality of the explorative contents is already impressive, as is the underlying hints at a story that, despite its superficial appearance, is equal parts endearing and tragic. You can tell right off the bat what a labor of love this project is for its creators, and a lot of their spirit--and raunchy humor--shines through in just about every aspect. With a game that centers upon building a family tree over generations, it is perhaps not unexpected (but still a little disarming) just HOW BADLY this game wants you to have sex. "Bugger someone," it seems to chant through thinly-veiled innuendos. "Woo them. Knock naughties already. What's that? You still haven't lost your V-card? Time's a-ticking, lads and lasses, so please, porker your neighbors already. Have smoochy time with someone. ANYONE. They already married? Worry not, it's all free real estate. Get to it. Now. GO." That being the case, it is almost depressing at just how bland the myriad of other characters are. None of them are exactly a knock-out in appearance, and they all have the same phrases they tend to repeat on a daily basis, so really, you might as well marry the 100-year-old naked hermit that lives next to your farm, since he has the same amount of personality and charm as the blacksmith, the woodsman, the shop owner, the other farmer, the other other farmer, the other other OTHER farmer, and so on, and so forth.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave this game a real shot. I really did. It was one of those games that I have waited for years to finally come out of early access and while I did have my doubts about how ambitious it sounded I was also optimistic and excited for it.Unfortunately, after having played for almost 70 hours, I have to say that there's still A LOT of obviously glaring flaws that makes this feel like a very incomplete and unpolished game. While I appreciate that the devs have been pretty good with patching things and bugs as they get reported every few days since it's official release, I just think it's a shame that even after years of waiting that there's still a lot of things that don't work especially since this is supposed to be it's first version finally out of early access. Workers not gaining experience when they should (has been already fixed but I was thinking was something that should not have been broken to begin with, on release), stat line of parents from having kids seemingly not having any bearing (which is a shame really since the generational/legacy building part of the game was what got me most excited for this.), that, and your children turning out not looking anything like you. There are many other issues with the game but these things I speak of make the game almost unplayable for me at it's current state.I tried to enjoy the game for what it's supposed to be but I had to draw my line in the sand when, after almost 70 hours, I got to finally pass on my very first Kynseed and my heir is suddenly missing points from one of it's stats after inheriting the seed (8 whole points from Virility!). This just really killed it for me since trying to train your heir and completing the Kynseed challenges was supposed to give them more stats and the game not properly accounting for that just makes that whole 70 hours of play feel thankless and unrewarding.It is a beautiful game that has plenty of potential but sadly, after years and years of development, you would have hoped that a lot of those potential have already been realized. I cannot, with a good conscience recommend the game in this current state. I have been playing on Steam for years and this is the very first review that I have written because I want this game to succeed so much and live up to it's promises. Eventually, hopefully it will.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first steam review ever. I bought this game years ago when it was still in early access and impatiently awaited its full release.  I always find it odd whenever someone can play a game for dozens of hours of entertainment only to give it a thumbs down. However, this thumbs up is given more with a sigh of disappointment than with enthusiastic applause. Here goes.Overall: Kynseed is a fun game for anyone looking for a crafting/shop management/adventure game that offers more in the way of variety than depth. For example, there are a WHOPPING >80 npcs in the game, and I can only remember a few of them.My primary complaint (mild spoilers ahead) is with the title itself. The main "gimmick" of the game involves gaining control of your children (with stat bonuses based on your performance) as your previous character becomes too old and dies. Hence, "kin-seed." However, I expected a lot more than what was ultimately delivered. For example, when you pass on to the next generation, no dialogue options change. In fact, nothing changes aside from how all characters get older and some die. No one remarks how sad it is that your parent died. The rest of your family simply disappear from the map. There is no funeral. NOTHING. Even your first character's sibling is still referred to as "sibling" instead of aunt/uncle when you take control of your children. It is the most convoluted leveling system I have ever seen in a video game. They essentially created leveling with extra steps and no payoff. Oh, and by the way, you can EASILY beat the game without ever moving on to the second generation.The basic gameplay loop is fun. Crafting/gathering/combat/shop management all feel fun. But many aspects feel unpolished. You cannot customize your farm or your shops at all. No furniture placement. No changing floors/wallpaper. The only thing you can customize in this game is the color of your hair. That's it. This honestly feels like an unfinished product, and that the developers tried to rush out the game because they were running out of funds. Tldr: The game is fun but feels unfinished. They continuously are pumping out updates for the game so maybe purchase it on sale in a couple months after they've polished it up some more.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like your stardew valley with some weird twists and an interesting combat system. _childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Kynseed since it was in early access, and I'm really impressed with the final game. It's polished, fun, and a lot of minor annoyances have been addressed - I particularly appreciate that unfed animals are now automatically selected even if they're close to a fed animal, I don't have to keep track of which pig I fed already every day. The art has always been beautiful and the new world map screen is really nice, very fun and colorful.

_childDocuments_.review: This game follows the foremost tenants of indie developer bible: Over-promise and under-deliver. Gameplay can be summed up as running around an overinflated and diluted map to different resource nodes and pressing E on them, sometimes with a tool equipped. Mining, harvesting, planting, fishing, relationships, etc all just static nodes you press E on. The soundtrack sounds like instrument soup and not the delicious kind. Kynseed? More like Inbreed. Seriously why can you marry your sister? Now I got you wanting to play it don't I? Weirdo.
_childDocuments_.name: Kynseed

_childDocuments_.review: The core gameplay loop gets old very fast and holds few, if any, surprises; I can't imagine actually playing long enough to reach a point where I move on to the next generation. Outside of some brief quest chains, the overarching story seems to fizzle out after you move on to adulthood. There's no sense of urgency, and the game doesn't make it easy to set meaningful goals for yourself. You don't need to eat, sleep, or feed your animals; some farm animals don't even seem to serve a purpose beyond providing fertilizer. Penalties like failing to do offerings are easily reversed. It's incredibly easy to upgrade tools and even that seems to serve next to no purpose. Festivals and events like pig auctions are forgettable.Game feels incomplete. Frequent instances of placeholder text in dialogue and descriptions, which makes already bland NPCs feel even more bland. Multiple items and ingredients appear to have no use (and some outright say they do not yet have a use). Poor balancing on certain crafting and gathering tasks as well as shop management, imo, making them incredibly tedious.At least one cheeky reference to forthcoming DLC, which was kinda what made me put the game down. Why advertise in-progress DLC when your game feels like the early access dust hasn't even been swept up yet?
_childDocuments_.name: Kynseed

_childDocuments_.review: Cons: It is spread a bit too thin. The farming aspect doesn't have a lot going for it. NPC convos get boring after a while.Pros: The pixel art is gorgeous. Especially when it rains. Combat is fun, so are the smithing/cooking mini games. The humor is great. I like the kinda creepy lore. Also, this game is the only time I've ever been actually scared in a farming sim. Curse you Tommy Hookfingers!Edit: The Big Build Update is awesome. Adds a lot of new features.
_childDocuments_.name: Kynseed

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed it until I got through the prologue.The prologue lasts about two in-game weeks, which took me all day with other stuff going on.The writing is solid. The game mechanics are enjoyable. There's a few bugs but it's not so hard to reload at the start of the day — though there should be a quicksave.My issue isn't with the gameplay, but that the story gets really dark. It feels like things turn on a dime. It's like someone took the aging mechanic on Story of Seasons: A Wonderful Life and then turned it up to eleven.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome RPG that continuously improves! I initially started playing after the full release and have found myself coming back often. The mechanics/story lines/goals, etc. have become more balanced and fleshed out over time, which is great for keeping you interested and striving towards rewards. The addition of customization is one of my favorite developments since the release! It is so nice to rearrange things and add decorations on my own farm.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE 21/03/2024Kynseed recently got a HUGE 1.1 update that added lots of content AND improved a lot of the pre-existing systems, with more to come in the future. Kynseed has only gotten better with time. The devs are dedicated and passionate! I highly recommend this game!UPDATE 18/08/2022Updating again because a small thing has changed: the roadmap was abandoned ages ago, so don't bother looking at it (sadge). Currently the devs have decided to stop updating the game until the big 1.0 date, which they hope will come out this year. If you're looking to buy Kynseed, I recommend waiting until that update: the full experience is so close!Also still stand by everything. It's continued to improve and I'm very excited for 1.0.UPDATE: 12/08/2021Just updating to say I stand by what I said, and that every update since has been excellent in quality and content. This game is shaping up to be something very special!The game isn't finished, but whats here is engaging, and the developers have done nothing but consistently demonstrate how trustworthy and hard-working they are. From their Pixel Count Post where they post brief updates on their work, to the indepth roadmap where all future updates are lovingly detailed - these dev adore their game, and want us to adore it too.Even ignoring that, the game is really fun. Theres heaps to do, lots of explore and discover. Even with half the systems not implemented, you can still get a sense of the experience theyre going for. The game is also extremely pretty; I don't think Ive ever seen such detailed pixel art. Kynseed is an excellent early access game that promises only to get better. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Mile wide, but inch deep:Kynseed has the foundations to be excellent life sim/farming story driven game that adds something new to the genre, but in its current state it seems incomplete and unfocused.  The farming, crafting, store management systems have good foundations in the form of interesting mini games, but little content and purpose behind them.  The lack of meaningful day-night cycle (yes, your character is an android who never sleeps) breaks immersion or any sense that you are struggling to restore your family's farm.  Check beck in few months when the design direction is a bit clearer.'Assad or we burn the country'.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: Game has a great foundation and could be incredible in the future, but for now feels like its still in early access. I have very high hopes for it assuming the devs plan to keep pumping out updates. It is worth $20, but I think it could be one of those gems that you replay super often after some more content/updates.---Some of the thoughts I had after sitting down and thinking about it after my 50 hours:Character customization is incredibly limited, can only pick gender, hair color and a few options that affect basic stats. Would've been nice to invest points like an rpg or something to make a more rounded character, like make a character with higher charm/barter but is bad at combat or something, but for now the most you can do is like +2 to barter, or +2 to stamina. They did just adjust the heir system recently though, so at least your children should have a better mix of stats, supposedly. The combat is very simple and I'm not a huge fan of it, it can be frustrating and getting new gear/upgrades doesn't feel like it does much to help you. Farming mobs to buy upgrades feels more cumbersome than it should, and I love grinds so that's saying something. Combat stamina doesn't feel great, the grind to unlock your 3rd attack is annoying, the 'added damage vs enemy type' some weapons have is basically not noticeable at all. There's a lot of small things they could adjust that'd just make it feel so much better, like adjusting how often enemies attack/adjusting how often they use certain moves, making the pets feel more impactful/useful, etc. It's probably the thing I dislike the most in the game currently. With an heir with like 15+ strength, who knows maybe combat would feel better, but with your starting character with the +2 strength you can choose it doesn't feel good. Farming, it's okay. Would love to see some more upgrades, some of the deals you can take with Mr. Steal-your-soul do nice things, but it'd be cool to have like a sprinkler for your crops, or more field to plant stuff on, more fruit plant options, something you know. Your spouse can water plants for you and that's nice but that's not really what I'd have in mind. Upgrading tools doesn't change anything, even using the best hardest to work with metals. Would be cool if cutting a weed with a better scythe would give you better items or something. Marriage. Love that it's an option, love the idea of the heir system, but the dating mini-game is kinda basic and had a date in the shingles just bug out and not progress at all, and even when it does work its just kind of whatever. I don't expect a dating sim, not sure I'd really want it to be either, but kinda just feels like something to rush through and not care about. Wish getting married would do more, like you'd have cool things pop up to do with your spouse or something, idk. For now you kinda just pick a spouse that has good stats and either employ them somewhere or let them water your plants. Would be cool to bring your spouse into battle or something for like combo attacks or noticeable stat boosts. Could fire arrows as support idk. Fishing, it's very simple, could be better could be worse. Not much to say. Kinda wish there was a bit more to it, but having something like the smithing/cooking mini-game to catch a fish each time would probably drive me nuts. Crafting. Loved it at first. After about 10 hours got kinda tired of smithing swords every other day. First character I had didn't have any great arcane deals to pick from, horny mirror and a fog horn, guess it's randomized items idk. Made a second character and had a swiss army knife that made it so anything I made at the smithy made double which was life changing. If the game has/had more stuff like that, more upgrades, would love it. Doing the mini-games over and over can be tedious though, but it's not any worse than doing the fable 2 mini games for gold. Animals, gotta feed them too often and they don't feel like they do enough to justify getting them. Wish I didn't need an upgrade to auto-feed them every day. Not having a fast travel point at your house by default is pretty lame. I dunno, I could probably go on if I sat down and made a list but that's what comes to mind for now. Still, I do really like the game, and the devs seem very active both in the forums and in updating, so I think it has great future. It's just a little too unfinished feeling right now. More bang for your buck than a lot of $20 games on steam though.

_childDocuments_.review: So i would give this game a seven out of ten and for many reasons. You cannot get stronger in any way aside from raising children which forces you to try and find a spouse or adopt early game to improve on your abilities. Since you cannot get stronger going into dungeons or places with monsters is pointless because its far to difficult to go anywhere stronger for your first character. Also somewhat aggregating many npc's have HIGHER stats then you. The crafting system is extremely complex when you go to potions to the point where you could be put off because you craft differently depending on what your using. Blacksmithing seems to be the easiest crafting system and doesnt put you off. The Npcs are also somewhat bland and dont have any type of personalityAside from those three major put offs the game is good, i feel the game would have been more better had the story been deeper. Your children had a much more diverse and interesting set of personalities, strengths and weaknesses and that your default (beginning) character could  get stronger over time through doing certain tasks. But then having a limit to how strong a generation can get and then have to continue with that when you play as a child.The game was not bad... i tried to get deep into it but i couldn't. However the developers definitely put a lot of heart in soul in the graphics and it can be seen when in game its windy, raining, and night time. Hoping more success for the developers so that they can achieve and make better games from this.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, shame on the devs for calling this buggy, incomplete mess a full release when it’s clearly still Early Access.With that said, let’s talk about the good, the bad, the ugly, and the worst aspect of all when it comes to Kynseed.Let’s get the good stuff out of the way first. This won’t take long; it’s a short list.The world looks gorgeous. The hand-drawn pixel backgrounds are lush and beautiful, and each area looks distinct from the others. This is enhanced by the music, which gives each area its own background track. It makes the world feel expansive.And it’s not a small world, either. This is easily the largest life sim game I’ve played in terms of overall area. It took me a long time to explore it all, and based on the roadmap there’s even more to come.The combat system isn’t terrible, and can get tense on higher difficulties.There. That’s it for the good stuff. Now let’s talk about why none of these things matter.The world is big, yes, but it’s also extremely shallow. Once you’ve explored everything, you’ll find there’s actually very little to do. Many areas exist only to run through, and that’s only if you don’t bother to use one of the game’s fast travel systems.Playing the game involves engaging with a bunch of tedious mini-games that fast wear out their welcome. They also aren’t balanced – some are so easy they feel pointless, while others are frustratingly tricky, and all feel like they’re only there to take up your time. The devs have admitted that they need to rebalance these, but they’ve known this for years and have yet to actually make it a priority.This is made worse by unfinished content. There are items that quite literally say “This doesn’t do anything yet.” NPCs and books reference events that don’t actually occur at the time of this writing (e.g., the music festival). There are bugs galore. None that I’ve encountered are game-breaking, but all these little bugs add up, and they quickly become frustrating, particularly when they intersect with unfinished content. An example of this from my playthrough: I was trying to unlock a late-game ability, which required me to collect a number of rare items. Thanks to a bug, one of the items was impossible to acquire directly – you have to use a roundabout method of sending family members of expeditions and hoping for the best from the RNG. This made it take (no joke) about fifty times as long as it should have to acquire.Nevertheless, I put in the grind and eventually got enough of this item to unlock the skill. Turns out the skill in question doesn’t do anything – it helped with a mini-game that was  because it was too tedious and repetitive (which, given the nature of the mini-games they left in, is really saying something.) The devs didn’t bother replacing the ability with anything else for the , so all that grinding was for nothing.The characters are all ugly. This is something I thought I’d get used to, that maybe it would work with the admittedly gorgeous pixel backgrounds, but no… The sprite designs are all a bunch of ugly blobs or stick-limbed creatures, and the portraits (you have two different style options for portraits) are somehow even worse regardless of which version you use.The writing is steeped in cringey attempts at humour. It’s not funny, btw, unless you consider fart jokes, innuendo, and obvious references to other video games hilarious, in which case you’re in for a treat! But the worst attempts at humour, by far, are the fourth-wall breaking jokes. These tend to occur whenever any sense of immersion might, against all odds, threaten to grab you, bam, you’re hit with some dumb joke reminding you that you’re playing a video game. These include the references to more famous video games, mentioned above, but go beyond that as well: “Fetch, boy!” says a passing NPC to my pet dog. “Just kidding,” he adds, “I don’t actually have any throwing animations.” It’s like the game is embarrassed by its status as a game and wants to keep you at arm’s length lest you actually engage with it earnestly.Even if you could engage with the characters and the world, there’s little point. The NPCs almost entirely lack personality. With the exception of your uncle, your sibling, and the Masters, all the characters draw 95% of their dialogue from the same pool, so they all end up saying the same things to you over and over and thus feel bland and generic. You can date anyone 18 or older, and marry anyone as well regardless of their gender or current marital status (there’s an in-game explanation for why this is if you go looking for it), but it doesn’t matter much – one spouse is pretty much the same as any other.Look, the game’s claim to fame, its central conceit, is that it’s a multi-generational life sim. Characters are supposed to live, grow up, marry, have kids, and die, then one of your character’s kids picks up where you left off and the story continues. And the world itself also follows this rule, with generations growing old and dying, and new ones coming up.Sounds great, doesn’t it? I thought so, too, which is why I bought it during Early Access.There’s supposed to be a genetics system that has your offspring inherit stats and traits from their parents, which allows you to build ever-stronger characters to face the challenges in the world. This doesn’t exist – the devs supposedly added something along these lines in a recent update, but wouldn’t you know it… It’s bugged, doesn’t work.Let me say that again: And the world’s generational mechanics also don’t work. Started NPCs aren’t replaced fast enough by new arrivals, which makes areas start to feel kind of like ghost towns… And those new NPCs that do get introduced are somehow even more bland and generic than the ones they’re replacing. At least what little personality Isiah Green had matched the sprite design, but when he was reintroduced as Billy Scrumpy he just became generic NPC #85.The thing is, even if these generational mechanics were complete and functional, it wouldn’t matter. The game’s challenges aren’t significant enough that they can’t be tackled by your starting character, and the gameplay isn’t rich enough to want to play out the generations anyway. The devs clearly had an admittedly great idea for the game’s hook, but had no idea how to actually make it mesh with the game in a meaningful way.I haven’t come into these opinions lightly. Between Early Access and “full release,” I’ve put in almost ninety hours into Kynseed. I’ll admit – at first, it was fun. The game showed lots of promise. But the little annoyances, bug-related and otherwise, added up. It soon started feeling more like a chore – grinding out items to give as gifts to improve friendships to unlock things to grind out items better, a gameplay loop that would be rewarding in a better game but here is just tedium repeated ad nauseum. I kept hoping that the game would redeem itself somehow – some new area or mechanic or even late-game challenge that would make it all click. That never happened, though. Even if I got my money’s worth in terms of time played, in the end almost none of it has been a satisfying experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Giving this a positive review because I've played it so much, but if I'm brutally honest it also feels 20% unfinished. I agree with all of the major critiques which have been given.1) You should be able to name your sibling2) Blacksmithing and many other skills don't give you a sense of being able to practice steady progression - like why can you make 5 different kinds of swords right away? Why are they all 4 star from 1 star ore? Meanwhile some basic food is hard to make more than 1-2 star.3) The two small talk dialogue options should just be removed. Honestly do not see the point.4) Early quests should not be impossible to do based on recipes, accessible areas, etc.5) Maybe some relationship quests would be good? Like with older platonic folks? 6) Develop some of the characters please. It shouldn't be impossible. Like what is up with the giant naked man?7) I can't tell what level up mechanics exist and what don't. Is blacksmithing improving something? Farming? I need clear, tasty leveling.8) The reputation level should also feel more tasty to level up, I think. Some sort of unlockables?9) Similarly - quests to unlock areas? Deliveries? Needing all mapstones from a previous area? Idk, something.10) The delivery quests need to be a little more balanced. It's either 1 item or 45 items.11) The writing suddenly is crass and breaks the Fourth Wall way too muchI can't help asking a really basic question: isn't this game... not... really... like Fable? Is there any way to be evil, for example?It seems more like you can work on whatever you want, like Fantasy Life, but that it should be about the satisfaction of incremental improvement, and that you may as well make some unique partners to court.

_childDocuments_.review: You've been given the Kynseed, a mystical acorn that grows into a family tree where your choices manifest in its branches. Raise a family, farm the land, run shops, and explore a world where everyone ages. When you die, step into the shoes of your children and continue your legacy.

name: Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodhunt
detailed_description: Bloodhunt is a thrilling free-to-play battle royale game set in Prague consumed by a ruthless war between vampire factions. Use your supernatural powers to hunt and outsmart your rivals and Inquisition soldiers in this third-person action shooter. Gear up, feed on potent blood to grow in power, defy gravity to strike from anywhere, and dominate the night! SUPERNATURAL WAR Whether you prefer a sneaky surprise attack or dive straight into battle all guns blazing, choose your clan allegiance to define your playstyle with unique supernatural powers. RUTHLESS DOMINANCE Roam from the deadly streets to the rooftops of Prague preying on mortals to grow in power. Finish off or commit diablerie on every enemy that crosses your path to be the last one standing. UNHOLY ALLIANCES Hunt as a solitary predator or rally your friends to join you and go into visceral, fast-paced fights where teamplay and strategy are essential. STYLISH PREDATORS Create your most unique looks for rivals to remember you by. Customize your appearance with stylish outfits, timeless hairdos, piercings or tattoos, and show off your personality with looks that truly kill. VAMPIRE: THE MASQUERADE LEGACY Set in the World of Darkness universe, Bloodhunt draws from this grim version of our modern world where vampires hide in plain sight and fight against hunters, other vampires, and their own worst instincts, all while struggling to maintain The Masquerade.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Note. The fact that we can only say yes or no to recommendation when writing a review is so dishonest. I like the game enough that I want it to succeed but I hate the practice of taking these universally accepted narrative driven games and forcing them into an online competitive multiplayer space especially battle royale. So I recommend, but I'd prefer it to be known I'd rather be playing Bloodlines 2 or even just a TTRPG set in this universe.I don't understand why anybody thought appealing to a wider audience by making a World of Darkness game in a Battle Royale format was a good idea. Don't get me wrong, I mostly like the game. I however, am not so out of touch that I don't realise most people don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about Vampires, much less like them. Majority of my friends don't care for them, they may like a character here and there but for the most part they'd rather have a story involving their destruction rather then being one of them. I blame Interview With a Vampire, Twilight, and Vampire Diaries for this. Buffy may or may not have helped in that sense as well with Angel and Spike but I digress. One even asked "Why would I want to play a tween girl's fantasy" -_-.WoD is unique in it's take on more then just Vampires, but werewolves, changelings, wraiths, mages, and even the Hunters have personal horror aspects to their stories, and the fans of this lore are already starved for content passed the TTRPG's (and some of us are baffled and frustrated with V5 in that regard) that making games like this is kind of unnecessary and kind of a false hope scenario (just like Legacy of Kain and Nosgoth). I don't think appealing to a wider audience when it comes to niche settings/lore/fictional worlds like WoD is a brilliant move. I actually think it's dumb because you alienate the fan base that don't want this to begin with or if they do enjoy it still would rather play something else and on the flip side the public already has almost no interest in it and if they do give it a shot, it is short lived. This game was hot for a month and then dropped as quickly as it grew.For the love of Caine... and Kain the other one, stop making this mistake.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, simply put, the best Battle Royale game out there. That's a bold statement, I know, and maybe you might not feel the same way. Though I'd like to break down a bit what this game does differently, and why it works.Let's start with the obvious: The setting. There's a lot of Battle Royales out there, but there's one key factor that they're all missing and that's lore. Now, why would you need lore for a BR? You don't. This is personal preference, for sure. Most BRs take place in unique universes specifically created for the game itself, most notably PUBG, Apex Legends and Fortnite. There's a handful of BRs that draw from existing franchises, but those usually don't go deeper than a couple games in, or just simply borrow the name, such as Firestorm, Battlerite Royale and another game close to my heart, Eternal Return.What differentiates Bloodhunt is that it can draw upon a  backlog of existing lore material, being part of the "World of Darkness" universe, and more specifically, being a "Vampire: The Masquerade" game. Longtime fans of these universes will immediately feel drawn to that, and as such, cannot help but speculate about all the unique ways they can implement existing lore. You simply just don't get that from PUBG or Fortnite.But if lore was all that mattered, someone would've done this long ago. No, in fact, it's got another strong thing going for it, and that's gameplay. Gunplay is alright, personally I'm really no expert on the subject. Some people will either love or hate it, but it's really not what sets it apart for me. No, the key part, for me, is the traversal. The ability to simply scale any wall, at any time, leap off of any building in any direction of your choosing. This game is a blast to jump around in. For the lack of a better word, it's giving hard "Spiderman" vibes, and that's high praise.But all that climbing wouldn't be much fun in an open field, right? And that's kind of what most other BRs do. They have big, empty spaces with a couple of houses and "notable locations" strewn about where the action takes place. I find that so incredibly bland. Bloodhunt puts you in the middle of a city. And I mean that quite literally, it feels like a city. We only have one map so far, but it's phenomenally detailed and even during night feels very lived in. There's a natural lack of driving cars, for better or for worse, but the fact that one of the key mechanics is to suck blood from roaming NPCs leads the city to be quite populated. And because of that, you never run out of things to climb or traverse. It almost gives the entire game another layer, as there's strategies to sticking on the ground as well as jumping on the roofs. It's brilliant.All that being said, why's the rating so low right now? I've spent a good couple hours trying to understand just why people seem to dislike it, and there was a seeming outrage toward some Anti-Cheat the game used, but that hardly speaks for the quality of the game. In my opinion, the biggest drawback of the game right now are the loading times. Personally, I don't mind them too much, but I am a patient man. I know there's a lot of people that cannot wait to leave and rejoin the next map, and with the way the game is structured, it can take a minute or two to have that happen. It's not even queue times, it's just the fact that the game loads so long. I've also had a bit of stuttering happen here and there, but the game's in early access, I'm not going to dunk it for that.All in all, I heartily recommend you try the game. I mean, , it's free, what more of an excuse do you need? It's well worth a try and I mean it when I say that this game is the best BR out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Shows promise! Can't tell what the hell is happening most of the time, though. Things are too dark/unsaturated. The "vampire sense" mode is jarring, it's hard to tell enemies and civilians apart, and you can't take the time to figure that out or you'll be shot. It's too fast paced of a game to allow you to take the time to acquire your target, which I think is the biggest problem. When you can't identify your target because of either the same-ness of it all, whether that be the color of the everything or the actual textures of the characters, there's a problem. You get noticed for shooting or using powers in front of civilians, marking you for everyone else to see. That's flavorful, but bad design, ESPECIALLY when [insert things I've already said]. Gunplay is also meh. Every gun feels the same, whether it be shotgun, sniper, LMG, etc.The 'drop screen' is also somewhat of a de-volution, imo. You select your preferred spawn location on the map before the round starts, you don't drop from a ship or anything. You get to see if an opponent is dropping close to you, and you get to see the high-value loot locations on that selection screen.Powers are fun, though! That's the one big up-side. Granted, not as fun/varied as Apex, but fun nonetheless. Right now, I wouldn't spend time playing the game much. It's kiiiind of a mess. Once they fix some of these things, maybe I'll pick it up again. Wouldn't say DOA, but..It's not got much going for it that hasn't been done already, save for the Vampire flavor, and the cool-ish powers. If you REALLY like VtM, I.. dunno if you'd like this too much tbh. Just a 'meh' BR with VtM branding/whatever on top of it.Needs improvement, is what I'll say.Edit to add:Sure. If you've managed to play 9 hours of this game in a day, you'll be able to discern, for example, the differences between civs and hostiles. I don't have that time to play a game I don't enjoy playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I have friends that like to play this game and I like playing it with them. Aside from that, it's a pretty painful experience:1) The game hasn't improved measurably since the "early access" and subsequent betas. Most of the notable bugs in those are still present here. That ranges from significant things like getting stuck on geometry or having your mouse become unresponsive to minor annoyances like being unable to clear the markers from your collection that mark things as new and un-viewed.2) Because of the aforementioned bugs, it can be difficult to know if you're dealing with a bug or one of the many hacks available for this game. 3) The game is basically a third-party simulator, due to the high mobility. If you can hear someone fighting, you can probably get there before it ends. This can be annoying in trios but it's painful in solos and promotes a passive playstyle and mostly involves hiding your way to the end of the match.4) They tried to shoehorn in a story to capitalize on the VtM license. It's pitiful. Honestly, if they were going to get more lore into the game, they should have just waited until they were ready to do it right.On the flip-side, the game can be fun and I've had some really good moments with it. Unfortunately, that fun is often marred by the aforementioned issues and can lead to a lot of frustration. If you're super into the VtM world or have friends that want to play, it isn't the worst way to spend your time.

_childDocuments_.review: since Nosgoth, i miss having a gothic pvp game with vampires. i certainly find this premise more interesting than your usual military shooter, so i want to like this game but i am once again just reminded of why i just for the life of me cannot enjoy the Battle Royale genre, which is made worse by the serious bug issues this game suffers from as it is an early access. First of all, the performance is dreadful on smy gaming laptop, it does reach the minium requirments to run the game, but it still struggles. first time i played after downlading it, it would lag and tank like crazy everytime i joined a match. so i went through updating my graphic card, and even cleaning my laptop for more space. yet after that, it somehow got worse, the game breaking completely and just giving me a black screen with distorted noise when i joined a match. i try the game again a few days later, now it suddenly works fine, though i still have to play at the lowest graphics, so it's not a particularly good looking experience. i play a couple of rounds until i run into a bug where i am stuck in the loading screen when the match starts. i can hear the game playing in the background and that my character has spawned on the map, but i can't see anything since i am still stuck with the loading screen. this happens 3 times in a row until i give up on the game for that day. (i also had several minor bugs with the UI and buttons not working correctly)today i try again. i avoid the loading screen bug, but the game perfomance is still extremely inconsistent, it is a very "jittery" experience on my laptop, which doesn't exactly make aiming very fun. and now several chunks of the city would not render or load in properly when playing the game. the map turning into mushy polygon squares that you can't touch or walk on, resulting in your character being stuck in a falling animation that just floats around the unrendered map and buildings. Battle Royales are probably one of the least newbie-friendly genres there is. at least if you don't have anyone to play with like me, and have to often play games solo. the learning curve of a BR becomes the equivalent of slamming your head against a wall. this game is no different in that regard. the game forces you into a tutorial after downloading it, but after completing it, i don't see anyway to replay it. if there is a way, i couldn't find it. which makes the game harder to get into as there is no training mode for you to go back into to better familiarize yourself with controls, abilities and the various weapons.  the traversal is a double edged sword. i love the easy movement and climbing which gives alot more satisfying freedom in how you play, but at the same time, all this verticality makes it hard to keep track of where players are located in relation to each other. combined with a fairly short time-to-kill, this becomes particularly annoying in a Batte Royale where you only have one life. suddenly you are killed by a player who came up (or down) behind you because they were at a different height level.my opinions on this might change with more experience. but the problem is getting there with all of these performance issues that makes the game practically unplayable (on my gaming laptop) in it's current state. as with most Early Access games, you get a glimpse of a game that might become something but doesn't work properly most of the time.in accordance to my experiences so far, i can't recommend this early access unless you are super obsessed about the Battle Royale genre, that said, it's not exactly revolutionary for the genre, while it has a few ideas in relation to the vampire stuff, the focus on guns does boil the game down into being another shooter BR. if you are on the edge or unsure about games like this, then this game will definently not convince you otherwise in it's current state, even if you love vampires.

_childDocuments_.review: I have some ideas for Bloodhunt to be more than a battle royale.Insert character creation, like an RPG sheet. That's right, instead of giving the player pre-set kits "Siren, etc.", the player distributes points in Physical Attributes (strength, dexterity, stamina); Mental (perception, intelligence, reasoning) and social (charisma, manipulation, appearance) attributes. This will impact gameplay, for example: strength increases melee damage (melee), dexterity impacts speed in climbing and/or running, stamina (hit total, damage resistance). Perception helps to "see" things when we sharpen senses with "X", intelligence impacts the performance of disciplines (powers), reasoning when opening cars, locks. Social attributes impact npcs: in how they react to player mess on the map (the lower they are, the more they give away the location of the players). Vampire disciplines can also be placed on the sheet, for players to choose which ones will have greater power. Can add tb Abilities such as dodge for bonuses against damage; firearms, melee weapons, for bonus damage; medicine, to raise up fallen teammates. Think of Bloodhunt as a scavenger hunt where each player builds his or her character through an RPG token.Virtues impact map issues. The cathedral is on fire, roll a test... a vampire with low courage goes into a frenzy and the player loses control of the character when they get too close to the flames.Finally, some experience character progression system to improve his token attributes and improve his character in general, where he learns xp playing, and spends improving his Vampire through points. Maybe a penalty, suffering a diablerie makes him lose points, with some daily/weekly limit.Each vampire within the arena will be unique in the amount of possible combinations. Bloodhunt will not be just another battle royale, but a BR with RPG elements of Vampire: the Masquerade.

_childDocuments_.review: Full Release Update 27/04/22:Despite some bugs lingering from prior playtests (Taking damage from the red gas zone despite you visually being within the zone, or bullets fired at Ventrue not registering randomly), the full re-release has been both successful and very enjoyable. There's the addition of a Mastery tab that shows a bunch of challenges that you can complete to unlock rewards, crossplay has been added so queue times are drastically reduced (In the UK, my queue times are very often <30 seconds), and plenty of balance adjustments for the weapons, though IMO they've always been fairly balanced as far as BR's are concerned. They've also added levelling up for each Archetype (classes) which allows you to unlock perks, giving additional value to trying each class and adapting playstyles.Will definitely continue playing this into the future - highly recommend--------------------------------------------------Original Early Access Review:After getting more time into this title, I can still wholeheartedly recommend this if you're a fan of BR games. It expands on a standard formula but incorporates elements of the VtM universe very well, such as avoiding using powers around civilians, drinking different blood types to gain buffs for skills and a whole subsection of lore, quests and collectables. Is it 100% lore-friendly? Not entirely - but if you're here to play a BR game with tight movement and gunplay, well-balanced classes and meaningful abilities then I think you'll have a lot of fun with this.Addressing hackers, I can only speak from personal experience but after 43 hours I've only had one or two encounters I'd even consider 'suspicious', not definitive. I can only assume either the hacker amount on EU servers is very low, or the reports are greatly exaggerated and people are too quick to call hacks. Make of that what you will.I think it's very admirable and frankly impressive to see a BR VtM game done to such a quality as this, and it's a huge shame that it was review-bombed early in its life. I'm very hopeful that when we see the return of this game in 2022, a majority of the minor outstanding issues will be ironed out

_childDocuments_.review: Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodhunt is a console ported third person Early Access multiplayer only PvP arena/Battle Royale.  The game is branded/licensed with White Wolf's successful Vampire: The Masquerade mythology, but has little to nothing in common with that universe apart from featuring three of the Camarilla clans (Brujah, Nosteratu and Toreador). There's a distinct, dramatic irony of a game about immortal undead being dead itself before it's even born.  The game probably won't make it far out of Early Access.  The developers have made a number of crucial design and strategic flaws that have pretty much killed the game.  The first is the most obvious.  The developers made the terrible mistake of launching a multiplayer only game in Early Access.  This is almost certain to kill the game.  Most gamers will evaluate a game only once.  If they do so when the game is incomplete, they will check it out, then abandon it (just like the developers will).  When (IF) the game eventually does get around to release, there will be no players, because the developers burned the first impressions through their faulty Early Access experience.  Players who saw the game and didn't like it because it was incomplete .  Multiplayer games must have a large population if they are to go "viral" and succeed, especially without single player content to fall back on.  Releasing a multiplayer only game into early access kills the game population, and thus the game, before the game even launches.We can see the player numbers dropping sharply, now commonly less than 10% of what they were on launch.  The developers doubled down on their apparently deliberate failure by not including servers in most regions, for a game they designed to be a low-latency twitch reflexes PvP Battle Royale.  That's a very quick and easy way to alienate gamers and drop your player counts by an order of magnitude.  The developers failure here shows... I waited around 10 minutes and I wasn't even able to get a match.  This is a dead game walking.  And it won't be walking for long. The second fault from the developers is a bit more serious.  To thine own self, be true... and this game is a sheer insult to Vampire: The Masquerade.  It has nothing to do with the cult classic tabletop RPG.  There's no appeal here to fans of Vampire.  The three Clans represented aren't reflective of how those Clans work in the game universe, and have abilities nothing like the RPG counterparts.  This is just a random BR game that they slapped a Vampire skin on.  Instead, you get "vampires" that have sonic boom attacks and they can all climb up walls looking like rabid, demented monkeys.  Nice work, slow claps for that. So this has no appeal to fans of Vampire: The Masquerade apart from giving them something to be insulted by.  Vampire is all about a strong, rich, deep storytelling RPG experience.  The game system isn't called "Storyteller" for nothing.  The yokel developers decided to take Vampire and rip out all the storytelling, leaving an empty, generic shell of yet-another content-free BR game that nobody asked for, in a saturated market full of far better competitors.The questionable and poor choice of branding will do nothing but discourage the actual target audience (Fortnite players) from even bothering to try this.  Sharkmob have done an incredible amount of work on making a not-bad console port with pretty decent graphics (for a console game), and then made sure it appeals to absolutely nobody!So, despite apparently setting out to fail deliberately, with a multiplayer game in Early Access with dwindling player numbers, horrible treatment of a once loved RPG franchise, on a game that won't appeal to fans of the franchise and won't appeal to fans of Battle Royale games, Sharkmob have succeeded in insulting all gamers everywhere with a full, ridiculously greedy, overpriced microtransaction shop.  It's like $30 to buy a cosmetic outfit, I'm not joking.  You can get a Vampire: The Masquerade rulebook for less and actually enjoy yourself with a bunch of friends, rolling dice and playing something with some meaning.  It's a very basic rule that you don't monetise Early Access games this badly, that's appalling and insulting to gamers and to the industry.  But as you can see from the litany of failure here, that's just what we should expect from this team.  This dead Early Access game isn't even worth the download.  And the biggest shame of it all is that the industry will point at this failure and say "Look, gamers don't like Vampire: The Masquerade, so let's not make any more Bloodlines games."All I can do is quote Vito Corleone: "Look how they massacred my boy."

_childDocuments_.review: * * EDIT AT THE END * *	Bloodhunt is an odd beast to be sure. With the recent inclusion of a team deathmatch mode the game finally begins to move toward something resembling enjoyable. As its systems stand, however, I still couldn’t recommend it to anyone. The battle royale mode that is the main focus is still an extremely unrewarding, messy and frustrating experience for a casual player. Matches for any mode, but especially the battle royale can take up to 5 minutes possibly longer to load into; couple that with the combat’s quick time-to-kill and you’ve got a huge problem. Waiting so long for matches that can be, and often are for me, over within a fraction of the time it took to enter is a horrible feeling to say the least. If load times and match start were quicker this would be less egregious, but with low player count and region based matches this issue will likely persist until one of the only two outcomes of a live-service game come to be.	Team deathmatch, while having similar, if a little shorter, queue times is ‘usually’ a more fun affair. The smaller zones players fight in make encounters more frequent and less stressful. It’s more freeing, you can take more risks, be more aggressive in TDM than in the other mode. Since players are given small xp bumps for kills, assists and damage done to enemies this feels, to me, like what the game was meant to be. Similar to Fortnite starting as a horde-shooter with a battle royale mode as a side thing that later takes off as it’s main selling point, Bloodhunt feels like this in reverse. Starting as a battle royale whose new game mode feels better by far. Now if only we could fix xp.	As of this writing the summer season’s battle-pass has a great hoard of vanity items that I just will not acquire. One level of the battle pass takes 28,000 xp to complete. Doing damage generates few points, but in TDM, if I’ve done a descent job, I’d generate roughly 1,000 I believe. Eliminations are a few hundred each and assists are somewhere south of 200. There’s also “placement” xp which I’ve only seen in the TDM, but may also be in the BR mode as well if you’re the last player standing, or top 5, though I wouldn’t know from playing. However, in TDM placement xp is usually pretty low. Getting mid placement on the winning team it’s only a few hundred. The boosts the paid battle pass gives strangely only effect placement xp which makes it nearly useless to a low-teir player.	While there are dailies and weeklies to complete for bigger xp gains, the long wait for matches paired with mode, weapon and character specific challenges can make the system feel like a wash. Simple ones certainly exist; play a certain archetype, kill a certain clan type, just get hits, run around the city, play matches for 15 minutes cumulatively. But then there are some weeklies that are too specific to do on accident, while others have high bars to clear that likely take longer than a weeks worth of casual play to complete. All that to say that for a garbage-baby tier player like me the xp rewards for just playing a match feel stunted while challenges don’t feel like they stack up much vs the requirements to clear just one point on a timed 100 tiered battle pass.	Admittedly, I’m bad at pvp games and that’s Bloodhunt’s entire bag. I want to play in the VtM universe, but if this is all there is, I’d rather fall into torpor.Edit:As of this edit, the game has entered a state of play I find much more agreeable! Wait times for the Battle Royale mode be you solo, duo and on seems largely addressed! Firefights feel much more fair, I don't know if that's due to the inclusion of bots or the improvement of gamepad support, but games last longer within the BR mode more often than not. And then, what's more, the required XP for battle pass progress has been more than halved. Now with any given match you stand to get at least one level on the pass, which is free at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshingly well made Battle Royale game!I will admit, as a World of Darkness/VtM:B fan I was put off by the idea of a VtM br but... it is what it is. This game gets so many things right and it seems like so many other reviews are just completely ignoring. All I see is outrage over the anti-cheat and conspiracies about how its Chinese spyware. My guy, every app on your phone is either Russian or Chinese spyware, sorry to disappoint you. The last thing you need to be worrying about is anti-cheat in your vidya, I don't care that it's running in your precious kernel.PRESENTATION: The animations, gunplay and graphics are all phenomenal and have no business being as good as they are. After playing countless indie/cash grab Battle Royale games, I am pleasantly surprised by the level of detail in a game developed by this studio I had never even heard of. Character movement isn't stiff or clunky, gunplay is fantastic, animations are smooth and aesthetically pleasing. Environments are absolutely STUNNING and puts even Warzone to shame. Gothic architecture with noire aesthetics lit by neon signs a la cyberpunk. Rain, puddles and reflections are almost indistinguishable from raytraced assets despite presumably utilizing SS. I have no idea how they pulled it off. Oh, and did I mention EVERY ROOM in EVERY BUILDING has a room inside it, making the map feel alive. This is a welcome feature that I wish more games implemented. It's always an amazing change of pace from your average opaque windows where you can just so easily tell every building is but a facade.PERFORMANCE: There are some reviews reporting poor optimization but I have yet to run into any issues, personally. I do have a rather powerful rig but even for a 3070 FE, 120+ FPS on max (ultra) settings at 1440p is pretty insane considering how absolutely stunning this game is. I am happy to report I have yet to suffer a single crash, however I did have to force quit the game on two occasions after getting stuck in a loading screen with the spinny wheel going on forever. This seems more like a network issue than something with the actual client though.LORE: This was always my primary concern. How are they going to implement tenets of the Masquerade into a battle royale game? Do the Camarilla abide these giant battles in the streets between immortals? How much suspension of disbelief am I going to have to engage in to enjoy this? Is this just PUBG with a Vampire skin? Well, I'm happy to report that I had no reason to worry. I'm actually shocked at the level of detail the developers went into building this game from the ground up with the Vampire the Masquerade/World of Darkness universe in mind. This is not just a reskin -- sure, it has all the standard BR elements. An ever closing ring, a single victor, varying tiers of loot, a battle pass, etc... but it truly stands on its own. Using your supernatural abilities, feeding/killing or diablerizing in view of humans reveals you to the map, essentially putting a bounty on your head (aka a "Bloodhunt"), which is a really cool way of implementing a punishment for Masquerade violations.

_childDocuments_.review: Hyperscape, but spooky, and also fun!Good, modern, class-based BR for those that want a little more forgiving gameplay while still playing around with powers. Has some fresh ideas like picking up quests in the lobby which encourage you to explore the over world and occasional modifiers that will pop up during some matches. Chasing targets while running up walls and bounding buildings is a lot of fun, and there are some tense moments trying to feed for powerups without getting spotted. In a way the navigation, powers, and gunplay remind me of the *good* parts of Saints Row IV -- take that how you will.I can tell the player count is a little low because I see familiar faces in the lobby, but I never had trouble getting into a match. The queues show fairly accurate estimates, and you have a bit of time to run around and turn in quests between matches. I don't know if they're going to break through the BR market before it's too late, but it's not too late to play it and have a bit of fun right this moment.For WhiteWolf fans, they do a good enough job of keeping the lore: The Masquerade is to be maintained ruing the hunt, and killing civilians or being spotted feeding puts a bounty on your head for a time. The loose idea is that the other players are anarchs, and you are attempting to hunt them down to service the hierarchy. There are some loose threads of questing and exploration that will probably be fleshed out over time, which give a purpose to exploring both the lobby and battle map. The classes are the clans which offer fairly unique gameplay opportunities. There is a reasonable (for a BR) character customization system (limited variety as the game is still in the first season), and good emotes and a lair which functions as a lobby that should offer some RP opportunities for those seeking it (though that's not for me).

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start? There's two game modes: Solo Battle Royale and 3 man squad Battle Royale. In solo you'll load in and then in under 30 seconds someone will have gotten a machine gun and you're dead unless you found the machine gun, in which case everyone else is dead. There's no real balance to mention. In three person squads you'll frequently get people that will just run off in whichever direction and die instantly against a full team of three and then they'll quit out entirely, leaving you down a man, because they still get full rewards upon quitting the match. Every weapon in the game deals way too much damage and you'll die almost instantly from anything, so basically it's a game of "Be the first one to shoot". The "masquerade" portion is pointless because the "reveal" is muddy and hard to see amongst all of the dozen random things all over your screen at any given moment. It's somehow both too bright and too dark at the same time. It's impossible to see anything, and entering the "Enhanced Senses" mode actually makes it even HARDER to see. There's no color and no clarity. It's near impossible to tell apart civilians from other players, and shooting a civilian "reveals" you, which would be a problem if being revealed even meant anything. There's also an over-long list of weapons for no reason with several of them doubling up on each other's functionality. There's no less than six different automatic rifles for example. The class and clan abilities feel weak and pointless. The Brujah leap doesn't offer any more maneuverability than simply slide jumping, the Nosferatu stealth run lasts less than 2 seconds (and leaves a smoke trail), and the Toreador teleport is both slow to execute and only moves about as far as... a slide jump, again. Class specific skills are even worse, including a gas trap that deals the same amount of damage as a crossbow gas cloud, but minus the damage of shooting someone with a crossbow, the Brute "punch" has limited range and is less effective than just using a melee weapon or shotgun, and the "blind" ability takes as long to activate as it blinds the enemy with the bonus downside that you can't shoot while activating it but the enemy can still shoot while blinded, actually leaving you at a DISADVANTAGE if you use it in combat.Seriously, the tl;dr version is that this game has ZERO playability. Which is a shame, because it has a nice aesthetic. Shame the developers forgot to make a good game to go with the style.
