_childDocuments_.review: I have more cons then pros about this...Pros: Beautiful art design, awesome game concept, decent size map (could be made slightly bigger), character design isn't too bad, lovely video quality (if you have a high end PC).Cons: Hit boxes are ungodly small, doesn't make much sense that pistols are stronger then most guns (i got downed in 2 shots), i noticed some people got headshots almost every single match so i'm assuming auto aim, reaaaaally laggy even on low end settings in game from all the rain, map definitely could be a bit bigger so everyone isn't spawning on each other, not huge on how you can see everyone on the map just before loading in, few npc's to suck blood from, and the list goes on. I do like the idea and concept the game has, the only problem is that this game is going to be made strictly for high end pc's that costs thousands upon thousands of dollars which makes it a bit unfair for medium or low end pc users. Most players I saw on there are CoD/Fortnite sweats which make it not really fun to go against. It feels like when you're running around and looting you're playing fortnite. I'd rather have the first person point of view when you're in combat. Running around in 3rd person does make it easier, but in terms of combat stuff it's hard to actually get a good shot on people since half the time you can barely see them even with brightness up. Granted I didn't play for a super long period of time, but it was enough to gain a small amount of idea about the game before it's full release. Honestly I feel like the rain in it is making the game more heavy on frames which will make PC's run harder then they need to. I honestly wouldn't complain if it had less rain in it. Even if it was a small shimmer of rain it wouldn't be as hard on PC's and the frames wouldn't struggle as much. In the current state I wouldn't suggest it to certain people, but I mean if you're a tryhard gamer then go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love the World of Darkness franchise, and this game has a TON of potential in it.As of now there are only 3 clans, and 2 archetypes in each one, for a total of 6 variations. The customization options are limited, but the AMAZING part is that you can alter your appearance and style and even your gender as you see fit. So you are never stuck with just one main, and can express yourself whenever you like.The game is loads of fun, fast paced, and full bodied... but the learning curve is extremely steep, and those who don't have a lot of experience with Battle Royale games are gonna feel the pinch the hardest. After 15 hours of playing, I finally won my first match, and it felt amazing and it was incredibly satisfying which will keep me coming back for more.Some basic pros:Free customization whenever you likeMovement is fluid and fun... I rather enjoy sliding and brujah lunge jumping everywhere.Combat is logical... headshots are key, armor is important, good strategy and movement make a difference.The worldspace is gorgeous and you want to see and explore everything.The lore is detailed and you can get lost for hours just reading through everything.Secrets are hidden throughout the city, which can win you hidden free customization rewards.The meta play is fun and engaging, stacking the right blood resonance for your build/playstyle can mean the difference between winning and losing a fight.Weapons are somewhat varied in functionality which can be fun to experiment and toy with.Cons:The character models are... clunky, especially the fashions. Sorta bland and not terribly detailed or interesting. Most of the battle pass has t-shirts with jeans combo... very meh.Steep learning curve, particularly if your not a seasoned veteran of BR games.Servers can be HORRIFYINGLY laggy, and can cost you a pivotal battle with a badly timed lag spike.Skill based matchmaking is nonexistent. Expect to get absolutely ganked from all sides immediately. Until you learn the mechanics, and the layout of the map... expect to get poo'ed on.Battle pass progress is painfully sluggish. After 15 hours of playing, I am at rank 8 out of 100, and that's with BOOSTED exp they patched in recently. Unless you get 1st place, or grind out daily/weekly challenges, or kill half the server... don't expect to gain more than a 1/10th of a level per match.Extremely low variety in customization options, store options, only one medium sized map, clans, game modes... to be fair tho, it's still in early access so you can't expect them to have it all right out of the gate.All in all, for a free battle royale game, I highly recommend it, particularly if your are a fan of Vampire the Masquerade. Also, the sheer volume of potential once this game reels in some more content, is staggering. It's a 6.5 out of 10 for me in it's current state, but has nowhere to go but up once they start fleshing it out. I will stick around for awhile and see where it goes from here.-Luna :D

_childDocuments_.review: Vampire: The Masquerade - Battle RoyaleBloodhunt is a TPP action game belonging to the battle royale subspecies. Players take on the role of vampires fighting with traditional weapons and numerous powerful supernaturals. The production is based on the free-to-play model.Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodhunt (initially known under the working title Vampire: The Masquerade - Battle Royale) is a third-person online shooter belonging to the battle royale sub-genre. The project uses a free model with micropayments. The title was developed by Sharkmob studio, founded by former Massive Entertainment employees who previously worked, among others, over Tom Clancy's The DivisionPlotThe action of the game is set in the World of Darkness universe, created for the needs of "paper" RPG systems such as Vampire: The Masquerade.In Bloodhunt, treason leads to a war between vampires. Worse, the bloodsuckers are targeted by a mysterious organization known as the Department. Players take part in the conflict to win their side and restore the Masquerade, a pact designed to protect the creatures of the night from being discovered by mortalsMechanicsBloodhunt is an online action game. We observe the events from the camera placed behind our character's back, and the fun comes down to skirmishes with other players. We all control vampires whose physical abilities go far beyond human abilities. Warriors can, for example, jump long distances or climb walls. There are team variants and all against all. The game continues until only one person or group is left on the map.We can play the role of a vampire from many different clans, offering unique special abilities. Each clan has two separate archetypes to choose from, also with their own abilities, which further increases the variety of characters in the game. During the skirmishes, we use both traditional firearms and melee weapons, as well as numerous supernatural powers, allowing, for example, to teleport short distances or create blinding walls of light.In addition to player-controlled vampires, there are AI-controlled civilians on the maps. We can attack them and suck their blood from them, which allows us to regenerate our character's strength and health, as well as develop abilities.The masquerade is not just part of the storyline here. If another AI character sees us drinking mortal blood, then for a short time all other players will see our location on the map. In addition, units of hunters controlled by artificial intelligence will start hunting us.Game modesVampire: The Masquerade - Bloodhunt allows only multiplayer games.Technical issuesThe game offers eye-catching 3D graphics. The maps have a lot of detail and are vertically expanded, and the characters of vampires are characterized by a lot of variety.Game mode: multiplayer Multiplayer mode: InternetAge requirements Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodhunt: 18+my opinion is 6.2

name: Hammerting
detailed_description: Hammerting is a vertical dwarven mining colony sim with RPG elements. Manage a clan of colourful Dwarves, establish an epic mining operation, craft legendary swords and delve deep for greater glory, riches... and danger. With conflict raging on the surface, the Dwarves pledge to delve deep and as master craftspeople, will produce and supply what is needed to support their allies. From humble beginnings, you start with a handful of Dwarves who need to set up their operations quickly. However, as you progress, your small clan will expand and become known throughout the Overworld for their skill and premium craftsmanship. Crafting for Victory Allies on the surface will have all manner of requests. Dwarves may find themselves asked to craft a plethora of silver swords against an oncoming army. With the Overworld in need, every successful delivery takes you one step closer to triumph. As your Dwarves grow in skill and your base expands, build conveyor belts and elevators to free them of manual labour. Colorful Personalities Does Åglöf’s fancy ancestry clash with Vargskreva’s humble upbringing? Is your explorer afraid of the dark? Has your master crafter reached their Ballmer Peak? Aim for success and exploit the strengths of your Dwarves, as well as their weaknesses. Each Dwarf is richly and uniquely defined through its stats, Dwarven ancestry, traits, abilities, equipment, move-set and much more, as they are shaped by events occurring in their lives. Skilled Craftspeople Anyone can craft an Iron Sword, but only Dwarves can dig down into the depths and cart up boatloads of diamonds and bones and use it to craft the... Iron Sword +2. With every strike of the hammer on an anvil, a skilled Dwarf has a better chance of achieving a critical result, giving you better and improved gear. Living Cave It is as they say – “Fortune favours the bold”, and only in the deepest depths will you find the most powerful materials, the warmest magma, the rarest treasures, but also the most dangerous conditions. Figuring out the fastest and safest route down - and up again - is a chief concern, but you’ll have plenty of unique Dwarven mechanisms to help you to do so. Hammerting features liquid and physics mechanics for pumping sizzling lava to your hearths, brewing hoppy beer, tossing burning torches down shafts to light up the unknown and more! Online Co-op Mode A Dwarven king once said: “A single axe is easily blunt, but an army of axes is unbreakable!”. You might want to explore and populate the depths of Mara on your own, but you can also partner up with jolly comrades and run a dwarven colony together. It’s all about synchronization, companionship and common goals!

_childDocuments_.review: November 19th 2021, V1.0 release review: Sadly this just didnt live up to my expectations. There are certain areas of the game such as the overworld that have seen a huge upgrade which is fantastic but it seems as though this has left gaping holes in the core gameplay in the cave.THERE IS SO MUCH MICRO IT IS NOT FUNNY. Trying to re-equip your units with better tools is just a nightmare. Here is a quick breakdown: You select the type of handle, then you need to make sure you pick the kind of metal you want or else it will pick whatever it feels like, then you need to select the type of "head" you want on it (for example a pick) and select the metal and then you need to select the BLUEPRINT and build that whilst also selecting the parts you just made... like what in the actual hell... this does NOT need to be this convoluted.There are so many aspects of the flow of the game that are just missing for new players to understand and it just feels as though the vast majority of improvements were not actually in the mountainhome.That isnt to say there arent good things that have been done since its time in alpha but simply put, it does not justify the pricetagFebruary 8th 2021 Early access release review:A few simple things about the game both good and bad:1. The game has unique mechanics that separate it enough from games of the same style/genre to make it interesting2. There are quite a few bugs but nothing "rage quit" worthy from what ive seen3. The progression of item building is quite convoluted and the UI doesn't do an overly great job of making this process as simple as it could be (feels like its made more complicated for the sake of being more complicated).4. The work order queue is pretty darn solid and I havent had any issues with dwarves not doing their jobs which is fantastic for a game like thisPoint 3 is probably the thing I have the biggest problem with in terms of the game at this point. building tools etc is really cool because there are a lot of options... but at the same time its quite complicated to keep track of with different materials, types of pieces etc etc and eventually it just gets annoying.I will still recommend this game because I think its quite unique and offers players a different experience to similar style games.

_childDocuments_.review: PROSBest Dwarven hold or mining simulator currently available. Nice and atmospheric. Lots of Mist under the Mountain.Reclaim ancient sites and knowledge from a Fallen Realm. (Edited - Inclined rails are here!)Dwarves go off exploring on their own, watching them leap chasms and struggle up cliffs is endearing, and they don't get killed (too) often.CONSThe pesky Surface-dwellers keep pestering me about some war or something up above. It doesn't take long to address their needs once the hold is up and running, but takes precious seconds away from planning my next mine shaft. Carts and Elevators can be a bit fiddly, making proper Dwarven logistics a challenge, but this is Right and Proper. (Edit - this is possibly fixed post Update 8. I will update review after playing around with it - Huzzah!)Learning to equip Cooks with a ladle so Proper brewing can commence wasn't obvious, and took some trial and error.Not nearly enough Ancient and Terrible Foe in the deep (at present). Obviously we aren't digging too Deep or too Greedily (yet).Swords seem to be better than Axes in combat in the early game. This is a Travesty. This cannot be!(Edit: Minecarts go up and down inclines, and many other things have been changed. This review is from during development in Early Access. But I shall let it stand from now as a record of a dark and grim early Age!)

_childDocuments_.review: Elevators and storage rooms are the key to all your problems.This game is still in early access, and while that shows -it's already improved a lot since the demo, with the devs teasing juicy updates and improvements on the discord. Despite some frustrations with a steep learning curve due to a lack of tutorials, and a lacking system for controlling your dwarves -the game is already a massive time-vampire. Looking at the roadmap for the game it's only going to get a lot better when you consider what extra polish and features like automation will add to the experience.The basic premise is that you control a small band of dwarves that have set out to colonize a long abandoned mountain, whilst being a part of an alliance currently at war in the overworld. Exploring the mountain gives you "mountain lore" which allows you to advance your technology and start to put the mountains resources to work. However to fuel your operation you will also need resources that are scarce to come by underground -like leather and lumber, and this means you'll need to accept trade missions with the overworld. Overworld trade nets you "trade lore" that also unlocks more technologies. In addition you'll also encounter "war omen" missions where you need to support a battle-site in the overworld with trade missions, lest the alliance will lose a strategic location to the horde -in turn losing you the resources they provide.As you delve ever deeper into the mountain you'll find better resources and harder enemies, each rewarding you with materials that'll boost your operation's efficiency. It might be worth waiting a while longer before you purchase this game as I'm sure it'll be MUCH better down the line, but I'm already having a blast playing it.A pro tip for beginners is to leave a six blocks wide gap vertically for where you want an elevator shaft later. That equals the same space as a scaffolding block with one free block either side.I recommend exploring horizontally before you start delving vertically just because replacing scaffolding blocks with elevators are a pain in the ass, while building elevators is super easy. Also: BUILD STORAGES EVERYWHERE and sort what you want to store in them. It will make your dwarves more efficient as they will spend less time hauling stuff in total.

_childDocuments_.review: A little difficult to learn and perhaps easy to master but the journey was interesting!  This game is a little bit of a puzzle in that you have to learn how the logistics system and crafting system works - the tutorial (Such as it is) is very light on but all the details are available, just not easy to identify. E.g. Dont forget the control key to open tooltips when you look at items! Trial and error will definitely be part of your first game!It took me 72 hours to complete, albeit I knew I'd win after about 30-40 hours sin o the rest was a bit of slog. While there is conceivably alternative ways to play, the tactics aren't deep enough that I'd try this game again, maybe a speed run but for that sort of time investment, I doubt it!I'd say its worth a buy given the amount of enjoyable time you'll get out of it and it shouldnt leave you feeling like you've been robbed. It was a memorable experience. It wont be one of those games you clock up hundreds of hours on though.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this in the Humble Bundle. I used to want this game... but it's a total mess. Everything below was apparent within less than half an hour of starting the first game.The tutorial is the first problem. It's not interactive... it just talks *at* you and shows you things, without actually giving you guidance. It's like having a cram session before a test. I don't need the tutorial to show every tool tip one at a time... I need a tutorial to guide me through the basics of the game loop.Then there's the UI. It's a lot, and it's not common stuff. It doesn't follow many conventions, and while that could be interesting if the "tutorial" was in better shape, it makes understanding everything more arduous. Some of the odd choices include requiring a character's stats to be visible when you want to control them directly -- and that information takes up an entire section on the side of the screen. It also has pop ups everywhere... on both sides, in the middle of the top, two bars overhead, another in the middle of the bottom, plus whatever you click on. It's a lot to take in, and it gets difficult knowing where to look.Then the actual gameplay, is also a mess. One of the many overlays on the screen is a list of seemingly random objectives. More appear as you complete previous ones. You are not at any point told how to complete these objectives; you have to hunt through the horde of windows to figure out where something might be. Sometimes, it isn't related to a window, and it seems to imply you're meant to explore randomly... except, you can't explore anywhere without having a character selected, and they can only go as far as your current "vision" scope (you can't access everything you've explored; it's grayed-out). In other words, you have to baby-sit a character, forgoing all building and production, to go searching for... whatever it might be. Another oddity I encountered was the ability to COMPLETE a mission without ACCEPTING one... and there was no indication as to how I was supposed to accept it. It seems like it should be straightforward, but nope: there was no button to accept, just a list of things to do and I was able to complete them and get credit for it, but could not actually get the mission to consider itself "accepted" in any way.All in all, the game is quite messy and lacks intuition. I generally enjoy Team17, but I've been quite disappointed in the last couple of games I picked up from them. Hopefully the final release is far more polished than it is currently.

_childDocuments_.review: Mildly recommended, but late game left a bad taste.This is a good colony sim with lots of exploration, base building, crafting and combat. Most of it works well, with nice graphics and animations, variety in the biomes, tons of items and an interesting trade system. The end game is a major grind, AI can sometimes get wonky and the enemy waves have insanely high difficulty spikes that will crush you. In the end, I definitely enjoyed my time with this game, but the end game needs work.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Buy it if you like Dwarf Sims and can enjoy an unfinished early access game with some flaws. Updates are steadily coming.Hammerting has a huge amount of potential. I love what this game could be. It has what I want from a dwarf colony manager: mining, smithing, and delving deep into a hostile mountain. There's even some automation with drills you stick to a wall, and with more support for automation to come. But there are flaws. Dwarf job management is bad, to be frank. Something similar to job priories like Rimworld has are sorely needed. It can be a struggle to get your dwarves to do what you want. Additionally, your dwarves will get stuck.  The main way to explore deeper is to build stairs/scaffolding down. Your dwarves will often stop building and instead jump off the scaffolding, leaving themselves stranded until another dwarf comes to finish the job. I enjoyed my time with it, but I'll wait for some patches before picking it up again.

_childDocuments_.review: After spending some time with it, I've deemed it not worth purchasing at this point. Received as part of the Humble Choice program. The most glaring issues have to do with the Dwarf AI. They don't eat, they don't take trips to buy things (unless you're also selling something), and worst of all, they don't heal themselves. As far as I could tell the only way to get a dwarf to heal was to specifically have that dwarf craft the healing item they were to use. Otherwise, you can craft as many as you want, but the dwarves won't use them. Instead they'll just let themselves die. Dwarves seem to ignore equal-priority tasks depending on proximity. If you've got some stuff to do near them, none of them will bother to run out to the thing you want them to do far away. Combat is also "janky", with Dwarves sometimes running right into enemies despite their lack of health, but also sometimes refusing to fight at all, instead just running back and forth in a circle a few feet away from the enemy as they destroy your buildings.The game has promise, and at the end of the dev cycle it may very well be worth playing, but I've put enough time into it to know that any MORE time would be a waste OF time. It's just not in a truly fun state, and I don't have an ocean's worth of patience to wait for the devs to gradually fix all the current issues. I'll come back to it once it's launched and replay and review. For now, though, it's very much in a beta state and not worth the $25 price.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was inspired by another really old and fun game, similar to this one really... called Wiggles at first, and then changed the title to Diggles. Wiggles/Diggles was unsucessfull because the developers did something huge mistake and ruined the optimization of the game horribly at the end. They couldn't fix it unfortunetly so the game became a big failure. This game is MAYBE trying to copy exactly the Diggles but doing it wrong at the moment..Diggles could be a real gem with it's unique room bulidings under the ground, etc.. the dwarves even had hamster power generators etc.. it was a real fun and joy to see your little dwarves doing their job. Changing of day and night time was also interesting method because you had to set the rest and working hours for them so they had enough time for each other as well, because they were in couples, marriage, children etc. The cute character design was one fo the best thing in it and this game does not have that. However, maybe they don't want to have that of course.. just saying because the outlook of the characters gave a lot to the atmosphere of the game.I think, Hammerting is trying to provide everything Diggles game had.. building rooms for various porpuse under the ground, farms for food, mining minerals, exploring for exciting things.. but the characters are literally "hammering" everything.. even the water. :D That was a little bit too much for me. Don't have day, night time changing either and the characters are not so cute but they are OK for one..In my opinion, you should create remastered, and properly optimized version of Diggles for a deserved huge success! ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from someone who enjoys his colony sim games, take this review with a grain of salt.Hammerting does many things right, but there's so much more I'd wish the Dev's did better. With a stylised yet functional art style, limited animations, and a disjoint between your dwarves drawn portraits and their 3D model, this game didn't do much to initially endear me. As I progressed I found the usual gameplay loop of specializing your colonists, setting build orders, and organising my base fairly satisfying, albeit again limited. Still, for every system Hammerting introduces, it doesn't go as far as other games in the genre, ala Rimworld, Banished, ect.So why am I giving this a thumbs up? Despite not giving the player fine detail control over their colony's functions, it does just enough to be a satisfying gameplay loop. If you do want the fine-grit controls, you'll be quickly frustrated by the lack of detailed colonist systems; but if you can put up with the limitations, you'll find a game that lets you be a Dorf exploring your mountainhome, pickaxe in one hand, mug of ale in the other.

_childDocuments_.review: Regretfully switching once again to not recommended. The changes they tried to make were only half-formed. I somewhat enjoyed another few hours of play because I am a nut for cave-delving, but everything else about the game is poorly executed in their "final" product. If discovering new caves a la Terraria fills you with unimaginable glee (like it does for me) than maybe this game is worth it on deep discount. For the rest, probably not.Update as of the November 27, 2020 patch:Switched rec to yes. They've smoothed out the really annoying launch blips, and while I hope to see them add more to the game (they've mentioned an expanded and deepened overworld experience which is a great idea) and maybe remove/simplify some other things (individually leveling your dwarves is tedious and for now kind of pointless) the experience is now well on its way to a great game, and fun enough for quite awhile in its current state.Original review:Can't recommend just yet. I'm a sucker both for the game type and the theming and I don't regret buying the game at all. There's a lot of good stuff here and I hope that with a couple patches I'll switch my recommendation to yes, but there are a number of bugs, erroneous values (keeps tools from working as intended) and missing - fairly basic - content (jewelry recipes, some key resources nearly impossible to find, etc) that need to be smoothed out before this has appeal beyond people like me.

_childDocuments_.review: Build an underground kingdom for your dwarves and mine the depths for more treasure. You get plan out your buildings and choose what to mine, but otherwise your dwarves do all the actual work. You can assign them preferred jobs so they'll focus their skill in one area. Most of the game is spent exploring the mountain to find new ores and get points to research new technology. As you progress you can craft better tools and equipment to make your dwarves more efficient. There's an overworld map where you can send you dwarves out to do some trading with the humans. The overworld is pretty boring though, you'll only need to use it to make money or buy resources that are hard to find underground. Most of the time you spend underground managing the expansion of your kingdom.The base gameplay is really quite fun, but there are some annoying bits that could be improved. Sometimes your dwarves get stuck and its not entirely clear why they can't move past something. It's really easy to miss a tiny connection in your rail line and no way to tell where it's disconnected. Laying out track can be really fiddly and the overlay is not great at showing you what is happening. You can't directly control movement of goods and the dwarves don't always make good decisions. It would be great if all the emerald could be transported directly to my whitesmith in a big batch. Buying stuff from the overworld is really tedious, why can't I just always buy all the hides they have every month? Even with all the little annoyances, the game is really fun and I thoroughly enjoyed it.A few tips that might help you starting out:- Rail is the fastest way to travel, make rail lines everywhere- You can put rail over your buildings, your dwarves can quickly move around your home base with it- Dwarves can only get off the rail line at stations, then they can walk around- Build elevators with scaffolding on the side to prevent dwarves from getting stuck- The mine cart (not the hand cart) is automated and can pickup or deliver goods anywhere on the rail line- Build a drill when you find a rare resource, this will get you much more ore/gems out of it- Check out the guides (AKA spreadsheets) for optimal crafting

_childDocuments_.review: This is a reskin of Oxygen Not Included where you have to research how to eat food. At first I thought this was a remake of Diggles: Myth of Fenris but this game is far worse than that game. For some reason, dwarves cannot climb like they could in Diggles, and the trading system is utterly broken. There are also these big grinders you can build to mine from the map, but they often just sit idle for no reason. Every dwarf has to be individually upgraded and equipped; they won't automatically pick up tools or level up. This adds a lot of needless busywork to the games already rife busywork. There is this really linear tech tree that requires you to reveal more land, so the game wants you to rapidly explore instead of citybuilding. A lot of time will be spent trying to figure out the strange/obscure rules the dwarves use to pathfind. I want to remind you a 20 year old game handles this better by allowing the dwarves to climb on the background. In order to recruit new dwarves, you need money that you get from the overworld (instead of minting them out of the copper/gold/silver you mine for some reason); Granite is woth a lot, rare metals are worth a few pitiful coppers, and items made out of those materials are exactly the same cost as buying a singular ingot of metal. So you're going to be starved for money because you're getting ripped off by the humans above; because your characters are too stupid to forge coins.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game at its core. They've done away with a ton of the annoying micro-managing games like Oxygen Not Included have (as much as they're great games), and have a set up an interesting and rewarding progression system. I've really enjoyed it. My following critiques are mainly on areas it can improve.There's still a lot that can be developed, and improved upon. The talent tree is really bad for example. It's set up in a way that every dwarf is essentially running the same talent path with very minimal diversity. The talents themselves aren't conducive to develop a particular talent and force you into a sort of jack-of-all-trades result.Equipment/tools is half-way there in terms of its use and ease. For example the auto-equip rules I discovered rather late and it's just not quite obvious in its design. Some of the UI and GUI can be a bit clunky. I had no idea how storage worked for the first 4 hours because never, in any game, have I see a storage that automatically turns itself off when built. That's a weird design choice. Also the combat mark makes everyone attack the enemy, including those you turned combat off for. I only want my proper militia to attack so that's a pain.It's way too easy to get more dwarves. I have 14 now and can have up to 23, but I don't want more. It's a pain in the ass to equip and manage a new dwarf and they don't offer that much value to make it worth it. A couple of suggestions: make individual dwarves more meaningful (example; improve and expand the talent tree; make crafting levels harder to gain and more rewarding) and remove sovereignty from the knowledge tree. Make it only found through exploration, as that's what you want the player to do, because finding the statues and gaining sovereignty is great and really fun to do. Getting a huge amount randomly in the knowledge tree makes it too easy to get dwarves.The overworld is problematic in its current state. My initial impression was that you, as dwarves, were going to supply one kingdom/alliance with your gear to support them and in turn they'd help defend your mountain. I thought it would be some type of world war/battles where you would help support a side to gain victory or dominate. That is pretty interesting to be honest. It gives the player a lot of agency in their impact on the overworld, without requiring them to participate directly in it. It also makes the crafting and the developing you do worth it as making really good equipment could potentially have an impact on the strength of your supported kingdom/s. However right now the overworld is purely an area for resource exchange. Which is super boring.Exploration feels fantastic. I love finding stuff like the sacred well, those big statues, and the mineral motherlodes. It's a ton of fun. Discovering new locations are super cool too. Monster spawning areas are well designed. Exploration is by far the best part of this game and kudos to you guys for making it so fun to mine around. I'd love to see more diversity in what you encounter as you progress (basically more content).Enemy waves and base defense are really bad at the moment. To begin with enemy waves are pointless. They're tiny amounts of easy to defeat enemies that act as nuisances rather than any sort of challenge. I'd love to see this changed and made to be a legitimate problem that impacts your base expansion. This would include base defense as currently that too hardly exists. Doors are optional and actually impede your pathways and there's no real defense besides the dwarves themselves.Which sucks. Dwarves are builders, creators. We should see things like turrets and strong doors and traps and other things. I would love to see enemy waves be something you face periodically as a significant challenge, with their strength increasing by exploration percentage / base expansion. You'd then have to consider your defenses when you expand and build in all sorts of ways to defend against the waves. This is a way to give player challenges in their exploration and advancement and reward them for making quality bases. Right now I just throw ♥♥♥♥ everywhere with my base because there are no consequences.So that's my thoughts. I've really enjoyed the game. It has a lot that it can develop and improve on, and could become a really fantastic game. I hope it does.

_childDocuments_.review: I finally played through a game to the end without encountering a game stopping bug, but at this stage it's a no from me.  My main concerns are pacing problems and very low replayability.  Both issues don't appear to be being addressed as early access progresses.Following the tasks list, you quickly build a quarry, smelter and forge.  Lots of interesting things going on as you unlock new techs, discover what each buliding does and your dwarves are exploring the immediate surroundings and ferrying resources around.  This initial game experience fades very quickly with subsequent playthroughs.I usually recruit up to 8 dwarves fairly quickly and top out at 12, but each dwarf wants its own dwelling and the dwellings are as large as the forge and quarry, so you end up digging a massive area with lots of poorly trained and poorly equipped dwarves for the rest of the early game.  The purpose of a dwelling is so that the dwarves can pilfer your gold and move it to their home, thus satisfying their greed meter.  It's a cool idea, but it's not clear why you care about the greed meter and for that matter building houses for them only serves to make an alert go away.  You only use gold to recruit new dwarves and making gold is easy as you get plenty through trade and you can sell anything you make.Next you build farm, cookhouse, infirmary; all of which serve to replenish your dwarves energy and health bars.  At the moment, dwarves aren't sensible in which items they consume.  So they will for example drink water instead of beer to replenish morale, even though water is an ingredient in beer and beer is notionally the thing they say they want to fix morale problems.  They will run all over the map to eat raw mushrooms, instead of using a bandage or eating something you've cooked.  Either way, these buildings allow you to survive exploring the map, where you run in to various monster lairs.More pacing problems emerge in the mid game with the main problem being that the map is far bigger than the current content warrents.  Dwarves take a long time to traverse the map.  You can speed that up by building rail (horizontal) and elevators (vertical), but that tech comes a bit too late.  The mid game goal is to find certain biomes and lairs.  In theory this would provide you with new resources to do new things.  In practice, you make tools and weapons out of copper, then iron and then there is a huge delay until you find something better.  Even if you find better ores, you can't use them until the very end of the tech tree.  For all the variety available with (after iron) orichalcum, adamantine, hard metal, platinum and mithrill, most of those late game metals have the same properties, so it feels like there are really only 3 teirs.  After making some hard metal picks and then oricalcum weapons, I found there was no compelling upgrade for the last half of the game.The last half of the game was spend just digging downward to find the bottom of the map.  At the beginning of the game you are told to find the God of the Forge.  When you do, it's just a passive monument and that objective is ticked off.  No bonus, nothing else to do.  Hopefully this is an EA limitation with the content being witheld.  The final objective was to wait for enough overworld battles to occur before the good guys won.  Honestly, the overworld feels so disconnected it could be replaced with a trade screen where you can set recurring trades and get access to new trades as your fame increases or something.I have played the early/mid game a handful, but there hasn't been a lot of variety in how I've done that.  The map being random is of no significant conseqence to the way I would approach either building the main part of the base, or exploring the map or building transportation routes.  Speed: fastest; shift-queue long elevator segments, wait for dwarves to gain visibility on the next few tiles down and place the next evelvator segment.Other issuesAt the moment there are just 16 buildings in total.- The Tavern and the Great Hall are completely passive.  You get nothing from building them, they can't do anything and your dwarves won't interact with them in any way.- The Foundry and Smithy are functionally identical to their small versions, with one exception.  The small quarry can't build one item that is needed for the largest buildlings.  Really pointless teiring at the moment, and those buildings are obnoxiously large.Jobs/tasksYou can specialise your dwarves through a typically clunky tick-box grid of all dwarves and all possible jobs.  The more you specalise, the more dwarves will invariably be doing nothing at certain points in the game.  If you allow a stonemason to haul, he will make one brick and then haul it to a trade deal, while other haulers stand idle.ZoningYou can't control where dwarves go.  The only way to keep your stonemason and blacksmiths near their respective workshops is to forbid them from having mining and hauling jobs.  Worse, when it comes to combat and lairs, it's very difficult to prevent your dwarves from attacking once they can path to a given lair.  Often, one lone explorer goes in and dies.ScarcityYou either have a resource in total abundance or you have none.  It felt like I smelted a million copper but there was still plenty around.  Conversely, to equip all of my dwarves with good equipment, I needed less than 50 oricalcum.  When you finally find saphire/diamonds, the are in absolute abundance.  Unfortunately there is really no significant use for them apart from making a dwarf spend ages cutting and polishing them in to ever more valuable versions before selling them.ChallengeChallenge really only comes from combat and unfortunately you have very poor ability to control how combat plays out.  You hope you've equipped and leveled your dwarves well enough.  You could micromanage a dwarf on low health to try and run away.  The overworld is no challenge at all.  You might fail to meet their demands once by accident but there's plenty of slack there.TLDRThis game is much closer to Craft The World than Oxygen Not Included, but where Craft The World knows it could be a flash game and keeps things nice and cartoony-simple, Hammerting has a lot of unnecessary complexity for what it's trying to do.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a shame this game has been review bombed. I actually got more hours out of this than ONI and arguably more enjoyment. It doesn't have the depth nor does it have the complexity of that title, but in my experience that was actually a positive. It is more of a relaxed gameplay loop.The graphics are great and they have nailed the environment and the atmosphere. I love the different biomes and the satisfaction you get from exploring new tunnels and new depths. As others have stated, the overworld system is lacking and was never fleshed out with any depth, but it didn't really detract from my experience. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed my 40+ hours and will definitely be coming back to it for another playthrough. It's just a shame the game was never finished.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is frequently updated. Very playable. Not experiencing any crashes.I enjoy exploring the mountain and building up my colony. It can still be a little tedious, requiring some micromanagement. But overall the need for micro has been much improved.After expanding my colony further, I can't recommend this game since its not reasonably possible to achieve a win condition.The game speed slows down as you expose more and more water or lava in the game. In my latest game, playing on fastest speed is now more like playing on the slowest speed. This occurred gradually as I exposed more and more pools of water. Eventually I exposed some large pools of lava and then performance got really bad.Second reason is that the dwarfs are super inefficient. Spend many hours and get really large in the game. Naturally you'll have building required at your base and at your farthest expansion point. This is when you'll start noticing that your dwarfs are crazily inefficient. They will travel the full length of your rail network to pick up one item and return with it. Travel the full length of your rail network to only dig one or two blocks and then return for food. This occurs constantly and really impacts progress in the late game.High priority on foundries also exposes crazy inefficiency. Long trips to collect one or two ore. Built a second foundry to try and improve things, I don't think it helped.

_childDocuments_.review: VERY tentative thumbs up (edit: months later, still not a challenging game at all; thumbs down). This is another case of "needs a thumbs-sideways". The state of the game right now is that it's a very playable "build your own dwarf hall" and "mountain exploration" simulator. There are a few buggy quirks and areas where the development had got ahead of the manual (and the tutorial) but nothing you can't work around.A lot of people might find it very enjoyable in the present state because I know a lot of people enjoy games that just revolve around building and setting things up efficiently without the risk of being blown out. Personally, though, I like risk and consider it the real heart of games like Dwarf Fortress and Rimworld: it's not just about building, it's about building to handle disaster, eventually getting killed and having the enjoyment of starting over and THIS time making DIFFERENT mistakes that kill you.The present state of Hammerting, however, is that you pretty much can't fail. Dwarves don't really die. I mean, I had one get himself stuck and downed by a swarm of enemies but he just laid there til we eventually got to him. If there's a death timer it's super long. Enemies can damage buildings but all they really seem to do is shut them down until you fix it. Morale and other stats are very easy to maintain. The game is basically "easy mode".In the end, it's a game more of building and discovery. Maybe you're into that so "thumbs up". If you prefer the challenge of games like Dwarf Fortress or Rimworld where mistakes can mean death and starting over, then I don't think it's here. I kinda keep playing and digging hoping maybe the real challenge just has to be uncovered but I kinda think it's just not in the game at all. Will they add it? Who knows. I feel like if they wanted it to be a challenge, they would have already implemented some of that by now.

_childDocuments_.review: Prefacing this with that I'd like to give this a *mixed* but of course that isn't possible. So what about this game? It's a promising little colony management sort of game but really has a long way to go before it is good.To start off with, what's good about this game. Well for one I really enjoy the concept, and using different stat bars besides just food and water to keep people alive is a pretty interesting idea even if it's not super fleshed out right now. There is also a sort of level up or progression system that is nice but also comes at the downside of being incredibly complex and really confusing. I list that in the positive section because that's more of a personal preference and not necessarily a negative, but I don't like it. The biomes are interesting but that comes with its own downside I'll mention later. Something a bit different for this genre that Hammerting includes is  somewhat mobile characters, able to jump over gaps and literally climb straight up 90 degree cliff faces on their whims. I enjoy this as it ... helps to avoid trapping your characters... sometimes. The concept of forging great weapons in the forge is nice, but right now it's pretty limited and you start the game crafting SPEARS. The inventory menu is pretty extensive, and you're able to equip your characters with stuff like chisels and rakes which specialize them at certain jobs, however there is no way to make sure a certain well kitted dwarf does a job at the moment but it is planned I hear. Alright now stuff I didn't like. Storage and transportation in this game is an absolute *mess*. If you mine a bunch of resources, your dwarves will walk over to a resource, grab one, and place it where it needs to be, then go back and grab another one. It's extremely inefficient and consumes absolutely absurd amounts of time. You can get storages later in the game, but they are almost useless as they take up a huge amount of space and store relatively few things compared to spamming storage chests? The best play I think is to just let the dwarves utilize their building storages and simply leave all of the rest of the things you use on the floor. You'll find yourself crafting hundreds of chunks and blocks, and if you want to store it all waste massive amounts of space. Not worth it. You can grab skill upgrades to somewhat remedy this problem, but again, this doesn't help a lot when your dwarves just do any task they want. The absolute worst part of this is when you want to construct something like a ladder/stair and they'll just grab a single chunk, bring it, and make 2 trips for this one building! It takes several minutes because of this to build small ladders/staircases. Next I'll just skim over the details and say that equipping dwarves with items right now requires tons of clicking off the menu where the item is to each dwarf to see which ones you gave items, this is just something that needs menu improvement. Overworld is really basic, they request stuff and just sort of annoy you every now and then. Not a bad idea but is pretty barebones right now. Oh yeah that reminds me, how about timber? It's a really important resource used in so many buildings and you have no reliable way to get it, just rummage around and hope you happen to find one. I'd like to see this changed. When I first started playing I placed dwellings in bad spots for my crew, and decided to tear them down and move them one block. Oops! Now I don't have enough lumber for beds and one of my dwarfs sits near my farm slurping down my water to not lose all of their morale. Just the brief bit I wanted to add to exploration, it's very hard to explore right now. The biomes are neat, but it's very easy to softlock a character by just digging around into a bad spot, and finding the biomes themselves takes *forever* as you can only dig a few blocks at a time. A way for the dwarves to hop to a flat surface opposite of the one they're on would help so much. Silly things now. First, I thought the characters looked weird and their animations are super rough and whatnot. But I think the main reason the characters have an uncanny valley feeling to them is because they are dwarves without beards? That and, early game you equip your guys with spears. Dwarves with spears! Again, I think this game has potential, and I'm not just trying to rag on it.

_childDocuments_.review: -Music and charming visual presentation-Surprisingly competent mining AI-Does the core gameplay loop of explore-gather-build-upgrade-repeat pretty well-Took a total of 15 mins to encounter the first crash, experienced the next one 25 mins later-Character portraits and sprites don’t match making it hard to identify dwarfs on sight-Slow, maybe even sluggish gameplay-Easy to get lost in both the UI and the game mechanics (I still have no idea how to track resources or where my crafted medicine disappeared)I only stumbled across this title via Humble Choice and I’ve only spent a limited time with it, so take that into consideration. So far, Hammerting seems like something that carries potential but definitely needs more work to join the club of titles such as Rimworld or Oxygen Not Included. Characters sprites don’t match their portraits (not even regarding gender) and that annoyed the hell out of me.  The amount of content is getting there, but still a long way to go. _childDocuments_.review: Ah, yes Hammerting. A glorious DWARVEN colony management game. This game could have a stairway to heaven...  if the elevators to hell would not exist.OK jokes aside. Currently, the game is more like a graphically refined good idea than an "actual game". Yes, I know that is an early access game and bugs should be expected. But pathfinding, certain bugs and the "stupid" combat system are more than flaws in my opinion.Instead of ranting like a moron I will try my best to suggest some ideas and options of improvement with this review.But before starting with the good points let start with some nice words.First of all. The graphical style of this game is something that deserves praise. I love it, and it is really pleasing to my eyes. Also, the idea of a colony sim with a dwarven setting is pretty interesting. The more or less existing quest in the game is also pretty neat.This all good and nice, but let us look at the not so golden side of the game.First on the not so great list. Bugs should be squashed and exterminated like every monster attacking your colony. Critical bugs should be fixed instantly if they are known.Second point on the list. Doors. Could you possibly add some more functionality to them? Maybe make them a defensive structure and a point of access that only allows some dwarves to enter an area.Third thing. Retreat during combat and automatic attacking. Sometimes I've got the feeling that my dwarves are suicidal as hell. Attacking enemies with no way of retreat or retreating far to late is a problematic thing in my opinion. Dwarves are known it fantasy books for using various tactics during combat, so I think it should be possible to let them attack as a group. Also, could it be an option to set certain areas or enemies to a zone of no attack to not provoke some kind of retaliation?Fourth thing. Cargo transport feels like a drag. This point is more an idea for later updates, but the cargo transport should be improved by cargo lifts or cargo carts.Fifth and last point on the list. The equipment.  It would be really great to introduce equipment policies like in Rimworld. I don't like equipping everything manually, and also I have the feeling that some materials have no use.With this I would like to conclude my list for this game.Will I consider rating this game with a "thumbs up" later if certain bugs will be removed, quality of life improved and more content be added? Definitely YES because the potential of the game is extremely vast.Would I recommended this game in its current state? Not so much.I am sorry if some people have a problem with the quality of this review. My English sucks and I have no experience in writing such stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting is a super fun game! There's a fantastic game idea here and a great time to be had, there's just one issue......the game wasn't really ever completed.The game left Early Access months ago, and did so mostly "feature complete" but it was still a performance mess, had bugs, clear placeholder content in areas, an at times iffy AI, and was missing advertised modding support.  As of 3/17/22 on a forum post, this game has been abandoned and will no longer be worked on.  In addition, in a dev post in same thread they stated they were removing the posted planned modding-support from the store page, straight pulling away a feature listed on a page for a NO LONGER Early Access game (they didn't change the plans in Early Access, they let you support the Early Access then pulled the rug after you supported).  In my personal opinion, Steam should be harder on companies that borderline-abuse the Early Access function like this and should be limited from future Early Access titles on Steam, but that's another discussion.I could tell you all the details and features about the game and how it's fun and a great idea, but what it really all comes down to is this:Hammerting is a super-fun game idea that will give you many hours of fun.  This fun will encounter bugs now and again that you'll have to at times live with and work around.  Further, even if you have a computer which meets or exceeds the recommended requirements, the game will HORRIBLY bog down to single-digit frames-per-second when you have a reasonable population or play on the larger map sizes built into the game.  These performance issues make it a feat of absolute patience to reach any of the end-game goals or get any of the harder end-game achievements unless you are willing to slog through horrible performance for endless hours of fast-forward at 5 fps just waiting on the game to be done lagging (which doesn't happen).  Sure you can help the issue by not letting more workers come live in your mountain, or making sure to not leave anything sitting on the ground which can eat at performance over time, however even if you do this constantly you will NOT make it to endgame without lagging.  Period.  You want the achievement for 40+ dwarves?  Be prepared for lag.  You want to complete all the endgame goals?  Lag.  You want to fully explore a large mountain all the way to the bowels?  Brace yourself, lag is coming. If you can get this on sale for $15 or less and are OK with a game you'll never really complete, but will have fun in starting over with procedural maps playing to late-mid game until performance makes you so mad you give up and start over on repeat, then this is a fun experience.  Modding support was planned and advertised, it has been removed from the plan and store page and will no longer be added.  RIP if you got the game to support in Early Access based on planned features to now learn that it's being left as-is.And I really don't want to bash the fun here, the game is a LOT of fun and a GREAT idea, sadly it just never got to a point where it's a smooth and seamless experience.  This experience led to iffy reviews, which led to iffy sales (after months post early-supposed-access), which has led to it being abandoned.  I guess if you don't make millions in a few months, it's time to abandon and move on if you work at these companies. Short-short version:OK to buy if $15 or less DO NOT pay full-price. Fun game, some bugs, at-times questionable AI, really bad endgame performance.  New features added last-minute to game just prior to being development being stopped, so some features not fully tuned or balanced.  Lots of graphics and features -- while technically functional -- have a very strong feel of being placeholders to be improved on or replaced later which will never happen as game is abandoned (graphics in some places that don't move but clearly should, 2D stuff in place of 3D in clear placeholders, lots of overworld gameplay feels like it's early access and not a finished product.)  A fun game if you can get it in the bargain box and understand the issues prior to purchase.  The recommended requirements should be taken as minimum requirements; if you just barely meet recommended you won't have a great time.Cannot overstate end-game performance issues, be prepared to not fully complete any game runs because it just gets to be your patience vs bad performance for endless hours.

_childDocuments_.review: I played about 200 hours of this game, trying to go around the plethora of issues it has, unsuccessfully.First of all, the interface is horrendous, you have buildings with 'charges', like farms' fertility, that regenerate over time, if you use it too much, you need to wait for these 'charges' to recharge before using it again.What is the most obvious way to solve this issue? you build more farms, but you can't copy settings from one building to another.If you want to have the same set of production of water and a dozen crops over 10 farms, you need to manually input the production one by one, which takes forever, oh, you expanded and want to move your farms. Need to do these settings all over again.And that goes for ALL production buildings, there is no way to copy these settings to multiple buildings, want to have multiple crafters working on the same production across multiple buildings? be ready to manually configure every single buildings, even though it's the same items you want to craft, you need to do that over and over and over again.And this issue of poor interface extends to the entirety of the game.You build a storage, what will dwarfs store then in this storage building? nothingUntil you manually select what you want them to store, the storage buildings will hold nothing.And be ready to have to do that for every single storage, because if you have food on the ground, it can be raw, it can be cooked, doesn't matter, and there is no storage to put them on, dwarves will starve, same goes for all their needs, like water, ale, whatever, if it is not stored somewhere, they can walk around the hallways kicking it, but won't touch it to consume.The same thing happens to dwarfs, you need to manually set their professions, until you do the game bothers you that there are dwarfs that are not 'specialized'.You want to copy those settings to a new dwarf? which of the over a dozen professions it will do or not, and which of the 30+ talents it needs to pick once it levels up? be ready to set it manually, over and over and over again, you want to have 4 builders/miners with the exact same settings? be ready to have to click stuff two hundred times because you can't copy these settings from one over the others.Upgrading houses is another asinine interface, there is no 'tree' of upgrades for houses, you can make them all, but be ready to click 20 times to select the upgrade, then click build, select next one, click build, and so on, and on, and on, and on, you need to build them in order, like one requires previous upgrades, but you need to manually click them one by one, you have 50 dwarfs and want to upgrade all houses? you guessed, you need to manually select each house and upgrade each option manually through multiple clicks per single option.And that is when the game works, you click too fast on the dwarfs bar to the right? crash to desktop.You place too many orders on the map, like mine this, build that, etc. They stop doing them all.You want to prioritize haulers to send resources to specific buildings? you can't, they will do whatever they want and you can't prioritize which building you want to be always ready for production, there is an option to incrise priority, but the dwarfs that you set to haul resources ignore it.You need to do something far away from where your city is? like pump lava to use as fuel or plant stuff? be ready to, with luck, have a dwarf do half a dozen pumps before he has to run back home.Oh, you want to split your colony so you have buildings close to where you want the dwarfs to do these far away stuff? you can't set where you want dwarfs to get stuff to consume, like food or water, you can have two storage buildings for those, but the haulers will fill one, then the other, and dwarfs from either colony will run across the map to get stuff on the other colony.The game itself is a great idea awfully implemented, and it is not worth buying at this point, maybe if they solve these issues in the future, but not right now

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those Early Access games which "released" but is really still feels very much Early Access.I've been wanting to play a more accessible Dwarf Fortress like game for a long time as I just couldn't get past DF's insane learning curve. This game is certainly more accessible, and it was of course always going to be much simpler than DF, but it feels as if key bits of gameplay are just not there or not finished. Specifically:1. Lack of Failure conditionsOnce you have the basics set up, i.e. water, basic food, basic medicine and a quarry and a forge, the colony is basically self sustaining. My first game I failed at this because the game didn't explain very well what was needed, but my second colony had no problems surviving. There doesn't seem to be any failure states your colony can get into once the basics are covered. No diseases, spectacular mental breakdowns, supply chain collapses etc. Your farm will reliably create food and water. Your dwarfs will reliably do their jobs. Advanced resources like Beer instead of water just make them work longer. Morale seems to be barely a concern. This means that failures are not threatening but irritating. For example I couldn't get a hold of lumber for a while due to not finding the right mushrooms to chop down and my trade partner was getting steamrollered in a war so I couldn't buy from them. This just slowed down some construction projects while I explored further to find lumber and waited for the geopolitical situation to calm down. 2. Lack of External ThreatsMonsters spawn in the dark (like minecraft) and from spawn points you discover and can destroy in the mountain, but they never feel like much of a threat. Rarely a couple of rats or slimes might come and start chewing on a building, but it's an annoyance. I've never seen a dwarf killed in combat or a building actually destroyed. Similarly there's an overland map with kingdoms fighting each other, but you seem to be an entirely neutral party in all this. Nobody attacks you, their armies ignore your traders etc. This is reflected in the complete lack of defensive structures to build. Doors are the only fortification you have, and they are just to slow down monsters while your dwarfs run over to kill them. Maybe this was never intended for the game but it feels like it's crying out for traps, fortifications and a need to build them to protect yourself from the overland world and the depths.3.  "Personality" except notOne of the key selling points on the store page is "Personality", and yes each Dwarf has different attributes, but they all become interchangeable pretty quickly, especially because you can't assign them to specific parts of the colony. You give a "explore here" order and it could be any of them show up - one of the guards, your cook, the stonemason, etc. They don't so much hold down jobs as run around fulfilling whatever need is closest. Obviously to some extent this is necessary due to the scale of the game (i.e. lots of jobs, few dwarfs), but this coupled with the lack of failure states mentioned above, means that I don't really care which dwarf is doing what, only that it gets done. Overall it feels like it doesn't quite know what it wants to be. Does it want to be Dwarf Fortress Lite? If so it doesn't have enough threats to your colony to compare. Does it want to be a chill management game about dwarfs? A sort of underground Rollercoaster Tycoon? If so it doesn't focus enough on the personalities of the dwarfs or make you care about who is doing what. Does it want to be focussed on the overland world and the dwarfs place in it? If so, it doesn't give you enough ways to interact with that overland world, or enough risks for doing so (e.g. being seiged). Whatever it wants to be it is missing features or not balanced in such a way as to achieve it, leaving it feeling half finished and unfulfilling.Edit: Originally I said give this game another year and see if it improves, but since then the Devs have declared it finished. Therefore, you should steer clear. This game is half-baked and poorly thought out.

_childDocuments_.review: *Updated Review - April 2021*I find that if you are going to leave a negative review and the game changes you should at a minimum see if anything has changed for the better.  So this review is a follow up. Finally, elevators are fixed. Pathing is much better as is the AI in general. I mean you are still going to get the occasionally stupid dwarf that opts for hanging off the side of a cliff and starves to death, rather than simply climbing up or dropping down, but the elevators and bases themselves no longer bugged out on me or ground to a stop towards late game. Yes, you read that right... ELEVATORS ARE FIXED. Also, bone supplies have been corrected so the game is not artificially bottle necked. Those were my two main issues with the game in my previous review, and both have been corrected. So I have changed my recommendation from "No" to "Yes". That said, I still find the game a bit dull after the first couple of hours into a new base. It has potential, but it lacks depth. The skill tree is a nice start, but the reality is that I found very little use in it and started just mindlessly filling it out on each dwarf without paying much attention to specialization of skills. I don't have a real reason to connect to or care about my individual dwarves or the battle raging on in the overworld. It still seems like an annoyance to fulfill requisitions, rather than a battle I have any real stake in. Plus, ugh that page to get overworld orders needs an overhaul, it's not streamlined or intuitive. Perhaps a way to opt out of requisitions that I don't need anymore, and then a click all for the rest, etc. Bottomline: The latest update solved many of the core issues with gameplay, they have started adding depth with skill trees and improved AI. For a $25 early access game that has involved developers it becomes an easy game to recommend. I hope the future of the game doesn't stop there and they figure out a way to breathe some soul into it --either with more individualized dwarves I care about or with a flushed out overworld that is more involved than just fulfilling the same orders over and over again.*Previous Review - Jan 2021*I keep going back to this game hoping it has improved enough to be playable past the initial early buildings. Unfortunately, it's still very broken. As others have stated, I will repeat... DO NOT BUILD ELEVATORS. It will break your base. Your dwarves may not get stuck at first, but they will eventually, and en masse. Stick to stairs and scaffolding. It stinks and is slow, but do not be tempted to build elevators until they actually fix them. I write this mid-January 2021. After a major patch, and yes they are still broken and your dwarves still have terrible pathing.To slow the pace of the game, they have bottle necked building larger buildings by making you use bones, which can be a serious pain. No real way to farm them as your dwarves will simply go wipe out the graveyard and cut off your supply. Beyond the initial hour of getting things set up and not starving in the process or getting murdered by rats/slimes the game gets tedious pretty fast. By mid to late game all you are doing is supplying the above world which quickly becomes boring. This game lacks a grander purpose past fulfilling supply orders, I keep going back hoping for some sort of magic to have happened but other than building an initial base over and over and then watching it grind to a halt as all the dwarves get stuck, there isn't much to it. Fun for an hour or two, then usually the base gets scrapped and it's time to start over because there isn't really anything exciting left to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting is a competent city builder in the spirit of Oxygen Not Included where you control a clan of dwarves.  At a high level it plays very similarly to ONI - there's a 2D side-scrolling perspective with a grid of voxels where you can carve a stronghold for your dwarves into the heart of the mountain, and there's a hex grid overworld where you can trade with other factions.  Hammerting is much more forgiving than ONI - the oxygen IS included for once.  This will likely make it a much more palatable experience for folks that aren't into the whole "losing is fun" modality.  Exploration feels satisfying so far, tech unlocks feel meaningful, and I like how the trade missions give you a little dynamic direction as you unlock new trade partners.I've enjoyed the time I've spent with Hammerting so far, but I have a hard time recommending it to anyone that isn't an enthusiast for the base-building-delving-city-builder-game subgenre.  There were a number of bugs that limited my enjoyment of the game:1) Player-placed blocks seem to interact with the building or fluid systems, and they will often disappear for no apparent reason.  This resulted in a wall on my filled reservoir disappearing, and the bottom half of my fort flooding in one particularly bad incident, but also frequently results in gaps in walls or floors which can create navigation or cosmetic issues.2) Dwarf navigation seems to get... confused some times?  Occasionally a dwarf will catch itself in a loop (e.g. jump up on scaffold to deconstruct it, then jump down next to the scaffold to decon it, then back up, then back down....).  You can fix this by issuing a move command but it results in semi-frequent time losses.3) Some dwarf statuses "strobe" on and off - which can make the outliner jump around (making it difficult to  interact with).I hope these issues get ironed out, there's a need for more accessible city builders and I really like Hammerting outside of these frustrations.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has potential - but not worth the money at this point.Others have posted lists of the current bugs and crash issues - so I won't repeat those.My major gripe is with the save game mechanic.  The current implementation isn't just bad..  it's probably one of the WORST designs I've seen in years.  There are no date/time stamps on any of the save files - so there is no way of determining when the backups were taken.  You can load the last auto save (and ONLY the last autosave) - the last manual save - or pick a save file from a nondescriptive list (SAVE0, SAVE1, SAVE2, etc).  I had my first game come to a point where the game would just freeze repeatedly - no matter what I tried.  Started a second game and was making good progress when I noticed two of my guys had died to some generic rats for some reason.  When your dwarves are fighting - you get a little icon in the upper right corner - but it's easy to miss that when you're focused on mining tunnels and building.  You get no audio warnings they're in trouble unless you're looking right at them.  So of course, the autosave feature took a snapshot AFTER they died - and I hadn't done a manual save in several hours - so I'm basically out of luck.I can handle some bugs in an alpha release - it's expected.  But this is a design flaw that is just plain sloppy/lazy.If you're interested in the game - wait for a month (or two) and see where things stand.  I'm hoping the current save mechanic is just a temporary placeholder for something better.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like recommending against a game, especially when there's caveats, but since it's not early access anymore I feel like it's fair.Hammerting is the stereotypical result of a studio of artists and level designers making a game. Behind the beautiful aesthetics it's just a mess of over-simplified gameplay and unnecessarily complicated systems. It's full off odd decisions like the talent tree. The stats system is great, the talent system is great, but why are there are so many talents that boost irrelevant stats? The tiers in the talent tree make no sense either, they don't get any stronger as you work your way down. I understand that the effects are cumulative but why do I have to unlock multiple paths to get max boosts to whitesmithing? And why do my whitesmiths have to unlock stonemasonry and farming skills to progress?Research is even more messy. Advanced Casting (metalworking), Complex Stonemasonry and Woodworking are all tier 3 but you can't build the large foundry without unlocking woodworking and stonemasonry first. So if you spend your points thinking that iron weapons and tools might be nice then congrats you just soft locked yourself and now you have to focus on exploring until you can get enough points to unlock the other two. Oh, and you can't unlock masonry without first unlocking... farming... and arcana...? Dwarfs starving at the beginning of the game? Oops you have to unlock the almost completely useless early game tech of fishing before you can learn to cook a simple meal. Cave farming doesn't actually farm anything anymore, it's just a way to get water for free. If RNGesus is good to you then maybe you can get some wheat, which you can't use without unlocking... fishing...?The overworld is a bit of a missed opportunity too. There's no reason to have to map fogged out at the beginning of the game, all it does is arbitrarily limit the trading you're allowed to do, which is already extremely limited and very tedious. Why can't I just build a trade hub in my mountain and set up automatic routes to get the stuff I need? The war is basically meaningless because I don't care about any of the above ground civilisations, none of them are a threat and once a town is captured and rebuilt it's trade as usual with just a change of flag. Sometimes you get good prices for things so a town can rebuild but your gold already builds so quickly it becomes a meaningless number. Dwarfs should be the peacekeepers, if one faction becomes too powerful they should attack the player and trigger a loss rather than have the player win the game. That way you would always have to walk the tightrope of helping out the underdogs to maintain the status quo instead of just befriending the winner. Things would have to happen more slowly so the player could keep on top of them, but they could have quests to send dwarfs on diplomatic or combat missions to give a decent boost if things start to tip too far in one direction.The UI needs some tweaking too. Things like making sure the professions are in same order for every dwarf, as would having the appropriate modifier at the top of the attribute and talent tool tips (some stats improve a skill by +1 and some by +2, in the tool tip for attributes and talents these seems to be in a completely arbitrary order, just put the +2 at the top and the +1 under those for easy reading).Exploration is heavily encouraged, but largely unfulfilling. Once you unlock drilling machines ore is essentially unlimited and a single tiny patch can feed your fort indefinitely without the need to explore for more. The places you find are as beautiful as the rest of the game, but mostly meaningless. Deeper ore makes stronger or more expensive items, but the game is easy and gold quickly becomes meaningless so... why am I digging for it?Those are most of the (hopefully) objectively inexcusable problems I have with Hammerting. The caveats to my negative review are mostly subjective things like how easy the game is. Comparisons to Craft the World are unavoidable, but there's genuine conflict in that game that takes genuine strategy and work to overcome. Hammerting is extremely sedate by comparison, which is great for casual gamers who just want to watch their ant hill grow. The problem is that Craft the World also has a far more flexible building system that lets you customise your ant hill in fantastic ways. Hammerting looks amazing aesthetically, but the variety between your subsequent forts will quickly approach zero. They've tried to add a thin layer of customisation to dwarf rooms, but they all have the same upgrades that go in the same places.In conclusion: Craft the World is superior in basically every way. If you want something to doodle around with while you watch something on a second monitor then Hammerting might be good for you, if you want a rewarding challenge then maybe not so much. I alternate between the two so I'm a bit ambivalent about posting this but ultimately there are better doodling games out there and better challenging games out there than this one. I hope they keep developing it because it seems a bit half baked at the moment. Thanks for your time.
