_childDocuments_.review: EDIT 5/17/2022: Developers have abandoned the game, very sad to see, this could have turned into Dwarf Fortress lite. Developers stated they will be moving on to other projects, however, I'm not sure it is realized by them that quite a few players will never purchase another game by them due to what feels like a very quick 'give up' on this game. Overall this is one of the better dorf simulators that has come out recently. It does need improvement, but the devs have shown that they are actually competent; they will fix issues in a timely manner. This is obviously a passion project for them, and I think it will turn into a good game in this genre.The crafting system is overall the highlight of the game; different materials have different attributes to them that impact the ability of a tool to perform a specific labor or for a weapon deal damage a certain way. This is multiplied by making items consist of components that multiply the attributes of the material. To simplify:For example, to make good pick-axe: You need a handle & a mining head. Mining speed is largely increased by the weight of the pickaxe & the hardness of the material, and is decreased by how 'precious' the item is. You have a choice between two handle types, a straight handle and a curved handle. The curved handle has a multiplier increasing the 'preciousness' of the material used. The straight handle has a multiple decreasing the 'preciousness'. Therefore, you should use the straight handle to make the pick-axe. As for the material, you will want to use the heaviest, hardest material available to you. Gold is very heavy, and is surprisingly hard. However, it is quite 'precious', which will decrease the mining speed of the pick-axe. With the multipliers of the components & item, it could make for a decent pick-axe. However, a material such as iron is also heavy, hard, and is not precious at all. Therefore, iron would likely be the better choice of material. The pick-axe is a pretty straightforward tool to make and figure out best materials. But this system applied to everything your dwarfs will make - including some tools such as a hammer that can serve multiple purposes. It is a fun system not found in many other games, and you will find yourself striving to figure out how to make the best tools to equip your dwarfs with. There is a good deal of room for improvement, namely in stockpile management, expansion of systems such as the overworld & farming, pathfinding & labor assignment - and most importantly: story-telling. I think this will come with time as the devs continue to work on this passion project. If you like this genre, it is worth picking up & supporting developers like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Given that development of the game has been discontinued without fixing many core problems, I cannot recommend purchasing it at the $30 CAD price point it has as of this edit. However, if the price is dropped substantially and you are desperate for a dwarf-hold builder game, below is my original review:===A decent time killer as-is, but released far too soon for the ambition they sought to achieve.- Settlement milestones are sparse and largely uninteresting, with few "make your own goals" opportunities to fill in the blanks. You will pretty much always build the same structures in the same order, and most structures are not actually all that useful.- Overworld is shallow and brainless, with pawns moving around for the sake of moving. Factions have no personality or storyline aspects, and the "war" has nothing to make it compelling or interactive. This is actually a bit of a downgrade from the initial concept at the start of Early Access, where there was at least a good vs. evil kind of thing going on.- Money is worthless aside from being a "score" of sorts, as is the Trade Lore resource, both acquired from trading with factions. It is impossible to spend faster than you can make money.- Trade is the main Overworld interactive activity, with nothing worth buying from anyone outside of novelties like deciding all your cloth will be made of beaver hide instead of rat hide- Crafting system suggests considerable flexibility and depth, but it turns out there is no actual reason to use that fancy beaver hide for anything. Just grind up a crafter and have them make 300 of the item you want using a low-tier abundant resource, and your colony will be swimming in highest-grade items.- The default mountain is absurdly big, and almost totally empty of notable things to find. It is impossible to be resource-challenged aside from, perhaps, some of the later game minerals (which you don't need, since the crafting system gives you overkill gear long before you get to it)- Dwarf skill, attribute, and talent advancement are not really worth much attention. The talent tree, in particular, needs a lot of work before it can be useful for specializing dwarves in meaningful ways.- Numerous long-standing bugs, particularly around enemy spawns and fluid sources (the latter of which are, again, almost totally useless)- Strange income/output imbalances for many resources, because these were not yet adjusted with a fully-scoped economy in place- It is frustrating to build vertical shafts, with dwarves often ending up in awkward, isolated situations due simply to the build order of certain jobs. Long stretches of elevator shafts are pretty much mandatory if you want to explore the deep () depths.It is a charming game, with many little flourishes that show the team's desire to make something cool, and many of these problems will likely go away if time/funding permits the development team to continue, but it is difficult to recommend as-is. If nothing else, at least it's not a $60+ game at launch; you might find it fine for $20 - $30 (CAD) to burn off some hours here and there while it improves over time. If it does, of course. (narrator: it did not)

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Expect bugs and missing content. I have a soft spot for dwarf themed games so personally I love it. Overall, be realistic with your expectations. You may find a solid 10 hours of content here but also expect to find some pathfinding issues, some poor performance as you get further and further along. I even experienced two crashes but progress is saved fairly regularly so it wasn't heart breaking. It doesn't take forever to progress thankfully it doesn't feel like a grind at all.Don't buy this game expecting to have endless hours of bug free fun, it wont happen. _childDocuments_.review: Hammerting has beautiful graphics and an incredible concept, but the game is lacking in both content and quality of life features in a way that most casual players will find it better to just wait a bit longer, mainly given its costly launch price. Considering the good communication devs kept with the community I think it will be a matter of time until I change this review.Since most good reviews are exalting the good points of Hammerting, I’ll give focus to the major negative points (IMO) currently present within the game. I’ll not discuss technical issues as those are constantly being fixed and calling out the devs for this kind of thing on an early access indie game is just plain lack of spirit. My main points of concern for the game are micro and macro management mechanics. Hammerting stays in a gray area of gameplay progression, almost like it does not know what to ask from itself OR the player. Micro and macro tasks are all mixed up, to the point where I left the game with a bitter taste of “okay, am I playing this how it’s intended to be played?”. These problems come to light when talking about the player's mine scalability – as the game progresses, it will expect the player to do tasks at a non-enjoyable pace while offering no tools or easy ways of doing any of them. Even though controlling a few dwarves and buildings will seem easy at first, you'll soon find yourself wondering what is going wrong, why no resources are made and why you have five idle dwarves complaining about having no health. It is not easy to come by. The game's UI looks pretty and well themed, but it also looks old in terms of game design. It is not easy to look at and information isn’t given easily by it, and it’ll get really tiresome given the size of your mine and how many dwarves you're controlling. There's no unified "log of events" window, so you'll lose important events (or dwarves) without knowing it. There's also no easy way of organizing your resources, so you'll find yourself clicking around ostensibly on multiple chests and storage rooms. I'll leave an honorable mention to the Ledger, even though it lacks a lot of QoL features. I feel like Hammerting tries to make itself simpler than it actually needs to be. Most stuff will get done on its own and your job is basically hiring dwarves, asking them to mine ores, building stuff, and telling each building what it must be doing so your dwarves can get it done. You are the taskmaster, but you give basically no orders. That is good considering the gameplay will evolve naturally, giving players the freedom to not worry about everything, but sometimes you will want to move some dwarves, tell them to ignore foes and fall back, or even to queue items to be crafted in a certain order, and all that is very hard to come by. There is basically no easy way of commanding a group of dwarves, but you can give orders to each one of them, which is really, REALLY tiresome. It is lacking. There's basically no way of creating chains of commands or even production lines. Every craft is done manually. Even though mine carts and elevators are a thing, they suffer from simplicity problems cited above – you have zero control over them and they'll work on their own. Devs have already expressed their concerns about have more rules over the crafting system, but I think just being able to "craft item X until a certain condition is met" is not enough. The game needs some logistics complexity. Even though Hammerting never sold itself as a "Lord of the Rings Factorio", automation should be an important aspect considering the gameplay flow and amount of crafting variety devs have chosen for the game. The overworld feels weird. You'll find yourself doing tasks for the overworld as a sort of war "main story" progresses, but it seems purposeless and too much of a time taker. The thin connection between your mine and the overworld is basically centered around a single chest located by the mine's main gate, so it feels like it's all for nothing. The overworld in general has a mobile game vibe to it, so it ends up looking like a different game is attached to Hammerting. A lot about the overworld has been said in other reviews already. It has a bad flow. Trading is not easy since there's no good storage management system or even a focused market building. You'll find yourself selling single cabbages that are covering your mine caves by clicking a thousand times on each single one of them or selling all of a certain item by accidentally clicking the "Sell all x(s)" in the Mountainhome Ledger. Dwarves also take coins to fill their "greed" bars at non paced intervals – and since there's no log of events, you'll only notice you are short on money when you run out of it. Money flow in general is no good. They need an overhaul. Dwarves are not the smartest guys around. Even though the AI is enough for making the game bearable, it needs a lot of work. You soon find dwarves dying or getting themselves trapped in stupid situations. Movement in general needs a lot of polishing. Personally, I’ve seen the pathfinding system to be really glitched given certain maps layouts. Speaking about visuals, all dwarves look more or less the same and you'll probably not get fond of your fellow workers, considering they have no "visual personality" and look nothing like their pictures or traits. Currently, they feel somehow disposable. Having a better appearance diversity, different clothes for different professions, or having some interactions and random talk lines would do the trick. Dwarves have levels and they get XP automatically by doing many tasks in the caves. You are given the option to level up their DWARF (Deftness, Wisdom, Awareness, Robustness, and Fervor) skills individually each time they level up. Each skill gives dwarves bonuses on certain professions, but there's no practical reason for doing it since assigning jobs is too much of a burden and you'll probably leave your dwarves on "be all do all" mode. I've seen the devs talking about remaking the job assignment window, but I have not seen anything said about the skills system and how weird it feels. Honestly, going through all dwarves and leveling up their skills is boring, and it feels like a useless action to the point where you'll just forget to do it. In my opinion, the skills system needs to be somehow more integrated into professions, as the relation between skills and jobs is not very easy to understand. Most tool-related systems need work. Hammerting has a mechanism where different resources can be used when making tools and their properties will conjointly result in different stats and specifications for the resulting tool. One concern I have here is that this system is so obscure within the game that most players will end up ignoring it. The second point of attention is that you have no control over which resources will be used. Dwarves will use whatever they have available first. It doesn't matter if you want an iron tool. If copper is available, it'll be used. The game needs some sort of UI for allowing players into deciding not only which tool to make, but with what resources. Showing up the resulting tools that will be produced (or mass-produced) and the weight of each one of their materials over the resulting tool’s properties would be an “easy” fix to these issues. Equipping tools is also a burden as it is upgrading dwarves’ skills – you'll need to do it for each dwarf individually. Allowing dwarves to equip different and new tools on their own would be a great improvement, and I've seen devs talking about this as a possibility.I feel like Hammerting still has a long way to go, but it seems like a possible path. Devs are working a lot on the game and I expect most points cited to be changed in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I have to say I like the game concept, environment and ideas. 1º - AI: The thing that totally killed it for me was the AI. It has the most horrible AI I have ever experienced in all games of this style. Its so bad that you often see dwarves doing absolutely nothing even with all the factors required for work are present. Dwarves try to load storages even with the said storage completely full, which makes all the items in it pop around the exterior, only for the dwarf to try store them again, over and over. Dwarves goes for a building, stops middle way, and another dwarf takes to the build, stops middle way, the other dwarf go for the building. I have a lot of playing experience in games like Oxygen not Included and Rimworld, and neither I had any issues with AI at all. 2º - Less important, but nevertheless an issue for me, was the designation of tasks and priority system. You don't have a level of priorities, like 1,2,3,4,5,6,7, from the lowest to the highest; it just has do and don't do, high, standard or low. Even buildings or tasks set with higher priority have no marks or illustration regarding them as such, and the dwarves totally ignore it; only the do and don't do works. I really appreciate all the new stuff the devs added for it, like the karts and world trade exploration, but the AI system should have been the core of the development, the angular stone from which everything was build around. So until they fix this horrible AI, this game will not be present in my library for anything and I will not recommend it to anyone until they fix this horrible AI.

_childDocuments_.review: Really great game, and i do recommend playing if you like Dwarf Fortress and oxygen not included. I only have a few gripes, and i hope the Devs are listening!We all know the inspiration for this game is Dwarf Fortress, which I've played, and am happy to play something similar with a nice visual style and more simple UI.However, some things just don't add up and I do feel it was a little early to release from Early Access. In the game many things are unclear, but i eventually figured them out. Better tooltips and more in depth explanation would help a lot. The book of tings isn't quite advanced enough. For instance, is gloom flour flour? is vendari lumber, count as lumber? How about reclaimed lumber? These things if igured out eventually, but it certainly confused me at first.Farming seems broken, many many objects get left on the ground with no way to pick them up or move them. For instance mushrooms are just over populating and no one is picking them up and storing them, even though i have dedicated farmer. In Dwarf Fortress you can designate certain areas for to store and place objects, like lumber goes into this area for storage, so anytime there's lumber, it gets stored there. I feel Hammerting really needs that. Often there are valuable resources laying around and the dwarves never pick them up or move them, they just get left in some far reach of the mountain till they're needed and the dwarf has to run halfway across the map to get it. Makes no sense.When building multiple scaffolds my dwarfs only carry 2 granite chunks, but have way more capacity to carry more according to the slots and hauling weight in the inventory tab. But they only carry two, then run all the way back to pick up more, back and forth. The dwarves almost never use their inventory. I don't know if it's a bug or just needs to be tweaked, but that's my biggest annoyance right now 13 hrs into my second campaign.  When there's an object on the ground, a bone for instance, i can right click on it and it gives me options, but they're always grayed out. Obviously i can't equip a bone, or drop a bone if it's already sitting there, so why even give me the option to right click on it? why not right click and send to storage? That would be great, right now it seems broken.Lastly, i'd love to see something where i can cancel their standing orders, because exploring the mountain is already such a pain. Even if i designate a dwarf just to exploring they still want to run back and do something else. if i tell them to pick up something, they just walk past it. Would be great to have the option to rummage and bring things back while exploring, but right now they just ignore my requests.Great game and having fun, just seems it needs a bit more work to make it a bit less tedious, so we can focus more on the grand scale and less on the micro managing of tiny things that you can easily miss.Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: Update (17/3/22): Unfortunately, the devs have announced that they are no longer planning to support Hammerting going forwards. This is a shame, as the game is a true unpolished gem that really could benefit from continued support beyond critical bug fixes. I understand and appreciate the reasons by the studio has had to stop supporting Hammerting at this time. With that said, I have enjoyed my time with the game, and continue to enjoy it, and I would recommend the game to anyone who likes the genre, and is willing to put up with the rough edges that the game still has.Update (19/11/21): Hammerting launched on Tuesday, 16th November 2021 with version 1.0.12.0. I still play it solidly, but it's quite clear that Hammerting really deserved another year of Early Access. Unfortunately, the devs don't neccessarily set the release date for games, and it's clear that there wasn't really any wriggle room here. However, the devs have worked tirelessly to get the game into a playable, if not fully polished, state. I still like where this game is going, and think that the devs deserve the time to finish it. They have a robust post-launch support programme, and this is the next best thing to remaining in Early Access in my opinion.My original review is down below:This game is best described as Terraria meets Oxygen Not Included with Dwarves. Although it's still in Early Access, I like where this game is going, and have been playing it solidly ever since it was included in July '21's Humble Choice...

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as part of Humble Choice, so although I paid for the game in a way I'm still marking it as free since this was more or less an afterthought.OVERALL:-Is this game fun? Yes, somewhat. It's my first colony sim and I'm digging them now. But there are a lot of major gripes with the game so far.-Do I regret the time I've put into it? Not at all. It's quite addicting, if unfinished as of now.-Is it worth the cost right now? No. It's still in a beta phase, and it feels like it. The game lacks the depth it seeks as of now, but I'll revisit both the game and its review with each major update. It seems promising.-Do I reccommend it?No. It's simply not worth the purchase right now, but if you can get it heavily on sale and you seem interested, give it a shot.ISSUES:-Dwarves have poor work efficiencyA rather key flaw, very frustrating on the whole. Often if you have a large mining or building project, dwarves will often get themselves stranded and end up being unable to complete a job. This is especially true for large projects, as they'll tend to do the minimal amount of the nearest job and end up blocking the remainder of the work. Building large things is an exercise of micromanagement and patience more often than not, but mining seems to go just fine most of the time.-Lack of money utilityGoods are too cheap, and there is no true value to money. For a game that emphasizes the importance of hoarding money, there is pitifully little you can do with it.-Too little storage spaceRather straightforward but frustrating. Not enough space to store your things, if dwarves need something, they'll waste a lot of time running to and fro just to pick up one coal. Even with a dozen storage rooms, you'll run out of space. Item stacking would be a godsend.-There is too little tech, and the costs are too cheapAfter you figure out the basic systems on your own and how to get the currency for tech, you'll be rolling in it withing a few hours and you'll have maxed out the tech tree and trade relations. There is simply too little to spend it on, and the costs are too little.-Game information isn't clear and the tutorial is minimalThe advanced information hovering with the cursor is great, but there is little explicit information as to intimate details; how basic things work and where to find certain items is basically all word of mouth as of now.-The game is very CPU intensiveIf you're doing a large project, have a lot of dwarves, or have too many orders at once the game will chug and your PC will start whirring. My PC runs modern games rather comfortably.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview: Hammerting is a Colony/City/Civ builder game type thing with a side view setup. The general idea is that you play as a fledgling Dwarf colony digging into a mountain and make a mine into a city into a ...whatever?Verdict: I like the idea. I like the art. I like the gameplay. It's hard to tell if the game is intentionally difficult, poorly designed OR if I'm just dumb. I'm having a good time trying to figure it out though and that's what you pay your money for.Pros: - The game has decent art, an ok looking ui and is generally acceptable in appearance.- Gameplay is "setup tasks watch minions do things" and is pretty hands off on interaction. This could be either a positive or a negative. Depends on you.- The idea is pretty complete and plays pretty well to  certain point. (I have noticed some lag at the later game on fast forward so...meh)Cons- I'm not sure if it's broken ai or a feature but sometimes your dwarves will just stand there doing nothing. Sometimes they'll ignore some jobs despite set priorities. and they will always- Task ai is kinda wonky in bits as I haven't really figured out how to set task priority for multiple jobs on a single entity.- The tutorial is kinda lacking in advanced features and does a poor job of setting up meta features like material control and advanced task control but I've figured out the basic bits and I'm figuring out more advanced stuff with a few searches of the web.- I have NO idea what is going on on the surface. The guides I see talk about a battle between good and evil and monster invasions and I have seen NONE of that in 20+ hours. I might just be obtuse but the surface is a chaos of factions and battles and I have no idea what is going on up there.

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to note that if you can find this game on hefty sale then I think you will enjoy your time with it.A few things that ultimately stand out as why I would not overall suggest this game.- The concept of the Overworld at war is a really neat concept that I think can be built out. That being said none of the factions mean anything to you or your player. They market that you can support a faction of your choice, I found myself not caring and just selling and buying to whoever offered the best deal or had what I wanted.  Theres no real downside to supporting anyone over another as I couldnt get them to attack me as promised without hamstringing myself in trade to start.- The Overworld has one war. When one side wins the war the novelty of the Overworld is gone as they stop moving or doing anything at all. They stay in the same alliance and just sit there for the rest of the game. This happens fairly early on as well.- The pacing of leveling up and teching up does not match the speed in which the Overworld progresses. So while the Overworld is dead you are only on Tier 2 tech.- Optimization isn't here at all. At around 30 Dwarves you will start to see the ultra fast speed lagging and at 35 dwarves you will have to switch to the speed below it. At 40 dwarves you might as well play on normal speed.  I would have loved to see a bustling underground empire of dwarves but with the game struggling with 40 dwarves on top of not seeming like it intends to be that in the first place was a bit of a let down.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR yes it has some issues, but at the time of writing the game sits at 23% and it is nowhere near that badThe good:- fun colony sim with dwarven theme- good enough base game loop to have fun for ~20h. Explore, mine resources, craft things, unlock more things- interesting progression with railways as a logistics upgrade and being able to craft many items out of different materialsThe bad:- The biggest problem: in the late game the game crawls to a halt. inefficient job assignments, workers idling / flat out refusing to do certain jobs. Jobs will either take ages, or if anything is time critical (like reviving a downed dwarf) it may simply fail and there's nothing you can do about it. If there's no time limit, it will just take a really long time to get things done.- lack of polish in balancing (example: why the hell are 2 tile wide stone stairs actually worse / slower than basic one tile stairs? also there comes a point where you'll just unlock a ton of materials at the same time and you can simply skip a lot of the intended progression)- trade system ends up just being incredibly fiddly (having to manually check 20 cities for best price to sell or buy something is not engaging, just frustrating busywork)- individual skill trees and equipments for dwarves is too much micro management for my taste and i ended up just ignoring it for the most part- and making all the downsides even worse: no more game updates. So these issues are here to stayI still had a bunch fun for around 20h before the game basically just breaks, which is honestly not that bad for a game you can get for around 6€ on a sale. It's not amazing, but an okay value in my book.If you're looking for a game to play long term and enjoy having a huge, sprawling base then the game won't be for you.If you enjoy colony sims and are happy to put away a game after a few dozen hours of enjoyment, maybe worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It is extremely buggy though. I'll update the review once I feel like I can write a complete honest review.UPDATE:So after playing for whatever amount of hours. I am at an midpoint.The game is frustrating.The game has multiple speed setting (which can be adjusted while playing) that is helpful in speeding things up.  As it turns out, I spent the first 8 hours at normal setting & I will have to say, it becomes painful. The game itself is extremely engaging due to all the micromanaging you would have to do. (If you love to micromanage, this game is for you.) I enjoyed it immensely during the play through but after I believe making the cart & elevator, the game start to become a pain.Before I dive in why it's a pain, let me explain what the cart & elevator does. Both are a mode of transportation, the game is immense which I love but it is time consuming waiting for your dwarf to reach one side of the map from the other side. At normal speed, you can probably find a snail moving faster than your dwarf moving. So the cart exists to speed that up. On top of that, your dwarves also need to pick up materials that drop on the ground. So imagine that happening at a normal speed many times, you can easily consume a lot of time before you get anywhere in the game. (I really love the speed up feature, I praise them for adding it to the game) The elevator works the same way. Instead of going left to right, the elevator goes up and down. Same idea, time consuming watching your guys going up and down. Now, the problem comes in when both are either created or you create the elevator or the mine cart. (I'm not sure which one of the problems it is but it's one of them.) The dwarf would literally not move. I mean dead set stuck in the elevator waiting for the platform or mine cart to show up. I swear it's like watching someone waiting for an angel. The worst part is when it does show up, your dwarf does not move. I mean literally do not move just standing there. How is that bad you ask? Well, your dwarves all have HP bars. They also have something called a Greed bar, Energy bar, & a Moral bar. (If you want to know what they are, go to wiki or buy the game). If those 4 bars decrease to 0. POOF, there goes the dwarf. Oh, don't worry. There is revive in the game. But now the second problem comes in. After they revive, you would assume the AI would require the dwarf to fill up on the bars, but that is not the case. They are literally still standing there waiting for their angel to arrive. And then they die again, So the cycle goes on. It is funny to watch but also makes your overall system less efficient since you have some of your men/women doing nothing but dying. Worst part is, eventually multiple dwarves do it at the same location. one cancer AI seems to effect all the healthy AI. This all happens I believe 4-6 hours at normal speed in. It also depends on how fast you are in the game. If you are playing at higher speeds, you will run into this problem at 1- 2 hours in. Don't worry, there is a brightside to all this. Its actually quite simple. RESTART THE GAME. It helps initially but the problem will happen again. Oh, I forgot to say a few things. When you encounter all of the problems, you will not be anywhere near completing the map. I ran into the problem after a few hours & I was done exploring 1/20 of the map.Resource is great. I think they have it pretty fairly generated. You can feel like the game is short on some resources but more than anything, it's you not exploring enough. I did have a few issues with the enemies. First was their constant desire to attack a dwarf who is running away like another dwarf is attacking it. It's like watching a Lion hunting a cat which is hunting a mouse. (Actually that is a pretty good description of what happens). second is their ability to spawn at random locations in your area. Slimes to be the ones that does it. It's annoying since they can destroy your structures.Item management is neutral. Filter is probably the main reason why I stand neutral. It needs a little more fine tuning. Automation is until cart & elevator comes in. The quests will become tedious. Do understand it is extremely early phase so do not be upset about it. I would say the quests are about all the same. Overall, I would say the money is worth it. Despite the issues, the exploration part is immensely rewarding. Watching your dwarf find a location to mine, it is immensely rewarding finding the rare gems or ores. I don't really care for the quests at the moment, but they will change those as the updates roll out. So why am I neutral in the game? Mainly because the issues balance out the fun I was having in the game. Once the game is officially released, I would say buy it. It's won't break your wallet & it's a game you would put immense time into. I'm sure other players have other issues as well which I'm probably not aware of. HF & GL

_childDocuments_.review: So sad to give a negative review so soon but that game has some issues.It starts already with the tutorial which is spamming dozens of popups and arrows telling you things you really don't need to know. If the game really needs to show me where my resources are, something went wrong with the UI / UX.And this is far not the worst. Jumping right into the game then, you basically have no idea what to do.You get some tasks to fulfill (a bit like CryoFall) which is supposed to help you with the first steps. But they are just not reachable. After 20 minutes I understood how to see what resources are missing. However - unlike other games - there is no clear way of finding what is missing.So the mission states to build a vault. First of all, I don't have that technology. Takes some time to find out what is wrong and how one could be planned. Then, when trying to build one, it tells you you need copper bars. So you search around in the messy UI trying to find how and where to make copper bars only to find out you need copper and fuel for the forge.So you start wondering around how to get both since you basically have only one other building: the quary. But it only produces stones.After a while I found out that I can dig in the background image of the cave and some of the blinking "stones" seem to be copper. So I gave another command to dig there and got some copper, only to find out I have no idea how to get fuel in a cave? Is there wood? Coal? Do I need to buy this? But all you do is veeery indirect. Selling stuff means clicking on the "town" and some buttons. They end up in a list and if one of my lazy dwarfs feels like, they are selling things.This can also be modified in "task priorities" - similar to Rimworld - but sadly everything is clumsy and needs a few too many clicks to achieve. Maybe as a smaller example: when you want to produce something (say 1 copper bar) you click on the forge, then on the item "copper bar" and then need to confirm you want to produce it. Why not just simply clicking on the item itself (or if safety is required, make it a double click). Especially for a game that needs crafting and digging, all those extra clicks are annoying.So, well, I did not play that much yet. But I still feel annoyed by unorganized UI/UX.Since the game seems a mixture, I would actually suggest any of these 3 other games instead:1.  - a similar dwarf management game. Less content but faaar easier playability. Surely fun for a while if you like the theme and want an easier approach. Also allowing Multiplayer Coop!2.  - Colonly sim, with digging, science, survival and resource management. The theme is different (surviving on an asteroid) but the graphics are nicer. It is a bit harder perhaps, but better polished. Sadly no multiplayer. But if you can live with that, this is by far the better game!3.  - Sadly this one is only multiplayer with workshop mods, but the game itself is by far much better in so many aspects. Mentioned task priority list is better to maintain. You also get a better understanding of your pop's needs. In this game the dwarfes sometimes show icons above their head (as Craft the World does, too) indicating something. Imagine "an apple" for "is hungry". But then some things are really hard to understand. What does a scroll mean? Do they want to read something??? And then there are 10 popping up at the same time without understandable feedback. These things are far better organized in Rimworld (even though different so perhaps you don't like that). And the workshop content alone for it justifies the higher price alone. So yea, maybe I give it another chance one day. But for now, the game sadly did not convince me.

_childDocuments_.review: ---Updated Review Post Fluid Update---When I wrote my original review I had less than 2 hours. I was so annoyed by the number of bugs that I had no desire to continue.After seeing the Fluid Update and the long series of bug fixes I decided to buy the game again and give it another shot.At the time of this update I have nearly 16 hours and am happy to say this game is my current gaming addiction.*Things I like*Improved Resource Queue / PathfindingI saw that they improved resource queues and pathfinding. I mentioned before that my cave farm randomly stopped working in my pre fluid patch play through. With my 14 hours of Post patch play I have not encountered any issues like that.FluidsThis is a nice addition. I haven't made it far enough to see all the usage for fluids but the fact that it provides an easy early source of water outside of your farms is a very nice addiction.ResearchSomething I hate in most colony sims is the "researcher" trend. Where you have one or several colonist that are basically useless as they spend long quantities of time at a research bench / lore book. Hammerting rewards you with research points in two ways... completing objectives and exploration. I love this system because it feels organic. It encourages you to push further and further into the dark creepy caverns. Rewarding your Dwarves risk with lots of new goodies via research.DirectionI like that the objectives and overworld missions guide you towards what research is valuable to learn, without telling you how you should play. want to focus on building powerful tools first? You can. Prefer to be a farmer? You can do that too.*Suggestions to Team17 and Development* ClimbingThis patch has made Dwarves getting stuck and falling into caverns a lot less common which I like, however I still think there should be another option outside of scaffolding. There are rare cases when all dwarves fall into a hole and digging your way up isn't always an option if you're enemy enemy lairs. Some ideas: Allow placing dirt blocks. If this is too convenient maybe make them crumble upon a single dwarf leaving that block to avoid them replacing scaffolds. Another idea is to maybe allow crafting temporary tools that allow dwarves to dig up while attached to a wall.Mountain LedgerPlease allow us to set the quantity to sell and not just sell all.Sometimes I get large quantities of an item that I'd like to sell but I don't want to sell the entire stack.TeardownPlease improve AI when removing scaffolds. Primarily making dwarves remove them from the top down. Removing scaffolding currently requires a lot of micromanaging.-Will add more as I play----Original Review Pre Fluid Update---I bought this and unfortunately refunded it. I will start by saying that this game has tremendous potential and was actually quite fun. Enough that I will more than likely purchase it again in the future.So why do I not recommended it? The bugs... I get that it's in early access. I have a massive library of games and a long history of purchasing early access titles. However it isn't often that I encounter bugs so early into a play session and with the level of frustration I experienced here. There's also some mechanics that are quite clunky.A couple examples:1. It's really easy to get your dwarves stuck in places. I ran into a bug where it looked like a dwarf had a block beneath him that maybe was removed. He hovered in mid air and refused to do anything. Not even manual move commands. He sat there defiantly opposing gravity until I sent another dwarf to place a block beneath him, then he was happy. Normally this would not be an issue but it happened deep down, in front of a rats nest which spawns large numbers of enemies continuously. 2. I've seen numerous threads of people complaining about getting dwarfs stuck in holes.... Something I liked in Craft the World is that you can place dirt blocks in an emergency. This game requires you to build scaffolding, which means your Dwarf that is stuck must first build a quarry, which means you have to first get a particular resource, which is based on mining a particular block with a less than 25% success chance to drop the resource you need. It's a clunky mechanic that is made worse when you're trying to work your way around other bugs.3. My Cave Farm randomly refused to work. I had plenty of the green resource required to grow (I forget the name), as well as all required ingredients for the recipe. However there was what looked like a tiny red cancel icon on the farm indicating something... but what? I have no idea. No tool tips, no info, nothing. The game has a notification panel that indicates when a job is unreachable or missing ingredients... but in this case there was nothing. 4. This could be user error but I didn't see a way to force dwarves not to engage in combat. There's a fog of war system in this game and anytime they uncovered an enemy lair, they would ignore any orders I gave them and ran straight for their death. Controlling them in combat was also kind of clunky. I'll remove this is if I find a feature I missed for this scenario.By the time I experienced these issues I had played for only about a little over an hour. I was just over it at that point and moved on.My suggestions to the Hammerting Team. There's a lot of comments about bugs, its sort of become a running theme. I get this is early access but please try not to get carried away with providing new content before the core systems function properly. Quality over quantity.

_childDocuments_.review: So Im 8-9 hours into my first session of the game, got pretty far tech wise, enjoying things so far but there are a few issues.Early GameplaySo in the beginning of the game, its very difficult to figure out what to do, the quests sort of lead you to stuff, but its not enough for anyone not experienced with colony sims. If you don't explore like every single panel in the game, you're gonna get lost. Also, Water and healing in the beginning is so difficult, it severely limits your gameplay. The dwarves need to be babied through every single excursions into the deep mines or they'll get knocked out by a simple skeleton. Crafting is a mystery at first, but the deeper you go, and the more buttons you click, the easier/more intuitive it actually becomes. For anyone whos struggling to upgrade your dwarves tools/armor/weapons, You can change the material types used for recipes when you select them by clicking the little buttons that are the cost requirements, if the game explains this, I honestly didnt see it and I tried to read all of the tutorials as I went.Water In GeneralAlright, so, I kind of love and hate water so far. Its interesting to mess with, I made a proper aquifer next to my production area and I started to pipe water in from areas above and even set up a very clean trench to flow water from a couple of wall sources. Pretty neat. So whats my issue with water? Things don't drown. Water just gets in the way, nothing else, its not actually a risk. Put a dwarf in it to test, buried him in a watery tomb, came back to check like an hour later with the game on fastest mode. Little bastard must have gills. Also, the fact that I cant build like aqueducts is kind of disappointing.FuelOkay... so I understand a need to heat your furances and such as that... but the teeny amount of coal on the map is INSANE. It only spawns in the very beginning section from what I've seen and there are only two alternative fuels, both of which are horrendously involved to acquire. PLEASE increase the loads of coal and make coal spawn throughout.Ore TypesOres Ive found so farCopper - So abundant I vendor it.Iron - Found a motherlode of it, wasnt even excited, there were sapphires in the load, so at least thats kind of cool?Mithril - Final smelting tier, found it stupid early, super rare and currently useless to me.Orichalcum - Same as Mithril but I found a ton of it and now it just lives in my storage taking up space.Some wierd crystaly stuff in the green area - Forgot the name of it, its useless. I cant even find a crafting use for it and it doesnt show up on the trade menu to sell it, wtf?Creature CavesOkay, so I had hopes for this, and then they were dashed. I came upon a creature cave, and I was like, "Ooh boss or mini boss or something! Cool! Lets get the dwarves here and rock!" Only... that isnt what happened, my dwarves ran up to the cave and buried it, in seconds, on normal speed... without weapons... Really hope they make these into something cool, maybe up their health and spawn rates to make it challengeing to kill them, throw in a boss that triggers when you attack it at first or when it hits half health (Or both, both is good).TradingThe game actually has a decently interesting trade map, but none of the locations resources make sense, they should be a lot more defined and have bigger variances in market prices. Single copper for generally rare items is sort of insulting. Also, the Overworld Market button only  displays buyable stuff, but not sellable. I get that all the markets have different prices on goods for how much theyll buy your stuff for, but theres gotta be a way to allow a selling section into the game thats better than checking every single individual town. Also, auto-sell would be kind of nice, because as big as the gold goals in the game are, and how fast storages fill, being able to just constantly sell junk to trickle in copper would be fantastic.Game SpritesAlmost all the sprites look the same, I'm hoping they add in more detail and make the female dwarves look like female dwarves. Also, altering appearance with armor would be cool.CraftingMy only complaint here is I want to be able to assign specific dwarves to specific facilities, not just specific jobs, without having to hunt them down. I kept really close watch on this as my very first dwarf ended up being my master smith (He's only a little bit away from having fully talents, which feels kind of broken). Also, needs more talents for other professions, heavily focused on smithing, needs a divide between armor and weapon smithing. Need more readily available leather as well, rat holes are super rare and low spawn rate even once located (got 6 rats from one, never saw any others and I didn't kill it)OverallI would recommend this game. Its fun, its a good time sink, and honestly, I feel like I did a lot for the 8 hours I played. I plan to play a lot more of it and see it through to completion (for whats available) I hope the developer looks at comments and feedback from their community and continues to develop this gem of a game into something incredible. Overall I give the experience so far 7/10, and I look forward to future development with this game!

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Flipping this to a 'Do Not Recommend' due to the game being abandoned incomplete. Do not buy this gameI'm going to go ahead and give this a thumbs up, but please know that that is only because the game has a lot of potential in the future. Right now there are just too many bugs for the game to really be enjoyable for long.These are the main issues that need to be addressed before the game can really be great.1. Pathfinding.This is the biggest issue by far. I've started 4 or 5 games and every time, once I started digging a certain distance from my home base, my dwarves just lost their minds and starved to death since they couldn't figure out how to use the stairs or elevators to get home all of a sudden. 2. Building priorities.This one is a problem because the dwarves just don't seem to want to build certain structures at all, but they will immediately run to other structures even if the distance is much greater.  Adding a way to set priority would solve this issue.3. Direct commands.There needs to be a way to issue direct commands to your dwarves. There will always be situations where you just need to have a dwarf drop what their AI is telling them to do and run to something else. having this ability would help to cover over some spots where the AI is weak.4. Misc. issues.The talent tree is kind of lacking in choices, as talents further down the tree require all talents at the top. Storage becomes more and more of an issue the further you go. Not so much that you have too many items, but more that you struggle to find specific items when you need them. Adding a set of tabs at the top of storage containers with item types would help a lot I think. Perhaps even add a global storage list to see everything you own would be a good idea.Combat is an issue currently since you can't issue direct orders. You can only issue attack orders on an enemy, then all dwarves rush to attack it, but this is a problem since most of the time, a single dwarf will be much closer than the rest, and they will rush to their death before they have backup. Adding a direct command option would resolve this.There are other issues to be addressed, including adding a little more variety to the underground and interesting overworld events, but these are all do-able if the devs stick with it. I have a lot of hope for this game in the long run.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting is a colony builder revolving around supplying a war in the overworld where your contributions influence the outcome of the battles. But there is so much more to this game. And to everyone who thinks, this looks like Oxygen Not Included but with oxygen, yeah you are right but there is also more to it. The core gameplay is to build you colony make your dwarfs happy and provide materials for the overworld either for war efforts or for trading for goods that you are in need off and cant get in your mine, for example algae for your farms.But I digress so let us get to my pros and cons:-	Each dwarf can be individual skilled, equipped and assigned to tasks-	Different sites and loot can be found and explored throughout the map-	Resources can be obtained Overworld tasks (they mentioned it to be dynamic in the roadmap, so I am looking forward to that big time)-	As far as I can see you can either play minimalistic or go as big as you want and still win so individual play styles are possible-	Different maps so no two similar playthroughs (except the weekly challenge map)-	For me, the game was intuitive and easy to understand and control-	You cannot take control of a dwarf and tell the dwarf what to do (lost more than one dwarf because of that)-	The save game management maybe that is just me but thus far I have not found an option to delete save files, name save files or overwrite save files-	No priority settings for tasks -	Dwarf seem to be prone to stand on scaffoldings while demolishing it and then dropping all the way down not being caught by a scaffolding below themAll in all, I say this is a game worth getting when you like  colony building and survival games and of course dwarfs. It is a lot of fun to play  and I am looking forward to what the roadmap has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting:~~~~~~~~~~ The raging war between the Leagues of Methis and the Dread Horde has intensified on The Overworld. To help the war effort of the Leagues of Methis, a group of dwarves are heading to the highest peak of the Mara mountain to a cave that was abandoned by their race a long time ago. There, they will establish a camp and dig in all directions to find precious minerals to make weapons for the League of Methis. Not only that, the food supply and all the other commodities need to be set up to keep these little fellows happy in their new camp. After all, who knows what they will be crossing path with while digging day in day out. I have a feeling that these 4-foot-10-inch people are taking on a difficult challenge, way beyond their height. Their morale and confidence has hit the roof since they heard that you’ll be the one who will steer them through the tunnels of Hammerting!Hammerting is a strategy/colony sim/resource management game developed by Warpzones Studios and published by Team 17 on the 28th of October 2020 on the Steam platform.  The game has been released as an early access and therefore is under development.  Some of the games released as an early access do not have a tutorial, and Hammerting falls in that category. If you are slightly familiar with this genre of game, you’ll probably figure out what to do reasonably quickly. If not, it will be a trial and error type of gaming experience until you get up and running.They are two main screens in this game, which are inside the mountain (mine) and The Overlord map. On the map, you’ll have several towns and other locations where you’ll be able to monitor the battle between the leagues of Methis and the Dread Horde. As you progress through the game, orange and yellowish arrows with an exclamation point on them will appear, which indicate missions that you can accept and complete. Most of these missions are to provide specific goods to that location, and you’ll be rewarded with land resources or coins. But the main gameplay is the mine screen which is where you’ll start the game with three dwarves. On the top left of your screen, you’ll find a tab with several icons. The most important icons (buttons) are the Overworld map which you can refer back to in order to see the evolution of the battles and to access missions as well. There is also a small technology tree, mountain lore, trade points and how many dwarves you have in your colony. And of course, currency. Make sure you have enough mountain lore and trade points, as you’ll need them to learn new technologies.On the right side of your screen are displayed your tab dwarves, active missions (cave and land) and a few other bits. And at the bottom of the screen you have all the actions, such as building new structures, scaffold stairs, attack, dig, mine etcetera.I like the fog of war within the mine and you have to send your dwarves to explore or dig to see further inside the mine. And let me tell you it is a big map! Not only will you receive Mountain lore points for exploring, but you might encounter strange creatures, skeletons, and rats that will attack you on sight. You’ll also find graves of fallen heroes, old camps, carts, plenty of mushrooms and a few other things to rummage. You can sell them if you’d like to.The most important thing is to keep your dwarves’ colony stocked with plenty of commodities, as well as paying them so they keep their morale up and greed satisfied, otherwise you’ll be stuffed!  I had several plays through and each time I seemed to make progress with the cave, land missions and exploring the mountain even further, but I kept hitting a wall with the currency system in the game. With three dwarves it was ok, but very slow in terms of buildings rooms, crafting or just transporting goods to the storage room and chests, even with accelerating the gameplay. But with 4+ dwarves I would keep hitting the number 0 at some point in the game and then it would all go pear-shaped. I like the character menu, which you’ll need to use frequently as each of your little fellows will gain experience each time they mine, explore and complete tasks, but there are no key bindings so you have to constantly click on the individual tab to have their menu pop up so you can distribute the achievement points you receive into their 5 different attributes. It’s madness!I experienced several bugs which made me restart the game a few times. The main one is when one or two of your fellows are making some sort of protest by being stuck to the wall, and that’s it, you can’t do a thing!Don’t get me wrong, I actually like what I’ve seen so far, and I like that each of my plays through was different as the cave is randomised at the start.  Most importantly, I had fun. I would not have persisted if I didn’t think the game had a solid base, and the developers also give you some information on what’s coming up when you login into the game. Graphically, the game looks great! It’s important to remember that this is an early access game.   Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Nice graphics+	Each playthrough is different+	Good character menu (attributes, skills etcetera)+	Fun and addictive gameplay+	Trading cardsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	No key bindings-	The currency system is not quite right-	Several bugs-	No achievement as yetExplore and mine the highest mountain in Overworld to support your allied war efforts in Hammerting.6/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Updated Review:The key quotes from my early review were, "I barely recommend this game" and "the 1.0 version is a lesser game than the earliest version I played". Unfortunately, the team has had to make the hard choice to stop updating this game. I was hopeful it would be updated to the point that the systems made sense and the overworld map had a point (like the earlier versions did) but that's no longer the intent. This game is playable but many systems are unfinished and represent reboots after deeper versions were already released and clawed back. This is abandonware. Do not purchase.OLD REVIEW:Before getting into my review, I have to say, I barely recommend this game. I've enjoyed it a lot, there are parts of it I love, but it has balance and design issues and in some ways, the 1.0 version is a lesser game than the earliest version I played in Early Access. Somehow, they brought in working multiplayer near the end of Early Access. That's amazing and a big value added feature so it tipped me to recommending. It's very possible they add modding support eventually which I think could allow the community to balance the game for them and would make a big impact on the design issues.The Good: Beautiful game lovingly made. This is a group of good illustrators and animators with good intentions who have a real affection for the dwarven mythology found throughout other fantasy games. The game itself is an innovative idea, too! What's it like to run one of these fabled dwarven mountainhomes that are always either abandoned or playing a supporting role behind the scenes in fantasy games? Content wise, there's great grist for the mill here. Lots of crafting with different materials and experimentation available to find the best handle, head, and materials to make each tool class based on what you have and can work at any given moment. There's a trade system you interact symbiotically with to get things you're bad at producing (foodstuffs and materials only available on the surface, for example) in exchange for stuff you're great at producing (stone and metal objects of great quality). It's a fun concept and the loop can be enjoyable.The Bad: Numerical balance, challenge, shallowness of certain systems, bizarre depth to other systems. There are a number of choices available in your mountainhome's development and each character's development that just don't make any sense to take. Once you reach certain technologies, you automate mining at a much higher efficiency than before and you no longer need to explore further. If you understand the need to trade things you have a fundamental advantage in producing (early on, that's structural materials) for items you need to survive (food, drink, money), the game is easy on the hardest difficulties. Every one of your characters can hold three tools so there's never any survival pressure or intense management. At worst, you notice you're not producing something as fast as you would like, go searching for a new recruit on the dwarf market, and suddenly your production woes are much improved and they probably contribute as a hauler and a warrior you didn't really need to boot. The "Battle for the Overwold" is supposed to be the main victory condition. It existed in the very first version I played, then it was removed, it was restored just before release but it's VERY shallow.

_childDocuments_.review: UpdatedI have explored the game a fair amount, and there is a great deal of creativity and potential here.  Many of my frustrations have to do with how little is explained.  If you're ready for things that aren't intuitive and answers are hard to find, you will also find some fresh and dwarvish fun here.  For example, it took a silly amount of searching to find the buttons that allow you to customize crafts.  They're just lost on the interface.  And if you want to store mushrooms, be ready for your dwarves to go crazy harvesting them all over the explored map, putting your colony at risk.  And building elevator shafts just isn't worth the headache, in my opinion.  But exploration is pretty fun. There are really no tools to assist you in collecting and processing materials. Ores, food, coal, and other materials are left scattered about the floor and sometimes fall into deep chasms.  Eventually you can have adequate storage, but it is not organized.  Until then, a dwarf goes running off - sometimes a great distance - to pick up a resource.  I have not figured out how to see how much of a given resource I have; it's just a matter of waiting until you suddenly can't build something.Your dwarves will eventually die, unless you manufacture healing items.  These are made from monster parts.  So your healing economy depends on getting attacked, rather than making the place safe.  My first colony died out from hunger and exhaustion.  There were no messages indicating a problem, I just eventually noticed that everybody's health bar was very low.  Imported food is prohibitively expensive so early in the game.  I had built rooms for the dwarves, which are too large use up valuable space and seem to serve no purpose, except that dwarves will deposit their wages in their rooms.  They don't rest and recover in their rooms, and none of the mechanics needed for survival are explained anywhere.  Live and learn.I don't mean to badmouth the game that this wants to be.  It will be a good game, if the devs think about what they are doing and continue their work.  The idea of influencing overworld events via production is a really good one, and the game has an economic system that Craft the World, for example, lacks.  I'm just saying it's not quite ready for Early Access, and some of the oversights concern me.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit:So after playing this for about 15 hours, the negetive reviews are 100% correct. Or at least the top rated ones are. At a glance, this game looks like it's as deep as an ocean with how complex it is. Though when you try to take a step into it, you realize that not only is it not an ocean of depth, it's not even a pond, or a puddle. It's just a very realistic painting of an ocean. I don't say it lightly that NONE of the mechanics of this game actually matter. If you have a few farm plots and some water generation, then you have zero threat. This game has zero threat, zero consiquences, zero challenge. Once you learn how to farm food and get water, which you can do in literally minutes of starting, the game is functionally over. - Upgrading? meaningless, the stat's don't do enough to matter- Talent points? You can go the entire game and not touch any without noticing a difference- Overworld relations? It's extremely easy to make everyone an ally with very little effort- Overworld wars? You can't make any enemy hostile. Even setting them to the lowest relation has no effect.- Trading? Once you can earn 2 gold reliably, in a game where you're expected to earn thousands, you can buy everything in the game. LITERALLY EVERYTHING with just 2 gold. cash is meaningless- Food and Drink? Why bother making better food when the basic mushroom and water does the exact same thing as the end game top tier food. There's no reason to give them any luxury- Improving dwarf homes? The upgrades give such insignificant bonuses that it would take you actual years to notice a difference based on current stat change rates.- Upgraded buildings? they give you 1 new item of 8, and take up more than twice the space. You're better off with 3 basic buildings- Armor and Weapons? You'll never need this, and likely wont ever notice your dwarves surviving longer or killing faster with any form of upgrade.I don't say it lightly that nothing in this game actually matters, assuming it functions at all. The starting options say that there's a wave based assault that (should) happen to your base. This NEVER happens. You can sometimes get a small handful of enemies that spawn, but a single door will hold them off almost forever, and 2 dwarves can kill anything. Nothing matters and no feature actually means anything.Original:I don't want to say the negetive reviews are wrong exactly, but this game's insane scale and list of options is staggering. Yeah there's definitely issues that need to be ironed out, and I really hope the devs do fix the issues people mention. However, this game has a really legit shot at being up there with Rimworld in scope of both how much you can do, and how insane the worldbuilding really is. This is rough around the edges, and my god the UI needs an overhaul... but it's definitely worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting works very well as a game already at the early access release. It has some minor quirks here and there, but most of the time you can play for several hours without problems. And because of the autosave function, you don’t have to be afraid of losing a lot of progress.You can also save manually, but at the moment it is not possible to name savegames and start several different games in parallel. There are the default 4-5 saves and if you start a new game, the saves of the previous game will be overwritten. What I’m still missing are some comfort functions like certain hotkeys, maybe a minimap, and the options menus and the save system could really use a thorough upgrade.For the early access state, I can say, the basic functions are mostly all included in the game and you can play through it from front to back without any problems. I have already saved the upper world once, it took about 10 hours. But since the map is randomly generated, you can easily play through the scenario several times without it getting completely boring.From a graphical point of view, the mountain, its caves, the five different underground biomes offer something for the eye. It’s all very fancy and the many, many different goods, objects, and materials are all easily recognizable and clearly distinguishable. As far as weapons and armor are concerned, the game still lacks a bit of graphical variety...... (Read full article for more details)Let’s summarize, Hammerting already shows a positive impression. The game runs stable, offers a coherent gaming experience, and is, therefore, worth its price. And this with the prospect of improvement and expansion through further development by a capable team.For this, I would like to award a base score of 85%. The very rare crashes, small deficiencies in handling and menus, and the expected gaps in the game content in an early access title let me deduct 3% here. So I now have a very good 82 % rating for Hammerting for the Early Access Release.But since Warpzone will surely continue to work on the game for some more time, I see a lot of potential for Hammerting. Depending on the amount and quality of the upcoming patches, the rating for the game could rise up to 90%.EN DE

_childDocuments_.review: Do you love sinking a lot of time into a game, only to run into unpassable bugs about 3/4 of the way to the end?  This game's for you.  There are horrible scale problems that only show up after you've sunk a bit of time.  They ruin the game but you keep putting in more time trying to fix it, in vain..  Basically, once you reach a medium size, resource management falls apart.  Dwarfs stop following professions and priorities.  Commands are ignored.  Since in most cases crops are the same as seeds, this becomes an quick failure loop once priorities and professions become unbalanced.  Cooks will use the crops to create food while farmers ignore commands to re-sow crops.  You can't set a reserve, so you end up with a massive food supply but no ability to replenish it.  Then your dwarves eventually eat everything and starve while you wait for them to just walk over and plant the crop you see in your storage and sitting on the ground, but they won't follow the commands.This is not a release-quality game.  The game-trashing bugs aren't even early access expectation, they're what you'd see in an early alpha.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm hoping to change my "thumbs down" later but for now I just can't recommend this game. Below is a list of my biggest issues with the game, at this time. At the right of the screen is your main information for the game. This includes "cave missions", "overworld missions" "dwarves" info and other such info needed. I find this screen obnoxious. There is too much going on here and it's very hard to keep up with it all. Likewise, the info panel for the dwarves themselves seems to also have too much going on and it's very hard to really get a grasp for what it all means.Your dwarves seem to have some sort of leveling system where they will become better at certain tasks for doing said tasks but controlling what they do does not seem to be possible at all. It seems up to them, or random, for who does what task when you set up tasks. Or a higher level in something seems not to really matter when you cannot control what tasks they do.Dwarves can only be given orders one by one. In otherwords, if you want to explore a new part of the map and want backup, you have to click on one dwarf, give him a move order, click on the next, give him a move order and so on and so on. There is no way to select multiple dwarfs at one time and order them all to move to one location together.My main reason for not recommending this game, at this time, is the dwarves are just dumb. And I mean dumb! I discovered an area in my game that is some kind of atrium. In front of this atrium is something, I cannot, for the life of me, figure out what this something is, but it's mine-able. When my dwarves insist on mining this spot, without orders or my ability to stop them, they spawn a bunch of slimes that attack them. The dwarf is eventually overrun by the slimes and begins to run away. I will set the slimes to be attacked but, instead of anyone attacking them, they will simply run past their fellow dwarf (now running for his life) passed the horde of slimes chasing him (that I've tagged to be attacked!) and go find some food in the same, newly discovered, area or collect some ore. Eventually the running away dwarf will turn around, run right passed the slimes that are still chasing him, and go to find some food himself. Until, the inevitable happens, and he is downed by the slimes. The slimes will now begin chasing another dwarf, if the slimes manage to be brought down... guess what happens...? Another dwarf walks right over to that invisible mining spot, starts to mine and spawns more slimes! Eventually all my dwarfs will be downed by these slimes. This is unplayable.I will continue to return to this game to give it more tries as I really, really love this type of game. I have played "Craft the World" probably more than any other game between my PC and tablet. I want to see this game become something I can play.

_childDocuments_.review: Bad things first.(When reading, keep in mind that this describes the . I did not inform myself about potential fixes, gave it a 22h-try and now wait for the full release. Then I may rewrite this review.)1) When crafting, you need to click the Icon first, and then hit "Craft". This is in particular annoying because later on you are mostly spamming the "Craft"-Button. So you do a click on the item, and then on the "Craft"-Button, while you could actually have a "non-craft-selection-click" and a "selected-do-craf-click".When accepting Quests, you may wanna do it as fast as possible because they are repetitive - and you need to fly with the mouse across the screen to first click it and then fetch it. No, nobody reads the quest instructions. You could have simply have a list of what is required, a reward-list, and then an "accept"-button on one side.The cherry on top: as soon as all materials are gathered, you need to do it again. Click Quest, click "Complete". Especially when everything got fetched, and it the request is timed, I would prefer an auto-submit!"Hey, that is no biggie! Why are you mentioning that at all, considering that it will be probably fixed later on and was primarily made that way because for example AI got priority?"- "Because I think it is noteworthy."2) ... in the current state. I see how that may be developed, but right now the gameplay it is mostly spamming production - the RPG-aspects only happen in your head. I played the "Main Quest" and received an utterly anticlimatic text.3) I wish there was an auto-equip function. Currently it is hard to tell whom to give which Item; it is hard to figure out who is carrying something already; it is annoying to figure out if somebody is currently already grabbing an item; sometimes it is even hard to find the item.The more dwarves you get - the messier it becomes.4) I am not sure if I like it or not.Example: you want to craft a Sword. You craft a sword blade, a sword handle.. and then tell the Dwarf "put handle + blade together!"If you got a Bronze Blade and a Mithril Handle, then both will be put together. Looks quite unique.But: you got no control over what is being put together!The dwarves run around like ants, pushing Items into the working locations, and I think the only way how you can influence what is put into which spot is by blocking the inventory for particular items.So on the one hand the idea of "Dwarves grab what is available and put it together" makes things much easier - on the other hand the player loses control, and if they want to regain it, need to micromanage more than without those "easy craft"-Mechanics.By the way: this is the source of one bug which always occured for me. After figuring out why that happened it was no biggie to fix, but it is rather annoying and only happening because of the "AI-driven-crafting"-System:Sometimes you may not be able to craft an Item. Especially Support Beams or Gems are having those issues. Reason for that is that a Support Beam needs for example 2 Copper Platers.. or 2 Iron Plates.. but if you only have 1 Copper Plate, then it will wait for another Copper Plate instead of grabbing an Iron Plate. So you need to somehow get some Copper... and craft a Copper Plate. But: there is always a chance that a Dwarf will feed the Smithy... Iron! And then you have more Iron Plates! But still lack the Copper Plate - and the production is stuck.Best solution: go into the Inventory of the Crafting Station, sell the Copper Plate, and then try again.Same goes for Gems. If you only got 2 Gems of the same type.. perhaps sell them. Or end the production-queue, wait for a dwarf to fetch the Item... and then try again!Oh, one more thing:If you craft Chests or Storages, then by default THEY DO NOT WORK. First you need to tell the box which Items are allowed to be stored inside! Otherwise dwarves will just drop everything onto the ground like Aunt Petunias spoiled fat Turkey she calls "Dudley".5) A quest wants you to fetch a diamond. You never found a diamond. The quest is stuck for ages; till you find a diamond.You finally got some money and can recruit some Dwarves. First they cost a few silver - now you gathered some gold and most cost one gold or more. So eventually you need to horde more gold, just to see the prices rising even more.That is balancing, though. Should come later on.What I am concerned about, though: some resources are finite. Meaning: there is a chance that eventually the whole map got farmed empty, leaving you short on all those important resources.6) Dwarves run somewhere, mine stuff. Stuff lays on the ground. Nobody cares.Dwarves kill a rat, rat loots stuff - nobody cares, it just lays around.Suddenly you get a quest - rat hide? I dun' have any! Suddenly dwarf picks up some rathide which he remembered would lay somewhere in a dark tunnel.No fuel in the kitchen anymore. Some dwarf runs to a coal vein, because the ground is covered in coal. Dwarf picks +1 (ONE!!) coal. Dwarf drops one Orichalcum Bar in exchange. Finally the kitchen can finish a rat on a stick.Genius.The good things:1) The current music might be annoying after 22 hours, but in general I like the feeling. You go deeper into different cave bioms, you try to build your base. It's fun. I like it.Though I must admit that I love Dwarf-Games in general.2) Yea, I said something negative about the AI above already. But in general I was rather happy how well it runs. It prioritises the important things, like sending supplies with a countdown.Needs some time to figure it out, but in general it was fun to watch how everything came together.3) ... how this might develop."Eh? That is really specific.. and why do you have a recommendation considering that most aspects you named are negative?!"- "It is simple: I enjoyed the game. I do not know exactly why. Perhaps because I just wanted to have something amotspheric and relaxing, where I build thousands of storages and let some dwarves be productive, while I am just doing some general mangement and still feel satisfied seeing how everything works out."Conclusion:It is still Early Access. I cannot play more than 22 hours currently without getting too bored.But so far: it is fun!It might be worth your time if you are into dwarves and into building (general) structures.I am curious how this game develops.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really review games often, but I wanted to try to give this game a fair shake based on the mixed reviews.  It's early access.  Yes, I know what I'm getting into.  That being said, after 8 hours of pretty solid play, I've come across one bug (The curved handle ladle not working) and some annoyances that other reviewers mentioned(Movement loop jumping across a construction block - Cancel and requeue and it was fine. Stuck drawves twice - mine the block next to them and they were free. Scrolling scaffold issue, annoying but cancel and reclick and I could continue.)Nothing I have come across has made my game unplayable, but I have found it a relaxing, chill simulation game.  My biggest complaint is that I would like the drawf pawns to look like their portraits or at least the same gender, but that's just me.   I've found it enjoyable to gather resources, complete quests and explore to gain lore.  Worth $30?  Maybe not in it's current state, but I've dropped more on AAA titles that I've gotten less enjoyment out of.  If you like simulation/basebuilding games and are looking for one that is pretty relaxing and low stress to play after a long day of work, you will probably enjoy this like I have.
