_childDocuments_.review: You know what? I tried to enjoy this game. But this game has been released insultingly early.I've had my fair share of early-access colony management sims, ONI, Stonehearth, Rimworld etc. But this. This is possibly the most infuriating early access sim I've played thus far.So, here's the story:I worked around some of the game's broken features (don't bother with rail, an older version required you to keep your farms at max fertility to avoid wasting precious lime, storerooms are inferior to chests etc.). This is of course, the norm for early access games. That's fine, I can still try to get some enjoyment out of it. But what follows are issues that aren't excusable, and I just cannot fathom why the developers decided to go early access this early.Unsurprisingly, one of the core activities of this game is to dig down; and as stated earlier, mechanical platforms won't work  (on reloading the save, dwarves get stuck). This means you have to rely on good old fashioned stairs to make your descent. Problem is, the dig command has a higher priority than the build command, so your dwarves are more than happy to dig themselves into a chasm since they won't build the stairs first (no, you can't change priorities). To compound issues, each set of stairs requires two chunks of granite; but for some reason, dwarves will only carry one chunk at time. This leads to absolutely game-stopping flow, where you have to wait two minutes for a single set of stairs to be built. Of course, all your dwarves are happy to idle during  construction (no, two dwarves can't work on the same set of stairs, union rules I guess). What finally broke the camel's back is, this issue is absolutely lethal to a dwarf if a mob spawner is located in the chasm. You cannot tell the rest of your colony to speed up construction to save the dwarf. Why bother with a management game, when you don't have the management tools?Speaking of which, why are basic tools missing? There's no way to designate which material is used for which items, which is important when the stats of the item depend on the material. Also, there is no way to 'maintain X', I hope you enjoy micromanaging productionOverall, please avoid this game. Ambition is fine. Early access missing some features is also fine. But a game being released this early tarnishes the reputation of Steam early access as a viable route for other games.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to like this game.As an experienced player of Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld and O.N.I I'm quite familiar with the concept and was looking for something nice-and-easy.So, while the visuals are quiet nice compared to the other games, there is a proof-of-concept for gameplay basics, but what is needed now is a real game designer, to stitch together all those loose ends and imbalances..Examples: Import/export, Goal setting, difficulty (much too easy), Millions of food, Dwarf skills and charaterisics don't matter really, etc.So I will put it back on the shelf and wait another year for some major overhaul or mod support; until then I don't recommend buying as you will be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: they made a few “quality of life” updates during 2022 AFTER release which was back in November 2021 after five years of development. They have to move on from the game and shift their focus to other projects as well, you know, they are humans with families and need to make money to live (who would have known?) and fund development of other games (no way, right?).The game is playable, it has a niche in the sandbox genre and I was looking forward to a game with simpler approach compared to “No Oxygen Included” plus I like dwarves so it was a no-brainer to pick it up. I was pleasantly surprised by the challenges it comes with.I play it from time to time to relax and wish I could give it more time because every time I start a new colony I find something new. I like to design my dwarven “mountainhome”.I tested it some months before release during EA, the updates always brought improvements, with a couple of exceptions for the overworld map and dwelling, I wish there was an option to choose the preferred version.During my playtime I didn't encounter tremendous bugs or game breaking issues, if you aren't ready to pay for the full price, wait for steam sales. It currently is 90% off which really is a bargain. I got it as a key with Humble Bundle, so I count myself lucky for getting to know it.You aren't sure about buying it? Watch a couple of gameplay videos and then make your choice, this genre is not for everyone. at least be honest if you don't recommend it instead of putting them under a bad light with just one line of text saying: "gaem bad, no update after release :^( ". Did you really think they would post updates forever after release? I get it, some things like end-game could have been handled better, but judging the overall picture it holds up nicely, I still have to see something so bad that it makes me not recommend this game, you're probably just not used to sandbox god-games.If I'd like more features or aspects being developed? Of course, but I'll be glad to pay for a DLC or expansion if they come back to the game. I'm looking forward to what they will develop in the future.The game is fun to play, which is the most important thing. The only thing I miss was the old hand-drawn map for the overworld, not a huge fan of the 3D rendition but it's okay, I can get past that choice.But come on, imagine posting a bad review bragging about lack of updates after the full release (which is factually untrue since they updated ) like they owe you something indefinitely. This is not a game as a service nor minecraft with its billion of copies sold. You might have recommended it to people to help them with more sales and funding, but since that's not the case, it's quite delusional that you hope for a dev to keep up something that stopped selling after a while thus not generating enough income for them to keep it going. Games rely on word of mouth as well, not solely on marketing, so you had a chance to speak about it.In the past even I was a bit pissed off about the choice to stop updates, but they've been developing it since much earlier than I've jumped aboard. If you bought it during Early Access, you already knew it was a beta phase. After releasing it they needed to move on as sales declined. I figured it was the best choice, I prefer them to make other stuff rather than see them close shop, either way you wouldn't get your precious updates, right? You should realize it and if you don't... well, welcome to life, it's tough.Thank you for the "exhilarant" award, glad you found it funny ;D I'll buy an emoticon to honor your quirkiness.

_childDocuments_.review: if you didn't buy it yet, wait for a few updates. this game has a lot of potential!!hammerting is fun to play, although it feels a bit slow paced, if you dug deep into the mountain like i did.bigger buildings are not worth it, since they give only one working place more and are 4x bigger than the smaller ones.while your base gets larger, you need more dwarfes to operate, and at the same time, you are progressing on the overworld and become overflooded with quests. you slowly run into the issue of lacking dwarfes to farm ressources, selling stuff, to recruit more dwarfes, running out of ressources to craft stuff to sell or complete quests with. -> see where this goes?this game feels like, it needs automation (ore farming) and a possibility for endless ressources. yes, we have drills, i know, but those dont farm forever. when the ores in the wall are gone, you can basically destroy the drill.since ressources aren't endless (for drills), you are forced to dig deeper, further. running paths get way to long for building, crafting and farming at the same time. _childDocuments_.review: This game was not ready for release at release.This is mostly due to a known issue since the farming update in which certain crops are both the product of farming and the seed for farming.  Meaning that in many cases the farming item is used in crafting, meaning your dwarves don't replant it and thus run out of the resource with no good way of recovering it.  On the forums the developers have said that they are aware of this issue and have a fix, but that will be in a later update.  In other words, the game was released with a game-breaking issue that they knew about and failed to fix before launch and rather than delaying the 1.0 release until the issue was resolved called it good for launch anyways.These are the kinds of issues that one could and should expect during early access, not on a full release.EDIT:  As of 12/22 the farming issue has been fixed and the game just seems to run much more stable in general as of this release.  If the game was in this state at launch I wouldn't have left a negative review.

_childDocuments_.review: Read this first!  Don't buy it yet, give it time.The AI seems to get worse later in the game, where your idiot dwarves will move back and forth as enemies hit them. There aren't items to add energy, so you have to micromanage just to try and save it, but EVERY dwarf will go right for it.Basically, you will waste about 15 hours until the game will say it's time to end (even on easiest difficulty). _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed what I played of this! The art design caught my eye at first, and colony sims/resource managements are (one of) my cup of tea.I like the overworld missions mechanic alongside farming materials underground.  Not sure if I was managing my money incorrectly or if that system needs tweaking, as I couldn't keep my bank above 0 between paying missions at later stages in game (with no more than 4 dwarves requiring wages/compensation/greed fulfillment)No tutorial other than an introduction to the UI. If you're familiar with the genre its not hard to pick up.My version did seem to get more glitchy the longer my run got.I hope there will be more individualized control over each dwarf. At times they seem to queue tasks in odd ways. I know the job management isn't polished yet and would like to see a prioritization mechanic. Occasionally the ai would freakout and a dwarf would loop until another dwarf overrode a task that had the other in a pickle. _childDocuments_.review: As much as I enjoy the spirit of this game, it's just too buggy to be worth it.  Sometimes your dorfs will be unable to reach targets despite a clear path.  Sometimes you will be attacked and your dorfs will run back and forth in one location while seemingly trying to choose a target.  I watched a group of rats destroy my entire base while my 5 dorfs just ran back and forth in a room just below the action.Or you might have fun trying to exit the game only to be unable to click the "Exit to Main Menu" and "Exit to Desktop" buttons because they are superimposed on top of each other, thus rendering each useless.On my system, running the game on an SSD, I still see stuttering whenever textures are loaded - every single time I click any of the action/building menus there is a slight pause while the menu renders.  These are very noticeable and not small pauses.The lack of a tutorial makes it tricky to produce food and keep dwarves alive in the early game, and as you proceed to build a bigger colony, the bugs seem to get worse.  Every time the game autosaves or transitions to the overwold map, expect a pause for 10-45 seconds as there is no threading and the game fully blocks until these actions are completed.  If I experience these issues on my machine, I suspect the issues will be amplified for those closer to potato level.AMD Ryzen 9 16-core128GB DDR4 RAM16GB VRAM

_childDocuments_.review: So I waited a while and after coming back to the game after a year and a half, I was excited to see a lot of new features. Sadly, most of the problems I had with the game are still there.Improvements I enjoyed are: jobs can be automated and level-up perks can be queued. That's all.The interface that was looking lke a placeholder and could use a full rework just got polished up a bit. Mouse clicks lose focus and start selecting things when I'm trying to give orders. Game only lets me build one block or stretch at a time, then you have to re-select the tool. And once again I had to google how to cancel building in progress because "cancel order" doesn't work on that, you have to click a small icon that you won't even notice is there unless you know what you're looking for.But the worst part again is the AI. You're not playing against the computer or the environment, you're playing agains your dwarves' ambition for the Darwin award. They frequently get stuck in place or in a loop, even in combat. They dig under their own feet and fall to their deaths or into a deep pit they can't leave unitl they starve. They run halfway through the map just to forget what they were going to do and switch to a different task on the other side of the map, finishing nothing. They ignore their priorities and the tasks in their immediate area and do whatever's the least necessary at the moment. I had a dwarf get knocked out because while running away from the enemies with almost no health left, he ran past a workshop and decided to stop there to finally get some work done.I guess I'll try again in a year or two.Previous comment from 29.09.2020:Nice idea worth checking out, but it doesn't feel polished yet.There's lots of tedious manual work, like you have to order the crafting of every single piece of stone, and you'll need thousands of them. Dwarves have extensive skillset that they can improve by performing work and gaining XP, but you have to manually assign their level-ups and there's little reason to specialize them since you don't seem to have any control over what work they'll do. The biggest challenge seem to be keeping the dwarves from committing suicide or getting stuck. I gave up when I found two of my dwarves dead in a walled-off section of the cavern that they had no physical means of entering, followed by a game crash.I'm not refunding it because it shows potential, but I'll wait a while before I'll play it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Hammerting

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting is a cute and enjoyable vertical dwarf colony game. You hire in dwarves to join your colony, build and explore to advance your knowledge, and craft wares for trade. Rats, slimes and other THINGS all lie in wait and can attack in waves. You build and improve homes for your dwarves, hone their skills, and throw your diplomatic weight around in the distant surface world; every metal you mine has different characteristics allowing uniquely useful (or useless) tools, weapons, and armour. Meanwhile improved food and drink keeps your dwarves happy and productive.It's a fun game, more relaxed than a lot of recent games.Early access of course had issues, and the devs have worked hard and consistently to address those.EDIT: the game is now more or less unsupported, which is sad. There are some bugs that show up intermittently. It's still worth a go if you get it cheap, but be warned.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the perfect podcast game. In that it's perfectly able to hide its red flags long enough to suck you into listening to better productions while making you think you're doing something when really you're just sighing in exasperation as the dumbass AI dwarves fall into a pit and get stuck because Dwarves can't mine without being micromanaged and you just keep playing because we live in a Capitalist Hellscape and this is the only endorphin release you can get anymore. The first red flag should have been the "Tutorial" which somehow explains a lot and yet nothing. The second red flag would be the single track of music for the OST. Maybe there's more, but I sure didn't hear it for the first five hours. The third was that nothing you do in the Overworld matters and will not affect you at all because anyone who declares war on you can just be bought off easily. Barely an inconvenience. The fourth is that there are literally unimplemented or poorly implemented game mechanics still present in the "final" release. And attackers are of so little concern I started ignoring their attacks and someone would just rebuild the base anyway. The fifth is that the optimization is terrible. 10 hours in and the game is stuttering like hell. Nothing about this game is elegant, it's a hell of a lot of clicking to get ♥♥♥♥ done and I can't go through everything wrong because this game doesn't respect your time so why should I respect it. But hey, 20 hours of Hammerting let me catch up on my podcast queue. So, that's. Something.

_childDocuments_.review: I've experienced everything this game has to offer and I really have mixed feelings about it.I'll start with the good... The graphics are nice and the sounds are decent. The management is fun for a little while until you get far enough that it becomes essential to micromanage everything every dwarf does without being able to directly tell them what to do...And the bad... Almost nothing is explained minus very rushed tutorial screens that give you no clear direction, they just highlight things that they don't adequately explain. I never use wikis and I couldn't have gotten far in this game without one. That's a clear sign of a poorly designed game.The AI is ridiculously dumb. You can have a group of dwarves designated to do hauling and building, a dwarf will haul the required materials to a build site and then -drumroll- they walk away and another dwarf halfway across the map makes their way over to start the build.  It makes everything take so incredibly long for no reason. Additionally when you try to build several buildings of the same type (for instance building several dwellings at once), hauling dwarves will supply one building's materials at a time despite having room in their inventory to bring more from storage. Just really, really poorly designed AI all around.Late game, the speed up is insufficient for making meaningful progress and the game becomes INCREDIBLY CPU heavy. After building enough structures or having a sizable amount of dwarves, my game would freeze every second. Awful optimization and then to recommend an i5 implies that the developers don't expect you to make it far enough for it to matter anyway.Overall, I wouldn't suggest anyone get this game. But don't expect anything._________________________________________________________________________Old Review:Potential spoilers ahead.PROS:- frequent updates.- interesting roadmap- lovely game design and artwork (finding big ore veins is always a 'WOW' moment).- cool fantasy theme (if you like LotR you prolly gonna like this game too).- fast and easy to learn.- there were bugs obviously, but it was okay since there werent any game breaking ones- time flew by playing this game (finished this game in one playthrough of ~12 hours - enough for a early access/demo imo).- kept on digging for another 3 hours after finishing the main objective just because I felt like there are more secrets to unravel.CONS:- that being said, I felt like there were big secrets hidden in the depths, sadly I couldnt find any.- each overworld city has only one repeating quest, at one point I just memorized what they wanted and set those things on autobuild, the war efforts quests cycle a bit more but are in general the same ones too.- youre skipping ore tiers alot of times so there is little to no use in building low tier ores, i.e I found silver before iron and mithril before orichalcum.- money is a bit useless right now since there is no trading and the better dwarves to hire only cost up to 80 silver - I had masses of gold coin in silver tier selling silver tools.- also a lot of items have almost no use right now (i.e. there is no reason for me to craft ruby gems since I cant do anything with the money).- AI is quiet clonky right now, for example dwarf 1 is bringing all the materials for a bridge but now has to wait for dwarf 2 who will finish the bridge while dwarf 1 is standing right next to it doing nothing (or another task) instead of building it himself- it feels like clearing monster caves doesn't matter because they just keep spawning randomly in dark places- was bit disappointed finding out the explorable regions are only around 2/3 of the whole map.- was a lot dissapointed finding no big boss monsters like gold hoarding dragons.IDEAS:- obviously improvements to the bugs and the AI- some secrets of the mountain would actually make it worth to keep on digging even after finishing the main objective/finding big nodes of top tier ore (maybe giving you buffs like faster digging or increased combat strength after finding them, or in order to activate a ancient statue it needs 3 stars of mara etc.).- make quests more random; maybe introduce a time limit for ALL quests.- give a reason to follow the tier order, I'm thinking of 'you need tier 3 to dig this deep' or 'you need iron tools to mine silver'.- introduce trading, I'm having some sort of reputation system in my mind linking to the quest system.- BIIIIIIGGER map; overall we are inside the highest mountain of these lands and not inside some hobbits' backyard hill (not just downwards bigger but also upwards - maybe digging out of the mountain peak and building on top?).- make monster spawns a tiny bit more predictable; random spawning is okay but not randomly in my base just because a brazzier is a bit out of touch.- big boss monsters?- my favorite idea: the evil forces from the war effort campaign are invading you at random moments, coming through the mountain entrance, trying to stop you helping the good guys - like the game gives you a 5 minute timer to ready up in advance (would also be a good opportunity to tie in a rep system i.e. if you have good rep with your neighbors they'll send you reinforcements or thin out the enemy army before the battle or they ignore you if you didn't finish their quests).TL;DR: Pretty good early access. Needs some good polishing though but overall its worth trying out or at least keeping an eye out.Thank you for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing for 25hrs and beating the game with a "Diplomatic Victory" I'm not recommending others buy the game in its current state.There are many MANY minor issues that add together to make an overall frustrating experience. The "heavy micro" problem others have said isn't really true, its just what one youtuber said so the pack picked it up and ran with it.The real problems with the game stem from:- The standard mountain size is too large. There is too much space to explore and too little variety filling it up. I had 1600+ mountainlore sitting there at the end of the game with every upgrade unlocked.- The war on the surface is pointless. You can repair your allies fortifications but forget about helping them get armies out. Your contributions to their food or weapons do so little that the un-aided enemy can keep up easily. So get ready to sit there an repair their walls for hours on end until they eventually capture a city...and go immediately into a truce.- Due to the above point the only way to win is to get max rep with all the surviving factions. I had 3 allied factions in the end....makes me feel less like I made a choice of who I wanted to support and more that I just had to do it to get the game over with.- Due no doubt to the size of the mountain, once you hit around 15-20 dwarves your entire supply chain starts to fall apart. I sat there for 30 minutes on fastest waiting for my dwarves to plant a crop that they had haulers, farmers and plants available to do. The crop was even set to "high priority" with a yellow triangle on the craft symbol. IT TOOK 30 MINUTES. The AI needs massive improvement to make it workable and remove the feel of micro managing.- Too little direct control of the dwarves to be able to take over when their standard AI fails as mentioned above. I could have solved bottlenecks in seconds if I could override all commands on one dwarf and get him to do one critical step rather than hit a feeble high priority button and watch as the dwarves do tasks that have a lower priority.- Trading with the other races is tedious. Even when using the trading window you have to scroll through the entire list, hunting for every scrap of hide or whatever it is you need at that moment. Add a filter, add a search bar or something ffs. Let me type "hide" and it filters to all items with "hide".- The dwarf buildings get very large and the "grotto" areas become impassable roadblocks. Have one spawn where you're expanding into? Too bad, you can't build there. Let players cave-in the grotto's and build over them. They serve no purpose other than aesthetics.- The HAMMERTING. The thing that shares its name with the game!....is utterly useless and pointless. It feels so lacklustre, the bonuses are pathetic and have zero impact on the gameplay. Want to know what has more of an impact than the bonueses? The time your dwarves spend when you do the hammerting and they all run there and talk for ages. - Some buildings are almost entirely useless. Arcana and Tailor have one or two things you need and then....forget about them. The healing building doesn't get any new recipes from the start of the game. Want more advanced medicine? Use a random shrine that spawns....forget researching something using higher level materials.- The higher level materials don't feel like they make any impact at all. Nothing changes when you get orichalcum, or tomb lotus or diamonds...you can just craft another thing that makes some kind of difference but nothing that is readily apparent to the player or has any impact on gameplay.- Auto-equip upgrades doesn't extend to rings and armour. WHY NOT!!?? Holy crap is it tedious to go through 20+ dwarves and check their 2 rings and armour. So guess what, I didn't do it and it made 0 difference. Raises the question of what's the point of having that mechanic?Edit: don't know how I left this one out as it's my number 1 frustration- When harvesting crops the dwarves do not reserve a plant to re-harvest. So you'll be sitting at 100-200 mushrooms for example and go "yay I can use those for food/yeast etc now". Then 30 minutes later you have a crop of mushrooms with a red ! across it because they've used all the mushrooms and now you have none. Begin the process of pausing everything that uses mushrooms, hunting down more and re-growing your crop. While the crop bit might sound annoying...now imagine after encountering that and trying to control it you then have it happen 3-4 more times with mushrooms, twice with sugar beets, 5-6 times with gloom wheat....until you just give up and rush the win condition so you can be done.I could go on even longer with this but you get the point. So many frustrations with this game. It needs more dev time. It needs polish. It needs someone to stop and have a hard look at what the systems are doing and what they're trying to accomplish because right now it plays like an indie demo, not a full release game deserving of a mid-market price point.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a nice fishbowl filled with Dwarves, this game in its current state might be your thing. It excels at the "build some stuff and watch the beautifully rendered ants scurry about" vibe, but sadly the game part is hampered by some serious issues:Firstly, the job broker is seriously broken. Especially late-game, when the distances within the colony are HUGE, your little dwarves will travel great distances to pick up 15 pieces of ore... Only to drop them all moments later because they've decided they're hungry/greedy/sleepy/just feel like dropping stuff. Instead of delivering 20 tracks so a whole segment can be built in one go, dwarves just carry one piece of track to one particular segment, and then truck all the way back to whatever they were doing. This goes for building as well. Finishing a piece of track some way off the main part of your colony can therefore take up to HOURS.Secondly, this game touts you can assist the raging war on the Overworld. This part of the game has enormous potential, but apart from not making that much of a difference in battles if you do decide to meddle in the affairs of Orcs & Humans, there eventually is no point: groups never take over each other's settlements, and if a group does raze all the other groups' settlements, the losers just get put on time-out and will join the pointless fray after a while. You can kind of influence the spawn rate of armies, by supplying food for manpower and weapons for might. But the spawn rate does not seem to change that much if you max the stats. Also, even if you supply vast amounts of weapons, it does not influence the actual armies: they are still fueled by some standard RNG, resulting in all your boosted armies biting the dust due to unlucky rolls. Its often best just to ignore the Overworld, and just finish all the quests when your colony is all set up.Thirdly, the game obviously got rushed to 1.0. Apart from all the game design flaws, there are some glaring reminders that the game just isn't finished. First and foremost the building called "Tavern Small", which has no bigger counterpart because that probably got scrapped. The tech tree seems to rush you with cool stuff to play with, but the latter tiers fall on their face entirely, providing you another mostly useless foodstuff or drink instead of giving you faster modes of transportation or ways to manage the various fluids in the game.Fourthly, some resources are only acquired via trade. This wouldn't be such a problem if they were plentiful, but some crucial resources have a damning low spawning rate. Yes, there are buildings you can construct to speed this up, but like most of the Overworld mechanisms, they do not affect it well enough. Apart from the trading, some resources such as slime are dependent on mobs, which may or may not spawn, often the latter. Even if you leave the lairs in tact, that's no guarantee the mobs will spawn frequently enough to supply enough resources. Other mobs are often a hindrance. It would be so much better if there were ways to effectively control the spawning of mobs and farm them when needed with a walling/defense system.Lastly, when you expand far enough and get an interesting amount of dwarves, the game starts to chug. It seems like the code is as optimized as the job broker of the Dwarves themselves.That being said, it did grip me for almost 50 hours, mostly because the art style is just really lovely and the fact that this game seems to have a lot of potential. Sadly, after seeing all there is to see, it feels like a game that's rushed to a release and probably won't get the Dev love and attention it deserves to make it great.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to give this game a good review, but at this time and where Hammerting is thus far, I can not. Please do me yourself a favor, WAIT ON THIS GAME. _childDocuments_.review: Did you enjoy Dwarf Fortress? Gnomoria? Towns? Any other games where you start with a small group of colonists and have to attract more along the way?This game is excellent and has many of the great features that made me love some (or all) of these games. You can do a tight, cramped, crowded base that develops organically. You can build a planned colony with lots of room that kind of sprawls out. You can basically finish the game without building rails. You can also make a base that exclusively uses rails.There are some fun, decorative bricks you can place in the foreground and background, but not as many as I'd like personally (given the variety of stone types you wind up digging through). That's a fairly minor issue, though, as the decorative blocks they DO have do connective textures and make some pretty gorgeous features.I find a bit of performance issues once you have a large enough base with 30+ dwarves, but if you don't try setting it to max speed (just using normal and fast) it still runs pretty decent. My system's no potato, but it's also a few years old this month (yesterday, happy birthday!)The keyboard commands integrate REALLY well with the mouse so you can quickly stamp a thing (room, block, whatever) multiple times. I'd love the ability to copy and paste a layout you've done (sort of like blueprinting) as I'm particular about the design of my stairwells and fancy them up a tad.All in all, for a game I got through my Humble subscription, I feel VERY inclined to support them in further endeavors as this game is excellent and they've done at least four major update releases since the game left early access, showing their intent to continue supporting the community even AFTER getting their money. YAY, integrity!!The music might very well be the best part of the game, as excellent as the graphics, design, interface and controls are. I can just sit and listen to the music and kind of zone out while watching the dwarves do a massive build project I plopped down. The names being taken from Norwegian and actually translating to things (like Dragonhammer, or Leadback) is exceptionally cool to me. I know a bit of the language, and a guy FROM Norway who's confirmed my translations and offered many of his own.I feel like 327 hours (at this point) is lowballing the time I've put into the game, but I suppose that goes to show how much enjoyment I've really gotten out of it, that I feel like I've had the game longer and played it more than 13-going-on-14 solid days. O.oEDIT: I forgot to mention. Don't be an idiot like me, and actually try to change which metals they will use for industrial crap like rails and machine parts. I'm not going to admit how many of those 327 hours came before figuring out you can control THAT element.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, this really scratches my Diggles: The Myth of Fenris itch. Or at least the early game does.The game starts strong with promises of exploration and expansion. You discover a few landmarks, see the hints about a cool crafting system, build your "small" tier buildings, get new quests, explore the over- and under-worlds.But the further you go, the more things seem to just... wobble apart. You still keep discovering new landmarks, but it's now the same nine landmarks on repeat. The variety in crafting system just ends abruptly, as if they added the system but never finished filling it. The "small"-tier buildings remain "small" for the most part. Over-world quickly reveals its placeholder nature, considering how you can't even remove your upgrades from your enemies or take part in battles yourself until the very endgame. The UI, comfortable to use with 7 dwarves, becomes a nightmare of micro-management with more than a doesen. Not to mention that they never figured out why you want certain elements to remain static when someone is trying to interact with them (good luck selling all of your pickaxes instead of five kegs of beer if unpaused). And the worst offender - the more of the map you uncover, the more dilated the time becomes. This does not affect any of the graphics, amusingly. But your dwarves will be moving at 0.3 FPS while the drill behind them still gets perfectly animated at x3 speed.This boils down to the endgame being a nightmarish slog, and that's without counting the insane scaling enemies get at maximum depth. I've never even found the mysterious God of the Forge, because every single action a dwarf wants to take in hell will require a five-minute roundtrip per action, per dwarf, not counting the absurd time slowdown.Given some polish and a few updates this could have been a great game. But from what I've seen, people say that it's abandoned in its current state? This wouldn't have been that much of a problem, but there's no workshop functionality, despite the foundations for it clearly being there.As it is, if you're someone who likes playing through your games to the end, I would recommend you steer clear of this until it is, if ever, improved.

_childDocuments_.review: Not good at guiding the player through the gameplay. There are essential resources such as lumber for building and food for your dwarves that is severely lacking and has no obvious way to obtain, so you the barriers come up very quickly where the dwarves have no food and no resources to get more food.The UI is a bit of a mess, and it is hard to tell how much of certain resources you have available for crafting. Trade is difficult to understand if you are doing it right, and the research points for exploration and trade are not easy to acquire.There are too many interwoven objectives and for success you have to do them in the right order so there is a lot of either research or learning from failure required.I like the automation aspect and the 2D grid style makes base building cool, but this is all potential as there is not a good groundwork there to start.This game was not ready to be released and seems to have been abandoned.

_childDocuments_.review: This game still has a long way to go before full release, but it's coming together nicely. I'm changing my review from 'No' to 'Yes' because the recent updated added some QoL to hauling and I still got 20+ hours of enjoyment out of the game.I won't go into all the negatives because it's Early Access and the devs are making improvements all the time. If you love colony building games, especially dwarf themed, go ahead and get Hammerting in early access. If you aren't that die-hard, maybe wait for full release.Devs:1) Increase the priority of building scaffolding and laying bricks. These tasks are usually bottlenecks. I'd suggest making the priority just below combat. It's that important!2) If a dwarf is going to build infrastructure (scaffolding, lay brick, rail line, elevator shaft), look to see if there are multiple adjacent pieces to build. If so, gather the necessary resources and then go build all the pieces at once. THIS! This is huge. Otherwise, it takes too long and feels bad.3) Give Storage Rooms higher priority. For example, I tried to use a storage room to store all of my old weapons and tools, but the task is such a low priority that the dwarves were always busy doing something else. Then I have to go look around the map for secondhand picks and hammers... ugh!4) Force dwarves to empty their inventories. My guys were running around with extra tools in their inventory for the entire game. This kills their carrying capacity.5) Before a dwarf returns to base, look around the immediate area for valuable resources and take them back to base if you have a storage place setup. For example, when my miner gets done excavating a mithril vein, I want him to pick up as much as possible and take it to the storage room dedicated to ore.6) Storage Rooms default to 'Everything'. I did not select a filter on a storage room and it started to fill up with junk. No bueno. It should default to 'Nothing'. Add a filter option for 'Everything'.Good luck with the development process. I'll be back for full release!Old Review:

_childDocuments_.review: Another EA game that is a gem already and far better than a lot of completed titles that are out there today.  If you like dwarves and building games, this is definitely one you should pick up. Bugs are few, even in an EA game, and I ran into none that were game-breaking. I could stand to see a little more of a challenge on monsters. At this point, you deal with rats, slimes, the occasional rare (unfortunately) skeleton, and a couple of other minor baddies. But for dwarves delving deep, it would be nice to uncover a balrog or dragon or other major baddy that could really put a dent in your growing kingdom. I would also like to see something in the way of expanded crafting to let dwarves create treasures that could be sold for a decent profit to the outside world. And of course, maybe a dwarf king?  Additionally, there are a couple of buildings that are nice visuals, but really offer nothing in the way of really adding to your kingdom.I played a couple of games to start and get a feel for it, then completed a full game to victory. As long as you are taking care of the quests on the outside, victory is pretty much assured while you dig and build. When I hit the victory point, I hadn’t hit the last tech tree level and hadn’t found several of the hidden places underground. So there is still plenty to do even after victory. So I like that you can continue.Overall, a definite winner here. I look forward to the completed product and seeing what else is added to the game going forward.

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game very enjoyable, but extremely akin to Oxygen Not Included's early access. There are a few things on the horizon that the dev's are planning to implement, much of which I feel will be amazing. On the positive scale, I played the game for roughly 8 hours straight before I ran into my first major issue that nearly ended my run. The game has an active trade-based mission system with the Overworld that you also use to move the Overworld Campaign in your favor. Other, minor missions are available for general resources such as wood, which you'll find a stark lack of in your mountain hold. Your dwarves are fairly beefy - they are dwarves afterall - and pretty forgiving if some random under-mountain beastie tries to feast on their organs. Lots of construction options are available, ranging from your standard production facilities and rooms, nothing too outrageous there. Equipment is upgradeable for your dwarves to improve their ability to do tasks, and there is a task system to disallow certain dwarves from performing tasks. That said, it's a yes/no system, not a gradient, and that can be problematic for if you have some dwarves that are good at a task, but a mile away through the many chasms, caves, or channels you've had them carve through the stone around you, then you won't be able to have those closer dwarves handle it if you've disabled them (you can honestly leave everyone active on everything). Also, your dwarves can level up as they perform tasks and allow you to allocate skills to several different facets of their being. Without fail I increased carrying capacity, movement speed, and vigor, which are represented by differently named stats. Good system, but you do get penalized for some of the stats, such as reducing movement speed for having a really thicc boi/gal who can carry a great deal or is particularly full of vigor. Some bad things that you should know before you buy; the trade system for ordinary items is NOT refined, building downwards with scaffolding (or destroying said scaffolding when your dwarf should be trying to do so sanely) can sometimes result in your building team breaking the ground out from under them when you know there's empty space beneath that very last tile. Instead of the scaffolding being 'soft-installed' and catch your dwarves, they instead plummet sometimes vast distances to the ground where they may or may not have a way up. Note, this doesn't happy if you're already building one of these things in open air and the dwarves don't have to mine anything, but if they have to mine out a location first, then you're gonna hurt, especially because they like to stand on top of tiles they're mining.  Remember up there where I mentioned the first major problem I ran into? Yeah, full team of seven dwarves went one after the other in rapid succession right off the side like this, and couldn't get access to materials to build scaffolding.If there's a Dev that reads these (though highly unlikely, you never know!) the easy way to hotfix that particular problem would be to make the small quarry buildable without resources, or with resources that can be gained by simply cracking some stone open. As is, you're granted the resources to build one at the beginning of the game, and then require granite blocks constructed from that very same building to make any more. You'll only ever really need one in your main base, but if you ever get trapped down below any reasonable way up, then being able to crank one out to build scaffolding back upwards to your base would be amazing.Now, on to what I had to do to save my run. I had my guys run right to no avail (two graveyards full of the undead and a dwarven mosh-pit to destroy them was hilarious, though) as I hit a pretty massive crevice into empty space. The other direction was better, and I had to serpentine cut my way up 'S-shaped' until I ran into an area with accessible copper. I could have technically just kept doing this until I reached an area in my admittedly massive homestead, but I also had technology for elevators ready. All those needed was copper ore, which I then just constructed at the base of where I fell and had it set up to go up to where I'd fallen from. Problem solved.I could go on and on about suggestions on improvements beyond that, but that's just what I'd experienced. Point being that there are workaround to most of the issues you'll find in the game, and that I love the game enough to be thinking on how it can be improved, rather than how much it just isn't worth it. This game has the potential to be absolutely amazing, and already bears a sort of rugged shine. So, should you buy it? Personally think that you should wait a bit for a sale, or until they come out with a few more updates. BUT, it's perfectly playable and scratches the itch for an Oxygen Not Included game with the added flavor of trade missions, and far more updates on the horizon. If you've got a few games worth of an allowance to yourself, take the jump!

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting is a side-view colony manager, quite similar to Oxygen not Included, though more approachable. You manage a colony of dwarves by helping them satisfy their basic needs, expand the colony by digging to the depths below, and build the economy to help in a war against the forces of Evil happening in the overworld.The game is rather bare-bones content-wise, and there are bugs, but all that is to be expected from its Early Access status. Serious, game-crashing bugs are fixed quickly and with priority. There is also a playtime-limited demo that has no restrictions otherwise, which is more than many other Early Access titles can claim. The devs hang out in their discord and can be approached anytime for bug reports and suggestions. Overall, they are hard at work improving the game, so I am optimistic for the future of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very pretty and I liked the gameplay at first but as I've played more it's become apparent that the game is quite simple and very easy after the early game. I've explored far enough that I only have two techs left to unlock (tech is unlocked by exploration and trading), and most of the techs are pretty useless. For example I've bought half a dozen or so techs that unlocked all sorts of random foodstuffs and booze which I see no reason to make over the initial ones. Maybe they heal you more or something but once your dwarves have a few levels combat is completely trivial and they don't take much damage anyway so who cares? I've unlocked a whole bunch of gem crafting tech which as far as I can tell only exists to give you more stuff to sell but I have more money than I know what to do with and keep having to build more vaults just for somewhere to put it. Same deal with unlocking different sword blades and spears and better metals etc when I was already rolling everything with copper axes.I've done all the quests that have popped up except the one to build a large vault and fill it. For the vault I'm missing adamantium which I can't seem to find now matter how deep I dig. Digging deeper doesn't even seem to get noticeably more dangerous or difficult. Occasionally I bump into a lair or some new enemy but my dwarves just roll it effortlessly and loot a couple of minecarts for some more copper or iron sheets as if there wasn't more copper and iron ore hanging off the walls than I could ever mine let alone put to use. The stats/perks system feels kinda homogeneous. I tried specialising some of my dwarves but there doesn't seem to be any real reason to, and the higher level perks require so many of the lower level ones that everyone ends up taking most of the same picks anyway. Even the later level perks are like +1 to a couple of stats and +2 to a skill you have a ton of levels in already, and honestly I don't notice any difference between my dwarves however I build them, and definitely don't get attached to them like I do to say my Rimworld pawns or XCom soldiers. Even the base stats are all just like +1 and +2 to a whole bunch of different skills and it all just feels like a bunch of meaningless number salad.The game pitches the overworld as being something you affect through who you support and trade with but as far as I can see it's just an overly long list of towns with slightly differing prices they'll buy your stuff for and different junk for sale, most of which you won't ever have any reason to buy anyway. If they've been fighting each other or something I haven't noticed and it hasn't affected my game in any way.I feel like the bones of a fun game are there - a mix of Terraria and Rimworld which sounds great on paper, but ultimately nothing you do feels rewarding, whether it's exploration, combat, building, crafting, commerce, or research. Hopefully it's something the devs can remedy moving forwards.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting promises to be an engaging dungeon building game. The graphics are awesome, the music soothing and the map huge. It still has some bugs and issues that need to be addressed but when they do, this could seriously turn out to be a very addictive game you can even play for only 15 minutes at a time and still enjoy a lot.----------------- So we're now some months along since I last wrote the above I think, so here's an addendum to that.Hammerting has been steadily releasing new patches to the game with bug fixes but also a lot of new content, new skills, etc. The mods really listen and help out. I've encountered a few bugs and have been communicating with the mods, who are in direct contact with the developers, about the bugs I've encountered, trying to fix them.Is it ready for release? No, there's still some tweaking to do and the main story line could use more content.Is it fun to play? Hell yes, it's even very relaxing. The fullfillment of the main story doesn't mean the end of the game. You can, as I have, keep digging more of that mountain, creating more rooms, find more treasure, hire more dwarves. I've found that part to be most relaxing to be honest.Even with over 80 hours playing this game, I still feel I could do more in the game and considering they just released a new patch with new content, I can hardly wait to either continue on my 'old' save games or start a new mountain and start exploring all over again!Got questions about this game? Let me know, I'm happy to answer them!----------------- So I thought it was time for a new update. I'm 185 hours in this game and I still seriously enjoy it a lot. Somehow it's soothing to the soul. The mining of ore, the building of new rooms, the laying of tracks, the crushing of the skulls of skeletons and rats....This game has been receiving a continues stream of new updates, adding new features, new goals to clear (one of which is filling a 50k treasure room which is no small feat!), new stuff to wear (armor, bracelets, rings) and an increase in difficulty when encountering the deeper hidden domes. All in all I still recommend this game. It's about to launch (mid november 2021) and still they're adding new content. Widescreen support is being added, as well as fishing and a slew of other stuff. If the developers keep pumping out new content at the rate they've been doing so far, I doubt I'll ever start any of the other games I have on Steam.

Crashes when I open page 2 of the job manager (there was another crash in the open world (I was trying to get my dwarves to heal a downed dwarf), but I'm not sure what caused that). Vulkan issue when another Vulkan game runs fine. Sometimes dwarves just get stuck (jump/drop loop), which can be fixed by moving the dwarf manually or reloading, or the game forgets that a dwarf has an item equipped (the later is rare and can be fixed by saving and loading the save). (Crashed while trying to do some crafting/disassembly tasks in the new relations update).Lots of issues with priorities as well. Dwarf unconscious? For some reason, the game wants to do everything else first before reviving them, even when your dwarves have everything but healing turned off, they'd rather just idle. So instead, you need to haul all the materials to your storage, finish all your trades, THEN your dwarves will go: okay, time to heal. Fueling and repair have similar issues as you can't seem to put these in the queue manually.The UI also has some issues where the game doesn't show you the locations of certain discovered items (also, holding down a vision entry seems to dismiss the notification and end up loading the logbook instead, so you have to tap the eye). Would be nice if there was a UI entry for renewable resource nodes and things like hand pumps. Unfortunately, at this time, you have to memorize where they all are or find them (good luck on a large map).Speaking of UI, there are no special overlays. Some games of this style have overlays where you can see clearly any discovered resources or specific buildings or w/e. For example, you might have an overlay that shows the player all player built objects in yellow or w/e, which would help players find those objects quickly.Some cities quickly become useless because they will only sell x ore/pelt/wood before they stop selling these. Not sure if a bug or intended. There are limited resources in the game except for gems and coal and certain other special nodes. Deconstruction has to be done manually (you cannot group deconstruct), which is really annoying because scaffolding is extremely useful early game, but deconstructing scaffolding takes a very long time as you have to go one by one as your dwarves are not smart (your dwarves will kill themselves by getting stuck instead of jumping off a slightly high edge and conversely, will drop themselves to their doom if you try to break multiple scaffolding at once. Similarly, they can get stuck when excavating as they don't prioritize blocks that will cause them to get stuck. This means you break the last block and instead of falling to safety, they get stuck, sometimes seemingly in midair.). Also, you do not recover resources for deconstruction, so make sure you don't build in the wrong spot.Extractors can be build from any side, but it looks like you need to be in the center and bottom of the extractor to actually make use of them (it could also be left side specific). This is especially annoying since extractors are more efficient (grab more ores) than your dwarves manually mining.All buildings are one directional. This means, for example, the rail ramp rises from left to right. There is nothing in the game I found that tells you how to rotate buildings.The water pump can be built with natural terrain blocking the liquid area, but if you have any non-natural terrain (such as scaffolding), it won't work. This can be annoying if you ended up with water in your base that you want to get rid of. Similarly, water sources can be partially blocked by natural terrain, but you cannot fill in these spaces with placed blocks.It is really annoying and lengthy process to replace buildings. For example, if you want to change a long rail to a long rail station, you can't just place the long rail station on the long rail, you have to destroy the long rail (which will break your railway), then put in the long rail.Building is also annoying. Your dwarves have 12 inventory slots. They will use 1 inventory slot. Maybe 3 if you are lucky. And they are more than happy to run over and deposit the item, then leave, requiring a second dwarf to run over and actually build. They are also more than happy to go all the way back to base to stash their items and then pick up a copy of the material instead of picking up the materials right next to them! This is with inventory space and weight available.Repeat crafting can also get annoying when the game wants to use a specific material when you have other materials. You can get around this by manually selecting the ingredients and doing something like making 4 different repeat builds - one for each ingredient. This was supposed to be fixed, but only when the output item all count as the same item.Selling items is a bit of a mess as items will keep jumping around. Sell all only sells up to 256 of the item (and doesn't always sell everything even when you have less than 256). Note: up to. If you have 257 of the item (such as if you are selling water because you are clearing out the map of water and your pump is active while selling (really fun because you can't really pick to sell from pump only or to auto sell to highest), you will keep just selling 1 unless you manually first sell several items to drop yourself below the 256 threshold, then sell all. And don't think you can just spam because if an item jumps up, the sell all will change to that item instead of following the item you clicked sell all for. And good luck unselling 256 adamantine ore when your selling list is full of 10000+ water and 1000+ molasses (an amazingly well selling item for the effort needed). You have to not only find those 256 adamantine, but you also have to unsell them by dropping them... one at a time.... before they end up on the overworld.You can sort of work around some of the shop options by pausing the game, but the game already takes a long time to beat as is, pausing every time you want to empty your pumps of water (another option being to break them and rebuild) will make it all the longer.You can beat the game without equipping past copper tier gear (you might be able to beat the game with grandfather tier gear if you gather the max dwarves, all personally selected over several hours for the best traits and attack enemies as one large unit, but I didn't try that), but it will take a very long time. Ideally, you want a slime spawn, a mushroom or skeleton spawn, and maybe a rat spawn near your base as resources for various high value items. Obviously, selling better gear will net more money and if you are making those, you probably want to equip your dwarves with that better gear to make battles easier.Note: if you defeat a spawn, the enemies will stop spawning (they also seem to stop spawning if you maintain vision on them). For this reason, it is often better to not defeat spawns except for ones further down where they are far enough from your base that they aren't much worthwhile to seek out.Apparently the devs want to remove water from the farms, which will limit the water you can obtain, making the water sources actually useful instead of nuisances to seal off. Honestly, I think that is just going to make the game less fun and more tedious, because now your dwarves have to run around even more than they already are. (Note: this is how I initially played the game because I didn't realize you had to craft certain items to unlock further recipes and running around trying to find and tap into water sources just wasn't much fun).The devs removed the ability for dwarves to eat off the ground? When a dwarf is stranded and low on stats, I probably want them to do exactly that. Sadly, personal orders are limited (for example, you can't tell a dwarf to specifically demolish an item or jump to safety (if the jump height is too high for the ai).These are just some of the issues with the game (text limit)

_childDocuments_.review: An unjustly maligned game, but one worthy of comment for being a little bizarre. I'm not offering a full-throated recommendation for this game. Actually, it's probably more of a thumbs down-- but it's a lot less harsh than others have been.The central play loop is a somewhat humdrum worker management game, the likes of which you'll have seen done better in other titles, many of them even featuring dwarves.Combat is just another work type, and requires nothing from you- even healing and leaving combat is managed by the troops themselves. Your dwarves have a bad sense for priority and make poor choices when it comes to where to fulfill their individual needs which can lead to a lot of frustrating waiting for things to get done that shouldn't take half as long.What really makes this game interesting and sets it apart is in a secondary layer to the game. You can sell your products to other races, currying influence and using it to whisper rumors (lies) in their ears to get them to like or dislike you as you see fit, or to turn them toward or against the other races as it suits your needs and revealing a (much more intersting) way to play and win the game-- one that gets away from the main loop and leans more into a somewhat alternate mode.I'm a big fan of that part of the game. It's not mind-meltingly unlike anything you've ever seen before, but it IS unique to play as what is essentially a Dwarven Illuminati CEO, deciding not only what wars you want to fight, but what wars are to be fought. It's an new idea, and it's a good one.But the criticism here is that Hammerting isn't doing a great job of being two things. Some games pull that off fine, but with Hammerting, you're left with the impression that the main loop needed a lot more of a fun injection. It feels to me like the devs started making a dwarf fortress game, then struck gold with this Dwarf Illumanti idea, but were already too deep into making a game they never really found the pulse on. But I don't want to slag off the main loop totally. It is 'okay'. And the co-op idea in this style of management game was an interesting addition that I've also never seen in a game of this type. The multiplayer works very well, though it doesn't allow assignment of units or resources, so it's very easy to step on each other's toes when trying to get things done. If you're interested in trying this in co-op, I'd suggest only going in with people you know, get on discord, and keep your number of players low.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: The game sucks. Great graphics, fun idea: all of that squandered on crappy AI and terrible controls/options.Longer version: I've been playing since late May, in Early Access. It's definitely pretty, and there is a technology tree to explore, but... Why? I've been waiting for a purpose to be introduced to the game for over 6 months, and at this point I'm giving up waiting.There are players out there that like to do the same thing over and over, without the merest hint of a thought passing through their heads. "The game is obviously a grind" they might respond, bizarrely thinking that "a grind" is a good thing. I'm not interested in repetitive tasks with no interesting goals in sight. Accrue 5000 gold? Why? Unite all the surface folk (who have zero personality or ability to meaningfully interact with you)? Why?The dwarves here have zero personality. There's mention of them being of different clans, and that there is friction between them because of this: I've never noticed anything of the sort. Perhaps they idle longer? Socialise longer? I have no idea, it has zero impact on gameplay = irrelevant.You can access most all of the materials in the game before you're 1/2 down the mountain. You haven't yet hit the final biome, and thus lack a critical food ingredient (wtf...), but you will have found every ore and gem in the game at this point. Certainly, the rarer ores were slightly more rare, but not by much. I had also researched the whole (short) tech tree: why continue?Up until 2/3s down the mountain, creatures were simple to beat. And this is a central issue with this game: the enemy creatures have almost no AI at all. They will randomly spawn in the darkness and just sit there, forever, until a dwarf comes within their view. Oftentimes I'd get a message that a dwarf was under attack only to find it was a dwarf in a minecart that had whooshed past a random fiendish imp. Right-click on the imp, and a bunch of dwarfs kill it in seconds. The enemy runs at the dwarves, the dwarves run at the enemy = squished imps.Don't worry, they'll respawn again in about 10 min. And again. And again. And again. And again. And again. They won't do anything differently. The dwarves won't do anything differently.Likewise with the lairs: creatures just sit there, waiting for dwarves to appear. When they do, the creatures attack, and they typically get squashed.For the most part. Until the last lair I hit about 2/3 the way down.For context: None of my dwarves were equipped with armour. I hadn't even crafted the early leather you get access to. I had crafted zero weapons. For 15 hours, the combat was a cakewalk.And out of the blue there's slimes that are suddenly just eating my dwarves. Taking roughly zero damage, but knocking them down in 4-5 hits.While that's a crappy way to make the game more difficult (just increase their stats), at least it was a change. I started crafting armour and weapons. But wait... Another dwarf is suddenly unconscious...One dwarf decided to 'aid' a dwarf that had been dropped, so they were also dropped.Another decided that they *really* needed to move something from that area into storage, so *they* dropped.Have you played Rimworld? Where you can mark an area as off-limits to your colonists? That's not an option here.Or you can set your colonists to run from enemies? Nope, not in Hammerting.How about Oxygen Not Included, where you can build a door and deny access to your colonists (thus stopping them from going somewhere)? Also not an option here.In short, the only way to stop my dwarves impersonating lemmings was to go into the Job Manager, go to the second page, and then try to figure out which task was sending my dwarves to their doom, and turn it off. There was a task for every downed dwarf. There was a task for every dropped item. There was a task for every piece of ore and plant that had been dropped, not to mention the food that was brought down to 'aid' the downed dwarves.What. The. ♥♥♥♥.If you're looking for, essentially, a rollercoaster simulator for dwarves, this is the game for you.Otherwise, this is kinda crappy, and I regret backing it in early access.[I'll leave comments on for a bit until the trolls become boring]

_childDocuments_.review: Currently the game needs several reworks in key areas to be good but the devs are focusing on new content rather than fixing the spine of the game so I would check back in 2022 and look at the updates at that time. Right now I would not recommend this game due to the sheer number of annoyances and anti-fun mechanics there are.- The RP aspects for the Dwarfs are pretty good with their own clans personal regions on the map with some in depth thinking about what items/equipment/talents you can employ for them.- Nice artwork for the player's mountain area internally and across the biomes- Pathing is a huge part of the game but it simply isn't working as intended. The logic for it works about 95% of the time but the other 5% is frustrating and time consuming enough to remedy that in an already whack-a-mole type game (more on that below) that it's something that ruins the game.- The Overworld map looks like it's from Mobile game which admittedly has been addressed by the developers is still a big break of the immersion.- "Questing" system needs a complete re-work. As I alluded too early, it's essentially a whack-a-mole system where you are getting new quests as fast as you hand them in leading you to have so much clutter on your UI. The quests themselves are very mundane as they are 100% "give us very basic materials in exchange for incredibly useful materials and points that you require for researching tech. Hours in and I am still flooded with them asking for Copper which is mined from the first few seconds in the game in exchange for materials you have a much harder time getting yourself such as meat/lumber/furs.- Progression system for your dwarfs is incredibly imbalanced to a point where you probably won't care about it too much unless you are overly invested in the game. Your skill point acquisition is incredibly low so you really have to pre-plan your build on each individual dwarf and also remember which build you plan on going on you simply won't be able to interact with some of the late game buildings.- Tech tree is insufferably wide from an early point forcing you again to pre-plan every move you make or really overbear a new player. Unless you know what you are doing then tech points are not that fast to acquire so you will probably end up with a list of quests you can't complete because they are locked behind tech you don't have. It should be much thinner but wider with a clearer choice for a route of progression rather than a ramble to what you can afford the quickest.- Ores/Minerals are attached to the background meaning you can walk past them without ever mining them. Whether or not this is a good idea is made irrelevant by the the fact that half the map isn't something you are mining out but is just empty requiring you to develop, produce, acquire and then craft hundreds of tiles worth of means of passage like scaffolds, stairs, bridges, rail, lifts etc.

_childDocuments_.review: *Edited at bottom after the most recent patch.Hammerting is a game of dwarves and mining. You start the game with just a few dwarves and must explore and expand your underground empire finding new materials and discovering new technologies on the way.My take on the game is this. It can seems a little overwhelming at first due to the complexity, but once you get the basics of what to do it becomes fun and interesting to send your little minions delving into the earth, and finding some of the big mineral veins is a truly great experience.That said, the game is rather poorly optimised, and when you have 20+ dwarves and have discovered most of the map, it lags like crazy, and the AI of the dwarves themselves needs work. They often have all the materials available for cooking, but wont cook, leading to food issues, and they will regularly travel all the way to the far corner of your mine, drop off the materials to build what you want built, and then you have to wait for another dwarf to come and actually build the thing because the delivery dwarf has already run off to go do something else. You can try to solve this by manually telling the dwarf to do the task, but this sometimes doesn't work. If it weren't for the crazy lag in the end game this wouldn't be too much of an issues as they can travel very fast, but with the lag, prepare to watch your construction efforts take a long time.I did and do very much enjoy the game, but having "beaten" the game now, I will probably not play it again for a while until the above issues are fixed.TLDR: Recommend if you enjoy colony sims and digging for gold, but expect a learning curve and some AI issues.Pros: -nice graphics, particularly on the ore seams-fun colony sim-crafting system has depth and is interesting to exploreCons:-AI can be rather stupid-The "Overworld" basically only exists to sell your materials, and is a bit bland-Lags badly when the colony gets bigger-Cooking in particular can be tough to manage*After the latest patch, the farming / cooking issues are much much better, and the game is very playable and much more fun. The AI and the lag have also been improved, but still have work to do when the colony gets very big and you have explored much of the mountain. I now would certainly recommend this game, with the caveat that there is still a bit of a learning curve, and that you may want to play on the "small" mountain size to reduce lag in the end game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tried it again two months after release. 2hours in and I honestly have no need to update my review. I'm just overwhelmed by information from the very first minute, notifications don't stop coming in, the first dwarf drops dead while others are idle. No sound or special effect would notify me of that, it just gets lost in the flood of other infos popping up all the time. I'm sure this game can become quite enjoyable, but it severely lacks polish. It's exhausting to play.I enjoy the art art style of the environment, buildings and UI quite a lot.The game had much more to offer than I had expected.Chill colony builder, as I had hoped.If the following downsides weren't so stressful, this game would make a great addition to my chillout game section.The game completely crushed me with the amount of information. I thought I had seen everything after Oxygen Not Included and Factorio, but figuring out the details comes close to Europe Universalis frustration levels.The UI looks good, yes. But there's two things wrong: First, it overloads you with text and stats about every little part of what you are about to craft. Second, it provides you no easy way of making sense of some highly interweaved mechanics (dwarf stats and crafted tool stats).Dwarves have stats and a skilltree both of which influence their effectiveness in given jobs. Naturally I would soon begin to specialise them into basic categories like fighters, metalworkers, stoneworkers, etc.However each of the stats influences about 6 different jobs and every job has a primary and secondary attribute. If you want to find out what jobs should be blocked for that dwarf, you have to do a whole lot of reading back and forth between the stat infopanels. In fact, I've spent about 2 hours total doing just that over the course of a long gameplay session.Because it gets even more convoluted with the skilltree. It usually adds either stat points or job proficiency. One would assume that there are several career paths to be followed but it becomes very quickly obvious that the skills are even more locked to each other, wildly distributed over all stat points, that specialising is too tiresome and not worth it. In fact I stopped distributing skillpoints and only blocked jobs where I knew I had at max one dwarf working it (e.g. cooking).But that's not it, sorry.I'm glad we have equipment to craft and it even has different parts which affect the effectiveness of the given tool or weapon. It furthermore affected by the chosen material. Now it becomes really complex ... there's no easy way to know in advance which combination works well. So you got to craft a prototype of every combination first and try it. Doing this means going through 3-5 submenus depending on what you're doing for dozens of different parts. This is extremely time consuming in itself making up easily a third of my gametime.At the very last chosing the loadout for a single dwarf brings us back to the skillpoint problem again as it is not clear what kind of specialty he has (I mean it is, if you invest another 5 minutes figuring it out). And if you don't block the jobs in all dwarves, unspecialised ones will block the working areas of your specialists.Oof, this all boils down to ...The aforementioned is already very tiresome, but you also need to equip every single tool manually to every single dwarf. If you want to explore somewhere, you have to do it manually. If you give far away work orders, they will probably not do it by themselves. If you craft something with a auto-order without checking from what parts it was made, it could fill up the storage with parts made from the wrong material and you have to redo that again as well. I have spent a ton of time clicking through crafting menus and modifying the proper amounts for auto-crafted parts.After about 8 hours into the game I now experience frequent crashes to desktop. This is the second within the hour. Will check back with the game when the next update comes.I like it - I almost gave it a recommendation. But the needless complexity through obfuscation and micromanagement hell are more stressful to me than relaxing.I was thinking a few times about refunding (because major flaws like these are rarely fixed during Early Access). I definitely got a false impression from the reviews before buying and expected something simpler but much more polished.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this game, the devs have put in a lot of work, but I'm not necessarily recommending you buuy the game in it's current state. This was one of my top games in this months humble bundle pack, and now it's my greatest disappointment. _childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a recommendation between 'yes' and 'no', because that's what I'd give this game.The graphics are nice. In early game it feels good to play. As you can see from my play time, if you're just looking for something pretty to escape into for a short time that doesn't stress you out too much, this game is ok.Then in the later game things fall apart. The game gets laggy. There are occasional bugs here and there with movement and crafting. The overworld battle system is shallow, and frankly, involving yourself in it meets that saying about insanity doing the same thing over and over but expecting a different result. Your involvement in the overworld system really has little effect. You craft a mythic heavy metal armored ring with 10+ defense stats in each of crushing, piercing and slashing damage, afix a star of mara jewel to it in the expectation those defense stats will be boosted, only to have the resulting jewel afixed ring have worse stats than an un-afixed uncommon iron armored ring (ie 5~). (That was the thing that just now pissed me off enough to write this review.) There's no way to order surplus items get auto sold off based on their quality.I always play on the largest map size and have yet to dig deep enough to find those sulpur sprouts. I don't think I ever will, because before I get down there I get bored and/or frustrated with the other mechanics.Given the amount of play time I've had I won't go so far as to say I regret buying the game but ... In it's current state I wouldn't regard it as polished enough to be considered a finished game.So, if you only ever really play a short, casual game  for an hour or two at a time, and you like pretty graphics, then this will do you, because you likely won't have a play session long enough to experience the problems that do exist.If you're looking for a deeper game experience, it's a no.
