_childDocuments_.review: I stopped playing this game when I realized I'm only playing it because I want something like it to be good, rather than because it _is_ good.There is a ton of micro needed that really shouldn't be there - Having to manually manage scaffolding or dirt block removal because the dwarves will remove the closest one, preventing them from removing the rest? In a game largely about digging? Or only being able to mark ~10 blocks to be dug out at a time in a direction because you can't mark anything beyond your field of vision? Or manually adding upgrades to individual dwarf homes when it's normal to have 10-20 dwarves? This game is filled with tedium.There's also almost no actual pressure in the game - swarms aren't a threat, and you can block them out trivially with a few placed blocks.Each additional update should be a clear improvement, but they've been hit or miss, and they (at least recently) have missed the mark at actually making the game better - they just make it more complex. The game didn't need relationships between the dwarves, and, even after a release focused on that, they don't actually seem to matter to your settlement. Adding farming in the dirt (instead of it being in a building) now makes farming something that you can't manage the same way you do all of your buildings' work. Epic crafting (leveled gear) is neat, but no one is going to buy this game for RNG-driven leveled crafting. In the mean time, the only win condition is amassing a truly enormous amount of money (again, only achievable through tedious repetition), because the devs removed the main story line 6 updates ago.Did I mention this game is leaving early access in a month?

_childDocuments_.review: Keep in mind that this game is in Early Access, so things will change.I am a big fan of games like Dwarf Fortress and Rimworld, this is similar in the aspect that you don't really have direct control over your Dwarves, you issue build orders and plan your mining/construction and wait for it to happen.I really like the quests in the  Overworld that contribute to the war effort, that adds to the overall sense of contribution that your Mountainhome is providing.Overall, this game is definitely worth playing.A few things that took me far too long to figure out myself:- Granite blocks and crushed gravel repair buildings.- Your Dwarves can only hold 3 tools, and there are more than 3 jobs.  If you want a Dwarf to cook or make Jewellery, you have to make the tool and equip it on them. (I spent far too long wondering why no one was cutting gems)- Your shops reserve based on what is first in inventory.  If you want your new Pickaxe to be copper, make sure the first items available in the Smith is copper.- Since your shop reserves first based on inventory, if you don't have enough of the first item, the shop won't automatically switch to or substitute.  You have to cancel the queue, drop that item from the shop, queue it up again.- The Overland quests cycle in what seems to be two batches.  You need to do them to get the next batch, this is important to get wood.- The quests don't currently pay enough coin.  Make a billion pillars and sell them. (or copper weapons, copper sells for more than iron does)With these basic hints, you'll be well on your way to enjoy the early access version of the game.cheers,

_childDocuments_.review: ***EARLY ACCESS REVIEW***I gotta say, so far, I like this game. I can't decide whether or not to recommend it just yet due to some rather annoying and outright idiotic behavior on the part of our little bearded axe wielding friends. In keeping with my belief that one should never present a problem without simultaneously presenting a solution, I offer some suggestions that I hope aren't exceedingly stupid or just plain impossible. 1- Pathfinding - SERIOUS issues here. It has gotten a lot better, but there are times when a dwarf either runs back and forth in a hilarious impression of Butthead dancing, or simply refuses to moved until a "dig" or "mine" command is issued close to him. That seems to force a path recalculation and snap them out of it. There needs to be a fail-safe in place to prevent this. Maybe a script that checks to see if the dwarf needs to move but can't find a way. If yes, compare the current path to the last few and make sure the dwarf isn't stuck in a pathfinding loop. Maybe count the number of tiles the dwarf needs to travel through before reaching his destination, and if this number hasn't dropped by a certain percentage since the last check, force a recalc (I'm a coding noob, forgive me if none of this is possible).The second part of pathfinding I find annoying: Dwarfs wandering off into the caves, jumping or falling off a ledge, and getting stuck in a pit. They also dig themselves into situations like this with annoying regularity. I'd like to think that most Dwarfs are smart enough to look over the edge of a cliff and make sure they can climb back up before they just jump off, and seeing as they live underground and dig tunnels constantly, they should not be digging the ground out from under their own feet if there is naught but empty space below it.  Maybe some kind of "reverse pathfind" that assesses the path from where the dwarf will land back to their current position? And perhaps a "Stonesense" skill that allows them to see under the ground at their feet, so they don't pull the Dwarf equivalent of sawing off the limb upon which they are sitting. And while we're on that subject, how about making sure that other Dwarfs aren't total A-holes? I've lost count of how many times one Dwarf has dug the ground out from under another's feet and sent the poor bugger hurtling to the bottom of a mine shaft. And here's an idea to fix a lot of the Wile E. Coyote behavior, while at the same time giving those squishy explorers a better chance of survival: GRAPPLING HOOKS. Give them a rope and a hook, and let them spelunk to their heart's content. Don't have a grappling hook? "Explore" job is disabled. Can't go wandering off on your own. Simple as that. Whilst exploring, avoid combat as much as possible. And try not to kite the entire population of the seventh layer of Hell back to the colony, please? 2- WEAPONS - Dwarfs need crossbows. No question. Ranged weaponry is a must. Maybe even guns at some point, especially after Chymical Forging is unlocked. And how about some magic users? Dwarfs can be mages, too. 3- GUARD POSTS - They need these, too. A race of people who live among subterranean horrors of all shapes and sizes should have a basic grasp of defense, which includes doors that can be locked, defensive traps, permanent outposts bristling with spiky things, siege engines, angry little beer-swilling axe hurlers, and maybe even some allies from the surface to lend a hand in defending the only source of Dwarf weaponry to which they have access. Just a thought. 4- HAULING - This really needs fine tuning. I tried to build a drill, and simply could.... not... do it.... because the dwarfs kept stealing the metal plates from each other and running them back and forth all over the mountain like they were playing some weird underground version of rugby. That's when I noticed that the only building that has a "Priority" setting built right in is the warehouse/storage/whatever I can't recall its actual name at the moment. I had to shut down all production at both of my smithies to finally get the little buggers to quit screwing around and deliver the plates to the drill. Also had a similar problem where the farm was stealing all the lime, and I couldn't make any mortar because of it. There needs to be a supply priority system that the player can change. It could be done at the building level, much the same way the warehouse is currently implemented (setting that joker to "High" makes every dwarf run about the place picking up everything in sight), but more granularity might be required (per production order, for example). 5- COMBAT IN GENERAL - I didn't know that being short could make someone so suicidal. I had a dwarf that simply WOULD NOT do anything except run off and fight spiders. I spent 15 minutes trying to convince the little twerp to do anything else. Manually issued orders to pick up shrooms, mine ore, dig tunnels, walk around aimlessly, all sorts of things, in hopes that he would finally let go of his hate and stop acting like a Troll Slayer in search of a mighty doom. Didn't work. Dude might as well have been named Snorri Nosebiter. As soon as I turned my back, he took up his axe, gave a mighty war cry, and ran off into the dark to meet his end. I only knew he had fallen when I heard his death cry echoing through the cavernous halls.I guess his buddies hated him as much as he hated spiders (and himself), because they did NOTHING to help him when he was unconscious. I had a well-stocked infirmary and there was a clear path to the place where he fell, but the rest of the dwarfs did nothing for the poor little wretch, even when I sent a party out to retrieve him. They could have dragged him back to the infirmary, at least. Well, such is the life of a Dwarf. His bones now lie mouldering in the cloying darkness 'neath the Mountainhome. May his soul find peace in the realms beyond.One last Combat related item: Monsters currently have limitless and completely irrational hatred for all things Dwarf, so much so that they will pursue a Dwarf to the very ends of the Prime Material Plane to separate soul from flesh. Please give the enemies a "chase distance." If a Dwarf is outrunning a monster, and the monster's home is safe, they shouldn't follow the Dwarf all the way home like some kind of twisted, evil, murderous lost puppy.All jokes aside, there needs to be a "Stance" function that affects all dwarfs at once. "Offensive" means they can team up with other angry Dwarfs and go attack things, "Defensive" means they will only attack things that attack the colony, or approach too closely. Not sure if there is a need for individual stance manipulation, but it could be done based on each Dwarfs combat ability. And they should never, ever run off alone to be murdered by ill-tempered eight-legged freaks. And lastly: can we have a sandbox mode, please? I'd like to just build a colony without all the surface world drama. Blasted manlings and pointy-ears can handle their own problems for a change!These are the most glaring issues I have seen to date. I am actually loving this game in spite of the problems, and I really hope it succeeds! Keep at it, devs!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, Hammerting is a pleasant experience for those who want to focus solely on base building. That said, it does have a few issues, namely the fact that there is just a general lack of things to do once you establish your colony with proper food supply and mining mechanization. For me, the game was engaging up until I started mechanizing everything and adding railway lines everywhere, on top of having a never ending food supply. My suggestion to add more content to the game would be to focus more on how the Dwarves impact the overworld, such as being able to customize embassies established in other nations instead of it just being a task on a missions sidebar. I would also suggest the ability for Dwarves to be able to more directly influence nations of the overworld, such as establishing mechanized trade lines with railway tracks to increase trading speed and maybe even being able to take "bulk orders" or weapons or armor in order to expedite the process. I would also suggest adding ways for Dwarves to participate in overworld battles in some way. I recommend the game on sale, but I can't say in its current state that it's worth the full price, as current tasks become monotonous and non-engaging once you reach a certain point in the "end game".

_childDocuments_.review: So...Hammerting.  Ultimately I had to decide between a "yes" or a "no" for this game.  What ended up deciding it was if the game was worth it currently (as of 04/2022) and the answer for me was a begrudging yes.  Did I enjoy the first 20 hours of gameplay?  Absolutely.  Trying to dig hard/deep while keeping my delicate balance of systems intact was fun and warding off attacks from both outside as well as the deeps seemed to prove a worthy challenge.The problem?  It is terribly shallow, does some impressive stretches to enlarge the time sink,  all the while doing an awful job of explaining itself.-You need to know what materials are best for each profession's tools or weapons?  Tough ♥♥♥♥.  Seek out a spreadsheet on the forums.-Got the min-max materials from the spreadsheet?  Oof, too bad your uberskilled dwarf had sausage fingers when rolling item stats and your expensive ring is now effectively a paperweight.  Try again and GIT GUD!-Get geared out finally?  Great, tough titties you dig into a rat hole in the 9th circle of hell and they dog pile your poor dwarf before running up the stairs +slaughtering all 35 geared/leveled dwarves of your colony.  Turns out, even though its the same few mobs copy pasted all over....but different biomes have arbitrarily boosted stats to extend difficulty.  So... THOSE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ had resistance levels to all  weapon damages/armor mitigation that would allow a snow man to tan while eating tamales with Satan in Cancun.  -Didn't leave a slime spawner alive?  Dont be jelly  you have to limp through the rest of the run without multiple food/medicine types because you cant buy it at all.  Several goods are NOT buyable or a few are ONLY buyable (nicest wood/hides) and in very low quantity forcing you to go back frequently to click several times for a few items.-Overworld trade/war?  Just spam trade currency and the world will eat ♥♥♥♥ off your boots.  Just dont ask itself to explain quests, how to join a faction, or really participate in anything at all.-Automated selling/buying of goods?  goodluck figuring that out, only got part of it before my 80 hours were up and im still not sure if the auto buying is a thing so you have to micromanage the damn thing.- the game LAGS horribly as time goes on because your dwarves drop crap by default or if you over Q a building.  To compound this, its the lowest priority by default to clean it up so until it starts to set in you might not realize it.-Dwarves like to chill out until they starve on stair edges and will be "unreachable" if downed in this spot so they will absolutely die unless you destroy the stairs in time.To top it all up, rumor has it that the development team is now calling it quits with updates/tweaks when the game still feels so empty/superficial.So...why recommend the game?  I got it on sale and it happily killed a few evenings to make it worth the price I paid.  I will not be reinstalling it as it has no replay value to me.  If you want a more replayable/in depth/polished equivalent then go look at Oxygen Not Included.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT : Changing my review to positive. The game is being patched, improved, bugs are being fixed. It looks good! Still wish we could rebind keys though, moving the camera on an AZERTY keyboard is a bit annoying (Z is considered a cancel action).-----------------------------------I'm a bit annoyed because I almost never give games negative reviews, and I have to do it for this one, at least temporarily.It's early access, but it's -too early- access.No way to mute the game or change the volume, no way to rebind the keys (problematic for non-qwerty users), bugs upon bugs (dwarves getting stuck in stairs a lot), and a UI that could seriously be improved (if you make it mandatory to right click an item to give it to a dwarf, at least make it easy to find every item from the ledger).  There's a ton of good stuff too. The graphics are nice, it feels very "dwarfy", the way depth is handled for stairs and rooms is very clever. The skill system looks cool. The research tree is very short but that's excusable for an early access. I'm sure the game will get better, and I'll gladly change this review to positive when it does, but for now I think you should just wishlist it and wait for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Oi! Ye! Aye, ye!Ye be a dwarf, ye say?Is yer belly filled wit’ ale and yer pockets ‘eavy with gold? Do ye fancy yer women folk wit’ glorious beards as thick as yers? Do ye feel the call o' the stone beckoning ye to take yer grandfather’s pickaxe an’ hack into the depths of a mountain?Will ye bolster relations wit’ yer dwarven brethren from rival clans?Are ye excited ‘bout forging an’ maintaining the next dwarven kingdom to rival the grand halls o’ Moria an’ save the fragile surface world? - ...cause we always do!Aye, you say?Aye… perhaps ye be a dwarf, down ‘ere where it counts – at the beard, ye git! So, what are ye waiting fer? Grab yer ale, enter the Hammerting and start digging! The gold an’ glory won’t dig themselves out!What is Hammerting?Hammerting is a base builder with colourful and cartoonish graphics, which gives a sense that this game is meant for a casual player, yet it contains depths that appeal to less casual players. Hammerting’s premise revolves around a colony of dwarves establishing their base in the depths of a mountain, all the while war rages through the surface. The main task is to forge and manage a colony of dwarves and aid their allies on the surface.I would like to start with the state of the game and why I believe this is a product you should keep an eye for.While many reviews state that this game is not yet ready for release, I’d argue that the base game is ready. By base game, I mean that it is playable and has no game-breaking bugs. I am not saying that this game is, by all definitions, bug-free or that it doesn’t require additional features. I am stating that it is playable at its current stage based on my personal experience with Hammerting. Moreover, I want to point out that the game was developed by a small development studio called Warpzone Studios and is their first project. While the development team is small, they are skilled and dedicated, with many years of experience in their respective fields and prior experience working in the game development field. This is why Hammerting is a product the members of Warpzone Studios hold dear to their hearts and want to develop it until it reaches the potential they saw in it back in 2016 when the development process started.Let’s talk about the dwarves:The dwarves, it seems, are inspired by Tolkien and D&D concepts of dwarves, which makes them very lore-friendly, fitting in a high fantasy world-setting. From the art style used to draw the dwarves to the fact that female dwarves also have a beard are good attention to detail and a homage to the classical high-fantasy dwarven races. Another aspect is the different clans, which also draws inspiration from the same sources. Other dwarven clans have their own cultures and ideologies and can’t always get along. This feature is represented by a variety of clan symbols and via relationships between the dwarves. This is also a task that you, the player, must maintain.Your dwarves and their lack of control:As much as we like to micro-manage each player character’s tasks and movements, the Hammerting allows us only to push the dwarves into the general direction of our goals. It is up to the dwarves to decide where they should go, what should they forge and when to run away from a fight. While it takes from micro-managing your units, it provides a sense of autonomy out of our control, which forces us to create an environment where you anticipate the dwarves actions and plan for them. More speed… moar speed!A common feature in base-building games is the ability to set up and speed up time. After learning a base building game, we usually tend to set the time speed on its fastest setting and see our bases sprawl like a flower blooming on a sunny summer morning.After playing the Hammerting a couple of times, the game’s average speed felt too slow. Tasks felt tedious. Travel was excruciating, and combat lasted forever. Therefore after learning the basics of the game, I’d crank up the speed to the fastest  After playing on higher speeds, I can’t find myself getting back to average speed again. Gameplay-wise, Hammerting draws you into its grasp with surprisingly calming and repetitive music. When loading the game, I expected thumping music and a dark atmosphere akin to what you should expect from Tolkien-inspired dwarven society. Instead, I was introduced to calming and repetitive music, which looped from the main menu into the actual game. While initially, I considered it a design mistake, the music gently drew me deeper into the game. Combined with sound effects with speed set on fastest (more on that later), I ended up playing for hours while remaining calm and collected with my crafting decisions.Moreover, the calming music track enhances the graphics’ colourful, cartoonish, and lighthearted setting.In conclusion, Hammerting is a game I am actively playing as a proud dwarf, and I highly recommend giving it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting mix of Craft The World and Oxygen Not Included. It doesn't reach anywhere near the level of complexity of Oxygen Not Included though.The general gameplay loop feels fairly relaxed. Once I had placed my initial production buildings and figured out the basics I never felt particularly challenged. There are odd rats, slimes and other enemies that appear from time to time and as you explore you will come across various enemy holes in the wall to clear. But none of them ever seem to be a threat. There are no organised attacks on your home. This may be something that is changed when the overland diplomacy features are added.I didn't encounter any majors issues with the AI getting stuck. The handful of times that someone got stuck was usually due to me telling them to do something dumb like digging straight down. In fact, I was quite impressed that the AI actually factors in blocks required for support when digging out large areas and then clears those blocks at the end.There is definite room for improvement, especially when it comes to QoL items. Being able to track resource totals more easily would be a big help and a bit more depth to the crafting systems to allow more intelligent choices of what materials to use would be nice.It would also be nice if the dwarves themselves had a bit more character. Each of them belong to one clan or another and have a few traits but ultimately it didn't seem to have any real impact. Deeper social interactions and character flaws would add some nice variety to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hammerting is very promising. Though it's early access there's quite a lot of mechanics in play that impressed me. There's great depth in Dwarf stats/skills/perks/equipment progression. The Win/Loss condition is very unique and fits the theme for Dwarfs. Replayability definitely will come from trying to min/max your building, gathering, tech, and combat effectiveness. There's a lot of quality of life additions I'd love to had added such as a tab to see every resource available that you've mined (kinda like RimWorld).Check out my gameplay preview for Hammerting here: Disclaimer: I received this game for free. I was not paid to promote or write a review. All thoughts are solely my own. Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: -INTRODUCTION-So I got to try the demo and was hooked up to it and bought the game. Bought this for $28.99 but tbh it feels like it should have been at $15-19 at its state.-PROS-You can get easily hooked with the game if you're into builder-type game. Not really much story into it yet but at considering it is EA, it kinda suffice.-CONS-Again, EA stuff. Lots of bugs. _childDocuments_.review: I will start by saying I only recommend this game if you get it for *quite* cheap and tend to enjoy colony sim games, like many others I got it from Humble choice and I thought it was quite the interesting game. I actually enjoyed the few hours I put into it, the game is interesting, it looks nice (apart from some of the guis) and it is an incredibly interesting concept. I usually find myself playing colony sim games in a binge format which is possibly the least healthy way to digest these but whatever. My point for stating this is that you tend to find the flaws of a game like this when you play for several hours in a row and let me tell you, this game has flaws. Just to start...* No priority queue, there is only low neutral and high, and the highest isn't always prioritized* the AI for the colonists (dwarves) is not the brightest tends to get stuck, and gets sidetracked easily (this would be remedied by better priority)* placement of anything can be weird, with no snappoints (tracks can be placed anywhere not just on a station, meaning you can miss a gap and spend lots of time finding it)* Money is ultimately meaningless and only used to sustain your colonists* Reputation with other nations means nothing, just better prices for nothing specifc.* Lumber, a very important resource is incredibly sparse, unreasonably so.* research is incredibly cheap, meaning you will have all tech within a few hours.All of those flaws being listed, I would still recommend the game, but not in the state that it is in today. There is a lot of room for improvement and honestly most of those are QoL changes, and generic improvements like making the game make more sense, balancing resources more so that you actually have to manage what your colonists are doing, or face consequences. things just to make things that happen in the game more ***meaningful*** to something. TL;DR this game is REALLY(!!!) cool and I thoroughly enjoyed it through what would usually be game breaking flaws, namely the meaninglessness of most mechanics. The only reason is because its a new(er)-ish take on a colony sim, and has a lot going for it, as well as visual appeal. The only reason I dont regret paying (through humble choice) is because I got it for pretty cheap and the game is in Early Access being updates as little as a month ago (at the time of writing).

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I like the game, but in its current state, it is not worth the price.**This review may contain minor spoilers**I like this game, but it feels like its missing something. On the surface it checks all the boxes. Have a bunch of characters, each with their distinct traits, build, mine, trade, explore. But it feels like this game is just "going through the motions" of a colony building game. There is no substance to it. I like the idea of dwarves digging a mine, which is pretty much the only thing keeping me in the game. There is no "oomph" here. So let me go through the points one by one.Characters: Although the characters are all distinct, they feel exactly the same. I feel no need to treat my pawns as individuals. Let me use Rimworld as a counter example: When I have a bad cook in my colony, I know I very much don't want this person to cook. Because when they do, the food will come out bad, which can make other people sick or I have to throw it out. This forces me very strongly to look at the strengths and weaknesses of my pawns and assign them the right tasks. In Hammerting however, everyone of my dwarves feels like a villager in AOE.Building: Building is very shallow. Plop the building down, done. Buildings are very simplistic in funtion. Mostly you put coal in as a fuel, have some raw materials and produce cut stone or whatever. Since pawns are basically all the same, someone will produce things eventually. If you feel fancy you can assign someone a "favourite" job, but thats like whatever. Production chains dont really feel meaningful. You can produce honey and from honey you make mead, and sometimes your dwarves consume mead (I think). But never once was there a point where I was like "O damn I need more mead NOW!". There is nothing forcing you to keep the wheel spinning. Just set your buildings to produce a bit of everything and you are good.Same thing with weapons and tools. There is a bunch of different ways to make your tools. Is one of these ways better than another? Maybe. Does it matter? Nah.Mining/Exploring: Mining is also kind of whatever. Mark the blocks, someone will go pick them up sometime. Sometimes you will find open space with something in it. But findings never feel impactful. Find a rat nest? Destroyed. Find a graveyard? Destroyed. No meaningful changes in gameplay or mechanics. Mobs dont really pose a threat ever. Sometimes you also find new production buildings, but those are also meh. Nothing really screams "Oh yeah now you can do THAT cool new thing!"Trade: Trade seems like it should be a key mechanic in the game, but its also very shallow. Instead of missions of "Buy X or sell Y" I'd like to have trade agreements. "Sell this one town 10 spears each month" or stuff like that. Then make it so that the production is actually plannable. Like "I assign this guy to produce shafts and if I always have the materials he makes 10 shafts per month. So if I assign 2 people to produce this other thing I need, I have such and such many spears each month." This would automatically put more importance on each dwarves differences. There should also be something that constantly drains your money. For instance buildings that need maintenance. Some need wood to maintain, so you always have to buy some wood from somewhere, which costs money, which forces you to somehow make money constantly, which forces you to think about your production and what you want to sell.All in all the lack of urgency makes this game feel pretty bland. Its an OK game but it could be so much more.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Not yet, it is still in Early Access. Starting with 3 dwarves (more can be hired), you build a dwarven colony on the peak of a mountain. Your dwarves have a lot to do, they need to dig into the mountain, mine minerals or stones, build structures underground and craft stuff. Growing food or fighting other mountain dwelling creatures should also not be neglected.I'd suggest to build a quarry first, otherwise you will soon have no stones to build anything anymore. Not that this happened to me, of course. Then a foundry is a good idea, cause dwarves are the best smithies. Then maybe something where your dwarves can rest when they don't work. Or a cave farm to grow some mouldy mushrooms? You get the picture - collect ressources, build structures, don't starve or otherwise die. Explore the mountain by digging deeper and deeper, research new technologies and abilities - you give orders to your little greedy dwarves, and they obey as long as they have the required materials. Combat happens automatically when cave creatures are found.When your dwarves work, they gain experience and you can improve their attributes. While you build and craft and the time flies by, there is a war going on on the outside, and your colony supports one side. Deliver them the ressources they require, and help their war effort. You receive valuable ressources from the outside in return. Do not send them ressources, and your side will lose the war to "The Horde", and that's something you do not want to happen.The game reminds me of "Oxygen Not Included". Instead of a space rock you now dig into a mountain, but many of the game elements are similar. This is not a bad thing of course, "Oxygen Not Included" is a fantastic game. Although still in Early Access, I did not see any features obviously still missing. There are a bunch of planned features, but they will all improve the current game and are not necessary to play it.Build a dwarven colony inside a mountain and help them to survive and thrive.

_childDocuments_.review: I was in the mood for a colony management sim in a generic fantasy setting and Hammerting is 100% that. Its core structure is pretty similar to Oxygen Not Included: recruit workers, excavate a giant grid of various kinds of dirt and stone, build workstations, and convert raw resources into goods to satisfy the various needs of the colony. But where ONI is a brutal (if inconsistent) physics simulation, Hammerting is less gritty and more forgiving. Much of the game is still about making sure your workers can efficiently get to places and diagnosing where a production problem is happening, but there's much less focus on automation and exploiting physics cheats. I didn't have to spend nearly so much time with a wiki. Which is good, because there's hardly anything in the Hammerting wiki. Also, it's much, much prettier than ONI.That said, if you're NOT very much in the mood for this specific subgenre, I'm not sure I can recommend it. The main problem is that you quickly become self-sufficient, and once you do most of the purpose drains out of the game. Effectively colony sims constantly lure you into thinking that if you just complete this  life will be golden. They push the state of colony self-sufficiency back as far as possible while making it feel like you're on the cusp. The thing is, Hammerting already has the necessary tools to make surviving an ongoing struggle. Where ONI is a constant battle with entropy, Hammerting has much more literal battles both within and beyond the mountain. The issue is that these just don't scale with your colony and barely qualify as a nuisance. On Hard enemy difficulty I never had a single dwarf in danger with any attack. After several tries on Very Hard it was obvious that you need a lucky start, but if you get it you'll still outgrow all your enemies. Just increasing the number, variety, and challenge of the enemy waves as time goes on would help create the tension the game is currently lacking. As it is, Hammerting commits a cardinal game sin: your victory becomes inevitable a long, tedious time before the game makes it official.The overworld is a potentially compelling addition that is entirely wasted. It feels like an artifact from an early alpha. "Armies" are giant statues that slide around the map without animation, "fighting" by flinging out sprays of blood icons. Factions have nice descriptions of their home biome, but all the visible terrain consists of just grass and snow. Each faction has an opinion of you, but all this affects is how much you buy and sell for. Factions will never attack you or your traders. Because you quickly have way more money than you need (money is consumed by dwarves like food, but very slowly) and almost never actually  the goods the factions sell, the only reason to engage the overworld is to slowly grind towards a diplomatic victory. A faction's opinion of you doesn't seem to connect in any logical way to your own actions unless you spend trade points to manually change it. In my current run I picked Generic Paladin Faction to be my besties. I spent enormous effort hauling granite blocks to their capital to keep it intact in the face of relentless orcish raids, sold them all the weapons I could produce, and was rewarded by their steadily falling opinion of me. (The orcs in contrast held steady at dead neutral.)  The game could also use more attention to detail. A dwarf's AI will sometimes hang and have to be manually instructed to move. Pathfinding is not terrible given the map complexity but still inconsistent. A number of building and infrastructure options appear to be straight noob traps: staircases for example are both more expensive than simple scaffolds to build and also much slower for your dwarves to traverse. The game wants you to specialize your dwarves, but the skill tree actively defies your efforts to specialize; it merges instead of branching. The tutorial is inadequate, so your first playthrough is likely to involve a bunch of googling. On thing I will say though: I was very impressed with the way mining dwarves "reserve" blocks of terrain for last to make sure they'll be able to reach the higher spots you've indicated for mining. Kudos to whoever on the dev team is responsible for that.Overall, the game needs to better balance for mid- and late-game difficulty, a more robust overworld game, and some additional quality of life passes. In its current form it's a pleasant, low-stress way to kill some hours in a soothingly familiar fantasy setting rendered in a very pretty style. If that's what you're hankering for, I recommend it. Otherwise at $25 I'd have to say you should wait and see what additional content the devs add.

_childDocuments_.review: In an industry ripe with sub par colony management games, it doesn't take long for a gem like Hammerting to stand out from the rest.The music and ambient design is very fitting for this game and even after hours of play it still is a joy to listen to.Building and structure management has an interesting and very successful approach. It has a fun first and planning second approach by separating things into 2 layers. The first layer is where walkways, bridges, and extra elements like doors or torches are built. the 2nd layer goes behind the first with rooms built into the walls behind it. It allows for fun and interesting layouts where you can design layouts orderly or slam them in chaotic and all over the place with walkways be built before, during or after the process.There is no immediate doomsday approaching like we see in games like Oxygen Not Included where unbalanced systems or too slow of progressiom result in the collapse of your colony. In Hammerting you get to choose the pace. You decide how and when to expand, you decide how and when to explore, you decide how and when to learn new things. Instead, the challenge comes from how complicated you decide it will be.There is an overworld element where a war is raging between the forces of good and bad and you are the dwarves not fighting in it (yet. who knows if its a feature being added in later) but you are the driving force behind equipping your side with items, tools, and even food they may need. Its really fun.In terms of the challenge it can come in several different ways. You can open up lots of paths to explore and risk more ways monsters can approach from, or even what monster lairs you will discover. You can create custom items and tools for each and every dwarf customized to their specific tailored tasks using different types of handles, heads, and even the ores used in its crafting. You can even take on lots of different crafting jobs and try to keep up with the demand of all of them working simultaneously together. You are always in control.The game is currently in early access and there are some bugs in it but they are all minor in the sense that all of the major game functions still work. For me personally I've encountered doors not working properly so everything passes through them like they aren't even there, and dwarves get stuck on the elevator you can start to build later on. But other then that the game works great and the developers are already working on fixing them.And for the streamers and content creators, all your dwarves names are customizable which is always an added plus.If you are on the fence about the game, you should get it. its fantastic for both new players to this type of genre and veterans will find some new fun elements added in to everything they already love.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is quite fun, and it should be noted that this is still Early Access so some quirks are to be expected. _childDocuments_.review: Edit: I've edited my original review, after playing a bit on release version. If you want to read original review, scroll down - though a few things I pointed was changed and fixed.The game improved a lot since the early access version I started playing (0.6 or 0.7), but I still cannot recommend it on full price unless you're die-hard fan on dwarven colony sim games. While there is a roadmap and planned features, and the development is very active (and friendly!), this is purely sandbox experience even when playing on highest difficulity.- Old Review -I really wanted to like this game.I'm a fan of all things dwarfish, and spend a ridiculous amount of time playing original DF and games inspired by it (the only notable worth mentioning is Craft the World, but I personally doesn't like its childish graphics) - Hammerting looked like it could cure the itch, and allow me to happly dig down to ultimately find my doom. And then repeat this again.The game aestethics looks great, carverns, buildings - okay, maybe 3d models are not really that good - but pretty much everything looks pretty. Crafting system is interesting, with different material stats contributing differently to finished items. Tools system is quite nice, limiting the dwarf to three professional items or weapons.But even on the highest difficulty, the game is... ridiculously easy. It's just grindy and tedious, and two last updates as of writing this review (Relationiship and Farming) did not make it any better. Perhaps even made it worse.Notable faults:- They removed the war, I had no chance of playing it as I bought the game after they removed it but its still mentioned everywhere.- Every playthrough looks the same. - Construction removal and digging is tedious (order of things doesnt matter, the dwarfs just deconstruct the closest stairs until you manually change priorities aftewards, which is tedious multiplied by its square).- Dwarves frequently stucks while digging, hugging to walls when they could just drop by like four tiles without even health damage.- Dwarves are immortal - when downed, they get rescued and healed back. No real risk.- Leveling up is ridiculously easy - especially for farmers and masons. You just need to make production take all storage space within the building and they will keep producing stuff indefinitly (corps and stones doesn't require any special resources). Bam, you have a lvl 50 dwarf 25 minutes into the game.- Monster 'Waves' are a big, laughting joke.- AI, AI, AI... Why even with turned off Militia skill the dwarves bravely rush to fight enemies marked to kill?- Trade is meh. Town markets are fixed per playthrough, past early game you don't really need to buy anything anymore, except for wood for more dwellings, you cannot place any buy or sell orders, you need to manually click for stuff to happend. You can easly cap all relations for best prices with all factions by spending few trading points. Nothing makes sense here...- Combat is implemented poorly - while there are multiple damage types and resistances, and lots and lots of weapons, it really doesn't matter. What matters is to have best quality stuff made of best materials and your dwarves will beat the crap out of enemies even when heavy outnumbered.I really wanted to like this game, and this is bordering on neutral opinion, but the game is almost out of early access. Two last patches did not added any value to the game. Even when half of my dwarves hated other half, never once a fight broke between them which would cause a tantrum spir... wait, wrong game.Improve the combat, improve the AI, make better economy both within the region and within the hold, allow us to place buy/sell orders or even just filter the damn trading screen, make monster waves actually be something to fear AND BRING BACK THE WAR.

_childDocuments_.review: Important: The Devs stated on March 17, 2022 that they will no longer be working on the game or doing any major additions to it -- Aside from bug fixes and fixing major issues. If this changes, I'll adjust that in the future.Hammerting is another entry in the "Dwarves build a fortress and try not to die" genres. It has a lot of promise and some really good systems setup, but they lack the polish and expansion that is desperately needed to be a truly great game about Dwarves. The AI is buggy and there is slow down that occurs when you get to the deeper part of the mountain and start having 40+ Dwarves run around.There are also some strange decisions with tech tree layout, progress, monster spawns, the over world map/interactions, over world missions (and lack thereof), end game grind (victory conditions are literally big time sinks), etc. etc. -- It's your Early Access that released too early issues. It's pretty much a dime a dozen these days.Now, apart from all that -- I thought this game was an absolute joy to play, issues aside. I found it relaxing and let me sort of progress at my own pace. I actually really liked the presentation and artwork for the game and the music, albeit repetitive, was rather pleasing to listen to. I couldn't put it down until I finished my first play through after about 35-40 hours. I am thinking of strategies for my next run and what I would do different in terms of base layout and stupid Dorf goals to achieve.Pick it up on a sale, I don't think it's quite ready for a $25 price tag, but for $15 or less -- Definitely, especially if you like this genre.Edits: Grammar/spelling.

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't recommend it at $25. I got it as part of Humble Bundle many moons ago and aside from that, I don't think I would have purchased it. Enemies are lackluster except for a few at the absolute bottom of the map which takes hours upon hours just to get to... and I'm not saying that based on research or anything game specific, it's based on how slow your dwarves move and how the AI is abysmal because once you get that low, they'll pick up a single object then run all the way back to the top to drop it off then run all the way back down to pick up another that was right next to the first.Gold is absolutely worthless. At the start of the game, everyone on the "overworld" is fighting so you can pick a side to support in their war efforts or alternatively, you just sell to the highest bidder which ends up making everyone hate you. Then with your pockets full of cash, you can just buy out entire cities/towns of supplies and still have an absurd amount of gold. Then because you've got gold and the cities hate you, they attack you, but again, enemies are absolutely meaningless and zero threat so your dwarves roll them easily.All in all, it's alright to spend some hours in but the two end-game achievements are simple to get, just very time-consuming. _childDocuments_.review: As of 11/1/2020I'm really enjoying this game!*  It's a blend of hardcore dwarf fortress mechanics, with the world diversity and exploration offered by games like Terraria with a hint of Dungeon Keeper or War for the Overworld.*This is a good foundation for a game. I've played through all of the content offered in about 14 hours. There are more places I could explore but there are no more technologies or quests to get. Not all games come to Early Access with the same amount of content and I understand that. What they have here is very enjoyable but what we need is more of everything, more techs, more quests, more stuff underground, more overworld map, etc, etc.There are also a bunch of issues and bugs to work out.-The pathing on the dwarves needs help, they get stuck in random locations and the way they prioritize multiple tasks sometimes stands them or makes the other tasks impossible to get to. For instance, if you try to deconstruct three scaffolds that are all on top of each other they will deconstruct the bottom scaffold leaving the other two above it impossible to deconstruct. Another example is that if you ask them to dig out a 10x10 square they seem to end up at the bottom leaving the top 3x10 impossible to get to without constructing scaffolds. They just seem to "paint themselves into corners" a lot stranding themselves so it requires more micromanagement then it should.-We need a way to better prioritize tasks. I've had the Omens of War quest time out fail with the required items in my storage because my dwarves were busy with other tasks. I shouldn't have to cancel all of my orders all over the underground and redo them later just to do the quest. I also shouldn't have to disallow digging in the labor allocation menu for them to do a quest or another important job.-Everything is super cluttered, half of my base is storage, I have literally 26 storage rooms for 9 dwarves, at least half of that is dedicated to specific types of items to streamline crafting (Ores next to foundries etc.) and I still don't have enough storage. Because of this, a mission that requires 15 swords overwhelms the iron ore I have on hand and then my dwarves have to go out and collect more ore to finish a single quest.-Storage hauling priorities. I have at least two storage rooms for silver ore, plenty of silver mined on the ground, my labor allocation heavily favoring hauling and no silver ore in my storage. Also, It seems like they aren't using their full hauling capacity or they are only collecting a single ore to meet the demand of the current project.-The item crafting needs some sort of automation, every time you create an item you have to manually create all of the parts required to make the item and you really need to specify what materials the item should be made of. Maybe allow us to create blueprints for custom items and add it to a list so I can just click my custom "gold ball-peen hammer with curved copper handle" from the list and it inputs the pattern for a gold ball-peen hammer head and the curved copper handle and the assembly.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:*** Abandonware! Devs released the game unfinished. Buyer beware! ***Original review:I am only recommending this for other optimistic buyers like me! If you believe in the power of Early Access and want to take a chance to support these devs, this game comes highly recommended.In its current state as an Early Access game, Hammerting lacks a lot of QoL features that make it easily enjoyable. Currently, there is not much to recommend it over any other colony sim, but once deeper exploration mechanics are implemented, it has the potential to become something really special.Enjoyable things:- Exploration feels deep and mysterious. Hammerting really pushes you to dig deep and dig greedily.- The lore is very well fleshed out and fun to read! Almost everything has a nice flavorful description.- Really looking forward to when dwarven clan mechanics are implemented. Right now, dwarves belong to clans that give them certain bonuses. You can build a Great Hall where your dwarves will hold their ting (a moot, or a meeting of clans), but it doesn't seem to do anything as of yet.Some grievances:- You can't directly control your dwarfs to expedite certain jobs, there is no way to prioritize tasks, crafting lacks a "create forever" or "create until you have X" features, etc.- High degree of micromanagement. To make a singe pick, you have to click three things in the crafting menu. After it's created, you have to manually assign it to a dwarf by right clicking. Over time, this becomes very tedious. Luckily, tools don't break so you don't have to do this often. Additionally, manually assigning skill points on your dwarves feels meaningless and tedious.- How the hell do you get bones?? You need bones to eventually make mortar, which is needed in the construction of some high end buildings. As far as I can tell, the only way to get bones is to kill skeletons, which are spawned from randomly generated tombs. Currently, there doesn't seem to be a way to stop your dwarves from destroying the tombs, so good luck finding a renewable source of bones!

_childDocuments_.review: is a colony builder / simulation game with a fantasy setting that is out in Early Access now. It's missing some basic things, like an interactive tutorial, so it's a bit hard to get into unless you do a lot of trial and error. It seems rather challenging, but maybe it's because I don't quite understand all of the mechanics yet. If you want to be a part of how the final game will shape up by offering your thoughts and suggestions, now is a good time to get into it, otherwise, it's reasonable to wait for the full release.You control a group of 3 dwarves to start and you will be able to hire more. Their job is to build a city underground. You start with mining and this creates paths through to the caves where you will get your raw materials, and so of course as building simulators go, you will be able to gradually use your resources to progress the game.You will see some objectives on the right-hand side of the screen. By completing the objectives, you will earn knowledge points. The points can be used to unlock new things, like new rooms, etc. It's somewhat akin to research upgrades, because these newer rooms will allow you to use the materials that you have found or mined and make other things.You will also have other objectives in the overworld. In order to be successful in this game, you will need to finish those. You have competitors/enemies, and you will want to try to do everything efficiently and quickly, in order to always be a step or two ahead of the others.Be careful when navigating the caves and tunnels, since you are digging deeper underground. You may have trouble getting back up if you fall down ledges. You will also have to face enemies who spawn underground and they can and certainly will kill you when given the chance.As mentioned, the game in its current state does not have a tutorial. There are some written information that pops up to give you some instruction but I do feel that an interactive tutorial would be so much better for this game. I hope that will be added before the game's release.There is not a difficulty setting either, I do think that would be helpful for different people of varying skill levels as well. Newcomers to the genre may want an easier difficulty to get used to both the style of play and also the game itself. In some parts you can face a lot of fights, so having some extra room to breathe as an option would be nice.The graphics are very nice, the details are smooth even when zoomed in.I like the music because it's very relaxing.The game can be fully played with a mouse and a keyboard.€24.99 for an early access game isn't cheap. One would expect a finished game for that price. The game does offer a lot of content. is a quite good building simulator with its own unique style and gameplay. The fantasy setting will appeal to those who like that. There is a good amount of game content already even though it's in Early Access. If you want to help with the game's development by playing and providing your thoughts and troubleshooting any issues, now is a good time to get into it. Though if you would rather wait for a full product, definitely come back to it once it's done, because it's definitely a game worth playing in the genre.With the lack of an interactive tutorial in its current state, I had trouble with understanding everything that was around me and I have died three times so far. So I do hope that is implemented before the full release. It's rather challenging as a game but also because there are some parts of the game that you have to learn through trial and error, so expect to make some mistakes in order to improve.I enjoyed my time with the game, and I think you will too.

_childDocuments_.review: So. This game came out as a "Release" around the time I'm writing this. Reviews are very mixed, and with good reason.So let's start with the main thoughts: This game is very much your standard Colony Sim where you set priorities and they do things. All the systems are fairly solid, and I've enjoyed the game "for the most part". It has decent depth and options, though not quite as deep as bigger names like Dwarf Fortress or Gnomoria, but is simultaneously less annoying than Oxygen Not Included (no silly gas systems)Some reviews complain about awful AI and getting stuck; I'm pretty sure those folks have never touched a game like this before, because that's normal and something you just have to think ahead about. Prioritize your jobs well, and disassemble scaffolds 1 at a time and you'll never have an issue. (Though let's be fair, the AI SHOULD at least be smart enough to not do something that will result in the unit or another unit being stuck with no exit path)Some reviews complain about this game not really being ready for Release - Those are 100% true; They only JUST added farming + fishing and Multiplayer a month ago. Neither of which are fleshed out or properly bugtested/tweaked:1) Farming: Planting Shroom Trees & Cloth-making Troll Tails will generate Material + Seeds. Neither of these is super valuable, but having renewable Charcoal from the "wood" is useful. However... Mushroom Paste, Mushroom Oil, etc is EXTREMELY common in a lot of recipes, and your Mushrooms do NOT generate seeds/spores for replanting; it generates multiple mushrooms, which your Dwarves tend to eat before they can re-plant if you don't Prioritize the planting well. Same for other Plantable things. This is Colony Sim 101, you should know better than to not have a Seed system for every plantable, let alone an extremely commonly-used-but-also-food one. And the things that DO have seeds? There's nothing you can do with excess Seeds. You have no pet animals like chickens to feed. You can't sell them to the Overworld dinguses. You just store 'em or let them litter your base. Which is a HUGE oversight.2) Lack of Animal Taming - You want a renewable supply of Leather? Too bad, you gotta buy it or leave Rat Holes un-destroyed and deal with constant attacks for meager supply over time. I understand they value the Overworld Trading system as an important part of the game, but I've got more Trade Lore than I'll ever need, and with the over-zealous War system, the bases are destroyed and lacking buyable useful stuff like Leather half the time anyways.3) Which brings me to...the Overworld system. It feels...tacked on at best. The Dwarves are basically Sweden, staying out of it, while they fight. And they fight. CONSTANTLY. As soon as you start the game, someone is sending a team of enemies to attack the nearest other faction, and might even wipe it out before you can buy anything from them. Sure, it means I can sell them stone to repair their towns, but then you have to wait for buyables to restock. I saw their Road Map on the reddit, and half the stuff isn't even in yet..I'm sure they have legitimate reasons and/or publisher pressure for going for a Release now instead of waiting to implement more or even refine the stuff they JUST added and is CLEARLY not ready for Retail.My final thoughts: This is a pretty good game for what it is, I've thoroughly enjoyed it in spite of the above. But I'm still very disappointed in every developer/publisher in the last decade or so that has a "We'll fix it with a Day 1/post-launch patch" instead of the late-1990s Blizzard motto of "It's done when it's done, because we want to do it right" mentality. Blizzard (back then) was respected for that decision (regardless of how fubar they are now lol), and any other dev/publisher that has the balls to be honest about the QUALITY of their game should be respected for that, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this for a few hours a few months ago, didn't like it for a variety of reasons (mostly related to the way overworld quests, the only source of money at the time, worked), set it aside.Came back, and was surprised to discover that it had turned into a decent game, with ongoing developments, mostly oriented at quality of life improvements.This is a sandbox game, in the purest sense of the word.  It isn't Dwarf Fortress, and, as far as I can tell, you aren't expected to lose; if you come in expecting that experience, you'll likely be disappointed.  You're building a dwarfhome in a not-particularly-perilous-mountain.  It's more of a relaxing experience than a significant challenge, even on the hardest difficulty mode; it's more like a dwarf garden than a dwarf fortress.My only note of advice, which may suggest something about the gameplay itself, is to play on the smallest map available, it's still far more space than you will ever need; all the extra distance will only hurt you in the long run, particularly given some of the quirks of the AI, which isn't great at dealing with traveling long distances to do tasks.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR? Sorry about that, I couldn't resist.  I'll be serious from here on out. (Probably...)Hammerting is generally a pretty laid back experience and it's fun.  If you like ant colony style building (think Fallout Shelter, Craft the World), dwarves, exploration, trading, crafting, and of course digging holes (See?  I just couldn't resist.  Again.) this might be a good game for you!Want more detail?  Read on!The game has a good UI and I like the graphics.  The sounds are okay, if sometimes a tad repetitive.  Gameplay is centered around exploration while digging tunnels, building workshops and other buildings in an ant colony style layout.  There's also a lot of crafting and trading.  It's got fairly complex crafting that, so far, hasn't managed to feel like it's too complicated.You start off with a few dwarves and recruit a few more provided you have earned enough coin to pay them to come and work for you.  Don't like the traits a potential dwarf has?  Dismiss them and wait for someone better to show up.  Some dwarves show up with no negative traits, some show up with mostly negative traits.  It seems fairly balanced most of the time, and many negative traits also have some positive aspect to them.As you explore, trade resources with overworld communities, and build you will unlock research and trading points that you use to unlock new technology.  Sometimes this will be a new workshop and new items, sometimes a new product for an existing workshop, and sometimes a simple bonus like an increase to the total capacity of dwarves, or a stat bonus.Each dwarf has a clan background which means they may not play well with others from different clans, especially if they have certain negative traits that makes them less socially competent than other dwarves.  If they don't get along, and their needs fall too low, they may not function as well as they could.Luckily there are perks you can unlock as your dwarves gain levels that make them better at, well, everything including being more adept at talking to and getting along with other dwarves.  Some perks require certain prerequisite perks or technologies to unlock but this system seems very well though out and it's easy to use.  The game also lets you pick a top tier perk, double click it, and it will set up a progress path to auto-buy each prerequisite perk as soon as it's available.  Keep in mind that if you have a technology requirement then a path may be locked until you research that tech so it's possible to set up a progress path that can't be reached.  You can manually adjust this at any time, or manually add other perks as long as the dwarf has perk points to spend.Dwarves also have equipment slots, and equipment can make a big difference in effectiveness.  They show up with a grandparent's old hammer, axe, and pick that will do the job until you can make better gear.  They have three slots for equipment, and as you progress you will want to specialize.  You can make rakes for farmers, ladels for cooks, weapons for militia, hammers, axes, picks, and other items as well.  There are also two ring slots, and an armour/clothing slot.Building can be a bit tricky to understand at first, unless you watch a tutorial or do a bit of reading about the systems, but once you understand how it all works, which shouldn't take too long, building becomes very easy.  Crafting is the same, it takes a bit to figure it all out unless you do a bit of research first.  Luckily it doesn't take too long to get used to and it was fun learning it as I played.One of the best crafting features is the ability to set an overall inventory at a crafting room, or set a per-room inventory.  You can tell a crafting room to make x number of an item and maintain that number in the entire community, or to make x number of the item and keep that amount in that room.  This way you can set rooms away from where you're expanding to maintain an overall minimum for the community, and rooms near areas where you're building to keep a room inventory.  Why is this important?  The dwarves won't have to walk as far to get what they need to build.  Another great crafting feature is the ability to select components.  Run out of copper for that order of axe heads?  Use iron instead.  No more of one type of mushroom for that soup?  Use a different mushroom.  There's also a benefit to using better materials, or different types of components.  Iron is generally better for weapons and tools than copper, fetches a higher price on the overworld (usually - depends on the needs/wants of a community), and usually is more efficient meaning crafting, digging, etc. with iron tools is faster and better.  There's also a bonus system in place so that sometimes better quality items are created, and this depends on quality of materials, tools, and skill of the dwarf doing the crafting.Dwarves all have a huge number of stats/skills to consider, plus positive and negative traits.  You can min/max by assigning certain tools to dwarves that are better at certain tasks, but if you don't want to micromanage that much you don't have to.  It's usually worth it, but I found it was not generally necessary to spent much time on it.  Give a dwarf the proper tools for the jobs you want them to do and you should be fine.  Since a dwarf can only hold 3 tools (weapons, lanterns, tools all use the same slots) you can customize what jobs they can do by giving them only the items that they need to do those jobs.  Want a dedicated miner/hauler?  Give them a pick and a bag.  Militia?  Weapon but no crafting or digging tools.  They've also got an in progress job board so once that's done it looks like you're going to be able to really fine tune what each dwarf prefers doing.This game has some small bugs and minor issues at the moment, but nothing game breaking.  The worst issue is when the AI gets confused about what it's doing and runs back and forth between two points.  This can usually be fixed by either directing the dwarf to run to a specific spot or cancelling whatever order it's trying to do.  Every time I've done one or both of these things it will solve the problem.  A bit annoying, not game breaking at all.  This game is in EA so this is to be expected.Some players have found that the AI gets worse as the game progresses and the colony gets bigger.  I have noticed it seems to struggle at times, but I have also noticed that sometimes it's due to the orders I have given to dig, build, craft, etc. Sometimes it's the game, but again - it's an EA game so sometimes things won't quite work properly.  The more I play the more often I find I can prevent AI pathing or task issues, or fix it quickly if issues happen.  You do need to be aware that you could cause some issues if you set certain tasks that can't be completed due to location or lack of resources.There are also a few aspects of the UI that could be improved, but it's generally pretty good.  I'd like a better system to manually equip the dwarves with certain items, but you can set them to automatically upgrade their tools when something better is available which is a very nice feature.  I've noticed that when a new dwarf shows up one of their first actions is to go directly to a storage area and pick up better gear since I usually have a half dozen or more of better versions of each starting item (pick, axe, hamemr) kicking around.Right now this is a very solid 7/10, but it's in EA right now and I think it's only going to improve.  If you're a fan of this style of game I highly recommend you give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of reviews compare this game to others. However, the one i didn't see much of was that this game is closer to Oxygen not Included and a little bit of Craft the world. I haven't played the dread horde so I don't know how similar the game is to that.However, if Oxygen not Included (O.N.I) was enjoyable than this game will have a high probability of giving you the same enjoyment of managing a group of dwarfs that are building and exploring in a  mountain home.  Though the game is similar to O.N.I it definitely has a different feel and very different mechanics that make more than just a re-skinned O.N.I game.At this time the game really shows promise of what it can be. Though the game is riddled with strange and incomplete features that are expected from a game this early in it's development. A small list of pros and cons from my playtime.PROS:  * The overworld quests are a nice feature to the game that gives the player a break in the explore, build, and manage units loops * The art style and theme is on point with Dwarves and a general Norwegian / viking vibe * The game does provide decent cues and notifications when just about anything needs your attention CONS: (Some of these may not apply in the future if the game addresses) * The money mechanic as it is, is very much incomplete. Making money is unusually difficult and the greed status along with the dwarves hoarding money you can't use doesn't feel good. As a result having more than 4 dwarves (3 of which are starters) to work with makes the game really slow death and more things need to be done and getting more units is hard since money is required to hire new units. *  Units in the game will just get stuck with no way correcting it. Usually due to a pathing errors, my last dwarf died stuck on a wall with nothing to do game over...not fun. These things obviously may or may not change as the game develops. There many things still one can enjoy with the game in the current state. I hope the continues to grow and be just as fun as other games like it. I think this game has the real possibility of that because it already feels really  different enough yet still at it's core a good management sim kind of game.

DONT BUY.--------------------------------------------------------------------------Early access review: there seriously needs to be a mixed review button on steam...This game has potential to be really great, but it is currently being held back by hoard of small annyoances and problems. There is probably more to explore and find out about the game, but this is just a first impression after roughly 8 hours of play. Given its still in early access I believe that many of these kinks will be ironed out before final relase.+ subtle music background music+ very nice art+ no game breaking bugs/chrashes or performance issues (I feel like this one is really important, considering current state of game development in general)+ catchy gameplay+ UI is relatively easy to understand (tho I think it could use some improvements)+ fast loading times+ game is suprisingly small for how good it looks+ ability to sort and designate warehourses/storage rooms for only specific stuff- Missing ingame tutorial!! tho there is a help/encyklopedia of some kind which is instantly thrown at player as a whole it doesnt really help as I dont want to spend half an hour reading stuff. I want to play...- Missing gather this button (dwarves do gather on their own but in rather random way or only when its needed to craft something)- Whats the point of the doors if they dont work and enemies go right trough...- Advanced buildings are unnecesarily large while offering little to advantage over smaller buildings- there is no easy way to get bones (you can get some from dead bodies of adventurers but only if you are lucky and game spawns them somewhere relatively nearby in a cave) which are required for mortar to build  some advanced buildings- You are literally swamped by requests from the overworld after short initial period, up to the point I cant even change equipment for my dwarves bcz everyting is going outside to help war effort. - You are often asked for items you can't really make yet very early (looking at you swords and machine parts) which are locked behind some additional expensive research- Building of scaffoldings and placing blocks could be much easier. _childDocuments_.review: The game is visually well done and the concept is interesting.  However, it feels very unfinished.  The economy is rinse and repeat with no real consequences. Combat is clunky and impossible to manage. And production lines feel very thin with there often being only one thing to craft from a resource rather than a single resource being used to make various items.  This game looks like it has a lot of potential and feels like Oxygen Not Included but with Dwarves.  However, it is either unfinished, or has been released in a very poor state.  Still, I've had some fun playing around with it.  Just don't expect to become invested in your mountainhome the way you would in other similar games.  Great concept, very little depth of gameplay, feels like a beta.UPDATE:Well the game is now declared "finished" by the developers.  It very clearly isn't.  There are incomplete mechanics, tooltips, items, etc.  You'll very rapidly get the sense that things were never fully implemented or developed because the starts and half done concepts are quickly visible in the game. They didn't finish this game, they were simply finished with it.  It's worth a few bucks to pass the time, but you'll probably never feel you got a complete game.  It's a shame because based on the limited progress, it feels like the developers have some very good instincts in game design. But I hate to say that I will look at any of their future projects, particularly any "Early Access" content with great skepticism.  They've left this gamer with the impression that they don't have much dedication to finishing projects once the early access money dries up.  Which is a real shame since I like the way that feature supports smaller dev teams.  I can understand a project taking longer than expected or time to finesse.  A reputation for a lack of follow through, however, is not a way to get me to pitch in for future projects.

_childDocuments_.review: "Hammerting is a vertical dwarven mining colony sim with RPG elements."That is how the game is sold, and it sounds pretty good, you are in charge of a mine, you have control of dwarves, you build, craft and fight. Surely this is Dungeon Keeper for 2020 right? Not quite.So, the basic story is that there is a war going on overground, dwarves are working underground to help their allies overground, you start with just a few Dwarves but you can then hire more, you upgrade them, and so on. When you click on the door to the mine, you see a map and are able to choose challenge to accept. This all sounds pretty simple doesn't it, and if it was simple, then I would love this game, the problem is, that it is not simple its overly complicated and confusing.The first hour of gameplay I was literally trying to figure out how to get a dwarf to just do what I wanted it to do, you see you can't actually tell a dwarf to do a specific task, you have to instead queue up tasks and then the dwarves will decide themselves what to do, the problem is half the time they just seem to stand about idle, or do not go where you need them to, and this is not on purpose either. The game is full of bugs, and because you can't physically tell a dwarf to do something, you will soon get massively frustrated by these bugs.Another problem with this game is that it is a vertical builder, but you mine into the wall you are looking at, so despite you having what should be a 2D area that you are interacting with, you actually end up with 3 layers, which just adds to the confusion. It also doesn't help that the tutorial to help you start is utterly useless. Remember how I mentioned Dungeon Keeper earlier? Remember how each level you would be eased into things, gathering gold, building, mining and so on, this game just kind of throws you in there.The layout is also poorly designed, for example I knew that I had to access the inventory, but there is no inventory button anywhere on the screen, after giving up a few times and then emailing the PR person promoting the game, I eventually figured out that each room you build has it's own inventory that is a box to the side of the pop up window when you click on it. I can moan about this game for ever but I will stop here, the game is still Early Access, and it has lots of potential, the team who are developing it are quick to reply, they are open to listening and trying to improve the game. There is also a free demo you can play, I advise you to check out the demo, and if you like it and want to stick with it and watch it grow, then go for it. But for me, even if this game was perfect, I don't think it is worth £20. This could be a browser game. Dungeon Keeper it is not.Such a shame as just the description of the game had me so excited. Maybe after a few months when the bugs are all fixed, and they improve the interface, and make the game more playable, then I might come back and give it another go, but even after trying so hard to enjoy this game and putting a solid 6 hours into playing it, it just doesn't work for me.But don't take my word on it, download the demo, give it a chance, remember this is early access, and hopefully will improve over the coming months.
