_childDocuments_.review: The game feels prematurely launched, though playable and enjoyable. Steam only allows for recommended or not, and in good conscience, I cannot recommend it to most buyers in the current state. A few more months of development and patches will definitely make a far more enjoyable experience. Here are my thoughts after some about sixty hours of playtime.Games like Hammerting and Oxygen Not Included sort of function through entropy. You must complete the game before resources run out. Advancing allows you to stave off entropy to a point where it may no longer even really be a factor, lending the end game to being more of a sandbox. Hammerting doesn't feature much - if any - of an entropy system. By mid to late game, the systems allow unlimited water, unlimited ore (i.e., ore crushers), and even the dwarves themselves don't seemingly die. This isn't necessarily bad, as the game could be oriented toward a more relaxed approach. ONI requires you to fundamentally grasp heat capacity, physical states of materials, and more. It isn't a game for everyone. Hammerting could appeal to a more casual crowd, however you cannot entirely let your foot off the "challenge" gas without having sufficient alternative systems to keep players engaged. I feel like those systems are lacking.Exploration is not particularly exciting. The lack of entropy in resources means that the value of discovering a huge vein of copper is exceedingly tempered. An ore crusher on even a small vein of ore means you now have - what appears to be at least - an unending supply of minerals. A new statue? That'd be neat if I could move it to my base as a decorative item, but the passive bonus to more headcount is nice if you are really in need of more dwarves. Mountain Lore is crucial currency at first, but by mid to late game, it serves almost no purpose. You will have hundreds with very little effort. Dwarf Tombs give grave poppies, but those are really only useful for a limited number of diplomacy quests but after that don't offer any value. Jackpot Mines seem a bit unnecessary given ore crushers. Springs of Life are likely the only ones that I still find to be useful and always great to uncover. Building suffers from a lack of variety both in decorative or functional items. In my game, waves of enemies stage themselves in dark halls, however never seem to attack if blocked by a door. Defensive traps, barriers, etc., all could have made for a more engaging building experience. Waves of more aggressive enemies could deepen your militia requirements and yet I never found a need for more than three or four. Requiring more dwarves could require more food, which could require more dwarves, etc., pushing the concept of entropy more to the forefront. Even outside of that pressuring system, there are few decorative options. Some background bricks, a few different types of bridges, but otherwise nothing that plays out in a truly functional or aesthetic way. Essentially, for a game about delving into the depths of a mountain it is a comparably shallow experience. I simply believe this game needs a bit more development to be a rewarding experience. I don't think you'll find the money wasted, especially for a price point < $20 and ongoing patches/development are likely to improve the experience substantially. I can't say I disliked my experience at all and I am looking forward to mining again once the content improves.

_childDocuments_.review: I had originally chosen not to recommend this game after it's official release due to a number of balancing issues that seemed to impact gameplay--in particular, that a substantial portion of map seeds lacked initial access to a number of vital resources necessary for survival.  The devs have been hard at work correcting these and other issues, and as a result, this game has gone from being a hopeless slog at the beginning to being a challenging but fun strategy and management simulation.There's a fair bit to think about in the game, even in the very first stages, and early missteps can lead to some serious problems later on--albeit problems that can be solved, though usually with some sacrifice involved.  Once a colony gets going, the engagement of the player with the simulation really begins.  Good decisions are rewarded and bad decisions punished--often in fairly brutal fashion.  Nevertheless, I'm motivated to keep playing in order to see the colony develop and continue expanding through the mountain home.Each seed comes with its own problems to overcome.  Some seeds give the player massive veins of various resources to mine near the entrance, but also several enemy lairs nearby.  Others give scant but adequate nearby resources, thus requiring more immediate exploration to develop the mountain home.  Still others may have a good balance of nearby resources and enemy lairs, but be laid out in such a way as to require significant build-out and modification of the mountain interior before structures can be logically laid out.  Because of these and similar factors, each map is not only unique, but also feels like playing a different game.  There's little repetition between map seeds.In the middle and late games, there are a variety of surprises waiting for your dwarves as they hack through the rock.  These require the player to innovate--what worked before may not necessarily work again.  In short, the game has ways of keeping you on your toes.A few stubborn problems remain, though these are far less noticeable than they were in previous versions of the game.  First, there is the occasional map seed that still leaves the player too little in the way of starting resources to have any reasonable chance of surviving.  These are rare, however, and the easy solution is just to start with a different map seed--the ones that don't have enough resources initially are easy to spot within the first five minutes or so.  A slightly more serious problem is that sometimes dwarves have to be micro-managed, and the AI sometimes prioritizes tasks in an obviously dumb way--I watched one of my dwarves fall unconscious after being unexpectedly swarmed by rats, the other dwarves come to her rescue by killing the rats...and then, rather than revive her, they collected all the rat hides and took them to storage, and then ran back and forth over her for a good five minutes while they completed other fairly insignificant tasks.  Finally, two dwarves (one of whom thought of the fallen dwarf as his best friend per the relationship panel) made for the spot, and had a 30-second-long conversation before finally reviving the fallen dwarf.  Still, such occurrences are fairly rare.Overall, after some initial struggle, the game seems to be living up to the promise it had in early access, and is now a very engaging and enjoyable colony management and strategy simulation game, and fans of either genre are likely to find plenty to keep themselves entertained.

_childDocuments_.review: There really isn't any other game like this; that was true when it was a Kickstarter demo(which I backed) and it's still the main reason to play it. It is as straightforward and linear as your usual Final Fight or Streets of Rage style game, and it has most of the familiar elements from those games, but when you attack, you can plan a combo with an RPG-style menu. That's it. That's really the main proposition here. If that sounds too niche or gimmicky for you, then you may want to steer clear, because it isn't going to give you a giant open world or minigames or other trappings, and it won't blow you away with graphical fidelity either.But if you're curious about the mechanic, you probably want to know, "how does that work?" Well, it's a kind of push-your-luck system where you have both actions and attack power that regenerate over time. If you use your actions on weaker attacks, your chances of hitting are higher, and when you land a combination, you get a bonus that builds up your actions and attack power faster, so you can start to mix in your strong finishers if you use the right pace and weaken your opponents first. Then add in some of the usual RPG roles and status effects, adapted to brawler tropes(counter-attacks, grappling moves, charge-ups, weapons, biker gangs, etc.) and you have the gist of the combat. Like any good fight system, it's easy to learn and hard to master, with lots of matchup details to consider. Even past the four hour mark, the depth of it all is still growing on me, and the game continues introducing stuff at a careful pace which has given me a good share of "aha" moments. The game is fairly generous with healing items and even makes sure to have you try every character's playstyle by having occasional "grudge fights", so you never feel like you're missing out or are uncertain of how well you did - it's easy to tell if you played a fight optimally or not by looking at how much damage you took. It's all combat, but it's very good, tightly designed combat and each fight does something different.The NES-style graphics and sound are mostly iconic and cartoonish, but distinctive; like many beat-em-ups, the game can barely take its plot seriously and most of the dialogue is over-the-top, which works well with the aesthetic. At the same time it manages a very authentic and heartfelt portrayal of the diversity, personalities and politics of the real NYC, and so while a lot of the game's writing is typical scenario-building filler - it labors hard to contrive reasons for encountering the same few dozen people over and over and fighting them - the moments where the characterization touches on the real are uniquely compelling, and the characters have grown on me over the course of my playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Treachery in Beatdown City takes me back to the days of Double Dragon, River City Ransom, Bad Dudes, and all the other NES-era beat 'em ups with some OG Final Fantasy under the hood to create a sweet 8-bit fighting RPG. For the first time in literal decades, I found a game that  exactly like ones I'd played in the 80s, but also has new elements added that make it interesting and fun.The gameplay starts out with basic moves and combos that are unique to each of the three playable characters. Aside from certain story-mode fights, you can choose any character/fighting style and rock your enemies in a number of different ways. You can find items along your journey that will aid you in battle. The writing is extremely tongue-in-cheek, never takes itself seriously, lampoons just about everyone and everything, and (again) really feels like writing you'd find in any old NES game. As the story progresses, the complexity of battles and combos ramps up alongside a level of difficulty that is expertly dialed in. Fights start out very easy to allow you to find your way, but become increasingly more challenging. While the going gets quite tough toward the end, nothing in this game ever feels impossible. If you died, it was your fault. I like this because the game is a challenging enough to be engaging - it never gets boring because it's too easy nor does it get frustratingly difficult of sadism. In addition to great balance/difficulty, I have to shout out the items and inventory system. Each item is single-use and you can only find them along the way, preventing item hoarders like me from stockpiling ungodly amounts of items and ruining the gameplay balance. Instead, players have to be judicious about when and where to use items to maximum effect or when to take the L and rotate to another character. By the end, I had  items on hand to beat the last few encounters.The addition of hidden combo techniques keeps fights interesting as well. You can inflict additional status effects that are more or less effective depending on enemy types. The list of possible moves accumulated by end allows for a staggering amount of different combinations. I still haven't found all of the hidden techniques as of the time of this review and something I plan to do using the chapter select unlocked by beating the game.The banter between characters will either land with you or not. Some jokes made me laugh out loud and some fell a bit flat, but the overall style and content kept me entertained throughout the whole game and was another area where I felt the nostalgia shine through. It felt like I was reading text that would be in an 80s game: direct and to the point, somewhat ham-fisted and goofy, but updated with modern references. If it's not your jam, you can always just skip the text, but there are some good gems in there worth reading.Soundtrack is bangin!Lastly, this game is perfect on the Steamdeck. Even though TiBC is not fully verified as of the time of this review, I had  issues playing on the deck. The turn-based nature of the combat in this game made it easy to enter a game-and-chill flow state on couch with some TV on in the background, making it a ultimate relaxing nostalgic gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: I've been eagerly awaiting Beatdown City for a long time, and Nuchallenger/Hurakan Works have delivered something really great. "What if Double Dragon used Fallout's VATS system?" or "What if Slay the Spire was a beat-em-up?" All that and a bag of chiptunes. If that piques your curiosity, know that there's nothing else quite like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Beatdown City is a cool genre mashup that does something very new with the mechanics of a classic NES action games like Double Dragon and JRPGs like Dragon Warrior. The odd combination delivers more thought than the former, and more fun than the latter, while wrapping itself in a bizarre and aggressive parody of modern politics through the lens of 80s cheese.This game won't be for everyone. Fans of traditional action beat-em-ups will find the pseudo-RPG style of its combat too much to think about, and turn-based combat fans might be nonplussed by the simplicity of its stat system. It's most likely to satisfy those of us who've grown tired with genre convention and just want to play something new and unique.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: I love the idea, the music, the look, (some of) the humor, and the game play mechanics are fun.  However, the controls are horrible, and there is no way to remap them.  The button set up is just awkward and follows no standard gaming conventions.  So, the game ends up just being annoying, as you try to navigate clunky menus with counter-intuitive controls.  I really wanted to like it, and played it many times, but always end up turning off after about 15 minutes.  (I play with a keyboard.)
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Treachery in Beatdown City is the most refreshingly unique take on retro-aesthetic beat-em-ups I’ve had the pleasure of playing in quite some time. Both for its gameplay and message. If you enjoyed series like River City or Streets of Rage, or perhaps even oldschool RPGs like the original Final Fantasy, then the turn-based combo-creating nature of Beatdown City should prove an interesting, and if you’re anything like me, satisfying addition to the format.Described in a few words, Beatdown City is creative and cathartic. It rewards you for doing more than just the barebones of combos, with the ability to chain more moves and take down obnoxious people more effectively. Its retro aesthetic is realized flawlessly, with a kickass chiptune soundtrack to boot.The game is priced at $20. Some may see as a little high given the repetitive nature of gameplay and shorter campaign, around six hours for the first and currently only episode. I personally thought the experience was worth the cost. Especially given that the future addition will be free. And I’m always willing to cut more slack about cost to indie devs, in the name of supporting their lives.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: My arm is tired from holding down the button to make the endless ENDLESS endless boring (and stupid) dialog go, line by line by line... press S to start, press S to end, press S to block, press S some more,  press S to read, press S again, press S and press S and press S S S and sometimes press A, but usually press S over and over and over. What a boring piece of junk. I wish I hadn't wasted an entire ten dollars on it.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: So, 3% of players have beaten the second boss. And there's a reason for this.Treachery is a semi turn based brawler. You navigate a city map, get into scuffles, and during fights you can pause time and program in strings of attacks.Problem #1 - Nearly everything you do can be countered, and enemy counter rates are based on their current hp. This means you need to whittle them with low damage high acc attacks before you start opening up, but sometimes they just counter the low damage high acc attack and it's rng.Problem #2 - Resources are limited, maps are big, and movement is ungodly slow. You might think I'm exaggerating, but half of the reason I burned out of this game on my second hour (and 97% of players burned out before then) is because walking between two points on the map takes a genuinely comical amount of time. Backtracking to grab more items from a side route feels like a punishment for being thorough.Problem #3 - The writing feels like an episode of Archer, but only in a bad way. And there's a ton of it. And the provocation for most fights is that there's a character being annoying. This means you're spending most of your time reading, and you're specifically reading about characters being annoying. If it bothers you even a little, it'll wear through faster than flesh touching pavement at 75mph.Despite all of this, I do think there's a good *idea* in here. A lot of thought has gone into the mechanics, and if the game clicks with you there's a ton of content. It did not click with me, and it did not click with 97% of players, but who knows. Maybe you'll be the one.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Combat system doesn't feel very good. I guess the expectation is to be able to press attack to punch as a beat em up, but the turn based system really kills the flow. Not enjoying it. Would probably enjoy it more as a straight up turn based system where I didn't have to real time worry about spacing and dexterity speed in conjunction with a non transparent turn based wait on actions. if I have to wait my turn anyway would have more fun not having to time out the long delays between actions. Would skip this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Somewhat short right now (I managed to get to the end of Chapter 1 in 4 hours), but still an enjoyable beat'em up/turn-based strategy RPG.The custom combo system, while a bit tough to understand at first (and the fact you don't start fights at full FP means you'll be starting nearly all fights the same way), does lead to fun when you can chain several powerful techniques together to pummel your enemies with a hail of blows. I've only had a similar experience with two other games, Slay the Spire and Library of Ruina, so it's nice to see another one that's added to the list.One thing I have to take issue with is the rates at which enemies counter attacks, especially grabs. Despite my best attempts to weaken foes before grabbing them, occasionally I would get countered even when the enemy's health was rather low. I recall one time I got countered by an enemy who only had 1 HP left... They still got KO'ed in the end, but I wasn't too happy.Still, the game itself is on the easier end of things despite the counters - healing items are rather common.The levels are mostly linear, with the occasional side route to pick up items with.Somewhat worrying is the fact the end of Chapter 1 promised a new chapter in about May (Though I'm not sure I remember the message quite right). Still, there's not much to do about that besides wait and have faith.While the price is a bit much, the game still has a good deal of heart. If you're into RPGs, or beat 'em ups, this might be worth a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent, uniquely enjoyable game. Imagine someone had the idea of making a game where Streets of Rage was just the mana-harvesting part of a turn-based battle system. Then imagine that they actually committed to making that game, not as a simple novelty or parody but as a fully-realized game that stands on its own. Then imagine that that game included a fleshed-out world filled with extremely current social commentary and satire. That's Treachery in Beatdown City. This is not just an homage to old arcade/16-bit brawlers, but a triumph on its own in terms of both writing and innovative mechanics. Because the battle system is so ambitious, it's not quite perfect, and someone in the future will probably come along and further evolve these mechanics, but this game is an easy recommendation to anyone who likes retro games, old-school brawlers, turn-based combat systems, and storytelling that is both funny and relevant.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad by any means, but it was way too repetitive for me to finish it. The overworld is almost pointless and the game really just boils down to walking from one fight to another with the same enemy types and same strategies over and over again. Once you figure out an optimal series of moves, there is almost no reason to deviate from that and breeze through most fights. As for the dialogue, it is occasionally funny but more often than not, it overstays its welcome too, constantly making the same types of social commentary jokes over and over again.If it was just a quick 2 hour game for a few bucks, I feel it would be a much easier sell
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely fun, unique blend of beat-'em-ups and JRPGs, which results in deep tactical gameplay. Don't play this if you're looking for an arcade game - in fact, I'd say this game makes much more sense to RPG players than beat-em-up fans. Obviously, if you're into both, this game is a delight to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing Treachery In Beatdown City, all I can say is that this game SUCKS, and it is one of the worst games I've ever played. This game has so many issues that it would be impossible to point them all out here, but I'll try:Firstly, let's talk about combat. It is not a usual beat 'em up game. The developers tried something different, and it's more like a turn-based game. This combat system ruins all the fun and enjoyment. Would you like to play a game where, most of the time, you are waiting for a bar to fill up so you can execute a move? If you answered yes, then go ahead and buy this game, but if you answered no, stay away. You wait for a bar to fill up and gather FP so you can pull off some powerful moves, but it's a miracle if you can hit enemies with these powerful moves. Because enemies counter your stronger moves, all your resources are gone. The whole combat system is fundamentally flawed. As if this isn't enough, the game introduces different mechanics after mechanics, different enemy types after enemy types. It unnecessarily complicates things. It turns the combat system into f*cking rocket science. This dog sh*t game could have been ten times better if it had a simple combat system.Secondly, the writing. OH MY F*CKING GOD! The writing isn't just bad. It's unbelievably bad. The dialogue tries to be funny, but fails. It is CRINGE! The last act of the game is a pure nightmare. It was just text after text, dialogue after dialogue. The writer thought of himself as Hideo Kojima, I guess. I thought the latest Disney shows had bad writing. Those shows are Shakespeare compared to this junk.Thirdly, the graphics. In-game graphics are decent, but the cutscenes are eye sore. Not a single character looks like a human. They are hideous and vomit-inducing. Seriously though, what's the point of designing these characters so ugly?Overall, this whole game is a dumpster fire and beyond saving. You might be thinking, Isn't there anything nice about this game? The answer is no. God-awful combat, vomit-inducing graphics, dialogue that is more cringe-worthy than My Hero Academia fan fiction. Mix it all together, and you get a sh*t show. This sh*t show is called Treachery In Beatdown City
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting combo mechanics using menu. It would help to know exactly how FP (fight points) are generated other than "strike hits and you may get some" but fight flows relatively well. As long as you can generate FPs somehow, fights are actually kinda fun.An issue is that the grapple resist mechanic on enemies not nearly dead makes grapple basically finshers and strikes are what you will be using most of the time so the strike guy is clearly the most viable one and the grapple guy the "joke" one. This may change if grapples are more effective in the future from the start of the fight and not just when guys are almost dead anyway. The fact that resisted grapples waste LOTS of FPs do not help at all.This is actually a game that I enjoyed playing but it is simply too short for its price tag and feels unfinished with the amount of content it currently have (despite having its release almost 3 years ago). Devs seem to be working on updates so it may change at some point and would be glad to recommend it then but for now, it just feels like a very promissing (paid) demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: From the anthemic slogan "Beatdown City -- we gon' whoop your ass!" to the epic trailers and artstyle-defying promotional material, Treachery in Beatdown City forebodes a world full of pixelated punches.Each fight is presented as a vignette between one of three playable characters, and various enemies each personified with a name and archetype. Beatdown City has many types of foes, including bicyclists, preps, cheerleaders, grifters, gym junkies and rent-a-cops.It follows good game design by easing in mechanics, enemy types, and difficulty. With that said, the "tutorial" is a tad too long, arguably it could be cut to a third of its length and still be effective. The multitude of short battles (each 1-5 minutes in length) can feel repetitive, but the variety in enemies and tactics required in overcoming them keep it fresh.A special note to keep in mind: one time my save file got corrupted via Steam Cloud, I let the dev know, and they sent me a backup save file. That was incredibly kind of them to do.Outside of fighting, the writing's some of the most hilarious American social commentary you've seen in a video game. Nobody's spared the rod of "social justice", everyone gets whacked with it a few times for good measure.This is definitely a love letter to older games and it's made with passion. It's neither too difficult or too easy, and its unique charm in the realm of beat-em-ups will keep you coming back for another fight.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those ideas that looks terrible on paper but somehow actually works in practice. Instead of taking a beat em up and shoving RPG mechanics into it, it's an RPG with beat em up mechanics worked in. Really fun, original and engaging once you get the core mechanics down. This isn't something where the ideas are just thrown on a dart board randomly either. The way difficulty scales in a way that forces you to adapt to different strategies and fighting styles is all by design, showing a lot of thought went into the process. Hope to see a sequel or further installments one day. This game's a gem. #BlackLivesMatter
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game and truly unique.  It's pretty rare for American minority creators have access to the resources required to create video games; and even rarer for a game to provide explicit social commentary on the casual everyday racism and misogyny that minorities & women encounter in the US. If you are a black or brown person and live in the US, you will find this game's social commentary to be hilariously refreshing (without being too cynical).   Looking forward to future content in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: - Important game from a minority creator- Shows what it's like to face racism around every corner (literally)- Great scrolling beat-em-up, which innovates by merging the genre with RPG tactical combat- The RPG influence extends to the world map and narrative, creating a long-lasting and immersive singleplayer experience- 8-bit loveliness in the graphics, sounds and animationLove this game. I like scrolling beat 'em ups, but I always feel a sense of shallowness and repetitiveness after a while - the narratives always feel kinda optional, and after a while the combat feels samey.Enter Treachery in Beatdown City, which brings some RPGness into the mix and gives the genre the much needed longevity I've been missing. There's a whole world map to explore, tons of character dialogue that is sharp and funny and dripping with satirical social commentary. Hell, I heard about this game through a website encouraging people to support Black developers, following the killing of George Floyd, and right away in the first few areas there's a scene depicting police brutality. It's a great game, but also important insight for white players like myself to see how far racism is etched into society.The game uses an RPG-like combat system: you can punch enemies outright, but the meat of the combat comes from dipping into the menus to choose and chain together a wide variety of moves (whose roster increases as you level up) in interesting ways. Navigating the menus pauses the game, and makes you stop and strategise your next move, considering the enemy type and your own health and action points.That might sound overwhelming, but fights, at least so far, are nearly always one on one. It's not technically a "scrolling" beat-'em-up in that the level doesn't scroll with you as you progress. You traverse from point to point on the world map, and at the destination enter into a one-on-one fight (sometimes two-on-one so far, and looking at the screenshots, even-more-on-one later) - but it's not Street Fighter 2; you still have the depth of the screen to move in and out of, and move around. So the fights play out more like the Duel/Battle mode in Streets of Rage 2 (and possibly in the new SOR4, though I've not unlocked that mode yet - I'm actually spending more time on this game instead). Position is very important, as you sometimes need to step back while your action points recharge, though be careful you don't get attacked from behind!I don't know how long the game is, but it feels like the story is only just beginning; and looking at the screenshots, there are clearly new enemy types, locations and moves I haven't even seen yet. The story is pulling me along, and I want to keep playing to see where it goes. I've just reached unlocking the third playable character, and each time the story swaps them in you get another point of view on the story; I genuinely feel like I'm getting to know these people. It definitely feels more like a long-play RPG than an arcadey beat'-em-up, and that's a positive turn for the genre in my eyes.The 8-bit graphics look gorgeous on my 4k monitor, and the music and sound effects are totally on point.I really don't have any areas I would have liked to see improvements. At first I missed the use of WASD for directional control, but it soon becomes clear the game's keyboard layout is well-suited, with arrow keys for movement, and the WASD area used for navigating the combat menus. The subtitles in the intro movie were too fast for me to read, though I got the gist of the backstory; with repeat watches though (it plays each time you launch the game), I was soon able to read them. (The subtitles in-game are player-forwarded which is cool.)The tutorial prompts are extensive, and even now 1.7 hours in they are still teaching me new things. But they are drip fed at a good pace for me to take everything in, and coming back to the game each time I feel like I can remember what to do - the info has clearly sunk in.It's a blast of nostalgia to classic scrolling beat-em-ups, with a modern genre-bending and social sensibilities.P.S. When can Blake Orama become president again? (When I find him I guess!)

_childDocuments_.review: Twenty-second read. Combines the forces of the masked Ryu (Ninja Gaiden (NES)) and Final Fantasy VII with a side-scroller brawler (Streets of Rage, Double Dragon) in an 80s setting similar to Final Fight (Arcade). The world map borrowed from Super Mario 3 (SNES) and the political themes alas Orama etc. stretch the games' twenty-dollar price tag over a twenty year conversion period; does anybody really think noone had thought of making a turn-based, side-scrolling beat-em up game 🎮? Is just a game that has been politicized openly yet in enigmatic ways with a cast of characters that appear to be part of a Blackmirror (Netflix) sequel. Just my two cents.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll admit to being a little disappointed when I saw it wasn't a traditional brawler, but the gameplay is still a very fun mix of turn based and traditional brawler mechanics. Love the general vibe of the game too; the writing is sharp and the soundtrack is a banger. Seems like it'd make a great Steam Deck game.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Been a long road for this game (longer if you backed via Kickstarter like I did nearly a decade ago, so there's my disclosure), but it's been worth the wait and there's still more coming.This game is a beat-em-up with a twist - most of your actions and moves are executed in a turn-based style, via a menu. This gives the game an incredibly fresh feeling, with some deep strategy at play given your moves require both action bars (may not be the real name, sorry) and fight points (FP). Are you willing to risk a low accuracy but high damage move against an enemy you know can block? Or would you rather play safe with grapples, even though this enemy can break your combo and counter them? You also have three characters, with their own playstyles, strengths and weaknesses.I don't entirely care about the story the game is telling, but the writing is excellent and downright brilliant in individual moments (the devs using NPCs on the overworld to deliver some funny meta-commentary is one highlight). The music was done by Inverse Phase, who can nail these retro-style chiptunes soundtracks - this one is no exception.The most recent update has improved the game tremendously, added more content and seems like it's just the start of a lot more. Even if it isn't, this game is well worth your time as is.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: (I purchased this game on itch.io and received a free Steam copy.)Treachery in Beatdown City combines turn-based RPG strategy with fast-paced beat-em-up action, and it works really well. If you're at all interested in the premise of the game, it's well worth your time and money. Right out the gate this game oozes charm with its bright, retro graphics and its witty, satirical dialogue. The plot is a bit silly: President Orama is kidnapped by Terrorist Ninjas, and a group of ragtag street fighters team up to investigate what's really going on. There's nothing too serious going on here, but you will encounter characters and scenarios which touch upon the problems of modern-day America, particularly what it's like living in a big city. So while the conflicting tone may put some people off, I think it works pretty well. There's a few moments where the dialogue's a bit over-the-top, or the comedy just doesn't land, but I found myself enjoying what the game had to say despite the humor not landing.My main critique of the game as it stands is that the gameplay can get boring fast. There's not enough variation in the core gameplay loop to keep interest for very long. Despite this, the gameplay is still pretty solid. It's satisfying pulling off a big combo, or going for the risky hit just to finish your opponent off early. What doesn't work for me is that there's not a lot of enemy variation, and you're essentially doing the same thing over and over.There's four main enemy types: brawlers, dirty-fighters, grapplers, and supporters. Supporters will mostly run around and cheer until they've got nobody left to support, and then they become brawlers. That leaves you with essentially three enemy types, and while the game sort of presents this as a rock/paper/scissors system where you should grapple the brawlers, beat down the grapplers, and outsmart the dirty-fighters, I really just did the same thing to every single enemy. All you need to do is get a big combo off and then you're golden, you'll have so many hits coming at an enemy that they'll just die. On the contrary, grappling is REALLY strong but REALLY risky, I found that it was 50/50 whether or not my big grapple combo would land or not. This is what contributed to me getting a bit bored of the game after playing it for ~30 minutes.BUT, it is a lot of fun in short bursts. There's enough strategy there to keep your interest, there are some challenging fights where you need to make sure you're using the right attacks, and each character is fun to play since they have their own advantages and disadvantages. Because of that, I'd highly recommend picking this up if you're interested in a blend of turn-based RPG strategy and beat-em-up fun. It goes together like peanut butter and jelly!I feel like I should point out that as of writing this review, this game has been out for well over 2 years and there's a second episode that's yet to be released. I'm not sure when that episode will come out but I've got a feeling that it'll provide more enemy variety as well as some improvements to the core gameplay loop. The second episode will be a free update to this game, so I'm more than happy to play & review it whenever it comes out.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game because of the promo song. The content release so far (Ep 1) took me 4-5 hours with lots of laughing breaks, looking forward to more episodes! I think it's well worth buying and playing as-is, though.The gameplay is a really interesting mix of fighting game and RPG mechanics, with position and spacing, combo bonuses and momentum, and dynamic resource management. I was constantly gauging my FP vs. action points to pick moves, decide whether to pummel one enemy or knock them down and switch targets, or maybe keep something back for defense. Once you get the hang of keeping momentum, the game is pretty easy- I had to take a 2nd try at 2-3 fights but generally rolled over the idiots. Struggled to get Brad rolling with his low accuracy and vulnerability to counters compared to Lisa and Bruce, but landing a big throw was always awesome.The dialog is hilarious, the enemies are oh so punchable, and the gameplay is unique and cool. Two thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but the whole reason I bought it was for the wrestling references and moves, and the grappler character is completely hamstrung by the combat system. There is no reason to use Grapples because you will be countered 90% of the time. I understand the mechanic that grapples do big damage so you have to wear down your opponent before you can use them (basic wrestling psychology), but I feel the implementation is not balanced at all. At least give the grappler more wrestling related strikes (clothesline, big boot, dropkick).Overall it's a cool idea but needs to be balanced better.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance you might think Treachery in Beatdown City is an average beat em up game that aims to remind you of the days back when. And in some rights that is true, but to say it is only that would degrade the game and what the devs have achieved here. Beatdown City manages to blend that beat em up style with a semi turned-based RPG to create an entirely new type of experience. It's fluid, allows for multiple combo variations. Add that in with multiple enemy variants and combat never becomes dull. With a funny story and amazing writing to go along, this is definitely a game worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: So far its been good and fun. Feels like mashup from the ole Double Dragon of NES and Final Fantasy turn battle game. You walk in "world map" like in Super Mario 3, and there's enemy waiting to battle. When you reach the enemy, the screen turn into closeup sideway look of the map and you can move freely. When  you want to start to attack the enemy you get bunch of option from light punch, kick etc. Each of the attack have an Action Point much like x-com game. I can't get the detail but there's more to it. You just have to play the game your self.  I dig the art style. Too bad it doesn't support ultrawide but that's Ok for me. Playing in  21:9 there's a blackbar on each side of the screen.I haven't finished the game so I can give my full review about all the enemy type and character's move set. But I really like the game loop mechanic so I want to give it an early review.I'm one of the backer of this game and I'm glad it was what I expected, a classic mix of my favorite genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Treachery in Beatdown City

_childDocuments_.review: Beatdown City's gonna whoop yo ass.  If there's a downside, it's that I played through the game in a day, but I really do like the combat system.  It makes button mashing useless, turning what could have been a twitchy mess into a beautiful strategic masterpiece.  Okay, not really a strategic masterpiece, but it's pretty sweet.  I do kind of wish that the advantages/disadvantages were slightly more influential.  I love the way weapons are handled.  Costing more FP to use them and limiting defensive actions focuses the combat towards disarm.  And it feels really awesome to throw a Mexican Suplex on some dumbass fool stupid enough to get in your way.Of course the social commentary and unique comedic voice is really what sets the game apart.  I enjoyed beating up people who deserve beating up, and not having to worry about having moral quandaries about whether I'm the good guy while satisfying my virtual violence quota.Highly recommend.  Can't wait until the sequel is released.

name: Afterparty
detailed_description: New From Night School About the Game In Afterparty, you are Milo and Lola, recently deceased best buds who suddenly find themselves staring down an eternity in Hell. But there’s a loophole: outdrink Satan and he’ll grant you re-entry to Earth. Control Milo and Lola with an intelligent conversation system that changes the story and your relationships based on every decision. Uncover their personality quirks and foggy history during the wild events of the night. Every step is up to you as you stumble through the underworld. Go on a hellish bender, uncover the mystery of your damnation, and drink Satan under the table. Afterparty Features: An intelligent conversation system that allows you to change the story and your relationships based on every decision An underworld with an interconnected network of islands via the River Styx A variety of libations (over 30), each changing your dialogue choices and personality A large, outrageous cast to interact with, each with their own unique set of problems Demonic activities including beer pong, dance-offs, and chugging competitions An original soundtrack by scntfc, the composer from Oxenfree Starring: Janina Gavankar as Lola Khoi Dao as Milo Ashly Burch as Sam Erin Yvette as Wormhorn Dave Fennoy as Satan Music and Sound by SCNTFC

short_description: In Afterparty, you are Milo and Lola, recently deceased best buds who suddenly find themselves staring down an eternity in Hell. But there's a loophole: outdrink Satan and he'll grant you re-entry to Earth.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have any memories of what bar crawling and club hopping is really like - by which I mean, if you remember how much of it consists of schlepping two blocks down to the next place, feeling antsy and bored as your buzz begins to wear off, wondering if you're really having fun and if the people you're hanging out with are really your friends - then you might like Afterparty. That is not an insult. Afterparty is a game about alcohol and relationships and the ways that both can leave you unfulfilled, and I really, really liked it. And I especially liked those dull moments, steering Milo and Lola back to the cab stand, listening to the ambient sound of the city at night, because the way the silence would get itchy and drag a little bit too long made me go, "Ah. This is exactly what it was like. This game gets it."If anything, I think marketing this game as a gleeful romp through hell to outdrink Satan was a mistake. Don't get me wrong - the writing is witty, the voice actors turn in top notch performances, and the cocktails themselves are delightfully creative. But playing it, it's obvious that Afterparty was never really out to capture the joy of being raucously drunk at a killer party where that's a welcome thing to be. It set out to capture the uncertain misery of dragging yourself back home in the grey light of early morning, feeling the beginnings of your hangover-to-be through your fading buzz, already regretting some of the ♥♥♥♥ you said to the person dragging themselves back home beside you. And it nailed that.Honestly, I wish it got a little more respect for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: Despite what others might think, to me, afterparty is actually quite a good game. It's a walking simulator, which most might already expect, especially if you were an Oxenfree fan. What comes down to whether you would enjoy the game, mostly depends on how you view the story. Afterparty is not the hyper and edgy party-animal game that some trailers might falsely portrait. It gives more of the "afterparty" vibe as a teenager barhopping and feeling like trash and... not really having a good time, when you feel like you should be. That's what it felt like to me. You're dead, you're in hell, and everything is sadistic and sucks. Kinda like life, but you make the best out of it.The taxi rides are supposed to be awkward. Lola and Milo are supposed to not be perfect friends. And that's okay. It makes the game feel real.And oh, I recommend forfeiting the drinking competition in the end, at least for once. There were some interesting and even philosophical dialogues. And don't be afraid of "bad choices". There are none, only "different" choices. 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like Afterparty. Oxenfree was great, The premise is interesting, and the chromatic-aberration art style is trippy in a good way. I was really bummed out when they announced the Epic exclusivity, and really excited to play it when it popped up on the Steam store. But man... was it not worth the wait.Just to get this out of the way, the game had a surprisingly high number of bugs over its 5-6 hour runtime. I had multiple gamebreaking bugs that required not just a reload of the save but a hard restart of the game and some experimentation to fix, as well as non-gamebreaking bugs that really hurt immersion. To give an example of each:1. In one bar, pressing space on the 'exit' door would play a character animation of opening the door, but not actually open the door, and then the character would be unable to take any other actions. Eventually had to restart the game, go use another door a couple times, and then come back to the door I wanted to use to fix the issue.2. At certain points in the game, your narrative decisions will be briefly reviewed and commented on. In one such section, the game thought that I had made the *opposite choice* to what I actually did, and the characters got into an argument over events that did not occur in my playthrough.Separately from the bugs, the game's story just isn't up to the task of carrying a narrative-driven game. It spends its first 3 hours introducing a variety of subplots, depending on the choices you made, and then seems to realize that it needs to wrap up its main plot and either drops or abruptly concludes each subplot. There are several moments where characters caution you about decisions you're making, in a "Clementine will remember that" sort of way, only for that character to never reappear in the game.It also struggles with meaningful narrative branching -- when I asked another character for a stamp of approval, they asked me to do a favor in return and then we'd play a drinking game for it. When I refused to do the favor, they kind of went "eh, whatever" and played the drinking game with me anyway. When I lost the drinking minigame because it was timed and there were no controls given to me (I assume there was supposed to be instructional text that bugged out) they just gave me the stamp of approval anyway. Why even give me the choice, if the narrative structure can't handle it?The last thing I'll mention is the minigames' unhealthy prominence in the narrative. There are three, and each showed up twice for me, usually at pivotal story moments. Without any way to really practice them in advance, my performance in them was based on whether I had played a game with similar mechanics before, which led to me performing perfectly on the DDR-esque minigame, while it took me one loss in the drinking game to understand the controls and a second loss to understand the goal. The game even seems to understand that this is a problem, with one character jokingly breaking the 4th wall and offering to reload the save for you. This turns all the game's key narrative moments into these sort of goofy Warioware-esque segments, which completely deflate the narrative momentum and tension.I'll still look forward to Night School's next game, but this was a miss for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: Never played Oxenfree or even watched a play through of it but I saw this game pop up on the featured section of my store page and I had some money left over in my steam wallet, a day of nothing to, and an interest in the concept so I figured why not. Let me tell you I didn't regret a single cent of my purchase. This game captivated me so much I ended up completing one entire run in a single sitting, all 5.3 hours. Due to the decision making and different types of alcohols that can affect your dialogue options at the very minimum this game allows up to three full play throughs. Most dialogue options are given in threes, A, B, or nothing. The dual protagonist method really helps this game a lot especially if you choose the silent dialogue options because normally either Milo or Lola will cover for the other in that event. This game touches very well on some very heavy and serious topics without it feeling like it is saying them to say them. It treats serious issues with respect and integrity. Would highly recommend even if you haven't played Oxenfree.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a “maybe” option between just “yes” and “no” for recommending a game. I really loved Night School Studio’s first game, Oxenfree. It’s probably one of my favorite games of all time. I’ve replayed it dozens of times and I’m still not sick of it. And technically, on paper, the mechanics of Afterparty aren’t any different… but they FEEL like so much more of a boring slog. The choices you make throughout the game hold no meaningful weight and have no real lasting consequences. The dialogue doesn’t feel nearly as organic. The atmosphere doesn’t hold up beyond the first 30 minutes or so. The premise stops being engaging after the second time you go to outdrink a demon and realize that the entire game is just walking through Environment A, ordering a drink, talking to Demon A, walking through Environment A again to talk to Demon B, ordering another drink, playing a drinking game, reporting back to Demon A, and then walking back through Environment A to go rinse and repeat the entire process 2-3 more times. There’s just not a lot of depth to this game. Even player choice doesn’t actually matter that much. You can choose any random dialogue options at any given point and it barely matters, because you’ll almost definitely still get what you want/need in the end. You can be a selfish, uncooperative jerk and deliberately fail at every task you’re given the entire time and it will barely affect the end results of your playthrough. The narrative moves along at a snail’s pace with zero sense of urgency or suspense and very little variety. If you replay the game and pick all the opposite options from what you originally chose, you’ll still end up with almost the exact same gameplay experience and the exact same choices of ending. And unlike in Oxenfree, the relationships between characters in Afterparty just feels a bit forced. Milo and Lola talk often about what good lifelong friends they are, but apart from occasional inside jokes and references, you never really get the feeling that they have anything more than a surface-level friendship of proximity rather than one of actual love or affection for each other. There’s nothing overtly WRONG with this game, which is why I really hesitated to say I wouldn't recommend it. The graphics are good, the voice acting is great, the narrative is fun and interesting, the characters are cool, the gameplay is amusing. And yet, every time I play Afterparty, even during my very first playthrough, it just ends up feeling like a chore that I have to push through. If it's on sale and these kinds of games are your jam--then go for it. Give it a try; maybe you'll enjoy it more than I did. But if it's NOT on sale, or it's between this game and another one... I'd probably recommend that you go with the other one.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Oxenfree which is why I decided to buy this game. Honestly the acting and the graphics are amazing. I do like the side scroll play style too. However thats where it really end for me. The story could've been better. I think the idea of the plot is a good concept, I just don't think the plot was well executed. At times I felt like it was too slow for my taste. And the side conversations are pointless. I would listen to the whole conversation just to get nothing out of it. My choices didn't really seem to affect the story that much either. I think if the developers added more backround story at the beginning and added more meaningful conversations to the main plot would make it better. If I had to rate this game I would say 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Afterparty is a story driven game from developers who made another amazing game called Oxenfree. Afterparty retains similar gameplay and amazing artstyle.You end up in hell where you feel like... in hell. Although after some time it seems that it's a pretty fun place to be. People are tortured there for years, decades, eternity. But it's a fun place. There are parties, everyone has their job, some work as bartenders, some work as taxi drivers, some work as torturers and so on.So after  Lola and Milo die they end up in hell and want to go back to the world of living and for that they need to speak to Satan. They venture forth to enter the Satan's party only to realize they need to get seals and then outdrink the Satan. Fun isn't it?The game is very simple yet extremely fun. You basically walk/run back and forth in a side-scrolling manner. No puzzles like it was in Oxenfree but instead you get mini-games which are really challenging. But those are mainly tied to achievements.The game is pretty short and has few mini-games. Those are dance and pong games. Dancing mini-game is simple – you must repeat the moves of your competitor which is simply pressing the buttons in the right order after they show on screen. Now in beer-pong you must throw a ball into a cup and if ball gets into a cup that person drinks the cup. Simple but this is actually very challenging.You'll play these few times.You need to speak to other characters, do some tasks and travel to different districts of hell. You also can drink, drink a lot, countless of different cocktails to choose from. Drinking opens up new dialogue choices which often involve lots cursing. Oh yeah this is has a lot of cursing, love it. Drinks also may have an effect on mini-games.The game is full of humor, good humor. Actually the humor is a big part of the game. Did you know that Jesus Christ could be shortened as JC? Yep. Cool. Oh and that line about turtles and titties...i just don't know what to say, i laughed my ass off.There also are some choices which affect achievements so you'll need to replay the game for those. Although the replayability value isn't great. I wish you would be able to get all the achievements in one playthrough because it feels like a waste of time.Graphically the game is stunning. Technically nothing impressive but the artstyle is amazing and the graphics look very clean and full of details. All the characters are different, animations are very good and  overall the game looks beautiful and makes hell a wonderful place.Game works in ultrawide with a simple fix. I don't why it doesn't support it out of the box, the game looks beautiful in ultrawide and has no issues.Performance obviously is great although there are some occasional barely noticeable stutters which most likely are connected to autosaving which happens very often.Now sound. The soundtrack is good but you'll probably won't remember it. It's great when you hear it but nothing to listen to when not playing the game.Voice acting on the other hand is is outstanding. Huge thumbs up for getting all these amazing voice actors. I can't describe with word how good it is, you need to hear it. And voice acting plays a huge part in such game. Combined with awesome writing and humor it's simply amazing, you will never want for characters to stop talking.Overall a very good game for those who are into narrative games and loves humor. Although the game is definitely not for children. Get this on sale at least, it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: : This game features a lot of dark and crude humor. There are many mentions of horrific ways to die or be tortured, but none of it is graphic. All nudity is pixelated, but some scenes might make the player uncomfortable. It also makes a mockery of religion (mostly Christian mythology), so if you’d take offense to that, don’t play the game.As the game description mentions, it’s about two friends – Milo and Lola – ending up in Hell together. They don’t remember how they died. They feel that they don’t belong in Hell, so their journey begins in trying to find a way out. They learn that Satan will release souls from Hell if they can out-drink him in a drinking contest, but of course, it can’t be that easy. Milo and Lola trek all over the wastelands that are Hell for their quest, but also realize some of the mistakes they made in life along the way.    • Great voice acting. Ashly Burch! <3    • Fun music and sound effects definitely add to the ambiance of the game.    • Striking visuals and environments.    • Low-key psychological analysis of people’s actions combined with philosophical thoughts on what is considered “good” or “bad.”    • Some branching paths, choices, and results.    • Depending on what alcoholic beverage the (in-control) main character is drinking, dialogue options change. That’s neat.    • The two main characters are nice racial representation. Milo is Asian-American (heritage not specified) and Lola is black American.     • Even in Hell, it isn’t cool to be racist.     • You  pet the dog.    • Rarely, audio cuts out too early or doesn’t quite sync with the scene, but it wasn’t a big deal.     • Writing inconsistencies. For instance, if you don’t wish to use a comma for addressing people directly, then don’t do it at all. Randomly using it sometimes makes it look like several mistakes rather than a chosen style of writing. So, it could just be several typos throughout the game, if that wasn’t the intention.    • The mini-games can be a bit unfair, especially since the player is thrown into them without any clue on how to play them. The initial directions are there for about a second, and I’m just like, “Uh, wtf am I supposed to be doing?” There should be a way to practice outside the story events. I hate the shot glass stacking one.     • There are moments in the game that put a lot of emphasis on individual responsibility when it comes to issues in the world, especially climate change, but that’s problematic. The one true way to fix the problems of the world is to eliminate capitalism. Climate change? It’s because of capitalism. Profits over environment. Non-stop war? Capitalism. War is profitable. Exploitation? It’s f*cking capitalism. Profits over people. If there’s money to be made by doing something horrible, capitalist opportunists will hop right on that. I’m not saying people should stop recycling or doing good things for their community, but putting the blame and responsibility on  for the world’s problems is just downright wrong. Even if every individual person stopped harming the environment, it would put a rather small dent in preventing climate change. I’d recommend this game to those who liked Oxenfree. It has the exact same sort of gameplay (plus mini-games), but instead of horror, you get dark humor.

_childDocuments_.review: Hmm, I guess my rating would be more of a neutral if Steam allowed it. I hate to say it, but this is boring - and not because it's a dialogue focused story game.I loved Oxenfree, and numerous games like this one, but Afterparty is...just kinda hollow. Every area just feels a little bit barren once you look past how nice the visuals areOne of the main features is that you can get various alcoholic drinks and drink from them to unlock new dialogue. All this really does is give you a third option in conversations where your character cracks a sarcastic or jokey response, that is immediately forgotten by everyone elseThere are simple minigames thrown in every so often but they come at you unexpectedly and give the player little to no time to practise. Since they're a little bit clunky in controls, I found myself failing them before I really had a chance to try and succeed The two main characters I actually like quite a lot, although I don't know if the game does a totally amazing job at convincing you that these two are lifelong buddies There also isn't much of a focus on why these two characters are in hell which felt like a missed opportunity

_childDocuments_.review: Lola and Milo, two fresh college-grads who are yet to start their life, find themselves in Hell with amnesia roaming their memories. What did they do to deserve this ticket for eternal damnation? They have no idea as they try to accept this new horrifying reality. Here is food for thought, what did they do to deserve something else? People who don't have enough good deeds in their balance go straight to Hell, even if they didn't commit horrendous crimes; that's according to the beliefs shared within the Afterparty universe. Ironically, Afterparty doesn't have enough balance to make me recommend it.Later on, they learn that in order to escape Hell, they must beat Satan in a drinking contest. That sums up the plot, and here is where it fails. So why did it work fine with Oxenfree—Night School Studio's previous game—and didn't work in Afterparty, although they share nearly the same mechanics? The answer is simple: the suspense is missing. Oxenfree did a fine job in interconnecting both the character-driven and story-driven elements of the plot, weaving a thrilling experience filled with mystery that enthralls the interest, making the player engaged with the story and always eager to strive for more. On the other hand, it won't take much effort to uncover the entire plot within the first hour of gameplay in Afterparty, leaving a boring story with some comedic drama to charge up the entertainment.The adventure is simple: interact with NPCs, choose the desired dialogue option, play some minigames, and enjoy the show. Of course, the speech-bubble dialogue plays the heaviest emphasis on the overall gameplay with a new formula to the mix: alcohol intoxication. Booze in Hell has more to it than to inebriate. Each Hellcohol has a mystical toll on its drinkers, as it unshackles them from their previous concerns of societal appropriateness. Such effects are not limited to enhancing confidence, double-talk, flirting, intimidation, etc. Consuming these beverages while talking with someone unlocks new dialogue slots, adding more room for exploring different scenarios within conversations but doesn't have any solid consequence in the flow of the events.No objection to the overall quality of the voice performances; it's very professionally delivered. As for the writing, it's subjective. To put it straight: sometimes, the humor-themed dialogue goes very well with the events at hand, and other times, it becomes either awkweird or boring. It depends on your taste in comedy. Everything is a joke; nothing to worry about; everything is fine! It doesn't take itself seriously, and the game knows it. For the record, it isn't for children, sensitive, or religious people, as there is no limit for the humor here. The final result of the script: I didn't care much about any moving thing in the game. Also, I am not a fan of the game's mechanic of randomly switching between Lola and Milo while traveling or in the middle of a conversation.No matter what you do. No matter what you choose. You'll always wear the dunce cap, all thanks to Sister Mary Wormhorn, an anthropomorphic form of psychological torture in Hell who will mostly judge your choices, making them all look stupid no matter your decisions. The more I play, the more it becomes linear that I stopped caring about any choice I make. The game is point A to point C. You can't deviate off the direction to explore B or go back to A. The exploration is tied only to conversations, and after all, it doesn't matter much in the end. It's more like a fixed-path dialogue-interactive animation movie. The game has three endings that entirely depend on the very last portion of gameplay. All the choices you've made throughout your playthrough till that point are pointless.A fancy introduction themed by neon-colored fluorescent lights accompanied with a superb piece of music! These people don't mess around in terms of grabbing one's attention. Body language plays a remarkable role in covering up the lack of detail regarding facial expressions due to the far camera's point of view. As for environmental sound design, I find it quite generic and can get boring over time. The soundtrack is fine, with "Schoolyard Strangler" being the finest. The latest game build supports full point-and-click controls for mouse-only gameplay. I did encounter a total of 3 annoying bugs that required me to exit and start from the last checkpoint.I did my best to like Afterparty, but eventually, I failed. I consider it a wasted opportunity for a solid concept and excellent art direction. The shallow depth of the story, the futile choices, and the linear level design; all don't befit what the game intends to be, hence wrecking the entire experience. In addition, its humor didn't suit my taste, but at the end of the day, comedy is subjective. Worthy of mention: there is a twist in the story, but it didn't work for me, as I didn't care much about the characters in the first place. In brief, this game will work for you if you're interested in its characters, and its comedy matches your taste.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: If this game got your attention, go play Oxenfree instead. You'll thank me later.This game isn't bad, but it left me pretty disappointed. This game starts off super strong, the moment to moment dialog, animation and art style are on point, from the word go the story has you hooked. You're in hell, the only way back to earth is to out-drink the big bad of big bads, the ultimate party master, Satan himself. Sounds good, lets roll. However, by about the one or two hour mark the game starts to lose the thread, and it slowly dawns on you that the game popped off almost all its creative ideas in the beginning, and the "hell is just one big nightclub and Satan is a high-functioning alcoholic, isn't that funny lol" bit, along with witty and punchy moment to moment dialog, is really all the game has to cover the next three-four hours. The story also feels like it's building to some big twist at the end, like it's all going to come to a head. But then it just kinda, ends? Hope that's not a spoiler.Night School might be their own worst enemy here. Oxenfree set the bar so dang high with this style of game that they really had to swing for the fences on this one, and (in my opinion) they missed, which is fine. Can't win em all.My hope is that they learn what worked, and what didn't, and pour all of that knowledge and creative energy into Oxenfree II, which already looks to be quite promising. P.S., whoever thought up the mechanic that you only have access to your third dialog option if you drink deserves a high-five. I spent every second I could absolutely sloshed on any bevs I could find just to see what the third choice would be, and it was worth it ever time. Hands down the best part of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: After Oxenfree, the devs put themselves in a tricky situation, Oxenfree was REALLY amazing, so the expectactions were high for me.And sadly, they failed to meet them. The premise, concept, aesthethic, amazing, but the story, the KEY part of it all? Lackluster.It's not that it's awful or anything, it's just bland.The pacing and the story itself just don't hook you in, it doesn't leave you wanting more, the world feels full yet empty, with little to do other than walk to point B. This could've been an open world RPG if I'm honest.I waited what felt like an eternity for this to come out due to the Epic Store exclusivitiy, and I ended up being disappointed in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: I was somewhat disappointed by this one. I bought Afterparty on the merits of the trailer and the young studio's previous game, Oxenfree. This is NOT on the same level as Oxenfree. The developer is going with a similar recipe, but this game is under cooked. It starts off strong, with good dialogue, a compelling premise, but never seems to go anywhere with it. The story ends up feeling short, shallow, and the ending is weak. It's unfortunate, considering how rich the world feels. There is strong world building at work here. Rich environments and music. But not enough to do. On a few occasions I would wonder, as the characters are running: "I've never been so bored looking at such nice pictures". The game has it's funny moments. You can feel that a lot of care went into things like the names of the drinks, and the lore of the world... But after a few hours of play, you start feeling like the whole thing is stalling. I kept waiting for the second act to drop... For some twist, or for the stakes to rise... At some point I though: ok, the good part is coming, I can feel it... But it was the ending already and the game was over. I cannot recommend this one. Just go replay Oxenfree.
