_childDocuments_.review: Don't buy this game, there's a serious bug that prevents you from completing it if you choose a certain option.  When you are in a club if you choose the second option - when you are meant to jump down, you select the option and then - nothing. You can then no longer move or interact with anything. It seems to affect multiple players and the only suggestion I've found seems to be to reinstall, play back to the same point, and *hope* it doesn't happen again!  Steam won't refund the game as it's too far in on the game and I contacted the developer directly and got no response. Really disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: Okay boring at first but gave it a chance and actually finished it. Now I'm playing a second time because just like Oxenfree, I wanted to see what other decisions I could've make to bear different results. Despite being in Hell and trying to outdrink Satan, it has a good moral story about friendship. Milo and Lola were strangers to me at first, but as time went on pieces of their lives were unveiled, and I realise how these two are inseparable but also sometimes to their detriment. I came to understand and love their friendship by the end of the game. Love the drinking mechanic, different drinks, different dialogue effects, that's genius. Also I can't stop admiring the visuals, the colours, the designs they're just too good, night school studio never disappoints :')
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: The reviews were good, the idea was interesting, the atmosphere seemed to be there, but the whole experience was 8 hours of disappointment. 8 hours of excruciatingly boring gameplay and endless dialogues. This game could have easily been 3 hours, I don't know why this effort to stretch every situation and conversation for no particular reason - and of course let's not forget the additional glitches to spice things up for us. I don't have a problem with the walking simulator type of games as long as there is a story to walk through but it does not exist in this game. I can't comprehend how this game gets to be called "story-rich". Visuals and music are cool but that's all there is. There is an illusion of choice but it is not like a choice that actually matters. It says it is a "dark comedy" game but for me, this game was neither funny nor dark. 3 hours in and I was just begging for the game to finish as I do not like to leave games unfinished but oh boy, it was a painful decision. I respect everybody's opinion about what is "comedy" so let's just say that I have a different sense of humor and a very different set of expectations from a game. So if you are actually looking for a "dark humor", "story-rich", "drama" where "choices matter", I do not recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: Although the subject matter and setting are ripe with potential, the humor ultimately killed any desire I had to play the game.I had a very hard time following dialogue, because characters would frequently interject their own sarcastic opinions, non-sequiturs, and philosophies. It was very distracting. It is possible that one may like this kind of humor, but I did not. It was almost entirely referential and obscure. There was one reference to a district attorney who died several decades ago. I genuinely spent 20 minutes trying to figure out why this person would be referenced, to no avail. On the occasions when I did get the references, I sometimes couldn’t understand why it was funny. There was one joke about how Toronto looks like New York. I mean I guess? Is this a thing that people joke about? I honestly have no idea why anyone would care if these cities do or do not look alike, or why it would be funny.Occasionally I got glimpses of what could have been. There are themes of conflict, either between friends, between family, or interpersonal. There is also a revelation at the end that adds some weight to the story, but I this came too late. I do believe there is potential here, I just think it was squandered.Gameplay wise you are mostly just walking around and talking to people. Dialogue options will come up organically as the character is speaking, as they did an Oxenfree. I think here they are a little bit more janky than they were in Oxenfree. There were times when I would choose a dialogue option, and it would interrupt the character currently speaking in an unnatural manner. There are a few mini games, such as dancing in the club or drinking games. They offer a nice break from the story, but I think they are too few. I am OK with the game having only a little interactivity if there is a strong story, but with the story leaving much to be desired, the lack of interactivity was more noticeable.The game is pleasant to look at. There are not too many environments that you get to explore; it's mostly just clubs and bars. But they look good, with bright neon lights contrasting with the darkness of Hell in the background. My only complaint is some of the character animations. You will play as two characters, and sometimes I will move one character, and the other one is kind of lagging behind, so they will be in a weird position while conversations are happening. It takes you out of the experience.All said, I really can't recommend. I just wasn't able to get into it with the attempts at humor being such a large part of it and falling so flat.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: This game is sloppy but fun. If you like graphical adventures, and can put up with the bugs, it is worth it. That might not sound like a solid endorsement and, well, it isn't. This is not a masterpiece. It feels like a rush job. The studio was going through some things while this was in production and it shows. They cut corners to get it out the door and the game suffered for it. But, if you can overlook the flaws, there is a fun story to be had. I enjoyed it enough to give it a weak thumbs up.Pros:Good voice actingGood soundtrackCool art directionFun settingNot overlongCons:BuggyGlitchyShallowNo puzzlesOnly the briefest of mini-gamesNot really worth replayingThis game does have issues. Read the other reviews. Sometimes you will encounter game breaking bugs and you have to restart the game. It isn't that long so you aren't going to lose 40 hours of progress but it does suck. I didn't have that issue but, based on the overall level of polish, I can see it happening. It is also glitchy. There are A LOT of clipping issues. Satan's back pokes though his cape, the NPCs walk through you and each other all the time, the voices of some characters will randomly become very quiet, characters rubber-band a lot, Milo and Lola will be looking off into strange directions during dialogs, all sorts of strange things. This is also not a traditional graphical adventure. This is not Monkey Island or Kings Quest. It is more like a visual novel presented in the style of a graphical adventure. I only encountered 3 different drinking minigames during my playthrough and I only played them a half dozen times. The story has branching paths, so maybe I would see others if I chose different dialog options but I'm not going to play it again just to see what i missed. This game is mostly just talking. If that is enough for you and the story seems interesting, grab it. Finally, this is a one and done game for me. There are branching paths in the story that effect the finale but the different ending simply don't seem that interesting to warrant a replay. I watched the others on Youtube after beating it.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: I love Oxenfree and had high expectations for Afterparty. It looks great, but that's where it ends. Everything about it feels so hollow. The worlds are empty and although the characters talk much, they don't say a lot. I truly wanted to like this game, but on my second playthrough I'm still not feeling it.

_childDocuments_.review: 12.3h (100% achievement, finished game 1.5 times) 7.8h No (2 can be grindy depending on your playstyle). Yes (17 achievements). No. tells the story of Sam and Lola in the depths of hell. You'll visit several places with a bar in them, try out different drinks, and follow the story. Some minigames are included as well, which might or might not include drinking in them.- Slight differences in dialogues depending on your response throughout the game- 3 endings- Boring story- Unable to fast-forward the dialogue for the second playthrough- BugsIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 is displayed in 3D visuals, albeit in a sidescroller format. The dark lighting with neon signs also makes the 3D models not that apparent, giving a unique style to it. The interface is also simple and nice to look at.There is a party, and you just died.  gives a sharp turn at the beginning, forcing you to figure out where you are and how you can get out of your predicament. You'll go on an adventure; the hell doesn't seem to be that different from the world we are in, except with some demons and their torture-related job, and most importantly, there are bars that you can visit to get drunk and forget your worries.I like that people talk like humans. They all bicker with each other nonstop, with you having to cut their sentences to talk or risk not getting a say in the dialogue since you missed the timing. Moreover, NPCs have varied dialogues, making it not boring when you have to talk to them several times.However, I found the topic to be boring. Just like how it is in real life, people are talking about nonsensical stuff, which sometimes was done just for the sake of making a conversation. I don't mind if it's done in real life, but I find them to be empty when it's applied in a game. does a good job of mixing drinking into the gameplay elements. For starters, the whole premise of the game is to find something or someone to drink with. Each bar has its specialties which can give a new option to what you can say. One drink can make you drunk, another can make you talk like a pirate. You need to drink it first, though, and be in an effect of the drink to make the dialogue option available. The new dialogue might not change the story as a whole, but it still gives a nice variation to the story.Three minigames are available to play. All of them are only available during a certain point of the game, which is usually required to progress the story. One is a beer pong where you need to throw a ball to a cup, another is a glass-stacking game where you need to stack a glass while being drunk, and the last one is a dance game where you need to mimic someone's movement. They are easy to beat, although you are usually given second chances if you lose the mandatory ones.The rest of the game is mainly playable in a sidescroller format where you need to walk from point A to B. The thing is, the walk can be lengthy, and sometimes you need to wait until the characters finished talking before you can interact with something. It makes the game to be tedious, especially in your second playthrough since you can't skip any dialogues.I finished the game in 7.8h. You need to finish the game three times if you want to get all achievements, or make a backup save and played the game 1.5 times. I did the second option, and it took me an additional 4.5h (12.3h total) to get everything. The game has a replayability value since people will react differently based on what you did, but I don't think it's worth another playthrough, especially with how tedious the game is. I even dozed off several times when I played the game at night, even in my first playthrough.There was an instance when I couldn't progress the game since a cutscene didn't trigger. It took me minutes to figure out that I had to restart the game to trigger it - I thought I lost my 4h progress and had to restart from scratch. I found that there are similar bugs that people reported in Steam's discussion thread, so I was being careful not to trigger another bug while playing. might have an interesting premise and cool presentation, but all of it was shadowed with boring dialogues. You have to deal with the tedious walking, only to hear people talking endlessly. It might work in  () since it has more suspense and mysteries, but I don't think it works in this game due to how straightforward it is. That being said, I'm afraid I can't recommend this game as I didn't enjoy playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: The real hell is enduring the dialogue that this game thinks is funny.If you’re like me and enjoyed Oxenfree because of the premise, the setting, the intriguing mystery and naturalistic dialogue, this game is going to be a hard disappointment because it’s lacking almost all of that. By the time you get past the description of Afterparty, the joke’s already been worn out.It still shares the same problem Oxenfree had, that is, characters cutting their own dialogue off because you walked past a certain point, and you always miss out on the few lines that are interesting, without fail. Yet surprisingly, when you try to walk away from some of the annoying lines the characters spout, the screen will lock, forcing you to stay and listen to their ceaseless drivel. Other times the dialogue ends way too early, leaving you to stroll along for several minutes in awkward silence. When the only string to your game’s bow IS the dialogue, it’s quite a misstep. When none of the characters present act like they care, why should you? That’s the major theme to take away from this title. It honestly makes you want to reach through the screen and punch them in the head until they can learn to speak without wrapping everything in 15 layers of irony and snark.There’s one part where you have to take several elevators up multiple levels in order to get to the top floor, only to have to turn around and return to the bottom, but now there’s an option to jump right to the ground floor, or vice versa if you’re returning. Why wasn’t that a choice from the beginning? Because the game hates you and wants to waste your time with inane banter.I tuned out during one of the bits where the game tries to make fun of your choices, aside from probably making some writers sad, I don’t think I missed much. And neither will you, if you choose to pass up this irritating test of patience.

_childDocuments_.review: Some pros and cons, but on the whole game boils down to a ~6 hour bar crawl through hell. : Visually charming, similar to Oxenfree or Night in the Woods in that regard. Voice actors were very good, too.: Without spoiling anything, the plot is nonsensical. The dialogue was written by somebody who was trying  hard to be witty. The game is short - only about 6 hours - and is very much on rails, not many decisions to make and they don't seem to make much difference anyhow. The mini-games have no preparation or instructions, and aren't always self-explanatory enough. Overall, it's tough to recommend this game. It's definitely not as charming or well made as Oxenfree was, but if you're *really* a sucker for a quaint side-scrolling jaunt through hell, then this might be a good way to kill an afternoon.

_childDocuments_.review: This is no Oxenfree, but as a short story-based game without that level of expectation it is fine.The high points are the voice acting and art style. Writing is hit and miss. It's sometimes funny, but it does suffer from being too Whedonesque; when almost everyone is constantly trying to be witty/snarky the impact is lost, and characters lack their own distinctive voice. The narrative also feels too obviously on rails; by the late stage of the game I didn't care too much about a choice which was seemingly contrary to my objective, as I had no doubt that the game would conspire to put me back on track.It also feels very janky. Dialogue being cut off was an annoyance in Oxenfree but it's particularly grating here. Too often I just had to put the controller down for a while for fear of interrupting a conversation, while at other times I was left wandering aimlessly (and slowly) trying to trigger the next event. Still, you can't go too wrong with an occasionally funny, visually appealing and well-voiced story which doesn't overstay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: is Night School Studio's second graphic adventure game. Like  before, the game tells a dark and surreal story using the same gameplay formula, this time involving two college grads who recently died under mysterious circumstances and got a one way ticket to Hell.A fantastic duo of best friends who face eternal damnation. There is only one way to escape from Hell: outdrink the Lord of Darkness himself, Satan. if they succeed, they can safely return to the world of the living. It's just as simple as that. No surprises or big twists around the corner; it's a story that mostly plays by itself. Despite being a game of choices that partially affect the plot and what other characters say about Milo and Lola, there are only two predefined endings. What I feel disapponted about is that there is only one way of interpretation, but you understand that only during the credits.The game is about alcohol and relationships, and how they affect us. It's nothing philosophical and it's always kept funny by clever dialogues and great sense of humor, though there are some jokes that can be only understood by americans and christians (and those who know these two well enough). Milo and Lola are inseparable, but you can only play as one and swap at different times. This way you get to know both, while their subconscious is constantly brought up by a personal demon who torments them every now and then.A new mechanic is also introduced. Throughout this hell of a journey you will visit many bars and clubs where you can order different types of drinks that change your attitude and expand dialogue options. For instance, you can , be a , or just a . It's a nice addition that adds some variation to conversations, but it also feels like a wasted opportunity since it doesn't have much effect on gameplay.Aside from drinking and talking to demons and other condemned humans, there is not much else to do in Hell. A few mini-games (like Beer Pong) are available during some crucial parts of the story, while overall there is a huge lack of interactivity with the level design. From the main menu you can access a Social Network which works exactly like Twitter, except that you can only read other people's tweets, so it feels quite passive.The quest for salvation brings Milo and Lola through different neon-lit districts of the Underworld. If you got yourself at 2am walking on a street filled with closed shops while looking for a bar that is still open, you will get that sense of loneliness. Once you find an open bar, it's gorgeous (and you get to know lot of people), but again, there isn't much to do. I often explored areas that didn't have anything to show, not even a dialogue between random characters, except for a few tweets notifications.Voice Casting is phenomenal and clearly the major reason for feeling so attached to all characters, along with the fun writing and deep characterization.,,,. If these names don't ring any bell to you... well, they should. It's rare to see a cast like this in a small indie game.Music is a great part of the journey, always following Milo and Lola inside and outside clubs. The mesmerizing soundtrack has been composed by who previously scored Oxenfree as well, among other titles.The game runs flawlessly and overall I didn't encounter any issue, except for one time when the camera got stuck in one place and I was forced to quit and reload the save. There are some minor glitches as well, but nothing game breaking.Afterparty is a charming dark comedy with superb voice acting and a wonderful imaginary. It plays a lot with the sense of freedom, but except for a few moments where you will be asked to do A or B, it's quite linear and after nearly 10 hours I don't feel like playing it again to discover the other routes. The Epic Store deal clearly put a shadow on this game during its full year of exclusivity, but you don't want to miss it if you enjoyed Oxenfree. Just don't expect the same tone and atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I want to recommend this game, I simply can't.Pros: Looks good. Well animated. Good voice acting and a fun idea for a plot.Cons: Every mini-game you see in the trailer is used once or twice, not regularly, and with no instructions on controls. Story is over in about 5 hours. The effect you have on the main characters is minimal, even though you are controlling them. There is a point where the two characters get mad at each other and split up, even though I chose every dialog option for defusing the situation - for both of them, but it didn't matter. While it might seem re-playable, I can't say that I would want to, knowing that the majority of the pieces I experienced would likely be the same no matter my choices. Some world building would have been nice, but a character in the game breaks the fourth wall and says they didn't want to do that.Overall, I really wanted to like it, honest. I loved Oxenfree and wanted another interesting romp like that. I was left with 5 hours of my life gone. Not all bad, but certainly not worth the $16 I paid on sale. _childDocuments_.review: I love Oxenfree by the same creators so I figured this one would be similar. It's stylistically somewhat similar but without the key elements that made Oxenfree so special. This time, you play as Milo and Lola, who are inexplicably in hell after dying on their college graduation. They learn that the one way out is by outdrinking Satan. You get to embark on tedious, boring tasks till it's finally time to play two drinking games and either beat him and be alive again, or stay in hell for a bit and then be offered the chance to leave because of some loophole. The game sprinkles in some minor trauma but it doesn't feel nearly as heartfelt as Oxenfree. The characters aren't very likable and are honestly a total bore. I didn't even get into the glitches! That's a very important part of why I don't recommend it. The game lags at times, making the dialogue take forever and sometimes the characters can't access exits unless you run to the other side of the room and then try again. It's exhausting. The game should take 6-7 hours tops but it somehow took 12 because of this. So I say this as a big Oxenfree fan: do not buy this game. It'll leave you feeling unfulfilled and make you wonder why you  wasted $19.99 on it instead of something better.

_childDocuments_.review: Warning: There is a game-breaking bug currently present in the Afterparty where your character will get stuck on a ceiling walkway, not allowing you to advance. Unfortunately it's right near the end of the game. I ran in to this issue. This review encompasses about 90% of the game's contents.Afterparty's premise is interesting. Milo and Lola have just died, and awoken in hell. Cue an adventure that skirts the beaucratic process of checking in and out of hell, while exploring it's booze and party soaked streets. At its core, Afterparty is a walking simulator with light dialogue-based puzzles and a few drinking-inspired mini-games. The gameplay primarily involves moving left or right, listening to conversations, and making dialogue choices—usually between sarcastic and even more sarcastic responses. Although the game teases a branching narrative based on whether you favor Milo or Lola's choices, there is really only one significant branching points. Ultimately, regardless of your decisions, the story proceeds in a linear fashion, making the branching narrative feel superficial. You can even let the dialogue timer run out, and the characters will continue regardless of if you chose something, which undermines the impact of your choices. The drinking mechanic offers different dialogue options depending on your drink, but this doesn't add much to solving the dialogue puzzles and is mostly just flavour text.The artistic design is a highlight. Hell is depicted as a series of neon-lit back alleys, packed with dive bars across various islands on the River Styx. While Afterparty has its unique style, it's clear that it draws inspiration from Grim Fandango and Tim Burton's Beetlejuice in both its visuals and storytelling.However, the writing, particularly the dialogue, is a weak point. Though the game aims to be a comedy, the humor quickly wears thin. It falls into the trap of being overly crude and snarky, with insincere, sarcastic characters and clichéd writing tropes. The characters frequently launch into long-winded rants and monologues that add little value, only deepening your frustration and dislike for them. The story, despite its promising setup, fails to deliver. Milo and Lola are supposed to confront their fears through their personal demons, but any introspective moments are shallow, leaving you wondering what the point was. The demons themselves are good-natured and respond to Milo and Lola's quips with sarcasm, making nothing feel consequential. The script seems more concerned with showcasing the writer's wit and ability to cite obscure references than with delivering a coherent narrative. The result is an endless stream of rants, obscure allusions, and strange analogies (such as the tone-deaf rant about chocolate milk and animal abuse).In the end, Afterparty is a game with a promising concept and an interesting art style, but the limited gameplay, poor writing, and unlikeable characters make it a forgettable and frustrating experience. For me, it was one of the least enjoyable games I've played in a long while. I would recommend passing on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: One of those mixed reviews.I give it a positive because obviously a lot of work were put into making this game, and the voice acting is as perfect as it was in Oxenfree, but the game itself...You never know if you must take it seriously or not and end up never getting into it. _childDocuments_.review: A superb story driven game, although unfortunately held back a little by the lack of unique world design.The game does a good job of building the general identities and relationship of the protagonists in a natural pacing, and the game found quite a clever way to give players backstory on the protagonists through certain recurring events. As a whole pacing is a stronger point of the game. Apart from a few sequences of quiet travelling, there's always some form of dialogue taking place while the story keeps the experience relatively fresh throughout. The presence of multiple endings, choices and dialogue options gives players a reasonable amount of control over what happens. The complete voice acting also really helped to bring the story to life, all the voice actors did a fine job.The main weakness of the story-telling itself is that players cycle between playing as each protagonist while they progress. Consequently players never get to really settle down in a given identity or establish any sense of in-world perspective as they are constantly swapping roles. It also makes things somewhat confusing because players control the decisions that both protagonists make, which further degrades their sense of individuality as characters.The game attempts to use its drinking mechanic as the main, unique draw to the gameplay itself. Players have two default dialogue options they can make in a conversation, and the third option is determined by the type of drink they consume. This usually gives players access to intense behaviours independent of their character's identity, often unproductively absurd ones. Furthermore players often can only pick one type drink for the entirety of the conversation, a choice they must make ahead of time. As a whole the feature just feels like a devolution from simply giving players access to more dialogue options, and mostly only serves as a limited way to allow players to be unproductively silly.The world is aggressively built on human mythology. It would of been much nicer and more exciting if the developers created their own unique afterlife instead of just vaguely copying all the names and themes from human myths. It really doesn't add anything to the experience beside capping the creative potential of the world in exchange for acquiring a premade foundation for it. This all coincides with the somewhat immersion breaking elements of the world, such as the fact that demons all talk with completely average human voices; and that the demons are overly aware of human history and culture. Demons drop references to human history and culture constantly, generally more than they make references to their own history and culture; which betrays the fact that this story was written by humans and so the world is biased by that.There are some other more gameplay oriented problems such as characters occasionally having awkward pathfinding, walking conversation dialogue being interrupted by story events, characters standing in awkward places or clipping through things. Nothing majorly damaging to the experience but still cumulatively bothersome. The worst is that during the minigames, players only get one chance at it but also no tutorial. So the first time the player does the minigame it is frustratingly unknown, yet will have story consequences all the same.It does very well to carry its comedic story telling during the whole experience, and while endings may vary the one I got was quite satisfying. Unfortunate that the experience is addled by its desperate clinging to human mythology as a substitution for building a unique world; but the story that takes place within that world is still great.If you're interested in finding more games like this I've probably reviewed quite a few on my curator page .

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who really enjoys dialogue based stories that kind of send you into existential dread, I found this game oddly comforting and I enjoy looking back at the conversations written in the game. I came into this with no prior expectations and without playing the studio's previous game, Oxenfree, and I will have to say that its understandable on why this game is a hit-or-miss. I'll start off with the negative things.For people who enjoy more action filled games or a lot of other things to do to fill in the gaps, I wouldn't say that this is the best game for them as it does sometimes have very long pauses in places and kind of forces you to process everything that's happening in the game. Walking between places can be pretty slow as well. I've seen that there have been some bugs in other people's games, personally mine worked fine on a Macbook Air. I will have to say that there were some spots of dialogue that seemed confusing and out of place and there were certain actions that seemed slightly tedious such as getting the coat to meet a certain someone. There are slight inconsistencies and it would have been nice for a little bit more meaningful conversation in certain things like why Milo and Lola were such close friends in the first place and why they became so codependent on each other.However, I did find this game incredibly charming. I loved the colours and the art in the game. They were absolutely captivating and I really enjoyed seeing all the little details while walking to the next task. As a person who tends to overthink small phrases and tones in dialogue, the spaces of silence served well for me to marinate in my thoughts as someone would say something bizarre once again and I would get a hefty laugh. I found Milo and Lola to be endearing protagonists and I could see a lot of people I know in them as well as me, which is obviously extra points for relatability. It also brought up a lot of food for thought when I was also away from the game.I have to bring up that I do have some level of relatability to these characters so I had an easier time connecting with their stories and thoughts, which may be harder for others to grasp. This story isn't about learning who was who or what's right or what's wrong. What I took out of this game was just slight comfort. Comfort knowing that everyone is somewhat a douche in some way and that it just kind of matters if you were there at the right time and place. People get screwed and screw over others and when you follow Milo and Lola, you'll start to feel a certain sadness and grief. As the game continues on, you realise that whatever it is you're going through, it's just another instance of our messy beginnings and endings. It takes a while to digest what this game has to offer to you and that's not for everyone.So that being said, if you're a person who doesn't like to think a lot and you don't like to spend your time just sitting with a certain feeling, I wouldn't recommend this. BUT, if you are the type of person to be open to just listening to more conversations, looking at amazing art and sitting with a slightly unsettling feeling then yes, I would recommend getting it when its on sale or gifted. These kind of games take patience so if you feel like you wouldn't take the time, please play something else. I highly enjoyed this game but I do have very niche tastes so please treat this game gently and you'll be able to get something out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: I wholeheartedly wanted to like this game, but I can't recommend it to everyone.TL;DR it looks great, the premise is great, the voice acting is great, but it doesn't feel great.I'll start off with some positives:-I absolutely love the aesthetics. The artwork and the lighting and effects are fantastic.-The environment is extremely detailed and there are plenty of background conversations to eavesdrop on.-The voice acting is pristine, with a few exceptions.-Meeting the Greater Demons was really cool.-I enjoyed learning about Milo and Lola's friendship and seeing them adapt to their situation.Now, I'll try not to be too negative, but  here are some of the issues:-The dialogue. The script can't go two lines without making some obscure reference. For about 10-20 minutes into your first play-through you go "yeah, ok this seems witty, but not ". Eventually, when you start to realize that 99% of the characters speak that exact same way . It starts to get a bit tiresome. References are not jokes. Obscure references at every turn are exhausting.-Replayability. At the time of writing this, there is no way to skip dialogue. Considering you are given two or three conversational options, I figured I'd be able to have some influence on the conversation. On my second play-through, I found this NOT to be the case. You'll get maybe a unique line here and there, but without the ability to skip through parts you've already heard, consecutive play-through's become a chore.-The "choices". There are only about  distinct dialogue options that actually determine your endgame. Several times you are presented with what looks like an alternate path for your objective, aaaaand it is completely unexplorable. Why bother offering the option if the game immediately pulls the rug out from under you?-The minigames.  Don't get me wrong, in a story-driven game like this, minigames should not be that important. Except that your performance in these minigames WILL affect your outcome! What's more insulting is that there is background dialogue to suggest that you've "had plenty of practice", as if you've been given multiple opportunities to play them!-Exploration. In such a beautiful world, there are very minuscule rewards for taking the time to enjoy it. The dialogue between the characters will only last you long enough to get from point A to point B. If you meander about on path C, you get one or two points of interest leading to a dead end. You are then left to wander in complete silence back to your original destination.And finally:-The main characters. As mentioned before, the dialogue is overwritten; even for our two protagonists. Milo and Lola are given an epic quest, but if ALL of the characters sound like pretentious philosophy majors, the lines start to get blurred. The game gives you "choices", but it doesn't seem like there's ever a wrong answer. The duo's relationship is explored... .I know making indie games is hard and I'm open for discussion, so feel free to let me know if I've been unfair in my criticism.

_childDocuments_.review: I think Oxenfree is a truly amazing game, and I found Afterparty disappointing. There are plenty of professional reviews out there about how the mechanics of the game are either the same as the developer's prior work or different and not quite as good, but what stood out to me as a fundamental difference in the first hour of play is the tone and characters. In Oxenfree, the tone is pretty consistent. It's clear that something a bit spooky may happen from the very beginning, and by the time the prologue ends with the protagonist's trip through a cave, there's a sense of excitement, and dread. What's more, Alex as a character is pretty well-developed, both by your dialog choices during a game of truth or dare and by learning what motivates her. It made me as the player care about her journey, and to be invested in her as a character.I spent a little over an hour with Milo and Lola, and while the stakes are higher in that they woke up in hell, they can stay there for all I care. Other than the fact that these two people are friends, nothing about them is particularly sympathetic, and also while "escaping eternal damnation" seems like a pretty good motivating factor, every character in Hell itself seem pretty blase about the whole thing, as if an afterlifetime of eternal torture is no big deal. There's no real sense of stakes, and I found the characters off-putting, and obnoxious. Since the point of this game is to help these characters (and listen to them talk endlessly) for several hours, it's gonna be a no from me.

_childDocuments_.review: I had this for years and started it in 2020 or 2021, I think, then under Linux. Played about 2 hours, then forgot about it. It's not bad, although the one-dimensional humor is as often tedious as it is funny. Nevertheless, I was on board with seeing it to its end. Until a game-breaking bug, when Lucifer, his cronies and my two characters all failed to walk up a wall and simply got stuck half-way. _childDocuments_.review: Having played, and enjoyed, Oxenfree I gave this a go because it was (is at time of writing) on sale.TL;DR - underwhelming and janky. Worth a shot for the sale price. Can't give a neutral review; hence negative.If you're not familiar with Night School Studio's previous entry it's a walking sim (/pos) with some story and simple puzzles thrown in. It was an enjoyable experience that was written well enough to keep me engaged. I honestly can't give a deeper summary than that without revisiting it first, but my overriding memory is of enjoying the experience. So with that earned goodwill in its favour, this game made it onto my wish list where I promptly forgot about it among the 100 or so other things in there. Seeing recently that Afterparty and Oxenfree 2 were on sale at a deep discount, I bought them and started with Afterparty as I want to replay Oxenfree 1 before going on to 2.I'm not sure if I was more forgiving of the wonky elements of Oxenfree or if they are more jarring here, but it feels a lot less polished than the prior release despite the several years between their releases. Considering they are both made in much the same way, I would have thought that they would have improved on these elements in the intervening years.First, having been spoiled by 'Slay the Princess' (in more ways then one), I  sorely felt the absence of a user driven save system. The auto save in Afterlife is a bit flaky; I lost progress because I quit out of the game after a conversation but the game had not yet saved. I can understand that this might be to negate save scumming as a strategy to explore all the options, but they could have implemented a save on quit function. There are places in the game where the dialogue audio drops off for your characters compared to the others to the point where I switched on subtitles for the rest of the game. It's nice to see that accessibility settings are there for those that need them, but it's a shame that these had to serve as a crutch for patchy QA. Often the cues to leave an area would not appear and sometimes the pacing into and out of set pieces would feel stilted, like the game was struggling to load the next events (to be clear I'm running a 5900x which was high end when this was released, and a 4090 so it should not be a hardware issue). Also when moving from one point to another, the dialogue  would cut out if you reached the exit point for the area, assuming you would want to immediately transition from there to the next point of interest. This led to me slowing down to listen to what the characters were saying and then traversing large tracts in silence which really hit the pacing hard. As for the dialogue itself, it was funny in places, eliciting a quite few outbursts of laughter from me, but in others it felt overwrought. I did not appreciate the fourth wall breaks, especially one lamp-shading the mini-games you have to play (for example: a rhythm game dance competition which was used at least twice). It felt less like a 'you're just a mouse in a maze hoping for that hit of dopamine when you get the treat at the end' style critique and came off more as an embarrassed apology for including them. Worse still, these repeated fourth wall breaks run the risk of reminding the player that they are not in this world, and they can always play something else. I think that this last point might be a symptom of the game's age. By 2020 we had had two Deadpool movies and a solid decade of MCU tie-ins with their Wheadon-esque quippy dialogue, referential humour, and forth wall breaks. Four years on from that, and many of us have tired of these elements dominating media. The originators used them well and to good effect, but too much of a good thing...The drunk dialogue system.When you drink alcohol you get an extra dialogue option in conversation, which drink you choose at the bar determines the tone of these options. This was one of the thematic elements that I really enjoyed; it was fun choosing which kind of approach I wanted to take with each person based on what I had learned about them ahead of time. While I am quite sure this had no mechanical effect on the conversation, it was fun for immersion's sake. I should also add that the voice acting throughout was excellent; no complaints. This alone carried a lot of the clunkier writing.Let's be honest, what narrative driven games, often disparagingly called walking sims, lack in core mechanics they have to make up for with engaging characters, an interesting world, and a story with stakes that you care about. If you get these core elements correct, it allows you to forgive some jank; but there is a limit. If the walking sections are filled with long silences because of pacing issues caused by clunky transitions, or if the transitions into and out of conversations are stilted, if the dialogue itself feels overwritten in places or worse is barely audible in a Narrative. Driven. Game, then the whole thing starts to come apart. Then you start to notice that the walking sections didn't need to be this big and the world feels empty, or that the mini-games are a bit rubbish, or worst of all, you stop caring before the end. The final act had the potential to be poignant, but because of quality issues and the inconsistent writing I had already disengaged and that is a great shame. I didn't hate this game, far from it. By the end I simply didn't care and that is a much greater sin. If I had to sum up my feelings about Afterparty, it would be this:So much wasted potential.Which, ironically, is thematically appropriate.

_childDocuments_.review: For some reason, all the voice actors were told to speak quickly, as if they were constantly in the middle of a panic attack. In addition, the main character acts in a drunken voice from the first to the last second. This makes the game annoying and boring, because if you convey anxiety you have to compensate with emotions and there are no emotions. I struggled to finish this game. As I continually found better things to do (including cleaning!), I forced myself to go back and finish it. And that cost me a few hours, as you can see: for a game that lasts 6 hours, I spent over 70 hours trying to escape it.That said, it is a casual game, almost a walking simulator. There is no challenge, no risk of losing, and the ending is decided in the... ending!There is a lot of talk but it's fluff. Lots of useless words to fill in the dead time. The impression is that the developers found themselves with a 2-hour game and stretched it a bit to justify the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is best in the first few hours but as it goes on it becomes increasingly clear the main characters barely have personality and the dialogue options you get are often just be nice or a bit of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, with the additional ones being funny to listen to without really influencing the conversation or adding to the personalitys. The minigames aren't fun either.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: This one is...a damn shame, honestly. Potential spoilers ahead.I really fell in love with Night School Studio with Oxenfree, and incredible mystery thriller with horror elements where choices mattered. I was expecting a similar chassis with more of a light-hearted spin, with drinking tournaments and relationship struggles backlit by gorgeous environments.It's unfortunately lacking. The hook is really strong getting into the game, but there's really not a lot of...out-drinking folks in this game. No 'drink out these lesser demons and work up to the big S himself!' type deal. You use drinks to open up a third dialogue option flavored by the drink of your choice, but there's not much to it beyond that. There's like, three -total- beer pong games, and beyond your personal demon (literal, in this case) hounding Lola and Milo about their family issues and accidental betrayals? There's really not much that defines them as friends, or awful people. Hell, you only get to know key details about them if you stumble into the dialogue options.The game builds up (over an excruciating amount of time) that there's some shadow conspiracy to over throw Satan, mostly out of sight, mind you, so you aren't too distracted from having to walk from point A to point B, y axis to z axis, talking to the Demon of the moment and fix their problem to you can get closer to doing Satan's drinking contest. And it is a -slog- to get through with how slow the characters move, the unskippable animations and dialogue, and the snail's pacing of the story itself. Turns out, it's actually an  Frankly, I think it would've been a far more engaging element to have sprinkled through out the whole story, making addiction and anxiety overarching themes rather than a twist bit shoe-horned into the ending of the game. Milo and Lola also just, need some serious fleshing out in general.So, lightning-round nitpicks and a summary of gripes. There's no checkpoint right before the contest starts and no manual saves, so good luck winning the beer pong. There's also...really not much of a need to open your phone menu through out this whole experience, I forgot it was even there. The game's humor is weirdly almost Family Guy like, beat-for-beat, to the point that there were a lot of obscure references and jokes that weeere not landing (that's most of the games tone by the by). I don't feel like Milo nor Lola really grew as people, and I honestly think this would've benefited more as a game that has a lot of drinking mini-games, that lets you bond with the NPC's more naturally, that tackles trauma, substance abuse, social distance, and the human condition as the themes.Unfortunately, this not it. I'd save my money for Oxenfree, and I hope Oxenfree 2 ends up just as good.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended with caveats. If you enjoyed the quirky dialogue style of Oxenfree, and you're a fan of absurdist humour, this is a fun game. It's short (I finished in six hours) and the storyline is a little more muddled than Oxenfree's. I was confused by the end about exactly what kind of game I was playing. The characters were interesting, and the story enjoyable, but not great. Overall, a C+ kind of game. The levels felt strangely large for the amount of content, as if the devs intended to put more content in but never finished. And the end was fun, but not thrilling. Worth a runthrough if you can get it on sale and liked the dialogue style of Oxenfree.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but the story is very disappointing and feels like a step back from what we saw in Oxenfree. I'm writing my review largely as a comparison to that game, hopefully it'll still be helpful to you if you haven't played it. There will be minor spoilers probably.Rather than focusing on a tight and compact cast of characters, there are two specifically main characters and a larger cast of supporting characters. As far as the characters go, they're unfortunately not at the level of Oxenfree. Milo and Lola are fun but they mostly fall flat, I personally don't empathize with them or their problems to the level I did with the characters in Oxenfree. It feels less... this is such an arbitrary and subjective thing to say, but it feels less true to life, and I think that's mostly due to the jokey setting, but it also has to do with the fact that Milo and Lola's problems feel very generalized and un-fleshed out. The cast of characters is larger than the cast in Oxenfree, but that's a double-edged sword since the cast also has less time to shine individually, and some of them just feel like complete joke characters. For the ones who are more serious there's a feeling of... 'okay, why should I care about your problems though?' In Oxenfree, the characters are all part of the same social circle, but in Afterparty you've just met them and the goal of the game is to go home and never see these people again.Additionally, there are tonal issues with the story, it's mostly a comedy but the level to which it's a comedy makes the serious moments mostly fall flat. Like, the main characters have gone to hell and they want to get out, but there's never any real sense of urgency or danger for them remaining in hell. All the other helldenizens are very blase and chill and acclimated to their fate, and the game is more interested in providing funny moments than gripping or scary moments that help you empathize with the characters. The most antagonistic force they encounter is a personal demon who follows them around trying very hard to say mean things to them. All of the above is fine, but it's disappointing to me personally as I expected something more tonally similar to Oxenfree - not horror, I don't think anyone could look at the advertising and expect this to be a horror game, but a game where the stakes matter and you care about the characters.like we are supposed to be concerned about the eternal damnation of a character who is literally named ronaldo spaghetti, the narrative beats are completely at odds with the need to have Funny Witty Writing at all times.Gameplay-wise it's basically just oxenfree stuff, but your choices matter less. In that game, the main elements of choice you had were interpersonal relationships, who liked or hated you at the end, who you chose to hang out with, etc etc. That's obviously harder for a game with a wider scope like this, but it's still disappointing that seemingly the only choice which 'matters' comes at the very end of the game, with nothing else you've done really affecting the outcome overall. The big gameplay draws of the game - special mixed drinks which change your personality - are underutilized. For the mixed drinks, basically they just give you a third dialogue option that's Whacky based on The Drink You Consume. you generally speaking want to always take the third dialogue option if it's available, so the specific drink you choose doesn't have an effect, nor does being a weird drunk ever backfire. It would be cool if you could have taken a drink that makes you a raging ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to solve a solution by beating someone up, or a drink that makes you a flirter to flirt your way past them, and so on, and so forth, but that never really materialized.  There are also fun little drinking minigames, but those are mostly unimportant and are underutilized, only appearing during main story beats.The environments are big and pretty, but they're also rather sparse in terms of things you can interact with. There aren't really any any side quests or incidental NPCs you can interact with which aren't connected to the main quest, which is fine, but it leaves the experience on rails and feeling a bit underutilized. Travelling from story location to story location could essentially have been a cutscene at all times.With all those negatives out of the way, I don't hate this game. It's charming at times, and Wormhorn is best girl by far. It is just really frustrating, because it had the potential to be so much BETTER but that potential never really materialized. If you have a dire need to experience this game, get it on a big sale and try not to expect much more than a fun comedy romp, it's good at being that.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: It starts off strong with a cool premise, somewhat relatable protagonists (socially anxious cynics), an interesting setting and great performances (which thankfully stay consistent until the very end). Unfortunately it becomes clear very quickly that this game needed a lot more polish before coming out.First of all, the performance is not good for a game of this "caliber". I played it on the Steam Deck and despite it being verified I was met with frequent audio issues (more specifically Milo and Lola's dialogue playing at lower volume than everything else) as well as FPS drops (when capped at 40...). Bicker, which is like an in-game social medium you can open by pressing select didn't work at all, seemingly because the game didn't recognise the deck as a controller.Gameplay-wise, the devs clearly wanted Afterparty to resemble Oxenfree as much as possible, but they completely overlooked some aspects that weren't relevant in their first game. For example NPCs - there are tons of them in this game, but they NEVER talk. You literally walk among hundreds of people / demons in complete silence - even the main characters are silent for like half the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game, seemingly just running out of stuff to talk about (and they are supposed to be lifelong BFFs). To be fair, if I had to walk through these long-ass levels with hardly any soundtrack or ability to interact with anything I would quickly run out of ♥♥♥♥ to talk about as well - hell has actually never before been this boring. There are a ccouple of locations in this game, but they are all equally boring and soulless. Even the demons all look the same. There is that one side-character demon named Fela - he has a VA and is somewhat involved in the main plot, but he looks exactly like one of ~3 generic demon types present throughout the game.The writing is (for the most part) passable. If it comes to jokes hardly any of them landed for me. There's plenty of american deafultism - demons making jokes about cbs, "foreigners" just speaking English with an accent instead of their native languages (which would actually make a good joke if you put a minimal amount of thought into your worldbuilding - something the devs frequently brush off in the game by breaking the fourth wall and essentially saying that nobody cares about that). Story-wise it's decent. The idea of outdrinking Satan to get out of hell hardly makes any sense, but it's not really supposed to so it's fine. There's a nice twist at the end and the player is met with a choice - an interesting one, without an obvious answer unlike in for example Life is Strange, so that's nice. What's not nice is the game autosaving right after making the choice, essentially preventing the player from seeing other endings, but I guess it wasn't like I wanted to play any more of this at that point so get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ owned.I mentioned that the main characters are initially likeable, but they get more and more infuriating as time goes on. I blame the dialogue options for that as we only get two instead of three like in Oxenfree (unless you drink, which gives you an additional option, that most of the time is so stupid that it's really a non-option). The options themselves more often than not are almost the exact same and / or stuff I just didn't want to say. You can always just choose not to say anything, but the time it takes for the game to acknowledge it is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ long even the characters you talk to shut up before you do, seemingly begging you to say something. Oxenfree had an achivement for stayng silent the entire game, Afterparty passively discourages it, making itself even more sloggish than it already is. But to be fair, it's not like Milo and Lola themselves are particularly interesting - character-wise they're alright, but their relationship is subpar to pretty much any duo involving Alex in Oxenfree. Most of the time I would just pick a "leave him / her alone demon!!!" dialogue option instead of a "join the demon and laugh at him / her" one and choose to believe this is how friendships work.In general the game kind of feels like a Netflix movie (which isn't that surprising, as Netflix actually owns Nights School). Quality-wise I would be willing to compare it to someting like "To All the Boys I've Loved Before", but all the flaws in gameplay and design place it closer to "Red Notice". I originally planned to finish this in 2-3 days, but it took a whole week so yeah...

_childDocuments_.review: is a gorgeous, funny, and sometimes emotive game about death (surprise!), the fine line between friendship and loneliness, and the difference between living and . The characters are compelling, the voice acting is  and the story manages to carry itself through its ~5 hour runtime (for one playthrough). Regardless of its minor graphical and dialogue issues, this is a recommended game if you're looking for a game to spend a reflective, but entertaining, afternoon with.You play as Milo and Lola, two newly-graduated teenagers who have known each other since forever and now find themselves in Hell. In order to leave, they must beat Satan at his own game: drinking. Satan loves a drinking game. However, the road to leave-Hell is paved with many roadblocks, and so Milo and Lola must choose between multiple decisions in order to both convince Satan to play and to prepare for the final drink-off.The general gameplay consists of: point-and-click (quite linear and obvious), decision making through dialogue choices, and - well, wouldn't you know it! - drinking. Before having conversations with most people, you can go to a nearby bar and take your pick of one of four drinks (you can switch between drinks too). As is the case with alcohol, each cocktail can change your personality somewhat, giving you extra dialogue options that may help or hinder your conversations: you can be a witty hardass or a pirate (arrrrr, you read that right!) for example, or even just a plain ol' drunkard. These can help you overcome obstacles to objectives in the most efficient way, but choosing the wrong one just means that you might have to do things slightly differently and take a different, longer tact or route. For ~reasons~, the game definitely encourages multiple playthroughs (at least two). There is no manual saving or chapter select for exploring different decisions, but I imagine that each playthrough will feel notably different (not just minor story beats, but pretty big decisions throughout), which lessens the blow of starting the story from the beginning again.- : Holy moly, guys, the voice acting is fantastic! There was no character that felt out of place or poorly delivered. The voice actors managed to convey a variety of easy, conversational tones, exasperated snark, and quite emotional story beats with seeming ease. I would say that, if for nothing else, the voice work in this game is worth the price of admission.- : This game is pretty, well, pretty. The neon-by-night look really shines through the story and the feel of this kind of Hell - boozy, wayward, and a little depressed - is significantly carried on the back of the environmental and character designs. Clearly, much thought has been put into each character's designs and I was very impressed throughout (even with very minor characters).- : Despite it being, y'know, , I found myself liking more than loathing the demons I met along the way. I don't mean like as in 'I would be friends with the person' but that they were multi-faceted and often not all they seemed to be on first meeting. Lola and Milo are great protagonists for this kind of story about moral greyness because they are both likeable and frustrating, as humans are wont to be.- : The story was fairly strong and kept me interested throughout the game - there was sufficient mystery, breadcrumb clues, and twists to keep it ticking over. I mostly enjoyed the  in which the story was told - there were a number of fourth-wall-toeing moments that were quite arresting (in a good way) and it felt purposeful when you felt you weren't being told everything that was going on. I also very much enjoyed the "intermissions" with a certain character-I-shall-not-name-here-for-spoiler-reasons.-  There were a handful of instances where you were 'walking and talking' with another character and the talking would stop/be overridden by another set of dialogue once you'd passed an invisible trigger line, and you couldn't get that previous dialogue to play again. I understand that this is important to story pacing, and I could have easily stopped to let the dialogue play out, but there were definitely a couple of times where it felt like the game wanted you to be moving while talking ('hey, we don't have a lot of time, just come over here a second') and the abrupt halting of dialogue felt jarring and a bit frustrating. -  The movements of characters/figures in the world can be a liiiiittle janky (standing on top of each other, getting caught on a pole) and there were multiple instances of texture clipping. Also, despite being on ultra settings, there were times where jaggy lines (aliasing?) were noticeable. All these are really minor nitpicks for a very impressively constructed game.

_childDocuments_.review: On a positive note: while playing this, my insomnia was temporarily cured since I slept through at least a couple hours of the "played" ones. And I mean it literally. This game is boring. No nice way around it. I mildly appreciated the character design ( even those were kind of meh after a while ) and the voice acting, but that's about it. I'll just highlight the pain points in my opinion:The level design is non-existent... lots of walking without a reason for it. Silent walking endlessly from point A to point B even multiple times. And since there is no objective map, which would be fine if only the path was structured in a consistent way, you can miss talking to a character who gets referenced later on by accident. Not that it matters since the game acts like you did meet them anyway ( which makes no sense since when you do they then act like they didn't meet you, of course ). If you think there is a point in the choice between going to/from Satan's party one "floor" at the time or directly, I'll just save you time: there is none. It's just one of the many game mechanics with no thought behind it.Normally I don't have an issue with dialogues options which feel like they have no impact at all on the story, but here the conversations are just so dull and pointless that having to wait for the option to pop up so you can just click through and move on HOPING that the conversation will soon be over, is just frustrating. Also at some point one of the dialogue options was late in popping up and created this awkward staring contest between the characters and Satan that makes no sense. I believe it might be a bug, but I wouldn't be surprised if it was a choice considering the dullness of this game.It feels like the writing is trying for clever and funny, but it doesn't deliver. There are a couple times that the game tries for more interaction with the player by transforming its own mechanics to become a fast clicking memory battle with the AI, but it honestly is not engaging and the already weak atmosphere of the scene is completely ruined by these attempts.I'm sure people working on it really tried, maybe there is a bunch of beginners developers in their first project ( this is what it feels like - I refuse to believe that the same people who worked on Oxenfree also worked on this """game""" ) and I can just hope they'll get better. If you are still curious about this game and want to try it yourself, find it on discount or in a key shop, because the full price feels like a scam.

_childDocuments_.review: The game, in comparison to Oxenfree, seems severely lacking in...well, everything. The setting is neat and it's really pleasing to look at the set pieces, but they're no more than decoration for a pretty bland story.The two main characters have no chemistry (claiming to be best friends, no less). The alcohol plays little to no role in the game, yet it was marketed to be an important mechanic. The game is about outdrinking the Devil himself, for Pete's sake!But what got me the most was one of the characters breaking the 4th wall by saying "That's for your other playthrough". I get that this is the studio's gimmick, BUT WHAT IF I DON'T WANT A SECOND PLAYTHROUGH? I get the allure of multiple endings and yet I'm opposed to the idea of "Play this one more time to get the REAL deal" (this appalled me in Oxenfree, to be honest). It's as if you've finished a project and then your boss says: "It sucks. Scrap everything and do it again."I was really eager to play Afterparty, but it turned out to be the recycling of old ideas without the charm of Oxenfree.

_childDocuments_.review: Afterparty is an entertaining barcrawl though the underworld.  The design is delicious and the dialogue is witty and and the characters are delightful.  I only wish it was longer but just finishing up my first run, I'm sure I haven't mined all the choices and dialogue yet (a play through is ~6 hours). _childDocuments_.review: Unlike Oxenfree with its intriguing story, Afterpaty is extremely boring.Visually, it looks great. The idea of going to hell and discovering yet another interpretation of how could it look like is interesting. But a lot of references and jokes are based on stuff that probably only people living in a religious society can fully understand and relate to. Otherwise, the story doesn't work: it's getting more or less good in the final hour, yet the final is crumpled.Dialogs are terrible. They talk too fast and use too much slang, it was hard to follow even with subtitles.There are probably two or three minigames that took maybe ten minutes of the total playthrough. Othether than that, I was just running from point A to point B. It's not even a good walking simulator compared to Oxenfree and many other story-driven games.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: It's somewhat interesting, but the 2d sidescrolling suckss.. the characters move pretty slow and just the fact it is 2d sidescrolling makes it hard to get engaged with the story. There were several times just walking to the next objective really took me out of it even though it was only a few minutes. Also it does not show you what the next objective is at all, its not particularly hard to figure them out but sometimes it takes a little walking back and forth and it can be very annoying. Frankly it would be a lot more bearable if it was purely a decision making visual novel but the character movement just ruins the game I likely would have been able to finish it if it werent for the movement. Same art style but just a pure visual novel would have been 10x better

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever played Oxenfree you know what to expect here. It's basically that but with a different setting. It even has the same virtues and shortcomings. What I liked in oxenfree were the conversations and I disliked everything else. The story seemed interesting at first but got worse the further I got and ended on a low note. The little gameplay that was there I didn't like and there was a LOT of walking and backtracking.I could just copy past my oxenfree review if I ever wrote one.Developer Night School Studio is very good in conversations. Oxenfree excelled at it and so does Afterparty. The writing and voiceactors do a good job at being witty but at the same time it feels like a real conversation. This one lacks depth though I think most people will find Afterparty very funny. The jokes didn't really work for me though. Part of it might be that I'm just not into the setting but it's also because the voice actors are speaking too fast and you can't really let anything sink in. You'll again do a lot of walking around while listening to conversations. One thing I noticed though. When walking to your next objective when you get there the conversation is cut short when you reach your destination. So a character will be in the middle of a sentence and then suddenly it stops and goes to whatever was coming up. It's probably the last sentence so you don't miss much in terms of story but it annoyed the hell out of me (pun intended). It not only breaks immersion but you'll miss parts of the one thing Afterparty excels at: conversation. Oxenfree never had this issue, the parts in between were perfectly timed where the conversation would come to a natural conclusion right before arriving at the destination.I know I keep comparing the two games but it's difficult not to when they are so similar. I wasn't the biggest fan of their previous game though and this just feels like the same game but just about everything is done less well, even the parts that weren't good to begin with.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I even start? This game is such a regression from the studio's previous game.Oxenfree was uncharacteristically open for an adventure game. Edwards Island was structured like a web, similar to (though much less complex) than the map of metroidvanias. In addition, there were quite a few reason to backtrack or venture on your own, from the adler letters, to hidden frequencies, to optional conversations. The game also allowed Alex to free-roam the Edwards Island for most of the game.Afterparty took away all of that. Hell is fragmented to smaller 'worlds'. And you can't diverge from the storyline and go to a 'world' you're not supposed to. If the story demands me to go to A or B then I have to go to A or B, I can't go to C. And even once you're in those smaller 'worlds', there's little to no reason to explore them. Go to the bar and do what the game demands you to, that's it. Not only that, you can't even backtrack to 'worlds' you've been to.Oxenfree has 2 plots. The 1st plot concerns the island and its ghost. The 2nd plot concerns the interpersonal relationship between the characters.This is a recipe that Afterparty adopt, but executed horrendously. The 1st plot concerns Milo and Lola attempt return to the real world, while the 2nd plot involves their relation and friendship. The problem is, the 1st plot hogs so much runtime that the 2nd plot is suffocated. So when the 2nd plot reaches climax its undercooked and feels out of nowhere.The 1st plot isn't even believable. Imagine if in Oxenfree insted of saving Ren or Clarissa, you instead go to the gift shop to change its lightbulb because the ghost ordered you to. That's what this game is.Remember how almost all of the dialogue in Oxenfree has 3 choices? This game defaults at 2. You want a 3rd dialogue option? You can only do it in a bar while being drunk. This is the equivalent of a hardware company clawing features from its low-end products and giving it back at the higher-end. More dialogue options if you use the drinking mechanic! Except that it should've been the baseline.And this game barely qualifies as a 2.5D sidescroller. There's no section where I could just move my joystick up and down to get my character to move forward and backward. If you want your character to move forward and backward, you can only do that in specific sections such as a tunnel or a lift that you press X to get into. And you're instantly transported, no input or player agency here.So you really can only move along a 2D path. This was fine in Oxenfree because most of the environment is just hiking path or narrow rooms, and when they aren't, such as the beach or the parking lot at main street, you could move forward and backward. But many part of this games doesn't take place in narrow paths. You're in a bar that visibly has depth but you can only move in a straight line left or right? What design choice is that?Sure, the environment is much more vast and substantially more gorgeous than Oxenfree. Hell may be as wide as an ocean but it's only as deep as a puddle. They could've made a smaller game that has more depth, figuratively and literally, but no.I suspect that Night School Studio had bigger plans for this game, and this isn't what they had in mind when the concept of this game is still in development. But when they were screwed over by Telltale Games sudden closure, they had to release this game as soon as possible or risk bankruptcy. Which causes them to cut some plot points and many of the planned bell and whistles. That's probably why the game was an EGS timed exclusive. But these are just my conjecture.

_childDocuments_.review: If Oxenfree is a 10, then this is like a 4...at best.There are some fun conversations and the different effects of alcohol are interesting, but choices don't really have much of an impact, the relationships between the characters don't really seem to change as much as they did in Oxenfree, and the game just loves to waste your time.Your constantly using elevators in which you wait like 10 seconds, ordering a drink clocks in at 30+ seconds of downtime (like seriously, who thought this long-ass animation was a good idea) and at the beginning you'll often still run all the way to the egde of the islands, thinking there might be some interesting interaction or a possibility to open up another path, but really it's usually just barren and you wasted your time going there.Overall I thought this was, unfortunately, rather disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: It's the first game in a while I've been able to sit down and play in one day because it's kept me interested. While there's not too many places you go and visit, for the length of the game it was probably a good call on their part. The places you do go to are beautifully designed and interesting visually.There is a few small bumps such as characters pausing during conversations until the game loads up the choices which breaks the flow a little and models glitching out/sinking into the ground/snapping back into place but it's nothing that impacts the overall gameplay. Bear in mind that Night School Studio only has 13 full-time employees.The dialogue is well written and I found myself pausing multiple times just to hear what random NPC's had to say as well as Milo and Lola themselves. While for the most part it's lighthearted and goofy it handles more serious topics and tones (such as their insecurities) well. Overall fun and engaging, I'm definitely going to do another playthrough :).EDIT: I think what might of helped Afterparty a little more if their advertisement went a little differently? For a game called Afterparty, you don't really do that much partying in hell. While it didn't bother me personally I can see why people felt a little misguided when they came to play it. Just as a heads up for people really looking forward to getting heavily drunk in hell.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game with high expectations and it was disappointing in every aspect but character/prop/set design. My main issue is that this game put the most weight on its writing, and the writing is...very cringy. It reads like older adults trying to capture the "college vibe" with dated slang and high school humor.  It's aesthetics, gameplay, writing doesn't feels very cohesive. While the visual design on its own is excellent, I'm not really sure what the plasticky, stop-motion-like visuals have to do with college, bar culture, or hell. The gamelay is done through drinking minigames, and feels a bit like a chore and also does not contribute to the theme in anyway besides subject matter. The voice actors do a good job with what they were given. The sound design pretty good. A lot of pieces on its own are polished and well made, but are not built to slot together seamlessly as a whole.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: Huh, this game was not at all what I expected. Overall the game looks great and I like a lot of the dialogue, however, after playing through a second time I found that my decisions didnt make much of a difference and its another example of a game that has 2 endings but is all based on a single choice you make at the very end. There is a little replayability for some alternate routes but not much and the fact that you cant skip dialogue makes a second playthrough a drag. I enjoyed a lot of the dialogue but the game still felt like it had some pacing issues. The minigames are disgustingly boring and make the game grind to an absolute halt which is a real shame. Overall this game is quite flawed, however if you enjoy visual novels and dont mind if theyre very on rail I would still recommend this game if you can get it on sale because it is still very charming with a unique and interesting story.
_childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: Dark humor version of Oxenfree. I was hoping for something with a Monkey Island vibe and initially it seemed like it might be, but the more I played the more it became a drag. This is a highschool drama with very shallow story, flat characters and pretentious writing that never shuts up, it's Oxenfree meets Borderlands 3.There's a severe lack of technical polish and it looks like a mobile phone game or a very old PC game.As for the barely existing gameplay, I didn't appreciate the minigames and the alcohol-drinking gimmick felt wrong, I guess it goes with the highschool theme ("we are young and awesome let's party and get drunk") but I'm too old for this stuff.It's not all bad, the writing is pretty good for gaming standards and some of the dialogues are fun, but not enough for a game which only selling point is precisely that. I really wanted to give this game a positive review, but it annoyed me more than it made me laugh, so I just can't.If you enjoyed Oxenfree and Borderlands 3's non-stop ranting go for it, otherwise I'd pass.

A brilliant narrative experience that got deeper than I thought it initially would.The voice acting is also phenomenal.Highly recommended.
