_childDocuments_.review: Afterlife is a perfect example of what i would call a ''fun game''.It's pretty short and filled with a sort of R-rated Terry Pratchett-esque humor. (dope)It's not like Oxenfree which is what I think a lot of people criticize about the game, it's very linear and sometimes feels a bit empty, and it isn't filled with nearly as many details and easter eggs so don't go into it expecting the same level of design. (seriously, very different games)It's not heavily choice based, most of the dialogue options (though very amusing) are in the end meaningless, and all choices will ultimately lead you to the same three ending choices. (if you're looking for something deeper, sorry)The art style is neat as hell (pun intended)And it's depiction of hell is pretty neat aswell (humor)Overall I think the games sheer charisma will satisfy most people as long as you know what you're getting into, I love the game and can't wait for more stuff from Night School Studio.

_childDocuments_.review: Ooof, this was a trudge.  At this point, I'm not convinced that the biggest mechanic, being able to add dialog options by drinking, actually does anything at all other than add flavour.  Plus, the other 2 mini games give you infinite tries, even in the finale. Also, throughout the whole game they make very obvious references to it being a videogame.  1 character literally says something about saving some exposition for your second play through.  So, any rational person would start thinking there's no context for so many comments like that... maybe there's some big meta twist... nope, just a boring trudge with dull mechanics and no way to actually lose other than choosing to forfeit.  For what its worth, the voice acting was good, and I liked the characters, and the dialog (excluding weird meta references) sounded realistic.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, creative, and aesthetically pleasing game. It's got a great narrative, excellent voice acting, and plenty of sass and drama to keep you entertained even through a second play through. If you liked Oxenfree, you'll like Afterparty. If you like stories about young people trying to escape the underworld (e.g. if you played SuperGiant Games' "Hades"), you'll like Afterparty. If you love cool club beats supplemented by neon colors and grungy city night life, Afterparty has it. It's beautifully designed and the characters are charming. Is it groundbreaking? No. How can you expect such a thing from a $20 game? Just enjoy it for what it is. Show your support for these small studios who are trying to bring interesting and experimental experiences. I believe this Afterparty is a foundational game; another step for Night School Studio that will move them towards making even better games.

_childDocuments_.review: Not bad. Kind of threadbare though. The choices don't matter all that much (you can basically fail everything and say anything and still get any ending you want [edit: and turns out two of the three endings are exactly the same]). The drink system is novel, but doesn't affect anything except having one of the protagonists say something wacky (which gets unacknowledged). Very buggy, despite having been out on EGS since March (including a bug that forces you to start over if you stop playing at the wrong place). However, the characters are entertaining. The dialog is almost as engaging as Oxenfree, though the buggyness undercuts it (some audio clips fail to play, or get significantly delayed). The setting is cool, if somewhat underrealized. The concept is strong, this game just doesn't manage to fully realize its potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Oxenfree is one of my favorite games. It's a game with great humor, a good atmosphere and a unique dialog system that I hope to see in more games. Afterparty is even better: It has better graphics, fantastic voice actors and the dialog system has a fun spin on it.And I don’t like it. The humor is way too cynical for me. I didn’t enjoy the atmosphere and the lessons that I took away from it are pretty pessimistic, which is not what I need at this time in my life. _childDocuments_.name: Afterparty

_childDocuments_.review: A short and sweet story about going to hell and drinking a lot of booze, held back by shallow gameplay and lack of consequence. The style and atmosphere aswell as the dialogue are definitely the best parts about this game, while gameplay and exploration fall short. There are no puzzles to speak of and every problem has a obvious solution, although sometimes you get choices that define the outcome of plot points thorugh dialogue. Drinking different booze to change your dialogue is a cool idea, although I feel like it is underused and I wish there was more to it instead of a single new choice that didn't seem to influence the actual dialogue at all. This reduced the whole system to a fun novelty and fluff instead of feeling like there are any consequences for spouting whatever ♥♥♥♥ the booze lets you say. Being only around 7 hours long, maybe 8 if you are taking in the sights and explore (latter has no use as there are no sidequests and you visit all locations during the plot anyway) actually helps the game, as it slowly unravels itself as a scarcely interactive visual novel the longer one plays. Being a visual novel at its core isnt necessary a bad thing, but it raises questions as to why I have to do so much uneventful walking around or why walking past certain triggers skips and breaks dialogue, or why dialogue options fade out rather quickly making the current protagonist say literally *nothing* instead of fumbling their words or picking *some* option available, if the focus is clearly on the story and characters. Why do you get all this interactive fluff when a lot of it doesn't add anything to the world besides the novelty of exploring it through your own halfhearted inputs?.In conclusion, it is a fun game with witty writing and the two protagonists are unusual and bring a good amount of charm to the setting. The devs have the style and atmosphere down and it really carries the ultimatively shallow gameplay and minigames. If the devs work on how to implement more interactivity into the gameplay and add smoother ways of traveling between and inside maps, their next work could easily fill over 10 hours without feeling slow or underdevelopped. As it stands right now, it is a fun adventure game with two loveable protagonists and well worth your time if you don't expect a lot of interactivity or fleshed out gameplay. Tl:dr: Go into it expecting a *Hell Themepark* with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of booze and you will have a fun ride.

_childDocuments_.review: In Afterparty, you are Milo and Lola, recently deceased best buds who suddenly find themselves staring down an eternity in Hell. name: Maquette
detailed_description: Maquette is a first-person recursive puzzle game that takes you into a world where every building, plant, and object are simultaneously tiny and staggeringly huge. Maquette makes it possible by twisting the world into itself recursively in an MC Escher-esque fashion. Head to the center of the world and you'll feel like a giant, towering over buildings and walls. But venture further out, and start to feel small as things get larger and larger - to the point where cracks in the ground become chasms. In Maquette you will explore the scales of everyday problems in a modern-day love story. Where sometimes the smallest of issues can become insurmountable obstacles.
about_the_game: Maquette is a first-person recursive puzzle game that takes you into a world where every building, plant, and object are simultaneously tiny and staggeringly huge. Maquette makes it possible by twisting the world into itself recursively in an MC Escher-esque fashion. Head to the center of the world and you'll feel like a giant, towering over buildings and walls. But venture further out, and start to feel small as things get larger and larger - to the point where cracks in the ground become chasms. In Maquette you will explore the scales of everyday problems in a modern-day love story. Where sometimes the smallest of issues can become insurmountable obstacles.
short_description: Maquette is a first-person recursive puzzle game that takes you into a world where every building, plant, and object are simultaneously tiny and staggeringly huge.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, let me start off by saying that I was really looking forward to this game, and I wanted it to be good, I really did. The premise is wonderful: a 3D puzzle game based on recursive geometry and scale manipulation. The trailer made it look like a game that I would be in love with. Annapurna Interactive has an unbelievably good track record in choosing the games that they publish, so when I see their logo next to a title, it is almost like a seal of quality for me. But Maquette... is not a good puzzle game, unfortunately. Nor is it a good story game. The camera and the controls are slightly jittery, which gave me a constant feeling of not quite being in full control most of the time, and that is pretty unpleasant. The puzzle design had a lot of potential, as this is a pretty brilliant foundation for a puzzle game, but it falls way short in terms of setting its expectations, and communicating the language of its world to the player. It jumps from idea to idea with very little in the way of connective tissue. Instead of building upon the puzzle language to create more and more intricate puzzles to solve that relate to the player's intuition in a fun way, it just discards ideas as soon as each puzzle is solved, and starts from scratch each time. Because of this, I rarely felt like I knew if I was doing what the game expected me to do, or if I was finding cheese left and right, breaking the fragile physics of this recursive world. In this way, solving the puzzles wasn't very satisfying, because I never really knew if I was actually solving them or not. I went into the game expecting a puzzle wonderland, akin to Superliminal, Manifold Garden, Portal, or The Witness and maybe that expectation ruined me, because it simply did not match up to my hopes as a puzzle game.I will say, however, that the final level is transcendent, and I kind of wish that the whole game was based on that final level, instead of whatever else was going on here. There is an ongoing story being narrated as you make your way through the puzzles, and in my opinion, the voice actors (who I later learned are husband and wife, which is adorable) are quite excellent, and they kept me engaged, despite the story being perhaps the most generic, bland relationship story I have ever experienced.  The story was connected to the puzzles by only the loosest of threads, so it didn't even need to be in the game, as far as I'm concerned. I'm sorry that this is such a negative review. I really had high hopes for Maquette, and I feel kind of deflated now that I've played it. My recommendation, if you are interested in Maquette, but haven't yet played Superliminal or Manifold Garden, is to play those first. I promise you will enjoy both of those in the way that you are hoping to enjoy Maquette. If you've played those games already and are looking for more perspective-bending puzzle games, I'd say give Maquette a try, but temper your expectations, please.

_childDocuments_.review: A good game, but not worth $20.I haven't kept up with this game much after the initial announcement but after seeing how cool it looked I decided to blind buy it.What I didn't realize is that this isn't really a puzzle game so much as the game is a medium to tell a love story. That's fine because other games like Edith Finch/Story About My Uncle have done this great, but my god I have not felt this disappointed in a long time.I expected some loose story to go with this game about wacky mindbending puzzles and I got the complete opposite.There's ~7 levels and maybe 4-6 "puzzles" per level, and a lot of them are "use this object to make a bridge" kind of thing.The puzzles are cool and surprisingly intuitive but the recursion mechanic is criminally underutilized. There's only 3 real recursions you explore: Small, Big, Default. It's very apparent why they did this, because in the bigger worldsyour movement speed is aggravatingly slow and terrible. Rather than find a solution for that, they kind of boxed you in with your mobility and ability to solve puzzles in your own way.If an object is too small, you can't grab it, there's only maybe 1-2 objects for you to use at a time, it really feels like they kept the baby gloves on for you.The gameplay does reflect the story in an interesting way sometimes, and some of the puzzles are really clever, but there's so few of them that not only am I left wanting more, I am thinking "That's it???"The amount of puzzles per level is so small for how big they are, I never felt like I really finished a level.THIS IS NOT A PUZZLE GAME, THIS IS A STORY GAME TOLD THROUGH THE LENSE OF A PUZZLE GAME. If the story was better maybe it could be justified, but I can't help but have a bitter taste from how cool and original of a mechanic this is and how they really wasted that on 10 puzzles.As with most games like this, it only gets interesting and difficult near the end for some reason the last half hour of the game is filled with fantastic, creative, out of the box puzzles. It's heartbreaking to play, not just becuase of the story, but because the better the puzzles get, the closer you know you're getting to the end. Really a tease.The game doesn't let you solve things your own way or explore more than the breadcrumb trail they left for you, which I believe is in service to the accesibility of the story and detriment of the gameplay. The biggest example of this is that sometimes you can hold an object and it will fit in a hole in the regular world, and you should be able to just grab it and place it, but the game says NO, you have to go to the small world and place the same object there, even though they are the exact same scale. There's a lack of room of outside solutions.This is a, good-ish game though. If you liked other games in this style you'll probably enjoy this for the experience, it's got nice music, the level design and puzzle design is intuitive and interesting. Surprisingly you won't feel lost, you're in a big plus sign and each arm has different environments. The recursion even gives you a little miniature world to look at and kind of use as your map in the hub. The recursion engine is really impressive in the later levels, the feeling of seeing a giant version of the object your holding in the distance is a really cool feeling the first time.I hate how short this game is, because it is really fun thinking with this mechanic and trying new things out, I would love to do more with it because the gameplay really is fun and solid.  If you loved other story based games then you'd probably enjoy this, the story isn't as compelling as other games but it's nice and the game is pretty and cool to play. For someone expecting a little bit more out of this game, you won't find it.I strongly believe that there are enough mechanics here to make a really good, compelling, challenging game and I'm really disappointed that it was so underutilized especially since now there's not going to be a game with this mechanic in a while because then everyone will way "they copied Maquette".That said, it isn't a terrible game, just when the lens of context is applied to it, it doesn't stand up to the hype it creates for itself.It's really strange that all these games are popping up with such similar "vibes" to them, I'm not sure if it's really a genre or just a new style that is being adopted. It's cool when used sparingly, but I think this one missed the mark.

_childDocuments_.review: For those whoe wanna check it out but concerned about the "MIXED" reviews.i must say. i came for the puzzles but stay for the plot,Yes, at the core the game doesnt push the boundaries of this brilliant idea of a world into a world.Yes, the story may be a little cliche.yes, they should improve the item locking and the use of the mouse.and yes it did crashed a like 3 times towards the end.BUT. its a debut game guys.which finally brings something new to the table.the story its not just a love story, its about growing up, overcoming.the complexity of the world that maquette brings to us, its equivalent as the complexity in each human being and how we develop according to the challenges we are introduce in the course of life.the game gets slower and harder at the moment the characters are experiencing the same. that was huge for me. i think its a great detail.the music is great, the voice acting too.it is for sure a game to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Maquette is a first person puzzle game centered around three models of a town. Each town is different in size and you can move between these different sized models solving various puzzles. Each town is connected and objects in one town are replicated in other towns but in different sizes. Your goal is to navigate out of the seven areas, each representing a stage of their relationship. Michael and Kenzie meet and instantly a spark is created. What follows is a relationship in bloom and we watch as events unfold, chronicling the ups and downs of their relationship together. The attraction started through their love of drawing and by solving puzzles within the Maquette, we see how the relationship evolves through hand drawn pictures and voice overs.  is a bit of a mixed bag and I would say its current mixed rating is about right. It is going to appeal to some people and not to others. I found the puzzles to be quite difficult. Some of them are extremely clever and do provide you with immense satisfaction when you finally work them out. Others, seem unfair or have their own set of rules which you are not privy to. The puzzles in Maquette are never explained. It isn’t as bad as The Witness for example, but the game leans in that direction. You are dropped into a scene and it is up to you to work out what to do and where to go. There are visual clues, and sometimes it is obvious, but other times the solutions seem nonsensical. The game at times encourages exploration but then blocks your passage; doesn’t let you drop items when there is no reason it should; the smaller Maquette can be painfully claustrophobic and awkward to place objects and the walking speed in the large Maquette is very slow. The game can be quite frustrating at times.The majority of the puzzles are clever, if a bit awkward to navigate. Puzzles are mostly solved by using objects which have to be rotated into place. The camera and the surrounding structures can prove troublesome but with perseverance it can be done. For some reason, my Xbox one wireless controller caused the game to lag severely although the developers said they hadn’t had this issue reported. I had to use the keyboard and mouse which wasn’t my first choice. The graphics are pleasant. The cut scenes are gradually sketched, like someone drawing the scene until it is completed. This was nice to see and well done. The voice overs are very professional and emotional. The story is just a typical relationship. It wasn’t particularly dramatic or memorable. The songs felt a bit out of place and would sometimes randomly kick in at inappropriate times. I think music could have been used better. If you are an achievement hunter then a third of the achievements are speed runs which I am not even going to bother with. I can only see that ending in tears!A Maquette is a model. The Maquette represents their kinship; where they met; memorable moments and past events. There are three Maquettes and each model represents a different size. By moving objects in and out of each model we can affect the object size and placing objects in one model will be replicated in the other two models but either smaller or bigger. If you drop an object in one model you can often see its bigger or smaller counterpart falling in another model in the distance. The game is a three dimensional puzzle game where size matters! By moving in and out of each three-dimensional model it feels like you are getting bigger or smaller, whereas in fact it is just the environment which has changed. You may no longer be able to climb stairs for example, as they are now too large. The objects in the large Maquette are too big to pick up but objects in the normal and small Maquette can be picked up, rotated and dropped almost anywhere. So, by placing an object on the stairs in the small or normal Maquette could possibly mean you could climb that object in the large Maquette and get up the stairs you previously could not climb.Walking speeds are affected depending on which model you are in. The large Maquette means you walk painfully slow sometimes, and some environments are quite big so this can take some time.There are no indicators as to where to go or what to do but there are sometimes subtle hints to guide you in the right direction. Some butterflies flying around a door; a coloured gem; or colour coded doors are all examples of visual hints. Mostly, you will just be trying to enter buildings to trigger small cut scenes of relationship moments. Along the way, you will see comments by Michael or Kenzie in the form of floating sentences, describing their feelings at the time.The visuals are okay. They look bright and cheerful. The cut scenes are nicely done by gradually drawing the scene as it unravels, as if they are drawing a sketch of an event. There are odd sporadic cases of songs bursting into the game. Sometimes, they make sense and add emotional weight to the story but sometimes they feel out of place and distracting. The songs are performed well enough but I’m just not sure they add to the experience. The object noises as they drop sound awesome. When you hear a massive key drop in the distance it sounds weighty and satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a mixed bag, and honestly not one I would recommend to anyone I actually liked. First, the good:- It's beautiful, and has nice animations and music to go along with the pretty visuals.Now the bad:- The puzzles are trivial for the most part.- Most puzzle mechanics are one and done. The crystals used to open doors exist for a single level before disappearing entirely. At no point does the game seriously make an attempt to challenge the player by mixing the mechanics, or adding greater complexity to existing mechanics such as more than 1 level of nesting to the Maquette.- Puzzles mostly boil down to, resize the thing, use it as a bridge, then get to the maguffin.- Player movement is fairly slow which is alright at normal scale but painful at small scale. A sprint button would be appreciated. - Options involving multiple different nested maquettes are ignored.- The story is mediocre, but fails to meaningfully connect with the puzzle solving you are actually doing.Now, the ugly:- The player character handles like dead fish. Controls for picking things up and dropping them fail to give you much precision, while forcing a slow mode on you during placement. When running into a wall with an object, the game will attempt to maintain the distance you have selected between yourself and the object by turning your view around.- Bugs. In the final level, attempting to pick up the maquette while standing on it, or on the lip will result in an instant crash.- The timed puzzle has a chance of completely bugging out and not opening the door requiring a level reset to try and make progress.- The key resizing puzzle can cause confusion due to small keys sinking into the floor of the very large room that the maquettes are mirroring. Combined with the poor lighting in the room, it can make it close to impossible to to find the key in the room.In summary: The game is pretty and well acted, but has no depth, few good puzzles, clunky controls, and weak integration between the story and the game-play. The game has multiple bugs, some of which are not immediately obvious to the player which completely lock off progression.Not recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 4/10, mostly from the milquetoast story and the frequent yanking of the controls for lame slow pan cutscenes.First of all, wonderful concept.  Shame that the story is so bland.  Like chicken seasoned with water.   The perspective of the storytelling feels like the standard fare of sad guy who has a bunch of red flag behavior and eventually has his relationship deteriorate for...  people growing apart?  Frankly, a lot of what Michael says early on in the relationship is like a big cry for help to go to therapy, and since the perspective is solely his we only see his flaws.   Which makes me wonder what the hell their chemistry is supposed to be.  Seriously, he downplays her constantly and basically isolates her with his anxiety.  Okay but enough about the story and how it feels like a 1st year college student journal, let's talk about the game.  The game has...some great puzzles.  Key word, some.  What holds back a majority of the puzzles is the god awful move speed, which is only slightly noticeable in normal sized sections but horrendously slow when you are smaller than the environment.  There are some hidden, inconsistent speed boost pads beneath the floor in some places, but frankly its not enough to make a failed puzzle solution feel any less punishing to trudge back through.   Additionally, the environmental indicators are dodgy, leading to some stumped moments because the cues are not there to get you to pay attention to the right spot.  Finally, there are sooo many opportunities to soft lock yourself, despite the game trying its best to not let you drop something in a location you can't retrieve it.  Lookin' at you, gear and red orb section.Frankly, the thing I can absolutely recommend about this game are the visuals.  Absolutely stunning imagery throughout, only marred by frequent interrupting cutscenes that yank your ability to appreciate the moving parts and changing environments, often heavy handedly pointing you to an important thing rather than letting environmental cues guide you there.  In summary, I would recommend this game on hefty discount, as the sparse, phenomenal puzzles and fantastic visual design are undercut by the lukewarm main character, what the textbooks tell you to avoid story, dodgy guidance, sluggish controls, and mechanics that never really bloom into something interesting.  What I can say to really wrap the game up in a neat bow is that everything in the game is simply a set piece, with no depth or  stability keeping it interesting or smooth.And don't get me started on the bugs, glitches, and performance issues.  I walked on a pile of wood and it flipped a switch halfway across the map for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game felt very "meh" to me. I typically like short games, I prefer short games with a bang over 80 hour epics In Which You Can Do Anything And Go Anywhere.However, I did not enjoy my time with this game:- The "story" (I guess it's more of an audio book that you listen to while you play the game) is pretty clichee: - The "Twist" is spoiled in the trailer, although I guess that's how you get people to buy this game- The game feels unfinished: Lots of invisible walls; there is somehow too much and too little handholding at the same time: If you miss the hint, you can wander around aimlessly for hours, turning every stone, wondering which of the things you can even interact with, until afterwards you realize that, oh, the thing you thought was gonna "Be it" from the very start, in fact "Was It", and it only didn't work due to janky controls/physics- The mechanic of "The Twist" is interesting, but IMHO barely explored properlyLike, I don't want to be too harsh, I can tell the developers tried, but... It just kinda wasn't good enough for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Maquette falls into that increasingly-common category of games with a creative puzzle mechanic that's tied together by a story with a heavy theme.  (See also: Monocage, Braid, It Takes Two, RiME, The Unfinished Swan, Superliminal, A Fisherman's Tale, Gorogoa, et cetera.)I found the story parts difficult to listen to, but not because they're bad in any sense: they're well-written and voiced, and mesh with the puzzles and level design in meaningful ways. You can skip cutscenes by holding spacebar, but I don't think you should (until you're ready to take a crack at the speedrun achievements anyway).It's fairly short: I completed the story in around 4 hours, then took another hour or so to complete the speedrun achievements.The core puzzle mechanic itself is unique, and each stage riffs on it in different ways, which combines with the game's short length to ensure the puzzles never have a chance to feel stale or tedious.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very limited. If you have played The Witness you'll know how this feels: You start to understand the mechanics taught to you and the game starts to open up a little. But then you try applying interesting puzzle solutions yourself, and the game punishes you for not finding the hints in the exact order it was designed. There is no space for you to puzzle in this puzzle game. I tried to shrink objects down to molecular size - not allowed. I tried to shrink myself down to fit through small holes - not allowed. I tried to place large objects in such a way that they form bridges over walls - not allowed, unless intended.There are some pretty clever ideas where an object has multiple purposes at different scales, but that is all that this puzzle gimmick entails. They stapled some tired love story to it and suddenly expect me to get invested? The gameplay has nothing to do with love, and the success of other puzzle games is a clear indication that you shouldn't need the story. This game could just have been a genuine puzzle game but instead environments are stretched out and dialogue is scattered throughout. Techniques are not expanded upon and the game quickly feels like a hunt for the one clue you missed. You start to think "What would the designer have intended for me to see" instead of "What can I do with the tools at my disposal." Again, not puzzling but just... intentionally having your hand held.Plain bad executions, sadly.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: When Annapurna publishes a game you know it has something special, so far all the games they have published I fell in love with after playing them so no wonder why this publisher became one of my favorite of all time, it’s a very simple rule, if it’s an Annapurna published game, check it out, and here we are with Maquette, the newest published game from this amazing company, will Maquette deliver? Well, let’s find out, shall we? Michael and Kenzie, two strangers who meet by accident and from that precise moment something sparks, a love story full of emotions, a journey through the memories and experiences of this couple that will bring up moments of joy and moments of sadness in an oneiric world in which each situation has a form. A letter, a sketchbook and the voice of Michael are the means by which the story is told.You can bet this is an Annapurna game because the story and narrative of this game is clearly their style, I must say something about it, the story is good and the plotline consistent, not only the voice work made it feel natural but also the relation between Michael and Kenzie felt like a day-to-day story and the way is being told is fantastic thanks to this floating sentences and the sketches from the book, however, I must say that I had a “Deja Vu” moment by the end of the game and that’s because this game reminded me to another Annapurna game, that will be explained in the next spoiler section and I won’t give too much details.I have mentioned a lot the sketchbook element of this game and not without a good reason, the visual aspects of this game are quite interesting and charming, first we have varied arquitectonic styles within the structures, from the main maquette to the different buildings, all of them have a different style, in addition to this, from time to time we will experience a beautiful effect of air traces painting an scene that represents part of a conversation, part of where the action is taking place or a visual representation of the feelings, really beautiful effect that helps the general atmosphere. We can’t forget about the main attraction here, size changes based on what maquette are you in, wait what? Yes, there are different “levels” of perspective to play, I will talk about the gameplay side of this later, right now I want to focus on the visual aspect of this mechanic, it’s simply impressive at times, it might now be something new as we have seen this mechanic used in different games, however, Maquette does use it with a few tweaks here and there that creates a visual illusion that at times is breathtaking, like an infinite horizon or creating an infinite sky box of the main maquette building, I won’t spoil anything but there are a few times that it will amaze you.When it comes to gameplay the game is very direct with the mechanics, on the one hand you walk, explore the environment and pick up things or activate mechanisms, on the other hand we have the perspective mechanic, what I was describing before it’s the main mechanic of this game, we will have to go in or out of the maquettes in order to get new objects, reach places that weren’t possible to access before.This mechanic in particular isn’t new at all but it’s really well implemented and they nailed it when it comes to puzzle solving, sometimes you will be amazed how easy something was and you didn’t see that coming, it is essential you keep your eye sharp because you will probably miss some details and mandatory elements to solve a puzzle or keep going with the story, that lever won’t be pulled alone and that gem won’t fit there, will it? As a note, I only had a few minor glitches in the game and all happened when picking up objects, nothing game breaking, just a few glitches here and there but that’s it.We talked about visuals and we talked about gameplay, what’s missing? Oh yeah, sound and music, another technical aspect nailed by the team, the OST is absolutely marvelous, such a great selection of tracks for each moment that brings up even a more powerful sense of the feeling they want to transmit with the letter but nothing does as much as the voice acting, they did an amazing job doing a very natural acting, joy, anger, sadness, each thing feels real, there is one dialog in particular mid-to-end of the game that woah, that anger was something else. In conclusion, Maquette was an “Annapurna seal of approval” game that was exactly what I was expecting, aside from the spoilered paragraph everything else felt really good, all the technical aspects were good, the story was good and in general I enjoyed my walkthrough.Do I recommend this game? Yeah, right now we need stories that bring us a bit of joy and human feeling to the heart and this game does it, it’s not too long, it is direct and it is a perfect game for a bit of passion and wholesome narrative, it might not be as lovely as you might find out, but hey, life is exactly that, experiences that we live and learn from. That being said, I do encourage you to play the game and hopefully you will enjoy it like I did. Goodbye, Sunflower.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been very on the fence about this game for a while, and to be honest I wish it weren't a game-crashing bug that pushed me off of it.  (I was prepared to call this "a qualified yes", but...)  Currently stuck in the final chapter, unable to finish, which is really unfortunate.Here's the thing: there's a lot to like in this game.  The puzzles are, generally speaking, very clever and interesting, and visually striking.  The voice acting is great!  The story is, well, OK, perhaps kind of a cliche (; this might have felt eye-opening and fresh when I was 20, but a quarter of a century later, not as much), but it's at least well-told.)But then...1. The gameplay is very linear.  That makes sense, to an extent, because the story is very linear.  (At least...kind of linear?  Honestly, it's told in flashbacks and memories, so maybe it didn't have to be!)  But it means that unlike other walk-around-and-solve-puzzles games, if you get stuck, you're stuck.  There's no walking off, looking at something else for a while, coming back with fresh eyes.  You're just stuck.2. The graphics are great, but there's a downside: it's sometimes very hard to tell what's important and what's just scenery.  We spent a lot of time walking over to every random bush, wall, corner, candle, what have you, trying to see if that's where we were supposed to do something.3. Not unrelatedly:  has that classic graphical-game problem where there's very little feedback.  At one point we were close to doing the right thing, but couldn't tell we were close, we could only tell that what we were doing wasn't working.  (For the record: .)  At another point we were really, really far from doing the right thing, but once again had no idea whether it wasn't working because we hadn't quite done it right or because we were in totally the wrong place.  (This one: .)4. The idea of puzzles that involve changing perspectives is really cool--and I wish so much that the story was about changing perspectives, but most of the time the puzzle mechanics and the story are completely dissociated.  (Not always: there are some places in The Spiral where, for instance, the text is about "not quite fitting" and the puzzle involves getting something to fit properly.  But mostly.)I see that this is the first game from these developers, and even with all that complaining, I'm genuinely looking forward to seeing what they do next; there's a lot in here that's good and I'm hoping that they can learn from the mistakes they made.  Especially the game-crashing ones.

_childDocuments_.review: Starting with the good stuff: The art direction is one of the BEST I've ever seen - the visuals are impressive and always bring something fresh from the beginning to the end of the experience, taking you by surprise with new colors, compositions and visual effects.The core mechanic is great, puzzles have some good "a-ha" moments, and each level's design is pretty fun to explore for the first time. However, the pacing is a little bit odd - there are plenty of difficulty spikes caused by not having properly prepared the player for some challenges - I usually like puzzles that don't underestimate the player, but when there is an exploration element to the game it's easy to get stuck because you simply didn't notice something that should be easy to see - like understanding whether a platform is reachable by a jump or not, or not being 100% sure if you messed things up to the point you created a deadlock state. That is not a good puzzle, it's just bad ergonomics.Also, although there are some interesting details in how the dialogue is written, narratively speaking Maquette unfortunately doesn't bring anything new to the table - other games have told the same story in very similar ways. There is a lot of influence from Florence but the use of "mechanics as metaphor" seem a little bit forced at some points, as the story feels a bit slapped on top of the "recursiveness" mechanic.There were also plenty of game-breaking bugs on the release day, which made me re-start the levels from scratch (and watch all unskippable cutscenes again) several times. But I assume this will probably have already been fixed by the time I post this.It hurts to give a "not recommended" because the visuals are amazing and the main mechanic is delightful to discover. A lot of work was clearly put into this game, but in terms of experience I think the full price is a little bit high,  especially in a world with so many great indie puzzles being released all of the time - many of them published by Annapurna itself. If you are curious, I would recommend waiting for a bigger discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game on my radar since I finished Outer Wilds and searched for what Annapurna published besides it.The trailers had me intrigued, so I got it once it got onto steam.I quite liked the game and would recommend it to fans of puzzles games, maybe to fans of narrative driven games as well.Both recommondations come with some caviats though:-Don't go in here looking for a long game. The game is short, I finished it in about 3h.-Don't go in here looking for hard puzzles. The puzzles are rather tame. I looked up 2 solutions. One of them was because the game bugged out on me and the (valid) solution I already tried did not work (or let's say, the whole puzzle didn't actually work). The second one was because the solution was (imo) way out of the box (the game kinda threw me a curveball on this one, probably on purpose).-Don't go in for a really deep story. The story is rather clichee imo, but it is well delivered and has an emotional effect.Since the game is cheap, I am fine with it's shortness. I feel like the story wouldn't have been able to get stretched out further anyhow, so it's a plus that it did not drag on. I am a bit sad that the game is so short because the general puzzle mechanic this game uses is quite unique and I would've like more and more complicated puzzles using it. Oh and the KB+M controls can be really janky at times. It's not completely disfunctional, but some sections had my scratching my head. Also there are no graphics options to speak of, besides a resolutions, 3 presets and a FOV-slider (I had to turn that down though, as the highest option, 90, brings heavy motion blur with it).
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Up until the final level I would have said that it's worth buying discounted if you are into puzzle games and if you aren't easily frustrated.The game looks pretty nice and the core gameplay mechanics are kinda cool, which is great. What's not so great is that the controls are really weird. It is often harder to place the objects in the right spot than to figure out the right spot, which is frustrating. The story is also very superficial and told in a way that is not engaging at all. It's basically just text that pops up in the world and occasionally some dialog (audio only). It's supposed to be very emotional but fell completely flat for me. But other than that the puzzles are fun most of the time.However the final level is so broken that I can't recommend this game to anyone. The game will randomly lock up completely when you interact with a specific item. This happened at least 6 times in a level that's supposed to take approximately 15 minutes.Don't buy it. Not even if you are really into puzzle games and it is heavily discounted. This is not acceptable.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: I was really disappointed with this game having expected an experience in a similar vein to Superliminal. The puzzles do not feel mentally challenging at all. Instead it's more a case of walking around and trying to interact with everything, anything, only to find that one object is the only thing used through the majority of the level. There were also cheap tricks such as mechanics which only work once and then the rules seem to change without warning. In addition, you end up doing most of this in silence since once the song to enter the new section ends, no background sound/music is added thereafter. Lastly I found what I heard of the story cliche and the voice actors performances were not good enough to carry a sup par script with the female actresses interpretation being particularly irritating.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles are somewhat simplistic and the level design could do more to guide the player to solutions, especially early on, because even though the puzzles are simple, you may miss the solution because you just have no idea what you're looking for.The story is also simplistic, one-dimensional, and frankly, a bit played out. The pacing felt wrong, the relationship's turn for the worse seemed to happen quite suddenly, even though it was clear from the very beginning that's where the story was heading. In the end, I didn't really care about the characters, they're totally uninteresting. And the angry shouting match was completely unnecessary, and frankly, hard to listen to. Maybe the developers should try some nuance or subtlety in their next game.Movement was a bit janky, and so was the camera. I'm not sure what else I can say here.At around 6 hours, I'd complain about the game being too short, except by the time I reached the ending, I was happy to move onto something else.TL;DR: go play Florence instead. It's got a relationship, it's got ups and downs, it's got puzzles, and is a delight to play.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Maquette is a simple puzzler that presents itself as a metaphor/backdrop to a story told via voiced interludes and text throughout the environment. The story is bland, the puzzles are frustrating and unclear, the mechanics are underutilized, and the controls are incredibly clunky.The main gimmick for the game is recursion - each level contains a miniature version of itself that you can kinda interact with. A puzzle might require that you place an object inside the small version of the level, which then appears at that spot in the main level and can serve as a makeshift bridge to traverse a gap. Unfortunately, that is about the extend to which this mechanic is explored. The recursion mechanic is the main reason I was drawn to the game, so this was a huge disappointment. The one exception is the level which allows you to move the level around inside itself - this is really cool and I got excited for a couple minutes, and then the game ended. That last level felt like it should have been near the beginning, so the fact that it was supposed to be the high point is rather telling.The controls are nearly unbearable. Movement is slow and even slower when you walk into the larger version of the level, and the fact that the shift button  instead of sprinting feels like some kind of cruel prank. Picking up/moving items is imprecise and unwieldy and there is no clear indication of what can and can't be jumped over. All of this means that you often can't tell if you've done anything correctly or just glitched your way to the solution, all the while wrestling with the controls to do very basic tasks. The icing on the cake is when the game yanks away control out of nowhere with a slow-pan cutscene every few minutes.The game just feels like they didn't really know how to make a puzzler. Rules for solving puzzles are introduced and then immediately thrown out - things that worked before don't work in subsequent levels, and there isn't any kind of progression or escalation of the mechanics. Nothing is ever explained, which is fine, but when combined with this lack of consistency it's just a chore to figure out what exactly they wanted you to do. And again, it's usually not the main attraction of the recursive levels, but rather just a thing you gotta find to put somewhere to open something.The story is the most generic, bland narrative about a couple you could possibly imagine: . It is told via text found throughout the level as well as some voiced sections. The voice acting is great, but that's about it.Not all achievements are guaranteed - you have to go back and redo levels in a certain time limit. I didn't bother.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Maquette is a perfect example of why Steam review ratings need to be more granular than "yes" or "no".The story tackles a common life event that isn't all that commonly the focus of game stories, so is quite interesting in that respect. It is also told entirely through narration via some pretty good voice acting. I personally felt the female voice was considerably more convincing than the male voice, though can't really put my finger on why, but ultimately I felt the story was very well told.The gameplay has you exploring this artistically beautiful recursive world which hold elements of the memories of the two narrators. You move through these memories by solving puzzles which typically involve negotiating dimension bending big and bigger, and little and littler versions of the environment you're in. Conceptually pretty cool.Unfortunately, a lot of the puzzle solving is pretty janky and feels kind of half-baked in places. Some puzzles get you really thinking, which is a good thing, but other times you're left wondering if you actually did some puzzles right or if you just abused the game's mechanics and got away with it.Most puzzles are solved by picking up an object, carrying and moving it around, but the pick, carrying and moving mechanics just feel broken. Honestly, the unclear puzzles wouldn't even be half as frustrating if it just "felt" good to hold and move stuff.There's only a few "cut scenes" for when a puzzle is solved, the rest of the time you are left awkwardly platforming a slow moving, low jumping character over a bridge or ramp you have placed, struggling to reach the end and unsure if you've just missed something somewhere or if the actual intended solution is just this rough.Ultimately though, I enjoyed my time with the game. The way it told its story is unique and engaging, the world is beautiful and pleasant to be in, and the puzzle concept is interesting and fairly unique despite its roughness.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this, but it's too frustrating.  The concept of playing with size and worlds-within-worlds is good, but the puzzles are pretty simplistic, and don't really take much advantage of it.  The controls and also fiddly, making it difficult to place objects.  I've also had a few crashes as well.  Worst of all though is the drippy storyline of a couple getting together, splitting up, getting back together, blah blah.  It has nothing to do with the gameplay, and is just trying to give the game some emotional heft, but just ends up being annoying.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: It's alright, you'd expect explorations of fractal space from the trailer, and there's a tiny bit of that at the end of the game, but most of the game is a walking sim. The story sucks, there's very few puzzles and most of them are trivial, akin to a hidden object game where you have to click on the right thing.The idea is interesting and the last three puzzles in the game are cool, so a weak thumbs up I guess.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: I was sold on this from it's core mechanic of the recursive paradox world, but this has very few applications. With one or two exceptions the puzzles were quite simplistic. A lot of the interaction felt like padding to space out a fairly bland plot about a guy getting the feels over his relationship failing.Visually it's fantastic, but the excellent level design is eschewed for doodle like animatic scenes for all the plot, which serves to pull focus from the mechanical concept.  The plot and the theme might have worked well in a different game, but they had absolutely nothing to do with your actions in this game, and seemed to serve as nothing more than a distraction to space out barely an hours worth of puzzles in a world that is beautifully detailed, but interactively rather sparse.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, I really did. In theory it has a lot going for it from the interesting story to the absolutely beautiful visualss... but it just does everything possible to make liking it impossible. It's glitchy, there is no v-sync, you will be soft locked often, it crashes, the puzzles are unwieldy and most of them are pretty unengaging, the few puzzles that are actually difficult are only difficult because their parameters are poorly explained to the player or just not explained it all. The list of cons is a mile long.I'm sorry to the devs, but I DNF. I don't recommend. Skip.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: A short puzzle game with puzzles based around interacting with the same objects at different scales. Padded with a sequence of tedious but skippable spoken dialogs about a failed relationship.A few of the puzzles are unintuitive and/or involve a lot of walking long distances, and the last level crashes if you interact with the main object the wrong way (the object is recursive, and you have to be careful to select the outermost object; the game crashes it you accidentally select the inner one).It has a lot of promise, but the execution is underwhelming and timid. Toward the end I found myself just pushing through it as fast as I could and relying on FAQs for the more unintuitive puzzle solutions because I wasn't enjoying it anymore and just wanted to be done with it.

Not severely broken, but just enough that it doesn't work. A minor fix would solve it, but it appears no one's home to fix it. This sums up the game itself as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Maquette is a beautiful game with a few really good (and hard) puzzles, but it's little more than that. Only rarely does it flesh out its core mechanics to the max, allowing/requiring you to travel across more than one level of its fractal, recursive world. Most of the time you're dealing with only two levels, making items smaller or bigger to suit your needs (like in Superluminal). Maquette does shine, though, on a handful of puzzles which require a lot of spatial awareness and lateral thinking. It has charming visuals and an amazing soundtrack. Really, the songs are the best feature of this game. The length is also good, and the game doesn't overstay its welcome.The story is a bit lackluster, and doesn't add a lot to the enjoyment of the game. But what really tips the scale towards not recommending it is the glitches and bugs. This game could really use a few months of play-testing before being released. As of April/2021, and after some patches, it's still easy to get stuck clipping through objects. It does not encourage exploration also: I found a way to go one level higher, without exploiting any glitches, by using a staircase in Wedge. I thought there would be something there, or at least an achievement, but instead you're awarded with falling through the map forever. :(All in all, Maquette is still a decent game, and I had fun playing it. At a 40% or higher discount, I'd recommend going for it. But at full price, there are many better options out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Maquette promises a puzzle game built around their recursive world mechanic. But the game spends so much time ham-fisting dialogue-only cutscenes between each of its basic puzzles that it feels less like a game and more like an over-engineered walking sim with, in my opinion, an incredibly bland romance narrative that barely ties into the gameplay. 30  minutes was all I could take of this.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Neat idea, pretty visuals, but the actual puzzles are lacking in creativity. The recursive mechanic was rarely ever an integral part of the solution. There are so many cool ideas to be had here, but so few was used. Take for instance in one of the last levels you are able to pick up the recursive maquette, and when tilting it will tilt the gravity outside. However that mechanic was never actually used for anything, which is a real shame. When the game finally introduces some worthwhile mechanics, the game is already over.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzles designed not like:  here is ALL data about puzzle, figure out how to SOLVE (like Portal or Talos Principle)but  here is the level, GUESS about mechanics (except perspective, this moment devs deigned to explain) and data about puzzle, then solve.I dont like guessing in logic games. It is unfair - I can't know which level elements are pieces of puzzle, which not. I CANT GUESS THAT HERO THAT BARELY JUMPS CAN JUMP OVER ONE SINGLE PLACE IN LEVEL THAT VISUALLY DONT LOOK CROSSABLE AT ALL! Well, I can actually, but it boring and lazy design. I'm sure there are time limited and pixel hunting puzzles further in the game, don't want to check.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you ever have a friend that had a myriad of relationship problems. And when relating stories of his relationship woes, always reframed it to make the other person seem like the bad person. Watch this go on for years, and see them refuse to grow as a person, while everyone they ever date eventually gets sick of their ♥♥♥♥ and leaves? I hope you enjoy listening to them blame other people for their relationship problems, because that's the cringefest that Maquette is in a nutshell.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting mechanic that they seemed to struggle to find a good plot to go with it so they chose some sappy love story that you follow along  as you play the game but in the 4 hours I've played seem to have nothing to do with the "magic" of the game world, past they change some of the visuals to match the story, maybe in the end the extremely grounded love story comes together with the magical size shifting world, but so far the love story is just a nauseating slow down in the gameplay I wish I could just skip. None of the dialog seems to have anything to do with what's going on with the puzzles so you could just turn off the sound and ignore the text and do fine.The puzzles themselves are pretty decent though some are pretty out there, the few times I got stuck and had to get help online, most of the time I wound up thinking "yeah I should have seen that/thought outside the box, it's a new way of thinking" but a few of them are "ugg, really, how contrived and unintuitive from what we've seen in the rest of the game and can see in the puzzle itself."From a puzzle standpoint it still gets a slight yes, but the sappy love story is just ruining the experience. It might be cliche but I'd be a lot less turned off if it had something to do with "a wizard did it".
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: I very much enjoy puzzle games in this style, and Maquette seemed to have some potential. The early puzzles are kind of simplistic, but that's to be expected. However, the vocal interludes and other aspects of heavy stylization that will probably make this an indie darling turned me off hard and made me put it down before I got very far.Roughly - people who enjoy love stories but are only somewhat interested in puzzle games will probably be engrossed, people who like puzzle games but give romance a skip are going to find that the romance is way too front and center of what the game wants to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: A good demo of what this could have been: You loved the preview video? Well that's pretty much everything you will get.Excepted this good idea and the awesome artistic direction, puzzles are all really simple and straightforward: i feel like the point of the whole game is to keep you busy long enough to prevent refunds.2 hours to see the end of the game, just watch a walktrough, no point paying for it if you want actual puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine if Portal had a cutscene ever 30 seconds and made you listen to the Romance of Cave Johnson and Glados. There is very little gameplay in this game and even less puzzles. Make small things big to walk over gaps and make big things small to unlock doors. That's the game. I didn't like Superliminal very much already but compared to this game it was a marvelous experience far and above what this has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: It's... okay?Very similar to Superliminal, but the puzzles are not as good. Handling objects is often frustrating, and the story is .Accurately predicted the game was written and designed by the same person because it feels it.Game length is probably more like 2-3 hours if you don't get stuck, but there's very few puzzles you go "AHA" and feel like you achieved something. Quite a few of them are "oh I was supposed to touch [insert object that's just out in the open and not a puzzle here]".Would recommend on discount, but don't recommend otherwise.Soundtrack is pretty nice tho.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't finished the game yet, but I made sure I read a lot of reviews before buying this, since it's very mixed.Deciding whether or not you want this game depends on what you're down with.If you enjoy lovely art direction/atmosphere, decent writing with great voice acting, and okay use of recursion, then this will be a very pleasant experience for you, as it is for me.If you want something that provides comfortable controls, complex/clever puzzles, and an unpredictable story, that's not really what you'll get.This game has puzzles. But like many said, they're mostly simple with usually obvious solutions.But many people also said the world doesn't match the story, and I STRONGLY disagree.The use of colors, lighting, music, and locations match the feelings that this story goes through very well. Memories represented in an imaginary world we escape to, while reflecting on how we saw everything. Several visual metaphors are even used for puzzles.As for the story itself, it's fairly simple and predictable (so far. I haven't finished it yet, but reviews said the rest is simple), but executed very well by the solid writing of the dialogue, fantastic voice acting, and incredible cutscenes of animated drawings. I feel the puzzles are there for the sake of some gameplay, but mainly focuses on telling a story, kinda like What Remains of Edith Finch, which I personally dig.Now for the more objective issues.Controls for moving objects can be a chore. It's easy to forget what button is for dropping, holding out, and putting back. And when holding out an object, you move slow, and can't move your camera if you get too close to a surface.It can also be easy to miss clear solutions if you don't look closely enough, like gem-shaped holes that you need to make objects small enough for, or platforming over some rocks to get outside of your zone. Puzzles like these aren't good as much as they are confusing.Overall, if the lack of much real puzzle gameplay, and stiff controls won't get in your way of enjoying this pretty game and its decently told story, then it's a solid recommend on sale. I got it for 10 bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fusion between Manifold Garden and Superliminal, but with sappy romance instead of hard geometry. It goes without saying, but the visuals can be gorgeous.I finished it casually in less than 4 hours, but there are speedrun achievements, for those interested. See for yourself if it's worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Maquette

_childDocuments_.review: A work of art in every sense of the word! And it's much more than that! I expected just an experimental game built on the idea of the "fractal space" mechanics. And that is very cool and mind bending in itself, but this game delivers MUCH MORE. Before and after the levels centered around "the dome", there are other levels based on fantastic ideas and with incredible visuals. They could've got away with much less, just building levels and puzzles on the main idea, but they did more, and I'm extremely grateful for that.It's not a perfect game. Above all, I'm sorry they didn't get 5x the budget to make it look even more beautiful. It's gorgeous anyway but has a "low poly" feel to it, which I personally don't like, it feels cheap. I also felt zero connection to the story - it was cheesy and not very deeply written. And it had a few bugs too (frankly I'm surprised it has only that few, given the fractal mechanics - I'm sure it was not easy to program this environment). But all these can be ignored and one can just jump in and enjoy the ride in this unique and exciting world!I will definitely play it again!

_childDocuments_.review: The most puzzling experience that Maquette offers is the sight of its credits – to be exact, their length. It's surprising how many people worked on this game and it still got published as is.I have several issues with this product, the worst of which is the control scheme. However, even if technical issues were fixed in the future, the game is just not interesting as a puzzler nor as some plot delivery device.To pick up an item, you have to right-click it. This makes you carry it in front of your character, locking your camera straight onto it, and slowing you to a crawl. To unlock the camera and walk at normal speed, you have to left-click after picking up the item. To drop it, you have to right-click to carry it in front of you again, then right-click  to finally let go.I don't understand why these actions are bound this way. It's completely counterintuitive to me and made the gameplay so much worse with every item I had to carry. I've lost count how many times I've made a mistake in this mouse button dance – dropping an object when I wanted to walk fast, or hearing the annoying  when the game didn't feel like allowing me to do something.The controls are configurable, but . Restarting the game brings back the defaults. What's more, the bindings menu is a pain to use – scrolling through it is slow, clicking anything resets the view so you get lost, and there's no feedback upon overriding another binding.Since Maquette deals with variable sizes, it would be natural to include a sprint button to run through large areas. Nope! Holding Shift makes you walk . Why? There are exactly zero places where this is useful, as opposed to times where you fall asleep running from one area to another as a rat-sized character.Dropped items most often hover above the ground, which is very noticeable on levels where you need to climb them. Good luck jumping on top of these stairs! They're unreachable, go back and place them again.Loading a checkpoint can result in physics engine bugs, so that objects pass through the ground and there's no way to recover them. These stairs that previously were too high? Now they're underground.There are multiple issues with objects lacking textures, polygons that fight for z-index and missing apostrophes in sentences floating around. The game also decided to ignore my mouse input after one of the numerous cutscenes, so it was yet another forced restart.You know what? It's a puzzle game, so we should stop complaining about minute details such as nauseating camera, terrible controls and game-breaking bugs, and focus on puzzles!Yay!They're bad.Maquette throws ideas and discards them after one use. Instead of letting the player build up an understanding of the mechanics, the game introduces a thing, expects you to immediately divine what you're supposed to do, and proceeds to another thing.It has such a great core mechanic that it doesn't explore at all. The novelty wears off after a few minutes of playing with the sizes and there are very few puzzles that require mental effort. The objective is often not clear, so instead of wondering , you're left wondering .It's apparent to me that the game did not go through testing (with creative testers) before release, because players are finding ways to get stuck, the only way out being a level restart. Dropping a key behind a door it's supposed to open doesn't trigger any "you dun goofed" check, and you're forced to realize that yourself.And guess what? If you carry an object in front of you, it's larger than if you hold it to your chest. You can't fit the red crystal through the doors, but you can walk with it if you press the left mouse button first. How does that make any sense?!Nothing to write home about. It's not interesting, painfully predictable and doesn't fit the puzzles at all. If there is any connection between the plot and the maquette or traveling through recursive worlds, then I must have completely missed it. I also didn't really like the characters, but that might have been intentional.However, I need to praise the voice actors. They did an outstanding job, so even if the script was mediocre, their delivery was remarkable – most of the dialogue carried convincing emotional load. Their acting was emphasized with nice illustrations, cutely animated to fit the content. The quality of this aspect of the game really stands out.I was intrigued by other reviewers that praised the last chapter of the game, so I pushed forward to find out if Maquette was going to become another example of tedious game with brilliant final puzzle (like The Pedestrian). Unfortunately, even that's not the case. The mechanics change a bit, but the game continues its search for raison d'être with one-time puzzles that rely on clunky controls.Maquette fails as a puzzle game, fails with its storytelling, and wins in voice acting. But voice acting alone won't carry a $18 title which has barely more content than its Steam screenshots show.
