_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: I'm playing MNM on my Steamdeck and it is running very well. I estimate I am 80% through the story and I'm loving it. I love the silly, dry humour infused in the writing, I love the sentimental aspects of the story, and I love how the number of crafts and activities I can do continues to expand. If you like cozy, adorable games, this one is great. You're limited with what you can do at the start, but that changes as you advance the story. Cheers to Meowza games for making this. 😻💮
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: Mineko's Night Market is a fun game! At first, there is not much you can do, but you slowly unlock more areas of the map and even more things to do. The game can be a bit grindy when you need to collect resources for quests or to make items to sell at the Night Market. Also, there are some bugs such as playing the games at the Night Market can completely freeze the game and you are forced to close out of the game and lose your progress for the day, but this bug seems to have been fixed. I enjoy the story and I love all the cats as well as the Night Markets and how each Saturday is a different theme. I do recommend this game, but I do recommend picking up this game on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: Mineko's Night Market is a game that's more than just a relaxing farming simulator. It holds pros and cons:Pros:- Funny dialogue and interactions with some NPCs- Adorable development of a relationship between a father and daughter - Cute art style and character design- Comfy and relaxing music- You can interact with cats !!!!Cons:- Most NPC interactions are rather shallow, and most tasks given to you consist of having to collect/purchase items for them in order to unlock recipes- The game is slow to start up and feels as if it has a bit of a lack of direction- Under the guise of a cosy game, Mineko's Night Market is a very grindy game and your earnings from the night market relies on how effectively you manage your time by using your stamina everyday to collect items for craftingOverall, I do recommend this game as I have been enjoying it myself, but it does feel as if the game isn't finished, and I hope more updates are to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely a game where you can zone out and not really have to think for a few hours; it fits the "cozy game" genre perfectly. Some may find it a bit repetitive at times as you are just gathering and crafting 90% of the game but it's also nice to play when stressed to unwind. While I had the game on my wishlist for four or five years and I did expect more (more gameplay, dialogue, and overall game richness) I'm still pretty content/happy with what was put out. I do hope that updates, additional gameplay features, and outfits will be added into the game in the future and I encourage the developers to be mindful that many players are hoping for the same as well. If you're someone who gets bored easily but also likes mindless games, I definitely recommend waiting for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: Mineko's Night Market was a game that I waited since it first got showed to me when it was on Kickstarter. It was a highly anticipated for me since I'm a big Animal Crossing fan. I enjoy cozy games, but I do not like farming games as much as I easily get bored or get distracted at other aspects of the game. Games like Mineko's Night Market are ones I gravitate the most so I don't understand the people here that stated for others to "try other cozy games" because this genre of cozy game seems so limited to me. I can say, a con regarding this game is that there's things that aren't super straightforward, but it could also be that I get distracted at games super easily. I couldn't figure out the docks puzzle until I found a guide. That's fair though. A wayt to keep a counter of like stuff you need to do or for characters to repeat instructions more would be great. I got to say though, the start was a bit slow but as you are unlocking the stores in the night market, doing the mini games and everything else, it gets exciting.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: The game is definitely slow to start, but once you get through the first few objectives and start unlocking the different areas of the village/island you start to see the story piece together and suddenly you find yourself invested in Mineko (the protagonist) and Nikko’s (the elusive cat spirit) stories. The game’s strengths lies within its beautiful art style, witty humor, and cozy/repetitive game style. If you’re looking for depth and a mind-blowing experience this won’t be the best choice for you, but if you’re looking for a well-rounded before going to bed kind of game this is it.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this game for quite some time, so I'm excited to finally be able to play it. I'm working on my first play through and trying to accomplish everything. I enjoy looking at the little details in games. Overall, yes, I recommend Mineko's Night Market. The art style is wonderful. I enjoy the different music choices for different areas. You will be in these areas quite a bit to collect resources to craft with. It reminds me of Animal Crossing, honestly. You are doing the townsfolk favors for rewards...but also creating items to sell on Saturdays at the Night Market. The main story line is somewhat interesting and I'm hoping it continues to be so. Also, it has cats.It is not without it caveats. In short, it feels like it needed more. More time put into the game, more dialogue options, more things to do (especially if you're waiting on something you can't attain at the moment), etc. Completing the highest level of a relationship status ends up rewarding with a handful of items that I now have an overabundance of. Before this, you could receive crafting recipes. The milling of materials feels pretty soulless after awhile with no huge changes to the areas. or reasoning behind gathering. I've encountered a few problems in game play, but only one resulting in having the force the game closed.Annoyances: Crafting.one.item.at.a.time. Selling one item at a time or all. There is no in between. Characters with the same dialogue (I'm looking at you right and left cat). Lacking proper instructions for things like the metal detector. *Hint: use shift key. Showing instructions each time you go to use said metal detector. These are not a complete list.My hope is that the creators are able to add MORE and personalize this a bit. I think it's good, but it  could be GREAT.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 chill game, it has everything I love about a relaxing game: cats, story, and a cute market! I love how there are some small puzzles as you progress through the game and tons of different games for each market. It's so fun to watch the market level up every week! If you want to play a relaxing game after work, here it is!
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: I am absolutely loving this game so far - cannot express how much I love the vibes of this game. Very relaxing, simple, and cozy. MNM has some of the cutest cats I've seen in a video game. The pacing and progression is good. Looking at the achievements and map it looks like the game is going to open up, and I'm going to enjoy this ride. Edit: Just made it to 8 hours playing, and I think I'm going to play more. Please don't listen to the negative reviews in which the reviewer only played for an hour or two. This game is a slow burn and there is quite a bit more content than I anticipated. And the end is not in sight for me. This could be my most favorite cozy game this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely LOVED this game. The crafting, the agents, the side quests? 10/10Some people might think that it's boring and you need to grind too much, but for me, it was an almost perfect balance of story and exploring! I also liked the witty dialog :)Some things could still be improved, though: 1. The controls are kind of clunky (but maybe that's just a skill issue)2. You can't save until you go to sleep (this could be a pro, but a manual save option would be nice)3. You can't view the side quests (I'm a forgetful person, needing to go to every person individually to remember what they want is annoying)
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: At the moment, the game is a little buggy, some things are unclear for story progression, and some of the gameplay is somewhat repetitive or 'grind-y'. Yet, even despite the occasional bout of frustration, I still clearly really like this game, because I've been playing 5 hours a day for two days. Mineko's gameplay isn't the most innovative, but the charming art and feel to the story keep me coming back.And also how can you say no to petting cats and having a small army of them follow you around??
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this game since 2019 and it's finally here! Is it everything I hoped it would be? Not quite. Is it still a great game? Absolutely!  This is a fun cozy game and it's clear that a lot of love went into the making of Mineko's Night Market. I do hope the devs continue adding more to the game and making tweaks because there have been some minor issues, but overall I'm very much enjoying the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: I have been excited for this game for years, and now it's finally here. I understand and somewhat agree with the negative reviews, but I will still keep this game and keep playing because I'm having fun. The dialogue makes me smile, the music is calming. Very cute art, relaxing, simplistic. If that's what you're looking for, this is for you. Sure, $20 can seem like a lot, but you can play this nostalgic, Ghibli-feeling game for more hours than you could spend at a movie for the same price. Support the devs, they've done great work on this.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review: Super cute and fun game. Very relaxing, almost gives me like Dreamlight Valley/Animal Crossing vibes but a bit nicer. I love the art style of the game, and the activities keep you entertained and motivated to continue. The only mild (and I mean mild) complaint I have is I wish we could have the option to sell multiples of one item without having to sell either all of them or one at a time.
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

_childDocuments_.review:
Mineko's Night Market is a game that celebrates Japanese culture while introducing a heartwarming story about friendship, tradition, and many, many cats.

Play as Mineko, a curious girl who has just arrived at her new home on a struggling Japanese-inspired island at the base of Mount Fugu. The superstitious locals on the island worship the Sun Cat, Abe. What was always thought to be a long-told myth has the town puzzled, as sightings of Abe have begun to surface among the residents of the island in recent days.

Discover the secrets behind the town and restore the struggling village to its former glory. All the while, manage your daily activities, complete various jobs, venture on whimsical quests, and craft peculiar items in preparation for the weekly Night Market!
_childDocuments_.name: Mineko's Night Market

name: Wildermyth
detailed_description: Hear a Tale or Spin Your Own About the Game Wildermyth is a character-driven, procedurally-generated tactical RPG. Like the best tabletop roleplaying experiences, Wildermyth gives you choices and answers your every decision with consequences that drive your characters forward. Lead a band of heroes as they grow from reluctant farmers into unique, legendary fighters. Combat unexpected threats and strange monsters across interactive battlefields. Unravel mysteries and share pensive moments in an ever-new fantasy setting that blends hard truths and sacrifice with humor and personal storytelling. Where does your myth lead? Come help us uncover it! Reminiscent of tabletop roleplaying, unique heroes are born in unique settings every game. They age, transform, fall in love, disagree, and make harrowing sacrifices. Each hero brings their own organic history and personality with them, but your choices and combat skills are what decide their paths and outcomes. All heroes die someday… but you get to hold on to your favorites. Reintroduce them in the next adventure, and over many lifetimes the myths you make will form your own legendary pantheon. An Imaginative Papercraft World The Yondering Lands, where the game is set, is a richly layered world populated with hand-painted 2D characters and scenery. We’ve paid loving attention to breaking molds and exploring new ideas: no orcs, elves, or goblins here—but watch out for the telepathic insect-dragons and the clockwork undead. Extreme Character Depth Each of your heroes has their own unique generated history, personality, and appearance, and will form relationships with your other heroes. All of these elements change and develop over the course of a playthrough, as characters age, encounter mysteries, and overcome challenges. Choices That Matter Your hero may choose to trust the enigmatic wolf god, leading to a hair-raising change in their appearance and combat abilities. Or they may pursue a romance with a fellow hero, giving each of them a shared buff and more story opportunities. Encounters and events have permanent, character-defining effects, letting you craft the arc of each character. A New Approach to Death Did your favorite character get one-shotted by a tentacled horror-bear? Choose to let a hero 'fall back' with a maiming that will lead to some transformative new paths in their legend, or let them go out in a blaze of glory to be remembered for generations to come. Deep and Creative Tactical Combat Combat in Wildermyth emphasizes teamwork and careful positioning, as well as imaginative use of your evolving capabilities and surroundings. Walling and Flanking mechanics provide clear but conflicting incentives, while mystical interfusion lets you remake the battlefield with explosive magic. Multiple difficulty levels mean you can get as intense as you want to. Cooperative Multiplayer In a multiplayer game, you and your friends can each customize and control your own heroes as you play through a campaign. Recommended for up to five players—though in a typical campaign, you start with three heroes and pick up the fourth and fifth along the way. We also support Steam Remote Play. Endless Replayability Pick and choose from a huge bank of combat abilities as your heroes level up in each playthrough, and decide whether you prefer offensive or defensive tactics, brute strength, stealth, or magically flinging fire from a nearby lamp into your enemies' faces. Procedural generation gives you new heroes, new enemies, new story events, and new maps every time you play. A Custom Pantheon of Legends You’ll have the freedom to customize hero appearances, names, histories, and more. As time passes, heroes grow old and may retire, or else might fall in combat—and yes, some will survive all the way to the end. You can add your favorite heroes to a roster of legends and call on them again in later playthroughs. Build your own mythologies and share the awe-inspiring might of your heroes with others.

short_description: Wildermyth follows heroes over their whole careers, from their pitchfork days to their powerful primes, and on into old age and memory. It’s a party-based procedural storytelling RPG where tactical combat and story decisions will alter your world and reshape your cast of characters.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; A fantastic experience to play alone and really get drawn into the story, OR, grab a group of your friends and voice over your own characters. Slightly randomized character levelups combined with multiple unique build possibilities keeps the combat fresh and distinctive, and each campaign features one Main Enemy Faction (usually) with three side factions to mix up the fighting.If this game looks even remotely up your alley, buy it. This game takes a WIDE host of pre-written story frameworks (you'll recognize some after your second or third playthrough) and then proceedurally generates the details. The names, the characters, the interactions, and that last bit is the incredible part. More than just designing a character's face, you get to design their personality, and then watch them come to life. I have a set of archetypes that I frequently use as characters in RPG's, and I'll be damned, but this game did a bang up job of giving them personalities based on the parameters I set.And the writing. The writing in this game is something special. The only other thing I can compare it to is Cultist Simulator, which, if you haven't played it, every single written line of that game just OOZES with feelings of mysticality of the Occult. Wildermyth manages to do the same. The myths, the legends, the spirits, every interaction just soaks through with style.The combat? Excellent. Build variety with randomized level up perk rewards give this game a roguelike feel, which keeps the three base classes wonderfully fresh. You can easily have three of the same class in a party and have each one play wildly different.Bought this on a slight sale with my friends for a Lads Night, and it's turned out to be one of the best impulse purchases I've ever made.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Essentially unlimited replayability, lovely visual style, and tons of fun build options.  Unique playstyle for mages involves interacting with environment.  Themes let you transform your body and totally change how your character looks and plays.  Personalities and hooks influence the ways your characters act and which stories and choices are available to them.  Interesting twist on permadeath involves your character surviving but gaining a heavy debuff or dying but dishing out damage or a buff before they go.  Multiplayer with up to four other people.  Mod support.If you're a fan of roguelikes, games like XCOM or Wasteland, or both, this is highly, highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Combining evocative writing with procedural generation, Wildermyth takes a "best of both worlds" approach to storytelling that delivers on both the craft of a pre-written narrative and the wonderment of emergent gameplay. If you're the kind of person who played Darkest Dungeon and got really invested in a hero because of the quirks they developed, this game is for you. If you like the Sims, but you find yourself saying, "wow, I wish I could also be playing Fire Emblem right now," this game is for you. If you've wanted to play a game where, after being haunted by mysterious dreams, the hero is visited by a mysterious woman who transforms the protagonist's head into a crow head, stop reading this review and add Wildermyth to your cart immediately. Once you've poured a ton of hours into the game, the story events do start to get a little repetitive, but the game is highly moddable, and I haven't even scratched the surface of all the fan-made expansions the community has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Conk started life as a Farmhand working in the fields, every year he would head to the Faire and compete in the tournament, he got better and one year came in second. He swore his next year he would win it all. The tournament finally came around and he made it to the final, his opponent like him was training all year for this fight. They traded blows and drew blood but in the end Conk emerged victorious. Conk helped his defeated foe up from the field while his foes mother ran over from the crows to tend to him. After the ceremony Conk spent time with them at the next attraction which was a local mercenary recreating a battle with a captured Lizard folk she kept as a slave. However, a bird swooped down and attacked the mercenary just as the Lizard thrusted with his spear killing her before she hit the ground. Suddenly from the stands more lizard folks appeared and began killing the townsfolks, Conk his foe and foes mother joined forces and vanquished the lizard folks. However, in the battle the main Lizard landed a maiming blow into Conk which infected his leg and had to be amputated giving the Lizard time to escape.Conk now with a pegleg spent years with other mercenaries tracking the lizard. Every battle though Conk was too slow not able to get to the fight before his able-bodied companions could dispatch the enemy. During one of the seasons of peace Conk set out to find the mystic knights of legend who could walk between shadows. He ignored people who said they were just legends and not real and one day he found them. He trained with them for years and they taught him how to be a shadow walker. When he finally got to confront the lizard who took his leg and his prime he used everything he knew to defeat him swiftly. And while the lizard lay there dying Conk didn’t feel satisfied. He knew it wasn’t the end of his story. The Lizard was taking slaves and digging up ancient burial sites for a reason.Years went by and eventually that reason manifested itself, local townsfolks were losing their farms to fire and raids by the lizard folk so Conk and his band of warriors set out to get to the bottom of it. After months of searching and fighting they found the lair of the Lizards, they had no idea what they were about to discover. When they went into valley they saw something of legends, a Dragon. No one has seen a dragon for thousands of years and were thought to be a myth, Conk who already lost a leg and figured he had nothing left to lose used his shadow walk ability to get next to the dragon and lodged his battle axe into its chest, hitting him over and over before the dragon could react. While this didn’t kill the dragon it open up a vulnerable spot that the Legendary Hunter Redla was able to hit with an arrow which wounded the dragon making him flee. The Dragon retreated and years of peace fell across the valley, Conk was finally at piece and when he returned home everyone shouted Conk the Dragonslayer, Redla took no insult to this as Conk was the one that truly saved the day, she just did her job and was already a legend of her own several times over.The following years of peace were good to Conk who retired from adventuring and settled back down into farming for his twilight years, sometimes teaching other how to fight through loss of limbs.However, the dragon was not defeated12 years pass and the Dragon flew into a town landed, larger than ever before. It is clear the dragon spent the years getting stronger, and he bellowed a challenge to the townsfolks, telling them to send Conk and anyone who wished to face him to the Nearby volcano by years end or he would burn all of humanity.Word got to Conk who could not even lift his battle axe anymore due to age, he went to his companions of old and passed on all the information he had. The companions took the challenge and went to the volcano to meet the dragon. They battled through hordes of Lizard to get to the summit where the dragon came down to meet them, he was twice as big as they remembered and for a minute were left speechless and in awe. The feeling soon washed over them as they remembered who they were and the actions they took to get here, each companion, a hero, recalled what it means to be a hero. They recalled Conk who never hesitated in front of the Dragon, Redla shouted "For Conk" and Into action they leapt using everything they learned to slay the dragon. The battle was longer than the first encounter, many taking wounds and scars from the Dragon but the outcome was always known to them. Eventually Redla finished what Conk started and the arrow found the dragons heart and it came crashing down, dead. What lizards remained ran in fear. The day was won, no hero fell that day. And the Valley knew peace at long last, thanks to Conk the Dragon-slayer.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game! It is tons of fun and definitely worth the price I paid, which was around 20ish USD. It has okay storytelling, if a bit predictable once you've done a couple campaigns, and character customization is really good. THAT BEING SAID:I feel like this game is missing a feature of being able to go into towns and interact with regular villagers and actually be IN the world. I feel like this element would add a lot of gravity to the stories already being told and would also allow players to tell their own stories through the emergent gameplay of an intricate town system for the major settlements. Anyhow, if you are on the fence about buying it, it essentially boils down to more of a roguelike for me than an RPG the way it currently is. I love roguelikes and rpgs, so I still had a ball playing it, but if you don't like roguelikes this probably won't be for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews, but I think this one deserves it. Yes, it is not a perfect game (give me an option to rotate the camera), but the narrative potential is incredible.Here is a little story about one of my characters called "Mirko".Now, Mirko was a warrior, and on one point she gets stucked in some caverns due to her bulky build. Since she has a rivalry with the archer, she says something like "unlike you, I have warrior hips", which means she is proud of her body.After some years, Mirko starts to get old. We get a story panel of her where she starts to feel hey body straining, since she is not as young and strong as before, but she is too proud to tell the rest of the party member. She has a son, an archer called Yrborn that joins the party. Tragically, he dies on his first battle. Mirko then gets a story panel where she mourns the death of her son, shouting to the skies "Why did you not take me instead, death? Was I too old, too leathery for you?" (something like that). In that way, you get the feeling that how proud she was of her body relates to her son's death.On the last quest to save the world in the campaign, my party was about to die, Mirko is fatally wounded, but she sacrifies herself to give the archer, her lifetime rival, enough chance to survive for her to give one final shot, which she does and kills the boss.I like to think that Mirko died not just because she could not bear keep on living while her body decays, but because now she can runite with her son.This was not a scripted story. This happened due to various circunstances on the campaign. And a similar experience might happen to you if you play it.10/10, I miss Mirko so much...

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing this game so far. As of writing this, I did the first three chapter campaign, a generic three chapter campaign, and the enduring war. Wildermyth brings all the feelings of a tabletop DnD campaign to a really cool game. There's a lot of focus on character development. Gameplay-wise it's similar to XCOM's tactical turn-based tile system. I would definitely recommend playing this if you want that epic DnD feel in your video games.The non-generic campaigns are well-written though not particularly groundbreaking. The game's story lets you fill in the blanks just enough in your head to fit your own interpretation of the narrative in. I think that is an effect of the story being procedurally generated. It has to be vague enough for the parts to fit together cohesively. Nonetheless, I thought the themes of the story, especially in the Enduring War (a 5 chapter campaign that allowed them more time to explore their theme in depth), came out really well.The bulk of the work in the procedural storytelling goes into the character development of your party for sure. It's a complex system that takes into account previous actions, established character relationships, and leads to some really cool setups. On one of my campaigns, I had my rogue character and warrior guardian (who became a half-bear), be rivals from beginning to end. Their bickering, snarking, and one-upping was amusing at times, but the narrative gave it a satisfying conclusion that they do really care about each other and ended up retiring together.Basically, the collection of small side-quests, one-off events, become part of what makes every tale, every campaign you go on, so gripping, weaving in and out of the main campaign. About 80% of the story's strength comes from those individual one-off events. Would I like to see the main stories get a bit more of an oomph? Probably yeah. but I think that could get in the way of the flexibility needed to make the procedural story generation work so well. At the very least, the main threat helped add more weight to the character development.If you're familiar with the XCOM series, you won't find too many surprises in the way the combat works in this game. There's only three classes in this game, but every level up, you can pick from a variety of abilities, essentially letting you split the classes further into several specialisations. I think there's enough variety to make each class feel really well fleshed out. You can also further specialise your characters with the types of gear you choose for them, finding what works best for each build.I did not find the tactical combat to be particularly hard on the standard difficulty. The difficulty curve as the campaign progresses occasionally doesn't feel right though. When you're just starting out and are underequipped, the game feels a lot harder and the RNG can occasionally ♥♥♥♥ you over. You have to be -really- careful to not get maimed in the beginning.As you progress, your party will basically become so powerful that you have a near infinite amount of safeguards against RNG-based misses, dodges, blocks, etc. Your health is no longer so low that an unexpected ganging up on can lead to a one-turn knockout of one of your party members. I'd even say it made the final fights in the campaigns, led up to as this big "this will be our last stand" sort of thing, feel too easy in comparison.The overland view is interesting. You essentially secure tiles as you go along, build settlements which provide resources at the end of each chapter (necessary for gear upgrades), and every time you travel, you can get some random story events for every place you discover (which in turn can give you bonuses, story progression, unique gear, cool transformations, etc.) Strategising your resources also becomes easier overtime as your party grows and you can have one team sent out to do fighting on the frontlines, and another team securing settlements and building up defences.Those defences are a necessity against the incursions, which are basically time-based events. After a certain amount of in-game days, the enemies will muster up forces and attack your settlements. You can stop them by basically stopping the force as it marches through, defending your town, and defeating them. Managing the incursions together with the main quest, and character development events, etc. was a bit tedious. There were times where I just could not be bothered doing a random character development opportunity (despite it sounding really interesting) because I knew there was gonna be an incursion coming up that I had to deal with in a few days.The incursions do do a good job of adding more of that looming threat to the campaign. Peace is fragile after all, but yeah, sometimes it got in the way of doing the actually interesting storytelling quests and opportunities as I allotted my resources to defending against this constant threat.There's also the calamities. These are cards that grant your opponents new buffs throughout the campaign every certain number of days. You can spend legacy points (a resource that kind of represents your heroes' fame) to cancel these power-up but I never felt like it was worth the effort as you could also spend your hard-earned legacy points on upgrading your equipment, recruiting new members, etc., and like I said in the tactical gameplay review section, the combat felt like it got progressively easier anyway.Wildermyth is a great game, with its procedural storytelling shining the most in character development. You will make heroes that you'll cherish for many days after the campaign is finished. The overarching themes of the campaigns are not the most groundbreaking, but they do help add weight to all your character development and decisions you make along the way.Gameplay wise, there's a few annoying aspects in the strategic gameplay that sometimes got in the way of the more fun story bits, and I felt like the game gradually got easier, leading to the final battles often getting a bit curbstompy. But all in all, it's a great game, and I enjoy playing it, and I want to recommend it to everyone who wants the DnD storytelling feel in a video game.7.5/10 game for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Bland and boring, with an underdeveloped combat system. If only some care and effort went into making the combat tight and actually challenging; for there are some good ideas in there (mostly thinking about the magic mechanics here), and the game has beautiful visual design. As is, it is just a disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is one of my top 3 game of 2019, and it's still in Early Access, which says a lot. It's an amazing blend of tactical RPG and procedural narrative construction, something I've only felt playing table top RPG.Don't let the time played showing at the time I write the review, I've been part of the beta for more than 6 months now and I've enjoyed this game, upgrade after upgrade. The folk working on this game are true artist and dedicated workers who are delivering a solid gaming experience. I can't wait to see what else they have in store.But you can already play full games, with two complete campaigns available and two sandbox options. Plus, you can already mod the game to add your stories/villains. This is a truly amazing game, with very deep tactical options and stunning writing. Game is tough, you'll create beautiful backstory for your characters, they'll love, they'll fight, they'll die. Or they'll transform, get pets, learn to fly and many other activities that fits heroes. Until they can join your legacy and come back for more adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Bought after seeing rave reviews. Ultimately disappointed. Storytelling isn't as good as people make it out to be; it failed to grab me or make me emotionally invested in the characters. Artwork is mediocre. Board game "paper" visuals is a cute touch but falls a bit flat- compare to Darkest Dungeon which uses a similar style but presents far more evocative art. Mechanics are okay I guess with some neat ideas but feels too RNG-dependent from my admittedly limited experience.Ultimately didn't really have fun. Not recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I think this is a great take on the tabletop videogame genre. I really only have one complaint with it, and thats with the MP. when playing with others only one player has access to the camera controls which makes it really quite annoying to think about your moves when your friend is the active controller. but other than that I genuinely enjoy playing this game and its still tolerably enjoyable with friends. Unsure if an update has been made yet, but will change once Ive confirmed.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I was breathtaken by my first playthrough. From what I had previously read I was excited to see how many ways the story can alter for my parties on future playthroughs. Unfortunately by the end of my second campaign I had become completely disillusioned to where this game is in its development. There is very little reason to actually play a second time as it is right now. For now, variance only appears in a few personal quest triggers, but otherwise -most- events will be almost identical.I'm voting this up because I had a blast for the first playthrough (about 5 hours?). This game is in early access, so I expect there will be more legitimate variance in the future and I can't wait to see that.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah it's pretty fun. I do get repeat events constantly but they don't really take away from the experience. I really wish there was more permanence of characters though. The only relationships that are consistent through the campaigns are parental relationships, and it's kind of sad that marriages and rivalries aren't kept.

_childDocuments_.review: I've now completed one of the campaigns, and can say without reservation that this is easily one of the best games I've ever played. It is mechanically fantastic, its procedural content is well executed, the mod tools are beautiful, and for the first time in a considerable amount of time, a game made me tear up a little.I don't want to go in to a deep dive on this really, because no matter who you are, from first time gaming to tactics veteran, you're going to find something you *love* in this humble offering. It's simple to approach, but wonderfully deep and intricate. The concept is phenomenal, and well, well, well worth the money.Seriously, buy this game.Okay fine I'll actually review it.Good: Charming hand drawn papercrafted style. Comic book cutscenes with modular characters for truly procedural storytelling. Simple to play but delightfully robust combat system. The first story I've played thus far was delightfully written, and I was very surprised how cohesive the story ended up feeling. Active dev community that responds to fan requests. Adorable elemental pets. Real, organic, interesting character relationships. Strong modding community. Bad: Not. A. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Thing.Ugly: Okay. Fine. Gun to my head, there's one criticism I have. There's only three classes, though each have randomized class abilities that come together in a really interesting way. There's only three "character dynamics"- Friends, Lovers, and Rivals. This game might benefit from some more official content along these lines, though I think you can mod new stuff in, which would help tremendously. Though, just saying, devs, release DLC classes and story packs and I'll be first in line with bells on.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: A great leap forward in theory, a modest hop at the moment. The potential of Wildermyth's gameplay model and procedural approach to storytelling has a very high ceiling. In theory. At the moment however, the game's depth is only about an inch or so. The levelup system is pretty bare bones, and while this does help emphasize strategic use of the environment, by the end of your first campaign, you'll realize that you've already seen most of what there is to see. The game is also so intent on short vignette-style cutscenes that the attempts at character customization come across less like they're developing in front of your eyes and more like 3 slack-jawed yokels rambling about the countryside aimlessly.tl;dr: This games meh, but modding or the original developers could make it something really special in time.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed on this one, it's an alright game, but what exists so far isn't quite amazing. My thumbs up is a bit hesitant, it's more of a maybe, and one of those games I very much wish I could give a neutral review for.To start with, probably the biggest hook the game has pulling people in, is the procedural story. I feel like this is a bit misleading. There are 5 story campaigns, and 4 options of randomized campaigns. The story campaigns have a fixed story, with sometimes a single choice to make during it. How the game plays out, is you are given an opening event which introduces your starting characters and a main enemy, then you get a world map with about 8 tiles to explore for random events, then you tackle a chapter battle and get portion of the chapter story, then you move into the next chapter and the next 8 or so tiles to explore. This is how every chapter in every campaign works, sometimes there's a time limit and you don't have to explore all of them, otherwise you have to explore all or most of them. Each tile contains one of maybe 50-60ish random events, these short events are unrelated to the chapter story and the outcomes are often a dice roll that determines if you get a small buff or debuff in the battle that's about to happen on that same tile. A few of them provide an item reward or special bonus to a random character. The random events and story related events, always play out pretty much the same way, with some of them having a choice of 2-3 options at the end. The dialog is mostly identical, a few of the fluff lines are occasionally swapped based on the personality score of the characters involved, but generally once you've seen an event once running into it again isn't going to feel any different. In a few cases having a character with a specific item or personality trait will open up an additional option and slightly different reward.The procedural part is mostly the names and appearances of characters, and the shape of the world map. Otherwise, every campaign honestly feels the same, and by the 3rd or 4th it starts getting a bit repetitive. A 3 chapter campaign can take you 2-4 hours, a 5 chapter one is more like 4-6. At the 25 hour mark I've finished 5 campaigns and almost every event I run into at this point is one I've already seen a couple times. I would say the procedural storytelling in this game is rather poor, mainly because there is too much fixed story in the mix. Rather than an actual procedural or player created story like you might get out of something like The Sims or RimWorld, or even by just running around doing radiant quests in Skyrim/Fallout4, Wildermyth gives you a string of hand sculpted stories in a random order, it fills in too many of the blanks for you and with very repetitive content. It's like reading the same choose your own adventure book over and over, but you always flip to a random page instead of getting the choices, and some of the names and adjectives are randomized each time.The actual gameplay of the campaigns is a bit wonky as well. Every action you take in the world takes time, and your characters age and eventually retire and/or die. In addition, timers are counting down that increase the difficulty of enemies over time. By clearing the map of all enemies you are "rewarded" with bonus years of peace which happen between campaign chapters, during these years of peace your characters age, quite a bit, and that's about it. Why would you want bonus years of peace? Why is it rewarding? Gameplaywise, you wouldn't want them and it's not rewarding, the game punishes you for doing well. By not clearing everything you get fewer years of peace which keep your characters younger and stronger, and you also get fewer difficulty increasing effects making the game easier in later chapters, but you get less loot and exp. Overall it doesn't feel very good, but the game is not difficult enough for it really matter in the long run.Once you finish a campaign you can take all those characters and add them to your legacy, allowing you to bring them into future campaigns. They don't remember their old stories or mention them ever during any events, they only keep a basic form of their weapons and lose their other gear, and they get reset to a lower level based on their legacy tier. One thing they do keep is their completed "hook" quests. Each character has 3 "hooks" that trigger a specific side quest randomly during a campaign, they are pretty rare and you usually only get 2-3 per campaign total (after 5 campaigns I only have 2 characters with 2 hook quests completed, none with all 3). The main benefit of these hook quests though is they raise the retirement age, and with a couple of these completed your legacy characters don't really have to worry about retiring anymore. So that sort of negates the odd mechanics mentioned in the last paragraph.Combat is very simple, there aren't a lot of mechanics going on and very few active abilities outside transformations. For the most part warriors and hunters just attack with their weapon, mystics have an interesting mechanic where their spells require consuming nearby items on the map, limiting which spells they can use and how often to what is laying around. You usually have what you need to kill enemies quickly though, it's more a question of whether you bash enemies with a rock spell or strangle them with a vine spell, and when leveling up they can focus on making certain objects provide stronger spells or other benefits.Transformations are my favorite mechanic of the game. Some of the random events cause one character to develop some sort of mutation, and over time between chapters this can grow and take over most of their body. These transformations can turn characters into anything from giant bird people to living flame or walking crystal monsters. As the transformation progresses the character gains abilities from their new limbs, but also loses the ability to equip things onto those limbs, including weapons. This eventually feels really bad when all of your characters are transformed (and they will be pretty quickly if you don't refuse the transformation) and weapons are no longer useful to you, and you miss out on some of the special effects found on artifact quality weapons. The transformation powers themselves are strong enough to get you through a campaign without weapons if you pick the right skills, but often not as strong as a normal character with a good weapon.So for my recommendation, I would say if you are interested in a fairly short and basic strategy game with some interesting stories to read, this is pretty decent. Do maybe a couple campaigns and call it good, seeing all the events for the first time is pretty entertaining. If you are thinking, "Oh, it's procedural, that means lots of replayability!" I would say, maybe pass on it, it gets stale very quickly. I will say I am looking forward to any future content the game might offer, another wave of random events and some new classes would be fun, and hopefully they will rebalance some of the areas that don't feel that great by then.

_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: The game creates an immersive, emotional story. It is amazing how quickly you get attached to your characters and watch them not just have adventures but develop relationships and live their lives and pass the torch on to future generations of heroes. The gameplay is reasonably good. You're probably not going to come back to this game for the combat alone, but when combined with the emergent storytelling, it fits in just fine.If you like narrative games, this is one of the best.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best D&D style RPG games I've ever played, simple yet engaging mechanics, interesting stories to follow, incredibly character/party evolving systems to tell a great tale just like in actual TTRPG sessions, without even needing anyone else to play with (though it certainly wouldn't hurt)If you're a fan of TTRPGs or even just RPGs in general, DO NOT SKIP THIS ONE!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is a fantastic game that continues to get content updates (as of this writing, a new patch just dropped with some rewritten events and a new event, plus Deck verification and Portuguese support). The campaigns are interesting and well written. And when you've finished them, the procedural event generation is actually really good. As someone who generally runs for the hills when seeing "procedural generation" in a game description, I find it fairly well executed here. A lot of the joy for me in these types of games are the stories we create for our characters - that 1 battle where your clutch archer saved the day. The map where you lost everyone but your wizard. The events and legacy system really enhance that experience, creating heroes you'll want to revisit time and time again.

_childDocuments_.review: The bones are there. I really like the main campaign stories. But for an interactive story, event repetition starts happening almost immediately. Almost every playthrough has featured the majority of the same minor events happening, maybe with some minor changes (thee innkeeper was "jolly" instead of "gregarious"!)  Meanwhile, the Life Changing Events that can happen to your characters all seem to be minor variations on a theme. Basically, it feels like a couple of neat short stories stretched into a a bunch of extremely repetitive paint-by-numbers novels, overlaid onto a basic gameplay engine.Love the concept. Uninstalling it now b/c I can't see getting much new out of more play.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game. The combat is pretty fun and tactical but the main reason I play this game is the storytelling. I like watching the characters grow and change over the course of a campaign. I like the legacy hero system also so characters from old campaigns can show up in new ones. If you have friends, this game works pretty well for multiplayer too.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: You can usually tell how good a game will be in the end based on how good their Early Access is.This game is still in very early access and it is one of the best games I've played in quite some time. It's fresh, original, and has that feel of games like Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, the good parts of XCOM (without closely as much random), and Dungeons and Dragons. It's a very cool and unique game. Buy it. It's great!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: The game is more than just spectacular.I could finish my review here, but I still have some words to say and some emotions to share. I'll not deepen on the extremely fun tactics and class system - it's just too good not to try if you love XCOM or Dragon Age or JRPGs.This game hooked me in and I've played 21 hours of it in two days. The procedural storytelling leaves you no chance but to fall in love with your characters, that grow, fall in love, make rivals and get injuries. The legacy you build is something only YOU can fully appreciate. The dialogues and writing is captivating, therefore you shouldn't ever skip it.I love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game that succeeds at giving generated and/or custom characters a personality and making you care about them. - The characters develop friendships and competitive rivalries (think Legolas & Gimli).- The events you encounter will leave a mark on your heroes, so they might end up with a unique scar, an eyepatch, or some much more interesting things that I won't spoil here.- Your characters also age over time, their hair starts to go white and they can eventually retire, entering your "Hall of Fame".- In your next campaign, you can summon your favourite characters from your "Hall of Fame" to tell alternate stories about them.- Decisions have interesting consequences later on.Best game with semi-procedural content since Shadow of Mordor / Shadow of War.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get why this has such positive reviews.  The story text and dialogue seems procedure driven and as a result, doesn't make much sense and gives the impression it was written by someone who doesn't understand English very well.  Classes (three?) seem boring and that it would quickly become repetitive.  I really thought I would like this game as it seemed right up my alley, but I honestly can't get past the weird displaced feeling I get reading everything.  Maybe you're supposed to play this intoxicated or in an altered state of mind in order to look past the goofy sounding writing - it's just not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: The emergent narratives are fun, and I imagine as soon as I start seeing them repeat, the game is basically done for me.The tactical combat is too simple and probably too easy on Normal difficulty, but I recognize advance difficulties exist.  But there's just kind of a lack of depth in the combat (and what I think are probably some imbalances in the characters) that the fights felt more annoying to me than challenging.  Like I want to get to the weird stories, but instead I have to slog through a fight.  Maybe there are stronger tactical considerations at higher difficulties or vs. enemies I haven't faced before.Also, controller support is available, but I found it to be pretty unwieldy to actually use.Overall though, despite the complaints, the strength of the emergent stories and how they endear certain characters to you is why I would recommend the game.  If you're looking for an intense tactical RPG, this isn't it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't seem like it would be anything spectacular, but it really lives up to everything it claims to do. Dynamic character development, simple yet addicting combat, and procedural storytelling are very difficult things for a game to accomplish yet these devs have achieved all 3. I look forward to the many hours I will continue to spend in the world of Wildermyth and the stories of legend that will come from it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: One of my characters had a parasite in his body, his immune system manifested as a pig to explain the importance of eaten a balance diet. I instructed my character to negotiate with the parasite to agree to live in harmony, of which he was successful. My character's immune system represented by a pig was not amused by this agreement and transformed into a devil pig. I then had to fight the character's immune system and kill it. Now that character has a bond with said parasite in his body instead of an immune system and they both seem very happy with the arrangement. This was just a random character sidequest..I think I love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR After 30 hrs of play this game is worth the price! First, Wildermyth is a work of art, but don't let the storybook feel deter you.It is a real RPG that brings your characters to life and builds a story around them based on decisions you make for the direction of the story itself. Each adventure is divided by chapters. At the end of a "book" there's an epilogue of all the player character's whichis very rewarding in itself. The game allows you to bring back your  "Legacy Players" in follow on games too.I only wish is that equipment was interchangeable between players but the fact you can't brings a complexity of it's own in that it encourages you to "free" more lands to look for more items and purchase upgrades with the resources from the map.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: To call Wildermyth a turn-based tactical game would be to do it a disservice. Each play-through is like a pen-and-paper-RPG campaign where you create and evolve a party over time. Starting as young adults, your characters age (c. a decade between chapters), eventually having offspring that take up the adventurous call, retiring due to old age, or even heroically sacrificing themselves to save the group. One thing is certain, your characters will have changed greatly by stories end.Truly in great shape for a game in early access!What I would like to see added in the future:* more story arcs (campaigns) and mini quests to add to replay ability* more collections of enemies (currently 5 major groups of foes)* more varieties of player cosmetics, especially hair. The gents lack a decent selection of facial hair* more music, it's SO good !
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: So... awesome...!The way this is structured and the way it immerses you in the story is fantastic!Imagine all RPGs were like this, where your choices actually affect your character and the story alters them!Not like in most RPGs where the story is set in stone and doesn't change regardless of your character or what happened to them!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a really nice art style and the combat board with the cardboard cut-out figures makes it feel like your playing a board game with someone.  the main story lines in the campaign are engaging and really tug at your heartstrings while the randomly generated character stories make for a unique playthrough every time with tons of choice available.  The legacy system makes sure you can keep your favorite characters again and even have them powered up for future campaigns.  I absolutely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Not your run of the mill turn-based tactical rpg, Wildermyth offers stories you can care about and characters you end up attached to. Never before have I recognized such artificial decision pressure in a way that has made me think "I can't wait to make the other choice next time." _childDocuments_.review: The story aspect keeps this fresh, but the battling becomes a slog.  I enjoyed playing through several generations to see how characters developed and to be able to use them in future/later adventures.  For me though, the battles became too repetitive.  I also was not a big fan of the amount of time required to traverse the map.  There are a number of things to do on the map, but actually doing them requires so much time, and uses some of your characters, so I rarely would craft new weapons or prepare defenses or recruit new characters since the enemy gets stronger faster than you can prepare, so it's better to just run into battle with as many people as you can.  This leads to battle, battle, battle, battle, end of scenario and peacetime, back to battle battle battle battle.Eventually you will have 8 or 10 characters and be able to either: Battle and Prepare, or Battle on Two fronts.  Guess what?  Battle on two fronts still makes more sense, so no time for preparing defenses etc..Maybe after another 10 hours I would have enough characters to Push the enemy back, Intercept incursions, and Prepare defenses.  Don't know.  Still a good game and worth a good 20-30 hours of entertainment.  Recommended.

_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun game. The art style is simple but charming, I especially love the backgrounds. The music is good too, I can listen to it for hours, and not get tired of it. The turn-based combat is also very fun. It's simple enough to understand from the first fight, but can be made more complex as you develop strategies around your characters and their abilities that develop over time.I sometimes wish that time would progress slower at the campaign level, or that my characters would have children/recruit more often. It's sad when a character you get attached to is going to retire at the end of the chapter.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is nearly universally acclaimed for good reason. It's a great character generator that weaves together a bunch of randomized story bits that mold to your party's specifics and your choices and result in lasting effects upon each of your characters. As with any work of interactive fiction, you can't overdo it within a short period of time without hitting repetitive content, but it's a great way to spend a reasonably contained amount of time now and then. There's a huge variety of weapons, equipment, skills, pets, and personal modifications that when combined with a healthy amount of aesthetic variation leads to no two characters ever really looking the same. It's a great system that allows you to bond with your characters and get invested in their progression and in their relationships with one another. The fact that they age with time, have children, and progress to a legendary status at the end of a campaign that allows them to appear in future playthroughs is all exceptionally well done. The tactical system and combat get a little repetitive if you play too long at a stretch, but this is a great gaming experience that you should definitely try if it sounds at all interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent framework that just needs more content now. More of everything really, Thankfully at this stage of its early access we can likely expect exactly that.What it does right is make you feel like you're playing a game of Dungeons and Dragons, and the DM is naturally changing up the story depending on your previous interactions. The way your characters get tagged by various story events and how those then generate chances to better your character is reminiscent of Sunless Sea/Sky and I mean that as praise. The story quality isn't quite there but then those games were highly scripted, and this is all generated from a pool of events. Story vignettes that I hope will interact more with each other later once the pool from which they are drawn grows larger.The style is quite basic out of necessity but the variety already in afflictions, weapons, armour, and clothing means it needs to be to keep up with the almost puppet-show like cut scenes. The written story campaigns are by far the better experience, but the more random 3 and 5 season campaign options are perfectly decent. The quantity and depth of the vignettes shipped with 1.0 will ultimately decide whether this ends up a great game of one of the best. It really did almost capture the feeling of D&D, which hasn't happened for me since Baldurs Gate twenty years ago.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I have just finished the first campaign (3 chapters).   It is a very good game given it is still in early access.  I did not encounter any crash (10 hours of playtime according to Steam) although one of the tool tips looks like the programming commands are still showing.  Very stable.  It is a procedural generated story that is very personal to each of your heroes and the story, while has an overall arc, grows organically based on your choice and decisions.  It is *your* story based on your "head canon" of how these heroes played out.  I believe it has replayability although I have not gone through the second round.  Someone says it has a strong tabletop RPG feel and I completely agree.  It was what sold me and it delivers.  So if you want a light, solo TTRPG experience, this is the game!  I bought it at the summer sale for less than US$10 and I spent only 10 hours so far.  So a buck an hour (probably less if I play more) is a very good entertainment value!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is almost everything I enjoy in a game. Its got character customization, its got class systems, its got grid based combat, and it has relationship mechanics. Its all there, so of course it was a buy for me. And then I learned the true gold mine the game has: its characters. You wouldn't think that in a game where you create all the people you play with would do well in the character department, but it does. It somehow manages to make each character their own person, despite the fact there are so many different ways to craft a character's personality. So many times I've watched a scene unfold and go "Yup, that's exactly what X would do". Its incredible how much life each little person has. Even in the runs where I don't play one of the campaigns, I end up falling in love with the people I make, ESPECIALLY the joke characters. I don't know how they've managed it, but this game is perfect at crafting both a beautiful story and a beautiful cast. If you're the type that gets attached to characters like I do, this is the game for you. I cannot wait to see what other campaign ideas they come out with, and I cannot wait to create the stars of said story
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't look like much visually, or at least the style isn't my thing personally (though the monster designs are growing on me fast).  But wow the narratives it builds are great and I know I'm just scratching the surface at 6 hours in.  I think this is the fastest I've felt like recommending a game, which is made easier since the game is actually pretty easy to start playing mechanically.Definitely get it if you are an RPG fan (tabletop or video game)!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Easy to become invested in your starting characters and their legacy.Wide range of difficulties and separate options for overworld and battle difficulties, very approachable for all skill levels.Five properly structured narratives which range from good to great and several options for 'random' campaigns. 'All the Bones of Summer' and 'Monarchs Under the Mountain' are especially good, offering some memorable impacting choices that change your character's paths.'Just one more turn..' levels of addicting.Campaigns can last upwards of 70 years. Your characters can retire. They are replaced by their offspring or brand new recruits, who are significantly weaker and undergeared. This can make the end game especially difficult, given that enemies get a lot stronger with time. While this helps in making those 'replacements' feel like legends when they succeed, it can also just be frustrating, especially since their offspring are randomly assigned a class you don't need or want.Minor text bugs can make some events appear to be nonsense.Only 3 classes and little depth between them. After your 2nd or 3rd campaign you've seen every skill there is to see and a lot of them just aren't very good or fun to use.A good amount of information for features just isn't properly explained, requiring you to seek that information outside of the game. Don't let the cons give the wrong impression. What is great about this game outweighs the negatives. Overall, this was worth it just for the 5 structured stories alone. I haven't even touched the random campaigns. I've now got a wide cast of memorable characters from each campaign, including one who saw all 5 thanks to the legend system allowing you to pull one character from a campaign into the next. He is a storm-touched werewolf by the name of Bo Legthane Stormhowl. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth has this wonderful almost organic feeling to the adventures your characters go on. Seeing the main heroes from a previous campaign in a new one feels like bringing back old favorites and reconnecting with old friends and favorite stories. I cannot recommend it highly enough.
