_childDocuments_.review: Oh my god.I finally finished the first tutorial chapter and that was by far the most fun I had in playing an RPG. The procedural events, the random skills when you level ups, choices that DO matters in the story, what else can I say about this game.The papercraft comic and combat grew on me and I grown so attached to my band of heroes that when one of them actually died in a blaze of glory, it actually made me tear up.Brilliant game for anyone that loves RPGs, especially the tabletop era. A lot of reading but this is a true character-driven, story driven, procedurally generated RPG and I can't wait to start another story,Not to mention the modding scene for this game is thriving as well as multiplayer that allows up to 5 players.What else are you waiting for? This a love letter to all RPG fans out there, are you going to read it?
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I've only just started playing this game but I've been through the first two campaigns, and after being hit a bit emotionally on the second with real attachment to my characters, I felt compelled to add my voice to the heaps of good reviews out there. This is a fantastic game, with elements of all of the things I really enjoy about RPG, tabletop gaming, open world, and fantasy.  I use open world a bit freely here, but it still scratches an itch for me in that I don't typically enjoy linear games that force you down a direct path quite as much. Others have pretty much covered all the stuff that's good about it. I'm a really picky gamer and I'll circle a game for a while before pulling the trigger, making sure it'll be worth my while to learn the game and become good enough to enjoy it. So if you're fussy like me, and you don't like to have a huge learning curve, you will probably enjoy this if all the other boxes are ticked for you. The only thing I would change is perhaps the music because it does get a bit repetitive on longer playing sessions especially.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Procedural story-telling done right, personality traits/character hooks/relationships affect dialogue and event types. Decent weapon variety.Thematic transformations, collecting elemental enhancements, artifacts, mix-and-match abilities and cross-campaign progressions provide ridiculous number of build options and give the game a Pokemon "Catch 'Em All" appeal.Writing is great and really sets the mood despite the lack of voice-acting. 5 different campaigns with original and engaging storylines. No boring elves/dwarves/orcs as enemies, you get to fight lovecraftian horrors, steampunk abominations, corrupted cultists, ethereal bugs and lizard men instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Great experience, overall. The way the stories are being told by fusing predefined beats with randomly chosen events is fantastic, and it's quite easy to become invested in the characters involved. The Thrixl campaign was particularly enjoyable.Strong combat helps, with a great magic system easily being the highlight, although it's somewhat marred by the relative lack of content: you only need a playthrough or two to see pretty much all the equipment (weapons' elemental varieties take a while to unlock, sure, but there are only four elemental effects in total, and finding artifacts isn't exactly reliable, so they matter little), as well as most of the class abilities and all the basic enemies. I also think it's strange that there's no way to manually choose where your characters spawn when you defend against incursions (as in, when already present within the location that's about to be attacked), but in the end it's a minor annoyance at worst.Some shortcomings aside, Wildermyth is a fantastic ride. Not sure if I'll be giving randomly generated campaigns a go, but I'm perfectly content with what I got out of the game as is.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: For an early access game, Wildermyth is in a very good stage of development. Not many bugs, and most, if not all, of the gameplay features function perfectly. At this point, this game is in early-access because the devs are getting rid of the few remaining bugs and are also asking for feedback from the community to further round out the game by either adding in more gameplay and/or narrative features.This game is not necessarily easy, as there are 4 different factions of enemies with many unique unit types that mix-and-match different abilities. The enemy variety is therefore far from boring. As your characters level up, you can select which one of three randomly generated abilities they get, ensuring ability variety among even characters of the same class. The three randomly generated abilities are taken from a larger pool of class-related abilities, some of which overlap with other classes.In Wildermyth, the general gameplay loop is the following: Start with 3 randomly generated characters with randomly generated backstories and personalities, and embark on an epic quest that may or may not involve picking up more characters to join your party. Movement on the campaign map is tile-based, in that you move your heroes to a region, scout it out, and do battle or a narrative event. Characters often have narrative events with each other, especially after battles in which they fought enemies while next to each other, and the pre-generated dialogue is based off the personality traits they rolled. The more interactions characters have, the higher their chances of landing a critical hit when two or more characters are adjacent to each other, and also the more narrative events they may have. Characters that fall in love with NPCs off-screen can give birth to children who can join your party after some time. The story-telling is delivered through simple but effective comic strips.With a game like this, the big allure is the narrative. I can tell you that the writers put a lot of time into this and that there is currently a wide enough variety of personality traits that can lead to a good variety of narrative events and dialogue. Of course, there will come a point in which some of the narrative events begin to repeat themselves. Now here's the best part: You can make your own comic strips (therefore your own narrative events), your own dialogue, and your own campaigns. You can also access the custom comic strips, dialogue, and campaigns of other players through the Steam Workshop. In other words, Wildermyth technically has an infinite amount of variation.Like DnD, Wildermyth introduces players to stories of unlimited variety because the devs open up all the narrative elements to the modding community (in addition to the gameplay elements like weapons and equipment). I encourage people to purchase this game to help build this world, this Yondering Land.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't a fan of the story for this game.  Every story arc, no matter what choice you made, always ended up being bland inspirational garbage.  If you're the type who has "Live Laugh Love" written on your wall you might like it.The combat was the only redeeming part of the game, but by itself it's not enough to make a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: A procedurally generated tactics rpg with some roguelike elements.Like tactics rpgs? This isn't the deepest tactical rpg but it is fleshed out enough to leave many builds unexplored by the end of 2 longish campaigns. 3 initial job paths branches out through the use of cards you draw upon level up.  Unique events in any hero's life can further detail those characters personality or past, and expand their roles beyond the base rogue/ranger, warrior, mage classes.Procedurally generated characters manage to take on their own personality through the personality system and random life events that happen to them during their campaign.  Choices you make will permanently affect characters, those characters can then be found in future play long after you've completed their campaign.  There's nothing like meeting one of the heroes you shaped from your first play through midway through a new campaign and adding them to the party, expanding on their story even further.Each campaign can take a few hours or more easily, and the replayability with multiple constructed campaigns and the option of more vanilla randomized short and long campaigns leaves the door open to many play throughs and eventually dozens of legendary heroes in your stable.This game does an extraordinary job of fleshing out the quite literally cardboard cutout looking characters into interestingly deep protagonists. World building and cheeky cardboard cutout art style give a contradictory feeling of these 2d characters with hidden depths of personality and backstory, revealed in or experienced through campaigns, that I will keep coming back to.Do you have 2 hours and want to start a new somewhat casual RPG experience? You'll be thrilled with this game... and find yourself wanting to make more time and roll more characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: The game has lots of replayability and the situations you can put your characters with endless potential into are absolutely hilarious. One of my characters turned into a man/crow hybrid and another lost his limbs but got  the power to shoot fire from his arms that are on fire.The $25 is worth it, 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite aspects of Wildermyth is that you can customize the appearance/names of all your heroes. Neither appearance nor romantic interest has to be tied to a character's gender which is really cool! The open customization makes for some pretty funny games (I played one as the Scooby Doo gang) in which you get invested in the stories and the aging of your characters. There's no need to feel sad at the end of the game; you can recruit old heroes (regardless of whether they died or retired) in future games and continue to build on their abilities. I love the strategy elements to this game. There are many times in which the enemies feel overwhelming, but the challenge of figuring the best way to stack/set up attacks and beat the odds is thrilling. There are plenty of story campaigns to play and I like that you can have the game randomly generate regular/legacy character campaigns. Many of the choices you make will affect the campaign, whether it be just for the next round or for the entirety of the game. Definitely my favorite game of 2021 and will be on my overall favorites list for a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I have never had a game where I fell in love with characters so much - their weird generated names (my Mythwalker hero Onus Ardene), their weird traits (poetical greedwagon - yes please!), pets (I love me a fire chicken), transformations that can give you a wolf's head and/or a skeletal hand PLUS you get to age and not be the eternally young hero but a old lady with a skeleton hand and fire chicken who can kick the asses of some mindworm bugs that are trying to take over your fantasy, medieval-esque world.I've only played singleplayer because gaming is my escape from other people but it's been a lot of fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: FF Tactics meets Xcom, Divinity OS 2 and Tabletop goodness :)Wonderful rpg, probably the Game Of The Year for me so far (Up there with Valheim, Chivalry 2, RE: Village and Going Medieval). It has many elements that are more gamey and also elements that are more tabletop style. It is a really wonderful mix, on top of that it is playable in coop with a friend and it is a blast!There is also mod tools that the community has already been going hard on and creating some great stuff. The gameplay is fantastic, the level up system is great to (makes things alot less grindy than many other rpgs).Coop reminds me of Divinity OS 2, The combat reminds me of Final Fantasy Tactics/Xcom, Many elements that remind me tabletop games and it has many ideas of its own to.Probably my favorite coop rpgs since Divinity OS 2, but also fun solo to. This game came out of nowhere for me and it has been a real blast playing it. Despite many AAA big budget games out there, this game has managed to make a better job, roleplaying videogame fans and tabletop fans, JUMP ON THIS GAME! :)
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I made a bad call, and my warrior got knocked out of battle in the first game. I let him retreat, only for him to return with a permanent hook with where his arm used to be. The snarky rivalry banter between my hunter and my intellectual was entertaining, and I will forever be grateful that I made them rivals. I also turned my warrior blue, and my intellectual almost lost an arm in a dungeon. I finished the first campaign without too much trouble and immediately started the second one. The unexpected nature of my choices made the game very entertaining, and the battle was fun as you work on trying to keep everyone alive. I had a blast playing this game, and I really appreciated the depth of RPG elements that felt like I was playing with a DM. The music was fitting to the game. The graphics look simple but were used very well. There's a lot of replayability. Would highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a single-player game while you wait for AAA games to come out, this is the one! If you don't like the battle animations, don't even bother. As in 3/24/21, I just finished 3 playthroughs (30.5hrs) and I gotta say, as an x-com fan, this game is a decent squad-based rpg which reminds me of battle brothers, banner saga and massive chalice (characters getting old), yet it surpasses them with their character development and the different stories each character may have/develop. The 'story-making' is unique and gives the game decent replayability. The legacy system creates the opportunity to bring back heroes from other playthroughs to new ones, etc. I didn't encounter any crashes nor glitches so far, which makes the game pretty polished for an early access game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game within the week it came out of early access, and man, what a fantastic way to spend a summer! It popped up in my Discovery Queue, and the well-made trailer convinced me to try it out. I played through all of the campaigns and loved seeing my characters undergo different changes, internal and external. Wildermyth is one of the best indie games I played from its gameplay, the art-style, and storytelling.The only things I wish we have access to are the ability to handpick the personality traits for each hero and the option to establish familial relationships (parent and child, siblings, etc.) from the start. While these additions aren't fundamental, it would be nice to customize characters in this way even further.Overall, very delightful game for those into narratives and strategy RPGs.9/26/23 Edit: Thank you Trekopep for letting me know that I can indeed change the personality traits before starting a campaign! I admit I'm kinda embarrassed that this is how I learned what the 3 arrows are used for, but better late than never.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely worth buy. I was initially holding off hard due to the theme, since I wanted a more serious and darker tone to the aesthetics, dialogue, and whatnot, but the sheer polish of the random quests, relationships, and how it legit confuses me if they are part of the scripted railroading of the campaign or just complete random developments is just absolutely awesome.PROS:- Random relationship developments that feel scripted. When I say this, I mean that they feel like they are not random at all.- Random events that also feel natural. Some characters may discover "Opportunities" that can either give items, perks, pets, or whatnot, and they are so integrated properly and happen naturally that it also feels scripted. Sometimes, the character they are travelling with also gets intertwined in the dialogue.- Great balance of map pressure and relaxation. You have an allowance of scouting areas, crafting stuff, waiting maybe a day or two for your captured tiles to produce enough resources for you to craft things, but the sense of urgency timed events give also makes things active and engaging.- Great difficulty balance. The first two difficulties do a great job of introducing the game's unique systems properly. A new player will properly learn the game and not get punished too much for making mistakes. I am not sure about the higher difficulties yet, but I am planning to play some campaigns with the them.- A great sleu of pre-made campaigns. Unlike some other game that copies Trials by Fire (The Hand of Merlin), this is cheaper, if not at the same price, but offers far more content and build variation, with very engaging mechanics happening seamlessly as you play. (Meanwhile The Hand of Merlin's 3-level campaign is padded by artificial difficulty, and it's so damn short even compared to the 3-chapter beginner campaign of this game)- Fun, unique classes. My favourite class so far is the Mystic, with so much flexibility of doing AoE, going pure melee, or doing single target attacks. I don't like mages, but this class is just so unique and flexible (you can possess clutter items and use powers depending on the properties of the clutter. e.g. rocks), that I was inclined to toy around with it alot.- Mutations. This can happen to weapons, or a character. This may require you to sacrifice some body part depending on the mutation, and this happens via random events that happen to said character. This though offers a new set of "toys" you can utilize to make battles more interesting! They can even be upgraded depending on if you want the mutation to progress.BAD:- Wish there was more dark and serious tone to random dialogue, but the current format of things fits the game's theme I suppose.- Some very minor, random typos. This is probably to the randomization of dialogue in the game.- Lack of helmets and equipment. There's 3 levels of weapons, and 2 levels of armour, each with 2 subtypes, and can "mutate" depending on RNG. In the first campaign, I only had the opportunity to mutate 2 pieces of items out of my 6 characters, and I wish there was a lot more, plus helmets just to make gearing and crafting much more interesting.TL;DR: The game has very unique mechanics in terms of class abilities, and systems, and it's a game of its own class. If the theme does not turn you off, BUY IT, or even if it does, try it, and I can almost guarantee you'll love it. With the amount of content it currently has, and the still consistent updates, I would urge you to buy the game full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game around noon.........it's 9pm now and I just remembered I exist outside this game, it's amazing.If you like any kind of RPGs or tabletops try this game. The semi-random procedural generation makes this game feel infinitely replayable.This may be my new favorite game, gonna go set up alarms on my phone to remind me to eat and sleep before going back in.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly avoided this game for a while because I didn't like the art style, but I'm glad I gave in when it went on sale. "Charming" is a really succinct word to describe this game. You campaign with your customized heroes, and even though a lot of the gameplay elements are technically repetitive, they feel fresh in the context of the varied storylines and characters that come through. The writers definitely deserve a special mention here. The banter in the interactions makes the characters feel very alive. This is a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. As a big fan of X-Com and a few other turn based games, I found this game to be fun and provide a bit of strategy. I really enjoy that the characters age and retire. I also like that they can pass a bit of knowledge (experience for levels) to the younger characters, especially when their retirement is making me scramble to fill the gap.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting little game. It has a beautiful art style, simple but rewarding gameplay that reminds me a bit of X-com, and some very funny and surprising moments as a result of the randomly generated stories.Speaking of, it does a great job of keeping track of what happened and trying to link together various stories into a coherent whole. Things that happened in the past will be referenced hours down the line, and the game will remember the injuries or transformations your characters went through.The game though can be quite easy. I might need to increase the difficulty, but outside of the first few missions, it seems like the difficulty curve lags behind your characters' increase in power. I found myself one-shotting certain mini-bosses later on and not having to think that much about my strategy. I'm playing on Normal, so it is probably the reason why.The last thing to mention is the esthetic, which are really nice, from the character and location design to all of the little comic book strips you get to see.Overall, I really recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: The storytelling and character interactions is some of the best writing I have ever seen in a game. I am a voracious fantasy reader and this world was well developed, the dialogue is actually funny, the language used is just absolutely beautiful. I love how the relationships build and grow over a campaign, characters fall in love, they have rivalries, we can even recruit their kids as new party members as ours age and eventually retire. I play a lot of rogue-likes so I'm used to not getting attached to anything I play, but damn it if I don't get fully emotionally attached to my little group.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really looking forward to seeing how the mod scene for this game develops. It's early, but fantastic and engrossing. I've played through the initial 3 chapters and a 5 chapter game. I'm hoping for more development of characters from game to game so that you can have long winding character based stories as well as each campaign's arc.Really a very different style of game. Really enjoy it.Con: Having a bunch of characters retire early. I'd love to see it where you can choose when to retire a character, but as they get older, they get worse or gain additional maladies. Or, alternatively, that you're able to offload their gear some.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore any bad reviews of this game! I have only played the first chapter so far but I was hooked the entire time. The game feels like playing dungeons and dragons with the different storylines and characters along the way. My main warrior got turned into this bird like creature randomly as I was venturing. This game will always keep you on your toes knowing that the more time that passes the more difficult enemys get. The only thing I wish I could get more of in this game is more classes like a rouge/assassin who duel wields.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Are the graphics a bit corny? Sure, your characters are little 2-D figures that bounce around the screen. But the storylines? The stories are fantastic! The choices that you get to make for your characters are fun and you can play the same campaign multiple times that still come across new stuff. Its amazing!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first play through and I really enjoyed the game. I would say based on the time I've clocked in so far (7 hours) and the quality of the game, I could recommend it already. But I know this game is also supposed to have a lot of replayability and I look forward to jumping back in. Game has a really nice art-style and I love seeing the characters age and change. The music is nice. The combat system is pretty decent and is one of the better turn-based tactical combat games I've played.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I came back to play this the other night and BAM, all of a sudden my wife came in and and asked if we could go to bed already because it was already 1 and we had to work in the morning. In my cynical old age, very few games engross me like this. My stoic warrior touched a blue pillar and became a flighty, but deadly, blue woman of death. The obvious sexual tension between my charismatic wizard and boring vanilla hunter dudes was destroyed when the wizard became facially scarred and a grim loner. And my hunter, so vanilla and boring who kept trying to hide his attraction to the wizard by going super hetero on the warrior finally got a personality at the end of the first chapter by throwing himself into research and discovering the apparent plans of the gorgons.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool game. A lot more than meets the eye at first glance. The stories that unfold are adorable, and the character growth during each playthrough is an absolute blast to witness. You never know what's around the corner, and driving it all is an actually pretty awesome "light weight" x-com style game play loop.So far in my 3 hours of gameplay the battles have been on the easier side, but I suspect they will get harder in later campaigns.Two thumbs up!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is a game which managed to captivate me from the very first minutes after launching the game. It's immersive as hell, and each experience is unique, so the replayability is HUGE.First of all, the characters, except for the starter 3, are completely randomized, with their own personalities, back stories, looks, tastes, and so on. It is very fun and interesting to see your already existing characters interacting and forming relationships with the newest additions to the party.Randomness is my favorite aspect of this game. Characters can form relationships as time goes by, have children, get married, form rivalries, and so on. Another thing that plays a big part in the game is events, which are random comic book panel-style cut scenes where the characters interact, and where you can make choices that drastically and permanently influence the rest of the story and the future of your characters. Moreover, characters from previous campaigns, even dead ones, can make cameos or play important roles in future campaigns. Nobody is ever forgotten, as each character is added to your legacy.The artstyle is charming, and I can't really imagine a better one for this type of game. It's a very well designed game, HOWEVER, there are some things that can be a bit annoying or immersion breaking at times for some people:- Some events can be repetitive. Not drastically, though. I think only once or twice I got the same event in two different campaigns. They are planning to add more events in the future though, and you can also do that yourself with modding.- The combat is... meh. While I like how some events or getting injured can influence the combat style of your characters, it's quite slow and repetitive. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I don't think the game has a 2x speed option for combat YET. And that can be a problem when there's like 20 characters on the board, and you have to wait for each one to finish their turn.- Reading is an important aspect of this game, so if you're not into that, it's not really the game for you. The game is only in 1.0, and it's already AMAZING, at least for me. I haven't even finished the 2nd campaign yet, and I am already in love. It's also highly moddable, so there's plenty more content available. I can't wait to see what this game will become in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game makes a promise, and on that promise, it delivers.Grid based strategic combat, that is often challenging and requires a mix of good planning and a bit of luck, mixed with randomized, emergent story telling. This has been said 100 times already, but this is as close to a video game representation of playing in a DnD world as I've ever seen. Also, the choices this game makes regarding skills and magic use are unique and fun to customize and play with.In short, play this game. It is fun, and challenging, and rewarding.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that knows when to make your characters into heroes, and let them be people. It knows to let them feel a range of human emotion, not just different flavors of "determined to win." When to let you guide their path, and when for them to act as themselves. It knows to make magic feel like something that is other and unknowable, yet still usable. It knows the difference between rivalry and hostility. It knows when and how to inflict a change that will really make a character.I honestly can't recommend this enough. It's got tactics just complex enough to stay interesting without becoming cumbersome, a beautiful atmosphere that sells mystery (Seriously, it's like the distilled essence of a foggy mountain forest), so many choices, and characters that are about as cohesive as randomly generated characters can get.Chances are, in each campaign, you'll have a favorite, and that favorite will come with stories to tell. And then, when some new heroes are fighiting a new dire fight, those favorites will earn themselves a few more stories.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Glorious.Its a bit like fantasy X-Com, but the combat is simpler, there  is not much economy. You scout the world map, which is divided into parcels. Each parcel triggers a fight, after some fights, the enemies get tougher, but so do you. Each owned parcel grants ressources at the end of a chapter. These resources are spent on better gear. Gear can also be aquired after clearing a parcel and securing it. Enemies can take territory back and will try at unfixed intervals. Doesnt sound like much. But, each component is polished to near perfection. Especially the fact that heroes return in your legacy is fantastic. (Meangin, they can be recruited in later campaigns)If you have ANY love for tactic-rpgs with story that can change drastically, then this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Token, after turning into a werewolf, sunk his teeth into the huge rain causing monstrosity, dealing the final blow to the beast that was throwing other beasts at the Archers whom had joined his party. Overwhelming Positive reviews are where this game is and deserves. I rarely buy games at full price but did so with this game and I"m fully satisfied having found a gem that will provide many hours more of excellent storytelling wonder and excitement.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Okay here it goes. This game is really good. I thought it was going to be bunk, ugh Paper characters? Though I tend to kinda drop that outlook with playing it. Its so immersive engaging and very, very random. So many choices makes me want to start over all again. Tons of campaigns I have yet to unlock but the joy that I can unlock them. I would also like to say that its supported by steam workshop which is great edition. Very dnd like and the magic system is fun. Try it out you will love it and I think there is more to come with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Played through the first chapter and I must say I'm very impressed thus far.Visually the game has a beautiful hand drawn aesthetic. It's really captivating.Combat in the game has a simple turn based system in play similar to other games of its kind. Using a form of action points to move, attack, or use other items/abilities. You're able to flank enemies and defensive bolster allies when adjacent to them. It also has a unique magic system where instead of having your typical spells, you 'link' to environmental objects on the map which allow you do use spell like abilities. (Using a large boulder to hurl stone shards at enemies, or a bush to use its branches to entangle a foe).After each battle your characters gain experience and once they level you're offered a choice of upgrades to enhance that character. Likewise you might find new items or equipment or you're able to craft new items at a town you've rescued. The real selling point is the story, and how things that happen within the game and the choices you make actually have a real time effects on everything (story, characters, and combat). Random story beats might pop up to give you a chance to make a decision on how a character would react or what they'd do in a situation. -TL,DR-There's so much to this game that I can't put it all into words. I would just say that if you enjoy story, character customization, turn based tactical battles, and fantasy settings... this game is worth diving into.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a remarkably charming game that despite relatively simple gameplay and dialgoues manages to make you fall in love with your randomly generated gang of adventurers. Seeing them grow. age, and eventually retire or die throughout a campaign made me feel legitimately attached to all of them. I would say that even in its current early access game this game is incredibly fun and will be enjoyed by those who liked games both like final fantasy tactics and FTL.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I made my family my crew of characters.I died protecting my wife.She died later, despite being a ridiculously over-levelled mage.My heart stuck in my throat.I'm now taking a new generation of people I don't know into this world of chaos. They'll die too, in the end, in one way or the other, and that also will break my heart.I've only been playing this game for a few hours but it's absolutely amazing.In all seriousness; it's a sort of RPG/adventure/turn-based strategy hybrid where the point is that you know your characters are either going to die in battle or of old age. But their friends and children will continue the fight! The graphics are primitive - actually (and probably deliberately) reminiscent of table-top games - but the writing is witty, fun and engaging, and makes up about half of the game. I struggle these days to get really into games, which is probably a symptom of age and my own fault, but this is... well, play it. Write your own story into stone. Make your own history. It's beautiful. If you're okay with a lot of text and graphics reminiscent of a well-drawn comic book then I cannot recommend it highly enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Tactical roguelike games have existed for a long time, and Wildermyth doesn't stand out as one. It's got good combat, makes it easy to figure out what the enemies could do, and gives you good options, both before combat and during combat, to deal with them. Each different weapon has slightly different strengths and weaknesses; each class gets two choices for armor as well as a variety of special abilities they can learn as they gain experience; and there's a lot of synergies to be discovered or forced.The magic system does set it apart a little. Instead of giving characters spells, your characters instead "interfuse" with terrain elements, which have things they can do: plants can grab enemies and drag them around; lights blind; wood objects splinter; fires burn; and so on - but all of it damages the environment. Sometimes, that's a good thing, as you turn your enemy's cover against them - but sometimes you need to be careful, choosing between using some spell or keeping the terrain around as cover.But what really makes Wildermyth stand out is the story system. Relationships between characters grow organically, which also feeds into combat (lovers take revenge on enemies that hurt their lover; rivals top each other with stunts; and friends stand together, protecting each other); but also drives the story forward. Events in the game grow over time: a chance encounter might result in a character's slow transformation into any number of forms; gaining unique equipment or pets; or  just shaping the story, chapter after chapter. You watch as your characters age and mature - often guiding future generations: one of my favorite things is to finish a given campaign with the children and grandchildren of my first adventurers, finishing what their parents and grandparents started.Tactical roguelike game have existed for a long time; but never before have they come with a storytelling system that lived up to everything else they've done well.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a special time, my first review on Steam.  I'll use it for what I believe is a special game.  This... may be a long one.    Read more if you want to know why.Wildermyth is, beyond an amazing pun, a game that shows great potential.  It reminds me of the plucky hero who has been chosen by destiny to save the world - but still has to contend with tripping over his feet when he attempts to swing a sword.  Eventually though, you know that young one will grow up to be the legendary hero.  I usually avoid Early Access because of one too many bad experiences, but this was recommended to me at such a high level, I needed to see for myself, and I believe it is worth your time too.  Also, I believe it will  only get better (and it has, since I bought it, steadily).The young, legendary hero is probably a fitting comparison - since Wildermyth is all about stories of heroes from humble beginnings.  So I will talk about the 'story' first.  I had a great deal of enjoyment early on just randomly generating heroes, and throwing them at adventure, letting chips fall where they may.  The variance in events and character dialog based on character personality traits is very impressive.  Eventually you will definitely see repeating events in multiple playthroughs, but there is potential there for many more to be added.  Even more will be added by the community in the long term, so I am not worried about this in the least.  Campaigns can be plot driven, scripted stories, or random campaigns against marauding monsters.  There are multiple races of opponents to contend with, and all of them bring their own challenges to the table.  Both have their benefits, but the plot-driven campaigns written by the developers showcase how deep the story can actually go.  They have included some truly harrowing events and character choices which I will not spoil here.  In the case of graphics and sound, this game is adequate to above average.  If you grew up, looking at a tabletop gaming board, and moving minis around a grid, you will be right at home.  Do not expect much more than that.  Characters stretch and warp to show movement and action, but that is about the extent of their animation.  That would be seen as a negative - but they also use a 'paper doll' style... which shows a character's full equipment on them, even down to rings on their fingers.  It's always impressive to see a fully decked-out adventurer at the end of the campaign - covered in magic items.  A special nod in graphics needs to be given to the story events, which are told in an amazing comic-book style fashion which needs to be seen to be believed.  It may improve even further in the full release, but I was quite pleased with it here.  The sound design is above average, up to good.  There's some standout sounds, especially in the ambient category, which is different for each enemy type.  Though one of my most disliked sounds is also in that type, but that's personal preference.  There's some very excellent musical pieces in the game, which I hope are expanded upon in the full game.In regards to gameplay, it is a relatively simple, turn-based affair.  There are rules in place that are similar to what someone would know, coming from D&D or another tabletop game.  Even with no experience though, the combat is easy enough to pick up on.  There's also an overworld map for the macro aspect of gameplay, which is a balancing act of managing time vs your resources.  Difficulty levels of all of these are able to be adjusted to suit your preferences.  There are definitely gameplay balance issues with some enemies/powers/weapon enchants - but the developer has been addressing these even in the brief time I've been playing the game.  Characters gain permanent damage if they are severely injured in battle, and some events can completely change what a character is capable of, granting them a theme.  They may become infused with an elemental, or become a wolf-person.  Some unfortunate might end up turned into a frog!Characters grow old, retire, and can permanently die.  This is just the way of things.  They can also fall in love, form friendships and rivalries, and have children.  This is all done pretty seamlessly - but it has effects on the tactical gameplay, as well as the story events in the game.  As an aside - I need to shout out the Legacy system in this game.  Since the game takes place in a Fantasy Multiverse of sorts, true heroes never die, or fade away over time.  They can become part of your Legacy - sort of a collection of folk tales - the Paul Bunyans of your fantasy world.  You can bring them back into your 'new stories', other campaigns and progress them further from there.  They may not keep their gear, but they do keep their abilities and themes they have gained.  Eventually, your Legacy roster of heroes will be a list like the cast of certain superhero teamup movies.  'Getting the band back together' in a campaign is an exhilarating moment once you have a decent sized pool of heroes.  So there you have it.  My thoughts after playing this game for quite a long time, considering the content available.  I decided to write this review after acquiring every elemental enchantment, figuring that it was definitely time.  This game also deserves a shoutout for the lack of bugs, despite being an early access title.  With how the developers seem to be listening to the community, I expect my few gripes will be dealt with before full release.  I hope you all choose to support the developer, and enjoy your time in the Yondering Lands as much as I did.  + Story and customization  + Strategic combat feels right to a tabletop player  + Legacy system  + Permanent character growth/changes  + Paper doll inventory system  + Overworld management strikes a good balance  + Music  + Comic panel 'cutscenes'  + Incredibly few bugs  - Some sound design misses the mark  - Paper doll animation  - Could use more random story events  - Some balancing issues

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really nice take on the old turn-based RPG, but with a range of different campaigns of offer, serving as the basis for procedurally generated stories. The character each have their own quirky traits and relationships, and it's nice watching your party grow old with characters retiring and new ones coming in as a story progress. It's not your typical high fantasy CRPG fare, with detailed lore, epic stories, tonnes of different classes and complex game mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most remarkable games I've ever played. When you hear the pitch, "Procedurally-generated storytelling," you're like, "Okay, sure, we'll see." But like. Wildermyth pulls it off, and pulls it off *well*. The writing is excellent, and the procedural pieces fit together in ways that create something much more than the sum of their parts. Case in point: I'm playing through my third campaign right now, and two of my characters have fallen into a rivalry. So they're constantly one-upping each other and snarking at each other, which is not unusual; rivalries happen frequently enough. But, for whatever reason, the game keeps centering these two and their dynamic in a way that I haven't seen in previous campaigns. They keep on having events together, and these events keep deepening their relationship dynamic. And then a random opportunity presents itself: one of these two is sick with a seemingly incurable disease, but a pilgrim happens along with a potential remedy. They go off on an adventure together with this pilgrim. It's long, and heartfelt, and emotional, and culminates with the sick character sacrificing her chance at a cure in order to save someone else. Suddenly there's a new respect between these two characters, and it becomes clear that their rivalry was masking some romantic feelings.None of this was central to the plot. All of it has been the result of procedural encounters and my own choices. And, somehow, these two have become the emotional core of this story. It's really remarkable.Anyway, two thumbs up. If I had more thumbs, I'd stick them up, too. 16/10, would buy again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fantastic example of what can be accomplished with lower scale graphics and alot of creativity.  Wildermyth is a RP game presented in comic book styling with an AI-like adventure generation element giving a rogue-like experience.  Played out in various campaigns with different stories and which can even be creatable by players, the game is highly customizable and extremely varied.  No two playthroughs will be the same!  Get some friends or go solo, enjoy insane adventure and romance in in this story generation game!Combat is very flexible and played in a strategy 3d playing field with interesting abilities with powers that can be gained or discovered via random events and mini storylines that pop up during a campaign.  The best example of this is the Mystic class which is a mage that interacts with the environment around them to produce a large variety powerful magic effects depending on your build and what you interact with.  Torches can allow you to leash it's flames to move around the battlefield.  Cause a bookcase to shatter and explode to harm enemies.Forget the pros and cons!  It's a charming and hilarious game with good battle systems, alot of character customizability, is multiplayer and even supports Steam Workshop!Get this game!

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy tabletop RPGs, character building, and heroic fantasy adventures, you'll probably like Wildermyth. The graphics harken back to a simpler time of tabletop RPGs played with printed paper figures and theater-of-mind antics. It has quite a bit of content - In the 10 hours I've played, I've completed two campaigns, but each has replay value to some degree, and there's still more campaigns for me to explore!I love that I have the option to create new characters for each campaign OR to bring along my heroes from previous campaigns, building their stories and abilities through multiple adventures. The procedural events make for an interesting method of character-building and storytelling, and so far, I've felt like it's executed quite well.I do have one criticism, though: the writing can be... rough in places. The odd flow of writing and grammar mistakes make understanding the narrative difficult at times. I have to re-read text multiple times to try and understand what they're trying to say. If I had one suggestion for the game, I'd suggest they get an editor. Otherwise, I enjoy the humor and the vibrant descriptions!I give Wildermyth a solid 8.5/10 👍

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: Even in early access, this is a thoroughly charming game with fewer issues than some released AAA titles.  I got it on sale, but it was entirely worth the money.THE BASICS:Wildermyth is straightforward and streamlined tactical RPG with some light strategy elements on the overmap.  You create a trio of characters and then set out into the world to solve problems, mostly through tactical battles, but occasionally through choose-your-path cut-scenes. Actions on the overmap--moving between areas, scouting, building fortifications--all take a certain length of days.  The calendar speeds between significant events, so years can fly by pretty quickly.  Your characters age and eventually retire, but the most significant effect of passing time is that the enemies will grow stronger--gaining new sorts of monsters, stronger versions of monsters, or inconveniencing tactical effects--and periodically invade map areas.  As you explore the map, you gain Legacy Points which can be used to cancel some of that strengthening, as well as securing settlements, building new settlements, and recruiting new adventurers.  Mostly on the overmap you find and defeat monsters, and eventually explore your way to the main enemy base, where you fight a boss to end the chapter.The tactical battles are the bulk of the game, and though rather simple are satisfying, especially if you develop an affection for your ragtag group of heroes.  At lower difficulties the AI is genuinely stupid, and at higher levels makes some choices that are either such genius that I can't understand them or, well, still stupid.  But the scenarios themselves are usually enough of a challenge when areas are filled with hordes of high-damage high-HP monsters that splash poison whenever they die.  Each turn you can do two things, usually move and attack.  You can gain special abilities that shift that up a bit--letting you move twice and then attack on the enemy turn,  letting you attack twice on your own turn, letting you save an attack between turns--but mostly you'll do the same things a lot.  There are the usual effects like hiding and flanking, plus something called stunting which is a tweaked sort of critical hit.  Each of the three classes--soldier, hunter, mystic--has its own value, but the real stand out is mystics, who do something called "interfuse" with furniture in the room rather than casting spells directly.  This gives them extreme range (even around corners) and a spectacular array of offensive effects. (Why cast magic bolts when I can make the rubble that you're standing beside explode?)The real heart of the game is the story.  Each character has a personality of sorts derived from a ranking of a dozen characteristics.  If you experience the same cutscene with different characters, their dialogue will be different (although not necessarily their options).  As you advance through story chapters, you get updates on what characters did during the peaceful interim, updates that usually follow from either the character's backstory or choices that were made in the last chapter.  Each chapter has a story too usually, which build to the final boss fight at the end of the final chapter.  Some story choices grow across successive chapters, so that you can see long term results of choices.  Other choices are just flavor, not seeming to add anything mechanically, but work surprisingly well the first time you encounter them.  Also between chapters you can buy new equipment for your characters with resources you earn based upon how many settlements you control on the overmap.PROS:CONS:

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely rate or review games, but this one deserves it. The graphics may not be the best, but that's part of the charm. The real magic is in the stories and conversations between the characters. Each custom character from story to story changes and becomes more and more unique as their personality is shaped every chapter of every story. How they look, how they act, the decisions they make, how good they are at fighting... it all becomes altered ever so slightly with every story. Just because your favorite hero 'retires', doesn't mean (by any means) that they are out of the game. They live on as a legend, to come back in future stories, or to start off future stories as previously capable fighters! There are only 3 classes, but each one can be built completely different. -Warriors who are all about intercepting attackers, warriors who are all about defense for themselves and others, warriors that are more than capable archers, winged warriors who literally soar into battle... -Hunters that are assassins with 2 handed axes, archers who are my hardest damage dealers, alchemists who blind and poison groups of enemies, and (my favorite) a magical scout with a burning arm to create walls of fire between enemies and allies to give time to escape. -Mystics who wade into the fray, dealing AoE magic damage to things they come close to, magic werewolves who use nature to stealth and leap onto unsuspecting enemies, and pyromancers who just burn... well. Everything.

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game maybe a day after saying openly to the universe "I need a high fantasy X-Com."And oh my does Wildermyth deliver! EDIT: To compare this game to XCOM is to do both a disservice... but my point is; this is an absolutely, wonderfully made tactical turn based strategy with a basic "grand strategy" world map that ties individual scenarios together by providing a background world to adventure in. With a charming storybook, artistic flavor; over an otherwise grimmdark, world cataclysmic, choose your own adventure with infinite replay-ability.  This may be my new favorite game.If you like tactics/strategy or just great fantasy, YOU SHOULD BUY THIS GAME. If you happen across this game on sale, YOU SHOULD DEFINITELY BUY THIS GAME.I would buy ten more copies as gifts if i could get a bulk deal. j/k Pay full price and let these devs get sandwiches.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. I bought it because I was frustrated with BaldursGate releases. I thought it would be a quick fill-in, in the turn-based story generation game. _childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: It's a successfully executed, marvelously designed take on fantasy XCOM.In this lovely piece of art you control the fate of a company of heroes, one much like hundreds of thousands of nerds assemble them every week in their mother's basements. You defeat monsters, collect their stuff, and hunt the Big Bad.The loop is simple, but extremely up my alley. You direct your party to scout locations on the map, and subsequently exterminate dens of evil. Every time you do, there will be a story event (much like a yarn spun by your DM) told in the form of a short cartoon visual novel which culminate in a choice of actions. Then a battle takes place on a grid-based map, using a turn-based system that's roughly a fusion of XCOM and D&D. Once the battle is over, you collect loot, assign it to one of your heroes, possibly promote one of them to the next level, and move on to the next location on the map.A detailed character creation system ensures that no two heroes look the same, and that's before the various story events or injuries in battle physically transform them even further. There is even a personality system than helps guide their actions and ways of speaking during story events. It's the closest thing to playing a tabletop RPG with unique, diverse characters you can get sitting in your room without having to interact with anyone. Bliss!Truly eradicating evil, however, can take several lifetimes. From time to time, a chapter in the tale ends, and heroes grow old and may even retire, while younger recruits or even their own offspring take up the sword to continue the quest. Or they don't retire, and you get to field a party of warrior grandpas and grannies to make the final stand to save the world.The Early Access state of development is felt in the stability - from time to time I've seen crash bugs due to memory leaks and such that make me grateful there's a very robust autosaving system. Abilities and Weapon properties are still in flux; the latest patch reworked one of the three main classes. There are additional pre-written campaigns planned to complement the existing two, but the main attraction in my eyes are the fully procedurally generated "generic" campaigns (Three Chapters and Five Chapters) that give the game a ton of replayability already. What's more, every time you complete a campaign, the heroes that accompanied you on the journey become part of your "legacy" and can be recruited (youth regained) in future campaigns, and continuously developed to become ever more legendary asskickers. A system that's almost necessary, I would assume to succeed in H.P. Lovecraft, the game's highest difficulty rating. (So far I've stuck to G.R.R. Martin, which is plenty challenging!)I would go remiss if I didn't mention that all the story events in the game have the name of the author attached to them, and that I let out a bit of a fanboy squeak to see Ursula Vernon among them.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put only 33 hours into this game so far and I love it. It's creative and fun, and I love the artwork and stories. Pros - artwork and stories, as above.- Easy to take or leave in small bits of time or bigger blocks. I can play for ten minutes on my lunch break, or sit down on the weekend for a couple of hours.- Love the legacy aspect, and being able to revisit past heroes. Cons - events and random encounters seem slightly repetitive so far. I'm hoping they get a bit more diverse as more content is added.- Relationships between characters (both good and bad) could use some fleshing out as well as some continuity between the chapters. I enjoy the character development as much as the sword-and-board.Really looking forward to continued development. As far as playability, I have had no issues with crashes, bugs, or anything at all. It's been fine since the initial download.

However the main campaign plot is always written perfectly and so far each campaign has been very interesting.And that's where my only complaint with this game ends, the rest of it is truly amazing and I'm shocked I haven't discovered it sooner. The gameplay is addictive and the combat is somewhat simple, yet deep enough to hold your interest.Worth the $25 without a doubt, never been more satisfied with a purchase in almost a decade.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just fantastic. It has the vibe of the kind of D&D campaign you've always wanted to play. _childDocuments_.review: A procedurally-generated tactical RPG that is equal parts Fire Emblem and your Thursday-night DnD campaign.: Combat rarely drags and gets really exciting at the higher levels. The interfusion/scenery system in general is brilliant - it makes the entire battlefield worth engaging in, and the enemies will use it against you as well. Interfusing with a rock wall that an enemy is using for cover, then blowing up the wall to cause damage and remove the cover simultaneously is a great example of how tactical this system can get. Each character can specialize in one of three classes (Warrior, Hunter, Mystic) that grant specific abilities on level up, but all classes can use all weapons and off-hand items and it works extremely well. Since gear is so rare and offers such great effects, I found myself spending more time deciding which gear to assign to my characters than I spent deciding which abilities they should upgrade. The combat abilities all have great flavor and seem to be based on sub-classes of the base classes - for instance, the Hunter can acquire archery-themed skills (like a ranger-type class) or stealth-themed skills (like a rogue-type class). Additionally, abilities have no pre-requisites, so you can assemble whatever combinations you like. Combat is intertwined with the story on many levels - heroes that are maimed in battle carry lasting effects through the campaign and beyond, but story events and decisions made between combats can offer bonuses and strategic advantages in upcoming battles. Managing your heroes' agendas in the overworld actually feels like strategizing in a war effort instead of just directing your party to go to the next story event. Between major story events there will be long periods of peace - your characters will age, have families, and go on individual adventures. It's honestly REALLY cool to see my team of grizzled 70- and 80-year-old warriors that are all close to max level absolutely demolishing enemies, since fantasy parties are often portrayed only as young adults/adults during a specific campaign. The infestation/incursion system can get kind of annoying in the later chapters of long campaigns if you don't patrol frequently, but that's kind of the point so it's not really a negative. After completing a campaign (or dying gloriously in battle), characters can become part of your personal legacy (a sort of permanent stable for your favorite heroes). These heroes can then be recruited into new stories as younger versions of themselves (while keeping some advanced abilities). : The writing is full of heart and it's obvious that the creators share a deep love for lampshading fantasy/gaming tropes. The main enemy types are all interesting variants of classic fantasy creatures, and I've only played three campaigns so I haven't experienced half of the enemy types as main villains yet. There are a ton of credited authors for this game (and the author is even credited in each story within the campaigns), and the story beats vary in tone from contemplative and mystical to zany and slapstick. It's this kind of low-grade inconsistency of tone that makes it feel like playing a tabletop RPG with your friends - lots of tongue-in-cheek references but also a real desire to develop each other's characters. Like with any procedural story game, you're bound to get repeat events as you play, but many of the events have branching paths to explore on a later run. I also found myself not minding the repeat events/items/etc. as much because of the legacy system - since eventually my most-played characters will see most of the events anyways, I can focus more on the mechanical bonuses and skip through story beats that I'm familiar with.: I think the art style is really impressive considering how the portraits are generated - the facial expressions are well-designed and even with similar features I can distinguish my characters easily. The blended 2D/3D combat is gorgeous, and reinforces the tabletop elements even further. The comics that serve as story events and interludes are very well-drawn and serve as unique breaks from the procedurally-generated battle areas. The music is a little repetitive and grating, especially in some of the generic battle sequences, but it's a really hard job to do so much music for a procedurally-generated game like this so it's not a major issue. The SFX are good at conveying what's going on in the battle and distinguishing certain abilities/events (the stunt sound effect combined with a slow down visual is a dopamine machine) but they seem a little flat when paired with the really good scenery and character art.

_childDocuments_.review: Beware innocent review reader, this game will suck you in stories you craft, heroes you get attached to, worlds you will build and come to cherrish.Peril lurks in every encounter and victory is never assured.And the biggest peril being "oh, just one more turn" and then it's way past bed time...Now a bit more on the gameplay it's self:You lead a party of adventurers. Starting as ordinairy folk who rise up in the face of a threat (or is it destiny's calling?), recruiting partymembers, earning skills to level up in turn based combat, allowing you to specialize as the story unfolds.There are two game phases, the world map mannagement, where you decide what your party will do and the combat phase, when your party runs into enemies or side events, that can devellop into side quests. The combat is party-turn based and I enjoyed taking my time to think the fights, the targets I wanted to take down first, the risks I was ready to take...And when a story ends, you can "save" your heroes in your legacy and have them reappear in future stories.The game also has multiplayer but it is a feature I'm not keen about so I haven't explored it.The one regret that I have is that the side events only happen once and, after 58h of play (the time it took me to finish all the stories and a bit), I fell like I have seen most of them (though not explored all the possible issues).

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is a tactical RPG with a campaign mode, a turn-based combat mode, and story sequences, and features papercraft art. All elements we have seen before, but they come together to create a game that is absolutely wonderful. It truly captures the feel of a pen & paper roleplaying game, following your characters through a grand campaign that covers decades within the story. The characters, whether randomly generated or customized, are brought to life by the story sequences. Instead of characters just being a shallow list of statistics, the stories make you grow attached to the members of your party as they grow old, face new challenges, develop relationships, and eventually find their destiny. The way the stories draw on the personality stats to flesh them out and make each character’s journey unique gives you a reason to care about them, such that you’re sad to see them eventually go. Thankfully the Legacy system gives you a chance to bring your favourites back. I have never seen such good writing in a game, and I’ve been playing games for over 40 years. The writers have done an amazing job crafting poignant, touching stories, and evoking a truly mythic, fairytale feel. I am constantly delighted by the creative and original use of words in novel combinations, which contribute to the mood and other-worldliness. I was skeptical of the art style at first, but it quickly grew on me. The campaign map is fine, the character and monster designs are whimsical and illustrative without trying to be too realistic, leaving room for imagination. Again, you are really given the sense of looking down on a pen & paper battle map. But it is the visuals during the story sequences that make the game feel like you’re living through the pages of a fairytale fantasy.The tactical component of the game is very solid, providing reasonable challenge (I haven’t tried harder modes beyond adventurer yet), and the character advancement and loot system provide a constant sense of progression and getting ever stronger, to face the growing threat of the monster forces. The core gameplay is strong, and while it may seem simple at first, there’s many options to develop interesting  character builds and party combinations.Wildermyth is a rare gem of a game, and I heartily recommend it to anyone who enjoys story-driven RPGs, or who wants that sense of playing a classic pen & paper roleplaying game, bringing their own characters and stories to life.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is good. Why is it good? Scenarios generated are modular but assemble themselves in a fun way to tell a story you can always buy into and feel invested in. There's always a small surprise you didn't expect and some deep themes you don't normally see explored in a turn based game. Legacy characters are underrated as story generators and help a player benefit from multiple play-throughs.Could it be better? Yes. The power ceiling isn't clear for certain skill choices. The mechanics are simple and easy to pick up however "paths" like the infusion magic system could benefit from a less random approach to choice. Something that helps users plot their path towards a particular build in game would be invaluable.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply wow...This is a game that came out of nowhere for me. I was going through my queue and stopped at Wildermyth on a whim. I was skeptical about the tone and art direction as most people fail to make this kind of thing work, but the trailer won me over enough to give it a chance. Let's start with the non-gameplay elements. The music truly engrosses you into the fantasy setting, and is simply a pleasure. Beyond the quality, the music is used for great affect. Action scenes feel actiony, scary scenes feel scary, and thrilling scenes feel thrilling. Obviously this is a combinations of everything, but the music plays it's part well. Outside of the music there really isn't much audio design. No lines are voiced with the exception of some grunts and various other sound effects. The sounds that do exist in game perfectly match the paper craft art style. While most games go the realism route of audio design, trying to make the audio seem feasibly real, Wildermyth goes the stylistic route. The intent is to make the player feel like they're reading a story, and the audio design reflects that. The art design might be the hardest sell for a lot of people. Most games are either Anime-esque or an attempt at invoking a sense of realism. Off the wall styles are rare, and ones that work even rarer. Fortunately the devs really pulled it off here. The art is stellar and really does make me feel as if i'm part of some grand adventure or story, which is ironic considering the dominant tone of the industry today. This game is a throwback to an age where creators had the skill to bring stories to life without the need to plagiarize the natural world; an age where simple graphics, some music, a tad of writing, and a tinge of imagination conjured up wondrous scenes of life.This leads me to the writing. There're two sides to this game, the main campaigns and the procedurally generated ones. The main campaigns are constructed as your typical RPG kind of stories. There is an overarching plot, a recognizable villain, side characters, and of course the heroes. The procedurally generated ones largely follow the same format but lack the added depth of a named villain or a supporting cast. There're side characters, but not to the same degree as the linear stories. The writing is simple and mildly changes depending on the personality of the party. and each personality will have some unique scenes and quests. Despite the simple nature the writers nailed it. They bring these scenes, and the characters, to life. It may not be Bioware level writing, but for a character driven RPG without any real characters I was impressed. Choices seem to matter and can lead your party down some interesting paths, sometimes directly impacting a coming battle.As for the gameplay... The turn based style combat is simple yet engaging. There're a lot of different ways you can approach each scenario and I never felt bogged down by the game. The AI knows how to play the game, for the most part. I have seen the AI target my squishies, lay traps, and attempt to bait me, they even try to pull units out of combat rather than just sit still for me to kill them. I find even the easier modes to be a fair enough challenge and am excited to try the other difficulties. That's the key here, they made the game challenging not simply difficult. Melee characters are pretty standard, as is the ranged combat. Magic, to be touched on later.There is a siege system in this game where large enemy armies will form and attack player controlled territory. This is the biggest challenge outside of traditional combat. The player can build defenses in tiers of 3, on controlled territory on the campaign map. Each tier slows the enemy and gives more benefits to the defensive battle. Once an army attacks a territory it will eat away at it until they're defeated or they destroy the tile in which case they move on to a new one until all human tiles are destroyed.  Players can intercept the enemy and fight an aggressive battle, or fight on friendly territory in a defensive battle, as mentioned earlier. If fighting defensively the player will get several advantages: some kind of buff, random villager units, and a rain arrows ability. The sieges are longer than normal missions and offer a break in normal gameplay loop.Enemies will gain advantages over time through The use of a "deck" system. Every faction has their own deck and more cards are added to it after each battle with more coming after some days have passed. The cards can be buffs or even new monsters for the AI to use. The player can spend "legacy points" to get rid of cards before they're added to a deck, but doing so means it will be more difficult to craft items and recruit heroes as they also cost LP. The enemy roster is varied and each faction feels unique. Now for my favorite part, the magic system. It's easily the best I have seen implemented in an RPG. Mages use an ability called interfuse to link themselves with object in the environment allowing them to cast spells depending on what they link with. Wooden objects can explode into splinters, fire from a lamp can engulf an enemy, and the trunks of a tree can ensnare your opponents. Magic feels both powerful and grounded. Forcing mages to link with objects adds a layer of strategy and forces proper planning and map control. Now for some negatives...Not everything is perfect despite me talking the game up. While generally the writing is good, there is not enough variety in the random events or scenes, I didn't even manage to finish the second campaign before I saw the same candle in the window, or romance on a mountain top scene. In a game like this you need a good amount of variety in the random scenes for it to work, I can forgive it a bit due to the nature of the game but I can't forgive seeing the same scenes again and again. It's especially bad because the writing is quite good; after my first story I was thirsty for more so the repetitiveness really hit hard. There're a lot of missed opportunities as well. As an example, characters can start families, but outside of how characters identify each other, like instead of friend they say love, I have not seen any scenes related to family. I had one hero with 3 daughters but they never had any sister moments, nor did they have any mom and pop moments. It was simply "blank's daughter is old enough to join the party". This kind of thing really stands out despite how great the game is. It could be I am just unlucky and haven't seen it yet, but considering how often scenes are reused I doubt I missed it.More ability variety would be great as after one or two runs you have likely tried everything, at least when it comes to the traditional leveling system. Besides those few issues nothing significant jumps out at me except for some things I personally disagree with in terms of world design, but I don't feel like it's important for this review.EDIT: After upping the difficulty I have noticed a significant improvement in the AI, resolving all my concerns with the AI's behavior. However, there is definitely a balance problem with 5 chapter campaigns. With the age and retirement system your heroes will likely retire by chapter 4 leaving you with under-leveled characters. Sometimes it's not a problem, but when you're playing on higher difficulties it becomes mighty annoying.Overall it's a great buy and one of my favorite releases in recent years, I wholeheartedly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique game that is a good balance of party RPG fighting, adventure (chose where to go or what to do on the map), decent options within those story points (so the choices are impact to the character), customizations (though I recommend checking out workshop items), and comic-like story. The story itself is sort of predictable, but in a way that it's appealing to someone who wants to check off their favorite tropes. I do have some thoughts on the "personality" aspect of the characters which I'm a bit confused on how it works (it never really gave much explanation for it). The story and game-play does get repetitive at a point, especially when it comes to fighting certain monsters, but I feel like there's a good amount of variations for how the "roleplaying" aspect turns out.
