_childDocuments_.review: "Finished" the game around the 30-40 hour mark, and by that I mean going once through all written campaigns, including 2 with a total of 3 friends. Last tracked hours were faffing about doing stupid builds.What is it?- I'd describe it as a light classic RPG with linear overarching story progression but complete freedom for wild and interesting scenarios for the "in the chapter" part of the story. Playing this solo or with friends always turn up unique due to the great storytelling AI they have in the background. Close comparison could be a streamlined DnD/Pathfinder or hex and tile combat system mixed with basic campaign planning. The game wants you to PLAY rather than neckbeard min/max stats, and I am fine with that.RATING: 9/10GOOD:A. Great art style and character reflections: While basic in nature, the evolving art style as your character becomes more deformed through doing stupid things is a really welcome addition, just because of how ridiculous you can make it. The Enemy/Campaign/Character/Boss designs are top notch, with a clear amount of effort making each one unique. No such thing as cookie-cutter mooks here.B. Legacy and AI storytelling - I think both of these systems are really seamless in how they present the player with "progression" as well as situations to make decisions. There are alot of scenarios written, each one with a unique outcome that allows for the truly unique campaign by campaign gameplay. The Legacy/retirement system is something more games should really take note off in how its done and how well it was implemented. Kudos to the design/playtesting team for putting this one out. It may not be the first system ever, but the first I've seen translated well to a video game.C. Seamless multiplayer - Simple connection, and quick to start the campaign. I would say that getting a bunch of friends to play this over the weekend as a standalone adventure is super fun. You can all easily take part in both the campaign and battles, with no connectivity issues experienced for the majority of both my sessions with friends.- Minor improvement: Enable options to fast forward text scenarios to progress. Sometimes when a few friends are AFK and we've been through the dialogue, it can stall the game. While it may be an issue implementing this in public servers, I don't think it would need more than a gentlemen's agreement to not abuse it. YMMV.- Minor improvement: At the start of the battle, you should have a prompt to give certain characters to players for commanding. This can speed up who controls what and avoid confusion where 2 people try to control a neutral/later game character and basically end up messing the whole action turn.D. Simple, but effective combat system - Not much more to say here. This is a tried and true AP based hex and tile combat system with 3 effective main classes to choose from. Combat is streamlined, with surprisingly alot of depth if you play long enough to learn the quirks of the system. - Minor improvement: Enemy abilities are not always the easiest to read off the profile cards for some reason. I think a handy summary of the enemy types and role at the start of the battle would give players a sense of what they need to prioritize. The rule of bigger is badder is pretty evident, but not always the case.MIDDLEA. Explanation or customization of player characters - Wildermyth has pretty minimal customization options provided to the player stat wise, and not much of an explanation what or how you get better at being an adventurer. Maybe this is the developers goal to avoid min/maxing perfect stat builds, but I would recommend an "unlocked" or even a respec pathway scenario for legacy or just old characters to be upgraded.- Potential idea: It could actually be part of a radiant or uniquely written short campaign for your legacy character to quest for a "holy grail" or "an ancient one" or some big bad with the power to change myths and legends, effectively writing a change unto your character, probably at a cost. Do it too many times based on a roll% that decreases in success each time you run this questline and your character permanently gets written off.B. Sounds - Combat sound is fine and crisp. I played mostly with music off, but while it was on, serviceable though nothing to write home about.NEEDS IMPROVEMENTA. Slightly clearer description of what abilities work with what deformations. I re-call on my earlier playthroughs that it wasn't explicit what kind of deformations will work with abilities.- Improvement idea: Either at the scenario screen or post chapter fusing, list the abilities that would not work if your character accepts the transformation. B. Transformations - Extremely neat in idea, and probably a developer decision, but I've noticed that most fully transformed characters are just outclassed by partially transformed or "bred for purpose" chimera characters during the mid-endgame, even with any potential boost provided for a fully transformed status. - Improvement idea: Instead of an overhaul, you could provide a substantial boost to a character based on a single, but full transformation. However, the character's playstyle will be very specific to the traits of the transformation, eventhough amplified. C. Equipment and dummy testing range during post chapter sequence - A pet peeve of mine where weapons are not immediately unique enough to gauge how well they work in scenarios. - Improvement idea: Provide an optional training ground/dummy post that you can test out character weapon and item combos in their current state to check and see what kind of damage you can expect for performance gauging, rather than the "trial-by-fire" approach. Extremely useful for higher difficulties to work strategies out beforehand. D. The "Lived in world" - Wildermyth primarily focuses on hobbit-esque 3rd world early settler/iron age societies, with references to old kingdoms of ages past. Your adventurers are basically the heroes of the realm, and no one is somehow capable of establishing a city state structure during a multi-year campaign :/. Feels like all the people in the world acknowledge a big bad is coming for them, but expect 5 mutants / cripples to do something about it alone. PROBABLY true in real life if it ever happens, but this is a game, and there should be a better representation of humanity. - Improvement idea: Standing militia / men-at-arms or even equipped mercenaries should be an option to bolster your heroes during main battles and/or defences, provided you spend actual resources on them (not campaign time). They should still be led by a "hero" but can be customized from a "light" version of the 3 classes with some basic abilities and armour/weapons. TLDR: Farmers are trash tier mob infantry that are practically useless, and you can't upgrade them.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed the first (Gorgon) campaign so far, and oh boy. Was it an experience.Started off simple – a silly Mystic boy, a fiesty enby (yep, you heard it right) Hunter, and a stalwart Warrior young woman. The latter two were enemies and kept being at each other's throats throughout the first chapter. That's until, at some point, the adventures they had brought them together. They got together, went through a crisis of faith in their heroic dreams, and ended up having a wonderful Hunter daughter that took up the bow when her parent Hunter perished before the last boss. Never thought I'd see a non-cringey enemies-to-lovers story in a video game. Who would've thought that it would be through a randomly generated storytelling adventure such as Wildermyth! And that's just one such story of so many to come. It's a game where you build a legacy of legendary heroes and explore their stories. Some of them will build families and retire from adventuring, and some will perish in a burst of crystals before they even turn thirty. It's an incredibly unique, well put-together game, where it feels like your choices actually matter for once. If you're a fan of good stories, try it. It's enthralling 🤍

_childDocuments_.review: The strategy and battle elements are fine. But the writing is, to put it mildly, an insane word salad. I am shocked that anyone would call these randomly generated text snippets "great storytelling." As a strategy game, it's serviceable. But don't be suckered in by claims about the amazing writing. The story reads like it was (poorly) translated from another language, for example: "chew through fuel and turn it into deeds," fire "wriggling through the wood like a happy mud-dog," or describing the sun as a "glory-hoarding jerk."  That is...something. But it's not good writing, at least not in English. Other grammatical errors and oddities abound. Only a few hours in and I am already skipping past the nonsensical dialogue and plots. So take any claims about this game's story with a huge grain of salt. Or, be prepared to "chew through fuel and turn it into deeds,"as any competent, native speaker of the English language would say.

_childDocuments_.review: So I saw this game on sale, dug through some comments, and was like hey I'll buy this game, and boy am I glad I did. The Overviewin WilderMyth you start off with three random or custom hero's as they begin their journey to save the world from an overarching evil that grows stronger as time goes on. As your party adventures forward they will change and grow, from getting older, forming new relationships, changing magically or in personailty to even losing limbs. This focus on the change your hero's go through is quite fun, as a hero may start off a Greedy Romantic and end up a wolf god blessed married man whos now generous, has a wolfs head and missing an arm from battle. You can play through pre-written stories that have a focus, or a randomly generated one, battle is simple but always dangerous. Even at your hero's peak a situation could go wrong and you lose a hero, death of course is not the end as heros at 0hp can be saved, though they will be damaged usually missing a limb.The Pro's-High replayability, no story or heros will ever feel the same-One more turn Gameplay that will keep you playing for hours-You get attached to your hero's, how they change, and their realtionships-Updates from the developers as well as sources to talk to other players-Built in crafting kit to make your own content and eventsThe Cons-Story, Character History, and Coversations can come out a bit rough, sometimes being a bit confusing-Romances have events and buffs catered toward them but are never mentioned otherwise-The creation kit is complex unless your willing to put time in online to learn itFinal OpinionWildermyth is a fantastically fun game that I am even doing a Youtube Playthrough of, its rough at the moment but with love, care, and a active community this game is going places. Its always exciting to see your heros at the begining and wonder who they will be at the end, I HIGHLY reccomend this game if you're a TTRPG fan and love character growth.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly rarely driven to write reviews; normally, somebody else has already said whatever it was I was thinking to say and more.  In this case, however, I just had to add my thoughts to the pile, redundant though they may be.I'm not sure I've ever played a computer game that has gotten me as attached to my characters as Wildermyth.  It's much more akin to a tabletop RPG in that sense than a CRPG.  As you play though any given campaign, you not only experience the larger story but also briefer moments and narrative vignettes that bring to the surface the sort of individual personalities, relationships, and histories that make characters memorable.  It takes a mighty cold heart not to care about a hero after you've watched them struggle with loss, regain faith in themselves, possibly sprout a pair of crow wings, and now stand in what might be their final battle, holding the line against an endless swarm of mechanized bone-creatures while the other heroes race on ahead to reach the key objective.As the campaigns roll on, heroes age and survivors will likely retire at some point.  Along with fresh recruits and new faces, the children, or even the grandchildren, of the original group may be picking up the banner in their place.  There is a palpable sense of time passing, of the struggle against the various evils taking up most or even all of a hero's adult life.  There's a poignancy coming out of that which makes the characters feel even more rounded out.  Rather than just a set of optimized stats, they are individuals who might confess to a rival the trade they would have followed if things had gone differently, or ponder what it might have been like to be able to settle down and actually live in the town they just saved.There's a wry sense of humor throughout, however, and things are far from deadly serious.  Heroes can buy themselves a fox tail from a cursed merchant with a coin brought to them by their pet critter, save a fiery chicken from being used as bait, attempt to harvest stars off a magic tree, score a cool new frog-head, and so many other things, all as a part of the interstitial story moments that occur constantly through the game.At its heart, Wildermyth is a turn-based strategy game in which you pit a group of heroes against a variety of different foes on small procedurally generated maps.  Fans of X-COM, Xenonauts, or any of the many other spins on that sort of game play will feel quite at home.  The options available during a battle are not overwhelming or particularly complex compared to some offerings (about on a level with the Firaxis XCOM, albeit with a sane RNG), but the open-ended character evolution gives a hidden layer of complexity stemming from the player's ability to try many different approaches and strategies.At first, I was slightly disappointed to find there were only 3 character classes - Warrior, Hunter, and Mystic, but soon learned that any of those three can be spun in an impressive array of different ways. Characters select 1 of 3 talents each time they level up, plus there are a surprising number of different transformations that might permanently alter their abilities.  One Warrior might specialize in mobility, leaping automatically about the battlefield to engage approaching foes and making the most of an ability to perform multiple reaction strikes in a turn, while another might use their axe to shred foes' armor in combination with laying down flames with that left arm of theirs which was permanently changed to a fiery form in an earlier, randomly appearing story moment.Mystics specifically have turned out to be a pleasant surprise.  Rather than the typical concept of a mage, they are imagined as someone with the ability to "interfuse" with various inanimate objects, bending them to their will in order to perform a variety of effects depending on the terrain object being melded with.  It's a fresh concept, and the ability of Mystics to further specialize in different kinds of interfusions as well as other special abilities as they progress gives them every bit as much variety as Warriors and Hunters.  It's even quite possible to forgo the normal "glass cannon" stereotype and make a Mystic into a tanky bruiser, whose interfusions give them bonus armor even as they divert a portion of incoming damage into the objects they are interfused with.There's a light strategic wrapper around the tactical battles, and a small but varied array of equipment to secure for your heroes, but the other major feature of the game is the Legacy.  At the end of a campaign, heroes can be added to your Legacy.  This saves a snapshot, so to speak, of the hero as they were at the end of things.  When you are playing your next campaign (and I assure you, there will be a next campaign), you can bring heroes back off the Legacy bench and into the current story.  (The authors of the game compare this to the way mythological figures often feature in multiple different versions of their myths, including ones that are downright contradictory with each other.)  Depending on the hero's level within your Legacy, you can select one or more of their previously gained talents – and any transformations they undergone come along for free.  This gives you an advanced starting point for that hero which aims them in the same direction as their previous incarnation but also allows you to vary them and their skill set as you would.A Legacy character who survives to the end of a new campaign can also be promoted within the Legacy.  This replaces their previous "snapshot" with their new state and also increases the number of skills you can select from their updated list when bringing them into yet another story.  Promotion is optional – and, in fact, you will have a limited number of promotion opportunities at the end of a campaign - and that's a good thing if you just aren't satisfied with how they've developed this time as it gives more freedom to experiment.Nothing is perfect, of course.  I would very much like to see more of the small stories added into the mix, and a wider variety of events for the post-chapter/game end epilogues would be very welcome.  The multiple options available in each vignette and the varied personality-dependant variations that occur throughout definitely add to the replayability of those moments, but more overall would definitely be my number one ask.  There are a handful of UI tweaks that would be nice as well; for example, it is possible to check what resources are currently coming in by mousing over the name of the heroes' company, and that is very useful when trying to decide how to develop a newly secured area, but there's nothing that actually tells you that this info is available.  These are minor complaints, however, and I know the devs have stated they are working on more story content. In the end, it is often hard to express exactly what makes a game feel unique in just words.  If anything about the game sounds interesting, I would highly recommend giving it a try.  There really hasn't been anything quite like it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is highly addictive. When I first got this game I played through 8 hours in one sitting, it was incredibly immersive! The art and music is charming and tasteful. There are so many events, so many curveballs, and endless fun in this game. I feel like I experienced so many things in such short amount of time, and the fact that there are more consequences makes me giddy. I experienced my secured areas flooding. There was a time where my body became half fire. A character had raven wings and a dog-like head. I saved people and they joined my party. I let people die. A daughter in my party sacrificed herself to save her parents in a final boss battle. All these things shape your party members and makes them so unique. I love that I'm able to carry on their legacies in other campaigns as well.Whenever D&D sessions fail to operate with my friends, I play Wildermyth.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game because of all these reviews talking about amazing stories and so forth... I love me a great story that engages me on every level. Now, I wasn't expecting Detroit: Become Human levels of narrative excellence, but I do love DnD and a story doesn't have to be AAA quality to be amazing.Having said that, this is not what I experienced in this game. Sure, I may have only played for one hour, but whilst this game looks good on paper, the implementation of it was just awful in my eyes. The procedurally generated story that everyone is lauding about is just a bunch of random sentences and scenes that have nothing to do with each other, get thrown together. I was more confused at the end of the one hour I played then at the start, and not in a 'ooh I'm confused but invested I want to see more of this' way. When starting out, the game plays through introductory scenes for each member of your party - these are so random and without point that I immediately felt all the built up investment in my party that I accumulated through character creation, simply evaporate. And I modelled my party after my own DnD group so to make me lose interest in my own party is quite a feat.The combat is so simplistic that once you've finished a fight, the rest are basically the same. Having looked up late game combat scenarios on Let's Plays, my point still stands even with only 1 hour of playtime.Look, search up the game and watch the story and gameplay for a while - that's the best way of deciding for yourself whether you should buy this or not. Don't do what I did, don't read the Steam reviews then buy based off that. With that £20 you can buy your other half or your mama something nice instead and make their day. This will probably become an unpopular review but hey it is what it is. Either way, have fun =]
