_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Updating to affirm this still holds true as of the full version. WOW. This game is absolutely amazing. The first Early Access game I've ever bought and I am amazed. This I believe is the closest approximation of a tabletop-RPG experience in a video-game format. I can't be true, since I've never played any, but from what I have heard, yes. So it has one of the best procedural systems I've ever seen. The way it works is you have an overarching villain for each scripted scenario (of which there are 4 then there are 4 others divided in 2 sets that are procedural, 2 regular & 2 legacy more on that later), they are divided in 3 or 5 chapters. Within each chapter you operate at an overland map, which gives you a sort of strategy scenario where you take over areas (which gets into a combat situation, more on that later) or secure sites which gets you more resources at the end of the chapter (more on that as well). Along the way certain events pertaining to all or some of your characters will happen and they can range from them getting possessed by a crow spirit to them confronting something about their past to falling in love or getting married (by the no restrictions, wonderful character creator you can have nonbinary gender with either masculine or feminine body type or voice and have them fall in love with whoever you want). These can create some really wonderful situations as they build up over time and are magnificently written so that you get a sense of each character as distinct persons. A lot more small-scale, but brilliantly in that scale.  At the end of the chapter then you earn x amount of years of peace depending on how well you did. This makes a few things happen. First you get some nice stories about what the heroes have been up to between the chapters, but they also age, which is something you have to take into account. Not in a stat way, but they all have a retirement age, different from each characters and leveling up and certain events will influence it. For a 3-chapter it doesn't matter, but for a 5-chapter story at least some of your top heroes will retire and you need to prepare replacements. You also get to do some gear upgrading with the materials you got during the chapter, which is useful indeed. Then it's off to the next chapter and you repeat. Also calamity cards are added over time, this has a bit of a deck-building aspect. It's not a deck-builder, but more cards are added to the various enemy decks, which will make them more dangerous over time. You can stop some of them by using legacy points, which are also used for getting materials and recruiting heroes so they have to be spent wisely. Then after you win a campaign your characters become legacy heroes and you get to promote 1 or 2 of them to a higher tier. What this means is they can take part in legacy campaigns where you basically import old heroes with their entire story. They start at level one, but they will include their entire heroes, so 2 people who used to be lovers will be in love again, if they went through an animal or elemental transformation thing that will be set as well. They will also retain some abilities and even gear, it will be set to tier 1, but you can upgrade it. So I got a super rare axe during a scripted mission that Tauren, my super warrior got to keep. They get to retain 1 ability (of a max 5) for each legacy tier. So a tier-1 hero get to start with 1 ability, tier 2 2 abilities, and so on. You can't bring everyone with you, you are limited to a party of 3 for most missions, but it really holds promise. Even with only 4 scripted missions, I'm gonna keep playing this. Now, for the combat, which is amazing. It's a turn-based strategy/tactics system with a beautiful art-style that absolutely matches the tabletop-RPG thing they are going for. There's not much to say about it generally other than everything from abilities to range to much else is just amazingly polished, but I have to mention one thing specifically - the magic system. I have never seen a magic system this unique or this fun to use. Usually it's "unique and annoying" or "fun and standard" but they hit both. So the magic system doesn't have spells exactly, but rather a single spell called "interfuse" where the mystic "interfuses" with objects in the environment - fire, wood, stone, etc. and can use aspects of those - so they can shatter wood, throw a stone discus, or use fire to attack the enemies. It's incredibly fun. That to say, I'm absolutely in love with this game and if you love TBS/Tactics games or if the way it handles the tabletop thing sounds like your thing, I can heartily recommend it. I promise, it is super-good.

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanics are solid, art style is beautiful, that alone is worth the price tag. However I strongly do not recommend due to the following reasons that have left me deeply conflicted about the Wildermyth.As someone who played AI Dungeon religiously for the past 2 years, observing as the technology of NLP models progressed in scale and complexity, the 'writing' here sounds sounds as if took an old GTP-2 6b parameter model like AI Dungeon's old Griffin model or Clover, kept pressing enter, saved the output, and called it a day. The vignettes & campaigns by Douglas Austin suffer from this particularly as the output saved doesn't even appear to be cleaned. The other writers at least attempt to tidy it up to sound like human writing. I could be wrong of course, as this is purely anecdotal and I've not read any other reivews that state the same. But it really seems like the majority of the dialogue & scenarios have all the makings of machine generated language. Lovingly and beautifully illustrated, but devoid of coherency, logic, and tone apart from GTP-2 chaos.I understand this was made by a small team and if they did indeed use a GTP-2 NLP model to help create the huge number of scenarios, that's fair enough. The fact that it passes for 'great writing' by 98% of Steam reviewers, is also fair enough. I'm not a gatekeeper of fantasy writing. But the fact that it feels simultaneously lazy and high effort at the same time is what tears at me. I want to love this game. But I'm extremely disappointed by what was promised & reviewed to be a well written character-driven game with extreme character depth & choices that matter. Instead I feel like I bought an Interactive AI Dungeon / Novel AI Artbook. Which I guess is great if that's what you're looking for or haven't tried either of them before.

_childDocuments_.review: Best story-based game i played in a loooong time.the set-up is really simple, a bunch of nobodies find a reason to pick-up arms, and fight various evil beings, from lizard-people, to psychokinetic insects, or simple Cultists. the playable characters can be freely created to your desire add in some personality that changes how they react to events (as in, their personality changes the dialouge) and some hooks that lead them to personal quests. and you got a recipe for a nice story.on top of that, you can keep your custom characters after you Finish the story and make them a legend that can re-appear in other stories. who knows, maybe that person you rescue from a magic carpet turns out to be your favorite ranger from the last campaign you played.and if thats still not enough, you get a build-in editor to make your own custom events, set the parameter what has to happen for it to appear and share it within the steam workshop.word of advice however, don't be too puritan to how your character looks, some events can change the look for your characters permanently in various ways, maybe your warrior got defeated in battle and now has a fancy hook for a hand. maybe they disturbed a magic stone and got a gem lodged in their eyesocket. or maybe you just drank some magic water and the black guy is now looking like a smurf. so be warned, maiming and mutations await you, and who knows what'll happen. so if you re-create your OC's here. be prepared for them to lose or mutate a limb.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally! A tactical RPG that:1.) Meets the traditional definition of Role Playing Game. (You play as characters, and can make decisions that affect the story of the game as well as the character)2.) Is Inclusive! The character system supports all manner of gender and skin colors, with no obvious preferences given. 3.) Is well-written. RPGs have a long history of being paired with novels, largely because they both rely on good storytelling and world building.  Wildermyth's stories feel plausible within its fantasy world. The characters stories are integrated into the game, and the player's choices along the way have meaningful consequences. Once in a while you'll pick from the standard "charge/feint/ambush" type decisions standard in tactical RPGs, but mostly, players are picking the direction of the story, which feels much more satisfying than hitting "charge." for the 300th time.  The game is fun. It's currently playable and worth buying. I put 100 hours in, happily. That said, it is in dire need of balancing... it's current state allows the easier difficulties to support all tactical playstyles, which is nice, but as the difficulty goes up, it becomes clear that there's really only one viable class: hunter. Hunters get the most mobility, the most damage, free stealth, huge AoE's and free action points with kills. They are invisible killing machines that outrun everyone.  Entire chunks of the game can be avoided by entering combat with only hunters.  Anyway, what I'm trying to say is that Wildermyth is young. It is at a point in its life where it has met all the requirements to be a fun role playing game, and it's way above average already. It's combat system has it's flaws, but overall it's already more fun than some of the 3/4 view blockbusters that compete for the same audience's attention.  I've been playing RPG's since before there were computers, and have played almost all of them.   My predict: Wildermyth will become one of the best SRPG's of all time. I'm not quite sure everyone will notice, but sooner or later, they'll have to. Wildermyth shines with potential like nothing I've seen before.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This may not be a "hardcore" RPG but give it time and it will suck you in with its gentle charm, decent learning curve and brilliant story telling.The brilliance of the story telling allows a natural story of heroes who have been brought together and are now fighting the over arcing bad guy of that chapter.The story telling brings little moments outside of the grind of the hero and lead to all manner of moments that live on (or bring a swift end) for those involved.The legacy function of the game allows you to recruit heroes from a previous story, paying for the upgrades you want to take and their story can grow from there, I cannot stress how much you will start feeling for your little rag tag band of heroes.The combat is simple enough with magic being played in a different manner than the usual as scenery empowers your mystics, Close combat comes with some very defensive set of skills, while Archers can spec multiple different ways.I love this game, I love the design and I love my poor Heroes who suffer so the world can be free from enemies!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: A procedurally generated RPG storyteller.A mix of XCOM (combat), Rimworld (character depth), Mount & Blade (overworld), recent Fire Emblems (character romance / children in party), and Miitopia (surprisingly the most similar title to this game). If you like any of those games, you're very likely to enjoy this one. The combat and RPG mechanics are solid, with a lot of distinctive choices to be made. Your characters develop over time and are molded by a handful of (semi-random) elements, and there is some inter-campaign progression as your old characters will appear or be referenced randomly in new stories.If you like the idea of randomly generated stories and characters (that can be shaped by your actions) this one is a no brainer, because there's nothing close (except in a different way Rimworld, and at a much smaller scale Miitopia). The biggest difference I would say is Rimworld procedurally simulates the nitty-gritty details of individual scenarios (in effective real time), while Wildermyth procedurally generates an entire lifespan of a party of heroes through distinct story beats.Effectively an infinitely replayable tabletop RPG comic/VN.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played 1.5 campaigns but the game has been fantastic so far.  The story is presented as a graphic novel, the characters in tactical combat look like 2D cutouts from a cheap board game, and the strategic map is relatively normal, but somehow it all works brilliantly together.  So far I've had one character have an eye replaced by a gem and later retire to become a Seer, 3 characters maimed in combat (a choice allowed when they would have died instead), 4 killed in combat, one is transforming into a bear, one into a crow, and one into a wolf due to story opportunities and choices I made.  The son of one of my characters has just joined my team and his mother is getting close to retirement age.  The default "Adventurer" difficulty level is providing some challenge for me while remaining doable.  All around it has been great fun so far.  You should play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly wonderful.  Even in early access, it's a completely playable and satisfying experience.  I'd describe it as a delightful turn-based RPG with a strong emphasis on randomized events, dynamic narrative generation, character building, and inter-party relationships.  In many ways it's very close to a tabletop experience where you start with a group of fledgling heroes and then build them into badasses among the background of a rising threat.  Much of the game is played on a campaign map where your party moves through areas and combats threats, investigates sites, and/or builds defenses.  There are many story events (although I assume there'll be more in the future) and often you're managing the relationships of your party which have tangible effects in the game.The turn-based combat is very tactical; a surprising high point given the strong narrative components of the game.  During combat, your party moves about the battle map and engages with various enemies.  Hero placement, enemy positioning, and environmental effects are all important aspects to consider in the combat system.  The magic system is also very innovative: nearly all of your "magic" is environmental.  Your mystic infuses with various items around a room (a fireplace, a brick wall, a tree, etc.) and then has a variety of spell options based upon the environmental object.  It's great.I can't say enough about this game... A true surprise.  Really hoping to watch this develop into a classic.

This comes really close to what I want from my tabletop RPGs when I'm wanting a more old-school feel.

_childDocuments_.review: Friendly if you're looking for story but difficult if you like that.  Memorable, surprising, occasionally sad and painful, satisfyingly long arcs to the stories of the many many characters you'll get to know over your play time.  Character modification is limited visually, but in combination with skill trees and classes and personalities there's a wide field.  I haven't yet tried writing my own stories (I'm just enjoying playing them without knowing the possible effects of my choices in-character)... Combat graphics is all a very heavily styled 3d so plan a trial or search for some video to see if it's going to be acceptable - they focused on the tactics and development and story rather than blow a ton of development $ and disc space on sparkly graphics.In summary: great to play for story and there's lots of challenge to reach into when you're interested.  AI is plenty acceptable and enemy variations/development is, too.And They're Still Adding Content!  Happy to see growth continue like that, really making the most out of the constancy of internet access.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Story is not bad, gameplay is pretty solid though it would be better if movement wasn't tied to the action economy.The art style looks offputing at first but don't let that dissuade you there's quite a bit of care that went into this.The Legacy character system is really well handled because even if a character dies or retires of old age you can use them again in a new campaign and they go back to a young age, unfortunately I wish this would give them back their limbs because I love using 2handed weapons in games. Maybe make this optional?My one criticism is the inclusion of genders that do not exist, stop being brain washed by old pseudo science being pushed by a pedophile rapist named John Money(do your research) who pretended to by a psychologist and scientist. Though in the recent social climate I can understand why such a thing would be included but it is cringey and we will look back on this one day and facepalm. But I suppose no game can be perfect.There is one annoying glitch I encountered in multiplayer where it kept popping up with a story board menu and closing it in an infinite loop and both me and my friend couldn't progress without reloading a previous save. Also there's this one final level where you have to destroy pillars and kill a boss to win but the center of the stage will shoot you with lightning or something and knock you back and this would be fine but it can sometimes get caught in an infinite loop and just kill several of your charactesr from full health between turns.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: this game is DND lite for a solo player (though you still can play this game with your friends), as quoted from many other reviews.the storytelling in this game is so engaging and fun! the stories/banters that happens during random intervals or after some plot hooks really breathed life into the characters and make you care for them that when one of them gets maimed or killed during battle you can't help but feel bad when it happens.just wish it's easier to incite the hooks for various relationships between characters like friendship/rivalry/romance w/o playing with cheats from the very beginning bc sometimes i prefer to play the matchmaker and make characters frienemies lol
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game allows the player to develop groups of heroes in fantasy-themed campaigns by exploring the world and surviving turn-based combats.  The heroes will learn skills, gain equipment, and acquire transformative 'themes' over the course of the campaign.  Afterwards, heroes can be saved to the player's legacy, and recruited in later campaigns so they can become stronger.   The variety of character traits available allows for fun experimentation; combining skill sets and themes to create optimized heroes requires patience (or activating developer mode).  With several fully scripted campaigns, a nicely implemented random campaign generator, and variable levels of difficulty, this game offers great replayability for anyone who enjoys table-top style fantasy games.  Nice artistic style as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: ( Edit edit: So after more time playing - it seems really inconsistent when you can or can't use legacies, as well as when they retire, and plenty more. Dunno if it's bugged or not. Several characters were set to retire an djust.. didn't. A new story I could start with legacies when before I couldn't. Some of the transformations make ranged weapons unusable and kinda put your ranged characters in a weird spot if you don't know that beforehand. Events do start repeating kinda fast, easily by the time you're in the second campaign, which isn't too promising. Ultimately, I don't think the game is BAD, I think it makes some bad decisions - it would have been a thousand times more enjoyable as a single long campaign with a NON-procedural story/world, especially one that spanned maybe four or five generations at most.. as is you somehow have children and parents all getting super old in the same campaign, there's no "pass the torch" feel at all. Also - a character dramatically sacrificed themselves.. then showed up in a midpoint cutscene and is still available as a legacy.. What's the point of a sacrifice, then? )( Edit: Yikes. Beat the first whole campaign and went to start the second and.. you just start over? Lose all your heroes and items and such? Blegh. Awful, hate it. No new options for characters, no starting differences, just.. three random dingdongs from scratch? I looked it up and I guess you have the "possibility" of recruiting past heroes, but even then they don't save any changes or upgrades/etc. during that campaign unless spending other points. In my opinion this might be the worst approach you could take to super story-tell-y and procedural as a combo, it's just.. eh. Unless you REALLY like making a warrior/mystic/ranger and running those three over and over while pretending they're super unique despite being the same at the start every time, well.. this  might be a hard pass for you. If I at least got to keep building out characters and such I'd be more into it, but this falls really flat if you ask me. Some great ideas and some awful ideas make a mediocre soup at the end of the day. It also doesn't help that the first campaign is hardly more than a few hours long, so in one sitting, as you get a feel for the game, the heroes you maybe started to enjoy building and caring about are just done, save if you pay to recruit them later and then pay for ONE of them to retain any changes. On top of the combat being so tactically one-dimensional and heavy-handed with one-round kills.. I fear this is a total flop in my opinion, which is really quite a shame given the aesthetic and some of the good ideas in combat and whatnot. )Y'know, I hate to say it.. overall I "kinda" like it, but several things drive me a little crazy and make it a lot less fun than it could be.Enemies AND allies hit way too hard. Almost anything dies in a hit or two - you and foe alike. Which means you basically one-round most foes before they can act- or they one-round you. That's not particularly fun combat. Since the devs chose to go with a "all your allies go then all the enemies go" this turns immediately into the usual dogpile tactics that plague this style of "tactical" combat. Hammer foes repeatedly before they can act, or get ganged up and wrecked before you can react. Which is unfortunate because, truly, a lot of the ideas and systems seem pretty neat - but you don't really get to thoroughly explore them. Healing is also super slow and, in combat, appears to be basically non-existent, which further punishes any kind of actual risk taking or playstyle that doesn't lean on hanging back, reacting, and ranging foes in one turn each.But moreso, I *really* dislike all the huge time constraints that constantly come up, especially when you can't reasonable gauge the time cost for making multiple moves and events in succession, forcing you ignore tons of optional, potentially interesting or fun, side events or whatnot to make sure you don't get totally screwed by the time limits. It doesn't help that limits are often 100-200 days at most - moving a single tile takes 10-15, and *doing* anything takes 20-30, suddenly you're out of time in a few tiles without hardly realizing it.The events and such seem quite varied and neat, but I felt so constrained by time limits and the combat is SO heavily one-sided or the other that it's tough to really just enjoy the rest of it as a result. It's also near impossible to track what resources you need for upgrades, what upgrades come from where, and what you will have available at the end of a chapter for upgrading.I like a lot of the ideas and bones here, but the way it comes together as far as gameplay, turn order, and combat, just falls kinda flat for me. I understand the reviews - the aesthetic is lovely, the skills are fairly unique for being nothing more than 'wizard, rogue, warrior' options for characters (which is usually an instant buzzkill), the 'story' of sorts is cute, but.. all that doesn't quite stand on its own in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I really like this game!It's graphic style is different than many games, very simple, 2D cutouts that feel like playing a D&D game. The writing is interesting, with twists and turns and choices that make you feel like it's a choose your own adventure book.Combat is tactical and turn based. I thought I'd find it boring when I first started it, but turns out that there are a number of cool bad guy abilities, and an original magic for combat mechanism that I'd never seen before. I like how it plays out and how they handle the pre-fight and post-fight scenes.To make a very long story short, I like the game and it's a ton of fun. Look at the graphics, if you can live with them and you want a nice, story telling, game where your older characters can give new abilities to your new games, this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: After I finished the base campaign I couldn't be bothered to play the others. There is a lot of dialogue choices but restarting stories over and over with the same plot isn't necessarily "fun" in this game.As others have mentioned the combat doesn't have much depth and somehow it doesn't give nearly enough excitement that other turn-based combat games offer.Final verdict: Not worth the current price. Get this on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the first campaign(the one that starts with the tutorial).This game is stellar. I randomized all my characters including my starters and yet by the end of the campaign, I felt as though I had spent hours carefully crafting them in an character editor. The game literally makes them yours along with the story itself. I'm excited for my next campaign.Other quick notes. (mind you I played on the standard difficulty)-Considerable learning curve but you are tested on it too quickly. The game offers a lot over time.-Lot of potential depth but you don't have to dive to deep if you don't want to.-You can take your time maintaining your territory or literally hit the key missions and cruise to the endI highly recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game about stories.It's not a perfect game. I can't tell you that the tactical combat is strategically amazing (although it's extremely well-balanced and satisfying) or that the graphics are top-notch (but the simple, papercraft look works so well and the art is frequently take-your-breath-away beautiful). What I CAN tell you is that Wildermyth understands storytelling better than any game I can think of.My heroes grew together. They bled together, and talked years later about their scars and missing legs. They loved each other, and got married, and had children. My top warrior Cass was a loving, if insecure, spouse to the hunter Willow, and together they fought [REDACTED] in the final battle of the first campaign. Cass gave their life in that fight, but died in a blaze of glory defending the woman they loved. I cried.It's not going to be the best game you'll ever play in terms of graphics or even gameplay. But the stories you'll be part of will hook you in and stay with you.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth: or the game I wanted but didn't know existed.This game is, in my opinion, a must buy for any fan of D&D. The stories I've enjoyed in my meagre nine hours playtime are already extremely memorable. The characters I've played with came to life before me in painted beauty. When they died, I felt sad. When they triumphed, I was elated. Their tales of love and rivalry captivated me. I have not felt a connection to procedurally generated characters before this.Granted, the base campaigns in the game are short, and the combat relatively simple (but studded with enough loot and abilities to sate my metagaming mind) - but the game really shines in the storytelling. I have had a hunter become a wolfman, dispassionate towards the rest of his party, only to show his true humanity in a sacrifice as he took out a gorgon with his jaws and blade, dissolving in its acid as he bolstered his companions with his last words "For The Ragged Watchers!"I have had a mystic become wreathed in flames, cackling as she embraced her newfound power. These moments evoke that pen and paper rpg feel for me - that feeling of character progression.Perhaps most importantly - the developer of this game rocks. The game has been developing for years now, and just discovering it upon early access release I have a ton of reading to do. The dev has a blogspot where they document design philosophy, and also help you construct your own campaigns. The game has a build in editor - and the developer has tutorials on constructing battles, campaigns, compelling villains, you name it.I see a vibrant future of community content because of this, and hope to be part of that.Buy this game, and make me a story please!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: At 19 hours, I have played one three-act tutorial campaign and two acts of a procedurally generated campaign in singleplayer, and the first three acts of a five-act campaign with a multiplayer party. There are several other scripted five-act campaigns, each with a different core storyline and predominant enemy race, I have yet to touch. Suffice to say this game has a lot of content if the formula appeals to you.And that formula, from where I'm standing, is an epic multi-generational Fire Emblem and XCOM-esque tactical RPG with some of the most interesting kit/terrain synergies the tactics genre has seen since Into the Breach. And it really works.Whereas you might have to put in some elbow grease to see your XCOM marines as living, breathing characters, Wildermyth does the heavy lifting for you via a robust catalogue of dilemmas and narrative hooks that will see your characters live and fight their whole careers until death or retirement, growing, forming relationships, and earning battle scars along the way.Also extremely notable is the stability and amenities of the multiplayer. As someone who has always wanted a multiplayer XCOM campaign, this has turned out to be shockingly better than what I'd dreamed that would be.If you're a fan of any of the games previously listed, or you're just generally intrigued, you won't regret getting off the fence and buying it. If there's any justice in this world, studios will be taking pointers from Wildermyth for years.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I've only gotten through the first campaign, but wow has this game touched me. The overly saccharine phrasing and sometimes a bit amateurish prose aside, you do feel very attached to your heroes as they grow old, get married, have children that join your party, and go about the world together. My absolute favorite parts so far have been the side-quests that only involve two of your party members, they lend so much to the experience and that is where I have found the most touching writing in the game (thus far). Highly, highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: My adorable rascally hunter married my burly warrior dude, they had kids, then a grandkid, then she turned into a wolf. Wolfgrannie and her family then slaughtered the lizard emperor and his army without mercy. 10/10, should have bought this sooner. Extra thoughts: -Simplified XCOM with a light, fluffy, fantasy atmosphere-Great random stories/interactions that pop up-Simple but enjoyable turn-based combat with simple resource/gear system-Warriors with cleave are literal gods -- melee is very strong, so mages/archers feel a little weak in comparison so far
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game as I do many others: I'm bored and hoping it will be good.  Wildermyth was like striking gold.  This game is amazing, and I'm nowhere near done playing.   There is so much to do and I haven't even started checking out the community mods for the game.  I've gone through the story campaigns and a few random ones.  The premise of the game is fantastic, it's not too complicated, it's rewarding, and can be challenging.  The Devs are constantly working and communicating with the player base (their Discord channel is great!).10/10 would buy this game again.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything you read and all the praise is deserved. It succeeds in every aspects. The fights are satisfying ; the character management is interestingly unique, in a rogue-lite way ; the numbers of events and the procedurally generated maps grant new stories every playthrough ; the campaigns are beautiful and well written.. The storytelling is globally excellent and on point. It feels like playing a pen and paper RPG or a table-top game, with a game master. In top of that, it's visually beautiful (in its genre of course) and the soundtrack fits perfectly.I would have bought it on release if I had known. Don't miss it.EDIT : a new campaign was added for free and it's excellent. This game (and its devs) keeps on giving.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: A fresh take on a turn-based strategy made by only a few people. It is story driven, very well written and plays well. There are plenty of random events with various outcomes, characters have personalities, friendships, rivalries and there is assortment of weapons to choose from.Graphics are an interesting choice of putting 2D cardboards into a 3D world but works surprisingly well. Music is great, gameplay and UI elements are intuitive and flawless. I really have nothing to complain about. Although it tends to get repetitive over time as there are only 3 classes with little varieties in skill pool. And eventually even the random events start to repeat themselves. But I'd say the current content is well worth the price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: REALLY confusing! Nobody knows how to play the game and you spend 90% of the time flipping cards and basically just waiting "for the game to begin" and 10% of the time trying to figure out wonky mechanics. Is it turn based or not? Who has the controls over the characters? Why can we both move all characters at the same time? Really weird also with the "read along" button. Sometimes it works sometimes it doesn't and when it works it just feels weird. All in all - this isn't a multiplayer game. Cannot recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute treat, I love party based RPG's because of the idea of forming friendships between npc's. But rather than me having to roleplay in my head about the relationships, I have a game here that organically forms the relationships based on their personalities. The way the story generates and proceeds is  fantastic and get's you attached and hooked to certain characters. As far as the combat goes it's a solid 7/10. Enough to keep your interest but not an intricate combat system that will blow your mind. But overall it's more about the storylines and watching your characters grow than simply the combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I am pleased to say I was delightfully surprised with this title. Ever since the lockdown I've been in an endless loop of boredom replaying the same stuff over and over again. However, Wildermyth is refreshing as it does bring new elements to a genre that has been asking for legacy driven story play for years. Wildermyth delivers on good story telling with characters that you create and watch develop and grow.  Your characters are damaged, create families, rivalries, and bonds while affecting the world map. Its a good blend of RPG elements and RTS. A grid system for fighting and easy to follow mechanics. The game also has an easy to follow crafting system with in game events to make items legendary. I recommend it for those looks for a good RPG without too much depth that allows multiple runs without getting bored.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I keep seeing glowing reviews about the stories... but the scripts felt bland and uninspired to me. I enjoyed combat at first, but after almost 2 hours I was just too bored with it to continue. Figuring out how to use the mystic efficiently was probably the highlight. The art is beautiful, and the soundtrack is great. The plot just did not grab me at all, and I developed no fondness for any of the characters whatsoever.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I turned 50 this year. I am an old-school D&D player from the 80s.  This game is the first time since the 80s that I've truly felt that same rush, holding your breath as you make your choice and hope the dice fall your way. Mainly because, as you play with your characters and develop them and their superhero powers through multiple stories, it feels like playing with IRL friends.If you love the story and not just the combat, if holding your breath because you're sincerely worried you're about to kill your favorite character sounds like fun, do the thing. Buy the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic!      +Pros and Features that I love  Nice art style that really grows on you  Easy to learn combat, yet does not skimp on depth  Beautiful storytelling  Player choices to grow characters  Permanent consequences Semi-permanent death (Characters saved in a legacy menu where they can be reused in other campaigns!) Characters have Legacies Weapons and Armor are beautifully designed Characters fully customizable, yet develop their own personalities based on your choices or responses to events Random generation of the stories and events is thoughtfully and beautifully done! -Cons    No "Bag," or player inventory, or even a generalized party inventory.  Your characters are limited to what they can hold.          (This is also a good thing however, as it adds weight to weapon choices, and really makes you think about what you            do with a new item that you obtain.)  Looting is limited to four in-game events; There are Elemental spirits you chase to obtain an enchant, after battles and   also building a town, or some event cut-scenes. No chests, or containers to loot.           (I feel this was done in order to add a certain emotional attachment to these weapons and armors your characters             find, as each one is tied to a special random event or moment of significance.) I find myself wanting the towns to be something more. They are an area for you to craft weapons and recruit, but beyond  that, they are just for those purposes.  I feel the devs will eventually expand on it, if not, I'm sure someone will take a crack   modding it. Taverns maybe, so your characters can interact with NPC's, maybe make bad decisions drinking. Maybe those  decisions will increase drama or tension between other characters. Or perhaps your characters just blow off steam, relax a  bit. This would make them something to cherish, or something that would be worth defending from enemies, not just a tile  that pumps out a resource or two.Extended ReviewDon't let the visuals put you off if you're not into them. My initial interest was almost swayed by the visual art style, as I'm not always into games that have movement animations that are for a lack of a better term ,"static."  This was my biggest mistake; I thought that if the characters aren't moving, that I wouldn't be very attached to them, because they don't seem alive. I'm telling you, Don't make that mistake. I played the "tutorial campaign." I had three characters, two in a relationship, and one was a rival. The relationship dialogue is uplifting and adds a nice flavor to the game. The rivalry adds humor to the game, as your characters are constantly trying to get a leg up on each other,  even in battle they will mock each other, trying to show off. It makes you jump when your first character gets defeated in battle. I don't want to spoil what happens here. I found myself watching my characters grow and progress from barely winning, to actually holding their own against the enemy forces. They physically age, some obtaining scars from battle, a transformed body part, or even lost limbs. Some characters getting married and having children. Those children sometimes going on to follow their parents footsteps and help in battle.  I found myself satisfied, even after a three chapter campaign. In fact, my eyes were welling up a little bit from beating a campaign. You know what I mean, that heavy-hearted feeling you get when you beat one of your favorite games, knowing that it's over. I got that feeling from a campaign, and there are several of them. Yes, even after the second campaign, that feeling was replicated. It's a really amazing game if it can do that, not many games I played were able to give me that feeling.  Try out the game, if you've never played a turn-based RPG, let this one be your first one, as its storytelling is ultimately in your hands, which really makes it special. Don't let the "rogue like" components off-put you, on an easier difficulty, my characters rarely died throughout the entire campaign. If you want to play on a harder difficulty, I highly recommend that you do NOT reload when a character dies. Just keep going, it'll make the story more interesting. It really makes you feel more attached to the decisions your characters make, and it will really put some weight on your conscience, as they aren't invincible heroes who can just quash any problem they face.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I'm shocked at how well this game procedurally creates characters, a world, and a story you actually care about. The legacy system makes this feel even better because it allows your characters to live on past your initial playthrough with them.On top of all that the multiplayer works great and allows up to five players. Great game. Well worth 25 bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This has been an amazing game so far. Remarkable well polished considering it's currently in Early Access. With player made content so easy to create, expect this game to just keep on giving. The papercraft art style is endearing and the enemy types are varied in appearance. The world and stories flow well, and dialogue differs even in the same story depending on your character traits (be sure to get a Snarky character for some of the funniest dialogue) even events you've already witnessed differ slightly per playthrough. Heroes age, get hurt, become posessed, or reveal ancient artifacts entrusted to their families over time. Recruit more people, attempt to bargain with devils to regrow limbs or even banish spirits (just hope your own soul doesn't get lost in the process) 11/10, and it's just starting.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game. The stories are procedural but actually done really well, without the algorithmic stink that similar systems tend to have. It's easy to develop attachment to the characters, and heartbreaking to see them age out of adventuring. Mods are a thing, although I found them a bit sparse, and quite a few seem to cause gamebreaking problems. Overall I'm really enjoying this so far. Time will tell if the replayability is there... I wonder if there's really enough content to support multiple playthroughs, but for now it's an engaging, interesting, and well-told story.I recommend giving it a shot for its uniqueness more than anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Tactical combat is solid.  Dialog is surprisingly well written at first blush.  Setting feels as mythic as promised.  Balance is a bit questionable in places, but overall it feels satisfying at multiple difficulties.  After 2 and change campaigns I can recommend it so long as the paper doll graphics and super basic animations don't really bug you too much.Now 60 hours in I can say the game has not disappointed.  The novelty of being surprised by new encounters ends after about four campaigns, but that was still about 30 hours so I can complain.  My main complaint is currently how poor a choice pretty much all arm transformations are and the leg transformations aren't much better.  Basically, there isn't much reason to go further than the head unless you want to intentionally nerf a character or have already lost a limb.  Hunters seem weak compared to the other two classes.  Even with my tactical RPG chops I still take injuries in any difficulty higher than adventurer from time to time.  All that said, I'm happy with this game at full price, as is, as I totally got my money's worth out of it, and it seems like it's still getting developed.  Aside from the graphics and animation during battle, this is one of the best tactical rpgs I've played.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is a wonderful game from a small indie game studio. The comic book story events and papercraft battle scenes are beautiful and make it approachable for both young teens and adults. The turn-based tactics and character development has real depth. In fact, the character development adds to the emergent narrative and emotional experience. It is reminiscent of games like Rimworld, Crusader Kings 2, and Fire Emblem: Three Houses, which have character traits, moods, and preferences.As described above, I did run into a couple of issues with the game that hopefully will be fixed before release.I recommend this game for players that appreciate character depth, and fans of party-based, turn-based tactics games (that respect your time).I was able to learn the basics of gameplay fairly quick and there are many nuances to grasp in later playthroughs. It’s great to have an excellent, approachable game with procedural content generation and all the gameplay benefits it can provide, without being overly repetitive or the least bit bland.Read full review at Emergent Mage:
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Am struggling whether to recommend this or not, would give it a 6 out of 10 as it is. The game is decent to good, so why the negative review? Because it is definitely not as good as some people both here and in the media make it out to be. The basic premise of the game is great and when I played the first campaign I was really in awe and looking forward to more of the same in later campaigns. Turns out this is exactly what you get...the same. Already in the 2nd campaign the same random events start to repeat. The turn-based battles play out basically exactly the same no matter which opponent faction you fight against and the options you have on the map, well you guessed it, are exactly the same limited options you have in the first campaign. So what was a really fresh take on turn based tactical RPGs becomes repetitive rather quickly. Don't get me wrong I applaud the team for the game they created and I love Indie games like this one in principle. However as it currently stands the game is simply overhyped in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Do you want to fight elderitch mutated horrors with a party of lesbian warrior moms? Do you want to train a man to leap all over the place whenever an enemy violates his personal (read, 30 feet) space? Do you want to find a ghost bear, kill it, and then  a bear? if so, you have incredibly specific tastes. But don't worry, Wildermyth fills that niche, much like I fill my many abandonment issues with comfort eating.Overall 9/10 would start band of lesbian warriors mothers again
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: The tactics gameplay is good, as well as the character leveling/progression. However I found the procedurally-generated stories and characters unengaging. The writing/prose throughout the game is unique but I didn't like it. Was excited to love this game but I bounced off and haven't wanted to pick it back up.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I don't typically leave recommendations but this game has been such a standout in my library that I felt compelled to do so. I played this both solo and with a friend. This has become one of my top 10 of all time. The stories that emerged while traversing the campaigns have stuck with me long after the conclusions, so much so that several characters have become mainstays in other games and media for me. I have very few criticisms or hangups other than wanting more. More campaigns, more customization options, more weapons and armor. Just more. The developers have continued to add to the game with updates, DLC and another upcoming DLC, so my wants are being met. So I very much recommend this game. Thank you Worldwalker Games and I hope for your continued success. Take it easy all.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Casual RPG engine with intensely captivating mechanics. If you like the Final Fantasy Tactics style team building RPG you'll love this game. I was hooked with the Multi-Generational Hero system it has in place. Top Notch RPG with Workshop Access to Create Your Own Campaigns gives this gem Endless Playability.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Simple fighting with enjoyable stories. Lots of different play options whether you want to rush through to avoid early retirement or do every single thing, totally up to you! I've played through 3 of the available campaigns and have pretty minimal overlap of random events and i do ALL the things. 50 hours of enjoyment for $20? Well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: These characters are not only yours, but you get to watch and experience each and every turn and twist that a real character would have in their lives, while KNOWING that they're your very own. I've been surprised by the shocking twists of my own creations, especially when my original plans for the characters are suddenly turned onto their heads.This ends up leaving you with a near infinite amount of characters that you end up loving and engaging with, whether it be rambling to your friends about your adventures, committing yourself to writing a short story, or simply fondly remembering the feelings you felt when the character you didn't pay attention to initially ended up sacrificing themselves for their friends, only to revive again in a completely different campaign, ironically through another person's sacrifice.This game is a treasure. I highly recommend, especially if you have a good imagination and love creating fictional characters.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Plenty of things to like, but I wouldn't recommend at full price.PROS:The writing is amusing. The gameplay and progression systems are quite fun. Combat rewards being clever, and random events that permanently alter your characters are very exciting. Legacy aspects are a nice addition for something that affects your game over the long-haul across multiple campaigns.CONS:The music gets really monotonous and isn't particularly engaging. There's only a small handful of tracks and all seem to feature the same melancholy strings. The songs aren't bad per se, but compared to what you get out of a typical RPG they're disappointing.The art and animations are not good. Sure the studio is indy, or wanted to go storybook, or are being avant garde. Whatever excuse you like, it's REALLY hard to say the visuals don't look budget. I don't hold that against them; but it is the reality, unfortunately.Finally, while combat is fun, the abilities don't seem well balanced, with some clearly outshining others. Additionally, I love the system with which enemy forces strengthen over time, however the individual enemies themselves tend to be predictable, which quickly flattens combat despite the apparent variety of monsters.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This charming turn-based tactical combat RPG comes pretty close to the experience of playing a pen and paper RPG. Build up your party of heroes through progressively more challenging encounters through a procedurally generated storyline, facing off against a wide range of bad guys. Sounds ho-hum, but is actually incredibly engaging thanks to the stories which intersperse the combat encounters. These little vignettes slowly build up a back story to each of the members of your party, occasionally giving you the opportunity to make meaningful and lasting choices which can subsequently affect gameplay in small or large ways. For instance, encounters with magical beings or ancient statues can effect a variety of transformations upon your heroes, from turning them into half-man-half-wolf creatures, to converting limbs into stone and pure energy. And much more besides. These transformations can then progress as the story runs on --or not. The choice is usually yours. They give a variety of bonuses in combat, but are balanced with drawbacks. The combat itself is superficially simple but hides significant complexity and depth in its systems. The magic system, for example, is something I really like. Instead of being able to simply cast fireballs or lightning, mystics must "interfuse" with objects on the map. Depending on which object you interfuse with, your mystic can activate different abilities: interfuse with a skeletal carcass and cast bone lance at enemies, or interfuse with a pile of rocks and cast a defensive wall, a tree stump could reach out and pin an enemy, or explode in a blast of damaging splinters. There are loads of tactical options just in this one system, and each of the classes has similar depth and range of abilities to choose from, and upgrade as they accrue more experience.Each campaign takes places across a world map which takes days to weeks for your heroes to traverse. There are sometimes difficult strategic decisions about whether to split your forces to shore up defences in one area or keep them together. Between each campaign there are a variable number of years of peace (depending on how well you did) during which your party ages, forms relationships, breaks up, takes up new hobbies, has children, and more. All of these events again have small and large effects on the gameplay in the next campaign. And yes, eventually your heroes get old enough to retire. Or maybe they die in combat and their next of kin vows to take revenge.So the graphical style is simple and not to everyone's taste, but it's clear enough and it isn't going to need a beast of a PC to run it. It's also pretty cheap so really what's to stop you taking advantage and giving it a go? It's well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Something new for a change!  What a great little game. At first the art style and battle-graphics turned me off and had me "ignore" the title on steam.  With so much basement-developed shovel-ware on the platform, I worried this was another lazy amateur effort that wouldn't be worth my time.  Thankfully I started seeing it talked about on all the end-of year "Best of" articles in the gaming media and noticed the reviews were raving about it.  After a little bit of research I discovered this would totally be my type of game and the only worry I had was that the promise of procedural stories and deep character customization would be underwhelming.  I was not disappointed.  The graphics in this game, albeit primitive, are lovingly drawn and really fit folk-tale vibe the game has.  It's dark and mysterious and the stories are original and interesting.  The combat is every bit as deep (IMO) as something like XCOM but at the same time it hits the RPG notes so much better.  It's a blast to play and your party's leveling up and customization is RNG procedural as well.  You could play the same campaign 5 times and each time you'd end up with a very different party with very different parties.  Some of those parties will be much stronger than others, and you just have to make the best of the party you get.  I can't wait to play this game more.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Words can't describe how impressed I was with this title. The trailer looked incredible but of course I entered with caution and was not disappointed in the slightest. It's hard to believe this is Early Access and I'm extremely excited to see where this goes in the future. It's so rare to find an RPG where you can create your own characters and see them interacting and come to life on the screen and this game does this beautifully. I didn't want to risk messing up with characters I cared about so I simply let the characters be generated at random and wound up caring for them anyway and watching them age and have their appearances change based on what happens to them in the story is just a wonderful feeling. The randomly generated (I assume) events that occur between the characters and throughout the story really add a sense of excitement and not knowing what will happen next and I love that you are often given choices on how to handle situations, with varying degrees of success depending on the characters themselves. The combat feels great and (at least on the difficulty I played on) the overworld management didn't feel too brain-taxing and overwhelming like in other games that try similar mechanics. Overall just extremely satisfied so far and I cannot recommend this game enough :)

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is an absolutely beautiful game which blends the feel of fairy tales with an xcom style approach to tactical combat. With a dreamlike sense of time and place, the setting itself brings to mind the Otherworld of ancient Celtic Mythology. Fans of things like the Mabinogian or the Ulster Cycle will certainly appreciate it. If you aren't a mythology buff, the game itself still has so much heart and so much charm that I think you'll fall in love with The Yondering Lands all the same.The comics containing characters are surprisingly in depth, and even seeing the same event multiple times rarely gets old because there are so many dialogue variations available based on minute differences in character's personalities. Combined with the transformations that your heroes can acquire as they adventure, and the Legacy system, each character comes to life and becomes a story of their own - Something which is, I think, really quite rare for these kind of games.It has a ton of replay value, as such, and the procedural are handled in a way that they still feel like a concrete narrative - again, something quite rare for the genre, where it's often easy to see past the smoke and mirrors.Definitely worth picking up if you're a fan of storytelling, D&D and/or Xcom.

_childDocuments_.review: Never thought I could become emotionally attached to some randomly generated cardboard cutouts. _childDocuments_.review: My wife and I bought this game on a whim after looking for something new to feed our turn-based RPG cravings. Neither of us had heard of this game, but the style looked interesting. Since then we have played 11 hours in 2 days. That should give you the gist of everything below. To give some context, we are both traditional table-top gamers when we can get a group together. We ran a Pathfinder campaign out of our house, and had another campaign going by another friend. But as with many a table-top group, life got busy, and we moved far enough away that doing a campaign was difficult. So we have playing through tactical rpgs to feed our missing itch. We played through Divinity Original Sin 2 a couple of times, and started Pillars of Eternity Deadfire in turn-based mode, but we are always on the lookout for another game. This was the first that we played through, and then immediately started looking up the modding guide for how to run your own campaign in this game. The ability to do steam remote-play as well as the extensive modding support mean that this game can be so much more than simply a basic tactical RPG. If I have one complaint it is that the modding documentation is still meager, though the devs and community seem to be working on that.We played though the first campaign and loved every minute of it. The story is generic, but the fact that the game encourages you to make meaningful decisions and generates story made it so interesting. We invited to a friend to play though part of it with us using steam remote play. This worked ok, as we were using controllers, and for some reason she couldn't use her keyboard/mouse. She could see the screen, and directed us what to do, but she couldn't interact herself which was annoying. A specific word on multiplayer as this wasn't clear to us by reading the product page, this game technically has no limit to the number of players, but you shouldn't play with more than 5. This is because for most missions you can have up to 5 heroes. Additionally, everyone plays on the same screen, which can lead to all players fighting over the camera or switching characters/abilities. This can be mitigated by limiting which players can control which heroes, but it is definitely a different approach than you might be used to. We just learned to coordinate over voice chat who was controlling when.We played through the first campaign in those 11 hours and had a great time. The random events and story elements made the game fresh and unexpected. We had our hunter adopt a squirrel and our mystic attacked by a demon ghost bear. The combat wasn't too difficult on the default 'adventurer' difficulty, but we did almost have a few characters die. Hero death is considered a normal part of this game, and the game makes it easy to recruit new heroes. Some just join as part of events.Overall, I highly recommend this to those looking for a table-top like experience they can share with friends. Even alone I could see myself losing hours into the included campaigns.

_childDocuments_.review: I could say a lot about this game. I would like to say a lot about this game. Yet I know it would not be enough, my words would not do justice to this work.I have been playing video games for almost forty years and I have loved so many games, but some are real milestones.In the last twenty years I can say that I have had two great video game epiphanies: one with Dark Souls, which has put me at peace with the world of action video games, and the most recent with Wildermyth.I love the great classics in the world of CRPG, such as Torment, Arcanum, the Fallout series (the Black Isle and New Vegas chapters), Bloodlines and other more recent titles, such as Tyranny and Disco Elysium. Some elements of their stories, certain characters are engraved in my mind even after years.Wildermyth, after a few hours of playing in which I was trying to understand what was in front of me, struck me with a revelation that is incredible, like faith for an atheist: a game with randomly created characters and a procedural structure (and with many little stories written in a delightful way) can leave in me deeper marks than enormous works studied and meticulously written from beginning to end; its characters, born from the chaos of chance, are as dear to me if not more than the memorable ones from the games I mentioned earlier.Since I was a teenager I have played with the pen and paper roleplaying game, a fantastic gym for the imagination, for the ability to let go, to empathize and detach from oneself.No video game can give me the sensations of role-playing at the table with a good close-knit group, yet Wildermyth succeeds in the titanic feat of touching the same keys and evoking similar sensations. As far as I'm concerned it is one of the most incredible results achieved by a developer, and I wish these developers a life full of professional satisfaction (which would also translate into many fantastic video games for me).As I said initially, I could spend tons of words on this game, but I'll just mention one aspect, because it's something you never see in video games and that I love: this game tells great stories, extended over time; decades will pass, you will see heroes die, on the battlefield, from illness or old age, you will see delicate loves, you will see children take the place of their parents in a great and personal epic. This game will create a mythological body of stories, as done in the past by so many peoples, with all its amazing aspects, its contradictions, its ability to explain humanity through incredible stories. If you share with me the passion for video games, role-playing games, mythology, history and great stories, buy this game. The asking price does not do any justice to the splendid work of the people behind it.In closing, I take the liberty of giving one piece of advice to the players, and one to the developers, humbly hoping that it can be heard.Players, abandon yourself totally to the stories that this game tells you and accept the consequences of your choices and what happens in the world that is beyond your control. Do you make a mistake? Accept it. Is something overwhelming you? Accept it. An event pains you and you would like to go back? Don't do it, accept it. Great stories are made up of tragedies and victories, of joys and sorrows, of bright and dark days.Don't use your save files as a safety net, but always go ahead and eat one of the most amazing pieces of cake of your life.Also as regards the level of difficulty, try to understand which is the most suitable for you, so as to always have a real challenge, which is not unnecessarily frustrating but always puts you to the test, making you proceed but without opening the door for you, making you bleed.Developers, you have created an amazing game engine. What in my opinion would make the game, which already has an incredible quality, take a further qualitative leap, is a greater quantity in various aspects: many more classes for the characters, more skills, more stories, more objects. In short, most of all, so that the elements are repeated less and less between one game and another, making it a game with an incredibly extensive replay value. Give me ten, one hundred, one thousand DLCs, I'll buy them all. Just a little while ago I bought the Gorgon plush to gift it with a copy of your game. In short, as the internet teaches us: just take my money!

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: Wildermyth mixes TRPG, resource management, choose-your-own adventure and semi-persistent character options into an brew that creates your own epic stories.  A "mythology" creator, you can set forth on campaigns, have characters evolve, die, and retire - then some become legends that can appear in other tales.  A must-buy game for fans of story-driven and character-centric RPGs.Wildermyth is a game about legendary heroes - who are built from the ground up.  Starting armed with shovels and branches, your heroes battle monsters, save towns, and might just become spoken of in tales.  They may even cross over with each other as you create your own unique set of heroic stories, and their legends will grow.The game has several distinct elements that come together to make something truly great.THE SETTING: The setting is the Yondering Lands, a world of magic and spirits, old gods and new problems.  There are powers older than man both benevolent and malicious, creatures from beyond the world, and strange ancient experiments lurking.  The world feels alive, vast, and with something around every corner - and there are little setting details included in dialogues and scenes.CHARACTERS: Start out with a mix of randomized personalities.  Fitting one of three classes (Warrior, Hunter, Mystic) and chosen skills, they enter the world through a selected campaign.  You have customization options, but it's fun to just roll with what you have and be surprised!  Personalities will influence later events and choices in the game.CAMPAIGNS: There are set of story campaigns, as well as options to play ones with no overarching plot except "battle these monsters."  As the lands and events are randomized, no two games are alike.STORY MOMENTS: As you play, story moments appear, many based on character backgrounds, personalities,previous occurrences and your choices.  These can range from little character moments to life-altering transformations.  Build some backstory, get a cute pet, find some gear, or turn into a werewolf.RELATIONSHIPS: Characters relations change with each other.  Characters form rivalries, fall in love, become friends, have kids, etc.  Each relationship affects gameplay mechanics and in-game dialogue.  You also get options to make decisions based on these and have some power to control them.AGE AND CHANGE: Characters age change over time.  Eventually in long campaigns they may retire, passing on wisdom to the next generation - perhaps their own children.  Others may meet more interesting fates depending on your choices.OVERLAND: The overland game involves wandering from place to place to scout areas, recruit people, build defenses, etc.  As you play you are constricted by time, so you have to decide what to do carefully - as time goes on monsters invade areas, disasters happen, and other challenges may occur.  Fortunately you can split the party - which requires some planning and strategizing.BUILDING, CRAFTING, RESOURCES: As you travel and scout, you can secure areas that can yield resources, chances to recruit, places to rest, etc.  If you're worried about monster invasions, you can take time to build defenses.  You may also have to carve passes or build bridges - which permanently alter the land.  These too take time, so chose carefully . . .BATTLE: Battling is done on turn-based tile boards that delightfully resemble pop-up books.  Battles are EXTREMELY tactical and require thought even on average difficulty.  Scenery provides cover and is destructible.  Doors can hide enemies.  Fire can rage out of control - or provide needed illumination.  Different skills provide different advantages.  Finally magic is unique - mystics "interfuse" with objects and that provides them and their party various attacks and boosts.BECOME A LEGEND: Character death, retirement, or campaign completion can lead to characters becoming part of your Legacy.  These are heroes you can call on again and again, creating a web of adventures with "new" versions of them. Legacy characters can be upgraded by winning campaigns, making them more powerful next they appear.THE STYLE: Wildermyth does all of the above with a delightful storybook style - everything looks like pop-up books, comic pages, etc.Wildermyth is your personal fantasy adventure-drama.  Reunite characters with lost parents, build a tomb to a great hero and write their name in legend, visit ancient spirits to receive strange and wonderful blessings, and more.  It's not just a game - it feels like a revolution.This all being said, the game has a few flaws.  No show-stoppers, more ones to be aware of:- Difficulty even on the average adventurer level doesn't leave room for carelessness.  This is a game that requires you to think.- The overland elements where you travel, scout, and build are simple at heart - but can be overwhelming when you're juggling time and a large party.  These take more thought than is obvious, and it would be nice to have a few more time management tools.- The game is engrossing, but intense.  It's one you need to take a break from, as delightful as it is.- The game is randomized.  It is possible (and I have personally experienced this) to have unfair maps for battle or overland adventure.  Difficulty can be "swingy."- The help is basic and honestly needed more detail or an optional tutorial.Because of the challenges, save often and don't feel bad reloading an older save.  These flaws are, again, minor.  They in no way detract from what this game is - an achievement.Wildermyth is a game of human moments and large scope, a game of playing epic tales of very human people.  It's a milestone in RPGs that others will - and should - hold up as an example.For some, this is going to be your new obsession for a long time - and maybe one you return to.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Suddenly one of my favorite games. Queer-friendly. The stories feel relatable, and often use themes that feel integritous to me. I'm getting attached to the characters. The procedural generation feels smooth and organic, I can feel my choices determining the story in complex ways. Mod-friendly. Just a wonderful feeling game overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I would best describe this game as a love child between RimWorld (creating narratives, randomized events, survival elements, crafting, customization) and D&D. There is a multiplayer option but playing this solo is a fantastical adventure I highly recommend. You have the ability to build up a heartfelt campaign and lay stepping stones leading to how you want the story to (hopefully) end. The story telling elements are magical, the graphics feel cozy and solid, and combat feels easily sleek. Gameplay could potentially be confusing at first to those who have not played similar games before. Try using your first campaign as a "practice run", which will help you understand the basics better before hopping into a dedicated save.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Really loving this game!Playing with a friend and we are both totally in love with the art style and the story. The combat has been fun, and the perks are interesting. We have been a little confused on how exp is calculated, but we aren't bothered by it (was just something we weren't sure on).If you like story RPGs with a load of cuteness, consider Wildermyth recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I was intrigued after seeing the "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating on Steam despite never hearing about this game before, and after beating the first campaign I will say it deserves the praise it gets. Reminds me a lot of Rouge Legacy meets XCOM. What I think what will keep you playing is the war stories you will generate.For example on my first clear:- My leader who is a romantic tried to start an affair despite their spouse being there and almost wound up getting enslaved by monsters.- Said spouse wound up transforming into a Crow Man wizard with wings sprouting out the back and their arm turning into Raven talons. He would later become a Medieval Fantasy AirBnB agent.- Their best friend whose been there since the beginning wound up getting mutated into an Gorgoniod and getting a ethereal bunny that used to be a sword as a pet.- One of my new recruits, a Cowardly Poet, wound up with a peg-leg after getting separated from the group during a major battle (whoops). But then...- ...he had a daughter who joined my heroes and wound up ALSO getting maimed and got a hook to replace the left-hand that got chopped off. Like father like daughter!In short, I do recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game enough.In my last battle, the heroes defended a keep, a rookie, a warrior with a clockwork axe and an aged hunter, George. The defence started well, with the heroes boldly meeting the attackers and fending them off from the east, whilst George took some farmhands protecting their village to the south to meet the enemy. The battle seemed in our favour, the rookie slayed his first enemy whilst the warrior took on the biggest enemy she could find. George and the other defenders had engaged on their side too, and they seemed to have the high ground for a while, until more came. Huge lumbering creatures had appeared, and ran down the farmhands, who had bitten off more than they could chew. George knew he had to regroup with the others, like they had done when their allies had fallen before. He hid himself in the keep and began moving up towards his comrades. He had almost made it when they came, a horde of monsters larger than anything he'd seen in all his 30 years of adventuring made it through the west gate, cutting him off, they had found his hiding place. George had seen bad situations before, but this felt different. Like there was no way out. And so he ran, he ran as far and as fast as he could, just barely making it beyond his loyal warrior friend. She had set up a defensive line, but it was thin, and they were closing in fast. Worse still, they hadn't finished cleaning up the east side of the keep, and swiftly another beast turned on Ryvon, forcing him to turn tails and flee, his face gashed that would leave a scar for life.George shot down the fell beast in a single strike, but it was too late. With their enemies on the west side, the pair decided to disengage slowly, striking the furthest enemy from the pack and making a swift retreat again. The warrior, Hyuna, managed to slip back into the castle to face off against the foes moving to flank them, but the beasts burst their way through the wall, catching her off guard. She thought about how she would spend her last moments, the people she'd saved and the regrets she had garnered along the way, but in that moment, she got a lucky break. Her clockwork axe had taken the hit, and although she couldn't fight this battle, she was able to escape with her life.Only George remained now, and he was outnumbered 8 to 1. He resorted to guerilla tactics, weaving in and out of range and vision, his years of experience doing the work between volleys of arrows. Only one remained now. Though they both fired a shot, neither of them landed against their target. Breathing heavily from his prior wounds, he turned to face the creature one last time. He fired a shot. It landed. But the beast was only maimed, and fired back with a shot of its own, dealing him a serious injury to his arm. His story might have ended there if not for his instinct to counterattack. With the last of his strength, he fired one last arrow, taking it down and successfully repelling the invaders. By nothing short of a miracle, he survived (seriously, 0 hp), but it came at the cost of his hand. He would never fire his bow again.Whilst this story was a highlight for me, stories like this happen every 15 minutes in this game. Yes, it's a little slow to start, but once you get a feel for those characters, their choices, mistakes and their eventual deaths are all yours. If you're intrigued by this game and this sounds like your cup of tea, I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal! _childDocuments_.review: A lovely game, full of action, simple yet beautiful artwork and (this is the best part imho) epic stories.Though round based fights with a maximum of steps/actions usually aren't my thing I still enjoyed the game so much since all the different characters, their relationships, moods and development are priority number one.I'm looking forward to many future adventures <3
