_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game! Had a random character during my first campaign lose her arm. The party made sure she got to safety, then after she recovered she came back ready to go with a hook hand. She even gained a new ability from it! The level of character depth feels very engaging. Can't wait to play with some friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking for a game with tabletop role-play and strategy elements for some time now. There are many that fill this requirement, but what I was *really* looking for was a story that was catered to my characters and usually the characters are just tokens in a pre-established world with very little variation from your decisions. Well, it looks like Wildermyth managed to toss all my wants for a game at this time into the mix, sprinkle in some great art, mellow celtic-like music, developers from the great nation of Texas, and charm to last for eternity. Wildermyth in a nutshell.I was skeptical of the various reviews saying that you'd become attached to your various random characters but after playing the first campaign, the reviews weren't far off. The game's ability to do procedurally generated story elements is just pure genius. I quickly grew to like my characters and even after one of them was maimed and had a strange stone face mask affixed to their face, I ended up liking that character even more. They grew and changed as the story went on and I was sad to see them retire or die. My fighter, Sam, was a Guardian pretty early on and in true role-play fashion, the game came up with a story beat where he joined a group of turtle-like beings to become a real "turtle" like fighter. Looking at it objectively, it's a little cheeky, but the game managed to make it profound and memorable while I was playing through his story. Each of the three main characters had a great story beat and even my "turtle" and "stone-faced" lady ended up having a child that joined the journey (though she was never developed by the end of the campaign, sadly).If you're looking for a game with mellow vibes, good music, fantastic visuals of the water-color paper-craft variety, and a story that changes with each play through, then, really, look no further. Last, this game can be played on a baked potato, so there's really no reason *not* to get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is a very special kind of game.  One part tactical combat, two parts storytelling.  There are scripted campaigns as well as "legacy" campaigns that proceduraly generate a narrative in a way that does not seem artificial.  As events unfold, it feels like the choices you make in early chapters shape how your characters grow and develop relationships.The legacy aspect of the game is one of the strongest features.  At the end of a campaign, you can take a number of your current characters into "legacy," meaning that they will join a stable of previous characters that can pop up in subsequent playthroughs with some of their previous abilities pre-built into them.  The more times you choose to bring forward a character, the stronger and stronger they become.  This is reminescent of folk heroes recurring in multiple myths and legends across cultures.  Much like how the King Arthur romances of the Medieval period drew on Welsh legendary figures, combing them into new narratives that matched the needs of the present day.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game! I enjoy the paper "pop-up" book art style. The stories that are in here are fantastic. I play with my friends and fiance and we (try our hardest) to voice act our characters out and say our lines while we play it makes the game 10000% better, even though its already a fantastic game! Its challenging, and fun. I suggest anyone thats played D&D and/or divinity to give this a shot. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased Wildermyth expecting a 'Darkest Dungeon for kids' type game, and was blown away by how wrong I was. While the game is very accessible and appealing to all ages, it is definitely in its own category. My first play through felt vital and engaging, and I found myself quickly investing in my party members. While being entirely different from any TTRPG I've played, it did a great job capturing the feel of a traditional tabletop game.The dialog can get repetitive after a game or two, and it can be a bit over the top even from the beginning. I think the writers took a lot of chances to give that 'storybook' feeling, and not all of them paid off. I still find the stories enjoyable, even if I roll my eyes occasionally.As far as actual game play, it is extremely easy to learn and enjoyably challenging to master. I found myself trying new combinations of skills and equipment, feeling out different play styles and systems. Players of all experience levels will be able to engage in combat - and likely succeed!I give this game 4.5 out of 5 stars. It has a great deal of style and heart, and I love going back to it again and again. The occasionally amateurish writing and somewhat shallow game play mechanics set it back slightly, but only just.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun game. Watch zeroes become heroes. Combat feels like it has weight and it's satisfying to use the magic system once you figure it out. Save towns from roving armies, take on random quests to earn special gear for your characters. Bring back a legend from an old campaign into your new one.The game is great. The only downside is that the conversations are a bit hard to follow at times. "Poetic" personality characters especially talk a lot of nonsense from out of nowhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. The writing is insanely charming and well done. The art is absolutely amazing and beautiful. The combat is fun enough. I really grew to love my characters and found myself save scumming to make sure none of them die until /I/ was ready for them to go. There's a lot to do and I can see it's easy to get lost in this game for hours. I almost didn't get this game because the screenshots don't do it justice. If you're even slightly interested in what you see, just get the game. It's 100000% worth it. Oh, and it also has a modding community which is an added bonus.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game very swiftly hooked me, and it's really good.The biggest chunk of gameplay is the combat, and it's the standard turn-based affair with skills and cooldowns and whatnot. It's satisfying and feels good to pull off some plays.What really sets this game apart though, is the way your characters have so much narrative focus. Events happen on the overmap and before encounters, and they are written so well and it adds so much. It's like a randomly generated Dungeons and Dragons campaign, and it's so captivating. You can feel genuine connection to these heroes you watch grow and become stronger, all the while forming relationships and interacting with the zany fantasy world you're in. The world really feels alive.It's got that 'just one more turn' quality to it, and I write this after my first foray into the game that turned into an almost ten hour session. My eyes burn.Not only is this game massively replayable, but it's also moddable! Easily so, too.If you like story generators like Rimworld but ever wanted one to be a turn based RPG, here is your answer! Go nuts, this game is .

_childDocuments_.review: What a snoozefest. 3 classes, two of which are extremely uninspired (warrior and hunter). The mage is interesting, but ultimately not as useful as the warrior or hunter due to limitations in the environment.The auto content generator is super dumb. After trying to understand what was happening for the first 30 minutes, I just started auto skipping everything. The conversations make zero sense. GPT-2 storytelling systems are not ready for primetime.The XCOM style map system was lame as well. There was almost no agency to anything I chose to do. The only major choice was to rush secure or get an item. After equipping my team, I never chose item as the wasted time made no sense for an item that probably sucked anyway.End of era crafting was ok, I guess, but ultimately left me wanting. I just don't see how this is overwhelmingly positive. There isn't a single system that does anything particularly better than the myriad of other games that exist out there doing the same thing. In most cases, the systems are barebones and oversimplified. 4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth's a wonderfully charming RPG that introduces surprisingly involved and oddly coherent stories as you journey with your characters. Stories that morph and change between chapters while your favourite little heroes in each campaign build upon who they are in your mind, through your choice of actions and their consequences. Allow yourself to get invested in them, their triumphs, defeats, banter and quirks-- and you'll be rewarded :)
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game. It gets the feel of playing D&D down better than any other game. Now, that is the "feeling" not the mechanics or lore. While games such as Baldur's Gate might get the mechanics and lore down very well, and games such as Pillars or Divinity try to also capture a similar mechanics and a similar feel, none of them truly captures the feeling of a group of friends sitting around a table playing D&D like Wildermyth. It has different mechanics and lore, and actually goes out of its way to present a fantasy world that is actually purposefully different than the more traditional LoTRs copy fantasy worlds, but it captures that feeling of playing D&D with a group of friends shockingly well. A mixture of fairly good comedy, a simple but well working Xcom-like mechanics system, a lack of an inventory system that surprisingly makes the game flow a lot better than most other RPGs, very simple and easy modding system, and a procedural generation system for campaigns/quests/maps/characters that actually works smoothly enough to not feel like sudden random bits are being forced together which most games that feature procedural generation can feel like. Now that all said it is of course in early access and has some bugs and rough edges and all that. But with that "feeling" of playing a game of D&D combined with Xcom-like mechanics, Wildermyth is a good game that has a ton of potential. Easily worth a buy even in its early access form! 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: If you like DnD style story telling that doesn't take itself too seriously. If you like Fire Emblem style battles. If you like randomness. This game is for you. I am addicted to this game. For a little title, it's taking all of my time. It's fun and I cannot wait for future updates. I see the base of a truly classic game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is a beautiful game that will satisfy players who appreciate atmosphere, character permanence and build experimentation.The mechanics and modes all come together to provide a tale of your heroes. None of the gameplay mechanics or modes are great on their own, but they all work together to push forward the tale of your characters.  Capturing the atmosphere and feel of your characters is where the game really shines.  The writing and artistry are beautifully weaved with procedural generation. You will have certain characters become your favourites and appreciate the losses they suffer, even if they are technically gameplay setbacks!  There's also enough variety in character options and builds to make everyone feel distinct.The only advisory I have is for those searching for pure gameplay in tactics and strategy.  While the systems in this game are good, there are better options out there that focus on those gameplay aspects.If you have interest in developing characters and experiencing charming tales through gameplay, check out Wildermyth!

_childDocuments_.review: I played this for a few hours and it is one of my favorite games ever. It is like 1-player DND, and can be more. Easy character creation (though, I would have liked a bit more customization in stats), simple but memorable quests, and plenty of role-playing options.Edit: I played longer and it's not in my favorites anymore. It's still good, but the flaws are seen clearer now.--Issues--Combat: the reverse button works when it wants to. You only get one reverse per character per combat. This wouldn't be a problem if the fighting controls weren't so prone to mess up. You'll hit Z by accident and end your turn, or click the wrong square and do the wrong thing...and everyone will die.This game relies on the risk of failure, but you can easily fail by a mistake of sloppy game design.Music: They have like 2 music tracks. It gets repetitive and annoying fast.They should update that.Lighting: It's kind of hard to see some things on screen since objects become see-through and the cursor jumps all over the places randomly. No actual bugs, just kind of sloppy design there.Keyboard vs controller: You CAN use both in theory. In practice, use a keyboard.Story quality: The gorgon story is great. But they get progressively less interesting and the writing gets worse as they progress. By the time I was on the final one, I felt like I was watching a cartoon for kids. And calling characters "duckie" is not a personality.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: i avoided buying Wildermyth for a long time because i figured it would be a moderate time sink for me. That wasn't wrong. Some of the pros:- Native Linux support. At nearly 17 hours in it's run flawlessly for me on Linux Mint 20.1 on a moderately-powerful i3-based NUC computer. (Trivia: turning down the "light points" config option to 10 reduced its CPU load/temperature *considerably* on this machine.)- Beautifully-crafted. Vaguely reminiscent of Microprose's *Darklands* while being nothing at all like it. The papercraft-style artwork is outstanding.- Gamepad support. A couple aspects are considerably easier with a mouse (specifically, upgrading items via the crafting interface), but the game is otherwise comfortable to use with a gamepad.- Forces difficult choices. Its minimalistic inventory system forces the player to carefully choose who gets what equipment and what they'll discard if their space runs out. There is no inventory micro-management: assigning equipment is permanent.- Forces other difficult choices. Numerous random encounters force the player to make choices which the player "knows" will change the game, but may not know exactly how. (i'm still waiting to find out what chaos my inadvertent releasing of the Vulture Queen will cause.)- Characters age and retire and some die of disease or as a side-effect of encounter choices. This forces the player to keep an influx of younger folks to take over party roles as the older ones cycle out. This part of the game is largely background noise, though - there's no micromanagement involved. Sometimes the PCs will have kids (all "off screen" - that's not an active part of the game) and they'll join the party automatically when they get old enough.- When a PC is knocked out in a fight, the player is given the option to have them retreat but be permanently maimed (e.g. losing a leg) or to have them go out in a blaze of glory (dealing a massive blow before they expire).- Multiple difficulty settings which can be changed at any time, with the minor caveat that starting off at one difficulty and changing it later will still have some aspects of the original difficulty (namely, timer-based effects which have shorter or longer timers on different difficulty levels are not adjusted retroactively when changing the difficulty).- It has about 8 or 10 campaigns, two of which allow the player to reuse characters which completed, or were retired from, a previous campaign.- A great deal of randomness in events and storylines, adding to the replay value of any given campaign. Four(?) of the campaigns are composed entirely of random events, so are extremely replayable.- Though fantasy-themed, this is (thank goodness) not an elfgame. There are neither elves nor dwarves nor orcs. There are many fantastical elements, but its human-centric.Neither pro nor con:- Short campaigns. At nearly 17 hours in, i'm just over halfway through my 3rd campaign.- Characters who complete a campaign or retire during it are added to one's "Legacy" - like a history of characters. Those characters can be re-used in later campaigns, but only in those campaigns specifically designed to include Legacy characters. This Legacy system, and the way Legacy characters are *slowly* improved over time, will appeal to those who feel compelled to Collect 'em All. That's not me, but some people enjoy that type of thing.- Full control over character gender (including the 21st-century "non-binary" designation), sexual preference (for purposes of almost-entirely randomly-assigned romantic pairings within the game), and appearance.- Lots of reading is required. The random encounters are almost entirely mini-stories, often with choices to be made. They're well-written and thematic, but sometimes we just want to hack and slash.Cons:- Aside from a few minor UI-related quirks, none at all, and certainly nothing game-breaking nor rage-inducing.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly addictive turn-based party RPG with a ton of storybook charm in which you can customise all your characters, navigate a story with them and watch as they suddenly adopt pet squirrels, have babies, or develop crazy magic limbs or tails. 𝓰𝓪𝓶𝓮𝓹𝓵𝓪𝔂It's a grid-based, turn-based strategy game where you control a party of characters when fighting, and out of the fights you wander around a map overworld. In terms of the battles, it's typical turn-based fare, with attack ranges, varying weapons and skills, sneak attacks, crits, hit chances and damage displays. Think X-COM, but less guns. The skills you get for your character are rogue-like, in that when you level up, you get a choice out of a pool of skills to pick from, so you don't have complete control of your character tree, but the options are always fairly solid. The magic system in this game is fun and different -- you don't just pick a group of spells and sling them, but rather the environmental cues around your characters (like mountains of stone or stacks of firewood) dictate what spells you have access to and your spell range.On the overworld, you basically explore regions and fortify cities that grant you resources at the end of each section of your campaign, and sometimes there are objectives to carry out (go to X city, defeat Y at Z). Like X-COM, there are timers of when enemies grow stronger and gain additional traits, as well as timers for when invasions happen. The interesting thing in this game is that your characters will age and develop relationships as your game goes on, so you'll end up fighting with the children of your starter characters. If your characters get incredible, you can add them to your game's Legacy, where they'll show up in future games in different ways. This last bit is very cool and fun.There are a variety of difficulties in this game, ranging from very easy, where you can focus on enjoying the story, to modes where it gets harder and you're having to manage your characters, recruitments and LP very wisely (if a character falls in combat, they can either get maimed and fall back, taking on stat penalties for the rest of the game, or they'll die permanently). During my first campaign in the normal difficulty, my characters got maimed constantly, but by the second campaign I had learned how to manage my characters and upgrade my gear, and I had a much easier time (maybe too easy). I'm going to bump it up further next playthrough, but it's good to keep in mind that the battle system isn't immensely complex, so if you're looking for Fire Emblem-style difficulty and planning, you won't find it here.𝓼𝓽𝓸𝓻𝔂This game is so incredibly fun and mischievous! There are larger campaigns that you can run, and in the campaign there's a main narrative but also just a TON of random encounters that can happen as you progress. These random encounters seemed to be pulled from a pool of events, and they're all written so cheekily or so superbly. You'll get strangely poignant moments, laugh-out-loud references or meta-moments, and you'll come to grow attached to your characters as you navigate them through these events (there are usually dialogue options or story direction options). Essentially, in each campaign you're leading a bunch of characters through a sort of "legend" or "myth" where you basically fight and vanquish the bad guys. The overarching story isn't really why you're here -- it's all the moments and choices along the way. Sometimes half of your party will be pulled away for a character's side-quest, delving deep into their past, or other times your character might suddenly decide to chase down a creature. You, of course, get the options to pursue these side-quests or not, but they're always fun and lead to character development and stat bonuses or great loot.With workshop and the ease of adding narrative encounters, the sky's going to be the limit for this game. One thing is that I think the game would benefit from more tags that your characters can acquire  -- so, your characters can be cowardly or brave or a leader, etc., but I think if characters picked up traits from encounters that lead to subsequent related encounters (eg. a character likes baking, takes on more baking quests), you'd get a bit more depth with character-building in this choose-your-own-adventure format.𝓶𝓾𝓼𝓲𝓬It's fitting and very D&D/bard-esque, if that makes any sense. It matches, it's appropriate and it's catchy. Not much to say here.𝓪𝓮𝓼𝓽𝓱𝓮𝓽𝓲𝓬𝓪𝓵𝓵𝔂Don't let any graphics snobbery get in your way of experiencing this game -- it is absolutely charming. The simpler art style and paperlike style works because it feels like you're watching a storybook adventure unfold before your eyes. It may look average at first, but it quickly grows on you and is incredibly quirky and well-done. It's coherent and detailed where it needs to be, and all the items and bits of gear are things that you can see when you equip them on your character, which is always nice. They've done a really excellent job of making you feel like you're inhabiting the world of a storybook or -- dare I say it -- a book of myths. Ha ha.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I bought it on a Friday afternoon and played 14 hours by Saturday night. It's like playing tabletop with yourself. It's a tactical RPG that steals the best things from so many places. Like the best roguelikes, the abilities you get are transformative and feel game-breaking. The missions are quick and violent, and remind me of Gloomhaven, but less tedious. The storytelling reminds me of the rich, moody experiences of King of Dragon Pass or Fallen London. But really it takes inspiration from those things and creatives an innovative, creative new whole. It answers the question of whether games are art.To get the most out of the story you really have to take your time and engage with the characters; care about their connections and uniqueness. Pay attention to the emergent stories they create with each other and fill in some of the blanks yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This just wasn't for me. There are just many, many sentences where one of four things seems to be happening:1. Somebody was a creative writing major in college and thinks this is what "literature" should sound like.2. It was AI generated and never read by a native English speaker.3. It was procedurally generated and never read by a native English speaker.4. It was shoved through a google translator and never read by a native English speaker.The bigger problem is, it's not even consistent in its weirdness. There are at least two people writing this, based by the "written by" bylines (which is immersion breaking to have in game, but whatever). One of the writers abuses purple prose like it hurt him as a child - something doesn't die, "its bones fold", rocks don't "clatter", they "chatter" like teeth. The other writer writes simply and with characterization, and her writing is much easier to engage with. Having both styles in the story is a poor storytelling decision, because there's no consistent tone being used to engage the reader. It also makes it harder to pick up the meta-humor in the game - is this deliberately self-reflective? Is it just really bad purple prose? Who knows.Most games these days use multiple writers to craft an entire game's story, but there's a reason you can't tell who wrote what by the time it's published - it's all ultimately one cohesive story being told by a single narrator. Even D&D style single player games do this - think of the narrator from Baldur's Gate 3 or Pillars of Eternity II. There's a clear, natural "voice" in their writing that makes the world easily accessible. You can argue that this doesn't have that kind of big studio funding, and I agree, but writing is generally the cheapest and easiest thing to fix during game production. Wildermyth fails to do that, and it's so consistently immersion breaking, I ended up getting a refund.All that being said, the art is charming and the gameplay is fun. If you're on the fence, watch some gameplay videos and see if you're going to love or hate the style of prose this one guy writes, because that really will make or break the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Feeling like micro-4x, Wildermyth combines turn-based strategy with dynamic character building on the "campaign" map. Replay grants both meta-progression for your favorite characters and a newly generated story each play. 100% recommend this game for fans of rogue-lite strategy with a heavy lean towards dynamic character based storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This is currently one of my favorite games of all time. Being able to create your own pantheon of heroes is amazing, especially because you do grow attached to them throughout the course of a campaign. Seeing them in future play throughs is amazing, and being able to watch their lineage grow so you can play with their children and sometimes even have those kids in the same campaign as their parents is another nice twist. Character customization is strong, too. Each hero has their own unique personality, and their own side quests that explore more of who they are -- while also boosting their retirement age! That's right, if your heroes don't fall in battle, they'll retire!The writing is wonderful, and helps bring the game to life in a way that makes you care about the world these characters inhabit and the characters themselves. It's also pretty funny at times, and the way the characters speak to one another has made me laugh out loud on more than one occasion. Gameplay can be adjusted to be welcoming to newcomers of tactics based games. And for those who've got more experience you can adjust the difficulty to your liking. Difficulty also scales up throughout the course of the campaign. The classes balance against one another nicely, and each role contributes to the success of the campaign. I've completed all of the story campaigns, but keep going back to play the procedurally generated ones that are literally made up on the fly as you go. No hero has the same story, and no play through is the same. Seriously. Get this game! It's hard to find anything to be disappointed about in its style.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much better than expected.Its a digital tabletop game basically, with a strategic map where you have to scout and annex territories and deal with events (really cool ones, that cause shapeshifts, magical incantations that change character classes, etc), and combat takes place in tactical, turn based maps with a lot of interesting abilities and quick gearing and leveling.As time passes by, several enemy types "decks" keep beingu pgraded, so you never face overpowered or underpowered fights, and being efficient is rewarded.It has one of the most interesting and inovative magic system in a LONG while. You bind to objects in the scenario and those items have unique effects you can activate - destroying the object, so actually that's what counts as caster "ammo", not spell slots, mana, etc. Those bound items can also provide other bonuses depending on your character upgrades (I.E. give buffs like flaming attacks to close allies, ensnare close enemies, etc).This is a high quality game, it's hard to describe in a few words. If you like strategic campaigns/tactical combat games, give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, I'm not sure that most of this game is fun, exactly. The battle camera is a bit annoying, there isn't a lot of engaging audio-visual synergy and a lot of the time, it feels as though there isn't really a decision to be made, either in battle or on the campaign map. These parts aren't bad, they just feel like they're lacking a bit of spark.What the game certainly is in spades though, is interesting. The story elements are really imaginative and the presentation of those sections is a real pleasure. That whole part of the game is ultra well done. The reason that the battles and campaign map feel lacklustre is that the story sections are just so good that it's hard for the supporting sections not to be left behind.I've played through the first campaign and so far, I'd give it not quite 9/10, but close. A sequel that leaves the story sections as they are and works on making the other parts more fun and engaging could be 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: When I started this game I was excited to play, looking into the customization options I noticed a 'they/them' option, as well as an attraction option, a giveaway that a game supports the message. I told myself if it's just an option and the default is standard opposite gender attraction basic pronouns then it was OK. But it's never just an option. It's an agreement to be bombarded with the same tired narrative though every form of media consumed. The further I got into the game the more I came across it, a woman mourning the death of her wife... Not much... but when the topic is brought up I can't help but think about how we were sold that lie. That Gay people just want to love each other, but Pride becomes ever more about fetish, obscenity and orgies... All while we are told that our kids must attend or we are bigots. So all I can see in a loving gay couple in a story is the grooming of children. As far as the game play of this game goes, it is a mix of X-com and visual novels. Lots of story which changes your characters, gives them abilities or transforms them. Combat is turn based with using the abilities of your team to defeat monsters as well as using terrain to reduce damage. I very much enjoy that the campaigns are 3 or 5 chapters long, long enough to tell a story, short enough to let you have a break. I would say I could also enjoy a long story SAGA, with the generational aspects of the game it would be really cool to see multiple generations in a game
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love it! The only challenge is choosing to raise which character up to mythwalker legacy level as I have grown attached to most of them.I love all the transformations of my characters too, especially the crow, celestial and wolf look. Fantastic!Would like more enemies and campaigns as I already beat all of them! Looking forward to DLCs <3
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: What a refreshing game.  If you are looking for something in the old-skool pen and paper catagory, to entertain you OR you and four friends (or just you and a single friend)... get Wildermyth.  Yes, it has some reading.. a fair amount of it, however, this is part of what I'm liking.. this "refreshing" take; you will want to read it to see what has happened to you.  It's funny and will definately get the discord/teamspeak laughing. The legacy system lets your children.. yes you can get married and have children that eventually take over the adventuring for you, build upon your family story. The three class archetypes of Warrior, Hunter and Mystic can be fully customized as you level and select a new skill line. The forge lets you gear-up, incursions into your secured lands get larger and larger, players can be maimed (eye removed, limb amputated and so forth) or even mutated. Give Wildermyth a try.. at only 15.74€ its SOLID entertainment!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game worth buying?YesThis is a game where you make choices. Those choices have consequences, and they may end up killing your entire party. If your hardcore like me you can even make it so those choices are written in stone with no due overs. Great game for those who like that kind of thing. Does this game get repetitive ?At times.. However, I still love this game. You can find your self wanting to play through it over and over regardless.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool art style. Characters have personalities, and their stories and interactions in your company really compliment the story lines in the campaigns. You characters can have children, die, and pass along their legacies. And your really good characters can live on in the next campaign. Interesting board game, turn-based combat. Great music. Not typically my kind of game, but this one too fun not to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Been playing this literally all weekend during a heat wave and can't put it down which is a HUGE endorsement. Just...get it if you like ttrpgs, tactics games, or if the concept sounds even vaguely appealing to you. Super looking forward to any/all updates and new additions to this game, but there's also mod support, which is pretty sweet.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing this game while it was in early access and i was unsure at first but once i finished my first campaign I was immediately hooked and i waited in anticipation for each update and i watched as my character created an intricate and complex lore and fell in love, made mortal enemies, got married and had children of their own who then continued down there parents path and finish what they started. There were some emotional moments when some of my favourite heroes fell in the fray and we buried them in a dignified grave and carried on. This game never tires me and whenever I'm having a bad day i just boot it up and play a chapter. Each different enemy faction is so diverse and unique and each character so different. I can truly say that this game is a timeless gem of amazing stories, laughs and lore. I highly reccommend this to people who love a good story and a bunch of laughs. I guarantee you will have a good time!
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: Wildermyth is definitely an interesting game but it just wasn't for me. The over the map gameplay feels simple, slow and uninteresting. The resources and craftable items feel kind of bland. There isn't a lot of challenging elements to plan for. You just go from tile to tile and scout, fight, build and move on; there isn't a lot of reasons to do anything other than that so you don't make many important choices which is what I missed in general. The game also feels sluggish all around. The zoomed in combat sequence can be challenging at times but often feels boring due to the slow animation speed and having to walk from one end of the battlefield from the other in turn-based mode. The speed of interaction seemed to drag on whenever I wanted to control my heroes. One thing I liked about the game was that you could customize quite a bit of things with your characters and it was entertaining to see your heroes go through permanent changes like getting maimed or being influenced in persistent ways by story segments. It was also fun to see your characters' avatar change as they pick things up in the world. They not only change in the combat area but also in the story segments. I will also add that I liked the unique storytelling in this game though I found myself skimming the text quite often which is not something I do as I love getting lost in the writing. I do think it has a lot of great moments but didn't quite come together as an engaging experience in the end. It is hell of a production but was unfortunately not something I wanted to keep playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Wildermyth

_childDocuments_.review: is a turn-based battle RPG where you gather a small band of wannabe heroes and help them grow into legendary monster-stompers. Use the three classes of warrior, hunter, and mystic to create a crack company of heroes, and take up to five into battle at once. With the ability to randomly generate campaigns, maps, and personalities of your heroes, expect many hours of hunting down Gorgons and bringing peace back to the land.:Characters, monsters, and battlefields are drawn in a charming storybook style, which really adds to Wildermyth's goal of presenting a good story with every playthrough. Admittedly, the characters sometimes look a bit awkward in story cutscenes, as characters are always in their default action poses, which makes them look a bit tense even when it doesn't make sense storywise. This is a minor gripe though. It will be great to see if the developers decide to add other playable races later on. :Two main aspects: the campaign map and the battlefield. On the campaign map you direct the movements of your company in their various tasks, from preparing the defenses of tiles to recruiting new members, building bridges to attacking monsters, and so on. Securing tiles will give you resources that can be used to improve the gear of your heroes. Overall, depending on how many chapters a given campaign has you will direct the company to its goals, with most moves and events culminating in a battlefield skirmish.On the field of battle, you will direct up to five members of the party as they confront one of the various "decks," or different special armies, of monsters. Each side taking turns, develop strategies based on the strengths and weaknesses of the different hero classes to master the field. Be warned, with every victory the "deck" of monsters improves against you, either gaining a new monster type or gaining buffs in health or damage. Be sure to distribute loot strategically to your party members, and make sure to level up weapons and armor with the resources gained. After campaigns are completed, you have the option to add your favorite heroes to your Legacy, which will give you the ability to play as them in future campaigns. Over the course of multiple campaigns then, you can promote your favorites five ranks from Folk Hero to Mythwalker, writing countless stories and smashing infinite monsters. Overall, Wildermyth is very enjoyable, and its great to see devs that are working on implementing more and more game elements. The workshop is at the time of this writing lacking somewhat, but there is potential for a great number of mods that could add much more variety. Certainly worth full price, especially worth it if on sale. What stories will you tell?:

name: NUTS
detailed_description: Gear up your research caravan, boot up your GPS, spread out your map and head for the depths of Melmoth Forest. As a rookie field researcher, you’ll place cameras during the day, and watch the footage at night, tracking the movements of a scurry of squirrels. Where do they hide their nuts? What puzzling routes do they take? And why do they behave so strangely? Includes Gameplay based around surveillance and tracking An immersive story with full voice acting Bold visuals and foley sound effects envelop the player in a vibrant forest GET TO WORK You are a tiny cog in the ever-grinding machinery of Viago University’s research efforts. As a recent graduate, you’ve been sent on assignment to live alone in a dinky caravan in Melmoth Forest. Your job? To figure out exactly where the native squirrels nest. But the longer you spend in the forest, the stranger things begin to seem. ARRANGE YOUR CAMERAS Each day, your mission briefing will give you a starting point, but it’ll be on you to determine the optimal layout for your equipment through trial and error. Explore the wonders and mysteries of the enigmatic Melmoth Forest at your ease during daytime, until night falls… ANALYZE YOUR FOOTAGE … when you can review all the content you captured in your DIY control center. Comb your footage for the information needed to complete your mission and send proof to your boss Dr Nina Scholz back at the research institute. With each new day, things get weirder and weirder. But with both of you working on the case, maybe you can figure out what’s really going on? ACCESSIBILITY See a list of accessibility features on The Family Video Game Database:

short_description: NUTS is a single-player walking simulator surveillance mystery. Record the squirrels, report your findings, and piece together what’s really going on in Melmoth Forest.

_childDocuments_.review: Nuts is a fantastic little game with fantastic art and sound design. I played the demo when it was released and immediately fell in love with the look and feel of the game. The best way I can think to explain the extreme appeal of this game to ME is that it feels like you are occupying a liminal space. Like you are on the threshold of two planes of existence. From the desolate bus stop that you initially arrive at to the wide empty forests with these strange little squirrels being the only living things besides yourself… it’s strange, perhaps even a bit eerie in later chapters, but overall peaceful. Your goal in each chapter is to photograph the paths of squirrels and track them back to their nests. Nina calls you to tell you about your goal and where the squirrels end their path. You trek out into the woods to set up video cameras, hit record every night, wake up in the morning and play back the footage to see how you need to adjust your cameras, go out and place your cameras in different spots accordingly, and day by day make progress on tracking the squirrels back to their nests. There are five locations, each with different goals, each with different color palettes and interesting environmental objects to wander across. It’s calming and nice. I don’t really care to compare games to other games as I think most of them stand perfectly well on their own two feet regardless of where they pull inspiration from, but I very much feel that Nuts was not just inspired by Firewatch, but was nearly a copy of Firewatch. Without spoiling anything, they're just too similar in too many ways. This is not a bad thing, especially not if you love Firewatch, but I can’t not point it out.I only really have two complaints about Nuts, and admittedly they are minor, but are worth mentioning.1. At times, the gameplay can feel a little tedious and causes the pacing of the story to stutter a bit. Each chapter starts out fun enough but sometimes Nina updates your goals to something… less fun. One mission being, ‘I need you to fax me shots of the squirrel at 0:10, 0:20, 0:30, 0:40, 0:50, 1:00.’ But why? Not a big deal to me considering the length of the game, but could turn some people off. 2. Much like Firewatch, a mystery begins to unfold. Any time this happens in a game I get VERY excited. And like many other games, I was VERY disappointed. There was really nothing much to the story in the end and the mystery also did not affect gameplay in any way (in a game where the primary gameplay mechanics are setting up videocameras and reviewing nighttime footage… nope, didn’t utilize that). The game shines in many ways but would have been infinitely better with a stronger, punchier story.However, at the least, the ending (despite not resolving any part of the mystery, really) was satisfying and strange and beautiful. Perhaps not QUITE set in a reality that we’re familiar with. Somewhat folklore-ish. I loved it. You’ll just have to see for yourself.I do highly recommend this game. Maybe on sale, though. It's a bit short.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished the game (2.9 hours), I can't quite bring myself to recommend it at its current price point (£13)PROS:NUTS is a wonderful idea with an appealing aesthetic, and has a story with a decent premise. The voice acting is good - not What Remains of Edith Finch or Gone Home good, but it holds its own. Moving around is generously easy, which is important given the sparse visual cues, and the in-game equipment is a joy to play around with.CONS:I very nearly fell out with the game immediately for not offering any kind of control customisation beyond mouse sensitivity. As a lefty mouse user, my right hand is now a palsied claw from three hours of WASD, Shift, C and Spacebar. I know from experience it takes less time to implement control customisation in Unity than it takes to complete this game; there is no excuse for omitting it. At all.The second con is performance. I know visual simplicity isn't always simple to achieve, but a laptop that is quite happy playing Assassin's Creed: Odyssey should not be making noises like an experimental jet engine rendering three squirrels and twenty yards of purple trees. This won't affect everyone, but be aware the system requirements are steeper than the visuals suggest.The thing that stops me short of recommending NUTS, however, isn't the brutal lack of control customisation or the bitcoin-mining levels of juice it consumes. It's the fact that NUTS stops well, well short of fully exploring the space it creates, and left me with the sense of an opportunity squandered.After the initial couple of day and night cycles, I was SO excited - and I mean first couple of Portal puzzles excited. I was ready to spend in-game months out there, piecing together clues. But where Portal goes on to expertly wring every drop of value from its premise without outstaying its welcome, NUTS leaves the lion's share of its potential on the table. I want to avoid spoilers, so let's put it this way: NUTS didn't do any of the things to me that I got excited thinking it might do. I mean, come on: it's a game where you place surveillance cameras in a supposedly deserted wood, and then watch the recordings huddled in your little mobile cabin at night! I'm not entirely sure how they managed to pick their way between the opportunities to mess with my head, so thickly did they abound, but manage it they did.And then it ends. It ends very nicely, but it also ends very soon. The implication in the trailer (repeated in the in-game voiceover) that you might still be out there in the woods on night 23 of a particular section is borderline disingenuous. (The night count resets in each new location, which together with the repetition of (spoiler) briefly convinced me the squirrels had me trapped in a time-loop; I was disappointed to discover otherwise). It's very short, and I got no sense there was anything significant I had missed.Perhaps it's unfair to rate a game based on what it could have been, as though it were a Star Wars film. But here there was so much clear potential, so much anticipation, that I'm finding it impossible to get past the fact that, at the end of the day, I just spent three hours watching five or six one-minute-long animations from a bunch of different angles.

_childDocuments_.review: I really expected to like this game, and am disappointed that I didn't. I did really enjoy the camera-based game play, and the graphic style, and even the voice acting. But the story fell really flat for me. Honestly I feel like the game trailer tried to actively trick people into thinking there would be an intriguing story, maybe something with conspiracy or supernatural elements. There isn't. It was just a standard evil-companies-tries-to-build-something-in-a-nature-reserve tale, with no twists or surprises of any kind. You can find tape recordings around the forest from a previous researcher, but there is nothing mysterious or interesting about them either - they may as well have just been a piece of graffiti saying "Nora was here, 1982." There are things around you wouldn't expect in a nature reserve like an abandoned church and a pile of cars (?), but they don't matter at all and the game has nothing to say about them.The ending is abrupt, doesn't answer anything, and felt really unsatisfying. It also didn't actually have anything to do with the evil company either.Yeah, no thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I am the perfect audience for this game—I love Firewatch, Gone Home and almost all first-person adventures / walking simulators. Recently I've enjoyed Call of the Sea and Old Gods Rising, despite their flaws. But Nuts left me very unsatisfied.The success of a game like this rests on three things: The game world, the puzzle mechanic, and the story. Ideally, all three would be great, but usually one of them is weaker. So, Firewatch has an incredible game world and characters, but weak puzzles. The Witness has an incredible game world and puzzles, but no real story. Sadly, Nuts has an incredible game world, but the puzzle mechanic and plot just did not work for me.The idea of surveilling and tracking squirrels sounds great, but turns out to be rather less fun as implemented. I found the process of dragging cameras around and watching the subsequent footage to be frustrating and quite dull. Even the visual atheistic, while striking, actually works against you in some ways. Yes, you can see the squirrels very easily, but the lo-fi nature of the environment makes everything look very much the same through the cameras lenses.It's possible to imagine a version of Nuts that went much deeper on its puzzle aspect. There could have been different types of evidence of squirrel activity that you had to locate, different types of sensor and detectors you have to deploy. But instead it barely progresses beyond what you do in the first area.The shallowness of the puzzle mechanic could be forgiven if the story and characters were compelling enough, but while the story has a lot of promise, it is mostly squandered. You are teased with the idea of a big evil corporation, up to no good, and a population of squirrels displaying some very strange behaviour. And you're alone in the woods, at night, with who-knows-what going on around you. There are a lot of intriguing possibilities as to what's happening, and what could happen to the player, none of which are explored. Instead, you get a bunch of phone calls where a character tells you about stuff happening elsewhere that never pays off. Just when I thought the game was about the open up and give me some answers, it ends.Finally, the decision to have a nameless, faceless, personality-less protagonist is, in my opinion, a major mistake, and a failure to learn from what works in this genre. I think game designers imagine doing this makes it easier for the player to identify with the protagonist, but this is wrong. I wouldn't ever go and study squirrels in the woods for real, so I can't put myself into the story. Instead, like with Henry in Firewatch, or Norah in Call of the Sea, I want to get inside the mind of someone who would put themselves in this situation.And the decision to have a silent protagonist hobbles the rest of the characters, because they have nobody to interact with. Compare the funny and moving conversations in Firewatch between Henry and Delilah with the expository phone calls you get in Nuts. Which seem more natural and real? Which draw you more into the game world and the plot? If you're telling a story, you need a main character, and simply relying on the player to invent their own does not work.I feel bad to be so down on Nuts, especially when it's clearly a labour of love, and has some very talented people behind it. Part of me wants to say "not for me" and move on, but this a genre a love, and games of this ambition and potential don't come along very often. So it's disappointing when they fail to hit the mark, particularly due to what seem like errors in game design that could have been avoided with more critical thought about what really works and what doesn't in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, it's was well worth the almost 3 hours I put into it. Grab it on sale or wait for it to inevitably end up in Humble. That being said, and spoilers ho,You left two incredibly large loose ends in the plot there and those not being resolved kinda leaves the already sparse gameplay kinda bare.  These were 2 of 3 of the kick-off points for the entire mystery and they just didn't resolve. Ingenious setup and no punchline is the issue here. You know, there's this great christian sci-fi time travel movie (Not time changer... the name eludes me right now) that has one of the most insanely well written and tacked down time travel plots I've ever seen in a film, period. The effects, sets, and production are amazing and it carries over some minor nit-picks like some not so professional acting. And then, 30 minutes into the movie, it ends just before we hit the climax point. Apparently, the project had already run it's 10k budget dry and was forced to stop production before the director went bankrupt. Frankly it's a tragedy because it could've been a huge cult classic sci-fi film. Nuts is exactly like this. Really good art style, super puzzle mechanics, and all wrapped up in a neat bow of sinister intrigue. But 2 hours into the game, it ends just as it hits the climax. Did you guys run out of budget? Time? Did apple arcade screw the pooch? I'm not sure we'll ever get those answers. It's a tragedy, because this really should've been one of the finest indie hits around, locking arms with Return of the Obra Dinn or Baba is You. But unfortunately, in this state, it'll never be anything more then a drop in the sea of B+ games

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games (minor spoilers ahead).NUTS is a walking simulator where you play the role of a recently graduated biologist that has to conduct a study on the local wildlife. You’ll have cameras and tv sets that you set up during the day to record the squirrels later at night. The cameras need to be placed at specific points and the irregularity of the terrain makes it harder than it looks. The story is interesting The graphics are stylized and the color palette changes in each chapter. Personally I like this original take but it might be a bit weird looking until you get used to it. The voice acting, sound effects and music is very good and creates an interesting ambiance. The gameplay, as mentioned, revolves around placing the camera and photographing the squirrels and while it seems easy the path taken by the rodents is often unpredictable and trying to guess it cost me a few wrong tries a couple of times. My advice is keeping each camera in the frame of the others so you can figure out the right direction more easily.  6 Achievements. 3 hours on my own, probably half with a guide. Easy. Easy, but there are a few missables that can be replayed using chapter select. You need to . The rest can be obtained by playing the game and reaching the end. NUTS is an interesting and original walking simulator with a bold visual style and excellent sound design and voice acting. The gameplay is fun and challenging, as keeping track of the animals is harder than it looks.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS IS NOT a "surveillance mystery" game, as it claims to be. Yes, they INTRODUCE a bunch of VERY intriguing mysteries, but you never get to actually "piece together what’s really going on in Melmoth Forest" because the game just... ends abruptly without answering any of the mysteries it sets up. THE GOOD STUFF: - The basic game mechanics of positioning your cameras during the day and then huddling around the monitors at night to see what happened was very interesting and new. - The visual aesthetic keeps things simple and beautiful. MORE BAD STUFF: - I was hoping there'd be something creepy going on... something supernatural going on... maybe we see something scary or sinister happening on camera -- But nope. You never see anything running around except the squirrels. - Having a silent protagonist made "conversations" over the phone very awkward. OVERALL: Extremely cool concept and setup, but squandered and wasted potential. Also, it's extremely short. Not worth $20 unless they add WAY more into it. Buy it on sale to at least experience the cool camera mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: aaaaaaa! I didn't see the end coming and I really really should have. I loved it.This is a really fun first person puzzle/exploration game about exploring Melmoth forest and the spirited creatures who live there. You are essentially tracking squirrels over a series a days, by using a limited number of cameras and trying to pinpoint where they go. Do you play super cautiously and place each subsequents day's camera close to each other, or do you try and outwit the squirrel and guess where they might go and fail horribly losing them...I loved the art. It's almost monochrome, which gives the game a dreamy vibe, but each level's colours reflect a certain mood and style. The environment is nice too. I particularly dug the remains that were left behind, which hinted at an older and ongoing story, one maybe relevant to themes of the game.The story was well told, with lots of nice thematic touches actually. It's told largely through phone calls at the beginning and end of every mission but also there are a few secret audio logs to find about a past mission to the forest. At first this seems like just a simple job, but quickly it becomes something bigger and by the very end starts moving very quickly. It's not handed to you and there is some level of putting it together which I appreciated. I enjoyed the change of pacing in the end most of all. The whole game rushes to a energetic finale and a beautiful credits sequence, that would be perfectly at place in a Werner Herzog film. On the 'negative' side, you never get a chance to pet the squirrels. Maybe in DLC. xD

_childDocuments_.review: NUTS is an extremely unique game. From the art style, to the gameplay, so much of it, is unique and felt brand new to me. I was honestly shocked I had never even heard of this game before today. You play as a researcher in the field, studying squirrels and their movement patterns. There's an ongoing story about how your research is to protect them and the environment and an overarching theme about protecting the environment. The story was fine and did the job but I found the gameplay far more engaging and interesting. The normal price of $20 is too high in my opinion, so I'd recommend getting it on sale.The game uses a very unique art style, especially for a game largely taking place in the woods, a scenery that would normally be full of different colors. Every level is made up primarily of only 2-3 colors. This worked exceptionally well to my surprise. It really allowed you to focus on the squirrels, and the colors often fit the mood of what was happening in the story at the time, something I greatly appreciated. The music is well done, and often fits the mood. It's at its best in the later levels when it can be more atmospheric. The voice acting is also well done. The voice actors do a good job and you can tell what emotions they're trying to convey.The gameplay of NUTS centers around using cameras to track squirrels and their movement. This is done over the course of multiple days since you can only set up a couple of cameras in fixed positions. This means you have to strategically place them in order to give yourself the best chance to see where the squirrels go. After you place the cameras where you want them, you go into a room and watch the cameras in order to either figure out where to place them next, or take the photo you need in order to complete your research. The game does a very good job of adding variety to the gameplay loop such as having you find out where the squirrels come from instead of where they end up, or tracking them yourself without the cameras. These little changes go a long way in keeping gameplay fresh and engaging.The story takes you on your journey as a field researcher, doing research on squirrels for a company who wants to stop a dam from being built. Your only connection with the outside world is through the person who takes you to each station, and the only character you physically talk to, Nina, a former researcher herself. Throughout the story you uncover the mystery of the company you're trying to stop, and some shady practices they're taking part in. It moves along at a nice pace and accompany's the gameplay quite well, giving you a reason to do what you're doing. My only real complaint with is it that the ending isn't that good in my opinion but it's not a big deal since the gameplay outshines it. NUTS is a really unique game that was a breath of fresh air. It definitely won't be for everyone since it's a lot of repetitive tasks, but I found it highly enjoyable. It's a really relaxing, if not short experience. If you're a fan of unique puzzle games, definitely give it a shot, but only on sale. It's definitely not worth the $20, for the sale price of $7 is much more reasonable. For more reviews, follow my

_childDocuments_.review: Quick points:+ Placing cameras to track squirrels is interesting at first but gets tedious quickly+ Story is interesting and ominous, but never really amounts to anything+ Stylistically beautiful, nice use of shaders, especially differentiating between night time and day time+ Simon was such a great guy that I suspected that he was actually evil (especially when Nina mentioned his other job but didn't sound too sure about what it was)+ I liked the ending but not in the context of the story. In regards to the squirrels, it felt appropriate that they basically accepted you but in regards to the corporation stuff, it felt like there was just no saving the forest?Overall, this game is made up of many beautifully crafted pieces but the glue holding them together feels like it was giving out. It's such a short game that I didn't really feel any emotional attachment to anything... The maps are awesome but it feels like you barely even get to explore, rather you just sprint between the path of the squirrel and the caravan over and over and over.... It never feels rewarding to discover a nest, rather, it feels more like a sigh of relief that you can stop running back and forth in the same area.... Also, the story is basically about how beautiful nature is. Nina even mentions in one of the found tapes that someone should bottle up the smell of the forest after rain and then corrects herself quickly to say that it's better to experience it in person. That being said, at no point did I feel immersed in the worlds I was in. There was no rewards in exploration and just wandering around in the environments, rather, the concrete goal is to take pictures of the squirrels and get out of there as quickly as possible. The audio feels well designed and immersive, but the game play and the visuals in the environments don't seem to match up. It's weird how (for most of the game) you only get to see the squirrels through a TV but when you go outside, there doesn't seem to be any sign of life whatsoever (maybe a few butterflies and whatnot but it doesn't feel like a forest).
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Really not what I expected at all - for some reason I thought this was going to be a zany psych-horror-comedy about a researcher being driven mad by squirrels, and instead it's actually a rather serious environmentalist thriller. Basically a much better Firewatch in some ways. The puzzle elements are rather unique, as you have to place video cameras during the day and study the footage at night, essentially making this a very unconventional detective game. I can understand why some might consider this mechanic rather finicky, but as someone who had messed around with amateur audio editing in the past I found that element rather well done - you do need a sense of perfectionism.To lightly touch upon a major spoiler, I can understand why some might be disappointed by the ending - I'm generally not a fan of open endings, especially in games which feature such deadpan social commentary as this - but I feel like it works here - the pro-conservation and anti-corruption themes are very much relevant right here, right now, a happy ending would be disingenuous and ruin the message of the game somewhat, while a bummer ending would just be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ strange.About performance issues - I did suffer a rather surprising FPS drop on the Steam Deck, which surprised me, but I'm not someone who really cares about that kinda stuff - it's just kinda rare, especially for an indie title. I wouldn't try to run this on a potato laptop.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, despite the fact that this game was cute and (mostly) well made, I can't recommend it.It just did not have enough substance to it. I finished it in 2.6 hours, and I walked away a couple of times. There are a total of 5 areas, and the first four are effectively tutorials. When you finally get to the fifth area, you actually get to put everything together and do it yourself... sort of, as the mechanic introduced in the 4th area is only used for that area and nothing else.The entire gameplay is "watch squirrels on camera, move camera 20 feet, repeat until you find their nest". It would be a great game at $5. _childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is fairly simple and gets monotonous and easy very quickly. At its most complex you predict the movements of squirrels through a level that typically has one to two areas that could function as intricate "jungle gyms"but these never get used. Typically you just try to predict the movement of a squirrel through a fairly plain and monochrome landscape.One would expect the art and story to carry it, then. While the style is unique, the game feels it necessary to remind the player of the beauty of nature, which is woefully marred by the simplistic style used here. The forest is completely devoid of life, bar the squirrels, and while birds can be heard chirping I saw not a single one flying in my two hours. While the flag flaps defiantly in the wind, trees don't sway so much as jiggle their bush-like canopies meant to simulate leaves.The story is a heavily summarized plotline to a 90s TV special bar any kind of internal logic. The scummy corporation intent on burying the forest can get away with such an obscene amount despite the player's report being necessary under law. At any point I feel like the employees really ought to be in contact with at least one government official who can stop the dam, let alone the fact that they don't contact another newspaper who I'm sure would be happy to bury the other, corrupt one.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. Long version here, tl;dr at the bottomI really enjoyed it since my first demo playthrough, so I immediately bought this game on release. Art style is memorable, ambient soundtrack and sound effects are gorgeous, voice acting is great! Forest sounds so real and fantastic, you will look around "wait, is someone here?" often and it's really great feeling of being lost in the forest. Game really reminds me of Firewatch, which I truly love. Just go on walk, take pictures of squirrels and "find what's really going on in Melmoth Forest".But premise "find what's really going on in Melmoth Forest" (it's a quote from the main description of the game) is not fulfilled. Yeah, many strange stuff is going on in this game, but you never will actually find out what the heck is happened. In fact, the amount of knowledge about plot of this game I had before playing is equal after I've finished it. This game really reminds me of Firewatch, especially story-wise. If you've finished Firewatch, you know what I'm talking about. In the middle of the game story becomes really strange and creepy (in a good way - no jump scares or other horror stuff), I had a lot of goosebumps while playing and this part of the game I really enjoyed. But after credits roll, none of this is actually matters in terms of story. Yeah, I just spent 3 hours watching squirrels.I had so many expectations from this game, but many of them didn't come to live. There is only 6 short "missions" (different locations with some tasks to do), the gameplay is almost the same on all of them and gameplay-wise it never actually evolves. Find squirrel, place some cameras, watch where that small beast goes at night and take a photo of it. Sometimes it's three squirrels, sometimes they walk in strange paths, but the core gameplay loop is actually the same - place camera and watch. I can't say it's boring or something, I really like the part of "reverse engineering" squirrel paths, but I just want you to be aware of the main gameplay. Developers could evolve the gameplay, bring a new "toys" to play or change old ones, like "squirrel movement path is not static now" or "squirrel walk where you walk" or something like that. Or maybe developers tried this and it didn't worked, that's why this game is so short. I dunno, I'm just a stupid text.But I actually enjoy this game. Again, sound effects and voice acting is great, visually this is piece of art and the story is WOW up until the end. If you liked Firewatch (even the ending of it), you definitely will fall in love with NUTS. Game is short, very chill and awesome, so I can recommend it for walking simulator fans.tl;dr: NUTS looks and sounds awesome; gameplay is kinda repetitive, but game is short so you're not bored; story starts WOW but at the end it's just meh; if you like Firewatch you should buy NUTS.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: This is a first person........well, shooter doesn't really apply, so let's go with puzzle game.....where you attempt to slowly but surely use captured night-time footage (let's all ignore the fact that most squirrels in Europe....or anywhere else for that matter....are diurnal, not nocturnal.....I mean, really, just ignore it, otherwise this rather major scientific inaccuracy will drive you, well, nuts) to determine the paths taken by some squirrels as they move back and forth from their nut stores/dens/whatever.It is quite fun, with a really great gameplay loop, but it is not without its flaws.....**-Gameplay-  It's pretty addictive, ONCE you can actually figure out how the mechanics of the game actually work.......see below as a "meh"......-SFX-  They're quite good and really help set the scene and create a sense of place.**-Voice acting-  It's serviceable, but nothing special, and truth be told it vacillates between average and not really great at all (could be the line reading, could be the heavy accents and lack of English as a first language, it's hard to pin-point why it doesn't always land well).-Graphics-  They're highly minimalistic and stylized, but you can definitely tell what you're supposed to be looking at, and in a strange way they might just work better than realistic landscape and environments.....but for the most part, while they are functional, they're still kinda underwhelming.-Gameplay-  It was fun, but it took awhile to figure out how the game's mechanics actually work and how to proceed through the game (the game itself doesn't really do a great job of tutorializing {not a real word} the mechanics at all.  Thankfully there are no real time limits, so even though it may take you three or four days/nights (or five or six or......) to figure out exactly what it is you're supposed to be doing and to not place a camera so close to the objective marker on the map that you can't see what the game assumes you're going to be seeing, you'll inevitably figure out how it all works.  It's never frustrating, but I definitely made a mental note that I was wasting a lot of time just trying to get a handle on the central gameplay controls and how to interact (successfully) with the narrative.**-Plot-  Imagine eating a fabulous meal that just tickles your tastebuds for the first 80% or so of the meal, but then, for whatever reason, the last fifth tastes like someone slid rancid garbage and diarrhea into your repast.  It wouldn't matter that you'd totally been into the food for the majority of the time, you're only going to remember the waste and effluent flavour that you finished with.I'm going with this analogy because the first four acts or so of the game work hard to set up an underlying plot with industrial machinations and skullduggery lurking behind the bucolic splendour of the forest (and not just with dialogue either but with regions within the woods that you can happen upon that further relay that there's definitely some anti-environmental stuff happening behind the scenes).  And then the final act just tosses it all away, leaving you with a relatively action-packed finale (relatively is doing some  heavy-lifting here....) that has NOTHING to do with what the rest of the game was about, and none of those interesting plot-points get  kind of resolution.  NONE.So, I did have fun and very much enjoyed myself (once I figured out what I was supposed to be doing gameplay-wise), but the game absolutely has some warts.Recommended, but YMMV.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: *Spoiler Alert*What initially drew me into buying this game was the thermal vision artistic effect and that it looked similar to FireWatch. The color effect is in my opinion the most successful aspect of the game for a couple reasons. Firstly the play areas are very small, but it doesn’t feel that way. This game would be almost impossible in large areas, and the odds of getting the cameras in the right spots would be quite a challenge in a large map. With the colored effects it was hard to see distance so the small maps never felt small. The visual effects also made it easy for the designer to highlight important objects and make them stand right out for the player. I also enjoyed the technology the game used, the surveillance system, fax machine, tack board, phone, etc...all felt very realistic and was a nice touch.So there are a few things I just didn't love about this game. First off I hated the phone calls with Nina. She calls, states a fact to you, and abruptly hangs up. This to me is just not realistic, people just don’t talk on phones that way. I also hate that your own character never has any opportunity to speak or offer any thoughts or input. Not being able to talk and just be talked at by Nina made it hard for me to get any emotional connections with the characters. Now the biggest flaw that I couldn’t get past was the story itself. I don’t know anywhere in the world where a forest would be protected for squirrels. Squirrels are an extremely common animal of least concern on the conservation status. The idea that people would be paid to watch and protect basic squirrels just did not work for me. And lets not forget the most frustrating aspect of all, the ending or lack of. The story offers no closure and leaves a lot of loose ends.All things concerned I do think this game is worth playing. I loved how quick and low commitment it was. The story itself has a less is more approach that I can appreciate. I think the art was pretty brilliant and I’d like to see more.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore the silly and misleading name. This is a lovely little game that combines clever surveillance mechanics with minimalist nature exploration and a bit of tension and mystery. Be warned that gameplay can be quite slow and tedious. This is not an action adventure. There's very obvious inspiration from  in the setting, story, and even mode of storytelling. Perhaps too much inspiration. I can forgive this blatant rip-off because the gameplay is otherwise original and delightful. Throughout the story there are several variations on the basic formula that keep it interesting. It's not that deep, though, so luckily the game is short enough that its core mechanic doesn't overstay its welcome. The visual style is also quite nice. It's been done before, but it's done well here, with a striking color palette and suggestive geometry.There are some rough edges that could have been avoided with better design. For one, affordances and controls and not so great. I played with an Xbox controller, which is supported but very poorly, and it took me a while to realize this. Play with keyboard and mouse! Then, it's not clear what is clickable, and unfortunately the color coding of objects is misleading in this regard. Finally, and worst in my view, there are secret little documents you can find along the way that do a lot to enrich the story, but ... they are secret and easy to miss without a walkthrough. Why not let players experience this more readily? I see no point in keeping these secret.As for its difficulty, I found all the tasks easy enough to complete with some patience, but the final puzzle was very annoying, because it introduced a mechanic that was never used before in the game. How was I supposed to know about it? Affordances! Provide them! Spoiler: All in all, recommended for fans for indie walking-sim puzzlers.

Adding more bits of lore from previous research expiditions for example, would have been nice (you can find a few tapes from when your supervisour where in the forest years ago and (disregarding the logic in how tapes survived 15 years with no degredation) having more of that would have been nice, It's worth playing, but get it on a sale, 17€ is a bit steep IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: The idea is really solid.You set up cameras to track a squirrel, wait for nightfall and then you try and follow the squirrel back to it's destination through a period of a few days as you narrow down where it's going.But in execution it's rather tedious having to run all the way back every single day and pressing the record button for what is almost always only about 30 seconds of footage or less at a time and repeatedly doing that over and over again.The second issue that partially makes this not as bad but introduce a whole new problem is the end location is always very obvious. Meaning you most of the time just see a landmark that sticks out and see the nut pile there and can just skip the entire journey by placing a camera there early.Which is a huge issue, I finished every single scenario under 1 week each; most in just 2 or 3 days.Big spoilers for the ending.Overall for the rather big price I have a very hard time recommending this game.I really think there is a cool idea to be expanded and improved upon and I hope the devs do someday.
