_childDocuments_.review: I may have spent more time thinking about this game after completing it than playing it itself. It’s just on the edge of a positive review, but there is too many thing going against it.Nuts has an eye-catching shell that hides an empty core that pretends to be minimalistic. Everything at first glance looks interesting: graphics, gameplay and story, but when playing, you really feel ripped off, as if you were lied to. What you get is exactly what you see, .Nuts is a beautiful game with unique appealing graphics. The gameplay is also fairly innovative. During the day, you plant down cameras to record the squirrel activity of the night and figuring out where they go. It’s interesting, because you have to guess where they are going and what’s the best possible angles to capture the most potential movement. And you have to review the footage with zoom and fastforward/backward, hunting for any activity captured.  But that’s all that the game has for itself.In term of story, you get a line phone with your research director, you have to listen to her short monologues (because your character is mute) between missions.I think the game promises a lot, but delivers barely anything. Yes the “surveillance” gameplay is here. But can you really call it “surveillance?” It’s more like wildlife observation. Yes there are some “weird” things going on with the squirrels. But given the language of the promotional material, I was expecting actual weird, not just unusual stuff. This, with how the gameplay works, gives the impression that the game will iterate on the loop and improve it, make it more interesting (because toward the end, it really feels repetitive.) Instead… It’s more of the same, barely any spin on the same loop of planting cameras, looking at footage, repeat until you get to your objective.I think the game tries to impart a sense of isolation to foster reflection in the player, but it fails. For one, the areas are too small to give you a sense of being lost in a large place and the art style with low details is actually quite claustrophobic. For two, there is human activity traces all around most maps. I think it also fails to evoke a sense of wonder for nature.  The only visible lifeforms, the squirrels, act like robots, and the low complexity art style doesn’t do justice to nature. I was legitimately expecting more dynamic behaviors from the squirrels.The game has basically multiple story lines that diverges, you expect some follow up on previous plot points, but nothing. I couldn’t connect with the player character or Nina, because they don’t really exist as people with personality, they are mostly here to advance the game. The squirrel feel like alien entities with motivations very unlike humans, so I didn’t feel a connection to them.The game doesn’t know where it wants to go and at the end the devs just give up and say “sure, let the player decide.” It feels like the game ends midway through something great and just leaves you hanging.I also want to point out that the system requirements for such a graphically simple game are not acceptable. Level 3 has a graphical bug: with my Ryzen 3900X and Radeon RX 5600, the game couldn’t hold 30 fps at 1080p. To be fair, the rest of the game runs at 4K 60 fps fine.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: "This lady sounds NUTS!"NUTS is an unusual game, and that made me like it. You are tasked with researching squirrels, and to perform this task you must set up cameras in the forest, let them record animal movements overnight, and then review the footage you got in the morning. Maybe you pointed the camera the wrong way and got nothing, maybe you got precisely what you needed, or maybe you need to go back, readjust and try again the next night to learn something new. It's a very neat concept and not one I've seen done with this much freedom for the player!The sounds of the forest, and the minimalist ambient music, also work well to build up an atmosphere. There is a great sensation of potential during the early moments of the game, of something greater eventually coming our way. Even the plot, focused around your research being used to prevent some greedy corporation from ruining the forest by damming the river, seems to hint toward something more mysterious and nefarious.It is here, however, that the game lets the player down a little. A lot of the potential of this setting, and the gameplay mechanics, are never fully realised. It is my understanding the game was developed with limited time and resources, and the developers have done some great things, but as much as I like the idea of NUTS, I was left wanting something more.There is also the minor gripe I have with the only voice actor of the game. Her voice and accent are fine for her role, but her delivery leaves much to be wanted, with some lines delivered with too much haste, not flowing naturally. I think you can tell the actor isn't a native english speaker, and this might have made it difficult for her to feel natural when doing her lines.Finally I must also warn the reader of the colour scheme of NUTS. While I found it endearing in the way it uses limited colours and contrast to paint its world, several people I showed the game to complained that it was unpleasant to look at. I feel this will come down to personal taste and preference, so do take a good look at the screenshots in the store page before you take the plunge.Still, even for a short game with a lot of potential left untapped, I have to recommend NUTS. It's not an action packed experience, nor will it envelop you in a grand story full of twists and turns, but if you'd like to spend an evening doing something no other game lets you do, toying around with mechanics no other game offers, NUTS is a good investment.Playtime: 3+ hours (Single playthrough)Ratings (1-10)Visual: 7Audio: 8Story: 5Gameplay: 8Overall: 7

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where you pretty much immediately know whether you'd like this or not. So if you think this is up your alley, then go ahead, I promise it's satisfying and plays well. You won't be disappointed. The gameplay loop for the most part is simple. You set up cameras, you wait until nightfall, and you review footage. Then, the next day, you set up cameras based on what your findings from last night were. Rinse and repeat. It's pretty fun and engaging, really. If that sounds boring to you - trust me, it's not. It really makes you feel like a detective, of a sort. A squirrel detective? And then of course there are twists and turns in the story. They really keep things interesting. If you think this game only pretends to be about squirrels... hah, I could tell you whether that's true or not, but that would be a slight spoiler, wouldn't it? Nah. I won't. The game manages to go in the face of your expectations quite expertly. I'll leave it to blow your mind.And of course there's the visuals. They really make you feel immersed in the world. That's what they're for, right? They also look rather pretty. But for the most part, they're transparent; what you see is the forest around you. You're really there. The great soundscape also helps achieve this effect.If you're worried if this is a horror game - I'd say answering this is a spoiler in itself, so I finished in one day. I'd recommend it to anyone who likes nature, a good story, and appreciates cute animals.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: I generally like photography and slow methodological games, and nuts is it. Putting you in the role of a naturalist documenting squirrels in a reserve threatened by corporate greed, you have to capture these illusive rodents through careful placement of cameras which will test your observation and pattern identification skills. The story line isn't anything out of the ballpark but still compelling enough as you go through your assignments. And whatever it is, squirrels are cute and fuzzy. Short but challenging enough not to frustrate anyone to rage quit.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: The game really draws you in, Firewatch style. It presents a basic, nature-watch story that quickly turns sinister. Then, it puts you in a B-plot, resolves the B-plot, and ends the game. The main story, what happens to the other characters, and the whole purpose of the first 2 thirds of the game just get flushed down the drain. Not to mention I stumbled upon the end of the path for the final puzzle before the rest of it, so I never figured out on my own what you're supposed to do. The character never picks up on it, and what's set up kind of defies the logic it presents, so I had to look up a walkthrough just to beat the game. There isn't really a lot of logic behind why you do what gets you out, and it has nothing to do with the presented objective. Imagine an escape room where you stumble upon the button that unlocks the main door out immediately by accident. You press it, nothing obvious happens, and you assume it must be to something else. Then you solve the main puzzles up to where you get the to the button, and don't realize the button went to the main door, and that the door was unlocked. You'd be stuck forever.Even if you ignore that oversight, the fact that the story sets up so much so well and resolves nothing makes the game really not worth playing. In the end you haven't really done anything.To compare it to Firewatch again, imagine if in Firewatch, after you get knocked out, you wake up in a ravine. After you escape the situation you're in, the helicopter picks you up and the credits roll. No dialogue, you just leave and the game ends. That's pretty much what happens here. Really it feels like the story team quit 2 thirds of the way into the game, and they just kinda had to cobble an ending together asap.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Recently I had a game that I was excited for. A game that might seem similar to this even. Mysterious woods, investigating, a story that's mostly narrated and so on... and wow, it turned out to be a massive disappointment. I thought that perhaps I was too excited and ruined the game. In comes NUTS and I'm even more excited. But this time it was not a disappointment. It was in fact a very lovely experience. Visually this game's simple, yet really thought out. The colors invert based on night and day and each area has its own color scheme. They all look good, though at times it was very bright and a bit heavy on the eyes. I'm using a monitor with good colors though, so maybe on a TN panel the colors feel less vivid and this problem might not exist. Everything's easy to understand. The gameplay is simple and streamlined, yet still engaging. The bulk of the game has you tracking squirrel movements. Set up cams during the day, evaluate recordings during the night. You snap from day to night in an instant when you want to move on and it's just perfect for keeping a brisk pace. Your movement's also not restricted at all. If you manage to climb a rock and set up a camera at a vantage point, then you can do it. No invisible walls, no linearity. The story is compelling, but sadly nothing gets answered. Like seriously, nothing. Not even a single thing. This is like Act 1 of a longer story. I felt like I was half-way compelled into the story, waiting for the mysteries to get cranked up and focused on a bit more, only for it to just... end. Literally some of the stakes set up were pretty big too and them getting left to the dust seems almost comically ridiculous. What's there is great. Just that hearing that there's a mystery, seeing weird things and having it end with no payoff is a bit disappointing.But honestly, regardless of that I enjoyed it. The squirrels are so cute and genuinely adorable to watch when they're doing their thing. The mystery being built is enjoyable, if you're ready to be left in the lurch with no answers. It's charming, to put it mildly. This game made me remember that expecting a game to be good isn't some insane request.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: NUTS is an adventure game where you are tasked with the surveillance of a group of squirrels inhabiting the Melmoth forest. Said squirrels are the last bastion of defense against the evil plans of a corporation, which wants to destroy the forest in order to get terrain to build on. Being the squirrels an endangered specie, you are tasked with tracking them and get the proof needed to stop the forest's destruction, but soon enough you'll start to notice very strange behaviours...Squirrel surveillance is not the easiest of tasks: the little creatures will in fact run around a lot before getting to their stashes and the fact that you can't follow them by foot makes it harder. Coming to your aid are three different cameras and monitors, that you can position around the map and will record a whole night of squirrel movements. While the squirrels' path will be the same each and every night, the fact that you only get three point of views makes it so you will need to repeatedly move the cameras around the find your objectives, which usually are the squirrels' stashes. Initially, the game plays in small maps to makes you accustomed with the system, which offers an unique gameplay to say the least, increasing the size of the pieces of forest you'll find yourself in when you'll be accustomed with the game.All in all, that's the main gameplay loop in NUTS: move a camera, follow the squirrel until it goes out of sight, move the camera the next day to have a better view or to follow him. A gameplay loop that could become really boring really quickly. Luckily, the differentiation of the maps and the mistery behind the story will keep you playing through the whole game... which isn't a whole lot of time! For the base price of 16.79€, I would've expected more than only two and a half hours of gameplay that hardly introduces many new mechanics to differentiate, making the game very pricey in my opinion.NUTS repetitive gameplay loop is articulated by its story: you are a researcher sent to the Melmoth forest to study an endangered specie of squirrels, which could be the only thing between the forest and the plans of a corp to build Panorama, a project which would destroy the ecosystem. Each level of the game asks you to take photographs of the squirrels' stashes, in order to confirm their presence in the area and thus stopping the construction plans. This seems very normal, until you find a stash that, between the heaps of nuts, has some dinamyte. From  there the story gets more misterious and you'll find yourself wondering about the squirrels' behaviours more and more.While the story starts off great, the ending is very lacking and (without making any spoilers) I really expected something more. In the end, a game like this should have an interesting story with an incredible ending, which is not the case here.The first thing you'll notice about NUTS isn't its squirrel surveillance gameplay or its story, but its beautiful and rather strange graphical direction. Every level will in fact used two different color palettes, one for day time and one for night time, with every object having almost monochromatic textures, making for beautiful vistas even in simple environments. This also allow to recognize the squirrels among the vegetation, since they will always have colors that stand out from the environment, something that would've been hard to do with a more "realistic" approach to graphics.Unfortunately, even the graphical compartment of NUTS isn't without faults: in this case I have to signal a rather unstable framerate that moved between the 40 and 60 fps. Not really the best for a game with such simple graphics.NUTS is a game with a really interesting art direction, interesting mechanics (that could however have been expanded more) and an overall lacking story, expecially in the ending. The low playtime with no replayability, when confronted with the asking price, makes me recommend this game only under a very heavy (75%) discount.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game both stylistically and functionally. It’s only you and the squirrels, but the game does an excellent job of making you feel like there is someone else lurking just outside of your field of vision. The camera puzzles take a decent amount of trial and error but never become frustratingly difficult. NUTS is a fantastic game and you absolutely should pick this game up now while it’s on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Completed with 100% of achievements unlocked. While photography-based games are becoming something of an expanding niche, 's premise as a "squirrel surveillance" game is still an intriguing one. The game tasks the player with tracking squirrels' night-time movements across a series of forest areas with strategically-placed cameras, with an environmentalist story providing some narrative drive. While fairly simple, this mechanic works pretty well, with a couple of minor twists - though the later scenarios (there are six) do start to show its limits, as with their longer length the downtime between placing cameras (via first-person exploration), watching back the recorded footage, repositioning and repeating becomes evident - the traipse to and from the caravan observation point becomes increasingly tedious, adding little to the gameplay (though the inclusion of "walking simulator" in the game's official description does, I suppose, give fair warning of this). Overall,  is decent while it lasts (somewhere around 3 hours), but I can't see it sustaining an experience that's much longer than that.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to peeping tom nature edition. You are a private investigator sent to uncover the seedy underbelly of the rabid squirrel population and take photos of their nefarious crimes to blackmail them. But be careful. Your boss will gaslight you at every turn as she never lets you talk. It's all about her feelings.In all seriousness, this is a remarkably entertaining game, given its simplicity and repetitiveness. Virtual nature is as relaxing and therapeutic as the real thing. An hour will go by, and you won't even know it. The story and gameplay take some interesting turns on your journey. While the ending is abrupt, you can infer what happens based on the credits and what Nina said.There are no manual saves, but each chapter should take about 30 to 45 minutes, depending on how good you are at using a GPS and placing cameras. The key is to think like a squirrel.There are a few quirky bugs, like you can answer the phone from the fax machine or your bed with the world's longest arm. The trailer door will automatically close when you answer the phone. I suppose it's a ghost, a squirrel, or the wind. It closed the door when I was outside on the phone, so the cord must go through the door. I found the bugs charming, though.I recommend it, but only on sale because $20 is a bit steep for a walking simulator.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute game! Love the graphics and unique gameplay! Your job is to fulfill certain tasks by investigating squirells and tracking their moves throughout the nights by deploying cameras. The are a few games with similar gameplay but NUTS still managed to be unique in its own way. The gamplay loop of placing cameras, watching the recording, moving cameras, watching the recording, etc is sometimes a bit too repetitive and annoying, especially when you have to walk a good bit from your trailer to where your cameras are but it's not too bad as to sour the game.I personally also loved the story, even though it is a very generic "evil companies are destroying nature" storyline. The game provides a nice mix of story, gameplay, cute animals, puzzle, exploration, as well as excitement and certain calming elements.I can only recommend you try NUTS for yourself! Maybe do pick it up on sale though because for 3 hours of gameplay the game is rather short :)
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend Nuts? Yes. It's a great idea with a very nice atmosphere. The game definitely left me wanting more - Not necessarily a bad trait in a game. I do wish it had been longer though, I don't feel like they got all out of the concept that they could have. There is definitely room for more levels with more "puzzles" and more story. None the less, I was thoroughly entertained for the 3-4 hours the game took. If they create a sequel I'll definitely play it.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: This game is OK.  The visuals and sound are nice.  The gameplay is relaxing, but nothing extraordinary.  Basically, use tripod cameras to track squirrels from point A to point B.A couple of spots, including near the end, the developers bring several identical squirrels into frame and they wrestle in a tight ball, leaving you unable to determine which squirrel is the one you are supposed to follow....so you guess and follow one after the other until you guess correctly.  I found that annoying, particularly because you can't save mid-mission.  So, you might expect a 15-20 minute mission but if you guess wrong, you could be looking at 30-40 minutes.  That's a lot to ask for a chill relaxing indie game IMO.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: I give a small thumbs up. It's a relatively short experience. I quite liked the mechanics of the game, however I wish that it was longer. I would have loved to do more complex photo missions. It was very good for what it was though. A nice little environmental game with pretty stylization and satisfying photo taking.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pleasantly relaxing game. I would suggest going in blind as far as the story goes, but the basic gameplay mechanic is a trial-and-error effort to track down squirrels to take pictures. It is not a big-time action game, but the story is nice and the reduced color pallet of the environments invites your brain to fill in the details. The two-tone forest felt more real to me than a lot of pixelated leaf textures. I beat the whole game and got 100% of the achievements in three hours. Whether that bugs you or not is a matter of preference.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a fairly original game mechanics. It has interesting plot and the game is short enough that the repetitive gameplay elements don't really start to bother you. Personally I don't really like the two-tone graphics and found the loose ends of thee plot a bit annoying, but it's well worth playing regardless.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, a little short (I paused a lot so my playtime isn't really accurate, it probably would've been more like 5-6 hours), but pretty and compelling. However it has one glaring flaw:NO REMAPPABLE CONTROLS.You cannot change the keybinds, which is very frustrating if you're left-handed like me. I had to awkwardly reach over to WSAD with my right hand for the entire game. Arrow keys work, but when you need to use left-shift to run and Space to jump, they're not really an option. I can also see it being a problem for people who are disabled and need specific keybinds to be able to play. In 2021, especially for a game made in Unity which has innumerable tutorials, this is an utterly baffling and inexcusable decision. It has been inexcusable for years.Also, some plot decisions are weird and vague and the ending is what I would describe as open-ended, so if that is something that bothers you in your games, you might want to avoid this. I'm still wondering (ENDGAME SPOILERS) But overall it's very pretty and atmospheric and a relaxing way to spend a few hours. The camera gameplay is fun and doesn't overstay its welcome. I hope to see more games from these developers.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Super-cute and weirdly-addictive squirrel surveillance game that feels like a love letter to Firewatch whilst bringing alot of neat new ideas to the table. The art style and audio are beautiful - emphasising the relaxing yet mysterious vibe of the forest - but my favourite aspect of the game was playing around with the various bits of tech you have at your disposal. It feels very nice to play, with a great sense of mystery throughout and a wonderful lead voice actress and story to spur you forward. Lovely stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: My friend bought me this game for my birthday, and I loved it.  The puzzle of the game is incredibly unique and interesting to think through.  I'd compare this mostly closely to Return of the Obra Dinn: Incredible (stylized) graphics, an interesting puzzle with open-ended solving. The game also has a great ability to build suspense despite being a game where you walk alone in a forest, where the scariest thing out there for you to find are some squirrels, tapes, and a guitar.The only other character, Nina Scholz, is also a lovely presence.  She really carries the kind-hearted tone of the game while being delightfully German (Ihr, Deutscher, koennt nicht "Eichhoernchen" auf Englisch sagen - aber ist okay, weil ich "einhoernchen" nicht so gut sagen kann)I only have 2 complaints:1) There is no "skip to night" option, you always have to walk yourself back to the campsite.  This is just a nitpick, but it's the most tedious part of the game because of how much backtracking there is just to hit "record" on the VCR and progress to the nighttime parts.2) The ending
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little indie game with really good production quality. Graphics/art style, audio, level design etc are all done to a really high standard.Intriguing story, but don't expect to feel stunned or in tears at the end of it. The gameplay is good but would mainly recommend for those with a bit more patience, experience in these kinda games, or a quiet night off, as it can feel a little repetitive or frustrating if you're not in the right mindset.The pricetag is maybe a bit too steep at £15 in the UK. I don't mind what I spent because it means supporting indie devs like this, but the game is roughly 2-5hrs long which is pretty short. A sale of 30% off and I would definitely recommend this to others. Think you can play for £5ish on iOS.Score: 8/10 (6 or 7 if squirrels don't appeal to you)
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: A first person exploration game that takes heavy inspiration from "Firewatch".Like Firewatch, the game tells the story of someone at a new job in isolated wilderness, with the entire story being told via communications with your female boss. Both games wrap an intense, conspiratorial story in fairly mundane gameplay - in this case, taking photos of squirrels.The environments are pleasant to walk through, save for the weird single-tone neon shader covering the entire game.  I'm not sure why the devs went with this aesthetic. It didn't actually bother me much, but several of my friends who were watching me play said they couldn't stand to look at it. Yes, the entire game looks like that.The voice acting is not great - the lady's German(?) accent was hard to understand at times - but otherwise the production value is pretty good for an indie game.There's about 2 hours of content, with no replayability.Overall, it's not nearly good as Firewatch, but fans of that game will probably still enjoy this one.  I'm not sure it's worth the full price of $20, but it is worth getting on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Highly stylized mystery thriller that takes you on a journey to photograph squirrels and their nut stashes. This game hooked me right out off the bat with its relaxing atmosphere, sound design, and general feel with its unique art style. The ending (with no spoilers) was a bit more open and probably added a few more questions instead of answering any. That isn't necessarily a bad thing though, I still felt satisfied even with that open ended-ness, it felt more appropriate for the game to end that way instead of knowing exactly what happened/what will happen. You could easily complete it in only one sitting, and I wish that I could experience this game again with a fresh mind!
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game that uses a game mechanic that is often unused. The use of the colors and music combined with the narrative helps to give the player a feeling of "I'm going to see something disturbing right now, ain't I?". Its a feeling that was enjoyable and keeps you wanting to find out more. Unfortunately, the is a bit short. But if the devs add a few more chapters, in which they totally can as the story felt like it stopped too short and there were questions left unanswered, then this would be a solid indy game.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Cute little game, I love the style. It was a lot of fun and quite satisfying when you get the photos right!Only thing I can criticize, I wish Nina had more lines. I sent a certain photo of something that was obviously out of place and Nina just told me to get on with it... Nina, this thing could be very harmful to us! But other than that, it's all positive from here. :)*Slight spoiler*Okay so I now get why some people are a bit miffed at the ending as it leaves it up to your imagination of what happens afterwards. Either that or it's a hook for Nuts 2
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: NUTS is the best game I have ever played. My life was in shambles before I bought this game, but NUTS has changed my life for the better. Seeing those little squirrels squirreling around for the first time is an experience that I will never be able to relive. This is genuinely the best game of this generation, maybe even ever. Games like The Last of Us, God of War, Red Dead Redemption have nothing on the world building, and rich atmosphere that is NUTS. When the credits started rolling, I burst out in tears. Tears of happiness. Thank you NUTS.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Had an absolute blast with this game! The whole thing is gorgeous, it's equal parts eerie and chill. Finished it in one 4.5 hour sitting with a fair amount of faff so you could probably finish it quicker, but at the same time you could really linger over the beauty of the different landscapes. Really fun, would absolutely recommend :)
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet, innovative gameplay and very atmospheric!Very Firewatch with a hint of Scanner Sombre, you're on your own in the forest with a mission to track the nocturnal habits of some squirrels, luckily they follow the same routes every night so with the aid of some trusty cameras, night by night you move your equipment around to follow their routes homeSome will find the gameplay repetitive by the end but I really enjoyed it, it kept it fresh and mixed up what was required of you every so often and the narrative moments are woven in beautifully
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: By it for on sale!The price of 15€ is on the edge on this. I really digged the gameplay and the squirrels. The story felt for the most part nice, but leaves an empty taste behind. It feels like there could have been way more. Since there is an obvious inspiration of games like Firewatch, I wonder why there isn't more to it? The end is... a great scenery, but I felt like I did something wrong and got... almost the bad ending. It just left too many questions unanswered. I wouldn't have any problem, if this game changed the gameplay at the end for the sake of telling a deeper story. The story felt best after chapter 5, but that's also way too short. Also it baits a lot into a mystic direction, but hardly goes that way. That felt like a letdown as well.I still recommend it, if you can buy it with a discount. It's not bad, a nice experience, I had fun, but it's on the short site after all.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: I had a fun 2.5-3 hours playing NUTS. The art style is stunning and the gameplay is intuitive. The narrative had me intrigued, but wasn't necessarily gripping. It had a twist or two thrown in that I didn't see coming. There were moments that felt tedious that I just wanted to rush through, but not enough that it detracted from the whole experience. The game has an ever-present faceless NPC with a kind voice who only communicates with you via telephone, which felt very Firewatch to me. I think they definitely relied on Campo Santo's masterpiece for some inspiration here.Overall, I'm glad I spent a few hours in this world and would recommend to other fans of slower-paced indie narrative experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice artstyle, the main mechanic is new and has some interesting variations, but not enough to keep it from getting tedious by the end.The story starts interesting and keep me hooked, but it ends up not resolving any of the plot points, and just ends in a very vague pro-environmentalism message.Would not recommend it, unless you want to feel frustrated with a story that seems to go somewhere, and the just doesn’t.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: As I played through Nuts, I found myself captivated by the question of what these squirrels were up to. The game tells a tightly written tale that reaches a satisfying conclusion without taking too many risks. While the gameplay revolves around positioning cameras to track the squirrels' movements, it doesn't evolve much beyond that. However, what Nuts does exceptionally well is its sense of style. The visually striking art design and minimalistic use of colors create a captivating atmosphere. The audio design also adds to the experience, with the forest sounds transitioning to a sense of eerie silence at night. The story unfolds as you aid the research efforts of Viago University and uncover the mystery of the forest. While the gameplay may become repetitive, Nuts is still a relaxing and intriguing puzzle adventure with a strong ecological message. It's a great escape into a lush forest and the secrets it holds.Curator Page:
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: It's a slow game and that's fine. The gameplay loop revolves around setting up caneras and following the path of squirrels in a nature reserve.The style is unique and enjoyable. The reason I don't recommend it is because the game becomes tedious before the story is told.In the third act, the assignment becomes particularly tedious and I watched how the game played out in a let's play instead.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely game with an interesting premise but fails to provide any closure and departs from the original theme of "what are the squirrels doing?".The game simply ends with no answers to the squirrels behaviour or any answers to what happened with the shady corporations and Nina.Fun to play but forgets to finish its own story leaving you unsatisfied.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: An overall enjoyable game that's fun and intriguing, but just like Firewatch was, the ending was disappointing,  Right up until the very end I thought they were gonna do something interesting with the story.as opposed to the player character becoming a squirrel and having the x-files theme play which would've been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Nuts is a touching and political work of art that invites you to question how you see nature and biodiversity in a very sensitive way, with an innovative gameplay of camera placement. Graphics and OST give the game an eery and beautiful atmosphere.Nust is also a very good product in terms of design. It's fluid and fun to play with just the good amount of challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: This could have been enjoyable IF almost everything about this game were different.  The concept is interesting!  The gameplay could have been enjoyable!  IF the whole thing didn't look like some kind of vaporwave migraine.  For a game that's all about seeing things, it's remarkably hard just to look at: it's all rendered in flat silhouettes of pink and purple such that almost everything, regardless of location or perspective, looks the same.  The camera view pans sickeningly and the angle of the field of view seems to have been chosen for minimum utility and maximum confusion.  As the lurid mauve cherry on top of this retch-inducing cake, it's impossible to take a break from this game as it only saves at the end of chapters, so you can't even parcel out the suffering into smaller doses.  In short -- I dislike this game extremely for its affectations and impediments to play, but I hate it because it really could have been something new and delightful.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept but absolutely horrible color palette for most of the time, hard on the eyes. Took me about 50 mins to figure out I was printing screenshots from the wrong monitor (yes, I did read the instruction book by the door). Also took me some fiddling to find where my photos were stored and how to access them in order to fax them. Took me around 90 mins to realize I could jump. Overall the controls are not very intuitive, and they are not explained in the controls menu.The gameplay of following squirrels movements via cameras is inspired, I give it that, and I loved that “scientific” aspect of it. I'd love more games that have you be a nature photographer, scientist or researcher of this sort. But further along it gets pretty tedious since they are very easy to lose track of. And at one point late in the game you're even meant to more or less make a leap of faith into something that the game has taught you is no way to progress. The story is progressively intriguing but leaves a lot, if not everything, actually, hanging in the air by the end.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: If on sale for a few bucks... I can recommend, halfheartedly.What others might be see as story I can only see as as excuse to give tasks to the player. I am still not sure if I successfully finished the game or if it was a glitch. nothing was resolved, all the explanations for why the player has to do what he was told to... all pointless.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: If you want something super deep and intense and puzzling, this is not the game for you. If you want something chill, intriguing, and a bit absurd if you think about it for too long, then here you go! The squirrels are up to mischief, and it seems innocuous enough until you learn about what's going on, and more importantly what's coming. The game *does* leave some unfinished plot lines, but they are beside your actual task of investigating the squirrels. This is interesting and a fun couple of hours!
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Sheesh.The game had me always asking questions, always wondering about something. And just when I think I have everything figured out, It flips me on my head. This game in both artstyle, and gameplay, is a marvel. With unique gameplay and a one-of-a-kind art style, NUTS kept me guessing through my whole playtime. However this game is VERY short. It took me about 2.3 hours to get to the credits. And I understand why it's short, the primary development team consists of 5 or 6 people. So I understand that there is a reason for the short length and high-quality, but damn, can't say I wouldn't have enjoyed it if the game was 5 or 10 hours. All in all, NUTS is a fantastic game with great ideas executed flawlessly, a fresh take on the surveillance idea of singleplayer games.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this but honestly the gameplay is so boring that I just can't. I'm going to return it actually. _childDocuments_.review: "Maybe it's just not your genre". That's what I keep telling myself.But I surely think that if your game is about nothing else but repetitive gameplay and a narrative, AT LEAST make the narrative something decent.Oh no. Yet another "something is happening - it's an eViL cOrPoRaTiOn vs nAtuRe - we couldn't think of (or agree on) anything else beyond that so we'll just whatever our way to the end" story. Emotional investment: zero. Story content / believability : ridiculously close to nothing, and that is not counting the "strange/surreal" events. The study premisse alone is dumb. Incredibly annoying "let me interrupt your repetitive game with an oh look the sun is shining comment on a dictaphone tape" or "hey i just need you to listen to my unskippable phone monologues 24/7 and oh no they're going to get us all by DoCtOrInG an ArTiClE" whinery. Just let me chase another squirrel. Or rather, tediously replace cameras because just following them on foot would be to obvious - except in that one chapter when you suddenly have to run after them because whatever. I mean come on, there's even typos in the name of the researcher character, using both Nona and Nina on the same memo page.Total gameplay until the incredibly "i guess we really can't figure out an end so we'll just stop writing and cash in" ending: a mere 6.5 hours, of which 1 hour was lost due to bugs and navigating the menus in search of my previously saved game. _childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR Review: If a walking sim about tracking squirrels sounds nice and you like the graphic layout based on the trailer, then this will likely be a decent break from more active gaming. Be aware, though, that tracking the squirrels is a hit or miss mechanic and the gameplay may get old fast. 6/10, barely thumbs up. Review: Well, fuzzy little creatures sounded nice.  With the bare bones color layout and almost night-scope vision of the forest, I thought this would be rather easy.  It wasn’t.  Tracking the animals paths was fun for the first hour or so, but then it became somewhat aggravating as I honestly could not guess where they would be headed next, which led to more of the same activity of squirrel tracking than I assumed would happen.On one hand, this came off as the most interesting idea I’ve seen in a walking sim since I played “Everything”. On the other hand, by the second hour of tracking squirrels I was more than done. As a matter of fact, I just wanted *something* different to occur because the constant mission objective of finding a squirrel, guessing its path, and putting up cameras to look at the video just went on for much too long.  The story elements helped, but at the same time never really played out the way I thought it would.  I did enjoy learning about the doctor, your boss, but it’s all one-sided and your main character has no interaction beyond that other than some written notes in a journal.  If you are looking for Firewatch Jr, this is not it.Style-wise, I enjoyed the graphics.  It’s not for everyone.  While playing I did have a bit of trouble distinguishing areas with all the monochromatic graphics, but I doubt real looking trees and shrubs would have helped much either. At least the squirrels are easy to spot, just hard to catch and harder than expected to guess where they are heading next.  I don’t think it was the difficulty that was off putting so much as I just got tired of the same squirrel tracking missions over and over.The game ultimately ended well and if not for that I would have left a negative review.  So, 6/10 for me. Grab on discount and play when you are not busy.

_childDocuments_.review: Classic pancakesIngredients for approx. 10 pieces with a diameter of 24cm:150g of wheat flourpinch of salt2 eggs250ml of milk100ml of sparkling mineral water (or milk)1 tablespoon of vanilla sugar (if you want the pancakes to be sweet)frying oil or clarified butterA method of preparing:Pour flour, a pinch of salt and vanilla sugar into a bowl. Pour the milk with water and stir vigorously with a whisk so that no lumps are formed. Add the eggs and mix again. (You can also mix the dough with a mixer). If there are lumps, you can pour the dough through a strainer. It is best to leave the dough for at least 30 minutes to rest (but not necessary).Preheat a frying pan (preferably a Teflon one). Add a little oil. (I recommend spreading the oil with a silicone brush). Stir the dough again. Pour a little dough with a ladle into the center of the pan and, agitating it, spread it over the entire surface. Fry until the bottom is browned, and the top is curdled, i.e. no longer liquid. Turn over with a spatula and fry for a moment until golden.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a unique take on a game about following and observing squirrels and uncovering mysteries.The recording monitoring mechanism used is something I have not seen featured in any video games before and it is refreshing after the first phase of frustration of understanding the strategy to pass the first two chapters since it is all a new experience.The graphic is also what makes this game special but the unnecessarily eerie background music and noise made me expect more from the world and story.I had hoped for a deep revelation or a twist but it was too subtle and not at all satisfying. It would have been a highly praised game if they had reworked the world building and ending.Without the closure at the end being unsatisfactory and the fact that I would have liked the game to have kept me for longer, overall, it was still an interesting game and did not overstay its welcome. I would recommend that you give it a try if you'd like a short and casual adventure/mystery game with a unique system, which I would love to see implemented more for other games as well since it is a neat idea.

_childDocuments_.review: I was given this game for free as part of a promotion. I figured it would suffice for an easy play through for something new to play on a weekday. This game can be completed in less than 2 hours on your first try, maybe an hour or less if you've played before. There isn't much variety here. The storyline is just......awful. It never concludes. It doesn't matter what you manage to do in the game, you'll never hear about anything by the time you jump your last jump. So I was left holding the bag at the end there going "WTF". The music is ominous at times, which idk why because it isn't a horror game. Graphics are that of a calculator on monochrome steroids. The premise is fun and playful, but this isn't worth $20. _childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: This was a cute, short game. It's a bit of a walking sim, which I love, where you set up cameras during the day, and at night, you track squirrels going around doing their business.The visuals were very vibrant, the music was atmospheric, and the sound effects were all inspired by nature. Honestly, it played on my heart-strings and I loved every bit of it.The controls were simple, though I sometimes switched to mouse when it came to pressing the tv buttons (play, pause, rewind, etc).The story reminded me of other games I'd played, like Firewatch, for example, but I could play a million games like this, so this was a plus for me.I recommend this game for those who like walking sims and zen-like games.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: NUTS in many ways is just another walking simulator that draws heavy inspiration from Firewatch. However, Firewatch is a good template to emulate and NUTS has a few tricks up its sleeve to help it stand out from other games in its genre.First of all, theere's the camera mechanic which both feels novel and well-implemented. Although the game is fairly short, clocking in at around three hours, the mechanic never grew stale keeps you engaged throughout.Secondly, the art style, ambience, and lonely nature of the game lends itself to an utterly amazing ethereal, and at times even creepy, atmosphere. Last but not least, and this might be a bit spoilery so look away if you want a completely untainted experience, the later parts of the game are a lot more surreal than one might expect, especially the ending, something which, in my opinion, lends itself really well to this type of game.Either way, NUTS is truly a work born out of love and should not be overlooked despite it treading a lot of the same ground as some other walking sims.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a pretty good little game. It reminded me of Firewatch, though it lacks a little something to make it something really great.The idea of following squirrel trails with the cameras is pretty neat, though it also gets a bit old. Luckily the game shuffles things around a bit between each chapter, so overall it is still a pleasant experience.The graphics look pretty nice and are pretty unique. I initially bought the game mainly because I was intrigued by its look. The sound design is also pretty neat.In the end the only thing that bothered me was that when I finished the game there were still a few questions unanswered, which felt a bit underwhelming. The replayability might also suffer from the main mechanic being kinda repetitive and the objectives for certain chapters being somewhat obvious.Overall the game is a rather unique experience and a pretty pleasant one too ! I would definitely recommend it if you like games that try to tell a story through unique gameplay. Maybe wait for a sale if you're on the fence about trying it out !
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it during a sale. Game was pretty cozy and enjoyable that almost touched on feeling like it overstayed its welcome.The mechanics of the game is simple enough and the art direction helps you focus on your objectives due to the strong contrast between them and the rest of the environment. This game would definitely have been a lot more difficult with another art style applied, and it really helped to keep the game enjoyable. The game is pretty short, like a longer movie or so in length and I don't think it would make it better if it were longer, I think it was just enough to stay good and not repetitive and turn boring.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot in common with Firewatch (it's the story of doing work alone in a forest, tethered to society through someone on the phone), so if you liked that you'll probably like this too. I would say this is a tiny bit less polished, a tiny bit less compelling of a story, but the central game mechanic of reviewing squirrel footage is more coherent and elevates this game above the average walking simulator experience. The monochrome art style is also pretty neat.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: A decently long game. If this reminded me of anything, it was Return of the Obra Dinn; excellent visuals, intriguing puzzles elements that have you visiting and revisiting the same areas to make minor corrections. About ~8 hours experienceI will say it's not perfect, but it is great! I kept hoping the story would go somewhere a little deeper, or the mechanics would be a little more complicated; you see some highlighted objects that you don't really do much with, some objects are interactable but for no real purpose. Really wish I could throw away or recycle the old junk, or have to fix the wiring on the van after a storm, or something. A lot of promise for a sequel or DLC if they ever had the desire!
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little game, I really enjoyed it!!  I liked the mechanics and thought the color/art design was cool too.  I bought on sale for a hefty discount and thought it was worth every penny. No bugs, no issues.  Some people complain about the ending, I thought it was fine. Can't really say more without spoiling it...
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Good mystery game about setting up a surveillance system to track subjects - in this case, squirrels. You only have a few cameras, so it will take multiple nights to figure out the squirrels' route on each stage. The story gets a bit strained as it goes on, but overall I had a nice time with this game!
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous little adventure with a satisfying gameplay loop! One would think running back and forth to place the cameras would be tedious but the back and forth of frustration and satisfaction when you finally catch the little rascals keeps it fun the whole time. the soundtrack is also worth mentioning! It compliments the gloomy yet peaceful atmosphere perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: A charming little game with an interesting mechanic and an intriguing story.Here are parts I didn't like:Unfortunately, at the time of writing this review I had 3.9 hours in-game and that's all you really need, even if you have to redo certain parts of the game to get a few achievements you may have missed, you will not get more than 8 hours out of it.Other than that, the colors can be way too vibrant, and last I checked (well, over a year ago...) there was no way to calibrate them in the name, requiring me to change my monitor's "contrast" setting.The story ends in a nonsensical way, it's clearly rushed, there's no way that it was someone's artistic vision for an ending.Now the good:The immersion and ambiance of the game is great. You feel alone in a vast forest. There are no jump scares or anything like that, but the devs capture well the feeling of having no outside contact in a dark forest.The player's main point of contact is done with a professor, a character who is very well-voiced and personable. I thought she had a very expressive personality, and was well-thought-out.Finally, the story (up to the ending) is pretty cool. It's about low stakes environmentalism. I thought it was well done and I liked helping this fictional research happen.Overall, I'd say it's a good pick on sale, but such a short game at full price doesn't really feel worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: NUTS

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- follow around cute squirrels & take pictures of them- try to predict and navigate their paths, which almost has a puzzle-like aspect to it - adorable art style - entertaining dialog between characters- i really enjoyed the morale of the story, about leaving the forest to the wildlife instead of trying to tear it down for corporate uses (which could also be seen as a con, since its a cliche morale that's been done many times before, "SAVE THE FOREST!" and all that. but i enjoyed it anyway)Cons:- short game, with very little achievements (which could also be seen as a pro for some people, if that's the type of game you're looking for)- game seems to end abruptly, with a very vague ending that you have to try and interpret for yourself. it left me with more questions than answers - while the art style is unique, it can also be a headache. the colors change every chapter, making the game look like it had inverted colors half the time (i didn't mind it, i thought it was kinda cool since i'd never seen anybody else do it before, but others might disagree)- glitches. there were a few times when i got stuck between some rocks and couldn't get out without restarting (one time i even fell completely through the map and got stuck in a big, black void), which brings me to my next point...- game saves. you have to play the game by chapter, and if you were to somehow crash, glitch out, or try to continue your progress later on, it would restart you from the beginning of that chapter.- pricing. i got the game on a discount, as i don't think there was enough content/gameplay that would make it worth $20Overall, the game is pretty average. I personally enjoyed playing it, trying to run around and predict where the squirrels paths were, hoping they'd show up on my cameras I had tried to strategically place around the forest. But, it might not be for everyone, so take this review with a grain of salt <3

_childDocuments_.review: I struggle to call NUTS good; I experienced 4 apparent soft-locks in the 3 hours it took to beat it, alongside a dozen other collision and movement bugs, but there was an indisputable charm to the game and its atmosphere. Like a lot of other people, I got it in a bundle, and I think that it is a little expensive for the experience. Only using two colors per level makes the visual design memorable and I really enjoyed the vibes of both the art and sound design. The lack of time-sensitive objectives makes it a really calm experience. My only other complaint is that the ending felt very "and then a bunch of things happened". Up to that point, the story felt slow with a budding story about environmental destruction and corruption, before 60% of the story happens in the last part of the final level. If the final story bits could have been spread out through another level or two, I think it would have improved the pacing a lot. In the end, while there were lots of bugs and some gameplay/story annoyances, I still came out feeling positive overall due to the unique gameplay, good visuals/audio, and that it feels like a game made by a passionate team rather than trying to follow a trend.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming little nature game that reminds me of Firewatch, but instead of someone's past haunting them, you get squirrels. You get a camera, then two, then three, and track squirrels during the night in order to fight back against a corporation that intends to demolish fictional Melmoth forest's wildlife all to build a dam. The squirrels are more intelligent than you think they are, and the whole story serves as a well-wrapped metaphor about the interaction between humanity and the natural world. If I had a penny each time I wanted to pet one of the squirrels, I'd be able to get a DSLR of my own. That said, the ending struck a warm note in my heart (especially the  and  )Your only human companions are Nina and Simon, the two people who help you along the way (one of them going missing later on but that's a mystery we may never uncover). You get tidbits of Nina's life when she was in your shoes years ago, and it's honestly really touching to see how empathetic she is of the natural world.This is the second time I've played a game like this one (Firewatch being the first) and I highly recommend it. I promise you it's not creepy even though the music makes it seem that way some times. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: When I saw 'NUTS' I immediately got excited, it reminded me a bit of 'Firewatch' at least when watching the trailer and even when you play the first few chapters. While they both do have big things happening in the background of the story, this game is not nearly as mysterious as 'Firewatch,' it's not a bad thing, but the tone of the game sometimes makes it feel like you'll be facing similar situations. You are playing as a ranger being sent out to different parts of the woods watching and surveying squirrels, where they go, where they come from, hidden nut stashes, their homes, etc etc. You do not want this mega corporation taking over, not when you can prove that their end goal is going to hurt the wildlife. A message we as humankind should be taking into account and listening to, but of course we do not.Gameplay well, it's a walking simulator most of the time it's you going into these targeted zones and placing cameras, you'll sit in your little camper with the tvs on just surveying where certain squirrels are going. I actually liked this part a lot, it gives you a different mechanic to use other than just walking, and you aren't rushed with it either, you can take as long as you need to finish up whatever you're surveying. It can be quite tedious especially towards the end, it might take you quite a bit of time just figuring things out especially in the junkyard. I also really liked the graphical style they went with, the color palette is a really good and a unique thing to see. I like how every chapter will change the palette as well. They do a great job of also highlighting interactive objects with abstracting colors, not too abstract to where it doesn't feel in the correct atmosphere, but enough to show you "hey you can use this."Overall I would recommend NUTS, however I would advise finding it at a lower price because for what it does it does really well, but there isn't a whole lot of content here to justify $20, I got this in a mystery bundle so I got it at a really good deal, but still just wait for a sale. Works great on Linux as well.

_childDocuments_.review: NUTS is a unique game with lovely mechanics, and an amazing art style. There are many photography games out there, sure. But I don't know about any others that allow you to place down the cameras and move them to your hearts content! And you can't forget the little camera in your pocket! Well, I did. The journal was also a great feature, in my opinion. It has your To-Do list and a way to store photos if you need to compare them to the cameras. You don't take fall damage, amazing! The creators didn't need the player to take damage to get the right feeling. The game feels ominous in a calming way. When I would walk around the woods or the swamp I wouldn't feel the need to turn around spontaneously or peek around corners, but I would often feel like something was watching me. Squirrels? Birds? People? But I would almost always forget that feeling, as it would be replaced by the joy of running around, placing cameras, then checking them.The colours are one of the most notable things throughout the game. I didn't know what to expect when I was downloading the game, but I was pleasantly surprised! The contrast of the squirrels to the backround is amazing. And they somehow hid thestashes while having them be as noticeable as black on white. The way the colours changed from when you wake up to move the cameras and when you sleep to watch the squirrles is amazing! It is so noticeable but when the colours do change my mind doesn't even achknowledge it.I personally think there should be more games with this style. It could be the new black and white! As I was saying earlier, I really enjoy the night and day cycle. I'm pretty sure there is no limit to how many nights you can stay in one place. Not that I know of. But the thing I truly love is the way you just click a button and (NIGHT 8)Then you go to bed or walk out the door and it abrubtly brings up a dark or light screen with (DAY 5) You get what I mean, right?The whole world feels alive. When you're on the phone talking to Nina, when you watch the squirrels in your caravan, even as you ponder "what could be happening here at Melmoth Forest?" as you walk around, placing cameras. Even the slighest touch that you think nobody would notice, has an effect. Because we do notice, even if we don't even realise it.The voice acting is amazing, so thank you Almut Schwacke. You can really hear the exitement or the concern in Nina's voice. The rustle of papers over the phone as you recieve a piece of paper a couple second after. The whole world, especially over the phone, feels alive. Even though you are in an area fenced off from the world with chain link fence, it feels that Melmoth Forest is endless. As I jumped onto rocks and crouch under bushes, I felt like I could get lost in this endless abyss. But then I look back down to my GPS, and realise "nope. I know where to go, I got work to do."Another thing that feeds the endlessness of the forest is that the player never sees a human throughout the game. Not once. Squirrels and that's it. No birds, no rabbits. Just squirrels sitting in a tree as the leaves sway in the breeze.SPOILERS AHEAD :So near the end you slip on some rocks and fall. Then you come across this other caravan, and you contact Nina. She says that is her old caravan. You then try to follow the squirrel Bella to get your journal back. I had seen the squirrels crossto the island and I didn't even think once about crossing myself, didn't think I would make it. On the stick, two squirrels merged to one. So I thought "Oh! One must have stayed on the tree and my journal is there!" No. I moved the cameras closer and THAT'S when I realised the squirrels merged. So, I watched a video and saw thatthe player crossed the stick. Okay. So I crossed the stick and the rest is history. That was just a little confusing for me. Now I realise that it was kind of obvious that I would also cross to join the squirrels, but I thought that would be immediate death. But nope.How the story ended was very interesting. No one expected it. I think the story is like a poem. The creator(s) had a specific meaning to it, but many different people interperated it in different ways. Personally, I don't know what to think. I have a feeling that it's meant to say something about human corruption and nature either being a victim to it, or being smarter than us. We should help nature, or follow it. One of those two in my opinion. I truly loved this game, yet it was so short. I think the world needs more of this. More games with this art style, more games that have a similiar meaning to it. More games that are so unique, that it's impossible to recreate. just like this one.I'm not saying there should be a sequal, or even something part of the same universe, (the story of Nina would be cool) but that more games like this should be created. A lot of people love this game, including myself. So I have a couple recomendations for you! Alba: A Wildlife Adventure. More kid friendly but similar story and length.Copoka. Haven't played it much, but it kind of gives off a vibe resembling NUTS.Shelter 1, 2, and 3. Kind of related to this game. I still think you should check them out.The Stillness of the Wind. It just gives me more mature vibes, as does NUTS.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, little indie games like this inspire me to write reviews because they're so clever and fun. Nearly everything about this game was awesome, and that "nearly" makes me want to point out the  minor things that could've taken it to a 10/10. I'll keep this spoiler-lite, but just know that this game gets a hearty recommendation from me, and if you plan on playing it, you should stop reading now and give it a shot.Pretty much the only pitfall with this game is that it's a puzzle game that doesn't require you to use the pieces to solve it. It's as if I gave you a jigsaw puzzle of a squirrel, and told you to figure out what animal it is, and after looking at the pieces you determine it to be a squirrel without putting any of them together. In this situation you're right and have done what I've told you, but you've missed the fun. You could still put the pieces together and probably have fun doing so, but if the goal is JUST to find out what the picture is, you'd have to flip them over and assemble them on the blank side if you're really going to engage with the "puzzle" in the way you're meant to. To meet the puzzle's design halfway, you'd have to flip the pieces.In this game you're tasked with placing cameras during the day to record the nightly activities of squirrels to find out various pieces of information on them. It's an incredibly satisfying core gameplay loop, especially when you go out of your way to engage with that system. However, the game doesn't restrict you from NOT using this mechanic to solve the puzzles.For example, one of the first tasks they do is ask you to track a squirrel to it's stash and take a picture of it. Now, I had played this first level before on my iPad (before deciding that the port to mobile wasn't the most optimal way to play the game and switched to the PC version). Since I had done this, I already knew where the stash was on my first night, and I just plunked the camera there and basically skipped the whole process. Nothing stopped me from doing this, and it made me wonder... if I just look around a little, couldn't I do this every level moving forward?Well, you technically can, and that sort of indicates my one problem with this game. The game didn't make me flip the pieces over, and I didn't flip them over myself.See, in later levels you'll be tasked with finding a few different things in that area of the forest, and, remembering my early experience, I gave the area a single walk through looking for interesting places, and I basically "solved" the puzzle the first night. Interestingly enough, the game is prepared for this, and had dialogue that essentially said "No, you're not supposed to do that yet," and then later the character was shocked, SHOCKED, about what I had found, as if I hadn't just submitted the literal same solution but only when the game expected me to.This left me with mixed feelings, because on one hand I knew I was breaking the rules that the game set out for me by trying to "skip to the end" as it were, but on the other hand the game told me to solve a problem, and I did. I just happened to do it in the least fun way possible. I think this could've been changed earlier on, perhaps having locations be abandoned if you disturb them during the day which would cause them to move, resulting in you having to know where your subjects are going  you go there yourself. This would also mean if you mindlessly explore, you'll disturb the squirrels and perhaps get a worse ending, or simply move where they go at night, making your previous research useless. I think this change would've made it far more interesting, having to carefully move through the forest and check your sight-lines carefully to capture (but not disturb!) the squirrels.Another (possibly far cheaper) solution could instead change the way points-of-interest are highlighted during the day. As they are now, they're typically highlighted in a contrasting color and it makes them incredibly easy to find by just having a wander. Perhaps the colors could've been made to be the same as the environment during the day phase where you're setting up cameras, and only highlight important locations at night. On top of that, perhaps sprinkling more locations that COULD be the final solutions so if you do wander you won't know for sure if the one you're at is the one you need to capture, perhaps even randomizing them between repeated plays.This only applies to some levels though, as one level circumnavigated this by (light gameplay spoiler)  If more than just one of the levels did this, I think I wouldn't even have considered my proposed "solutions" I talked about in the previous paragraph. However, given that the final level of the game can (and I mostly did) be solved by just... looking around and trying a few things without engaging with that AMAZING core gameplay mechanic, it makes me feel like something's wrong. I felt like I stumbled into a solution rather than having an "aha!" moment, and that weakened the cool ending for me.The stylized graphics, subtle but well composed reactive music, wonderfully written story with charming voice acting, the stellar gameplay... all of it was a fantastic time. Overall for a tiny little indie game it was well worth my support and I am extremely excited for what the devs do next. A couple of hours with this game was extremely refreshing and had me hooked from beginning to end, I just wish I could say it was perfect. If you've read this far and still want to play this game, which you absolutely should, just be sure to flip the pieces over.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think NUTS is perfect, but it's certainly beautiful in its own right - and if you're looking for a fun, 3-4 hour adventure/exploration game with a decent enough story, it's hard to go wrong. The clean, minimalist aesthetic is super cool, and each level's palettes feel just right. NUTS' soundtrack brilliantly captures the spirit of the setting, and the camera mechanic is fun - the way each level expands or alters the idea feels very natural, though you can solve most of the puzzles through exploration/brute force; in that regard, there's basically zero replayability once you know the solutions to each level.That being said, let's address the [squirrel] in the [nest]: the ending. NUTS' ending is beautiful in its own right, but it's very sudden and leaves a lot of lingering questions. I don't think that ambiguity is a bad thing, and I didn't feel unsatisfied by the time I reached the credits; as much as a part of me wishes there had been another chapter or two to slow down the pacing, I think NUTS' strength is knowing just when to end. While the story didn't fall flat for me, I totally understand why someone expecting a tense but generally satisfying climax in the vein of Firewatch - the sort of narrative the trailer plays up - would be disappointed. I don't think you can really go wrong with NUTS, though.
